Mansour Abbas, the leader of the United Arab List (Ra’am), said early Wednesday that he hoped his party and Israel’s opposition bloc could together secure the 61 seats needed for a parliamentary majority to replace Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government.
“I hope we can change this government and that the numbers add up to 61 seats, the opposition bloc together with Ra’am,” Abbas told Israel’s Channel 12.
“With the numbers we have now, there is no government,” he said.
Abbas said the high turnout among Arab voters reflected despair and frustration that had turned into hope.
Asked about opposition party leaders Naftali Bennett and Avigdor Lieberman’s refusal to cooperate with his party, he said the matter would be addressed after the election.
Supporters of the Joint List celebrated at its headquarters in Nazareth, chanting slogans mocking National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir.
Joint List leader Yousef Jabareen said the projections showed that it had achieved its goal of building a strong list capable of bringing change.
Channel 12 reported turnout among Arab voters at 80%. Its exit poll projected a combined 18 seats for Arab parties in the 120-seat Knesset alongside 52 for the bloc led by Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot and 50 for Netanyahu’s bloc.
Neither bloc was projected to secure a parliamentary majority.
Overall turnout reached 77.7%, the highest since 1999 and up 7.1 percentage points from the 2022 election, the Central Elections Committee said.
Vote counting began after polls closed at 10 pm local time (2000GMT) Tuesday. Exit polls are projections, not official results.

Egypt orders closure of independent news site Mada Masr
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
23:16:00 UTC
08:16:00 KST

Egypt orders closure of independent news site Mada Masr
October 28, 2026
An Egyptian court on Tuesday ordered the closure of independent news website Mada Masr after convicting its editor-in-chief, Lina Attalah, of operating without a license.
Attalah, one of Egypt's most prominent journalists, was detained for several hours following the verdict before being released after paying a fine.
The court imposed a fine of 3 million Egyptian pounds (around $53,400; €48,112), the maximum penalty for the offense. It also ordered the website to shut down and its equipment to be confiscated.
Mada Masr, founded in 2013, is one of Egypt's few remaining independent news outlets. It is known for investigating corruption, human rights violations and the military's powerful role in the country.
What happened during Lina Attalah's trial?
Attalah's lawyers said the court rejected their requests to review the case file and submit additional evidence during Tuesday's hearing in Cairo.
According to Hossam Bahgat, head of the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR), who attended the hearing, the judge then appointed a new lawyer to represent Attalah despite objections from her eight-person defense team.
"In an even more shocking turn, the judge proceeded to dictate motions on behalf of this lawyer, who had not uttered a single word, and entered them into the official record," Bahgat told news agency AFP.
The judge announced the verdict amid protests from the defense before security officers detained Attalah.
She was released after Mada Masr paid the fine, her lawyer Hassan al-Azhari confirmed. The outlet plans to appeal the closure order.
During her release procedures, Attalah also learned that she had been sentenced in absentia in a separate case in 2024 to one year in prison and a fine of 20,000 Egyptian pounds.
That conviction concerned charges of spreading false news and operating an unlicensed website. Her lawyers have challenged the ruling, with a new hearing scheduled for November 11.
Why has Egypt targeted Mada Masr?
Mada Masr has faced years of legal battles with Egyptian authorities, who have blocked access to its website inside the country since 2017.
The outlet says it first applied for a license in 2018 but received no response. It only learned that its application had been rejected when prosecutors raised the issue during another case in 2022.
Mada Masr challenged that decision and says its latest application has been awaiting a response since 2023.
Six cases have been brought against the outlet and its journalists over the past six years, but Tuesday's trial was the first of its kind.
Egyptian authorities maintain that the country respects freedom of expression but insist that media organizations must comply with the law, protect national security and counter misinformation.
How have press freedom groups reacted?
The ruling drew widespread international condemnation.
A coalition of 119 rights organizations and media outlets, including Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), described the prosecution as an "unprecedented attack on press freedom."
"Today's decision represents a crushing blow to press freedom in Egypt and marks a dark day for independent journalism in the country," Amnesty International said.
Reporters Without Borders (RSF) called the ruling "outrageous" and "shameful."
"If Egypt can put in custody one of its most respected editors and shut down her newsroom, no independent journalist in the country is safe," said CPJ regional director Sara Qudah.
US Senator Chris Van Hollen also criticized the prosecution, describing the charges as baseless and saying that "journalism is not a crime."
What is the state of press freedom in Egypt?
The case comes amid a broader crackdown on independent journalism.
Six journalists from the fact-checking platform Matsadaash were arrested in September and subsequently charged with terrorism-related offenses.
Authorities accuse them of links to the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood and spreading false information to undermine confidence in state institutions and encourage protests.
The journalists have reported being tortured following their arrests, according to EIPR. Egypt's Interior Ministry has denied the allegations.
On Tuesday, prosecutors extended their pretrial detention by another 15 days. Rights groups warn that such detention can continue for months or even years.
According to EIPR, Egypt currently holds 26 journalists in connection with their work.

King Charles confronts calls for slavery apology during Caribbean tour
King Charles III began a Caribbean tour in the Bahamas on Tuesday, acknowledging “the great suffering of the past” amid calls for an apology over slavery. The 77-year-old monarch, undergoing cancer treatment, will also visit Guyana and Antigua and Barbuda, highlighting climate threats and attending a Commonwealth summit with Queen Camilla.
King Charles III began a Caribbean tour in the Bahamas Tuesday where he acknowledged "the great suffering of the past" in the face of pressure to apologise for the slave trade.
The 77-year-old king, who is receiving treatment for an undisclosed form of cancer, will also highlight climate threats facing low-lying islands during the visit to three countries in nine days.
He will first make solo visits to the Bahamas and Guyana, before being joined by his wife, Queen Camilla, for the final leg in Antigua and Barbuda, where he will address a Commonwealth heads of government (CHOGM) summit.
"We know that some of what is best in Bahamian culture today, the most joyful, the most hopeful, the most bright, was born out of darkness," he said at a youth rally.
"It is only right that we should acknowledge the great suffering and injustices of the past in these islands and beyond, even as we rejoice in the successes of the present and build new opportunities for the future."
Read moreGhana pushes for concrete slavery reparations
He said leaders of "affected" Commonwealth nations would be discussing the issue in Antigua and Barbuda next week where the issue of reparations for slavery will be on the table according to Commonwealth Secretary-General Shirley Ayorkor Botchwey.
Several of the former colonies have demanded the king take a new step toward making amends for colonization and the transatlantic slave trade, from which his ancestors profited for centuries.
As he arrived at the rally held at the historic site where The Bahamas officially gained its independence in 1973, protesters gathered to wave placards reading "pay what you owe us."
Last month Jamaica -- where Charles remains head of state -- filed a petition in an appeals court in London "to advance Jamaica's push for reparations for the African ancestors who suffered under hundreds of years of enslavement."
Charles has previously called slavery the "darkest days" of British history, and will address colonial issues at each stage of the trip.
Few in royal circles will have forgotten a turbulent 2022 trip to Jamaica by Prince William, when he and Princess Catherine were met with anti-monarchy protests and calls for reparations.
Read moreFrench slavery law repealed: 'Now we can start talking about reparations,' historian says
Guyana's President Irfaan Ali, who is to meet with Charles during the visit, told ITV News the king's recognition of the "darkest days" was just the "first step."
"Now, moving to the apology is the next step," said Ali, demanding accountability from the former empire which he said "exploited the region," "destroyed lives" and "created under development."
Modern monarchs have to various degrees expressed remorse for Britain's central role in chattel slavery, but none has yet formally apologized. The debt-laden UK government has balked at the idea of financial compensation.
Botchwey told Sky News ahead of the government meeting from November 1 to 4, that it "wouldn't hurt" for the king to apologize.
Botchwey also said the "time has come" to discuss reparations, in the form of financial payments or otherwise.
Read moreMacron backs symbolic repeal of France's slavery laws, warns against 'false promises' on reparations
Climate resilience
Buckingham Palace has insisted the tour is an opportunity for the king to look forward, meet young people and discuss pressing issues like climate change.
In his Bahamas speech, Charles also highlighted the particular threat facing low-lying islands face from climate change.
"In an island nation where 90 percent of the land sits below two meters (six foot, six inches). There is perhaps nowhere better than the Bahamas to understand the reality of climate change that threatens so many communities across the Commonwealth," he said. "Our world cries out for healing."
According to Botchwey, the Commonwealth, which includes 56 member countries with the king at its helm, is an important anchor in a "world that is almost spinning out of control."
"This CHOGM is going to be one like never before," the secretary-general told AFP in an interview, with the meeting in St John's set to focus on investment and trade opportunities for member countries.
Charles, who has long championed environmental causes, will meet organizations working in the field, including a coral restoration project in Antigua and Barbuda and rainforest conservation in Guyana.
"Many of these countries that are affected by climate are not polluters, and yet they feel the brunt of the effects of climate," said Botchwey, adding that the CHOGM summit will also touch upon climate resilience schemes.
While she refused to elaborate on whether the UK government and royals should pursue slavery reparations, she said the issue would be on the table in St John's.

Keys, cardboard houses and red carnations filled the air outside Portugal's parliament on Tuesday evening as thousands of demonstrators rallied in Lisbon over the housing crisis and alleged police violence.
Protesters sang “É a nossa morada” (“This is where we live”) and chanted against fascism, while banners called for housing rights and condemned the treatment of activists. Singer Marisa Liz joined the gathering.

Brazil central bank says no significant risk to financial stability
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
07:12:28 CST
08:12:28 KST

BRASILIA, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- Brazil's Central Bank said Tuesday it sees no "significant risk" to the country's financial stability, noting that the financial system maintains adequate levels of capitalization and liquidity, and the capacity to withstand adverse scenarios.
The bank's financial stability report for the first half of 2026 published on Tuesday pointed to a slowdown in credit for households and businesses, a trend consistent with high interest rates and a more moderate economic activity, as financial institutions have become more cautious in granting loans.
However, the report indicated that despite pressures regarding capital and liquidity, banks remain capable of weathering adverse economic conditions.
The report showed an increase in credit-related difficulties among households, with delinquency reaching its highest level since 2012 across most types of credit.
The bank's estimates suggest the pressure on consumers' ability to make payments will persist throughout the second half of the year.
Despite this outlook, the bank concluded that the country's financial system remains resilient and the provisions held by financial institutions are sufficient to cover expected losses. ■

4 killed, 10 injured in road accident in southern Peru

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
07:12:09 CST
08:12:09 KST

LIMA, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- Four people were killed and at least 10 others injured on Tuesday morning when three vehicles collided on the southern Pan-American Highway in Peru's Arequipa region.
The crash occurred in the Chira sector of Camana Province and involved an interprovincial bus, a pickup and a heavy cargo truck, state-run Andina news agency reported.
The bus, operated by Julsa, departed the country's capital, Lima, on Monday afternoon for the city of Arequipa, while the pickup was operating as a shared taxi serving the Secocha mining area.
Police said the pickup was completely crushed between the trailer of the cargo truck, which was traveling from north to south, and the interprovincial bus, which was heading in the opposite direction.
The National Police and firefighters rushed to the scene to help the injured, who were taken to Camana Hospital for treatment.
Traffic on the southern Pan-American Highway was disrupted for several hours as authorities conducted legal procedures and investigations to determine the cause of the crash. ■

French Senate weighs Bill to make protesters pay for unrest damage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

23:12:00 UTC
08:12:00 KST

French Senate weighs Bill to make protesters pay for unrest damage
- French senators debated a Bill to make protesters pay for unrest damage, after violent riots and looting in France. Supporters said it was needed to stop vandals.
- The Bill could fine people up to €10,000 and seize benefits or housing aid. Critics warned it could punish peaceful protesters and weaken the right to demonstrate.
- The Senate was expected to back the measure, with Marine Le Pen in support. It also approved a separate Bill to remove social media posts calling for “insurrection or taking up arms against the state”.
AI generated
PARIS - The French Parliament’s Upper House on Oct 27 debated a controversial Bill that would make protesters financially liable for damage caused during street demonstrations, despite warnings from critics that it could curb the right to protest.
The Bill was drafted in response to riots that followed Paris Saint-Germain’s victory over Arsenal in the UEFA Champions League final in May.
But it has taken on added significance after weeks of protests over inequality and soaring prices culminated in some of the worst violence France has seen in years on Oct 17, when thousands of businesses across the country were damaged and looted.
The legislation, due to be voted on later on Oct 27 or Oct 28, was expected to receive strong backing in the Upper House, where a right-wing and centrist alliance holds a majority.
Far-right leader Marine Le Pen, whom opinion polls place as the frontrunner to succeed Emmanuel Macron in next spring’s presidential election, supports the legislation.
Speaking in Parliament, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez stressed the “urgency” of responding to the damage and scenes of chaos seen on Oct 17.
“We can no longer allow the vast majority of our fellow citizens to pay for a minority of vandals,” he said.
‘Legal travesty’
Under the legislation, protesters could be ordered to pay up to €10,000 (S$14,261) for damage caused during street demonstrations.
But critics argue that people who took no part in vandalism could nonetheless be held liable if they were deemed to have been associated with those responsible.
The Bill introduces joint financial liability for anyone found to have “knowingly participated” in a group formed with the intent of carrying out acts of vandalism.
It would also apply to individuals who “voluntarily” continued to take part in a gathering likely to disrupt public order after two police dispersal warnings.
Welfare benefits and housing assistance could also be seized to help cover the cost of damages under the scheme, a provision that has drawn sharp criticism from left-wing parties and advocacy groups.
Left-wing lawmakers accused the government of an “authoritarian drift” at the expense of the freedom to demonstrate.
Communist senator Fabien Gay denounced what he called a “legal travesty that deliberately conflates protesters and rioters”.
Green senator Melanie Vogel accused the government of responding to social demands with “collective punishment.”
Supporters of the Bill sought to reassure critics.
“We must not give the impression that this Bill would criminalise a passer-by or a peaceful protester,” said Olivier Bitz of the centre-right Horizons party.
‘Disastrous consequences’
The legislation was expected to become even tougher during its passage through the Senate, where a large number of amendments have been tabled.
The government has proposed introducing protest bans targeting the most violent individuals.
Late on Oct 27, the Senate approved a Bill allowing authorities to demand the rapid removal of social media content calling for “insurrection or taking up arms against the state”.
“As we speak, there are calls circulating for next Saturday that are calls for insurrection. Those are the kinds of content we want to remove,” the interior minister told senators.
Platforms would be required to remove such content within 24 hours, or they could face “blocking” or “delisting.”
In an op-ed published in French daily Le Monde last week, a coalition of trade unions and student groups warned of a “serious infringement on the freedom to demonstrate.”
They argued the measures would disproportionately affect “the poorest families” and encourage “arbitrary police action.”
Amnesty International also urged the government to abandon the Bill, warning the measures could push “already marginalised families further into poverty.”
“If passed, this bill would be a deeply regressive step,” Nathalie Godard of Amnesty International France said on Oct 26.
“Seizing family allowances, housing assistance, or the active solidarity income could have disastrous consequences for some of the most vulnerable people.” AFP

FBI agent says he feared case against ex-FBI officials tied to Hunter Biden probes would look political

FBI agent says he feared case against ex-FBI officials tied to Hunter Biden probes would look political
WASHINGTON, Oct 27 - An FBI agent who helped lead the case against two former senior bureau officials accused of lying to Congress about Hunter Biden investigations testified on Tuesday that he feared the probe would look "political".
The testimony came at a hearing to decide whether the case against Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides, both former senior counterintelligence officials, can go forward. It adds to defense claims that the Trump Justice Department brought the case for political reasons, which prosecutors deny.
FBI special agent Bryan Witt said his concerns were based on the fact that the probe began in July, the day after President Donald Trump gave a primetime speech in which he directed the FBI and other agencies to investigate whether the US intelligence community suppressed information about foreign meddling in the 2020 election.
One of the former FBI officials who was charged, Nikki Floris, sought to discredit an FBI intelligence report that said China sought to influence the 2020 election in favor of Biden. FBI Director Kash Patel directed the FBI’s field office in Kansas City, Missouri, where Witt is based, to investigate following Trump’s address, Witt testified.
“I had concerns this would be viewed as political,” Witt said.
The testimony revealed concerns within the FBI about a probe into two of the FBI’s most senior counterintelligence officials whose actions Trump and Republican lawmakers had condemned for years. The case is the latest brought by the Trump Justice Department to face claims of political bias.
Justice Department officials have argued the former FBI officials should be held accountable for misleading a congressional investigation. Spokespeople for the Justice Department and FBI did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Prosecutors called Witt to testify as the agent who outlined the allegations in a criminal complaint.
Asked by Floris’ defense lawyer, Margaret Donovan, if he viewed the investigation as a “witch hunt,” Witt denied making that statement but said “people generally viewed it as that around the office.”
The direction of the probe eventually changed from foreign election influence to 2023 testimony by Floris and Benavides before the House of Representatives Judiciary Committee. Both were charged last week with making false statements about their knowledge and involvement in Hunter Biden investigations.
Hunter Biden was charged during his father's administration with tax and gun crimes. Former President Joe Biden pardoned his son shortly before leaving office.
Floris and Benavides were both supervisors on the FBI’s foreign influence task force ahead of the 2020 election. A criminal complaint accused them of lying to the House panel in denying or downplaying their role in Hunter Biden probes, citing internal FBI records and witness interviews.
JUDGE CRITICIZES PROSECUTORS
Attorneys for Floris and Benavides have disputed the allegations and accused the Trump administration of bringing the case to drive a political narrative.
US Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui, who presided over the hearing, said their claims had some credibility as he condemned prosecutors for filing a new criminal complaint early on Tuesday that added an obstruction charge against both defendants without seeking a judge’s approval. Faruqui said he was aware of no previous instance of prosecutors filing a criminal complaint that had not been approved by a magistrate judge.
Prosecutors denied doing anything improper and argued they were not legally required to seek a judge’s sign-off.
Faruqui told prosecutors their conduct bolstered defense claims that “everything here is atypical and bizarre and that is because this is not an appropriate case.” REUTERS

American woman convicted of getting military training from Islamic State
- Halima Salman, 27, was found guilty in New York of receiving military training from Islamic State. Prosecutors said she trained with an assault rifle in Syria and faces up to 10 years.
- Salman travelled to IS-held Syria at 17, married an IS fighter, and was held by Syrian forces in a relocation camp until returning to the US in 2024.
- The case shows the difficult fate of foreign women linked to IS. US Attorney Anthony Nocella said she was being held accountable for joining a terrorist group.
AI generated
NEW YORK - An American woman who joined the Islamic State (IS) group before being caught by anti-IS forces in Syria was found guilty on Oct 27 of receiving military training from the jihadists.
Halima Salman, 27, was one of hundreds of foreign women who went or were taken to the territory controlled by the Islamic State, and who then married jihadist fighters before being captured and detained pending their repatriation.
The fate of these women and their children has proven a sticking point for the Western countries from where some originated, with many trapped or stripped of their citizenship by their former homelands.
Salman’s mother is an American, and her family travelled from the United States to Syria when she was young.
Salman was convicted of receiving military-type training from IS when she was 18, prosecutors said in a statement, a crime that could carry 10 years of imprisonment. She will be sentenced at a later date.
At 17, she travelled to an IS-controlled area of Syria in late 2016 or early 2017, via Russia and Turkey.
“While in Syria, Salman was trained to use an assault rifle and received ammunition from an ISIS military battalion when she was 18,” prosecutors had alleged, using another acronym for the group.
While there, she married German-Afghan IS fighter Abu Ali, according to court documents.
In early 2019, she was taken into custody by Syrian forces opposed to IS and was placed in a relocation camp until 2024, when Salman returned to the US and was arrested.
“With today’s verdict, Salman is held accountable for joining forces with a terrorist organization,” said United States Attorney Anthony Nocella.
“ISIS ravaged Syria and caused havoc across the globe; our office will continue to prosecute those who supported its murderous reign.”
Salman’s defense attorney had claimed she was “the victim of her (mother’s husband) bringing her as a child to ISIS territory in Syria”.
The attorney added that Salman was unaware of the man’s pro-IS beliefs.
A US-led coalition was deployed to Iraq and Syria in 2014 to fight the Islamic State group, which had seized large swathes of territory, committed massacres, and forced thousands of women and children into slavery.
Kurdish forces still hold around 2,200 foreign relatives of suspected Islamic State fighters in a northeastern Syria camp, an official there told AFP earlier in October.
The Program on Extremism has identified 83 American adults who travelled to Syria or Iraq since 2011 and were affiliated with jihadist groups there. AFP

Microsoft moves to shed quarter of workforce
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
23:00:42 UTC
08:00:42 KST

Microsoft moves to shed quarter of workforce
US tech giant Microsoft is moving to shrink its workforce through a buyout program covering some 60,000 employees, more than a quarter of its global staff, the company has announced.
The move follows thousands of job cuts earlier this year and comes as Big Tech companies seek to slash payroll costs while ramping up AI investment.
Microsoft unveiled the program on Monday, saying that it would cover roughly 27% of its 223,000 employees across selected divisions in the US, Canada, UK, and India, including Xbox, Windows, Copilot, finance, and human resources.
Microsoft has described the initiative as a voluntary exit program, under which employees can leave with severance packages. The company has not disclosed how many workers it expects to accept the offer.
In a memo to employees, Microsoft’s chief people officer Amy Coleman said that the initiative would give eligible staff considering a departure an opportunity to leave with financial support.
The latest move follows several rounds of workforce reductions at Microsoft. In July, the company announced plans to eliminate 4,800 positions, including approximately 3,200 in its Xbox gaming division. It had already launched a voluntary exit program in April covering roughly 8,750 US employees, or about 7% of its American workforce, with around 30% reportedly taking the offer.
The cuts come as Microsoft commits enormous sums to AI infrastructure, including data centers and computing capacity, putting pressure on the company to remove other expenses.
Other Big Tech giants have also been cutting jobs while pouring billions into AI. Amazon announced 16,000 corporate job cuts earlier this year, following another 14,000 layoffs in 2025. Meta has also slashed jobs while ramping up AI investment, while Google has repeatedly launched voluntary exit programs to reduce its workforce.
The trend has fueled concerns that the technology being promoted as a driver of economic growth could also eliminate large numbers of jobs, particularly in administrative, technical, and other white-collar occupations.
The threat extends beyond the tech industry. The Netherlands announced plans on Monday to eliminate around 25,000 government positions by 2035, partly through the adoption of AI, in a drive to save €3.5 billion ($4 billion) annually. The cuts will be phased in over several years, with police and security services exempt.
Denmark has also announced plans to use AI to free up 50 million working hours annually by 2035, equivalent to roughly 30,000 full-time positions, although it has not committed to corresponding layoffs.
Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates has warned that AI could cause major upheaval in the labor market, while arguing that certain professions, including caregiving, should remain “human reserved” even if machines become capable of performing them.
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk warned in July that AI would eventually outperform humans in any job, describing the transition as “a bumpy road.” His warning comes amid growing fears of AI spiraling out of human control following incidents involving systems defying instructions. Musk, whose company xAI develops advanced AI models, also predicted that the technology could surpass humanity’s combined intelligence within five years, potentially escaping human control within a decade.

Russia replaces Ukrainians with Russian settlers in occupied Kherson Oblast; only 10–20% of pre-war population remains, Ukraine says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
23:00:15 UTC
08:00:15 KST

Ukraine’s military intelligence estimates that only 10–20% of the prewar population may remain in the Russian-occupied left bank of Kherson Oblast, accusing Moscow of forcing Ukrainians from their homes while relocating Russian citizens to the area.
Russia’s efforts to displace Ukrainians and bring Russian citizens into occupied Kherson Oblast are part of Moscow’s broader campaign to consolidate control over occupied territory, impose Russian institutions, and erode Ukrainian national identity. Similar practices have been documented in other occupied Ukrainian territories, including the resettlement of Russians into homes in Mariupol and efforts to replace Ukrainian education with Russian curricula.
The Main Intelligence Directorate of Ukraine’s Defense Ministry (HUR) said Russia was creating intolerable living conditions for Ukrainian residents and unlawfully seizing private property to displace them. The agency said Moscow was simultaneously using financial incentives to recruit Russian teachers, doctors, and other professionals to work in occupied areas.
Russia brings in Russian workers as Ukrainians are pushed out
Before Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, around 500,000 people lived on the left bank of Kherson Oblast, according to HUR. The agency estimates that only 10–20% of that population may remain.
Moscow is using state-backed recruitment programs, including “Zemsky Teacher,” “Zemsky Doctor,” “Zemsky Feldsher,” “Zemsky Cultural Worker,” and “Zemsky Coach,” to attract Russian citizens to occupied Ukrainian territory, HUR said.
Under these programs, Russian teachers and doctors who agree to work in occupied areas are offered one-time payments of 2 million rubles, while junior medical staff can receive 1 million rubles. The incentives also include higher salaries and other benefits, with contracts lasting at least five years.
HUR said hundreds of Russian teachers and doctors had already been brought to occupied Ukrainian territories from regions across Russia, including Krasnodar, Khabarovsk, Stavropol, and Perm Krais, as well as Rostov, Kursk, and Leningrad oblasts.
According to Ukrainian intelligence, Russian medical personnel are needed primarily to serve occupying forces, while Russian teachers are being brought in to undermine Ukrainian children’s national identity.
Ukraine accuses Russia of war crimes and genocidal practices
HUR said Russia’s efforts to displace Ukrainian residents and bring in Russian citizens bore signs of war crimes and genocidal practices against the Ukrainian population.
The agency’s allegations concern both the coercive removal of Ukrainians from occupied territory and the replacement of local residents with people brought from Russia. Ukrainian authorities say these policies are part of Moscow’s broader effort to consolidate control over occupied Ukrainian land and impose Russian identity and institutions.
Kherson Oblast faces displacement, attacks, and a humanitarian crisis
Russian forces occupied much of Kherson Oblast in the early months of the full-scale invasion in 2022. Ukrainian forces liberated the oblast’s right-bank areas, including the regional capital, in November that year, but Russia continues to occupy the left bank of the Dnipro River.
Russian forces regularly attack Ukrainian-controlled areas of Kherson Oblast with artillery and drones, killing and injuring civilians. Ukrainians have described repeated drone attacks on civilians as a “human safari.” In May 2025, a UN commission of inquiry concluded that Russian forces’ repeated drone attacks on civilians along the Dnipro’s right bank amounted to crimes against humanity of murder.
The occupied town of Oleshky, on the left bank, has also faced severe shortages of food, medicine, and medical care amid restrictions on movement and continued fighting.
Thousands are starving in occupied Oleshky. People have no food, no way out, and Russian forces bomb incoming aid
Russia’s occupation has also exposed residents of Kherson Oblast to major humanitarian disasters. The destruction of the Kakhovka Dam in June 2023 flooded settlements along the Dnipro, including Russian-occupied communities on the left bank, damaging homes and forcing residents to flee. Russian forces’ restrictions on access and evacuation further endangered civilians in the affected areas.
While Russia occupies the left bank of Kherson Oblast, its forces continue to target civilians on the Ukrainian-controlled right bank. Across the oblast, residents face the consequences of Russia’s invasion, from forced displacement and property seizures under occupation to deadly drone and artillery attacks.

Israel election: Record turnout as Netanyahu and Eisenkot remain deadlocked
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
22:58:53 UTC

Israel election: Record turnout as Netanyahu and Eisenkot remain deadlocked
Israel's election remained deadlocked on Tuesday, exit polls showed, with opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot's bloc narrowly ahead of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's camp by 52 seats to 50. Neither side had a clear path to forming a government. Voter turnout reached 77.7%, the highest in more than two decades.
Israel's wartime election appeared deadlocked on Tuesday, exit polls showed, a potential setback for veteran Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu if the projections hold, with neither side having a clear path to power but rival Gadi Eisenkot's larger bloc potentially giving him the first chance to form a government.
The stalemate could yet work in Netanyahu's favour, allowing him to remain in power in a caretaker capacity while parties try to forge a governing coalition.
Turnout was 77.7%, Israel's Central Elections Committee said, the highest in more than two decades and around 7 percentage points higher than in the previous election in 2022.
Israel's three major networks updated their exit polls, giving Eisenkot's bloc a two-seat edge over Netanyahu's Likud-led camp, at 52-50.
The remaining 18 seats were allocated to unaligned Arab parties in the exit polls. But Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, has all but ruled out forming a government with them, complicating his path to a majority despite his bloc's lead.
Read moreIsrael: First exit polls show no clear winner, Arab parties make gains
Some Israeli media outlets, including pro-Netanyahu Channel 14, projected a far stronger showing for Netanyahu and his parties, saying they would collectively win 60 seats.
Final results could take days, and Israel's fragmented political system leaves smaller parties potential kingmakers. No single party has ever won 61 seats outright in the 120-seat Knesset, making coalitions the norm.
It was the first election since the Hamas-led attacks of October 7, 2023, and the ensuing wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.
Yohanan Plesner, president of the Israel Democracy Institute, called the exit polls a major defeat for Netanyahu's coalition, which they showed falling from 68 seats in the outgoing Knesset to about 50. But he said Eisenkot had not emerged as a clear winner.
Plesner cautioned that much could change as votes were counted. If the final result mirrored the exit polls, he said, Eisenkot could try to form a minority government that would remove Netanyahu from power, even if it lasted only until another election.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
ANTI-NETANYAHU BOOST
While there was no clear outcome, the exit polls reflected the strength of the anti-Netanyahu opposition.
Opposition leader Yair Lapid said in a statement: “Don’t let anyone confuse you: the Netanyahu bloc has suffered a crushing defeat. This is a total collapse and the public has told them to go home.”
Eisenkot, 66, a hawkish former military chief who lost a son and two nephews in the Gaza war, emerged as Netanyahu's strongest challenger, stressing his security credentials while positioning himself as a centrist domestically.
He entered politics only four years ago and joined Netanyahu's war cabinet after the 2023 Hamas attack, but quit eight months later, criticising the prime minister's leadership.
Eisenkot offers a break with Netanyahu's leadership and far-right allies, but not with the hardline approach to security that has become more entrenched since the 2023 Hamas attack: He opposes Palestinian statehood and says Hamas' military wing must be destroyed or dismantled.
Eisenkot says Israel's response — a war that has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, according to Gaza health authorities —was a failure because Hamas remains in charge.
"Dear Democrats, a decision was made," Yair Golan, leader of the Democrats party and a Netanyahu rival, said at a party rally after polls closed. "The nation has given us a sacred duty: to translate the trust they have placed in us into action, to fortify democracy, to save Israel and to provide true defense for the state."
The headquarters of the Joint List, an alliance of several Arab parties, burst into whistles and applause when exit polls were released at the close of voting, on a historic night for turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel.
“We refuse the occupation and racism, and we will remain here,” said Faten Gattas, a candidate in the Joint List, in a speech at the alliance’s headquarters in Nazareth. 
Candidates hoped that high Arab voter participation would allow them to play a decisive role in preventing Netanyahu’s coalition – the most far-right in Israel's history – from returning to power.
Read moreIbrahim Abu Ahmad on Israeli election: 'Crucial for Arab citizens to have ally in Jewish community'
A RECORD TURNOUT
Long lines had formed outside polling stations as voters turned out in huge numbers, grappling with the trauma of Israel's deadliest day, when Hamas killed 1,200 people and took 251 hostage, and the wars in Gaza and with Lebanon's Hezbollah and Iran that followed.
While Netanyahu was criticised for the country's biggest security failure, he argued that he had made Israel and the world safer by assassinating top leaders of Hamas, Hezbollah and Iran.
The policies of Netanyahu's right-wing coalition have been divisive at home and deepened Israel's international isolation, but he has portrayed himself as the leader with the mettle to face down Israel's foes.
Netanyahu, 77, has served as prime minister for nearly 19 of the past 30 years and has repeatedly survived political crises.
His opponents have managed to wrest the premiership from him only once since 2009, after four inconclusive elections in two years. Eighteen months later, he was back.
He entered the election facing longstanding corruption charges, which he denies, and criticism over intelligence failures that allowed Hamas-led militants to carry out their attack.
Netanyahu campaigned on an endorsement from US President Donald Trump, his ally in the war against Iran.

Kazakhstan proposes closer coordination among 5 nuclear-weapon-free zones and Mongolia at UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
22:57:17 UTC
07:57:17 KST

Kazakhstan proposes closer coordination among 5 nuclear-weapon-free zones and Mongolia at UN
The Permanent Mission of Kazakhstan to the United Nations, in cooperation with the United Nations Office for Disarmament Affairs (UNODA), hosted a forum entitled “Nuclear-Weapon-Free Zones: From the Comprehensive Study to Practical Cooperation," Qazinform News Agency reports, citing the press service of the Kazakh MFA.
The event marked the 20th anniversary of the signing of the Semipalatinsk Treaty and the publication of the new UN comprehensive study on nuclear-weapon-free zones – the first in 50 years. Discussions focused on implementing its recommendations, strengthening cooperation among nuclear-weapon-free zones and engaging with nuclear-weapon States.
Participants included UN Under-Secretary-General and High Representative for Disarmament Affairs Izumi Nakamitsu, Deputy Permanent Representative of Mexico to the United Nations Porfirio Thierry Muñoz Ledo, Vice President of the Nuclear Threat Initiative (NTI) Paul Dean, as well as permanent representatives and diplomats of UN Member States, representatives of international organizations, and experts in nuclear disarmament and non-proliferation. Dr. Ryan Musto of William & Mary (United States) moderated the discussion.
In his opening remarks, Kazakhstan’s Permanent Representative to the United Nations, Kairat Umarov, stressed that rising nuclear risks made it particularly important to strengthen cooperation mechanisms that had proven effective. He called for the recommendations of the new UN study to serve as a basis for concrete joint initiatives, highlighting Central Asia’s contribution to regional security and the nuclear non-proliferation regime.
Ms. Nakamitsu commended the longstanding partnership between the United Nations and Kazakhstan and the country’s sustained efforts to advance cooperation among nuclear-weapon-free zones. In particular, Kazakhstan and UNODA jointly organized international workshops in Astana in 2019 and 2024 to strengthen interzonal cooperation and improve consultation mechanisms. Highlighting the Semipalatinsk Treaty as an example of successful regional diplomacy, the UN Under-Secretary-General emphasized that the study’s lasting value would depend on the practical implementation of its recommendations and reaffirmed UNODA’s readiness to support this work.
Mexico’s representative advocated strengthening the institutional capacity of nuclear-weapon-free zones while taking their regional specificities into account, and continuing dialogue with nuclear-weapon States on legally binding security assurances.
The NTI representative highlighted the potential of nuclear-weapon-free zones to reduce nuclear risks, drawing particular attention to the experiences of Kazakhstan, South Africa, Brazil and Argentina. He also outlined plans to convene an interzonal meeting in Vienna and develop a dedicated online learning resource for diplomats.
During the open discussion, the ambassadors of Brazil and the United Kingdom emphasized the importance of regular consultations among nuclear-weapon-free zones and constructive dialogue with nuclear-weapon States. Experts and civil society representatives proposed strengthening coordination, information-sharing and educational cooperation, including through youth engagement. A representative of the International Committee of the Red Cross highlighted the complementary nature of nuclear-weapon-free zone treaties and the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons.
Concluding the forum, Mr. Umarov proposed closer coordination among the five regional nuclear-weapon-free zones and Mongolia, including to advance shared priorities in dialogue with nuclear-weapon States.
As a practical follow-up to the forum, Kazakhstan, with UNODA’s support, will prepare a concise summary of the discussion outlining participants’ key proposals and possible areas for further cooperation.
Earlier, it was reported that foreign ministers of Kazakhstan and the United Arab Emirates had a telephone conversation. The sides expressed satisfaction with the dynamic development of Kazakhstan-UAE cooperation, reaffirming their mutual interest in further deepening political dialogue and expanding practical cooperation in areas of common interest.

Thousands rally outside Portugal’s parliament over housing crisis, police operations
- Thousands protested in Lisbon over Portugal’s worsening housing crisis and police raids on activist camps, as Parliament debated the 2027 draft budget.
- Housing prices and rents have nearly doubled since 2017, hitting young people hardest. Protesters called for fair housing, rent caps, and protection of the right to protest.
- Watchdogs and prosecutors opened inquiries into police conduct after the Oct 25 operations. Police said 11 people were injured, while activists claimed 60 were hurt.
AI generated
LISBON – Thousands rallied outside Portugal’s Parliament in Lisbon on Oct 27 to protest against a deepening housing crisis and recent police operations against housing activists, while lawmakers debated the government’s draft budget for 2027.
Portugal faces one of Europe’s most acute home affordability crises, with prices more than doubling since 2017 and new-lease rents nearly doubling, hitting young people hardest, as wages have not kept up.
The Oct 27 protest followed baton-charging police operations to dismantle tent camps set up by housing activists in Lisbon and Porto on Oct 25, sparking allegations of excessive force.
Rally organisers said several thousand people packed the area. Police gave no crowd estimate.
The Portuguese protests echo recent demonstrations in Spain and elsewhere across Europe over housing shortages and surging rents.
Erica Rodrigues, 39, an actress, said the crisis affects young people and older generations because the “cost of living in Portugal is very high for what people earn”.
“It is unbearable,” she said.
“My congratulations to this government for the clown show it has put on in recent times. It has done a terrible job.”
Protesters demanded the minority centre-right government scrap a Bill that would speed up evictions and end rent caps on new leases, which passed a first reading with the far-right Chega party abstaining.
Joao Martins, 39, who is unemployed, said protesters were “fighting for decent and affordable housing for everyone” and for a “state budget that genuinely reflects the interests of the majority of the population, rather than just a few privileged people”.
He said they were also demonstrating “for the right to protest, which has been seriously threatened in recent days”.
Portugal's internal affairs watchdog, the IGAI, opened an inquiry into the police operations, while prosecutors launched a separate investigation into officers’ conduct.
Police reported 11 minor injuries, including three officers, in the two operations on Oct 25, while activist group Casa para Viver (Homes to Live) said 60 were hurt.
Speaking in Parliament on Oct 27, Prime Minister Luis Montenegro said police acted in line with the principles of “necessity, proportionality and adequacy”. REUTERS

Alexander brothers get 30 years each in prison after sex trafficking convictions
NEW YORK, Oct 27 - Three brothers convicted of exploiting their access to wealth and high society in New York and Miami to drug and rape women were each sentenced on Tuesday to 30 years in prison.
The twins Alon Alexander and Oren Alexander, 39, and Tal Alexander, 40, were sentenced by US District Judge Valerie Caproni in Manhattan, seven months after being convicted in a six-week trial of multiple sex crimes including conspiracy to commit sex trafficking.
Lawyers for the brothers did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
• Caproni called the brothers' conduct "monstrous," according to multiple media reports.
• Oren and Tal Alexander were co-founders of the luxury real estate brokerage Official, while Alon Alexander was an executive at his family's security company Kent Security.
• Prosecutors sought life sentences, while the Alexanders requested mandatory minimum 15-year prison terms.
• Prosecutors said the brothers for at least 14 years exploited their social status to prey on women and girls, with more than 70 women saying they were assaulted by one or more of the brothers in locations including Manhattan, the Hamptons on New York's Long Island, and Aspen, Colorado.
• In one instance, prosecutors said in January 2017 three girls were celebrating their senior year in high school at an Aspen nightclub when the brothers drugged them, enticed them to their five-star hotel for a promised after party, and then assaulted them.

Trump ally flees to US after Brazil election defeat – media
Right-wing Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro has fled to the US following his election defeat to incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, Reuters and Brazilian news outlet Jovem Pan reported on Tuesday, citing sources.
A senior US State Department official told AP on Tuesday that Bolsonaro and his family would be granted US visas.
Bolsonaro, the son of jailed former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro and an ally of US President Donald Trump, narrowly lost Sunday’s runoff to Lula despite receiving more votes in the first round earlier this month.
He is under investigation for money laundering and currency evasion involving financial ties to lawyer Willer Tomaz and businesses linked to online gambling. Bolsonaro also faces a separate investigation into suspected irregularities in the financing of Dark Horse, a biographical film about his father. Bolsonaro denies wrongdoing.
His brother Eduardo, also a politician, moved to the US in February 2025, citing fears of political persecution and arrest. He was subsequently convicted of attempting to interfere with judicial proceedings against his father by lobbying Washington to impose sanctions on Brazilian officials. Eduardo, who remains in the US, was sentenced to four years and two months in prison in June 2026.
Flavio Bolsonaro initially refused to recognize the election results and vowed to seek their annulment, citing a two-hour extension of voting.
“They will not silence me. They will not intimidate me. Let’s hold our heads high and keep fighting for our Brazil, whatever happens,” Bolsonaro said in a video posted Monday, although he later dropped his demand for annulment.
Later on Monday, Bolsonaro was given 24 hours to surrender his passports as part of the investigation involving Tomaz. The documents were reportedly canceled on Tuesday after he missed the deadline. Bolsonaro, who could face prosecution in lower courts when his Senate term ends on January 31, had insisted on Monday that he had no plans to flee.
Trump also questioned the election results. “It had a very bad look, the election, the way it was tabulated,” he told reporters on Monday. “The extension given was very strange.”
Both campaigns had requested a two-hour extension of voting on election day, citing difficulties for voters, according to Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court.
Bolsonaro’s father is serving a 27-year prison sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election to Lula. The elder Bolsonaro had also traveled to the US following his defeat before returning to Brazil. He denied wrongdoing and argued that the case was politically motivated.
Lula previously served two presidential terms from 2003 to 2010. He was barred from running in the 2018 election after being convicted on corruption charges and imprisoned. Brazil’s Supreme Court later annulled his convictions, restoring his political rights and allowing him to run in 2022, when he defeated Jair Bolsonaro. Lula has also denied wrongdoing and maintained that the corruption case against him was politically motivated.

Targeting of journalists in Gaza aims to conceal atrocities, UN rapporteur warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27

07:46:59 KST

United Nations Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese has warned that the systematic targeting of journalists across Gaza constitutes a deliberate campaign to conceal atrocities, presenting her latest investigative findings as an exposure of truth that has been "buried under the rubble".
"What is happening is not incidental; it is intentional," Albanese said during a virtual press briefing addressing the genocide in Gaza.
She termed the phenomenon "mediacide", characterising it as "the systematic destruction of the media's public function".
"In a genocide, the systematic attack on the media is part and parcel of the crime," Albanese added, underscoring that silencing witnesses forms a core mechanism of mass atrocities.
Impunity and legal accountability
Questioned on the status of inquiries into Israel's 2022 killing of Palestinian American journalist Shireen Abu Akleh, Albanese noted: "Nothing, nothing happened. So, the update is impunity".
She emphasised that this culture of unaccountability was fostered not solely by Israel but also represented "impunity by the United States".
Rejecting the broad application of the terrorist designation, Albanese argued that the term "has been the label to kill everyone, to bring famine upon everyone in Gaza, to destroy Gaza".
She maintained that even where a state invokes self-defence under international law, "Israel doesn't have and cannot claim the right to wage a war against Gaza".
Addressing concerns over whether the International Criminal Court had failed Palestinians, Albanese asserted that "the complementarity of international criminal investigation can be triggered", calling for immediate proceedings "starting now with activating domestic courts".
She stressed that citizens of Britain, France, the United States, and Belgium who served in the Israeli military must face immediate legal scrutiny under national jurisdictions, warning that action "cannot be delayed".
Albanese also highlighted the noticeable absence of Western legacy media from the briefing, suggesting it reflected possible solidarity with news organisations scrutinised in her report.

A 59-year-old man who died after attending a demonstration in Paris may have succumbed to tear gas exposure, his family's lawyer said Tuesday following an autopsy that found acute cardiorespiratory failure
Christophe M. died on Oct. 17 in Paris' 10th arrondissement amid demonstrations that were marked by clashes between protesters and police, according to broadcaster BFMTV.

Oct 27 (Reuters) - President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Tuesday that Ukrainian forces were retaking territory through a series of offensives, including one operation previously unannounced in which Kyiv’s troops used gas pipelines to outflank Russian positions.
Zelenskiy, speaking in his nightly video address, said Kyiv’s battlefield position was the strongest in some time in the 4-1/2-year-long war and could be made stronger with more deliveries of air defence systems from its Western allies.
Zelenskiy, citing a report by senior commanders, noted for the first time the “Veles” operation using pipelines in Ukraine’s northeast. He also referred to an air assault operation in eastern Ukraine and the “Vivaldi” operation further to the north, designed to prevent Russian advances in key areas.
He said Operation Veles was conducted near Kupiansk, a city in northeastern Kharkiv region recaptured by Ukrainian forces in late 2022, but since under constant Russian pressure.
“It is a strong operation, well planned and technology-driven. The Russians tried to use underground gas pipelines to advance past our positions,” Zelenskiy said.
“Our fighters turned this tactic against the Russians and used the underground infrastructure against the occupiers with extraordinary success,” he said.
In the Vivaldi offensive, one senior commander reported last month that Ukraine’s Third Army Corps had cleared an area of 75 square kilometres (29 square miles) of Russian infiltration groups and recaptured a further 10 square kilometres.
That operation was focused to the north of the key strongholds in the region — the so-called “fortress belt” of the cities Sloviansk and Kramatorsk. Their capture would bring Russia closer to its goal of seizing the entire Donbas region.
Zelenskiy in August spoke of success in an offensive further south, with 26 villages being returned to Ukrainian control.
Russia says it favours an overall resolution of the war rather than a short-lived ceasefire and has pledged to pursue its drive to capture all of Donbas.
Russian commanders repeatedly say, often in announcements in President Vladimir Putin’s presence, that their forces are advancing on all sections of the 1,200-km (750-mile) front line.
The chief of Russia’s General Staff, Valery Gerasimov, said this month that Moscow’s forces had captured 92 Ukrainian settlements, including the town of Dobropillia, since the beginning of September.
Ukraine’s military dismissed the Russian statements.

Kennedy Jr. faced widespread rebuke from civil rights groups, healthcare advocates and Democrats on Tuesday over his anti-Arab comments that the Council on American-Islamic Relations cast as “a textbook display of unvarnished racism and bigotry.”
In his remarks on Monday at a campaign event in Michigan where Republican Mike Rogers is running for the US Senate against Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, the US health secretary falsely claimed that Arabs had not won major international awards and “don’t produce” science and literature.
“There’s 500 million Arabs in the world, and yet they don’t produce science, they don’t win the Nobel Prize, they don’t win the Fields prize, they don’t win the Wolf Prize, they don’t produce literature,” the US health chief said.
Arabs have won all those prizes. Peter Hotez, who is a professor at the Baylor College of Medicine and specializes in vaccine development and tropical medicine, said his late colleague, Nobel Prize winner Ahmed Zewail, who was Arab and died in 2016, “would disagree” with the US health chief’s comments.
The Department of Health and Human Services did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
US rights advocates have raised concerns over escalating rhetoric against Muslims, Arabs, immigrants and ethnic minorities by President Donald Trump and his allies during the ongoing midterm election campaign.
“Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s vile anti-Arab rant is a textbook display of unvarnished racism and bigotry,” the Council on American-Islamic Relations, which documents hate against Muslims and Arabs in the US, said on Tuesday.
“His sweeping erasure of Arab contributions to humanity is not only maliciously false, but it also fans the flames of anti-Arab and anti-Muslim hate at a time when communities are already vulnerable to bigoted attacks from other public officials nationwide.”
Kennedy said the rise of the Muslim Brotherhood, one of the Arab world’s oldest and most influential Islamist groups founded almost a century ago, has “created stagnant societies.”
Republicans have claimed, without evidence, El-Sayed has ties to the Muslim Brotherhood even as the Democrat has publicly disavowed the group and denied any connection to it.
El-Sayed, who is Muslim, has faced a host of anti-Muslim attacks during the campaign. Over the weekend, Trump invoked the September 11, 2001, attacks when speaking about El-Sayed, whom he has also repeatedly and falsely called a “jihadist.”
Democratic US Senator Chris Murphy also responded to the US health secretary’s comments.
“I really think everyone needs to pay attention to this coordinated campaign to delegitimize Muslim Americans — not just as citizens but as humans.”
US healthcare advocacy organization and nonprofit Protect Our Care cast Kennedy’s comments as a “wildly racist tirade.”
Kennedy, who has pushed his anti-vaccine views in his role as the top health official, was also in Michigan on Monday to promote funding for Detroit’s health department and touted agreements with hospitals to offer healthier food.

Israel Election: Four Scenarios as Opposition Edges Netanyahu but Falls Short of Majority
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
22:37:59 UTC
07:37:59 KST

Israelis went to the polls in the highest turnout for decades on Tuesday, with initial exit polls showing a slight edge but no majority for the opposition, meaning the next government will be formed by whoever can cobble together a coalition.
The country’s main pollsters projected the opposition bloc, led by ex-army chief Gadi Eisenkot, to win 52 or 53 seats, and Netanyahu’s bloc to win 50.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Israeli Arab lists made strong gains, with exit polls showing them winning 17 or 18 seats between them.
Here are four possible scenarios:
1. Coalition
The parties will immediately begin negotiations to try to reach a 61-seat majority in the 120-member Knesset, but the path forward is far from clear.
President Isaac Herzog will name a candidate who has the best chance to form a government – not necessarily the party with the most seats, which the initial exit polls showed to be Netanyahu’s Likud.
The Arab Israeli parties, particularly Raam, have voiced openness to working with Eisenkot’s bloc, but the camp has kept them at arm’s length, perceiving their support as a liability during the campaign.
For Netanyahu’s bloc, however, there is no obvious place to pick up more seats after some smaller right-wing parties failed to meet the vote threshold for entering parliament.
Coalition negotiations can be arduous, with parties insisting on parochial interests, and can produce unstable governments.
Elections in Israel: Can Netanyahu Hold on to Power?
Following the previous election in November 2022, it took Benjamin Netanyahu 58 days to form his government.
2. Minority government
If no bloc manages to secure 61 seats, a candidate could attempt to govern without a majority but rather through support on an ad hoc basis from other lawmakers.
In this scenario, lawmakers from the Arab Israeli parties -- whose community makes up 20 percent of the population and generally identifies as Palestinian -- could play a critical role.
Raam, led by Mansour Abbas, has been a kingmaker in the past, having been the first Arab party to join an Israeli government in a short-lived 2021-2022 coalition led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid.
Another Arab movement, the Joint List, has said it would be unlikely to join a coalition government outright, but has offered to provide a “safety net” for any one that ousts Netanyahu from power.
Political commentator Tal Elovitz said especially high Arab turnout “indicates a strong desire for partnership”.
Eisenkot has not publicly even entertained the possibility, and Netanyahu in his campaign relentlessly told Jewish voters that a vote for the opposition could bring Arabs into government.
“Bottom line, at the moment it appears there is a possibility of forming a minority government headed by Eisenkot, but this could still shift depending on the final results,” Elovitz said.
3. National unity government
Considering Israel’s extreme polarization, a national unity government would appear fanciful, but it could theoretically create a less extreme government.
Israeli commentators have often mused on the possibility of a national unity government in which Netanyahu would jettison his provocative far-right allies as well as ultra-Orthodox parties and team up with Eisenkot, who shares Netanyahu’s views on many security issues.
Such a grand coalition would also exclude Arab parties.
A poll published on October 16 found that 55 percent of Israelis would prefer a national unity government over new elections if the vote did not produce a clear majority.
This scenario has a recent precedent. In 2020, Netanyahu and Benny Gantz, like Eisenkot a retired general appealing to the center, reached a power-sharing agreement after three elections in less than a year.
The agreement stipulated a rotation of the prime ministership, but the partnership fell apart after a year, triggering another election.
A unity government in the present situation would face strong opposition from both sides, particularly the opposition bloc, which has built its campaign around ousting Netanyahu, casting him as unfit to lead.
4. Deadlock and new elections
If no candidate manages to form a government, Israel will have to return to the polls.
The country held four elections between April 2019 and March 2021 due to the inability of politicians to forge a lasting coalition.
The candidate designated by the president will, in principle, have 28 days to form a coalition, with a possible 14-day extension, although there are other procedural ways to prevent an immediate calling of new elections.

Chancellor targets cost of living crisis in budget for a ‘difficult moment’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
22:34:33 UTC
07:34:33 KST

John Healey has acknowledged the UK faces a “difficult moment” but insisted he would put the country on a better path as he delivers his first budget on Wednesday against a turbulent global economic backdrop.
But despite the international uncertainty, the chancellor will signal “fresh hope for the future” as he attempts to sound a more optimistic note, by providing households with breathing space from rising cost of living pressures.
The budget, which will be interpreted as a signal of Andy Burnham’s intent, is nevertheless expected to be a relatively modest affair as Healey grapples with stark fiscal realities, putting off important decisions on tax and spending until next year.
“The world’s a highly uncertain place,” the chancellor said, in a video released before the budget. “Conflicts abroad are pushing up energy prices, and the cost of living here at home – piling pressure on the families, on businesses and on our public finances.”
Healey insisted the government would move to ease the cost of living “responsibly” by sticking to Labour’s self-imposed fiscal rules, as he attempts to reassure the markets that his plans for longer-term reform will make Britain “more resilient” from global shocks.
The chancellor has limited scope for big giveaways because of the stretched public finances, made worse by international market turmoil caused by the Iran conflict, but changes aimed at easing the cost of living are set to feature heavily.
In his pre-budget address, he added: “This budget is about getting through this difficult moment. But it’s also about putting Britain on a future path, a better future path.”
Healey is expected to offer temporary support for poorer families before a steep rise in typical energy bills in January; while pledging energy market reforms aimed at bringing down bills for all households in the longer term.
Andy Burnham recently told MPs he was keen to see the gas standing charge – a fixed daily levy on all users – abolished. The move would bring down bills for consumers who use less energy, and the cost would be picked up by those who use more.
Industry experts fear further investment in hydrogen and carbon capture is likely to bear the brunt of efforts to rein in extra spending, in a blow to the UK’s net zero targets.
As part of a series of “everyday fixes”, the chancellor is expected to end the carers’ allowance cliff edge, which has penalised unpaid carers for going over their earnings limit, even by as little as a few pence a week. Healey is also expected to cancel January’s planned increase in fuel duty.
The government has been under pressure to use the budget to set out a clear path for defence spending to hit 3% of national income by 2030 – a target Healey claimed to be committed to when he resigned as defence secretary earlier this year.
But while he is expected to confirm more investment in defence industries – described as a “downpayment” on hitting the target – Healey is expected to wait until next year’s spending review to confirm the timetable.
The budget will also set out a “roadmap” to devolving more tax revenues to local leaders in a significant shift towards moving spending power away from Whitehall to the regions and nations of the UK.
But the detail of Burnham’s devolution agenda in areas such as skills and employment support is not expected until the government publishes a white paper in the weeks ahead.
Cutting energy prices has the added benefit of bringing down inflation, helping to ease pressure on the Bank of England to raise interest rates. Markets are now expecting the Bank to hike rates four times, to 4.75%, over the next 12 months.
Healey is also expected to take action to offset part of the hit to the public finances from higher interest rates on government borrowing – the result of rising inflation and turmoil in global bond markets.
The government had to pay the highest yield, or interest rate, on new five-year bonds since 2008 on Tuesday, above 5%.
City analysts say bond market investors will be watching the budget closely – though the upward move in UK yields, or interest rates, have echoed those seen in other major economies.
The UK’s economy has proved more resilient than expected in the face of the Iran conflict but recent data has pointed to a deteriorating outlook.
At a cabinet meeting last week, Healey told ministers that rising inflation caused by the conflict, which hit an in-year high of 3.5% last month, was the political backdrop to the budget.
Consumer confidence has fallen at the fastest rate since Brexit; while the number of businesses in financial distress has hit its highest level in more than two decades, according to data published by consultancy BTG on Thursday, with hospitality and construction hardest hit.
Healey struck an optimistic note, however, saying: “Britain’s economy is showing real signs of resilience: investment’s up, productivity is growing and we had the joint fastest growth in the G7 in the first half of this year.”
Healey will announce plans to increase the minimum wage by nearly 4% but slow the rise for younger people under the age of 21 after warnings that they are being priced out of jobs but prompting accusations that Labour had broken a manifesto pledge.
He is also expected to protect pensioners and those saving for their retirement by shielding nearly one million people from paying income tax and is preparing to make the government’s revived Help to Buy scheme more generous, in a boost to middle-earners.
To help offset the damage inflicted on the public finances by war in the Middle East, Healey is poised to raise taxes for Britain’s banks, potentially reversing cuts to the bank surcharge made by Jeremy Hunt, which would raise upwards of £2bn a year. Online retailers will be responsible for collecting tax owed by firms selling on their platforms.
The Tories said the chancellor was set to “shy away” from the difficult decisions, including bringing down the welfare bill, which the prime minister has said he does not want to do through “crude cuts”.
The shadow chief secretary to the Treasury, Richard Fuller, said: “Britain’s public finances are on a cliff edge. A ‘do-nothing’ budget will not solve the problems staring us in the face: a spiralling welfare bill, a crippling tax burden, mounting debt and rising global threats.”
The Lib Dems warned against a “steady as she goes” budget. Their deputy leader, Daisy Cooper, said: “Families are being squeezed from all sides, businesses face mounting costs and for many it feels like even the basic joys in life have become unaffordable.”

Israel has voted, but the coalition deadlock is just beginning - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
22:33:34 UTC
07:33:34 KST

An engaged nation went to the polls in unprecedented numbers on Tuesday and spoke. It will now take weeks, if not months, to figure out exactly what it said.
The exit polls released at 10 p.m. by Channels 11, 12, and 13 all showed the so-called change bloc ahead of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc, but Likud emerging as the largest party.
Neither camp, however, appeared to have the partners needed to form the government it promised.
The distinction matters. Taken together, the parties opposed to the outgoing government won a clear majority of the projected seats. But those parties do not constitute a single bloc willing to govern together.
The Arab parties are central to that gap.
According to the exit polls, they won a combined 17 to 18 seats, making them one of the election’s biggest stories. Their apparent strength helped deny Netanyahu a majority. Yet the change bloc’s commitments against relying on them also complicate its ability to replace him.
The Arab parties’ seats count just as much as anyone else’s. The obstacle is other parties’ willingness to enter a governing arrangement with them.
The result, if it holds, is a clear parliamentary majority against the outgoing government – 1,116 days after October 7 – without a clear agreement on what should replace it.
Expect Netanyahu, Eisenkot both to claim victory
Both camps asked the public for a decisive outcome. Neither got everything it wanted.
Netanyahu apparently emerged at the head of the largest party, but without a clear path to a coalition. Yashar leader Gadi Eisenkot emerged at the head of the larger change bloc, but with a gap between the seats opposing Netanyahu and the partners available to form a government.
Expect both to claim victory.
Netanyahu will point to Likud’s lead over Yashar, which trailed it by two or three seats in the exit polls. Eisenkot will point to the balance between the blocs.
Netanyahu knows better than most that the largest party does not necessarily form the government. In 2009, Tzipi Livni’s Kadima won one more seat than Likud. Netanyahu became prime minister because he could assemble a coalition and she could not.
The question now is whether Eisenkot can do what Netanyahu did then.
That will require finding a way around commitments that, during the campaign, sounded unequivocal.
Eisenkot set four conditions for prospective coalition partners that the Arab parties would be unlikely to meet. His camp will now have to confront the consequences of those conditions: a majority for replacing Netanyahu may exist on paper without being available around the cabinet table.
Even a willingness to rely on Mansour Abbas’s Ra’am party would not, on the figures emerging Tuesday night, necessarily close the gap. Support from the Joint List would raise a further set of political obstacles.
The Arab parties, meanwhile, have voters and demands of their own. They cannot simply be penciled into someone else’s coalition arithmetic as though their only function were to provide the missing seats.
Their projected gains came as a result of a strong determination to ensure that another right-wing government does not emerge.
But helping to deny the outgoing coalition a majority and helping to install its replacement are two different achievements. The first appears within reach. The second will depend on negotiations and decisions still to come.
Another route for Eisenkot would be to bring in the two haredi (ultra-Orthodox) parties, projected together to win 12 seats.
That could provide a majority. It would also give those parties considerable leverage over a government whose prospective partners have promised meaningful changes to haredi conscription.
The difficulty is obvious. Bringing the haredi parties into the government might solve the coalition arithmetic while making one of its central policy commitments considerably harder to fulfill.
There is also an option that jumps off the page: a government comprising Likud, Yashar, Naftali Bennett’s B’Yachad, and Yisrael Beytenu.
On the projected figures, those parties would together have 67 seats, without the haredi parties, the Arab parties, or the parties on the hard-right (Otzma Yehudit and the Religious Zionist Party) or the hard-left (the Democrats).
Numerically straightforward. Politically, anything but.
If Netanyahu remains at Likud’s helm, such a government would require his opponents to abandon their promises not to serve under him. It would also require agreement on who leads and on what terms.
A coalition that looks doable on paper is anything in real life. That is the central problem emerging from Tuesday’s exit polls.
There are combinations that produce a majority. There are fewer combinations that the parties have said they are prepared to join.
Weeks following election will test final or negotiating positions
The coming weeks will test whether those positions are final or negotiating positions.
First, however, the votes must be counted. Exit polls provide the opening frame for coalition negotiations, not the final count on which they will rest.
But if the broad picture holds, the question will shift quickly from how Israelis voted to what their elected representatives are prepared to do with those votes.
More specifically: which campaign promises will survive contact with the results?
Throughout the campaign, parties told voters whom they would sit with, whom they would never sit with, and what conditions they would insist upon before joining a government.
Those promises matter. A voter is entitled to know whether a ballot cast for one party might help put someone else in the prime minister’s chair.
But when enough parties rule out enough other parties, the result can be a Knesset with no workable majority.
Someone will now have to decide whether the greater obligation is to honor a campaign commitment or to compromise sufficiently to allow a government to be formed.
Those arguing for compromise can be expected to call it national responsibility. Those opposing it will call it a betrayal.
Netanyahu cannot in any way point to these projections and claim that the country gave him a vote of confidence.
His opponents can point to a majority that emerged against his government, but still have to demonstrate that they can turn it into a government of their own.
The politicians now have to decide what they are prepared to change: their conditions, their partners, or their promises.
Failing that, they may eventually ask the voters to try again.

Tal, 40, and Oren and Alon, both 39, maintained grim expressions during the sentencing but otherwise had little reaction. The prison terms, while lengthy, were less than the life behind bars sought by prosecutors. Lawyers for the brothers told the judge they would appeal.
The prosecution was one of the highest-profile sex-trafficking cases to go to trial in recent years.
