By Simon Lewis
WASHINGTON, Oct 27 (Reuters) - The US State Department’s policy chief, Jeremy Lewin, said on Tuesday he was leaving his role after nearly two years in which he helped lead an overhaul of US foreign assistance and implemented President Donald Trump’s policies toward Venezuela and Cuba.
Lewin, a top adviser to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, said on social media he was leaving to return to the private sector.
“President Trump has put decades of post-Cold War malaise behind us — permanently transforming US foreign policy to put Americans first, keep them safe, and drive peace and shared prosperity in key regions,” Lewin said on X.
The 29-year-old joined the government as part of Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency and played a leading role in closing the US Agency for International Development. Trump and Musk justified the move by accusing the agency of waste, fraud and abuse.
Some programs were later restored or revamped under the State Department. Lewin oversaw that process as acting under secretary of state for foreign assistance, humanitarian affairs and religious freedom.
In late August, Lewin began his stint as the department’s director of policy planning, in which he focused on US policy toward Venezuela and Cuba, according to his State Department biography.
The biography says Lewin is the only person under 30 to serve in the policy planning role.
The US military captured Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in January. Washington has since controlled the sale of Venezuelan oil and holds the proceeds, and Trump has said no Venezuelan oil will go to Cuba.
That move cut off the main source of oil for Communist-run Cuba.

Yemen’s armed forces say they carried out ‘precise, direct’ strikes against Houthis

Jomaa Younis and Serdar Dincel
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
Yemen’s armed forces said late Tuesday that they carried out 1,382 strikes against the Houthi group “in recent hours,” describing the attacks as “precise and direct.”
The operations "neutralized" around 440 Houthi fighters and commanders and secured new field gains in Taiz governorate in southwestern Yemen, army spokesman Col. Majed al-Nuzaili noted on the US social media platform X.
The operations targeted “field command centers, fortifications, sources of fire, troop concentrations and reserves as well as reinforcements, transport and supply assets belonging to the terrorist Houthi militia," al-Nuzaili said.
In Taiz governorate, al-Nuzaili said army units and Popular Resistance forces backed by warplanes carried out coordinated airstrikes and attacks using various tactical methods.
The operations thwarted Houthi attempts to retake positions they had lost, resulting in new advances on the ground and stronger fire control over several strategic positions and highlands, he added.
Taiz has witnessed intense fighting between the Yemeni army and the Houthi group for weeks, with hundreds killed and wounded on both sides.
On the Bab al-Mandab, Dhubab and Al-Mudhariba fronts in Taiz, al-Nuzaili said army forces thwarted Houthi infiltration attempts and targeted their reinforcements and military vehicles.
He also said army units continued offensive operations along the northern and northwestern approaches to the capital Sanaa and on the eastern front, supported by armored vehicles, artillery and drones.
According to the statement, the operations targeted Houthi movements, command centers, weapons positions, ammunition depots and fortifications, limiting the group’s ability to maneuver and move reinforcements between fronts.
Al-Nuzaili said simultaneous military operations would continue across the front lines to secure further gains, while precautions were being taken to protect civilians and civilian infrastructure.
The Houthis did not immediately comment on the Yemeni army’s statement.
The developments come amid a military escalation in Yemen that began in July, described as the most extensive since the relative calm that followed the start of a truce in April 2022.
Operation Dawn of Yemen has been underway since Oct. 5. Presidential Leadership Council Chairman Rashad al-Alimi said the operation aims to restore state institutions from Houthi control and take control of Sanaa.
Yemen has been mired in conflict since the Houthis seized Sanaa and several provinces in September 2014, triggering a civil war. A Saudi-led coalition intervened in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government.

Australia's appeal to international students plunges over six months as visa rules bite
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
21:46:19 UTC
06:46:19 KST

In brief
- Australia's appeal to international students fell sharply in just six months.
- Migration changes and rising costs prompted students to look elsewhere.
Australia's appeal to foreign students has plummeted in just six months, a new report has found.
The crash comes on the heels of the hot debate over migration prompting Labor, the coalition and One Nation to narrow the gangway for foreigners wanting to study in Australia.
Labor will stop higher education entrants from overseas bringing along their families and ensure they can only move between institutions if they're pursuing a higher-level qualification, under measures Immigration Minister Tony Burke announced in August.
New figures from IDP Education, a migration agent, showed less than one in four prospective students put Australia top of their list of potential destinations, down from more than one in three six months ago.
The US, UK and Canada all became more attractive over the same period, hamstringing Australia in a much more fearsome competition for the world's best minds.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Constant chopping and changing of visa rules and fiddling with planning levels had made prospective students take notice.
"The world's best students have got so much choice," IDP's chief partner officer Simon Emmett told AAP.
"Once you've got that uncertainty, the shift to other destinations is something that's difficult to switch back on."
Australia is still considered as a destination by a world-leading 54 per cent of prospective students, IDP found, but that was down five per cent and possibly about to be overtaken by a surging UK.
In July, the cost of a student visa jumped to $2500 for undergraduates and $5750 for postgraduates, making Australia the world's most expensive destination.
Australia's visa refusal rate had the previous month also climbed to a 10-year high of 24.6 per cent, up from just 7.9 per cent a decade prior.
Mr Emmett said Canada, where international enrolments dived 29 per cent after a massive crackdown, should serve as a warning to other countries wanting to lower their migration intake by cutting foreign students.
"We need to be really careful we don't overcorrect on student policies," he said.
"You can make decisions that impact visa decisions now, but it's the prospective students who you'll also impact ... students consider destinations over a long period."
Students already in Australia were also finding life trickier, IDP's report found.
Almost half said finding part-time or post-graduate work was harder or much harder than expected, and more than one in three had trouble with the cost of living.

Journalists associations in the country leapt to their colleagues’ defense, calling the remarks a “death threat” and asking the United Nations special rapporteur for freedom of expression to intervene. The Trump administration is considering lifting sanctions on the Russian Direct Investment Fund (RDIF), on which the former Biden administration imposed sanctions in the early days of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Russian officials pushed for the move during discussions on RDIF’s role in Russian diesel exports to the US, The New York Times reported on Tuesday, Oct. 27, citing people familiar with the matter. An unnamed US official confirmed to the newspaper that the US Treasury Department was reviewing the fund’s application for delisting through its standard procedures.

“While officially a sovereign wealth fund, RDIF is widely considered a slush fund for President Vladimir Putin and is emblematic of Russia’s broader kleptocracy,” the Treasury said under the former Biden administration.
By contrast, the US official told NYT that the current review was a part of an effort to improve bilateral relations between Moscow and Washington, with the fund’s chief executive, Kirill Dmitriev, praised as a “helpful envoy” in ending the war.
RDIF was initially created in 2011, by the order of former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev and then-Prime Minister, current Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Diesel deal paves way for sanctions relief

‘Trump Is Cooked’: How Trump’s Russia Policy Is Splintering Republicans Ahead of the Midterms
Shortly after the deal’s announcement, the US Treasury Department authorized the sale and import of Russian diesel fuel through April 7, 2027.
The move came only three weeks after Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act into law on Sept. 18, appearing to completely disregard the bill intended to target Russia’s energy and defense industries, as well as networks close to Putin.
According to NYT, RDIF offered to handle transactions between Russian sellers and American buyers, while at the same time pushing for its removal from the sanctions list. To be delisted, RDIF would have to prove that the reasons for its original designation no longer apply.

It has since changed its listed destination from New York to “for orders,” meaning it has no discharge instructions yet.
From slush fund to trusted mediator
Eric Green, who oversaw Russia policy at the National Security Council under former President Joe Biden, told the NYT that lifting the sanctions would signal that Washington was abandoning its earlier position of keeping economic pressure on Moscow until a peace settlement was reached in Ukraine.

He also revealed that the US Treasury Department is working directly with Dmitriev.
On that same day, Moscow revealed that Russia and the US are discussing the future of sanctioned Russian oil giant Lukoil’s overseas assets, valued at approximately $22 billion.
The US also proposed restoring Russian gas supplies to Europe, including reviving the Nord Stream pipeline system, The Economist reported on Oct. 22.
Earlier on Tuesday, Le Monde reported that the Kremlin is courting Trump and his inner circle with economic deals, including those in energy, civil aviation, rare earth metals and artificial intelligence (AI), without first agreeing to a ceasefire.
According to the same report, Witkoff presented Ukrainian negotiators in Florida on Oct. 9 with a postwar “regional prosperity plan,” which envisaged fully restoring Russian oil and gas supplies to Europe through Ukrainian territory.

Around the same time, Trump claimed it was time for Ukraine to get a new president, while, days later, restrictions on Starshield, the military version of the Starlink satellite network, disrupted Ukrainian drone operations.
Elon Musk claimed such limits were ultimately decided by Trump, not his company; a claim the US president denied.

Around the time, Zelensky also suggested that Russia was offering Washington potential business ventures and economic projects to influence its decisions.

Israel election turnout hits 77.7%, highest in 25 years, as exit polls show 52-50 split
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
21:44:12 UTC
06:44:12 KST

Israel recorded its highest election turnout in 25 years on Tuesday, with 77.7% of eligible voters casting ballots by the official 10 p.m. closing time, according to the Central Elections Committee. Meanwhile, updated television exit polls showed a remarkably consistent picture: 52 seats for the bloc seeking to replace Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, 50 for his political allies and 18 for the Arab parties.
A total of 5,695,682 Israelis had voted by 10 p.m., an increase of approximately 7.1 percentage points compared with the same stage of the previous election in 2022. It was the highest turnout recorded at poll-closing time since 2001.
The figure is not yet final. Voters who arrived at their polling stations before 10 p.m. were permitted to cast their ballots even after the official closing time, meaning the total is expected to rise further.
The high turnout was reflected across the country, with particularly strong participation in several Arab and ultra-Orthodox communities. In two small communities in the Arava region, Paran and Shaharut, the reported turnout reached 100%.
Where Israelis voted: The major cities
Among Israel's larger cities, Modi'in-Maccabim-Re'ut recorded one of the highest turnout rates at 79.2%, followed by Bnei Brak at 77%, Kfar Saba at 74.7%, Petah Tikva at 73% and Rehovot at 72.9%.
Rishon LeZion and Herzliya each recorded 71.3%, followed by Ramat Gan at 71.2%, Ra'anana at 70.8% and Lod at 70.6%.
Turnout in Jerusalem reached 65.9%, compared with 65.4% in Tel Aviv-Jaffa and 61.6% in Haifa, Israel's three largest cities.
In other major population centers, turnout stood at 69% in Holon, 68.7% in Ashkelon, 68.5% in Hadera, 67.8% in Ashdod and Beit Shemesh, and 65.8% in Be'er Sheva.
Netanya recorded 60.2%, while Bat Yam had one of the lowest turnout rates among the major cities listed, at 55.3%.
Arab communities report strong turnout
Turnout was particularly high in several Arab communities, with Sakhnin reaching 86.8% and Kafr Qasim recording 84.9%.
In the southern Bedouin city of Rahat, turnout reached 82%, while Kuseife recorded 81.2% and Hura 79.1%.
Tayibe registered 79%, Shefa-'Amr 75.9%, Umm al-Fahm 75.7% and Nazareth 72.2%.
The figures came as the updated exit polls projected a combined 18 seats for the Joint List and Ra'am, giving the Arab parties a potentially important role in the parliamentary balance.
Ultra-Orthodox communities also see high participation
High turnout was also recorded in several ultra-Orthodox communities. Rekhasim led the group with 86.9%, followed by Elad at 84% and Modi'in Illit at 83.1%.
Beitar Illit recorded 80%, while turnout reached 77% in Bnei Brak and 75.1% in Emmanuel.
These figures come as the main ultra-Orthodox parties, Shas and United Torah Judaism, remain part of the projected parliamentary bloc supporting Netanyahu.
Updated exit polls converge on 52-50 split
The latest exit poll updates from Kan 11, Channel 12 and Channel 13 all give the bloc seeking to replace Netanyahu 52 seats, compared with 50 for the prime minister's allies. The Arab parties are projected to hold the remaining 18 seats in the 120-member Knesset.
The new projections represent a slight setback for former IDF chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot's change bloc compared with the initial exit polls, which had given it 53 seats in some surveys.
In Channel 13's updated poll, Naftali Bennett's Beyahad party dropped from 14 to 13 seats, while the Joint List increased from 10 to 11. The change brought the anti-Netanyahu bloc down to 52 seats, with Netanyahu's bloc remaining at 50.
Channel 13 projects Likud as the largest party with 25 seats, followed by Eisenkot's Yashar! with 23. Bennett's Beyahad receives 13, the Joint List 11 and the Democrats nine.
Yisrael Beiteinu, Ra'am and United Torah Judaism each receive seven seats, while Otzma Yehudit, Shas and the Religious Zionism-Zehut alliance each receive six.
Kan 11's updated exit poll also shows Beyahad dropping to 13 seats and the Joint List rising to 11, producing the same overall distribution of 52 seats for the change bloc, 50 for Netanyahu's bloc and 18 for the Arab parties.
Channel 12's update showed a different movement within the change bloc: the Democrats rose to 10 seats, while Avigdor Lieberman's Yisrael Beiteinu fell to eight. Its overall bloc projection remained unchanged at 52 seats for Netanyahu's opponents against 50 for his supporters.
The updated Channel 12 poll continues to show Likud leading with 24 seats, followed by Yashar! with 22 and Beyahad with 12. The Joint List receives 11 seats.
High turnout, but no clear parliamentary majority
Despite the unusually high voter participation and the narrow lead for Netanyahu's opponents, the updated exit polls still do not point to a clear parliamentary majority for either main political bloc.
The change bloc's 52 projected seats leave it nine short of the 61 needed for an outright majority. Netanyahu's 50-seat bloc is 11 seats short.
The Arab parties' projected 18 seats could therefore play an important role in determining the next government, although disagreements among the parties seeking to replace Netanyahu remain an obstacle to forming a coalition.
The final outcome will also depend on the official count, including special double-envelope ballots cast by soldiers and other eligible voters whose votes require separate verification.
The unexpectedly high turnout could also affect parties close to the 3.25% electoral threshold, with Ofer Winter's Amcha Yisrael, the joint party led by Yoaz Hendel and Yaron Zelekha, and the Haredi Public Party all projected to fall short in the exit polls.
For now, election night has produced a clear result in one respect: voter participation has reached a level not seen in a quarter-century. Whether that translates into a decisive political outcome remains unresolved.

F-16 Jets to Add Startup Castelion’s Hypersonic ‘Blackbeard’ Missile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
21:43:24 UTC
06:43:24 KST

The Air Force has awarded Castelion, a venture capital-backed defense startup founded in 2022, a contract to integrate its hypersonic Blackbeard missile onto the F-16 Fighting Falcon.
The announcement, which came from the company via social media on Oct. 26, marks a major advancement in the Air Force’s work on hypersonic munitions.
Neither the Air Force Research Laboratory, which awarded the contract, nor Castelion immediately responded to a request for comment.
The same day, the service awarded a $694 million contract to Lockheed Martin, a longtime defense prime, to begin production of the hypersonic Air-Launched Rapid Response Weapon, Air & Space Forces Magazine reported.
The Blackbeard missile has drawn strong interest across the Pentagon, with the Navy pushing to field the rocket-powered, boost-glide strike weapon with a nearly 500-mile strike range on the sea service’s F/A-18 Super Hornet.
Navy Development
The Navy’s Air Test and Evaluation Squadron 23 used the Super Hornet to conduct carriage and separation tests of Blackbeard on Sept. 18 at Naval Air Station Patuxent River, Md., which validated the weapon’s compatibility and flightworthiness on the aircraft.
The service selected Blackbeard as the winner in its Multimission Affordable Capacity Effector program, which shifted it to a program of record under framework contract orders of up to $200 million.
The company won a $105 million contract to integrate the missile on the F/A-18 Super Hornet in April.
The MACE initiative sought an affordable hypersonic missile about the size of an AIM-120 AMRAAM air-to-air missile.
In June, the service awarded the company its first production contract, worth $23.4 million, for 50 early operational capability pre-production prototype Blackbeard missiles.
Subsequent delivery orders from the Navy aim to speed up Blackbeard pre-production prototypes to EOC status and field the low-cost hypersonic weapon.
USAF Spending and Development
For its part, the Air Force has spent nearly $21 million to date on Blackbeard research and development, and AFRL added $16.4 million in a September contract modification for the missile.
Those dollars cover development through June 2028 under current spending and contractual agreements.
The USAF contract modification also pursues compatibility with the F-35A.
While the F-35 is the services’ main fifth-generation tactical fighter, the F-16, like the Navy’s workhorse Super Hornet, are workhorse fourth-gen fighters that can carry more munitions without worrying about compromising stealthy characteristics.
The Air Force has more than 600 F-16s in the fleet and recently moved forward with plans to upgrade the decades-old software system for those crucial aircraft, Air & Space Forces Magazine previously reported.
The Big Picture
The Air Force now has a three-pronged approach to hypersonic munitions.
These include Castelion’s Blackbeard, an air-to-air missile; the Lockheed Martin AGM-183A ARRW, a strategic strike-focused, exquisite, long-range hypersonic missile; and the Raytheon/Northrop Grumman Hypersonic Attack Cruise Missile, a cruise missile option to strike ground or maritime targets.
ARRW successfully completed booster and All-Up-Round tests and is poised to add terminal seeker and data-link integration for moving-target tracking in its Increment 2 tests. The strategic strike missile is envisioned for the B-52 Stratofortress and B-1B Lancer.
The AHM-4A HACM is built for internal or external carriage and geared for both fighter and bomber use to add high-volume magazine depth to the fleet. The missile achieved milestone flight tests over an undisclosed Australian range in late September, Air & Space Forces Magazine reported. Initial operational delivery of HACMs is slated for 2027.
Additionally, AFRL recently posted a request for white papers on developing a more advanced hypersonic rocket engine for its current and future munitions dubbed the Rotating Detonation Rocket Engine.
If successful, the more affordable, mass-produced engine could extend ranges, increase speed, and up the payload for future hypersonic, Air & Space Forces Magazine reported.

U.S. issuing visas to Brazil's Flávio Bolsonaro and family after he lost presidential election, official says

Bolsonaro, an ally of President Trump, and his family will be allowed entry into the U.S., the official said.
Bolsonaro departed Brazil for the U.S. following his loss to incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in Sunday's election, according to multiple Brazilian media reports.
A spokesperson for Bolsonaro did not respond to a request for comment. His campaign manager Rogério Marinho also refused to comment.

A warrant was recently issued for his arrest.
Mr. Trump did not offer a full-throated endorsement of Bolsonaro in the runoff against Lula, as he has with some other right-of-center candidates in Latin America. But he suggested on Monday, without providing evidence, that Brazil's election was "rigged."
Bolsonaro's decision to leave Brazil came as a deadline for him to surrender his regular and diplomatic passports expired at noon Tuesday. It remained unclear whether he had complied.
Bolsonaro was served with the order to surrender his passports Monday, a day after his stunning loss. Bolsonaro said he received it outside the home where his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, is serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest for attempting a coup following his 2022 election loss to Lula. After his 2022 defeat, Jair Bolsonaro fled Brazil for Florida. He returned three months later.
The sealed Supreme Court order, viewed by The Associated Press, was issued Sunday. Bolsonaro has refused to concede defeat and has made unsubstantiated allegations of election fraud.
Lula, who turned 81 on Tuesday, received more than 64 million votes, compared with fewer than 60 million for Bolsonaro, a margin of nearly 4%.

Rare Nanotyrannus skeleton sells for $47.3m at New York auction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
21:40:13 UTC
06:40:13 KST

A rare skeleton of a Nanotyrannus, a smaller relative of the Tyrannosaurus rex, sold at auction in New York this week for $47.3m, making it one of the world’s most expensive fossils.
The skeleton, named “Jodi” after the person who found the remains in 2019, sold at Sotheby’s on Tuesday for $47.3m, “after a twelve-minute bidding battle that saw six bidders compete online and over the phones, before ultimately selling on the phone”, Sotheby’s said in a statement.
Sotheby’s initially estimated that the skeleton would sell for $6m to $9m. Tuesday’s result makes “Jodi” the “second most valuable dinosaur ever sold at auction”, Sotheby’s noted. The buyer has not yet been identified publicly.
The skeleton, which was unveiled at a Manhattan auction earlier this month, was discovered by Jodi Pierson in 2019 on her privately owned land in the Hell Creek Formation in Garfield County, Montana, near the town of Jordan. According to Sotheby’s, the skeleton measures 19.6ft long from nose to the tail, and around 9.6ft tall on the armature, “comprising approximately 191 fossil bone elements”.
In a statement on Tuesday, Cassandra Hatton, vice-chair and worldwide head of science and natural history at Sotheby’s, thanked the team who assisted in the efforts to “excavate and save ‘Jodi’”.
“Their passion and expertise have been fundamental to Jodi’s story,” Hatton said. “From the discovery and excavation, their commitment to understanding and preserving this remarkable specimen has helped bring us to this moment, a testament to the fact that we can all make major contributions to science. This exceptional result is a wonderful recognition of that work, and of the enduring fascination with the Nanotyrannus.”
“Jodi” is one of only “three substantial Nanotyrannus skeletons known to science, and the first to come to market since the genus was confirmed last fall”, per Sotheby’s. Judging from the overall size and degree of bone development, “it can be determined that the skeleton belonged to an adult individual”, according to a description on Sotheby’s website.
Sotheby’s described the nanotyrannus as “a fast, highly specialized carnivorous tyrannosaurid that lived alongside Tyrannosaurus rex at the end of the Cretaceous, about 67 million years ago”. It added that “previously hypothesized by some to be adolescent T rex, Nanotyrannus has been shown to have over 150 morphological differences that distinguish it from its much larger cousin”.
The sale and cost of the fossil has prompted criticism from some in the science community.
Thomas R Holtz Jr, author and principal lecturer on vertebrate paleontology at the University of Maryland, said that as a “tyrannosaur researcher”, his “concerns about the sale of Jodi are the same general concerns about all these multimillion-dollar sales of fossils.
“At the same time this sale went on, some museums are closing (the Academy of Natural Sciences at Drexel in Philadelphia) or being threatened with closure (the Sternberg Museum of Natural History at Fort Hays State University) because of cost overruns literally only 1/10th that of the final cost of Jodi.
“So a person really interested in paleontology could do vastly more good by supporting the ongoing operations of multiple museums than the sale of one specimen. And indeed, the total cost of excavation, preparation, and mounting of a skeleton like this is probably on the order of $1m at most, possibly much less. So a well-funded museum would be able to gather multiple good skeletons for the price of this one ‘trophy.’”
He also emphasized that “potentially scientifically significant fossils” like Jodi “can be lost to research and the public when they are in private hands”.
“Now maybe the as-yet unidentified purchaser will donate it to a museum or similar institution, where the public can see it and where scientists now and in future generations can measure the bones, take samples and scans of the fossils, and apply current analytical procedures (as well as procedures no one has dreamed of yet) to help us better understand the biology of these ancient animals. But if it simply graces the lobby or ballroom of one of some billionaire’s mansions, unseen and unaccessible to all but their friends, servants and so forth, it is effectively lost to both the public and the scientific community. In fact, at that point, it is no different than if it had just been left in the ground,” he said.
Linda Ivany, a professor of evolutionary paleoecology at Syracuse University, echoed similar sentiments to the the New York Times: “These amazing fossils should stay in the public sphere for scientists to study, for children to be awed and inspired, and for everyone to be able to marvel at worlds long past and what we can learn from them.”

Oleshky ceasefire expands beyond occupied town as truce holds without reported violations
Unknown

2026-10-27
21:39:43 UTC
06:39:43 KST

The ceasefire around Russian-occupied Oleshky in Kherson Oblast has expanded beyond the town to provide safe passage for humanitarian convoys, US First Lady Melania Trump said on 27 October. The expansion is intended to facilitate aid deliveries to civilians trapped under Russian occupation.
Ukraine and Russia are observing a localized ceasefire to enable a humanitarian mission to reach Oleshky, where residents have faced months of shortages of food, medicine, and medical care under Russian occupation.
Trump said the ceasefire took effect at 04:00 Moscow time on 27 October, two days ahead of the original schedule, to protect civilians and facilitate the delivery of critical humanitarian aid. Russia’s chief of General Staff, Valery Gerasimov, had confirmed the arrangement, she said.
Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said no ceasefire violations had been recorded by 19:49 Kyiv time on 27 October, and Russian forces had made no attempts to advance. He added that he remained in constant contact with his Russian counterpart, Yana Lantratova.
Road to Oleshky must be cleared before aid can arrive
Lubinets said the ceasefire began at 03:00 Kyiv time and would remain in effect until 22:59 Kyiv time on 1 November. He reported no violations since it began and said Russian forces had made no attempts to advance.
The next steps are to clear mines from the road to Oleshky and deliver humanitarian supplies. Representatives of Ukraine, Russia, and the United States will be present once the route is cleared and the aid arrives, Lubinets said in an interview with Ukrainian broadcaster 1+1.
He added that everyone who wants to leave for Ukrainian-controlled territory would be able to do so and that assistance would be provided to everyone who needs it.
The Financial Times earlier reported, citing sources familiar with the negotiations, that residents who agree to leave Russian-occupied Oleshky during the ceasefire would first be transported to occupied Crimea or Russia before being allowed to return to Ukrainian-controlled territory.
Humanitarian mission follows months of efforts
Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since 2022. The town has been cut off for months, with shortages of food, medicine, and medical care worsening.
The White House announced on 23 October that Melania Trump had secured a localized ceasefire originally scheduled to begin on 29 October. Russia subsequently announced a ceasefire on the Kherson axis from 27 October, with preparations to secure a route for a humanitarian convoy.
Ceasefire planned for occupied Oleshky as residents face starvation and blocked escape routes, White House announces
Lubinets said efforts to address the humanitarian crisis in Oleshky began in late February 2026, but progress accelerated in September following Melania Trump’s involvement.
The expanded ceasefire area is intended to facilitate the humanitarian operation, but the route must still be cleared and supplies delivered before the mission can reach residents. The new boundaries of the ceasefire area have not been specified publicly.

what can looking at earth from space teach us about how we live on it?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
21:35:48 UTC
06:35:48 KST

what can looking at earth from space teach us about how we live on it?
bringing together more than 50 artists, astronauts, scientists, and cultural thinkers, 'inploration: art exploring space to understand earth' by richelle ellis and lawrence azerrad explores how art can turn the perspective of space exploration into a deeper understanding of our planet.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
inploration brings the overview effect down to earth
‘We are not observers of this world. We are participants in it. We always were.’ In an interview with designboom, artist Richelle Ellis and creative director Lawrence Azerrad discuss the thinking behind Inploration: Art Exploring Space to Understand Earth, a book published by DelMonico Books. Bringing together more than 50 artists, scientists, astronauts, ecologists, and cultural thinkers, the publication examines how exploring space can change our understanding of Earth, and how art can turn a sense of planetary wonder into a more active form of environmental responsibility.
The book takes its starting point from Earthrise, the photograph captured by Apollo 8 astronaut Bill Anders on Christmas Eve 1968. Not included on the shot list of the mission, the image was captured spontaneously, revealing Earth as a blue and white sphere suspended against the darkness of space, without visible borders. Its impact extended beyond the space program, offering a new perspective on the planet as a shared and vulnerable home. Nearly six decades later, Ellis and Azerrad return to that image asking how the Overview Effect can resonate with people who may never leave Earth. In a culture saturated with photographs, videos, and digital feeds, the challenge is not simply to reproduce the sense of wonder that Earthrise inspired, but to connect that perspective to the ways people live, make decisions, and care for the world around them.
looking outward to understand what is at home
For Richelle Ellis, the relationship between space and Earth extends beyond the astronaut’s view. Her artistic practice moves between deep space, the deep ocean, remote terrestrial environments, and analog space missions, including projects that send artworks beyond Earth. These different settings share a central question: what happens to our understanding of home when we leave the environments we know? The farther we travel from familiar surroundings, Ellis argues, the more apparent our dependence on Earth becomes. Space makes borders seem arbitrary, while the deep ocean reveals worlds that remain largely invisible despite their importance to planetary health. Both environments challenge the assumption that what cannot be seen or directly experienced is somehow separate from everyday life.
Art can bring distant or unfamiliar environments closer, helping people connect with ideas that might otherwise remain abstract. In Inploration, this is where art and science meet. The book brings together people from both fields to explore how we understand the world, what remains unknown, and how looking at things differently can change our perspective. While their methods may differ, artists and scientists share a willingness to ask questions, look more closely, and explore the unfamiliar. Among the contributors is Amber Straughn, deputy project scientist for the James Webb Space Telescope, whose work helps communicate the significance of images made by the observatory. As she puts it, ‘Astronomy can lead us to think about bigger things rather than just the facts’. The telescope’s images allow viewers to reconsider time, scale, and humanity’s place in the universe. As Straughn explains, ‘we’re literally seeing them as they were further back in time.’ The publication also responds to changing ways of seeing. Its cover and back cover were updated at press time to include images from the Artemis II mission, many taken by crew members using their iPhones. Placed alongside the Hasselblad film photography associated with the Apollo era, these contemporary images point to how space exploration is documented and shared across generations. The tools change, but the challenge remains: how can an image of somewhere remote alter our understanding of where we are?
from the voyager golden record to a new earthrise
Azerrad brings another perspective to the project through his work as a creative director and his involvement in the 40th-anniversary edition of the Voyager Golden Record. Launched aboard NASA’s Voyager spacecraft, the record was designed as a message to potential extraterrestrial life, assembling images, sounds, music, and information intended to communicate something about humanity. Its audience may be unknown, but its message also turns back toward Earth. The act of selecting what to send into the cosmos requires a decision about what matters enough to represent us. The Golden Record is as much an exercise in collective self-understanding as it is an attempt at interstellar communication. Azerrad approaches Inploration in a similar way, as an attempt to prompt new ways of seeing Earth. His creative process begins with listening and asking questions, allowing different perspectives to sit alongside one another.
The work of artist Cai Guo-Qiang offers another perspective on humanity’s relationship with time and the planet. His pyrotechnic works exist only in the moment of their creation, demanding the viewer’s attention before disappearing. Reflecting on his practice, Ellis and Azerrad share that it reminds them that ‘our only true relationship with the planet exists in the finite moment we are in. The past and the future are really just ideas.’ The observation connects Cai’s ephemeral works to the book’s broader argument: planetary awareness begins with paying attention to the world as we experience it now.
whose cosmology, whose responsibility?
The section on Indigenous knowledge and cultural cosmologies expands the book’s exploration of how different ways of understanding the universe shape our relationship with Earth. Rather than treating the cosmos solely as something to observe and measure, these perspectives connect knowledge to relationships among people, land, other living beings, and future generations. The difference is not simply between scientific and spiritual understandings, but between the ways knowledge informs our responsibilities to the world. Where some Western approaches have treated nature as a resource to study and extract, many Indigenous cosmologies emphasize reciprocity, care, and the obligations that come with being part of a living world.
Artist Cannupa Hanska Luger expresses the relationship between cultural knowledge and scientific understanding directly. ‘The stories are the cosmology. The cosmology is the science,’ he notes. Here, storytelling is not an alternative to knowledge but a way of transmitting an understanding of how the world works and how people should live within it. Other contributors bring the discussion back to the scale of everyday responsibility. Artist Tavares Strachan asks us to reconsider the geography of care: does responsibility extend to someone twenty miles away, or only to the person next door? Artist Rebeca Méndez poses a more fundamental question: ‘What does the Earth need from us?’ These questions complicate the familiar image of Earth as a single, unified home. Seeing the planet as a whole can produce a sense of collective belonging, but that feeling must extend beyond the photograph. It requires attention to the unequal ways environmental harm is experienced, to the knowledge held by communities whose relationships with land have endured across generations, and to the consequences of decisions made in the present. Physicist and systems thinker Fritjof Capra also highlights the importance of slowing down enough to recognize relationships that are otherwise easy to miss.
MAKING THE FUTURE TANGIBLE
Inploration: Art Exploring Space to Understand Earth also asks how we move from understanding environmental crises to feeling able to respond to them. Climate change, biodiversity loss, and the complexity of planetary systems can be difficult to grasp on a personal level. Faced with a constant stream of alarming information, it is easy to feel overwhelmed rather than empowered to act. Art and design offer another way to engage with these challenges by translating complex ideas into images, sounds, and experiences. As musician and artist Beatie Wolfe observes, data alone cannot always convey the emotional weight of an issue. Art can help people connect with information that might otherwise feel distant. Astronomer Janna Levin captures this role succinctly: ‘The point is to move people with the knowledge.’
For artist Lita Albuquerque, understanding our place in the universe begins with locating herself within it. She describes her cosmic address, tracing her position from a specific date and time through the Solar System to the Laniakea Supercluster. ‘I don’t feel overwhelmed,’ she says, adding, ‘I feel connected.’ Her perspective suggests that looking beyond Earth can reveal the connections that make life possible. Design offers another way to consider our relationship with the future. Designer Forest Young notes that ‘any brief is an exercise in futuring,’ describing the act of creating as an exercise in imagining what comes next. He follows this with a question: ‘What is the thing we’re steering away from?’ His approach asks us to consider the choices shaping the future now. Activist Van Jones makes a similar point: ‘The future is not something we enter. The future is something we create together.’ The book carries this thinking beyond its contributors through a series of self-directed exercises that invite readers to reflect on their own relationship with the planet. A related program is planned for MASS MoCA in November 2027, alongside a companion LP to be released through Magnolia Record Store.
NO ROCKET REQUIRED
For Richelle Ellis and Lawrence Azerrad, the Overview Effect is not limited to astronauts looking back at Earth from space. It can start with looking up at the night sky or noticing details of the world we often take for granted. As they suggest throughout Inploration, we do not need to leave the planet to see it differently. The harder part is carrying that perspective into how we live. How do we account for the generations that come after us? Who do we include when we talk about humanity, and what do we owe the planet we share? The Earthrise photograph changed how millions of people saw Earth, even though most would never experience that view for themselves. With Inploration, Ellis and Azerrad hope art can prompt that same sense of recognition today, by paying closer attention to the world we already call home.

authors: Richelle Ellis | @richellellisart and Lawrence Azerrad | @lad_design
publisher: DelMonico Books | @delmonico_books

====================================================================================================

MusicSA chair on 'post-apocalypse' industry ahead of Good Music Month
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
21:35:46 UTC
06:35:46 KST

MusicSA chair on 'post-apocalypse' industry ahead of Good Music Month
Australian music is caught in a paradox.
Original acts are pumping out excellent music with an edginess fitting of a troubled era, yet local offerings account for only 8.5 per cent of what is being streamed in the country.
APRA-AMCOS reported this month that 91 per cent of the music we streamed in the 2025-26 financial year was imported, with Australian music down 37.5 per cent in five years.
It has previously blamed the situation on global algorithms preferencing music from countries such as the US.
This is despite an original music scene bursting at the seams with excellent rock, indie, blues and psychedelic acts in a revival that's been underway for most of the decade in pockets across Australia.
South Australia is riding the same wave.
At small venues such as The Hotel Metropolitan, Jive, Ancient World and Memphis Slim's House of Blues, as well as at mini-festivals at locations like the Fleurieu Peninsula and Adelaide Uni Bar, young people are regularly packing rooms to see local acts they know well enough to sing along to.
A difference from golden ages like the 1990s, however, is that this scene is mostly being ignored by larger media outlets.
One needs to tune into stations like 3D Radio in Adelaide, Triple R in Melbourne or RTRFM in Perth to get a real finger on the pulse, pick up a street magazine for a gig guide, then get out the house to hear it in person.
In fact, the APRA-AMCOS 25-26 Year in Review pointed out, in a major study with Monash University, that 1.6 million Australians discovered local acts via community radio, and 1.5 million then looked them up on a streaming platform.
APRA-AMCOS has called for audio streaming to be treated the same way as radio and broadcast, as "critical cultural infrastructure", with local content obligations introduced that act in a similar way to commercial radio quotas to ensure Australian music is heard.
It's into this arena that Adelaide songwriter and lawyer Adrian Tisato has entered as the new chairperson of MusicSA, the not-for-profit organisation charged with promoting, supporting and developing the state's contemporary music sector.
"We are in the post-apocalypse,"
he said.
"Whether the apocalypse was Napster, or the post-Napster rollout of the delivery of music to consumers through digital streaming, whether it was COVID-19 or the combination of these events, it's the metaphorical apocalypse.
"But the truth is, we're still here, making music."
An 'electric buzz'
Mr Tisato has replaced John Glenn, who retired as MusicSA chair after nearly six years.
He believed Adelaide was in the midst of a "very important time as a music city" — one with an "electric buzz" that was attracting young and older music lovers to intimate live venues.
"The quality of music that's happening in small venues on the streets of Adelaide, in our regions and in mini-festivals, is outstanding, on a global level," Mr Tisato said.
Live shows have become more or less the only way local musicians can make money since the large-scale digital disruption of the industry and streaming left artists earning very little income from recorded music.
Much of it will be on show during Good Music Month, an open access program featuring local, national and international acts that kicks off with a street party at Hyde Street on Friday night, and runs at venues in Adelaide and across the state until November 30.
Wednesday to Friday will also see the national Regional and Remove Music Summit take place in Mount Gambier, a conference hosted by MusicSA that takes a "deep dive" into the state of music in Australia.
The not-for-profit organisation will also present the annual SA Music Awards on November 10 to "celebrate those South Australian artists who are excelling".
"The calibre of the finalists for each of our awards is extraordinary," Mr Tisato said.
A background in music
The son of Italian migrants, Mr Tisato grew up a Roman Catholic in Woodville and said his home was the meeting place for neighbours, friends and extended family, who would gather around after dinner and play Italian card games.
"They would sing Italian folk songs that had been handed down in the oral tradition, funny little melodic tunes that were sweet and poignant, sometimes containing ribald innuendo or telling tragic tales," he said.
"They'd be sitting there singing in two, three or four-part harmonies while we, as kids, would run around the house absorbing this music into our minds and bodies.
"Once I started to learn the guitar as a 15-year-old, I got involved in the church music group as a singer and guitarist."
Mr Tisato soon began songwriting and ultimately formed a trio with members from the church group. The band started playing parties and then performed in pubs and Adelaide venues.
Named Lookout Joe, the band was one of many enjoying Adelaide's vibrant live music scene throughout the 1990s.
Like the 1970s and 1980s, it was an era, Mr Tisato said, when people didn't question whether they were going out to see live music or not.
"They were going to see a band. It was just a question of which venue or venues they were going to,"
he said.
Mr Tisato also founded and ran an indie record label in the 2000s, and songs he has co-written in the last decade have been licensed to US and Australian television series.
Like most Adelaide artists, however, it was necessary to pursue a day job for financial security and Mr Tisato has been a commercial lawyer for more than 30 years.
A former Adelaide Fringe deputy chairperson and People's Republic of Animation chairperson, he has been actively involved in arts governance and is the current Art Gallery of South Australia Foundation chairperson and a gallery board member.
He has also served on the boards of the South Australian Film Corporation and the Motor Accident Commission.
'Quality trumps all'
Mr Tisato wants to see Adelaide continue to present itself to the world as a "global city of art and culture" and says he will bring his passion for music, business, governance and legal skills to the role.
With so much to on offer from homegrown artists, Mr Tisato urged commentators not to get stuck on whether or not the city attracted every big act that came to Australia.
"Over the years there's been an insecurity in Adelaide about the fact that certain artists don't come to Adelaide," he said.
"We need to let go of that. I actually think it's much more important to ask ourselves whether our own artists in intimate venues are great and thriving.
"Go see them perform live. They're brilliant."
Mr Tisato points out that despite the challenges in a post-digital disruption age, "quality trumps all".
"For musicians, for songwriters, however difficult it may be to make a living from this, the opportunity remains to find a way," he said.
"It starts with being great at what you do and writing extraordinary songs and performing them to audiences, and I still believe that for those who are doing that, the future is bright."

More Than 3% of Russian Men Aged 40–50 Have HIV as Epidemic Spreads in 27 Regions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
21:31:00 UTC
06:31:00 KST

- Category
- World
More Than 3% of Russian Men Aged 40–50 Have HIV as Epidemic Spreads in 27 Regions
The HIV epidemic in Russia has reached a generalized stage in 27 regions, Vasily Akimkin, director of Rospotrebnadzor’s Central Research Institute of Epidemiology, told Nezavisimaya Gazeta, as reported by The Moscow Times on October 26.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
A generalized epidemic means the virus no longer threatens only high-risk groups but is spreading among the broader population. In these regions, HIV is diagnosed in more than 1% of pregnant women.
The most affected regions are Kemerovo, Irkutsk, and Sverdlovsk, where more than 2% of residents are infected.
Among Russian men aged 40 to 50, the virus is present in more than 3%, stated Natalya Ladnaya, a leading researcher at the institute’s department for HIV/AIDS prevention and control. She noted that the average age of infected people has risen from 32 to 44 over the past 15 years. About two-thirds of new transmissions occur through heterosexual contact, Ladnaya added.
An infographic illustrates the scale of Russia’s HIV. (Data: Rospotrebnadzor via Nezavisimaya Gazeta and The Moscow Times)
Insufficient treatment coverage remains a central problem. Only half of the people living with HIV in Russia have a suppressed viral load, Ladnaya explained, meaning at least 600,000 people continue to transmit the virus. Among patients receiving antiretroviral therapy, viral load is suppressed in about 77–78%, compared with the 95% target set by the World Health Organization.
In 2025, Russia also recorded the highest number of bloodborne infections in medical facilities in 15 years, mostly HIV and hepatitis C, reported Elena Igonina, head of Rospotrebnadzor’s Department of Epidemiological Well-Being of the Population.
Investigations are ongoing into 11 clusters of such infections across ten regions. In 2026, authorities also identified two cases of HIV transmission through blood component transfusion, the first in six years.
Igonina attributed the infections mainly to violations of sanitary and epidemiological rules, including the use of the same catheters and glucometers for multiple patients.
According to Rospotrebnadzor, 30,000 to 34,000 people have died of HIV annually in recent years, an extremely high figure. For every death, there are 1.5 new infections. The draft federal budget for 2027 provides additional medication for 30,000 HIV patients.
That funding falls short of the number of new diagnoses, which stood at about 52,000 in 2024 and 45,000 in 2025.

As I see it
For its autocratic African ally, Taiwan bites its tongue and opens its wallet
Democratic values don’t stop Taipei from offering aid and debt-trap loans to eSwatini – its sole remaining diplomatic partner on the continent and Africa’s last absolute monarchy
3-MIN READ3-MIN
2
 Listen
Alex Lo has been an SCMP columnist since 2012, commenting on China and international affairs. 
Eswatini probably does not register on most people’s mental maps. Its relatively recent name might sound unfamiliar as many people still know it as Swaziland.
That it demands attention from pundits like yours truly has much to do with it being the only African country that still formally recognises Taiwan. It is also the continent’s only absolute monarchy. The two facts are closely connected. Recognising Taipei makes little sense when every one of eSwatini’s neighbours recognises Beijing, but it makes perfect sense for the only system of government this kingdom of about 1.2 million people has known since independence from Britain in 1968.
King Mswati III is the son of King Sobhuza II, the first post-independence ruler, and one of his 70 wives. The kingdom briefly made headlines in 2023 when human rights lawyer Thulani Maseko, who had spent years agitating for an end to absolute monarchy, was shot dead in his home. The government denied that its security forces were responsible. While major governments condemned the killing, Taipei stayed silent.

High voter turnout leaves small parties below electoral threshold | This is who missed out
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
21:28:46 UTC
06:28:46 KST

High voter turnout in Israel's 2026 election left little room for smaller parties, all of which fell below the electoral threshold, according to television exit polls. Three parties stood out in recent weeks: Amcha Yisrael, the Reservists-Economic Party and the Haredi Public Party. The first two had hovered around the electoral threshold in the latest polls, while the third generated momentum on social media that, according to the exit polls, failed to translate into votes.
Amcha Yisrael
Among the smaller parties, the collapse of former IDF brigadier general Ofer Winter's Amcha Yisrael party was particularly striking. The party initially polled in the single digits in Knesset seats following its launch, but slipped toward the electoral threshold in recent surveys as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu intensified his attacks against it. According to all television exit polls, it has now failed to cross the threshold.
Winter, who commanded the Givati Brigade during Operation Protective Edge in 2014, retired from the IDF in December 2024 with the rank of brigadier general. About a year and a half after leaving the military, he announced the establishment of Amcha Yisrael, naming pro-Israel advocacy activist Yoseph Haddad as his No. 2 candidate.
Netanyahu waged an aggressive campaign against Winter in an effort to pressure him to withdraw from the race, amid polls suggesting he was at risk of failing to cross the electoral threshold. But Winter, who had announced at the beginning of his campaign that he would recommend Netanyahu for prime minister, refused to drop out. His decision appears to have cost Netanyahu's bloc tens of thousands of votes.
Sources close to Winter told ynet Tuesday evening that he had spent recent days crisscrossing the country, persuading voters, making phone calls, joining family WhatsApp groups and fighting for every vote against the odds while facing what they described as an "insane campaign" against him.
They argued that had Winter not entered the race, Yoaz Hendel and Yaron Zelekha would certainly have crossed the electoral threshold, giving the anti-Netanyahu bloc another four seats.
"We fought until the very end despite Netanyahu and his allies' violent, disgraceful and ugly campaign," a party source said. "We have a solid base of voters," the source added, claiming that more than 100,000 people had voted for the party.
Amcha Yisrael officials insisted that Netanyahu had made the strategic mistake, arguing that his effort to draw votes away from their party had cost his own bloc valuable Knesset seats.
"We could have won today," a party source claimed. "But the unhinged campaign by Netanyahu and Smotrich, who talked about Judaizing the Galilee and the Bedouins in the Negev, drove Arab voters to the polls in huge numbers instead of keeping them at home."
Looking ahead, party officials maintain that Amcha Yisrael has established a solid voter base. They suggest that, much like Itamar Ben-Gvir, who ran unsuccessfully several times before gaining substantial electoral support, the party could return in the next election and attract more votes.
The Reservists-Economic Party
Yoaz Hendel and Yaron Zelekha, who joined forces on a single electoral list under the Reservists-Economic Party banner, also failed to cross the electoral threshold, according to the exit polls.
Hendel and Zelekha explored several possible political alliances before ultimately joining forces. In some of the final preelection polls, their list appeared to gain momentum, reaching the equivalent of four Knesset seats. But when voters went to the polls, the exit surveys indicated that Israelis had opted for larger parties.
Hendel, who served as communications minister in the previous change government and, about 15 years ago, headed Netanyahu's National Information Directorate, established the Reservists Party last year. In July, he announced a joint run with Hili Tropper's party, but after Tropper joined Gadi Eisenkot, Hendel aligned himself with Zelekha's Economic Party.
During the Swords of Iron war, Hendel was called up for reserve duty, participated in combat operations in Gaza and established a new battalion made up of former special forces soldiers who had passed the age of mandatory reserve service.
Hendel previously belonged to Moshe "Bogie" Ya'alon's Telem party, which later joined Benny Gantz's Blue and White alliance. He was also a member of Derech Eretz alongside Zvi Hauser and New Hope under Gideon Sa'ar, and signed a merger agreement to establish the Zionist Spirit alliance headed by Ayelet Shaked.
Economist Yaron Zelekha, ranked second on the list, served as the Finance Ministry's accountant general from 2003 to 2007. He ran independently in the previous two elections, receiving less than 1% of the vote each time and failing to cross the electoral threshold.
Third on the list was Einat Wilf, who served in the Knesset from 2010 to 2013 as a member of the Labor Party and later Ehud Barak's Independence faction.
Hendel said Tuesday evening that he was counting on the double-envelope ballots, which include votes cast by soldiers.
"By the end of the week, we'll know the results from IDF polling stations," he said. "We experienced incredible momentum. Let's see the actual results. In any case, we fought very, very hard. We're fighters, we work hard, and we'll fulfill our ambitions for the State of Israel and the Jewish people. Nobody here is giving up. That's the first thing."
Hendel also thanked Winter for what he described as the "difficult road" he had traveled.
The Haredi Public Party
The third party that appears to have attracted some support but failed to cross the electoral threshold is the Haredi Public Party, led by Moti Leitner. Netanyahu also campaigned against the party in an effort to pressure it to withdraw from the race.
Leitner sought to offer ultra-Orthodox voters an alternative to parties that support sweeping exemptions from military service and oppose the inclusion of core curriculum subjects in religious schools.
While Israel's established ultra-Orthodox parties, Shas and United Torah Judaism, have pushed for military service exemptions, restrictions on core curriculum studies and the allocation of welfare funding, Leitner presented a more pragmatic ideological approach.
Throughout the campaign, he claimed that support for his party was growing among younger members of the ultra-Orthodox community. According to the exit polls, however, that support ultimately proved insufficient to carry the party across the electoral threshold.

Trump showcases Venezuelan oil as he seeks to rally voters in Texas
US president seeks to underscore Latin American military operation, as Iran war causes midterm affordability threat.
United States President Donald Trump has featured a ship he said is carrying Venezuelan oil during a visit to Texas, where he will hold two rallies one after the other in the hopes of boosting Republican chances in a make-or-break Senate race.
Speaking at Corpus Christi on Tuesday on his fourth trip to the state this campaign season, Trump pointed to a ship in the distance.
“It’s got 1 million barrels of oil on it from Venezuela,” he said, adding the cargo was “thanks to our big victory in our recent war with Venezuela”.
The emphasis on the oil comes as US consumers have wrestled with high fossil fuel prices amid the US-Israel war with Iran, a key issue in the upcoming midterm elections.
“We’re celebrating the greatest oil victory in history,” Trump said.
It was not immediately clear under what pretext the oil had been shipped or whether the details Trump gave were correct. The US had received crude oil shipments from Venezuela before the US abduction of Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro on January 3, but those transfers have increased this year.
In August, the Trump administration announced a deal giving the Pentagon a 35 percent stake in North America Blue Energy Partners, a new company overseeing 65 billion barrels of proven oil reserves. The White House said in September that the first shipment from the deal would likely hit US reserves in November, although experts have cast doubt on whether the deal will have any short-term impact.
Speaking to reporters earlier in the day, Trump referred to the shipment as a “gift” from Venezuela. The country’s interim leader, Delcy Rodriguez, has not commented on the specific shipment.
At the rally, Trump also floated making Venezuela the “51st state”.
Key race
Trump’s frequent visits to Texas underscore the state’s significance for Republicans.
Trump endorsed Attorney General Ken Paxton in the Republican primary over incumbent Senator John Cornyn. The scandal-ridden Paxton now faces a punishing contest against Democrat James Talarico, a Presbyterian seminarian.
Polls have regularly shown Talarico leading Paxton, although that lead has largely remained within the margin of error. A RealClearPolitics average of polls had Talarico leading Paxton by 1.7 points.
Talarico’s victory would mark a sea change in a state that has not elected a Democrat to statewide office since 1994.
It would also represent a major rebuke to Trump, whose Republican Party is fighting to maintain its narrow control of the Senate. Democrats are widely projected to take control of the US House of Representatives in the November 3 vote.
Talarico has used the final stretch of the race to focus on years of corruption allegations against Paxton, while drawing a contrast to voters’ affordability concerns.
“Ken Paxton represents everything that’s wrong with this broken, corrupt system,” he said during an event in Houston last week.
Paxton has sought to portray Talarico as too “radical” for Texas, saying his policies would hurt a state known for its pro-business policies.
Trump and other administration officials, notably Vice President JD Vance, have regularly focused on cultural issues, distorting Talarico’s past comments on transgender rights and border security.
Speaking in Corpus Christi, Trump repeated those attacks and urged his supporters to vote as if he were on the ballot.
“If you go out, and if you all vote, we win in a landslide,” Trump said.

Boeing Bullish on Defense Sector After Fighter Wins, Shunning Fixed-Price Deals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
21:24:29 UTC
06:24:29 KST

Fresh off Boeing’s victory in the competition to build the Navy’s sixth-generation F/A-XX fighter, CEO Kelly Ortberg on Oct. 27 expressed confidence that the darkest days of the company’s beleaguered defense sector are in the past.
A year ago, Boeing expected its Defense, Space, and Security division to see revenue growth in the low single digits, Ortberg told investors in an earnings call. Now, the company is projecting defense revenue growth in at least the mid-single digits or higher.
Ortberg pointed to Boeing’s Sept. 29 win of both the $20 billion F/A-XX contract and a $2.38 billion Air Force contract for 22 more F-15EX Eagle II fighters as examples of the tailwinds boosting Boeing’s defense portfolio. The F/A-XX win followed the Air Force’s March 2025 selection of Boeing to build its F-47, putting both the U.S. military’s sixth-generation fighter programs in its portfolio.
In the first three quarters of 2026, Boeing’s defense sector brought in $23 billion in revenue, with earnings of $710 million. That’s up from $19.8 billion in revenue and $379 million in earnings a year earlier.
Ortberg also said the company’s decision to swear off risky contracts—such as the fixed-price contract for Boeing’s KC-46 Pegasus program, which has lost the company billions—has helped put its defense sector back on course.
“The important part is, all these programs are also being underwritten with the right contract type,” Ortberg said. “So not only are we booking more orders, we’re booking more orders that won’t result in some of the challenges we’ve had.”
The F-47 contract is a cost-plus deal, Ortberg said. He declined to identify what type of contract Boeing signed for F/A-XX, but said it is “an appropriate contract type.”
In 2022, Boeing put executive Ted Colbert in charge of its defense sector, who pledged to not agree to further fixed-price contracts with the Pentagon. A few months into the job, Colbert told reporters in London that Boeing had passed on competing for the Air Force’s Survivable Airborne Operations Center, or SAOC, in part because it would have required agreeing to fixed-price elements in the contract.
Colbert also said fighters remained an important part of the company’s business, even though the firm then had not landed a contract to create an entirely new fighter in years. Later in 2022, Colbert reorganized Boeing’s defense sector in an effort to stop it from bleeding revenue and fix persistent quality problems.
Two years later, Boeing Defense appeared increasingly troubled. Financial losses piled up, and the company fired Colbert in September 2024. Labor troubles between Boeing and its machinists led to a massive strike in 2024, and a smaller one a year later, further complicating the firm’s outlook and slowing its F-15EX delivery pace.
But this year, Ortberg said he saw more reasons for optimism. Boeing’s T-7 Red Hawk trainer for the Air Force and MQ-25 Stingray for the Navy both achieved their Milestone C approvals and moved into low-rate initial production this year as well, which Ortberg said was a positive sign for the company.
“We’re not done with the development programs until we’re done,” Ortberg said, adding that the defense team is “doing a really good job of finding win-win scenarios with our customers to get these projects moved forward.”
“So the outlook is strong, our products are in strong demand, and the budget supports additional growth,” Ortberg said. “I think our defense portfolio is a little bit of a sleeper.”

“People are living in a daydream that someday they will benefit from the drugs prices control order (DPCO)... The policy is only to give benefit to the corporate. We are thinking from the point of view of poor patients,” SC observed. Bhati, thereafter, submitted that medicine prices in India are among the lowest in the world due to free market and govt cannot take control of the entire pharma market, but the bench told her, “You are either not aware about the problem or not keen to solve the problem.
.. Why is the entire system working for the benefit of few people?”“Ordinarily, where there is substantial competition, there is no need to regulate prices. It is not that the govt has left the market unregulated but the complete control of the market is not feasible,” Bhati said, adding that the issue pertains to economic policy and commerce and the court should desist from interfering. Not convinced by this, the bench said, “Should they (pharma companies) be allowed to run amok? What is the justification for the difference in prices? You are not able to come with an answer. We have asked you 30 times. Do not talk about control... You are talking about economic policy and commerce. Is commerce more important than the life of citizens and be given precedence?”

Satellite images confirm damage at Russia’s largest known air defense storage base after Ukrainian drone strike
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
21:20:46 UTC
06:20:46 KST

Satellite images show signs of fires at the 75th Arsenal facility in Serpukhov in the Moscow Region, around 60 miles south of the Russian capital, Greenpeace analysts who examined the imagery told The Insider. The site was struck by Ukrainian drones overnight into Oct. 22. The target was the largest known Russian storage base for air defense equipment.
Satellite images from Oct. 26 show changes compared with earlier imagery. Greenpeace experts who analyzed the data told The Insider that burn marks are visible in the upper left of the image. Additional signs of fire can be seen in the center near a hangar and in the lower left.
The Ukrainian open source intelligence (OSINT) project Oko Hora ✙ News and Analytics claims that the strikes hit workshops No. 24 and No. 25, which specialize in repairing and restoring components for Russia’s S-300V and Buk surface-to-air missile systems, its Tunguska-M air defense systems, and radar equipment. The site, formerly an arsenal of the Russian Defense Ministry’s Main Missile and Artillery Directorate (GRAU), only became the largest known storage base for air defense equipment in Russia after the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion.
OSINT analyst Jompy wrote in March 2024 that researchers had identified an air defense equipment storage base at the 75th Arsenal site in Serpukhov, adding that the facility had originally served as an artillery depot before being repurposed to store air defense systems. Satellite images show numerous hangars at the site that may contain systems including the Buk or S-300. The analyst said it appeared to be the largest known storage base for air defense and surface-to-air missile systems in Russia.
Another OSINT analyst, Athene Noctua, wrote in June 2024 that the 75th Arsenal base held about 60% of the identified reserve of Russian Ground Forces air defense equipment — 574 out of 950 units.

German special forces have begun preparing for a possible war with Russia – the military is changing tactics and combat scenarios
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
23:18:00 EET
06:18:00 KST

German special forces have begun preparing for a possible war with Russia – the military is changing tactics and combat scenarios
Kyiv • UNN
The KSK has changed its training to confront Russia, focusing on prolonged operations and battles against heavy weapons. The unit numbers around 1,500 personnel.
Germany is redirecting the training of its elite KSK special forces unit toward a possible military confrontation with Russia. The soldiers are being trained for prolonged operations, countering heavy weaponry, and conducting combat operations in extreme conditions. BILD reports this, citing KSK commander Andreas Kühne, UNN writes.
Details
According to the general, the German command has already changed its approach to training special forces. Whereas previously they mainly practiced short operations lasting approximately three days, they must now be ready to remain in the field for significantly longer.
We are very specifically orienting ourselves toward Russia as the adversary
German special forces are being prepared for confrontation with the Russian army
The new training program provides for operations against an adversary equipped with tanks, artillery, drones, and modern electronic warfare capabilities.
Particular attention is being paid to preparing for prolonged stays directly in the combat zone, when servicemen cannot count on a swift return to their permanent bases.
The special forces are also practicing carrying out missions in extremely low temperatures. This is connected with the possible conditions of combat operations on NATO's eastern flank, particularly in the Baltic states.
According to Kühne, during exercises in the Baltic states, German servicemen have already demonstrated the capabilities of their special forces units. Such training is intended to show Moscow that an attack on NATO would have serious military consequences.
What is known about the elite KSK unit
The KSK Special Operations Command is based in the city of Calw near Stuttgart. The unit's total strength is approximately 1,500 servicemen.
Approximately one-third of the personnel carry out combat missions directly. The remainder provides training, command, and operational support.
Selection for the KSK is considered one of the most difficult in the Bundeswehr. According to the data cited, only about 15% of candidates can successfully pass it.

War update: 178 clashes on front line, Pokrovsk sector remains hottest
As reported by Ukrinform, this was stated in a report by the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine on the situation as of 22:00 on Tuesday, October 26.
“A total of 178 combat clashes have taken place since the beginning of the day. The enemy launched one missile strike and 46 airstrikes, dropping 171 guided aerial bombs. In addition, they used 5,942 kamikaze drones to strike targets and carried out 1,563 shelling attacks on settlements and the positions of our troops,” the report said.
In the Northern Slobozhanshchyna and Kursk sectors, Russian forces carried out 27 attacks on the positions of Ukrainian troops and settlements, one of them using multiple rocket launchers.
In the Southern Slobozhanshchyna sector, the enemy attacked Ukrainian positions five times toward the settlements of Okhrimivka and Mala Vovcha. Two of these attacks are still ongoing.
In the Kupiansk sector, Russian forces made three attempts to improve their positions, conducting assault operations toward Radkivka. Fighting is ongoing.
Four attempts by Russian forces to advance were repelled in the Lyman sector, toward Nove, Stavky, and Lyman.
In the Sloviansk sector, Ukraine’s Defense Forces stopped two attempts by Russian troops to advance near Yampil and toward Orikhuvatka.
In the Kramatorsk sector, Russian forces launched one assault toward Malynivka.
In the Kostiantynivka sector, Ukrainian Forces repelled 13 Russian assaults near Kostiantynivka as well as toward Raiske and Pavlivka. One enemy assault is ongoing.
Russian forces launched 24 attacks in the Pokrovsk sector. They attempted to advance near Sofiivka, Vilne, Vodianske, Vasylivka, and Molodetske, as well as toward Toretske, Kucheriv Yar, Dobropillia, Hannivka, Novohryshyne, Hulive, and Serhiivka. One combat clash is ongoing.
According to preliminary estimates, 23 Russian troops were killed and eight wounded in the sector today. Ukrainian forces destroyed five vehicles and one piece of special equipment. Three vehicles, one electronic warfare system, one UAV command post and 39 enemy shelters were damaged. A total of 173 unmanned aerial vehicles of various types were destroyed or suppressed.
In the Oleksandrivka sector, Russian forces did not conduct any assault operations.
In the Huliaipole sector, Ukraine’s Defense Forces repelled 16 enemy attacks toward Ternuvate, Dolynka, Hirke, Charivne and Yehorivka. Fighting is ongoing.
Russian forces conducted no assault operations in the Orikhiv and Dnipro River sectors.
No significant changes in the situation were reported in other sectors of the front.
As reported by Ukrinform, the Vivaldi operation by the Ukrainian Defense Forces pushed Russian troops back and liberated significant areas north of Lyman, but the threat to the Sloviansk-Kramatorsk agglomeration still remains.
