UK Defense Chief Calls on NATO to Brace for Potential Confrontation With Russia
British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting warned that Western allies must prepare for a scenario where the United Kingdom and NATO could find themselves in a direct military confrontation with Russia.
Speaking alongside Polish Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz in Warsaw, the official stressed the necessity of strengthening deterrence capabilities across Europe, as reported by The Guardian.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Addressing joint defense efforts, Streeting pointed to historical precedents regarding official assurances from Moscow prior to Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
“We must be prepared for a scenario in which the United Kingdom and the NATO alliance find themselves at war with Russia. Not because we want war—we have no quarrel with the Russian people and do not seek war with Russia; NATO is a defensive alliance—but when Putin assures that he has no intention of provoking a war with NATO, we remember what he said about Ukraine just a few days before the invasion,” he noted, The Guardian reported.
The defense minister reaffirmed the alliance’s readiness to defend all member territories while maintaining active support for Kyiv.
“The more we are prepared to stand up to Russia, to defend every inch of NATO territory, the less likely we are to find ourselves in such a scenario,” he added.
On May 27, 2026, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk and British Prime Minister Keir Starmer signed a historic Security and Defense Partnership Treaty in London, officially designating Russia as the primary threat to European stability.
The agreement was designed to elevate bilateral military cooperation to its highest level and enable rapid, direct defense responses in the event of a regional crisis without awaiting unanimous consensus from NATO’s 32 members.
Tusk underscored that while Poland remained fully committed to the transatlantic alliance, building swift, bilateral mechanisms with key allies like the UK and France was essential to counter regional aggression effectively—particularly as Washington prepared to gradually reduce its military footprint on the continent.

Russia and US exploring Arctic cooperation – Putin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:37:44 UTC
05:37:44 KST

Russia and US exploring Arctic cooperation – Putin
Russia and the US are exploring opportunities for cooperation in the Arctic, President Vladimir Putin has said, stressing that Moscow is ready to work with partners genuinely interested in joint projects.
Speaking at the eighth summit of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) in Moscow on Tuesday, Putin highlighted growing global demand for natural gas and Russia’s efforts to expand production, particularly in the Arctic.
Natural gas already accounts for a quarter of the global energy mix, and Russia, which holds the world’s largest reserves, is investing in infrastructure and technologies designed to operate in extreme northern conditions, the president noted.
“Russia is systematically strengthening its technological sovereignty,” Putin said. “We have also taken a major step forward by creating our own proprietary [liquefied natural gas] LNG technologies, which are already being deployed in the harsh conditions of the Arctic.”
Moscow is “open for cooperation,” including in the technological field, Putin maintained, adding that it is “actively working with many nations” in the Arctic. “Now, we are exploring avenues for joint work with American partners,” he added.
Earlier this week, the New York Times reported that Moscow and Washington were discussing a potential venture to use Russian technology to extract natural gas in Alaska, liquefy it and export it.
The proposed company, dubbed Polar LNG, was reportedly discussed last month by Putin and US President Donald Trump’s special envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. According to the newspaper, Russian gas producer Novatek has helped finance the venture through a UAE-based firm and is considering taking a minority stake.
Western energy companies have largely scaled back their Russian operations since the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022. US energy giant ExxonMobil withdrew from the Sakhalin-1 oil and gas project, although the Wall Street Journal reported last year that it was considering a return.
ExxonMobil and Chevron nevertheless retain stakes in the Caspian Pipeline Consortium, which transports Kazakh oil through Russia to the Black Sea.
Several major European energy companies have also exited Russia, although France’s TotalEnergies retains stakes in Novatek and the Yamal LNG project.
The EU, meanwhile, has adopted an increasingly militaristic approach to the Arctic. Its latest Arctic strategy identifies the region as a potential flashpoint for confrontation with Russia, declares that the bloc itself “is part of the Arctic,” and outlines a range of military objectives.
In August, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov warned that the EU was seeking to turn the Arctic into a new “hotbed” of tensions. He accused NATO of “driving the region towards militarization” through its military buildup, while stressing Moscow’s commitment to “preserving the Arctic as an area of peace and cooperation.”

Egypt orders closure of leading independent news site Mada Masr
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:35:18 UTC
05:35:18 KST

Egypt orders closure of leading independent news site Mada Masr
Editor Lina Attalah was freed once a $53,400 fine was paid, only to learn of a one-year sentence passed in her absence
An Egyptian court has ordered the closure of Mada Masr, one of the country’s last prominent independent news outlets, and fined its editor-in-chief, Lina Attalah, three million Egyptian pounds ($53,400) for running a website without a licence.
The New Cairo Misdemeanour Court also ordered the confiscation of the outlet’s equipment and devices. Attalah was taken into custody after Tuesday’s ruling. She was released several hours later, after Mada Masr paid the fine in full.
During the release procedures, Attalah learned that she had been sentenced in absentia in 2024 to one year in prison, on charges of publishing false news and running an unlicensed website. Mada Masr said Attalah’s lawyers have challenged that ruling, and a retrial hearing is scheduled for November 11.
In an editorial published hours after the verdict, Mada Masr said it had entered court “with a measure of faith in the law and the justice system”. It added: “But what we found in court left none of that faith intact.”
The outlet said the court refused its lawyers’ requests to review the case file, submit additional evidence and call witnesses. According to Mada Masr, the judge then appointed “an unknown party” to act as Attalah’s defence lawyer, even though eight of her own lawyers were in court and she herself objected. The editorial said the judge wrote that lawyer’s requests himself “before issuing a verdict carrying the maximum penalty, with no review and no defence”.
Hossam Bahgat, head of the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights, attended the hearing. According to Mada Masr, he said the court went ahead with the appointment despite Attalah’s own objection to being represented by a court-appointed lawyer. Mada Masr’s lawyer, Hassan al-Azhari, told the Egyptian outlet Zawia3 that the court rejected the defence’s requests and then appointed a lawyer, a step Attalah and her team objected to.
Egypt’s website laws
Tuesday’s ruling is based on Article 105 of Egypt’s 2018 media law, which sets fines of one to three million Egyptian pounds ($17,800–$53,400), plus closure and confiscation, for operating an unlicensed website.
Mada Masr says it applied for a licence from the Supreme Council for Media Regulation in 2018 and again in 2020, without a reply. It says it learned of a rejection only when prosecutors raised it during a previous case in 2022. In 2023, an administrative court upheld the council’s refusal, citing the absence of proof that the outlet’s trademark was registered, although Mada Masr’s lawyer said he had submitted a trademark registration certificate. A new application has been pending since June 2023.
There was no immediate official comment on the verdict.
The head of the Journalists’ Syndicate, Khaled el-Balshy, said the union would take legal action to appeal the ruling.
Mada Masr was founded in 2013 and has been blocked inside Egypt since 2017. It says it has faced six cases in six years, and rights groups say this is the first to reach trial.
“We tried to defend the law,” the outlet wrote, “just as we tried to defend ourselves.”
Amnesty International’s senior director for regional impact, Yasmine Ahmed, said in a statement, “Today’s decision represents a crushing blow to press freedom in Egypt and marks a dark day for independent journalism in the country.”
“This draconian ruling is the culmination of years of relentless harassment and unjust proceedings designed to shut down one of the country’s last remaining independent media voices,” Ahmed added.
The verdict came on the same day that Egypt’s Supreme State Security Prosecution, which investigates national security cases, renewed the detention of six journalists from the fact-checking platform Matsadaash for another 15 days.

Former Met officer who served in same unit as David Carrick and Wayne Couzens found guilty of sexual offences
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:34:59 UTC
05:34:59 KST

A former Metropolitan police officer who served in the same unit as Sarah Everard’s killer, Wayne Couzens, has been found guilty of sexual offences against a woman he met through his work as an officer.
A court heard that Mark Tyrrell raped the woman – who cannot be identified for legal reasons – by having sex with her after she repeatedly said no.
The 57-year-old was then said to have told her “I don’t believe what’s just happened” and “do you realise that what I’ve just done, that was rape?”
Tyrrell had been attached to the parliamentary and diplomatic protection command, which is where the convicted rapists Couzens and David Carrick both worked.
He was convicted of one count of rape, three of sexual assault and one of perverting the course of justice after a trial at Southwark crown court.
Prosecutor Catherine Farrelly KC alleged that when the woman resisted Tyrrell’s sexual advances “he simply chose to take what he wanted”.
The court heard that concerns were raised after officers attended her address for a separate matter and found Tyrrell hiding by the side of her bed.
The former PC was found guilty of perverting the course of justice by attempting to delete messages with the woman.
In one message, the court was told he said he was “sorry” for “being a sex offender” and “for ruining your life by being in it”.
Jurors found him not guilty in relation to 13 other charges, including one count of rape.
In his evidence, Tyrrell claimed sexual intercourse between them was always consensual and “there was never any forcefulness to it”.
Ch Supt Sara Leach, commander within specialist operations, said: “This kind of conduct is abhorrent but even more so when it is carried out by a serving officer, who had gained the trust of the victim.
“We remain appalled that someone like this was serving within our organisation and it is right he has been brought to justice.”
Tyrrell previously admitted misconduct in a public office. He also pleaded guilty to perverting the course of justice by persuading the woman to lie to the police about why he was in her bedroom.
The defendant, of Meltham, West Yorkshire, will be sentenced on 16 December.
Everard, 33, was kidnapped, raped and murdered by then Met officer Couzens in 2021. He was later given a whole-life order.
Carrick, 51, who previously served as an armed officer in the Met, is serving 37 life sentences after attacking more than a dozen women.

The $9 billion fuel bill raising questions about Australia's energy security
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:32:19 UTC
05:32:19 KST

In brief
- Australia paid a higher price for imported diesel than any other nation during the fuel crisis.
- New analysis linked billions in extra fuel costs to energy security risks.
Australia has paid more than twice as much as any other nation in additional diesel import costs during the global fuel crisis, with a report putting the toll at $9 billion over six months.
The added cost equates to $324 for every Australian, exceeding the bills incurred by Brazil, South Africa, France and the UK.
The Climate Council released the figures from its energy security scorecard on Wednesday, which also found Australia paid an extra $1.6 billion for petrol imports.
The findings come days after oil prices reached a six-month high amid escalating threats in the Middle East.
The council's report, called Crude Awakening, analysed Australia's energy security, its exposure to rising global fuel prices, and policies and progress towards electric transport and renewable energy.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
It found Australia was the world's largest seaborne importer of diesel, with imports responsible for 90 per cent of its supply.
Diesel use in Australia had also more than doubled since 2000 to 33 billion litres in 2025, with about a quarter used in mining.
Australia paid $9 billion in additional costs to import diesel between March and August, compared to an extra $3.5 billion in Brazil and $3 billion in the UK.
The nation also paid an additional $1.6 billion for petrol, or $56 per person.
Climate Council spokeswoman and economist Nicki Hutley said those costs had a widespread impact.
"We're seeing costs (rise) right through the economy, whether it's in inflation at the supermarket or all the way through the supply chain," she told the Australian Associated Press news agency.
"If we keep relying on imported oil, that is leaving our energy security in somebody else's hands, and we're seeing that this year."
Moves to renewable energy had saved Australians from some higher costs, the report found, with electric and hybrid cars cutting $1.7 billion in costs and saving the equivalent of 17.4 million litres of petrol and diesel per week.
Australia was still slow to adopt electric trucks, with the vehicles representing 0.7 per cent of new sales compared to nine per cent worldwide, and had one public charging point for every 41 electric cars, compared to the global average of one for every 11 EVs.
Electrifying more vehicles and removing diesel fuel tax credits could help to protect Australia from future fuel shocks, Hutley said, and state and federal policies should support the transition.
"Every crisis should be seen as an opportunity, and we shouldn't waste that opportunity," she said.
"The best time to do this was yesterday, as they say, and the next best time is today to say what will set us up for a long-term future of energy security at lowest cost to Australian taxpayers."

Ukraine intercepts nearly 60% of Russia’s Geran-4 jet drones, General Staff says, as Kyiv races to counter evolving threat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:28:36 UTC
05:28:36 KST

Ukraine’s air defenses have been intercepting nearly 60% of Russian Geran-4 jet-powered attack drones over the past three months, with the interception rate reaching 80% during some attacks, Ukraine’s General Staff said.
Russia has increasingly used jet-powered drones in its attacks on Ukraine, adding a faster-moving threat to the Shahed-type drones Moscow deploys against Ukrainian cities and infrastructure. Ukraine is working to improve interception rates while reducing the cost of countering these aerial threats amid shortages of surface-to-air missiles.
The General Staff’s update did not mention interception rates for Russia’s more advanced Geran-5 jet-powered drone.
F-16s, Mirage jets help intercept Russian drones
According to the General Staff, tactical aviation plays a significant role in destroying Russian jet-powered drones. Ukraine uses F-16s, French Mirage aircraft, and MiG-29 fighters to intercept them.
The military is also strengthening what it calls “short-range air defense” as Ukraine faces a shortage of guided anti-aircraft missiles. These systems include Gepard and Shilka anti-aircraft guns, newer Skynex, Skyranger, and Terrahawk Paladin systems, interceptor drones, and mobile fire groups deployed by different branches of Ukraine’s Defense Forces.
Mobile fire groups are equipped not only with machine guns and supporting equipment but also with man-portable air-defense systems (MANPADS). Ukrainian troops have been successfully using these missiles to shoot down Russian jet-powered drones, the General Staff said.
Denmark rushes 50,000 cannon rounds to Ukraine to help F-16s hunt Russia’s advanced jet drones
Ukraine tests cheaper drone interceptors
Ukraine is also seeking to lower the cost of countering Russian aerial attacks by testing new interceptor drones.
According to the General Staff, some models have already downed dozens of Russian Geran jet-powered drones. The military did not provide further details about the interceptor models or the number of drones destroyed.
The rising interception rate reflects Ukraine’s efforts to adapt its air defenses to Russia’s evolving drone campaign while preserving scarce and expensive air-defense missiles for threats that require them.

Trump weighs lifting sanctions on Russian fund once described by U.S. Treasury as Putin’s ‘slush fund,’ NYT reports
Unknown

Trump weighs lifting sanctions on Russian fund once described by U.S. Treasury as Putin’s ‘slush fund,’ NYT reports
President Donald Trump’s administration is considering lifting sanctions on the Russian Direct Investment Fund (RDIF), sources familiar with talks between Russia and the United States told The New York Times.
Russia is pressing for sanctions relief for RDIF so the fund can take part in supplying Russian diesel fuel to the United States, the sources told the Times.
The U.S. Treasury Department is reviewing the fund’s application for sanctions relief under its standard procedures, one source said. RDIF will have to prove that the reasons it was sanctioned no longer apply.
RDIF is headed by Kirill Dmitriev, a key participant in the talks between Russia and the United States. He is leading the Kremlin’s push for possible joint business ventures between the two countries.
RDIF was established in 2011 to attract foreign investment to Russia. The best-known project it helped develop was Russia’s Sputnik V coronavirus vaccine. Dmitriev and his wife, Natalya Popova, are believed to be close to Russian President Vladimir Putin’s younger daughter, Katerina Tikhonova.
President Joe Biden’s administration imposed sanctions on RDIF on February 28, 2022, four days after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. “While officially a sovereign wealth fund, RDIF is widely considered a slush fund for President Vladimir Putin and is emblematic of Russia’s broader kleptocracy,” the U.S. Treasury Department said at the time.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu berated Itche Dzalovsky, the operator of an ultra-Orthodox information hotline, on Tuesday evening. In a recorded phone call, Netanyahu can be heard demanding to know whether ultra-Orthodox Jews were going out to vote. "What's happening with the Haredim?" the prime minister asked. 
Dzalovsky replied: "What's happening is that they're very angry that, to this day, all the promises about conscription and the ultra-Orthodox community..." Netanyahu interrupted him, shouting: "Tell me, are they crazy? Do they want a left-wing government? Are they crazy? We'll die."
Dzalovsky, a member of the Ger Hasidic community, tried to explain: "They want a government that will deliver on what it has repeatedly promised." Netanyahu continued shouting angrily: "Do they want to die? They want to destroy the Torah world, and they're not coming out? That's what I want to know." The ultra-Orthodox activist replied: "They want ultra-Orthodox Jews to be able to observe the Torah and its commandments to the depths of their souls, without having their religion trampled."
The prime minister continued: "So, in short, they're not coming out to vote. That's what I'm asking. They're not coming out. Is that the point?" Dzalovsky replied: "They want to come out, but after seeing those promises honored over time." Netanyahu responded: "What do you mean, promises being honored? In another hour and a half, they're going to establish a government of Mansour Abbas, who says he's going to destroy the Torah world." Netanyahu was referring to the leader of the Arab Islamist Ra'am party.
"But they've had four years of promises being broken consistently," Dzalovsky said. Netanyahu replied: "Fine, but that's not the question right now. Are they going out to vote or not? That's what I'm asking."
The ultra-Orthodox activist responded: "They're not convinced there's anyone who will keep his word."
"What? What?" Netanyahu asked.
"They're not convinced there's anyone who will keep his word," Dzalovsky repeated.
"So that means they're not going out. That's what you're telling me," Netanyahu replied.
The information hotline operator continued along the same lines: "I get the impression that it's very difficult to convince people who received promises that weren't kept."
The prime minister asked: "So they're not going out, okay. Is there anything we can do about it now, with an hour and a half left?"
Dzalovsky replied: "I think if you call and promise to provide guarantees to the leading rabbis, members of the Council of Torah Sages and other rabbinic authorities..."
Netanyahu interrupted: "I'm going to give them guarantees now, with an hour and a half left, tell me?"
"What hasn't been done for four years is certainly very difficult to do now," Dzalovsky replied.
At the end of the call, Netanyahu made one final attempt to appeal to the ultra-Orthodox activist: "So, in short, you're telling me there's nothing to be done, right?"
"That's what I think. I think it's really, really impossible," Dzalovsky answered.
"Thank you, Itche. Goodbye," Netanyahu said.

Arab voter turnout surges as parties projected to nearly double their seats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:25:16 UTC
05:25:16 KST

Amid historic voter turnout in Israel's 26th Knesset election, large numbers of Arab citizens turned out to cast their ballots Tuesday. According to television exit polls, the Joint List and Ra'am are projected to win a combined 16 to 18 seats, up from just 10 in the outgoing Knesset.
As of 8 p.m., nationwide voter turnout stood at 74.3%, with particularly high participation recorded in many Arab communities, including Bedouin towns and villages. In the village of al-Aryan in Wadi Ara, turnout reached 90.7%, followed by Sakhnin at 83.5%, Kafr Qasim at 81.3%, Rahat at 79.8%, Kuseife at 78.6%, Bir al-Maksur at 77.6%, Tira at 77.5% and Hura at 76.3%.
However, turnout in several Arab communities remained below the national average. In Shefa-Amr, 72.5% of eligible voters had cast ballots, compared with 70.1% in Umm al-Fahm, 70% in Nazareth and 73% in Tel Sheva. In Tayibe, turnout stood at 74.3%, matching the national average.
Among Bedouin communities, turnout reached 87.3% in Bir Hadaj, 85.2% in the Abu Qrenat tribal community, 84.2% in Kabu'a and 71.3% in Ar'ara in the Negev. In the Galilee, the Bedouin village of Dmeideh recorded 87.9% turnout, while Shibli-Umm al-Ghanam, at the foot of Mount Tabor, recorded 74.3%.
By comparison, turnout in Arab communities was considerably lower during the previous Knesset election in 2022. In Sakhnin, 68.4% of eligible voters participated, compared with 66.88% in Kafr Qasim, 60.6% in Rahat, 57.7% in Tayibe, 51.5% in Shefa-Amr, 49% in Hura and 48.3% in Nazareth.
The most dramatic increase was recorded in Umm al-Fahm, where turnout reached 70.1% by 8 p.m. Tuesday, compared with just 38.3% in 2022, nearly doubling. One possible factor behind the sharp increase is that Joint List chairman Professor Yousef Jabareen is a resident of the city.
Most Arab voters support the Arab parties, the Joint List and Ra'am, which could play a significant role in determining the composition of the next government.
According to the exit polls, the opposition bloc may need the support of these parties to advance measures against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc, including legislation that would bar a politician under criminal indictment from serving as prime minister, replacing Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana and potentially establishing a government dependent on their support.
However, Gadi Eisenkot, chairman of the Yashar! party, who appears positioned to receive the first mandate to form the next government, has already declared that he would establish a coalition only on the basis of a Zionist majority.
The Joint List and Ra'am: From 10 seats to a possible 18
The Joint List is an alliance of three Arab parties: Hadash, Ta'al and Balad. Hadash is headed by Yousef Jabareen, who succeeded Ayman Odeh. Ta'al has been led since 1995 by Ahmad Tibi, who has served continuously in the Knesset since 1999. Balad is led by Sami Abu Shehadeh, although he will not enter the Knesset after the Central Elections Committee disqualified his candidacy.
During a hearing on an appeal against the disqualification, the Supreme Court recommended that Abu Shehadeh consider withdrawing his candidacy to avoid the need for a ruling. The Balad chairman subsequently withdrew.
At its peak in 2020, the Joint List won 15 Knesset seats, although all the major Arab parties, including Ra'am, were running together at the time. A year later, when the Joint List ran with the same three-party composition as today, it secured just six seats.
Ra'am has been headed by Mansour Abbas since 2019. The party is considered the political arm of the southern branch of the Islamic Movement in Israel. In the two previous elections, Ra'am ran independently, winning four seats in 2021 and five in 2022.
Following the election to the 24th Knesset, and after also holding coalition negotiations with Likud, Abbas and Ra'am backed the so-called change government, the coalition that replaced Netanyahu. That decision prompted fierce attacks from Netanyahu and Likud, which continued throughout the current election campaign. Netanyahu's central campaign slogan was "Right or Palestine."
This time, for the first time, Abbas placed a Jewish candidate on Ra'am's electoral list: former deputy public security minister and retired police major general Yoav Segalovitz, who was ranked second.

Arab voter turnout would have been lower had there been any other outgoing government - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:25:01 UTC
05:25:01 KST

Throughout this campaign and into its final hours, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu sounded the same alarm he has sounded throughout his political career: Arab citizens are flooding the polls and endangering his rule. For once, the outgoing prime minister was telling the truth. Arab Israelis are voting today in numbers not seen in decades, and they may well bring his reign to an end.
The last time this happened was 1999. In one of Israel’s few direct elections for prime minister, Arab voters turned out in large numbers to back Ehud Barak almost unanimously, helping oust Netanyahu for the first time and opening the door of the prime minister’s office to Barak, Israel’s last left-wing prime minister.
Sixteen months later, in October 2000, police under Barak’s government opened fire on Arab demonstrators protesting Ariel Sharon’s visit to the Temple Mount, Al-Aqsa Mosque. Twelve Israeli citizens were shot and killed. The Or Commission of Inquiry later confirmed what every Arab Israeli had already known: There were grave failures in how the police and the state treat Arab citizens. It surprised no one that no police officer was ever charged.
October 2000 became an open wound in Arab Israeli collective memory and a reason to keep a distance from the Israeli mainstream. That memory has kept many Arab citizens home in every election since.
This time is different.
Netanyahu's coalition has abandoned, betrayed Arab citizens
The memory of October 2000 has not faded, but it has been overtaken by the reality of the past four years, under a government that has done far more than neglect Arab citizens.
Israel’s outgoing coalition, the most radical in the country’s history, not only tried to import the reality of the West Bank across the Green Line and into Israel proper. It also taught Israel’s two million Arab citizens that a bad situation can always get worse if they accept their own political marginalization.
This government left Arab communities at the mercy of criminal gangs, living amid anarchy and state absence, with little urgency from those responsible for public safety. Meanwhile, its mouthpieces in the media spewed relentless incitement against Arab citizens: doctors, journalists, elected officials, bus drivers, ordinary people. Without that, Arab turnout today might well have continued its decades-long decline. Instead, the government that did the most to push Arab citizens out of Israeli politics may be the one that brought them back.
The easy reading of this historic turnout is that Arab citizens rallied behind their parties. That reading is wrong. The Arab Israeli political establishment is widely seen as a closed, exclusionary club: outdated, ineffective, and recycling the same faces and the same speeches. Some Arab citizens voted for Jewish-led parties today. Many who voted for Arab lists did so without enthusiasm.
They came out of a sense of citizenship and shared responsibility, just as they did in October 2023, when they stood shoulder-to-shoulder with Jewish Israelis in the country’s lowest, most painful moment. Then and now, they showed that they belong to this state, that they are willing to carry its burdens and share its fate, and that they will not be written out of it. For a community so often accused of standing apart, and even branded an enemy within, today’s turnout declares the opposite. It is a cry from below, from people who have spent four years under the most far-right government in Israel’s history.
Arab citizens, Israel's 'kingmakers'
In 2021, the only government to unseat Netanyahu in over a decade came to power because Ra’am, an Arab party, provided its majority. It was the first Arab party ever to join an Israeli coalition. The opposition took power on that basis and then spent years acting as though it should apologize for it.
In this campaign, its leading figures refused even to say they would govern with an Arab-Israeli partner.
Arab citizens know they are once again the kingmakers. They have put aside their doubts and shown up to defend a democracy that has not always defended them. Voting in such numbers while carrying the memory of October 2000 is an act of extraordinary trust, and trust given twice is not guaranteed a third time.
The opposition need not embrace every Arab politician or every platform. But before coalition talks begin, it must say plainly that at least one Arab party is a legitimate partner in government.
Anything less sends two million citizens a message they have heard before: Your vote counts when it is useful, but your voice has no place in shaping this country.
The hand has been extended. The Jewish-majority opposition can take it, and with it lead Israel toward a different future.
Or it can confirm everything October 2000 taught Israel’s Arab citizens and hand the outgoing coalition the deadlock it desperately needs to stay in power.
The choice is the opposition’s alone. Will Israel be a democracy among the nations, where every vote counts? Or will it keep sliding toward an isolated, undemocratic, and racist ethnocracy?

All three new parties polling near Israel's electoral threshold were projected to fall short of entering the Knesset, according to exit polls published by Channels 11, 12, and 13 on Tuesday night.
People of Israel, led by former IDF Brig.-Gen. Ofer Winter, the Reservists-Economic Party, led by former communications minister Yoaz Hendel and economist Yaron Zelekha, and Haredi Public, led by Moti Leitner, were all projected to fall short of the 3.25% electoral threshold required to enter the Knesset.
People of Israel campaigned on a right-wing security platform, advocating tougher action against Hamas while also supporting greater ultra-Orthodox participation in military service.
Winter declared his party to be part of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc but challenged the prime minister on several issues during the election campaign and repeatedly called for new faces in Israel's parliament.
Despite challenging the establishment, new parties projected to fall short of Knesset
The Reservists-Economic Party campaigned on expanding military service to include more ultra-Orthodox Israelis and addressing Israel's economic challenges. Hendel did not commit to joining either political bloc, instead calling for a broad Zionist government to be formed following the election.
Haredi Public sought to offer an alternative to the established ultra-Orthodox parties, Shas and United Torah Judaism, with a focus on representing the Haredi (ultra-Orthodox) public.
The parties' failure to clear the threshold could affect the distribution of Knesset seats among the parties that qualify, as votes cast for parties that fall short are not included in the allocation of seats.
The exit polls are preliminary projections. The final outcome will depend on the official vote count and the allocation of Knesset seats.
People of Israel officials: Winter's campaign did not cost Netanyahu’s bloc seats
Officials from Ofer Winter's People of Israel party said, following an initial analysis of the exit poll results, that the seat distribution would have shifted against the right-wing bloc if Winter had withdrawn from the race.
They claimed that Yoaz Hendel and Yaron Zelekha would have passed the electoral threshold, adding four seats to the left-wing bloc.
The officials also argued that the vast majority of votes cast for Winter came from voters outside the governing coalition, dismissing claims that the party had wasted votes as “absurd.”

Israel election exit polls: Netanyahu, Eisenkot deadlocked as both blocs fall short of majority
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:24:44 UTC
05:24:44 KST

No clear winner emerged in Israel’s election, according to exit polls published by Channels 11, 12, and 13 on Tuesday night, all of which showed both Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc and the opposition bloc seeking to replace him falling short of a 61-seat Knesset majority.
The opposition bloc, comprising Yashar, B’Yachad, Yisrael Beytenu, and the Democrats, was projected to win 50-52 seats, compared with some 50 for Netanyahu’s bloc. Channel 13 exit polls published at 1:00 a.m. projected that both Netanyahu's bloc and the opposition bloc were tied at 51 seats each. Channel 13's poll data predicted Likud winning 27 seats, with Yashar projected to win 22 seats. Neither side appeared to have a clear path to forming a coalition, though the opposition bloc declared victory shortly after the exit polls were released.
The Joint List and Ra’am were projected to win a record-breaking combined 17-18 seats, potentially making Arab parties pivotal to coalition negotiations. However, opposition leaders have largely ruled out forming a government with the Arab parties, barring the Democrats' Yair Golan.
Netanyahu’s Likud was projected to receive 24-25 seats and was set to remain the largest party in the next Knesset, while Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar was expected to win 21-23 seats, according to the exit polls.
Most recent polling ahead of the Tuesday vote had shown neither Netanyahu’s bloc nor the opposition bloc as managing to secure a 61-seat majority. Voter turnout reached its highest level since at least 1973, according to Central Elections Committee records, which have tracked turnout at set times throughout Election Day since then.
The final voter turnout number came out as 77.7% when polls closed at 10:00 p.m., according to the Central Elections Committee (CEC), up by 7.1% recorded in the 2022 election.
The small right-wing parties hovering near the electoral threshold, Ofer Winter’s People of Israel and Yoaz Hendel’s The Reservists-Economic party, were both projected to fall short of the required 3.25% threshold, potentially further complicating efforts by Netanyahu’s bloc to secure a majority.
Could Israel be heading toward a unity gov't - or another election?
The prospect of a unity government involving Netanyahu and Eisenkot has appeared unlikely, as Eisenkot has rejected serving under Netanyahu, including in a rotation government. Other opposition leaders have also ruled out joining a coalition led by the prime minister.
Eisenkot has called for the leader of the largest party in the opposition bloc to become its candidate for prime minister, though no agreement on the arrangement has been announced within the bloc.
The exit polls also raised the possibility of a minority government that could win a Knesset confidence vote without holding an absolute majority of 61 seats. However, opposition within the bloc to relying on Arab parties could complicate such an arrangement.
Official results to be determined after ballots are counted
The exit polls have differed from final results in previous elections, and the official results will be determined after ballots are counted.
The political deadlock could ultimately lead to another election, although coalition negotiations may still produce an agreement between the parties.
In the opposition bloc, Naftali Bennett’s B’Yachad is projected to be the third-largest party, receiving 12-14 seats according to exit polls.
Avigdor Liberman’s Yisrael Beytenu was projected to receive 7-9 seats, while Yair Golan’s Democrats stood at 9-10, exit polls showed.
Meanwhile, in the Netanyahu bloc, National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir's Otzma Yehudit party was projected to win 6-7 seats, while the Religious Zionist Party-Zehut, led by Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, was projected to win 6 seats.
The major (haredi) ultra-Orthodox parties are set to receive a combined 12-13 seats, with Shas getting 6 seats and United Torah Judaism (UTJ) earning 6-7 seats, according to the exit polls.
Opposition leaders declare exit poll results a victory for bloc
Eisenkot and other opposition party leaders declared the initial exit poll results a victory for their bloc, stating that Netanyahu’s camp had been defeated.
“The initial exit poll results indicate a complete lack of confidence in Netanyahu and his October 7 government among the Zionist majority and the majority of Israeli citizens,” Eisenkot stated.
“If these are the final results, they represent a victory for Israel’s national-minded, Zionist majority,” he added.
“I will act immediately to implement the people’s decision, replace the Netanyahu government, and establish a Zionist government committed to military conscription as soon as possible,” Eisenkot said.
Opposition leader Yair Lapid also declared Netanyahu’s bloc defeated.
“Don’t let anyone confuse you: The Netanyahu bloc has suffered a crushing defeat. This is a total collapse, and the public has told them to go home,” he stated.
Democrats Party chairman Yair Golan said the results presented an opportunity to establish a new government.
“The public has spoken. It has fired the Netanyahu government. We have been given a historic opportunity to establish a genuine government of change in Israel, and we have no intention of giving it up,” Golan said.
“We are ready to work with all our partners, bridge the gaps, and take responsibility,” he added.
If Eisenkot were to become prime minister, he would oust Netanyahu, whose right-wing government was in power during the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led attacks and went on to serve its full term. Netanyahu is Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, having held the office for more than 19 years in total.
Following the October 7 massacre and the ensuing war, the opposition bloc has called for Netanyahu to be held accountable for the attacks, arguing that he should no longer serve as prime minister and calling for a state commission of inquiry to be established.

Shas, UTJ projected to win 12-15 seats in next Knesset, election exit polls predict
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:24:24 UTC
05:24:24 KST

Israel's two main haredi (ultra-Orthodox) parties, Shas and United Torah Judaism (UTJ), were projected to win six to eight and six to seven seats, respectively, according to exit polls published by Channels 11, 12, and 13 on Tuesday night.
The projections would give the two parties a combined 12 to 15 seats in the 120-member Knesset.
The results could have significant implications for coalition negotiations and the next government's ability to secure a parliamentary majority. However, exit polls are preliminary projections, and the final distribution of seats will depend on the official vote count and the allocation of Knesset seats.
Both Shas and UTJ are part of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s political bloc, and their combined seat total could prove crucial in determining whether he can secure the 61 seats needed for a Knesset majority.
Neither party has committed to joining only a Netanyahu-led coalition, and Shas’s spiritual leader has indicated that he would be open to joining a government led by prime ministerial candidate Gadi Eisenkot. This challenges the assumption that a vote for Shas necessarily translates into support for a Netanyahu-led government.
Shas, UTJ back Torah study law amid criticism over haredi draft exemptions
Both haredi parties pushed for legislation, recently passed by the Knesset, enshrining Torah study as a fundamental value in Israel’s Basic Laws. Critics argued that the legislation would encourage draft evasion, while the haredi parties defended it as a measure to protect the religious importance of full-time Torah study.
Regarding Gaza, Shas has broadly supported efforts to dismantle Hamas and demilitarize the Strip while opposing indefinite Israeli control of the territory.
Shas and UTJ have maintained close political cooperation, signing a surplus vote-sharing agreement earlier this month ahead of the October 27 election and pledging to continue working together in the next Knesset.
Another central issue for both parties is the relationship between religion and state. Shas and UTJ seek to preserve Israel’s Orthodox Jewish character and maintain the authority of religious institutions, particularly the Chief Rabbinate.
Both parties have strongly opposed expanding alternatives to religious marriage, including civil marriage, and support maintaining the existing system in which Jewish marriages are conducted through the Rabbinate.
Shas, UTJ reaffirm cooperation with vote-sharing agreement ahead of election
Announcing their surplus vote-sharing agreement, Shas chairman Arye Deri and UTJ lawmaker Yaakov Asher said it reflected the “continued cooperation between the factions, in accordance with the instructions of the generation’s leading rabbis and Torah sages.”
Despite their longstanding partnership in Netanyahu’s coalition, Shas and UTJ have faced growing criticism over their opposition to haredi military conscription amid the IDF’s severe manpower shortage.
Both parties pressed Netanyahu’s coalition to advance conscription legislation that critics argued would fail to significantly increase haredi enlistment during the government’s term.
They also boycotted coalition votes, declaring that they would not resume cooperation until progress was made on the contentious legislation they had been demanding.
Shir Perets contributed to this report.

Olivia Chow elected as Toronto mayor for second term in victory for progressives
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:23:46 UTC
05:23:46 KST

The mayor of Toronto, Olivia Chow, promised more rental housing, free school lunches and reduce fares for frequent transit riders after she was elected to a decisive second term as mayor in a wave of support for progressive councillors.
The tightly fought election saw record turnout but Chow ultimately turned in a dominant 13 percentage point win over her rival, Brad Bradford, receiving 54% of the vote compared to his 41%. Many had been expecting a far closer race, given weeks of polling that suggested a dead heat between the pair who presented differing visions for Canada’s largest city.
Chow bet that voters would accept her policies to confront a mounting affordability crisis that has engulfed major cities around the world. On Monday night, she thanked her supporters and Bradford.
“I know we share a love for Toronto and a belief in its future,” she told a jubilant crowd. “We can disagree on how we get there, or what it looks like, but I do not doubt we both want what is best for our city.”
Chow, 69, has long been a fixture of the city’s politics. She previously served as a school board trustee, city councillor and federal member of parliament. Her total of more than 532,000 votes nearly doubles what she received in 2023.
Bradford, a former city councillor and urban planner, spent much of the campaign focusing on what he said was Chow’s failure to stem the rising cost of living and to address crime. He told residents crime was so bad in Toronto that he slept with a baseball bat next to his bed.
While auto theft and high-value property crime have risen, most other categories – including homicides, firearms related violence and assault – have all dropped significantly in recent years.
Bradford said more police were needed, and pledged to cut taxes and city spending.
In a city that has experienced antisemitic vandalism and shootings at Jewish schools, Bradford aimed to ally himself with Toronto’s Jewish community, and said that Chow’s decision not to attend a debate on antisemitism meant she wouldn’t be an effective voice to combat hate. For her part, Chow increased the size of the police department’s hate crimes unit and pushed a “bubble zone” bylaw that barred protest within 50 meters of places of worship, schools, childcare centers other vulnerable institutions.
In his concession speech, the 40-year-old took a conciliatory tone. “I want her to succeed. And my supporters and the nearly 400,000 people that cast a vote for us tonight, they want her to succeed too,” he said. “We all love this city. We know it can be better.”
Bradford also acknowledged the daunting odds against his candidacy: no incumbent mayor who has sought re-election in Canada’s largest city has ever lost.
Chow also benefited from her apparent ability to manage a fraught political relationship with the Ontario government and its premier, Doug Ford. When she was first elected in 2023, Ford said she would be an “unmitigated disaster” for the city. While Ford did not endorse her in this election, he told reporters the pair had a “phenomenal relationship” and said people should “read between the lines” when it comes to his preferred candidate. However, the two are likely to spar in a fierce battle over the city’s bike lanes.
Like other major urban centers, Toronto remains locked in a battle over affordability, an issue that is expected to remain a challenge for the incoming council, where a large number of progressive candidates both returned and won for the first time, including Diana McNally Chan, a well-known advocate for unhoused people, who will be the first renter to sit on city council.

UN rapporteur says impunity prevails for killing journalists in Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:23:07 UTC
05:23:07 KST

Merve Aydogan
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
UN Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese said Tuesday that the targeting of journalists in the Gaza Strip is part of a deliberate effort to conceal atrocities, describing her latest report as an examination of "truth" that has been "buried under the rubble."
"What is happening is not incidental; it is intentional," Albanese, who briefed reporters virtually, said about the genocide in Gaza.
She said she provocatively called the phenomenon "media side," describing it as "the systematic destruction of the media’s public function."
"In a genocide, the systematic attack on the media is part and parcel of the crime," she added.
Asked for an update on the investigation into Israel’s 2022 killing of Palestinian American journalist Shireen Abu Akleh, she said: "Nothing, nothing happened. So, the update is impunity."
She noted the impunity was not only by Israel but also "impunity by the United States."
Rejecting the terrorist label, Albanese said it "has been the label to kill everyone, to bring famine upon everyone in Gaza, to destroy Gaza."
Even if Israel has a right to self-defense under international law, she said: "Israel doesn’t have and cannot claim the right to wage a war against Gaza."
Responding to a question on whether the International Criminal Court (ICC) had failed Palestinians, she said "the complementarity of international criminal investigation can be triggered," urging prosecutions "starting now with activating domestic courts."
She said citizens of France, Britain, the US and Belgium who served in the Israeli army could face scrutiny, stressing it was "something that cannot be delayed."
Albanese also pointed to "the absence of so many media, especially legacy media" from Western countries, saying she read it as "possibly an act of solidarity" toward outlets named in the report.

Israel election: Anti-Netanyahu bloc ahead, but no majority
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:21:00 UTC
05:21:00 KST

Israel election: Anti-Netanyahu bloc ahead but without a majority
Published October 27, 2026last updated October 27, 2026
What you need to know
- Israelis have voted, at a high turnout, in a parliamentary election that appears to have produced no clear winner
- The pro-Netanyahu bloc is on 50 seats, with the anti-Netanyahu bloc on 53, according to public broadcaster KAN
- Two Arab parties have gained 17 seats between them
- At least 61 seats are needed to form a secure majority
- Israel election committee reports highest voter turnout on record as of 2 p.m., halfway through the voting day
- Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister, faces a staunch challenge to his grip on power
- His chief rival is former military chief Gadi Eisenkot
Follow below for all the latest on the Israeli election on October 27, 2026, and its aftermath:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
Eisenkot says he is ready to form a government
Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the opposition bloc, said the election results pointed to a "complete lack of confidence" in Netanyahu and his coalition.
"I will act immediately to carry out the people’s mandate, replace Netanyahu's government and form a Zionist government committed to military conscription as soon as possible," Eisenkot said in a statement.
A former military chief, he made the issue of eliminating exemptions from military service for Ultra-Orthodox men central to his campaign.
Majority of Israeli public voted against Netanyahu, exit polls show
Much of the Israeli media labeled the Israeli election an opinion poll on Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
If the exit polls of Israel's main news outlets are anything to go by, the Israeli public voted against the country's longest-serving prime minister.
While Netanyahu's current coalition includes 68 seats, the exit polls gave his bloc between 50 and 51 seats.
The Israeli prime minister is unlikely to concede defeat despite his coalition having taken a significant hit, but it remains to be seen how Likud's own ranks, as well as its coalition partners, will react to the exit polls.
Ra'am party becomes political power broker
The success of Ra'am, which exit polls predict will take seven seats, means no Israeli government can be established without the religious Muslim party playing some part.
The party already made headlines after appointing Yoav Segalovich, a Jewish former high-ranking police chief, as the number two candidate to leader Mansour Abbas. The raging criminality and violence across the Arab and Palestinian community, as well as the war in Gaza, both could have played a role in Ra'am's result.
Both the Likud-led coalition and large parts of the Israeli opposition may have ruled out a coalition with Ra'am, but the current results may leave them little choice but to seek some form of cooperation with the party.
As one Israeli pollster put it, "Tonight, Israelis were reminded that their population also includes Arabs and Palestinians with Israeli citizenship."
Netanyahu's bloc trails in Israel election, exit polls say
Exit polls from Israel's major television networks project that a majority of Israelis voted against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition, but his Likud party has emerged as the largest single group in the Knesset, with 25 projected seats.
Challenger Gadi Eisenkot's bloc has emerged as the largest group with a projected 53, just ahead of the ruling coalition on 50, but well short of the 61 needed for a majority.
Neither bloc has a clear majority without the support of Arab parties.
These projected numbers are from public broadcaster Kan 11; other numbers vary by channel, but only slightly.
Polls closing around the country
It's now 10 p.m. across Israel, which means that polling stations around the country either should have closed or should be making preparations to do so as the last people in line cast their ballots.
Exit polls should follow shortly on Israeli television. These have a fairly good reputation overall but of course are only projections.
Results will start to trickle in through the night and are unlikely to be finalized until Wednesday.
And of course, there's every chance that even once the dust has settled and the final results are in, we will have a longer wait until there's clarity about who might be able to form a coalition government.
In any case, stick with us and we'll keep you posted.
Election commission sees 'no need to extend voting hours' after Netanyahu request
The Central Elections Committee has rejected a request by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party and some other groups to extend voting beyond 10 p.m. (2000 UTC/GMT).
"High nationwide turnout across all sectors of society reflects strong public engagement in the democratic process, and no need to extend voting hours was identified," a commission statement said.
The committee noted, however, that this decision was based on the circumstances "as things stand," leaving open the possibility for matters to change.
For instance, voting hours have been extended in some areas, including a polling location used by Israeli settlers in Hebron, in the occupied West Bank, where a power outage led to an extension of the closing time from 8 p.m. to 10 p.m. Polling stations with fewer than 350 eligible voters typically close two hours earlier than larger polling stations in urban areas.
The commission has also said several times that anybody who started queueing before closing time will be given a chance to vote.
IN DEPTH: How AI reshaped Israel's election campaign
Artificial intelligence is emerging as a major factor in Israel's election campaign, with political parties using AI-generated videos, automated calls and online content on a large scale.
DW's Josh Axelrod examined the growing role of AI in the campaign, as researchers and analysts raise concerns about misleading content, bots and deepfakes ahead of the vote.
High turnout could spell problems for Netanyahu's bloc
The expected high turnout means the number of votes needed to cross the 3.25% threshold to enter the Knesset, the Israeli parliament, is going to be higher, meaning smaller parties are at risk of not making it.
According to opinion polls from last week, the two parties that are on the threshold limit are Amcha Israel, a far-right party led by former military commander Ofer Winter, and the Reservists Party, which has not declared support for either main bloc.
Winter repeatedly said he intends to join a Netanyahu coalition, and a scenario in which his party doesn't make it to parliament puts Likud's chances of a future coalition at risk.
Either way, Israel's Central Elections Committee will have to make a decision on the matter within the hour.
Turnout reaches 2 in 3 voters by 6 p.m.
Voter turnout reached 66.7%, or roughly two in every three eligible voters, by 6 p.m. local time, according to an update from the Central Elections Committee.
This remains the highest partial turnout figure since such records were first taken in 1973.
The level is only slightly clear of the previous high of 65.2% in 1973 and 1988 — but it quite considerably surpasses the 57.7% who had voted by this time in 2022.
And that figure had already been the highest 6 p.m. turnout of the 21st century before being surpassed today.
WATCH: Could Arab voters hold the key in Israel’s election?
Arab voters could play a decisive role in Israel's election. With neither Benjamin Netanyahu nor Gadi Eisenkot expected to win a Knesset majority, Arab parties could become key to forming the next government.
Activists worked to boost voter turnout, especially among young voters.
Netanyahu emphasizes Arab turnout in appeals to his own voters
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu continued issuing appeals to supporters to go out and vote online as the day progressed.
One common theme was apparent in almost all of the posts: warnings about high turnout in Arab and to a lesser extent left-leaning communities.
"We're at war for our home," one of Netanyahu's posts read, using a phrase that appeared repeatedly in his messaging. "Muslim Brotherhood supporters are raiding the polling stations and stealing the elections. Go out and vote, recover it!!"
In another post he showed an image claiming to show a long line of voters queueing in Rahat, with a crowd of women wearing niqab coverings prominently visible at the front of the queue, suggesting that they were Muslim Palestinian voters.
Sami Abou Shahadeh, the leader of the Balad party, which is part of the alliance known as the Joint List, in turn called on his supporters to vote before the deadline expired, also highlighting similar appeals to voters from the leader of the far-right Jewish Power party, Itamar Ben-Gvir.
"There is one response to the incitement by Ben-Gvir and Netanyahu against the Arab citizens that has been going on all day: go out and vote for the Joint List!" he wrote.
President of German-Israeli Society, Volker Beck, says a change would be 'good for Israel'
The president of the German-Israeli Society, Green party politician Volker Beck, said in a TV interview on election day that he believed a change in leadership might be in Israel's interests.
"It would be good for Israel, if it were to come to a change, because I believe that [Prime Minister Benjamin] Netanyahu has squandered a great deal of trust in recent years, both in foreign and domestic policy," Beck said in an interview broadcast on sister channels RTL and ntv.
Beck, a Bundestag lawmaker for more than two decades with the Greens who was perhaps best known as a politician as a campaigner for LGBT rights and advocate of an uncompromising Israeli foreign policy, is not typically associated with stern criticism of Netanyahu or his government.
"Although he has also done some things right and has done some necessary things, a change is really needed" to allow Israel to recoup support among the international community, Beck said, as Netanyahu becomes an increasingly polarizing figure on the world stage.
He also criticized domestic efforts by the Likud-led government to reform the legal system and its influence over politics, saying this would "fundamentally change Israel's character, and should be stopped."
Beck said he hoped that a functioning majority would emerge from the vote, but acknowledged that pollsters anticipated a stalemate. In that scenario, he said, he would personally favor a national unity government incorporating all the major players.
But at present he thought the "divide between the two camps is so deep, that it really would be a bit of a masterstroke to be able to bring them together." He made a similar comment online, saying such a unity govermment "would be good" but was "not very likely."
Likud says online that it has requested an extension of voting hours
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party wrote on the Telegram social media channel that it has submitted a request for polling stations to stay open later.
"Likud: We have submitted a request to extend the voting hours!" the post said.
It offered no further details, for instance, how long an extension it was seeking or whether it was to be nationwide or at individual polling stations.
The Ultra-Orthodox Shas party also joined the petition, according to the Times of Israel, saying: "The parties are trying to prevent a situation in which citizens waiting in line won’t be able to vote."
The main opposition Yashar party rejected the extension, saying: "No exceptional incident has occurred that would justify granting this request, which is intended to lay the groundwork for allegations challenging the integrity of the election, continuing the lies Netanyahu has been spreading since this morning."
Politicians of all stripes have been trying hard to mobilize voters for what's expected to be a tight race. Turnout has also been high so far, with long lines at some polling stations as a result of this.
Voting was already set to continue quite late into the night, with polling stations scheduled to close at 10 p.m. local time. Voters who are in line at polling stations at closing time will still be allowed to vote.
Who are Israel's first-time voters projected to support?
Polls show Israel's many young voters are more likely to vote for far-right parties, particularly Itamar Ben-Gvir's Otzma Yehudit (Jewish Power) party.
An opinion poll by Agam Labs at Jerusalem's Hebrew University predicts that supporters of Otzma Yehudit are younger than the average Israeli voter, with as many as a third voting for the first time.
Over 500,000 Israelis have reached voting age since the 2022 election. Of those voters, three in every four define themselves as right or center-right, according to a recent poll for Channel 12. The poll did not survey Palestinian citizens of Israel.
First-time voters were teenagers when Ben-Gvir joined Netanyahu's incumbent government in 2022, making up Israel's most far-right government to date.
A year later, they witnessed the Hamas-led October 7 terror attack which killed 1,200 Israelis, mostly civilians, and saw some 251 others taken hostage and brought to Gaza. The attack triggered a 2-year war on the Palestinian enclave that resulted in tens of thousands of Palestinians killed and intensified settler violence against Palestinians in the West Bank. Hamas is designated as a terrorist group by several countries.
Previously, Otzma Yehudit's support was concentrated primarily among settlers in the occupied West Bank.
WATCH — Author, politician Avraham Burg on why a Palestinian peace process barely featured in the campaign
While security remained the dominant issue for Israeli voters, one topic was largely absent from the election campaign: a peace process with the Palestinians.
After years of conflict and failed negotiations, that debate has been pushed to the political margins.
Has Israeli society abandoned the idea of coexistence?
Avraham Burg, an Israeli writer and former Speaker of the Israeli Parliament, shares his insights with DW.

To hike or not to hike? And will today’s CPI answer the question?
The old joke goes: "Ask five economists and you'll get five different answers — six if one went to Harvard."
For the sake of blogging brevity, we'll keep it binary. Here are two different takes on the same result — the trimmed mean CPI coming in at 3.6% yoy.
Pause: CBA senior economist, Trent Saunders
CBA's economics team, which is tipping the consensus result of the trimmed mean CPI coming in at 1.0% over the quarter (3.6% yoy), is leaning towards the RBA holding next week even with a result that is a fair bit higher than the RBA's forecast.
CBA senior economist Trent Saunders says it's not all about inflation, noting that the recent easing in the labour market and subdued consumption growth also come into play.
Saunders points out the oft-quoted RBA deputy governor Andrew Hauser last week was suggesting the board faces hard choices — a difficult trade-off between responding to persistent inflation pressures and avoiding unnecessary further weakness in activity and employment.
He says while the November meeting will be "live", that is a hike is possible, a pause is more likely.
"While our baseline remains for the RBA to leave the cash rate unchanged, the decision will depend heavily on the outcome and composition of [the] CPI print."
Hike: UBS senior economist Stephen Wu
The UBS belief that the RBA will hike next week is also strongly influenced by Hauser's comments last week but is more focused on the "inflation outlook looks materially worse than we projected in the August report" bit.
UBS senior economist Stephen Wu says Hauser was effectively conceding that absent a big downside surprise in the monthly CPI for September, the quarterly for Q3 inflation will be higher.
"Overall, UBS still expect a 25bps hike to 4.85%, most likely in November 26. The likely trigger remains a 1.0% q/q Q3 trimmed mean, alongside upgrades to the RBA's inflation profile," Wu said.
How's the Aussie dollar tracking ahead of the decision?
CBA's FX team has just fired in its morning note saying the AUD/USD consolidated about 0.7030 during the overnight trading session as markets positioned ahead of key risk events.
"Domestically, the Australian Q3 26 CPI is under the spotlight today. With the market pricing an around 60% chance of a 25bp increase in the cash rate next week, the CPI will make or break the case to increase the cash rate."
CBA's Australian economics team has pencilled in a trimmed CPI slightly lower than consensus.
"The upshot is AUD/USD could move sharply down today, possibly testing support at 0.6951," the CBA FX strategy team wrote.
CPI — the numbers that matter
Just a quick primer ahead of the consumer price index (CPI) inflation release at 11:30am (AEDT).
While the CPI is essentially backwards-looking — measuring the price changes of a basket of goods and services in the three months to the end of September (Q3) — the real significance is next week's RBA meeting.
Too high and there's a very strong likelihood of another interest rate hike.
A lower-than-expected result may keep the RBA on hold.
Before the CPI release, the market is pricing in a 60% chance of a hike.
Trimmed mean CPI
The most "policy-relevant" number to look out for is the trimmed mean CPI.
The consensus is it will have increased by a firm 1% over the quarter, taking the year-on-year figure to 3.6%.
If the consensus figure is delivered, that would be the fifth consecutive quarter of the trimmed mean being between 0.8% and 1.0%.
It would also be well above the RBA's August forecast of 0.8%.
A rate hike trigger? Perhaps.
It's worth noting that since the August forecasts were published, deputy governor Andrew Hauser noted last week that the inflation outlook now looks "materially worse".
A surprise on the downside is always possible.
A trimmed mean CPI below 0.8% may be good enough for the RBA to keep its powder dry.
September CPI
As well as the quarterly data, the most recent September numbers will be broken out.
The trimmed mean is expected to come in at 0.3% over the month.
Headline inflation is expected to have accelerated in September, largely due to a jump in fuel prices, which are thought to have been up around 10% on ABS measures.
A 0.7% jump in headline inflation in September would deliver a 4% year-on-year result.

Exit polls from Israel’s election show no clear winner
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:18:18 UTC
05:18:18 KST

Exit polls signal blow for Netanyahu but no clear winner in Israel election
Israel’s first election since October 7 attack appears deadlocked, with neither Netanyahu or Eisenkot on track for a majority.
Exit polls from Israel’s election show no clear winner, with neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nor his main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, on a clear path to a governing majority.
Polls from Tuesday’s election, described as the most consequential in Israel’s history, projected that the bloc led by Eisenkot, a former military chief of staff, would win 52 seats in the 120-seat Knesset.
The bloc supporting Netanyahu was projected to win 50 seats.
Either side would need 61 seats to form a majority government.
Arab parties are projected to win 18 seats collectively.
The election is largely seen as a referendum on Netanyahu’s handling of the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led attacks and the ensuing genocidal war on Gaza, as well as the attacks on Lebanon and Iran.
The exit polls – released by the major Israeli television networks – are subject to potential error. Preliminary results are expected in the coming hours, and may vary from the exit polls.
An inconclusive result would leave Israel in political limbo, allowing Netanyahu to remain in power in a caretaker capacity while parties try to forge a governing coalition.
‘Crushing defeat’
Eisenkot said the exit polls show a “lack of confidence” in the current prime minister.
Yair Lapid, the current opposition leader, echoed the sentiment.
“Don’t let anyone confuse you,” he said. “The Netanyahu bloc has suffered a crushing defeat. This is a total collapse, and the public has told them to go home.”
Yair Golan, the leader of the opposition Democrats, meanwhile said Israeli voters have “fired the Netanyahu government”, pledging to work with political partners to form a new administration.
“We have received a historic opportunity to establish a true government of change in Israel and we have no intention of giving it up,” he wrote on X.
But Gideon Saar, Israel’s foreign minister and a member of Netanyahu’s Likud party, said the opposition’s celebrations were premature.
In a social media post, he criticised the “pronouncements of biased commentators” and said: “Likud is the largest party in Israel. It is always good to learn something from the past.”
Netanyahu, who is 77 and heads Likud, has served as prime minister for nearly 19 of the past 30 years and has repeatedly survived political crises. His opponents have managed to wrest the premiership from him only once since 2009, after four inconclusive elections in two years.
Meanwhile, at the headquarters of the Joint List, an alliance of Arab parties, supporters erupted in whistles and applause as the exit polls were announced, capping a night of historic turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel.
Yousef Jabareen, leader of the Joint List, called the election a “historic day” and said voters had delivered a “clear and sharp” message. “The ‘government of bloodshed’ must go!”, he said in a statement.
“We have proven that we are a political force that cannot be ignored, and that a future here cannot be built without our voice.”
Mansour Abbas, the leader of Ra’am, or the United Arab List, also hailed the projected results. “We will transform the mandate we received into a new reality in the country,” Abbas told reporters, according to Israel’s Channel 12.
While the exit polls suggest the Arab-led parties could emerge as kingmakers, both Netanyahu and Eisenkot have ruled out partnering with the parties, citing a lack of shared values.
‘Difficult task’ ahead
Ehab Jabareen, a Palestinian political analyst and researcher in Israel, told Al Jazeera that the early exit poll projections show “a clear weakening of Netanyahu’s bloc” but expressed caution about “declaring either a Netanyahu victory or the end of his political career”.
“The exit polls suggest that his bloc has lost its majority, but they also suggest that his opponents face a difficult task in building one,” he said. “If neither side can form a government, Netanyahu could remain in office as caretaker while the negotiations continue.”
Polling stations had closed at 10pm local time (20:00 GMT).
The Central Elections Committee said some 77.7 percent of eligible voters – or more than 5.69 million of about 7.33 million voters – turned out to cast their ballots in Tuesday’s election.
The figure is about 7.1 percentage points higher than the 70.63 percent recorded in the previous election in 2022, and the highest turnout in a Knesset election since 1999, when 78.7 percent of eligible voters participated.
Earlier in the day, the committee rejected a request from Netanyahu’s Likud party to extend voting hours.

Australia clawed its way back into the third Test, but big challenges await
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:16:44 UTC
05:16:44 KST

It was, in the final analysis, close to the perfect day of Test cricket: ebbing, flowing, intriguing, with 10 wickets falling and 329 runs-worth of enterprising batting fulfilling Les Favell's trusty old criteria for an entertaining day on the hill.
There was a six-fer for Mitchell Starc, another bundle of tantalising, shot-filled knocks from South Africa's underappreciated batting stars and a pair of remarkable sequences in which Australia took 5-29 and 4-2. Both sides will, in some ways, feel they got the better of the other for telling periods.
The nagging doubt, after day one of the third and deciding Test, is how badly Australia's chances had been damaged before a ball had even been bowled. Not sufficiently recovered from his neck injury, Steve Smith withdrew. Not sufficiently superior to his colleagues in most facets of the game a week ago, Scott Boland was dropped for Nathan Lyon.
Then there was the toss. The minute Pat Cummins won it and elected to bowl first under sunny skies, on a perfect-looking pitch — not exactly a ringing endorsement of Australia's remade top six — it was hard to stop one's mind from wandering away from Newlands and back through time in search of precedents.
The obvious destinations were Edgbaston in 2005, the scene of Ricky Ponting's ill-fated decision to bowl first in that classic nailbiter, and Brisbane three years earlier, when poor old Nasser Hussain got it even more horribly wrong.
By lunch at Cape Town, Cummins's Australians were fighting an unwelcome omen: South Africa's domineering 0-140, obtained with a procession of boundaries off the most credentialed bowling attack in world cricket, comfortably shaded both England's 1-132 at Edgbaston in '05 and Australia's 1-125 in Brisbane in '02. Was Cummins coming similarly a cropper?
Cricket history tends to write inconvenient facts out of these stories. Few remember that in the immediate aftermath of Nasser's nightmare, for instance, Australian skipper Steve Waugh admitted he probably would have bowled first, too, albeit with a caveat. "The significance of the toss is overrated," Waugh explained. "Whatever you do first, you've got to do it well."
To say Australia didn't bowl or field well in the first session of this crunch game is an understatement. The vaunted quicks misfired early. To staunch the bleeding, Lyon had to be deployed in just the 11th over. Normally apt to suffocate opponents with sharp fielding, tight lines and partnership bowling, Australia managed only two maidens in the first 25 overs.
Proteas opener Marques Ackerman, who'd never batted at the top of the order in first-class cricket until his Test debut last week, attacked the bowling like prime David Warner, clubbing 12 fours and two sixes in his run-a-ball, thrill-a-minute 95. With Aiden Markram, he raced to South Africa's first 150-run opening stand in nearly a decade.
Of particular concern for Australia was the captain's bowling performance, the tone of which was set in his first over when Markram freed his arms, swivelled into position as though the ball was travelling in slow motion and cross-batted Cummins over the fence at cow corner. Cummins would finish the day with 0-73 from 18 overs, having extracted almost nothing from the pitch he'd so liked the look of in the morning. South Africa played him as though intent on showing a competitive disrespect.
But at first, slowly, and then in two manic bursts, Australia did pull things out of the fire somewhat from their dismal early position.
Lyon, whom Ackerman had taken a particular liking to, kept his head amid the onslaught and had the left-hander stumped, later roaring back into the game at a critical juncture and sneaking one past Temba Bavuma to bowl the Proteas skipper for a duck. Australia stemmed the flow of easy runs — from 5.18 an over in the first session, down to 3.11 in the second.
Reprieved on 39 when Travis Head dropped a sitter at short cover, Markram had doubled his score but looked set for even bigger things when he fell into a trap set by Hazlewood to be caught on the fine leg boundary. Matthew Breetzke was too casual against Cooper Connolly's spin, the left-armer reviewed an LBW shout cannily to claim his first Test wicket.
In the above-mentioned half-hour of head loss, South Africa lost 3-13 and squandered its momentum. Immediately after tea, the Proteas were even more culpable for failing to resist what appeared to be a very obvious temptation: an outer ring of catchers scattered around the boundary from fine leg to deep mid-wicket and Starc banging it in short.
David Bedingham, who'd reached 50 without much trouble, was the first to fall for it, hooking recklessly to be cleverly caught on the fine leg rope by Hazlewood. Two balls later, Wiaan Mulder tried an equally daft hook and feathered an edge to Carey behind the stumps.
If South Africa is destined to win this match and with it the series — and unfortunately for Australia, there is an air of destiny about that result at the moment — perhaps the Proteas' 97-run seventh-wicket partnership will be looked back on as a critical period. Ryan Rickelton, out of form with the bat until that point, contributed a patient 42 as all-rounder Marco Jensen battered a typically confident half-century.
The latter fun, which threatened to take the game back away from Australia entirely, ended when Starc took the second new ball. Calling it a clinical demolition of the tail would undersell him: with 4-2 in the space of seven ruthlessly full and straight deliveries, the Australian paceman took his 20th Test five-wicket haul and finished with 6-72 from 16.3 overs.
Once the day's surges of chaos were done with, a comment by Cummins before play seemed worth revisiting. Boland's omission, the Australian captain claimed, was that great cliché of cricket team selection: "a good problem to have".
But is it? Perhaps Cummins was implying something else, that Australia's other selection problems — replacing three of its top-six batters with players assuredly not in the same class as Boland — are bad ones to have. Ones that may shape this game more than what happened on day one.
Which brings us to another of cricket's enduring clichés: don't judge a pitch until both teams have batted on it.
