Exit polls on Tuesday showed that the opposition bloc led by Israeli opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot gained a narrow edge over Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud bloc in the Knesset, setting the stage for weeks of jockeying to form a government. The day's vote was marked by decades-high turnout in the country's first election since the October 7, 2023 attacks. Follow our liveblog for the latest updates.
Eisenkot says Israel has chosen change, hopes to form government
Opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot said early Wednesday said Israel had chosen change after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and that he would seek to form a new government.
In remarks to supporters, Eisenkot also warned Netanyahu: "Don't you dare use Israel's security for your political needs," in a likely reference to his threats of new strikes on Iran.
Eisenkot warns Netanyahu not to 'use Israel's security' for political ends
Israel's elections: What happens next?
Here are four possible scenarios:
1. Coalition
The parties will immediately begin negotiations to try to reach a 61-seat majority in the 120-member Knesset, but the path forward is far from clear.
President Isaac Herzog will name a candidate who has the best chance to form a government -- not necessarily the party with the most seats, which the initial exit polls showed to be Netanyahu's Likud.
The Arab Israeli parties, particularly Raam, have voiced openness to working with Eisenkot's bloc, but the camp has kept them at arm's length, perceiving their support as a liability during the campaign.
For Netanyahu's bloc, however, there is no obvious place to pick up more seats after some smaller right-wing parties failed to meet the vote threshold for entering parliament.
2. Minority government
If no bloc manages to secure 61 seats, a candidate could attempt to govern without a majority but rather through support on an ad hoc basis from other lawmakers.
In this scenario, lawmakers from the Arab Israeli parties -- whose community makes up 20 percent of the population and generally identifies as Palestinian -- could play a critical role.
Raam, led by Mansour Abbas, has been a kingmaker in the past, having been the first Arab party to join an Israeli government in a short-lived 2021-2022 coalition led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid.
Another Arab movement, the Joint List, has said it would be unlikely to join a coalition government outright, but has offered to provide a "safety net" for any one that ousts Netanyahu from power.
3. National unity government
Considering Israel's extreme polarisation, a national unity government would appear fanciful, but it could theoretically create a less extreme government.
Israeli commentators have often mused on the possibility of a national unity government in which Netanyahu would jettison his provocative far-right allies as well as ultra-Orthodox parties and team up with Eisenkot, who shares Netanyahu's views on many security issues.
Such a grand coalition would also exclude Arab parties.
4. Deadlock and new elections
If no candidate manages to form a government, Israel will have to return to the polls.
The country held four elections between April 2019 and March 2021 due to the inability of politicians to forge a lasting coalition.
The candidate designated by the president will, in principle, have 28 days to form a coalition, with a possible 14-day extension, although there are other procedural ways to prevent an immediate calling of new elections.

Iraqi court jails French nationals for belonging to IS

Breadcrumb
Iraqi court jails French nationals for belonging to IS
An Iraqi court on Tuesday jailed seven French nationals for belonging to the Islamic State group, after they were transferred along with dozens of others from Syria last year.
Six of the defendants were handed life sentences, which under Iraqi law are equivalent to 20 years in prison.
They were found guilty of belonging to IS and "of having contributed, together with members of the group, to spreading terror", according to an AFP journalist at the court.
The judge told the defendants the court had "commuted the death sentence to life imprisonment, given that you are young, to offer you a chance...to get your life back on track".
The court sentenced a seventh French national to 15 years in prison. The now 24-year-old had been taken to Syria by his mother, who joined IS more than a decade ago.
All seven were part of a group of 47 French citizens transferred from Syria last year.
The larger group includes Adrien Guihal, who claimed responsibility for the 2016 Nice attack for IS.
"These sentences offer a certain form of relief, especially for the families, because the death penalty was legitimately feared," said Matthieu Bagard, the French lawyer for four of the seven defendants sentenced on Tuesday.
He told AFP, however, that it "did not make a difference to everything we have denounced".
"There are French citizens being judged without a fair trial," he said, mentioning "the torture they suffered and the forced confessions".
Marie Dose, the lawyer for the now 24-year-old, reproached France for accepting "that this fate should be reserved for children who have become adults, who bear no responsibility whatsoever for their parents' choices".
The jihadist group swept across Syria and Iraq in 2014, committing massacres and forcing women and girls into sexual slavery.
Iraq, backed by US-led forces, proclaimed victory over IS in 2017, and the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces ultimately defeated the group in Syria two years later.
Iraq is nonetheless still reckoning with the group's legacy, with mass graves still being uncovered and testimonies of IS brutality yet to be investigated.
For years, its courts have handed down hundreds of execution orders and life sentences to those convicted of terrorism offences, including foreign fighters.

AI generated
PARIS - Paris department store BHV Marais, which courted controversy in 2025 with a partnership with Asian fast-fashion giant Shein, said on Oct 27 it had sought bankruptcy protection to protect its operations and jobs.
The bankruptcy procedure “is part of BHV’s relaunch, not its failure,” the company said, adding that the landmark store opposite Paris City Hall that employs 700 people will remain open.
The store’s previous owner already had problems with brand-name boutiques it hosted over payment delays before it sparked controversy in 2025 by announcing that BHV Marais would host Shein’s first physical permanent store.
The announcement struck a raw nerve in a French public concerned about the disappearance of local jobs amid a flood of Asian imports, and triggered the departure of a number of brands.
The owner finally sold the business to a number of its managers in June, who promptly parted ways with Shein.
The new owners said that as part of that deal the ownership of part of the building was transferred, but they had yet to receive the funds, which adversely impacted their plans to revamp the business.
The owner of the building, the Canadian asset manager Brookfield, rejected that assertion, saying it does not have any outstanding sums due to BHV Marais.
French labour inspectors believe that BHV Marais has not been making payments, which its management has denied. AFP

Ukraine Holds Its Strongest Frontline Position in a Long Time, Zelensky Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:10:53 UTC
05:10:53 KST

President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Tuesday, Oct. 27, that Ukraine’s frontline positions are currently the strongest they have been in a long time, pointing to the country’s three landmark battlefield operations during this year.
In a statement on Telegram, Zelensky placed Operation Veles, an underground operation conducted by the National Guard’s Khartiia Corps near Kupiansk, as the third of those operations. The first two were offensives led by the Air Assault Forces (DSHV) and the 3rd Army Corps.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“It is important to note that this year, Ukraine’s positions on the frontline remain the strongest they have been in a long time during this war,” Zelensky said, noting that Ukraine would be in a much better diplomatic position if partner support was equally strong, particularly in the field of air-defense systems.
Air assault gains and Operation Vivaldi
According to Zelensky, the offensive led by DSHV has liberated more than 800 square kilometers (309 square miles). The campaign ran through Jan. 29 through Aug. 12, liberating 26 settlements spanning across three regions – Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, and Zaporizhzhia.
The second, Operation Vivaldi, was carried out by the 3rd Army Corps near Lyman in Donetsk region from July until mid-October. According to Zelensky, Ukraine’s Defense Forces liberated more than 200 kilometers (124 miles) there, in an area where Russia had concentrated its assaults.
POW Dispute: South Korea Pulls 8 Diplomats From Ukraine
When the operation ended on Oct. 14, 3rd Corps commander Brig. Gen. Andriy Biletsky said his forces had retaken 277 square kilometers (107 square miles) and more than 16 towns and villages, while inflicting at least 8,000 casualties on Russian troops.
The offensive, he said, pushed Russian forces back from the Slovyansk-Kramatorsk highway, a key supply route for both cities.
Turning a Russian tactic against Moscow
In a separate statement earlier on Tuesday, Zelensky said he had been briefed on the operation’s results by Commander-in-Chief Mykhailo Drapaty, Deputy Head of the Presidential Office Pavlo Palisa and Brig. Gen. Ihor Oboliensky, the Khartiia Corps commander.
According to the report, Russian forces had previously tried to use underground gas pipelines to slip past Ukrainian positions and launch assaults. Ukraine’s Defense Forces then adopted the method and refined it, making it “far more thought-out and technologically advanced,” Zelensky said.
Repeating figures Khartiia’s Corps first released on Oct. 22, Zelensky confirmed that more than 30 Russian soldiers have been captured, while Russian losses exceeded 100.
At the time, it was reported that more than 30 Russian prisoners were captured, with the maneuver described as the world’s first full-scale underground counteroffensive.
Without any GPS or daylight, Ukrainian troops pushed through more than 15 kilometers (9 miles) of underground infrastructure before emerging behind Russian positions overhead.

Israel election exit polls: Opposition edges Netanyahu, Likud largest as Arab parties surge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:08:41 UTC
05:08:41 KST

The Central Elections Committee announced that official election results have begun to be released. So far, results from 15 polling stations have been received, representing 2,679 voters."Throughout the night, the official results will be updated regularly on the Central Elections Committee's website and interactive results map as vote counting, data processing and verification progress," the committee said.
"The figures at this stage are partial and may change as counting and verification continue."
Israel's first election exit polls pointed to a narrow lead for the bloc seeking to replace Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, but neither side is projected to win the 61 seats needed for a parliamentary majority. While Netanyahu's Likud emerges as the country's largest party, Arab parties are projected to make substantial gains, potentially complicating efforts to form the next government.
According to Channel 12's exit poll, the bloc seeking political change wins 52 seats, compared with 50 for Netanyahu's bloc. The two Arab parties secure a combined 18 seats, leaving neither main bloc with an outright majority in the 120-seat Knesset.
Channel 13 projects a slightly larger advantage for the change bloc, giving it 53 seats against 50 for Netanyahu's allies. The Arab parties receive 17 seats in that projection.
The results represent a significant shift from the final pre-election opinion polls, which had consistently placed Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar! party ahead of Likud. Both exit polls instead put Netanyahu's party in first place, although the broader political balance remains narrowly tilted toward his opponents.
The projections are based on surveys of voters and do not constitute official results. The allocation of seats could change as ballots are counted, particularly for parties close to the electoral threshold.
Channel 12: Likud leads with 24 seats, Yashar! follows with 22
Channel 12's exit poll projects Likud as the largest party in the 26th Knesset with 24 seats, followed closely by Eisenkot's Yashar! with 22.
Naftali Bennett's Beyahad party is projected to win 12 seats, while the Joint List, an alliance of Arab political parties, reaches 11.
The Democrats, led by Yair Golan, and Avigdor Lieberman's Yisrael Beiteinu each receive nine seats. The Islamist Ra'am party and the ultra-Orthodox United Torah Judaism party are projected to win seven seats apiece.
Shas and the Religious Zionism-Zehut alliance each receive six seats.
Together, the four main parties seeking to replace Netanyahu hold 52 seats, compared with 50 for the prime minister's political allies. The Joint List and Ra'am account for the remaining 18 seats.
Channel 13: Opposition bloc grows to 53 seats
Channel 13's exit poll presents a similar picture, although several parties receive different projections.
Likud leads with 25 seats, followed by Yashar! with 23. Bennett's Beyahad party wins 14, while the Joint List receives 10 and the Democrats nine.
Yisrael Beiteinu is projected to win seven seats, alongside Ra'am and United Torah Judaism, which also receive seven each. Shas and Religious Zionism-Zehut are allocated six seats apiece.
The overall distribution leaves the change bloc with 53 seats, Netanyahu's bloc with 50 and the Arab parties with 17.
Despite the differences between the two surveys, both point to the same central political challenge: neither main bloc has enough parliamentary seats to form a government independently.
Arab parties emerge with 17 to 18 seats
One of the most striking developments in the exit polls is the increased representation projected for Israel's Arab parties.
Channel 12 gives the Joint List 11 seats and Ra'am seven, for a combined total of 18. Channel 13 projects 10 seats for the Joint List and seven for Ra'am, bringing their combined representation to 17.
That marks an increase from the final pre-election surveys, which projected 14 seats for the Arab parties on Channel 12 and 16 on Channel 13.
The gains could have significant implications for the parliamentary balance. With the two main political blocs separated by just two or three seats, the Arab parties' positions may become an important factor in the political negotiations that follow.
However, neither exit poll indicates an outright majority for the bloc seeking to replace Netanyahu, even as it holds a narrow advantage over his allies.
Three parties fail to cross the electoral threshold
Both exit polls also project that several smaller parties will fail to enter the Knesset.
Ofer Winter's Amcha Yisrael party remains below the 3.25% electoral threshold, as does the Reservists-Economic Party led by former minister Yoaz Hendel and economist Yaron Zelekha.
The Haredi Public party, which has attempted to attract ultra-Orthodox voters dissatisfied with the established religious parties, is also projected to fall short.
Under Israel's electoral system, parties that fail to secure at least 3.25% of valid votes receive no parliamentary seats. Their votes are excluded from the allocation of seats among qualifying parties, potentially affecting the balance between competing political blocs.
With record voter turnout, the absolute number of votes required to cross the threshold is higher than in previous elections. Final results could therefore change if parties finish particularly close to that mark.
Record turnout, but the final result could take days
The exit polls follow a day of historic voter participation. According to the Central Elections Committee, turnout had reached 74.3% by 8 p.m., the highest rate recorded at that hour since 1988.
A total of 5,449,277 Israelis had voted by that point, out of 7,331,981 eligible voters. At the same hour in the November 2022 election, turnout stood at 66.3%.
The final distribution of seats may remain uncertain for several days because of the large number of special double-envelope ballots, including votes cast by soldiers, diplomats, hospital patients and voters away from their registered polling stations.
More than 650,000 such ballots are expected to require separate verification and counting. Central Elections Committee officials have warned that the process could continue until Friday morning.
For parties hovering around the electoral threshold, those votes could be decisive, potentially changing not only their parliamentary representation but also the overall balance between political blocs.
Even once the final results become available, Israel's next government will not necessarily be determined. President Isaac Herzog must consult the elected parliamentary factions before assigning a lawmaker the task of forming a coalition.
With both exit polls showing a divided Knesset and no immediate majority for either main bloc, the central political question remains unresolved: which combination of parties, if any, can secure enough parliamentary support to form Israel's next government?

SAN JOSE, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Costa Rica has locked up the first 123 inmates in a new mega-prison, built with the help of the Salvadoran government in the outskirts of capital San José, the country’s justice ministry said on Tuesday.
The ministry shared images showing rows of inmates dressed in orange, seated with shaved heads bowed and their hands behind their necks, in poses resembling photographs from El Salvador’s Terrorism Confinement Center (CECOT), the mega-prison where President Nayib Bukele’s government holds tens of thousands of gang members and suspected gang affiliates.
Costa Rica’s maximum security prison, which it calls the High Containment Center against Organized Crime (CACCO), has been presented by the government of President Laura Fernandez as a symbol of a new “tough on crime” approach championed by her administration in response to a security crisis facing Costa Rica, once one of the most peaceful countries in the Western Hemisphere.
“Costa Rica is writing a new chapter in its penitentiary history,” Justice Minister Gabriel Aguilar said in a statement. “CACCO is a monument to national security, a forceful response to organized crime, and a guarantee that the state will exercise its authority without hesitation.” Aguilar has said the new facility will also help reduce overcrowding in the prison system.
The prison has a capacity for 5,100 inmates, equivalent to 20% of the country’s prison population.
Costa Rica, long regarded as one of the safest countries in Latin America, has in recent years experienced a sharp rise in violence linked to drug trafficking and organized crime. The country recorded a record number of homicides in 2023, although figures have since stabilized. Authorities attribute most killings to disputes between criminal groups over drug trafficking routes and markets.

EU burying its own economy – Putin (VIDEO)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:06:01 UTC
05:06:01 KST

EU burying its own economy – Putin (VIDEO)
The EU is burying its own economy by rejecting Russian energy supplies, Russian President Vladimir Putin has said.
European nations have faced soaring energy costs since imposing sweeping sanctions on Russia and its hydrocarbon exports following the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022. Brussels has pledged to eliminate Russian gas imports entirely by 2027, despite opposition from several member states.
Speaking at the eighth Gas Exporting Countries Forum summit in Moscow on Tuesday, Putin warned that efforts to push Russia out of the global gas market were hurting European industries and households.
“[Europe] is dealing a blow to its own industry and social sector by abandoning Russian energy supplies and tearing up long-term contracts,” he said.
There is a saying in Russia: ‘Don’t dig a pit for someone else, or you might end up there yourself.’ In my view, that is precisely what has happened today in the countries of the European Union.
Putin also accused European nations of hypocrisy over their approach to fossil fuels, arguing that they had built their own prosperity on resources they now discourage developing countries from using.
“The economy of modern Europe was built precisely on coal and hydrocarbons,” he said.
Yet those same countries reopened coal-fired power plants “when they found it more difficult to address their own energy challenges,” Putin added.
European gas prices surged to their highest level since December 2022 on Monday, briefly exceeding €97 ($108) per megawatt-hour as supply disruptions linked to the Iran war and forecasts of colder weather rattled markets, according to Trading Economics.
Germany, Europe’s largest industrial economy, has been particularly hard hit by the loss of Russian gas. The country suffered two consecutive years of economic contraction in 2023 and 2024, while its energy-intensive industries, particularly chemicals and metals, have struggled with higher production costs.
German industry is shedding around 15,000 jobs a month, Tanja Goenner, head of the Federation of German Industries, warned in July, citing structural weaknesses, US tariffs and mounting competition from China.
Economic pressures have also fueled public anger across Europe. Rising living costs, stagnant wages and government policies have triggered protests in France, Belgium, Italy and other countries this month, with demonstrators demanding relief for struggling households.

Germany’s Helsing promises jet-drone-hunting missiles at under $100,000 a shot—its CEO doesn’t expect them on the market before 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:04:58 UTC
05:04:58 KST

German defense AI firm Helsing has unveiled Contra, an AI-run air defense system and two interceptor missiles designed to chase Russia’s jet-powered Geran drones, the company announced on 26 October. Officials pitch it as cheap, but it won’t reach the market this winter.
That leaves Ukraine on its own defenses as Russia shifts to jet drones. By early October, jet models made up about 40% of Russian drone launches, and Ukraine’s own interceptors for them won’t arrive in needed numbers before late November, Air Force Deputy Commander Yurii Cherevashenko said.
Two missiles, one AI brain
Contra is the command layer of air defense: it links radars and other sensors, tracks incoming drones and missiles, and assigns a weapon to each target, while people keep control over decisions, Helsing said. Besides the company’s own missiles, it can also use other firms’ interceptors, lasers, guns, or nets. AD-1 Inferno is jet-powered and designed to loiter, swarm, and re-engage targets, while AD-2 Ambush, a solid-fuel rocket, is designed to reach Mach 2.5, over twice the speed of sound, and a range of more than 20 km, the company said.
Inferno, with a 700 km/h speed and a 20-km range, would be the everyday shooter. Ambush would handle “leakers,” drones about to hit the ground, said Maxwell Adams, Helsing’s senior product director. Each shot should cost under $100,000, company officials said.
Built for the faster Gerans
Ukraine once downed 90% of Russia’s slower, propeller-driven Gerans, copies of Iran’s Shahed, Defense News reported. Russia has since fielded thousands of jet Geran-4s and Geran-5s flying at 400–700 km/h, and almost half now get through, Helsing co-founder and co-CEO Gundbert Scherf said.
Ukraine’s own nightly rates swing widely. On 28 September, President Zelenskyy put the shoot-down rate for jet drones at 57%. Overnight on 7 October, it exceeded 82%, National Security and Defense Council Secretary Ihor Klymenko said. Russian output of the two models has reached 4,000 a month, Helsing said, citing unspecified intelligence reports.
Helsing has signed one Contra contract, Scherf said, but the system is still in testing, and he expects it on the market in the second half of 2027. Ukraine already uses Helsing’s HX-2 strike drones. Scherf said they should be integrated into a system like Contra.

MOSCOW, October 27. /TASS/. Russian President Vladimir Putin is holding talks with visiting President of Equatorial Guinea Teodoro Obiang Nguema Mbasogo, a TASS correspondent reported.

Diplomatic relations between the former Soviet Union and Equatorial Guinea were established on December 7, 1968. From the 1990s through the 2010s, bilateral dialogue was maintained at the level of the foreign ministries. In June 2011, President Teodoro Obiang Nguema Mbasogo, who has been leading the country since 1979, visited Russia for the first time. In July 2013, he participated in the Gas Exporting Countries Forum summit in Moscow, and in October 2019, he attended the Russia-Africa Summit in Sochi. On both occasions, he met with Putin. In November 2023, he paid an official visit to Russia.
According to Russia’s Federal Customs Service, trade between Russia and Equatorial Guinea was $1.7 million in 2021 (further updates are unavailable). Meat and meat products accounted for 86% of Russia’s exports, which also included cardboard, paper, and timber. Timber and charcoal accounted for 100% of imports.
Currently, Russia and Equatorial Guinea are discussing Russian companies’ potential participating in the Central African gas transmission system project. This refers to an agreement reached in September 2022 by seven oil-and gas-producing countries, namely Angola, Gabon, Cameroon, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the Republic of the Congo, Chad, and Equatorial Guinea, to build a network of major oil and gas pipelines, oil refineries, and power plants to reduce dependence on the refining capacities of developed countries.

Rates, not tax changes, the main driver of house price fall: Treasury
Liberal Andrew Bragg is probing whether Treasury stands by its view that the budget's capital gains tax and negative gearing changes would have a modest effect on house prices.
Yes, says Jenny Wilkinson. She says the "most significant" factor behind falling house prices at the moment is the four rate hikes delivered by the RBA this year. The fall, she says, is broadly what you would expect from that many hikes.
The budget changes have "some effect", but she calls them "structural" rather than "cyclical". Decoded, that means she thinks the tax changes will change long-term patterns but are not so influential in the short-term.
And she sees some signs that the long-term changes are what the government wants to see: in the aftermath of the budget, she says, there has been a 13 per cent drop-off in loans for property investors buying existing homes. But property investors are still investing in new homes, and first homebuyer loans are tracking better.

That scheme, which was partially paused in July 2024, when concerns it may have been operating unlawfully first arose, has now restarted, with advocates warning the problems have not been fixed.

The changing face of youth extremism
What drives a 12-year-old child from a loving, stable home to absorb violent online propaganda? That is a core challenge facing the Australian Federal Police amid new data tabled to Senate estimates.
The AFP analysed the histories of 55 radicalised youths and found online extremism is impacting children who show no history of family trauma or obvious vulnerability.
Every subject studied was male, aged between 12 and 17, and radicalised at least in part online. But while violent jihadism and white supremacy dominate, AFP Commissioner Krissy Barrett warns that investigators are seeing a messy shift toward "mixed/hybrid ideologies, unclear/incoherent ideologies … and ideological fluidity."
While some of the radicalised youths faced trauma or lacked stability, Barrett notes that others came from completely secure family environments.
The AFP's deep dive into youth radicalisation did highlight a few common threads: 13 per cent were suspended in primary school, over one-third were kicked out of high school, and three in five had received mental health treatment.
With no single profile or predictable pathway, the AFP hopes this data will help police, educators and parents spot early warning signs, long before an online rabbit hole turns into real-world violence.

It's full steam ahead for AUKUS following the arrival of a US nuclear-powered attack submarine — USS Colorado — at HMAS Stirling yesterday for scheduled maintenance.
The visit serves as a trial run of sorts for the Submarine Rotational Force–West (SRF-West) plan.
What is that? Well, starting in late 2027, SRF-West will establish a permanent presence of up to five US and UK nuclear subs in Western Australia.

This week's maintenance work is basically an opportunity for Australian and allied technicians to show they're up to the task of servicing these high-tech submarines. Israel election 2026: What happens after polls close and when will we know who won?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:01:40 UTC
05:01:40 KST

At 10 p.m. Tuesday, most polling stations across Israel will close and the country's three main television networks will release their exit polls, offering the first indication of the outcome of the election for the 26th Knesset. But the end of voting will mark only the beginning of a process that could take days to produce definitive results and weeks or even months to determine who will form the next government.
With voter turnout reaching historic levels, hundreds of thousands of special ballots still awaiting separate counting and several smaller parties potentially hovering around the electoral threshold, the results projected on election night may look considerably different from the final distribution of parliamentary seats.
Beyond the count, Israel faces another series of deadlines: the publication of official results, the swearing-in of the new Knesset and the president's decision on which lawmaker will be given the opportunity to assemble a governing coalition.
What happens when polling stations close at 10 p.m.?
At 10 p.m., Israeli television networks Kan 11, Channel 12 and Channel 13 are expected to publish their exit polls, providing the first estimates of how the Knesset's 120 seats will be distributed among the competing parties.
The exit polls are based on surveys of voters and are not official results. While they may indicate which political bloc is ahead, they cannot determine with certainty which parties will enter parliament or who will ultimately become prime minister.
One of the most significant uncertainties concerns parties close to the 3.25% electoral threshold. Parties that fail to reach that percentage of valid votes receive no seats, meaning even a small change in the final count could significantly alter the balance between rival political blocs.
The official counting process will begin as polling stations close, with results gradually transmitted to the Central Elections Committee. The first counted votes are expected to become available during the night, providing a clearer picture as the hours pass.
Although the scheduled closing time is 10 p.m., voters who arrive at a polling station before the deadline will still be allowed to cast their ballots, even if they remain in line afterward.
When will the final election results be known?
The counting process could continue well beyond election night, primarily because of the large number of special double-envelope ballots.
More than 650,000 such ballots are expected from soldiers, diplomats, displaced residents, hospital patients, voters with disabilities and others who cast their votes outside their registered polling stations.
Unlike ordinary ballots, double-envelope votes require an additional verification process to ensure that each voter has cast only one ballot. The identifying outer envelope is checked before the anonymous vote is added to the count.
Central Elections Committee officials had initially hoped to complete the count by Thursday, October 29, but acting Director-General Dean Livne warned that the number of special ballots could be higher than anticipated, potentially delaying the process until Friday morning.
The committee is expected to publish a clearer picture of the election results by Thursday, although the final tally may take longer. Under Israeli law, the official results must be published by November 4.
The distinction is important: even if television exit polls show one political bloc holding a parliamentary majority, the actual allocation of seats could change as the special ballots are counted and parties near the electoral threshold learn whether they have secured representation.
Historic turnout: 74.3% by 8 p.m.
The election has already been marked by unusually high voter participation, with turnout reaching 74.3% by 8 p.m., the highest rate recorded at that hour since 1988.
According to the Central Elections Committee, 5,449,277 Israelis had voted out of 7,331,981 eligible voters, compared with 66.3% at the same hour in the November 2022 election. The increase amounts to eight percentage points, or approximately 12% in relative terms.
The latest figure also surpassed the previous election's final turnout rate of approximately 70.6%, with two hours still remaining before most polling stations were scheduled to close.
Earlier in the day, turnout stood at 66.7% by 6 p.m., compared with 57.7% in 2022. By 4 p.m., it had reached 55.7%, compared with 47.5% four years earlier.
Participation was also particularly high among military personnel. According to the IDF, 68% of eligible service members had voted by 5 p.m., compared with 65% at the same hour during the previous election.
The surge brought long lines to polling stations in several cities, while severe weather and flash floods in southern Israel complicated voting in some communities, particularly in the Arava region, where road closures prevented some residents from reaching their designated polling stations.
Election committee rejects request to extend voting hours
The combination of exceptionally high turnout, lengthy waits and severe weather prompted a political dispute over whether voting should continue beyond 10 p.m.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party submitted a request to extend voting hours. The proposal received support from Shas, led by Aryeh Deri, Otzma Yehudit, led by Itamar Ben-Gvir, and Ofer Winter's Amcha Yisrael party.
Opposition parties, including Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar!, Naftali Bennett's Beyahad and Yair Golan's Democrats, opposed extending voting hours.
Following a discussion, Central Elections Committee Chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg, deputy president of the Supreme Court, decided not to approve the request, leaving the scheduled closing time unchanged.
The committee nevertheless emphasized that voters arriving before 10 p.m. would be allowed to vote even if they remained in line after the deadline.
Violence and confrontations throughout Election Day
Tuesday's voting was also accompanied by several reported incidents of violence, intimidation and confrontations between political activists.
Israeli singer Ofer Levi was questioned by police on suspicion of incitement to violence after a video circulated online allegedly featuring calls to execute left-wing voters. Levi denied making the statements, claimed the video had been manipulated using artificial intelligence and warned that anyone distributing it could face legal action. He was released under restrictive conditions following questioning.
In Rahat, a Bedouin city in southern Israel, a brawl broke out near a polling station following arguments between voters.
In the ultra-Orthodox city of Modi'in Illit, youths burned pictures of Moti Leitner, chairman of the Haredi Public party. Campaign booths belonging to the party were also vandalized in Beitar Illit and Bnei Brak, while activists were reportedly called "traitors."
In Haifa's Bat Galim neighborhood, a confrontation erupted between city council member Yaniv Ben Shoshan, who heads the Likud faction on the council, and activists at a Democrats party campaign booth. The activists alleged that pushing had occurred.
In Bat Yam, Deputy Mayor Kati Piasecki of the Democrats and five other party activists were reportedly assaulted near a school.
Earlier in Tel Aviv, police arrested a man carrying a knife who approached Democrats leader Yair Golan during a tour of the city. Golan's party alleged that the incident was an attempted attack, while police confirmed the arrest but did not characterize it as an attempted stabbing.
The incidents underscored tensions surrounding the election, even as millions of Israelis continued to cast their ballots.
November 10: The new Knesset will be sworn in
Once the official results are published, attention will shift to the composition of the new parliament and the process of forming a government.
The 26th Knesset is scheduled to be sworn in on Tuesday, November 10, exactly two weeks after Election Day. Its 120 elected members will formally take office, even if negotiations over the next government have not been completed.
Unlike in presidential elections, Israelis do not vote directly for a prime minister. They vote for party lists, with parliamentary seats distributed according to each party's share of the valid vote, provided it crosses the electoral threshold.
A party's position as the largest faction in parliament does not automatically entitle its leader to become prime minister. Instead, the president must determine which member of the Knesset has the best prospect of assembling a governing coalition.
To do so, President Isaac Herzog will consult representatives of the parties elected to parliament, with each faction recommending a candidate to form the next government. The candidate selected by Herzog will then be tasked with securing sufficient parliamentary support.
How long does a candidate have to form a government?
The first candidate chosen by the president will have 28 days to form a government. Herzog may extend that period by up to an additional 14 days, allowing a maximum of 42 days for the initial attempt.
If the candidate fails, the president may assign the task to another member of the Knesset. That second candidate would receive 28 days, without the possibility of an extension.
If the president concludes there is no viable candidate, or a second attempt fails, a further 21-day period allows at least 61 members of the Knesset to submit a written request asking the president to assign the task to a particular lawmaker.
Should such a request receive the necessary support, the designated candidate would have 14 days to form a government.
The president's role is therefore central to the post-election process, particularly if the parliamentary balance is divided and no political bloc can immediately secure the support needed to govern.
And if nobody succeeds?
If every attempt to form a government fails, the Knesset would be dissolved and Israel would return to the polls for another election, to be held within 90 days.
Until a new government is sworn in, the outgoing government remains in office in a caretaker capacity.
That means the first exit polls at 10 p.m. may offer only the opening chapter of a political process whose conclusion could remain uncertain for weeks. Even after the official votes are counted and the new Knesset convenes, the question of who will lead Israel may still depend on negotiations between political parties and their ability to assemble a governing majority.

Export hurdles and visa waits for Ukrainian companies force Pentagon to slow its drone contest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:01:15 UTC
05:01:15 KST

Export hurdles and visa waits for Ukrainian companies force Pentagon to slow its drone contest
A soldier holds a remote controller near a GARA unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) at an unnamed location in Donetsk Oblast, Ukraine, on Oct. 16, 2026. (Dmytro Smolienko/Ukrinform/Future Publishing via Getty Images)
One morning in June, the head of export at Ukrainian drone company Stellarion found himself unexpectedly in need of a U-Haul outside the Detroit Metro Airport in Michigan.
Stellarion was set to test its drones in front of American soldiers at a competition organized by the Pentagon at Camp Grayling, a military base three hours away. But while many of its 48 invited competitors were American companies that had had weeks to modify, prepare, and fit warheads onto their drones, Stellarion was facing a last-minute scramble.
The company's drones had landed that very morning, slowed by Ukrainian export controls and lengthy shipping times, Stellarion's head of exports, who requested anonymity for security reasons, told the Kyiv Independent.
Stellarion performed strongly enough to advance in the competition, but the Ukrainian company's ordeal reflects a broader problem.
Interviews with Ukrainian manufacturers competing in the Pentagon's Drone Dominance Program (DDP), a contest to procure drones for U.S. defense, revealed the companies’ struggles with export controls, shipping times, and visa approvals, sometimes resulting in late product arrivals and rapid turnarounds before competition.
The obstacles to Ukrainian companies are serious enough that, in early October, the Pentagon announced it was pushing back the next phase of the competition, Phase 2.5, which focuses on bomber drones, to November. About half of the 17 companies invited to participate are Ukrainian, a sign of how much the U.S. procurement strategy now depends on drones made in Ukraine.
read also
It is the first time the program has been so visibly forced to accommodate its rules and timeline to meet the needs of Ukrainian companies.
In a statement to the Kyiv Independent, the Pentagon said that "Ukrainian companies have the most battlefield-tested Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems products in the world, and have scaled. We have a responsibility to give American soldiers and Marines the benefit of the best materiel."
The DDP, initiated by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in a July 2025 memorandum, is the U.S.’ flagship effort to procure drones at a time when Russia and Ukraine each plan to produce 7 million in 2026 for their respective war efforts. The program is funded to the tune of $1.1 billion and initially aimed to procure 340,000 drones, according to the Request for Solutions released in December 2025.
The Pentagon has prized speed, stating in February in a press release: "We are buying what works — fast, at scale, and without bureaucratic delay."
In the spring, Phase I tested classic one-way attack first-person view (FPV) drones. Over the summer, Phase II tested long-range strike drones and those that operate in close quarters. Other than the U.S. itself, no country sent more competitors to those initial phases than Ukraine. Other competing countries included Israel. Croatia, the U.K., among others.
In July, the Pentagon announced the names of the 17 companies that would be invited to compete in Phase 2.5, spending $30 million to acquire up to 1,200 bombers, according to the Request for Solutions released in July.
Unmanned bombers, which can carry heavier payloads, have played a crucial role in Russia's war against Ukraine. These drones have increasingly been used for logistical, resupply, and rescue missions, with one drone airlifting a 42-kg E-bike to a wounded soldier in July of 2025.
Eight or nine of the companies invited to Phase 2.5, according to the Inside Unmanned Systems blog, have Ukrainian origins: UFORCE, Gurzuf Defence, Skycutter-Skyfall, Meta Bureau, Grim Tech, and F-Drones are publicly Ukraine-based. Two other companies, listed as Achiever UA and UA Defense Tech, have no public presence, nor does the Areya corporation. Ukrainian companies need a registered legal entity in the U.S. to enter the competition.
read also
Ukrainian companies have long struggled with the DDP’s tight turnarounds. In late July, the DDP put out a "Request for Solutions," or an invitation for companies to pitch the Pentagon on participating in Phase 2.5. Responses were due by Aug. 10. Invitees were announced publicly on Sept. 21, and given until mid-October to ship six ready-to-test bomber drones — which can cost up to $20,000 per unit to produce — to Camp Grayling.
But the export obstacles that Shtylyk faced in June are still present.
Ukraine has worked to streamline its export approvals, aiming in July to shorten the approval process to 30 days, but it can still take weeks to approve drone exports. Phase II of the DDP required a special deal to get Ukrainian drones out fast.
But shipping the drones to the U.S. can add another two or three weeks, leaving Ukrainian companies with practically no time to make needed modifications or prepare in an on-base testing environment.
A number of Ukrainian companies therefore considered or decided to withdraw from the competition. One is Skycutter-Skyfall, a partnership between a British defense tech startup that works closely with SkyFall, which produces drone hardware in Ukraine.
Skycutter-Skyfall placed first in Phase I of the DDP in March, earning an order of 2,560 of its one-way-attack FPV drones, according to the DDP’s online leaderboard. Yet, Skycutter was the last of 11 companies to deliver its drone contract, the leaderboard shows.
Gurzuf Defence told the Kyiv Independent that it had notified the Pentagon of its withdrawal from Phase 2.5, while another Ukrainian company told the Kyiv Independent, on condition of anonymity, that it considered pulling out of the competition before ultimately deciding to attend.
As of Oct. 13, at least four companies — a quarter of all those invited — declined to audition their drones at Camp Grayling, according to the DDP website. Two of the four were Ukrainian companies.
Now, the Pentagon is postponing Phase 2.5 to November "to best position all participants for success," according to the Drone Dominance website. The Pentagon reached out to companies that had withdrawn to ask them back to the competition. Gurzuf, for its part, still declined, telling the Kyiv Independent it would take them until December to be fully ready.
The Pentagon told the Kyiv Independent that Ukrainian export controls and shipping times were not "in themselves a factor" in the decision to postpone Phase 2.5. Instead, they emphasized that the decision "included a recognition of the time-consuming U.S. visa processes."
The U.S. Embassy in Kyiv does not process traditional business visa applications, meaning Ukrainian applicants need to travel elsewhere to complete the process, which can take weeks or months, depending on the location.
The Pentagon maintains that it holds Ukrainian companies to the same standards as all competitors. In the first two phases of the program, run between February and August, multiple Ukrainian companies, on condition of anonymity, said the Defense Department’s attitude to supply chain challenges could be boiled down to: "These are the rules. You knew them in advance."
The Pentagon’s decision to postpone signals a shift in approach, suggesting the DDP cares more about encouraging Ukrainian participation than preserving its initial, rapid timelines.
The DDP is the largest drone procurement initiative in the world outside Russia and Ukraine. It is a central part of the U.S. defense modernization effort.
A Grim Tech representative, who spoke on condition of anonymity, told the Kyiv Independent: "If you want to access the American market, you need to be there." In its request for Fiscal Year 2027, the Pentagon has asked for $54 billion for drone warfare and procurement. Companies that succeed now stand to benefit from large future American contracts.
Ukrainian companies also know domestic wartime demand will not last forever. Some have begun to modify their products and form new partnerships to make themselves attractive to foreign governments, the Pentagon most of all.
In March, Ukrainian drone producer General Cherry announced a partnership with American military producer Wilcox Industries to produce hardware in New Hampshire. F-Drones, another Ukrainian company, announced in June a major production project in Ohio. Both General Cherry and F-Drones advanced in earlier phases of the DDP.
But these partnerships don't come cheap. As Grim Tech’s representative put it, "We are finding reliable partners in the U.S., but we're still thinking about what we can do. Because it's a high cost. It's a big investment to set up."
Stellarion’s head of exports put it similarly: "Companies that already have some strong representation in the U.S., some U.S. partners, are in a much better position."
"We had to navigate challenges on our own."

Tanzania’s jailed opposition leader Tundu Lissu ends brief hunger strike
Lissu, who faces treason charge carrying a possible death sentence, refused food after being denied access to lawyers.

Lissu, who leads the opposition’s Party for Democracy and Progress (CHADEMA) and came second in the 2020 presidential election, began refusing food on Monday after his lawyers were denied entry to the prison where he is being held, party spokesperson Brenda Rupia wrote on X.

‘Treason’
Accounts of Lissu’s protest have differed. While CHADEMA spokesperson Rupia said on X that Lissu began refusing food on Monday, Nshala told AP that the strike began on Tuesday morning, after promised private consultations failed to take place.

Could tomato paste help your brain? A three-month trial points to modest gains in attention and memory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:00:07 UTC
05:00:07 KST

Eating concentrated tomato paste every day for three months was linked to better performance on tests of selective attention and face-name memory in healthy middle-aged adults, according to a clinical trial published in Antioxidants. A small brain-imaging subgroup also showed changes in how certain brain networks communicate, and levels of a protein involved in brain cell growth showed a borderline increase. The findings suggest that a single, common food may help support cognitive performance during midlife.
Dietary patterns rich in plant-based antioxidants, such as the Mediterranean diet, are often linked to healthier brain aging and a lower risk of cognitive decline. A primary component of the Mediterranean diet is the tomato, which serves as the main dietary source of a natural pigment called lycopene. Lycopene belongs to a family of fat-soluble plant compounds known as carotenoids, which give red, orange, and yellow fruits and vegetables their bright colors.
Among all dietary carotenoids, lycopene is especially effective at neutralizing unstable oxygen molecules in the body. It is able to cross the blood-brain barrier, a protective layer of tightly packed cells that prevents harmful substances in the bloodstream from entering the brain. Once inside the brain, lycopene is thought to help reduce brain inflammation and oxidative stress, which is cellular damage caused by a buildup of reactive molecules.
Animal and laboratory experiments have helped clarify how this compound protects neural tissue. For example, a 2018 study in mice found that lycopene supplementation prevented inflammation-induced memory loss and reduced the buildup of harmful amyloid proteins linked to Alzheimer’s disease. Lycopene is also thought to support neuroplasticity, the brain’s ability to adapt and form new connections, by regulating brain-derived neurotrophic factor. Often referred to by the acronym BDNF, this protein acts like a growth factor for the nervous system, helping existing neurons survive and encouraging the growth of new ones.
In human populations, several observational studies have connected higher blood levels of carotenoids to better mental performance. In a 2019 neuroimaging study of older adults, higher blood concentrations of lycopene and other nutrients were linked to better memory and more efficient communication across brain networks. Similarly, a 2019 clinical trial in young adults indicated that taking daily supplements of lutein and zeaxanthin, two carotenoids other than lycopene, for six months boosted circulating BDNF levels and improved cognitive scores.
Despite these encouraging connections, direct clinical trials testing the cognitive impact of tomatoes in humans have been rare. Past trials typically combined tomato extracts or lycopene with several other vitamins, herbs, or berries, and they focused mostly on older adults. Because these studies mixed multiple ingredients together, scientists could not tell whether the cognitive benefits came from the tomatoes or from the other substances.
To isolate the effects of tomatoes alone, Ricardo López-Solís, Marina Corrado, Rosa M. Lamuela-Raventós, and their colleagues at the University of Barcelona designed a randomized clinical trial focusing on healthy middle-aged adults. By studying people between the ages of 40 and 55, the researchers aimed to see whether eating tomato paste could support brain health before age-related cognitive decline typically becomes noticeable. They used a crossover design, meaning that every participant completed both the tomato diet and the control diet at different times, allowing each person to serve as their own comparison.
The researchers recruited 47 healthy, non-smoking adults from the Barcelona area who had no history of chronic diseases or cognitive impairment, and 42 participants completed the full study. The participants had an average age of about 47, and two-thirds of the sample were women. Nearly 93 percent of the participants had completed higher or postgraduate education.
Each participant completed two three-month dietary phases separated by a one-month break, known as a washout period, during which they mostly returned to their normal eating habits before avoiding lycopene-rich foods in the final week. During the tomato phase, participants ate concentrated commercial tomato paste containing only tomatoes and salt every day alongside their regular meals, either raw or cooked. The daily dose was tailored to each person’s body weight at 0.5 grams of paste per kilogram of weight, which worked out to an average of about 35 grams of paste (roughly two tablespoons) containing 38.4 milligrams of lycopene per day.
During the three-month control phase, participants followed a low-lycopene diet that restricted tomatoes, watermelon, papaya, pink grapefruit, guava, and any food products made from those ingredients. To help participants keep the rest of their diet consistent, the researchers provided a recipe booklet offering paired meal options, such as dishes made with tomato paste for the active phase and similar tomato-free dishes for the control phase. Throughout the trial, the researchers monitored participants’ broader diet, sleep, body composition, and physical activity using food questionnaires and wrist-worn activity trackers.
At the beginning and end of each three-month period, participants provided fasting blood samples to measure their blood levels of lycopene and BDNF. They also completed three standardized cognitive tests measuring different mental abilities. One paper-and-pencil test evaluated selective attention and visual processing speed by asking participants to scan rows of letters under time pressure and mark only specific target letters with two dashes.
A second test measured associative memory, the ability to learn and remember the relationship between unrelated items, by showing participants 12 pairs of faces and names and testing their recall 15 minutes later. A third test used a card-sorting game to measure executive function, which includes mental flexibility and the ability to adapt when rules change unexpectedly. In addition, a smaller subgroup of 14 participants underwent resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging, a type of brain scan that measures how different regions of the brain communicate while a person is lying still and not performing a specific task.
Blood tests indicated that lycopene levels responded to the diets as intended on average, while participants’ overall calorie intake, sleep, and exercise habits remained unchanged. Based on a blood-lycopene cutoff, however, the researchers judged that 14 of the 42 participants had not fully followed the diet in at least one phase. During the control period, average blood lycopene levels stayed flat at 0.40 micromoles per liter, whereas during the tomato paste intervention, average blood lycopene levels more than doubled, rising from a baseline of 0.32 micromoles per liter by an average of 0.40 micromoles per liter.
Cognitive testing showed that eating tomato paste improved selective attention and one aspect of associative memory compared to the low-lycopene control diet. On the attention test, concentration performance started at an average baseline score of 171.0 points and increased by 7.8 points after the tomato phase, yielding an adjusted difference of 7.2 points over the control phase. Visual processing speed improved by a similar margin, rising from a baseline average of 188.3 points by 8.5 points after the tomato diet, for an adjusted gain of 8.3 points compared to the control period. These attention gains amounted to roughly 4 percent of baseline scores; in standardized terms, the authors describe the effects as moderate.
When the researchers excluded participants whose blood tests suggested they had not strictly followed the diet rules, these attention gains grew roughly twice as large, reaching a 13.7-point advantage in concentration and a 14.7-point advantage in processing speed. On the associative memory test, participants improved their ability to match faces with the correct names from a baseline average of 9.4 out of 12 points by 0.8 points over the control diet. The overall associative memory score, which combined all three parts of the face-name test, did not differ significantly between the two phases, however. In addition, the card-sorting test showed no meaningful changes in executive function during either phase of the study.
Although the trial’s sample size was originally calculated to detect changes in BDNF, blood levels of the protein showed only a borderline increase after the tomato intervention, with an adjusted average difference of 15.2 nanograms per milliliter compared to the control period (relative to baseline levels of 26.5 to 32.2 nanograms per milliliter).
The researchers noted that participants who completed the tomato diet first still had elevated BDNF levels when they started the control period a month later. An analysis restricted to the first phase, which avoids this carryover problem, found a consistent difference of 11.0 nanograms per milliliter. The authors suggest that this lingering carryover effect may reflect sustained biological changes triggered by tomato consumption that last longer than the four-week break between phases.
In the subgroup of 14 participants who underwent brain scans, the tomato diet was linked to reduced communication within two brain systems: the right frontoparietal network, which helps direct attention toward goals, and the auditory network, which processes sound. Larger drops in connectivity in these networks correlated with larger gains on the face-name matching task.
The authors suggest that this reduction in cross-network chatter may reflect greater neural efficiency, helping the brain filter out distracting background noise and sensory interference during visually demanding tasks. These brain findings came from 14 people and did not pass the study’s strictest statistical correction for multiple comparisons, so they are best treated as preliminary.
During the low-lycopene control diet, brain scans showed weakened connectivity within the dorsal attention network, a brain system responsible for sustaining focus. Across the study, bigger increases in blood lycopene levels were moderately correlated with stronger connectivity in the dorsal attention network and modestly correlated with faster cognitive processing speeds. The findings are consistent with research covered by PsyPost in 2024, which linked higher blood levels of carotenoids and other nutrients to slower brain aging and better cognitive performance in older adults, rather than directly testing a tomato intervention in middle-aged adults.
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider when interpreting these results. Because participants were eating actual tomato paste rather than swallowing an identical-looking pill, they knew which dietary phase they were in, and so did the staff who administered the cognitive tests. Expecting benefits could have boosted participants’ motivation during testing. The authors argue that the parallel changes in blood lycopene and brain scans make a purely expectation-driven explanation less likely.
The design of the control phase also introduces a question about what drove the differences between the two periods. Because participants had to actively avoid tomatoes and several red fruits during the control phase, the authors note that the restriction itself, rather than only the added tomato paste, may have contributed to differences between the phases, such as the weaker dorsal attention network connectivity seen during the control period. In addition, while lycopene was the primary compound tracked in the blood, tomatoes contain other beneficial nutrients like vitamin C, beta-carotene, and plant polyphenols that may have worked together to produce the observed effects.
The study sample was also relatively small, especially the 14-person brain imaging subgroup, and more than 90 percent of the participants had a university or postgraduate degree. Future studies will need to test larger and more diverse groups of people to see if the results hold true across the broader population. Longer trials with extended washout breaks and brain scans conducted while participants actively perform mental tasks could help clarify whether daily tomato intake provides lasting protection against age-related cognitive decline.
The study, “Tomato Intake Improves Cognitive Performance and Modulates Functional Brain Networks in Healthy Adults: A Randomized Crossover Clinical Trial,” was authored by Ricardo López-Solís, Carolina Donat-Vargas, Patricia Ramírez-Carrasco, Rocío M. Gutiérrez-Romero, Maria Pérez, Magda Castellví, Beatriz Bosch, Camila Arancibia-Riveros, Alejandro Hinojosa-Moscoso, Carlos Laredo, Emma Muñoz-Moreno, Ana Maria Ruiz-Leon, Rosa Casas, Ramon Estruch, Anna Vallverdú-Queralt, Marina Corrado, and Rosa M. Lamuela-Raventós.

Ukraine, Russia say US-brokered truce holding in ravaged city of Oleshky
- A US-brokered local truce in occupied Oleshky appeared to hold, with Ukraine and Russia reporting no violations as humanitarian aid and evacuations were planned.
- The city is badly damaged and nearly empty, with residents facing hunger and no medicine; former residents welcomed the chance to leave.
- Fighting continued elsewhere in Ukraine, with strikes on Kyiv and other areas, while talks may resume in November and leaders sought new ways to end the war.
AI generated
KYIV - A local truce between Ukraine and Russia aimed at allowing humanitarian aid into the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky appeared to be holding on Oct 27, with neither side reporting any violations after several hours.
Both sides said they began observing the truce at 3am local time (9am in Singapore).
The war-ravaged city in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region had been caught in the middle of fighting between the two sides since 2022, when it was seized by Russian forces at the start of their invasion.
Former residents told AFP in September that those remaining in the city were starving, lacked medicine and could not easily leave.
“The possibility of evacuation from Oleshky is very good news for me and for the people who are trapped there,” Olga, a former resident whose last name AFP is withholding for security reasons, told AFP on Oct 27.
“My acquaintances are ready to leave,” she said.
Announcing the truce on Oct 23, US First Lady Melania Trump said civilian officials from both Russia and Ukraine would visit residents in their homes and “determine the level of assistance they require”.
“Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine,” she said.
AFP was not able to immediately verify details about the humanitarian mission or whether there had been a decrease in fighting.
The Russian military does not routinely grant international media, including AFP, access to areas under Russian occupation.
Right-leaning US cable network Newsmax said it had been granted “exclusive television access” to accompany observers entering the city on Oct 29.
‘Biggest de-escalation since 2022’
David Arakhamia, a Ukrainian lawmaker who took part in peace negotiations with Russia in 2022, described the ceasefire as the “biggest de-escalation since 2022”.
Both sides were adhering to the truce as of 5.30pm (10.30pm in Singapore), Ukrainian human rights commissioner Dmytro Lubinets said in a post on Facebook, adding that it was scheduled to remain in effect until 10.59pm on Nov 1.
Russia also reported the truce was holding.
A staffer for Lubinets said the truce applied to the entire Kherson region.
Oleshky, on the southern bank of the Dnipro River, was seized by Russian troops in 2022.
The population has since dropped from about 24,000 to around 2,000 today, including as many as 50 children, according to Ukrainian and US estimates.
Former residents told AFP in September that some of those remaining in the city were hunting pigeons to survive and had “forgotten what bread is”.
The Ukrainian military has released drone footage of the town showing rows of empty apartment blocks, some charred by fire or partially destroyed by fighting.
Vladimir Saldo, a Moscow-installed official in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region, told Russian media that those wishing to evacuate could go to Russian-occupied Crimea or Rostov in southwestern Russia, but would need to wait until the heavily-mined road from the city had been cleared.
Air barrages elsewhere in Ukraine
Outside the Kherson region, Russia continued to pummel the rest of Ukraine with air strikes, officials said.
Ballistic missiles struck a university campus in Kyiv on the evening of Oct 26.
Another overnight strike hit the capital’s Southern Bridge – a major road-and-rail artery crossing the Dnipro river.
Images posted on social media showed a gaping hole in between subway tracks and a mess of twisted metal.
In Russia, two people were killed “as a result of explosive devices being dropped” on the western city of Bryansk, the regional governor said.
Ukrainian attacks on the Russian-occupied Luhansk region killed four people, the region’s Russian-installed governor Leonid Pasechnik said.
Hundreds of thousands of soldiers and civilians have been killed and millions forced to flee their homes since Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, a conflict that has spiralled into Europe’s deadliest since World War II.
Russia, which denies targeting civilians, now occupies around a fifth of its neighbour: the Crimean peninsula, which it invaded and later claimed to have annexed in 2014, most of the eastern regions of Donetsk and Luhansk – collectively referred to as the Donbas – and large parts of the southern Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions.
US-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine are set to resume in November, having been effectively frozen since the United States and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran in February.
Finland’s president and Norway’s prime minister held a surprise call with Putin on Oct 27 aimed at ending the war, which they described as “frank and substantive”. AFP

Ukraine says it has finished its part of FREYJA, Europe’s joint anti-ballistic project. Partners’ work is still underway

04:57:44 KST

Ukraine has finished its share of FREYJA, a joint European project to build a system against ballistic missiles, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told journalists on 17 October, Ukrinform reported. He added that Kyiv wants to test the first system as soon as possible.
Ukraine still relies on US-made Patriot interceptors to stop Russian ballistic missiles. Zelenskyy told ABC News on 23 October that Ukraine had received only 24 of them from the US in three months, while it needs 350 a month on average. FREYJA can not close that gap soon, because the system is still in development.
Ukraine’s missile and launcher, partners’ radars and sensors
Zelenskyy said the partners’ share of the work, with 10 countries taking part, is still underway. He also said he had discussed the project with French President Emmanuel Macron, and he named Norway as a key partner.
Ukraine’s missile, Europe’s sensors—FREYJA enters active development on an early-2027 clock
Zelenskyy did not say what the partners still have to deliver. In August, he said Ukraine is capable of making the missile and launcher, while partners would supply critical components such as radars and sensors.
One part not made in Ukraine
In May, Fire Point co-founder and chief designer Denys Shtilerman said all components of the FP-7.x interceptor are made in Ukraine except one. “As for that one part we don’t manufacture in Ukraine, we’ve contracted a certain quantity of it. We already have it,” he said, but did not name the part.
In June, however, Shtilerman told the Financial Times that mass production depended on an infrared seeker Fire Point hoped to get from Germany’s Diehl Defence. Neither statement says whether the seeker is that one part.
Fire Point co-founder Iryna Terekh said in September that FREYJA was going through testing and technical integration in combat conditions in Ukraine. The company plans its first intercept of a ballistic target by mid-2027.
The official timeline has since moved closer. On 21 October, Zelenskyy wrote that officials had identified where to speed up so FREYJA reaches testing by the end of this year. A test is still a step short of an intercept.

Quebec’s separatist leader threatens to play spoiler at Carney’s EU summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
19:57:34 UTC
04:57:34 KST

Quebec’s separatist leader threatens to play spoiler at Carney’s EU summit
Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon says Ottawa would rather he “serve shrimp cocktail” at a function than stage one, and alleges a “serious lack of respect.”
Paul St-Pierre Plamondon walks to make a speech after winning his election to become the next premier of Quebec, in Montreal, Quebec, Canada, on October 5, 2026. | Andrej Ivanov/ AFP via Getty Images
Quebec’s new separatist government accused Ottawa on Tuesday of barring the province from this week’s EU-Canada summit in Montreal and warned it would have the last word on any deals struck there that concern its powers.
The dispute erupted Tuesday morning when Quebec Justice Minister Marie-Claude Sarrazin said in a statement that Ottawa had refused Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon's request to address the summit, which opens Thursday.
St-Pierre Plamondon said in a post on X that the decision revealed a “serious lack of respect,” adding that Ottawa would rather he “serve shrimp cocktail” at a function rather than address one.
Advertisement
Ottawa also turned down a September request from the previous Quebec government to host a reception on the sidelines of the summit, Sarrazin noted.
Prime Minister Mark Carney hit back, saying St-Pierre Plamondon had himself turned down an invitation to the Thursday night summit dinner. “It’s his decision to leave an empty chair again,” Carney told reporters in French.
The tiff threatens to overshadow an international gathering that Carney, Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa have billed as a step change in mutual relations, driven by U.S. President Donald Trump’s aggressive tariffs and scorn for the postwar Western consensus.
Early drafts of the joint declaration include a digital trade deal and a pact that lets the European Investment Bank finance Canadian critical minerals projects. Many of those deliverables fall under provincial jurisdiction, such as natural resources.
“'When you’re not at the table, you’re on the menu,' Prime Minister Carney told us,” Sarrazin said in her statement. “The federal government has chosen to prevent Quebec from having a say on its own territory.”
Whatever agreements are signed at the summit, “Quebec is sovereign in its fields of jurisdiction internationally, so it will have the last word,” Sarrazin warned.
Advertisement
Her statement evoked the 1965 Gérin-Lajoie doctrine, a principle of Quebec’s international policy that holds it can conduct its own foreign relations in areas the Canadian Constitution assigns to the provinces. It also noted that Quebec had a seat at the table during negotiations on CETA, the EU-Canada trade deal signed in 2015, attending more than 100 meetings.
Yves-François Blanchet, leader of the separatist Bloc Québécois in the federal parliament, also said he had been refused a request to attend. “You’re invited to come, but above all, keep quiet. Don’t speak,” he told reporters on Parliament Hill.
The plot thickens
On Tuesday midmorning Ottawa time, Trump congratulated St-Pierre Plamondon on his election victory — three weeks after the actual Oct. 5 ballot — sharing an article headlined “Separatists win Quebec provincial election in blow to Mark Carney.”
Trump and Carney have been at odds since the dramatic implosion of mutual trade talks in late August, with the U.S. president deploring the Canadian leader as “nasty.”
The Quebec premier, meanwhile, is all-in on sovereignty in a province where support for separating from Canada reached a three-decade low of 29% earlier this year.
Carney rejected St-Pierre Plamondon’s claims of exclusion, saying Quebec had been consulted on the summit. “We have had three consultations with the Quebec delegation already on the agreement with the European Union,” he said. Carney’s office told POLITICO on Tuesday that it had invited every premier to attend the Thursday dinner in Montreal.
Advertisement
St-Pierre Plamondon also skipped a federal meeting with Indigenous leaders and premiers on Monday, an absence Carney criticized.
Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said the premier was “welcome” in Montreal, but that the summit was a federal meeting, with geopolitics a federal area of responsibility. “With everything going on in the world, we just need to make sure we can reach an agreement with the European Union,” she said. “That’s what Quebecers want.”
Despite the public spat over the summit logistics, working-level officials described the relationship between the different levels of government as constructive.
Hélène Drainville, Quebec’s delegate general in Brussels, told POLITICO on Monday that federal and provincial officials have set up joint working groups to implement the summit’s outcomes.
Quebec is also in talks with the European Investment Bank and DG GROW, the Commission’s industry department, about the bank’s entry into Canada, she said.
“Right now, all the signals are green,” Drainville said. She underlined, however, that the province “has to be at the table” if Ottawa and Brussels strike deals in its areas of jurisdiction.
Mickey Djuric and Sue Allan contributed reporting from Ottawa.

UN chief urges greater role for women in peace processes as conflicts, sexual violence rise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
19:53:27 UTC
04:53:27 KST

Diyar Guldogan
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on Tuesday urged governments to strengthen women's participation in peace negotiations, restore funding for women-led organizations and ensure accountability for gender-based violence.
Addressing a UN Security Council open debate on women, peace and security, Guterres warned that gender inequality continued to undermine peace efforts despite international commitments to women's participation.
He cited Security Council Resolution 1325, adopted in 2000, which recognized the importance of women's involvement in conflict prevention, resolution and peacebuilding.
"But let's face facts: too often, it has resulted in a lot of talk, and not enough action," Guterres said, referring to the implementation of the women, peace and security agenda.
Guterres said the world was experiencing its highest number of conflicts since World War II, citing crises in the Gaza Strip, Ukraine, the Sahel, Sudan and Myanmar.
He warned that women and girls faced increasing exposure to armed conflict, sexual violence, displacement and restrictions on their fundamental rights.
"The number of UN-verified cases of conflict-related sexual violence has sharply increased, reaching over 9,700 last year – with the actual number certain to be much higher," he said.
Women and girls also faced growing risks from explosive weapons used in densely populated areas, including in Myanmar, Sudan and the occupied Palestinian territory, he said.
Guterres also raised concerns about rising maternal mortality in crisis zones, disruptions to girls' education and attacks on women leaders, journalists and human rights defenders.
3 priorities for governments
Guterres said women remained largely excluded from formal peace negotiations despite evidence that their meaningful participation could strengthen peace agreements and improve prospects for lasting stability.
Women accounted for just 5% of negotiators across 57 peace processes in 2025, he said.
Fewer than one-fifth of peace agreements concluded globally that year included at least one reference to women, girls, gender or sexual violence, he added.
Guterres urged governments and other participants in peace processes to introduce binding targets and quotas to ensure women's meaningful participation in negotiations.
He outlined three immediate priorities: securing women's representation in peace talks, increasing funding for women's organizations in conflict-affected areas and enforcing zero tolerance for violence against women and girls.
"Of course, these three priorities are not the only areas where action is urgently needed," he said.
Guterres called on governments to fulfill their official development assistance commitments and restore funding to organizations supporting women and girls in conflict settings, particularly those affected by forced displacement.
He also demanded full accountability for perpetrators of gender-based violence, including conflict-related sexual violence.
The UN chief urged authorities to remove restrictions on female humanitarian workers and strengthen protections for those delivering aid.
Beyond those priorities, Guterres called for stronger domestic laws addressing gender-based violence, improved economic security for women, greater support for grassroots organizations and better collection of gender-related data.
"Equality is not a dream. It's a decision," he said.
