How student assemblies brought down the Serbian government
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
18:58:25 UTC
03:58:25 KST

How student assemblies brought down the Serbian government
A list of academics, engineers, artists and activists chosen by Serbia’s student assemblies defeated long-ruling president Aleksandar Vucic's right-wing Serbian Progressive Party Sunday. The shock victory comes after nearly two years of student-led anti-corruption protests – and may serve as a model for other movements hoping to turn street demonstrations into concrete political change.
Almost two years ago, a concrete canopy at a freshly renovated railway station in Serbia’s second city of Novi Sad collapsed. The falling canopy, which the country’s protest movement has blamed on widespread corruption, killed 16 people. Now, it has brought the country’s ruling party down with it.
Serbia’s right-wing populist president Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat in the country’s parliamentary elections on Sunday. Just who exactly he has conceded to remains harder to judge. The force that won the popular vote, and a clear majority of parliamentary seats, is not a traditional opposition party – or any kind of party at all.
Instead, the seats will be filled by candidates belonging to the Student List, a collection of little-known academics, economists, athletes, engineers, artists and activists chosen by majority vote by the nameless student assemblies that have sprung up in the universities occupied by demonstrators for almost two years.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
These plenums, as they are known, have served as the guiding hand of a protest movement that has brought tens of thousands of people into the streets to overturn what demonstrators described as a culture of corruption and cronyism that had taken root under 14 years of Vucic’s increasingly authoritarian rule. Now, it falls upon them to determine which of the candidates will serve as Serbia’s next prime minister and which will run the country's ministries.
All power to the plenums
London-based political scientist Branislav Radeljic said that the student assemblies had been crucial in channelling the public fury unleashed by the Novi Sad collapse.
“The student plenums helped turn mass mobilisation into institutional change through collective decision-making, decentralisation and a deliberately broad agenda,” he said. “Organised at individual faculties, the assemblies allowed students to debate demands, agree on tactics and vote on key decisions. This created a sense of shared ownership and legitimacy, while requiring activists to justify proposals to their peers rather than defer to a single leader.”
You don’t have to go all the way back to the Petrograd Soviet to find precedents. Nebojsa Vladisavljevic, a professor in Serbian politics at the University of Belgrade, said that these experiments in direct democracy had been a staple of student protest movements across the Balkans for years.
“This horizontal model of organisation, highly decentralised, is not that novel when it comes to this region – students have organised themselves in this particular way via public assemblies, or plenums as they call them, for probably about two decades now,” he said. “And that includes Belgrade students, but also students in Zagreb, Croatia, Sarajevo and Tuzla in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Skopje in North Macedonia.”
Read moreWhy has the EU kept silent on Serbia’s massive protest movement?
Students have served as the vanguard of Serbia’s protest movement since November 2024, when suspected ruling party supporters set upon a silent vigil organised by students and teachers at Belgrade’s Faculty of Dramatic Arts. The students swiftly occupied the building, setting off a wave of university blockades that shut down classes across the country.
“The protest spread out widely,” Vladisavljevic said. “All faculties or schools of all state universities were under blockade for several months, and during this period, students made all their decisions in these plenary sessions and working groups on all sorts of issues.”
Behind closed doors
The rules are simple. Every student has the right to participate in plenary sessions. In occupied university buildings across the country, students put forward proposals to be debated by their peers, often over multiple sessions. Decisions pass by majority vote.
Ana Jovic-Lazic, a senior research fellow at the Institute of International Politics and Economics, said that the plenums had been crucial in building trust both within and without the growing student movement.
“In a political environment where parties are often strongly identified with individual leaders, the students offered a different way of organising and making decisions,” she said. “The emphasis on collective decision-making gave participants a sense of ownership and responsibility. It also helped the movement maintain its independence from established political parties, which was particularly important given the widespread distrust of traditional political actors.”
By deliberately casting itself as a leaderless force, Vladisavljevic said the student movement was also shielding itself from being singled out for slander by a media that has been tightly controlled by the ruling Serbian Progressive Party.
“It has to do with the nature of regime that we had in Serbia for about 10 or so years – which is not just authoritarian, but also personalist, and which is based not purely on repression, but is specifically on media manipulation,” he said. “They specialised in targeting a prominent opposition personalities and government critics. And in that way, they successfully undermined opposition in previous years.”
Eric Gordy, professor of political and cultural sociology at University College London’s School of Slavonic and East European Studies, said that the lack of public-facing figures had made the student movement more difficult to undermine than its predecessors.
“It's a leaderless movement, which in terms of the media environment where there is a constant effort to try to discredit movements of opposition, they become a much more difficult target – they’re a moving target,” he said. “You can't discredit the movement by concentrating on a personality and defaming them.”
Direct action
Unwilling to let the traditional broadcast media set the narrative, students instead organised their own outreach to the wider public, holding public rallies and marathon cycling trips across the country to connect directly with communities outside the major cities.
Students also called on people across Serbia to set up their own local assemblies, or zborovi, to spread their experiment in direct democracy off campus. Scores of these assemblies have sprung up across the country since March – though their painstakingly debated demands have had little success in eking concessions from local government officials.
“What I find especially significant is that the students managed to connect their demands with concerns shared by people well beyond the universities,” Jovic-Lazic said. “Their insistence on accountability and functioning institutions resonated with a much broader public.”
Read moreSerbia’s student-led protesters wanted accountability. Now they’re calling for elections
Having failed to secure its demands for accountability for the Novi Sad collapse through more than a year of mass street demonstrations, the student movement set its sights on more traditional organs of state power.
The movement began pushing for early elections, and a slate of parliamentary candidates began to emerge behind closed doors as the student assemblies voted and vetoed a list into shape.
“By entering electoral politics and involving student assemblies in candidate selection, it sought to transfer collective authorisation into formal institutions,” Radeljic said. “The key test now is whether the decentralised practices that sustained mobilisation can also deliver accountability, coordination and effective government. Given the calibre of the people selected by the student movement, I believe they can.”
The mass line
The movement’s minimalist political programme has also played a core role in the Student List’s mass appeal.
The 11-point programme that emerged from the student assemblies combines a raft of targeted anti-corruption measures with broader social policies including providing young people with affordable housing and investing in rural healthcare.
While its supporters paint it as a blueprint for dismantling more than a decade of authoritarian control of the country’s judiciary, media and civil service, the programme deliberately steers clear of the thornier policy discussions that would reveal deep divides within the broad-church movement.
Gordy said that the intentionally expansive outreach to people from every corner of the political spectrum meant that representatives from the radical left were rubbing shoulders with right-wing nationalists.
“There are at least three different currents within the student movement. You have one that's a radical democratic current that's saying, ‘Let's try to remake the society so that authoritarianism and corruption are eliminated and don't return’,” he said. “Second, you have a procedurally democratic group saying, ‘Let's try to establish rule of law, but basically our role is not political, and what we want to do is create the conditions for the political parties to take over.’"
“And then third, you've got a so-called ‘national group’ – that is, the ones who are more radical on these questions of relations with other states in the region than what has been,” he added. “They've sort of declared a truce in order to face the election, but they're going to be competing for power and control of the government now.”

Money for shifting electricity consumption: how Ukrainians will be able to receive a reward
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:57:44 EET
03:57:44 KST

Money for shifting electricity consumption: how Ukrainians will be able to receive a reward
Kyiv • UNN
The NEURC approved an aggregation project that provides for a reward for changing the consumption schedule. The system will operate after the rules are approved.
Ukrainians and businesses are being offered payments for changing their electricity consumption schedule—for example, shifting appliance use from peak hours to another time. To participate, it will be necessary to conclude an agreement with an aggregator—a company that represents consumers in the energy market. On October 27, the National Energy and Utilities Regulatory Commission of Ukraine (NEURC) approved a draft of amendments to the retail market rules. UNN explains how to participate in such a project, what to know about the compensation, and how to receive it.
How the mechanism will work
The NEURC explains the two-zone electricity consumption mechanism as follows: demand for electricity changes throughout the day. When people switch on household appliances at the same time, the power system needs additional capacity. Changing the operating schedule of appliances will help distribute the load on the system more evenly.
The aggregator will combine participants’ capacities to change their consumption and provide the relevant services on the market. A consumer will be able to receive compensation by meeting the conditions. It should be noted that the project provides both for shifting consumption and for temporarily reducing or increasing the load at the aggregator’s command in response to market needs.
Who will be able to participate in the program
The regulator lists households and businesses among the potential participants. For an apartment or house, an example could be changing the operating times of household appliances; for a business, shifting some production processes. Having one’s own solar power plant is not identified as a mandatory condition in the NEURC’s announcement. However, participation will depend on the final rules, the technical possibility of metering, and the aggregators’ offers.
We emphasize that participation is voluntary. Current legislation allows consumers to join an aggregated group without the consent of their electricity supplier. There is no need to change the company supplying the electricity: the supply agreement and the agreement with the aggregator are separate.
How to receive compensation: a step-by-step plan for Ukrainians
After the rules are approved and offers become available, the following steps will need to be completed in sequence in order to receive compensation.
First, find an aggregator. To do this, determine whether the company works with household customers or the relevant type of business and what terms it offers. You can check the company in the NEURC’s licensing register via the link. At the same time, it is worth remembering that the law provides for cases in which a separate aggregation license is not required.
Second, clarify metering issues. Ask the aggregator and the distribution system operator whether the existing meter is suitable, whether additional equipment is needed, and who will pay for it. A meter that shows only total consumption will not indicate how much electricity was used during specific hours. Most likely, a two-zone meter will be needed to participate in the project.
The next step is concluding an agreement. The draft resolution provides for a written agreement specifying the equipment, management procedures, settlements, and payments. It is worth clarifying how commands will be delivered, whether they may be disregarded, how the result will be determined, and what costs the consumer will bear.
After that, it will be necessary to notify the supplier if the final rules require this. A written notification can be sent to the authority’s postal or email address, or submitted through the electronic account within three business days after concluding or terminating the agreement. The notification must specify the relevant electrical installations and metering points.
Afterward, the person will only need to comply with the conditions and check the calculations. The project provides that the aggregator will inform the participant of the results at least once per settlement period. The payment information must specify the cost of services, incentive payments, and the deadlines and methods of settlement.
What compensation will be available
It is not yet possible to name an amount, since the NEURC has established neither a single rate per kilowatt-hour nor a guaranteed monthly payment. Under the project, the procedure for calculating the results and payments will be determined by the agreement in accordance with the market rules.
Therefore, before taking part in the program, it makes sense to find out exactly what the payments will cover, how changes in consumption will be measured, and whether there are aggregator service fees or equipment costs. In addition, expenses and possible taxes should be taken into account. The latter will depend on how the payments are formalized and on the recipient’s status.
Which appliances can be used at other times
First of all, attention should be paid to appliances whose operating schedule can be changed without harming household activities or production:
-  washing machines and dishwashers; 
-  water heaters, if their control system allows it; 
-  charging electric vehicles and storage systems when the appropriate equipment is available; 
-  some production processes, if they can be safely and technologically shifted. 
The hours will depend on the contract and the situation in the energy system. For example, on October 27, Ukrenergo asked people to limit the use of high-power appliances from 4:00 p.m. to 10:00 p.m.
In addition, refrigerators or medical equipment should not be switched off if they need to operate continuously. After power is restored, all high-power appliances should not be turned on at the same time — this could overload the grid.
Nighttime tariff: how to save money already
Aggregator remuneration and a two-zone tariff are different mechanisms. In the first case, the payment is for an agreed change in load; in the second, it is a lower electricity price at night when a two-zone meter has been installed and programmed.
For most household consumers, the price is UAH 4.32 per kWh. With two-zone metering, from 11:00 p.m. to 7:00 a.m., half of this price applies — UAH 2.16 per kWh. The current prices for households have been extended until April 30, 2027. For certain categories, including consumers entitled to a preferential tariff for electric heating, the calculation may differ. If 100 kWh of monthly consumption is shifted from daytime to nighttime hours, the difference in payment under the general tariff will be UAH 216.
When the system will start operating and how it will help the energy sector
As of October 27, 2026, the NEURC had approved only a draft of the amendments. It is planned to put it up for discussion, but the regulator has not yet announced a specific date for adopting the new rules and launching payments.
According to the NEURC’s plan, Ukrainians’ participation in the aggregation program will help reduce peak loads and maintain the balance between generation and consumption. However, energy-sector experts are already warning that the outcome will depend on the number of participants and the remuneration terms.

Egypt’s parliament approves military support for Saudi Arabia amid Houthi attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
18:57:06 UTC
03:57:06 KST

Egypt has approved military help for Saudi Arabia if requested as Houthi attacks threaten the kingdom and Red Sea shipping. The vote comes as Saudi officials hold talks in Iran amid regional efforts to prevent a further escalation of the fighting.
Egypt’s parliament on Monday authorised President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi to provide military assistance to defend Saudi Arabia if the kingdom requests help, following a wave of attacks by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis.
The House of Representatives said the decision passed with the required two-thirds majority. It allows el-Sisi, in coordination with Riyadh, to take measures to protect Saudi territory, sovereignty and holy sites against external attacks.
Parliament’s statement did not specify what assistance Egypt would provide or announce that troops were being sent.
On 17 October, Yahya al-Raei, speaker of the Houthi-controlled parliament in Sanaa, warned Egypt against military involvement, saying it would endanger Egypt’s own security and stability.
El-Sisi said last week that any Egyptian military role would be limited to defending Saudi territory and borders, ruling out attacks on Yemen.
The vote came as Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman joined Pakistani and Turkish officials for talks with Iranian leaders in Tehran. The Saudi foreign ministry said the visit aimed to open channels for negotiations and prevent further military escalation.
Approval after three closed sessions
El-Sisi first sought parliament’s backing on 17 October. MPs met behind closed doors on 18 and 19 October before postponing the decision until Monday.
Deputy Speaker Assem El-Gazzar said nearly 500 MPs had asked to speak during the discussions. Most parties supported the request, but some lawmakers questioned the terms of a possible military mission.
The Egyptian Social Democratic Party instructed its MPs ahead of the vote to abstain. It said parliament had not received enough information about what Egyptian troops would be asked to do, how long they would stay, what the operation would cost or the risks they would face.
While supporting Saudi Arabia’s security, the party warned against an open-ended military commitment and urged Egypt to leave room for diplomacy.
The National Defence Council, chaired by el-Sisi, had endorsed support for Saudi Arabia on 18 October. However, Egypt’s constitution also requires approval from two-thirds of MPs before its armed forces can be sent on combat missions abroad.
Attacks continue as diplomats meet
Saudi, Pakistani and Turkish officials met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and other senior officials in Tehran on Monday. Pakistan sent army chief Asim Munir, while Turkey sent intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin.
Fighting continues between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen’s internationally recognised government.
The Houthis said on Monday they had attacked pumping stations on Saudi Arabia’s East-West oil pipeline and King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh. There was no immediate Saudi confirmation of those claims.
The Saudi-led coalition separately said it had intercepted a missile heading towards Riyadh. It also said it had destroyed Houthi missile launchers and storage facilities in Yemen.
The fighting threatens shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The waterway forms the southern entrance to the Red Sea and is part of the route to Egypt’s Suez Canal.
Egypt’s main stock index closed 1.7% lower on Monday ahead of the parliamentary vote. Trading had been halted for 30 minutes on Sunday after the broader EGX100 index fell 10%.
Saudi Arabia is a major political ally and financial supporter of Egypt. It provides aid, energy supplies and deposits at Egypt’s central bank.
Egypt joined the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen in 2015, mainly through naval operations. Its combat role was limited.

We have published mobile phone numbers for collecting information. We are gathering information on our side, and the Russians are doing the same on theirs. We are also compiling verified lists specifying what assistance each person needs,” Lubinets said.

All government agencies are working on this under our coordination,” Lubinets said.

“They are closely monitoring what each side must do and what commitments it must honor. From the 23rd to the 27th, several days have passed. During this period, we have already gone through several stages, and each side has fulfilled its commitments in full,” Lubinets said.
As previously reported, US First Lady Melania Trump said she had secured a local ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine covering only Oleshky, a town in the temporarily Russian-occupied part of the Kherson region.
According to the White House press office, the parties agreed to temporarily cease all military operations in Oleshky to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and prepare for the evacuation of civilians through an agreed safe corridor.

Poland to Host €227M Patriot Missile Service Center
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
18:54:13 UTC
03:54:13 KST

Poland has announced that it will be hosting a European service center for US-made PAC-3 interceptor missiles, aiming to cut repair times for weapons that are already in short supply worldwide and critical to Ukraine’s defense against Russian ballistic missile attacks.
Polish Deputy Defense Minister Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka, who led Warsaw’s negotiations, called the decision “historic” in a statement on Tuesday, Oct. 27. Three other countries had competed to host the facility, she said, naming Germany, the Netherlands and Norway.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“This success was not a given. It is the result of many months of negotiations and the hard work of the entire team,” Sobkowiak-Czarnecka wrote, noting that the Polish bid had been the highest rated since the application stage.
According to TVP World citing Sobkowiak-Czarnecka, the hub would be the only one of its kind outside the United States. Its cost would be roughly 1 billion Polish zlotys (about $253 million) and would take about a year to become fully operational.
In her statement, the defense minister thanked Poland’s Prime Minister Donald Tusk and Deputy Prime Minister and Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, who appointed her chief negotiator.
The outcome showed what was possible when the government and the country’s President Karol Nawrocki pulled in the same direction, she added.
POW Dispute: South Korea Pulls 8 Diplomats From Ukraine
Short repair times for scarce interceptors
PAC-3 missiles, used in US-made Patriot air-defense systems, are currently shipped to the US for servicing, which led Washington to seek a European site to cut turnaround times, TVP World reported.
The US, Poland, Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden signed an agreement with manufacturer Lockheed Martin in July, in an aim to explore setting up such a hub.
According to the broadcaster, Warsaw has long pursued the project with hopes that it would eventually lead to Patriot missile production in Poland.
Plant near Warsaw seen as likely site
Although the government did not officially name a location at the time of the report, TVP World reported that the WZE electronics plant in Zielonka, located about 15 kilometers (9.3 miles) northeast of Warsaw, is widely seen as the leading candidate.
In September, Sobkowiak-Czarnecka toured the plant with US Under Secretary of State Thomas DiNanno. At the time, the US Embassy in Warsaw noted that the visit highlighted bilateral cooperation on critical Patriot components.
Under a 2019 agreement with Lockheed Martin, the plant already produces and services key PAC-3 MSE components, TVP World reported.
Ukraine facing critical shortage
As of Oct. 15, Ukraine has reportedly depleted its stocks of Patriot interceptor missiles.
For the country, the PAC-3 is currently among the very few weapons capable of intercepting Russia’s Iskander-M, a ballistic missile carrying a half-ton warhead strong enough to tear down a quarter to half of a typical apartment block.
The shortfall was particularly felt during Russia’s large-scale attack overnight into Wednesday, Oct. 14, when most incoming ballistic missiles reached their targets. The strike hit three power plants in Kyiv and energy facilities in Kharkiv, killing four people and injuring at least 25 in the capital.
According to CNN’s exclusive, Ukraine fired its last remaining Patriots as the Air Force shot down four Russian ballistic missiles during that same attack.
Around the same time, the US aerospace giant Starlink tweaked parameters and limited terminals above 160 kilometers per hour (100 miles per hour), crippling Kyiv’s drone operations, including interceptor drones used against Russian jet-powered Shahed drones.
As of Oct. 1, Lockheed Martin is in advanced talks over PAC-3 production outside the US over tripled demand, as countries seek to rebuild their stocks amid the war in Iran and Russia’s escalating rhetoric towards Europe.
For much of the year, Ukraine has repeatedly appealed to its Western partners for faster deliveries of Patriot interceptors.
On Sept. 8, German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said Germany would deliver PAC-2 missiles to Ukraine from it’s own Bundeswehr stocks, while Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara said contracts are being signed with partners for about 1,000 Patriot missiles.
During the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York, US President Donald Trump said he made a “final decision” to grant Ukraine the licenses to produce Patriot missiles domestically, after backtracking on the previous July commitment.

built from upcycled timber and iron, portable micro-barn wanders through japan
dobedo studio develops ehho!², a portable micro-pavilion that reinterprets the traditional japanese kago, hand-carried by two people.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
DOBEDO builds PORTABLE PAVILION FROM DEMOLISHED JAPANESE BARN
Designed by DOBEDO STUDIO, EHHO!² is a portable micro-architecture engineered from materials salvaged during the deconstruction of an agricultural barn in Gunma Prefecture, Japan. The mobile timber structure draws functional and formal inspiration from the traditional Japanese kago (palanquin), carrying architectural remnants of rural infrastructure into the urban public realm. Upcycling weathered corrugated iron sheets, structural logs, reclaimed timber boards, and hand-woven ropes, the project translates rural material memory into a compact, deployable social pavilion carried by two people.
CORRUGATED METAL AND TREE-BRANCHES DETAIL LOW-TECH ASSEMBLY
The tectonic assembly by DOBEDO STUDIO balances low-tech mechanics with site-adaptive details. The rusted corrugated metal sheets are bent to form a protective curved roof, utilizing decades of atmospheric weathering as a natural, textured exterior skin. Hinged timber side panels fold downward to function as exterior benches, exposing a contrasting crimson-painted interior inspired by the seasonal bloom of local red spider lilies (higanbana). To secure the folding benches during transport, the studio integrated small wooden branches as tactile latch pins. If misplaced during transit, these fasteners can be replaced using fallen twigs sourced directly from nearby urban trees, establishing an intuitive, maintenance-free locking mechanism.

Rada withdraws bill that threatened journalists' work – MP
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:53:13 EET
03:53:13 KST

Bill No. 10242 has been withdrawn from consideration by the Verkhovna Rada, according to MP Yaroslav Zhelezniak (the Holos faction).
"Yes, I would like to report that following constructive negotiations with Andriy Motovylovets, first deputy head of the Servant of the People faction, and the parliament's leadership… Bill No. 10242 has been withdrawn from consideration – both for tomorrow and for the rest of this week," Zhelezniak said on his Telegram channel.
The bill in question provides for amendments to Articles 361 and 361-2 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine, increasing penalties for acts involving unauthorized access to electronic systems and the dissemination of restricted information.
According to media reports, the bill was proposed for the agenda by Andriy Motovilovets, first deputy head of the Servant of the People faction.
The bill had already been considered in 2024 – on December 4, 2024, the Verkhovna Rada did not support the bill in its second reading and sent it back for a repeat second reading. Prior to that, on December 2, media and human rights organizations called on the Rada not to support the bill due to threats to freedom of speech, the work of journalists, and the protection of journalistic sources and whistle blowers in Ukraine.
Chair of the Committee on Freedom of Speech Yaroslav Yurchyshyn called on his colleagues in the Verkhovna Rada to remove Bill No. 10242 from the agenda and draft a new one that takes into account the rights of whistle blowers. However, two weeks later, the bill reappeared on the agenda. On December 17, Media Rukh, along with media and human rights NGOs, appealed to lawmakers for a second time, urging them to withdraw their support for the bill and noting that the revised version had not eliminated the risks. Proposals to introduce effective protection mechanisms for individuals who disclose confidential information in the public interest-particularly journalists and whistleblowers – were not taken into account.
On December 18, 2024, the Verkhovna Rada did not consider the bill, but it was not withdrawn from consideration.
In January 2025, the bill was once again added to the agenda of the Verkhovna Rada sessions without consultation, even though the Committee on Freedom of Speech had previously sent a list of editors and media experts who would be proposed for a meeting to reach an agreement. Shortly thereafter, the bill was again removed from the agenda, as some members of parliament emphasized during the discussion that they were unwilling to support the bill until it had been agreed upon with the media community.

Pro-Ukraine demonstrations took place in more than 10 cities across Europe, North America, and Australia over the past week, with protesters opposing US President Donald Trump’s agreement to resume Russian diesel shipments, the easing of sanctions on Moscow, and restrictions affecting Ukraine’s military support.
The protests were organized by Ukrainian diaspora groups and international supporters of Ukraine, who called on Washington to maintain pressure on the Kremlin, restore Ukraine’s access to Starlink, and stop using military aid and intelligence sharing as leverage against Kyiv.
The International Center for Ukrainian Victory (ICUV) said the actions reflected growing concern over US decisions that could benefit Russia while its war against Ukraine continues.
The demonstrations followed Trump’s announcement on 9 October that Russia would supply diesel to US and global markets. The US Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control subsequently issued a temporary license authorizing transactions involving Russian-origin diesel, including imports into the United States, through 7 April 2027.
The decision reversed part of Washington’s restrictions on Russian fuel imposed after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
“We are witnessing a dangerous situation today: Russia, which attacks Ukrainian cities every day, is being offered economic agreements and sanctions relief, while Ukraine is being asked to make concessions. But Ukrainians cannot simply stop fighting. For us, this is a matter of our state’s existence. Our future cannot be the subject of agreements between Trump and Putin. It belongs to Ukrainians,” said Olena Ivashchenko, founder of Campaign for Ukraine.
Protests target Russian fuel deal and pressure on Kyiv
In London, hundreds of protesters gathered outside the US Embassy on 16 October, according to organizers from Campaign for Ukraine and partner groups. Participants included Ukrainians, Britons, Americans, and members of other national communities. British lawmakers also raised the issue in Parliament.
Demonstrators carried signs reading “How Many Ukrainians per Barrel?” and “Occupation Is Not Peace,” calling on Washington to preserve sanctions and reject pressure on Ukraine to make territorial concessions.
Trending Now
Protests also took place in Edinburgh, Chicago, Houston, Boston, San Diego, Prague, Rome, Stockholm, and Sydney. In Prague, two Ukrainian activists staged a protest outside the US Embassy on 21 October, pouring a red liquid resembling blood onto the road to symbolize the human cost of the policy.
Participants in several cities also condemned restrictions on Starlink, delays in ammunition supplies, and disruptions to intelligence sharing with Ukraine.
The diesel agreement has drawn criticism in Ukraine because Russian fuel exports generate revenue for Moscow while its forces continue attacking Ukrainian cities and infrastructure. A Russian diesel tanker carrying 40,000 metric tons of fuel departed Russia’s Baltic port of Primorsk on 22 October bound for New York, according to shipping data reported by Reuters. It was expected to arrive on 7 November.
Organizers warn against easing pressure on Moscow
Protest organizers argued that restoring Russian fuel sales and relaxing sanctions risk helping Moscow finance its war. They also opposed any US effort to secure concessions from Kyiv without requiring Russia to end its aggression.
The demonstrations reflect concerns among Ukraine’s international supporters that Washington’s pursuit of economic agreements with Moscow could undermine efforts to isolate Russia and strengthen Kyiv’s position.
Trump has defended the diesel arrangement as a way to increase fuel supplies and lower prices. His administration has also presented engagement with Moscow as part of its broader effort to end the war, while critics question whether easing economic pressure will produce meaningful concessions from the Kremlin.

Even American Monsters Need Mechanics: Ukraine Reveals What’s Under the MaxxPro

Even American Monsters Need Mechanics: Ukraine Reveals What’s Under the MaxxPro
Ukrainian military mechanics have revealed what lies beneath the massive armor of the US-made International MaxxPro, sharing rare close-up photographs of the heavy-duty suspension and mechanical systems that keep the mine-resistant vehicle operational on the battlefield.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
On October 27, Ukraine’s 146th Separate Repair and Recovery Regiment released photographs showing its specialists maintaining and restoring armored vehicles used by Ukrainian forces.
The images show a MaxxPro positioned over an inspection pit inside a military repair facility, where two Ukrainian servicemembers are working beneath its front section.
With the undercarriage exposed, the photographs provide a detailed look at the vehicle’s enormous suspension springs, reinforced control arms, and other components designed to support several tons of armor.
Despite its imposing appearance, the MaxxPro relies on complex mechanical systems that require regular maintenance, particularly after operating on damaged roads and difficult terrain.
Modern versions of the vehicle, including the MaxxPro Dash, use independent suspension systems designed to improve mobility, stability, and handling over uneven ground.
Another notable feature visible in the photographs is the additional metal mesh protection installed around the vehicle’s body. Similar screens are widely used on Ukrainian military equipment to provide an extra layer of defense against Russian FPV drones.
The International MaxxPro belongs to the Mine-Resistant Ambush Protected (MRAP) family of military vehicles, developed to protect personnel against mines, improvised explosive devices, and ambushes.
One of its defining features is a V-shaped armored hull, which helps redirect the force of explosions away from the crew compartment, reducing the impact on personnel inside. Depending on the configuration, MaxxPro vehicles can transport troops, support frontline operations, and evacuate wounded servicemembers from dangerous areas.
The vehicle’s protective capabilities have already proven critical during combat operations in Ukraine. In November 2025, soldiers from Ukraine’s Syla Svobody Battalion survived an anti-tank mine explosion while traveling in a MaxxPro to evacuate fellow servicemembers.
Earlier, in June 2025, a Canadian-made Roshel Senator MRAP was filmed evacuating wounded Ukrainian soldiers in the Donetsk region despite losing a wheel in a mine explosion. The armored vehicle continued moving on just three wheels, highlighting the importance of mine-resistant designs in protecting troops and maintaining mobility under battlefield conditions.

Italy Delays 13th Military Aid Package for Ukraine as Meloni Waits for US Midterms
Italy’s 13th military aid package for Ukraine is ready but remains frozen as Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s government waits for the outcome of the US midterm elections, La Repubblica reported on October 27.
The package has already been delayed several times, first from July to September, then until after the League party congress, and now potentially until after the November 3 US vote.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to La Repubblica, the government had previously assured French President Emmanuel Macron and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy that the package would be approved by the end of October. With four days remaining in the month, however, Italy’s parliamentary intelligence committee, Copasir, had still not been called to review the decree.
Italy has not sent a new military aid package to Ukraine since December 2025.
The new package is expected to include Aster 30 missiles, which Ukraine needs to strengthen air defenses protecting Kyiv and other cities from Russian attacks. Italy and France are the only countries able to supply the missiles, according to the report.
Italian Defense Minister Guido Crosetto has continued to publicly support military assistance to Ukraine and is pressing for approval of the package.
The interministerial decree requires signatures from Crosetto, Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani, and Economy Minister Giancarlo Giorgetti. La Repubblica reported that Giorgetti has been hesitant amid concern over opposition from Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini, though the final political decision rests with Meloni.
Crosetto has privately told colleagues that a political obstacle still needs to be resolved, according to the newspaper. Government officials interpreted this as a lack of final approval from Meloni’s office.
La Repubblica reported that some government sources now favor waiting for the US midterms to assess the direction of President Donald Trump’s next two years and calibrate Italy’s policy accordingly.
Domestic politics are also weighing on the decision. Salvini’s League has opposed further military support for Ukraine, while former Prime Minister Giuseppe Conte has continued campaigning against weapons deliveries.
Italian officials have informally urged Ukrainian counterparts to remain patient, according to La Repubblica, arguing that an immediate confrontation over the package could create additional political difficulties for Meloni.
Italy and France had committed to supplying the missiles by the end of October. With Copasir still not convened to examine the decree, another postponement remains possible.
Earlier, UNITED24 Media reported that Italy’s 13th military aid package was expected to include four SAMP/T NG air defense batteries, Aster 30 interceptor missiles, and seven long-range radars, with part of the Aster 30 stockpile planned for transfer by October.

Flight data, satellite images reveal growing US role at Ecuador air base

Flight data, satellite images reveal growing US role at Ecuador air base
- Taura air base in Ecuador has become a growing hub for US anti-drug operations, with around 20 military flights, new construction and signs of a longer-term presence.
- President Noboa backs closer US cooperation, but a former air force chief warned it may be illegal or unconstitutional, and he was removed two days later.
- Local people say the area feels unsafe and neglected, with cartel violence, no drinking water and anger over military abuses, while some welcome foreign troops.
AI generated
TAURA, Ecuador - An isolated Ecuadoran air base has quietly become a key hub in Washington’s expanding war on drug trafficking, according to flight records, satellite imagery, witnesses and military documents uncovered by AFP.
Hidden among shrimp farms and teak plantations about an hour from Guayaquil – the Pacific port that has become the biggest gateway for Latin American cocaine bound for the United States – the Taura complex plays an increasingly prominent role in President Daniel Noboa’s security alliance with Washington.
AFP observed significant works at the decades-old facility, identified around 20 US military flights between June and mid-October, and obtained documents referring to the presence of US troops at the base.
The buildup comes less than a year after Ecuadorans voted against allowing foreign military bases, and has prompted questions from even within the highest ranks of Ecuador’s armed forces.
In a letter obtained by AFP dated Sept 8, then Air Force commander Mauricio Salazar warned the top brass at Joint Armed Forces Command that hosting US troops at Taura, supporting the US Air Force and receiving ongoing flights by US personnel might be illegal or unconstitutional.
His letter states that the US Air Force would “use and modify infrastructure at the base” and operate “temporary support flights” from there.
Two days later, he was removed from his post.
Flight records reviewed by AFP show repeated arrivals at Taura by US military aircraft, including C-130 Hercules and C-17 Globemaster transport planes, V-22 Osprey tiltrotor aircraft and Black Hawk helicopters.
Several of the flights connected Taura with facilities in the United States, including the Cherry Point Marine Corps Air Station in North Carolina and Dover Air Force Base in Delaware, with stopovers in Puerto Rico and Panama.
Satellite imagery also shows the base undergoing significant construction work in recent months.
Several hectares of vegetation have been cleared, new operational areas have appeared around the airfield and dozens of structures consistent with rapidly deployable military tents have been installed inside the complex.
A larger structure measuring roughly 40m by 20m resembles a retractable aircraft maintenance hangar.
Outside the facility, guarded by camouflaged soldiers, AFP observed three construction trucks entering and leaving the base within 10 minutes.
Taura is the only Ecuadoran air base reserved exclusively for military use and boasts a runway of more than 3,000m, longer than that of Guayaquil’s international airport.
President Noboa announced in September that he was working with the United States so that “any type of cooperation” between countries could be carried out there.
“I think it is much more appropriate to move everything to Taura,” he said.
The Ecuadoran Air Force did not respond to a request for comment.
The Pentagon said to contact US Southern Command, which did not immediately answer questions from AFP.
Details on security cooperation closely guarded
Details of the cooperation between Quito and Washington remain closely guarded, with only occasional announcements about the arrival of aircraft and equipment.
The flights detected by AFP arrived as President Donald Trump has expanded military support for anti-cartel operations across Latin America and the Caribbean.
Ecuador’s defence minister announced in August that the United States would deploy three Black Hawk helicopters as part of bilateral security cooperation.
The following month, Noboa said Ecuador would operate two MQ-9 Reaper drones, a platform used extensively by the United States for surveillance and strike missions in conflicts in the Middle East and Africa.
Retired Air Force colonel Roberto Marchan told AFP the aircraft and facilities observed at Taura suggest preparations for a long-term operational presence.
The transport aircraft identified by AFP would allow troops and equipment to move rapidly across the Andean region, he said, while some of the newly installed structures appear suitable for aircraft maintenance and logistical support.
“The US military is establishing a capability there,” Marchan said.
He also argued the growing American presence “diminishes sovereignty.”
“There is some discontent among the rank and file, but they keep it to themselves out of respect for the institution and fear of losing promotions,” he added.
‘Nobody comes around here’
Outside the perimeter fence, daily life bears little resemblance to the military activity unfolding inside.
A few kilometres from the base lies the town of Taura, a community of around 9,400 people connected by dusty roads and surrounded by shrimp farms.
Despite its proximity to one of Ecuador’s most strategic military installations, the town lacks access to drinking water.
Residents say the area has become increasingly associated with cartel violence.
“Nobody comes around here. They think it’s dangerous because sometimes bodies are found dumped,” community leader Fidela Martinez said.
In 2025, the bodies of four boys were found in scrubland near the town after they were tortured, killed and burned by soldiers in a case that shocked Ecuador.
Others have noticed more immediate effects from the expansion of the base.
Alma Goya, 40, runs a small food stall nearby. She said a medical centre inside the military installation no longer serves the public.
“They told us it was because of the state of emergency,” she said.
Not everyone opposes a foreign military presence, in a country that recorded South America’s highest homicide rate in 2025, with 51 killings per 100,000 inhabitants.
“I saw a big plane coming in to land,” said 68-year-old resident Tito Henriquez, who owns a small restaurant, adding that it would be “wonderful” to see foreign troops arrive.
As C-130 transport planes continue to arrive, bulldozers are clearing new sections of land inside the Taura complex. AFP
