How brain implants turn thoughts into speech
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
18:35:43 UTC
03:35:43 KST

How brain implants turn thoughts into speech
Casey Harrell lost his voice to ALS or amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. As a volunteer in a clinical trial, he’s helping scientists test a brain-computer interface. Electrode arrays that are implanted in Casey’s brain send signals to nearby computers, where those signals are translated into words he intended to say.
Casey uses this system every day to talk with his wife, daughter, friends and work colleagues. The moment he realized that it worked was “pure joy,” Casey says. Even though the researchers scripted his words for that first test, “it was a profound moment,” he says. “The possibilities for the near future for me and the rest of humanity were overwhelming to realize.”
This episode of The Deep End: Talk to Me follows Casey and the fast-moving neuroscience that enables him to speak.
Episode 4 transcript
Patients paralyzed from the neck down can manipulate robotic arms with their thoughts. The woman in this video is controlling a robot with her mind. The so-called BrainGate system relies on a sensor of electrodes implanted in the motor cortex of the brain. Researchers hope by implanting electrodes in the brain it can read the brain signals meant to move the muscles involved in speaking, and translate the person’s intention to speak into comprehensive speech produced by a computer.
Laura Sanders: Controlling things with your mind. It sounds like science fiction, but it’s definitely real. Today, we’re going to explore what it’s like to communicate with a brain implant that decodes your thoughts and turns them into words.
[voices] Hey mom, can I tell you something? The voice is absolutely an integral part of your identity. Hello? That added layer of it being you. Do you want to talk? Your voice. Hi. Your voice is you.
Sanders: From Science News, I’m Laura Sanders, and this is The Deep End, Talk to Me. Okay, so what is BrainGate? It’s an experimental system that connects electrodes that are implanted in a person’s brain to a nearby computer. It’s called a brain-computer interface, or BCI. The goal here is big: to help people with paralysis or brain injuries or missing limbs regain control over their world.
Leigh Hochberg: BrainGate clinical trials have now been going on for nearly 22 years. It’s 21 point something at the moment.
Sanders: Leigh Hochberg is the director of the BrainGate Consortium and Clinical Trials. He also has a job at Massachusetts General Hospital, Brown University and the VA.
Hochberg: People who may have had a brainstem stroke and suddenly lost the ability both to move and to speak, or for somebody with ALS who is progressively losing the ability to move or to speak, there’s long been a hope that particularly implantable brain-computer interfaces could restore communication and could restore mobility.
Sanders: In 2004, a BrainGate device was implanted into a person’s brain for the very first time. That person was a man named Matthew Nagle, and he had been paralyzed in an accident. With BrainGate, he could control a computer cursor with his thoughts. Here’s a 2008 report from IT World.
Technology gave him hope. He was one of four testing BrainGate, a new technology where a chip is implanted in the brain that picks up electrical impulses. A computer then interprets those impulses as actions.
Hochberg: Those early studies have been really encouraging, and I think speaks to the potential for the field.
Sanders: Over the years, there’s been amazing examples of people using BrainGate. People have used it to click around on the internet, play video games, one woman who was paralyzed was even able to drink a cinnamon latte with a robotic arm.
Hochberg: And she was able to think about using her own arm and reach out with a robotic arm and pick up that thermos and bring it to her mouth, and tip it towards her mouth, and then put the straw in her mouth and then to take that sip. And while it wasn’t the first time in nearly 15 years that she had had something to drink, it was the first time that she was really able to do so solely of her own volition. I remember the smile on her face when she did that.
Sanders: Over the decades, BrainGate has had a lot of research success in a lot of ways. But what about talking? Hochberg says that when it comes to decoding speech, the science here is still very, very young.
Hochberg: We are at early days, just to be super clear. This is the very beginning of this field. There are only a small handful of people in the world who have had any type of implantable BCI that has been decoding speech.
Sanders: Where does the science stand when it comes to decoding the intention to talk? In the past few episodes, we’ve heard the stories of people who have lost their ability to speak. One of those people was Casey Harrell, and Casey also happens to have a BrainGate device implanted in his brain.
Casey Harrell: My name is Casey Harrell and I am 47 years old.
Sanders: Casey wakes up in the morning, and plugs in.
Casey: The first thing I will usually do after getting out of bed is to plug into the Matrix, so to speak.
Sanders: By that, he means attaching two wires to two pedestals that come out of the top of his head. These two black wires then snake down to nearby computers. Collectively, these electrodes in Casey’s brain, wires from his head, and computers are called the BrainGate 2 neural interface system. So Casey gets it all fired up and then he’s off.
Casey: Unless I have a medical appointment or something that will move me out of the house, I will sit in this position for most of the day, with specifically small breaks in between.
Sanders: All the while, Casey is generating brain signals as he thinks about saying words. These are small, precise electrical pulses made by Casey’s neurons, specifically the cells in his speech motor cortex. Remember how we learned there are over 100 muscles that are involved in speech? These are the parts of the brain that control those muscles.
Casey: I am using a decoder for about ten to 14 hours a day, seven days a week, for the past almost two years, making me the world’s biggest power user of the brain-to-computer interface known to man.
Sanders: Like Jules, Casey has ALS. The disease has slowly taken away his ability to move and to talk.
Casey: I began to lose my ability to talk shortly after my diagnosis in 2020. Then it became a slow motion car crash of multiple years before almost no one would be able to understand me.
By the time of my surgery, only my assistant and my wife, Levana, could really understand me fully. A few other friends who were around often would be able to understand some of what I was saying. I relied upon my assistant and my wife to basically serve as my translators to other people. I did not go anywhere, even a video call without them, either one or both.
Sanders: In July of 2023, Casey volunteered for a clinical trial called BrainGate 2. A UC Davis neurosurgeon put four small electrical arrays onto the left side of Casey’s brain. I wanted to know more about how these arrays worked, so I talked to the neurosurgeon who put Casey’s devices into his brain.
David Brandman: My name is David Brandman, and I am the co-director of the UC Davis neuroprosthetics lab, developing next-generation neurotechnology to help people with paralysis. A brain-computer interface is a device that records brain signals from people that are paralyzed and then translates those brain signals to allow people to control objects in their environment using their minds.
Sanders: Casey’s implant is made of four arrays. Each of them are square and they’re about as wide as a peppercorn. Each array has a bunch of pointy ends that go down into his brain. They look a little like those metal cat brushes. Altogether, the four arrays contain 256 electrodes. These electrodes are all listening to Casey’s brain activity when he thinks about saying a word.
Brandman: The way this device works is by recording the electrical activity of the brain as he tries to speak.
Sanders: The wires from Casey’s head carry those neural signals to nearby computers. That’s where machine learning algorithms attempt to do a very complex sort of matching. The algorithms match Casey’s brain activity patterns to the patterns that predictably occur with certain sounds called phonemes.
Brandman: We translate his brain signals into one of 39 different English phonemes. Now, a phoneme is a building block of language. So if I say the word hello, the word hello can be broken down into ha, uh, uhl, and oh. Hello.
Sanders: Next up, those algorithms assembles these phonemes into words by making its best guess about what Casey wants to say.
Brandman: So I translate this brain activity into a phoneme and then, using artificial intelligence, turn phonemes into words, words into sentences, and sentences into paragraphs.
Sanders: So that’s the process, and it allows Casey to type messages on Slack, text his friends, and send emails. Sometimes in his emails to me, he includes a tagline at the bottom: “Sent from my brain,” with that cute little pink brain emoji. His setup also lets him convert these typed messages into spoken words. These words show up on a screen for him where Casey proofreads them. If everything looks good, Casey gives the go-ahead and the system speaks the words out loud. Brandman tells me that when Casey tries to speak naturally, he can say about six understandable words per minute. That’s pretty slow.
Brandman: Using this prosthesis, he’s in the ballpark of 50 words per minute. Now, as I’m speaking to you right now, I’m speaking on the order of 120 to 150 words per minute, depending on how excited I am, right? So we’ve got him back to about a third of how quickly he spoke as an able-bodied person.
Sanders: I had emailed Casey some questions a few days before our talk. But he didn’t answer them by email. He used his brain-computer interface to answer my questions in real time just by thinking about the words he wanted to say to me. As we introduced ourselves, I saw how the timescale had stretched.
Casey: It’s a challenge because we can have this conversation, but I am slower than the average Joe, even where we grew up.
Sanders: Casey and I both grew up in the south, Casey in the Atlanta area and me in middle Tennessee. But he’s lived in the Bay Area for over 20 years now. And like me, his accent had faded. 
Casey: And yes, I do not have much of a Southern accent anymore. But I love my roots, and I would love to show my daughter where and how I grew up. But it is exceedingly difficult to travel when you cannot move.
Sanders: Before his mobility was limited, Casey did a lot of cool things.
Casey: I spent most of my professional career as a climate campaigner and have went all over the globe, fighting companies who are destroying the Earth and trying to bring some justice to our planet and the people who inhabit it. I am very fortunate because I have been able to do something that I love and also develop some deep friendships and relations with other phenomenal people.
Sanders: My interview with Casey was unlike any I’ve ever had. I’m used to being flexible for interviews. There’s time zone problems, language barriers, mathematicians who sometimes answer my questions in symbols and formulas. But when I logged on to Zoom to talk with Casey, I quickly realized this conversation would be different. I was self-conscious at the beginning of our talk. I fumbled around too much. I’d ask Casey a question and then another one before he had a chance to answer. I accidentally interrupted him a few times. Sometimes I wasn’t sure if he was composing an answer or just waiting for me to say something else. This poor performance on my part wasn’t unusual for Casey at all.
Casey: It is hard for people in your position to stay focused because you were not used to the cadence of a conversation this slowly.
Sanders: He’s right. I was not used to it. And timing, in conversations and in life, is everything. Here’s Greg Bryant of UCLA.
Bryant: Turns, conversational turns, happen at the level of hundreds of milliseconds at the longest. Two hundred milliseconds is a long turn. That’s a fifth of a second. I mean, that’s really fast. So if you are slow at all, it’s noticeable. We have to coordinate our talk so our terms make sense. I can’t take too long or be too quick to respond to your questions. I have to know when to stop and start. We get into this flow, kind of a dynamic, and that is hugely consequential for how we feel about the conversation, the other person, ourselves. You know, it’s all timing.
Sanders: Let’s turn to Jules. His words start in his brain too, but then they take a different route. He types them by looking at letters on a screen, then his voice clone says them. It’s also a slow process and one that takes a lot of mental power, too. At one point in our conversation, MA describes the effort this requires of Jules.
MA: And in his brain, you know, you can imagine he’s doing all these mental gymnastics, to, right now, he’s listening to us. He’s writing something with his eyes, like letter by letter to contribute to the conversation. Plus, he has the answers that he pre-wrote, of the questions that you asked. So it really is like, there’s a whole lot happening behind the scenes that of course anybody who doesn’t have to think about their voice takes for granted. So I’ll pause to let him complete what he’s saying.
Sanders: MA and I wait here for Jules to weigh in. So far you’ve heard ten seconds of the pause. The full length of the pause was a minute and 18 seconds. 
Jules: It is a challenge to communicate with people who don’t interact with me on a daily basis. I have a major bottleneck from my thoughts to actually speaking.
Sandes: And as with Casey, these pauses can introduce difficulties. Here’s speech pathologist Jessica Pietrowski with more on that.
Pietrowski: Humans are not very comfortable with silence, especially communication. And when we’re talking to one another, we fill in the silences, it’s less awkward. And so, someone who’s communicating with a device is probably very used to those latency periods and some more silence and they’re comfortable with it. Whereas the person they’re communicating with is like, let’s keep it going, like this is, I want to help, I want to fill in the blanks, I don’t want this to feel awkward, but in turn, might make it a little more awkward than they think.
Sanders: Jules hates when people read his screen before he’s ready to say what he wants. This particular hate inspired a joke in his stand-up routine.
[Jules audio]: People read off my screen while I’m typing and try to finish what I am saying. It’s like having to constantly deal with an over-competitive charades partner.
Sanders: Jules and Casey encounter other people’s impatience constantly. Not that it isn’t well-intentioned but still, it does not help. Even worse, they face other people’s misconceptions about what they’re capable of. Casey is an interesting, funny and compelling conversationalist. That might not be apparent to everyone who doesn’t slow down to hear him. And that’s an assumption that really bothers him.
Casey: It is incredibly undignified and a terrible consequence of the health care system to treat me like this very quickly.
Sanders: Brandman has seen this dismissal, this mistreatment too. It happens with some of the volunteers he works with on the BrainGate 2 project I mentioned earlier. That’s the same trial Casey’s in.
Brandman: I think as healthcare professionals, we conflate the inability to communicate with the lack of understanding. And I’ve witnessed this firsthand as I’ve watched doctors and nurses interact with my BrainGate participants and then treat them as if they are invalid. Or they’re not there because they’re unable to express themselves. And in fact, I go out of my way in the intensive care unit on the wards and dealing with anyone who’s dealing with my participants to say, look, you know, they’re inside. They’re there. They can understand everything that’s happening. They just happen to not be able to speak. And so please treat them with the respect and dignity that they deserve. And it’s a constant challenge for the participants that I work with. And it’s the reality of which we face and it’s the bias that we have against people that can’t speak for themselves.
Sanders: Casey and the other people with ALS are not alone. Many people who have trouble talking or who just need more time can be judged this way. Here’s Karina Nagin from Bridging Voice.
Nagin: It’s how people see you. And so when you have ALS and you cannot move and you don’t even have facial expressions and you’re hooked up to machines, people assume you’re not there. And we see this every day where people either don’t talk to the person with ALS, assuming that they can’t respond. They speak really loudly and slow. Their mind is completely working.
Sanders: For now, Casey’s words may be slow. But despite all the drawbacks, they are still an absolute marvel. Remember Hochberg from the start of this episode? He’s one of the neuroscientists who works with Casey, and he told me a story from the first few days of testing after Casey’s BCI was implanted.
Hochberg: We gave him a 50-word vocabulary on day one. And even on day one, he was able to say some key sentences from those 50 high-value words.
Sanders: At this point in the testing, Casey was asked to say some pre-specified sentences so researchers could test their system out.
Casey: Most of the sentences were what we called closed loops.
Sanders: That means that the researchers already knew what brain activity patterns should go with the words Casey thought about saying. It was a test to see if the system was working.
Casey: The decoder would be able to verify whether I was right or wrong, giving me short preloaded sentences to say. I was asked to say, “What good is that?”
Sanders: “What good is that?” is not the most poignant sentence ever uttered, but it had a big effect both in the room and for researchers joining remotely by video.
Casey: “What good is that?” Everyone is crying after I am successful.
Sanders: Later on, there was time for Casey to actually express himself.
Casey: It was only after the first few sessions that I had any real time to say what I wanted for a good amount of time in relative privacy. That said, it was pure joy, even though I wasn’t getting to say what I wanted to say in that moment. It was a profound moment for me. The possibilities for the near future, for me and the rest of humanity were overwhelming to realize.
Sanders: Things only got better from there. To set the scene here, during this session, Hochberg was in his office and Casey was at his home, sitting in his living room. Hochberg was watching Casey on a screen.
Hochberg: On the second session, came back and gave him the full 125,000 plus word English dictionary to be able to select from. That is, the decoders and the AI and the machine learning language models would be able to select from basically a full dictionary. And the first thing that he said was something along the lines of, “Is this thing on?” Kind of a funny statement.
The next thing that he said on the second day of using brain-computer interface, or the second thing that we decoded was, “I’m looking for a cheetah.” And it’s the second day. We know there’s all kinds of opportunities for decoding errors. And when I saw that, I said, you know, there’s no way that the second sentence on the second day of using an implanted brain-computer interface is going to say anything about a cheetah. You know, that’s obviously a decoding error and that’s fine.
Sanders: Hochberg could see Casey on the screen, but he couldn’t see something really important that had just happened in the room.
Hochberg: His four-year-old daughter had just walked into the room dressed as a cheetah.
Sanders: Here’s Casey remembering the same moment.
Casey: Yes, I remember this time very well. It was the second session of talking that I experienced early in August 2024. My daughter was incredibly cute in her cheetah outfit. This was one of her favorite animals. They were going through a phase where everything they did was super fast, running from thing to thing. Everyone was thinking that it must have been a mistake that I could not use this language. It was so random. This was only from the people like Leigh who were not in the room with us. The researchers who were there could validate that, yes, I said this. I meant it because of the unique context.
Sanders: It’s one of those moments that many parents have. A kid does something cute, a parent plays along. But in this moment for Casey and his child, it was anything but ordinary.
Hochberg: And she was born around the time that he was diagnosed with ALS. And one could imagine that because the voice that was coming out of the computer was a version of his own voice, and then the rest of the interaction was between dad and daughter. And it was between parent and child.
Sanders: The BCI had given Casey something priceless, a minute to play with his sweet little cheetah.
Casey: I was quietly confident that it would work the way it ended up working for me. I had done a lot of research and the thing was that the technology was on the cusp of a breakthrough. And why not me? I asked myself.
Sanders: Early on in the research project, Casey and his wife had been told not to expect it to work. This was an experiment and the outcome was far from certain. Casey, however, was optimistic.
Hochberg: So to me, seeing it work that quickly and that powerfully really, really emphasized that these are technologies that are going to be able to restore not only activities of daily living, not only key kind of instrumental activities of daily living, but they’re going to restore communication between parent and child. They’re going to restore communication between friends and family and care partners and health care providers.
Sanders: Because this is a podcast about the human voice, I’ve been asking people I interview what their voice means to them. Here’s Casey’s answer.
Casey: It means so much. I think it is the most important thing that I have lost in this whole disease.
Sanders: Getting it back, even in a limited form, is everything.
Casey: It was so amazing to be able to be understood right from the get-go and to be able to talk and respond, respond to my daughter, especially because that was lacking completely from my life up to that point.
Sanders: Casey’s restored voice changed his life.
Casey: It is the ability to parent my daughter. It is the ability to connect with my wife. It is the ability to make a wry joke with my friends. Timing is everything, and that is why having nothing, this is completely revolutionary. And to look back on my previous answer, it is something that really can still improve.
Sanders: At the beginning of the experiment, the research team had told Casey and his wife that they’d be able to try using the BCI for casual chats just a few hours a week. Those hours felt like a huge gift at the time, considering that they hadn’t been able to talk meaningfully for a long time. Here’s Brandman.
Brandman: As we kept coming to his house two or three times a week, things kept getting better and better. And it got to a point where Casey wanted to use the system to say all the things that he wanted to say.
Sanders: Early on, only the researchers could set Casey up with the system, plugging him into the Matrix, as he puts it.
Brandman: And so our research technologist would start coming to his house three, four, five times a week to don and doff the system to enable him to communicate so that he could go about his day. And so at a certain point, we saw, well, he really wants to use the system. Can we streamline this for him? And so we petitioned the FDA to actually allow us to change the clinical trial protocol slightly so that we could train his care partners to don and doff the system without us being there. And so since then, he’s been a near daily user of the system.
Sanders: That’s a far cry from a few hours a week. I’m going to read you some numbers from a research paper Brandman and his colleagues published about Casey’s BCI in Nature Neuroscience in June of 2026.
“Over nearly two years, the participant, that’s Casey, used the BCI for more than 3,800 hours at home with no researchers present to maintain rich, interpersonal communication with his family and friends, independently control his personal computer, and sustain full-time employment, despite being paralyzed. He communicated 183,060 sentences, totaling 1,960,163 words, at an average rate of 56 words per minute. He labeled 92 percent of sentences as being decoded at least mostly correctly.”
Those numbers in this very bare-bones science kind of way are dry, if we’re being honest. But when you stop to think about it, each sentence, each of those nearly two million words, is a tether that connects Casey to his life. They’re messages to his daughter, jokes with his partner, texts to his friends. They’re games of Wordle with his wife and kid. Here’s Casey and his family in a video shot by UC Davis Health.
Okay, so no A, but we got an E. M-I. O. M-I. Good job, team. We are almost there.
Sanders: We’ve talked a lot about words here and the fundamental ways that Casey’s BCI has restored his ability to say them. But Casey’s BCI goes a little bit farther than that. It gives him the ability to add some extras. He’s got some bells and whistles up his sleeve.
Casey: It is really a communication device, first and foremost, and less of a tool that I use to make funny remarks. But I do have that as well in my repertoire. For example, I have the ability to add sound effects to what I am saying. 
Sanders: For instance, Casey has a sad trombone sound.
[sad trombone sound]
Casey: So if I find something funny and want to say, LOL, the theme from the TV show, Seinfeld, will play.
[theme song]
Sanders: This is what he means. These jokes make me think of Jules, which made me wonder if Casey, like Jules, could also swear with his system.
Casey: To answer your question of whether I can curse with this device, I most certainly [beep] can.
Sanders: So for all your inquiring minds, there you have it. Looking ahead a bit, there’s a lot happening on the horizon. The science here is moving fast and many companies are working on similar systems. We’re going to cover that in a few episodes. But for now, Casey is alone. He is an N of 1, as the scientists say – the only person using a brain-computer interface for communication this heavily.
Casey: I hope to have this changed very soon because I feel like everyone who wants this should have the opportunity to have it, especially those who are with my disease.
Sanders: Hochberg tells me that this drive to help others is common among people who volunteer for these sorts of clinical trials.
Hochberg: Each participant in the trial has been just so generous and so clear that they recognize that it’s early days in the research, but they’ve told us that they want to help other people with paralysis. They want to be able to allow people with brainstem stroke or cervical spinal cord injury or ALS or other paralyzing illnesses or injuries to have improved function, to be able to regain control over that computer or regain the fluent speech and communication that they had previously. So it’s that generosity of spirit that has really defined the participants in our BrainGate studies.
Sanders: Casey’s generosity, his drive to help other people, really shines through as we talk. But I want to get back to him. I ask Casey what it’s been like to have this technology in his home, in his brain. He tells me how precious our voices are, and how easy it is for many of us to forget that.
Casey: We take them for granted. The ability to scream when you are running and want to get out some stress. The ability to say sweet nothings into your partner’s ear. These are the things that life is all about. And when you are robbed of those times, you want them back at all costs. And this is why this is good enough for now, and we should have accelerated approval for devices like this.
Sanders: Casey’s BCI is slow compared to the pace of a normal conversation. And it gets things wrong occasionally.
Casey: Sorry, I am trying to answer you. And it is changing what I want to say. And I am being stubborn instead of trying to say it another way, which I will do now.
[Sanders audio] I’m not in any rush. You take as much stubborn time as you want. 
Sanders: And it needs an internet connection and power. And let’s not forget that Casey has an adapter coming out of the top of his head. But these are solvable problems, one that scientists are actively working on. So not perfect, but as Casey puts it, good enough for now.
Scientific efforts to restore voices have been transformative for Jules, Casey, and others. But the ability to separate a voice from a body also raises new possibilities for our societies and for our lives.
MA: His voice will live on in whatever videos or things we’ve captured, whatever he’s left us intentionally, and that’s as far as that goes.
Sanders: On the next episode, we’re stepping out of the lab and into a strange new digital world where voices might not be what they seem.
Hany Farid: And so we are living in, I think, in equal parts an exciting time and a terrifying time. And somehow those are coexisting.
Sanders: What changes are coming in a world where voices can be so easily cloned?
Farid: Today, with nothing more than a keyboard and an internet connection, you can type and you can get an image, a voice, a video of anything, anybody doing or saying anything.

The WhatsApp ‘general’ behind Lula’s election comeback in Brazil
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
18:35:05 UTC
03:35:05 KST

The WhatsApp ‘general’ behind Lula’s election comeback in Brazil
Andre Janones built a WhatsApp army of nearly 11 million subscribers. Did it help Lula win?
As Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva celebrated his election victory on Sunday in Sao Paulo, he placed his hand on the head of a man standing beside him and beaming in a green and yellow Brazilian football jersey.
Lula thanked him for his role in the campaign, calling him “our general”.
Andre Janones, a 42-year-old Brazilian congressman who had spent the final weeks of the presidential run-off building a mass online movement to get Lula re-elected, then embraced the president.
“He played an exponential role in this campaign in lifting the morale of our troops every day, morning, noon and night,” Lula told thousands of supporters who packed Paulista Avenue, the city’s main artery.
Just three weeks earlier, the president seemed to be in trouble. He had finished behind his right-wing rival Flavio Bolsonaro after the first round of voting, his campaign struggling to keep up with the right’s powerful social media operation.
Janones, who had also helped coordinate Lula’s digital operation in his run-off against Jair Bolsonaro in 2022, was convinced Lula’s campaign needed a change – and that he could help turn things around.
He posted a video declaring, “We are going to win this election. Lula will be re-elected president of Brazil.”
His plan centred on a WhatsApp channel he had launched months earlier.
Called Exercito do Lula, or “Lula’s Army”, it had about 60,000 followers after the first round.
By election day, Lula’s Army had grown to almost 11 million subscribers, with Janones widely credited with helping Lula stage his comeback.
How Andre Janones built Lula’s WhatsApp army
Janones is a lawyer and congressman who grew up in a working-class family in Minas Gerais. He made a name for himself through his social media commentary during Brazil’s 2018 truckers’ strike and was elected to Congress that year.
In 2022, he dropped his own presidential bid to endorse Lula, joining his run-off campaign.
“At the time, he became widely known for employing tactics similar to those used by Bolsonarism, despite operating on the left,” said Viktor Chagas, a professor at Fluminense Federal University who studies digital politics and online campaigning.
Janones coined the term “cultural Janonism” to describe his approach, which relied on urgent messages, memes and calls for supporters to take action, as well as what Chagas described as the occasional use of negative campaigning and “content of questionable origin”.
But the scale of Lula’s Army in 2026 was unprecedented, Chagas said.
In the video declaring that Lula would win, Janones urged supporters to enlist as “soldiers” by posting saluting emojis and joining his WhatsApp channel, where he assigned them what he called “missions”.
The tasks were simple, from recruiting three friends to sharing campaign videos to promoting hashtags.
They came in a relentless stream of messages from Janones himself, often written in capital letters. Supporters couldn’t reply, but they could forward the messages or react with emojis, often doing so in the tens of thousands.
Chagas described the strategy as a form of “electoral gamification”, with Janones setting targets for supporters to reach together.
For Andre Pagliarini, an assistant professor of history and international studies at Louisiana State University and the author of a book on Lula, the appeal of Janones’s approach was giving people something they could actually do to help Lula win.
“It became an organising platform that grew exponentially because it spoke to a desire that many Lula supporters evidently had to do something tangible to defeat Flavio Bolsonaro,” he said.
How Lula’s campaign changed its message
But the path to victory wasn’t just about mobilising supporters online.
Pagliarini credited the campaign for also finding a more effective way to tell the story of the president’s working-class past.
“The campaign’s mistake in the first round was to present this history as a finished monument, worthy of admiration but distant from the lives of the people it was meant to represent,” he wrote.
After Bolsonaro mocked the president for having nine fingers during the final televised debate, for example, Lula responded by recalling how he lost a finger at 17 while working a night shift at a factory. He then linked his experience to workers injured as a result of employers’ negligence.
“Unlike Flavio, he reminded voters, he knew the world of work because he had lived in it,” said Pagliarini.
After the debate, Janones spread the message online, promoting the hashtag #SomosTodos9Dedos, or “We Are All Nine Fingers”. Supporters shared the slogan, with some posting photographs of their own amputated fingers in solidarity.
Janones had also publicly called for simpler, less polished campaign videos that showed a more relatable side of Lula, drinking coffee, visiting people’s homes and talking to ordinary Brazilians. Around the same time, the campaign started posting more informal, selfie-style videos.
“Lula was looser in his political communication, less mediated,” Pagliarini said.
Did Lula’s WhatsApp army help him win?
It is difficult to establish whether Janones’s digital army actually delivered votes.
“I am not sure there is a way to empirically connect the group to the outcome,” Pagliarini said.
But he believes Janones helped turn the campaign around.
“Janones himself became a kind of character in the campaign, a cheerleading strategist who seemed confident in a plan that had been missing throughout much of the race,” wrote Pagliarini.
Chagas agreed that it was “difficult to imagine the outcome we achieved without Lula’s Army”, adding that the channel brought together left-wing supporters who had previously been scattered across fragmented online communities, and gave them a way to work together.
The challenge now is keeping that momentum going, Chagas said, pointing to the far right’s use of “permanent campaigning”, maintaining the engagement of supporters between elections.
On election night, at least, Janones kept his soldiers busy.
“EVERYONE TO PAULISTA TO CELEBRATE,” he wrote, urging them to gather on Sao Paulo’s Paulista Avenue. “NOW.”
Later, he asked them not to go to sleep, adding that he’d let them go once he got back from the celebrations.
“Then we’ll discuss a few days off for you,” he joked in a message that drew more than 225,000 reactions.

Russell Brand told police he led a ‘very promiscuous’ life, trial hears
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
18:32:46 UTC
03:32:46 KST

Russell Brand told police he had led a “very promiscuous” life and consensual sexual encounters had been “unfavourably reframed decades later”, his trial has heard.
The 51-year-old comedian blamed the allegations on “defamatory and fictitious” media reports. He said in a statement that he had had sexual encounters in countless locations and scenarios and kissed hundreds of people in public while trying to be “friendly, consensual and warm”.
Brand is accused of seven offences against six women in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999. He denies all the charges.
Wearing a grey suit and pale blue shirt, he sat in the dock on Tuesday as his statements to police were read to Southwark crown court in London.
The jury was told Brand was interviewed four times between November 2023 and July 2025, when he read prepared statements in which he insisted he had “never engaged in any non-consensual sexual activity”.
“I led a very promiscuous life in the past, which I have spent years openly denouncing,” he said in his first statement on 16 November 2023.
Referencing joint reporting by Channel 4, the Times and the Sunday Times, Brand added: “On 16 September 2023, a defamatory and fictitious documentary was broadcast in conjunction with the publication of two national newspapers containing false, anonymised allegations which led to unprecedented media reporting.
“Subsequently, both the media and the police publicly invited additional allegations to be made, which resulted in further encounters being invented or reimagined.”
Addressing an allegation that he had touched an MTV worker’s breasts before dragging her into a toilet and raping her in 2004, he said he did not recall meeting the woman.
“At no point would I have touched [her] breasts unless it was consensual,” he said. “I have had consensual sex in toilet cubicles during parties. I have never forced anyone into a toilet and I have never forced my penis into anyone’s mouth.”
In a statement on 14 December 2023, Brand said he did not remember the women who had come forward to accuse him.
But he added: “It is entirely possible that I may have encountered them and that we may have engaged in consensual sexual activity or physical contact that has since been reimagined.”
Brand described aspects of his past celebrity lifestyle, saying: “My engagement with interested members of the public was friendly, consensual and warm. There was often physical contact. At live shows, press events, junkets and book signings I did my best to be accessible, non-discriminatory and loving. I spent a lot of time at these events.
“I have shared kisses with hundreds of members of the public during press events and photos of many such kisses, in front of hundreds of people, are available online. Everything I did in public once I was famous could be photographed or recorded and end up in the tabloids – I was aware of this.
“I routinely made provocative jokes or comments both with members of the public and during live performances and broadcasts.”
He also went on to detail his promiscuity, saying: “I did on occasion find reasons for leaving, or for asking partners in casual sexual encounters to leave, shortly after the experience had concluded.
“I had sexual encounters in countless locations and scenarios often with people I had just met. The way of life that I have described, the magnitude of the promiscuity, deceptively rendered in recent media attacks, accompanied by advertisements for complainants, have caused consensual encounters to be unfavourably reframed decades later.”
Brand gave similar statements to police in his subsequent interviews on 17 January 2024 and 17 July 2025. In response to police questions after each statement, Brand said: “I have nothing further to add at this time.”
Brand is accused of three counts of rape and three counts of sexual assault. On Tuesday, an allegation of indecent assault was changed to a charge of attempted indecent assault. He has pleaded not guilty to all charges.
The trial continues.

Iraq sentences seven French nationals to prison for belonging to Islamic State
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
18:32:24 UTC
03:32:24 KST

The men were deemed "particularly dangerous because of their role in threatening Iraq's national security, destabilising Iraq and Syria, and their involvement in inciting terrorist operations in other countries," a court statement said.
An Iraqi court sentenced seven French nationals to prison on Tuesday for belonging to the Islamic State group.
Iraq's Supreme Judicial Council sentenced Lakhdar Sebouai, Adel Bou Aoun, Anas Abdul Rahman, Ziad Ahmad, Mehdi Sida and Benjamin Van Han to life imprisonment, which under Iraqi law is equivalent to 20 years.
The seventh defendant, Amza Benabed, 24, was given a 15-year prison term. They now have 30 days to lodge an appeal.
Under Iraqi law, decisions handed down by criminal courts are also subject to review by the Court of Cassation, whether or not the defendant has filed an appeal.
The seven men were deemed "particularly dangerous because of their role in threatening Iraq's national security, destabilising Iraq and Syria, and their involvement in inciting terrorist operations in other countries," a court statement said.
They were among 47 French citizens suspected of links to IS. Held in Syria until last year, they were transferred to Iraq so they could stand trial.
Defence lawyers and representatives of the French embassy were present at the hearing.
Islamic State
The Islamic State group swept across Iraq in 2014, seizing vast swathes of territory in the west of the country and in neighbouring Syria, where it established the seat of its self-proclaimed caliphate.
Although the organisation lost control of these areas several years ago, it still has active cells that periodically carry out attacks in both countries.
Iraq is currently holding thousands of people suspected of belonging to IS. They include more than 5,700 detainees transferred from north-eastern Syria after fighting broke out in January between Syrian government forces and the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF).
The latter had long been guarding the detention centres where jihadist fighters and their families were held following the fall of the caliphate.
Some detainees linked to IS managed to escape during the January clashes, fuelling fears of larger-scale breakouts and leading to the transfer of the remaining prisoners to Iraq.
Iraq's national security adviser, Qasim al-Aboudi, said earlier this month that Syria had requested the transfer to Damascus of around 4,000 Syrians suspected of belonging to IS so that they could be tried there. Baghdad, however, rejected the request.
Al-Aboudi said that once their trials in Iraq were over, some detainees could be sent back to their country of origin to serve their sentences there. It is still not known whether the convicted French nationals could be repatriated.
In the past, Iraq has frequently executed people convicted of terrorism, prompting criticism from human rights organisations. However, the country does not apply the death penalty to foreign nationals whose home country does not provide for capital punishment.

Factors contributing to the death—which was "hypoxic in

Exit polls on Tuesday showed that the opposition bloc led by Israeli opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot gained a narrow edge over Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud bloc in the Knesset, setting the stage for weeks of jockeying to form a government. The day's vote was marked by decades-high turnout in the country's first election since the October 7, 2023 attacks. Follow our liveblog for the latest updates.
Eisenkot says Israel has chosen change, hopes to form government
Opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot said early Wednesday said Israel had chosen change after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and that he would seek to form a new government.
In remarks to supporters, Eisenkot also warned Netanyahu: "Don't you dare use Israel's security for your political needs," in a likely reference to his threats of new strikes on Iran.
Eisenkot warns Netanyahu not to 'use Israel's security' for political ends
Israel's elections: What happens next?
Here are four possible scenarios:
1. Coalition
The parties will immediately begin negotiations to try to reach a 61-seat majority in the 120-member Knesset, but the path forward is far from clear.
President Isaac Herzog will name a candidate who has the best chance to form a government -- not necessarily the party with the most seats, which the initial exit polls showed to be Netanyahu's Likud.
The Arab Israeli parties, particularly Raam, have voiced openness to working with Eisenkot's bloc, but the camp has kept them at arm's length, perceiving their support as a liability during the campaign.
For Netanyahu's bloc, however, there is no obvious place to pick up more seats after some smaller right-wing parties failed to meet the vote threshold for entering parliament.
2. Minority government
If no bloc manages to secure 61 seats, a candidate could attempt to govern without a majority but rather through support on an ad hoc basis from other lawmakers.
In this scenario, lawmakers from the Arab Israeli parties -- whose community makes up 20 percent of the population and generally identifies as Palestinian -- could play a critical role.
Raam, led by Mansour Abbas, has been a kingmaker in the past, having been the first Arab party to join an Israeli government in a short-lived 2021-2022 coalition led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid.
Another Arab movement, the Joint List, has said it would be unlikely to join a coalition government outright, but has offered to provide a "safety net" for any one that ousts Netanyahu from power.
3. National unity government
Considering Israel's extreme polarisation, a national unity government would appear fanciful, but it could theoretically create a less extreme government.
Israeli commentators have often mused on the possibility of a national unity government in which Netanyahu would jettison his provocative far-right allies as well as ultra-Orthodox parties and team up with Eisenkot, who shares Netanyahu's views on many security issues.
Such a grand coalition would also exclude Arab parties.
4. Deadlock and new elections
If no candidate manages to form a government, Israel will have to return to the polls.
The country held four elections between April 2019 and March 2021 due to the inability of politicians to forge a lasting coalition.
The candidate designated by the president will, in principle, have 28 days to form a coalition, with a possible 14-day extension, although there are other procedural ways to prevent an immediate calling of new elections.

The Guardian view on supporting carers: the DWP’s problem is deeper than IT | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
18:30:40 UTC
03:30:40 KST

The reform of carer’s allowance – a benefit paid to people who spend 35 or more hours a week caring for a disabled relative – is overdue and welcome. The cliff-edge design that forces claimants in England and Wales to forfeit their entire payment if they breach an earnings limit of £204 a week by as little as a penny is wrong in principle and made much worse by the appalling way in which rules have been applied.
A Guardian investigation revealed that the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) failed to warn thousands of people who it knew were being overpaid. This resulted in debts and hardship, and hundreds of criminal convictions for fraud. Carers in already difficult personal circumstances described feeling driven to desperation and illness by what one called a “catch-out culture”. Most claimants are women on low incomes; the allowance is £86.45 a week.
The plan to replace this outdated, blunt tool with a taper is a good one. The disincentive to employment built into the existing system is perverse. Adults with caring responsibilities should be encouraged to do paid work in addition to their roles at home if they can. As with child benefit, the promised taper will mean that earnings over the threshold lead to a diminution rather than a loss of the allowance. Demands for repayment should be drastically reduced. Thousands of low-income households with disabled members will gain more freedom as a result.
Details of the policy’s implementation have yet to be set out. But after years of delay and inaction, the main concern is timing. A DWP whistleblower first raised the overpayment issue a decade ago, only for their complaint to be shut down. Successive Conservative governments did nothing despite a detailed 2020 report from the work and pensions committee. Finally, last November, Liz Sayce’s independent review led to the recruitment of extra staff and a new approach. Ministers committed to correcting past errors, including the way that claimants had been unlawfully blocked from averaging their earnings. But progress has been slow, and with the taper expected to be rolled out in 2030-31, the injustice of the current situation looks set to continue for several more years.
The benefit system is complicated, and it is better to make changes properly than to rush through a botched job. But the overhaul of carer’s allowance should not be mistaken for an IT problem. The deeper issue is the ongoing failure to get to grips with the fundamental challenge of care in our society, and to take on board the extent to which millions of people’s lives are shaped by the needs of dependent adult relatives.
Louise Casey has made it clear that her social care commission will deliver recommendations about what it is reasonable to expect of families, as well as the state. There are grounds to hope that her forthright style and years of experience, combined with Andy Burnham’s strong commitment to reform, will finally lead to a breakthrough. In the meantime, the DWP must do all it can to put right the wrongs done to carer’s allowance claimants. There has still been no satisfactory explanation about how such a punitive culture developed. But the new commitment to tapered support is an encouraging indication that the government is now moving in a more compassionate direction.

The European Union remains determined to increase pressure on Russia and engage in meaningful peace negotiations following recent phone calls between the leaders of Finland and Norway and Russian President Vladimir Putin, the bloc's spokesperson told Anadolu on Tuesday.
"We take note of the call, which took place solely on a bilateral basis, and is a follow-up of the meeting in Oslo on 20 October," an EU spokesperson said, referring to recent contacts between Finnish President Alexander Stubb, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store, and Putin.
"On the EU side, we are united in our commitment to put an end to this horrific war of aggression by Russia and to achieve peace that will be just and sustainable. The European Council made clear it remains determined to further increase pressure on Russia so that it stops its brutal war of aggression and engages in meaningful negotiations towards peace," the spokesperson said.
European leaders also underlined the importance of sustained efforts to provide military support to Ukraine, adding that "Russia has not shown any signs it is willing to end its war of aggression."
The EU's remarks came amid criticism from some European leaders.
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen voiced skepticism over what she described as an "uncoordinated" initiative, saying the calls had not been coordinated with other European countries.
She also warned against individual diplomatic approaches to Moscow, arguing that European countries should maintain a united position.
"I think that we should keep Europe together instead of going solo," she added.
The foreign ministers of two Baltic countries, both bordering Russia, also weighed in.
Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna called for increased pressure on Russia, saying every contact with Moscow must convey Europe's unity and determination to support Ukraine.
Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys similarly stressed that Europe must be represented in any negotiations on Ukraine but should not act through fragmented diplomatic initiatives.
"Any contact with Russia must be backed by a united position, real leverage and a list of European demands," Budrys said on US social media platform X, adding that engaging with Putin "individually and without a clear agenda had never worked for Europe."
Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson also reaffirmed his country's support for Ukraine, saying Russia has shown no signs of seeking peace but rather wants submission, which Europe could never accept.

Around 1,000 soldiers from El Salvador have deployed to Haiti, source says
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
19:30:15 CET
03:30:15 KST

By Sarah Morland
Oct 27 (Reuters) - Around 1,000 soldiers from El Salvador have been sent to Haiti after four Salvadoran members of a UN-backed force went missing during a gang ambush on the outskirts of the capital Port-au-Prince, a security official in Haiti told Reuters on Tuesday.
It remains unclear who will command the new Salvadoran contingent, which arrived in a series of flights following the October 18 ambush, how long it will operate in the Caribbean country and how many more soldiers could still be deployed.
The Haitian and Salvadoran governments did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The security official in Haiti spoke on condition of anonymity due to the sensitive security situation.
The surge in deployments comes as the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force has reached about 2,000 troops — just over a third of the planned size a year into its mandate — with limited impacts on Haitian security.
GSF did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Armed gangs in Haiti have for years expanded their influence over the capital and surrounding regions through extortion and brutal attacks that have displaced nearly 1.5 million people and battered its economy and institutions.
Haiti’s leadership has since 2022 requested international security support, despite a difficult history of foreign interventions, after the assassination of President Jovenel Moise a year before led to a sharp rise in gang violence and left a power vacuum.
Successive transitional leaders have since postponed elections due to the violence, and lawmakers’ terms were left to expire.
El Salvador President Nayib Bukele last week announced a military operation to recover the missing Salvadorans, who have been unaccounted for since leaping from a burning vehicle during an ambush, but did not disclose how many troops he would send.
A US military official said the US Southern Command had provided C-130 military transport jets to partially help bring the Salvadoran troops to Haiti.
Other flights between San Salvador and Port-au-Prince, both commercial and military, have appeared on tracking website Flightradar24 and some were reported by the Miami Herald.
NO CLAIM OF RESPONSIBILITY
Bukele has won broad support at home through tough-on-crime policies that several other right-wing governments in the Americas have sought to emulate. Human rights groups say this has come at the expense of due process and hundreds of deaths in custody.
Bukele said the missing Salvadorans were GSF air force technicians returning to base from a market and that he believed they were being held hostage by criminal groups.
No Haitian gang leader has taken responsibility for the attack. Gang leader Wilson Joseph of 400 Mawozo has released videos in which he denies holding the Salvadorans hostage and rejects responsibility for what happened to them.
Prior to the ambush, El Salvador had deployed at least 124 troops as part of the UN-backed force, according to a United Nations report. Bukele later said they were pilots and technicians sent to evacuate injured soldiers, not fight.
While Haitian authorities awaited more deployments for the Gang Suppression Force, the government also contracted a private military company run by Blackwater founder and ally of US President Donald Trump, Erik Prince, that has since 2025 run anti-gang drone operations.
President Luis Abinader of the Dominican Republic, the only country to share a land border with Haiti, said at a press conference on Monday that he was prepared to provide logistical support to the Salvadoran arrivals.
(Reporting by Sarah Morland in Mexico City, Gerardo Arbaiza in San Salvador and Harold Isaac in Port-au-Prince; Editing by Daina Beth Solomon and Bill Berkrot)

Louise Doughty, a judge on the 2026 Commonwealth Short Story Prize whose winner was accused of AI use, thinks so.
"We're only at the beginning of understanding the depth of that threat, and how we can combat it,"
she said.
Readers struggling to 'keep up' with evolution of AI text
How do we even tell whether a book is AI-generated?
ABC Radio National's Critics Corner spoke to Matthew Rubery, professor of Modern Literature at Queen Mary University, trying to answer this big question plaguing some readers.
He said individual readers could still broadly discern whether a text was AI-generated, through "tells" including:
- "It's not X, it's Y" constructions
- Always giving three examples
- Laboured metaphors
But Dr Rubery said the signs of AI usage "change a lot" and it was "very tough to keep up with it".
One potential solution to the issue is a "human-authored" certification.
Many certification schemes are gaining traction around the world, using a range of methods including interviewing the author, asking for their edit history and using AI tools to analyse their work.
Trevor Woods, CEO of the human-authored certification company Proudly Human, said he expected the AI tools to get less and less effective over time.
In the meantime, however, the service has attracted a spike in interest which Mr Woods said could birth a "brand new industry".
Loading...
He predicts the certification industry could be worth "hundreds of millions or billions of dollars" at its height, adding that individual authors, publishers and writers' groups would be footing the bill.
When asked whether big tech companies or governments should be paying for the schemes, he said that was not a realistic aspiration.
"It's like asking the bad guys that have robbed you of everything to then give you a little bit of money back to try and make you feel better about it,"
he said.
Beyond the issue of writers bearing the cost of relieving readers' uncertainty around AI, Ms Doughty expressed concern about the emerging trend of using AI tools to detect AI-generated writing.
She said the tools were used to level accusations at this year's Commonwealth Short Story Prize winner, despite the prize's own investigations finding the winning work was human-authored.
"It's important for the industry to be aware of and guard against frivolous or malicious accusations of AI being used to derail a writer's career," she said.
She said the accusation "will always be easier to level at new authors" who did not have a body of work that AI tools could refer to, producing false positives and degrading reader trust.
"Absolutely, we must not end up with books written by AI, but we must also view AI diagnostic tools with the same level of scepticism,"
she said.
Ultimately, Dr Rubery says, "there will be too many challenges for this to be successful" in the long run.
But advocacy groups have tabled another solution at last week's Joint Select Committee hearings on artificial intelligence.
Groups like the Australian Publishers Association say the government should enact laws requiring the disclosure of AI use in texts, among other improvements.
However, there are fears that the government is going the other way, favouring the interests of tech companies over authors and publishers.
Copyright changes to 'displace' authors from the book market
A proposal leaked last month revealed the government was considering watering down copyright law to create an "opt-out" system where tech companies could train their AI models on authored work without permission until rights holders told them to stop.
At the Joint Select Committee hearings last week, writers and publishers urged the government not to pursue the changes.
"AI companies seeking an opt-out model are asking government to reverse a basic principle: if you want to use someone else's work, you should first seek permission," Hachette Australia and New Zealand head Louise Stark said while fronting up to the committee.
"An opt-out model shifts the burden onto the very people whose rights should be protected."
A submission by the Australian Society of Authors noted it was not a future issue.
Tech companies have already scraped vast amounts of authored work in what a Microsoft executive termed "the largest theft of labour in human history".
The ASA also cited a UK report which found 86 per cent of authors surveyed reported a drop in income due to generative AI.
Kylie Moore-Gilbert, author of The Uncaged Sky, attributes a drop in income to AI-generated summaries and knock-offs of her memoir posted online.
"If someone wanted to read a condensed version of my book in a couple of hours without paying for it, they could listen to this instead," she said.
"Each time a reader watches or listens to such a clip rather than reading or listening to my book is a sale I lose and royalties I don't receive."
Although more than 150 legal cases have been launched in the US over the use of generative AI, the courts have not yet provided definitive answers about enforcing such copyright infringements.
It means AI-generated books are free to "displace" writers from receiving compensation for their own work, says Australian Publishers Association head of policy Stuart Glover.
Dr Glover, who also fronted the Joint Select Committee last week, said it was difficult to determine just how hard AI displacement had hit the publishing industry overall.
However, he attributes the softening of the non-fiction book market to AI.
He said instructional books such as travel guides and cookbooks were at "particular risk".
"Anything which has a hard reference edge to it I suspect is in a kind of terminal decline," he said.
"It's very much a mixed picture, and it requires responsible regulation by the government."
A crackdown on copyright would put more legal pressure on publishers to ensure their writers were not using AI.
"For copyright to subsist it must be created by a human author," Australian Copyright Council CEO Eileeen Camilleri said.
She said using an AI spell-checker or editor would not void an author's copyright, but "where you put in a prompt and get it to generate … copyright is unlikely to subsist".
Dr Glover said that was because "copyright is vested in the expression … the kind of words that you use to create a work".
"It's not vested in the underlying ideas," he said.
"If you generated an output through a machine, even if you had a really great underlying idea but you used the machine to write the idea, then you've got no way of protecting that work and anyone can copy it."
If an author has used AI and it is discovered after their book's release, the publisher may not be able to sell it exclusively.
As a result, publishers have become more vigilant about the work in their submissions inboxes — from updating author contracts and applying for human-authored certifications to getting cold feet about publishing new writers.
The Joint Select Committee on Artifical Intelligence's final report is due on November 30.

The New Relationship Minefield: Your Partner’s AI Chats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
18:29:22 UTC
03:29:22 KST

Lindsey Hall’s boyfriend was asleep on her shoulder when she accidentally discovered what he’d been telling ChatGPT about her.
Her phone had died, so she picked up his to look up something for work. Then she noticed a chat titled “Relationship Issues and Uncertainty.” Inside, she says, were complaints about her appearance, doubts about his attraction to her, and a sentence she still remembers verbatim: “I’m just not proud of her.”
While he peacefully snoozed beside her, she learned that ChatGPT had issued a verdict on the state of their relationship: Her boyfriend needed to end it.
When she first saw the chat title, Hall figured it was about a familiar disagreement: She loved her three cats; he wasn’t an animal person. “This is probably about the cats,” she remembers thinking. She hadn’t expected a list of complaints about her. “Nothing was positive,” she says. “Not one thing.”
Hall got up, collected her toothbrush and charger, and slipped out the front door. “I just had nothing to say,” she says. “I had nothing but rage at that point.”
Couples have long had ways to discover things they weren’t supposed to know about each other: rifling through a journal, stealing a glance at incoming texts, poking around in Instagram or Snapchat DMs. Now, there’s another place to look—and plenty to wish you hadn’t seen. Therapists say they’re working with couples who have discovered their partners asking AI whether they should break up, sharing sexual fantasies, or contemplating how to bring up something they were too nervous to say out loud.
Why a partner’s AI chats can feel like a betrayal
Reading the chats doesn’t necessarily tell you what the other person meant. Was your partner venting after a fight or seriously considering leaving you? Were they asking for help talking to you—or finding a way to avoid it? And who owes whom an apology: the person who read the chats, or the one who shared intimate details about their partner with a chatbot?
When Ilana Grines, a licensed marriage and family therapist in Los Angeles, works with couples, her first question is now: “What have you told AI?” She wants to know if and how both people are using it, what they’re sharing, and whether they’ve discussed any of that with each other. Most haven’t, she says.
“We don’t have a language around our conversations with AI,” Grines says. Couples may understand that a journal is private without having discussed whether the same goes for a chatbot conversation. When someone discovers their partner’s chats, “it creates this huge rupture where one person accessed the other person’s history,” Grines says. “And then it’s nuclear.”
One couple Grines worked with paid for a single AI subscription. The wife, a teacher, used it to grade papers. Her husband used it to explore sexual fantasies, apparently without realizing that conversations from his computer would be visible through their shared account, Grines says. His wife discovered the topic in the platform’s sidebar.
“We know about a third person entering our relationship,” Grines says. “But we don’t know about this third space that we’re creating.”
Sometimes, one partner doesn’t even know that space exists. They might be aware their partner asks AI for help with work or vacation planning—not that they’re also discussing their sex life or wondering whether to stay together. Hall used chatbots herself, but discussing her relationship with one hadn’t occurred to her. “I just didn’t think of it as a tool for that,” she says.
Part of what stings is realizing your partner talked to a chatbot about something they felt like they couldn’t bring up with you, says Shemiah Derrick, a relationship therapist in Chicago. You might also wonder how long they’ve been feeling this way—and whether you would have known if you hadn’t read the chats.
Derrick has seen couples finally talk through a problem—only to start fighting when one person admits they used AI to figure out what to say. The other person’s reaction, as she describes it: “You had to go to chat for us to do that?”
In those cases, Derrick points out that the person turned to AI because their usual way of bringing up problems wasn’t working. They wanted to get through a tough conversation without having the same old fight. “They were trying to do something different,” she says.
What AI chats can reveal about relationships
Giulia P. Davis, a licensed marriage and family therapist in San Francisco, recalls working with a couple after one partner read the other’s AI chats without permission and found complaints and doubts about their relationship. The person who wrote them was still sorting out how they felt. Their partner assumed they’d already made up their mind.
“The partner didn’t find a straightforward confession or plan to leave the relationship,” Davis says.
Davis helped them distinguish “what you really think” from “what you might think about.” Someone might complain to a chatbot after a fight or ask what would happen if they broke up, for example, but not feel that way once they’ve cooled down.
If you find these types of messages, you should ask your partner how they’re feeling, Davis suggests—not assume everything they typed is something they’ve been hiding from you. “A person can have private thoughts without being deceptive,” she says. “Couples need boundaries around private digital spaces just as they do around journals, therapy, or conversations with trusted friends.”
A chatbot also does something a journal doesn’t: It answers. But remember that it’s getting only one side of the story, says Shayce Johnston, a licensed mental health counselor in Gainesville, Fla., and the founder of Human AI Dynamics, which explores how people form emotional and relational bonds with AI. If your partner complains about you and the chatbot agrees, they may feel that someone else has confirmed you’re in the wrong. Johnston describes the reaction this way: “Even the AI agrees with me.” That doesn’t make it true.
How to set boundaries around AI in a relationship
Don’t assume you and your partner agree on what should stay private, says Tammy Nelson, a psychotherapist in Los Angeles and author of Open Monogamy: A Guide to Co-Creating Your Ideal Relationship Agreement. You might think nothing of opening their ChatGPT account; they might consider it the equivalent of reading their journal. Talk about that before you’re staring at something you wish you hadn’t seen.
“What parts are private?” Nelson asks. Keeping a password to yourself, for example, doesn’t automatically mean you’re concealing something that would hurt your partner. “I really do think that it’s important to revisit that conversation pretty often,” she says.
Reading the chats is only part of the issue. What’s OK to put into them? Johnston works with couples in which one person uses AI enthusiastically while the other has privacy, ethical, or environmental concerns. Your partner might be fine with you asking for date-night ideas but uncomfortable with you pasting in their texts or describing your sex life.
Grines suggests starting with a question: “Can you share something you’ve asked AI about our relationship?” You can also ask whether there are subjects they find easier to discuss with a chatbot than with you. The answers can help you get specific about what you’re both comfortable with: using AI to prepare for a difficult conversation, for example, or talking through an argument afterward. Discuss whether those exchanges will stay private or whether you’d like to share what came out of them.
If you’re tempted to skip the conversation and start scrolling through your partner’s chat history, Nelson suggests asking yourself why. Has something happened that makes you distrust them, or are you feeling anxious and hoping what you find will reassure you?
As Davis puts it: “What gets in the way of asking your partner directly?”
What to do after reading your partner’s AI chats
If you’ve read something upsetting, ask your partner what it meant before assuming you know. Davis encourages couples to wait until they’re calm enough to have that conversation. The person who used AI can explain what they were working through; the person who read the chats can explain what hurt.
Johnston wants couples to stop treating the chat history as a verdict on their relationship. Instead, she helps them understand “what the need was, what the fear is, and where the disconnection was that led to the conversation in the first place.” That means making room for both people’s feelings: You can be hurt by what your partner wrote, and they can be upset that you read it without permission.
There may still be a useful role for AI in the relationship. Grines has worked with couples who use their therapy notes to ask a chatbot for questions they can discuss together at home, for example. Johnston sometimes encourages clients to rehearse a difficult conversation with AI before having it with their partner.
“I don’t think AI is inherently anti-relationship,” Grines says. But she wants couples to consider whether it’s helping them talk to each other—or becoming the only place they’re willing to be honest. “AI can be a bridge into communication,” she says, “or it can be a place where communication goes to die.”
For Hall, finding out how her boyfriend used AI made her question conversations she’d once felt good about. Before meeting in person, they’d spent months messaging. He’d seemed warm over text, she says, but could be colder face-to-face. She’d wondered: “What am I doing wrong?”
His chat history offered a possible explanation. When they’d discussed serious or emotional subjects, she says, he’d pasted her messages into ChatGPT and asked it to help him respond. She remembers his instruction: “Placate her.”
“It’s horrifying,” she says now.
She still wonders whether he would have spoken so harshly about her to another person, or whether something about talking to AI encouraged him. “Would you have said all those things to a person in that way?” she asks.
After she left his house, he began texting her. She turned off her phone. When he later came to her home, she told him she’d read the chats. By then, she says, she felt there was little left to discuss: “I just read exactly how you feel.”

Rights groups say proposed French law to make rioters pay for damage is anti-democratic

Rights groups say proposed French law to make rioters pay for damage is anti-democratic
Critics have said that a proposed French law that would make rioters liable to pay thousands of euros for any damage they cause is anti-democratic, as it could undermine the legitimate right to protest. The government put forward the law in a bid to quell looting and vandalism on the fringes of ongoing national protests over poor conditions in French schools and the high cost of living.
A proposed French law making rioters liable to pay up to €10,000 ($11,150) for damage they cause faces a backlash from rights groups and some lawyers who say it attacks the basic democratic right to take to the streets to protest.
President Emmanuel Macron's government, under pressure to quell social protests accompanied by some of France's worst unrest in years, says the law is needed to compensate victims of the vandalism that often follows protests, such as the looting and rioting seen across the country on October 17.
Read moreFrance faces reckoning with public order policing after violent protest weekend
But critics say the draft bill, being debated in parliament this week, is worded in such a way that legitimate protesters who happened to be close to the scene of any violence could also be deemed legally responsible for it and face prosecution.
"Around the edges of a protest there can be those who engage in violence or damage with no involvement from the vast majority of peaceful, legitimate demonstrators," said Hanna Bouchareb, a Paris-based lawyer who represented some of those accused in fast-track trials of taking part in rioting on October 17.
Read more'I didn’t know it was theft': Trials begin in Paris following October 17 violence
"It's very problematic because it undermines the right to protest," she told Reuters.
The text states that anyone who knowingly formed part of a group of people would be held jointly responsible for any damage caused by any member of that group.
It further allows the state to seize welfare entitlements of those convicted, or those of their parents if they are minors, to help pay the costs.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
French businesses and retailers say they have lost millions of euros either through looting or vandalism or by being forced to shut their shops and board their windows during protests.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez, who offered his resignation to Macron last week after security forces were overwhelmed by the unrest, rejected arguments the law undermined the principle that individuals were only accountable for their own actions.
"What this draft law changes is that we are creating a joint responsibility – not a collective one," Nuñez, whom Macron asked to remain at his post, told broadcaster TF1.
That is a distinction rejected by France's Human Rights League (LDH) and a group of trade unionists who signed a column in Le Monde newspaper this weekend demanding it be scrapped.
Police were accused in 2020 of using excessive force against "yellow vest" anti-government protesters and there was criticism then of a subsequently watered-down law banning circulation of images of police officers in some circumstances.
In recent weeks, protesters have again accused police of heavy-handed tactics against the student protesters while lawyers including Bouchareb have raised legal concerns over the fast-tracked convictions of some of those accused of rioting.
Backers of the proposed new law point to surveys showing broad public support for it. The National Rally (RN) party of Marine Le Pen – the far-right frontrunner for next year's presidential election – said it would go even further.
"The vandal's law is good in that it recognises the principle of joint responsibility," RN senator Edwige Diaz told French television. "But not with a cap at €10,000."
