File photo: Two people holding an umbrella brave strong winds and rain as high tide waves hit the coast ahead of the impending landfall of cyclonic storm 'Arnab', in Visakhapatnam, Andhra Pradesh.
NEW DELHI: The ministry of civil aviation on Tuesday reviewed aviation safety and operational readiness as Cyclone Arnab is expected to intensify into a very severe cyclonic storm and cross the Andhra Pradesh coast on October 28, bringing winds of 125–135 kmph and gusts of up to 150 kmph, according to the India Meteorological Department (IMD).In a statement issued by the Press Information Bureau (PIB), the ministry said flights to and from coastal Andhra Pradesh and southern Odisha, including Bhubaneswar, were expected to be among the most affected. Hyderabad, Varanasi, Prayagraj and Gorakhpur could also see knock-on delays depending on the storm’s track.
The ministry reviewed preparedness with the Airports Authority of India (AAI), Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA), Bureau of Civil Aviation Security (BCAS), IMD, airlines, airport operators, the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) and disaster management authorities in Andhra Pradesh, Odisha and West Bengal, among other agencies.
Flight operations suspended at three Andhra airports
According to the ministry, operations at Visakhapatnam airport were suspended from the afternoon of October 27. Flights at Vijayawada and Rajahmundry airports were suspended after 7pm the same day. The Delhi–Bhogapuram–Delhi service has also been cancelled for October 28.Airlines have announced cancellations and operational changes:Air India: Six cancellations on the Delhi–Visakhapatnam–Delhi route on October 27 and the Delhi–Vijayawada–Delhi route on October 28.
Air India Express: Thirteen cancellations, mainly affecting Visakhapatnam services to and from Hyderabad, Bengaluru and Vijayawada. Varanasi–Bangkok and Bangkok–Visakhapatnam flights have also been cancelled.IndiGo: All flights at Visakhapatnam have been suspended, along with services at Vijayawada and Rajahmundry after 7pm on October 27. The ministry said cancellation figures were provisional.Akasa Air: Delhi–Bhogapuram and return flights scheduled for October 28 have been cancelled. All other flights were expected to operate.Alliance Air: Operations were continuing normally, with no cancellations reported so far.
Passengers advised to check flight status
The ministry has advised airlines to follow operational guidelines for adverse weather, inform passengers about delays and cancellations, and comply with applicable rebooking and refund rules.
Passengers have been urged to check their flight status through their airline’s website, app, helpline or SMS before leaving for the airport, and not to travel unless their flight is confirmed. They have also been advised to allow extra time for their journeys, as waterlogging and road closures are likely in coastal Andhra Pradesh and Odisha.The ministry said the aviation secretary had asked airlines and airport operators to provide additional assistance to senior citizens, persons with reduced mobility, parents travelling with infants and passengers requiring medical support.Passengers with unresolved complaints have been advised to approach the airline first and then escalate the matter through the AirSewa portal or app.The ministry said passenger safety remained its top priority and that further updates would be issued as weather conditions changed.

The Guardian view on the far right’s plans for Brussels: doing the work of Xi, Putin and Trump | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
18:25:40 UTC
03:25:40 KST

Following the Brexit referendum in 2016, Marine Le Pen was in a predictably celebratory mood. Britain’s vote to leave the European Union, she told one interviewer, was the first breach in the “Brussels Wall”. Ms Le Pen’s Front National party was at that point committed to taking France down the same path, given the chance. But as the UK’s self-inflicted economic wounds became a cautionary tale for the rest of Europe, the notion of Frexit was put on ice.
Instead, Ms Le Pen now hopes to lead far-right allies in hollowing out the EU from within. This month, both she and the leader of Alternative für Deutschland, Alice Weidel, outlined their visions of a “Europe of nations” in which EU institutions would be stripped of both cash and power. Ms Weidel’s “new deal for Europe” would abolish elections to the European parliament, and seek German opt-outs in areas such as migration, defence and common borrowing. Ms Le Pen’s party, now called National Rally, proposes slashing French contributions to the EU budget by 60% over a five-year presidential term, and ending the role of Brussels in proposing common policies for the 27 member states.
Similar ideas have long circulated in far-right thinktanks. But they are now in the programmes of parties that lead the polls in France and Germany – Europe’s historic engines of integration. Ms Weidel has targeted 2029, when the next German election is due to take place, as the year in which a critical mass of anti-EU leaders can begin to effectively unravel the European project. By then, Eurosceptic ultra-nationalist parties could conceivably be in power in France, Italy and Poland.
Faced with plotting in plain sight and a putative timetable for action, the response of pro-European forces has been distinctly underwhelming. From the economy to the climate emergency and security, Europe faces challenges that can only be properly addressed through the greater pooling of resources, allowing it to punch its continental weight. Mario Draghi, the former head of the European Central Bank, has warned that without an industrial policy to compete with China and the US, the continent faces an existential struggle. But other than the beleaguered and soon-to-be-departed French president Emmanuel Macron, it has been hard to find any EU leader speaking with the same sense of urgency.
Ms Le Pen and Ms Weidel’s interventions should be treated as a wake-up call. The kind of Europe they envisage would be less than the sum of its parts, distracted and weakened by competing national interests. In relation to defence, the moves towards European strategic autonomy would be undermined. The green transition, in the absence of collectively agreed goals, would stall. Adopting such a direction of travel would be an act of continental self-harm, opening up vulnerabilities that Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin (and any Maga successor to Donald Trump) would eagerly exploit.
As a pivotal period in the history of the EU approaches, the time to start making such counter-arguments is now. The case for a strong Europe at a time of geopolitical volatility and anxiety is overwhelming. But it will need vigorous advocates as a battle for hearts and minds looms. For the time being, to paraphrase WB Yeats, the pro-Europeans appear to lack all conviction, while their opponents are full of passionate intensity.

How a 16th century pirate accidentally spawned a centuries-old math problem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
18:25:19 UTC
03:25:19 KST

This article is from Proof Positive, our friendly newsletter that explores the joys and peculiarities of math. Sign up today for a weekly math essay and puzzle in your email inbox.
Opinions about Sir Walter Raleigh, who sailed the seas in the 16th century, vary widely. Was he a gifted navigator and explorer or a brutal pirate who terrorized the waves? According to one legend, Raleigh was gentlemanly enough to place his cloak in a mud puddle so that Queen Elizabeth I wouldn’t get her feet dirty. But less well known is that with a simple question, he profoundly influenced an area of mathematics that experts still puzzle over today.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
During his expeditions, Raleigh’s ships carried cannonballs on board for protection against enemy attacks. He wanted to quickly know how many he had at a glance, so he presented his scientific advisor, Thomas Harriot, with a seemingly simple task: calculate the number of cannonballs stacked in a pile. Harriot quickly found a convenient formula for how many were arranged in a square pyramid based on the number in the bottom row and was able to present Raleigh with a satisfactory solution.
But Harriot wondered whether that arrangement was truly the densest possible packing of spheres. What if there were an infinite number of cannonballs to consider? In 1606 Harriot wrote a letter to astronomer Johannes Kepler outlining this question. Five years later the scientist published a hypothesis that went down in history as Kepler’s conjecture. To create the densest arrangement of spheres, you start with one sphere in the middle and add six more around it to form a hexagon pattern that can be replicated across an entire plane. A second layer is then formed by nestling the spheres into the resulting spaces like eggs in a carton. The third layer corresponds to the first—and the arrangement continues. Kepler was able to calculate how much free space is created by such stacking: about 26 percent.
It’s worth noting that a finite number of spheres can be arranged much more efficiently; for instance, they can be lined up like a sausage. But Kepler’s problem revolves around an infinite number of spheres in three spatial dimensions. Other configurations Kepler investigated produced larger gaps.
In 1773 physicist and mathematician Joseph Louis Lagrange proved that in two dimensions, the hexagonal configuration is indeed the most space-efficient. It results in a density of about 90 percent, meaning there is only 10 percent empty space. And in 1831 the exceptional mathematician Carl Friedrich Gauss was able to prove that Kepler’s conjecture is correct if you assume that the spheres are arranged only in regular lattices. In this case, it is possible to distribute the first few spheres in space and arrange all the others according to the same pattern.
Gauss could not rule out the possibility of an even denser, more chaotic arrangement, however. This possibility makes the problem considerably more difficult because in this case, every sphere could be placed anywhere—and not just the first few objects. More than a century would pass before the next significant breakthrough.
Because it is impossible to test infinitely many cases, Kepler’s conjecture needed to be reduced to a problem in which only a finite number of configurations are relevant. In 1953 Hungarian mathematician László Fejes Tóth proved that this is indeed possible. The basic idea is to divide three-dimensional space into infinitely many regions and prove that the Kepler configuration is densest in all regions—because then it is also densest in all of space.
More specifically, Fejes Tóth used a kind of diagram in which he created dots representing the center of the spheres—ensuring each was the diameter of one sphere apart—and then drew boundaries halfway between each point of neighboring points to create a series of separate cells. These so-called Voronoi cells, Fejes Tóth conjectured, must be at least as large in volume as a regular rhombic dodecahedron surrounding a sphere of radius 1. (The rhombic dodecahedron is the shape produced by the most efficient sphere packing in Kepler’s conjecture.) He then considered up to 13 cells and formulated a new problem: if it could be shown that the volume of Voronoi cells is always larger than that of rhombic dodecahedra, then Kepler’s conjecture would be true.
Instead of running through an infinite number of possibilities and checking whether the corresponding packing density is always lower than that proposed by Kepler, Fejes Tóth had proposed a way to examine just a finite number of cases. Even so, the number of arrangements to be tested was enormous—beyond human capabilities alone. It wasn’t until 1992, when American geometer Thomas Callister Hales began working on the problem using a computer, that the effort moved forward. Hales, together with his student Samuel Ferguson, sought a way to work through the numerous cases to prove Kepler’s conjecture, building on Fejes Tóth’s preliminary work. They examined more than 5,000 different arrangements of spheres and showed that their density was lower than that proposed by Kepler, a task that involved approximately 100,000 problems for a computer to solve. The complete implementation took four years.
Hales finally submitted the 250-page proof and three gigabytes of computer files to the prestigious journal Annals of Mathematics in 1998. The reviewers took another four years to examine the proof and concluded that they were 99 percent certain of its correctness.
Although this confidence was sufficient for publication in the journal, Hales was still not satisfied. He worried that he might have made a mistake or overlooked a special case. So in 2003 he launched the Flyspeck project (from the acronym FPK, short for Formal Proof of Kepler) to have his calculations checked by a computer-aided proof assistant. It took 11 years to complete that project, but computers fully verified Hales’s work—and found that the proof was correct.
More than 400 years passed between Sir Raleigh’s original question and the complete solution of the problem. But mysteries remain around dense sphere packing, particularly if you consider the question in higher dimensions. As Henry Cohn, then a mathematician at Microsoft, told Scientific American in 2016: “Part of what I love about the sphere-packing problem is that every dimension has its own idiosyncrasies ... Some dimensions just behave much better than others.”

‘If they’re honest’: Trump casts latest suspicion on US midterm elections
Trump’s comments come as his administration files legal challenges to Democrat-led US states over election integrity.
United States President Donald Trump said he would respect the results of next week’s midterm elections if they were “honest,” as his administration expanded a legal battle to assert power over state authorities running the highly-watched contest on November 3.
“I will if they’re honest elections,” Trump responded to reporters on Tuesday when asked if he will respect the outcome even if his Republican Party loses control of the US Congress.
Trump’s remarks came a day after his Department of Justice (DOJ) threatened the northwestern state of Washington with legal action if it did not remove around 400 people it claims are not US citizens from its voter registration rolls.
“The timing of this request—one week before the General Election—is no doubt intended to cast unfounded suspicion on the results,” Washington Secretary of State Steve Hobbs said in a statement on Monday, addressing the request received in a letter that gave the state until Wednesday at noon local time to respond, or face what the DOJ called “emergency relief”.
Hobbs’s office said it was reviewing the list of 400 alleged noncitizens, but had already found some of them to be based on outdated information. The DOJ was citing a record from 1994, for instance, to claim one person was a noncitizen on its list, Hobbs said.
“Washington elections are secure. Cases of voter fraud, including noncitizen voting, are incredibly rare, and every voter attests to their eligibility by signing the declaration on their ballot return envelope in every election,” Hobbs said in the statement.
Last month, the state of Washington successfully argued in a lawsuit that it was not obligated to turn over its entire voter list to the DOJ. It was among dozens of Democrat-led states to have faced the demand from the Trump administration and had courts side with it.
Despite the setbacks in court, Trump’s DOJ has continued to try and cast suspicion on the outcome of the November 3 elections, in particular by attempting to claim large numbers of noncitizens are voting in Democratic-led states, a claim that has been repeatedly dismissed by bipartisan voting rights groups.
Last week, the DOJ filed a lawsuit against the state of Alaska, saying it would seek to block certification of its Senate election if the Republican incumbent, Dan Sullivan, did not win. The DOJ said because the state was allowing another candidate who was also named Dan Sullivan to appear on the ballot, local authorities were failing in their responsibility to fairly run the election. On the ballot, Senator Dan Sullivan appears with information indicating that he is the incumbent.
The Senate race is one of several around the country that could go the way of the Democratic Party and see Trump’s Republicans lose control of the legislative body. On Friday, Trump said he personally had told the DOJ to file the lawsuit against Alaska.
Earlier this month, California said it had received a letter from the DOJ saying the state must review a list of around 20,000 noncitizen voters. California authorities said a large percentage of those on the list were in fact people who appeared to have been born in the US, which would automatically make them eligible voters.
The DOJ has also said it is planning to deploy a record number of election observers across the country on November 3 to watch for any irregularities, despite the objection of local officials in several Democratic-led states, including New Jersey and California. Historically, the DOJ has sent observers to watch for issues at places with a record of civil rights violations and obstacles that would keep minorities or disenfranchised groups from the polls on Election Day.

Russian steel lobby still blocks Ukraine's access to EU market – Metinvest executive
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:23:12 EET
03:23:12 KST

A Russian metallurgical lobby remains active in the EU, actively obstructing Ukrainian metal products from accessing the European market and seeking to push Ukraine out, Oleksandr Vodoviz, head of the CEO's office at Metinvest Group, said during the panel "Global Markets: Closed Doors or New Opportunities" at the 12th Kyiv International Economic Forum (KIEF) titled "People. Business. Economy. What's Next?" on Monday.
"We see that the Russian lobby is also present in Brussels. They hire companies and fight to keep Ukraine out. And when we enter certain offices there, a Russian delegation is leaving them," Vodoviz stated.
He recalled that after the outbreak of the war, Europe imposed sanctions, Russia stopped supplying almost all steel products to the European market, and Ukraine managed to partially replace those supplies. However, Vodoviz noted that there are now efforts to bring Russia back to the European market, while quotas for Russian slabs have effectively not been reduced.
The head of the CEO's office specified that, in addition to Europe, China had historically been a key market for Metinvest, to which the group supplied iron ore. However, due to a significant increase in production costs and logistics expenses, the company had to abandon supplies to distant markets, and Europe will remain its key sales market.
Regarding Europe, he identified the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) carbon levy and the quotas introduced in July this year, set at 670,000 metric tons annually, as barriers to entering the market. Previously, supplies to the EU amounted to approximately 2 million metric tons. He said Metinvest had recently acquired a pipe plant in Romania, but the EU introduced quotas two months later, meaning the group can no longer supply Ukrainian steel to the plant for pipe production.
"I know that the Romanian government also raised this issue at the meeting of foreign ministers in Dublin, but there were no answers, and there still are none," Vodoviz said.
According to him, the European Commission has broken its promises to Ukrainian steelmakers regarding CBAM and quotas, and its overall policy is unpredictable and unfair, given that Ukraine is at war, plants in the industry have been destroyed, and the sector has been deprived of access to financing.
"We are asking the European Commission and the EU to take a somewhat broader view of financing for Ukrainian metallurgy and Ukrainian metallurgical companies' access to the European market," Vodoviz said.
The senior executive expressed concern that, because plants in Ukraine have been idled as a result of shelling, the group may be unable to use its EU quotas. In December 2026–January 2027, the European Commission could use the quota data for those six months to make a final decision and introduce quotas for the next five to 10 years.
"We are very concerned that our plants have been destroyed and we cannot supply products, while they could take these six months and set some minimum quota for the next 10-year period. That could also happen, which is why our government is currently engaged in a very difficult negotiation process," Vodoviz said.
Asked what the state could do to help in this situation, the head of the CEO's office noted that it was difficult to ask anything of a state that was essentially bankrupt, given that 51% of Ukraine's budget is financed from abroad. He said one could only sympathize with officials who receive a huge number of requests from businesses seeking assistance.
"But there are things that do not require money. For example, there is a war-risk insurance fund that the state wants to establish. We support this idea. The question is: where was everyone over the past five years, and why didn't we do this in the very first year? There is also the issue of compensating war-related losses using funding from European donors. At present, we have funds blocked that flow directly into the state budget. But this money could be used to finance funds for the recovery of strategic industries. We know that the Ministry for Communities, Territories and Infrastructure Development has established such a fund, and it is operating," Vodoviz stated.
Metinvest is a vertically integrated group comprising mining and metallurgical enterprises. The group's enterprises are located primarily in Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Dnipropetrovsk regions. The holding's principal shareholders are SCM Group (71.24%) and Smart-Holding (23.76%), which jointly manage it. Metinvest Holding LLC is the management company of Metinvest Group.

Anthropic Flags Gas Supply as One of Its Biggest Near-Term Risks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
18:20:28 UTC
03:20:28 KST

Data centers’ reliance on private natural gas plants is a key near-term risk to Anthropic. In the company’s IPO filing on Monday, it warned that the data center gas buildout could drive prices higher in some regions, affecting its AI ambitions and other data center operators around the country.
As America’s data center boom keeps growing, the facilities are set to consume a staggering amount of natural gas, with many companies opting to build their own plants rather than wait years for grid connection. Energy analyst company Cleanview estimates behind-the-meter gas projects in development as of October 2026 at 110 gigawatts, up from just 20 gigawatts in July 2025.
Competition from other natural-gas-fired data centers could leave Anthropic exposed to “fuel price volatility and supply disruptions that are outside of [its] control,” the company wrote in its IPO filing, and “could drive up the price of natural gas in such areas and may adversely affect [its] ability to contract for firm fuel supply.”
The surge in demand for gas comes on top of an already tight market for natural gas. US export terminals are sending more gas abroad for a variety of reasons, including geopolitical conflicts and federal support for exports. Export demand is expected to double over the next decade.
Still, data centers could add a hefty chunk of demand, even if just some of what’s in the pipeline is built. BloombergNEF estimates that grid-connected data centers alone could add an additional 15 billion cubic feet per day of natural gas demand by 2035, a 15 percent increase in overall demand. Adding on a conservative estimate of onsite gas capacity in the pipeline would add another 3 billion cubic feet per day by the next decade.
Anthropic has traditionally relied on renting compute from major cloud service providers. Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and SpaceX are specifically named in the IPO. (Anthropic is renting server space from the latter’s Colossus data centers in Memphis, Tennessee, which is facing a lawsuit for relying on unpermitted gas turbines.)
But the company has moved in recent months to directly lease and develop data centers, in a bid to lessen its reliance on other tech giants and more directly control its own data centers. In the IPO, it singles out its $50 billion partnership with Fluidstack, announced last year, which “provides data center development and operations services” for the company. It has announced data center sites in Texas and New York.
Doing so, though, exposes it to more risks, including the rises in natural gas prices. The company has also been tied to developing data centers with major onsite gas projects in states as spread out as Louisiana, Texas, and West Virginia. The latter could eventually be among the largest gas plants in the US, according to developer Nscale’s own IPO filing.
The geographical dispersion of its data centers opens Anthropic up to regional gas supply shocks and markets. That’s particularly true in the Southeast, where projects will have to compete with LNG exports.
“It wouldn’t be surprising if you start to see gas start to get more expensive in Louisiana and Texas, where all the LNG projects are concentrated,” says Enrique Gonzalez, BNEF’s head of gas research for the Americas.
Texas is also the national hot spot for behind-the-meter data center development, putting multiple developers in competition for the same, potentially limited gas supply. Anthropic acknowledges this risk in its IPO filing, writing that “we expect increased competition among users for the same natural gas supply and pipeline capacity in those areas. This competition could drive up the price of natural gas in such areas and may adversely affect our ability to contract for firm fuel supply.”
Any strain on gas supply could have knock-on prices for home energy bills. Gonzalez thinks that natural gas producers learned their lesson from the energy crisis of 2022, when high gas prices caused production to increase, in turn knocking down prices. While markets are unlikely to be that extreme in the coming years, “if hub prices rise, there’s a chance—unless you have legislation—that it goes to consumers,” he says.
One solution for this is, of course, to look at renewables, which also have the added climate benefit of being carbon-free. But Anthropic mentions them once in its IPO filing, and only to dismiss them. “Newer sources of generation, such as solar, wind, battery storage, nuclear, and geothermal power, may not be available in the quantities or on the timelines we require, or may be available only at higher cost,” the prospectus states.

X-Bow to build boosters for CoAspire’s CHAOS cruise missile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
18:19:04 UTC
03:19:04 KST

- CoAspire selected X-Bow Systems to develop and produce booster motors for its ground-launched cruise missile under the U.S. Navy’s CHAOS program.
- The U.S. Navy awarded CoAspire a $70 million CHAOS agreement in July; the value of X-Bow’s subcontract has not been disclosed.
X-Bow Systems will build the solid rocket booster that launches CoAspire’s ground-based cruise missile under the U.S. Navy’s CHAOS program, an effort to give allied nations a low-cost weapon for striking ships and land targets.
The Albuquerque, New Mexico, company said Tuesday that CoAspire, the prime contractor, selected it to develop and produce the ground-launched solid rocket motor boosters for the Coalition Heterogeneous Affordable Offensive Strike program. Neither company disclosed the value of the subcontract, the number of motors involved or a delivery schedule.
CoAspire’s CHAOS weapon is a ground-launched version of its Rapidly Adaptable Affordable Cruise Missile-Extended Range, or RAACM-ER, which cruises on a small turbojet. Because a turbojet cannot get a missile off a launcher from a standstill, a solid rocket motor fires first, pushes the missile clear and accelerates it until the wings and jet engine can take over, after which the spent booster falls away. The Tomahawk, the Harpoon and the Naval Strike Missile all use the same arrangement when fired from ships or ground vehicles, so the concept itself is long established; what CHAOS changes is the price target and the intended buyers.
The U.S. Navy selected CoAspire for CHAOS on July 17 under a $70 million prototype Other Transaction Agreement covering Phases 1 and 2. The agreement tasks the Virginia company with designing, building, testing and delivering the ground-launched RAACM-ER to the Navy’s munitions portfolio office and its PMX-201 program office, and CoAspire said at the time that the system would pair the missile with a booster and launcher designed specifically for the program. Tuesday’s announcement identifies who will make that booster.
The Navy intends to offer the missile through Foreign Military Sales to allies and coalition partners that need an affordable maritime strike weapon that can be produced in large numbers, although neither the service nor CoAspire has named the countries involved. CHAOS grew out of an earlier requirement known as Coalition Affordable Maritime Strike, which sought a missile costing about $1.5 million that could hit ships at least 140 nautical miles (260 km) away with a warhead under 500 pounds (227 kg). The Navy has not published a unit price target for CHAOS itself.
CoAspire is not the only contractor in the program. In September, the Navy awarded Zone 5 Technologies $65 million to build a maritime strike version of its AGM-188 Rusty Dagger, and the two companies also compete in low-cost missile efforts run by the U.S. Air Force and the U.S. Army.
The RAACM family began as an air-launched weapon roughly the size of a 500-pound Mk 82 bomb. CoAspire builds much of the airframe through additive manufacturing, which the company says frees internal volume for fuel and lets it introduce new variants without retooling a production line. The larger RAACM-ER is the basis for the CHAOS missile, and CoAspire claims it can reach maritime targets at up to 1,000 nautical miles (1,850 km), a figure that has not been demonstrated publicly. A closely related ground-launched version called GHOST, which also relies on a solid rocket motor to leave its container, is CoAspire’s entry in the Pentagon’s Low-Cost Containerized Munition program.
“Rebuilding the nation’s arsenal demands a fundamentally different industrial base,” said Jason Hundley, founder and CEO of X-Bow. “Our digital-first manufacturing and proprietary Additive Manufacturing of Solid Propellant technology are built to deliver advanced, reliable systems at a cost and velocity the legacy industry can’t match.”
Conventional solid rocket motors are usually produced by mixing propellant in large batches and casting it into motor cases, a process that involves long curing times and dedicated tooling for each design. X-Bow uses an additive process that it says shortens that cycle and adapts more easily to different motor sizes, and it opened a production site in Luling, Texas, in late 2025.
The CHAOS selection is X-Bow’s third booster award in three weeks. On Oct. 7, the company received a U.S. Navy prototype agreement worth up to $69.7 million to develop a booster for a next-generation Navy weapon and to install tooling in Luling for up to 500 motors a year. Five days later, Leidos picked X-Bow to supply booster motors for its entry in the U.S. Army’s Low-Cost Containerized Munition program, with full-rate booster production

Türkiye's Erdogan chairs cybersecurity meeting on digital sovereignty, AI threats

Türkiye's Digital Sovereignty Strategy, aimed at strengthening the country's sovereignty in the digital sphere and reducing dependence on foreign technologies, was presented to the Cybersecurity Board on Tuesday, according to the country's Communications Directorate.
The board met under the chairmanship of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and discussed the implications of global and regional geopolitical developments for the cybersecurity environment, as well as recent cybersecurity incidents worldwide and evolving threat dynamics, the directorate said in a statement.
The board was briefed on how developments in artificial intelligence are affecting the nature, scale and speed of cyber threats.
It also assessed the effects and risks of algorithmic manipulation and cognitive influence activities carried out through digital platforms on national security and societal resilience.
The meeting stressed the importance of digital sovereignty for national security, identifying the protection of critical infrastructure, strengthening national cyber resilience and deterrence capabilities, and achieving technological independence as strategic priorities in Türkiye's security and development policies.
Against this backdrop, the strategy was presented to the board with the aim of "strengthening Türkiye's sovereignty in the digital sphere, reducing dependence on foreign sources in critical technologies, and developing national technology capacity," the statement said.
The board decided that measures taken in line with the strategy's objectives would be implemented by relevant institutions and organisations within their respective spheres, while implementation processes would be effectively monitored and progress regularly assessed.
The meeting also focused on strengthening interagency coordination, developing joint risk assessment capabilities and ensuring consistency in implementation, given the ability of cyber threats to spread rapidly and affect multiple sectors simultaneously.
The board reaffirmed its commitment to deepening cooperation among public institutions, the private sector and academia and developing a comprehensive cybersecurity ecosystem, the statement added.

Budget 2026: six charts that reveal the economic realities facing the chancellor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
18:15:29 UTC
03:15:29 KST

John Healey will deliver his first budget on Wednesday as UK households and businesses come under pressure from the unfolding economic shock caused by the war in the Middle East.
Against a febrile backdrop in global markets, the chancellor is facing a delicate balancing act to provide “breathing space” measures to ease the cost of living crisis while increasing growth and sticking to the fiscal rules.
Healey will also flesh out Andy Burnham’s pledge to deliver “good growth in every postcode”, with measures to hand local leaders more money and power.
Here are six charts that will underpin the chancellor’s decisions.
Sticking to the fiscal rules
At the spring statement, Healey’s immediate predecessor, Rachel Reeves, left herself £23.6bn of “headroom” against the fiscal rules, which require day-to-day spending to be matched by receipts by the end of this parliament.
 
However, the buffer is widely expected to have been slashed by a surge in debt interest costs, as the war in the Middle East causes a global inflation shock that is rattling the bond markets.
The Resolution Foundation estimates headroom has been halved to about £12bn. Much will depend on the judgment of the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), the independent Treasury watchdog, which will take into account the hit from rising debt costs, but also other positive and negative developments for the public finances – including inflation, pay growth, employment and productivity.
Healey is thought to be willing to allow the buffer to take a hit. However, jittery bond investors will be looking for him to retain some headroom to guard against further negative shocks, with at least £14bn thought to be needed to avoid provoking a bond market reaction.
‘Breathing space’ measures
The chancellor has pledged “breathing space” measures for households and businesses grappling with the cost of living crisis, as the energy price shock fuelled by the Iran conflict hits consumers.
Petrol and diesel prices have surged close to record highs and energy bills are forecast to increase to £2,000 a year from January for the typical household. Since 2021, consumers have paid almost £14,000 on average in additional costs for mortgages, loans, energy and water bills.
Healey is thought to have earmarked more than £1bn to help energy consumers, the bulk of which will go on increasing the discount given to households on certain benefits. He has also vowed to help businesses, and has been urged to extend a cut in fuel duty.
Alongside energy support, Andy Burnham has already promised Labour will cut living costs through other measures – including a new mortgage scheme for first-time buyers, and a pledge to build more social homes.
Rewiring the state
Burnham has made “growth in every postcode” his top political slogan since becoming prime minister. With devolution likely to be a central theme of the budget, a raft of measures are expected to add some substance to the rhetoric.
Central to the devolution package will be plans to allow local leaders in England to retain a share of income tax, alongside a new £1.5bn borrowing facility for directly elected mayors.
Britain is the most centralised G7 country for tax and spending policy, and is among the most economically unequal, according to the Centre for Cities thinktank. The aim of redrawing the political map – including establishing a new hub for No 10 in the north, based in Manchester – is to increase regional economic growth, and with it the performance of the UK economy at large.
Burnham has also signalled that a strengthened industrial strategy will be key to his agenda, as well as measures to support high streets and towns.
Tackling the youth jobs crisis
The prime minister has said Britain is facing an “economic catastrophe and a moral failure” after a rise in the number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) to almost 1 million.
Tackling the youth jobs crisis will be a key budget theme. Business leaders have pressed Healey for tax cuts and help with labour costs to encourage youth recruitment, while ministers have explored options for overhauling the benefits system and making changes to apprenticeships.
Healey has indicated that welfare reform will be critical. There could though be costs attached – as any savings from changes to the system could be offset by higher spending on employment support. The government is handling the process carefully to avoid a repeat of the welfare rebellion faced by Keir Starmer, and is still awaiting recommendations from two key reviews – by the former Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn and the Department for Work and Pensions minister Stephen Timms.
The government is understood to favour handing local leaders more power and money to support young people as part of the solution. Analysis from the Youth Futures Foundation, a charity, shows the risk of a young person becoming Neet is geographically uneven: rates are significantly higher in Blackpool, Birmingham, and Bradford than in Bath, Harrogate or Guildford.
Increasing defence spending
Having resigned as Starmer’s defence secretary over funding, Healey is widely tipped to use his budget to find more cash for the military. Burnham has also spoken of the importance of the defence sector for his reindustrialisation plans.
First, the chancellor will need to find an additional £1bn a year to fund Labour’s defence investment plan. Announced by Starmer in his final weeks in office, that put defence spending on track to reach 2.7% of gross domestic product by 2029.
However, Healey has expressed an ambition to spend 3% by 2030. The Institute for Fiscal Studies estimates an extra £11bn would be needed in that year. Longer term, the government is targeting spending of 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035. This is equivalent to a £25bn increase in today’s terms.
Repairing the economic damage of Brexit
Burnham reopened the debate over Brexit in his speech to Labour conference in Liverpool, arguing that leaving the EU had damaged the UK economy and failed to bring the benefits promised.
This week’s budget is expected to underscore the economic hit, including from a drop in net migration.
Net migration to the UK has fallen sharply from a record peak of almost a million in 2023. Earlier this year, the Office for National Statistics downgraded its estimate for the long-run figure to settle at about 230,000 annually, down from a previous assumption of 340,000.
On average, immigrants are net contributors to the exchequer, and so how the OBR accounts for this drop in its forecasts will be critical. Should it adopt a similar approach to the ONS, the Resolution Foundation thinktank estimates this could lead to a drop in tax receipts of £4.7bn by 2029-30 relative to previous forecasts.

====================================================================================================

Why Dangerous Fungi Are on the Rise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
18:15:07 UTC
03:15:07 KST

In the winter of 2015, Dr. Tom Chiller received a call from public-health officials in Britain.
They were panicking. A new fungus was causing devastating infections at a large London hospital. “They weren’t able to get rid of it,” says Chiller, who was then chief of the fungal-diseases branch at the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). “They didn’t know what to do.”
The British officials said the fungus—a kind of yeast called Candida auris—appeared to be spreading from patient to patient. The officials said they were going to shut down parts of the hospital to curb its transmission. “That was just mind-boggling,” Chiller says.
At first he was more confused than alarmed. Candida is a kind of yeast that causes some of the most common fungal conditions, including thrush and vaginal yeast infections. Some species can cause severe illnesses, including bloodstream infections. But Chiller knew of no Candida species—indeed, no life-threatening fungus of any kind—that could spread so easily among people.
“I’ll never forget that call,” he says. “At first, I didn’t really believe it. Suddenly we have a yeast acting like a bacteria? It was weird.”
First discovered by doctors in 2009 in the ear of a patient in Japan, Candida auris behaves differently from most other fungi. It can survive at higher temperatures and in saltier environments, making nooks like a human ear, armpit, and groin ideal places to grow. It is exceptionally sticky and clings doggedly to people’s skin and hair follicles, and to surfaces—including slick ones, like hospital floors and beds, that are designed to repel germs. It is highly resistant to antifungal drugs, hard to kill with standard disinfectants, and can cause terrible, often deadly illnesses. Also, as British officials were starting to notice in 2015, it spreads easily through physical contact between people and via contaminated surfaces.
At the time of the call, though, much about Candida auris remained unknown. A few countries had reported a smattering of infections, but it hadn’t seemed like a big deal. No cases had yet been reported in the U.S. “It was a wake-up call,” Chiller says now. “We realized that, huh, maybe this little ear fungus isn’t just a little ear fungus anymore.”
In the decade since that phone call, that realization has cemented. When about 200 people—mostly doctors and researchers—attended a three-day conference about fungal diseases near Denver in September, Candida auris was the first topic on the agenda. To a nonscientist, the talks were dry, technical presentations on the pathogenesis and epidemiology of the disease, but to the attendees—and “almost everyone who works in mycology is here,” said Dr. Luis Ostrosky-Zeichner, an infectious-disease specialist at UTHealth Houston—they were red flags we should all be taking seriously.
Candida auris has rapidly gained ground since 2015. It has sickened tens of thousands of people in over 80 countries and six continents. The World Health Organization (WHO) has designated it one of the world’s highest-priority fungal threats. The CDC on Oct. 27 listed Candida auris as one of four top-priority drug-resistant pathogens that require "urgent and aggressive action." Thousands of cases are now reported in the U.S. every year. The CDC said this summer that the fungus had already infected more than 3,000 people this year in 27 states. Up to 60% of people who are infected die.
“In some U.S. states, it’s just endemic now. It’s there to stay,” Chiller says.
Deadly fungal diseases were once considered very rare, but the proliferation of Candida auris points to a troubling trend: dangerous fungi are increasingly finding new opportunities to infect us, and human activity is spurring them on.
From the climate we’re warming to the medical treatments we use, we are creating conditions that allow fungal pathogens to thrive, infectious-disease experts say. Rising global temperatures, they say, likely led to the emergence of Candida auris and are driving the evolution of other fungal pathogens never seen before. Changing weather patterns are pushing some fungi to expand their geographic range, and the overuse of antifungals in medicine, agriculture, and livestock farming has driven them to develop resistance to these drugs.
“We are creating an environment that is favoring pathogenic fungi and drug resistance,” says Dr. Andrej Spec, a fungal-disease specialist at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis. “That means they are likely becoming better at infecting us, and also at evading our treatments. That’s a bad combination.”
Fungi are ubiquitous organisms. They live in, on, and all around us. Every day, we inhale thousands—if not millions—of fungal spores. There are an estimated 6 million species of fungi on the planet, but only about 300 of them cause diseases in people. “We are protected by our temperature and our immunity,” says Dr. Arturo Casadevall, chair of microbiology and immunology at the Johns Hopkins School of Public Health. The human body is too hot for most fungi to thrive, but as the earth warms, fungi are adapting.
Researchers think Candida auris, which likely originated in marine ecosystems, evolved a tolerance to salty conditions and high temperatures over time. The yeast can now survive at 107°F.
Candida auris is not the only threat finding hot new hosts. A new fungal pathogen is disfiguring cats and people in South America, and certain molds, which once infected only plants, are now sickening people too. Spec published a report in 2021 describing the first case of a person infected by a mold that had previously been known to damage only trees. Since then, two more people in the U.S. have been infected, Spec says. “It’s gone from never causing human disease in the history of medicine to three new cases of it in the last five years,” he says.
In October, the CDC said that cases of a different mold—a brain-attacking variety—have jumped fourfold in the past two years. “This is a nasty pathogen,” Spec says. It infects even healthy people and causes brain abscesses that in up to 70% of cases are fatal.
“We’re seeing a lot of these molds that were once rare pathogens becoming more common,” Spec says. “A lot of us are leaning toward the idea that this is probably being driven by climate change.”
Spec and other doctors are working with public-health officials, patient advocates, and drug developers to try to stem the rise of threatening fungi. They’ve made some progress in recent years: raising awareness, doing more surveillance, and developing new drugs and tests, but the challenge is formidable.
As fungi develop mechanisms to better infect us, more people are becoming vulnerable to serious fungal diseases—because of advancements in medicine. Today, to fight autoimmune conditions and diseases like cancer, millions of people take drugs that suppress their immune systems. But immunocompromised people are at higher risk of contracting severe fungal infections. Thanks in part to those therapies, the growing population of immunocompromised people in the U.S. is now estimated to number at least 7 million.
“We have people who have immune conditions like multiple sclerosis, Crohn’s disease, and rheumatoid arthritis who might have died from these diseases in the past but aren’t dead thanks to these therapies. But they’re also immunosuppressed, so we have a bigger pool of people who are at risk,” Spec says.
More people are also being kept alive by invasive medical devices, such as heart-lung machines and ventilators, which can create pathways for germs including fungi to enter the body. “We’re making all this medical progress,” Casadevall says, “but that progress comes at a cost.”
Ryan Zwick, a healthy 22-year-old, had just graduated from nursing school when COVID nearly struck him dead in December 2023. The virus, which research shows increases the risk of cardiovascular disease, severely damaged his heart.
Zwick spent a week in an intensive-care unit in Las Vegas before he was airlifted to a hospital in San Diego to receive more advanced care. He was intubated and sedated; his lungs, kidneys, and heart had all started to fail.
He was attached to a heart-lung machine, a life-support device that pumps a patient’s blood outside the body, via tubes placed into his sternum. “His chest was basically open for like a week,” his wife Emmy remembers.
Candida auris took advantage.
When Zwick finally woke up more than a month after being admitted to the hospital, doctors told him he had a severe Candida auris infection. The yeast, they said, likely sneaked into his body through the tubes in his chest. “It got into my bloodstream and kept causing a lot of issues throughout my body,” he says.
He was treated aggressively with antifungal drugs, which kept the infection under control. But the fungus lingered.
Zwick was discharged from the hospital in April 2024, but he returned to the emergency room a couple of weeks later because blisters had appeared at the incision site on his chest. He soon learned that the Candida auris infection was causing osteomyelitis, a serious and painful condition in which bone tissue becomes inflamed. “They took out a bunch of bone and stuff, and put me on more antifungals,” he says.
More than two years later, Zwick, who works as a nurse in New Hampshire, continues to receive weekly infusions of a potent antifungal drug to manage his infection. His doctors have warned him that he will likely have to take them for life. “It’s basically chronic now,” says Zwick, who still sometimes has swelling and blistering at the incision site.
Zwick worries that available antifungal drugs could one day lose their sting. Candida auris is highly resistant to many antifungals; a growing number of infections are “pan-resistant,” which means no medicines are effective against them. “I just hope these drugs keep working for me,” Zwick says.
When Candida auris first emerged in the U.S. a decade ago, it was a very rare and often severe disease whose victims were usually sick, elderly, and immunocompromised people in hospitals and nursing homes. But the yeast has been expanding its reach: not just infecting more people, but a broader range of them, and causing a wider variety of illnesses too.
“Ten years ago, we’d maybe see one Candida auris patient every few months,” says UTHealth’s Ostrosky-Zeichner. “Now, we have several cases per day in Houston.” Texas, New York, Nevada, Florida, and California are among the U.S. states with the highest number of cases.
More young people, like Zwick, and people who aren’t immunocompromised are getting infected, doctors say. The yeast is also starting to cause new types of hard-to-treat infections. Spec says that this year, for the first time, he treated a woman with a vaginal yeast infection caused by Candida auris. She had diabetes that was well-controlled and was otherwise healthy, says Spec.
The woman had come to see him after getting recurrent yeast infections that hadn’t responded to standard treatments, he says. She recovered only after being treated for several days with an IV antifungal drug more powerful than what is usually used to treat such infections, Spec says.
Vaginal yeast infections are very common, with an estimated 3 in 4 women having at least one in their lifetime. A class of antifungals known as azoles are typically used to treat such infections, either as a cream, suppository, or oral pill, but Candida auris is more than 90% resistant to azole drugs. “It’s no joke when you have to tell a woman that she has a vaginal yeast infection for which you usually take one pill and move on, but in her case, she needs to get on IV medication,” Spec says.
Doctors say Candida auris is also emerging as the cause of another common disease: urinary tract infections (UTIs), which roughly half of women will experience at least once. Doctors have known that Candida auris can cause UTIs in people with catheters, but they are now seeing cases of people with tough-to-treat infections who don’t have any medical devices or major health complications.
Public-health experts worry that the fungus could become as widespread as pathogens like MRSA: methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, a superbug bacteria.
“Initially, we tried to stomp it out, but we realized early on that Candida auris was here to stay. It was going to be more like MRSA,” says Chiller. “MRSA used to be hospital-only, and now it’s on every skin boil on the high school wrestling team.”
After Chiller got off the phone with his British counterparts in 2015, he went on a quest to better understand the fungus that he suspected would soon invade the U.S. He first wanted to know if Candida auris was already on U.S. soil but doctors had just missed it. Under his direction, the CDC sent out an alert to hospitals and researchers, asking them to test samples of unidentified fungal pathogens in their repositories going back decades. “We didn’t find Candida auris historically,” he says.
The CDC also collaborated with public-health officials in parts of Asia, Africa, and South America, where Candida auris cases had been detected. Together, they studied samples of the fungus in an attempt to understand how it emerged. They discovered something remarkable: at least three distinct strains of Candida auris appeared nearly simultaneously, over the course of a few years, but separately—in different corners of the globe.
Many fungal-disease specialists and researchers now think climate change likely drove the yeast’s transformation from non-threatening environmental fungus to deadly pathogen. “It’s hard to explain the emergence of Candida auris simultaneously on all these continents and not include climate change as part of it. It just has to be. There’s no other good explanation,” says Dr. Peter Pappas, an infectious-disease doctor at the University of Alabama at Birmingham.
Fungi are sensitive to heat, but they are also very adaptable to rising temperatures. In laboratory experiments, researchers have put different fungi in incubators and, by steadily raising the temperature, have spawned fungi that are more tolerant to higher heat.
“It’s actually not that hard,” says Casadevall, who studies how fungi cause disease and was the first to publish the theory that global warming spurred Candida auris’ rise. “The slower you raise the temperature, the more the fungi can tolerate it. It doesn’t take a lot of mutations,” he says.
A study he published with colleagues last year showed how different microclimates within the same city can trigger changes in fungi. “We went to Baltimore and looked for fungi on the sidewalk in a cool part of town, where they had nice trees and it’s shaded, and then the same fungus in a warm part of town,” Casadevall says. “We found that even within one city, just two miles away, the fungi from the warm neighborhood grow at higher temperatures. So, it’s happening.”
Fungi are already a major threat to many plants, insects, and cold-blooded animals. Frogs everywhere are being wiped out by a fungal disease; rice and banana crops have been decimated by fungi; and millions of bats, which drop their body temperature when they hibernate, have recently died in North America because of a deadly fungus. Until now, however, most mammals have been protected by our high body temperatures.
The emergence of Candida auris is a “shot across the bow of humanity that these things can happen,” Casadevall says. “We can have an organism come out of nowhere, and begin causing disease.”
Many other fungi are changing in ways that are worrying and, in some cases, dumbfounding doctors. As temperatures rise and rainfall patterns shift, some are spreading to new places. The soil-dwelling fungus Histoplasma, which had historically been confined in the U.S. to central and southern regions, has been steadily moving northward, eastward, and westward. U.S. cases have increased twofold in the past decade.
Valley fever, caused by inhaling microscopic fungal spores, is estimated to sicken up to 360,000 people in the U.S. yearly. The fungus was primarily found in the arid American Southwest until about a decade or two ago, when it began spreading to states like Washington, once considered too wet or cold for it.
Even fungal diseases considered mundane and easily treated, like ringworm, are evolving in alarming ways, doctors say. A new species of ringworm that can be resistant to all antifungal drugs has been spreading from the Indian subcontinent to the Middle East, Europe, and the U.S. in recent years. This new ringworm, which is highly contagious, causes chronic, inflamed, and itchy skin plaques all over the body.
“Think of athlete’s foot, but it’s now athlete’s body, and it’s untreatable,” Chiller says. He predicts this new disease, which experts think evolved in response to the overuse of over-the-counter antifungal medications, will become the predominant ringworm found globally in the next decade.
In Brazil and South America, outbreaks of a fungus that causes a disfiguring and sometimes fatal skin disease have been sickening cats, dogs, and people. Like Candida auris, the pathogen has mysterious origins. The fungus was first identified as a threat in 1998 after an outbreak in Rio de Janeiro. First, cats started showing up to the city’s clinics very sick and covered with lesions. Then, people and dogs did too. Infectious-disease doctors identified the culprit of these illnesses as a type of Sporothrix fungus. Infected cats were spreading the disease to dogs and humans through scratches, bites, and even sneezes.
That explanation didn’t seem to make any sense at first, says Dallas Smith, a fungal-diseases scientist at CDC who tracks emerging pathogens including Sporothrix.
A species of Sporothrix fungus called Sporothrix schenckii had long been known to doctors and scientists. The pathogen causes what is often referred to as “rose gardener’s disease” because the fungus, which lives in the environment, typically infects people who work with dirt and plants. “Gardeners would get pricked by a rose thorn, and that would provide the opening for the fungus to enter,” Smith says.
The fungus was known to infect cats, but that was exceedingly uncommon. The disease itself was also very rare. At the largest hospital for infectious diseases in Rio de Janeiro, the Evandro Chagas National Institute of Infectious Diseases, doctors typically saw two to three cases a year before 1998, says Dr. Dayvison Freitas, an infectious-dermatology researcher at the hospital.
But seemingly out of nowhere, something incited the emergence of a more virulent Sporothrix species spread by cats and not plants. It isn’t clear what pushed it to evolve to so effectively infect cats. “Is it because of climate change or environmental change or some other pressures that we don’t understand?” Smith says.
Sporothrix brasiliensis was named as a separate species in 2007. Infections caused by the fungus can result in multiple lesions in people, sometimes all over the body and face. It almost always leaves lasting scars, which are often dark and raised, says Freitas.
In up to 10% of cases, usually involving elderly or immunocompromised people, the fungus can enter the bloodstream and cause destructive illnesses. “The fungus can affect any organ or system, including the bones, joints, lungs, throat, brain. It can cause a kind of meningitis,” Freitas says. “If this happens, it is very, very severe, and the death rate is high.”
Brazil has seen an explosion of the fungus in recent years. “Cats are spreading this disease among themselves, but also to humans at an alarmingly high rate,” Smith says.
From 1998 to 2001, fewer than 180 people, concentrated around Rio de Janeiro, fell sick with the disease. In recent years, thousands of people across the country are infected annually, Smith says.
The disease is now even infecting people in remote villages in the Amazon, Freitas says, and has emerged in other countries too. Cases of Sporothrix brasiliensis have been steadily sprouting up across South America in countries including Argentina, Paraguay, and Chile. Uruguay experienced its first outbreak of the disease in 2025, and Peru reported its first case this year, Smith says. “It’s just a matter of time before it ends up in the United States” and beyond, he says.
Sporothrix, says Chiller, is one of a growing number of fungi that are “dramatically changing our understanding of how we think fungi are supposed to act.”
At the Denver conference, a line of scientists followed Chiller wherever he went. Everyone there wanted to bend his ear. Chiller was decked out in his usual professional attire: a well-cut jacket with a colorful, bespoke fungi-print lining and a matching pocket square. (Chiller, whose grandfather was a tailor, has about 15 fungi-themed custom jackets.)
“In every generation, there tends to be a few people who are a force multiplier,” says Spec. “They change the field. In the case of mycology, the success that exists is often due to Tom Chiller.”
Chiller has been working for decades to draw the world’s attention to fungi’s gathering threat. He was the deputy director of the CDC’s fungal-diseases branch for about 10 years and its chief for another decade. Under his leadership, the department doubled in size to about 45 people and expanded its work to include surveillance of priority fungal diseases, including Candida auris, and research into emerging pathogens, as well as new treatments and diagnostic tools.
He was instrumental in the development and widespread use of a cheap, simple, and accurate test, using just a pinprick of blood, for Cryptococcus—an environmental fungus that can cause meningitis. “It’s definitely saved tens of thousands of lives,” Chiller says. “I’m very proud of that.”
Chiller left the CDC last year after 25 years at the agency, months after Robert F. Kennedy Jr. was named head of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. Chiller says he had been growing increasingly disenchanted at the agency since COVID. “During the pandemic, it was turmoil for everybody. CDC took a big hit reputationally,” he says. Then Kennedy took the helm, and Chiller’s team was cut by about a quarter, he says. “We had to prioritize what we could do.”
Chiller says he felt “handcuffed” by restrictions imposed on CDC staff in the spring of 2025. “They cut all our travel, they canceled all meetings. We didn’t really have budgets,” he recalls. “I thought to myself, If this is the future, it’s not for me.” Chiller is now chief medical officer at IMMY, a company that develops tests for fungal diseases. He’s also a board member of the nonprofit Global Action Fund for Fungal Infections and of MyCARE, a fungal-disease patient-advocacy organization. Now, he gets to do what he loves most: advocating for fungal-disease awareness.
In September, he attended a roundtable discussion about fungal diseases with Kennedy and other U.S. health officials. Chiller, who helped coordinate the meeting, says it was the first time in his career that he had been in a room with a U.S. Health Secretary to talk only about fungus. That felt like progress, he says.
Chiller knows just how critical it is for health leaders and professionals to be familiar with fungi. “Think Fungus” was the catchphrase of the CDC’s first Fungal Disease Awareness Week, which Chiller helped launch in 2017. Doctors often miss fungal diseases because they fail to think of them, research shows.
Though the spread of fungi in a warming world may seem like an impossible foe, there is hope in the fact that diagnosing fungal infections early makes it much more likely that a patient will survive—and researchers, including Chiller, are working to help patients take advantage of that edge.
They’ve got a long way to go: a 2019 paper showed that almost half of some 270 patients in Arizona with valley fever—a fungal disease Chiller studied as a young doctor—weren’t diagnosed correctly for a month or more.
Justin John lived that nightmare. The 27-year-old software engineer from Arizona was wrongly diagnosed with COVID, the common cold, and irritable bowel syndrome before doctors realized—more than six months later—that he was sick with valley fever.
There were “lesions literally everywhere inside my body,” he says. After lumps caused by the fungus started appearing on his forehead and neck, doctors discovered that the fungus had eaten holes through parts of his spine and skull. He underwent two surgeries to insert a metal plate into his forehead, and replace a part of his vertebrae with a metal disc. “The vertebra was so dissolved, they couldn’t save any of it,” he says.
John says he was healthy, active, and had no underlying medical conditions before he got sick. “It’s in the dirt. You can get it anywhere at any time,” he says. “I could have gotten it when I was walking to Walmart.”
Blood tests are currently used to diagnose valley fever, but false negative results are common, causing many missed diagnoses. IMMY is developing a new rapid urine test for the disease that it says will be easier to administer and more accurate. “So many patients, even here in Arizona where this disease is endemic, get missed,” says Dr. Fariba Donovan, a valley fever specialist at the University of Arizona who treated John. “This test could really decrease that delay in diagnosis.”
These are steps in the right direction, but Chiller says we need to take greater strides if we want to win in the race against fungi. Many decades ago, after encountering very sick and dying valley fever patients, Chiller says he “learned a lot about how devastating and complex fungal diseases can be.” He’s still waiting for the rest of us to catch up.

American, Israeli Jews report stronger bonds despite challenges of recent years, survey finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
18:14:31 UTC
03:14:31 KST

A new survey commissioned by the Jewish Federations of North America (JFNA) has revealed that a large majority of American and Israeli Jews feel a deep and growing sense of shared connection, defying prevailing narratives of a widening chasm between the two communities.
Mimi Kravetz, chief impact and growth officer at JFNA, told The Jerusalem Post, “Over the last three years, a surge in Jewish engagement here at home has come alongside a rising sense of connection to Jews in Israel too.”
“Now there’s an opportunity to strengthen those connections using the kind of relationship-building strategies our data show work, including travel, shlichut [emissary work], and community partnerships that our communities have invested in for decades,” Kravetz told the Post.
Writing in a JTA op-ed on Monday, Kravetz and Rebecca Caspi, senior vice president for Israel and overseas and director general of JFNA’s Israel Office, shared the survey's findings, noting that the survey forms the first part of a two-part analysis exploring where the two communities are aligned and where they differ. “Part two will address where American and Israeli Jews see things differently, and why.”
Caspi and Kravetz pointed out that the last three years have been historic for both communities, marked by the trauma of October 7 and ensuing wars in Israel alongside a dramatic rise in security threats, antisemitism, and attacks on Zionism faced by American Jews at home. While it would be understandable if these separate challenges drove the two populations apart, the data reveals that they actually feel closer to one another than they have in years.
JFNA surveys over 4,000 American, Israeli Jews on shared identity and connection
The findings are detailed in the 2026 JFNA Bilateral Relationship Between American and Israeli Jews research initiative published on the Berman Jewish DataBank, which examined attitudes on peoplehood through two separate national surveys conducted earlier this year. The research comprised a national survey of 2,836 adult Jewish Americans conducted by Burson via text-message recruitment between May 4 and May 27, and a parallel survey of 1,323 Israeli Jewish adults conducted by Shmuel Rosner utilizing the Madad Israeli panel and a haredi (ultra-Orthodox) panel between May and June.
The study explored how both populations view their bilateral relationship, tracking a noticeable rise in what the report termed the “rise in peoplehood” since previous major assessments. According to the survey data, 75 percent of Israeli Jews reported feeling “a lot” or “some” commonality with Jews in the United States. On the American side, 72 percent of respondents reported feeling a similar connection with Israeli Jews, rising significantly from 59 percent in a 2020 Pew Research Center survey, with those reporting they have “a lot” in common jumping from 19 percent to 29 percent.
This strengthening bond is also reflected in how members of both communities characterize their relationship through family metaphors. Among American Jews, the share describing Israelis as extended family or part of their community climbed from 46 percent in 2021 to 62 percent, while those feeling no real connection dropped by more than half from 28 percent to 13 percent. Similarly, the proportion of Israeli Jews categorizing American Jews as extended family or part of their community rose from 45 percent to 53 percent, while those reporting nothing in common dropped from 14 percent to 10 percent.
When asked whether Jews around the world, regardless of where they live, share a common fate and must act accordingly, 78 percent of Israeli Jews and 56 percent of Jewish Americans agreed. Furthermore, strong majorities in both countries rejected the notion that diaspora life is a problem to be solved, with 72 percent of American Jews and 72 percent of Israeli Jews affirming that the Jewish Diaspora is a legitimate form of Jewish life.
The research highlighted that this connection translates directly into action, particularly through philanthropic support following the events of October 7, 2025. The Jewish federation system raised $908 million through its Israel Emergency Campaign to fund recovery efforts on the ground. 79 percent of Israeli respondents and 67 percent of American respondents agreed that American Jewish philanthropy remains important to Israeli society, while 68 percent of Israelis stated that post-October 7 giving made them feel Diaspora Jews genuinely care about Israel.
Travel to Israel strengthens American Jews' sense of shared identity
Beyond broad sentiment, the data demonstrates that physical presence and direct engagement dramatically multiply feelings of commonality between the two populations. Among American Jews, travel frequency correlates directly with a stronger sense of shared identity; those who have traveled to Israel once are 1.7 times as likely to feel real commonality with Israeli Jews, those who have traveled more than once are 3.8 times more likely, and those who have lived in Israel are 11.2 times more likely.
A similar dynamic exists on the Israeli side, where casual tourism does not significantly shift connection levels, but deeper immersion does. Israelis who participate in Jewish communal life while visiting the US are 2.8 times as likely to feel a sense of peoplehood, and those who serve as emissaries, work at summer camps, or live inside an active American Jewish community are 2.6 times as likely. Overall, 87 percent of Israeli Jews with real, engaged contact with American Jews feel commonality, compared to just 52 percent among those with no contact.
When American Jews were asked in open-ended discussions why they feel connected to Israel, the responses revealed a consistent set of core motivations. Respondents frequently pointed to seeing Israel as a safe place for Jews, viewing it as the historical homeland where Jewish identity began, and maintaining a belief that Jews are responsible for one another alongside religious or biblical ties. Others highlighted feeling more whole in Israel, recognizing the necessity created by the Holocaust, viewing Israel as part of their own culture, and taking personal pride in Israelis themselves.
Caspi and Kravetz noted that this reawakening of shared peoplehood directly corroborates findings from a separate, comprehensive study conducted by JFNA that tracked trends in Jewish life in the United States. That separate survey revealed that heightened community engagement, known as the “Surge,” had evolved into a sustained behavioral shift rather than a temporary reaction.
Specifically, the research showed that 38 percent of the American Jewish community is part of the Surge and has maintained an active increase in participation across three distinct areas: communal involvement like attending synagogues or joining advocacy groups, educational exploration, and social connection such as hosting private Shabbat dinners or participating in workplace affinity groups.
“We are in another challenging season for the Jewish people,” Caspi and Kravetz said. “It would be easy to conclude that we have more differences than we have commonalities, and to approach discussions from a place of distance and division. But there is an opportunity in this tense moment to recognize our deep sense that we are one community.”
JFNA urges greater investment in travel and community programs to strengthen Jewish ties
Regarding their recommendations for moving forward, Caspi and Kravetz stated, “Our data confirm that today we feel closer than ever, and we recognize that our lives are shaping each other’s. Perhaps even more importantly, our data show what we can do to strengthen and perpetuate this trend. We need to keep investing in things we know build a connection: more travel, more Israeli emissaries in North American communities, and more programs that put people in real contact.”
“And we need to scale innovation that will enable shared volunteer projects, philanthropic partnerships across both communities, stronger business and professional ties, and digital opportunities to learn from one another. These opportunities can ensure impact when travel is impractical, reach those who are less engaged, and ensure that this sense of connection to and understanding of Jews across the world is accessible to everyone in our greater Jewish family and community,” Caspi and Kravetz said.
