France and 10 European countries plan to deploy nuclear-capable French jets to deter Russia, WSJ reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:57:51 UTC
01:57:51 KST

France and 10 European countries plan to deploy nuclear-capable French jets to deter Russia, WSJ reports
France is working with 10 other European countries to establish a new nuclear deterrence framework aimed at Russia, The Wall Street Journal reported.
The initiative, which President Emmanuel Macron called “forward deterrence,” was unveiled in March 2026. It calls for deploying nuclear-capable French Rafale fighter jets to other European countries. Participants also intend to create a joint system for early warning and intelligence sharing.
The United Kingdom, Germany, the Netherlands, Belgium, Poland, Greece, Finland, Norway, Sweden, and Denmark have joined France in the initiative. The three Baltic states, which are most vulnerable to Russian aggression, are not part of the project, while Italy declined to participate. Finland said it would like to take part but does not plan to host nuclear weapons on its territory in peacetime.
French officials believe the new deterrent could be more credible because the security of France’s European neighbors matters far more to Paris than to Washington.
European officials also emphasize that the new system should supplement, rather than replace, the American “nuclear umbrella” over the continent and create further strategic uncertainty for Russia.
Experts say the French ASMP-A cruise missiles carried by Rafale fighters are more effective in modern warfare than American B-61 nuclear bombs. The American bombs were developed in the 1960s, and advances in Russian air defenses limit their use.
Macron also said France plans to resume producing nuclear weapons for the first time in decades. The country currently has about 290 nuclear warheads but will no longer disclose information about its arsenal.
In practice, however, France will retain full control over its nuclear forces. “The French will let us participate in their nuclear deterrence as much as the Americans,” said a minister from one of the countries involved in the project.
France is holding bilateral talks with its partners and has set up 10 separate groups for those discussions. Defense officials across Europe have had to hold frequent calls to keep one another informed about the negotiations, military officials said.

Guidance: Defence Safety Management System (JSP 815)
United Kingdom

Defence Safety Management System (JSP 815)
Joint Service Publication 815 provides the Defence Safety Management System framework, enabling Defence organisations to develop and implement tailored safety management systems.
Documents
Details
Joint Service Publication (JSP) 815 is the Defence Safety Management System (SMS) and provides the framework, direction and guidance to enable Defence organisations to develop and implement their own safety management systems tailored to their business.
Purpose and Structure
JSP 815 is comprised of Defence SMS Framework and Defence SMS Direction and Guidance.
Defence SMS Framework
Defence SMS Framework provides the elements, expectations and performance statements that must be achieved to move Defence to a highly resilient and proactive organisation. The policy has been developed to align with ISO 45001 requirements.
Defence SMS Direction and Guidance
Defence SMS Direction and Guidance provides the direction and guidance which is to be used by all Defence organisations to assist them with the successful implementation of the requirements set out in the corresponding 12 elements.
Defence Safety Function Operating Model
The Directorate of Defence Safety and Support page holds the latest version of the Defence Safety Function Operating Model (1 September 2026) which should be read alongside JSP 815.

Weighing dependence on Washington: Trump between Zelensky and Netanyahu
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:55:14 UTC
01:55:14 KST

Within eight days in October, US President Donald Trump made two statements about two wartime leaders that, placed side by side, read like a confession. On 10 October, speaking to reporters as he left the White House, he said of Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky: “I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president.” He accused Zelensky of passing up the chance to settle the war with Russia “many times, many many times” and of driving up diesel prices by striking Russian oil refineries: “He wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers, with diesel fuel.”
On 18 October, Trump posted a letter on his Truth Social platform describing Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu as “a Great Warrior Prime Minister, and an even greater Partner for Peace.” In the letter, he gave Netanyahu his “Complete and Total Endorsement” nine days before Israel’s general election on 27 October.
Trump’s endorsement of Netanyahu was expected, given Washington’s long record of backing Israel. His remarks on Zelensky, by contrast, shocked many. They revealed the real logic of the Trump administration: politics driven by calculations of interest rather than by allegiances or alliances. Together, the two statements hold an important lesson for anyone who believes American support is a promise rather than a calculation. They also expose Zelensky’s own strategic failure: he relied on a foreign power with its own interests instead of honestly weighing his own capabilities in the conflict with Russia.
A card that no longer plays
Zelensky’s fall from grace was triggered by a dispute over diesel. On 9 October, after a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, Trump announced a deal under which Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel, followed by 500,000 tonnes in November and larger volumes after that. The Kremlin said Russia was ready to supply “the American and global markets.” Zelensky condemned the agreement as “an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged,” and warned that Russia would “repay” the diesel “with further terror and perfidy.”
Trump responded with fury. For weeks, he had pressed Zelensky to halt strikes on Russian refineries, which had cut Russian diesel output and pushed up global fuel prices. A US official told Axios that Trump struck the deal with Putin after Zelensky ignored his requests. Driven by his own political calculations, Trump wanted Ukraine to stop unilaterally and made no matching demand of Moscow. “We said you could do whatever you want to Russia, don’t hit the refineries,” Trump told reporters. “So what does he do? He goes and hits the refineries.”
The domestic context was decisive. The US was just over three weeks away from the midterm elections on 3 November. Diesel prices were close to record highs, driving up the cost of almost everything. Trump’s approval rating had fallen to the lowest point of his presidency amid the war on Iran, which the US and Israel launched in February. That war, and to a lesser extent the Ukrainian drone strikes, lay behind the energy crisis. By blaming Zelensky, Trump sought to shift responsibility for rising prices onto a foreign leader at a moment when American voters were preparing to punish the party in power.
The episode shows that Zelensky’s abandonment is not tactical but structural. He is no longer a useful card in American domestic politics, where Ukraine has no lobby to match the influence of pro-Israel groups. The Trump administration, along with other Western political circles, appears to have concluded that the war against Russia cannot be won.
Behind Trump’s insult lie facts about this war that are hard to deny. Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022 was an act of aggression in breach of international law. Yet even if Western countries encouraged Kyiv to keep fighting, the choice to pursue the conflict on the battlefield rather than at the negotiating table was ultimately Zelensky’s, and he bet everything on Western support. His former spokeswoman Yulia Mendel has claimed that he undermined around seven attempts to end the war, an allegation his office rejects as baseless. In October 2022, he also signed a decree declaring negotiations with Putin “impossible”. The result is plain: having relied heavily on foreign powers, he is now stuck in a quagmire, with foreign support shrinking and no prospect of gains on the battlefield.
A war criminal who remains indispensable
Netanyahu is a different calculation entirely. In November 2024, the International Criminal Court (ICC) issued a warrant for his arrest for war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza. The warrant remains in force even though Washington has sanctioned the court’s judges and deputy prosecutors and its president. He is a fugitive from international justice. Yet a sitting American president has endorsed his re-election in the most personal terms available.
Why? Because Trump needs him, both for his war on Iran and for electoral calculations shaped by pro-Israel lobbying networks in American politics. The most prominent of these is the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), which a US senator says plans to spend $233 million to defeat candidates critical of Netanyahu’s government. If Trump abandoned Netanyahu now, he would be abandoning his own decision to go to war with Iran. He believes the Israeli leader is central to the future of the US confrontation with Iran, and he does not want to carry on alone, which would become far more complicated if Netanyahu loses. Trump spelt this out himself: “If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so.” The endorsement was not moral; it rested on political calculation and self-interest.
The lesson: interest, not values
The contrast between Zelensky and Netanyahu is not one between good and bad. It is a practical lesson in how far a leader can rely on a foreign power. Netanyahu remains indispensable not because the case against him has gone away, but because he remains useful to the man who endorsed him. Zelensky was discarded because, at least in Trump’s view, he had become useless, with no domestic constituency in the US to protect him.
The difference is not between two leaders or their conflicts. It is between an asset and a liability. It is Zelensky’s own fault, not anyone else’s, that he failed to recognise the limits of American support when he chose to continue the war rather than settle it through direct talks. He believed a foreign leader would back him without exacting a price. Trump sees Netanyahu as an asset he would like to keep in power, while Zelensky was traded for a diesel deal that carries electoral value for Trump and his party in the upcoming midterms.
Return, finally, to the two men. One is a wanted war crimes suspect who received a presidential endorsement in a public letter. The other is a wartime president who was told publicly that his country should find someone else. The contrast is not an anomaly to be explained away; it is an instruction manual. Those who place their fate in Washington’s hands should study Zelensky’s path and adjust their expectations of a foreign power, whose support will never come at the expense of its own interests. That is American politics today.

Israel’s genocide in Gaza never stopped – UN commission
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:54:21 UTC
01:54:21 KST

Israel’s genocide in Gaza never stopped – UN commission
Israel has continued committing “genocide” in Gaza despite last year’s US-brokered ceasefire, while also perpetrating crimes against humanity in the occupied West Bank, the UN Commission of Inquiry has concluded.
The October 10, 2025 truce was meant to end Israel’s Gaza offensive, which was launched after the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attack in which around 1,200 people were killed and around 250 were taken hostage. The retaliatory campaign has killed tens of thousands of Palestinians and displaced most of Gaza’s population. Israel, however, has continued the strikes, accusing Hamas of ceasefire violations.
In a report published on Monday, the UN Commission of Inquiry accused Israeli forces of deliberately targeting Palestinian civilians, including children, under “discriminatory” rules of engagement and with near-total impunity.
Since the ceasefire and by September 30, it claimed, Israeli attacks killed 1,431 Palestinians in Gaza, including 300 children and 130 women. Israeli forces also killed 1,080 Palestinians and injured 10,940 in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, since October 2023. The overall Palestinian death toll across the occupied territories, according to the report, now exceeds 75,000, including at least 21,500 children and 11,000 women.
“While Israeli authorities and security forces continue to commit genocide in Gaza, the situation in the West Bank has deteriorated drastically,” the commission said. It described military operations and settler violence as a “widespread and systematic attack” on civilians. They also documented rape, torture, and sexual violence intended to “fracture, expel, humiliate, and subjugate” Palestinians.
The findings build on the commission’s initial September 2025 conclusion that Israel committed genocide against Palestinians, citing four of the five genocidal acts under the 1948 Genocide Convention. International bodies, including Israeli rights groups B’Tselem and Physicians for Human Rights-Israel, have also accused Israel of genocide.
Israel in denial
Israel has rejected the allegations of genocide and war crimes. Responding to the new report, its Geneva mission demanded the UN commission’s dissolution, accusing it of a “misinformation campaign to demonize the state of Israel and portray its very existence as criminal.” Ambassador Daniel Meron said the panel seeks “to undermine Israel’s legitimacy and deny its fundamental right to exist and defend itself.”
Meanwhile, members of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition have called for control over Palestinian territory to be expanded. Earlier this month, Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich urged Israel to seize Gaza and launch a similar operation in the West Bank.
“Yes, we need to wipe out Gaza, for example. Not commit genocide, God forbid,” he said, calling the enclave a “terror entity with 1.8 million Nazis” raised to hate Israel.
What happened to the ceasefire?
More than a year after the truce took effect, its next phase – reconstruction, governance arrangements, and further Israeli troop withdrawals – remains deadlocked over Hamas disarmament.
Hamas has said it will not surrender its weapons without a complete Israeli withdrawal and an end to strikes. Netanyahu has demanded full disarmament and the dismantling of Hamas infrastructure before further withdrawals.
The prime minister also acknowledged expanding military control beyond the original Yellow Line, which initially left Israel holding around 53% of Gaza. With Israeli forces now controlling more than 60%, Netanyahu has ordered the military to extend that to 70%.
Netanyahu faces election reckoning
The UN report came on the eve of Israel’s first parliamentary election since the October 7, 2023 attack, with Netanyahu facing growing scrutiny over security failures, a widening regional conflict, and legal troubles.
Over the past three years, Israel’s Gaza offensive has expanded into fighting with Hezbollah in Lebanon and direct military clashes with Iran. Netanyahu has also faced allegations that he received advance warnings of the Hamas attack, which his office denies.
He is also on trial for corruption and faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza, adding to the pressures surrounding his bid to retain power.
Final polls show a tight race between Netanyahu’s Likud and former military chief Gadi Eisenkot’s centrist Yashar party, which are projected to win 18-30 and 21-23 seats respectively. Neither bloc is assured the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-member Knesset.

In Ukraine, 72% of the projected grain areas have been harvested: which regions are leading
Kyiv • UNN
Ukrainian farmers have harvested 72% of the areas and collected 41.7 million tonnes of grain. Odesa, Dnipropetrovsk and Mykolaiv regions are leading in terms of area.
As of October 27, agricultural producers had harvested 41.7 million tonnes of grain and leguminous crops from 8.3 million hectares, or 72% of the projected area. The Ministry of Agrarian Policy reported this, UNN writes.
Details
It is noted that the average grain yield is 50.2 centners per hectare.
The harvesting of late-season crops is currently underway. In particular, farmers have harvested 9.8 million tonnes of sunflower from 85% of the area, 7.9 million tonnes of corn from 29% of the area, and 3.2 million tonnes of soybeans from 91% of the area. They have also harvested 3.9 million tonnes of sugar beets, 60.1 thousand tonnes of buckwheat, and 89 thousand tonnes of millet. The total gross harvest of sunflower, soybeans, and rapeseed reached 16.9 million tonnes.
The wheat, barley, peas, and rapeseed harvests have been completed. The figures stand at 26.2 million tonnes of wheat, 6.6 million tonnes of barley, and 833.6 thousand tonnes of peas.
In terms of the area under grain harvesting, Odesa, Dnipropetrovsk, and Mykolaiv regions are the leaders in Ukraine. The highest average yields are being achieved by farmers in Sumy region (69.8 centners per hectare), Khmelnytskyi region (69 centners per hectare), Bukovyna (64 centners per hectare), and Vinnytsia region (63 centners per hectare).

Mbappe apologizes as Chinese sponsors drop him and TV broadcasts are halted over Mao dictator remark
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:49:00 UTC
01:49:00 KST

Mbappe apologizes to China over Mao dictator remark
October 27, 2026
France striker Kylian Mbappe apologized after apparently referring to China's founding leader Mao Zedong as a dictator in a video that circulated online.
The controversy prompted three major Chinese companies to sever sponsorship ties with the Real Madrid forward, while Chinese state television suspended broadcasts of Spain's La Liga.
What did Mbappe say about Mao?
The controversy began when a video circulated showing Mbappe discussing his favorite internet meme featuring himself.
In the clip, apparently filmed ahead of an appearance on the French online talk show The Bridge, Mbappe referred to an image depicting his face superimposed on the body of "some guy ... I think he's a Chinese dictator."
The image appeared to depict Mao Zedong, who founded the People's Republic of China in 1949 and ruled until his death in 1976. Jokes about country's former leader and descriptions of him as a dictator remain taboo.
Mbappe has previously been depicted as authoritarian leaders in online memes mocking his perceived influence over teammates and suggestions that he has the power to influence club decisions.
Mbappe has been nicknamed "the dictator" in the European press.
How did Mbappe apologize?
"My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world," Mbappe said in a statement.
"I apologize to everyone my words have upset. This was absolutely not my intention. I have deep respect for the Chinese people and their history, and I am sincerely sorry."
Chinese sponsors cut ties with Mbappe
Chinese beverage company Dongpeng, dairy producer Mengniu and cheesemaker Milkground announced they were ending their partnerships with the French international.
In similarly worded statements, each said that they oppose "any words and actions that hurt national sentiment."
China Media Group, which oversees state broadcaster CCTV, also suspended broadcasts of La Liga matches and removed advertisements featuring Mbappe.
La Liga apologized for the controversy, saying Mbappe's comments were made in a personal capacity and did not represent the Spanish league.
Chinese state broadcaster CCTV subsequently said it would consider Mbappe's apology but would also judge his future actions.
In response to a question about the controversy, China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Guo Jiakun said that "words and actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people will naturally be met with joint opposition from all sectors of Chinese society."
Why is Mao such a sensitive subject in China?
Mao remains a revered figure in China, where public criticism of the former Communist leader is politically sensitive.
His rule was also marked by disastrous political campaigns, including the Great Leap Forward, which contributed to a famine that killed tens of millions of people.
The ruling Communist Party acknowledges some of his mistakes but maintains that his achievements outweighed them, making criticism of his legacy politically sensitive.

From 97.9% to 13.2%: Where Israelis are turning out to vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:48:12 UTC
01:48:12 KST

Voter turnout in Israel's election for the 26th Knesset continued to break records Tuesday, reaching 74.3% by 8 p.m., the highest rate recorded at that hour since 1988, according to the Central Elections Committee. A total of 5,449,277 Israelis had voted out of 7,331,981 eligible voters, compared with 66.3% at the same hour in the previous election. But where has participation been highest, and which communities are lagging far behind?
Updated locality figures from the election data dashboard, last refreshed at 8:41 p.m., reveal striking differences across Israel, with turnout ranging from nearly 98% in one community to just 13.2% in another. The figures were updated at different times for individual communities, meaning they do not all reflect voting at precisely the same hour.
The highest reported turnout was in Bat Hen, a small community in central Israel, where 97.9% of eligible voters had cast their ballots. It was followed by Zavdiel at 94.3%, Beit Hogla at 92.5%, Timorim at 91.6% and Yuval, near the Lebanese border, at 91.5%.
Other communities reporting turnout above 90% included Megiddo at 91.4%, Hazon and Yesodot at 91.1% each, al-Aryan at 90.7% and Shorashim at 90.1%.
Several communities that had appeared among the highest-turnout localities earlier in the day also recorded increases. Asael reached 86.6%, while Shlomit stood at 84.8%. Melilot remained listed at 79.4%, although its entry had not been updated since the afternoon.
The communities with the lowest turnout
At the other end of the list, Sha'ar Menashe continued to record the lowest reported turnout, at 13.2%, according to an entry last updated at 6:16 p.m.
Other communities with particularly low reported participation included Yotvata at 21.4%, Aloney Yitzhak at 21.6%, Ibim at 24%, the Janabib tribal locality at 24.8%, Nir Oz at 25.2% and Holit at 26.4%.
However, some of the lowest figures had not been refreshed for several hours. Yotvata's 21.4%, for example, was last updated shortly after noon, making direct comparisons with localities whose figures were updated during the evening potentially misleading.
Several communities that had appeared near the bottom earlier in the day reported substantially higher turnout in the latest figures. Ghajar, near the Lebanese border, reached 43.5%, compared with 16.7% earlier, while Almon rose from 20.7% to 74.6%.
How are Israel's major cities voting?
Among Israel's larger cities, Modi'in-Maccabim-Re'ut stood out with turnout of 76.5%, followed by Rehovot at 70.3% and Petah Tikva at 70.2%. Herzliya recorded 69.2%, while Ramat Gan and Rishon LeZion each reached 68.6%.
In Tel Aviv-Yafo, turnout stood at 63.6%, compared with 62% in Jerusalem and 59.8% in Haifa. Ashdod recorded 65.3%, Holon 66%, Be'er Sheva 63%, Netanya 57.3% and Bat Yam 53%.
Other urban centers reported 72.5% in Bnei Brak, 65.9% in Ashkelon, 68.7% in Ra'anana and 79% in Rosh HaAyin. Eilat, meanwhile, recorded 48.2%, lower than most of the major cities included in the dashboard.
The new figures reflect significant increases since the afternoon. At 4 p.m., Tel Aviv stood at 50.4%, Jerusalem at 47.7%, Haifa at 46.2% and Rishon LeZion at 50.9%.
Tel Aviv challenges the official turnout calculation
Earlier in the day, Tel Aviv-Yafo Municipality issued an unusual statement disputing the turnout figures published by the Central Elections Committee.
According to the municipality, the city's actual turnout at 4 p.m. was 63.5%, substantially higher than the official figure of 50.4% reported at that hour.
"The source of the error is that the calculation is based on eligible voters registered in the Population Registry, rather than more up-to-date data from the Central Bureau of Statistics," the municipality said.
The municipality argued that the Population Registry listed 490,900 eligible voters aged 18 and older in the city, while Central Bureau of Statistics data from 2024 showed approximately 365,000 residents in that age group. It maintained that turnout should be calculated using the bureau's population figures rather than the registry.
The Central Elections Committee's later dashboard update placed Tel Aviv's turnout at 63.6%, but that figure refers to a later reporting period and should not be confused with the municipality's alternative calculation for 4 p.m.
Arab and ultra-Orthodox communities
Among Arab-majority cities, Rahat in southern Israel recorded turnout of 79.8%, compared with 60.6% at 4 p.m. Sakhnin reported an even higher rate of 83.5%.
Shefa-'Amr reached 72.5%, Nazareth 70%, Umm al-Fahm 70.1% and Tamra 76.8%. Tayibe recorded 74.3%, while the Bedouin town of Hura in the Negev stood at 76.3%.
In predominantly ultra-Orthodox cities, Elad led with turnout of 80%, followed by Modi'in Illit at 77.3%, Beitar Illit at 74.5% and Bnei Brak at 72.5%.
All four cities recorded substantial increases compared with the afternoon. At 4 p.m., Elad had reported 59% turnout, Modi'in Illit 58.8%, Bnei Brak 53.3% and Beitar Illit 52%.
Gaza-border communities and the northern frontier
In the Negev and communities near the Gaza border, turnout varied considerably. Netivot reached 75.2%, followed by Ofakim at 71.5% and Sderot at 69%.
In several kibbutzim affected by the October 7 attack, the reported figures remained considerably lower. Be'eri recorded 35.8%, Kfar Aza 33.6% and Nir Oz 25.2%. Holit stood at 26.4%, while Kissufim reported 54.8%.
Other communities near Gaza reported significantly higher participation, including Re'im at 71.5%, Nahal Oz at 70.7%, Nir Am at 70.3% and Zikim at 68.8%.
Along Israel's northern border, Shlomi reported turnout of 68.1%, Nahariya 65.3%, Acre 64.2%, Kiryat Shmona 59.3% and Metula 51.7%.
The differences were particularly striking when compared with Yuval, a community near the Lebanese border, where turnout had reached 91.5%.

Turkish parliamentary committee approves Mecca pact
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:46:08 UTC
01:46:08 KST

The Turkish parliament's Foreign Affairs Committee has approved a bill to ratify the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement between Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan.
The bill was approved on Tuesday following deliberations during which Deputy Foreign Minister Levent Gumrukcu answered lawmakers' questions about the agreement.
Speaking at the committee meeting, Gumrukcu said the agreement aimed to strengthen regional security through cooperation and collective defence.
“The Mecca agreement is not only an extension of the special friendly relations between the three countries, but also a concrete product of the regional ownership increasingly needed in our region,” Gumrukcu said.
He recalled that the agreement was signed in Mecca on August 7 by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, Saudi Crown Prince and Prime Minister Mohammed bin Salman, and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif.
He said Saudi Arabia and Pakistan had completed their domestic ratification procedures and submitted the required official notifications.
Gumrukcu said the agreement marked an initial step towards establishing a regional security framework based on cooperation and collective defence, adding that the three countries aimed to take responsibility for addressing regional challenges rather than waiting for solutions from outside the region.
He said the framework was intended to contribute not only to the security of the three signatories but also to that of the wider region by strengthening dialogue and cooperation based on mutual trust and promoting lasting stability.
Deal ‘envisions integration rather than bloc-building in region’
Gumrukcu stressed that the agreement was entirely defensive in nature and did not target any country.
He said it was open to all regional countries that respect international law, including the principles of state sovereignty and territorial integrity, the prohibition of the use of force except in self-defence, the peaceful settlement of disputes and non-interference in internal affairs.
“The agreement envisions integration rather than bloc-building in the region, embracing an inclusive rather than divisive vision,” he added.
Defence cooperation and NATO commitments
Gumrukcu said the agreement envisaged strengthening collective deterrence, holding regular consultations on international security issues and improving interoperability between the countries' armed forces through personnel exchanges, joint training programmes and military exercises.
It also provides for closer defence industry cooperation, including joint production and technology sharing, stronger joint counterterrorism efforts and logistical support between the parties in implementing the agreement, he said.
The deputy foreign minister emphasised that the agreement would neither replace nor undermine Türkiye's obligations under its existing alliances and agreements.
He said the initiative was expected to complement Türkiye's participation in multilateral platforms, particularly NATO, by contributing to security and stability across the broader Middle East and supporting European security in light of the interconnected nature of the two regions.
Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Fuat Oktay also dismissed concerns that the pact could constitute an alternative to NATO.
“There were questions about whether an alternative to NATO was being created. Absolutely not,” Oktay told reporters.
“This agreement will not undermine the territorial integrity or sovereignty of the three countries, nor any agreements they have concluded to date,” he added.
Oktay said the pact would not alter the countries' legal standing, sovereignty or foreign and defence policies, stressing that it would not disrupt the coherence of Türkiye's foreign policy.

Libya's maritime deal: Why Haftar is turning towards Turkey
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:45:36 UTC
01:45:36 KST

Breadcrumb
Libya's maritime deal: Why Haftar is turning towards Turkey
Tripoli, Libya - Six years ago, Libya’s Benghazi-based House of Representatives (HoR) unanimously rejected the 2019 maritime memorandum of understanding (MoU) between Tripoli and Ankara.
Under Resolution No. 6/2020, the House severed political ties with Turkey and accused the former prime minister, foreign minister, and interior minister of high treason, referring them to the Attorney General.
Yet on 20 October 2026, the eastern-based HoR abruptly reversed its position, unanimously approving the maritime deal.
Parliament did not ratify the accompanying security pact, nor did it repeal the 2020 treason referrals - leaving it unclear if the Attorney General will act on a dormant mandate while the accused officials live openly in Tripoli.
The 2019 Istanbul agreements were born of an existential crisis for the Tripoli-based Government of National Accord (GNA). As Khalifa Haftar’s Libyan National Army (LNA) advanced within 10 kilometres of the capital, Ankara provided a vital military lifeline at a heavy political price.
The package comprised two parallel instruments: a security pact deploying drones and mercenaries to rout the LNA, and a maritime MoU securing Turkey’s Eastern Mediterranean ambitions.
Both pacts sparked immediate outrage, with critics arguing a besieged GNA could not bargain freely. One Libyan border expert, who wished to remain anonymous, told The New Arab that the arrangement was a clear “case of blackmail” of a desperate government.
Others, however, reject that description. Mohamed Taher Siala, Libya’s foreign minister at the time and one of the agreement’s signatories, told The New Arab that criticism of the deal would only be fair “if it fails to serve the [Libya] country's national interests”.
In his view, Tripoli conceded nothing to Ankara. Instead, it secured a substantial expansion of its Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ), unlocking vital offshore oil and gas reserves.
That perspective is shared by Baghdadi Saleh, a retired Libyan border expert, who verified that the maritime MoU does not deprive Libya of a single square meter of territory. Speaking to The New Arab, Saleh noted that the deal effectively “does not infringe” on Libya’s rights.
Yet, despite these potential territorial gains, the circumstances of 2019 have rendered both MoUs deeply controversial. Besides the HoR’s rejection, regional countries including Greece, Egypt, and Cyprus rejected the maritime boundaries as a direct violation of their own rights, while the European Union declared the deal legally null and void.
This history makes the HoR’s ratification of the deal all the more striking, raising the central question: what has changed in 2026 to make former adversaries embrace an agreement they once condemned as high treason?
Haftar's shift towards Turkey
Between 2019 and 2026, two developments help explain the HoR’s reversal. The first is the change in its leadership, with Al-Salhin Abdulnabi replacing Aguila Saleh, who had occupied the speakership since 2014.
The second, and likely the most important, is the recent pragmatic rapprochement between Haftar’s camp and Turkey.
Seven years after the military conflict, the former adversaries are moving closer. Ankara has consolidated its position in western Libya while increasingly engaging with Saddam Haftar, who is not only deputy to his father but also hoping to become president of Libya one day. Closer relations with Ankara could certainly serve his ambitions.
For Khalifa Haftar, meanwhile, cultivating ties with Turkey offers a way to advance his family’s political influence, even if his own long-standing ambition of governing Libya remains unrealised.
The 2019–2020 LNA military campaign on Tripoli was accompanied by a bitter war of words that makes today’s rapprochement all the more striking.
At the time, President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan branded Haftar a “putschist,” while Haftar denounced Turkey as an occupying power and called for mobilisation against a “Turkish invasion”.
Egypt, meanwhile, backed Haftar fully. In June 2020, as Turkish-backed forces advanced toward Sirte, President Sisi declared the city a “red line” and threatened direct military intervention - a move publicly backed by then-HoR Speaker Aguila Saleh.
This confrontation went far beyond maritime boundaries, with Ankara and Cairo backing opposing camps and raising the spectre of a wider regional conflict.
Regional tensions
Reactions to the HoR’s reversal came quickly, led by Greece and Egypt, which rejected not only the agreement but also the legal effect of its ratification.
The Greek Foreign Minister declared that “the memorandum will not be implemented under any circumstances” because “it is illegal.” Cairo stated that the ratification had no “legal consequences for Egypt”.
The European Union followed, with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa reiterating the bloc’s opposition and expressing solidarity with Greece and Cyprus.
Meanwhile, the EU’s foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, issued a further statement reiterating the EU’s rejection. Israel also strongly condemned the ratification while accusing Ankara of destabilising the region.
Washington’s response was more restrained. On 22 October, a US State Department spokesperson urged all parties to resolve maritime disputes through negotiations. Greece briefed the UN Security Council on the matter.
The controversy surrounding Turkey’s footprint in Libya is not confined to high-level diplomatic calculations or military bases - it extends directly into daily life in the capital.
In Tripoli’s Zawiyat al-Dahmani neighbourhood, the Turkish Embassy’s long-standing closure of a primary public road has become a persistent local grievance.
Security roadblocks have exacerbated the city’s severe traffic congestion, disrupting local businesses and often obstructing emergency access to the nearby Eye Hospital. The Turkish Embassy was contacted for comment, but no response was received by the time of publication.
The dispute serves as a local microcosm of the broader friction defining the Turkey–Libya relationship: a dynamic where foreign security arrangements regularly override public accountability and everyday Libyan rights.
Maritime ambitions, uncertain returns
In August 2022, then-Oil and Gas Minister Mohamed Aoun expressed approval of the deal, saying it gave Libya access to “vast maritime areas”.
His point is echoed by pro-Haftar commentator Ahmed Alhossein, who told The New Arab that the MoU should be viewed positively “as long as it secures Libya’s interests”.
But for other analysts, the main question is whether Libya is actually ready to exploit this vast maritime area.
Since 2011, the country has been struggling to manage and develop even its less costly onshore oil production and its existing infrastructure, let alone attract the huge investment needed for offshore exploration in disputed waters.
In the politically unstable country, violence could erupt at any moment and “oil production is regularly interrupted and sometimes stopped for months”, the Libyan border expert told The New Arab.
Major oil potential partners are unlikely to commit millions of dollars to contested offshore areas in this environment of instability.
The agreement has also put Libya at odds with Greece and Cyprus, backed by the European Union. The dispute could ultimately end up being decided through international legal proceedings, which are often lengthy, adding further uncertainty for investors.
Many Libyans argue that their country, already deeply weakened, needs fewer disputes, not more, particularly with its immediate neighbours and trading partners such as the EU.
Any potential gains from offshore resources must be weighed against the diplomatic, legal, and investment risks the agreement could create.
The question is not simply what Libya might gain, but whether those potential benefits will outweigh the problems the agreement could bring.

Cooperation in the field of introducing and translating the works of contemporary writers of both countries and designing an ecosystem for the Persian language in cyberspace were among other topics raised in the meeting.

This working group will be responsible for continuous follow-up and facilitating the process of implementing bilateral cooperation programs.
The 14th Dushanbe International Book Fair was held from October 22 to 24 at the National Museum of Tajikistan.
Iran Book and Literature House presented more than 300 titles at the fair, promoting Iranian literature and opportunities for cultural cooperation.
The Iranian pavilion featured classical and contemporary literature, Iranian studies, and children’s and young adult books.
Iran Book and Literature House also held meetings with Tajik cultural officials and participated in specialist sessions to explore cooperation in publishing, translation, and literary exchange.
Iran has regularly attended the Dushanbe fair, and Tajikistan has participated in the Tehran International Book Fair (TIBF). Tajikistan was the special guest of the TIBF in 2023.

James Tasamba
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
Early detection and contact tracing remain weak, helping push new Ebola infections in the Democratic Republic of Congo, officials said Tuesday, as the number of confirmed cases crossed the 10,000 mark, including nearly 5,000 deaths.
Confirmed cases have reached 10,060, including 4,887 deaths since the current outbreak was declared in May, Health Ministry data showed.
The fatality rate stood at 48.6% in what has now become the world's second-largest Ebola outbreak recorded.
Authorities said only about 12% of confirmed cases in Congo have been identified among previously known contacts, meaning some chains of transmission remain undetected.
The disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus strain has affected eight provinces: Haut-Uele, Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Bas-Uele, Tshopo, South-Ubangi and North Ubangi.
The World Health Organization (WHO) Africa region office said sustained efforts are essential to end the outbreak.
“This requires continued scale-up of key control measures, greater access to affected areas, and community outreach that builds trust and encourages people to engage with the response,” it wrote on US social media company X.
The WHO said in a report last week that of the 66 health zones affected, 50 or 75.8% reported at least one new confirmed case during the most recent 21 days.
The Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) is due to convene a high-level virtual meeting of African Ministers of Health on Wednesday to assess the situation, strengthen coordination across borders, accelerate support to affected countries and reinforce preparedness throughout the continent.
Uganda, France, Kenya, and Nigeria have reported cases linked to the outbreak in Congo since May.

Sardinian restaurants ban families from using phones at the table
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:43:05 UTC
01:43:05 KST

A group of restaurants in Sardinia are banning families from using smartphones and other devices at the table in a quest to encourage conversation.
The initiative, called A tavola senza schermi or At the table without screens, is being spearheaded by Anna Cau, the children’s ombudsman for the Italian island. It is part of a campaign to curtail excessive screen use among children and inspire interaction during meals.
Parents and their children will be required to put their phones away when dining at any of the 15 restaurants that have volunteered to participate in the scheme during a one-month pilot exercise beginning next week.
Cau, a former juvenile magistrate, said: “The idea is not to rely solely on prohibitions or to place the burden of responsibility entirely on parents, but to ensure our broader environment supports parents in their role and helps minors integrate with others.
“We need real-world settings that strengthen and accommodate the lives of both adults and children. This initiative is a small step within a broader philosophy that guides my approach to this highly complex issue.”
After families hand in their devices, restaurant staff will give them a “reunion kit” containing games and drawings. The kit, which has been designed by the Italian federation of paediatricians, is aimed at helping under-18s start conversations with their parents, such as sharing stories about their day.
The kit includes a brochure outlining the risks of digital overexposure and tips on managing social media use at home.
“The restaurants will offer an alternative activity in the form of a game which is intended to foster interaction,” said Cau. “Obviously, the games are structured with time limits within the context of a restaurant lunch or dinner.”
Cau worked on the scheme with the Sardinian wing of Fipe-Confcommercio, an association uniting the catering, tourism and entertainment sectors.
Emanuele Frongia, president of the federation on the island, said the 15 restaurants had readily agreed to participate. The plan is to expand the initiative on a voluntary basis.
“Restaurants play a vital role in fostering the intimacy that families rediscover when they dine out,” said Frongia. “Yet we increasingly observe that during these moments lively chatter is replaced with stretches of silence as people look at their devices. Often a child is handed one to keep them quiet.”

Kazakhstan, U.S. discuss prospects for small modular reactor technologies use
Kazakhstan and the United States have discussed prospects for the peaceful use of nuclear energy, the development of small modular reactors (SMRs) and scientific and technical cooperation, Qazinform News Agency reports, citing the Agency for Atomic Energy of Kazakhstan.
The issues were discussed at a meeting between Almasadam Satkaliyev, Chairman of Kazakhstan’s Agency for Atomic Energy, and Shawna J. Wilson, U.S. Deputy Assistant Secretary of State for Security Assistance Programs.

Following the meeting, both sides reaffirmed their mutual interest in further developing Kazakhstan-U.S. cooperation in the peaceful use of nuclear energy.

ENGLISH DIGEST 實用美語(空中美語)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:42:24 UTC
01:42:24 KST

Near the Bay of Naples in Italy, the ancient city of Pompeii stands as a remarkable time capsule. In 79 AD, at the height of the Roman Empire’s prosperity, Mount Vesuvius erupted with overwhelming force. Within hours, the city was buried under meters of ash and pumice. This catastrophe turned out to be an unintentional act of preservation, sealing an entire civilization in place for nearly 2,000 years.
Walking through Pompeii, visitors are struck by the sophistication of its urban design and the vivid traces of daily life it preserves. The ash sealed out air and moisture, leaving streets, buildings and everyday objects intact. The city’s well-organized roads, raised sidewalks for pedestrians and public fountains reveal the Romans’ advanced engineering techniques. Written messages can also be seen on walls, including election slogans, restaurant menus and graffiti by ordinary citizens. Together, these features offer a clear picture of a lively and orderly commercial society.
Perhaps the most haunting discoveries are the plaster casts of the victims. As bodies decomposed inside hardened ash, they left behind hollow cavities that retained their final postures. In the 19th century, archaeologists filled these spaces with plaster, capturing the victims’ final moments. Some figures appear to be shielding themselves, while others cling to loved ones or personal belongings. Such details transform historical facts into deeply human stories, connecting us emotionally to people who lived two millennia ago.
Photo: Flickr / 照片： Flickr
Today, Pompeii remains one of the world’s most important archaeological sites. As visitors walk through its quiet streets, they are reminded not only of Roman civilization’s brilliance, but also of this city’s sudden end. No matter how powerful or prosperous a society may be, it cannot escape the forces of nature. The ruins of Pompeii, frozen in time, continue to speak of human vulnerability and the fleeting nature of life.
在義大利的拿坡里灣附近，古城龐貝是一個十分特別的時間膠囊。在西元 79 年，羅馬帝國正值鼎盛之際，維蘇威火山以壓倒性的力量爆發。幾小時內，這座城市便被掩埋在數公尺厚的火山灰和浮石之下。這場災難最終卻成了無意的保存行為，將整個文明原地封存了將近兩千年。
走在龐貝城中，遊客會被它精細的都市設計，以及它所保存的鮮明日常生活痕跡所震撼。火山灰隔絕了空氣和濕氣，使街道、建築物和日常生活用品完好無損。這座城市規劃良好的道路、供行人使用的加高人行道，以及公共噴泉都展現了羅馬人先進的工程技術。牆上也可以看見書寫的訊息，包括選舉口號、餐廳菜單，以及普通市民留下的塗鴉。這些特色共同呈現出一個充滿活力且井然有序的商業社會清晰的面貌。
或許最令人難以忘懷的發現，是遇難者的石膏模型。遺體在硬化的火山灰中分解時，它們留下了保有最後姿勢的中空空洞。在西元 19 世紀，考古學家用石膏填滿這些空間，捕捉了遇難者最後的時刻。有些人形看起來像是在保護自己，有些則緊抱親人或個人財物。這樣的細節將歷史事實轉化成深刻的人性故事，在情感上把我們與兩千年前的人連結起來。
如今，龐貝仍是世界上最重要的考古遺址之一。當遊客走在它寂靜的街道上時，他們不只會想起羅馬文明的輝煌，也會想起這座城市突如其來的終結。無論一個社會可能多麼強大或繁榮，它都無法逃過自然的力量。被時間凍結的龐貝遺跡，持續訴說著人類的脆弱，以及生命短暫易逝的本質。

Ex-FBI director James Comey hit with fresh charges
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:42:23 UTC
01:42:23 KST

Former FBI director James Comey has been charged with allegedly disclosing national defense information, the third criminal case brought against the outspoken critic of US President Donald Trump.
In a criminal complaint unsealed on Monday, Comey is accused of communicating the information in October 2016, when he was head of the FBI, to a “person not entitled to receive it.”
Comey was charged in September last year with making false statements to US Congress and obstructing a congressional proceeding in what was widely seen as retribution by the Republican president against a political opponent.
Photo: AP
A federal judge threw out the case on the grounds that the US attorney handpicked by Trump who brought the charges had been unlawfully appointed.
Comey was indicted again in April, this time for allegedly threatening Trump’s life in an Instagram post that showed the numbers “86 47” spelled out in sea shells.
The Trump administration’s Department of Justice has claimed that “86 47” constitutes a threat to the president — “86” meaning to kill and “47” a reference to Trump being the 47th president.
Comey has denied threatening the president’s life.
In the latest case, Comey is accused of directing an unidentified person to “disclose national defense information to a reporter for a national news publication.”
“They’re back again,” Comey said in a video posted on his Substack in response to the latest charges.
“It would almost be funny if it weren’t such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice,” he said. “I’m still innocent. I’m still not afraid of these people, and I still believe in the independent federal judiciary.”
In a statement to US media, Comey’s attorney, Patrick Fitzgerald, said the charges in the latest case had been investigated by prosecutors during the first Trump administration and “the Government determined that no charges should be brought against anyone.”
The unsealing of the court documents came just hours after a US federal judge ruled that firing of Comey’s daughter, Maurene Comey, a former federal prosecutor in New York, in July last year was unlawful.

Super-rich cashing in on climate crisis, report finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:42:22 UTC
01:42:22 KST

The world’s wealthiest people are not just profiting from the polluting causes of climate breakdown, they are also increasingly cashing in on the catastrophic consequences, a study by Oxfam showed.
The global equality organization has found that the richest 0.1 percent of the world’s population are heavily invested in disaster preparedness, recovery and reconstruction — a market that is projected to grow from US$70 billion to US$92 billion a year by 2029.
This gives the planet’s wealthiest and most powerful people a “double dividend” from the climate crisis and, more alarmingly, an incentive to delay or disrupt action to solve the problem, the non-governmental organization said.
Photo: Bloomberg
It also worsens global inequality as those least responsible for global heating end up having to pay those most responsible in terms of higher food prices, repairing homes damaged by extreme weather or relocating to other areas.
Oxfam chief influencing officer Jean McLean accused billionaires of turning chaos into profit.
“The super-rich benefit at both ends of the crisis: First, through continued investment in polluting industries, and second, through investment in the booming ‘adaptation economy’ — recovery and rebuilding services are sold back to a warming world,” she said. “The populations who contributed least to the climate crisis are absorbing its worst consequences, while those who caused it are best equipped to protect themselves.”
The richest 0.1 percent on the planet, a group of 8 million people, are responsible for more carbon emissions than the poorest 3.5 billion combined, the report says.
As a result, the richest group have reportedly contributed by 125 times more than the average person to extreme heat events.
That is partly due to lifestyles. For example, private jets release more carbon dioxide in two seconds than most of the world’s people emit in an entire year, but the biggest impact of this group comes from their investments.
Oxfam’s new destroy and rebuild index identifies 217 corporations that either fuel climate breakdown or do business in adapting to it through provision of cooling devices, flood barriers, firefighting equipment, transportation, food, insurance and loans.
Last year, these companies made an average of US$1.8 billion and paid out US$1 billion in dividends to shareholders. Six major asset managing firms, which advise wealthy investors, are on this list in their own right and are heavily invested in other members. Two of the biggest, BlackRock and Vanguard, have shares in 92 percent of the companies in the index, worth a total of more than US$1 trillion, Oxfam said.
Similarly, it said that crises — caused by extreme weather or war — have tended to boost the profits of major food trading companies that are dominated by billionaires, whose wealth has increased by US$120 billion since 2020.
When drought, floods or storms hit crops, any subsequent increase in food prices tends to disproportionately benefit big corporations and their investors at the cost of small producers and regular consumers, Oxfam said.
The group cited the case of a 231 percent surge in cocoa prices after extreme weather in west Africa in 2024, saying that local farmers saw none of the gains.
Such inequality has consequences. The annual emissions for the richest 1 percent would cause 1.9 million excess deaths due to heat, Oxfam said, based on estimated impacts on human health, agricultural productivity and sea level rise.
More than three-quarters of those deaths would occur in low and middle-income countries, which are far less responsible for the crisis, because they produce only 8 percent of emissions.
Wealthy nations and wealthy people are somewhat insulated — at least for now — from the climate crisis, because they are more likely to be able to afford higher food prices, robust houses, emergency evacuation, private healthcare and personal security.
That makes them less likely to use their considerable lobbying power to support climate action, and might even encourage them to slow or block emissions cuts that could affect their personal wealth, Oxfam said, adding that instead, some use disasters to push privatization agendas or encourage poor nations to take out loans.
Alex Maitland, one of the lead authors, said the richest people were not just passive beneficiaries of the climate crisis.
“This is deliberate,” he said. “When you take into account their political influence, this is pretty damning evidence that they’re able to orchestrate that is happening.”
Oxfam is demanding higher taxes on the rich, private jets, oil and gas companies, and polluting companies. The group calls on the British government to improve international climate financing commitments based on grants rather than loans, and to end profiteering from climate disasters.
Nafkote Dabi, the climate change policy lead at Oxfam International, said: “What’s complex about talking about climate change is everyone likes to think it’s a shared problem, but it’s not. Addressing the climate crisis is really easy. Control the richest, curb their power, curb their emissions, and also tax their wealth.”

2026 Elections: Taiwan steps up to stop China election meddling
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:42:22 UTC
01:42:22 KST

The National Police Agency (NPA) will step up efforts to prevent election interference by China, gangs and local collaborators, Minister of the Interior Liu Shyh-fang (劉世芳) said yesterday.
Liu made the remarks during a plenary session at the legislature in response to concerns by Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Legislator Michelle Lin (林楚茵).
China’s transnational repression is having a direct impact on Taiwan, Lin said.
Photo: Tu Chien-jung, Taipei Times
Bulletproof glass has already been installed for DPP Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) amid heightened security concerns, she said.
Comedian Huang Yi-hao (黃逸豪) has also been subjected to surveillance and attacks allegedly carried out by local collaborators working on behalf of the Chinese Communist Party, while television host and writer Kevin Tsai (蔡康永) might have been pressured into issuing a public apology and saying he did not support Taiwan independence, Lin said.
Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) said that external forces have repeatedly sent military aircraft and warships to harass Taiwan, with these activities growing increasingly brazen and extending into Taiwan’s territory.
The examples cited by Lin clearly show that these operations are directed by foreign forces and carried out with the assistance of local collaborators, he added.
In Shen’s case, the Hong Kongers who allegedly commissioned and funded the operation have fled, Cho said, adding that the sequence of events appears to be a clear example of how transnational repression is carried out in practice.
Noting that effective countermeasures must be developed under the Anti-Infiltration Act (反滲透法) and through other relevant mechanisms, Cho said a task force has already been established, and at last week’s Cabinet meeting, he called for measures to protect public safety, including the security of all candidates and related individuals over the next month.
Liu said her ministry, through the NPA, would implement special measures to counter transnational repression, in line with directives from the Presidential Office and the Cabinet.
During the election campaign, enhanced security measures would be introduced for any candidate who experience a surge in online or media attacks, she said.
Since the beginning of this year, the NPA has launched three nationwide crackdowns on organized crime, she said.
Together with its ongoing crime-fighting initiatives, the operations have resulted in 483 cases involving 2,886 suspects, she said.
Some of those involved have ties to specific political parties, and authorities have seized more than NT$700 million (US$21.57 million) in illicit proceeds, she said.
With election campaigning entering its final stretch, Liu said the NPA would direct police agencies nationwide to step up efforts to prevent transnational repression and interference by local gangs and collaborators from affecting Taiwan’s elections.
Such interference would have a negative impact on the development of Taiwan’s democracy, she said.
Liu also called on the Legislative Yuan to expedite amendments to the National Security Act (國家安全法), the Anti-Infiltration Act and relevant laws, saying stronger legal tools would enable the government to take action against those who openly or covertly threaten public safety and national security.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Harry Kane on Monday became the first Englishman in 25 years to win the Ballon d’Or thanks to his prolific scoring last season.
Kane scored 73 goals for club and country last campaign — he was Europe’s top scorer — and smashed scoring records in Germany for Bayern Munich and at the FIFA World Cup, where he captained England to a third-place finish.
The 33-year-old Kane said that winning the prestigious individual award was built on so much more.
Photo: EPA
“Anything is possible with hard work, when no one else is watching, to go through the ups and downs, to learn through resilience, determination and self-belief,” an emotional Kane said in a message to young players after reflecting on his early-career struggles.
“My journey wasn’t straightforward. I wasn’t the kid who went straight to the top. I had to experience the downs,” he said. “I had to fight my way to be the very best right now. I hope that can give you inspiration as well.”
Kane was followed in the voting by Kylian Mbappe, Lamine Yamal — voted best young talent for a third straight year — 2024 winner Rodri and record eight-time winner Lionel Messi.
Kane thanked his teammates, coaches, parents, children and wife.
Kane led Bayern to the Bundesliga and DFB-Pokal double, scoring a hat-trick against VfB Stuttgart in the Cup final.
At the World Cup, he scored six times to pass Gary Lineker as England’s all-time leading World Cup scorer and placed himself among the all-time top five in tournament history. His lineup lost to Argentina in the semi-finals, but beat Mbappe’s France for third place, England’s best World Cup placing in 60 years.
An Englishman had not won the Ballon d’Or since Michael Owen in 2001.
“It’s massive for England, for our country. [The ceremony] being here in London was a good omen for me,” Kane said. “It’s been too long. Certainly [there have been] incredible English players... To put us back on the map, to put us here with this trophy I’m extremely proud. Playing for England is my biggest honor, the thing I love to do the most.”
England coach Thomas Tuchel told Kane that the Three Lions are “lucky to have you as our leader.”
“I ran out of superlatives to describe your performances a long time ago, but I’m delighted to see that you have now been formally recognized by the football world,” Tuchel said.
Kane planned to celebrate with family and friends, but just a little.
“We have a [DFB-Pokal] Cup game [against second-tier Magdeburg] on Wednesday, so it can’t get too messy,” Kane said, adding that he had an early flight back to Munich in time for team training.
Monday’s ceremony was held in London for the first time in recognition of the inaugural winner 70 years ago, England’s Stanley Matthews in 1956.
Earlier, Spain star Alexia Putellas won her record-equaling third women’s Ballon d’Or after leading her former club Barcelona to multiple trophies last season, including the Women’s Champions League.
Putellas, who joined London City Lionesses in the off-season, also helped Spain win the Women’s Nations League in December last year.
The 32-year-old midfielder ended Spain teammate Aitana Bonmati’s three-year reign.
Bonmati, who completed her women’s Ballon d’Or three-peat last year, was not on this year’s shortlist after breaking her leg in December last year.
There was not a women’s Ballon d’Or until 2018, when Ada Hegerberg won it.
Putellas urged young players to approach the sport with “love and passion.”
“Believe in yourself, that’s the most important thing,” she said. “If you have a dream, go for it, even if at some point you have to start from zero.”
Putellas had joined Barcelona in 2012 and called her time at the Catalan club “something special.”
“I’m really grateful for having 14 seasons as a player” at Barcelona, she said. “What I experienced last year was like a perfect story.”

Lai’s trust, approval ratings rebound

President William Lai’s (賴清德) trust and approval ratings rebounded to 53 percent and 52.2 percent respectively, both the highest since April last year, surveys released by polling expert Tai Li-an (戴立安) yesterday showed.
Only 35.4 percent of respondents said they did not trust Lai, the lowest rating since December 2024, the poll showed.
Regarding Lai’s overall performance, 52.2 percent of respondents said they were satisfied, while 37.6 percent were dissatisfied.
Photo: CNA
The polls also showed Premier Cho Jung-tai’s (卓榮泰) approval rating rising 5.8 percentage points to 47.7 percent, a record high since he took office.
Asked if they have a favorable impression of the following politicians, with respondents allowed multiple selections, former president Tsai Ing-wen (蔡英文) of the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) topped the poll at 61.7 percent, followed by three more DPP politicians — Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim (蕭美琴) with 53.5 percent, Lai with 49.7 percent and DPP Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) with 47.8 percent.
Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) politicians lagged behind, with Taichung Mayor Lu Shiow-yen (盧秀燕) and Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) each getting 36.9 percent, Legislative Speaker Han Kuo-yu (韓國瑜) 35.0 percent and KMT Chairwoman Cheng Li-wun (鄭麗文) 15.5 percent.
Another 8.6 percent of respondents did not provide a clear answer.
The survey was conducted from Tuesday to Thursday last week, collecting 1,075 valid responses with a margin of error of 3 percentage points.

NSC says latest Fukushima discharge won’t affect Taiwan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:42:18 UTC
01:42:18 KST

Japan’s latest discharge of treated wastewater containing tritium from the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear power plant is not expected to affect waters around Taiwan, the Nuclear Safety Commission (NSC) said yesterday.
The 25th round of discharges began Monday and is expected to continue for 19 days, with about 7,800 metric tons of wastewater to be released, the NSC said in a report issued to update the public on each discharge round.
The wastewater is expected to mainly affect waters off eastern Japan, while tritium concentrations in waters around Taiwan are forecast to remain below the minimum detectable level of monitoring instruments, the NSC said, citing forecasts by Taiwan’s Central Weather Administration and information from Japan’s Tokyo Electric Power Co (TEPCO).
Photo: Taipei Times
Japan began releasing treated wastewater from the disabled plant in August 2023. It has since completed 24 rounds of discharges, releasing a total of about 188,000 cubic meters of wastewater, according to the NSC.
Taiwan has also been monitoring radiation levels in surrounding waters. Since 2017, authorities have analyzed more than 20,000 samples of seawater, marine life, seafood, beach sand and seabed sediment, with no abnormal radiation detected, the NSC said.

Elderly traffic fatalities rise 3%, ministry says
Unknown

01:42:16 KST

The number of people aged 65 or older who died within 30 days of a traffic incident rose 3 percent year-on-year to 790 in the first eight months of this year, despite an overall decline in road fatalities, Ministry of Transportation and Communications data released yesterday showed.
The total number of deaths within 30 days of a traffic incident fell 2.8 percent to 1,777 in the January-to-August period from a year earlier, and was down 10.7 percent from the same period in 2023, the ministry said.
In the first seven months of this year, traffic fatalities among people aged 65 or older increased 5 percent, or 33 more than the same period last year, but for the first eight months, it was only a 3 percent rise, or 23 more deaths compared with the same period last year, Department of Railways, Highways and Road Safety Director-General Wu Tung-ling (吳東凌) told a news conference in Taipei.
Photo: Tu Chien-jung, Taipei Times
Deaths in the age group were highest in motorcycle-related incidents and incidents involving pedestrians, he said.
Among the three administrative regions that recorded the largest increases in elderly traffic deaths, the year-to-date increase in Taoyuan fell from 25 through July to 23 through August, the data showed.
In Hualien County, that figure fell from 13 to 11 for the two periods, while in Taichung, it rose from 14 to 20, the data showed.
Wu urged families to pay close attention to the safety of elderly relatives when they are on the road.
Overall, road safety indicators showed improvement, the ministry said.
In the first eight months of this year, motorcycle-related deaths fell by 217, or 17.1 percent, from the same period in 2023, while fatalities among children and teenagers declined by 29, or 52.7 percent, and deaths in drunk-driving incidents dropped by 99, or 56.6 percent.
Separately, 1,132 people died in “A1” traffic incidents — defined as those resulting in death at the scene or within 24 hours — in the first nine months of this year, down 14.2 percent from 2023 and 6.4 percent from last year.
Meanwhile, 377,039 people were injured in A2 traffic incidents — those resulting in injuries or deaths occurring more than 24 hours later — in the first nine months, down 6.1 percent from 2023 and 4 percent from last year.
Twenty-three fatalities involving drug-driving incidents were recorded in the first six months of this year, while 11 deaths were recorded in July and August, after the National Police Agency broadened the statistical definition, the ministry said.
However, road deaths within 30 days of an incident reached 177 in New Taipei City and 74 on national highways in the first eight months of this year, showing an upward trend compared with the same period in 2023 and last year, the ministry said.
Wu said that secondary collisions on highways were a growing concern, with six such incidents reported in August.
Motorists involved in crashes should move to a safe location away from traffic when possible, he said.
In incidents involving only property damage, drivers should photograph the scene and move their vehicles to a safe location before reporting the incident, rather than waiting for police to arrive, he added.

Taiwan, EU decide their ties, MEP says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:42:15 UTC
01:42:15 KST

Beijing has no say in Taiwan’s partnerships with European countries, Formosa Club acting chair Rihards Kols, a member of the European Parliament (MEP), told a forum in Taipei yesterday.
The Formosa Club, an interparliamentary group of European lawmakers, and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs cohosted the Trusted Technology Forum for Democracies, focusing on artificial intelligence (AI) and drone technologies.
In his opening speech, Kols said it is crucial that people meet and understand each other’s concerns, and work out how they can help.
Photo: CNA
The club has brought European parliamentarians to the second annual forum to understand Taiwan better and seek opportunities for collaboration, he said.
There is a lot of common ground between Taiwan and Europe, he said.
Both want people to live freely and securely, businesses to succeed and to “make our own decisions without someone else threatening to punish us for that,” he said.
There is also a lot the two sides can offer to each other, such as Taiwan’s strengths in semiconductors, electronics and its growing drone industry, and Europe’s experience in manufacturing and industrial technology, he said.
Europe has learned a costly lesson about dependence from treating Russia’s energy as a commercial matter and dismissing warnings about political leverage, and the same mistake cannot be made with the technologies that factories, communications and defense systems rely on, Kols said.
“Before we buy a system, we should know: Who controls it? Where does the data go? Can we repair it?” he said, adding that these questions become more important when hospitals, electricity network and a country’s defense depend on it.
Russia’s invasion of Ukraine has shown how quickly military designs change and the importance of quickly producing and repairing equipment, he said.
Parliamentarians should work to bring trusted businesses, researchers, investors and policymakers closer together for technology cooperation, he said.
“The European Parliament has called for better market access, greater certainty for investors and closer cooperation with Taiwan on critical technologies. That matters to the company considering an investor, a researcher looking for an industrial partner, or a manufacturer seeking a reliable supplier,” he said.
“Beijing[’s] objections cannot give it a right to decide whom Europeans meet or which partnerships we build,” he said, adding that Taiwan and Europe should be able to pursue opportunities that serve mutual interests.
AI and drones are rapidly becoming fundamental to economies and security, but they carry a heightened vulnerability, Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs Francois Wu (吳志中) said.
“In an age of geopolitical competition, authoritarian states are treating these technologies as tools of cohesion and related supply chains as instruments of power to challenge the status quo,” Wu said, adding that Taiwan and Europe feel it directly, from Russia and China.
“How do democracies keep the technologies they depend on in trusted hands?” he asked.
Taiwan stands at the heart of many of the world’s high-tech ecosystems, but its greatest contribution to the free world is not just what it makes, but that the nation’s partners can trust how Taiwan makes it and with whom, he said.
“Taiwan is committed to creating non-red supply chains that are secure, transparent and free of coercive control,” he said. “A stronger, more autonomous Europe and a trusted Taiwan are complementary, not competing.”
Europe leads industrial-based world-class research and a drive toward re-industrialization, while Taiwan leads in semiconductors, AI servers, and the coming wave of physical and embodied AI, he said.
“That combination makes us indispensable to each other,” Wu said. “Together Europe and Taiwan can widen the options available to democracies so that no single supplier and no single government can hold our shared future hostage.”

Xi’s lifelong presidency should be opposed: MAC head
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:42:15 UTC
01:42:15 KST

People of conscience should support calls to end Chinese President Xi Jinping’s (習近平) unlimited presidential term, Mainland Affairs Council Minister Chiu Chui-cheng (邱垂正) said yesterday.
Chiu made the remarks in response to media queries for comment about a petition reportedly circulating on Monday among Chinese university students from 14 institutions, including Peking University, urging the reinstatement of term limits for Chinese presidents.
Monday was also the opening day of the Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party’s plenary meeting.
Photo: AP
The petition, titled: “A Joint Appeal from a Group of University Students in the Republic,” was first posted on a Chinese-language Web site.
The petition, which was quickly taken down, demanded restoring constitutional term limits on China’s leaders and defining the office’s roles and powers.
It also called for initiating democratic constitutional amendments by convening a national conference of the people and improving the mechanisms for election, supervision and recall processes, and protecting spaces for people to discuss public affairs.
The open letter has also been published on other Web sites.
Chinese university students were “confounded and disturbed” by the authorities’ abolition of the constitutionally mandated term limits for the office of the Chinese president and vice president, the petition said.
“We deeply understand stability and continuity are needed by the nation for its development, but the source of stability should be the predictability of institutions, not dependence on an individual,” it said.
The party should reform itself to ensure that power is subject to term limits and checks, and respect the people’s right to criticize and advocate for public affairs, it said.
Xi in March 2018 oversaw the process for constitutional amendments that made him president for life, an act that allowed him to consolidate power and weaken institutional constraints.
A Radio Free Asia report said it was unable to determine whether the open letter originated in China, as the Siyuan Lake BBS Web site was hosted in South Korea, and no personal name was used.
In Taipei, Chiu told reporters on the sidelines of a legislative meeting that “every intellectual possessing a conscience would support the open letter,” regardless of its origins.
Chinese professors he had met in 2017 before the freeze in cross-strait exchanges had made similar objections to Xi’s move to make himself president for life, Chiu said.
The academics at the time said political tradition demanded that Xi nominate a successor as China’s president, not seek additional terms, he said.
Chinese intellectuals absolutely cannot accept Xi’s presidency for life, Chiu said.
However, after the Chinese Communist Party consolidated power around a single leader, the intellectuals’ ability to correct political errors “disappeared entirely,” Chiu said.
Screen grabs obtained by the Chinese-language Liberty Times (the Taipei Times’ sister paper) showed the petition had appeared in at least 17 forums with links to Chinese universities.
