Securities trading on typhoon days
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:41:45 UTC
01:41:45 KST

Each time a typhoon approaches, Taiwanese inevitably find themselves embroiled in a debate over whether a typhoon day off should be declared. The government must consider the severity of the wind and rain as well as safe commute, while the public is concerned with whether they have to commute during the storm. Financial markets face whether they have to suspend trading.
Yet, despite years of repeated debates over whether to grant a day off, Taiwan has given relatively little thought to a more fundamental question: Should financial markets follow local governments’ decisions to suspend work and classes on typhoon days?
Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Legislator and Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) has proposed that, as a major financial hub, Taipei should consider whether stock market trading should be decoupled from typhoon days off and whether financial institutions could adopt different contingency measures. The key question is whether ensuring the safety of commuters means that financial markets should also suspend trading.
The purpose of suspending work and classes is to reduce the risks people face when commuting during typhoons, whereas financial markets must consider whether stock trading and subsequent settlement can proceed normally. The considerations behind local governments’ decisions to suspend work and classes are not identical to those behind the decision to close the stock market, so the two do not necessarily need to follow the same approach.
With digital trading and remote work becoming increasingly widespread, the central government should reassess the system and explore whether financial markets could maintain some level of operation when local governments announce work and class suspensions.
Of course, keeping the stock market open does not mean employees should be expected to brave the storm to get to work. If the central government intends to implement such a policy, it should explore arrangements for remote work, staffing requirements for essential personnel and guidelines for handling situations in which employees cannot report to work due to transportation disruptions or safety concerns during their commute.
Otherwise, if the policy is only concerned with the operation of financial markets while shifting risks onto employees, it would defeat the very purpose of institutional reform.
The mayor of Taipei might not have the authority to unilaterally decide whether financial markets should close, but the city can put forward concrete proposals and coordinate with the central government and financial regulators to establish clear guidelines for work suspension standards, financial contingency measures and worker safety.
Shen’s proposal has given society an opportunity to move beyond the binary debate or whether to declare a typhoon day off. As remote work becomes increasingly common and financial trading methods continue to evolve, Taiwan should also rethink how to maintain financial market operations and protect workers’ rights while ensuring people’s safety.
Dino Wei is an engineer.

US bans vehicles from China’s BYD at base in Japan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:41:44 UTC
01:41:44 KST

One of the US’ biggest overseas military bases has banned vehicles made by the Chinese electric vehicle maker BYD Co (比亞迪) over security concerns, the US military in Japan said yesterday.
The ban, which went into effect this week at Kadena airbase on the southern Japanese island of Okinawa, has fueled speculation that similar measures could be taken at other US military facilities as part of Washington’s crackdown on Chinese technology it suspects of being used to collect sensitive information.
“These vehicles present an unacceptable and unmitigable risk to our personnel and our mission,” US Lieutenant Colonel Alli Stormer, a spokesperson for the US Air Force 18th Wing at Kadena, said in a statement.
Photo: Getty Images via AFP
ALL VEHICLES BANNED
The restrictions apply to all BYD vehicles, including privately owned cars, taxis and delivery vehicles, reports said, adding that security personnel stationed at the base’s gates had been instructed to block BYD vehicles and instruct drivers to turn around.
Kadena, the biggest US Air Force base in east Asia, would be directly involved in responding to a crisis involving China, Russia or North Korea.
Its inventory includes the powerful Typhon missile system, which is said to be capable of firing Tomahawk missiles as far as 1,600km, putting parts of China and Russia within striking distance. Kadena also hosts fighter planes and aircraft used for mid-air refueling, surveillance and reconnaissance, its Web site says.
The move comes amid concerns of potential information leaks via vehicle-mounted technologies such as cameras, sensors and GPS devices, South Korea’s Yonhap news agency reported.
US military officials have not identified a specific threat, but the ban is part of wider measures taken by the US and other Western countries to restrict Chinese smart technology in vehicles, mobile phones and other devices they fear could be used to “spy” on their owners.
GROWING LIST
In June, the Pentagon added BYD to a list of 188 Chinese firms it believes have ties to the country’s military, drawing a protest from Beijing. The blacklist also includes the automaker Inc (蔚來汽車), e-commerce firm Alibaba (阿里巴巴) and Internet company Baidu Inc (百度).
The US Department of Defense banned the sale and use of smartphones from Chinese companies Huawei Technologies Co (華為) and ZTE Corp (中興通訊) at military bases worldwide in 2018, again citing security concerns.
China has imposed similar restrictions on US-made Tesla vehicles. In 2021, it barred them from some government compounds due to security concerns over cameras installed on the vehicles. Beijing removed that restriction in 2024 after Tesla won an endorsement from the country’s top auto industry association.
BYD, which has not immediately responded publicly to the Kadena ban, overtook Tesla as the world’s biggest seller of battery-electric vehicles last year.
It is expanding overseas, including in the world’s fourth-biggest auto market, Japan, where in July it launched its Racco electric minicar in the hope that the small, cost-efficient vehicle would carve out a place in a market dominated by domestic brands.

Judge rejects prisoner’s challenge to Vegemite ban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:41:41 UTC
01:41:41 KST

A prisoner on Monday lost his challenge to an Australian state’s ban on inmates eating Vegemite after he argued in court that withholding the polarizing yeast-based spread breached his human right to “enjoy his culture as an Australian.”
Andre McKechnie, 55, who is serving a life sentence for murder, last year took his battle for the salty, sticky, black-brown byproduct of brewing beer to the Supreme Court of Victoria.
He had argued being refused Vegemite denied him his right under the Charter of Human Rights and Responsibilities Act to “enjoy his culture as an Australian in the community with other persons of Australian background,” court documents showed.
Photo: AP
Australian Justice Claire Harris accepted prison authorities’ refusal to allow McKechnie Vegemite “limited his cultural rights” under the charter.
However, she found the ban was justified in meeting authorities’ goals of removing illicit drugs and alcohol from the prison system.
“The limitation on Mr. McKechnie’s ability to enjoy Vegemite in community with other persons of Australian background is primarily that he is a prisoner,” Harris wrote in her 47-page verdict.
Prison officials testified at a trial in July that Vegemite had been banned throughout the state’s 12 prisons for the past 20 years, because it could potentially impair sniffer dogs’ ability to detect narcotics and could be used to brew alcohol because of its yeast content.
McKechnie, who represented himself in court by video link from maximum security Barwon Prison west of Melbourne, argued that the fact that neighboring New South Wales state did not ban Vegemite from its prisons was evidence that there were “less restrictive means reasonably available” to achieve such drug and alcohol outcomes.
Most Australians revere Vegemite as an unfairly maligned culinary icon, and more than 80 percent of Australian households are estimated to have a jar in their pantries. Vegemite is typically considered an acquired taste at best by those who were not raised on it.
The last US president to visit Australia, Barack Obama, once said: “It’s horrible.”

Photo courtesy of Kentec Inc
The company expects robust demand for AI data center system integration and steady expansion in EMS business to sustain its growth momentum into next year, he said.
Containerized and modular data centers are an important area of development for Kentec, Kuo said.

The company has completed development of its 2.5MW CDU, which is expected to enter mass production this month, while a new 3.5MW model is slated to begin validation next year, Chen said.

Populism’s next chapter is being written in continental Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:41:38 UTC
01:41:38 KST

Since 2016, the story of populism in the rich world has been dominated by the UK and the US — by the UK’s vote for Brexit and the US’ election of Donald Trump, not once, which might have been put down to naivete, but twice — but things are about to change: Over the next year populism is likely to fade in those countries, but burn ever brighter in continental Europe.
In the US, the Democrats are increasingly optimistic that they will take the Senate as well as the US House of Representatives, forcing Trump to spend the rest of his term dodging subpoenas. Democrats lead Republicans by 9 percentage points in the generic congressional ballot. Only 31 percent of Americans approve of Trump’s job performance. Looking ahead to 2028, no party has ever secured victory in a presidential race when the incumbent president has such a dismal number.
In the UK, Trump’s brother-in-arms, Nigel Farage, is sinking. His party’s approval ratings have been falling for months, thanks to Farage’s taste for pocketing gifts and his foot soldiers’ taste for bad-mouthing minorities. The great theme of British politics today is the recovery of the two-party system.
Illustration: Mountain People
If you like your politics hot, mainland Europe is the place to be. The continent is about to enter a year-long electoral super-cycle, starting with Spain’s general election on Nov. 29 and peaking with the French presidential election in April. Although Germany does not have a federal election, three state elections in April could topple an already doddering German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, if, indeed, he survives that long. Smaller countries that will go to the polls include Finland, Poland and Slovenia.
Even before France erupted in fire and fury on Oct. 17, the populist right was well-positioned to do well out of this super-cycle, thanks to rising living costs, a never-ending refugee crisis and general “grobulation.” Spain might be about to take a sharp turn to the right after eight years of Socialist Workers’ Party rule, with polls suggesting a clear majority for the center-right People’s Party and its putative partner, the radical right Vox.
In France, Marine Le Pen has been ahead in the polls before only to lose decisively in the second round, but this time her poll lead is bigger, and her potential opposition is weaker: So far, the center has been unable to produce a charismatic figure, and the left has united behind someone who is even more divisive than Le Pen, Jean-Luc Melenchon.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, who has led the country’s longest serving post-World War II government, is favored to continue her winning streak, while in Germany, the Alternative for Germany (AfD) is the most popular party in Germany with 28 percent of the vote (and in next-door Austria, the equally right-wing Freedom Party is even more popular, at 39 percent).
The riots in France would surely bolster the right’s position. French President Emmanuel Macron, languishing at 15 percent in the polls, contributed to the sense of centrist fatigue by delivering an address to the nation that one of his former ministers described as “rubbish.” Melenchon appeared to condone the rioting.
Right-wingers across the continent say that civilization is under threat from barbaric hordes. The leaders of Poland and Hungary declared that the riots proved the wisdom of their countries’ hardline policies on immigration. Meloni sent troops to Milan where riots had also broken out.
The populist right is also showing signs that it can harden as well as strengthen. Many centrists have comforted themselves with the idea that the right might be civilized by success: Meloni has governed Italy largely as a traditional conservative and Le Pen has rejected her father’s more revolting policies while adopting social policies that are more gay and female-friendly.
However, Meloni is moving back to the right to fend off criticisms from Roberto Vannacci, a former general who leads the National Future party. Many of Le Pen’s liberal social policies were adopted to strengthen her case against Islam. Meanwhile, the AfD has thrived on extremism.
What will this potential populist turn mean for Europe? The answer clearly depends on how far the populist turn goes — above all, on whether Le Pen wins in France. At the very least, the super-cycle would paralyze the EU machine. Focused on winning votes at home, national leaders would be tempted to play hardball in the EU, particularly on budgets, to curry favor at home. Eurocrats would be absorbed in watching national elections and calculating what to do about them.
A victory for Le Pen would be a bigger blow to Europe than the UK’s vote to leave the EU in 2016, given France’s role in both founding and steering the European project. Le Pen might have abandoned her earlier talk of “Frexit,” but she is nevertheless campaigning on a long-list of anti-Brussels measures, including an initial proposal (since moderated) to cut 11 billion euros (US$12.3 billion) from France’s contribution to the EU budget, pulling France out of the EU’s common asylum policy, giving preference to French companies in public contracts and unilaterally withdrawing from some aspects of the single market; in other words, a partial “Frexit” that would leave Le Pen with a seat on the European Council.
The most obvious winner from any rightward shift in Europe would be Russian President Vladimir Putin, the most obvious loser Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy. Le Pen (whose party took a 9.4 million euro loan from a Russian bank in 2014) has promised to stop aid to Kyiv for anything other than military training and to oppose Ukraine’s membership of the EU. Vannacci and Alice Weidel, the leader of the AfD, are loudly pro-Russian.
What about the wider populist project? The most important thing that a European tilt to populism would mean is survival. US commentators, being an introspective breed and fond of writing the end of things, would likely see a defeat for Trump as marking the end of populism. However, Trump is merely the latest manifestation of a much bigger movement.
The current populist wave arguably started in Europe rather than the US (or the UK). Jean-Marie Le Pen began his political career in 1956, when he was elected to the French Assembly, and made his first run for the presidency in 1974. Silvio Berlusconi, Italy’s four-term prime minister in the 1990s and early 2000s, prefigured all too many Trumpian themes, including mastery of the media, dark charisma, womanizing and self-dealing.
The shift to Europe could also mean the intensification of populist themes. The EU is the last great holdout of the neoliberal project of globalization and free markets. A significant populist advance would terminate that already fading project. Europe is closer to the Muslim world than the US and has a substantially larger Muslim population. Hostility to immigration in general and Muslim immigration in particular would be even more central to European populism than to Trumpian populism, spiced with worries about declining birthrates and “civilizational erasure.”
The next phase of populism would be less dominated by grumpy old men than the US phase, featuring women such as Marine Le Pen, Meloni and Weidel and well-coiffed young men such as Jordan Bardella. The populist operation could also become more professional. Trump was so intemperate that he often shot his own side: Ask Pierre Poilievre, who was heading for an easy victory in Canada before Trump announced that he wanted to annex his northern neighbor. Le Pen and Meloni are not only more experienced at navigating domestic politics, but are also more skilled at operating across national borders.
Over the past quarter of a century, we have become accustomed to thinking of the Americans as, on average, hard and the Europeans as soft. Robert Kagan even wrote a book about how Americans are from Mars and Europeans are from Venus. The next turn of the electoral cycle is likely to demonstrate that Europeans can be every bit as hardy as their cousins across the Atlantic.
Adrian Wooldridge is the global business columnist for Bloomberg Opinion. A former writer at The Economist, he is author of The Aristocracy of Talent: How Meritocracy Made the Modern World. This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.

Taiwan heads to the polls next month for local elections. Beneath the campaign ads lies a deeper question: What do we call this place and who gets to decide? In the pages of the Oxford English Dictionary (OED), that question has been playing out across three centuries. The entries for “Formosa” and “Taiwan” chart an island’s journey from colonial fantasy to self-named reality. Names are rarely neutral; they are the first act of possession. Nowhere is this more evident than in the OED, where the two entries serve as a linguistic seismograph for one of the world’s most enduring geopolitical fault lines.

Senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan on Monday held talks with Iran to stop the Middle East war from reigniting, with Tehran saying the discussions were “very good.”
Officials from the three Mecca pact countries flew to Iran as part of efforts to “de-escalate between the parties to the current crisis,” the Saudi Arabian Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement.
The talks, which included Saudi Arabian Minister of Defense Prince Khalid bin Salman, followed warnings by the US, Iran and Israel that hostilities could restart in the eight-month war.
Photo: West Asia News Agency via Reuters
It was the first joint visit to Tehran by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey since they in August formed a defense alliance in Mecca, the holy city in western Saudi Arabia.
The delegations met with Iranian President Massoud Pezeshkian and Minister of Foreign Affairs Abbas Araghchi. The meeting ended without concrete announcements, with the parties saying they “agreed to continue discussions,” Iranian state media reported.
However, Iranian Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council Mohsen Rezaei said the discussions in the capital, Tehran, were “very good,” state television reported.
POSITIVE ATMOSPHERE
“I feel that a new atmosphere is emerging in the region... I sensed a very positive atmosphere in the discussions among the gentlemen,” Rezaei said.
He said they agreed that security in the region “should be achieved by the countries themselves, and that we must prevent any kind of foreign intervention,” adding that emphasis was put on the Israeli occupation of southern Lebanon, southern Syria, Gaza and the West Bank.
Saudi Arabian Prince Khalid, Pakistani Chief of the Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir and Turkish National Intelligence Organization Chairman Ibrahim Kalin met Rezaei.
Regional tensions have risen ahead of Israel’s pivotal elections yesterday and next week’s US midterms, where US President Donald Trump’s Republicans are battling to keep control of both chambers of the US Congress.
As the talks in Tehran began, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said it was “essential to stop any escalation” in the Middle East.
“The risk to have the combination of an overwhelming military attack on Iran, and an overwhelming military attack by Iran on the countries of the Gulf, needs to be avoided at all costs,” he told a news conference in Cairo.
‘LAST CHANCE’
Saudi Arabian security analyst and researcher Hesham Alghannam posted on social media that “this historic meeting in Tehran may be the last chance before escalation spirals out of control.”
Fresh explosions rattled Riyadh overnight, which has suffered weeks of attacks from the Iran-backed Houthis, after the group claimed a new attack on the Saudi Arabian capital’s international airport on Sunday.
The Saudi Arabia-led coalition in Yemen later reported intercepting three Houthi-launched drones over southern Saudi Arabia and the Riyadh region.

The Tainan District Court on Monday approved a request by prosecutors to detain a man surnamed Lee (李) who is suspected of involvement in his wife’s death in Japan last week.
Wang Sheng-hao (王聖豪), a senior prosecutor with the Tainan District Prosecutors’ Office, yesterday said in a video briefing that Lee is suspected of being involved in the apparent murder of his wife and attempted fraud.
Prosecutors sought Lee’s detention on Sunday, citing concerns that he could flee or destroy evidence, he said.
Photo courtesy of the office via CNA
Lee’s wife, surnamed Ching (井), was found fatally stabbed at a hotel in Yamanashi Prefecture’s Fujikawaguchiko on Oct. 19, Wang said.
Japanese police arrested a suspect, a woman surnamed Yang (楊) who is also from Taiwan, for her alleged involvement in the case, he said.
On Thursday last week, Tainan prosecutors launched an investigation at the request of the Criminal Investigation Bureau’s International Affairs Division.
Prosecutors found that Lee, who traveled to Japan after his wife’s death to handle the funeral arrangements, had taken out two travel insurance policies on Ching prior to her death — one for NT$10 million (US$308,147) and another NT$20 million, Wang said.
Authorities arrested Lee when he returned to Taiwan on Saturday evening.
They searched seven locations, including his residence, on Saturday and Sunday, Wang said.
Prosecutors said they found records of contact between Lee and Yang, who Japanese authorities suspect of killing Ching, but added that the alleged coordination between the two and their respective roles in the case remain under investigation.
Japanese media last week reported that Ching was found dead on a hotel bed with extensive bleeding.
Yang, 27, was also in the room and later arrested after police found her in possession of a kitchen knife, on suspicion of contravening the country’s Firearm and Sword Possession Control Law.
The women were part of a tour group from Taiwan, the reports said, adding that hotel staff went to check on Ching after she failed to show up before the group’s outing that day.
Japanese police are continuing to investigate the relationship between the two women, with no further details released, reports said.
In Taiwan, the Ministry of Justice said that while the Tainan Prosecutors’ Office had not yet requested judicial assistance from Japan, the ministry would handle any such request in accordance with the law and maintain contact with Japanese law enforcement agencies.

Last year, the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) and the Taiwan People’s Party reinstated Taiwan Retrocession Day on Oct. 25 as a national holiday. It came under a broader program of “giving holidays back to the people,” adding four new or restored public holidays to the calendar. Naturally, people welcomed the change. But why must this particular holiday be tied to the historically and ideologically contentious “retrocession” day?
In 1945, the Republic of China (ROC) government accepted Japan’s surrender in Taipei, bringing 50 years of Japanese colonial rule to an end. At the time, many Taiwanese had high hopes for the new regime. What came next, however, was a chaotic takeover, the tragic 228 Incident of 1947, and the martial law and White Terror that followed. The end of Japanese colonial rule by no means meant that the people had gained their freedom.
The term “retrocession” means more than just a change of government; it is suggestive of liberation and celebration. The KMT might view Oct. 25 through the lens of victory in the war against Japan, but Taiwanese who experienced political repression also have reason to ask why it should be the day of post-World War II takeover that is designated for celebration. The end of colonial rule can be marked and acknowledged without needing to buy into a single interpretation of history.
Retrocession Day had not been a public holiday for many years. In 2001, civil servants moved to a five-day workweek and Oct. 25 became a day of commemoration without a holiday. In 2017, amendments to the Labor Standards Act (勞動基準法) to reduce working hours and improve leave entitlements saw private-sector workers also cease to receive the day off. Yet none of this made Taiwan any less able to study and reflect on the history of 1945.
The Legislative Yuan has the power to add public holidays, as well as the power to pick the occasion. If the goal is to protect people’s rights to rest and have time off, why not discuss holidays marking the lifting of martial law, freedom of speech or human rights? Why must it be Retrocession Day that is restored?
Expanding public holidays and choosing which historical events to commemorate are two distinct policy questions; the latter should not be swept away in a policy push for the former.
Last year, China established its own “Commemoration Day of Taiwan’s Restoration,” linking the occasion to its “one China” principle and calls for unification. In 1945, it was the ROC government that accepted Japan’s surrender in Taipei; at that time, the Chinese Communist Party had not yet been founded.
How Beijing uses narratives surrounding “retrocession” cannot determine how Taiwan should judge its own history. However, if Taiwan celebrates the day without critical reflection, it cannot avoid confronting the ongoing significance this term holds in cross-strait politics.
If the concern is truly about workers, then let us discuss working hours and the sufficient right to rest. If the aim is to face up to history, then different perspectives on 1945 must be allowed. Holidays with historical baggage means that people who simply want an extra day off are first asked to concede to particular interpretations of the past.
Oct. 25 can be remembered without being publicly designated for celebrations. Ultimately, what Taiwan should cherish most deeply is the democracy and freedom its people fought so hard to win.
An extra public holiday does not have to mean celebrating so-called “retrocession.”
Steve Ho is a retired engineer.

Government studying ways to compensate creators whose work is used to train AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:41:29 UTC
01:41:29 KST

The government is exploring ways to compensate authors and other content providers for materials used to train artificial intelligence (AI) models, but has yet to determine how content should be valued, licensed or paid for.
Democratic Progressive Party Legislator Michelle Lin (林楚茵) raised the issue earlier this month during a meeting of the legislature’s Transportation Committee.
She asked whether the Ministry of Digital Affairs would provide content free of charge for AI model training following efforts to obtain voluntarily licensed material from Taiwanese book publishers.
Photo: Reuters
She also asked whether the ministry was developing a mechanism for AI developers to pay news outlets for the use of their content.
Minister of Digital Affairs Lin Yi-ching (林宜敬) said the ministry is collecting four types of training content through its voluntary initiative: works whose copyright protection has expired and that are in the public domain, book descriptions provided by publishers, book preview material and works that authors have voluntarily licensed.
The ministry has not sought AI training material from Taiwanese news outlets, he said.
“We are aware that several international news media outlets have signed content authorization agreements with large AI firms, and we would work to facilitate such partnerships in Taiwan,” Lin Yi-ching said.
“Our ultimate goal is for large AI firms, particularly those based in the US, to pay for the content they use to train their models,” he said, adding that the ministry is considering only public-domain and voluntarily licensed material to avoid delaying Taiwan’s AI development through potentially protracted legal disputes over content use.
The ministry began building a corpus of high-quality traditional Chinese content for Taiwan’s sovereign AI models late last year, initially using materials provided by central and local government agencies. On Sept. 15, it announced rules governing the participation of private publishers and e-book platform operators, including provisions for voluntary participation, content authorization and the removal of works by authors who opt out.
As of the middle of this month, the corpus had accumulated 3.3 billion tokens — units of text that AI models use to process and learn language.
The government is also studying ways to encourage AI developers to pay for training materials, but has not specified how payments would be calculated, how any revenue would be shared or when a mechanism might be introduced.
At a separate meeting convened in July by the Taiwan Intellectual Property Office (TIPO), representatives of magazine publishers and broadcast media proposed measures to ensure AI companies pay for the use of their content.
The government should establish a licensing platform to allow media companies to register content for AI companies to use in exchange for payment, CommonWealth Magazine legal affairs director Chiu Ai-lun (邱愛倫) said.
She also urged AI companies to disclose the content they license and the sources of their training data.
Some international AI companies continued to scrape media Web sites even when the owners have explicitly prohibited such activity, Satellite Television Broadcasting Association secretary-general May Chen (陳依玫) said.
She also called for a mechanism to connect content owners with AI companies seeking to license their material.
TIPO’s draft Copyright Guidelines for Generative Artificial Intelligence (生成式人工智慧著作權指引) could give the impression that obtaining authorization was the only way to use copyrighted material, Taiwan Innovative Software and Services Association vice chairman Chang Jung-kuei (張榮貴) said.
Fair-use provisions, which permit the use of copyrighted material without the rights holder’s permission under certain circumstances, should remain available when data sources are lawfully accessed and the AI-generated output does not replace original works in the market, he said.
He also proposed exploring corpus-matching or collective licensing mechanisms.

Maintain control of Hormuz, Leader insists in meeting with security chief
TEHRAN — Leader of the Islamic Revolution Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Khamenei met with Major General Mohsen Rezaei, Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council (SNSC), for a review of the country’s situation across culture, politics, economy and security, and the region’s shifting order.
During the meeting, the Leader described the SNSC and its Secretariat as the “crossroads of policymaking” in the country’s affairs, stressing that culture, politics, economy and security are interconnected and that decisions in each field must be accompanied by appropriate supporting measures.
He said sound and well-grounded decisions require a roadmap based on a comprehensive understanding of each undertaking, from its starting point to its conclusion.
Unity, trust and constitutional capacities
Other key topics discussed included strengthening national cohesion and unity, as well as mutual trust between the people and officials.
The Leader underlined the need to make use of the capacities provided by the Constitution, particularly Article 176, to assist the President and executive bodies in facilitating and expediting the resolution of the country’s problems.
He described the enemy’s desperation as one of the fruits of national resistance, while emphasizing the need for proactive and timely communication to sustain the people’s continued participation in defending the country and the Islamic establishment.
The Leader also stressed the need to pursue the rights and interests of the Iranian nation and the Resistance Front by ensuring that the conditions set forth by the country’s officials for ending the war are met, and by bringing the current state of “neither war nor peace” to an end.
Safeguarding national and regional security by maintaining control over the Strait of Hormuz, and strengthening bilateral relations with neighboring countries on the basis of lasting and mutual interests, were among other points raised by the Leader.
For his part, Rezaei presented a report on the country’s situation in various sectors and ongoing efforts. He identified the pursuit of the Islamic Republic’s strategic policy of “establishing endogenous regional arrangements and order” as one of the initiatives currently being undertaken by the Secretariat of the SNSC.
From directive to action: quadrilateral in Tehran
Rezaei’s remarks after Monday’s quadrilateral meeting in Tehran — which brought together senior officials from Iran, Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia on regional security and stability — illustrated that policy in practice.
Speaking after the talks hosted by Iran, the SNSC secretary called for a regional security framework built by West Asian countries themselves and free from foreign interference, saying the meeting demonstrated that U.S. threats had failed to deter regional states from pursuing closer ties.
“Following the resistance of the Iranian nation and the strength of our Armed Forces, a new and positive atmosphere has emerged in the region and in our discussions with senior officials from Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia,” Rezaei said, adding that regional cooperation should have begun much earlier.
He said the results of Iran’s resistance were becoming increasingly evident and that the participating countries shared the view that regional challenges could best be addressed through cooperation among all four nations.
The discussions, he said, had led to a clear conclusion: security in West Asia must be generated from within the region, and foreign intervention must be prevented.
In a post on X, Rezaei reinforced that position, arguing that the United States had failed to bring security to any country in the region and that Washington’s inability to provide security guarantees had become apparent.
“Security in West Asia must originate from within the region itself, and any foreign intervention must be prevented,” he wrote.
Ghalibaf recounts Leader’s outlook on economy and war
In a related account, Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf on Tuesday gave MPs details of his own recent meeting with Ayatollah Khamenei, saying he found the Leader in full health, with strong spirit, hope, firmness, inner calm and full command of issues.
Despite the heavy personal losses he has suffered, this spirit reflects profound faith in God and deep trust in the people, Ghalibaf told the open session of Parliament in his pre-agenda remarks.
According to Ghalibaf, the Leader closely followed macroeconomic indicators and stressed that they must be assessed precisely, with neither overestimation nor underestimation.
Another major topic, raised by the Leader for the third time during the war, was securing production chains — from raw materials and production cycles to the supply of basic goods — Ghalibaf said.
Preserving people’s purchasing power and livelihoods, especially those of the Armed Forces and fighters on the frontlines who must remain the priority, was another point of emphasis, he added.
Ghalibaf said military issues, the war and the Resistance Front, as well as diplomacy, negotiations, and in particular the economic war, economic exclusion and the naval blockade, were discussed, with reports presented and reviewed.
The Leader, he said, also stressed service to the people particularly in the area of resilience, maximum unity among officials, adoption of firm and unified positions — especially at the level of branch heads — the latest state of relations with strategic partners, especially China, on which he regularly follows up, and cooperation between the government and Parliament.

EU proposes expanded Frontex powers beyond bloc's borders
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:40:00 UTC
01:40:00 KST

The European Commission on Tuesday unveiled plans to significantly broaden the authority of EU border agency Frontex, including allowing operations outside the bloc, following a surge in migrant arrivals at Spain's Ceuta enclave last summer.
The proposal would significantly broaden Frontex's mandate, allowing it to carry out deportations between non-EU countries, operate outside the bloc and deploy rapid-reaction teams in emergencies.
The proposed legislation is an attempt to make Frontex more reactive to large-scale arrivals at the EU's borders, such as in Ceuta on the North African coast, as European governments push for tougher migration policies despite concerns from rights advocates over accountability.
"Today we propose that Frontex becomes the central EU actor on returns," Magnus Brunner, commissioner for internal affairs and migration, told reporters.
"It will be able to act faster, with a quick reaction force that can deploy within 24 hours and spot risks early, before an event becomes a crisis," Brunner added.
But while the proposal would significantly broaden Frontex's role, it would also narrow the scope of its internal rights watchdog, with complaints referred to national authorities to handle.
The proposal comes as member states increasingly focus on returns, arguing that too many migrants ordered to leave the bloc ultimately remain.
Although irregular arrivals have decreased, the arrival of more than 72,000 people in Ceuta from Morocco in late July, most of whom later left, reignited debate over the EU's migration rules and was cited by several member states as evidence for stronger tools.
The plan envisages gradually expanding Frontex's standing corps to 30,000 officers by creating a new "European border and return reserve" of 17,000 officers by 2041, who would remain at the disposal of member states and could be deployed when needed, the commission said in a statement.
The proposal would create a new EU Return Coordination Centre within Frontex and expand the agency's role across the entire deportation process, from voluntary return counselling to organising returns and reintegration support, the statement said.
The agency would also be empowered to help organise and carry out deportations from one non-EU country to another, subject to agreements with the countries involved and international legal standards, according to the statement.
That would mean Frontex could, for example, deport a Bangladeshi national from Libya - one of the main launching points for migrant boats crossing to Europe - back to Bangladesh.
The proposal would also create a new online monitoring centre to track border-related developments on social media and support action against content linked to border security risks.
The Commission proposed allocating €11.8 billion to Frontex for the EU's 2028-2034 budget cycle, nearly double the almost €6 billion earmarked for the agency under the current 2021-2027 framework, as part of a planned expansion of its mandate.
The push comes just a few months after EU lawmakers approved new rules aimed at speeding up deportations and allowing member states to establish return hubs outside the bloc.
Tuesday's proposal was met with criticism from rights groups and some lawmakers.
"Working with third countries, without proper oversight or accountability, is a threat to fundamental rights and respect for international law, while leaving Frontex staff in legal limbo outside of European law," said Tineke Strik, a Dutch MEP from the Greens/EFA group.
"The Commission is pandering to populism and the far right on migration," she added.

Waltz returned to the embargo, pointing to US trade with Cuba as evidence that Havana’s description of the measures was misleading.

NEW YORK - Human rights monitors criticised senior UAE diplomat Lana Nusseibeh’s candidacy to be the next UN chief on Oct 27, citing her role in championing the country’s foreign policy and denying the UAE’s role in fuelling the conflict in Sudan.
Pushback against the prominent Middle Eastern candidate has gathered steam since her late entry last week.
Her bid upended the gridlocked race to replace UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, as he finishes his second five-year term this year.
Despite months of campaigning by several senior UN figures and former country leaders, the competition has struggled to produce a consensus choice among the Security Council’s most powerful nations.
Sudan’s war, which erupted in April 2023 following a power struggle between the military and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), has displaced more than 14 million people and created one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises.
“She has been asked about the UAE’s role in arming and supporting the RSF, and she just blatantly denies it without regard to the facts – that is not what we need as UN Secretary-General,” Kenneth Roth, former executive director of Human Rights Watch, told a webinar organised by the campaign.
A UN fact-finding mission said in September that foreign weapons, military technology, fighters and logistical networks – including individuals and entities in the United Arab Emirates, among others – are helping sustain Sudan’s conflict.
“This is the opposite of the kind of moral standing of the human rights leadership that we want from a UN Secretary-General,” Roth told the webinar titled “Call To Stop UAE Minister’s Bid for UN Top Job Amid Sudan Genocide”.
The webinar also featured Sudanese experts, as well as a survivor of the El Fasher massacre, on their concerns about Nusseibeh’s candidacy and its implications for the UN’s commitment to protect civilians, according to the organisers.
“Electing its senior diplomat as secretary-general would hand leadership of those same institutions to that government’s chief defender, at the very moment Sudanese civilians most need the UN to hold powerful states accountable,” said Husam Mahjoub a Sudanese advocate and founder of Sudan Bukra TV.
Asked about Sudan during the dialogue with the General Assembly on Oct 27, Nusseibeh said: “If I were to become secretary-general, Sudan would be a number one priority, as one of the most horrific conflicts we have seen in recent history.”
“The loss of human life on the ground is a tragedy, the atrocities committed by the RSF are atrocious, and I would support the work of all UN fact-finding missions for accountability and transitional justice,” she added.
Reached for comment on the criticism by the activists, she said: “I would put the UN’s full political and practical support behind ongoing efforts to reach a ceasefire and a credible and inclusive political process that reflects the democratic aspirations of the Sudanese people.”
Nusseibeh, 48, served as UAE ambassador to the UN for more than a decade.
She previously led the UAE’s successful campaign for election to the Security Council.
She is widely known by diplomats working in New York, who say she is a competent manager, skilled negotiator and clear communicator.
An informal council poll in October had placed former Costa Rican Vice-President Rebeca Grynspan as the narrow frontrunner in the race.
But she and all other candidates received two or more opposing votes from the ultimately decisive five permanent members of the council – Russia, China, the US, France and Britain.
Whoever wins will have to tackle multiple crises, including several wars, cutbacks in American contributions to the UN, and the 193-member body’s declining political relevance as Washington has pulled out of dozens of its agencies.
The next straw poll could take place as soon as Oct 30, but the format and exact timing are still being negotiated by the diplomats. REUTERS

It adds to a series of Russian strikes on Ukrainian publishing houses, printing facilities, and book warehouses that have destroyed millions of books and disrupted the country’s publishing industry.
KSD announced the strike on social media, saying it had planned to greet readers on the holiday and reveal its November releases but instead had to deal with the attack. The publisher said strikes in the area were continuing, preventing it from determining the full extent of the damage.

“We really want to show you the new releases we had prepared for November,” KSD said. “But for now, as we clarify the details, we cannot yet assess the scale of the destruction and understand how we will work going forward.”

Russia’s attacks devastate Ukraine’s book industry
KSD’s warehouse is the latest publishing facility affected by Russia’s campaign against Ukraine’s book industry. In July and August alone, Russian attacks destroyed around 13 million books, nearly a third of the number Ukrainian publishers printed in all of 2025, according to the Ukrainian publishing industry.
On 1 August, a Russian strike on a warehouse used by the Ranok publishing group in Kharkiv destroyed around 8 million books, including hundreds of thousands of school textbooks. A separate attack on a printing facility in July destroyed print runs and book materials belonging to numerous Ukrainian publishers.
In October, Russian strikes also damaged a Kyiv warehouse belonging to publisher Knyholav, destroying tens of thousands of books, including titles and reprints that had replaced stock lost in an earlier attack.
Russia has burned millions of Ukrainian books, striking at the infrastructure of Ukrainian culture
These strikes threaten more than publishers’ finances. Destroyed print runs and damaged warehouses delay new releases, deprive readers of Ukrainian-language books, and force publishers to spend scarce resources replacing titles instead of developing new ones.
KSD has not yet disclosed its losses or announced a revised release schedule for its November books.

American Airlines is raising the annual fee for two of its rewards credit cards for the first time since 2018 and adding new benefits like a TSA PreCheck credit and points from spending on hotels.
The fee on the Citi AAdvantage Platinum Select World Elite Mastercard will go up to $150 a year from $99. That is the first hike since 2018, when it raised the fee from $95 to $99, an airline spokeswoman said.
The Citi AAdvantage Business Mastercard will also have a fee increase and will now cost $150 a year.
Airlines and their bank partners have been steadily raising fees on rewards credit cards.
Those cards generate billions of dollars a year for airlines, which make money when miles are sold to banks, which then give them to customers. American's move, announced Tuesday, follows similar increases by rivals such as United Airlines.
Meanwhile, American Express last year raised the fee on its popular Platinum card, which comes with airport lounge access, to $895 a year from $695. JPMorgan Chase increased the annual fee on its competing card, the Sapphire Reserve, to $795 from $550.
The new perks for the American card include three times AAdvantage miles earnings on hotels booked through American's portal, a credit of up to $120 every four years for Global Entry or TSA PreCheck, and a $100 annual statement credit on in-flight purchases like food.
The new fees take effect Jan. 24.

Some 75% of Jewish employees find workplae DEI approaches inconsistent on antisemitism, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:32:33 UTC
01:32:33 KST

A new workplace study published on Tuesday has revealed that 75.5% of Jewish employees feel that Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI) approaches within their organizations fail to respond consistently to antisemitism.
The research report titled Yes, But... Antisemitism and the Limits of Workplace Inclusion was published by Pearn Kandola, a business psychology firm co-founded by Professor Binna Kandola. Pearn Kandola is a UK-based occupational psychology consultancy that specializes in diversity, inclusion, and unconscious bias training for corporate and public sector organizations.
The study follows the organization’s 2024 research on workplace antisemitism and Islamophobia, which tracked a nearly 50% increase in antisemitic incidents following the October 7, 2023 massacre.
Following a series of webinars held during Antisemitism at Work Week in June, researchers noted that Jewish attendees repeatedly described a lack of responsiveness from diversity teams regarding antisemitism, prompting a broader investigation into whether these experiences reflected an isolated trend or a systemic pattern.
The research combined a national survey of 1,002 Jewish employees across the UK with qualitative interviews involving participants from various sectors and organizational levels. The interviews included individuals directly involved in diversity and inclusion roles, with some working for large US multinationals and describing interactions with American diversity teams.
Majority of Jewish respondents have misgivings over practical application of corporate commitments to equality
According to the survey findings, while the vast majority of Jewish respondents acknowledged public corporate commitments to equality, major misgivings emerged regarding their practical application. Specifically, 87% of respondents agreed that their organization expressed a clear commitment to tackling racism and discrimination, and 83% agreed that the diversity function was visibly active on these issues. However, 75.5% agreed that their organization’s diversity approach was not consistent in its response to antisemitism, 72.7% noticed a gap between public commitments and actual responses, and 60.5% agreed that antisemitism receives less attention than other forms of racism.
The survey findings also highlighted a severe chilling effect on employee reporting and confidence. Only 15.9% of respondents said they felt able to raise concerns about antisemitism in the workplace. Furthermore, 70.8% of respondents agreed that they had avoided raising concerns because they were unsure how those reports would be received. The report analyzed this low reporting not as an indicator of low prevalence, but as a cycle of futility where employees conclude that speaking up will not yield understanding or action.
The study pointed to organizational listening as a central challenge. The report claimed that providing formal reporting channels or communication pathways is insufficient if institutions lack the capability and motivation to properly receive, interpret, and act upon employee feedback. When concerns are routinely minimized or misread, employees tend to withdraw, creating a dangerous paradox where a low number of complaints mistakenly bolsters corporate confidence that no underlying problem exists.
Problem goes beyond lack of understanding Kandola tells 'Post'
Professor Binna Kandola OBE told The Jerusalem Post: “Our research raises serious questions about the way Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion functions operate. We found that many Jewish employees feel overlooked by the very people whose responsibility it is to promote inclusion.”
Kandola added, “The problem goes beyond a lack of understanding of antisemitism. It concerns the assumptions and frameworks that some DEI practitioners use to understand discrimination. Jews are often stereotyped as wealthy, powerful, influential, and privileged. Because many are white, they do not fit comfortably into models of discrimination that see racism primarily through the lens of power and privilege. As a result, antisemitism can be minimized, explained away, or simply ignored.”
Through in-depth interviews, the research examined how diversity functions can fail to address antisemitism, identifying several recurring rhetorical devices and organizational responses. Among these, denial manifested directly or through silence and omission, such as when Holocaust Memorial Day events omitted references to Jews or when organizations remained silent following October 7. Reversal occurred when individuals raising antisemitism were repositioned as the wrongdoers or accused of self-interest. Liberal arguments regarding merit and fairness were also identified, where perceived Jewish success, wealth, or representation was used to imply that Jewish people do not experience racism or require inclusion support.
Deracialization emerged when antisemitism was reframed as a generic religious matter, an international political issue, or an interpersonal disagreement rather than a form of racial exclusion. Other identified mechanisms included distancing through inaction or framing incidents as isolated anomalies rather than systemic issues, positive self-presentation where inclusion credentials masked operational gaps, trivialization of Jewish safety by making it low priority, and empathizing primarily with perpetrators over targets.
Additional themes from the interviews explored the complexities of Jewish identity, which participants noted encompasses ethnicity, culture, ancestry, and peoplehood rather than religion alone. Interviewees also discussed the distinction between legitimate criticism of Israeli government policy and antisemitism, noting that difficulties arose when diversity teams viewed all Jewish concerns exclusively through the lens of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. Employee resource groups, while intended to offer support, were occasionally reported by interviewees as having been utilized by diversity teams to block action or contain antisemitism as a niche issue relevant only to Jewish networks. Furthermore, participants described heightened fear, visibility concerns, and the heavy emotional burden of acting as educators or public advocates for their community.
The report concluded by outlining several core findings regarding the limitations of current diversity practices. The report emphasized that diversity frameworks centered rigidly on power, privilege, and oppression can inadvertently obscure Jewish vulnerability due to persistent stereotypes surrounding influence and success. The report stressed that psychological safety remains ineffective without active organizational listening, and that professional expertise in antisemitism and prejudice cannot be assumed simply through a general commitment to equality or membership in affinity groups.
Professor Kandola told the Post, “Organizations need to take a critical look at their DEI functions. They should examine the assumptions that underpin their work, the evidence supporting their approaches, and whether they are applying the same standards of fairness to everyone. Importantly, these reviews should not be led by the DEI functions themselves.”
Professor Kandola further noted, “We also need to professionalize DEI. A commitment to equality, however sincere, is not a substitute for expertise in the psychology of prejudice, stereotyping and discrimination. Practitioners must be prepared to recognize and challenge their own biases, not just those of others.”
Based on these conclusions, the report provided six key recommendations for organizational leaders: reappraise the purpose and practice of diversity functions through independent review; redefine professional expertise by ensuring practitioners understand the distinct history and contemporary manifestations of antisemitism; separate representation metrics from inclusion experiences; clarify the role of employee resource groups so they do not act as expert advisory bodies or veto mechanisms; build genuine organizational listening capabilities into reporting structures; and introduce reflexive practice so that inclusion teams routinely examine their own underlying assumptions and potential biases.
“Our findings are not an argument for abandoning DEI. They are an argument for fundamentally rethinking how it operates. An approach to inclusion that fails to recognize discrimination because the people experiencing it do not fit a particular model is failing in its most basic purpose,” Professor Kandola told the Post.

Oman: No lasting Persian Gulf security without Iran’s participation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:32:06 UTC
01:32:06 KST

Oman: No lasting Persian Gulf security without Iran’s participation
TEHRAN — Omani Foreign Minister Badr bin Hamad Al Busaidi has called for an inclusive regional security framework bringing together Iran, Iraq and the six member states of the Persian Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), warning that any arrangement excluding Tehran would be inherently unstable and incapable of delivering lasting security.
Speaking at the University of Cambridge on Monday in a speech titled Inclusive Security in the Persian Gulf, Al Busaidi challenged approaches that portray Iran as a threat around which regional security arrangements should be built, arguing instead that stability depends on cooperation among the countries bordering the Persian Gulf.
He said existing security arrangements had been shaped by the mistaken assumption that Iran and the Arab states of the Persian Gulf were fundamentally hostile to one another, despite centuries of coexistence and shared regional interests.
With a population of approximately 93 million, a history spanning some 3,000 years and a coastline extending along roughly half of the Persian Gulf, Iran is an indispensable part of the region’s security equation, the Omani foreign minister argued.
Foreign military presence has carried political costs
Al Busaidi also questioned the long-term consequences of the Persian Gulf states’ reliance on foreign military powers, pointing to US military agreements, intelligence cooperation, naval deployments and air defense systems.
While stating that such arrangements had delivered certain benefits, he said their political costs over the longer term had been substantial.
His assessment reflects a broader debate over whether an enduring regional security order can be built through external military guarantees or whether it requires direct cooperation among the countries most affected by instability.
From this perspective, excluding Iran from regional security arrangements would leave a major regional power outside the very framework intended to address shared security concerns, undermining the prospects for a sustainable settlement.
Al Busaidi did not suggest that cooperation with international partners should end. Instead, he called for a shift away from military commitments toward investment, economic development and other forms of constructive engagement.
Iran-US negotiations and Strait of Hormuz security
The Omani foreign minister cited the Iranian nuclear issue and negotiations over maritime navigation through the Strait of Hormuz as examples of regional challenges that have been complicated by external involvement.
Oman has played a mediating role in indirect negotiations between Iran and the United States. According to Al Busaidi, Muscat facilitated five rounds of talks in April and May 2025 and three further rounds in February 2026.
He said substantial progress had been achieved, and an agreement had appeared within reach before the US-Israeli military aggression against Iran disrupted the diplomatic process.
Al Busaidi also reported progress in discussions between Oman and Iran on a preliminary framework for an interim maritime security agreement, while acknowledging that political obstacles remained.
The Strait of Hormuz is a vital international energy transit route, making security arrangements there a matter of importance not only for the Persian Gulf's coastal states but also for global energy markets and maritime trade. The Omani position points to the importance of addressing navigation and maritime security through engagement with the countries directly concerned.
Reviving a regional security initiative
As a way forward, Al Busaidi proposed reviving a 1976 initiative for collective security among the eight states bordering the Persian Gulf: Iran, Iraq and the six GCC members.
He identified a non-aggression pact as a possible foundation for an inclusive regional arrangement, suggesting that a shared commitment to refrain from aggression could help establish the trust needed for broader cooperation.
Such a framework would place regional states at the center of decisions affecting their security and provide a platform for addressing disputes through dialogue rather than military confrontation.
Al Busaidi's proposal also leaves room for continued international engagement but envisages a different role for external partners—one focused more on economic investment and development than on military deployments and security guarantees.
The central message of his speech was that lasting stability cannot be imposed on the Persian Gulf through arrangements that exclude one of its principal coastal states. Instead, he argued, security must be built through the participation of all regional countries and grounded in their shared responsibility for peace and stability.
The proposal reinforces the importance of regional diplomacy at a time when tensions involving Iran, the United States and Israel have heightened concerns over military escalation, maritime security and the wider consequences for energy supplies and regional stability.

Security and defence
An important item on the agenda was fostering Polish–Vietnamese cooperation in the fields of security and defence. Deputy Minister Robert Kupiecki took part in talks on the development of a military partnership, including between the defence industries of the two countries. Both sides also declared their willingness to strengthen cooperation within UN peacekeeping operations.
One key area of discussion was countering contemporary security threats. Poland and Vietnam announced the enhancement of cooperation on combating cybercrime, cross-border crime, human trafficking, and illegal migration, as well as on the protection of critical infrastructure and exchange of information and experiences.
Economy, trade, and transport
One of the priorities of the strategic partnership is to increase trade and mutual investment and to create more favourable conditions for entrepreneurs. Poland and Vietnam reaffirmed the importance of making full use of the EU–Vietnam Free Trade Agreement (EVFTA), reducing non-tariff barriers, and facilitating access to the markets in both countries. The development of Polish agri-food export, industrial cooperation, and modern technologies is of particular importance.
Regular meetings of the Polish–Vietnamese Working Group on Cooperation in the Field of Agriculture, the next session of which should take place by April 2027, will serve to further develop economic cooperation. The launch of a direct LOT Polish Airlines air link between Warsaw and Hanoi, scheduled for the first quarter of 2027, will also create new opportunities for businesspeople and tourists alike.
Regional cooperation and international affairs
During the talks, both sides reaffirmed their commitment to the principles of the UN Charter, international law, and respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of states.
Poland and Vietnam emphasised the need to achieve a comprehensive, just, and lasting peace in Ukraine, in accordance with international law and the principles of the UN Charter, including the prohibition on the use or threat of use of force.
The two sides also acknowledged the importance of peace, stability, and freedom of navigation and overflight in the South China Sea. They also spoke for peaceful resolution of disputes in line with the international law, particularly with the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS),
and agreed to strengthen cooperation in multilateral forums, including within the framework of Poland’s and the EU’s relations with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN). Vietnam expressed its support for Poland’s efforts to strengthen cooperation with countries in the region.
Science, modern technologies, and people-to-people contacts
The strategic partnership will also include the development of cooperation in the fields of digitalisation, innovation, scientific research, and the medical and pharmaceutical industries. Both sides announced plans to expand cooperation between universities and research institutes, to organise exchanges of students and experts, and to support the teaching of Polish and Vietnamese.
Interpersonal contacts remain an important element of relations, including the role of the Vietnamese community in Poland, which is instrumental in bridging the two countries.
The Joint Action Plan for 2026–2030 will serve to implement the agreed priorities. It is intended to translate the strategic partnership into specific political, economic, and social ventures.
Lastly, Prime Minister Donald Tusk invited Prime Minister Lê Minh Hưng to pay an official visit to Poland.

German court sinks bid to cancel Nord Stream trial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:29:36 UTC
01:29:36 KST

German court sinks bid to cancel Nord Stream trial
A German court has rejected an attempt to end the trial of Nord Stream bombing suspect Sergey Kuznetsov, after the defendant’s lawyers claimed that he cannot be convicted without a confession.
Kuznetsov, a Ukrainian military officer whom German prosecutors claim carried out the sabotage of the Nord Stream 1 and Nord Stream 2 gas pipelines in 2022, stayed silent in the opening hearing of his trial earlier this month. As Kuznetsov was an active duty soldier at the time of the bombings, his legal team claimed that he cannot be forced to defend himself without divulging state secrets, and filed a motion to dismiss the charges against him.
The Higher Regional Court of Hamburg rejected the motion on Tuesday. “According to German law, the defendant is not restricted in his defense,” presiding Judge Anne Meier-Goring told the court, explaining that the terms of Kuznetsov’s service in Ukraine do not apply in Germany.
Kuznetsov is accused of causing an explosion, disrupting public utilities, property damage, and being an “accomplice to war crimes.” He has neither admitted nor denied carrying out the attack.
Prosecutors claim that he led a seven-person team into the Baltic Sea on a rented pleasure yacht and planted timed explosives on all four individual lines comprising the Nord Stream 1 and 2 projects, three of which completely destroyed the pipes. They did this, prosecutors allege, despite the well-documented limitations of the yacht and the logistical and technical difficulties in carrying out multiple deep-sea dives in a single night.
The case rests on a relatively flimsy body of evidence. Although Kuznetsov was allegedly seen in Germany prior to renting the yacht in Rostock, his fingerprints were not among those lifted from the vessel, and a phone call to his wife in which he defended the bombing as “an official military operation” is the closest thing to a confession that prosecutors can work with.
Russia maintains that the version of events presented in Hamburg is implausible from the outset. “Five people were sitting around drinking, having a laugh, and decided ‘Why don’t we blow up the Nord Stream pipelines?’ They had diving skills, allegedly hired a little boat, sailed to the place where the Nord Streams were passing, went down, planted explosives and detonated them,” Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov commented in 2024. “If someone can actually believe this version, then it’s only people who are afraid of the truth and are trying to protect the criminal Kiev regime in any way possible.”
American journalist Seymour Hersh has put forward an alternate theory. Citing sources in the intelligence community, Hersh claimed that CIA divers, working with the Norwegian Navy, used NATO’s June 2022 BALTOPS exercises in the Baltic Sea as cover to plant remotely-detonated explosives on the Nord Stream lines, which were triggered three months later with a sonar buoy.
Another lead came from a Danish harbormaster, who claimed in September 2024 that he had approached a US amphibious assault ship – with its transponder switched off – at the location of the pipelines five days before the explosions. The harbormaster claimed that he was ordered to turn away by the Danish Naval Operational Command and forbidden from discussing the incident.
His claims were never investigated. Denmark closed its investigation into the bombings seven months before the harbormaster came forward with his claims.
Back in Hamburg, Kuznetsov’s trial is expected to run into the new year.

Bagheri: Tehran quadrilateral meeting reflects Iran’s defense capabilities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:29:12 UTC
01:29:12 KST

Bagheri: Tehran quadrilateral meeting reflects Iran’s defense capabilities
TEHRAN — Ali Bagheri Kani, deputy for international affairs at the Secretariat of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, has described the quadrilateral meeting between Iran, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan in Tehran as a product of the Iranian nation’s resistance and the courage of its Armed Forces, saying the gathering reflected a growing recognition among regional countries that 'lasting security must be built through cooperation and reliance on domestic capabilities.'
Speaking after Monday’s meeting, Bagheri Kani said the talks took place against the backdrop of major strategic developments in the region over recent months, the “brutal aggression” of the Israeli regime and the “terrorist US government.”
He said Iran’s resistance had thwarted Washington’s objectives and left the United States facing a difficult situation. He also maintained that developments following the Israeli regime’s aggression against Iran had not unfolded according to its plans.
Bagheri Kani identified two major outcomes of the confrontation: Iran’s ability to withstand military aggression through its domestic capabilities and the demonstrated effectiveness of its indigenous defense industry.
Indigenous capabilities and resistance to sanctions
The official said the Islamic Republic had relied on its national resources and domestic capabilities to withstand two separate acts of aggression, adding that Iran had succeeded in confronting both.
He noted that the United States and Western countries had imposed sanctions on Iran for decades, particularly targeting strategic sectors and restricting the country’s access to advanced military equipment and technology.
Despite those restrictions, he said, Iranian military personnel and specialists had made significant advances in defense capabilities, demonstrating their effectiveness under operational conditions.
He maintained that Iran’s experience demonstrated the strategic importance of developing indigenous capabilities rather than depending on external powers for national security.
The official also pointed to a broader lesson for countries across West Asia, saying some regional states had believed that aligning themselves with a major power such as the United States would shield them from security threats. In practice, however, he said, events had shown that such expectations did not necessarily correspond with reality.
He argued that regional countries therefore had growing reasons to pursue security through regional engagement, cooperation and the pooling of their respective capabilities.
Israeli policies and the case for regional security cooperation
Bagheri Kani said developments involving the Israeli regime had created an important basis for greater understanding among regional countries about the sources of insecurity and instability.
He argued that the regime’s actions, particularly following developments in recent years, had demonstrated its 'aggressive conduct and lack of restraint in pursuing its ambitions.'
Referring to the concept of “Greater Israel,” he said the idea encompassed a number of countries in the region and had reinforced concerns among regional states about the implications of Israeli policies.
According to Bagheri Kani, the growing recognition of the Israeli regime as a source of instability had helped create common ground for regional countries to work toward establishing security within the region.
He identified this assessment as 'one of the key points reflected in the Tehran meeting,' alongside the emphasis all four participating countries placed on self-reliance and the development of domestic capabilities.
The official said Iran regarded reliance on internal resources as a fundamental strategic principle and that the other participants had also acknowledged the importance of self-sufficiency.
“This is a very important point and a fundamental cornerstone on which we can move toward the future,” he said.
Bagheri Kani added that regional security could not be sustainably achieved by relying exclusively on external powers. Instead, he argued, countries in the region needed to strengthen their own capacities and establish cooperative arrangements capable of addressing shared security challenges.
How the quadrilateral meeting came to Tehran
Bagheri Kani also outlined the process that led to the meeting between Iran, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan, explaining that the initiative emerged from earlier consultations among the three other countries and their subsequent efforts to bring Iran into a regional dialogue on security.
He said Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan had previously held a meeting in Pakistan and had expressed a strong interest in Iran's participation. However, circumstances at the time had prevented the Iranian side from attending.
The three countries subsequently held another meeting in Turkey, where they again expressed their desire for Iran to take part in the discussions.
This time, however, they proposed travelling to Iran themselves to hold a quadrilateral meeting in Tehran, Bagheri Kani said.
He cited a previous visit to Tehran by Pakistan’s army chief, during which the Pakistani commander met Major General Rezaei and conveyed the three countries’ interest in convening a meeting in the Iranian capital.
Four countries seek a framework for broader regional engagement
The Iranian official emphasized that the meeting was not an attempt by any one participant to impose its particular outlook on the others. Rather, he said, the four countries sought to develop a common framework capable of accommodating their respective perspectives and encouraging practical cooperation.
He described this approach as a significant feature of the gathering, arguing that a cooperative framework among the four countries could also encourage other regional states to participate in efforts to strengthen security.
Bagheri Kani said Iran, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan had the potential to play an influential role both across the wider region and in the Muslim world if they worked together.
He stressed that their cooperation could serve as a foundation for broader regional participation, enabling countries to address shared security concerns through dialogue, coordination and the development of mutual capabilities.
Its emphasis on self-reliance, regional cooperation and the need for a common approach to security, Bagheri Kani said, reflected a shared interest in developing practical mechanisms for addressing the region’s challenges.
