Forced retreat of neighbors
Khorasan examined the reopening of borders by Iran’s eastern and western neighbors, Pakistan and Iraq, after a forced retreat from restrictive policies. The paper argued that recent statements by Scott Bessent regarding cooperation between Washington and Iran’s neighbors to limit land routes represented a new stage in economic pressure on Tehran. However, developments on both borders showed that isolating Iran through regional blockades is neither easy nor cost-free.
According to the report, Iran remains an important partner for neighboring countries in sectors such as energy and essential goods. Any political decision designed to pressure Tehran for a limited period could result in the long-term loss of valuable markets. The newspaper noted that Iran provides substantial opportunities for foreign exporters, manufacturers, and service companies. Restricting access to this market would reduce sales and may even negatively affect employment in neighboring states. For this reason, attempts to economically isolate Iran could ultimately damage the interests of regional countries as much as, or even more than, Iran itself.
Ettelaat: Shadow of war and a window for diplomacy
Ettelaat focused on the complicated relationship between military developments and diplomacy. It wrote that disagreements over negotiation terms have intensified the challenges facing both Tehran and Washington. Iran seeks relief from economic and maritime pressures as well as guarantees against future confrontations. The United States, in contrast, continues to emphasize nuclear restrictions and security arrangements. The analysis stated that neither side wants to enter negotiations from a position of weakness, making a comprehensive agreement difficult to reach. Declining trust is another major obstacle. When confidence erodes, even establishing common ground on basic issues requires more time and stronger assurances. The newspaper added that economic pressure may be increased in an effort to force concessions, but such measures can also reduce the likelihood of compromise. Successful diplomacy requires a willingness to understand the concerns of the opposing side and to search for realistic solutions rather than simply repeating demands.
Arman-e-Emrooz: Mediators on the move
Arman-e-Emrooz highlighted regional and international mediation efforts aimed at preventing further escalation. The paper noted that several actors are simultaneously attempting to create opportunities for dialogue. Qatar has sent a delegation to Tehran, Pakistan has expressed readiness to mediate, and Russia may assume a more active diplomatic role. According to the report, Iran has made clear that it is prepared for negotiations but only under conditions it considers acceptable. Issues related to the Strait of Hormuz and restrictions on ports are viewed by Tehran as interconnected and cannot be discussed separately. The newspaper argued that meaningful progress depends on confidence-building measures and practical actions by all parties. Maintaining stability is especially important because any serious escalation could affect neighboring countries, international trade, global energy markets, and broader security concerns.
Arman-e-Melli: Why Europeans have become active
Arman-e-Melli examined increasing European diplomatic activity toward Iran. The newspaper argued that since the outbreak of recent tensions and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, many analysts have viewed European countries as among the most vulnerable to the resulting economic and political consequences. As a result, Europe appears to be searching for a new path out of the current situation. The European troika is reportedly interested in playing a more influential role in future discussions between Iran and the United States through a revised framework for negotiations. Political and security indicators suggest that European governments are working to avoid becoming directly involved in policies that could deepen confrontation in the region. However, Europe faces several challenges. Among them are unexpected developments involving energy cooperation between the United States and Russia, as well as growing speculation about a possible accommodation between Russia and Ukraine. These factors have complicated European strategic calculations and encouraged greater diplomatic engagement.
Farhikhtegan: How Iran should deal with US
Farhikhtegan discussed strategic principles that should guide Iran’s approach toward the United States. The article outlined four main recommendations. First, Iranian proposals should be framed in terms of mutual interests rather than demands. This approach can present negotiations as constructive opportunities rather than confrontational exchanges. Second, if circumstances lead Washington to support ending tensions and pursuing an agreement, Iran should seek structural guarantees instead of relying solely on written or verbal commitments. Third, Tehran should expand the number and diversity of mediators, partners, and supporters involved in diplomatic efforts. Fourth, despite their limitations, international organizations should remain important instruments for advancing national objectives and protecting interests. The article concluded by arguing that the United States should be judged by its actions rather than its statements. Real policies, treatment of allies, and tangible outcomes are ultimately more important than public rhetoric in determining intentions and future relations.

The “Tiepolo 2026” Award to Giovanni Ferrero and Benito Tesier of Brembo
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
17:27:21 CET
01:27:21 KST

Giovanni Ferrero, executive chairman of the Ferrero confectionery group, and Benito Tesier Sierra, general manager of Brembo Iberia, are the winners of the 2026 Tiepolo Award, an honor bestowed upon business leaders who contribute to strengthening economic and commercial ties between Italy and Spain.
                                    
The award, now in its 29th edition and established in 1996, is presented jointly by the Italian Chamber of Commerce and Industry for Spain (CCIS) and the Spanish Confederation of Business Organizations (CEOE), under the auspices of the Italian Embassy in Madrid. The award ceremony will take place on November 17 at the Italian Embassy, in the presence of Ambassador Giuseppe Buccino Grimaldi and representatives from institutions and businesses in both countries.
                                    
The jury sought to recognize, in particular, the Ferrero Group’s strategic decision to focus on Spain as an industrial and technological platform for growth in Europe, as well as Tesier’s contribution to the development and consolidation of Brembo in the Iberian market.
                                    
The group, founded in Alba, Piedmont, in 1946, is celebrating 80 years of operation this year as a family-owned business, now in its third generation. As one of the world’s leading manufacturers of packaged confectionery products, it employs over 50,000 people, operates in more than 170 countries, and generates revenue of nearly 20 billion euros.
                                    
Its relationship with Spain dates back to 1985. In 1988, Ferrero Ibérica was established, with headquarters in Barcelona. Today, the company employs approximately 200 people on the Iberian Peninsula, across its offices in Cornellà de Llobregat (Barcelona) and Lisbon. On the Spanish market, the group is represented by the Ferrero Rocher, Kinder, Nutella, and Raffaello brands.
                                    
Under the executive presidency of Giovanni Ferrero, the group has also expanded its operations into the ice cream segment, identifying Spain as a strategic market for the development of this category. In 2021, it acquired Ice Cream Factory Comaker (ICFC), which has its headquarters and production facility in Alzira, in the province of Valencia.
                                    
The facility is set to become Ferrero’s European technology hub for ice cream production. To carry out the project, an initial investment of 140 million euros was approved, earmarked for technological and industrial modernization, the expansion of production capacity, and the introduction of new processes. The jury emphasized that this decision strengthens Spain’s role in the group’s European industrial strategy and serves as an example of how Italian investments contribute to the growth of Spain’s manufacturing sector.
                                    
The second award recipient, Benito Tesier Sierra, is the general manager of Brembo Iberia and a key figure in the development of the Italian group’s operations in the Spanish market. The jury recognized his contribution to integrating local entrepreneurial expertise into an international industrial and commercial strategy.
                                    
Brembo’s presence in Spain has evolved from its initial establishment in the Molins de Rei area, near Barcelona, to the consolidation of its operations in Aragon, in part through the collaboration between the Bombassei and Tesier families. The group has expanded its presence in the automotive sector and in the aftermarket—the market for replacement parts and post-sale services—including through the acquisition of J. Juan, a Spanish company specializing in motorcycle braking systems.
                                    
In his leadership role, Tesier helped integrate the expertise and business relationships developed in the Spanish market with Brembo’s technological, industrial, and international capabilities, fostering business continuity and the company’s growth. With over 30 years of experience in the automotive sector, Tesier has also served as president of Ceoe Aragón since January 2026. 
 According to the award citation, his career path demonstrates the value of collaboration between international capital and local entrepreneurial expertise in strengthening companies’ industrial capacity and international reach.

Explainer: Why the CPC puts people's well-being at the heart of self-governance
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
00:26:42 CST
01:26:42 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- In northeast China's Heilongjiang Province, eligible residents can receive certain forms of medical assistance and other support without submitting an application. Government departments share the information needed to provide the benefits.
The provincial bodies responsible for disciplinary inspection helped drive the change. They prompted civil affairs departments to build a data-sharing network connecting 33 departments and institutions, enabling 12 frequently used assistance services to be provided without applications.
The initiative offers a concrete example of how the self-supervision of the Communist Party of China (CPC) improve public services and help ensure that benefits reach those who most need them.
Earning public trust through tangible improvements in people's lives is a defining feature of the CPC's full and rigorous self-governance, which is high on the agenda of the fifth plenary session of its 20th Central Committee. The key meeting, which opened Monday in Beijing, is considering a draft decision of the CPC Central Committee on major issues concerning strengthening full and rigorous Party self-governance with perseverance.
COMMITMENT TO THE PEOPLE
The CPC constitution commits the Party to serving the people, and states that it has no special interests of its own apart from those of the working class and the broadest possible majority of the people.
Without seeking self-interest, the CPC can keep its spirit of thorough self-reform, and by swiftly detecting and resolving its own problems, the Party can prevent any interest group, power group or privileged stratum from preying on or corrupting its members.
Chinese President Xi Jinping, also general secretary of the CPC Central Committee, has led an unprecedented anti-corruption campaign since 2012, driven by a determination to "offend a few thousand rather than fail 1.4 billion." The campaign has targeted corrupt officials at both high and low levels.
Gyula Thurmer, president of the Hungarian Workers' Party, said serving the interests of the people is a central principle of the CPC.
He added that the Party's anti-corruption efforts have achieved significant results, strengthening internal discipline and helping implement major economic and social development programs.
SAFEGUARDING PEOPLE'S INTERESTS
Xi has called on Party members to bear in mind that "benefiting the people is their greatest political achievement."
An official review of work in 2025 reported that disciplinary and supervisory bodies nationwide investigated 967,000 cases of misconduct and corruption affecting people's daily lives, returning or helping recover about 77.6 billion yuan (11.5 billion U.S. dollars) in money and property to the public.
Faruk Boric, president of the Association of Friendship between China and Bosnia and Herzegovina, said China's efforts to pursue corrupt officials at both senior and lower levels send "a clear message that no official is above the rules, regardless of their position."
He said China's experience offers important lessons in linking clean governance with people's well-being. Protecting public funds, he added, helps direct more resources toward health care, education and other public services.
BUILDING BETTER GOVERNANCE
On several occasions, Xi has called for taking simultaneous, coordinated, and comprehensive steps to ensure that officials do not have the audacity, opportunity or desire to become corrupt.
In his article on the Party's self-reform, Xi urged efforts to improve Party conduct, enforce discipline, and fight corruption, while integrating Party self-supervision with public oversight to deeply advance the Party's self-reform.
Lyazid Benhami, a member of the Paris Association of French-Chinese Friendship, said rigorous Party self-governance can clarify officials' responsibilities, improve coordination and help sustain development programs.
He highlighted China's emphasis on long-term planning, infrastructure, education and research, adding that the country has achieved a profound transformation regarding such priority areas and improved the well-being of its people.
Those administrative strengths matter as China implements its 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030). In January, Xi urged efforts to confine power to an institutional cage in a more well-conceived and effective manner, and press ahead with the anti-corruption fight with a clearer understanding and stronger resolve, thus providing a strong guarantee for achieving the goals and tasks of the 15th Five-Year Plan period.
Volker Tschapke, honorary president of Germany's Prussian Society, said the CPC's courage to "turn the blade inward" demonstrated a "moral strength that I truly admire." He stressed that rigorous Party self-governance ultimately serves the fundamental interests of the people.

Iran opposes nuclear technology monopoly, calls for equal access to advanced technologies
TEHRAN — Iran has called for equitable global access to advanced nuclear technologies, urging the international community to eliminate discriminatory barriers, expand technical cooperation and strengthen protections for peaceful nuclear facilities.
Hossein Derakhshandeh, deputy head of the Atomic Energy Organization of Iran (AEOI) and chief executive of the Nuclear Power Production and Development Company of Iran, outlined four priorities for the equitable development of nuclear power at the International Ministerial Conference on Nuclear Power in South Korea on Tuesday.
He stressed the need to remove discriminatory restrictions, facilitate access to advanced technologies, broaden technical cooperation and reinforce international measures to protect peaceful nuclear facilities, warning against the use of nuclear technology to establish monopolies.
Derakhshandeh also called for equal access to advanced nuclear technologies in accordance with international law and without double standards. He reaffirmed the inalienable right of states party to the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT) to conduct nuclear research and development and use nuclear energy for peaceful purposes.
Emphasizing the importance of upholding the rights of NPT signatories, he called on the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) to function as an independent, technically focused and development-oriented organization, in line with its Statute. The Agency’s mandate includes promoting the peaceful use of nuclear energy and facilitating technical cooperation among member states without discrimination, he said.
However, Derakhshandeh argued that developments in recent years had shown the Agency to be increasingly influenced by political considerations, undermining its impartial implementation of its statutory responsibilities. He cited the US-Israeli attacks on Iran’s peaceful nuclear facilities as an example of the challenges facing the international nuclear framework.
He described the attacks as a flagrant violation of the United Nations Charter, international law, and IAEA General Conference resolutions prohibiting attacks on peaceful nuclear facilities. He also criticized the Agency for an 'inadequate response,' saying it had failed to uphold the fundamental principles of impartiality and professionalism effectively.
Derakhshandeh stressed that protecting peaceful nuclear infrastructure was a shared international responsibility. He also condemned 'international silence over violations of the Iranian people’s rights' in areas including energy, healthcare, food security, the environment and industry.
He further criticized the Israeli regime, the United States and certain European countries for 'politically motivated campaigns' against Iran, involving unfounded accusations and negative media coverage.
His remarks underscored Iran’s call for a nuclear order grounded in equal access to technology, respect for the peaceful-use rights of NPT signatories. and the consistent application of international law, free from political pressure and discriminatory treatment.

News Analysis: Burnham pushes for devolution, closer EU ties in first 100 days as PM
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
00:26:13 CST
01:26:13 KST

by Zhao Jiasong
LONDON, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- British Prime Minister Andy Burnham's first 100 days in office, which fell on Tuesday, have seen him put forward plans to devolve more power to the regions, reconsider Brexit, and pursue a more independent foreign policy.
Since taking office on July 20, the former mayor of Greater Manchester has helped the Labour Party recover from the stark drop in popularity it experienced under former Prime Minister Keir Starmer.
An analysis of polling data by the Press Association shows that Labour's average support has risen by around 10 percentage points compared with the period immediately before Starmer announced his resignation in June.
Nevertheless, Burnham faces growing pressure to turn his proposals into results, with constitutional tensions, the legacy of Brexit and disagreements with Washington testing his government.
DEVOLUTION UNDER PRESSURE FROM NATIONALISTS
Devolution has been central to Burnham's political agenda. After nearly a decade as mayor of Greater Manchester, he has brought his approach to regional governance into Downing Street.
Just three days after becoming prime minister, Burnham opened "Number 10 North" in Manchester, a government office intended to give regional development a greater role in national decision-making.
He also revived the National Economic Council, bringing together ministers and regional leaders to discuss investment and economic growth. His government has proposed giving local authorities greater powers over skills training, employment support and taxation.
Ian Scott, an academic at the University of Manchester, told Xinhua that the establishment of Number 10 North carries "considerable symbolic importance." However, questions remain over "how much decision-making power would actually move away from London."
He added that Manchester's experience, built over years of cooperation between local authorities and central government, could not easily be reproduced elsewhere.
Burnham's plans are also under pressure from nationalist parties in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.
On Sept. 14, leaders of the Scottish National Party, Plaid Cymru and Sinn Fein met in Cardiff and signed an agreement calling on the British government to prepare for constitutional change. The parties support Scottish independence, Welsh independence and Irish reunification, respectively.
Jennifer Todd, a political scientist at University College Dublin, said the meeting was "largely symbolic," given the different political circumstances and objectives of the three parties. She noted that Brexit had increased discussion of Irish reunification, though public attitudes remain complex.
Nevertheless, the meeting showed that nationalist parties are seeking closer cooperation as Burnham prepares to transfer more powers from Westminster. His government now faces demands for greater autonomy from parties that ultimately want to leave the United Kingdom (UK).
REOPENING DEBATE OVER EU RELATIONS
Burnham has also taken a different approach from his predecessor on Britain's future relationship with the European Union (EU), suggesting that the country should consider closer integration with the bloc.
In an interview with The Sunday Times published over the weekend, Burnham said Britain needed an "honest discussion" about restoring free movement with the EU.
He argued that immigration patterns have changed since Brexit, with more migrants settling permanently in Britain rather than moving between countries for temporary employment.
In the near-term, Burnham raised the possibility of Britain rejoining the EU single market or customs union, while in the longer-term, returning to the EU itself could be considered. The leader acknowledged that rejoining the bloc would require another referendum, while other arrangements might not.
The BBC reported on Tuesday that Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said British officials would discuss possible future arrangements with their EU counterparts, including free movement, ahead of a summit on Nov. 20.
For now, the government is concentrating on agreements covering food trade, emissions trading and youth mobility. Burnham has pledged to respect Labour's 2024 election manifesto, which ruled out a return to the single market, customs union or free movement during the current parliamentary term.
His comments have drawn criticism from Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, who accused him of betraying the Brexit vote. Some Labour lawmakers also fear that reopening the debate could alienate voters in constituencies that supported leaving the EU.
Britain continues to face trade barriers following Brexit, while businesses have called for closer economic cooperation with Europe. Burnham's challenge is to persuade voters that a new relationship would bring economic benefits without reviving the divisions that have shaped British politics for a decade.
UKRAINE, PALESTINE AND RELATIONS WITH WASHINGTON
In foreign policy, Burnham has continued Britain's support for Ukraine, while taking positions that at times differ from those of the United States.
On Aug. 24, he chose Kyiv for his first overseas visit as prime minister, where he reaffirmed Britain's commitment to military and political support for the country.
Differences with Washington became more apparent this month after restrictions on Ukraine's access to the Starlink satellite communications system raised concerns over Kyiv's ability to defend itself against Russian attacks.
During a telephone conversation with U.S. President Donald Trump on Oct. 23, Burnham stressed the importance of Ukraine having full access to Starlink.
He also acknowledged Trump's efforts to bring Russia to the negotiating table. The two leaders agreed to work with international partners towards ending the conflict.
Regarding Palestine, Burnham has supported stronger measures against Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
In September, Britain, France and Canada announced plans to ban imports of goods from Israeli settlements and impose targeted measures against those involved in settlement expansion. The three governments said such actions were necessary to protect the prospects of a two-state solution.
These measures drew criticism from Israel and the United States, pointing to differences between Britain and its allies over the Israel-Palestine conflict. ■

Owino began farming in 2021 through the Cereal Growers Association, cultivating grains, tomatoes, and other horticultural crops.

Today, his farm serves as a demonstration site where he trains and mentors young farmers. He also partners with UN Women to supply local subsistence farmers with fish fingerlings and modern agricultural techniques.

Feature: Lebanese artist turns war shrapnel into artworks of resilience
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
00:26:09 CST
01:26:09 KST

BEIRUT, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- For visual artist Lina Jouni, the shrapnel scattered across southern Lebanon is more than a remnant of war. In her hands, a jagged fragment of an Israeli missile becomes a Lebanese cedar, a flower or the image of a home.
In the southern village of Roumine in Nabatieh district, Jouni works beneath a pergola in her garden, with tree branches intertwining overhead. She collects metal fragments left by bombardment and transforms them into artworks that speak of memory, resilience and a commitment to life.
As she put the finishing touches to a metal sculpture, Jouni told Xinhua that the fragments were far more than discarded scraps.
"I do not treat these pieces as worthless remnants of metal. I see them as witnesses to what the people of the south have lived through, and to what happened to their homes, villages and loved ones," she said.
Her artistic project took shape after she returned to her home in Roumine following displacement during the 2024 war between Israel and Hezbollah. Finding pieces of iron and shrapnel scattered among the rubble, she decided to give them a new purpose.
"I decided to collect them and repurpose them in an artistic project that reflects my psychological response to what I experienced and gives what the war left behind a new meaning," she said.
Jouni examines each fragment's thickness, dimensions and curves to determine how best to reshape it. Using cutting, drilling and polishing tools, she gradually works the metal into shape before adding color and other elements. The process requires patience and physical effort as she experiments with bending and shaping the iron. So far, she has completed around 50 artworks.
Some of her works tell poignant stories of loss. One commemorates a mother killed alongside her two children, while another pays tribute to a man Jouni knew who was wounded multiple times before being killed.
Her most striking work began with a missile fragment that, she said, came from a missile that destroyed a three-story house in Nabatieh. She reshaped the metal into a Lebanese cedar, a tree deeply rooted in the country's national identity and long associated with resilience and continuity.
Jouni said art had given her a way to express the suffering of ordinary people, convey her views on what they had endured and affirm their determination to carry on.
"I do not claim that art can bring back the victims or erase the traces of destruction, but it can keep their stories from being forgotten and give people a space to express their losses and their determination to continue," she said.
Through her sculptures, Jouni tells a story of southern Lebanon that extends beyond its destroyed homes and landscapes to the determination of its people to remain rooted in their land.
For Jouni, the message is clear: "This is what I seek to achieve through works that make fragments a material for memory and creativity a means of confronting despair." ■

Pezeshkian calls for stronger gas cooperation, condemns US sanctions and military aggression

Pezeshkian calls for stronger gas cooperation, condemns US sanctions and military aggression
TEHRAN— Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has called on major natural gas producers to strengthen strategic and technical cooperation to safeguard global energy security, warning that unilateral sanctions and US military interventions in the Persian Gulf are destabilizing energy markets and threatening economic growth worldwide.
Addressing the eighth summit of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) in Moscow on Tuesday, Pezeshkian said geopolitical tensions and unilateral measures had exposed the global energy market to serious risks, emphasizing the need for coordinated action by gas-producing countries to maintain market stability, expand trade and strengthen investment across the natural gas value chain.
He condemned the US-Israeli military aggression against Iran, saying attacks on the country’s energy infrastructure and disruptions to energy transfers had endangered global energy security and the wider economy.
The Iranian president also denounced 'US economic coercion,' including unilateral sanctions, a naval and air blockade against Iran, and pressure on other countries to comply with the restrictions. He called on major energy suppliers to condemn and effectively counter such measures, arguing that US military interventions in the Persian Gulf had consequences far beyond the region by disrupting energy pricing, supply and transportation.
Iran ready to expand role in global gas markets
Pezeshkian said Iran, a founding member of the GECF and home to the world’s second-largest proven natural gas reserves, was prepared to play a more active role in multilateral energy diplomacy, technological cooperation and investment in gas infrastructure.
Despite years of unilateral sanctions, he said, Iran had developed its domestic capabilities and maintained its position as the world’s third-largest natural gas producer. He put the country’s annual gas production capacity at 280 billion cubic meters in his speech.
Natural gas accounts for around 70 percent of Iran’s energy mix, Pezeshkian said, adding that the national gas network covers approximately 95 percent of the population.
He invited foreign investors, particularly from GECF member states, to explore opportunities in Iran’s upstream and downstream gas industries, infrastructure development, and gas trade, citing the country’s strategic location along major energy corridors and its potential for mutually beneficial cooperation.
GECF urged to turn potential into joint projects
The president described the GECF as an important platform for multilateral diplomacy, the exchange of expertise and closer coordination among gas-producing countries. He called for the effective implementation of the forum’s charter, long-term strategy and summit declarations.
Pezeshkian said cooperation should focus on two principal areas: strategic governance and management, and technical and engineering operations.
On the strategic front, he stressed the importance of stabilizing markets and increasing natural gas trade at regional and international levels. On the technical side, he called for joint investment throughout the gas value chain, from production and processing to transportation and consumption.
He also emphasized the need to upgrade technological capabilities, improve productivity and reduce the environmental impact of natural gas production and use. Existing capacities, he said, should be translated into practical projects and shared economic interests, with cooperation aligned with long-term supply and demand trends.
Pezeshkian further called for stronger efforts to expand regional and global gas markets, maximize the value of natural gas resources and combat energy poverty.
Regional cooperation and multilateralism
The summit comes as Iran and Russia seek to deepen cooperation in energy and other sectors. Speaking to reporters upon arriving in Moscow on Monday, Pezeshkian said relations between the two countries had advanced beyond the signing of memoranda of understanding, with both sides working to implement their comprehensive strategic treaty across economic, scientific, cultural, security and political fields.
He described unilateralism and the use of pressure to advance national agendas as major challenges to international cooperation, saying Iran, Russia and other countries were working to strengthen multilateralism.
On the sidelines of the summit, Pezeshkian also met Qatar’s Emir, Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani. The two leaders reviewed bilateral relations and emphasized the expansion of political and economic cooperation, particularly in energy, trade and coordination among natural gas-exporting countries.
Iranian Ambassador to Moscow Kazem Jalali, meanwhile, said Iran and Russia had considerable potential to help shape a fairer global energy architecture. In an article published by Russia’s TASS news agency, Jalali argued that the future of the global gas market should be based on pluralism, diversified supply sources and respect for the sovereignty of energy suppliers.
The GECF summit brings together major gas-producing countries to discuss energy cooperation and the future of global gas markets. Pezeshkian concluded that constructive engagement among member and observer states could strengthen the security of supply and demand, support fair valuation of natural gas, and reinforce its role in the global energy mix while taking environmental considerations into account.

====================================================================================================

A 28-Year-Old DOGE Operative Gutted USAID. HR Had No Record of Him Working There
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:24:34 UTC
01:24:34 KST

On March 18, 2025, Secretary of State Marco Rubio handed the reins of the US Agency for International Development to Jeremy Lewin, a 28-year-old graduate of Harvard Law School, former investment banker, and affiliate of Elon Musk’s so-called Department of Government Efficiency. At the time, Lewin’s appointment drew criticism because of his lack of experience in government, diplomacy, or foreign assistance. But for career staff inside the agency, the issues surrounding Lewin’s new role were much more alarming than his thin résumé.
For at least two months, USAID senior staff had no knowledge of how Lewin, who appeared at the agency one day as a policymaker on an obscure detail from the General Services Administration, could have suddenly begun wielding the powers of the agency’s top official.
Internal USAID emails reviewed by WIRED reveal that during the three-week period of March 18 to April 4, during which Lewin began canceling lifesaving aid programs and personally signed off on the termination of thousands of USAID employees, he did not sign the paperwork typically required by law to begin work at the agency, despite repeated requests. In fact, his appointment was so mysterious that USAID security was unable to issue him an ID card because they had no records of his employment.
Lewin, currently director of policy planning at the State Department, tells WIRED that prior to Rubio delegating powers to him, he was “both detailed and dual appointed to work at USAID by Secretary Rubio according to well-established authorities and with the advice of State Department and White House counsel.”
Experts, though, say that while Lewin performed the duties of a top USAID leader under the title Rubio handed to him—deputy administrator of policy and programming and chief operating officer—it isn’t clear that he had the legal authority to do so. Questions about how DOGE affiliates like Lewin stepped into top roles at many federal agencies, including USAID, remain key to dozens of active lawsuits targeting DOGE and the Trump administration over federal workforce reductions, firings, and agency dismantlings.
Lewin has said, in a declaration submitted to the court in J. Doe 4 v. U.S. DOGE Service, that he began serving at USAID as a senior adviser as well as a director for strategy and programs on January 28, 2025. On March 18, according to court filings, Rubio, in his role as USAID’s acting administrator, delegated the authority of the deputy administrator of policy and programming and chief operating officer to Lewin, and also signed a document appointing Lewin an “officer of the United States.”
According to the emails reviewed by WIRED, on March 20, two days after Rubio placed Lewin atop the USAID hierarchy, White House liaison to USAID Adam Korzeniewski notified HR to begin the process of onboarding Lewin as a senior adviser performing duties as deputy administrator. Four days later, the emails reveal, after prompting from HR, Korzeniewski provided a proposed start date—March 18—and the next day, Lewin was sent a temporary job offer.
By March 26, the emails show, Lewin still hadn’t accepted the job offer, and had not filed his OF-306, the federal government's standard pre-employment background screening form; without this document, a federal agency cannot lawfully issue a final job offer or consummate an appointment. An HR executive noted in an email dated March 31 that Lewin had not completed the onboarding tasks required to initiate “the security reciprocity process,” which recognizes the transfer of an employees’ security clearance from one agency to another. (A detailing agreement between the GSA and USAID dated February 14—two weeks after Lewin says he began at USAID—specifes that “commencement of the detail is contingent upon the Detailee’s successful adjudication and receipt of any necessary security clearances and other pre-employment screening required by USAID.”)
On March 28, Lewin signed a letter terminating all remaining USAID staff. And as he executed sweeping powers to liquidate all 60 of USAID’s overseas missions and cancel thousands of lifesaving projects worldwide, HR repeatedly followed up with Korzeniewski.
More than a week after Lewin’s appointment, the emails show, a USAID official told Korzeniewski that the agency’s office of security was “unable to issue a USAID ID card to Jeremy Lewin as SEC [the agency’s secure database] did not have a record of Jeremy as an employee.”
“Until you’re onboarded at USAID, you aren’t even in the system,” says Natalia Machuca, a 15-year agency veteran who hired many staff. “You can’t get a badge, get into your computer, or even walk around the building.”
Lewin tells WIRED, “I was a regular government employee with a valid security clearance held by the State Department during this entire period. USAID HR was confused about this paperwork for a period of days, but this issue was cleared up once they were made aware of the dual appointment and my State Department position.”
But according to a top executive in HR, no one from their office saw any delegation documents until late April 2025. As one longtime HR executive at the agency, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said of Lewin: “He was the equivalent of an administrative ghost.”
“I think this creates a huge accountability problem if you have these actors who are making really consequential life-or-death decisions who didn't go through any standard confirmation process,” says Don Moynihan, a public policy professor at the University of Michigan, “or in this case didn't even complete their paperwork to become a formal employee.”
Lewin—who a White House official says submitted all the paperwork required for employment and clearance—provided WIRED with two documents, both dated March 18, 2025. One is an appointment and compensation waiver, signed by Rubio, naming Lewin director of strategy and planning, and stating that he would not be paid “pursuant to, among other provisions of law, 22 U.S.C. § 2385(b).” The other is a standard appointment affidavit naming Lewin USAID’s director of strategy and programs. A signature on the form appears to be Rubio’s, with the title given as “HRO”—usually an abbreviation for human resources officer. The State Department did not answer questions about this document.
To one former senior USAID official, Rubio’s use of 22 U.S.C. § 2385(b)—an obscure provision traditionally reserved for rapidly deploying emergency-response staff to disaster zones abroad—to appoint Lewin looks like a legal contortion.
“It is so unconventional that I’d never seen it used before I got to USAID,” the official said. “It was created for the purposes of scaling up really quickly if there was some outbreak of a virus somewhere and they needed to bring people on, then let them go.”
Brian Feinstein, a law professor at the Wharton School of Business, acknowledged that while using 22 U.S.C. § 2385(b) to appoint Lewin is complex, it appears to him to be legal. “Because Lewin's appointment is consistent with this law regarding USAID personnel,” he says, “his unusual status should not be a factor.”
Outside of this point, legal questions also remain about Lewin’s actions at the agency before he was appointed by Rubio, and his failure to complete the onboarding required to begin his initial detail period at USAID. During this time he was part of a team that issued sweeping orders, including one to then acting administrator Jason Gray to lock all USAID staff worldwide out of email and all communication systems, which could have put many staff’s lives at risk, and to terminate 57 of the agency’s top officials.
David A. Super, professor of law and economics at Georgetown University, describes Lewin’s failure to complete his onboarding as much more than an administrative slip-up. “You can’t just walk in the door of a federal agency and become an employee,” he says. Under federal law, a cabinet secretary can only assign the authority of a Senate-confirmed position such as USAID administrator to a subordinate official—an agency employee or officer who works under the supervision of a higher-ranking officer. These regulations, Super says, are a way for Congress to guarantee that “someone walking off the street should not be given these enormous powers.”
Nina Mendelson, who teaches law at the University of Michigan, agrees. She says the administration appeared to be trying to bypass the Federal Vacancies Reform Act, a federal statute that dictates how temporary vacancies in Senate-confirmed executive branch positions are filled. “The FVRA specifies who may fill in, for a limited time, when a Senate-confirmed post is vacant,” she says. “The possibilities are a first assistant, someone holding another Senate-confirmed post, or a longtime civil servant in the particular agency. Lewin doesn’t seem to have been any one of those.”
Lewin being placed atop USAID came in a specific context. In February 2025, shortly after the arrival of Lewin and other DOGE affiliates at the agency, two dozen current and former USAID employees and contractors sued Musk and DOGE in Maryland District Court. They successfully secured a preliminary injunction on March 18, on the grounds that special government employees—temporary hires from outside USAID and the government—lacked the authority to execute sweeping federal actions. That same day, Rubio delegated powers of the agency’s top job to Lewin.
On March 28, the Fourth Circuit Court of Appeals granted the Justice Department an emergency stay, pausing the injunction based on the administration’s argument that the actions were taken by Lewin in his role as a federally appointed official. In his declaration, Lewin wrote: “I am not, and have never been, an employee of Elon Musk or USDS,” adding, “I report directly and only to Acting Administrator Rubio” in his role at USAID.
The ruling gave Lewin the green light to fire thousands of career civil service and Foreign Service staff that very day, but the legal battle didn’t end there. The district judge has since allowed thousands of affected employees to sue DOGE and the administration as a group and ordered the government to hand over a trove of internal documents.
Kevin Byrnes, a veteran federal employment law attorney representing more than 170 former and current career USAID staff in a separate suit challenging DOGE’s role in the mass firings, says the fact that Lewin had not completed mandatory onboarding paperwork raises even more questions about the authority of nonconfirmed agency leadership, and potentially exposes Lewin personally.
“If Lewin didn’t even fill out the papers and was not authorized to take these actions, then he could be exposed to personal liability,” says Byrnes, who is asking the court to reinstate all the plaintiffs to their USAID jobs, with back pay.

Flávio Bolsonaro flees Brazil after presidential election loss, reports say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:24:15 UTC
01:24:15 KST

The far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro has reportedly fled Brazil and is on his way to the United States after losing Sunday’s presidential election to the leftwing incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.
A report by the news website Metrópoles, citing people close to the politician’s family, said he was en route to the US. “The plane is in flight,” Metrópoles reported, without making clear where it had departed from.
Bolsonaro allies told Metrópoles that he would land in Florida on Tuesday afternoon and planned to request political asylum. “The Donald Trump administration has been informed,” the website added.
Allies also confirmed to the Folha de S Paulo newspaper that he was on his way to the US, and said the escape plan had been “organized and enabled by a lawyer close to the Bolsonaro clan”.
“They say the flight should land in a few hours,” the newspaper added.
The news network CNN Brasil reported that Bolsonaro had fled to the US with his wife and two daughters in the early hours of this morning.
A US state department spokesperson said Bolsonaro and his family would be granted visas “to allow them entry into the United States”.
Lula slammed what he called Bolsonaro’s “shameful” decision to flee. “This is what the family Bolsonaro are like. Brazil is their second homeland. Their first homeland is licking the boots of the US, as he’s become accustomed to doing,” he said at an event celebrating his 81st birthday in Brasília.
“I keep imagining what’s on the conscience of a citizen who just lost the elections and flees his country … He who owes nothing, fears nothing. A citizen who sneaks out of his country owes something,” Lula added.
Lawmakers from Lula’s Worker’s party (PT) asked the supreme court to order Bolsonaro’s arrest and requested that his name be put on Interpol’s Red Notice list.
Bolsonaro had not been seen since Monday and missed a Tuesday-morning deadline to hand his passport to the federal police, fuelling rumours that he may have fled Brazil after losing on Sunday.
A report in the Brazilian newspaper O Globo said that during a meeting with friends and lawyers on Monday, the defeated candidate had appeared “possessed and made it clear he was afraid of being arrested”.
A supreme court justice cancelled Bolsonaro’s passport minutes after the result in a ruling related to a criminal case against the senator. He had until 11am to surrender the document to the federal police, but did not appear.
Bolsonaro has had Italian citizenship since 2023 and reportedly possesses a passport from the European country.
The Argentinian news website Infobae reported that on Monday night he reportedly fled to Argentina, where he was expected to board a private jet in Puerto Iguazú bound for the US, but the plane did not take off.
Bolsonaro, who has yet to concede defeat to Lula, posted a video on Monday in which, commenting on the cancellation of his passport, he said: “I never thought about leaving the country.”
One of the senator’s brothers, the former congressman Eduardo Bolsonaro, who is in self-imposed exile in the US, had said in an interview last Friday that his brother should leave Brazil if he lost.
The Brazilian newspaper Folha de S Paulo reported that allies in the Bolsonaro family’s inner circle had been told that he had indeed left for Argentina and intended to travel from there to the US.
As there is no record of him passing through any regular Brazilian immigration checkpoint, the federal police are trying to establish from Argentinian authorities whether there is any record of him entering the country.
The Argentinian channel Todo Noticias reported that the senator had reportedly crossed the border into Argentina on foot and abandoned plans to board the plane once news of his movements leaked.
Bolsonaro was told to surrender his passport over a criminal case in which the federal police are investigating him for possible involvement in a money-laundering scheme worth about £680m ($905m) involving betting companies.
The senator’s possible flight makes the future of the far right after the presidential election even more uncertain. The family patriarch, Jair Bolsonaro, is under house arrest for attempting a coup, and one of his sons is in the US and the whereabouts of another unclear.
Eduardo Bolsonaro has an outstanding arrest warrant against him in Brazil, after being sentenced to four years in prison for trying to interfere in his father’s trial by lobbying Donald Trump to impose sanctions on the justices hearing the case.
Political scientist Magna Inácio, a professor at the Federal University of Minas Gerais, believes a power vacuum may now emerge within the right.
“The resistance of Brazilian voters to handing victory to this more extremist camp sends a signal that the right leadership is now up for grabs,” she said.
Since Jair Bolsonaro, then a career congressman with few laws to his name, surprisingly won the presidency in 2018, there has effectively been no right wing in Brazil, only the far-right Bolsonarismo movement.
Camila Rocha, a political scientist who studies Brazil’s new right, believes the fact that three Bolsonaros are now potentially out of the picture could trigger a “shift in power” away from blood ties.
“I think there is a tendency for power to move away from the sons,” said Rocha, noting that before the election, polls showed Jair Bolsonaro supporters preferred other potential candidates over his eldest son, including Jair Bolsonaro’s wife, Michelle Bolsonaro, who was recently elected senator, and the São Paulo governor, Tarcísio de Freitas.
Flávio Bolsonaro reportedly did not want to run because he thought a presidential campaign would turn his life into “hell”, and believed his re-election to the senate was assured. But with Eduardo, his father’s “plan A”, now living in the US, the senator was chosen to run.
Most observers agree that Flávio lacks his father’s charisma. He had a 24-year political career in which he passed very few laws as a state legislator and senator, and the only previous time he ran for executive office was for mayor of Rio de Janeiro in 2016, when he fainted during a televised debate and finished fourth.
Speaking in Brasília, Bolsonaro’s campaign chief, senator Rogério Marinho, said he was surprised by reports of his candidate’s departure. “Because yesterday we talked about the need for Flávio, with the 60 million votes he received, to take on this role as leader of the opposition … since we were given a mandate by a significant part of the population,” he said.
Asked whether he believed Bolsonaro could lead the opposition from abroad, he said: “María Corina Machado did it” with her country, Venezuela.
Even in a family frequently embroiled in legal trouble he stood out, facing longstanding criminal allegations, including suspicions that he embezzled part of his staff’s salaries, as well as more recent accusations.
Even so, 48.21% of Brazilians voted for Flávio Bolsonaro on Sunday, which many analysts see as both an anti-Lula vote and a vote for whomever Jair Bolsonaro had chosen.
Inácio believes the struggle over the Bolsonaro legacy will also play out among family members who remain in Brazil, including Michelle and Bolsonaro’s other political sons, the senator-elect Carlos Bolsonaro and congressman-elect Jair Renan Bolsonaro, who publicly do not get along with their stepmother.
“Michelle clearly has a political project of her own, but she is likely to face strong resistance from the two stepsons who are in congress. It is only a matter of time before tensions between them grow,” said the political scientist.

Israelis living abroad spend thousands to fly in to vote in crucial election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:21:47 UTC
01:21:47 KST

Israelis living in U.S., other countries spend thousands to fly in to vote in crucial election: "My civic duty"
With a consequential election in Israel Tuesday, tens of thousands of Israelis living abroad have flown in just to cast their ballots.
Ronnie Teram Gil-Ad left Israel for the U.S. with her family a year ago. She shelled out about $3,000 to come back to vote.
"It is my country. The fact that I'm living abroad doesn't mean that this is not my home here. We wanna make a difference," she said.
Gil-Ad, who will fly back to Boston Tuesday night, will have been in Israel for just 36 hours.
"This is my civic duty," she said. And she's not alone.
Another voter, Yael Natra, told The Associated Press she spent thousands of dollars to travel from Toronto to Tel Aviv to be in the country to cast a ballot. It's the first time in the two decades since she left Israel for Canada that she felt she needed to vote in her home country's elections.
"The Israel that I grew up in is disappearing," she said in an interview from Toronto, citing an eroding democracy and deeply divided society. "If something won't change this time, I don't know what's going to be."
AID Coalition, a U.S.-based nonprofit whose stated mission is strengthening Israel's democracy, estimates that as many as 67,000 Israeli citizens have arrived from abroad to vote, based on surveys of expatriates and registration data gathered for its "Fly&Vote" initiative. It says about half have been flying in from the United States, with others from Europe, Canada, Australia and New Zealand.
Offir Gutelzon helped organize the flights that brought many Israelis to vote with the organization he co-founded, UnXeptable. They say their goal is to unseat Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who has dominated Israeli politics for 30 years.
Many voters said they see the election — the first national election since the deadly Hamas attack and start of the war in Gaza three years ago — as a referendum on Netanyahu.
Israel has parliamentary elections. The opposition bloc, which polls show will likely have a plurality of votes, is led by Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief of staff who left Netanyahu's government in 2024 accusing him of unnecessarily prolonging the war in Gaza and delaying a hostage deal with Hamas.
The mobilization of expats this year is notable, compared with past Israeli elections, Dahlia Scheindlin, an American-Israeli political analyst, told the AP. While many campaigns have focused on anti-Netanyahu sentiment, she said it's unclear overall how those flying in will vote.
"There are also expats coming in to vote for the pro-Netanyahu side," Scheindlin said.
Turnout is expected to be significant with predictions that up to 70% of Israel's roughly 7.3 million registered voters will cast ballots.
But the hard part begins after the polls close: forming a governing coalition that is stable.

Putin call pits Finland and Norway against Denmark and Sweden
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:20:39 UTC
01:20:39 KST

Nordic unity broke on Tuesday after the leaders of Finland and Norway held a 90-minute phone call with Vladimir Putin. The Danish and Swedish prime ministers publicly cast doubt on the diplomatic overture.
A rare Nordic split emerged on Tuesday as the leaders of Denmark and Sweden publicly rebuked their counterparts in Finland and Norway for holding a surprise phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
The call was the initiative of Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, who recently hosted a round of peace talks in Oslo.
The two leaders urged Putin to end the full-scale invasion of Ukraine and engage in meaningful negotiations to reach a stable, peaceful settlement.
"The discussion was frank and substantive," Stubb said.
"The outcome of this war will have a direct impact on our and the broader European security. Ending the war requires direct discussion," he added.
"We stressed the importance of de-escalation," Støre said.
The read-out made clear that Stubb and Støre had spoken to Putin as "leaders of their respective countries and did not speak on behalf of Europe as a whole".
Immediately after, Stubb and Støre phoned Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who thanked them for their "active" support.
But the choreography did little to mitigate the backlash from their neighbours.
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen was highly critical, pointing to Russia's escalation against Ukraine as evidence that Moscow is not serious about diplomacy.
The Kremlin's statement released after the call echoed Putin's maximalist tone.
"I am very sceptical about this independent initiative by Norway and Finland. It was not coordinated with any of us," Frederiksen said shortly after the call became public.
"I don't see any signs that Russia desires peace with Europe, neither in the hybrid warfare taking place every single day, nor in Ukraine."
Frederiksen questioned the effectiveness of the overture and drew a parallel with previous go-it-alone attempts, such as when former Hungary Prime Minister Viktor Orbán flew to Moscow to meet with Putin.
"I honestly don't know what they think can be achieved by this," she said.
"We have previously emphasise, with clear backing from the rest of Europe, that when others have gone solo and, for example, travelled to Moscow, it is crucial that we, Europeans, stand together. That is something many of us have fought for."
Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson also cast doubt on the initiative, albeit in less harsh terms.
"My impression is that everyone wants peace except Putin. I have pretty low expectations for this kind of (direct) talk," Kristersson said.
"Holding talks that risk splitting the European voice is risky. Now, I'm not saying they have done that at all. I don't yet know what those talks were about," he noted.
"Talks that make Russia more willing to make a decent peace on Ukraine's terms are, of course, good."
In response to the pushback, Støre said Europe should speak with Russia to complement the messages sent by the US administration, which has a different take on the war.
Stubb, Støre, Frederiksen and Kristersson were all in Helsinki, Finland, to attend a leaders-level session of the Nordic Council.
Tuesday's political split is significant given that the four countries always see eye to eye when it comes to Russia's war on Ukraine. They are among the largest bilateral donors to Kyiv and vocal advocates of applying ever-stronger sanctions on Moscow.

'They don't produce science': RFK Jr's anti-Arab claims checked
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:20:05 UTC
01:20:05 KST

Breadcrumb
'They don’t produce science, literature': RFK Jr's anti-Arab remarks fact-checked
US Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr has falsely claimed that Arabs do not produce science or literature and do not win prestigious international awards, making sweeping remarks that are contradicted by decades of achievements by Arab scientists, mathematicians and writers.
Speaking at a Republican campaign rally in Grand Rapids, Michigan, on Monday, Kennedy made the comments while supporting Senate candidate Mike Rogers, who faces Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in next month's election.
"There are 500 million Arabs in the world," Kennedy said. "And yet they don't produce science, they don't win the Nobel Prize, they don't win the Fields Prize, they don't win the Wolf Prize, they don't produce literature."
Kennedy went on to blame the Muslim Brotherhood for what he portrayed as the destruction of an earlier tradition of scientific and cultural achievement.
"They've created stagnant societies that do two things — hatred and war and victimization," he claimed.
But how much of what Kennedy said is actually true?
The New Arab examined his claims against the historical record and the achievements of Arab scientists, mathematicians and writers. The evidence tells a very different story.
Have Arab scientists won Nobel and Wolf prizes?
Yes. Egyptian-American scientist Ahmed Zewail won the 1999 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for pioneering the use of ultrashort laser pulses to observe chemical reactions.
Zewail, born in Damanhur, Egypt, had already received the Wolf Prize in Chemistry in 1993, directly contradicting Kennedy's assertion that Arabs do not win either award.
More recently, Palestinian-American chemist Omar Yaghi, born in Jordan to Palestinian refugee parents, shared the 2025 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for developing metal-organic frameworks.
These highly porous materials have applications ranging from capturing carbon dioxide to harvesting water from desert air.
Yaghi also received the Wolf Prize in Chemistry in 2018.
Kennedy's claim that Arabs do not win major international scientific honours is therefore contradicted by the records of the very institutions he named.
Responding to Kennedy's remarks on Tuesday, American scientist Peter Hotez pointed to his late colleague Zewail, with whom he had served as a US science envoy during the Obama administration.
"My late colleague and brilliant co U.S. Science Envoy with me in the Obama Admin the @Caltech Nobel Laureate in Chemistry Ahmed Zewail would disagree," Hotez wrote on X.
He also highlighted the contributions of medieval Arab scholars to preserving and transmitting scientific and philosophical knowledge, including the works of Aristotle, Hippocrates and Galen.
Have Arabs won the Fields Medal?
Kennedy also claimed that Arabs do not win the "Fields Prize", apparently referring to the Fields Medal, one of the most prestigious honours in mathematics.
However, Michael Atiyah, a British mathematician born to a Lebanese father and Scottish mother, received the Fields Medal in 1966.
Atiyah was recognised for groundbreaking contributions to mathematics, particularly in topology and geometry.
Although Atiyah was British, his Lebanese heritage makes him an example of internationally recognised scientific achievement among people of Arab descent.
The distinction matters: Kennedy made a sweeping claim about Arabs as a population, rather than limiting his remarks to scientists working in Arab countries.
Do Arabs produce internationally recognised literature?
Kennedy's assertion that Arabs do not produce literature is also contradicted by numerous internationally recognised authors.
Egyptian novelist Naguib Mahfouz won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1988, becoming the first Arabic-language writer to receive the award.
The Swedish Academy praised his creation of "an Arabian narrative art that applies to all mankind".
His best-known works include the Cairo Trilogy, which explores Egyptian society and political change across generations.
More recently, Omani novelist Jokha Alharthi won the 2019 Man Booker International Prize for Celestial Bodies, translated from Arabic by Marilyn Booth.
The award, shared between author and translator, made Alharthi the first Arab writer to win the prize.
Arab writers also claimed two major honours at the 2025 US National Book Awards.
Lebanese-American author Rabih Alameddine won the fiction award for The True True Story of Raja the Gullible (and His Mother).
Egyptian-Canadian writer Omar El Akkad received the nonfiction prize for One Day, Everyone Will Have Always Been Against This, which examines Western responses to Israel's war on Gaza.
These achievements directly contradict Kennedy's claim that Arabs do not produce literature or receive prestigious international recognition.
Have Arabs won the Nobel Peace Prize?
Kennedy's broader assertion that Arabs do not win Nobel Prizes is also contradicted by several recipients of the Nobel Peace Prize.
Egyptian President Anwar Sadat shared the 1978 award with Israeli Prime Minister Menachem Begin for their efforts towards a peace agreement between Egypt and Israel.
Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat shared the 1994 prize with Israeli leaders Yitzhak Rabin and Shimon Peres for their roles in the Oslo peace process.
Egyptian diplomat Mohamed ElBaradei shared the 2005 award with the International Atomic Energy Agency for efforts to prevent nuclear proliferation.
Yemeni journalist and activist Tawakkol Karman shared the 2011 Nobel Peace Prize for her nonviolent campaigning for women's rights and participation in peacebuilding.
She became the first woman from the Arab world to receive the award.
Tunisia's National Dialogue Quartet, representing trade unionists, employers, lawyers and human rights activists, won the 2015 Nobel Peace Prize for helping facilitate the country's democratic transition following the 2011 revolution.
The Nobel Committee credited its mediation with helping avert a potentially devastating political crisis.
Although peace prizes recognise different achievements from scientific and literary awards, these examples further disprove Kennedy's categorical assertion that Arabs do not win Nobel Prizes.
My late colleague and brilliant co U.S. Science Envoy with me in the Obama Admin the @Caltech Nobel Laureate in Chemistry Ahmed Zewail would disagree. God rest his soul he didn’t have to endure this, and of course RFK Jr forgets that it was the Arab scientists of the Middle Ages who kept Aristotle, Hippocrates, Galen alive to hand it down in the Renaissance. My favorite books on this topic attached
— Prof Peter Hotez MD PhD DSc(hon) (@PeterHotez) October 27, 2026
Did the Muslim Brotherhood destroy Arab intellectual life?
Kennedy also blamed the Muslim Brotherhood for what he described as the decline of Arab scientific and cultural achievements.
However, his explanation conflates centuries of intellectual history across numerous countries with the influence of a political and religious movement founded in Egypt in 1928.
The Brotherhood was established by Hassan al-Banna and developed into a wider Islamist movement advocating the organisation of society around Islamic principles.
Its branches and associated movements have followed different political paths across countries, including electoral participation and political opposition, while some offshoots have embraced violence.
It is not a single government exercising control over the Arab world.
Moreover, the scientific and literary achievements cited above all occurred after the Brotherhood's establishment, undermining Kennedy's suggestion that the movement brought Arab intellectual achievement to an end.
His remarks also overlook the contributions of Arab and Muslim scholars during the medieval period, when advances in mathematics, medicine, astronomy and philosophy helped shape scientific development far beyond the region.
The historical record does not support attributing the intellectual and cultural development of hundreds of millions of people across numerous countries to a single political movement.
Anti-Muslim rhetoric in Michigan's Senate race
Kennedy's remarks came as Republicans intensified attacks on Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, who is Muslim.
President Donald Trump appeared in Michigan on Sunday, where he called El-Sayed a "jihadist" and suggested he would need to pass through a metal detector before entering the Senate.
The comments prompted accusations of racism and anti-Muslim prejudice.
El-Sayed has denied ties to extremist groups and disavowed the Muslim Brotherhood.
Kennedy's comments targeted Arabs as an ethnic and cultural population, while his attempt to blame the Muslim Brotherhood introduced a religious and political dimension to his claims.
Arabs are not exclusively Muslim, and Muslims are not exclusively Arab. The distinction further exposes the problems with Kennedy's sweeping characterisation of hundreds of millions of people.

Finland and Norway Hold Direct Call With Putin, Prompting Criticism From Denmark
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:19:36 UTC
01:19:36 KST

- Category
- World
Finland and Norway Hold Direct Call With Putin, Prompting Criticism From Denmark
Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre called the Russian leader, Vladimir Putin, urging him to end the war in Ukraine and breaking with the recent practice of most Western European leaders avoiding direct contact with the Kremlin, Reuters reported on October 27.
The two Nordic leaders spoke with Putin before holding a separate call with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, according to a Zelenskyy aide cited by Reuters.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“The discussion with Putin was frank and substantive. We are neighbouring countries to Russia. The outcome of this war will have a direct impact on our and the broader European security. Ending the war requires direct discussions,” Stubb stated in a joint statement with Støre.
Støre emphasized the human and material cost of the war and noted that both leaders pressed for de-escalation. Finland and Norway also reaffirmed that their support for Ukraine would continue.
The Kremlin’s account of the conversation gave no indication that Putin had softened Russia’s existing demands, Reuters reported.
The Kremlin stated that a “just and long-term peace” would require Russia’s interests to be “fully and unconditionally” taken into account. It also accused EU and NATO countries of prolonging the fighting through what it described as confrontational policies.
A source close to the Kremlin told Reuters that Putin reiterated Russia’s demand to capture the entirety of Ukraine’s Donbas region. Stubb and Støre responded that any settlement would need to produce a “just” peace, according to the source.
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen criticized the decision by Finland and Norway to contact Putin directly, arguing that European countries should remain coordinated.
“I think Europe should stick together rather than going solo,” Frederiksen told Danish public broadcaster DR, while noting that she saw no sign that Russia wanted peace.
Stubb and Støre stressed that they had spoken as national leaders rather than on behalf of Europe as a whole.
Western European leaders have largely avoided direct calls with Putin since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, while increasing sanctions and military support for Kyiv.
Reuters reported that French President Emmanuel Macron was the last EU leader to speak with Putin by phone before the latest Nordic call. That conversation took place in July and produced no result, according to a source close to the Kremlin.
The call followed growing debate in Europe over who could serve as a direct channel to the Russian leader, Vladimir Putin, during negotiations over Ukraine. UNITED24 Media reported days earlier that European governments were considering appointing a representative to speak with Putin, with Finnish President Alexander Stubb among the names discussed.

European disease control center sends experts to Nigeria while Ebola cases surpass 10,000 in Congo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:17:14 UTC
01:17:14 KST

The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) deployed a team of experts to Nigeria this week as Ebola spreads across Africa, with cases reported in Kenya and Nigeria, the European agency announced on Tuesday.
With the Ebola outbreak continuing to spread beyond the epicentre in the Democratic Republic of Congo — where it surpassed 10,000 cases — ECDC sent a team led by its senior expert in epidemic intelligence to Nigeria, the fourth African country to report an Ebola case.
The ECDC experts are tasked with providing “advice and technical support to the EU Delegation in Abuja” and have offered to the Nigerian authorities to help with disease surveillance, contact tracing, infection prevention and control, as well as preparedness and response.
This is not the first time during this outbreak — the biggest that Congo has seen — that the Centre has sent experts to African countries. In May, a team was deployed to support the Africa CDC. The Centre also led a fact-finding mission on exit screening at airports in DRC and Uganda, while experts have also been deployed to South Sudan in June.
The outbreak began in Congo in May this year and has spread to Kenya, Uganda and Nigeria.
Kenya reported its first-ever Ebola case on 6 October. As of Monday, eight contacts of the confirmed cases had developed symptoms and tested positive for Ebola following laboratory testing. They were immediately transferred to the Ebola treatment centre in Nairobi, according to the United Nations. A further 20 contacts were released from quarantine in Kenya, the UN said on Tuesday.
The likelihood of infection among Europeans is very low, according to ECDC’s latest threat assessment. For those living or travelling to affected areas in Kenya and Nigeria, the risk is low.

New: Oxford Studies in Philosophy of AI and Computing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:16:23 UTC
01:16:23 KST

A new annual series and accompanying conference has been launched: Oxford Studies in Philosophy of AI and Computing (OSPAIC).
The executive editor of OSPAIC is Seth Lazar (Johns Hopkins). Its associate editors are Jeffrey Howard (UCL) and Rachael Sterken (University of Hong Kong). Ned Howells-Whitaker (JHU and Pittsburgh) is the assistant editor.
Lazar writes:
Rapid AI progress is raising so many philosophical questions; but philosophers aren’t as involved in the conversation as they should be, for many different reasons.
One is that, aside from some work in logic and philosophy of mind, philosophy of AI and computing has often sat on the margins of the discipline. One reason for that is that so many philosophers working on AI have had to do so basically on their own, figuring things out for themselves as they go along, without a real community around them.
OSPAIC is going to help fix this! We’re going to have an annual conference and volume. The conference (in DC! where much of the future of AI will be decided) is especially important as we think about the nature of intellectual life in a world where AI systems can one-shot a superficially-plausible philosophy paper. OSPAIC sees philosophical progress as being about more than just the accumulation of true claims. The conference is a big part of our vision for how we contribute to philosophical progress.
Just as other Oxford Studies in Philosophy volumes have accompanying prizes, so too will OSPAIC. The Cosmos Institute is running an AI and philosophy manuscript competition with a $10,000 prize.
Lazar adds that one aim of the conference and series is “to help philosophers be part of the broader public conversation” and “to that end we’re… encouraging everyone who submits to OSPAIC to also upload their draft to arXiv (at present, use keyword PFAI).”
Oxford Studies in Philosophy of AI and Computing‘s inaugural call for submissions is open.

Jailed Russian political scientist Alexander Kynev faces new ‘foreign agent’ allegation as broken leg leaves him unable to use cell toilet
Political scientist Alexander Kynev, who was arrested for allegedly attempting to sell drugs, has been cited for violating “foreign agent” regulations.
It is unclear what prompted the citation, which was filed with Moscow’s Perovsky District Court on October 27. No hearing has been scheduled.
Kynev has been in pretrial detention since September 25. He denies the drug allegations.
The Slovo Zashchite project reported that Kynev was beaten so severely during his arrest that his leg was broken. Political scientist Ekaterina Schulmann said the beating was an attempt to force Kynev to confess to treason.
On October 26, reports emerged that Kynev had stopped eating in pretrial detention because his broken leg prevented him from using the toilet in his cell. Kynev himself said the injury left him unable to move around properly.
Alexander Kynev is one of the most respected experts on Russian regional politics and elections. Russian authorities designated him a “foreign agent” in February 2026.
