UK urged to classify anti-Zionism as extremism, ban marches near Jewish institutions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:15:50 UTC
01:15:50 KST

B’nai B’rith UK has called on the British government to classify anti-Zionism as an extremist ideology, permanently ban al-Quds Day demonstrations, restrict protests near Jewish institutions and take stronger action against organizations accused of promoting anti-Jewish hatred.
The demands are laid out in the organization’s 108-page report, titled Antizionism: The New Face of Anti-Jewish Extremism. Written by Dr. Jeremy Havardi, the report was formally presented at the UK Parliament on October 20 at an event co-chaired by Labour MP Mark Sewards and Conservative MP Sir Iain Duncan Smith.
The report argues that anti-Zionism has become a predominant expression of modern antisemitism, drawing on Nazi propaganda, Soviet ideology and Islamist extremism, while presenting itself through the language of human rights and social justice.
It sets out 11 policy recommendations aimed at addressing what Havardi describes as an extremist movement that has contributed to the harassment, intimidation and exclusion of Jews from public life.
Among its principal recommendations is that the British government formally identify anti-Zionism as an extremist ideology and condemn political parties, nongovernmental organizations and civil society groups that promote it.
Restrictions on anti-Zionist demonstrations
The report calls for strict limitations on future anti-Zionist demonstrations, particularly those taking place near Jewish community institutions.
It stresses that “No march should be allowed next to synagogues, Jewish schools or Jewish social venues as this is a clear example of racist provocation.”
It also recommends the arrest and prosecution of demonstrators who incite violence against Zionists, including through calls for an intifada or slogans threatening Jews.
Although it acknowledges the importance of freedom of expression, the report argues that incitement should not be protected under the principle of free speech.
Havardi also calls for a permanent ban on London’s annual al-Quds Day demonstration, which he links to Iranian efforts to promote radicalization in Britain.
The proposed measures go beyond existing restrictions on particular demonstrations and would require further government action.
Universities, charities and public institutions
The report also proposes greater scrutiny of universities, charities and other public institutions accused of tolerating antisemitism.
It recommends mandatory reporting of antisemitic incidents and complaints across public bodies, including the measures taken in response, alongside the adoption of the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance’s working definition of antisemitism.
University administrators would be required to undergo antisemitism training, and institutions should appoint dedicated antisemitism officers when possible.
The report further calls for disciplinary action against university staff and students found to be glorifying Palestinian or Islamist terrorism.
Regarding charities, it urges the Charity Commission to shut down organizations promoting anti-Zionist violence or hatred, while maintaining safeguards for lawful advocacy.
The report also calls on the government to remind music, sporting, and cultural venues of their responsibilities under the Equality Act when responding to demands to exclude Jewish or Israeli performers.
Iran, Qatar and the Muslim Brotherhood
Beyond domestic activism, Havardi calls for the expulsion of Iran’s ambassador to Britain and the proscription of media channels promoting the ideology of the Islamic Republic of Iran and its regional proxies.
The report identifies several media organizations operating in Britain that it says are connected to Iranian influence networks, including members of the Islamic Radio and Television Union.
It also recommends that Britain ban the Muslim Brotherhood as a terrorist organization on national security grounds.
If the organization does not meet the legal threshold for proscription under the Terrorism Act 2000, the report suggests designating it an extremist organization, following the approach of German federal authorities.
The report further calls for Qatar’s funding of Islamist organizations in Britain to be identified and monitored, accusing Doha of using its influence to spread anti-Zionist and antisemitic narratives.
Anti-Zionism’s impact beyond Jewish communities
The report also argues that anti-Zionism has consequences for Palestinians, claiming that opposition to Jewish national self-determination undermines coexistence and prospects for a negotiated peace.
Havardi contends that anti-Zionist movements marginalize Israelis and Palestinians who pursue dialogue, while political rejectionism has contributed to lost economic opportunities for Palestinians.
The report cites previously published research, including figures showing that more than 160,000 Palestinians worked in Israel or Israeli settlements before October 7, 2023, to illustrate the economic importance of cross-border cooperation.
Havardi argues that these consequences contradict the British government’s commitment to a two-state solution and its support for regional normalization through the Abraham Accords.
The report’s recommendations have not yet been adopted as British government policy.

Likud officials sound alarm over voter apathy as Israel sees record-high election turnout
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:15:43 UTC
01:15:43 KST

Against the backdrop of unusually high turnout and reports of long queues at polling stations in strongholds of the change bloc and in Arab communities, Likud fears that even its traditional gevalt calls may fail to get right-wing voters out of their homes this election.
The party is concerned about the mobilization of the camp opposing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and the difficulty of generating enthusiasm among some right-wing voters as the battle for power enters its decisive hours.
Likud officials describe a particularly worrying picture.
“If we haven’t managed to make the right-wing public want to go out and vote by now, even a last-minute gevalt call will only help to some extent,” they said. According to them, “It seems that this time the public hears our gevalt calls and remembers the boy who cried ‘Wolf, wolf.’”
At this stage, one official added, “There isn’t even a single encouraging sign.”
Likud stronghold cities not as motivated to vote
One example is the relatively low turnout in Bat Yam, considered a Likud stronghold. The city’s mayor, Tzvika Brot, is also managing Likud’s campaign. As of noon, turnout in the city stood at just 23%.
It is important to note, however, that this figure represents overall turnout. It cannot be used to draw conclusions about the level of support for Likud or any other party.
Relatively low turnout was also recorded in other localities traditionally associated with Likud. As of noon, turnout stood at approximately 24% in Kiryat Shmona, 25% in Nof HaGalil, and 27% in Kiryat Malachi. In Ashkelon, Dimona, and Migdal Ha’emek, approximately 29% of eligible voters had cast their ballots. The figures were around 30% in Afula and 32% in Beit She’an.
These figures reflect overall turnout in each locality and do not indicate how many Likud supporters have voted or how much support the party enjoys there.
The concerns come as figures from the Central Elections Committee point to exceptionally high voter participation nationwide. By 10:00 a.m., 16.68% of eligible voters had cast their ballots, the highest turnout recorded at that hour since 1981.
By noon, national turnout had reached 31.5%, compared with 28.4% at the same time during the elections for the 25th Knesset. That represents an increase of 3.1 percentage points and the highest turnout at that hour since 1977.
The trend continued into the afternoon. By 2:00 p.m., turnout had reached 44.9%, compared with 38.9% in the previous election, an increase of six percentage points and the highest rate recorded at that hour since at least 1973.
The early turnout figures were presented at a press conference held at the Knesset’s command center by Adv. Din Livne, acting director-general of the Central Elections Committee.
Long queues at polling stations continue
Despite the high national turnout, the figures do not yet reveal how participation is divided between the political blocs.
According to an analysis by the Stat-Net Institute, the number of polling stations in Arab localities is lower than in the previous election, even though the number of eligible voters has increased. This may explain some of the long queues.
Voting patterns in Arab society are a particular concern for Likud. Polls published before the election estimated that turnout in Arab communities could reach approximately 60%–63%, up from around 56% in 2022. Such an increase could affect the distribution of Knesset seats and make it more difficult for Netanyahu’s bloc to secure a parliamentary majority.
The party is also worried about losing votes to smaller right-wing parties that fail to cross the electoral threshold, which would weaken the camp’s overall strength.
Likud’s concerns are not new. Even before Election Day, disagreements emerged within the party’s campaign headquarters. Some officials expressed confidence in the internal projections of pollster Shlomo Filber, while others worried about the opposing camp’s efforts to mobilize voters.
One official described the dispute over Filber’s projections this way: “Either Momo comes out a king, or Momo goes home”.
Another concern is voter apathy among Likud supporters. Their mobilization during the 2022 election helped Netanyahu’s bloc secure its electoral victory.
Likud fears the 'Wolf, wolf' warnings have lost their impact
Netanyahu himself is working to mobilize right-wing voters. In a video circulated today, he warned of efforts by the change bloc to bring voters to the polls.
“We are in danger, because the left is flying its thousands of people thousands of kilometers so that they will come to the polling station,” he said in an appeal to residents of the West Bank, asking them to help get voters to the polls.
Likud has prepared an extensive voter-mobilization operation, working alongside other parties in its political camp to increase turnout during the remaining hours before polling stations close.
The party’s efforts are further complicated by restrictions on one of the tools it used in previous election campaigns. Following a Supreme Court ruling limiting parties’ ability to track voter participation, Likud argued that its capacity to identify supporters who had not yet voted and take steps to get them to the polls had been impaired. Disagreements over the transfer of real-time voting data continued in the days leading up to the election.
Likud also remembers the 2022 election, when its voter-mobilization efforts helped Netanyahu’s bloc win 64 Knesset seats. At the time, the party succeeded in increasing turnout among its supporters by approximately five percentage points compared with the preceding election.
This time, however, the concern, according to a party official, is that repeated warnings about the danger of losing power are no longer eliciting the same response.
On the very day Likud needs its supporters to turn out at the polls, party officials fear that the public has stopped reacting to the repeated cries of “Wolf, wolf.”

Likud says it received 620 reports of 'suspected irregularities' at polling stations in Arab sector

16:15:43 UTC

The Likud party’s election integrity representative, Sagi Keisler, accused the Central Elections Committee (CEC) of ignoring alleged instances of voter fraud in favor of maintaining a high voter turnout on Election Day.
Likud claimed to have submitted 775 complaints to the CEC alleging documented incidents of improper conduct and attempted fraud at polling stations in Arab-majority localities.
Earlier on Tuesday, Likud said that it had received 620 reports of unusual incidents and suspected irregularities at polling stations in the Arab sector, collected through a network of over 1,500 representatives across the country.
About one-third of the reports concern the recording of voters' personal information and the transmission of information outside polling stations. Some 66 reports concern irregularities involving ballot papers and envelopes, 26 involve difficulties verifying voters' identities and exercising polling station committee members' authority, and 17 concern violence and threats.
The remaining reports involve staffing deficiencies, election campaigning, and documentation issues.
Envelopes reported missing
In one incident, 10 sealed envelopes were reported missing from a polling station in Fassuta and in another, a discrepancy of 11 envelopes between the number of envelopes and the recorded number of voters was found in Jadeidi-Makr, the headquarters said.
Likud's election integrity headquarters also criticized an instruction from the director-general of the Central Elections Committee to prevent overcrowding, saying it could undermine adherence to voter identification requirements and voting procedures.
"The Elections Committee is cutting corners precisely where stricter oversight is needed. We are receiving hundreds of reports of suspected irregularities, including missing envelopes and the unauthorized transmission of information.
"Instead of strengthening oversight, pressure is being applied to prevent overcrowding at polling stations. We demand an immediate investigation into these suspicions, the deployment of independent observers, and guarantees of a proper and transparent voting process," said Sagi Kaisler, head of Likud's election integrity headquarters for the Arab sector.

There is no alternative to the Southern Bridge: military expert warns of a transport collapse in Kyiv
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
18:15:37 EET
01:15:37 KST

There is no alternative to the Southern Bridge: military expert warns of a transport collapse in Kyiv
Kyiv • UNN
The bridge and metro were damaged after the missile strike. The expert warned of a transport collapse and new risks for crossings.
During the night of October 27, as a result of another Russian missile attack on Kyiv, a strike was recorded on the Southern Bridge, and metro tracks were also damaged. Military expert Oleh Zhdanov told an UNN journalist more about how long it could take to restore the damaged bridge, whether there is an effective alternative solution for crossing the river, and whether new strikes on the capital's bridges are possible.
Details
The Southern Bridge is one of the capital's largest crossings and has a significant load-bearing capacity, the military expert explains. In addition, he says, it is also used by the metro, and its prolonged closure will create an additional burden on the other bridges across the Dnipro. This, in turn, could complicate not only the movement of city residents but also the transportation of goods.
We have five road bridges, and one represents roughly 20%. And these 20% will fall on the other bridges. And considering that there also need to be roads along the Dnipro so that it is possible to get from one direction to another and reach another bridge—for Kyiv, this will be a collapse
Why the other crossings will not be able to replace the Southern Bridge
In Oleh Zhdanov's opinion, even if traffic is redirected to other bridges, this still will not fully solve the problem. Instead, not only the crossings themselves but also the access roads to them will face an additional burden, and as a result, traffic jams could spread across a significant part of the city.
When you remove at least one of the five bridges, a minimum of 10% of the traffic load is distributed among the remaining bridges. And possibly more. Plus, there are the access routes—all these streets will be filled with vehicles, both private cars and trucks
The expert also commented on the possibility of setting up ferry or pontoon crossings. In his opinion, such solutions will not be able to fully ensure transport links between the capital's banks, because ferry crossings require piers to be built on both sides of the Dnipro, as well as access roads for vehicles.
Water crossings over the Dnipro are being planned in Kyiv - Klitschko27.10.26, 16:28 • 3288 views
A ferry crossing is impossible because piers would have to be built on both sides. That's the first thing. And access roads to the places where vehicles can drive onto and off the ferries. And a pontoon crossing will not solve the issue
He also added that traffic across a pontoon crossing could likewise be quite slow because of the specifics of its design, which, in turn, would instead complicate the movement of vehicles and would not make it possible to provide the same capacity as a full-fledged bridge. In addition, the transportation of heavy equipment remains a separate problem.
A pontoon crossing is a last resort. It slows the movement of vehicles considerably. Therefore, this is a very complicated operation
How long could repairs take, and are new strikes possible?
Assessing the damage to the Southern Bridge, Oleh Zhdanov noted that he had not personally inspected the structure, so he could draw conclusions only from photographs. According to him, a bridge span was damaged, but it is unknown whether its load-bearing elements were affected, which is important because the complexity and duration of the restoration work will depend precisely on this.
To tie the reinforcement and pour the concrete takes about three weeks, and another 30 days are needed for the concrete to gain strength. Concrete can be loaded 30 days after it is poured. So, do the math: even at an accelerated pace—at least one or two months
At the same time, the military expert believes that Russia may continue attempting to strike bridges across the Dnipro, because such attacks could significantly affect the transport system and logistics, and crossings are particularly important for transporting military equipment and cargo.
They understand perfectly well: if they destroy even half of our bridges, traffic will collapse catastrophically—not by half, but several times over. Both on the railways and in road transportation. The bulk of logistics is based on road transport; low-loaders carrying heavy equipment are on the move
As an example of the possible consequences of a prolonged bridge closure, he cited a previous incident when, after a drone struck a support, the Southern Bridge was temporarily closed and considerable traffic jams formed on the roads. Now, however, if the bridge is closed in both directions for repairs, the situation could be much more complicated.
“Recall the first strike on the bridge, when a Shahed struck a support. The Southern Bridge was closed for three or four days then. What was happening in Kyiv? People stood there until midnight, unable to get from one bank to the other. Now imagine closing it in both directions for repairs. There you have a vivid example — it would be a one-hundred-percent transport collapse,”
Thus, there is currently no full-fledged alternative to the Southern Bridge, so the crossing must be protected and restored. At the same time, the exact repair timeline can be determined only after assessing the actual condition of the damaged structures.

Likud, Shas, People of Israel, and Otzma Yehudit push to extend voting times
Ofer Winter’s People of Israel, National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir's Otzma Yehudit, and the haredi (ultra-Orthodox) Shas party joined Likud in calling for an hour-long extension.

"According to the data we have, numbers like these have not been seen since 1973."
"There are massive lines at polling stations in Bedouin communities in the Negev and in Tel Aviv, yet, regrettably, in our own camp, among the Haredi and right-wing strongholds, there is a sense of complacency," Deri said.
Decision to extend voting hours can only be made by Sohlberg

The decision can only be made by CEC Chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg.

"No unusual incident has occurred to justify granting this request," the party stated, "which is intended to lay the groundwork for claims challenging the integrity of the election, in line with the lies Netanyahu has been spreading since this morning."

This 30-Second Habit Can Improve Your Balance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:14:42 UTC
01:14:42 KST

Standing on your own two feet might be no problem. Lift one up to balance, though, and you might have a few concerns.
Fortunately, there are ways to get a leg up on better balance. “Balance is not a trait—it’s a skill,” says Dr. Cory Calendine, an orthopedic surgeon at the Bone and Joint Institute of Tennessee. One way to practice: Stand beside a sturdy counter, lift one foot, and work toward holding the position for 30 seconds before switching sides.
Staying upright can be surprisingly humbling. “It’s free, it’s simple, but it’s also honest, brutally honest,” Calendine says. “It’s a good assessment of where you are.”
Here’s why it’s worth practicing, plus how to get started.
The benefits of standing on one leg
You might not give your balance much thought, but it helps get you through the day—from stepping into the shower to climbing upstairs when you get home from work. Even walking down the sidewalk involves briefly supporting yourself on one foot with every step.
There’s a lot going on to keep you from tipping over: Your brain processes information from your eyes, inner ear, and sensory nerves, while your muscles help keep you steady. When you lift one foot, for example, the muscles along the outside of your standing hip help keep your pelvis level. “All of these things are being coordinated for you to stand in one position without falling,” Calendine says.
Your balance can improve with practice: A review of 13 studies found that single-leg balance training improved balance performance in healthy adults. Calendine suggests working toward 30 seconds on each side, starting with however long you can safely manage.
Still, preventing falls takes more than good balance—you also need strong muscles to support you. A large Cochrane review found that exercise programs that focused on balance in addition to everyday movements, like getting up from a chair, reduced the rate of falls in older adults by about a quarter. While standing on one leg is a good start, it shouldn’t be the only exercise you do. “Balance is the front door, but strength is the whole house,” Calendine says.
How to stand on one leg to improve your balance
Find a sturdy counter you can hold onto, says Kevin Pozzi, an assistant professor in the doctor of physical therapy program at Johnson & Wales University in Providence, R.I. Check that the floor isn’t slippery, and give your footwear some thought: “Sneakers would be ideal,” he says, as long as “they’re tied well and they fit.”
If you’ve fallen before or had a significant injury or surgery involving your legs, hips, or spine, talk to a health professional before getting started. Pozzi also recommends getting help if you can’t hold the position for 10 seconds. A physical therapist can assess your balance and suggest a routine that’s safe for you.
Otherwise, start with your hands on the counter, stand tall, and lift one foot off the floor. Keep your core engaged and avoid slumping over, Pozzi advises. Bending your lifted knee so your foot is slightly behind you often feels most comfortable, though you can also lift it in front if there’s room. “See how long you can hold first while holding on,” he says.
If that feels easy, you can start easing up on your hands. “Maybe you go down to one hand,” he says. “Then lighten your grip even with that one hand so that you’re really not relying on it quite so much.” Keep it close enough to grab the counter if you need to.
Work toward 30 seconds, then switch legs. One side might feel easier than the other, especially if you’ve had an injury. “They’re not always the same,” Pozzi says. Once you can comfortably manage 30 seconds on each side, try repeating it a few times throughout the day.
And don’t expect to be perfectly still. “It’s normal to have a little bit of wobbling,” he says. You might feel your ankle moving or notice small shifts at your knee and hip as you try to stay upright. That doesn’t mean you’re doing it wrong. But if you’re wobbling so much that you keep grabbing the counter or putting your foot down, hold on and make it easier.
Don’t expect immediate results; this balance exercise takes time to work. Pozzi says people may start noticing changes after four to six weeks of consistent practice, including being able to hold the position longer. “Getting their socks and shoes on might be a little easier,” he says.
How to make balance exercises a daily habit
Calendine works on his balance while his coffee brews, both at home and at work, giving each leg a turn. “Nobody even knows I’m doing it,” he says. “They’re standing beside me, but you can kind of hide it, which is nice.”
Dr. Vonda Wright, an orthopedic surgeon in Orlando, practices so often that she sometimes catches herself standing on one leg while giving a speech. She also asks rooms full of executives to try it—and watches them struggle. “It may be one of the only things they fail at,” she says.
To make practicing easier to remember, she suggests pairing it with something you already do. Once you feel steady enough, try standing on one leg while brushing your teeth or taking a phone call beside your desk, with a sturdy surface nearby. “You’ve got to brush your teeth anyway,” she says. “Do it on one leg.”
When holding the position for 30 seconds feels easy, you can gradually increase the challenge. Wright suggests placing a folded towel under your standing foot, which makes the surface less stable. Another option is moving your arms while you balance. Change one thing at a time, with support within reach.
Think you’ve gotten pretty good at the whole thing? Try briefly closing your eyes; without being able to see, staying upright gets trickier. “Always be near something you can grab onto,” Wright says. If you lose your balance, put your foot down and start again. “We’re trying to make this a lifestyle,” she says, “not a workout regimen.”

Syrians bury victims of Jordanian airstrike massacre in Daraa

2026-10-27

Breadcrumb
Syrians bury victims of Jordanian airstrike massacre in Daraa
Residents of southern Syria buried seven civilians, including three children from the same family, on Tuesday following a massacre caused by Jordanian airstrikes on Daraa province, as a grieving grandfather described desperately searching through the rubble for his grandchildren.
The funeral procession began at Al-Sanamayn Military Hospital and travelled to the town of Al-Tuff in the Lajat region of northeastern Daraa, where mourners gathered to bid farewell to those killed in Monday evening's bombing.
The strikes killed seven civilians and wounded three others, bringing the total number of casualties to 10, according to information obtained by The New Arab.
Among the dead were three siblings, Yassin Hadi al-Sulaim, 11, Osama Hadi al-Sulaim, eight, and Lamis Hadi al-Sulaim, six, whose father has been missing since his detention under the former regime of Bashar al-Assad.
Their grandfather, Masoud al-Sulaim, told The New Arab that he had returned home on Monday evening after working at a well, prayed and eaten with his family before going to sleep.
He woke about an hour later to what he believed was thunder, accompanied by lightning and the sound of aircraft overhead.
Moments later, an explosion struck as he walked towards a wall, forcing him to take cover. When he emerged, he discovered that the place where his family had been staying had been destroyed.
"I called and called, but nobody answered. I just wanted someone to say 'ah', but nobody spoke, nobody opened their mouth," he told The New Arab.
He said he began searching frantically through the rubble, moving stones and debris in the hope of finding survivors.
His three grandchildren were among those killed.
Al-Sulaim said other grandchildren, from his daughter's family, had been inside a building made of concrete blocks and corrugated metal sheets when parts of its walls collapsed during the bombing.
Their mother managed to pull them from the rubble, and they were taken to hospital with injuries.
He said he had received telephone calls reassuring him that they were alive but had not yet been able to see them.
The other confirmed fatalities were identified as Lotfiya Hosni al-Ali, 64, Zaher Masoud al-Sulaim, 23, Riyad al-Karad, 65, and Mutlaq al-Sulaim, 70.
Mohammed al-Dukhan, a relative of the victims, told The New Arab that he initially believed the aircraft overhead were Israeli.
He said the strike hit a civilian tent sheltering an elderly woman and her three grandchildren, whose father had been detained in Syria's notorious Saydnaya prison in 2018.
Jordan acknowledges civilian deaths
Jordan expressed regret on Tuesday over the civilian deaths but defended its airstrikes, saying they targeted Islamic State (IS) positions linked to the perpetrators of a deadly church attack in the Jordanian governorate of Karak.
Government spokesman Mohammad al-Momani said the operation was based on intelligence about threats to Jordanian national security and claimed that more than 20 IS members had been killed and a large weapons depot destroyed.
Momani insisted that Jordan had taken precautions to avoid civilian casualties and deliberately avoided locations where civilians were believed to be present.
However, an unnamed Jordanian source told the state-owned Al-Mamlaka television channel that civilians had been killed when an airstrike hit a small concrete building near their tent.
The source claimed the building housed an alleged militant and that the force of the explosion killed an elderly woman and three children sheltering nearby.
Jordan's military said the operation, named "Jordanian Deterrence – Hammoud", targeted groups allegedly linked to the recent attack on Hammoud Church in Karak.
Momani said Jordan would work with Syria to establish a joint committee to investigate the consequences of the operation and improve security coordination.
Damascus condemns violation of sovereignty
Syria's foreign ministry strongly condemned the airstrikes, describing the bombing of locations in Daraa and the entry of Jordanian aircraft into Syrian airspace without prior coordination as a violation of national sovereignty.
In a statement on Tuesday, Damascus said the attacks were unacceptable under any circumstances and violated the principles of good neighbourly relations.
The ministry nevertheless stressed the importance of maintaining relations with Jordan and announced plans for an urgent joint security committee to prevent further incidents and improve border coordination.
Syrian Interior Ministry spokesman Nour al-Din al-Baba offered condolences to the victims' families and said authorities were working to establish the circumstances of the bombing.
He emphasised that protecting civilians must remain a priority in efforts to combat terrorism and cross-border crime.
The massacre has left several generations of one family dead, including three young siblings whose father disappeared into the prisons of the former Assad regime, as their relatives struggle to come to terms with another devastating loss.

Jonathan Kure, chairman of the independent investigative committee and a retired deputy director-general of the Department of State Services, presented the findings to Interior Minister Olubunmi Tunji-Ojo in the capital Abuja.

Tunji-Ojo pledged to implement the recommendations to ensure justice for those affected.
He also ordered the suspension of officers accused of cleaning the detention facility to destroy evidence, according to the report.
The deaths occurred on Sept. 17, when 37 of 67 artisanal and suspected illegal miners arrested during operations in the M.I. Wushishi and Lukoto areas of Niger State were found dead at an NSCDC detention facility in Minna, the state capital.
The federal government established the independent committee following public concern over the deaths and suspended officers implicated in the incident pending the investigation.
President Bola Tinubu had also called for a comprehensive and transparent inquiry.

Melike Pala

Authorities in France have declared 45 municipalities in the southern Herault department to be natural disaster areas following heavy rainfall and flooding that hit the region earlier this autumn, broadcaster BFMTV reported on Tuesday.
The decree covers damage caused by river flooding, surface water runoff and associated mudslides.
The recognition allows residents and property owners with insurance coverage to benefit from compensation under France's natural disaster insurance scheme.
The 45 municipalities include Montpellier, Castelnau-le-Lez, Lattes, Lunel, Perols, Baillargues, Castries, Grabels, Juvignac, Saint-Jean-de-Vedas, Vendargues and Saint-Gely-du-Fesc.

France has experienced several severe weather events in recent weeks, with torrential rainfall triggering flash floods across southern and southeastern regions.

IT Worker Jailed 13 Years in Russia After Binance Revealed He Donated Money to Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:07:25 UTC
01:07:25 KST

A Russian IT specialist has been sentenced to 13 years in jail on charges of financing terrorism after the cryptocurrency exchange Binance passed details to authorities in Moscow of his donations to Ukrainian fundraising campaigns.
A judge at the 2nd Western District Military Court on Monday found 49-year-old Yury Belenky guilty of the charges and sentenced him to three years in prison, plus an additional 10 years in a strict-regime penal colony, according to a court statement.
Belenky, who has a Bulgarian residence permit, was arrested in September last year when he flew to Moscow for a visit and has been in police custody ever since. He denied the charges, according to the court.
Documents showed that Binance provided Russian investigators with Belenky's transaction history last year, including records of transfers to Ukrainian fundraising campaigns, in response to a Russian request, and that the records were instrumental in prosecuting him, Reuters reported in August.
According to the records, Belenky sent more than $700 to the Ukrainian military in response to an online appeal by Arkady Babchenko, an exiled Russian critic of the Kremlin who supports Ukraine. Some payments went to the Azov Brigade.
"The response from Binance serves as key evidence in the criminal case against Belenkiy," said Yevgeny Smirnov, a lawyer with the rights group First Department, which helps people facing politically motivated charges in Russia.
Rights advocates who monitor such prosecutions say dozens of Russians have been convicted in recent years for donations made through cryptocurrency platforms to causes that authorities later classified as extremist or terrorist. Many used cryptocurrency because they believed it would keep their identities secret.
Asked on Tuesday about the sentence, Binance referred Reuters to a previous statement in which it said the exchange "does not make or enforce the laws of any jurisdiction, determine charges or decide how any government uses information in legal proceedings."
Binance said it does not comment on confidential law-enforcement requests or individual cases.
A lawyer who specialises in crypto regulation, Mike Bystrov, told Reuters in August that Binance, which left Russia in 2023 following the full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the subsequent imposition of Western sanctions, had been under no obligation to provide Belenky's data.
He said it might, in fact, have had obligations under European Union data-protection law not to do so because of Belenky's Bulgarian residency status.

Lula’s victory echoes across BRICS after fears of a Bolsonaro win
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:05:22 UTC
01:05:22 KST

Lula’s victory echoes across BRICS after fears of a Bolsonaro win
Lula’s fourth term may have spared BRICS an internal fracture at a time when Trump is trying to pressure countries back into Washington’s orbit.
When Brazil’s President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva scored his surprise election victory on Sunday, winning an unprecedented fourth term in office, his supporters were euphoric.
The joy they felt over Lula’s victory has echoed across large parts of the Global South – and could restore some hope to the grouping that has sought to give emerging countries a greater stake on the world stage, the BRICS alliance.
At a time when United States President Donald Trump is seeking to reassert US power and has cast BRICS as a threat to US interests, Lula’s victory in Brazil offers the alliance a measure of political reassurance, experts say.
A win by his rival, Flavio Bolsonaro, could have threatened Brazil’s commitment to the bloc, given his links to Trump and calls to reconsider the country’s role in BRICS.
Instead, Lula’s return gives the grouping one fewer reason to fear a retreat from within – as it continues to help forge a more multipolar future for a world dominated by the US.
As Esmat Zaidan, professor of public policy at Qatar’s Hamad Bin Khalifa University, told Al Jazeera, “The victory of Lula is important to BRICS’ political continuation in the current climate as it seeks to increase the bloc’s role and make it stronger in global governance.”
A spared fracture
It was clear to analysts that Lula’s win would safeguard the continuation of the BRICS alliance, while under Bolsonaro, its future may have floundered.
Lula himself was one of the architects of the bloc when it was founded nearly two decades ago, and has sought to advance its role on the global stage.
According to Zaidan, Bolsonaro’s desire to reconsider Brazil’s participation in BRICS and instead pursue closer alignment with Washington would have weakened the bloc’s political cohesion and potentially slowed cooperation on trade and financial reform.
Bolsonaro had reportedly also promised the US Trade Representative that Brazil’s Pix instant payment system would stay out of non-Western payment schemes, as the US seeks to safeguard global dominance of the dollar, said Imran Khalid, a geostrategic analyst and senior fellow at Foreign Policy in Focus.
“BRICS makes decisions by consensus, so one unwilling founding member can slow everything down from the inside. That was the real risk, more than Brazil walking out,” Khalid told Al Jazeera.
Still, Zaidan cautioned that continuity of the alliance does not amount to total unity within.
“The member countries of BRICS have distinctly different economic interests and geopolitical goals,” he said. “Therefore, while Lula’s victory makes it easier for the BRICS bloc to continue working towards a common agenda, his election did not eliminate these distinct differences.”
Guy Burton, a geopolitical and policy analyst, agreed that the bloc’s differences will remain unchanged with Brazil’s election result.
“BRICS matters because it represents a large share of the world’s population, economy and trade. But it has never really acted as a political unit. Its members are too different,” he said.
“The bloc now includes Iran and the UAE, which sit on opposite sides of the current war. That tells you how limited its cohesion is,” Burton added.
More multipolarity, but not a counterweight to Washington
The apparent relief in the Global South to Lula’s win reflects a broader concern among many emerging economies about their exposure to decisions made in Washington, “particularly regarding trade, tariffs and international economic relations,” said Zaidan.
“For these countries, the issue is not necessarily opposition to the US. It is about having greater room to make independent decisions and avoiding excessive dependence on any single global power,” he said.
Khalid pointed to China and Russia’s support for Lula, with Xi Jinping backing him against outside interference, and the Kremlin praising his work for the BRICS alliance.
“Most of these countries do not want a fight with the United States; they want the freedom to say no to Washington without being punished for it,” he explained.
“A strong Brazil inside BRICS helps protect that freedom.”
Lula has long advocated for a more multipolar international system, in which emerging economies have a stronger voice when it comes to shaping international rules and institutions, added Zaidan.
Burton said even countries and regions beyond the Global South are looking to lessen their reliance on Washington, including Europe, which is building its own security against Russia and in support of Ukraine.
“So states, whether in the Western camp or not, have accepted that they must pursue their own interests. That means working with whoever they can. We are moving into a genuinely multipolar world,” he said.
Still, BRICS’ diversity and its member states’ varied interests have meant it has never been a coherent counterweight to the West, experts said.
Many in the alliance maintain strong economic and security relationships with the US, said Zaidan.
“I would see Lula’s victory as strengthening the case for strategic autonomy rather than confrontation with Washington,” said the professor.
“BRICS is potentially more effective when it expands the choices available to its members, rather than defining itself simply through opposition to the United States.”
Burton agreed, pointing to Brazil’s changing ties with Trump over the years.
“Russia and China are the obvious US rivals. But India under Modi long had a close relationship with Washington, and with Trump in particular, even if that has weakened recently,” he said.
“Brazil, too, was close to Trump under Jair Bolsonaro, Flavio Bolsonaro’s father, when he was in office.”
Challenging dollar dependence
Among the BRICS’ many ambitions is to promote trade in local currencies rather than the US dollar – and Lula’s victory could provide the political foundation to build on these efforts, said Zaidan, given that Brazil is one of the largest trading economies in the bloc.
Khalid said that after the alliance scrapped the idea of a common BRICS currency at its most recent summit in New Delhi in September, its ambition for trade in local currencies has become far more viable.
“If the [BRICS’ New Development Bank] moves towards its goal of 30 percent of lending in member currencies, and Brazil and China settle more trade in reais and yuan as they agreed in 2023, reliance on the dollar falls step by step, without an open confrontation,” he explained.
But Zaidan said that political will alone is not enough.
“Countries also need reliable payment infrastructure, sufficient currency liquidity, appropriate financial regulations, and businesses willing to use these arrangements,” he said.
For now the dollar reigns supreme in foreign exchange transactions, and there may be no tipping point for another decade or so, Burton said.
Ultimately, though, Lula’s victory could help BRICS move from political discussions towards more practical financial cooperation, while reducing dollar dependence will be “gradual, uneven and driven as much by economic feasibility as by geopolitical ambition”, said Zaidan.
How Washington reacts to this is another variable; Trump’s government sits at the contradiction of wanting to remain the world’s superpower, while also retreating to a more protectionist America-first role, said Burton.
“Developments such as Lula’s re-election will only sharpen the pressures already building in the Global North,” said the expert.

====================================================================================================

Israel's exit polls show deadlock: What happens next?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
23:03:55 UTC
08:03:55 KST

Breadcrumb
Israel's exit polls show deadlock: What happens next?
Israelis went to the polls on Tuesday in the highest turnout in decades, with initial exit polls showing a slight edge but no majority for the opposition, meaning whoever can cobble together a coalition will form the next government.
The country's main pollsters projected the opposition bloc, led by ex-army chief Gadi Eisenkot, to win 52 or 53 seats, and ICC fugitive Netanyahu's bloc to win 50.
Arab lists made strong gains, with exit polls showing they won 17 or 18 seats combined.
Here are four possible scenarios:
Coalition
The parties will immediately begin negotiations to try to reach a 61-seat majority in the 120-member Knesset, but the path forward is far from clear.
President Isaac Herzog will name a candidate with the best chance to form a government, not necessarily the party with the most seats, which initial exit polls showed was Netanyahu's Likud.
The Arab parties, particularly Raam, have said they are open to working with Eisenkot's bloc, but the camp has kept them at arm's length, seeing their support as a liability during the campaign.
For Netanyahu's bloc, however, there is no obvious way to pick up more seats after some smaller right-wing parties failed to meet the vote threshold to enter parliament.
Coalition negotiations can be arduous, with parties insisting on parochial interests, and can produce unstable governments.
After the November 2022 election, Benjamin Netanyahu took 58 days to form his government.
Minority government
If no bloc secures 61 seats, a candidate could attempt to govern without a majority, instead relying on ad hoc support from other lawmakers.
In this scenario, lawmakers from the Arab parties, whose community makes up 20 percent of the population and generally identifies as Palestinian, could play a critical role.
Raam, led by Mansour Abbas, has been a kingmaker in the past, having been the first Arab party to join an Israeli government in a short-lived 2021-2022 coalition led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid.
Another Arab movement, the Joint List, said it is unlikely to join a coalition government outright, but offered to provide a "safety net" for any one that ousts Netanyahu from power.
Political commentator Tal Elovitz said especially high Arab turnout "indicates a strong desire for partnership".
Eisenkot has not publicly even entertained the possibility, and Netanyahu in his campaign relentlessly told Jewish voters that a vote for the opposition could bring Arabs into government.
"Bottom line, at the moment it appears there is a possibility of forming a minority government headed by Eisenkot, but this could still shift depending on the final results," Elovitz said.
National unity government
Given Israel's extreme polarisation, a national unity government may seem fanciful, but it could theoretically create a less extreme government.
Israeli commentators have often mused about a national unity government in which Netanyahu would jettison his provocative far-right allies and ultra-Orthodox parties and team up with Eisenkot, who shares Netanyahu's views on many security issues.
Such a grand coalition would also exclude Arab parties.
A poll published on 16 October found that 55 percent of Israelis would prefer a national unity government over new elections if the vote did not produce a clear majority.
This scenario has a recent precedent. In 2020, Netanyahu and Benny Gantz, like Eisenkot, a retired general appealing to the centre, reached a power-sharing agreement after three elections in less than a year.
The agreement stipulated a rotation of the prime ministership, but the partnership fell apart after a year, triggering another election.
A unity government in the current situation would face strong opposition from both sides, particularly the opposition bloc, which has built its campaign around ousting Netanyahu and casting him as unfit to lead.
Deadlock and new elections
If no candidate manages to form a government, Israel will have to return to the polls.
The country held four elections between April 2019 and March 2021 because politicians could not forge a lasting coalition.
The president-designated candidate will, in principle, have 28 days to form a coalition, with a possible 14-day extension, although other procedural measures can prevent new elections from being called immediately.

Israel before and beyond Netanyahu
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:04:18 UTC
01:04:18 KST

Breadcrumb
Before Netanyahu: the history behind Israel's policies toward Palestinians
If Netanyahu is the problem, why did it start long before Netanyahu?
As Israel’s elections approach, Western media and politicians often cast Netanyahu and his far-right coalition as the central problem in Israeli politics, promoting the idea that a change of government would lead to a change of policy towards Palestinians.
This is a fantasy. History suggests otherwise. It is a narrative that enables criticism of individual leaders without challenging the broader structures underpinning Israeli policy.
From its inception, Zionism presented itself as a colonial movement.
And since the state was founded, the occupation and dispossession of Palestinians have united successive governments across the political spectrum, from left to right.
Let's rewind to 10 March 1948, more than two months before Israel declared independence. Eleven men met and approved a plan codenamed Dalet.
Headed by Israel's soon-to-be first prime minister, David Ben-Gurion, they were creating a blueprint for ethnic cleansing.
The outcome was the Nakba: the destruction of at least 530 villages and the ethnic cleansing of more than 750,000 Palestinians in order to create a Jewish demographic majority.
Netanyahu wasn't in charge. Nor was Likud. It was Mapai, a democratic socialist party led by Ben-Gurion.
Fast forward to 1967 and Israel, still led by Mapai, occupied the remainder of historic Palestine. The party also oversaw a second mass displacement, expelling a further 300,000 Palestinians.
Then in 1968, Mapai merged into the Israeli Labour Party, and Israel's only female prime minister, Golda Meir, emerged as one of its leading figures.
She made clear her view on Palestinians in a 1969 interview: "There was no such thing."
A claim rooted in the early Zionist myth of "a land without a people for a people without a land".
After Israel occupied the remainder of Palestine in 1967, settlements began to spread across the newly occupied territories. These settlements created "facts on the ground" and remain among the biggest obstacles to Palestinian statehood.
Regardless of which political party was in power, they continued to expand. Even during the Oslo years under Labour Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin, settlement growth remained high.
So what does history tell us about Israel's elections?
They may change governments, but they have not changed the fundamental reality for Palestinians.
Regardless of who is in power, Palestinians remain occupied, dispossessed and denied their rights.

Oleshky truce appears to hold as two European leaders have ‘frank’ call with Putin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:03:09 UTC
01:03:09 KST

A local ceasefire in a southern Ukrainian city under Russian occupation appeared to be holding on Tuesday, with both sides ceasing drone attacks ahead of an apparent evacuation of about 2,000 trapped and desperate civilians.
The temporary truce began at 3am in Russian-controlled Oleshky. The city sits on the Dnipro River and is about 3 miles (5km) from Kherson, a larger city on the opposite bank. Ukrainian troops recaptured Kherson in autumn 2022.
Witnesses reported that the deadly frontline across the river was quiet for the first time in four years. The pause in fighting is due to last until 11pm on Sunday, Ukrainian officials said, and represents a significant if limited moment of de-escalation.
Finland’s president, Alexander Stubb, and Norway’s prime minister, Jonas Gahr Støre, held what they described as a “frank and substantive” phone call with Vladimir Putin about efforts to end the war in Ukraine. Støre indicated afterwards that big differences remained.
The two Nordic leaders said the call – a rare instance of direct contact between Putin and western leaders – was linked to upcoming talks between Russia, Ukraine and the US, expected to take place in Abu Dhabi next month.
The ceasefire in Oleshky appears to be an attempt by the Kremlin to curry favour with Donald Trump before the trilateral meeting and next week’s US midterm elections. The first lady, Melania Trump, requested the humanitarian mission, and in a post on X said it was brought forward by two days to allow the delivery of critical aid.
Its geographical scope had been extended beyond Oleshky “within the Kherson region”, she added, to provide safe passage for convoys. Calls for a ceasefire were also issued by Pope Leo, the United Nations, EU officials and the Council of Europe.
Between 1,500 and 2,000 people in the city have been living under a complete blockade by Russia. The last delivery of food to stores was in May, and many people are now starving and eating weeds. The Ukrainian military has airdropped food using drones but locals say Russian security forces detain anyone who takes it.
Russian soldiers have mined roads and use ruined buildings to coordinate round-the-clock strikes against Kherson. Some Oleshky residents have managed to escape, walking or cycling past bodies lying on the street and the burnt-out shells of vehicles.
Ukrainian observers say the Kremlin is planning a major propaganda tour this week in which Kyiv is blamed for Oleshky’s destruction. Trump-supporting US media channels have been invited to witness the evacuation, in which buses will take residents to occupied Crimea and Russia.
Ksenia Arkhipova, who fled the city in 2022 and now, as a volunteer, helps others leave, said some residents have told her they fear Russian officials may “filter out” evacuees with pro-Ukraine views.
“People say they are genuinely afraid that the Russians will check their phones and look for evidence of Ukrainian relatives or ties to the Armed Forces of Ukraine – something they have done repeatedly in other occupied territories,” Arkhipova told the Associated Press.
The ceasefire does not extend to other parts of Ukraine. Overnight, Russia bombarded Kyiv with drones and ballistic missiles, killing at least one person and injuring 15. It hit a university campus, wounding students, as well as a bridge over the Dnipro and metro infrastructure. Ten other regions came under fire.
The bridge remains closed to traffic, but some commuters walked across it to get to work. Writing on social media, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia “must stop dragging out this war” and said he welcomed European attempts to end it.
He said Stubb and Støre had briefed him on their call with Putin. “Alex and Jonas clearly conveyed to the Russian leadership the need for genuine steps towards de-escalation, particularly when it comes to our energy sector and infrastructure,” Zelenskyy wrote.
The Finnish-Norwegian initiative comes amid growing efforts by some European nations to establish a direct channel of communication with Moscow and secure a stronger European voice in negotiations. Stubb and Støre said they took part in the call as leaders of their respective countries and were not speaking on behalf of Europe as a whole.
European governments remain divided over whether direct engagement with Putin is worthwhile, given Russia’s maximalist demands remain stubbornly unchanged. There is little agreement on who should lead such talks. Stubb is seen by some EU officials as a candidate.
The divisions were laid bare shortly after news of the call emerged, when Denmark’s prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, criticised the move. “I am very sceptical about this independent initiative by Norway and Finland. It was not agreed with any of us,” Frederiksen said.
She added: “I see no signs that Russia wants peace with Europe – neither in the hybrid warfare it wages every day, nor in Ukraine, where brutal and aggressive strikes continue daily, claiming many lives.”
Russia’s foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, said the Europeans had offered “nothing new”, and were simply trying to insert themselves in the negotiation process.
This month Putin said he was willing to resume peace talks, but only on Russia’s hardline terms. They include the handover of the entire eastern Donbas region, including parts Russia has been unable to seize since 2014, as well as further territory in Kherson and Zaporizhzhia provinces.
Last week Zelenskyy said he was open to a peace agreement that would freeze the war along the current frontlines. “Yes, we are ready to stop this war as soon as possible,” he said in an interview with ABC News. He made clear that Ukraine would not recognise land seized and occupied by Russia as Russian.

‘Profiteering from pain’: Investments of super-rich fuel climate crisis and capitalise on recovery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:02:35 UTC
01:02:35 KST

Climate pledges fall short as Oxfam exposes how the super-rich profit from disaster.
A new UN report makes it clear we can’t depend on current national climate pledges to keep global temperature rise within safe limits.
The latest plans would reduce global greenhouse gas emissions by just six per cent by 2035, compared with 2019 levels.
This is down from last year’s projection of a 10 per cent cut, largely due the US’s withdrawal from the Paris Agreement. It remains far short of 60 per cent scientists say is needed to limit warming to 1.5°C, the threshold to avoid catastrophic and irreversible climate impacts.
Combining the pledges of 154 countries, the report covers 71 per cent of global emissions. Even if every country fully implemented their obligatory plans under the Paris Agreement and also met conditional targets, emissions cuts would still amount to just nine per cent.
To keep warming within the Paris Agreement’s fallback limit of 2°C above pre-industrial levels, emissions would need to fall by 37 per cent by 2035.
Even if efforts to cut emissions succeed, the UN warned earlier this month that the world is on track for a temporary or potentially prolonged overshoot of the 1.5°C limit. The news prompted an EU warning that countries must prepare for a potential 3°C temperature rise by 2100.
Could private investors move the needle on global warming?
In a second report, also published on 27 October, the UN found that global climate finance is increasing but still falls far short of what is needed.
Global climate finance averaged $1.9 trillion (€1.7tn) a year in 2023-24, up 32 per cent from 2021-22. The increase was driven largely by private investment in low-emissions technologies, including renewables, as well as household spending on electric vehicles, solar power and heat pumps.
So with government efforts failing, could private investment make up the shortfall?
A separate report by the charity Oxfam, published ahead of the COP31 climate talks in Türkiye, argues that for the wealthiest investors the incentives often steer them in the wrong direction.
Not only are the super-rich fuelling the climate crisis through polluting activities, they’re also “profiteering from pain” – sometimes reaping a “double dividend”: first from the industries driving climate breakdown, then from the businesses involved in disaster preparation and recovery, says Oxfam.
How are the super-rich profiting from the climate crisis?
Oxfam’s new ‘Destroy and Rebuild Index’, within the report ‘Disaster Divide: How climate chaos deepens inequality and enriches the few’, looked at 217 companies, some in industries that drive climate breakdown and others in industries that prepare for or rebuild after climate disasters.
The companies in the index not only made an average profit of $1.8 billion (€1.6bn) in 2025 but paid out more than $1bn on average to shareholders, according to the charity. The global disaster recovery market is forecast to grow from $70bn (€63bn) to $92bn (€84bn) a year by 2029.
Oxfam says the investments of the world’s 1,000 richest billionaires were linked to 486 million tonnes of CO2 equivalent in 2025. If they were a country, they would rank as the world’s 19th biggest polluter. 71 per cent of those investments are in high-polluting sectors such as oil, gas and chemicals.
Emissions of the super-rich linked to millions of deaths
Oxfam says the wealthiest also contribute disproportionately to the emissions driving the crisis. The richest 0.1 per cent – around eight million people – emit more than the poorest 44 per cent of humanity combined, accounting for around 3.5 billion people.
Oxfam estimates that emissions from the richest one per cent have been responsible for around 20 per cent of global warming since 1990. A single year of their emissions will cause an estimated 1.9 million excess heat-related deaths over the following century, according to the report.
Calling climate disasters “inequality machines”, Oxfam points to research published in the journal Nature showing flood deaths are seven times higher in more unequal countries.
Yet the wealthy are best placed to shield themselves, from buying safer homes to hiring private firefighters. Rich households can also absorb higher food costs and insure their assets. Poorer people tend to live in more exposed areas and in lower-quality housing, with fewer savings to fall back on.
Oxfam is calling on governments to curb the emissions of the super-rich, including those linked to their investments, to make rich countries provide far more grant-based finance for adaptation, and to end profiteering from climate disasters.

"Jagged" New York house is Aston Martin's first US residence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27

01:02:23 KST

“Jagged” New York house is Aston Martin’s first US residence
Automotive company Aston Martin has collaborated with US studio S3 Architecture for the Sylvan Rock residential compound in Upstate New York, conforming the metal roofline to the outcroppings of stone on the site.
Located in the town of Red Hook, Sylvan Rock features a faceted, black-metal roofline that angles with the house, which was built to follow the site’s slope.
At the low end, the roof meets the ground, covering a walkway that leads to the primary entrance.
“When designing, we always let the land speak first and respond to it,” said S3 Architecture partner Christopher Dierig.
“The roofline mimics the jagged edges of the rock ledge reaching down into the earth, as if the home is born of and launching from the landscape,” Dierig continued.
A stairway leads up from the lower entrance into the primary spaces of the house, which has two storeys on top of the outcropping.
Also on the lower level is a garage that forms a plinth for one of two swimming pool areas. Part of the garage was carved into the rockspace and the studio referred to it as “subterranean”.
The main, elevated body of the residence has glass walls interspersed with black metal panelling. Four bedrooms and five bathrooms are spread over this space.
Living and dining spaces are located on the ground plane, in line with the pool areas. A glass bridge connects an auxiliary spa and sauna space.
Luxury wood finishes and stone filter through the interiors, which are mostly monotone.
A floating staircase sits in the middle of the plan and provides access to the upper level, which holds the bedroom suites and features balconies that look out into the wooded landscape.
Wooden ceilings and beams lighten up the space and multiple fireplaces were included in the living spaces, including in the primary suite upstairs.
These interior spaces were designed by the Aston Martin team and also feature one-of-a-kind custom furniture by the brand.
Certain elements have direct reference to the company’s branding, including the brand’s lattice motif covering the wine storage in the primary lounge and a movie theatre that includes seating reminiscent of automobile seats.
The site also includes guest residences, a pavilion and a treehouse. The residences feature similar metal roofs and exteriors.
The house is one of two branded residences by Aston Martin planned throughout the world, with the other located in Japan.
It follows a trend of automotive brands entering the architecture field, directly designing residences and even skyscrapers, especially in the US.
For example, Bugatti unveiled a branded skyscraper design for Miami last month. Aston Martin completed its own skyscraper in Miami in 2024.

Israeli voters chose between ‘rabid yellow dogs and ravenous jackals’
TEHRAN — Israelis queued in numbers not seen in half a century on Tuesday, and Benjamin Netanyahu spent the afternoon begging his own voters to match them.

Channel 13’s last poll gave Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar 22 seats, Likud 19, Naftali Bennett’s Together alliance about 14.5, and Avigdor Liberman’s Yisrael Beiteinu 8. It put Netanyahu’s bloc on 50 and the opposition on 54, both short of the 61 needed in the 120-seat Knesset.

The day was ugly. Those Netanyahu warned about make up a fifth of Israeli citizens. Roughly three million adult Palestinians, in Gaza, the West Bank and East al-Quds (Jerusalem), have no vote in the government that controls their borders and legal status.
The military closed every West Bank crossing for the day. Near Nablus, settlers beat a man in the town of Burqa as Israelis voted.
Same pack, different coats
On September 26, five opposition leaders signed a pact pledging a “Zionist, statesmanlike government.” None accepts that Gaza is a genocide, and none has challenged Israeli strikes on Lebanon, Syria, Yemen, or Iran.
Their quarrel with Netanyahu is about management, corruption, and who failed on October 7. Daniel Levy, a former Israeli government adviser, says the treatment of Palestinians “is a consensus among Zionist parties.” Sociologist Yehouda Shenhav-Shahrabani sums up the field as “same lady, different dress.”
Iranians have a saying for similar situations: “Sage zard baradare shogqal ast.” (The yellow dog is the jackal’s brother.) The candidates amount to rabid yellow dogs and ravenous jackals.
Iran, Lebanon and Gaza get the same offer
There is precedent. In 2021, Bennett and Lapid ended Netanyahu’s twelve-year tenure. By August 2022, Israel was intensifying its campaign of terror and covert aggression against Iran while simultaneously bombing Gaza, killing dozens of Palestinians, including children, while illegal settlement expansion continued without interruption.
Iran shows it best. The United States and Israel attacked on February 28 in the middle of negotiations, and Trump has since urged Netanyahu to “finish the job.”
Eisenkot calls the war unfinished and mocks the U.S.-Iran talks as “a deal taking shape far from Israeli interests.” Yair Lapid wants “every Iranian energy facility bombed, Kharg Island first.” Bennett calls regime change “a must.”
Netanyahu posted an image of a mushroom cloud over an Israeli city and warned Tehran of “a devastating blow.”

Eisenkot wants troops to stay in the south, Bennett has said he would answer Hezbollah “by striking Iran,” and Liberman had described supposed limited operations as “complete madness.”
Israel holds about two-thirds of Gaza. 1,493 people have been killed since the so-called ceasefire, and Eisenkot promises “to destroy Hamas within 18 months.”
The records behind the slogans
Israeli and Western media have ludicrously tried to sell Eisenkot as the sober general and a loving father. And it has been approved.”
The Goldstone report described the doctrine as civilian destruction for deterrence. This year he told a conference he had applied it through “disproportionate strikes,” and in March he said it had never been more relevant for Lebanon.
Bennett’s “Octopus Doctrine” claims Iran is the head and Hezbollah, Hamas and the rest are “tentacles.” He once urged shooting Palestinians who cross into Israel, and he cheered the 2025 strike on Doha.
Liberman said there were “no innocents in Gaza,” proposed transferring some 300,000 Arab citizens to a future Palestinian state, and backs cutting Gaza’s water and electricity. Smotrich, who voted vowing to “Judaize” Hebron, wants Israel to “go to war” in the West Bank.
Analyst Ahron Bregman expects a new prime minister to calm the mood and little more, since any government will mirror Israel’s sharp turn to the right. Some analysts see room for E1 and settler violence.
Palestinians, Lebanese and Iranians have heard these men speak for years. They know what to expect. The yellow dog and the jackal wear different coats, but the governing machinery grinds forward with identical malice.

====================================================================================================

Autistic children’s brains respond less to the emotional meaning of sentences, fMRI study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:00:12 UTC
01:00:12 KST

A neuroimaging study in Hong Kong found that a brain region involved in language and social processing responded less strongly to emotionally meaningful sentences in autistic children than in non-autistic children. In non-autistic children, the left superior temporal sulcus responded more strongly to sentences describing people in emotional situations than to sentences about objects, but this tendency was reduced in autistic children. The paper was published in NeuroImage: Clinical.
Autistic children often differ from their non-autistic peers in social interaction, emotional processing, and communication. However, the neural differences underlying these patterns are not yet fully understood. While researchers have extensively investigated how autistic individuals process language and recognize emotions in facial expressions and tone of voice, much less attention has been paid to how they process the social and emotional meaning of words and sentences themselves.
Everyday language is filled with expressions describing relationships, social interactions, and feelings. Understanding words such as “friend,” “hug,” or “grief” involves more than recognizing their grammatical role and literal meaning; it also involves processing the social and emotional experiences they represent. Research suggests that autistic individuals often perform similarly to non-autistic individuals when explicitly asked to judge whether a word is positive or negative, but differ more consistently in how automatically they process emotional meaning.
Neuroscientists have identified parts of the brain’s superior temporal cortex, particularly the left superior temporal gyrus and the neighboring superior temporal sulcus, as important for processing both language and social information. A previous study of non-autistic adults found that these regions responded more strongly to sentences describing people in emotional situations than to sentences describing inanimate objects, a pattern called a social-emotional bias.
Study author Hanlin Wu of the Chinese University of Hong Kong and colleagues hypothesized that this social-emotional bias would already be present in childhood but would be weaker in autistic children than in their non-autistic peers. To test this, they used functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to examine how the brains of autistic and non-autistic children responded to spoken Cantonese sentences describing either people in emotional situations or objects.
The researchers recruited 78 right-handed children, all native Cantonese speakers attending mainstream schools in Hong Kong. Twenty children were excluded because they moved their heads too much during scanning, which can distort brain imaging data. The final sample included 58 children between the ages of about 8 and 12 (average age 10), of whom 37 were autistic and 21 were not, and 48 were boys.
The children completed assessments of autism symptoms (the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule, Second Edition), language comprehension (the Hong Kong Cantonese Oral Language Assessment Scale), and non-verbal intelligence (the Test of Nonverbal Intelligence, Fourth Edition). Parents also rated their children’s proficiency in Cantonese and English.
During scanning, the children simply listened to sentences without responding. Social-emotional sentences described people in emotional situations, half positive and half negative (e.g., “My older sister laughed at the joke” or “Chi-Keung feels he is no good”), while object sentences described non-human objects, events, or concepts (e.g., “Banana peels are yellow” or “The sun rises in the east”). The children also heard sentences played backward, which served as a non-language sound for comparison.
All sentences were eight syllables long and were matched on word frequency and grammatical complexity. They were generated with text-to-speech software using a single synthetic voice, so the two types of sentences differed in their meaning but not in tone of voice or other vocal cues.
Across both groups, the left superior temporal sulcus responded more strongly to social-emotional sentences than to object sentences, indicating that the social-emotional bias seen in adults is already present in children. When the groups were analyzed separately, non-autistic children showed a robust bias, while in autistic children it was weaker and did not reach statistical significance.
In one of four regions the researchers had selected in advance based on the earlier adult study, the middle portion of the left superior temporal sulcus, autistic children showed a weaker social-emotional bias than non-autistic children, a moderate-to-large difference. The groups did not differ in brain responses to backward speech or to object sentences, suggesting that general hearing and language processing were similar.
The difference appeared to be driven mainly by negative sentences, for which the gap between groups was largest. However, the statistical test comparing positive and negative sentences was not significant, so the authors treat this pattern as suggestive.
The group difference was not explained by children’s language ability. It could not be statistically separated from autism symptom level, because diagnosis and symptom scores overlapped so heavily, and within the autistic group, children with more severe symptoms did not show weaker brain responses.
“This reduced activity in the left STS [superior temporal sulcus] in response to social-emotional semantics may contribute to autistic children’s social communication challenges,” study authors concluded.
The study contributes to the scientific understanding of how autistic children’s brains process social and emotional meaning in language. However, the number of study participants was modest by current neuroimaging standards, and the non-autistic group was particularly small. Because of this, the study could reliably detect only relatively large differences between groups, and when the researchers compared the groups across the entire brain rather than in the preselected regions, no difference survived statistical correction.
Head movement led to the exclusion of 31% of autistic children compared with 13% of non-autistic children, so the findings may not extend to autistic children who have difficulty lying still in a scanner. Most participants were boys, and most autistic participants had at least one co-occurring condition, most commonly ADHD. Because the social-emotional sentences differed from the object sentences in both social content and emotional tone, the study also cannot separate these two factors.
The paper, “Autistic children show reduced activity in left superior temporal cortex in response to social-emotional meaning in language,” was authored by Hanlin Wu, Matthew Ganquan Shi, Phoebe Wai-Yu Chan, Peilun Song, Siu-Fung Lau, Gary Yu-Hin Lam, Xin Kang, Patrick C.M. Wong, and Xiujuan Geng.

Tennis player Osaka showed off a crane-patterned outfit in Tokyo before defeating Paolini
Kyiv • UNN
Naomi Osaka defeated Jasmine Paolini in the opening match of the tournament in Tokyo. The tennis player honored her Japanese roots with a kimono-style outfit.
Naomi Osaka honored her Japanese heritage with an outfit featuring a crane pattern before defeating Jasmine Paolini 6-3, 7-6 (7-4) in her opening match at the tournament in Tokyo on Tuesday. AFP reports, UNN writes.
Details
The former world No. 1 competed at the Pan Pacific Open for the first time in four years. She took to the court in a blue, long-sleeved outfit reminiscent of a kimono.
According to Osaka, the crane pattern was dedicated to her mother's homeland—the island of Hokkaido in northern Japan. The tennis player called her return to Tokyo a "return home."
"In terms of fashion, I have always created special looks for Grand Slam tournaments. And when I came back home, I wanted to do something special here as well," said the four-time Grand Slam champion.
Osaka is known for her eye-catching custom-made outfits, which regularly attract media attention.
At the US Open, she drew inspiration from the style of Allen Iverson—the former NBA basketball player known for his influence on sports fashion. At the tournament in Australia, the tennis player appeared in an unusual outfit inspired by a jellyfish.
At Wimbledon, she also highlighted her Japanese heritage by wearing a white kimono-style dress.
According to Osaka, the designer who created her new outfit for her appearance in Tokyo was the same one.
Asked whether she planned to unveil several more looks this week, the tennis player replied: "It would be fun if you followed me and then were surprised."
Osaka's last appearance at this tournament was in 2022. At the time, she withdrew from the competition because of abdominal pain before her second-round match.
Since then, the tennis player has become a mother. After the birth of her daughter, Shai, she stepped away from professional sport for 15 months and returned to the court in 2023.
Osaka faced a difficult test in her opening match: her opponent was world No. 35 Jasmine Paolini, who had defeated the Japanese player in their only previous meeting.
In the first set, Osaka's powerful and precise shots proved too difficult for the Italian. However, the contest was much tighter in the second set.
