‘Highest ever’: Israel election turnout hits 55.7% by 4 p.m., 17.2% above last election's pace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
15:11:39 UTC
00:11:39 KST

Israel's parliamentary election recorded its highest voter turnout at 8 p.m. since 1988, with 74.3% of eligible voters having cast their ballots Tuesday, according to the Central Elections Committee.
The figure represents a surge of eight percentage points compared with the same hour in the November 2022 election, when turnout stood at 66.3%. More than 5.4 million Israelis had voted, with two hours remaining before most polling stations were scheduled to close.
Acting Central Elections Committee Director-General Dean Livne announced the latest figures, continuing a day of unusually high participation that had already broken records at several earlier reporting intervals.
By 6 p.m., turnout had reached 66.7%, compared with 57.7% at the same hour in 2022. The nine-percentage-point difference represented a relative increase of 15.6% over the previous election's pace. At that point, 4,892,186 Israelis had already cast their ballots.
"By 6 p.m., we have surpassed the number of people who voted by 10 p.m. in the previous election," Livne said, referring to the number of ordinary ballots cast, excluding special double-envelope votes.
Earlier, turnout reached 55.7% by 4 p.m., compared with 47.5% in 2022, and 44.9% by 2 p.m., compared with 38.9% four years ago. Each milestone reflected the unusually strong participation throughout Election Day.
The latest turnout also exceeded the previous election's final participation rate of 70.63%, with two hours still remaining before the scheduled closing time.
Long lines and heavy demand at polling stations
The surge in participation brought long lines to polling stations in several cities, including Ra'anana and Ramat Gan, with some voters reporting unusually lengthy waits. Election officials urged the public to remain patient as the number of voters continued to climb.
Central Elections Committee Chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg said waits at some polling stations had reached 15 to 20 minutes. Officials stressed that anyone arriving before the scheduled closing time would be allowed to cast a ballot, even if the line continued moving afterward.
Participation was also high among military personnel. According to the IDF, 68% of eligible service members had voted by 5 p.m., compared with 65% at the same hour during the previous election.
At the Jalame military base south of Afula, unusually heavy demand forced the IDF to deploy an additional polling station after soldiers reportedly waited more than two hours to vote. Other soldiers reported waits of approximately 90 minutes at a base in central Israel.
The military said it had prepared for high turnout by operating more than 850 fixed polling stations, alongside mobile voting stations serving troops in the field, and was deploying additional facilities where necessary.
Where is turnout highest? Some communities surpass 90%
Figures published by the Central Elections Committee earlier in the evening revealed striking differences between communities and major cities across the country.
The highest turnout among regular polling stations was recorded in Timorim, a community near Kiryat Malakhi in southern Israel, where 91.6% of eligible voters had already cast their ballots. Close behind was Yuval, near the Lebanese border, with 91.5%, followed by Shorashim in northern Israel at 90.1%.
Other communities reporting exceptionally high participation included Bat Hen at 87.7%, Hazon and Shavei Darom at 87% each, Nataf at 86.4%, Netiv HaLamed-Heh at 86.2%, Yesodot at 85.3% and HaBonim at 85.2%.
Among larger cities, Modi'in-Maccabim-Re'ut stood out with a turnout rate of 70.1%, one of the highest among the major urban centers included in the committee's earlier update.
Tel Aviv recorded 58.6%, Jerusalem 55.3% and Haifa 54.5%. Rishon LeZion reached 61.3%, Petah Tikva 63.1%, Ashdod 59.4% and Netanya 50.6%.
In the south, Be'er Sheva recorded 55.8% and Ashkelon 58.8%. Holon reached 58%, while Ramat Gan recorded 61.9%, Bnei Brak 64.3% and Rehovot 63.8%.
Herzliya recorded 63.1%, while Bat Yam stood at 47.6%, one of the lowest turnout rates among the major cities included in the update.
The local figures reflect voting at regular polling stations as of the earlier reporting period and should not be confused with the updated nationwide turnout figure for 8 p.m.
Election committee rejects bid to extend voting hours
Israel's Central Elections Committee rejected a request Tuesday to extend voting beyond the scheduled 10 p.m. closing time, following a political dispute between coalition and opposition parties amid record voter turnout and long lines at polling stations.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party had submitted a formal request to extend voting hours, citing heavy turnout and lengthy waits. The proposal gained support from the far-right Otzma Yehudit party, led by National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, and the ultra-Orthodox Shas party, headed by Aryeh Deri.
Ofer Winter's Amcha Yisrael party also supported the proposal, calling for an additional hour of voting.
Opposition parties rejected the request. Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar! party, Naftali Bennett's Beyahad party and the Democrats, led by Yair Golan, all opposed extending voting beyond the scheduled closing time.
Yashar! said it "strongly opposes" Likud's request, arguing that no exceptional circumstances justified changing the voting hours.
"No exceptional incident has occurred that would justify approving the request, which is intended to lay the groundwork for claims against the integrity of the election, following the lies Netanyahu has been spreading since this morning," the party said in a statement.
Following a meeting of the committee's presidium, chaired by Justice Sohlberg, officials concluded that there was no justification for a nationwide extension.
"The high national voter turnout across all sectors reflects the public's strong engagement in the democratic process, and under these circumstances, no need was found to extend voting hours," the committee said.
Under the decision, most polling stations will close at 10 p.m. as originally scheduled. However, anyone who arrives before closing time will still be allowed to vote, even if they remain in line after 10 p.m.
The committee separately approved extending voting in Hebron until 10 p.m. because of a power outage that had disrupted the voting process.
Why the final results could take until Friday
A total of 7,331,981 Israelis are eligible to vote in the election for the 26th Knesset, with 12,018 polling stations operating nationwide. Most are scheduled to close at 10 p.m., when television networks traditionally release their exit polls.
However, the final results could remain uncertain for several days. More than 650,000 special double-envelope ballots are expected from soldiers, diplomats, displaced residents, voters with disabilities and others voting away from their registered polling stations. These ballots require separate verification and counting.
Livne warned that the number of special ballots could be higher than originally anticipated and that counting might not be completed by Thursday evening, potentially continuing into Friday morning.
"It is possible that the number of double envelopes will be higher, and it is possible that we will not finish counting them by Thursday evening," he said, adding that the count would be broadcast live.
The unusually high turnout could also have significant political consequences, particularly for smaller parties attempting to cross Israel's 3.25% electoral threshold. The threshold itself remains fixed, but as the total number of valid votes increases, so does the absolute number of votes a party needs to enter the Knesset.
With several parties potentially finishing close to that threshold, special ballots could alter the final distribution of seats and change the balance between rival political blocs.
The record turnout has already transformed the scale of Israel's election. Whether it will also transform the political balance will become clear only when the final ballots are counted.

Russians transfer Ukrainian prisoners from occupied Makiivka to Russia

Russians transfer Ukrainian prisoners from occupied Makiivka to Russia
Ukrainian prisoners of war and civilian political prisoners, as well as individuals convicted of criminal offences, have been transferred to Russia from penal colony No. 32 in occupied Makiivka, Donetsk Oblast.
Source: Novyny Donbasu (News of Donbas) news outlet
Details: According to the news outlet, some of the Ukrainian political prisoners and criminal convicts were transferred to strict-regime penal colony No. 1 in the city of Tambov. They were placed alongside Russian convicts serving their sentences there.
Another group of political prisoners and criminal convicts was moved to strict-regime colony No. 5 in the town of Morshansk, Tambov Oblast.
Several Ukrainian political prisoners remain in Makiivka penal colony No. 32 awaiting transfer to Russia. Their exact destination is currently unknown.
Meanwhile, about 100-120 convicts held in the settlement colony attached to penal colony No. 32 will remain in Makiivka for the winter period.
The transfer of prisoners from the Makiivka colony began in August 2026. The first to be taken to Russia were five Ukrainian servicemen and one civilian political prisoner.
The whereabouts of Ukrainian prisoner of war Vitalii Chmil, who was transferred from Makiivka in mid-August, have also become known. He was initially held in a pre-trial detention centre in Krasnoyarsk before being moved to strict-regime colony No. 1 in the city of Kyzyl in the Tyva Republic, near Russia's border with Mongolia.
The soldier was able to inform his relatives of his whereabouts with the help of Russian volunteers.
It is known that about 35 Ukrainian political prisoners and servicemen were held in colony No. 32, including five soldiers on the exchange lists.
Most of them have been in captivity for 7-9 years. The Russians sentenced them to 10 to 17 years in prison on charges of "espionage", "terrorism" and "extremism".
The administration of the Makiivka colony cited the inability to ensure proper living conditions in winter as one of the reasons for moving the prisoners to Russia. Specifically, this refers to a lack of funds to purchase coal for heating, as well as water supply interruptions and power outages in occupied Donetsk Oblast.
In addition, the relocation is linked to changes in Russian legislation, which stipulate that those convicted of terrorism and extremism must serve their sentences as far away from home as possible, as well as the fact that the premises of colony No. 32 do not meet Russian standards.
The vacated premises are already being refitted, including the installation of CCTV cameras.
Background:
- On 23 October 2026, two Ukrainian servicemen held in colony No. 32 returned from captivity during a prisoner swap: Anatolii Kapitskyi, captured in 2020, and Serhii Heremes, who had been in captivity since 2018.
- Meanwhile, over 30 Ukrainian prisoners from colony No. 32 who are on the exchange lists remain in captivity.

UK Home Office May Face Investigation Over Use of OpenAI Tools
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
15:10:26 UTC
00:10:26 KST

A UK government watchdog is considering an investigation into the Home Office’s use of generative AI tools to process asylum applications, WIRED has learned. The potential probe follows lawmakers and researchers publicly questioning the tools’ accuracy and the government’s secrecy around their use.
The Independent Chief Inspector of Borders and Immigration (ICIBI), which monitors the Home Office’s management of borders, immigration, and customs, has asked digital rights nonprofit Open Rights Group (ORG) to share more information on the tools as it draws up plans for the topics it will inspect next year, campaigner Sara Alsherif tells WIRED. ORG’s findings come from a six-month investigation into the tools, which involved 11 parliamentary questions, two ministerial letters, and 10 public records requests that attempt to pry details from the Home Office, which has withheld details on the tools.
The ICIBI tells WIRED it cannot confirm what topics are under active consideration before it publishes its annual inspection priorities, but it says it is aware of concerns about the use of AI tools and pointed to its findings last year that one of the tool’s “effectiveness and reliability were varied.”
“Asylum decisions are made by trained caseworkers, with AI tools used only to assist in navigating interview records and policy information. They cannot be used in isolation and do not make decisions on claims,” a Home Office spokesperson tells WIRED in an email. “We regularly monitor the performance of these tools alongside our established quality-assurance processes, and have already committed to publishing updated evaluations on their roll out.”
The Home Office uses the Asylum Case Summarisation (ACS) and Asylum Policy Search (APS) tools, built on OpenAI’s 2023 GPT-4 large language model and Microsoft Foundry, to summarize transcripts of interviews with asylum applicants and information about their countries of origin, according to documents obtained by ORG. The immigration and law enforcement authority started piloting these tools in late 2024 as the Labour government tried to clear a backlog of around 100,000 asylum cases, while staying on top of the tens of thousands of new applications the UK receives each year. While the department has made significant progress, halving the number of people waiting on an initial decision in the year through June, the number of appeals against decisions has ballooned.
Researchers are concerned about the accuracy of the AI tools–especially to decide something as high-stakes as whether to send someone back to a country where they fear persecution. ORG found that the percentage of summaries generated by the ACS deemed not fit for use—often because they contain factual errors or misrepresentations—is significantly higher than the published 9 percent error rate calculated in the pilot evaluation. There is no quality control for the summaries produced by the APS, it also found.
Asylum decision-makers use the tools to save time when reviewing asylum cases; when used together, the pilot showed the tools could save around an hour per case, according to government estimates. Caseworkers use the ACS to speed up their review of transcripts of interviews where asylum seekers explain how they were persecuted in their country and why they are afraid to return. They use the APS as a search assistant to find and summarize country policy information, which informs them whether the applicant faces a genuine risk of harm in their home country. In July, a UK judge accused the Home Office of citing an “AI hallucinated” document to refuse a Moroccan woman and her child’s asylum claim on the basis that her home country would be safe for her to return to.
“We’re dealing with people’s lives. We’re talking about people that have faced some of the worst circumstances, and we’re meant to be making decisions based on facts and on understanding harm,” Labour backbench MP Bell Ribeiro-Addy tells WIRED. “I just don’t think it’s appropriate that machines are doing that.”
A Home Office spokesperson says, “Use of Artificial Intelligence is just one of the tools at our disposal to protect our borders, and does not replace or automate the role of human decision-makers.”
Ribeiro-Addy, Alsherif, and the Public Law Project, which has separately been investigating the tools, also worry that well-documented “cultural bias” in GPT models could lead to language barriers and the loss of cultural nuances in the summaries, which could in turn result in discriminatory decisions. An OpenAI spokesperson highlighted to WIRED the company’s ongoing work to improve its models’ accuracy and pointed out that the company will be retiring GPT-4 in January.
In the absence of regulation, the UK’s “AI Playbook” mandates that departments must be transparent about the algorithmic tools they use in decision-making processes and make information on them available to the public, including listing those tools on a public repository. The Home Office’s case summarization and policy search tools are not on that list.
Asylum seekers are also not told when these AI tools are used in their case. “Migrant organizations, legal practitioners, not many of them know about the actual use of this tool,” says Alsherif, who leads ORG’s migrant digital justice program. “So we need to let them know about this, let them know how it works, so they can challenge it.” Not being able to contest an incorrect AI summary of their personal information may breach UK data rights laws, Cloisters lawyers wrote in an independent legal opinion commissioned by ORG. The Home Office states that parts of the decision-making process may involve automation in its privacy notice.
Both groups have sent their findings to UK data regulator, the Information Commission, which is currently investigating the Home Office’s refusal to tell ORG how staff use and were trained to use two AI tools.
Public Law Project senior research fellow Caroline Selman also notes that the ACS and APS tools are just two of the 11 high-risk AI systems that her team has found being used across government but absent from the public repository. She’s concerned there may be more deployed across government that even researchers, let alone the individuals they are being used on, are unaware of.
“Other tools are being used but not being publicized at all,” says Selman, “and you can’t even begin to ask questions about things if you don’t know that they’re being used.”

Hegseth heads to Manila to shore up US ties with Asia-Pacific partners
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
15:08:59 UTC
00:08:59 KST

Hegseth heads to Manila to shore up US ties with Asia-Pacific partners
The Iran war and Donald Trump’s criticisms of allies have led countries in the Asia-Pacific region to recalibrate their calculations.
US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth will attend a Southeast Asian defence meeting this week alongside his counterparts from India, South Korea and Japan as Washington looks to solidify ties with the region after a year overshadowed by the fallout from the US-Israel war on Iran.
The meeting will bring together defence officials from the 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) plus eight of the bloc’s dialogue partners.
Australia, New Zealand, Russia and China are also expected to send representatives to the talks, which run from Wednesday to Thursday in the Philippines.
Known as the ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting-Plus (ADMM-Plus), the meeting will be held alongside a parallel ASEAN members-only event for Brunei, Cambodia, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Myanmar, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, Timor-Leste, and Vietnam.
India is among the dialogue partners that will host bilateral meetings on the sidelines of ADMM-Plus to “review the ongoing defence ties and explore ways to further strengthen strategic partnerships”, according to state media.
William Yang, senior analyst for Northeast Asia at the International Crisis Group, told Al Jazeera that the focus will be on regional security concerns like Myanmar’s ongoing civil war and maritime disputes between ASEAN states and neighbouring China.
“The South China Sea dispute is going to be front and centre because the Philippines is the chair of this year’s summit,” he told Al Jazeera, adding that he expects Manila to push for ASEAN to finalise a code of conduct with China to outline how to approach maritime disputes and handle conflicts in the globally important waterway.
The Philippines, China, Vietnam, Malaysia, Brunei, and Taiwan all have overlapping territorial claims to the South China Sea, although Beijing claims most of it as domestic waters.
These disputes often leave Beijing at odds with its neighbours, and particularly Manila, as both sides claim the uninhabited Scarborough Shoal and parts of the Spratly Islands.
Tensions escalated sharply this month with at least “eight close encounters” in the South China Sea and nearby Luzon Strait, according to the US Naval Institute.
The spat turned into a war of words when Chinese Ambassador to the Philippines Jing Quan said Beijing could “easily win” a war with the Philippines, prompting a Philippine senator to call for his expulsion.
Beijing has yet to confirm whether Chinese Defence Minister Dong Jun will attend ADMM-Plus in person, but he could still make a last-minute appearance. The Chinese defence chief attended ADMM-Plus 2024 and 2025, according to Bonnie Glaser, managing director of the German Marshall Fund’s Indo-Pacific Program, and Hegseth’s presence could factor into Beijing’s calculations.
China and the US have spent the past year thawing their relationship. A face-to-face meeting between Hegseth and Dong could also lay the groundwork for two meetings between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping scheduled for later this year, following two previous meetings between Trump and Xi this year.
“It is certainly possible that he will attend again this year,” Glaser told Al Jazeera by email. “I would not be surprised if Dong meets with Secretary Hegseth, especially since China has repeatedly said that it attaches importance to strengthening crisis communications and preventing crises between the US and Chinese militaries.”
Analysts, however, say that the bulk of Hegseth’s work at ASEAN will be reassuring the bloc and its dialogue partners that the US remains committed to the region amid its months-long conflict with Iran.
The US has raised eyebrows in Asia over the past year by moving some of its military assets from South Korea and Japan to the Middle East, while Trump has also sent mixed signals on his views on Taiwan, another potential flashpoint for the region.
Trump has reportedly delayed a major arms package to Taiwan, an unofficial US ally, ahead of an upcoming meeting with Xi at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in November, before the Group of 20 (G20) Leaders’ Summit in December.
“What Hegseth says and does will be interesting,” said Ja Ian Chong, a political scientist at the National University of Singapore, because of recent comments by US defence official Elbridge Colby suggesting that Washington would focus less on empty gestures and more on substance in the Asia-Pacific region.
“How Hegseth keeps to these lines while trying to keep a US advantage will be interesting, since these are not easy calibrations to make,” Chong said.

The 4.5K 24-inch Retina display with 500-nit brightness and wide P3 color gamut remains unchanged. However, the iMac with the M6 processor has new Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 capabilities, as well as 2.5-gigabit Ethernet, providing 250 percent more speed than before. Unlike the latest version of the Mac Studio, it supports only Thunderbolt 4, rather than the twice-as-fast Thunderbolt 5. Nevertheless, up to two external 6K displays can be connected if additional workspace is needed.
Other features include a 12-megapixel Center Stage camera, a choice of seven colors, as well as color-matched accessories and Touch ID. Orders for the new iMac with the M6 processor will open on October 28 at a starting price of $1,499 with a 10-core processor, a 10-core processor, and 16 GB of RAM, or $1,699 with a 12-core processor and a 12-core graphics processor.

Israeli and US elections could hasten the end of Iran war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
15:07:05 UTC
00:07:05 KST

Israeli and US elections could hasten the end of Iran war
LONDON - Alongside military and economic calculations, the Knesset elections in Israel and midterm congressional elections in the U.S. are emerging as factors influencing the duration of the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran and the terms under which it might end. These electoral considerations also shape the relationship between Benjamin Netanyahu’s political future and Donald Trump’s decisions.
Netanyahu’s political future may be linked to the future of the confrontation with Iran. If Netanyahu loses the Israeli elections, Trump may have a greater opportunity to withdraw from the war while declaring that the United States has achieved its objectives.
Under this scenario, the withdrawal could be presented to the American public as a victory, even if the actual outcome more closely resembles Iran’s success in enduring the confrontation and maintaining its ability to shape the future of the region and beyond. In this way, Trump could end America’s direct military commitments while attempting to avoid admitting that the war failed to achieve its stated objectives.
However, if Netanyahu wins the elections, the confrontation could be prolonged, increasing the likelihood that it would continue for the remainder of Trump’s term. This would result from Israeli calculations favoring the continuation of the war and an attempt to avoid ending it before achieving results that could be presented domestically as an accomplishment.
Nevertheless, if Netanyahu remains in power, it does not necessarily mean that Washington will be able to continue the war indefinitely. American decision-making will remain subject to the costs of mobilization, attrition, the global economy and relations with allies. Elections, therefore, are not the sole factor determining the end of the war, but they could accelerate or delay the decision to withdraw.
What if Netanyahu and the Republicans in the U.S. lose the elections? In that case, political pressure to end the war could intensify, whether through an agreement or through an American withdrawal without an agreement. The ultimate outcome would depend on the nature of the settlement, the conditions of withdrawal and the ability to translate military results into political gains.
In either case, the central argument remains that electoral changes could politically provide the American administration with an exit from the confrontation. However, they would not guarantee that the strategic consequences of withdrawal would match the narrative presented to the public.
The United States, particularly the Trump administration, faces a dilemma that extends beyond achieving an immediate military gain. The American objective is not simply to leave the war, but to do so in a way that allows the outcome to be presented to the American public and allies as a victory.
The problem, however, is that Washington’s available options are now constrained by substantial strategic costs, meaning that none appears to be free of losses. These options can be summarized in three main scenarios: maintaining a state of neither war nor peace, withdrawing without an agreement, or withdrawing under an agreement.
Maintaining a state of neither war nor peace
This scenario involves maintaining the current situation without reaching a final settlement and without returning to open warfare at the same intensity. At first glance, this option may appear to offer a way to postpone a decisive outcome while keeping pressure on Iran. However, it raises a fundamental question: how long can the United States maintain this situation?
Keeping forces mobilized and on continuous standby, rotating units, securing supplies and covering military and logistical expenses all impose accumulating burdens. These burdens increase when troops are deployed far from American territory, particularly in a region of critical importance to energy security and global trade.
Withdrawal without an agreement
The United States may withdraw without reaching a comprehensive agreement, while maintaining its policy of sanctions on Iran.
Under this scenario, the Trump administration might attempt to construct a narrative of victory by launching a rapid military strike against Iranian targets, such as nuclear facilities and then claiming that the mission had been accomplished and Iran’s capabilities had suffered decisive damage.
However, such a declaration could be an attempt to disguise the withdrawal rather than a genuine indication that the confrontation had been decisively resolved.
Withdrawal under an agreement
The third option involves reaching an agreement that would allow the United States to end the confrontation on the basis of a memorandum of understanding containing 14 clauses. The memorandum itself calls the objectives of the war into question and grants Iran some of its rights. However, such an agreement would present Washington with a different strategic problem.
If the agreement leads to the lifting or easing of sanctions, the opening of economic and financial ties with Iran, and its reintegration into the regional and international systems, Tehran could transform its resources and capabilities into those of a major regional economic power.
Here lies one of the greatest concerns reflected in the agreement: the United States would appear to have been defeated and to have achieved nothing, while Iran, benefiting from economic openness, could become a regional economic giant—or what might be described as the “economic China of West Asia.”
Iran has demonstrated, through its development of national strength under sanctions, that it can mobilize its natural and human resources, geographical position and trade relationships. Without the restrictions imposed on it, Iran could become a major regional power and contribute to the establishment of a new world order.
An agreement that opens these doors could therefore alter the regional balance of power in ways that extend beyond the military results of the war itself.

More than 80% of Gagauzia residents expressed some degree of trust in Putin, the poll found. The poll surveyed a representative sample of 818 respondents ahead of elections scheduled for November to choose the head of the autonomy and members of the People’s Assembly of Gagauzia. The researchers estimated the margin of error at 3.4%.
The post of head of Gagauzia became vacant amid legal proceedings against Evgenia Gutsul, who was accused of violations involving the financing of a political party and sentenced to seven years in prison.
Gutsul denied wrongdoing and said that Moldova’s leadership spearheaded the proceedings against her. Her relations with Chisinau deteriorated after she won the 2023 election and announced plans to strengthen friendly ties with Russia.
After Gutsul was removed from office, Moldovan authorities amended the electoral code. Gagauz officials say the changes stripped the region of its right to organize elections for its own governing bodies independently. Only half of the political parties registered in Moldova were allowed to take part in the elections.

UN nuclear watchdog chief urges Iran to grant IAEA access to verify nuclear material

Merve Aydogan
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
The head of the UN nuclear watchdog on Tuesday urged Iran to provide the agency with the information and access needed to verify its previously declared nuclear material, including 440 kilograms (970 pounds) of highly enriched uranium.
The UN Security Council began the session by voting to adopt the agenda, with 11 votes in favor, two against from Russia and China, and two abstentions from Pakistan and Somalia.
Addressing the Council, Rafael Grossi, director general of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), said the agency continues to engage with Tehran, “seeking avenues to encourage it to clarify all remaining safeguards issues.”
“One area of particular concern is Iran’s previously declared nuclear material, which includes 440kg of High Enriched Uranium,” he said.
Grossi said the issues “have now been outstanding for more than five years.”
He recalled that the agency had to withdraw all its inspectors from Iran by the end of June 2025 for safety reasons after military attacks began.
“Inspectors have been available to return for many months now,” he said.
He stressed that Iran has not provided “the requested information and access so that the IAEA can verify previously declared nuclear material at Iran’s facilities under safeguards, both those that have been affected by military attacks and those that have not.”
Grossi said the only exception was the Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant, where inspectors were conducting verification activities.
“The one exception is the Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant (BNPP), where our inspectors are currently undertaking verification activities,” he said.
He added that the Atomic Energy Organization of Iran had engaged constructively with the agency to arrange the delivery of safeguards equipment needed to verify spent fuel before its transfer to a new dry storage facility, expected early next year.
Grossi also said the agency’s inspectors spent more than 14,000 calendar days in the field last year, conducting verification activities at more than 1,400 facilities and locations outside them, and were able to draw safeguards conclusions for 179 states.
“I invite Iran to work with the IAEA without any further delay to clarify outstanding safeguards questions,” he said, adding that Tehran must provide access “as is Iran’s legal obligation.”

‘Is This Real?’: A Serbian Investigative Journalist Reflects on the Country’s Stunning Election

I’ve seen some people from abroad commenting that they don’t have anything in their program about how they’re going to deal with Russia.
Russia, the EU, literally nothing. But that was super smart, because that's the only way to gather so much support. I think that was maybe the most important element.
And the third element was that the students were very open to learning. They know that they're new. They don't have much experience. But they were communicating. They were calling journalists, civil society organizations, everyone they could find who had some expertise, and asking them about how things work.
That was really important. We’ve never witnessed such a perfectly executed system of monitoring the polls. The students managed to cover all the voting places in Serbia. And the monitors did perfect work. They caught a lot of people who were trying to carry out some abuses.
They are not self-taught, they were getting help from other organizations who had expertise in this. I would say that these three elements for me are a kind of model, which managed to bring such a huge, huge victory.
You mentioned that the established opposition would stay in Belgrade and not go to the villages. Did the students make an effort to go to smaller places? I remember that was also a big deal in Hungary, with Péter Magyar’s campaign.
Yeah, that’s the fourth element … the students, they had a campaign called “a student in every village.”
And Vučić, of course, put a lot of lies about the students, saying that they work for the Secret Service and this and that. But when you see them going to the villages and talking with the grannies, with peasants, with farmers, when you have this real life experience, that really changed people and helped them to earn huge support.
I think that was one of the main focuses of their campaign. More than doing stuff in Belgrade. Belgrade is easy. You have the most progressive people, and it's easier to win. You don't need to really be there.
So that's one way of defeating a situation where the media is controlled by the government — you have to reach people in person, because otherwise the only thing they hear is the pro-government media.
Yeah, exactly. But usually, nobody will do that.
The typical opposition in Europe is complaining about social media. They complain that they cannot reach people because of these troll campaigns, but they will not actually go [in person]. But you really need to go to every village.
And that's nothing new. That's like old school politics, right? We just have to literally get back to the ways of how politics was done, and not allow social media to make you lazy.
The social media algorithms will always boost content that helps populists, right? All the hate speech, the anti-immigrant things, will always be pushed. So you have to literally meet people and talk. We in KRIK have a bit of experience, because we do a lot of crowdfunding, we have connections with our audience. So we understood how important it is to do that stuff.
So I hope, at least in Europe and the U.S., politics will return to this old-school way a little bit.
Turning to the future, what do you expect will happen now?
Now we have a lot of work to do. Now comes the really tough period. I think it's important to learn from history.
There’s a chance to change things, but Vučić left a really strong system. All the big businesses, the whole economy is in the hands of his oligarchs. Organized crime is powerful. So this will not be easy.
And we need to learn from what happened in the past. After Milošević was gone, [reformist Prime Minister Zoran] Đinđić was killed two years later, basically by a joint venture of the Secret Service and organized crime, because they didn't want to allow the country to reform.
So we can celebrate tonight, but tomorrow it's the beginning of a really big job. Now it’s really important that everyone really does their part of the work. We as journalists should continue to investigate.
I believe it will happen like in Milošević’s time — as we speak now, they'll start destroying evidence and documents, bribing witnesses. In the next three months, we're in a defining period where we need to discover as much as we can. And when the students constitute the assembly and the government, I hope that they’ll start prosecuting these people.
But it won’t be easy. Now the very difficult part is coming.
Who are the main entrenched forces that have to be defeated? Is it the security services? Is it organized crime?
Yes, the security services are one of the most difficult parts. And I think that was the biggest mistake [in the past].
[Đinđić] didn't ever really reform them. He basically just changed the bosses and kept on working with them. And in the end, they were the part of the group that killed him.
I think the students will do much stronger, deeper reforms, because the secret service we have now have been inherited from Tito and Milošević’s time. The people change, of course, but in a way it's the same structure, even with older people bringing their sons and daughters into the service.
It's kind of like the state within the state. When they say “deep state,” it really does work that way in Serbia. I think they’ll be able to really cut and reform it completely, which is important.
The second really difficult part is that it’s easy to remove the director of this or that state-owned company, or change ministers. But I'm really afraid about what will happen with the judiciary. Because this is a kind of a trick that Vučić performed with the judiciary. He adopted all the EU laws that offer really big protection to prosecutors and judges, so that they cannot be touched by politics. But the catch is he put his people in there. So what will happen now? Whoever comes, he'll really have a hard time changing the corrupt judges and prosecutors, because they're so protected that only the prosecutions and judges can change themselves. You will need to find a way to really clean them. I think you will need to kind of work with them. That will be really a hard thing to do.
Then, another really hard thing will be the Vučić oligarchs. They bought everything in Serbia. If you go from my office to the center of Belgrade, literally along the main street, and you look right and left, 90 percent of the businesses that you see — doesn't matter if it's a small coffee shop or some big company selling computer equipment — everything is owned by his people. In these 14 years, they bought everything, and they all opened businesses because they were harassing everybody who's not part of his party to prevent them from opening any business.
So now the question is, you take power, but the whole economy is in the hands of his people. There it will also be really hard to find a solution.
Of course, they will prosecute these people and they can seize their illegal money, but there'll be a lot of actual legal businesses still in the hands of his people. So he will go, but after so many years, everything from the business structure, secret services, judiciary, are [run by] his people.
Is it just about taking out his people and replacing them with your people? Don’t you have to change something about the rules of the game?
Yes, the point is to change the rules, not just replacing people. That's why people didn't like the [old] opposition. The opposition defeated Milošević and put in their people, who could be better than Milošević’s people, but the system still worked to their advantage, not for society.
So the whole idea of the students is that they will really try to change the system, which means not putting in our people to serve us, but trying to make the country really work. And I think they have a chance to do it for one simple reason — because they don't have their own people. They're just students.
We won’t have a government with all students. Now that they won the election, they gathered a list of people [to become members of parliament]. And none of them are actually students. They gathered different experts and professors. And many of them are not connected to the students. They were just picking people who they believe are clean.
It was really amazing because everything was built on trust that all of the students are honest and not corrupted. That's very powerful. If they use this model to change the system, that will work. I believe they will scan the system and pick the best people. There were still good people in the police. In every place, there are still good professional people. So I hope the students will recognize these people, who are not tied to them, and help them actually reach the top positions.
It will be based on a clean foundation. That's the kind of thing that I'm relying on most.
What about the criminal groups? They were heavily embedded in the Vučić regime. You've done a lot of reporting on that. Are they scared now? Are they running? Are they going to fight?
They will do what they always do. They will not run. I believe the criminals are now thinking of finding a way to approach the students. I believe they will not succeed, but that's how criminals work. They don't care, in the end, for Vučić.
But I need to say, this is really funny to see. So like I said, last night Vučić brought these strong police forces to the center of Belgrade, and all of these hooligans and criminals, a really big number of them, to this park next to the presidential building.
And in the moment when he declared defeat on TV, and people started gathering in the center of town to celebrate, there is a video, the criminals who in the moment start running, you know, and you have like tens of them just running, literally running from this park. They're only strong when they have protection, and when the police are working with them.
You sound pretty optimistic, because it seems like you really trust the students, is that fair to say?
I trust the students because I completely trust their intentions, in those terms I’m optimistic. But I'm realistic in what's going to happen now, it will be really hard.
Like I said, you need to reform entire structures — the oligarchs, the money side, the secret services, crime. I know they have good intentions, but it’s really hard to do it. We need to remember that Đinđić died and failed.
And the second thing, I'm really afraid what would happen — this also happened in the time after Milošević, when the democratic [forces] won — I think that we will feel in the following years a lot of the damage which Vučić did to the economy. I think it will be a hard period.
And I'm afraid of how people usually react — everywhere, not just in Serbia — if the economy isn’t perfect in two years, which is completely logical because we just now see how much devastation he left, if people aren’t happy in a year or two, they will not be able to make the connection to Vučić, they’ll most likely then blame the new power in Serbia.
And that was how Vučić came to power the first time, right? Taking advantage of disappointment with the democratic generation before him.
Exactly. They needed to deal with the country left by Milošević, which was under sanctions and embargos and completely devastated. But people will say, the ones now in power are the ones to blame. So I think this is a big danger.
The problem is also that journalists need to change how they operate. I don't think we can do old-school journalism anymore. So I think journalists can help, but also we need to find other ways to communicate these things and inform the audience. There's a lot of fighting to be done.
But literally everything changed — the atmosphere on the streets. Before the protests there was this kind of this dark atmosphere, cynical and dark, like there was no hope. Now it's like living in a completely different country. It is insane and very refreshing.

Coca-Cola on Tuesday raised its full-year outlook for the third straight quarter, despite lackluster demand in its home market.
For the full year, Coke now expects comparable earnings per share to grow at least 11%, up from its prior forecast of an increase in the range of 9% to 10%. The beverage giant also anticipates that its organic revenue will climb at least 5%, a slight increase from its previous outlook of approximately 5% growth.
CEO Henrique Braun attributed the company's strong results to its "speed and discipline" despite the "uneven environment," he said on the company's earnings conference call.
Looking ahead to 2027, the company expects consumer behavior to remain unchanged, CFO John Murphy said. In recent quarters, Braun and other executives have said North American shoppers are under pressure, stretched thin by inflation and economic uncertainty, and looking for value. But the beverage giant has also said consumers are still buying its drinks, from premium brands like Fairlife to its namesake soda.
Shares of the company fell less than 1% in morning trading on its gloomy forecast for the consumer environment.
Here's what the company reported compared with what Wall Street analysts surveyed by LSEG were expecting:
- Earnings per share: 91 cents adjusted vs. 88 cents expected
- Revenue: $13.4 billion vs. $12.92 billion expected
Coke reported fiscal third-quarter net income attributable to shareholders of $4.01 billion, or 93 cents per share, up from $3.7 billion, or 86 cents per share, a year earlier.
Excluding transaction gains and other items, Coke earned 91 cents per share.
Net sales rose 7% to $13.4 billion. Coke's organic revenue, which strips out acquisitions, divestitures and foreign currency, also climbed 7% in the quarter.
For the second straight quarter, the company's unit case volume increased 5%, helped by higher demand outside of North America.
Coke's home market reported flat volume. However, the company's North American business would have reported volume growth if not for the timing of the Fourth of July holiday and the monthslong shortage of Topo Chico, a sparkling water brand Coke owns, Murphy told CNBC.
"The underlying momentum remains quite strong," he said. "Consumer sentiment is largely unchanged in the sense that, wherever you are on the income scale, you're looking for value, and I think our system here has done a good job interpreting that."
In North America, Coke's at-home business is faring better than its away-from-home segment, which includes restaurants, movie theaters and amusement parks. The restaurant industry is still under pressure, and Coke expects that to continue through the rest of the year, Murphy told analysts on the company's earnings conference call.
Globally, Coke's sparkling soft drinks business saw volume increase 5% during the quarter, lifted by growth of Coke, Coke Zero Sugar and Diet Coke.
Diet Coke is having a "resurgence," Murphy told CNBC. Gen Z consumers in the U.S. have nicknamed it a "fridge cigarette," while consumers in India threw Diet Coke parties as shortages tied to the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran have made the drink scarce.
"It's a brand that's almost reinventing itself with the next generation of consumers," he said.
Coke has also gained market share as rival PepsiCo sees its soda business struggle, according to Murphy. Still, some of Coke's soda brands, like Sprite, have "some work to do."
Coke's water, sports, coffee and tea division also saw volume climb by 5%. Increased demand for its water, which includes its premium Smartwater brand, fueled the growth. Demand for its tea and coffee was flat, while sports drinks declined.
The company's juice, value-added dairy and plant-based beverages business reported flat volume, despite growth in brands like Fairlife and Minute Maid.

NEW DELHI: To improve last-mile connectivity in India’s broadband sector, the Cellular Operators Association of India (COAI) has urged govt to expeditiously notify the rule amendments enabling standard power operations in the delicensed lower 6 GHz band. An expert committee constituted by dept of telecom, that was led by IIT Madras’s Professor Radha Krishna Ganti had recommended enabling higher-power outdoor use at 36 dBm in the 5925–6425 MHz band. The industry has asked the telecom ministry to implement the same “without further delay”.COAI DG Lt Gen (retired) S P Kochhar said: “India's broadband sector has progressed significantly, yet last-mile connectivity gaps persist particularly in rural, semi-urban, and difficult-to-reach areas due to Right-of-Way (RoW) challenges, limited fibre availability and high deployment costs. The expert committee's recommendation to permit Standard Power (36 dBm) outdoor use of the lower 6 GHz delicensed band (5925–6425 MHz) remains a practical and cost-effective solution to this challenge — one that is yet to be operationalised through the necessary regulatory notification.”“Fixed wireless access (FWA) and point-to-multi-point (P2MP) deployments at standard power are suited for last-mile broadband delivery where fibre penetration is absent, economically unviable or physically impractical.
Enabling outdoor Standard Power operations ensures this 500 MHz of valuable delicensed spectrum is fully harnessed in service of national objectives and can be utilised by all service providers,” Kochhar said.COAI says once implemented, this move will not only expand broadband coverage but also substantially improve broadband utilisation, bringing high-quality, high-speed connectivity to homes, enterprises and institutions “that have long remained on the wrong side of the digital divide.”
“Enabling these operations will ensure that India's delicensed spectrum serves not just indoor enterprise and consumer Wi-Fi but becomes a genuine engine of rural broadband penetration and digital inclusion. Several months since the Expert Committee submitted its report, COAI earnestly requests the DoT to expedite the notification of the necessary rule amendments enabling Standard Power (36 dBm) outdoor operations in the lower 6 GHz band (5925-6425 MHz) for P2MP/P2P, so as to enable licensed and authorised entities to deploy these capabilities and bring the transformative benefits of high-quality, affordable broadband to every segment of our society,” he added.

US Justice Dept asks Washington state not to count ballots from possible noncitizens
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:03:49 CET
00:03:49 KST

By Luc Cohen
Oct 27 (Reuters) - The US Justice Department has asked Washington state not to count any mail ballots received from more than 400 residents who it says may not be US citizens, opening a new front in the Trump administration’s push to expand control of election administration ahead of the November 3 midterms.
The letter, which resembled a request earlier this month that California not count any ballots received from around 20,000 alleged noncitizens, marked an escalation in the Trump administration’s pressure on state election officials over alleged noncitizen voting. Multiple state audits and independent studies have found that voter fraud, including voting by noncitizens, is very rare and has not affected election outcomes.
The pressure campaign is a rare intervention by the Justice Department in the voting process in the weeks before an election. President Donald Trump’s fellow Republicans are locked in a tight battle to retain slim majorities in both chambers of the US Congress, and centrist Democrat Marie Gluesenkamp Perez’s campaign to hold onto her southwest Washington seat is one of 10 key races that could decide control of the US House of Representatives.
In the letter dated October 26, the top federal prosecutors in Seattle and Spokane asked Washington Secretary of State Steve Hobbs, the state’s top elections official, to determine whether the more than 400 people were in fact US citizens and to not count their ballots until their citizenship was determined. The letter said the Justice Department would seek “emergency relief” if the state could not take those actions by noon local time (1900 GMT) on Wednesday.
There were 5 million registered voters in Washington state as of 2024, according to the secretary of state’s office.
In a statement, Hobbs said his office would only respond to requests that follow due process.
“The timing of this request — one week before the General Election — is no doubt intended to cast unfounded suspicion on the results,” Hobbs said.
A Justice Department spokesperson said, “With his (Hobbs’) help, we can ensure that only American citizens vote in Washington’s elections.”
In California, after state election officials said complying with the Justice Department’s demand would be impractical and questioned the accuracy of its information on alleged noncitizens, federal prosecutors filed a lawsuit seeking to block the state from counting any ballots received from the alleged noncitizens.
A hearing is scheduled in that case for 1 p.m. PDT (2000 GMT) on Tuesday before US District Judge David Carter in Los Angeles. A federal appeals court on Monday night denied the Justice Department’s request to block California from counting any ballots before Carter had the chance to rule.
Democrats and voting rights advocates say federal data on citizenship is often outdated, meaning naturalized citizens registered to vote are often mistakenly flagged as noncitizens.
In its letter to Washington state officials, the Justice Department acknowledged that some of the individuals flagged as possible noncitizens may have since naturalized, but it did not say how many.
(Reporting by Luc Cohen in New York; Editing by Bill Berkrot)

Nigeria panel says 37 detained miners died from overcrowding and neglect
Italy

16:03:30 CET
00:03:30 KST

By Camillus Eboh
ABUJA, Oct 27 (Reuters) - A group of 37 suspected illegal miners died in detention in Nigeria as a result of severe overcrowding, poor ventilation and neglect, according to a government investigation into their deaths.
The investigating committee, set up after the deaths last month sparked outrage in Nigeria, rejected earlier claims by officials that an outbreak of disease was to blame and called for compensation for victims and survivors as well as an overhaul of the agency involved.
The deaths, which included many teenagers working in artisanal gold mines, triggered protests in Nigeria, raising fresh concerns about conditions in detention facilities and the treatment of suspects awaiting trial.
Jonathan Kure, chairman of the committee, said the deaths were “entirely preventable” and a result of severe overcrowding, deprivation of basic necessities and ignored warnings.
“The tragedy demonstrates the consequences of systemic disregard for detention standards, supervisory responsibilities, and the welfare of persons in custody,” Kure said after his committee reviewed evidence, including detention records, autopsies, hospital reports and communication logs.
NSCDC officials did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The evidence showed the victims died from asphyxia, an acute respiratory failure caused by prolonged confinement in a severely overcrowded, poorly ventilated cell, worsened by heat stress and dehydration, Kure said.
“The evidence did not support claims that the deaths resulted from a disease outbreak,” Kure said.
The Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC), the paramilitary agency that locked up the miners as part of efforts to regulate mining, initially suggested the detainees may have died from an unspecified disease before later saying the cause had not been established.
The panel recommended 30 million naira (about $22,500) in compensation for each victim’s family and 10 million naira for each of the 41 survivors.
The findings are in line with testimonies from survivors who told Reuters that dozens of artisanal miners were crammed into a small holding cell and repeatedly ignored after complaining of overcrowding.
The government has suspended senior NSCDC officials pending the investigation, but the panel called for a sweeping overhaul of the agency’s leadership.

Poorer Brazilians devote four times more income to credit card debt, central bank says
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:03:22 CET
00:03:22 KST

By Marcela Ayres
BRASILIA, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Lower-income Brazilians are devoting an increasing share of their earnings to interest on credit-card- and other high-cost consumer borrowing, prompting policymakers to consider how to reduce excessive debt.
The new central bank data point to a growing reliance on expensive forms of credit since late 2023, in the first year of President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva’s current term. Lula’s administration has long championed greater credit availability as a way to support economic growth.
But in its latest financial stability report, the central bank again flagged concern over the rising portion of household budgets absorbed by the servicing of high-interest borrowing and reiterated that it was studying macroprudential measures aimed at riskier lending segments.
Among borrowers earning up to twice the minimum wage, or 3,242 reais ($604) in total, the share of income being spent on credit card debt stood at 15% in June, close to historical highs and four times the 3.75% recorded among those earning more than 10 times the minimum wage.
The gap was also evident in unsecured consumer loans. For borrowers earning up to twice the minimum wage, the share of income committed to servicing that debt stood at 9.6% in June, compared to 3.1% among those earning more than 10 times the minimum wage.
The central bank said the rapid digitalization of financial services had significantly increased the availability of credit offers to lower-income consumers, and thus raised debt levels.
“In response, the central bank is considering macroprudential measures targeting higher-risk credit segments to reduce overindebtedness and strengthen credit sustainability and financial system resilience,” it said, without providing details.
The report said debt-servicing capacity is strained for both households and companies. Among families, debt burdens have reached their highest level in 21 years, with low-income borrowers bearing the brunt.
The central bank said credit risk has increased and is likely to remain elevated in the near term.
Troubled assets in household lending have risen across most credit segments to their highest levels since 2012, driven primarily by delinquency, while default indicators point to continued pressure through the second half of the year.
($1 = 5.3719 reais)

Critics attack ‘anti-democratic’ French bill making rioters pay
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:03:12 CET
00:03:12 KST

By Mark John and Layli Foroudi
PARIS, Oct 27 (Reuters) - A proposed French law making rioters liable to pay up to €10,000 ($11,150) for damage they cause faces a backlash from rights groups and some lawyers who say it attacks the basic democratic right to take to the streets to protest.
President Emmanuel Macron’s government, under pressure to quell social protests accompanied by some of France’s worst unrest in years, says the law is needed to compensate victims of the vandalism that often follows protests, such as the looting and rioting seen across the country on October 17.
But critics say the draft bill, being debated in parliament this week, is worded in such a way that legitimate protesters who happened to be close to the scene of any violence could also be deemed legally responsible for it and face prosecution.
“Around the edges of a protest there can be those who engage in violence or damage with no involvement from the vast majority of peaceful, legitimate demonstrators,” said Hanna Bouchareb, a Paris-based lawyer who represented some of those accused in fast-track trials of taking part in rioting on October 17.
“It’s very problematic because it undermines the right to protest,” she told Reuters.
The text states that anyone who knowingly formed part of a group of people would be held jointly responsible for any damage caused by any member of that group.
It further allows the state to seize welfare entitlements of those convicted, or those of their parents if they are minors, to help pay the costs.
French businesses and retailers say they have lost millions of euros either through looting or vandalism or by being forced to shut their shops and board their windows during protests.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez, who offered his resignation to Macron last week after security forces were overwhelmed by the unrest, rejected arguments the law undermined the principle that individuals were only accountable for their own actions.
“What this draft law changes is that we are creating a joint responsibility - not a collective one,” Nunez, whom Macron asked to remain at his post, told broadcaster TF1.
That is a distinction rejected by France’s Human Rights League (LDH) and a group of trade unionists who signed a column in Le Monde newspaper this weekend demanding it be scrapped.
Police were accused in 2020 of using excessive force against “yellow vest” anti-government protesters and there was criticism then of a subsequently watered-down law banning circulation of images of police officers in some circumstances.
In recent weeks, protesters have again accused police of heavy-handed tactics against the student protesters while lawyers including Bouchareb have raised legal concerns over the fast-tracked convictions of some of those accused of rioting.
Backers of the proposed new law point to surveys showing broad public support for it. The National Rally (RN) party of Marine Le Pen - the far-right frontrunner for next year’s presidential election - said it would go even further.
“The vandal’s law is good in that it recognises the principle of joint responsibility,” RN senator Edwige Diaz told French television. “But not with a cap at 10,000 euros.”
(Additional reporting by Elizabeth PineauEditing by Keith Weir)

Factbox-Who could Brazil’s Lula pick for finance minister?
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:03:03 CET
00:03:03 KST

By Marcela Ayres and Lisandra Paraguassu
BRASILIA, Oct 26 (Reuters) - A sharp selloff in Brazilian markets on Monday after leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva’s surprise reelection is pressuring the veteran leader to pick a finance minister who can send a signal of fiscal discipline and reassure markets.
Sources say Lula is likely to take his time to make a decision. But three sources who spoke on condition of anonymity said two key names have emerged: Vice President Geraldo Alckmin and Rafael Fonteles, the re-elected governor of Piauí state who revitalized Lula’s flagging campaign after trailing in the first round to right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro.
Here is a rundown of Lula’s choices:
WHO IS FONTELES?
Mathematician Fonteles, 41, is seen as a fiscally disciplined technocrat who could bridge the gap between Lula’s administration and wary investors.
He holds a master’s degree in mathematical economics and served as Piaui’s finance secretary from 2015 to 2022. He also completed two terms as head of Comsefaz, which represents state finance secretaries.
WHO IS ALCKMIN?
Alckmin, 73, comes from the Brazilian Socialist Party and was once the president’s center-right rival who lost to Lula in the 2006 presidential election. He is also a former two-term governor of São Paulo and ex-trade and development minister.
Reuters reported earlier this month that Lula was weighing Alckmin as finance minister to bolster his fiscal credibility and win over centrist voters.
WHAT IS WORKING FOR OR AGAINST FONTELES?
Fonteles gained prominence in Lula’s campaign after a shakeup that followed Lula’s first-round finish behind Bolsonaro.
A member of Lula’s Workers’ Party (PT), he is a close ally of Lula’s former education minister and senator-elect Camilo Santana. The two worked together on Lula’s campaign in Brazil’s Northeast, where the president secured a commanding lead.
In his victory speech, Lula thanked Fonteles for his role in the campaign, but noted that the governor still had a “mission to fulfill in Piauí,” which some allies read as a sign he may be reluctant to bring him into the cabinet so soon.
WHAT IS WORKING FOR OR AGAINST ALCKMIN?
In his victory speech, Lula lavished praise on Alckmin’s loyalty and even handed him the microphone before speaking himself. Lula wants a finance minister he trusts completely, one of the sources said. Alckmin is someone Lula trusts “100%,” another source noted.
“There are very few people outside the PT who have that kind of relationship with Lula today,” one of the sources said.
Lula, however, may ultimately decide to retain current Finance Minister Dario Durigan, said the sources.
While Durigan lacks the political weight of some rivals, Lula is said to value him highly and view him as an “effective operator,” according to a fourth source.
IT COULD COME DOWN TO THE CHIEF OF STAFF
The three sources said Lula’s choice of finance minister has become increasingly intertwined with whether Lula makes former Finance Minister Fernando Haddad his chief of staff.
Haddad, a member of the PT, left the Finance Ministry earlier this year to run for governor of Sao Paulo at Lula’s request - despite polls pointing to a likely defeat - to bolster the president’s base in Brazil’s most populous state. He lost.
Both Durigan and Alckmin, who are from outside the PT, are seen as having close ties to Haddad, which would also help ensure alignment between the Finance Ministry and the presidential palace.
Two sources also said that Lula understands that, given current market conditions, a PT figure alone would struggle to curb the slide in the Brazilian real or the surge in long-dated interest rate futures. This could boost Durigan and Alckmin’s chances of being finance minister if Haddad is chief of staff.
(Reporting by Marcela Ayres and Lisandra Paraguassu; Editing by Brendan O’Boyle and Alistair Bell)

GENEVA, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Israel continued to commit genocide in Gaza after last October’s US-brokered ceasefire in the enclave, a UN commission said in a report published on Monday that Israel dismissed as part of a “misinformation campaign”.
The report by the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including East Jerusalem, and Israel, examined violations against Palestinian civilians, including children, since the start of the war between Israel and Hamas on October 7, 2023, up to September this year.
It said Israeli authorities had kept committing “genocidal acts with the genocidal intent to destroy, in whole or in part, the Palestinians in Gaza”, and that the situation had also continued to deteriorate in the occupied West Bank.
Another report by the commission in September last year found that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza and that top Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu incited these acts — accusations that Israel called scandalous.
The Israeli mission in Geneva said the latest report was part of a misinformation campaign to demonize the State of Israel.
“The attempt to destroy the Jewish state … continues today through efforts by actors such as the UN Commission of Inquiry to undermine Israel’s legitimacy and deny its fundamental right to exist and defend itself,” Ambassador Daniel Meron said in a statement.
HEAVY MUNITIONS HIT POPULATED AREAS, COMMISSION SAYS
The commission found that Israeli forces continued using heavy munitions, drones, quadcopters, artillery and sniper fire in densely populated areas during the ceasefire in Gaza.
It said the “Yellow Line”, which was presented as a temporary ceasefire demarcation, was encroaching increasingly into Gaza, and becoming a de facto border, which the report said reflected Israel’s expanding territorial control of Gaza.
Palestinian authorities say more than 74,000 people have been killed in Israel’s assault on Gaza, launched after Hamas-led fighters killed about 1,200 people in southern Israel on October 7, 2023.
In its report to the UN General Assembly, the commission said the situation in the West Bank had also deteriorated sharply, with the number of Palestinians killed in airstrikes increasing from six between 2008 and October 6, 2023, to 254 between October 7, 2023 and September 30, 2026.
The report said Israeli military operations, alongside sustained settler violence, formed part of a widespread and systematic attack against the civilian population in the West Bank since October 7, 2023.
“The Commission concludes that the Israeli authorities and forces have committed the crimes against humanity of extermination, torture, rape and other forms of sexual violence in the West Bank, as well as persecution based on intersecting discriminatory grounds, with nationality, race and ethnicity at its core.”
Commenting on the report, the Israeli mission said the international community should reject what it described as distortions, and “repudiate the Commission’s findings”.
Commission Chair Srinivasan Muralidhar said the intentional killing of Palestinian civilians and destruction of homes in the West Bank formed part of a broader strategy to exterminate and displace Palestinians.
Military operations since January 2025 have led to the largest displacement of Palestinians in the West Bank since 1967, with 34,176 Palestinians remaining displaced as of August 2026, the report said.
The commission also faulted the Palestinian Authority, saying it had targeted Palestinians who voice dissenting views and that journalists and human rights defenders had been killed and injured.

It will also allow the two countries to share lessons and experience from developing frigate capabilities and increase defensive maritime activity in the Baltic Sea through exercises and regional coordination.
“The UK and Poland will also work together to further strengthen cooperation between their defence industries through closer defence procurement coordination,” the statement added.

LONDON, Oct 27 - A Russian IT specialist has been sentenced to 13 years in jail on charges of financing terrorism after the cryptocurrency exchange Binance passed details to Moscow of his donations to Ukrainian fundraising campaigns.
The 2nd Western District Military Court on Monday convicted 49-year-old Yuri Belenkiy and sentenced him to three years in prison plus 10 years in a strict-regime penal colony, according to a court statement.
Belenkiy, who has a Bulgarian residence permit, was detained in September last year when he flew to Moscow for a visit, and has been in custody since. He denied the charges, according to the court.
Belenkiy had responded to online appeals to help buy medical equipment for Ukrainian soldiers by transferring money from his Binance accounts to the Ukrainian military, according to Russian law enforcement documents seen by Reuters. Some payments went to the Azov Brigade or Azov Regiment, a particular bete noire for Moscow.
BINANCE ACCEPTED RUSSIAN INVESTIGATORS' REQUEST
The same documents showed that Binance provided Russian investigators with Belenkiy's transaction history last year, including records of transfers to Ukrainian fundraising campaigns, in response to a Russian request, and that the records were instrumental in prosecuting him, Reuters reported in August.
According to the records, Belenkiy sent more than $700 to the Ukrainian military in response to an online appeal by Arkady Babchenko, an exiled Russian critic of the Kremlin who supports Ukraine.
"The response from Binance serves as key evidence in the criminal case against Belenkiy," said Yevgeny Smirnov, a lawyer with the rights group First Department, which assists people facing politically motivated prosecutions in Russia.
Rights advocates who monitor such prosecutions say dozens of Russians have been convicted in recent years for donations made through cryptocurrency platforms to causes that authorities later classified as extremist or terrorist. Many used cryptocurrency because they believed it would keep their identities secret.
Asked on Tuesday about the sentence, Binance referred Reuters to a previous statement in which it said the exchange "does not make or enforce the laws of any jurisdiction, determine charges, or decide how any government uses information in legal proceedings". It said it does not comment on confidential law-enforcement requests or individual cases.
A lawyer who specialises in crypto regulation, Mike Bystrov, told Reuters in August that Binance, which left Russia in 2023 following Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the subsequent imposition of Western sanctions, had been under no obligation to provide Belenkiy's data.
He said it might, in fact, have had obligations under European Union data-protection law not to do so because of Belenkiy's Bulgarian residency status. REUTERS

More than 600 young people gathered in central Barcelona on Oct. 24 following a social media campaign promoted under the name Blocus.

A Telegram group operating under the name Blocus BCN has since circulated messages calling for another gathering on Oct. 31, encouraging participants to wear black clothing and Halloween masks to avoid police identification.
Promotional material also cited recent protests in France as an inspiration.
Catalan regional police are investigating who organized Saturday's violence, which they believe was coordinated rather than spontaneous.
Investigators have ruled out a political or ideological motive and believe participants followed instructions from unidentified organizers, according to Spanish newspaper La Vanguardia.
Study identifies nationwide network

The analysis traced the network's earliest known activity to Oct. 8 in Madrid.
Researchers found that organizers used TikTok and Instagram to recruit participants before directing them to private Telegram and WhatsApp groups.
The network operated through disposable accounts rather than a conventional organization, with the identities of its main operators still unknown, according to the study.
Researchers said participants identified luxury brands including Rolex, Louis Vuitton, Balenciaga and Hermes as potential looting targets.
Messages also discussed bringing heavy objects to break shop windows, confronting police and preventing bystanders from recording their activities.
The study identified further calls for gatherings on Oct. 31, Nov. 2 and Nov. 30, the day after Spain's general election.
Researchers also detected messages from accounts on US social media platform X based in France, Ecuador and Uruguay encouraging attacks on immigrants following the Barcelona riots.
They warned that the messages posed a separate risk of violent confrontations but found no evidence of coordination with Blocus organizers.

The signatories say the event “risks creating a hostile and exclusionary environment for students, particularly those of ethnic minorities” and “risks undermining Oriel’s role as a world-class educational institution” in 2026, the year of the 700th anniversary of its royal charter.
The letter accuses Cofnas of using his platform to assert discriminatory beliefs, and claims his blogging played a significant role in the coverage Arday faced.

Oriel College said in a statement: “Oriel College is committed to upholding freedom of speech within the law and has a statutory duty to do so. This includes the freedom to express views that many find deeply offensive. We are also committed to promoting inclusion and maintaining an environment that is free from all forms of discrimination and harassment, including racial discrimination.
“The college considers events booked by students who are committee members of registered societies according to our code of practice on freedom of speech. When an event is permitted, this does not imply endorsement by the college of the views of its speakers.
“When considering booking requests, the college takes seriously the security implications of events and the safety of its members.”

It added: “The Reform Society is committed to hosting Nathan Cofnas, and allowing attendees at the event to engage in respectful dialogue with the same.
“We find it strange that the University of Oxford or any of its constituent colleges should receive reputational damage in respect of this event. The decision to host Nathan Cofnas was made solely by the committee of the Reform Society, and responsibility for the event rests exclusively with the same.”
Cofnas was approached for comment.
