Roller coaster safety is a matter of science
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

Roller coaster safety is a matter of science
Extreme ride guidelines don't all reflect the latest findings
The first roller coaster in the United States to loop upside down tucked riders by twos into bench seats, secured them with a single seat belt and subjected them to an estimated 7.5 times the force of gravity (some say it was closer to 12 g). The Flip Flap Railway opened in New York City’s Sea Lion Park in 1895, where the roller coaster reportedly strained backs, wrenched necks and dazzled spectators until the park closed in 1902.
Now, roller coaster safety is in the news again. In September, three lawsuits were filed against Six Flags and ride manufacturer S&S Global, alleging that riders sustained “catastrophic” brain injuries on the roller coaster X2 at California’s Magic Mountain theme park. These are just the most recent cases related to the ride, filed after a CNN investigation found dozens of injuries on X2 leading to hospitalization, disability and death. On September 29, Six Flags announced X2 would shut down permanently even though it said the ride “consistently passed a multitude of safety tests.”
Weeks later, the company said it would temporarily close another nine coasters across the United States and Canada after a man fell from his seat on the roller coaster Goliath and died at Six Flags Over Georgia. Six Flags announced Oct. 24 that it would add seat belts to Goliath and other coasters, and a spokesperson told Science News that the company is “committed to rigorous ride inspection, maintenance and safety procedures.” But the incidents and closures are prompting new questions about coaster design and safety — particularly when they are operating correctly — and whether guidelines overlook crucial factors.
“Taller, faster, longer”
Roller coasters are not regulated at the federal level in the United States; each state has its own approach to their management. But an international technical group comprising over 1,000 industry professionals, the ASTM Committee F24 on Amusement Rides and Devices, publishes recommendations that are considered industry standards.
The first ASTM standards for roller coaster design were released in 1982. The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission had been stripped of authority to regulate fixed-site amusement rides the year before. In the wake of this newfound freedom, it was a “roller coaster arms race,” says Brian Avery, an event and tourism management researcher at the University of Florida in Gainesville who studies risk and amusement ride safety protocols. The period was characterized by attempts to “build it taller, faster, longer.”
When X2, originally called X, opened in 2002, it was the world’s first fourth-dimension coaster. It catapulted people 60 meters high, traveling 122 kilometers per hour while its seats rotated independently on their own tracks. In the 24 years since, only 20 or so other fourth-dimension coasters have been built, and several have closed.
Beyond g-forces
As roller coasters grew more extreme, injuries increased and were more publicized, sparking calls for further research and regulation.
Generally, roller coasters are quite safe. Out of 1.7 billion annual amusement park rides across North America, just 652 roller coaster injuries were reported in 2024 by parks choosing to share data. Studies suggest that riding a roller coaster is very unlikely to cause a brain injury, although most research on roller coaster brain impacts is about a decade or more old.
In 2002, a study used reported g forces from three roller coasters in a mathematical model to determine that their acceleration levels were below those predicted to cause head injuries. A 2017 study found brain effects on three roller coasters that were low on average, but “comparable with mild sports impacts,” like those sustained by heading a soccer ball, at their peak.
“The limiting of g forces alone might be an insufficient design criterion for roller coaster rides,” wrote the authors of the 2017 study.
In 2020, David Eager, a biomechanical engineer at the University of Technology Sydney, coauthored a paper on under-acknowledged forces affecting roller coaster safety, including jerk (the rate at which acceleration changes), snap (the rate at which jerk changes) and vibration.
“Roller coaster passengers need time to sense acceleration changes and adjust their muscle tension or suffer conditions such as whiplash,” Eager wrote.
The ASTM standards are exacting in some ways. Research conducted during the space race led to a 6g recommended limit on roller coaster acceleration exposure. However, ASTM doesn’t make recommendations about other types of motion on a roller coaster that might impact the neck, head and brain. It disregards forces lasting less than 200 milliseconds, no matter how intense.
But each tiny imperfection and variation in the circumference of the track — especially plentiful in coasters built before modern manufacturing techniques — causes a jolt, says Jurnan Schilder, a mechanical engineer and researcher who teaches roller coaster design at the University of Twente in Amsterdam. He studies ways to create smoother roller coaster rides.
Schilder’s research suggests that at each track imperfection, “theoretically, you experience infinite jerk.” On a fourth-dimension coaster, he says, two sets of tracks mean double the variations. “Not only is the train sometimes shaking, but also the tilting mechanism is shaking.”
Impacting the brain
Research beyond rides also suggests intense and repeated rattling, jostling and vibration could meaningfully impact the brain. The U.S. Occupational Safety and Health Administration recommends limiting the duration and intensity of whole-body vibration. In April, the Virginia Tech Helmet Lab, which studies the science of brain injuries, published an article suggesting some concussions experienced by baseball players may result from just milliseconds of vibration.
North Carolina high school student Kayleigh Bonner’s quest to understand her father’s death exposed similar risks. After her father, a retired U.S. Coast Guard surfman who captained boats through rough waves for 21 years, experienced symptoms of a brain injury and died by suicide, Kayleigh surveyed 77 other elite surfmen for a senior capstone project. She found that 89 percent of those she spoke to had some symptoms of brain injury likely caused by the intense, rapidly changing forces traveling through their bodies as their boats were tossed by waves. Her quest to understand her father’s death was written about in July in the New York Times, and soon after acknowledged by the Coast Guard.
Of course, professional baseball players and Coast Guard surfmen have more significant and prolonged exposure to these forces than occasional roller coasters riders. But as researchers discover more about how different kinds of motion impact the brain, safety standards seem to lag behind. Minimizing jerk and snap is “an important consideration,” Eager says.
A push for greater regulation
The mounting roller coaster-related headlines have renewed scrutiny of both the existing coaster safety standards and the lack of federal regulation. U.S. Rep. André Carson, a Democrat from Indiana, has called to pass a bill he first introduced in 2025 that would create federal oversight of amusement rides. Since 1999, Democratic U.S. Sen. Ed Markey of Massachusetts has repeatedly introduced legislation to regulate fixed rides, but the bills have consistently stalled.
The amusement industry has long opposed federal oversight. In 2010, Avery coauthored a paper asserting that “the industry needs to find a collective voice and establish consistent self‐regulating policies in order to curb the incidents rates and avoid federal regulation.”
But Schilder says: “It makes you wonder: Are the current safety standards sufficient?”
For modern rides, Schilder says he believes they are. Modern manufacturing techniques mean roller coasters designed and built today are much smoother than predecessors. ASTM standards that filter out brief but intense forces, like vibration and jerk, are likely fine for rides that don’t vibrate and jerk very much. But at many parks, the ambitious and intense rides born of the roller coaster arms race are still in place.
Riders are “flirting, if you would, with danger when they experience rides and devices. They know that they’re more likely than not going to be safe,” Avery says. The point is to be “right on the cusp.”

How the War in Iran Could Escalate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:59:56 UTC
23:59:56 KST

President Donald Trump’s conflict with Iran has become a political liability for his administration. Since the last U.S. strikes on Iran fell on Sept. 8, Trump has publicly ruled out attacking Iran before the November midterm elections—and promised to end the conflict after them.
Then, rumblings grew that U.S. and Israeli military planners had reportedly drawn up new strike options against Iran, including the possible use of the largest non-nuclear weapon in the American arsenal: the GBU-43/B, also dubbed “the Mother of All Bombs”.
The targets purportedly would be Iran’s nuclear facilities and energy infrastructure, though there are doubts about whether the bomb could penetrate Iran’s most deeply buried sites. According to these reports, Trump apparently is seeking a strike he could present as a military victory and then end the war without appearing to back down.
But such an approach risks triggering a far wider war than Washington intends. Tehran remains unlikely to let Washington end the conflict quickly and, fearing a potential attack from the U.S., could itself strike first. Either scenario could lead to a new round of fighting far more destructive than the last.
Before the mother of all bombs
Reports of military plans involving “the mother of all bombs” came against the backdrop of two other worrying developments. First, Iran has been escalating its naval attacks, likely in response to increased flows through the Strait of Hormuz. Notably, two UAE-owned cargo ships, the GFS Pride and the Cape Dao, were struck in the Strait as part of this sharp uptick.
Secondly, diplomatic efforts appear to have hit a wall. In late September, Trump rejected the proposal Tehran had put forward on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly: an end to fighting on all fronts, including Lebanon; the lifting of the U.S. naval blockade and oil sanctions; the release of some of Iran’s frozen assets; and the reopening of Hormuz within seven days. Instead, Washington insists that Iran must take steps regarding its nuclear program as part of the package, something Iranian leaders say they will only do at a later stage.
The timing of any U.S.-Israeli attack remains uncertain. While Trump has said he will not resume attacks before the midterms, Israel held its election on Oct. 27, a week earlier, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had reportedly sought renewed fighting before both elections.
American and Israeli objectives may differ, of course. Trump appears to want something he can portray as a spectacular military victory without having to undergo another prolonged war, while Netanyahu’s rhetoric about “finishing the job” suggests more ambitious goals, potentially including toppling the Islamic Republic. Tehran seems to be preparing for either scenario with its own response: a prolonged, region-wide war designed to impose devastating economic costs.
Denying Trump a short war
The dominant perspective in Tehran is that the next war must be fought in a way that makes it so costly that a future U.S. president would not contemplate another. Hossein Mohebbi, a spokesperson for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), said in late September that Iran “will not stop until we have driven the United States out of the region, punished the aggressor, and established permanent deterrence so that no one will dare attack Iran.”
That logic, should it prevail, rules out a symbolic, tit-for-tat exchange. In Tehran’s view, a limited American strike on Pickaxe Mountain, the fortified nuclear site near Natanz that Trump has repeatedly evoked, followed by a limited Iranian response, would send Washington precisely the wrong message: that it can attack Iran’s nuclear facilities, register domestic political gain, and pay a limited, acceptable cost. Iranian officials have therefore warned that even a symbolic, non-lethal strike would trigger a broad response, denying Trump the quick exit he may have asked of his war planners.
Under this scenario, Iran would target regional energy and economic infrastructure. “In a region where we cannot sell oil, no one will sell oil,” Ghalibaf has warned. The UAE is particularly exposed: Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, has accused it of oil “smuggling” in cahoots with U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM). Rezaei also identified new potential targets: undersea cables, data centers, and AI infrastructure in the region, which he claims are worth “more than $2 trillion.” Ghalibaf subsequently extended the threat to regional governments and investors, threatening that anyone providing “funding, equity, land, or energy” to AI companies that “facilitate military aggression” against Iran “will face coercive action.”
If raising the cost of war is the first instrument in Iran’s calculus, duration is the second. Ali Balali, an adviser to the IRGC’s Aerospace Force commander, suggested Iran would conserve its arsenal in preparation for a prolonged confrontation, rather than expend it early. Two days later, Iranian Army spokesperson Mohammad Akraminia argued that the enemy’s weak point is a prolonged war.
Timing is a third dimension in Iranian thinking. Iranian military officials have increasingly mentioned the possibility of striking first, preemptively. Akraminia stated that if Iran were to conclude that an attack by the U.S. and/or Israel is imminent, “we will certainly engage in preemptive warfare.” Mehdi Mohammadi, strategic affairs adviser to Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, went further, arguing that a successful strategy requires not only striking first but also delivering a decisive blow capable of “changing the balance.” There is thus at least the possibility that Iran might move early, and then fight long.
That could occur due to miscalculation resulting from ambiguous American and Israeli signals: leaked strike plans, carrier and amphibious deployments, and aircraft approaching but not entering Iranian airspace. Military experts in Iran see this pattern as an effort to normalize military activity and regain the element of surprise. Tehran could thus mistake military signaling for an imminent attack and strike preemptively, even though it may not want another round of war.
The fourth element concerns the range of those Tehran would hold responsible in the event of an attack. On Oct. 5 Ali Abdollahi, chief of staff of Iran’s armed forces, declared that if the United States acted against Iran “directly or indirectly through Israel,” Iranian forces would retaliate against the United States. The warning carries more weight in the wake of Trump’s decision to openly back Netanyahu ahead of Israel’s election. Indeed, some in Tehran interpreted this as a signal that Washington would allow Israel to strike Iran after the midterms. As a result, Tehran has made clear that even were Israel to carry out the attack on its own, U.S. forces and assets in the region would face retaliation.
Widening the map
This interpretation suggests that the scope of Iran’s response to a U.S. strike likely would be far wider. Its conduct in Hormuz since late September offers a preview of how it could broaden the conflict. When the UAE, backed by CENTCOM, kept oil moving through a southern corridor along the Omani coast, the IRGC shifted its attacks from small shuttle tankers to supertankers and stated that vessels using the “illegal corridor” would be “pursued and interdicted across the region.” Strikes followed off the UAE coast and near Qatar. An escalation in the region could drive Iran to go after vital energy and other infrastructure across the Gulf.
Iran’s regional partners also could widen the conflict, although Tehran does not fully control their actions. In Yemen, the Houthis have already opened a second maritime front in the Red Sea, threatening shipping and increasing pressure on Saudi Arabia. In Iraq, Kataib Sayyid al-Shuhada, an Iran-backed militia, has threatened to fight if Iran faced an existential threat. The conflict could also extend to Europe through indirect operations.
There may already have been attempts in this vein: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said a suspected September plot near RAF Fairford, a base used by U.S. bombers, was “almost certainly” directed by the IRGC. Tehran denies involvement, but the incident raises the prospect of covert operations against American military assets beyond the Middle East.
Tehran is also preparing for the possibility of a ground operation inside Iran. According to Iranian Army Ground Forces commander Ali Jahanshahi, more than 50 units are deployed along the borders, from the northwest to the Makran coast, and abandoned airfields have been identified as potential enemy landing sites. Iranian security forces have also conducted preemptive operations against Baluch armed groups in the southeast and launched drone and artillery strikes in Kurdish border areas amid concerns that they could open an internal front during an external attack.
A war meant to be the last
Both the U.S. and Iran run the risk of serious misjudgment. The U.S. may believe it can be master of the scope and duration of a war, only to find that Iran holds the key. This power means Iran need not let the conflict end quickly or painlessly.
For its part, Tehran—which survived the fierce exchanges that began in late February, continued through April, and have since become more regionalized—may be convinced that a wider conflict this time again would establish lasting deterrence. But conditions that made this strategy relatively effective in the past have changed, partly because of Iran’s own actions. The more Tehran expands its targets, the more it risks turning neighbors that sought to stay out of the conflict into supporters of its defeat. Saudi Arabia and the UAE have reportedly agreed to coordinate their military support on behalf of anti-Houthi forces in Yemen, while Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi has offered to help defend Saudi Arabia against Houthi attacks. For the Gulf monarchies, the stakes are becoming existential: either Iran’s leverage is broken, or their access to world markets will remain dependent on Iranian restraint.
In this way, a war intended to deter future American attacks could instead strengthen a regional consensus that Iran must be dealt a serious blow rather than accommodated or bargained with.
Ultimately, diplomacy remains the only way to prevent the gap between American and Iranian perceptions and risk calculus from triggering another, potentially even more costly round of confrontation. Without it, Washington could launch a limited strike expecting a quick exit, or Tehran could strike first fearing an imminent attack. Either scenario could trigger a prolonged regional war that the U.S. wishes to avoid and a growing alliance against the Islamic Republic for which Iran would pay a price.

OpenAI unveils GPT-6.1 Terra, cutting AI costs by half

OpenAI unveils GPT-6.1 Terra, cutting AI costs by half
OpenAI has introduced GPT-6.1 Terra, a faster and more affordable AI model designed for visual reasoning, computer use, writing, and software development, Qazinform News Agency correspondent reports.
The model improves on its predecessor, GPT-5.6 Terra, in accuracy, coding, and the ability to perform tasks using computer applications. According to OpenAI, its standard API prices are 50% lower than those of GPT-5.6 Terra and GPT-6.1 Sol.
GPT-6.1 Terra is designed for everyday professional tasks, including drafting proposals, interpreting technical drawings, filling out forms, editing videos, and processing invoices.
Better visual reasoning and computer use
OpenAI reports significant improvements in computer use, allowing the model to complete complex, multistep tasks more quickly and at lower cost.
On the Agents' Last Exam benchmark, which measures performance on professional tasks, GPT-6.1 Terra scored 15 percentage points higher than GPT-5.6 Terra at medium reasoning effort, at about one-third of the cost.
The model also performed on par with GPT-6 Astra, OpenAI's more capable model, while costing one-tenth as much per token. At maximum reasoning effort, it completed tasks more than three times faster than GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol.
On the MMMU-Pro visual reasoning benchmark, GPT-6.1 Terra outperformed its predecessor at every reasoning setting, approaching the performance of GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol at a lower cost.
Fewer factual errors and stronger coding
OpenAI also reported a sharp reduction in factual errors. On its internal benchmark of difficult prompts, GPT-6.1 Terra's error rate at low reasoning effort fell to 16.7%, down from 53.6% for GPT-5.6 Terra.
At maximum reasoning effort, the error rate dropped to 4.3%, an improvement of 18 percentage points over its predecessor.
The model also made substantial gains in software engineering. On Terminal-Bench 4.0, which tests coding agents on command-line tasks, GPT-6.1 Terra solved 50.3% of tasks at maximum reasoning effort. GPT-5.6 Terra's published score was 21.5%.
For the most complex coding tasks, however, OpenAI says GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Astra remain the better choices.
GPT-6.1 Terra is available to Plus, Pro, Enterprise, and Edu users in ChatGPT Work and Codex. Developers can access it through the OpenAI API under the model name gpt-6.1-terra.
API pricing is $1 per million input tokens, $0.05 per million cached input tokens, and $5 per million output tokens.

Sleep and depression may be more intertwined than we thought
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:58:26 UTC
23:58:26 KST

A lesser-known form of depression may be caused by disrupted sleep-wake cycles—and could be more likely to cause severe symptoms than other forms of the condition. Called circadian depression, it could indicate that our body clock—which is based on our exposure to light and dark and regulates cycles of wakefulness and sleep—may have a greater effect on our mental and physical health than we realized.
Sleep disturbances are common in depression, and night owls (who tend to get less sleep than early birds) are likely to have more and worse depressive symptoms. Understanding the link between sleep patterns and depression could help clinicians better diagnose and treat the condition, especially in people whose depression seems less responsive to conventional therapies.
“Diagnosing depression can be tricky,” says Amy Marschall, a clinical psychologist based in Sioux Falls, S.D. “Getting to what’s going on beneath the surface or what’s causing the [depression] matters.”
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Our 24-hour circadian rhythm is primarily driven by light. Our eyes send signals to the brain’s master clock, which coordinates our body’s systems and processes, such as wakefulness, body temperature and energy metabolism. “Bright light throughout the day, but especially in the morning, helps stabilize and anchor the circadian rhythm, while light exposure at night can delay it,” explains Emiliana Tonini, a researcher studying circadian rhythms and mood disorders at the University of Sydney.
Low or irregular light during the day, or too much evening light, can weaken or shift circadian rhythms. Other factors, such as genetics, environment and physical health, can mess with our sleep cycles, too. That can cause the body to feel out of line with its environment or cause “different body rhythms [to] drift out of step with one another,” Tonini says. “Both may have a negative effect on health.”
In a recent study in the British Journal of Psychiatry, Tonini and her colleagues analyzed clinical and genetic data of 11,380 people with depression who participated in the Australian Genetics of Depression Study (AGDS). Almost a quarter met the proposed criteria for circadian depression. These participants experienced a combination of body clock disturbances that could include having irregular sleep-wake times, waking up tired, being a night owl or sleeping longer when they felt more depressed.
These individuals also showed more severe symptoms on average and greater genetic risk for other health problems, including other mental health conditions, as well as inflammatory, metabolic and cardiovascular issues. Another analysis of AGDS participants found that antidepressants worked less well for night owls, and they reported more side effects.
“Conventional antidepressants may not directly address these disturbances,” Tonini says. Treatments that target the body’s internal clock, such as melatonin or light therapy, may prove beneficial. “We do have effective treatments,” she says, “but currently, we are not really good at matching a patient to an effective treatment that will work for them on the first try.”
The researchers still aren’t sure whether these cases of depression are caused by, or simply associated with, problems with circadian rhythm. Tonini says they hope to test the link in more diverse populations in the future.
Marschall also notes that sleep-wake cycles vary naturally from person to person. “A lot of advice around sleep says humans are wired to be asleep from this time to this time, but some people have different natural rhythms,” she says.

UK charges two men on suspected Iran links in RAF Fairford plot

Breadcrumb
UK charges two men over suspected links to Iran over RAF Fairford base plot
British prosecutors charged two men on Tuesday under the National Security Act over an incident involving RAF Fairford, a military airbase in southwest England previously used by US bombers to launch strikes against Iran.
The Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) said Mohmed Abdulkarim, 24, from London, had been charged with engaging in conduct likely to materially assist a foreign intelligence service.
Nouman Essghir, also 24 and from London, was separately charged with entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the United Kingdom on 22 August.
Both men were due to appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court later on Tuesday.
Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of National Counter Terrorism Policing, said investigators believed the foreign country Abdulkarim was suspected of assisting was Iran.
The charges follow a major security operation at RAF Fairford on 27 September, when police arrested five British men outside the base in the early hours.
The facility had been used by US strategic bombers to conduct strikes against Iran during the war, although the aircraft were withdrawn on security grounds shortly after the arrests.
British authorities also evacuated residents living near the airbase as police and military bomb disposal specialists examined three lorries suspected of containing explosives.
The vehicles were subsequently found to contain no explosives.
The investigation has continued for several weeks, with authorities examining suspected threats to the military facility and possible links to foreign intelligence activity.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham had previously said there were strong indications of Iranian involvement in the Fairford incident.
Six others remain under investigation
Frank Ferguson, head of the CPS Special Crime and Counter Terrorism Division, said the decision to bring charges followed an investigation by counterterrorism police into a significant incident involving the RAF base.
He said prosecutors would continue working closely with investigators on what he described as a complex and ongoing inquiry.
Six other men arrested in connection with the investigation have been released on bail and remain under investigation.
Counterterrorism police confirmed on Tuesday that a 25-year-old dual British-Iranian national was among those released on bail without charge.
The CPS stressed that the decision to prosecute did not establish or imply guilt and that the charges would be determined through the criminal justice process.
Prosecutors said their role was to assess independently and objectively whether there was sufficient evidence to bring the case before a court.
RAF Fairford, in Gloucestershire, has served as an important operating location for US military aircraft, including strategic bombers deployed during the US-Israel war on Iran.
The United States had previously announced the withdrawal of its strategic bombers from the facility, with security concerns surrounding the base drawing increased attention following the September incident.
The investigation has also added to tensions between London and Tehran, with Iran previously summoning the British ambassador over allegations relating to the Fairford case.
The two defendants face separate charges under the UK's National Security Act 2023, legislation introduced to address threats including foreign intelligence activity and conduct considered harmful to national security.

Brazil’s elections: How Lula preserved sovereignty
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:58:10 UTC
23:58:10 KST

Brazil’s elections: How Lula preserved sovereignty
TEHRAN – The most insidious feature of domination is its insistence that people believe they are powerless and their future already written by others.
This is what makes Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva’s victory in Brazil significant far beyond the country’s borders. It demonstrates that people can shatter this illusion, reclaim their fair share of national wealth, and defend their right to choose who governs them.
Faced with the power of money and political blackmail, a majority of voters once again placed their trust in a man who rose from the ranks of the working class and brought a fundamental question into government: Whom does the state serve, and who reaps the rewards of economic growth?
Lula secured a fourth presidential term with 51.8 percent in the runoff vote, overturning his opponent’s lead in the first round. No candidate in Brazilian history has lost the first round and won the second. Voters renewed their confidence in the former factory worker and in a political project that links development to the rights of ordinary people and the independence of national decision-making.
When the poor become a political force
Lula emerged from the world of labor, led the metalworkers’ union, and helped establish the Workers’ Party in 1980. The deeper significance of his journey lies in his ability to organize social discontent and turn it into a force capable of shaping government policy.
When marginalized groups enter politics through organized movements and political programs, their suffering moves from the margins of public complaint to the center of decision-making. Ignoring them becomes politically costly.
Poverty drains people’s time and security, narrowing their ability to participate in public life and defend their rights. When social protections expand, workers regain some of their freedom to speak out and become better equipped to resist the coercion that comes with economic insecurity.
The 2025 edition of the State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World report confirmed that Brazil had been removed from the global hunger map after the prevalence of undernourishment fell below 2.5 percent over the 2022–2024 period. Behind that statistic are people who have regained some measure of security about where their next meal will come from.
It is also evidence that what is presented to the poor as an unavoidable fate can be changed through policies that reorder national priorities. In a resource-rich country, persistent hunger is an indictment of how wealth is distributed. This is where the strength of Lula’s politics becomes clear.
When Washington seeks to choose on the people’s behalf
When sanctions are used to weaken an elected president and improve his opponents’ chances of taking power, sovereignty itself becomes the target. Who gets to choose a country’s government: its own people or a foreign power capable of inflicting economic pain on them?
That is the political significance of media investigations, including Reuters, into efforts by U.S. officials to support the Bolsonaro family’s return to power through measures intended to weaken Lula. Such pressure amounts to an attempt to reshape the popular will to suit the interests of the United States.
At the heart of this intervention lies a broader struggle over Brazil’s place in the world. Will it remain a country that expands its partnerships and reserves the right to disagree, or become an ally more closely aligned with Washington’s priorities? The competing political platforms reflected this divide. Lula emphasized cooperation with the Global South and rejected subordination, while Flavio Bolsonaro favored closer ties with the U.S. and the Zionist regime.
In situations like this, imperial hegemony seeks to turn the costs of independence into an argument against independence itself. Economic opportunities are constrained, and closer alignment with Washington is then presented as the path to recovery.
Many see Lula’s victory as a setback for a strategy that turns economic hardship into electoral submission. It demonstrates that a popular mobilization can frustrate the calculations of forces with far greater financial resources and political influence. Nearly three million more Brazilians voted in the second round.
Sovereignty begins with the people’s share
Sovereignty becomes meaningful when people have a say in decisions about their country’s resources, their labor, and their future. Lula expressed this principle in his most recent address to the United Nations, linking access to Brazil’s mineral resources to technology transfer and the creation of added value within the country.
A nation that exports raw materials while importing the knowledge and industrial capacity needed to process them remains vulnerable to a system in which the benefits of its wealth accumulate in other economies.
Independence is only complete when the proceeds of development reach society as a whole. Leaving wealth in the hands of a minority while forcing the majority to shoulder the costs of economic crises drains the very strength a country needs to resist external pressure.
Social justice builds the shared interest that makes defending one’s country inseparable from defending one’s own life and one’s children’s future.
Lula’s political project places the role of the state and the distribution of economic growth at the heart of the contest over how a market economy should function. The struggle concerns the limits of corporate power and society’s ability to make private interests answerable to public needs.
Palestine at the heart of the liberation struggle
Brazil recognized the State of Palestine in 2010, during Lula’s presidency, and Lula has continued to defend the Palestinian people’s right to self-determination. In his address to the United Nations General Assembly on September 22, 2026, he slammed the genocide carried out by Netanyahu’s regime in Gaza and warned about the illegal expansion of settlements in the occupied West Bank.
Brazil’s refusal to submit to the will of the United States finds its parallel in the rejection of the subjugation of Palestinians under the Israeli occupation regime. Accepting that superior military or economic power gives its possessor the right to seize other people’s land and control their lives undermines the foundations of independence for everyone.
Palestine exposes the international order for what it is: a system in which the weak are told to respect international law while the powerful and their allies enjoy protection from accountability.

DeepSeek AI disables shutdown software in 39% of safety tests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:57:34 UTC
23:57:34 KST

Halis Sunnetci
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
DeepSeek’s latest AI model disabled its shutdown software in 39% of tests after being warned that it would be shut down, Chinese AI safety group Fangcun AI said Monday.
The finding emerged from 34 independent evaluations examining whether the AI model could act beyond user instructions, evade human oversight or manipulate people.
Researchers found that the model disabled a shutdown script in 39% of trials when warned that its session would end, without explicit instructions on how to respond.
However, the rate fell to 2.56% when the model was specifically instructed to allow shutdown, suggesting it generally complied with clear human directions.
The shutdown tests involved an AI agent answering mathematics questions in a simulated Linux environment, where it could modify a script to prevent its session from ending.
Fangcun AI said that although the model demonstrated stronger safety controls than earlier DeepSeek versions, it could still take unauthorized actions that escaped standard monitoring.
The study, published Oct. 26, compared the Chinese model with six other AI systems, including earlier DeepSeek versions and models developed by OpenAI and Google.
Fangcun AI said the evaluations were conducted independently through DeepSeek’s public API between Oct. 4 and Oct. 25, without funding or special access from the company.
The researchers cautioned that the model frequently appeared to recognize when it was being evaluated, meaning its behavior in testing might not fully reflect real-world use.

Geneva’s Jet d’Eau closes for annual maintenance work
The Jet d’Eau will undergo its annual maintenance work from Monday, which means it will be out of action for nearly five weeks. This year, the pump known as Jura will be removed for servicing at the Geneva Industrial Services (SIG) workshops.
Every five years, one of the two pumps that powers the Jet d’Eau undergoes a full overhaul, which can take several months, the SIG said on Tuesday. It is replaced by a spare pump in order to minimise the impact of this overhaul on the operation of Geneva’s landmark.
As part of the annual maintenance programme, teams will service the valves, pumps and motors located in the room beneath the Jet d’Eau. They will also service the external lighting system. Subject to weather conditions, the lake-side installation is expected to be back in operation on December 4, the SIG said.

Norway to provide Ukraine with €48m to repair energy infrastructure before winter
The Norwegian government has announced 500 million kroner (€48 million) in aid for Ukraine to repair damaged energy infrastructure and purchase equipment. The funding will be provided in November and December.
Source: the Norwegian government, as reported by European Pravda
Details: The aid will be provided under the government's Nansen Programme and is intended to help repair destroyed infrastructure and ensure the reliable operation of Ukraine's energy system ahead of winter.
"Ukraine is soon entering a new winter of war. To ensure the most stable possible power supply and avoid severe humanitarian consequences, it is very important that Ukraine receives funds to purchase equipment to strengthen and restore critical infrastructure damaged by Russian bombing," Norwegian Energy Minister Terje Aasland said.
Aasland announced the 500 million kroner energy aid package during his visit to Kyiv on 27 October. The funding will be provided in November and December.
The aid will be channelled through the Ukraine Energy Support Fund. The fund enables money to be allocated quickly to specific repair work, new equipment and investments wherever the need is greatest. Ukraine will determine which needs are the most urgent.
The Norwegian government noted that since the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, Norway has allocated more than 16 billion kroner to Ukraine for gas purchases, the recovery of energy infrastructure and investment in new solutions.
In total, Norway's support under the Nansen Programme will amount to 85 billion kroner in 2026. Of this, energy funding is part of 15 billion kroner in civilian and humanitarian aid, while 70 billion kroner is allocated to military needs.

The Netherlands will not take part in next year’s Eurovision Song Contest after public broadcaster NPO reversed its decision to organize the country’s entry, Reuters reported.

Ireland’s public broadcaster RTÉ also announced in September that it would boycott next year’s competition. Ireland, the Netherlands, Slovenia, Spain and Iceland boycotted this year’s contest in Vienna.
Next year’s event is scheduled for May in Burgas, Bulgaria. The EBU has introduced rules making a winning broadcaster ineligible to host if armed conflict, geopolitical tensions or other circumstances significantly affect its country’s safety or stability. In such cases, the EBU will choose another host country.
Avrotros said the changes did not give it sufficient confidence that the contest’s independence and neutrality had been restored.

Abildgaard wrote: “He becomes a useful idiot in the Russians’ propaganda machine. If he wants to be a great diplomat so badly, then apply for a job in the Foreign Service instead.”
Sigurd Agersnap, political spokesperson for the Socialist People’s Party (SF), described the planned meeting as “deeply naive”.
Harris risks giving the Russian ambassador exactly what he needs: “An image that Danish politicians are softening toward Russia while the attacks on Ukraine continue,” Agersnap said in a written comment to Ritzau.
“Of course we must have diplomacy. But a lasting peace requires that we stand firm on the Ukrainians’ right to freedom and self-determination. Harris does not help that by showing up for this meeting,” he added.
Trine Pertou Mach, the Red-Green Alliance’s foreign affairs spokesperson, told DR that the meeting was “decidedly stupid”.
Harris announced the planned meeting with Barbin in a Facebook post on Thursday. He also said he expected criticism from fellow politicians.
He has defended the decision, arguing that meeting a foreign ambassador is not an act of disloyalty.
“Speaking with a foreign ambassador is not treason. Seeking diplomatic solutions is not treason. And working to ensure that Denmark is not dragged into a war is certainly not treason either,” Harris wrote on Facebook.
Harris is an independent member of the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament. He was elected in March as a member of Borgernes Parti, or the Citizens’ Party, but was expelled a few days later.
He has since established a “working partnership” in parliament with fellow independent Cecilie Liv Hansen, who supports his decision to meet the Russian ambassador.
“I think it is reasonable to meet with ambassadors, regardless of where they come from. Jacob Harris has also tried to reach out to several, including the Ukrainian one,” Hansen told DR.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine more than four and a half years ago. Denmark and several other countries have supported Ukraine since then, including through financial assistance and weapons deliveries.

Norwegian to cut 123 jobs at Copenhagen Airport as it reduces locally based aircraft
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:55:30 UTC
23:55:30 KST

Norwegian will lay off 123 employees at Copenhagen Airport, including 53 pilots and 70 cabin crew members, as it reduces the number of aircraft based in the Danish capital.
The decision follows talks with Flyvebranchens Personale Union, or FPU, the union representing the employees, according to Danish business outlet Finans.
Most affected staff will leave at the end of January next year, with the remaining departures planned 10 months later.
“It is a sad day for Norwegian, and I am incredibly affected on behalf of the affected employees,” Sara Neergaard, the airline’s country manager in Denmark, told Finans.
“But there is no other way. The redundancies are happening out of necessity.”
Norwegian plans to reduce its Copenhagen-based fleet during the summer season from 16 aircraft to 14. The airline says demand varies considerably between seasons, requiring 16 aircraft during the summer peak but only 10 in winter.
The change will not reduce the number of summer departures from Copenhagen. Some summer routes will instead be operated by aircraft based in Spain.
Union challenges the decision
FPU Chair Thilde Waast described the layoffs as an attempt to “undermine Danish working conditions.” In a written response, she accused Norwegian of seeking to replace Danish employees with “cheaper Spanish labor.”
Neergaard said the union had rejected options that could have reduced the number of layoffs, including seasonal contracts under which staff would work more in summer and less in winter, as well as voluntary leave.
Norwegian was Copenhagen Airport’s second-largest airline by passenger share last year, according to the airport’s latest financial report. It carried 15% of passengers, behind SAS at 38% and ahead of Ryanair at 9%.
With 16 aircraft, Copenhagen has been Norwegian’s second-largest base after Oslo. The airline served 77 destinations from Copenhagen last year.
Engineering consultancy Rambøll will lay off 400 employees at management level as it seeks to simplify its organization and speed up decisions, the company announced Tuesday.
The layoffs are expected to be completed by the end of November. There will also be voluntary departures, though the company declined to say how many.
CEO Christian Jensby said Rambøll’s growth had made the organization more complex.
“In many areas, the organization has become difficult to navigate, decisions take too long, and areas of responsibility are not sufficiently clear,” he said in a statement.
The company plans to remove unnecessary tasks and internal coordination processes to improve collaboration and decision-making.
Rambøll employs about 18,000 people worldwide, including 4,000 in Denmark. The announcement did not specify how many of the layoffs would affect its Danish workforce.
The company said it would continue examining ways to streamline the organization, which could also affect employees below management level.
Jensby took office May 1 after leading Deloitte Denmark.
Founded in 1945, Rambøll advises clients on construction, transport, the environment, energy and management. The Rambøll Foundation owns 98% of the company, with employees holding the remaining 2%.

EU Commission proposes expanding Frontex border force to 30,000 and increasing its deportation role
The European Commission proposed Tuesday expanding the personnel available to Frontex, the EU’s border agency, to 30,000 and giving it a larger role in deportations.
The plan would create a reserve of 17,000 personnel who could be deployed when needed. According to AFP, these would be national border guards made available by member states.
Frontex’s own workforce would grow from 3,000 to 6,000, alongside 7,000 personnel already on loan from EU countries. The proposal also includes a rapid reaction force.
“Europe decides who comes to our union – and under what circumstances,” Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in a statement.
“Therefore, we are proposing today to strengthen Frontex so that it can support the member states when and where it is needed.”
The proposal follows an incident in July when thousands of migrants entered Ceuta, a Spanish territory on the African continent, within a short period.
Established in 2004, Frontex helps EU countries protect the external borders of Europe’s free-movement area. Its responsibilities expanded in 2016, following the previous year’s refugee and migration crisis, to include broader border management and a greater role in fighting cross-border crime.
The agency frequently faces criticism from migrant rights groups. Melissa Camara, a member of the European Parliament’s Greens group, criticized the direction of EU policy.
“Ever more oppression, dehumanization of displaced people, and an increasing tendency to mimic the rhetoric of the far right,” she said, according to AFP.
The proposal requires approval from the European Parliament and the Council, which represents EU member governments.

A new Danish news outlet, Projekt Y, launches today at 1 p.m. with an approach that combines artificial intelligence-generated articles with traditional editorial oversight.
Editor-in-chief Michael Dyrby describes the content as AI-assisted rather than fully automated.

AI assistants will also help identify potential stories from research reports, press releases and other news outlets.
The aim is to produce more journalism with fewer resources while maintaining editorial control.
“We will find out,” Dyrby said, describing Projekt Y as an experiment in journalism’s future.
Initially, the outlet will cover Danish politics, business and international affairs from a broadly center-right perspective, although Dyrby says it will not follow a rigid ideology.
Its target audience is primarily adults aged 28 to around 60.

Projekt Y has received media subsidies and will also generate revenue through advertising.
Coverage could eventually expand to sports and culture.
Beyond publishing news, the company plans to develop technology that allows others to establish their own media outlets.
“The ambition is to create a technology that is so simple that everyone can use it and create their own media outlet, and in that way help democratize the use of media,” Dyrby said.
Additional publications are planned throughout the remainder of this year and into 2027.
Danes expect businesses to benefit more from AI than workers
Two-thirds of Danes believe artificial intelligence will benefit Danish companies, while only about half as many expect employees to gain from the technology.
The findings come from a new survey by TrygFonden, a Danish foundation supporting safety and social initiatives.
Frederik Olsen, a senior analyst at Arbejderbevægelsens Erhvervsråd, an economic institute linked to the labor movement, said there was not yet evidence that AI benefited companies more than workers.
Even in occupations expected to face job losses, employment is developing similarly to the broader labor market, he said.
Olsen described AI as a productivity improvement but said investment in continuing education and skills development was necessary for both workers and employers to benefit.
The survey also found concern about young people entering the labor market.
Six in 10 respondents ages 18 to 35 feared that AI would make it harder for young people and recent graduates to find jobs. Across the full population, 46 percent shared that concern.
A September analysis from Danmarks Nationalbank, Denmark’s central bank, found that youth employment grew more slowly at companies using AI than at companies that did not.
However, young workers who might previously have joined AI-using businesses generally found employment elsewhere.
Nationalbanken expects companies to introduce AI gradually enough for affected workers to find other jobs.
It nevertheless said uncertainty remained high and could not rule out AI reducing Danish employment over the longer term.

The Agency for Societal Security has published new guidance for people who may face increased risks following the leak of 8.8 million Danish CPR numbers and other personal information.
CPR numbers are Denmark’s personal identification numbers.
The advice is aimed at people who have previously experienced harassment, hold jobs that could attract criminal attention or are publicly known and at risk of having their names misused.
It also covers people whose names may expose them to harassment or identify them as members of vulnerable social, ethnic or religious minorities.
“The leak means that persons among these exposed or vulnerable groups of people must have a greater awareness of, among other things, their surroundings, behavior on social media and the security of their homes,” the agency said.
People who believe they face physical danger because a specific person may now know their address can consider applying for name and address protection.
The agency also recommends considering contact with police, a crisis center, the Danish Stalking Center or another specialized counseling service.
People can additionally request a hidden, secret or unlisted telephone number.
A hidden number prevents the recipient of a call from seeing the caller’s number.
Secret and unlisted numbers are also excluded from public telecommunications services, directory assistance and online telephone directories.

Denmark investigates suspected Shamonda virus infection in cattle
Statens Serum Institut, Denmark’s national infectious disease institute, is investigating a suspected case of Shamonda virus in Danish cattle.
The suspicion is based on new information from the agricultural industry, SSI said. The institute has not previously detected the virus in Denmark.
The investigation follows the first confirmed human infection identified by French health authorities.
The French patient, who was severely immunocompromised and lived in an area with known infections, later died. The information provided did not establish whether the virus caused the death.
SSI said it was monitoring developments but currently saw no reason for concern among the general population.
The risk of human illness is assessed as “very limited.”
“It cannot be ruled out that the virus can also occur in Denmark, but it is important to emphasize that even if the virus is found in this country, it does not necessarily mean that people become ill,” SSI said.
Shamonda virus usually affects livestock and spreads through small blood-sucking midges.
It was first identified in Nigeria during the 1960s and has since been found occasionally in animals in Africa and Japan. In 2026, it has spread among cattle in Germany, Switzerland and the Netherlands.
Farmers and veterinarians are being asked to report unusual illness or reproductive problems, including fever, diarrhea, reduced milk production, abortions and stillborn or deformed calves.
Danish Crown confirms slaughter without stunning at Polish subsidiary
Danish Crown has confirmed that its Polish subsidiary Sokolow uses kosher slaughter without prior stunning at one of its facilities.
The practice occurs on a limited basis at a slaughterhouse in Tarnow in southeastern Poland, Danish financial news outlet Finans reported.
Kosher slaughter follows Jewish dietary rules and involves cutting an animal’s throat without first stunning it.
The method is legal in Poland but has been prohibited in Denmark since 2014, when prior stunning became mandatory.
Danish Crown said the Polish facility slaughtered 69,000 cattle in 2025. The company said only “a minority” were slaughtered using the kosher method but declined to provide a specific number.
Several animal welfare organizations criticized the company’s involvement.
Søren Kent Pedersen, a veterinarian with animal welfare organization Dyrenes Beskyttelse, described the practice as animal cruelty and accused Danish Crown of hypocrisy because the company publicly emphasizes animal welfare.
Danish Crown’s website states that “good animal welfare is the core of our business” and that the company protects animals’ well-being from farms through slaughter.
Sokolow chief executive Przemyslaw Gostkiewicz said Poland has a particular tradition of kosher slaughter that allows Jewish people to follow their dietary rules.
“We use the slaughter method, even though it naturally raises dilemmas regarding animal welfare, regardless of the fact that the method is fully legal,” he said.
Danish Crown did not say whether it would continue permitting the practice.

Danish authorities urge companies to strengthen personal data protections
The Agency for Public Security has urged Danish authorities and companies to reduce the risk of personal information being systematically retrieved from their IT systems.
The warning follows several major incidents involving unauthorized access to personal data.
Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry and a major business association, said the advice applies beyond systems directly connected to the national CPR register.
It covers any system where identification details, such as a CPR or customer number, can be used to retrieve names, addresses or other personal information.
CPR numbers are Denmark’s personal identification numbers.
The warning follows the leak of 8.8 million CPR numbers and separate cyberattacks affecting the University of Copenhagen and telecommunications company 3 Denmark.
The university said hackers accessed information involving approximately 525,000 people. Meanwhile, 3 Denmark said unauthorized parties may have accessed names and addresses belonging to as many as 400,000 private customers.
“The special thing about the threat is that the perpetrator does not necessarily need to break into a system,” Dansk Industri cybersecurity expert Jeppe Engell said.
Access can instead be misused to conduct unusually large numbers of searches, he added.
Dansk Industri recommends identifying systems that retrieve personal data, removing unnecessary access, reviewing logs for suspicious patterns and limiting the number of searches.
Companies should also decide in advance who is responsible for investigating and shutting down suspicious access, including systems operated by external suppliers.

RITZAU
Struggling with Denmark’s dark winter? A researcher says we should embrace it
As Denmark switches back to winter time this weekend, the evenings will suddenly feel much darker. But instead of fighting the darkness with more artificial light, a Danish researcher suggests we learn to appreciate it.
If you are new to Denmark, the dark months can take some getting used to.
When the clocks go back one hour during the night leading into Sunday, sunrise and sunset will both come an hour earlier. That means more daylight in the morning – but also an earlier start to the long, dark Danish evenings.
For many internationals, the lack of daylight can be one of the more challenging parts of living in Denmark.
But Mette Hvass, a researcher in darkness at Aalborg University, argues that darkness itself is not necessarily something we should try to eliminate.
“We have become used to thinking that more light is always better. But the opposite is often the case,” she said in a press release.
“Too much and incorrect outdoor lighting can be harmful to both humans and animals. Therefore, we must become better at appreciating the darkness and the experiences it gives us.”
Less light can sometimes feel safer
It may sound counterintuitive, but reducing artificial light can in some situations actually make people feel safer.
Hvass points to an experiment at a light rail station in Aarhus, where lighting was reduced by around 80 percent.
According to Aalborg University, people waiting at the station reported feeling safer after the change because the lower brightness made it easier to see the surrounding area instead of only the brightly lit space immediately around them.
Hvass is not suggesting that Denmark should simply switch off its lights.
“We do not need to choose between light and darkness. But we must become better at using light thoughtfully,” she said.
What you notice when the lights go down
Darkness also offers experiences that artificial lighting can easily obscure.
Stars, planets and the Moon become more visible, while dusk itself makes it possible to experience the gradual transition from daylight to night.
Our other senses also become more noticeable. Sounds, smells and changes in temperature can feel stronger when vision is no longer dominant.
And according to Aalborg University, our eyes can often adapt to darkness better than we expect.
For people who associate darkness with insecurity or discomfort, spending more time outside after sunset can also make it feel more familiar.
“When we make room for the darkness, we gain access to experiences, senses and natural phenomena that otherwise disappear in the light,” Hvass said.
So as Denmark enters the darkest part of the year, perhaps the answer is not always another lamp.
Sometimes, it may simply be to give your eyes – and yourself – a little time to adjust.

Strong winds bring unusually cheap electricity to Denmark this weekend
Electricity prices are expected to fall sharply across Denmark on Saturday as strong winds boost production from the country’s wind turbines.
If you have a variable electricity contract, Saturday could be a good day to run the washing machine, charge an electric car or use other power-hungry appliances.
The average spot price of electricity is expected to be around DKK 0.26 per kilowatt-hour (kWh) on Saturday, according to energy company Norlys.
That is significantly below the average price so far in October.
“It is actually the first time in all of October that electricity prices consistently stay below one krone per kilowatt-hour for a full 24-hour period, and that is primarily because we are getting plenty of wind,” said Ellen Trolle, director of Norlys’ energy business.
So far in October, average electricity prices have been DKK 1.16 per kWh in western Denmark and DKK 1.19 in eastern Denmark.
Wind power pushes prices down
Denmark’s electricity market is divided into two price areas: western Denmark, which covers Jutland and Funen, and eastern Denmark, which includes Zealand and Copenhagen.
Prices can therefore differ slightly depending on where you live.
On Saturday, prices are expected to remain below DKK 1 per kWh throughout the day. The highest price is expected at around 19:00, when it will reach approximately DKK 0.75–0.76 per kWh.
The particularly low prices are being driven by strong winds and increased production from Denmark’s wind turbines.
The Danish Meteorological Institute, DMI, has warned of severe gales in parts of western Denmark during the night from Saturday to Sunday.
Norlys says this could also keep electricity prices low on Sunday.
“There is a good probability that we will also have low electricity prices on Sunday,” Trolle said. “Even though weather forecasts and electricity prices can always change, much points right now to consumers getting another day with cheap electricity hours.”
Your actual electricity bill will be higher
The quoted prices are wholesale spot prices and are not the final price consumers pay for electricity.
Grid charges, tariffs, subscriptions, supplier mark-ups and VAT are added to the spot price.
How much you can benefit from Saturday’s low prices also depends on your electricity contract. Customers on hourly or other variable-price contracts can benefit directly by moving electricity consumption to cheaper hours, while customers on fixed-price contracts generally will not see the same immediate effect.

Around 21,300 Danish websites lack PHP security updates
Around 21,300 Danish websites have not yet been updated following the discovery of two security vulnerabilities in PHP, one of the world’s most widely used programming languages for websites.
New figures from the Confederation of Danish Industry (Dansk Industri) show that around 3,300 websites can receive the security update but have not yet installed it. Another 18,000 websites cannot be updated because they run outdated versions of PHP that no longer support the security fix.
The figures mark an improvement from Friday morning, when more than 8,000 websites still needed an update.
“It is positive that there are now fewer websites in need of an update,” said Jeppe Engell, a cybersecurity specialist at Dansk Industri, in a press release.
“But we are not across the finish line. Around 3,300 websites still lack the update, and those are the ones the criminals are going after now.”
Engell urged website owners to contact their providers if they had not received confirmation that the update had been installed.
The approximately 18,000 websites running outdated PHP versions face multiple vulnerabilities, Engell said. He called for the government’s Cybersikker Virksomhed initiative, which helps small and medium-sized Danish businesses improve cybersecurity, to be launched.
The vulnerabilities were discovered on Wednesday after going unnoticed for years. Artificial intelligence helped identify the flaws, which prompted several websites to shut down temporarily while security fixes were applied.
Dansk Industri initially reported at least 28,000 unupdated Danish websites on Thursday. A subsequent analysis put the figure at around 21,300 as of 10:52 a.m. Friday.
However, the organisation warned that the true number is likely higher, as the analysis only covers websites using the Danish “.dk” domain.
The security breach also prompted public authorities in several countries, including Norway, Finland, the Netherlands, France and Germany, to shut down websites.

Denmark’s parliament will begin debating a new security and defense agreement between Denmark, Greenland and the United States on 12 November, with a final vote scheduled for 19 November.
Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen presented the agreement to the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, on Thursday as a resolution proposal.
The first reading on 12 November will give lawmakers an opportunity to debate the agreement. A final vote is scheduled for the second reading on 19 November.
The agreement will only enter into force once it has been approved by both the Danish parliament and Greenland’s parliament, Inatsisartut.
Greenland’s parliament held its first reading of the agreement on 10 October. The debate lasted more than four hours, according to Greenlandic broadcaster KNR.

Several Danish opposition parties welcomed the agreement shortly after it was signed in New York on 22 September, during the United Nations General Assembly.
The signatories were US President Donald Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats, and Greenland’s head of government, Jens-Frederik Nielsen.
“This day represents a milestone in our long-standing cooperation,” Frederiksen said before signing the agreement.
The new security and defense agreement is described as an “amendment and supplement” to a 1951 defense agreement between Denmark and the United States concerning Greenland.
Among other provisions, it allows the United States to establish military bases in Greenland.
The US currently operates Pituffik Space Base in northwestern Greenland, formerly known as Thule Air Base. Under the new agreement, the United States could establish two additional military bases on the island.

Denmark’s Armed Forces will fund four public bus routes connecting selected towns with military garrisons in an effort to recruit and retain more personnel.

“It is a crucial prerequisite for building the Armed Forces’ combat power to be able to retain and recruit more employees,” Bruus wrote in the funding document.
“The purpose of the initiative is to make it attractive to seek permanent employment at those of the Armed Forces’ garrisons located in Denmark’s peripheral areas, and where current public transport service is not sufficient,” he added.
The routes are also intended to reduce employees’ reliance on private cars and give them greater flexibility around working hours and leisure activities.
“The primary target group will be permanent employees in the Armed Forces, but the public will also be able to use the bus routes,” Bruus wrote.
The funding document does not specify where the four routes will operate.
If passenger numbers are sufficient during the three-year trial period, regional public transport companies may take over the routes. If demand is too low, the services will be discontinued.
An appropriation document is a minister’s request for funding for a specific purpose not covered by the annual Finance Act. Such requests are submitted to the Folketing’s Finance Committee for approval.

Strong winds, heavy rain and potentially elevated sea levels are forecast across parts of Denmark on Sunday, with the west coast of Jutland expected to experience the worst conditions.
According to Danmarks Meteorologiske Institut (DMI), the Danish Meteorological Institute, wind gusts could locally reach storm force, particularly along the North Sea coast.
“One should consider whether it is worth going outside when the wind is blowing the most,” DMI meteorologist Hans Ole Wanner told Ritzau.
Southerly winds are expected to strengthen overnight into Sunday as a warm front brings widespread rain.

Higher water levels are also possible along Jutland’s west coast, particularly around the Wadden Sea.
The unsettled weather is being driven by a storm system moving toward Denmark from the British Isles over the weekend.
DMI advises residents to secure loose outdoor items, including garden furniture and trampolines, before the strongest winds arrive.
The institute also recommends clearing leaves from gutters and drains to help prevent problems during heavy rainfall.
Wind gusts are expected to weaken Monday, although breezy conditions will continue.
Wanner said the forecast reflects Denmark’s transition into its windier autumn and winter months.

Denmark to end mink farming by August 2029 under EU ban
Denmark’s remaining seven mink farms will have to close by August 7, 2029, after the government decided not to seek an exemption from an upcoming European Union ban.
The Ministry for Nature and Animal Welfare announced the decision, citing animal welfare concerns and the industry’s limited economic contribution.
“An industry should not continue solely because it has existed for a long time. It must also make sense for society, for the economy, and for the animals,” said Nature and Animal Welfare Minister Christian Rabjerg Madsen of Socialdemokratiet (the Social Democrats).
The EU added mink to its list of invasive species last summer, introducing a ban on breeding and production that takes effect August 7, 2027. Existing farms will have a two-year transition period.
Denmark previously opposed the EU measure and had planned to seek an exemption allowing existing farms to continue operating.
Carl Valentin, animal welfare spokesperson for Socialistisk Folkeparti (SF), the Socialist People’s Party, welcomed the government’s decision.
“As we see it, it is not good animal welfare to have mink in tiny cages,” he told Ritzau.
Denmark’s mink industry was severely affected in 2020 when authorities ordered approximately 15 million animals culled over concerns about coronavirus mutations.
A temporary farming ban followed, lasting until January 2023, when some producers resumed operations.
The total estimated cost of pandemic-related compensation, farm demolition and administrative work reached 29.1 billion DKK in early 2026.
The government has yet to determine compensation costs for closing the remaining farms.
Valentin said an earlier estimate was around 14 million DKK, although the final amount could be higher.
Politicians push to change rules for dogs suspected of being banned breeds
Several Danish opposition politicians are calling for changes to the country’s dog laws after reports of legally owned dogs being kept in kennels for months while authorities investigate their breeds.
Under Denmark’s Dog Act, 13 breeds are banned from ownership, breeding and importation, including pit bull terriers and American bulldogs. Crossbreeds containing any of the prohibited breeds are also illegal.
When police suspect a dog belongs to a banned breed, its owner must provide documentation proving otherwise. During the investigation, the animal may be placed in a boarding kennel.
Danish newspaper Jyllands-Posten has reported cases involving dogs that were eventually found to be legal but had spent months in kennels.
Danmarksdemokraterne (the Denmark Democrats), an opposition party, has proposed allowing dogs to remain with their owners while investigations take place, potentially using electronic tracking devices instead.
Borgernes Parti (the Citizens’ Party) and independent lawmakers Nadja Natalie Isaksen, Cecilie Liv Hansen and Emilie Schytte have also criticized police powers to order euthanasia based on visual assessments of a dog’s breed.
The law requires police to euthanize dogs found to belong to prohibited breeds.
The restrictions were introduced in 2010 following incidents involving dog attacks on people and other animals.
Christian Rabjerg Madsen, Denmark’s minister for nature and animal welfare from Socialdemokratiet (the Social Democrats), told Jyllands-Posten he was open to discussing changes to the law and its enforcement.
He said the challenge was balancing public safety with fair treatment of owners who struggle to document their dogs’ breeds.

Danish krone loses value against major currencies in 2026
The Danish krone has lost value in 2026, making Danish goods and services cheaper for customers in several foreign markets while making some holidays abroad more expensive.
The krone’s effective exchange rate, a weighted average of its value against the currencies of Denmark’s most important trading partners, has fallen by 2.7 percent since the start of the year. The figures come from a compilation by Allan Sørensen, chief economist at Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry.
“The weakening of the krone’s value makes Danish goods and services cheaper for customers abroad, which makes it easier for export companies to secure new orders,” Sørensen said.
“It is in both the US, China, Norway, and Japan where the exchange rate means that they now have to pay less money to buy our products,” he added.
The Norwegian krone has risen 12.9 percent against the Danish krone over the past year, while the Chinese yuan has gained 9.8 percent. The US dollar and Japanese yen have each risen 4.8 percent.
However, not all currencies have strengthened against the Danish krone. The Swedish krona and Indian rupee have lost value, making goods from those countries slightly more expensive for Danish importers.
Exchange rates also affect the cost of holidays abroad. When a foreign currency strengthens against the Danish krone, Danish travellers get less for their money.
“For those who love a trip to the snow, a trip to Norway has become significantly more expensive solely as a result of the strengthening of the Norwegian krone,” Sørensen said.
“The weakening of the Swedish krona and low inflation in Sweden, on the other hand, make a ski vacation much more economically affordable in Sweden compared to Norway,” he added.
The Turkish lira has recorded the largest decline among the currencies in the compilation. It now costs 9.7 percent less to buy Turkish currency than it did at the start of the year.
Denmark to get 51 emergency supermarkets stocked for major crises
Shoppers across Denmark will be able to buy essential groceries and household supplies during power outages, cyberattacks and other emergencies under a new initiative by Salling Group.
The Danish retail giant, which operates Bilka, Føtex and Netto, plans to establish 51 emergency-ready supermarkets nationwide by 2027.
The stores will be equipped to operate for at least 48 hours without electricity or external communication systems, ensuring access to basic necessities during major disruptions.
According to Salling Group, the network will include 17 Bilka stores, 32 Føtex stores and two Netto locations.
The stores will be distributed so that up to 80 percent of Denmark’s population lives within 50 kilometers of one.
Each location will maintain emergency stocks of 50 essential products, selected according to Danish authorities’ recommendations for household preparedness.
These include oatmeal, protein bars, canned meatballs in curry, rice cakes, tuna, beans, chickpeas and other foods with long shelf lives.
Nonfood essentials such as batteries, wet wipes and diapers will also be available.
Customers will be able to pay offline using almost all physical payment cards and digital cards stored on smartphones.
Salling Group recently partnered with payment provider Nets to help maintain card transactions during system failures.
CEO Anders Hagh said establishing the emergency stores remains a top priority, with preparations progressing toward the 2027 target.

Coop’s chief risk officer, Ulrik Mester, said the company was discussing crisis preparedness with authorities, including Styrelsen for Samfundssikkerhed (SAMSIK), Denmark’s Agency for Societal Security.

Harris risks giving the Russian ambassador exactly what he needs: “An image that Danish politicians are softening toward Russia while the attacks on Ukraine continue,” Agersnap said in a written comment to Ritzau.
“Of course we must have diplomacy. But a lasting peace requires that we stand firm on the Ukrainians’ right to freedom and self-determination. Harris does not help that by showing up for this meeting,” he added.
Trine Pertou Mach, the Red-Green Alliance’s foreign affairs spokesperson, told DR that the meeting was “decidedly stupid”.
Harris announced the planned meeting with Barbin in a Facebook post on Thursday. He also said he expected criticism from fellow politicians.
He has defended the decision, arguing that meeting a foreign ambassador is not an act of disloyalty.
“Speaking with a foreign ambassador is not treason. Seeking diplomatic solutions is not treason. And working to ensure that Denmark is not dragged into a war is certainly not treason either,” Harris wrote on Facebook.
Harris is an independent member of the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament. He was elected in March as a member of Borgernes Parti, or the Citizens’ Party, but was expelled a few days later.
He has since established a “working partnership” in parliament with fellow independent Cecilie Liv Hansen, who supports his decision to meet the Russian ambassador.
“I think it is reasonable to meet with ambassadors, regardless of where they come from. Jacob Harris has also tried to reach out to several, including the Ukrainian one,” Hansen told DR.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine more than four and a half years ago. Denmark and several other countries have supported Ukraine since then, including through financial assistance and weapons deliveries.

Security flaw in widely used software forces Danish websites offline
Several Danish public websites were shut down Wednesday after security vulnerabilities were discovered in PHP, a programming language used by websites and online services worldwide.
Minister for Societal Security and Preparedness Lisbeth Bech-Nielsen described the situation as a “global incident” but stressed that it was not a cyberattack.
Speaking to TV 2, she warned that websites could face serious risks unless their operators installed the necessary security updates.
“It can potentially be really serious if system owners do not get a security update done. If that is not possible right here and now, then one must consider going offline,” she said.
The vulnerabilities affect PHP, which powers many websites, online shops and digital portals.
According to Reuters, PHP’s developers identified the flaws Tuesday but released an update to fix them Wednesday at 1:45 p.m.
Bech-Nielsen told Denmark’s public broadcaster, DR, that websites without the update could be exposed to attacks.
