Analysis: Why are Arab parties being ruled out of Israel’s next government, despite having served in a coalition before?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:23:49 UTC
23:23:49 KST

- i24NEWS
- Israel Elections
- Why can’t Arab parties sit in Israel’s next coalition? - Analysis
Why can’t Arab parties sit in Israel’s next coalition? - Analysis
“I get very upset when I hear politicians say that after October 7th, it is impossible to rely on the Arabs to form a coalition. We all experienced October 7th; Arabs and Jews alike were murdered."
“I get very upset when I hear Bennett, Lapid, or Eisenkot—or anyone else, for that matter—say that after October 7th, it is impossible to rely on the Arabs to form a coalition. And I ask: Why?”
This question, raised by Arab-Israeli political analyst Mohammad Magadli in a recent podcast, is also being asked by hundreds of thousands of Israel’s Arab citizens ahead of Tuesday’s elections.
Magadli continued: “Was there a single Arab citizen who participated in the October 7th attack? The answer is no. Was there anyone among the Arab political leadership who did not come out to condemn, denounce, and express shock—stating clearly that they condemn it? We all experienced October 7th; Arabs and Jews alike were murdered, and Arabs were taken hostage—we were part of this. Furthermore, in the subsequent wars—with Hezbollah and Iran—there were both wounded and fatalities from within the Arab community.”
The top contender to replace Prime Minister Netanyahu, Gadi Eisenkot, has set three conditions for any party joining his coalition: accepting Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, the values of the Declaration of Independence, and a duty of service, military or civilian.
He has since added a fourth: the next government’s basic guidelines, he said, will state that whoever does not accept that Hamas is a terrorist organization that must be dismantled will not be a partner. “And therefore,” he concluded, “I do not see an Arab party that accepts my principles.”
The head of the Ra’am party, Mansour Abbas, has accepted Israel’s Jewish character, albeit as “a fact imposed on us.” He has also backed a voluntary, Arab-led civic service with no military ties, though he opposes the existing national-service framework. The other Arab parties have not voiced support for civilian service, so this article will not discuss the prospect of their participation in the coalition.
But Abbas has repeatedly declined to publicly call Hamas a terror organization, a decision that has raised suspicion from many Jewish voters. Earlier this month, a member of his party, Yasser Hujirat, was asked in an interview whether Hamas was a terrorist organization. “This organization—part of which is essentially a charitable organization—also has a component that seeks to gain the right to exist and the right to be recognized as a state,” was his response.
As for Abbas himself, when asked a few months ago in a radio interview about his position regarding Hamas, Abbas replied: “I have an unequivocal answer, but I won’t state it. I am constantly receiving threats from Arabs, Jews, and criminal organizations.”
Abbas added: “We have condemned every act of terror and all the crimes that took place on October 7th—not only from a civilian perspective, but also from an Islamic religious perspective… None of us should be subjected to such a loyalty test. It is the wrong approach. People constantly fall into this trap set by extremists in Israel.”
Refraining from calling Hamas a terror organization is not a good look in Israel of 2026, especially ahead of the first national elections since the October 7 massacre. But making that the ultimate test of loyalty and a prerequisite to receiving a ‘kosher stamp’ to be part of the ruling coalition ignores reality, precedent, and deep sensitivities in Israeli society.
It ignores reality because if Eisenkot’s full “Zionism test” were to be applied on some of the current coalition parties, such as the ultra-orthodox, they would fail the test. It ignores precedent as Ra’am was already part of the coalition in 2021.
It ignores the deep sensitivities in Israeli society as many of Israel’s 21% Arab population consider themselves Palestinians, others have family in Gaza and the West Bank, and others consider themselves Zionists. Some Arab families will have all these identities living under one roof.
So the test should be in action. When Ra’am was in the coalition, it did not block a single military operation. Even when it froze its membership over the 2022 Temple Mount clashes, it returned. And since then, Ra’am has announced its separation from the Islamic Movement, which has been accused of having ties to the Muslim Brotherhood.
And what do the Arabs want? According to a May poll by Tel Aviv University, 77.2% of Arab Israelis said an Arab party should join the next government, and 75.8% supported voluntary civilian national service for Arab graduates.
As for the Jewish population, a majority of opposition voters favor forming a government supported by an Arab party, if the anti-Netanyahu bloc fails to win a majority on its own.
If the only thing that has changed from the previous time an Arab party sat in the coalition was the October 7 massacre, which saw no involvement by Israel’s Arab population, sorry, but that’s not enough
So what is really keeping them out? Magadli has his own answer:
"So, where does the problem lie? This is where the whole story begins: if it had served Benjamin Netanyahu's political interest—in terms of forming a government—to portray the Arabs as the heroes of this war, I can tell you that they would have become heroes. Those who stepped up, those who took part, those who helped, and those who suffered casualties—it simply does not align with Benjamin Netanyahu's political interests."

What to expect from the Fed as Warsh weighs hot inflation, oil and US midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:23:30 UTC
23:23:30 KST

The Federal Reserve is expected to keep interest rates on hold on Wednesday, six days before the US midterm elections, but with inflation at 3.7% and oil prices still elevated, investors see another hike in December as likely and will scour Chair Kevin Warsh's words for clues.
When the Federal Reserve announces its decision at 19:00 CET on Wednesday, it is widely expected to leave its benchmark rate unchanged at 3.75% to 4%, less than a week before Americans vote in the midterms.
However, with inflation at 3.7%, energy prices at the highs and another hike in December seen as likely, investors will be watching Fed Chair Kevin Warsh closely for clues about what comes next.
Markets put the chance of a hold at over 90%, but see a 73% chance of a quarter-point hike at the Fed's 8-9 December meeting, according to CME Group's FedWatch tool, which tracks interest rate futures.
That would follow September's increase, the Fed's first in three years. Since then, several senior officials have played down the urgency of moving again.
Vice Chair Philip Jefferson pointed in a speech to the jump in longer-term borrowing costs, adding that "my colleagues and I will need to come to our own judgment, which may take more time".
New York Fed President John Williams reiterated the same sentiment in a speech at the University at Buffalo stating that "there is no need for urgency".
Politics looms too.
"The Fed doesn’t want to poke the White House in the eye six days before an election,” said Joseph LaVorgna, chief economist at Japanese bank SMBC's US arm and a former Trump administration official.
Not everyone may go along.
Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack and Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan, who both say rates are not yet high enough to cool inflation, could vote for a hike, and as many as three officials could dissent.
Inflation runs hot as growth holds up
The case for tighter policy remains. US consumer prices rose 3.7% in September from a year earlier, up from 3.4% in August, while core inflation, which strips out food and energy, rose to 2.6%. Wholesale prices jumped 6.3%.
Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee stated the reading was "discouraging", saying underlying inflation at today's level was "not acceptable".
Petrol, which has topped $4 a gallon for the past three months, accounted for over half of September's price increase, according to the US Labor Department. Diesel hit a record $6.53 a gallon in late September, raising the cost of shipping almost everything.
Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, fell over 6% on Monday, from about $117.4 a barrel, its highest close since 19 March, as diplomacy over the Iran war seemingly gathered pace.
At the time of writing on Tuesday, it traded at roughly $110.8 a barrel, still far above the $72 it fetched before the Iran war began in late February.
Borrowing costs are biting too.
The average 30-year US mortgage rate hit 7.4% in early October, a three-year peak, before easing to 7.32% last week, against just under 6.2% a year ago. Research firm Oxford Economics estimates this year’s rise has priced 5 million more American households out of buying a home.
Expectations of further hikes have also kept the US dollar close to an 18-month high against major currencies.
The economy, meanwhile, is bending rather than breaking.
Employers added just 29,000 jobs in September and unemployment rose to 4.2%, yet the US economy grew at an annualised 2.2% in the second quarter, and the Atlanta Fed’s GDPNow tracker points to 3.5% for the third.
The next test comes straight after the decision.
On Thursday at 13:30 CET, the US publishes its first estimate of third-quarter growth and September data for the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index.
"Fed officials still appear broadly intent on tightening policy at a measured pace," Thomas Ryan, senior North America economist at Capital Economics, wrote in a note.
All eyes on Warsh
Warsh, who will speak to reporters at 19:30 CET, has offered few hints.
Speaking in Bangkok at the International Monetary Fund and World Bank annual meetings this month, he said the world had "broadly conformed to our expectations" since September.
"I don’t prejudge meetings," Warsh said while stressing that "at the Federal Reserve, we made very clear that we would deliver price stability."
He has long expressed opposition to forward guidance, the practice of signalling future moves to the markets, and has avoided it.
Aditya Bhave, head of US economics research at Bank of America, said a surprise hike could "end forward guidance by showing markets that they can't listen to the guidance anymore," though most economists doubt it.
The Fed Chair's independence is also under scrutiny.
Warsh defied US President Donald Trump's calls for lower rates in September, but Trump later said he had told Warsh he "might as well" vote for a hike, and has since stepped up his push to remove Fed Governor Lisa Cook.
Trump created a three-person committee to recommend whether he has cause to fire Cook over mortgage fraud allegations she denies. Cook is expected to appear before the committee next week.
As for Warsh, if his speech focuses on the fact that inflation must return to the Fed's 2% target faster, investors will likely read it as the confirmation for a December hike.

Polish cities mull cutting Ukraine ties over Nazi collaborators

Polish cities mull cutting Ukraine ties over Nazi collaborators
Several Polish cities have suspended or are considering cutting ties with Ukraine’s Lviv Region over a proclamation honoring Ukrainian nationalist forces that collaborated with Nazi Germany during World War II.
Last week, Lviv Region dedicated 2027 to the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), its commander Roman Shukhevich and nationalist activist Oleg Olzhich. The militia is loathed in Poland over its role in the slaughter of tens of thousands of Polish civilians during World War II in pursuit of an ethnically homogeneous Ukrainian state.
The government of Vladimir Zelensky has distanced itself from the move, even though the Ukrainian leader played a direct role in selecting nationalist figures for state-organized reburial in Kiev earlier this year.
The Przemysl City Council voted unanimously on Monday to suspend its partnership with Lviv. All 21 participating councilors backed the measure, arguing that the commemoration insulted the memory of UPA victims and warranted steps toward terminating the partnership agreement signed in 1995. Mayor Wojciech Bakun said the council “will not remain indifferent to provocative and anti-Polish actions.”
Similar proposals have been raised in Krakow, Wroclaw and Lublin.
Lublin Mayor Krzysztof Zuk opposed severing ties with Lviv, arguing that while he considered “publicly honoring a formation whose units committed mass crimes against Polish civilians” unacceptable, the decision had been taken by the Lviv Regional Council rather than the separate municipal authorities of the city of Lviv.
The Lublin Voivodeship, by contrast, has terminated its partnership with Lviv Region.
The original proclamation has since disappeared from the regional council’s website, but no formal retraction has followed. Lviv Mayor Andrey Sadovy and the city council have not publicly taken a position on the controversy.
The Polish-Ukrainian row over historic grudges reignited in May, when Zelensky granted an elite Ukrainian military unit the honorific “of heroes of the UPA.” The Ukrainian leader was subsequently stripped of Poland’s highest state distinction, becoming only the second person to lose the award.
Ukraine has also moved this year to establish a national pantheon of prominent historical figures. Leaders associated with the UPA and its political movement, the Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists, were the first selected for state reburial in January. Aleksandr Alferov, head of the Ukrainian Institute of National Memory said earlier this month that Zelensky personally determined the first five candidates.
The nationalist ideology associated with the OUN and UPA envisioned an authoritarian Ukrainian state headed by a supreme national leader-for-life and placed ethnic identity at the center of political life. Zelensky’s Jewish background would have disqualified him from the position under the proposed system.
Ukrainian ultranationalist militias played a critical role in the Western-backed coup in Kiev in 2014 and have since pushed for broader acceptance of their agenda. Moscow has cited legal restrictions affecting the Russian language and culture, as well as pressure on the Ukrainian Orthodox Church, which has spiritual ties to Moscow, as proof that modern Ukraine is captured by neo-Nazis.

Military matters are one thing, but the people who live there and continue to live there are another. In this respect, the experience could also prove valuable in organizational terms," Saldo said.
He added that the humanitarian operation in Alyoshki had been made possible through the efforts of Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova and President Vladimir Putin.
"This sustained effort may have paved the way for the first step toward achieving - or at least pursuing - mutual understanding on humanitarian issues concerning the people affected," the governor emphasized.
At 4:00 a.m. Moscow time (1:00 a.m. GMT) on October 27, Russian forces established a "regime of silence," or ceasefire, along the Kherson front to facilitate preparations for the humanitarian operation in Alyoshki.
Russia and Ukraine had previously agreed, with the assistance of US First Lady Melania Trump, to a ceasefire in the town to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and prepare for the evacuation of civilians through a designated secure corridor.
On September 21, Russian Presidential Press Secretary Dmitry Peskov described the humanitarian situation in Alyoshki as critical, saying that shelling and drone attacks by Ukrainian forces had made it impossible to deliver food and medical supplies to the town.
Of the approximately 20,000 people who once lived in Alyoshki, just over 1,000 remain, according to the report.

IN BRIEF: Key statements by Russian Deputy PM Novak at GECF summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:21:01 UTC
23:21:01 KST

MOSCOW, October 27. /TASS/. The position taken by some American politicians against the diesel deal with Russia is a bit surprising, as they are not acting in the best interests of their own citizens, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak told reporters on the sidelines of the GECF summit.
In particular, Novak announced that a fourth tanker carrying diesel is set to depart from Russia on October 28.
He also noted that liquefied natural gas (LNG) costs more for China than natural gas supplied from Russia.
TASS has compiled the key statements made by the deputy prime minister.
Diesel shipments to the US
Russia has already dispatched three tankers carrying diesel to the US, and they are currently en route: "There are three ships at the moment. The fourth has not yet departed."
A fourth diesel tanker is scheduled to depart from Russia on October 28: "We expect it to leave on the 28th."
American politicians who have come out in opposition of the diesel deal with Russia are doing their citizens a disservice: "Overall, it is certainly surprising to see the stance taken by Democrats, who speak out – or even take action – in a way that is not in the best interests of the residents of the United States of America."
On resumption of gas supplies to Europe
Russia is ready to resume gas supplies to Europe if European nations wish to do so: "For our part, we are ready. We have always been reliable suppliers."
Russia is capable of redirecting its entire gas volume to other markets if Europe rejects it: "If Europe chooses not to buy, we have destinations to sell our gas. You are aware that in recent years we have developed infrastructure to supply countries where consumption is actively increasing and economies are growing. Consequently, Russia faces no issues in this regard, the problem lies more with Europe."
Overpaying for LNG
Liquefied natural gas (LNG) is more costly for China than natural gas sourced from Russia: "From an economic perspective, it is currently far more expensive for them. In the face of gas shortages and a lack of affordable energy resources, consumers end up overpaying due to shortages and rising prices, buying more expensive liquefied natural gas with longer logistical costs and so on."
On future of the Nord Stream pipelines
In the long term, the Nord Stream pipelines will be needed by Europe for gas supplies: "Looking ahead, the development of gas pipeline infrastructure - which began in the 1970s and has continued into this century - is beneficial for both Europe and Russia. Russia is energy-independent and has the capacity to ensure the energy security of other countries that lack their own energy resources, Europe in particular. Therefore, I believe that from a long-term, strategic perspective, these pipelines will likely remain in demand."

Ukrainian comms and Danish space firms launch test military-purpose communications satellite into orbit
The Ukrainian company Himera and Denmark's GomSpace have launched Obria Nano, the first test satellite for a future independent Ukrainian communications network, into orbit. Its operation has already begun.
Source: Himera in a comment to Ukrainska Pravda
Details: Himera stated that the satellite was launched as part of the SpaceX Transporter-18 mission on 1 October 2026. It is successfully undergoing planned tests of the Obria satellite group's capabilities.
"The technical trials should provide the practical experience needed for the project's further development into a Ukrainian national infrastructure," the company explained.
The company emphasised that reliance on foreign technologies creates strategic risks, especially in wartime. The Ukrainian developer is convinced that building domestic capabilities will help the country diversify its communication channels and enhance strategic security.
Himera stressed that Obria Nano will be controlled by a Ukrainian operator and will serve Ukraine's strategic security needs.
The company added that the initiative eventually plans to deploy a satellite network that will provide communication coverage across the entire territory of Ukraine, as well as complement the capabilities of European satellite networks. This will lay the groundwork for an independent Ukrainian satellite communications system operating in the interests of national strategic security.
"An important next step will be the localisation of satellite and ground terminal production in Ukraine. This will allow us to develop our own expertise in satellite communications and gradually increase Ukrainian production capacity," Himera noted.
Background:
- Ukrainian company Himera is a well-known developer of secure communication systems. The company recently reported that its Himera G1 PRO radios and Himera B1 repeater were tested by personnel from a unit of Defence Intelligence of Ukraine.
- GomSpace is an international provider of small satellite solutions, with clients in over 60 countries.

The company is also working on a redesigned low-end MacBook Pro and the release of its first M7, M7 Pro and M7 Max chips in 2027. It is planning an M7 Ultra and a new Mac Studio in 2028.
Apple’s overhauled MacBook Pro with a touchscreen – coming on Oct 28 – will include a lighter and slightly thinner design, slimmer bezels around the display and OLED technology, Bloomberg reported.

Tusk shared a "very restrained optimistic" impression after the Europeans' talks with putin
Kyiv • UNN
Tusk said that the talks in Abu Dhabi are tentatively scheduled for November 4. He urged people not to have any illusions about russia's position.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk reacted to the talks between Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Finnish President Alexander Stubb with Kremlin head Vladimir Putin, providing details of the European consultations before and after the call. UNN reports this with reference to The Guardian.
Details
Speaking on October 27 ahead of a cabinet meeting in Warsaw, Tusk said that the call took place "after consultations with me, among others, but above all with President Zelenskyy and the American side,... that it would be good for European politicians to have a working contact, bearing in mind the planned talks on a ceasefire, which may take place in Abu Dhabi".
He said that talks in the UAE between Russia, Ukraine, and the United States were tentatively scheduled for November 4.
Tusk confirmed that he had been informed in advance about the plans for the call, and that Norwegian Prime Minister Støre assured him that he and Stubb were ready to assume political responsibility for this rare interaction with Putin and would adhere to the agreed position of the "coalition of the willing".
He said that after the conversation, Finnish Prime Minister Stubb informed him that "both sides are maintaining their positions", and that "the impression of the European side during the conversation was one of very restrained optimism" regarding the chances of making progress in Abu Dhabi.
Tusk said that he was "very cautious" about engagement with Russia, and urged Stubb and Støre to be "vigilant" in talks with Putin, since "Russia's agenda and interests are quite clearly defined, and one should harbor no illusions about reaching an agreement".
He said that Stubb and Støre also told Putin that the security of NATO's northern and eastern flanks "is not negotiable".
The Polish prime minister also stressed that, despite the resumption of dialogue, "nothing is changing" in Europe's "full support for Ukraine" or in collective views on the "[broader] security architecture and security guarantees for Ukraine".
"We must not have any illusions; it is clear what the Russian side is playing for, but I will maintain constant contact with everyone who has goodwill and faith that an agreement is possible – or, at the very least, a ceasefire before winter", Tusk said, summing up the talks.
Without specifying the source of his claim, Tusk said that "three or four nights ago" "Russia lost 2,500 people" in one night. "This gives us an idea of how horrific the further consequences of this war could be", he pointed out.
Recall
Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Finnish President Alexander Stubb on October 27 held a telephone conversation with Kremlin head Vladimir Putin – following talks in Oslo with President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy and U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner on October 20 and "in consultation with Ukraine".
Stubb and Støre, as noted by the Finnish president's office, "initiated the conversation to discuss Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine and diplomatic efforts to end the war and promote peace and stability in Europe".
"The purpose of the conversation was to convey a message directly to President Putin regarding future negotiations that would help end the war. The conversation concerned future meetings to be held in Abu Dhabi", Stubb's office said.
According to Støre , the conversation with Putin lasted 90 minutes, although it had initially been scheduled for only 20 minutes.
Afterward, Stubb reported having had a "good telephone conversation" with President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy as part of "efforts to seek a just and lasting peace" in Ukraine.
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy reported details of the conversation with the leaders of Finland and Norway. According to the head of state, they "clearly told the Russian leader that real de-escalatory steps are needed regarding our energy sector and infrastructure". They also discussed preparations for a trilateral Ukraine–U.S.–Russia meeting, scheduled for November at the team level, Zelenskyy said.

Türkiye to turn climate pledges into lasting action at COP31: official
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:17:57 UTC
23:17:57 KST

Türkiye's upcoming hosting of the UN climate summit COP31 will provide an important opportunity to share the country's vision for climate diplomacy with the international community, Communications Director Burhanettin Duran has said.
"COP31, to be held in Antalya on November 9–20, is an important opportunity for our country to share its vision in the field of climate diplomacy with the international community," Duran said at a panel titled From Zero Waste to COP31: Türkiye's Climate Diplomacy, held at the Communications Directorate on Tuesday.
Duran said that climate challenges, including biodiversity loss, ocean pollution, desertification, water-related problems, global warming and waste management, had long exceeded the capacity of individual countries to address them using national resources alone.
"Climate diplomacy is a concept we use precisely for this reason," he said, adding that government policies could become meaningful only through international negotiations, cooperation and shared commitments.
Duran said a climate diplomacy book prepared by the Communications Directorate aims to bring together Türkiye's experience, efforts and vision in the field and contribute to policymaking and further work.
Science and political decision-making
Emphasising that the consequences of the climate crisis were already being felt, Duran said international policies must balance countries' sovereign rights with their global responsibilities.
He said countries with greater responsibility for climate change were expected to build greater capacity for technology transfer and climate finance, while a fair negotiation framework was needed to reconcile national interests.
"Scientific knowledge is not enough. It must also be reflected positively in political decision-making processes," he said.
Duran cited political scientist Joseph Nye's description of climate change as a "threat multiplier" rather than merely an ecological crisis, saying the issue was directly linked to global justice and equity.
He also argued that conflicts in different parts of the world had serious environmental and climate consequences.
"Israel's unlawful attacks on Gaza not only threaten human life but also deepen the climate crisis through the intensive greenhouse gas emissions they release into the atmosphere," Duran said.
He added that carbon emissions caused by Israel's attacks since October 2023 had exceeded the annual emissions of hundreds of countries and the consequences extended beyond regional peace and security to the global climate.
Türkiye's climate policies and Zero Waste initiative
Duran said that Türkiye had adopted a comprehensive approach to combating climate change, ratifying the Paris Agreement in 2021 and setting a 2053 net-zero emissions target under President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.
Priority areas include improving energy efficiency, expanding renewable energy, reducing industry's carbon footprint, developing sustainable agricultural practices and protecting natural areas, he said.
He also highlighted the Zero Waste initiative led by first lady Emine Erdogan, saying the UN General Assembly's designation of March 30 as International Zero Waste Day, with support from 105 countries under Türkiye's leadership, reflected the country's efforts.
Duran said the initiative had given Türkiye a distinctive form of soft power in climate diplomacy by helping turn the Zero Waste approach into a global norm.
He stressed the need to support climate efforts with legal frameworks and warned that inadequate public communication could leave them vulnerable to disinformation and social resistance.
"My personal view is that conducting politics through social vulnerabilities will not carry us into the future," he said.
Duran said the Communications Directorate's Centre for Combating Disinformation monitored misleading campaigns on climate issues and other subjects, adding that authorities needed to build a bridge of communication between legislation and society.
He also urged the media to focus not only on the risks of climate change but also on solutions, warning that repetitive negative messaging could increase public anxiety and lead to "green fatigue."
Long-term communication strategy
Duran said climate change was a long-term issue that would affect future generations even more than the present one, calling for hopeful messaging across communication platforms.
He said Türkiye envisioned a multifaceted, long-term climate communication strategy, including age-appropriate environmental education for children through experiments, trips, books and stories.
He stressed the role of Turkish public broadcaster TRT in promoting environmental awareness through children's programmes.
Duran also cited Anadolu's "Green Line" project, launched in 2022, to provide accessible coverage of environmental and climate issues, and a joint statement on Mediterranean forest fires signed by news agencies from Italy, Spain and Greece.
He said environmental awareness needed to become part of everyday life, including home heating, transport, consumption habits, packaging and waste management, rather than remaining limited to expert opinions.
COP31 to promote shared solutions
Duran said Türkiye's vision for COP31 was based on restoring trust through dialogue and translating commitments into concrete results on the ground.
"Our goal is to help turn climate pledges into measurable and lasting action," he said, adding that Türkiye aimed to accelerate the implementation of international commitments, strengthen cooperation among countries and support tangible results in climate action.
The Communications Directorate was organising environmental and climate media tours, accrediting national and international journalists for COP31 and helping plan and establish the media centre at the conference venue, he said.
"Of approximately 3,000 members of the press, the procedures for 1,400 have been completed," Duran said.
He expressed confidence that the summit, to be hosted by Türkiye, would bring countries with different circumstances and priorities together around shared solutions, and wished the conference success.

UK government to give £15m to anti-misogyny fund amid ‘manosphere’ concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:15:50 UTC
23:15:50 KST

The chancellor will give £15m to a dedicated fund to tackle misogyny in workplaces, schools and public places amid concerns in government about the rise of “manosphere” influencers.
The women and equalities minister, Bridget Phillipson, will helm the UK-wide fund, announced last month, marking the first time there has been specific national cash to address misogyny.
The government said organisations could bid for money from the misogyny prevention fund to provide services including mentoring for young people, workplace training and awareness campaigns to improve safety for women and girls. Ministers will also seek match funding from corporate partners and philanthropists to grow the amount of cash available.
Campaigns that have drawn praise in the past – which could be funded nationwide – are Transport for London’s poster campaigns and adverts that encouraged other men to intervene when they saw abusive behaviour taking place, including the “Have a Word” and “Say Maaate to a Mate” campaigns to challenge misogyny.
The campaigns won advertising awards but some critics argued they had done relatively little to address the major threats of violence against women and girls.
Phillipson, who announced her misogyny prevention taskforce last month, said the fund’s aim was to educate and prevent everyday sexism.
“Day to day misogyny – from sexist slurs and harassment to workplace discrimination – quite simply has no place in modern Britain,” she said, announcing the funding.
“The time for talk has long passed, which is why this government is putting its money where its mouth is when it comes to supporting women and girls. This funding is a critical step as we work to confine misogyny to the history books, where it belongs.
“Government is leading from the front, but we all have a role to play. Everyone – from big business to members of the public – can do their bit to stamp out misogyny and improve the lives of women and girls everywhere.”
The chancellor, John Healey, who is expected to confirm the £15m in the budget on Wednesday, said: “Every woman and girl deserves to feel safe, respected and able to pursue their ambitions – at school, at work and in their communities.
“This investment will back practical action to tackle misogyny head-on, while bringing businesses and philanthropists on board so we can go even further – giving women and girls more opportunity to succeed and hope for the future.”
The government has previously announced a separate fund to tackle misogynistic influences in schools, as part of the violence against women and girls strategy. That £20m package is intended to provide new funding and materials for schools to address relationship issues, online misogyny and misinformation.

EU proposes giving Frontex power to carry out migrant returns between third countries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:14:51 UTC
23:14:51 KST

Melike Pala
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
The European Commission proposed Tuesday expanding the mandate of the EU border agency Frontex to enable it to support third countries in returning migrants from their territories to other countries, as part of efforts to strengthen the bloc’s migration management policy.
Under the proposal, Frontex would be able to provide technical and operational assistance to third countries and help organize and carry out return operations from one non-EU country to another.
The new mandate would be subject to an agreement with the third country concerned and would have to comply with fundamental rights and international standards, according to the commission.
“Of course, the main objective for Frontex will still be to increase returns from member states, but we also introduce the ability for Frontex to support third countries on returns,” European Commissioner for Internal Affairs and Migration Magnus Brunner said while presenting the proposals in Brussels.
“This will only be possible if there is an international agreement and where this is in the interest of the EU,” he added.
The commission said the proposed changes would give Frontex a more proactive role in coordinating returns, covering the entire process from strategic planning and identification to return operations and reintegration assistance.
The proposal also envisages establishing a dedicated “Return Coordination Centre” within Frontex to collect and analyze operational information and improve coordination among EU member states.
The commission also proposed gradually increasing Frontex’s standing corps to 30,000 officers through the creation of a new European Border and Return Reserve comprising 17,000 officers who could be deployed to support member states when needed.
The proposal includes the creation of a Quick Reaction Force, which could be rapidly deployed to the EU’s external borders to help member states respond to emergencies and sudden surges in migration.
Alongside the Frontex reform, the commission proposed a separate regulation to digitize return, readmission and reintegration procedures across the EU.
The proposals will now be submitted to the European Parliament and the European Council for consideration.

German court orders Nord Stream sabotage trial of former Ukrainian officer to proceed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:13:20 UTC
23:13:20 KST

Ayhan Simsek
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
A German court ruled Tuesday that the Nord Stream sabotage trial of a former Ukrainian army officer would proceed, rejecting defense arguments that secrecy obligations made a fair trial impossible.
The Hanseatic Higher Regional Court dismissed the defense's request on the second day of proceedings in Hamburg.
"According to German law, the defendant is not restricted in his defense," the presiding judge said, adding that foreign military service regulations could not limit a defendant's freedom to testify in Germany.
Serhii Kuznetsov, a former Ukrainian special forces officer, faces charges of war crimes and related offenses.
Prosecutors alleged that he led a team that planted explosives on the Nord Stream pipelines in the Baltic Sea on Sept. 26, 2022, seven months after the Russia-Ukraine war began.
Defense lawyers argued that Kuznetsov remained bound by secrecy obligations stemming from his service in a Ukrainian special military unit.
They said he risked severe penalties in Ukraine if he discussed the case with his attorneys or testified in court, making a fair trial impossible.
The court rejected the argument and ordered proceedings to continue as scheduled.
According to German investigators, Kuznetsov led a seven-member team comprising divers, support personnel, a medic and a captain.
Prosecutors alleged that the group used forged documents to charter a sailing yacht in the German port city of Rostock, which served as its operational base for planting explosives on the pipelines.
Kuznetsov was arrested in Italy in August 2025 while on a family vacation and was subsequently extradited to Germany.
The September 2022 explosions severely damaged the twin Nord Stream pipelines, which were built beneath the Baltic Sea to transport Russian natural gas to Germany.
The Ukrainian government has consistently denied involvement in the sabotage.
Media reports have alleged that the operation was overseen by then-Ukrainian army chief Valerii Zaluzhnyi without the knowledge of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Romania says Russian sabotage network set fire to Brașov defense plant, two Belarusians and a Ukrainian are suspects
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:11:49 UTC
23:11:49 KST

Romania’s intelligence service, the Serviciul Român de Informații (SRI), said it had uncovered a sabotage network coordinated from Russia. According to a statement from the agency, the network was behind a Sept. 14 fire at the Carfil defense plant in the city of Brașov.
An investigation carried out jointly with other intelligence agencies found that several people from former Soviet states were involved in the arson.
“The information obtained so far indicates that the network’s missions were not limited to Romania. Coordinators in the Russian Federation had assigned it a wide range of targets in the region: state-owned and private weapons production facilities, as well as other targets of military and industrial interest.”
Romania’s Directorate for Investigating Organized Crime and Terrorism, or DIICOT, separately said that two Belarusian citizens and one Ukrainian citizen are suspected of involvement in the Brașov sabotage operation. Romanian authorities have issued arrest warrants for all three individuals. Two suspects were detained in Germany “while they were preparing to commit similar acts,” DIICOT said. Another suspect is in Poland.
In recent months, investigations have also uncovered other attempted acts of sabotage in Romania, including at international military facilities and sites used to train members of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, the SRI said.
According to the intelligence service, operatives are typically recruited through social media. They are initially offered money to carry out a small task, such as watching or photographing a site, but the assignments then become progressively more serious. Over time, they can include assaults, arson, and even attempted killings. If a recruit refuses, the network’s handlers may resort to pressure and blackmail.
“These networks primarily exploit financial vulnerabilities, addictions, or criminal histories. To conceal their identities and movements, their members frequently use transportation, lodging, and payment methods registered under other people’s names, as well as communications via SIM cards from third countries and encrypted messaging apps.”
Authorities in Poland, Bulgaria, Slovakia, Germany, Lithuania, and Denmark have previously reported sabotage targeting defense companies and facilities involved in supporting Ukraine. Officials in those countries have accused Russian intelligence services of organizing the operations, while the people carrying them out have most often been Ukrainian citizens or nationals of EU member states.

Almost 400 migrants detained in Estonia since July
Since July, the Police and Border Guard Board (PPA) has detained 388 foreign nationals who arrived in Estonia without a legal basis after crossing the Belarusian border. Detentions in recent weeks have taken place exclusively in Tallinn.
As of Tuesday, 258 foreign nationals were being held at the detention center in Tallinn, while 148 people who entered the European Union via the Belarus-Latvia border have been handed over to Latvia.
"Each handover is essentially a logistical operation, the success of which requires verified information about the foreign nationals' routes, origins and intentions, as well as agreements between the authorities of both countries," said Indrek Aru, head of the border guard bureau at the PPA's Northern Prefecture.
Foreign nationals are transported back in groups.
Fifteen people are suspected of organizing illegal migration.
Medical attention
Detainees at the detention center have also sought medical attention due to health problems, including cold-like symptoms and skin rashes.
"Foreign nationals with high fevers were taken to West Tallinn Central Hospital, which provides healthcare services to the detention center. As of today, one foreign national remains hospitalized, and it is known that they will be able to return to the detention center in the coming days," Aru noted.
The hospital does not provide the detention center with detailed information about tests carried out or diagnoses.
"Due to personal data protection requirements, diagnoses are not disclosed to the detention center, but in the event of a health risk, the center's staff receive all the necessary information from medical professionals to immediately implement measures to limit the spread of disease, including isolation or quarantine," Aru said.

Political scientist Alexander Kynev stops eating after broken leg leaves him unable to use toilet in Moscow jail

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:09:12 UTC
23:09:12 KST

Political scientist Alexander Kynev, who is being held at Moscow’s Pretrial Detention Center No. 4 (known as “Medved”) is refusing to eat, as the injuries he sustained during his arrest prevent him from using the toilet in his new cell, Kynev’s lawyer Mikhail Biryukov wrote on Facebook earlier today. Kynev, a highly respected academic and analyst, was detained in Moscow in late September on drug distribution charges. He was beaten during the arrest and suffered a broken leg.
Biryukov described a colleague’s visit to Kynev at the detention center:
“My colleague visited Alexander Kynev today and said: ‘Alexander has been on a hunger strike since the weekend. He was transferred to Cell 213, the largest in Medved, designed for 34 people, but there are 35 detainees there. Instead of a toilet, there is a hole in the floor, and because his leg is in a cast after being broken in two places, he cannot use it. So he is not eating.’ We have taken every possible step to have him transferred today to conditions appropriate for his medical condition.”
As The Insider previously reported, Kynev was detained in Moscow on Sept. 25. He is accused of the illegal production, sale, or distribution of narcotics on a large scale under Article 228.1, Part 4, Clause “g” of Russia’s Criminal Code. The charge carries a prison sentence of 10 to 20 years.
On Oct. 22, Kynev personally told the Moscow City Court that he had suffered the injuries during his arrest. He said the officers did not identify themselves and that the force they used caused a serious double fracture of his right leg, along with multiple bruises. Kynev said he remembered little of what happened after he was forced to the floor. He also complained that he was not receiving necessary medical care and was having difficulty moving around the detention center.
Also on Oct. 22, the Moscow branch of Russia’s Federal Penitentiary Service (FSIN) said it had found no violations of Kynev’s rights. The legal rights project Slovo Zashchite (lit. “Word to the Defense”) reported the finding after publishing FSIN’s response to an appeal by urbanist Mikhail Popov, who had asked the authorities to investigate reports that Kynev was beaten. In its Oct. 22 statement, FSIN said Kynev’s detention conditions complied with Russian law and that it had found no threat to his life or health.
The agency also said it had found no violations of Kynev’s rights or treatment degrading to his human dignity. The published response, however, said nothing about the circumstances of his arrest, the incident during which Kynev says he was injured. Instead, the review concerned his detention at Pretrial Detention Center No. 1 (nicknamed “Matrosskaya Tishina”), even though on Oct. 14 he had already been transferred to another facility, Pretrial Detention Center No. 4 (SIZO-4 “Medved”).
Alexander Kynev is a political scientist who specializes in the structure of political power in Russia’s regions and analyzes election results at both the regional and federal levels. In February, he was added to Russia’s register of “foreign agents,” a politically charged designation that imposes extensive reporting requirements and restrictions and has been widely used against journalists, activists, researchers, and other critics of the Putin regime.
The Nobel Peace Prize-winning human rights organization Memorial has recognized Kynev as a political prisoner.

OpenAI announces 3 AI-generated discoveries in mathematics, computer science, physics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:08:50 UTC
23:08:50 KST

Halis Sünnetci
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
US artificial intelligence company OpenAI announced three scientific discoveries in mathematics, computer science, and theoretical physics, claiming its AI models produced proofs that address longstanding problems that have challenged researchers for decades.
The ChatGPT developer said in a statement Monday that its models produced a proof of the local smoothing conjecture in all dimensions, which would also resolve the Kakeya conjecture and Stein's restriction conjecture.
It said the proof, generated on Oct. 18, was formalized the following day using Lean, a mathematical proof-checking system.
In computer science, OpenAI claimed its AI had disproved the Exponential Time Hypothesis, a longstanding conjecture about the computational difficulty of solving certain problems that has underpinned hundreds of research papers.
Researchers from the University of California, San Diego, and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology will also examine the result, which was formalized in Lean.
In theoretical physics, OpenAI said its models had developed existence proofs for certain four-dimensional quantum field theories, including quantum chromodynamics, which describes the strong nuclear force.
The work also includes a proposed proof of the existence of pure Yang-Mills theory, addressing part of one of the Clay Mathematics Institute's Millennium Prize problems.
Nobel Prize-winning physicist David Gross will lead researchers examining the physics findings, which have not yet been publicly released.
OpenAI described the AI-generated manuscripts as raw research data, saying independent academic groups would examine and explain the findings. The company also pledged financial support for the process.

Europe is striking at its own industry and social sphere by rejecting Russian energy: Putin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:07:53 UTC
23:07:53 KST

Elena Teslova
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
Russian President Vladimir Putin said Tuesday that Europe is hurting its own industry and social sphere by rejecting Russian energy.
Speaking at the 8th summit of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) in Moscow, Putin said any attempt to exclude Russia from global gas market participants has serious consequences.
"Above all rising, exorbitant costs for foreign end consumers of gas: companies, enterprises, households," Putin warned. "This is exactly what we see now in Europe, which itself is striking a blow at its industry and social sphere by abandoning Russian energy resources and breaking long-term contracts."
Putin cited a Russian proverb to describe the situation in European Union countries: "Don’t dig a pit for another, or you will fall into it yourself."
Putin said the global gas industry is in a state of "uncertainty" due to the escalation in the Middle East, which disrupted usual logistics chains and supply routes, and what he called direct terrorist acts against Russian gas pipelines to Europe, which were blown up.
He also said some countries have put up barriers to purchases of specialized equipment and technology.
"Prices have risen sharply, but we understand that they can roll back just as sharply to the previous level," he said, adding that many investment plans have been put on hold, postponed, or canceled, increasing the risk of long-term market imbalance.
LNG not dependent on international pipelines
Putin said the main problem now is the disruption of gas supplies, with large volumes dropping out of the market while demand remains.
He proposed that GECF members optimize transport routes through mutual swap operations, noting that liquefied natural gas (LNG) accounts for about half of world gas trade and does not depend on international pipelines.
Putin also pointed to the OPEC Plus format as a successful example of balancing the oil market, while saying the gas industry needs its own mechanisms.
"We propose to expand consultations within our forum on crisis situations in the gas market in order to assess risks in a timely manner, including physical threats to gas infrastructure, and to coordinate approaches to deliveries," he said.
The Russian president also called for long-term contracts to support investment in new fields, processing capacity, shipping fleets, and LNG infrastructure, saying that such projects "cannot be guided only by the current high price conditions."
Putin also urged technological cooperation among gas exporters and said Russia is ready to share its technologies, including deep-horizon gas production, its own LNG technology used in the Arctic, and digital twins of gas fields.
Putin said that until recently European partners worked with Russia on its Arctic fields, and Chinese partners are still doing so.
"Now we are working on the possibility of joint work with American partners," he said.
Putin said GECF members hold 70% of the world’s natural gas reserves and about 40% of global exports. He said gas accounts for a quarter of the world’s energy balance, with consumption up 1.2% last year to 4.2 trillion cubic meters.
He said global demand is expected to reach 5.5 trillion cubic meters a year by the middle of the century, with international supplies rising about one-and-a-half times to 1.7 trillion cubic meters.
Russia ranks first in the world in natural gas reserves and second in production, Putin said, adding that it intends to remain a responsible supplier.
He invited the summit’s delegates to return to Moscow next year for the 10th Russian Energy Week.

Kazakhstan gets lower US travel risk rating than UK, Germany and Spain

Kazakhstan gets lower US travel risk rating than UK, Germany and Spain
Kazakhstan and three other Central Asian countries have received the lowest travel advisory level from the U.S. Department of State, while several Western European destinations are classified at Level 2, which advises travelers to exercise increased caution, Qazinform News Agency reports.
According to the department’s travel advisory listings, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan are classified at Level 1, the lowest of four levels used to assess safety and security risks for U.S. citizens traveling abroad. Tajikistan is rated Level 2.
Kazakhstan’s advisory, issued on Aug. 18, describes the country as “generally a safe destination for travelers.” The department recommends exercising normal precautions, while noting that flooding occurs regularly in the country.
Several Western European countries, including the United Kingdom, Germany and Spain, are rated Level 2. The advisories identify terrorism as a risk indicator for the United Kingdom and Germany, while Spain’s advisory cites terrorism and unrest.
The U.S. Department of State uses four advisory levels. Level 1 recommends normal precautions, while Level 2 advises travelers to exercise increased caution due to specific risks outlined in each country’s guidance. Level 3 advises reconsidering travel, and Level 4 recommends against travel because of serious safety and security risks.
The department emphasizes that its advisories assess potential threats to U.S. citizens, nationals and legal residents abroad. They are not a universal ranking of countries’ safety, and conditions can change at any time.
The latest travel advisories and country-specific guidance are available on the U.S. Department of State website.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported on the growth of Kazakhstan’s tourism sector, citing an increase in foreign visitor numbers and tourism-related revenue in 2025.

A former colleague of Polish President Karol Nawrocki from when he worked as a security guard in a hotel two decades ago testified in court that he told her it was possible to “make some extra money by bringing in girls”. She says she saw him escort a woman onto the premises.
The testimony was given after the president himself sued the owner of a website that, just before last year’s presidential election, published claims that Nawrocki had been involved in procuring prostitutes while working at the luxury Grand Hotel in the town of Sopot.
The court case began in September but, until now, hearings have been held behind closed doors. However, the judge decided that today’s session would be open to the public, with two former colleagues of Nawrocki giving evidence. The president himself is due to appear before the court in January.

Italy

2026-10-27

HEBRON, West Bank, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Israeli troops fired a stun grenade on Tuesday to disperse Palestinians who gathered to protest against an Israeli military operation that has displaced thousands of residents from a neighbourhood in Hebron in the Israeli-occupied West Bank.
The unrest, which follows the deaths of two Israeli soldiers shot by Palestinian gunmen at a checkpoint last week, unfolded as Israelis were voting in an election in which the country’s posture in the West Bank has been a major political issue.
Some Palestinian officials have accused Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of launching a crackdown in the West Bank to coincide with the vote, as a way to energise his right-wing supporters. The government says its operation is a response to the attack on its soldiers.
A group of Palestinian men, women, and children gathered at Tuesday’s protest. One elderly man held a placard that said: “No to collective punishment, no to closures, and no to displacement.”
The military said it had fired a stun grenade to disperse them so that its operation could continue.
On Monday, the United Nations said that over 3,000 Palestinians had been forced from their homes by the Israeli military operation, which targeted neighborhoods near the checkpoint where Palestinian gunmen killed the two Israeli soldiers on Friday.
“Collective punishment is a grave violation of international law,” said UN human rights chief Volker Türk in a statement. “Threats to empty and erase entire neighbourhoods also raise serious concerns of ethnic cleansing.”
The Israeli military said in a statement on Sunday that troops would carry out demolitions in the area. It said soldiers had not located any weapons in searches of the houses.
Since Friday’s attack on the checkpoint, Israel has blocked the entrances to most Palestinian cities and towns across the West Bank, severely curtailing Palestinians’ freedom of movement.
Noura Nassar, a displaced resident who attended the protests, said she had struggled to get medical treatment because of the blockages.
“Where is the democracy in all of this? Their elections are today, sure, but what about us? Aren’t we human beings? We want to go out, we want to visit the doctor,” said Nassar.
Netanyahu and his main rival Gadi Eisenkot both oppose the creation of an independent Palestinian state alongside Israel. Residents expelled from the Hebron neighbourhood said Tuesday’s election in Israel would do little to change the reality on the ground in territories Israel has occupied since 1967.
“Among themselves they will elect who is the oppressor and who will destroy the Palestinian people. That is their election,” said Sana’ Salman Abu Sneineh, another expelled resident.
Netanyahu’s government has presided over a rapid expansion of Israeli settlements, which are deemed illegal by UN bodies and most countries, though Israel disputes this. Under Netanyahu’s right-wing coalition there has also been a surge of militant settler violence against Palestinians.

Gold smuggling funds Islamic State-linked insurgency in eastern Congo, report says
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
15:07:11 CET
23:07:11 KST

DAKAR, Oct 27 (Reuters) - An Islamic State-aligned insurgency in eastern Congo generates most of its revenue from gold production and smuggling, allowing it to finance its own operations, a report said on Tuesday.
The Allied Democratic Forces, or ADF, which has killed thousands in attacks on civilians and security forces in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo over the last decade, generates between $1 million-$1.6 million a year from gold mining sites in one area of North Kivu province alone.
The gold is trafficked through trading hubs in eastern Congo and onwards to refiners and export networks in neighbouring Uganda, according to a report by The Sentry, a US-based investigative organisation that tracks violent conflict and illicit financial networks.
Uganda has deployed thousands of troops to Congo to help local forces fight the ADF, but the group has proved itself to be resilient, embedding itself deeply in local economic networks.
Revenue from gold has allowed the group to rely less on financial support from Islamic State since late 2024, when US sanctions targeted key facilitators in its networks, according to The Sentry.
Fighters also generate money from cocoa production, extortion and kidnapping, it said.
“The ADF has adapted to military pressure and sanctions by finding new ways to fund its operations, particularly through gold and other resource trafficking,” said Justyna Gudzowska, executive director of The Sentry, calling for governments to disrupt the ADF’s sources of funding.
“That means going after the financiers, gold traders, and facilitators,” she said.
Spokespersons for Uganda’s army, Uganda’s government and Congo’s government did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
ADF RESILIENT TO YEARS OF UGANDAN OPERATIONS IN CONGO
Established as an Islamist group in Uganda in the 1990s, the ADF had shifted most of its operations to eastern Congo by 2000. It then pledged allegiance to Islamic State in 2019 and has received support from IS central.
Since doing so, the ADF has combined a local insurgency rooted in the Uganda-Congo borderlands with transnational jihadist ambitions.
The group has carried out a number of bomb attacks in Uganda and has attracted a number of fighters from across the region.
Joint Congolese-Ugandan operations launched in late 2021 helped secure major cities and trade routes but the ADF has been fragmented, not defeated, and moved deeper into remote mining areas of North Kivu, Ituri and Tshopo provinces, the report said.
A representative of a Congolese mining cooperative said the ADF moved into the area in mid-2024, establishing bases near mining sites.
The representative, who requested anonymity for security reasons, told Reuters the group abducted miners and prospectors to extract, transport and sell gold on its behalf. Some residents cooperated in return for payment, he said, creating a system sustained by a mix of coercion and economic incentives.
The ADF continues to operate while most international attention remains largely focused on the Rwanda-backed AFC/M23 rebellion, now known as FRN, which seized large swathes of eastern Congo last year.
(Reporting by Clement Bonnerot and Fiston Mahamba; Editing by David Lewis and Susan Fenton)

====================================================================================================

A 'canary in the coal mine': Measles resurgence exposes weaknesses in U.S. public health, experts say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:07:03 UTC
23:07:03 KST

For nearly two years, the U.S. has had to swallow an uncomfortable reality: A highly infectious disease it once eliminated is spreading again.
More than 4,400 measles cases and at least three deaths have been reported nationwide this year, marking the country's worst outbreak in more than three decades. The spike followed nearly 2,300 cases in 2025. But many public health experts argue that the return of measles isn't the only concerning development — it's also what the resurgence signals about America that's causing alarm.
Measles is often described as one of the most contagious viruses, and it is uniquely unforgiving of weaknesses in public health defenses. A safe and highly effective vaccine has existed for decades.
But the virus's spread exposes declining vaccination rates, eroding trust in health institutions and growing challenges in persuading people to protect themselves, their children and their communities, experts said.
Together, those vulnerabilities have made measles a revealing test of the country's public health defenses. For some experts, the resurgence of a disease the U.S. eliminated more than two decades ago is a warning sign of its ability to contain future threats, from other vaccine-preventable diseases to emerging pathogens.
"Measles is the canary in the coal mine for so many different reasons," said Jennifer Nuzzo, an epidemiology professor and director of the Pandemic Center at Brown University School of Public Health. "It's the canary in the coal mine for other vaccine-preventable illnesses, where we could see a return of things that used to harm kids, but also for very acute, no-notice dangerous infectious disease emergencies."
The U.S. is on track to lose its official measles elimination status during an upcoming review by the Pan American Health Organization, which will meet in Washington, D.C., in mid-November.
"It says a lot about a country if it is unable to control measles," said Nuzzo, who is one of 10 experts CNBC spoke with about the ongoing outbreak and its implications.
Pockets of vulnerability
The U.S. has the tools to prevent measles from spreading. But pockets of low vaccination coverage are leaving the country vulnerable.
The measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine is about 97% effective against measles after two doses, while a single dose is 93% effective, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Yet data aggregated by the CDC shows that vaccination coverage for that shot among U.S. kindergarteners fell to 92.4% in the 2025-2026 school year, which is below the 95% threshold public health officials generally recommend to prevent sustained transmission.
That translates to 280,000 kindergarteners who did not complete their MMR vaccination series, according to the CDC. Childhood vaccination exemptions in the U.S. also reached a record high 4.2% for incoming kindergartners during the 2025-2026 school year, up from 3.6% the previous year, the agency says.
"The bottom line is that not enough people are vaccinating their kids," said Brown's Nuzzo.
While some cases stem from international travel, much of the recent spread has been driven by local transmission in "too many" communities where vaccination coverage falls below 95%, she added.
Among states across the U.S. collecting MMR vaccine data, 67% of counties and jurisdictions now have immunization rates below 95%, according to a September investigation by NBC News.
Recent U.S. outbreaks have often occurred in "closely knit communities" where people have frequent contact and low vaccination coverage, said Dr. William Moss, an epidemiology professor at Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health.
But declining vaccination rates do not mean most Americans have turned against immunization. Polling suggests broad support for childhood vaccines. A July KFF survey found that many Americans sit in a more uncertain middle ground about the shots, leaving room for conflicting information to influence their decisions.
"This is not an edge-case issue," Nuzzo said, adding that the vast majority of parents still vaccinate their children.
Even if outbreaks are concentrated in a minority of communities, it can create a "dangerous situation" far from those areas, she said. Infants too young to be vaccinated and people who cannot receive immunizations for medical reasons can be particularly vulnerable when the virus spreads into communities with high vaccination rates.
Those risks come as the Trump administration reshapes federal vaccine policy.
President Donald Trump signed an executive order in August suggesting that the combined MMR vaccine be split into separate shots, while repeating false claims about its safety. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has also overhauled a key federal advisory committee responsible for recommending childhood immunizations, though the changes are frozen amid ongoing litigation.
Several experts told CNBC that such moves risk further eroding confidence in vaccines and weakening efforts to protect children.
Public health infrastructure was also "really decimated by Covid," and the CDC in particular lost many experienced scientists and physicians "who had spent their lives working on vaccine-preventable diseases," said Scott Weaver, a virologist who is the research director of Galveston National Laboratory.
He added that the CDC, as of September, is also no longer immediately incorporating state-reported "measles-associated" deaths into its national published tally, making it harder to track outbreaks in real time. The agency lists three measles-related deaths in 2026, but Pennsylvania has reported at least five deaths.
"We have folks in federal health leadership right now that are throwing gasoline on the fire, and that is not helping the situation," said Jess Steier, a public health scientist and founder and CEO of Unbiased Science, an organization that aims to make complex scientific concepts understandable.
Consequences beyond current outbreaks
If the U.S. fails to materially improve vaccination rates, the measles resurgence could extend beyond ongoing outbreaks.
At "current" state-level vaccination rates, measles could become endemic again in the U.S., resulting in an estimated 851,300 cases over 25 years, according to a large-scale epidemiological model published in JAMA in April 2025 by researchers at Stanford and other institutions. Under that scenario, the model predicts the measles cases could lead to 170,200 hospitalizations and 2,550 deaths over that period.
The model, which simulated infectious disease spread in the U.S. at various childhood vaccination levels, relies on immunization data from 2004 to 2023 for that baseline scenario. The model assumes that diseases are introduced by someone who travels abroad and brings them back, most commonly a U.S. citizen who isn't vaccinated.
While many people are currently immune through vaccination, outbreaks can increase in size and frequency if immunization rates decline over a longer period.
Michael Osterholm, an epidemiologist and the director of the Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy at the University of Minnesota, said he views the measles situation in Canada as a direct warning for the U.S.
Canada lost its official measles elimination status in November after a multi-province outbreak that generated more than 5,400 cases across 10 jurisdictions in 2025. Canada has a population of more than 40 million people.
"We have a population of 350 million. If you extrapolate, if we had the very same experience that Canada had over the next year or two, that would be up to 50,000 cases of measles in the U.S.," Osterholm said. "I think that's a potential future we have to be mindful of."
Other vaccine-preventable diseases
An even larger measles outbreak isn't the only potential problem.
Vaccination coverage for other childhood diseases has similarly declined. The share of U.S. kindergartners vaccinated against polio fell to 92.4% in the 2025-2026 school year, while coverage for diphtheria, tetanus and acellular pertussis, or DTaP, dropped to 92%, according to CDC data.
The U.S. has already seen a sharp rise in pertussis, or whooping cough. U.S. reported cases reached roughly 43,300 in 2024 and nearly 28,000 in 2025, up substantially from pandemic-era levels, according to the CDC. Brown's Nuzzo said the resurgence reflects, in part, fewer people getting vaccinated and the fact that protection from the pertussis vaccine wanes over time.
The simulation model published in JAMA also examined how falling childhood immunization rates could affect the future spread of several diseases previously eliminated from the U.S. through vaccines. Under current vaccination levels, the researchers found that diseases including rubella and polio were unlikely to become endemic in the U.S.
But in a hypothetical scenario in which childhood vaccination rates fell by 50%, the model projected 9.9 million cases of rubella, 4.3 million cases of polio and 197 cases of diphtheria over 25 years.
Rubella can cause devastating complications when an infection during pregnancy passes to a developing fetus, while polio can cause paralysis and death, said Dr. Nathan Lo, assistant professor of infectious diseases at Stanford Medicine.
The projections are not predictions that these outbreaks will occur, but they illustrate how much risks could grow if vaccination coverage deteriorates.
"What vaccines often buy you is not just the protection, but also less uncertainty," said Mathew Kiang, an assistant professor of epidemiology and population health at Stanford Medicine who also worked on the simulation model. "I think even more frightening is just the really wide uncertainty that we just wouldn't be sure of what could happen."
Preparing for the next threat
The measles resurgence is also raising questions about how effective the U.S. can be at detecting and responding to emerging public health threats before they spread.
"Public health is all about prevention," said Dr. Manisha Juthani, president of the Association of State and Territorial Health Officials and commissioner of the Connecticut Department of Public Health. She said the country must maintain its ability to detect threats, invest in surveillance, and recognize that infectious diseases do not respect national borders.
Those capabilities are crucial for curbing emerging pathogens, especially when scientists initially know little about how a new disease spreads, how severe it is or how to treat it. A pathogen could spread before vaccines or treatments are available, making early detection, clear public communication and coordination especially important.
Other experts argue that weaknesses in those capabilities could also have implications for the country's defenses against deliberate biological attacks.
In an April 2025 op-ed, Steph Batalis, a research fellow at Georgetown University's Center for Security and Emerging Technology, argued that the measles outbreak exposed a broader vulnerability in the U.S.' biodefense strategy and, specifically, a weakened ability to deter potential biological attacks.
She argued that the country's struggle to contain a known, vaccine-preventable disease "might only embolden those who see our public health vulnerabilities as an opportunity."
But Osterholm, who works extensively on bioterrorism, said low MMR immunization rates and rising measles cases do not necessarily indicate that Americans would refuse a vaccine or antibiotic during a biological emergency. The shots and drugs used to counter biological threats can differ from those routinely administered to the public, he said, and the prospect of a severe outbreak could prompt urgency among the public to seek protection.
That point highlights an important limitation: The measles resurgence by itself does not establish whether the U.S. could withstand entirely different or novel public health threats.
But as a disease the U.S. knows how to prevent spreads, experts say the stakes of addressing those vulnerabilities extend to whatever might come next.

Few Young Bulgarians Report Long-Term Health Problems
Unknown

23:06:00 KST

Bulgaria Has EU’s Highest Road Death Rate
Bulgaria recorded the European Union’s highest road fatality rate in 2025, with 71 deaths per million inhabitants, according to final figures released by the European Commission
Bulgaria ranks sixth in the European Union for self-reported health among people aged 16 to 29, with Eurostat data for 2025 showing that a high proportion of young Bulgarians consider themselves to be in good or very good health.
Three other Balkan countries lead the EU rankings, with Romania in first place, followed by Greece and Croatia. According to figures released by the European statistical office, 98.2% of young people in Romania assess their health positively, compared with 98.1% in Greece and 95.9% in Croatia. Across the EU, the average is 89.7% for the 16–29 age group.
The results point to a strong presence of Southeast European countries among those with the highest levels of self-reported health. Bulgaria also ranks near the top, although it falls behind its three Balkan neighbors. Sweden records the lowest share, at 74.4%, followed by the Netherlands at 79.8% and Finland at 81.4%.
However, the figures require careful interpretation because self-assessed health is subjective. Responses can reflect physical condition, psychological well-being, personal perceptions and people's willingness to disclose health difficulties. Eurostat also notes that social and cultural differences may affect comparisons between countries.
In another indicator, Bulgaria has a relatively small share of young people reporting long-term illnesses or health problems. In 2025, Bulgaria, Romania, Greece and Italy were among the EU countries where the proportion of people aged 16 to 29 reporting such conditions was 5% or lower.
The EU-wide average was considerably higher, at 17.2%. Finland recorded the largest share of young people reporting long-standing health problems, at 39.9%, followed by Sweden at 25.1% and Estonia at 24.2%.
These differences do not necessarily mean that young people in Bulgaria are objectively healthier than their peers elsewhere in Europe. Although the low proportion reporting long-term conditions is a positive indicator, it does not provide a complete picture of the health of the country's young population.
Income-related differences in perceived health also set Bulgaria apart from most EU countries. Across the bloc, 85.6% of young people in the lowest income group rated their health as good or very good in 2025, compared with 93.7% of those in the highest income group.
Bulgaria and Malta are the only EU countries where the pattern is reversed. In Bulgaria, the proportion of young people reporting good or very good health is 0.1 percentage points higher among those in the bottom 20% of the income distribution than among those in the top 20%. Although the difference is marginal, it contrasts with the broader European trend.
Greece also shows only a small gap between the two income groups, at 0.3 percentage points, but the difference favors higher earners. Italy follows with a gap of 1.2 percentage points, while Belgium records 2.7 percentage points, placing both among the EU countries with the smallest income-related disparities in self-assessed health.

The portable system, known as Murdock, logged 20 flight hours across three airfields in three weeks in August and September, beginning during the Emerald Flag military exercises at Eglin Air Force Base in Florida, it said in a statement.

The company said the system is designed to support pilots while leaving all operational decisions and authority with flight crews.
Beacon AI plans to expand Murdock's capabilities in the flight lifecycle, from scheduling and flight operations to post-flight reviews, using data and feedback gathered during operational testing.
