King Charles’s Caribbean tour: Will he discuss slavery reparations?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:05:03 UTC
23:05:03 KST

King Charles’s Caribbean tour: Will he discuss slavery reparations?
King Charles embarks on a nine-day Caribbean tour amid monarchy questions and growing demands for slavery reparations.
The United Kingdom’s King Charles lll is travelling to the Bahamas on Tuesday, where he will begin a nine-day tour of the Caribbean.
The tour will take him to the Bahamas, Guyana, and Antigua and Barbuda, where he will attend the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) from November 1-4.
This comes as demands for reparations over Britain’s notorious role in the slave trade grow louder, and as the monarchy faces questions about its future in the region.
So what is the significance of this tour? And what does the Caribbean want?
Here’s what we know.
What’s on the itinerary?
King Charles will visit three countries in nine days.
His tour begins on Tuesday with the archipelagic country of the Bahamas, where he will be staying for three days.
Then he will make his way to Guyana, a former British colony that had more than 100,000 slaves when the trade was abolished in 1807.
After two days in Guyana, where he is expected to meet the president and elected leaders of Amerindian villages, he will head to Antigua and Barbuda for the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM).
The meeting, from November 1-4, is expected to include discussions about the environment and trade and development, although the question of British reparations for slavery is also likely to feature.
What do the countries King Charles is visiting want?
Government officials in the Bahamas and in Antigua and Barbuda – both of which are part of the British Commonwealth with King Charles as their ultimate head of state – have signalled that they want to become republics. Guyana gained independence from the UK in 1966, and has a president as its head of state.
Guyanese President Mohamed Irfaan Ali said in an interview with ITV News that while Charles “rightfully” recognised slavery as the “darkest days in human history” during a visit to Barbados in 2021 when he was still the prince of Wales, an apology should be his next step.
“You exploited the region. You destroyed lives. You created underdevelopment,” Ali said, in a reference to the lingering legacy of the British Empire and the slave trade.
In 2023, a Lord Ashcroft Poll revealed that 51 percent of surveyed respondents in the Bahamas wanted to become a republic, while 27 percent preferred to retain the British monarchy as head of state.
Niambi Hall Campbell-Dean, chair of the Bahamas National Reparations Committee, was critical of the king ahead of his arrival. “Why do we still have a king? What does this person really represent to us? Why is he coming and how will that benefit us?” she asked.
What do other countries in the Caribbean say about slavery?
Jamaica, which is not on the itinerary for this trip by King Charles, made its stance clear in September, when it filed a $10bn slavery reparations petition in London, addressing it to the king.
That was the first time a British Commonwealth state has taken legal action pursuing “the cause of reparatory justice”, as the Jamaican delegation called it.
The petition is due to be heard by a UK privy council in March next year. The UK has, so far, refused to formally apologise or pay reparations for slavery.
Also in September, Caribbean Community and Common Market (CARICOM) Secretary-General Carla Barnett said reparations are “fundamentally about justice”.
“It is about recognition, accountability and transformation, and about building a just and equitable future for the descendants of those who, as the chattel of colonial owners, endured untold suffering, loss of life and freedom,” she said.
The transatlantic slave trade was recently declared the “gravest crime against humanity” in a United Nations resolution in March this year.
The last time a British royal visited Jamaica was when Prince William and Kate Middleton, then the duke and duchess of Cambridge, toured the island in 2022 during their Caribbean Platinum Jubilee tour.
The more memorable moment of the trip was when the couple was pictured shaking hands with Jamaican children with a fence separating them, which many criticised for being “tone-deaf”.
What’s likely to happen at the Commonwealth meeting?
The meeting in Antigua and Barbuda is expected to cover climate resilience as well as trade and development.
Leaders and representatives of 56 Commonwealth countries will be attending. Many want an apology for slavery from the king, but Buckingham Palace recently announced that will not be happening.
“The visit programme will…not shy away from ‘the darkest days of our past’, as his majesty has described them, but – in keeping with the wishes of our host nations – it will principally be oriented to the vibrant present and promising future of each country,” a palace spokesperson said in a statement.
The palace added that it is “important” to acknowledge the “creative” ways that Charles has tried to right “enduring inequalities”.
The chair of the UK’s All-Party Parliamentary Group (APPG) for Afrikan Reparations, Labour MP Bell Ribeiro-Addy, said the royal family and the UK government had failed to recognise the demands of those wanting reparations.
“I think it would be wrong to think that we can continue with platitudes. You’ve got ‘atrocity’, ‘deep regret’, ‘sorrow’, and now they’re going to say ‘darkest days’,” she said. “I think the king needs to realise that people wouldn’t keep raising it if what he was doing was anywhere near enough.
“You can tell that the Commonwealth means something to the monarchy, and I’m sure he would not want to be the monarch under which it crumbles.”

Italian archaeologists discover links to tomb of Jesus underneath Jerusalem's Church of the Holy Sepulchre
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:04:50 UTC
23:04:50 KST

Italian researchers have found a burial ground beneath Jerusalem's Church of the Holy Sepulchre, matching biblical accounts of the location of Jesus' burial.
Whether God exists or not is a matter of dispute around the world. A large majority of modern historians are, however, convinced that Jesus of Nazareth was a real historical figure who lived in the 1st century and was crucified under the Roman governor Pontius Pilate. Christians across the globe have long believed that the tomb of the Jewish itinerant preacher lies beneath the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem.
The Church of the Holy Sepulchre, known to Orthodox Christians as the Church of the Resurrection, stands in the Christian Quarter of Jerusalem's Old City. It is one of the most important shrines in Christianity, as it is believed to have been built on what was thought to be the site of the crucifixion, burial and resurrection of Jesus Christ. It was commissioned by the Roman emperor Constantine the Great, and was built in the fourth century.
The first church was consecrated in 335 AD. Over the course of its history, the building was destroyed and rebuilt several times. It suffered particularly heavy damage in 1009 under the Fatimid caliph al-Hakim. In the following decades the church was partially restored.
After the Crusaders captured Jerusalem in 1099, extensive alterations were carried out. The church's present appearance is therefore the result of numerous phases of construction and restoration.
For a long time hardly any structural changes, renovation work or excavations were permitted, because several Christian denominations share the church and each feared that changes could weaken their rights and influence. Now the different parties have reached agreement. Since 2016 the Church of the Holy Sepulchre has been undergoing restoration, for the first time in more than 200 years.
Ancient tombs and a garden found beneath the church floor
In 2022 a comprehensive restoration of the church floor was initially planned. As work progressed, it turned into an extensive excavation project. Researchers discovered, beneath the church, an abandoned stone quarry, agricultural plots, a garden and rock-cut tombs.
The garden is of particular significance, as the Gospel of John mentions a garden at the place of Jesus's crucifixion. According to the Bible, the crucifixion took place close to the city limits of Jerusalem. The Letter to the Hebrews notes that Jesus suffered outside the city gate. This, too, is consistent with the archaeologists' findings.
Lead archaeologist Francesca Romana Stasolla of Rome's "La Sapienza" university interprets the finds as evidence of a burial landscape. The excavations suggest that cultivated land once lay between Golgotha, known as Calvary in the Bible's new testament, and the tomb, according to Stasolla.
The archaeologists also found traces of olive trees and vines, dated to around 33 AD, the period in which Jesus's death is usually placed.
According to Stasolla, the tombs carved into the rock also point to an earlier burial site. The Gospels of Matthew, Mark and Luke describe Jesus's tomb as a burial chamber hewn from rock, so this detail fits as well.
No conclusive proof
The finds do not provide scientific proof that Jesus was buried underneath the site of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre. There is no inscription to that effect, nor can it be shown that the tomb chamber was unused or belonged to Joseph of Arimathea, who, according to the Gospels, laid Jesus in his new rock-cut tomb. The plant remains also cannot yet be dated precisely to the time of the crucifixion.
The excavations therefore do not settle the question of Jesus's actual burial place. They do, however, show that the site venerated by Christians for centuries has geographical and archaeological features that correspond to the descriptions in the New Testament.

West trying to undermine Russia-Africa cooperation – Moscow
Russia and African nations must work together to counter attempts by Western countries to undermine cooperation in the information sphere, Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said on Tuesday.
Speaking to African journalists at the Russia-Africa Media Forum, Zakharova warned that outside powers seek to obstruct direct communication between Russia and African countries. She argued that restricting access to information and preventing independent exchanges between nations would deepen global inequality and reinforce divisions between countries.
“We must push back against this collectively... not individually, but by acting together,” she said.
Zakharova warned that efforts to limit international cooperation extend beyond the media sphere to cultural exchanges, energy, natural resources, and defense.
“African countries were pressured, blackmailed, and at times even threatened – while simultaneously being offered certain ‘bonuses’. They were told: ‘Renounce your cooperation with Russia, vote against Russia in international organizations, and in return, you will receive loans, food supplies, or political support.’”
Zakharova thanked African nations for standing firm under pressure, adding that it is “not just support for... Russia. It is support for the principles of justice, equality, and international law, and a rejection of segregation, humiliation, and blackmail.”
She expressed gratitude to the journalists who traveled to Russia for the forum, noting that some participants faced intimidation, “while others were lured with alternative events... to keep them from coming to Russia.”
Russia has also accused Western countries of trying to discourage African leaders from attending the Russia-Africa Summit, scheduled for October 28-29. In September, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov singled out France, saying President Emmanuel Macron would use a trip to Africa to persuade African leaders to not attend.

How has Andy Burnham used his first 100 days in power?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:04:23 UTC
23:04:23 KST

Burnham promised a more open approach to managing Labour, with greater consultation and less reliance on party discipline to suppress debate. Illustration: Guardian Design/Getty View image in fullscreen Burnham promised a more open approach to managing Labour, with greater consultation and less reliance on party discipline to suppress debate. Illustration: Guardian Design/Getty How has Andy Burnham used his first 100 days in power? From ‘everyday fixes’, party management and communications to long-term plans for care and pensions, the PM’s six key acts so far Andy Burnham arrived in Downing Street promising to transform the way Britain works, restore hope and bring an end to years of political division. One hundred days later, the prime minister has announced a series of measures aimed at making everyday life easier, he’s reopened the debate over Britain’s relationship with the EU and set out plans to overhaul public services. He has also managed to maintain an unusually visible public profile, appearing regularly on social media and even taking part in a charity edition of Channel 4’s Gogglebox. Burnham has said he’s been surprised by the public’s appetite for change, insisting his first budget on Wednesday would offer some breathing space for households and businesses. But the early weeks of his premiership have also exposed tensions between immediate political wins and the structural changes he has promised. Here is how his first 100 days have unfolded in six key ways. Quick policy wins Burnham made a series of what Downing Street calls “everyday fixes” central to his premiership, targeting everything from electricity bills and bus fares to misleading discounts, subscription traps and antisocial behaviour on public transport. One of his first announcements, the removal of VAT from domestic electricity bills across Britain, took effect on 1 October. The government estimates an annualised saving of £45 for a typical household, although the temporary measure is funded only until March. Other announcements have yet to take effect. A £2 cap on participating bus services in England outside London and new rules making subscriptions easier to cancel are due to start in January. The bus measure also involves trade-offs. It is partly funded by switching international climate finance from grants to loans, a decision criticised by development charities. The strategy is intended to demonstrate that the government understands ordinary frustrations and can respond quickly. Yet questions remain about whether a collection of relatively modest interventions can significantly improve living standards. The VAT cut on electricity bills is not likely to help struggling households, who are more likely to be reliant on gas than electricity. Rough sleeping and social care Ending rough sleeping was among Burnham’s earliest commitments, drawing on his experience as the mayor of Greater Manchester. The government initially allocated £442m to tackle the problem, and announced a further £432m on Sunday, bringing its commitment to £874m over different funding periods. View image in fullscreen Burnham speaks on a visit to St Martin‑in‑the‑Fields, a homelessness charity in central London. Photograph: Ian Vogler/Reuters Burnham wants everyone sleeping rough in England to be offered a route off the streets or appropriate support before Christmas. But the success of the initiative will depend on whether people can access suitable accommodation and the services needed to help them remain housed. And it remains unclear how exactly the prime minister hopes to keep people from going back on to the streets and not staying permanently in temporary accommodation. A big proposal is Burnham’s plan for a national care service in England, which he intends to help finance by reforming the state pension triple lock from 2030. The government plans to legislate during this parliament, while maintaining the existing guarantee until then. But the savings from changing pension uprating are uncertain and depend heavily on future economic conditions. Jonathan Cribb, deputy director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, welcomed Burnham’s proposed changes of the triple lock but said “it will not be the answer to funding universal social care”. Party management Burnham promised a more open approach to managing Labour, with greater consultation and less reliance on party discipline to suppress debate. His appointments have included members of the Socialist Campaign Group, bringing MPs from Labour’s left into government roles. But he has disappointed a lot of soft-left MPs who campaigned for him after the Labour conference in 2025, when he made a number of media appearances attempting to prove he could replace Keir Starmer. His failure to include many of those from Mainstream, Open Labour and larger soft-left factions has been noted from MPs in the new intake, and those who have been in the parliamentary Labour party for a long time. Disagreements have emerged, particularly over immigration. Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, faces opposition from Labour MPs and some cabinet colleagues over proposals that could require some migrant workers to wait 15 years before securing permanent residence. Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, declined to endorse the specific proposal before being forced to clarify her support for the government’s broader approach. Burnham backed the principle of earned settlement but stopped short of committing to every detail of Mahmood’s proposals. A government source believes Burnham has avoided public rows so far because he is “taking his time to get policy right”, but they added, “isn’t it strange that a sitting cabinet minister had to apologise for making a joke … clearly we’re not one big happy family”. Difficult decisions Beyond the everyday fixes, Burnham has begun confronting choices that divide opinion within his own party. He has reopened discussion of Britain’s relationship with the EU, arguing that Brexit has damaged economic growth and weakened immigration control. On Monday, he revealed his personal desire to see Britain rejoin the EU during his lifetime, while ruling out abandoning Labour’s manifesto red lines during this parliament. View image in fullscreen Activists from Fossil Free London stage a protest against the Rosebank oilfield and the Jackdaw gasfield outside the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero. Photograph: Vuk Valcic/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock Energy policy has presented another dilemma. Last week, the government approved the Jackdaw North Sea gasfield, arguing that domestic production would support energy security and employment. The development is expected to create only 27 new direct jobs and safeguard 273 existing positions. Environmental groups argue that further fossil fuel production undermines Britain’s climate commitments, while domestic gas does not automatically reduce household bills. Communication Burnham has drastically changed the way Downing Street presents itself. The prime minister’s social media updates, which are pretty much daily, his collaborations with public figures including Mo Farah and online creators, and his appearance alongside Steve Rotheram on Gogglebox have taken his message beyond the traditional Westminster audience or those who avidly follow politics. His approach has attracted substantial online attention and made short, accessible explanations of government announcements a recognisable feature of his premiership. Andrew Chadwick, professor of political communication at Loughborough University, has described Burnham’s collaborations with influencers as generating a “constructed sense of authenticity”. But there is a big difference between attracting audiences, of all ages and backgrounds, and explaining policy and persuading voters that measures will actually help them. What do the public think? UK poll averages graph Labour has recovered ground in the polls, although the measures of how satisfied the public are seem slightly more complicated. As soon as Burnham entered No 10, the party’s ratings rose to 23% then reached 26%, overtaking Reform UK on 24%. After the Labour conference, an Ipsos survey conducted between 15 and 22 October put the party on 32%, eight points ahead of the Conservatives, with Reform UK on 20%. But 66% of those surveyed expressed dissatisfaction with the government’s performance, against 23% who were satisfied. Meanwhile, YouGov polling conducted earlier this month revealed 46% viewed Burnham favourably and 42% unfavourably. His net favourability rating had fallen from 13 points in August to four points. Despite this, Opinium pollsters declared: “Burnham remains the only party leader with a positive net approval rating and holds a commanding lead over both Kemi Badenoch and Nigel Farage on who would make the better prime minister.” Explore more on these topics Andy Burnham Labour Social care Pensions Budget UK cost of living crisis State pensions features Share Reuse this content

Arab alliance accuses Netanyahu of using fake image to exaggerate voter turnout

27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
The Joint List, an alliance of three Arab parties in Israel, accused Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Tuesday of using a fake image generated by artificial intelligence to exaggerate Arab voter turnout in parliamentary elections.
Arab lawmaker Ahmad Tibi also challenged Netanyahu’s claims, saying turnout in Jewish towns remained significantly higher than in Arab communities.
Netanyahu posted an image on the US social media platform X showing people outside a polling station, claiming it depicted Arab voters in the southern city of Rahat.
“This is what is happening today in Rahat. You cannot stay home; go out immediately and vote Likud. We are fighting for our homeland,” he wrote.
The premier also shared a photograph of Tibi standing in front of a bus, which the Arab lawmaker had posted on his own X account several days earlier.
“Buses are heading toward polling stations, and reports indicate long queues in Arab towns,” Netanyahu wrote.
He claimed that right-wing strongholds appeared slow to mobilize, warning his supporters that failing to vote could result in a government led by Arab parties.
In a statement condemning Netanyahu’s conduct, the Joint List said the image purportedly showing voters in Rahat was “not real and generated by artificial intelligence.”
The alliance accused Netanyahu of using fabricated images to incite against Arabs.
“Netanyahu is afraid of high turnout in our community because he knows it will bring down his government,” it said.
The alliance warned that the image presented a misleading picture that could lull Arab voters into staying home by suggesting participation was already sufficiently high.
While turnout in Arab communities was encouraging, it said, a gap remained compared with the wider Israeli electorate, particularly in right-wing strongholds and settlements.
It urged Arab voters to continue heading to polling stations despite obstacles.
In a video statement, Tibi said Arab participation was being misrepresented by the Israeli right.
“Since the morning, turnout in Arab towns has indeed been higher than in the past, but turnout in Jewish towns is higher, and there is a large gap between turnout in Jewish and Arab communities,” he said.
Tibi urged voters to remain at polling stations until they had cast their ballots despite “obstruction and delays.”
He warned that the turnout gap could negatively affect the election outcome, while stressing that Arab voters could still narrow it.
There was no immediate response from Netanyahu to the Joint List’s statement or Tibi’s remarks.
Arab citizens account for 18% of eligible voters, Israeli citizens 77%, and people classified as having no specified religion the remaining 5%, according to figures released by Israel’s Central Bureau of Statistics two days earlier.
Polling stations opened at 7 am local time (0500GMT) and are scheduled to close at 10 pm (2000GMT)
Television stations are expected to release exit polls when voting ends, with preliminary results emerging early Wednesday. Official results are scheduled to be announced on Nov. 4.

What Lula’s victory means for Palestine solidarity in Brazil
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:02:11 UTC
23:02:11 KST

Breadcrumb
What Lula’s victory means for Palestine solidarity in Brazil
Over the weekend, Brazilians elected Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva president once more by a very narrow margin, defying polls that had him trailing. No candidate had won a Brazilian runoff from second place since 1989. That precedent is broken, and it was broken from below: by student-led rallies in Rio de Janeiro, São Paulo, Minas Gerais and Porto Alegre.
The rallies were called without Lula, by pop-star fan communities and influencers who injected energy into a campaign that had flagged all year, and by widespread mass communications like Deputy André Janones's WhatsApp channel, which passed 10 million followers. Many of those young figures have been vocal on Palestine. Their job now is to make sure their government hears them.
That mobilisation will matter all the more given the political landscape Lula faces. The Congress that convenes on 1 February will comprise 594 members, 513 deputies and 81 senators, with the right and its allies holding a comfortable majority in both houses. With 90 members close to the Palestinian struggle, the challenge will be to turn that support, alongside pressure from civil society, into concrete political action.
Palestine
Lula's words have been strong in recent years. He recognised the State of Palestine in 2010, the first in South America to do so, condemned the genocide in Gaza as early as October 2023, and did not back down when the Israeli colonial regime declared him persona non grata over his Holocaust comparison.
Brazil joined South Africa's case at the International Court of Justice and has had no ambassador in Tel Aviv since May 2024. His actions, however, were fewer. Diplomatic and trade relations with Israel were never fully cut. The Army’s planned purchase of 36 armoured howitzers from Elbit Systems was stalled in 2024 amid political opposition over military ties with Israel. The deal resurfaced in October 2026 after Brazilian defence company Avibras, reached an agreement with Elbit’s Brazilian subsidiary, AEL Sistemas, paving the way for local assembly.
The proposed purchase, worth almost $200 million, remained controversial after renewed public backlash, and the army subsequently cancelled the planned signing of the initial contract for two units. However, the wider procurement was not cancelled.
Lula has always been a conciliator. But a fourth and last term with popular backing opens room for much bolder steps, including ending trade relations with illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank, withdrawing from the Mercosur–Israel Free Trade Agreement, imposing a total embargo on weapons and technology transfers with the Zionist regime, and investigating and halting any indirect exports of Brazilian oil through third-country intermediaries.
The recognition of Palestine itself came at the end of his second term, and was then seen as his last.
For Palestinian solidarity movements, Lula’s victory above all means keeping the conditions they work under today, which are far more favourable than those a Flávio government would offer. The government remains open to dialogue with civil society, its own rhetoric lends legitimacy to the cause, and the state does not throw its weight behind the campaign against it.
Holding the line
Lula's government is not immune to Zionist lobbies, however. They continue to influence leaders close to the president and elected officials within his Workers' Party (PT) and Congress, where it needs centrist allies.
Even under Lula, part of the work will be to contest the government itself.
The institutional climate will remain turbulent. The reaction from Bolsonaro's supporters, especially if backed by Trump, is a challenge the PT anticipates. But the balance has shifted. Flávio will lose the privileged forum his Senate seat gives him, and with investigations advancing, he could face arrest.
Eduardo Bolsonaro, second in the family's line of command, is a fugitive in the United States after a Supreme Court justice issued an arrest warrant and cancelled his passports. He was sentenced to four years and two months for coercing the judicial process through lobbying Washington for sanctions against Brazilian magistrates.
From Florida, he has advised his brother to flee if defeated and joked about US Marines intervening. The family cannot hold political capital while their assets disperse.
Lula's path is to strengthen republican institutions – the Supreme Court included –, but he would be boxed in by a Senate taken over by the Bolsonarista party, which confirms justices and can impeach them.
Sustained public mobilisation in the streets and online could also help expose the networks of corruption and patronage that sustain the far-right’s power in Congress. Investigations into Banco Master and parliamentary budget amendments could weaken some of these networks and make it harder for politicians to convert economic power into political influence.
For the Palestinian movement, this matters. Challenging the interests that protect Zionist politicians is part of building a Congress more accountable to the public and less willing to enable complicity in the occupation.
Brazil’s importance in the region and to the cause is based on many factors; Brazil holds a third of Latin America's population and GDP, its main instrument abroad has never been economic or military might but diplomacy, and the country has built its influence on multilateralism, mediation and coalitions such as the BRICS. Gains made in Brazil tend to spread, as the wave of recognition of Palestine that followed 2010 showed.
In the region, Brazil is now an exception. Seven South American governments are aligned with Donald Trump, and Brazil is the largest country still holding out. Israel and the United States – as governments but also through Big Tech companies like META - invested here for years to change that. They have failed, for now.
Ultimately, a generation of young political figures carried this campaign, vocal on Palestine and with a strong presence online. In a contest increasingly fought on social media, a terrain the right had long dominated, the left has begun to close the gap. The platforms themselves are part of that dispute, and Meta's seeming interference in the campaign has become a matter of national and international debate.
The dispute over Brazil's public digital payment system (PIX) has also exposed US interest in challenging a model that threatens the dominance of American payment companies.
Furthermore, Brazil has a vibrant independent press that is often more receptive to the Palestinian cause. The country’s media landscape also includes major broadcasters such as TV Globo (formerly Rede Globo), Brazil’s largest television network and one of the country’s most influential media organisations. Its televised political debates attract large audiences and shape public discussion, with their coverage and political implications often resonating beyond Brazil’s borders.
Internationally, Lula's surprising victory and popular mobilisation must inspire and trickle to other countries where people are protesting in their masses against growing authoritarianism, fascism and neoliberal economic policies - all aligned with the Zionist regime - in France, India, Spain, and Serbia.
The pendulum is likely to swing in Brazil by 2030, and the next four years must be used to build irreversible actions toward liberation.
Rula Shadeed is the Co-Director of the Palestine Institute for Public Diplomacy.

Tashkent modernism enters the UNESCO World Heritage List
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:00:46 UTC
23:00:46 KST

Tashkent’s modernist buildings combine new architectural ideas with local materials, patterns and climate-conscious design. Ten landmarks are now included in a UNESCO World Heritage site.
Tashkent’s architecture reflects many layers of the city’s history. After the 1966 earthquake, a new generation of public buildings introduced modern forms, experimental materials and designs adapted to the city’s hot climate.
Many of these buildings remain in use today. Museums, concert halls, a circus and metro stations continue to serve the functions for which they were created, while their architectural value has gained wider recognition.
Ten modernist landmarks from this period are now included in a UNESCO World Heritage site.
Architecture shaped by Tashkent’s climate
The modernist architecture that emerged in Tashkent developed its own character by incorporating elements of local architecture and urban life.
According to Saidaziz Ishankhodjaev, Deputy Chairman of the Art and Culture Development Foundation, architects who came to Tashkent after the 1966 earthquake brought different approaches with them and adapted their designs to local conditions.
Courtyards, decorative patterns and architectural solutions associated with traditional Uzbek buildings became part of some modernist projects.
One example is the State Museum of History, where the architecture combines a strong geometric form with features designed for Tashkent’s climate.
A museum designed for the city
The State Museum of History was designed in 1968 by architects Rozanov and Shestopalov. Its white marble exterior, elevated position and distinctive form make it one of the most recognisable buildings in central Tashkent.
Jannat Ismailova, Director of the State Museum of History, says the building was designed with local conditions in mind.
Decorative grilles help protect the building from the intense summer sun, while the large staircase and central entrance give the structure a strong presence in the surrounding urban space.
Local craftsmanship was incorporated into the building as well. Carved wooden doors were made by craftsmen from Kokand, while traditional carved plasterwork, known as ganch, was used inside.
The building was completed in 1970 as the Lenin Museum. In 1992, the State Museum of History of Uzbekistan moved into the building, where it continues to operate.
Much of the original structure has remained intact, making the museum an important example of Tashkent’s modernist architecture.
A museum built around art
The Uzbekistan State Museum of Arts offers another example of how architecture was developed around a building’s purpose.
Construction began in 1967 and was completed in 1974. Unlike museums housed in adapted buildings, this structure was designed specifically as a museum, with exhibition spaces and storage facilities incorporated into the original plan.
Olga Udovenko, Head of the Department of Uzbek Folk Applied Arts at the museum, says the building was considered highly unusual for Tashkent when it was created.
Its original exterior used experimental panels designed to limit direct sunlight and help maintain suitable conditions for artworks. The material was later replaced, but researchers are now considering ways to restore the building’s original appearance.
Inside, the central atrium is surrounded by exhibition levels arranged around the space. Much of the interior has remained unchanged.
The building’s preservation has become part of a wider discussion about how modernist structures can meet current technical requirements while retaining their original architectural character.
A palace built for public life
Modernism also shaped spaces designed for large public gatherings.
The People’s Friendship Palace has hosted concerts, performances, congresses and other major events for decades. Its architecture incorporates decorative elements inspired by local traditions, including patterns and ganch-like details integrated into the building.
The palace has 3,816 seats, while its large stage was designed to accommodate major performances and events.
Its director, Isroil Gulomov, says the building was conceived with local architectural references in mind, including elements that could help protect the interior from Tashkent’s changing temperatures.
The result is a public venue where architectural decoration is closely connected with its practical function.
A circus with a distinctive form
Another landmark from the period was designed specifically for circus performances.
Construction of the Uzbek State Circus began in 1968 and was completed in 1976. The circular building includes performance and training facilities.
Its dome and exterior details were designed with references to the visual character of old Tashkent.
The building is now undergoing restoration, with authorities planning to retain its existing architectural appearance and historic elements.
For Rustam Majidov, Head of the Uzbek State Circus, the restoration is expected to improve conditions for performers while preserving the building itself.
Modernism underground
Tashkent’s modernist architecture also extends below the streets.
Kosmonavtlar metro station uses the theme of space exploration in its design. Its colours, walls and portraits reflect the fascination with science and space that shaped the station’s artistic concept.
Rustam Shafikov, Head of the Electric Train Depot, says each Tashkent Metro station has its own architectural and artistic concept.
The metro itself has changed significantly since its early decades. Its network has expanded, with new lines and stations added in recent years. Passenger numbers have also grown, reaching more than one million journeys a day.
Yet stations such as Kosmonavtlar retain their original artistic character while serving a modern transport network.
Preserving a living part of the city
The UNESCO recognition has placed greater attention on how these buildings should be managed in the future.
For Saidaziz Ishankhodjaev, preservation involves more than maintaining facades. Buildings need to remain safe, functional and suitable for contemporary use, while their surrounding urban environment also needs careful planning.
That includes assessing structural and engineering conditions, fire safety and the way buildings can be adapted without losing their architectural identity.
More than fifty years after Tashkent’s modernist architecture began taking shape, many of its landmarks remain active parts of city life.
Their significance lies in the way architecture, climate, local craftsmanship and public use came together in a particular period of Tashkent’s development. Their UNESCO recognition gives that architectural legacy a new level of protection, while their continued use keeps it part of everyday life.

Are seed oils unhealthy? Why are so many influencers speaking out against them? | Gideon Meyerowitz-Katz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:00:37 UTC
23:00:37 KST

If you’ve been online lately, you’ve probably been bombarded with the discourse about seed oils. Once a completely innocuous food that no one really talked about, they have become the enemy of the moment. Robert F Kennedy Jr, the secretary of health and human services in the US, has called them “toxic” and vowed to act against them. There are countless activewear-clad influencers online saying that nothing harms your health more than these products.
Which is odd, because the Australian dietary guidelines say seed oils are basically fine. You should limit them because they’re high in calories but otherwise there’s no major reason – according to the guidelines and most experts – why you should avoid them. As Prof Lauren Ball, director of the University of Queensland’s Centre for Community Health and Wellbeing, says: “There’s no convincing evidence that eating seed oils like canola or sunflower oil in normal dietary amounts harms our health. In fact, these oils contain unsaturated fats, which are generally beneficial for cardiovascular health.” Dr Jason Wu, a professor at the University of New South Wales, agrees: “The evidence base consistently points to health benefits of eating seed oils.”
So why the hubbub online?
Inflammation claims ‘not supported by evidence’
Seed oils are a group of cooking oils that are, unsurprisingly, extracted from seeds. They’re generally quite highly refined – although you can get less refined versions of many of them – and include canola oil, sunflower seed oil, rice bran oil, soya bean oil and corn oil. Most of the time vegetable oil is composed of seed oils – it’s often a mixture of sunflower seed and canola oils.
The concerns about seed oils boil down to one thing: inflammation. It is asserted that the omega-6 fatty acids contained in most seed oils such as linoleic acid can be harmful in large doses and may cause the body to become more inflamed over time. This isn’t entirely crazy – there is some evidence from rodent studies that omega-6s cause inflammation, and that having too many of them can have long-term negative outcomes.
The problem, of course, is that lab rats and mice aren’t people. Very high levels of omega-6s can cause liver dysfunction and gut issues in rats but that doesn’t mean that a bit of sunflower seed oil is going to destroy your intestines.
Data from humans doesn’t really show this connection. People who eat more linoleic acid have substantially lower risks of cardiovascular disease than those who eat less. Studies looking at supplementing seed oils in people’s diets have shown no major impacts – and sometimes even modest benefits – compared with placebos.
Human studies also don’t support the inflammation link. Randomised trials of omega-6s do not show an increase in inflammation caused by the fatty acids. A randomised crossover study in which the same people were randomly given either omega-3 or omega-6 fatty acids found that there was no difference in how they affected inflammatory markers. Evidence from careful analyses of genetics and causality in humans show little indication that omega-6 fatty acids are inflammatory. As Wu puts it, the pro-inflammatory effects of omega-6 fatty acids are “not supported by evidence”.
Scaremongering ignores the science
On the other hand, we know that animal fats are probably bad for you. They contain high levels of low-density lipoprotein – bad cholesterol – which goes on to clog arteries and cause heart attacks. Ball notes: “Replacing saturated fats, such as those in butter, with unsaturated fats in oils like canola and sunflower can lower LDL cholesterol, an important risk factor for cardiovascular disease.”
In other words, the scientific perspective is simple: seed oils are fine. They’re high in calories but otherwise perfectly healthy, and if you’re eating them to replace saturated fat then they’re probably going to improve your health. So why are there crazy-eyed men yelling at canola oil in the supermarket aisle on Instagram?
The story here is mostly about dietary fads. Favourite diets online now are quite high in animal fats. If you’re promoting your new book about keto diets, it’s not great for sales if everyone thinks that eating too many steaks is going to give them heart disease. Yes, there were some scientific concerns but those have been largely disproven in the literature already.
There are a lot of people scaremongering about seed oils online, which makes sense. You get a lot more attention for yelling that we’re all being poisoned than by calmly explaining the science. I doubt the furore about seed oils is going away any time soon.
But from a health perspective you’re probably better off eating seed oils than any other fats. You should limit consumption, because too many calories is not great, but whether you’re frying, making mayonnaise or whatever, it’s likely that the healthiest choice is a seed oil of some kind.
Dr Gideon Meyerowitz-Katz is an epidemiologist and science communicator and a senior research fellow at the University of Wollongong
Antiviral is a fortnightly column that interrogates the evidence behind the health headlines and factchecks popular wellness claims

Fresh isn’t always best: six easy ways to make better pasta, according to Julia Busuttil Nishimura
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:00:35 UTC
23:00:35 KST

Pasta is a well-loved staple in the kitchen. It’s something that many of us fall back on when we don’t know what to cook or don’t feel like anything too fussy. But if your pasta sauce is a little too watery, or lacks that oomph of restaurant dishes, there are a few simple tricks and techniques that can take your simple midweek dinner to new and delicious heights.
1. Fresh isn’t always best
While some might see fresh pasta as superior, true pasta lovers know that dried pasta has a very important role in Italian kitchens. There are many sauces that are simply better served with dried varieties, such as all of the Roman sauces: amatriciana, carbonara, cacio e pepe and alla gricia. Plus, dried pasta is very economical and a handy pantry staple. Look for dried pasta with a rough surface, perfect for sauce-catching, and a pale yellow colour, which indicates the pasta was dried low and slow, resulting in better texture and flavour.
2. Be generous with the olive oil
If a sauce is olive oil-based, such as aglio olio or alle vongole, or tomato-based, be generous with the extra virgin olive oil you use in the beginning. Particularly with an oil-based sauce, olive oil not only brings flavour, but also helps to emulsify the sauce once that pasta water meets the pan. Topping your finished dish with more extra virgin olive oil to finish is also highly recommended.
3. Cook sauce low and slow
When adding base aromatics for a sauce, make sure your pan and oil are only just warm, rather than very hot. Ingredients like chilli, garlic, onion and even parsley stalks added to a cold or warm pan with oil will slowly release their flavours and yield much more depth than cooking quickly over a high heat can achieve. Garlic, in particular, can become bitter and acrid if cooked over a too-high heat.
4. As salty as the sea?
When I lived in Italy, one of the first things I learned was just how important it is to salt the pasta water. Cooking pasta in unseasoned or underseasoned water results in, well, underseasoned pasta. But how much salt is too much salt? You’ve probably heard people say the water should be “as salty as the sea”, which if you ask me, is far too salty. I never measure, but if you want to, around one-and-a-half to two teaspoons of salt per litre is a good place to start.
5. Keep that precious pasta water
So your pasta is boiling (I like to cook mine for a couple of minutes fewer than the packet directions, and always taste mine towards the end of the cook time to make sure it’s al dente). Don’t tip that perfectly seasoned, now starchy, pasta water down the drain! Instead, keep the pot on the stove, scoop the pasta out either with a sieve for short shapes, or tongs for long ones, and place it directly into the pan with the sauce, which should now be at a fairly high heat. Have a ladle or a mug handy and scoop out some of that precious pasta water into the pan. Finish cooking the pasta in the sauce, adding more pasta water as needed. The starchy water helps both loosen and emulsify the sauce, so it clings to the pasta in the most pleasing way.
If making a sauce that doesn’t require any heat, for example a pesto, place the cooked pasta in a large bowl with the dressing or condiment, add splashes of reserved pasta water and combine until the sauce is glossy and coats the pasta.
6. No cheese, please!
All pasta dishes need grated parmesan, right? Well, I’m no absolutist, but some pasta dishes are simply better without a heaping of parm. Pecorino is the preferred cheese for certain dishes – I especially prefer it when making something with spring vegetables or lamb or those aforementioned Roman pasta sauces. Pecorino is a salty and sharp sheep’s milk cheese which is very commonly used in Lazio, in central Italy, and surrounding regions. I love how it builds a bold sauce when cooked with a handful of ingredients, and also cuts through the richness of ingredients like lamb and guanciale.
Generally fish and cheese don’t mix in Italian cooking – there are some exceptions, most notably mozzarella and anchovy or mussels with pecorino in Puglia, however using a strong cheese like parmigiano reggiano or pecorino with seafood is very uncommon. According to Hippocrates and ancient medicine, cheese and fish eaten together was said to poison the body. But I would just say that the flavour of strong cheese overpowers the sweet brininess of seafood and fish. Instead, try crunchy fried breadcrumbs scattered atop your next plate of seafood pasta.
- Julia Busuttil Nishimura’s cookbook, Simple Pleasures: Recipes to Fall in Love With Every Day, with photography by Armelle Habib, is available now through Pan Macmillan Australia, $44.99

In Gaza, no privacy, no peace: this is what our lives look like a year after the ‘ceasefire’ | Akram al-Sourani
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:00:34 UTC
23:00:34 KST

Every morning, I look at myself and my neighbours standing in the queue for water, and remember how each of us once had a life of our own, our privacy, our own toothbrush, our own home and our own bathroom. How we used to wash our faces and drink clean water without ever imagining that a day would come when these simple routines would become a battle with ourselves and with every drop of water. Even standing beneath a hot shower has become a dream postponed until further notice.
A year has passed since the announcement of the “ceasefire” in Gaza, yet the spectre of war, bombardment and death has never left our lives.
War is not simply the bombing of buildings or the evacuation of a residential neighbourhood. There are small wars inside this one enormous war. The tent is a war. The surveillance drone – the zannana, as we call it, for its incessant buzzing – is a war. Queueing for water is a war. Waiting to use the toilet is a war. The death of privacy is a war. Thirty people crammed into a single room is a war.
Every morning, the same question follows me: what will happen today? Will my children return from what remains of their school to what remains of our home, having walked along what remains of a street, when bombardment could take them from me at any moment?
They walk long distances because transport is difficult and expensive amid fuel shortages, repeated border crossing closures and the trickle of essential supplies into Gaza. It is as though life itself is being rationed to us, drop by drop.
In Gaza, waking up alive is not enough. You must also make sure that the place where you slept is still somewhere you can spend the following night. You must hope that your children can dream of an ordinary day – one in which obtaining a loaf of bread, an education or medical treatment is not an achievement worthy of celebration.
It is as though the ceasefire never happened. The sounds of bombardment, explosions and surveillance drones have continued to accompany our days and nights. What remains of our homes and tents trembles – and so do our hearts.
In Gaza, to be alive is to live on the edge of death. As though we are still trapped in October 2023, when the course of our lives was redrawn into a new geography, and evacuation became a matter of Israeli orders dropped from the sky on leaflets – orders to flee from one place to another, from one tent to another disappointment, from one dangerous patch of land to a corner that seemed slightly less dangerous.
On the morning of Friday 13 October 2023, the skies over Gaza rained down evacuation leaflets ordering us to leave our homes and head south.
We left the north, broken, and entered madness.
We left, but we have never truly returned to ourselves. We lost the people we were before the war. We are no longer who we used to be. The war has turned us into strangers, unfamiliar even to ourselves.
We left everything behind.
We left the stairwell, the curtains and the windows. The sofas, the router, the 55in television, the pressure cooker on the stove, the unwashed dishes – and half a lemon that, for some ridiculous reason, we always insisted on keeping in the fridge door.
We left behind conversations, arguments, disagreements, embraces and unfinished secrets. Stories told after dinner. A bunch of keys, and a never-ending chain of household troubles.
We left our photo albums, our wedding pictures, and the hairstyle that irritated me on my wedding night because of all the hairpins; the clutter in the storeroom, the gas lighter, the bathrobe hanging behind the bathroom door, the dining table, the backgammon table, and the water, electricity and internet bills.
And we left behind a precious set of drinking glasses, imprisoned in the display cabinet since 1997 on the charge of being “far too good to bring out for guests”.
After the bombing, they ended up out in the street.
And it turned out we had been wrong to punish our little boy for breaking a cup.
We never imagined that we, too, would be broken.
All of us were.
Three years have passed, yet we still fear hearing again the announcement that changed our lives: “Leave your homes immediately and head south.”
Three years of displacement, tents and fear. Three years in which school years have begun and ended without our children experiencing anything resembling a normal education.
For the first time, school years are no longer measured in grades and certificates, but in the number of years children have spent displaced.
Third year of tent school.
It is as though the words I wrote years ago had been waiting for me in the present. As though I had written an early warning that I myself failed to take seriously.
I once wrote, in my 2017 book What’s That:
“A tent that lets us down.”
And in a Facebook post that same year I wrote:
“We are all beggars in the making.”
I never imagined that the words I had written in satire would one day become the details of our daily lives.
From Gaza to Khan Younis, to Rafah, to al-Mawasi, to al-Zawayda, to Deir al-Balah, from a tent to what remains of our home, we have arrived safely in the unknown.
Our dreams have yet to arrive. Our hopes have yet to arrive. I fear they may have evaporated somewhere along the way.
And today, a year after the announcement of the “ceasefire”, I am still standing in queues: for aid, for cooking gas, for water – and in the endless queue of those waiting for the unknown.
I wait for my children to return from school, and I try to recover something of the life we left behind.
The name of this chapter has changed. But fear has not changed its address.
There is more to tell – if there is anything left of our minds, or our lives, to tell it.
- Akram Al-Sourani is a writer and poet from Gaza City, and the author of A Homeland Out of Coverage, Half-Baked Homeland and What’s That

News coverage of psilocybin often outpaces the science, systematic review finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:00:02 UTC
23:00:02 KST

News outlets and clinical studies report positive effects of psilocybin therapy at nearly the same rate, according to a new systematic review published in JAMA Network Open. However, while scientific papers tend to emphasize small sample sizes and study design flaws, news articles frequently present the compound’s medical benefits as established fact and extend them to conditions with little or no clinical trial backing. The findings suggest a gap between preliminary scientific evidence and public media narratives surrounding psychedelic medicine.
Psilocybin is a naturally occurring psychoactive compound found in hallucinogenic mushrooms. When a person ingests psilocybin, the body converts it into psilocin, a chemical that binds primarily to serotonin receptors in the brain and alters mood, emotion, and sensory perception. Medical researchers first began studying psychedelics in the 1940s, though legal restrictions in the 1970s slowed clinical studies to a near standstill for decades. Since the 1990s, scientific interest has rebounded, with modern researchers testing whether psilocybin can help treat mental health and substance use disorders.
Despite the surge in scientific interest, the clinical evidence supporting psilocybin remains in its early stages. For instance, a 2024 scoping review by several of the same researchers, which cataloged 193 published and 80 ongoing psilocybin studies, found that only 12 percent were randomized clinical trials, the standard medical test in which participants are randomly assigned to receive either an active treatment or a comparison substance. Most of the existing studies were small preliminary tests with a median of 22 participants.
Additionally, a 2023 systematic review of 10 psychedelic trials found that blinding, which keeps participants and staff unaware of who received the active drug versus a placebo, was either unsuccessful or never checked, likely because the drugs’ effects are so noticeable.
The authors argue that public interest has outpaced this preliminary evidence base. Between 2018 and 2021, the use of hallucinogens other than LSD, such as psilocybin, nearly doubled from 3.4 percent to 6.6 percent among young adults in the United States, and some people now use the substance off-label for mental health conditions without regulatory approval. Because many people rely on news coverage to inform health decisions, lead author Kim Madden of McMaster University’s Department of Anesthesia, senior author Anthony Adili, and their colleagues set out to compare the tone, safety details, and effectiveness claims in news articles against clinical trial publications.
“Psychedelics are having a renaissance, receiving increasing media coverage in recent years,” said Adili, a professor and vice chair of the Department of Surgery and an associate member of the School of Biomedical Engineering at McMaster University, as well as the chief innovation officer, head of orthopedics, an orthopedic surgeon, and director of the Centre for Health Innovation and Research in Psychedelics at St. Joseph’s Healthcare Hamilton. “While the socialization of these substances is helping facilitate research initiatives, we wanted to investigate how aligned media reporting is with the current published trials.”
To conduct their two-part systematic review, the researchers updated their earlier scoping review, searching four medical databases for English-language clinical trials of psilocybin targeting any medical condition between January 1, 2014, and October 10, 2024. They included randomized clinical trials and phase 1 or phase 2 nonrandomized trials, excluding review papers and studies on recreational use.
Next, the team searched the Factiva database for English-language news articles discussing clinical uses of psilocybin published between January 1, 2014, and April 22, 2025. They extended the media search six months past the trial cutoff to account for the delay between a study’s publication and subsequent news coverage, while excluding press releases, stock reports, and brief summaries.
Two reviewers independently screened and extracted data from every eligible trial publication and news story, with a third researcher resolving disagreements. For the trials, the team recorded the medical condition treated, sample size, dosing details, whether psychotherapy was included, safety outcomes, and the authors’ conclusions on whether the treatment worked. They also assessed randomized trials for bias using the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool. For the media articles, reviewers logged the target audience, specific health claims, discussions of side effects or drug policy, and overall tone, which they classified as favorable (combining optimistic and cautiously optimistic pieces), neutral, or skeptical.
The final dataset included 70 trial publications and 172 online news articles. Annual counts for both trial publications and media stories climbed starting in 2018, when trial publications rose from zero in 2017 to eight, and peaked in 2023. Most of the trials were conducted in the United States and the United Kingdom, while most news articles came from outlets in the United States and Canada. Nearly all media articles (163, or 95 percent) targeted the general public rather than medical professionals (9, or 5 percent), and 115 articles (67 percent) referenced at least one published clinical trial.
Of the 70 trial publications, 36 (51 percent) were randomized clinical trials, 30 (43 percent) were nonrandomized experimental studies, and 4 (6 percent) consisted of two nonrandomized crossover studies, one pooled analysis, and one secondary analysis. Nearly all of the trial publications described small sample sizes of fewer than 100 participants, accounting for 65 of the 70 papers (93 percent), and follow-up durations were often short or incompletely reported. Quality assessments indicated that 19 of the 36 randomized trials had a high or uncertain risk of bias regarding the blinding of participants and personnel, alongside concerns related to for-profit funding.
When comparing overall conclusions, trial publications and news stories reported positive outcomes at similar frequencies, though the two figures measure different things: a trial’s own conclusion about its main outcome versus any favorable claim in a news story. Forty-nine of the 70 trial publications (70 percent) concluded that psilocybin benefited patients on the primary clinical outcome, 5 (7 percent) reported mixed effectiveness, 1 (1 percent) found no benefit, 4 (6 percent) had inconclusive findings, and 11 (16 percent) provided no efficacy conclusion.
In the press, 125 of the 172 media articles (73 percent) made at least one positive claim about psilocybin’s effectiveness for a health condition, while 47 (27 percent) made none. In total, 122 media articles (71 percent) adopted a favorable tone, comprising 98 (57 percent) optimistic and 24 (14 percent) cautiously optimistic pieces, while 45 (26 percent) were neutral and 5 (3 percent) were skeptical.
Beneath those parallel numbers, scientific papers and news outlets framed the evidence quite differently. “The most practical significance of this systematic review is that there is a disconnect between media publications and the hard science,” Adili told PsyPost.
While trial authors routinely emphasized methodological limitations and the preliminary nature of their work, news articles tended to present benefits as established fact. Both groups focused primarily on depression, which was examined in 47 trial publications (67 percent) and mentioned in 138 media articles (80 percent). Other conditions examined in the trial publications included substance use disorders in 11 papers (16 percent), cancer-related distress in 5 (7 percent), headaches or migraines in 4 (6 percent), anxiety in 4 (6 percent), bipolar II disorder in 3 (4 percent), and body dysmorphic disorder in 2 (3 percent), plus single publications (1 percent each) on obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), autism, anorexia nervosa, and demoralization.
In contrast, news coverage frequently promoted psilocybin for conditions with little or no clinical trial backing. Most notably, 74 media articles (43 percent) referenced PTSD and 5 (3 percent) mentioned Alzheimer disease or other neurodegenerative conditions as clinical uses, even though zero eligible trials tested psilocybin for those conditions. Similarly, 72 news stories (42 percent) highlighted anxiety and 18 (10 percent) discussed anorexia nervosa or other eating disorders, despite the trial literature containing only four studies on anxiety and one on anorexia nervosa. Media reports also occasionally cited OCD (12 articles, or 7 percent), chronic pain (5, or 3 percent), and long COVID (4, or 2 percent).
The researchers also found differences in how treatment context and safety were reported. In 51 trial publications (73 percent), psilocybin was administered alongside psychotherapy, typically at doses of 25 milligrams or higher. While 107 news articles (62 percent) mentioned psychotherapy, 143 (83 percent) omitted dosing information entirely.
For safety, 31 trial publications (44 percent) reported safety outcomes, with 24 (34 percent) documenting short-term adverse events like temporary anxiety, nausea, or headaches, and only 4 (6 percent) assessing long-term safety. Media coverage addressed safety even less often, with only 51 articles (30 percent) mentioning adverse effects. When news stories did discuss harms, they focused on psychosis or challenging psychological experiences, with 12 articles (7 percent) noting potential long-term psychological risks that were not consistently tied to specific trial findings.
“Something surprising to me was how minimally media articles reported on safety,” Adili noted. “Based on the lack of safety reporting, we want audiences to be more aware that media articles may bias positive results without discussing safety concerns. As a result, patients may enter into trials with preconceived notions of the outcomes leading to potential disappointment if their expectations aren’t met.”
Policy themes were also widespread in the press. Across the 172 media articles, 48 (28 percent) discussed legalizing or decriminalizing psilocybin for clinical use, and 45 (26 percent) advocated for expanding patient access. Another 28 articles (16 percent) discussed reducing stigma around psychedelics, whereas only 8 (5 percent) mentioned the potential for misuse or abuse. The authors noted that pairing calls for expanded legal access with optimistic efficacy claims could foster public expectations that exceed the current medical evidence.
“We hope that the average person is more critical of overly positive media portrayal of psychedelics and is empowered to do their own research,” Adili explained. “When possible, reference the study that the media article references, delve deeper into potential safety concerns, and conduct further research.”
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. The findings concern how psilocybin research is communicated, not whether the compound works; the trials remain early-phase, while public enthusiasm and policy changes in places like Oregon and Colorado have moved ahead. Additionally, the media review was limited to English-language, text-based online news articles in the Factiva database, primarily from the United States and Canada. The analysis did not capture television, radio, podcasts, or social media, which may convey different narratives to the public.
On the clinical side, the 70 trial publications included several papers reporting different analyses of the same underlying trials, along with conference abstracts and a dissertation, so they do not represent 70 independent experiments. The review also relied on each paper’s own conclusions about whether psilocybin worked, rather than a formal grading of the strength of the evidence.
Evaluating the tone and messaging of news articles also involves some subjectivity. Even though two reviewers coded each article independently using predefined criteria, their initial agreement was moderate, meaning another research team might classify certain content differently. Moving forward, the authors suggest that scientists prioritize larger, high-quality randomized trials with longer follow-up periods and thorough safety reporting. The authors also suggest that media outlets can support informed health decisions by avoiding sensationalism and explaining study limitations, sample sizes, and remaining scientific uncertainties.
“At the Centre for Health Innovation and Research in Psychedelics (CHIRP), our next steps are to design and conduct rigorous randomized controlled trials to produce evidence and actionable outcomes that can improve patient care,” Adili added. “Long-term, we hope to provide novel solutions for patients with few alternate options across a wide range of subspecialties from gut-brain health to neurodegenerative disease, chronic pain, and women’s health.”
The study, “Clinical Evidence on Psilocybin and Its Representation in Media Reporting: A Systematic Review,” was authored by Kim Madden, Breanne Flood, Imad Kashir, Rayan Ahmad, Hiba Ali, Rotem Petranker, James MacKillop, and Anthony Adili.

New poll upends narrative that Democratic voters are split on El-Sayed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:00:00 UTC
23:00:00 KST

In the final televised debate for Michigan’s Senate race, GOP candidate Mike Rogers used his closing remarks to claim that Jewish Democrats were supporting him because they view his Democratic opponent, Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, as “too extreme” on the subject of Israel.
“Jewish Democrats who are afraid for their children when their daughters can’t wear their Star of David walking across Michigan’s campus, these are real,” Rogers told the audience. “My opponent’s rhetoric, his vitriol, is having consequences.”
The idea that El-Sayed’s criticisms of Israel have alienated Jewish Democrats is certainly not limited to propaganda from the Rogers campaign. In recent weeks, multiple articles have used this very narrative as their thesis.
“Michigan Democrats at odds over Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed as November nears,” a Quartz headline declares.
“Questions about El-Sayed’s stance on Israel, accusations of antisemitism, and his campaign’s relationship with [left-wing Twitch streamer Hasan] Piker have kept the party’s attention away from its general-election opponent, Republican Mike Rogers,” insists the piece. “The divisions come as Michigan’s statehouse and governor’s races are also closely contested.”
Division was also the theme of an NPR piece claiming that Democrats were trying to “unify” before the midterms. The article asserts that “healing the fractures is proving complicated” and quotes multiple Democratic voters who express reservations about the candidate over Israel.
“Democrats are still struggling to unite behind El-Sayed after the primary exposed deep disagreements over Israel,” says PBS News.
CNN said a “ruptured” Democratic Party is “trying” to unite around the candidate.
The Detroit-based Super PAC TFM is attempting to ride this purported wave, spending nearly $6 million on ad campaigns connected to a “Democrats for Mike Rogers” effort.
“We believe in the true spirit of the Democratic Party, always standing against hate and bigotry, no matter where it comes from, who it targets, or whether it is politically inconvenient or not,” reads the campaign’s website. “We believe every American deserves dignity, respect, and equal protection under the law.”
This past weekend, a planned “Democrats for Mike Rogers” rally in Pontiac, Michigan, drew almost no one.
The Bulwark’s Joe Perticone shared images of the event on Twitter, showing three people in an empty parking lot and one person operating a camera.
“When your astroturf campaign meets actual turf,” joked the liberal social media account MeidasTouch.
The low turnout probably wasn’t a surprise to anyone who read a recent Marist survey of Michigan voters. Despite the media narrative detailing a massive split among Democratic voters, 95% of Democrats say they’re voting for El-Sayed, and just 4% say they’re voting for Rogers. 3% of Michigan Republicans actually say they’re voting for El-Sayed, but this minuscule number certainly hasn’t led to a host of stories about divisions within the GOP.
“The Democrats have a six-point advantage against the Republicans on the generic congressional ballot question among Michigan likely voters,” reads a write-up summarizing the poll’s findings. “That leads opens up to 10 points among registered voters, little changed from the nine-point lead the Democrats had in September. President Donald Trump’s approval rating is upside down in Michigan, and a plurality of likely voters express worry about their personal finances.”
If this is reality, why do many articles on the race tell the story of a divided party, and why do they rely primarily on testimony from rare voters to convey a wider trend?
Furthermore, why do so few of these pieces point out that Israel has grown deeply unpopular among Democratic voters and that El-Sayed’s positions are consistent with the vast majority of the base? An April 2026 Pew poll found that 80% of Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents held an unfavorable view of Israel, compared with 53% in 2022.
This framing goes well beyond El-Sayed. The idea that the Democratic Party is divided on Israel is a consistent theme in the mainstream press, despite the fact that voters are effectively aligned on the issue.
“There’s only one problem with the tensions,’ ‘divided,’ and ‘wedge issue’ framing: It is not supported by any polls,” wrote media critic Adam Johnson in The Intercept earlier this year. “The ‘divide,’ such as it is, is increasingly not among Democrats or even liberals; it is between the supermajority of Democratic Party voters and party leadership. While party leaders such as House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and Senator Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, and big Democratic donors, are pro-Israel, actual Democratic voters have moved on from Israel with remarkable speed and consistency.”
The pro-Israel lobbying group AIPAC recently announced that it would stop issuing endorsements or directly earmarking contributions to political candidates. The move comes less than five years after the organization began making such endorsements. The shift exposes a clear truth: voters view AIPAC as a toxic entity, and their public support is doing more to hurt candidates than help them.
This was clear during Michigan’s Democratic primary, when El-Sayed highlighted opponent Haley Stevens’s connections to the group. An August Axios report showed that Mike Rogers even expressed concerns about an AIPAC endorsement, although he has since publicly welcomed their help.
This all seems relevant to next week’s election or, at least, more relevant than a split that doesn’t exist.

EU eyes better preparadness for climate risks with new strategy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:00:00 UTC
23:00:00 KST

The European Commission presented on Tuesday a new climate strategy aiming to better identify droughts, floods, wildfires and other effects of climate change and to manage the risks more effectively.
Climate resilience should be taken into account in all major EU policy areas in the future, the commission said.
"Europe is warming at double the global rate. To become truly climate resilient, we need to adjust and learn along the way," Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said.
"Today, we are presenting a European approach to climate risks, to anticipate, to prepare for and to manage. We are ensuring that climate resilience will be included in policies across the continent, supporting investment, innovation and long-term growth," she added.
A new Climate Resilience Act is intended to ensure that EU countries assess their climate risks and plan their preventive measures using the same basic assumptions.
The specific ways in which the member states protect themselves against heat, drought and flooding will largely remain up to the individual countries, depending on their risks and priorities.
A website entitled the European Climate Viewer will show potential hazards for specific locations and periods. For example, users should be able to identify railway routes that may be particularly exposed to high temperatures or heavy rainfall, allowing targeted protective measures to be planned.
Other platforms will help public authorities identify suitable, proven measures for addressing specific climate risks.
The aim of the initiative is to anticipate the effects of climate change and prevent damage through action at EU, national and local levels, the commission said.
According to the commission's estimates, economic losses caused by climate-related damage amounted to around 200 billion euros ($223 billion) between 2022 and 2025, or 50 billion euros per year.
In September, von der Leyen announced that the initiative would pursue a whole-of-society approach, down to the local level.
According to data from the EU Earth observation programme Copernicus, the past summer was the hottest on record for Western Europe.
Up to Sept. 2, the area of land that burned in wildfires in the EU was almost twice as large as the average for 2006 to 2025.
According to estimates by British scientists, heat killed around 50,000 people in European cities over the summer, more than ever before.
In Germany, some 16,000 people died as a result of heat, according to estimates by the Robert Koch Institute (RKI), a government health agency.
