UK Politician Jess Asato Got Deepfaked. Now She’s Taking xAI to Court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:29:41 UTC
22:29:41 KST

Few people understand the current deepfake epidemic better than Jess Asato. The British Labour MP has spent years campaigning against the use of technology to abuse women and girls. Then, after calling out Elon Musk during the notorious Grok Deepfake Scandal of 2025, Asato found herself caught in the very crisis she had been trying to prevent.
Disturbing and degrading deepfake images of the MP circulated widely. One appeared to depict a sexual assault. When Asato reported them to X, the platform repeatedly dismissed her complaints. So she decided to take the fight somewhere else: the courts. She is now pursuing legal action against Musk’s xAI, arguing that it unlawfully used her image without her consent. The case could help establish a precedent for holding AI companies accountable when their products cause harm.
For Asato, this is personal, but it is hardly new territory. Before entering Parliament, she spent years working with charities supporting survivors of domestic abuse and vulnerable children. That experience has shaped her political career, informing her push for stronger protections for women and children online. Now, she is confronting more troubling questions: What happens when the technology enabling abuse becomes ubiquitous, the platforms hosting it refuse to intervene, and the people targeted are left to fight back on their own?
At stake for Asato is more than the misuse of a single image. It is whether consent still means anything when AI can manufacture almost anything, and whether the companies building these tools can be made to answer for what they do. Asato is betting that the law can catch up with the technology. And she is prepared to take on Musk to find out. (xAI did not immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment.)
Also, before you read on, be aware that this interview includes references to sexual assault and child sex abuse.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
ROSIE SWASH: Jess, I just want to have a couple of warm-up questions before we get into it. Tell us a bit about your background, how did you end up becoming MP for Lowestoft?
JESS ASATO: Sure. So, I grew up in East Anglia in Norfolk and Suffolk, and in a not very political family. I got the politics bug in 1997 when Tony Blair was talking about education, education, education. Having experienced it, I felt that we could be doing a lot better in our education system. So I joined the Labour Party and got involved with my local groups.
Before Parliament, I worked for the largest children's charity in the UK for three years on their policy and public affairs, trying to change legislation on behalf of the most vulnerable children in the country. Six years prior to that I worked for a domestic abuse charity called SafeLives where we did huge amounts of work to try and improve the situation for survivors of domestic abuse, particularly through the Domestic Abuse Act.
Those twin issues of women and children have become my focus in Parliament, and I’ve been very clear that my reason for being here, my mission really, is to be a voice for women and children.
Well, that’s a good entry point for us to start talking about this year. So in early 2026, there was widespread reporting on Grok, xAI’s chatbot, being used to create sexualized images of children and women, and those images being circulated on X. How aware were you at this point of the phenomenon of deepfakes being used in this way?
Very aware, and actually had been working with survivors who had experienced deepfakes for quite a number of years. Ever since the advent of AI this has been happening to women, and there’s also been developing risks of children both being put into child sexual abuse material and also children using nudification tools on other children, thereby criminalizing themselves because these tools are so easy to access and often free.
So I was already very alive to the huge harms being created by AI deepfakes of both women and children before Grok ever happened. It was a known harm, which is why many of the tools from other companies had already taken steps to stop them from being used to create this kind of content.
There are a number of tools where, if you type in “nudify,” or “take the clothes off this person,” the tool will refuse to do that. So into that environment came Grok.
Was there a particularly egregious example or incident prior to Grok when you became aware of deepfakes that really stuck with you?
There is a brilliant campaigner who goes by the name of Jodie. I think it was probably listening to the experiences of Jodie, who was deepfaked, and it was such an affront to her that somebody would do this, and then she found out it was actually a friend. Such a betrayal of trust.
These things destroy not just the individual involved, but often families and everyone around them too.
For people who don’t know, who exactly was Jodie? Is this a constituent of yours or someone who came forward to you specifically?
No, no, no. She's a very well-known campaigner on this issue. That’s not her real name.
I know it sounds obvious, but what exactly is nudification?
It is where you ask an AI tool to take the image or video of a real person and use generative AI to make that person either nude, partially nude, or engaging in pornographic acts. This is something that, because of the photorealistic nature of AI images, it has become increasingly hard to see what is a fake image.
It can often look incredibly, incredibly real.
So what was it particularly about the Grok scandal earlier this year that made you want to raise this in the House of Commons?
It was the fact that we already knew that you could stop this from happening by designing the AI tool to reject the ability to do this.
This was completely avoidable. That’s why I spoke out, but also because I’d just spent a year and a half campaigning to get a ban on nudification apps, and here was an all-purpose AI tool becoming a nudification app.
It just felt to me as though we were making strides in the UK, and then the world’s richest man and his product decided to turn the clock back.
So what exactly did you stand up and say?
What I did was I talked about the need for the government to accelerate its ban on nudification apps, which it did. So the then secretary of state for science, innovation and technology, Liz Kendall, said that she was going to bring that ban into law through the Crime and Policing Act, which she did.
But I also said that it was very important that we went further than that, because, of course, Grok itself is not a sole-purpose nudification tool. It has a general use, and therefore we needed to bring all AI chatbots under the auspices of the Online Safety Act. That is also what eventually happened in the Crime and Policing Act, and we’re now waiting until that legislation comes into effect. There’s got to be a consultation, I understand, before it does.
So technically another Grok could happen in this period, but in the future there would be much stronger measures that we could take against tools like Grok creating nudification content.
So that’s a really positive outcome of your interjection in Parliament, but what else happened as a result of you standing up?
Well, one of the things that happened was that I posted on social media saying that Elon Musk should stop Grok from being able to do this.
And then, of course, I became a victim of the same trend. So Grok put this woman in a bikini. And most of the images were sort of pornified, I would say. They weren’t nude images, but they were me with inflated boobs in a bikini.
Then people tried to make it funny, I guess, by putting a swastika on me or hammer and sickles. Or making me pregnant with quintuplets and putting me in a kitchen. Because of course that’s the only use for women—birthing and making dinner. But the really disturbing one was a video of me being surrounded by a group of men, chloroformed over my mouth, and then I fall backwards onto a chair. Then my skirts are lifted up. So no nudity, but clearly the next frame is meant to be a sexual assault. So it was really distressing and disturbing.
That was the point at which a friend said, “You probably need to reach out to a lawyer.” Because each of these things we reported to X, and none of them contravened their terms and conditions. We just kept getting those sort of repeat emails coming back. “We’ve looked into this, and there’s nothing to see here.” So I did engage a lawyer, who sent a letter to X to ask for these to be removed, and they were.
But it was at that point that he said, “I think you might actually have a case. We think that xAI have broken the law.”
It’s impressive how you handled it, but it must have been really awful.
It was; it was awful. This is done to demean, to degrade, and to push women out of online spaces. From my perspective, I tend to use bad or difficult things that happen as a way of thinking about how we change this for the future.
My old boss was an amazing woman called Tessa Jowell. She used to say to me, “How do we change this negative energy into something positive?” “How do we work our way out of this into a place where we actually feel that we’ve learnt from it?”
So I guess she instilled in me that sense that when something bad happens you’ve got a choice. You can wallow in it, you can try and forget about it, or you can use it as a catalyst for change.
So I was quite trepidatious about the idea of taking on a legal action. Not least because of the person who is at the top of xAI, now SpaceXAI. [Eds. note: The company recently rebranded itself as SpaceXSI.] He’s the world’s richest man. But also because I didn’t want myself to necessarily be the story. Many, many women had things that were created of them through both Grok and other nudification tools that are much, much worse.
Having said that, I knew that if there was the opportunity to say that actually they’d broken the law, there was an important point of principle on behalf of all of the women and the children whose images were manipulated and misused by Grok, who would never, ever be able to bring a legal case. So I decided that I wanted to do this, because I wanted to be able to show that no one is bigger than the law.
Doesn’t matter how rich you are or how powerful you are or how big a reach you have in terms of your social media presence or who your friends might be at the top of various governments. If you break the law in our country, you need to feel the force of that. As an ex-lawyer and now as a legislator, it is important that we uphold our law where it has been broken.
So it’s also about giving control back, I think, to us as individuals, but also as a society. So many of these digital changes have been done without our consent or say, and I think there’s a feeling that there’s a sort of runaway train that we’re all on, whether we want to be or not, because we all need to use online spaces for our work, for connection.
And so my view is that we should be expecting companies to respect our law or at least make new laws to bring them more into line with what society really needs.
You said that you gave it some thought. In that moment of trying to decide how to respond, what are you weighing up? Who are you talking to? Are you going back and talking to your team or your family to work out how you should respond, knowing that it may invite further speculation and further attention?
My family mostly, my husband in particular. It’s one thing being a politician and arguing your case to change the law on behalf of women and children; it’s another having your own legal case.
So I was worried about the impact that that might have on my family, my children. I also know that this can bring danger to politicians. So I worried about the fact that I am obviously engaging and making the defendant somebody who has got this very wide reach on social media. However, I don’t like bullies. I very strongly believe that it’s important to fight on the field that you’ve got, and this was an opportunity I felt to make a difference.
So I weighed that up and thought that it was worth having that kind of attention and potential danger, because there is a bigger issue here that we need to get right.
When you say you don’t like bullies, are you talking about, let’s face it, men who used Grok in this way in the first place, or are you talking about Elon Musk?
I’m talking about the men who use this as a form of trying to push women out of the online space. Actually it was quite clear in quite a lot of the comments that they were saying, “Well, if you don’t like this, then get off the platform.”
Either that or, “If this is too hot for you, get out the kitchen,” which I always find quite funny because they put me in a kitchen. I think it’s really interesting when you look at X in terms of its demographics in the UK, it’s highly weighted toward men. I think some of that’s down to the fact that there is just so much misogyny and abuse on it. So I’m assuming, and correct me if I’m wrong, that the other side of the response to going public is that other women have come forward to you.
Absolutely. Actually, one of the heartening things has been people coming forward and saying, “Thank you, because this has now given me the license to actually accept that what happened to me wasn’t my fault. It’s not my shame.” So, in a way, what I’m hoping is that this has helped some victims to process what has happened to them and understand that this was not right.
I’ve also had emails from parents where they’ve said that this has happened to their daughter. It’s been done by boys at school. I’ve had teachers saying that boys have made pornographic AI imagery of them. And it’s something where we’ve just sort of let it happen and wash over us and accept that somehow this is now a part of the society we live in.
So yes quite a number of people have come forward. Obviously not all of their experiences have been through Grok, and I think one of the things is that often, when you see these films or images, you don’t know what platform they’ve been created on. I mean, the only reason why I knew it was Grok was because it was integrated with X, and you could see the commands that had been given by the users.
But much of the time, when this content is created, most victims don’t know by whom or on what platform. And so there’s really very little they can do about it. And I think it’s that sort of sense of helplessness that you have been violated, and that is the word that comes up so frequently from victims of this particular issue.
It’s not just that it’s nudified. Of course, much of my content wasn’t. It’s the lack of consent. And lots of people say, “Oh, but it’s fake. It’s just a laugh.” But what people don’t understand is that it is hyperrealistic, and it’s your face.
It’s a piece of your soul. It’s not just pixels on the internet. It is a person. And because obviously I’ve worked for a long time in violence against women and girls and spoken to many victims of sexual assault and to children who’ve been victims of child sexual abuse, it is the lack of consent that is so disturbing.
It can leave people with PTSD and quite deep trauma. And there have been a number of people I’ve met who have said that the world seems less safe to them because this has happened to them.
I think you’ve already touched on it, but what is the biggest myth around deepfakes that you would wish to dispel?
That it comes without any harm.
That it’s just a laugh.
There is clear harm, even when it’s not done to demean or degrade. So even if it’s done sometimes by friends, the fact is that you haven’t consented to that. There is something about the human psyche which is that when you see yourself so realistically created in a different situation or scenario, something that’s not something you would have done, I think it’s quite discombobulating.
I think your brain can’t quite process it because your brain knows it’s not true, but it looks very true. And I think psychologically we still don’t really understand how this content is going to change the way we think about our world, how we know what is true and what isn’t true.
Right.
Now, of course, you can do fantastic things with generative AI. All I’m calling for is that we respect people’s consent, and that’s why one of the things I’ve been working on since this happened is to look at whether we could create a system of consent to be manipulated by AI.
Could we create a greater right over our likeness online so that there’s a new social norm, which is that no, you can’t copy and paste that picture into an AI chatbot and do whatever you want with it. That’s not yours. It’s not your data. It’s their data, and you’re breaching the law if you do that.
I think if we were to do that, we could have a wide range of applications. It wouldn’t just be in this space of the sexualization of women and children. But also with political disinformation. We are so close to a moment where somebody produces a hyperrealistic video of a politician saying something that they didn’t, and then that leads to real-world harm. And so we’ve got to find a new social norm that says unless for public figures it’s parody or satire—and absolutely you’ve got to protect that—but in all other instances your picture, your voice, and your moving image is your personal data, and it’s not for anyone else to use.
So that’s interesting because you’re touching on new social norms and the possibility of new laws to keep up with this technology. But your lawsuit is specifically under a data law. Talk to me about that versus a law around consensual imagery or deepfakes specifically.
So, my case is brought under existing law, the GDPR, the data protection law, and it contends that Grok misused my data without my consent. It didn’t have consent to process my data, the data being my face and my likeness. But also under privacy laws that I had a reasonable expectation of privacy and that particularly the video of me being prepared for sexual assault reaches a criminal threshold and that nobody should be expected to be on the receiving end of.
Let’s remember, this is actually a product that has been designed by software engineers and developers, and that actually products should not lead to an invasion of privacy and the harm that I then experienced as a result of that, including distress and a sense that I was being harassed by this particular creation of this particular video.
So, it rests on good solid legal grounds, and we await the defense from SpaceX AI.
I don’t know how much you can say, legally, but what part of the process are you in? What happens next? What’s the timeline for a resolution to this case?
So like with a lot of legal cases, it’s very, very hard to pin down a timeline. But my understanding is that we should be receiving the response and the defense from SpaceXAI in the near future. But we don’t have a deadline or a particular time that I can put on it.
After that, my understanding is that the case will then be looked at, and if there is a case to answer, then it will go to a court hearing. But once again, no idea when that might be. And I think there’s lots of legal things that I don’t understand that need to be worked out in the meantime as well between my lawyers and their lawyers.
Have you ever had any acknowledgment on X itself from Elon Musk or anyone at xAI about this case? Has he ever spoken publicly about it?
No.
Would you expect him to?
I don’t think so. They clearly want to challenge this case, and so the best place to do that, I think, is in the courts and to leave it to see whether the merits of the case come through.
You were in New York recently to address the city council about your case. You didn’t get to speak to anyone directly at the company, is that right?
No. I mean, despite being subpoenaed, they didn’t turn up. Four of the other frontier AI companies did attend under subpoena. SpaceXAI didn’t, but they eventually did get their hearing with SpaceX in the city council. So, they have now had their opportunity to put questions and indeed did raise my case with them, I understand.
Was it a little enraging to attend a hearing like that where a company that you’re suing doesn't bother turning up?
I think it’s quite rude to the elected members of the New York City Council when you are a business that operates in New York. Indeed, I was told that they were just a few subway stops from City Hall. So I had traveled quite a long way from England to be there. And they couldn’t be bothered to turn up, which yeah, it felt arrogant and a bit of a snub, but they’ve now got there, so that’s a good thing.
Since you made the decision to take this to the courts, there have been a number of proposals in Parliament, notably there was a proposal for a kill switch bill at one point. Now I believe it’s dead or it’s not going very well. Is that right?
So, yes, there have been proposals put forward for a kill switch. And my understanding is the government rejected that. There continues to be strong calls for regulation of particularly superintelligent AI. We’ve heard various theories, whether it’s 2 percent, 10 percent, 20 percent risk of human extinction from this sort of race to superintelligence, a recursive AI, and we wouldn’t allow those margins of risk in any other sphere.
We would not allow it in bridge building or airplane making. They didn’t even allow it when they were testing the nuclear bomb and the Trinity test. It feels to me as though so much of this decision-taking is outside of democratic structures. It’s not with the public. It is being done by some incredibly, exceptionally wealthy companies and organizations who say they have the interests of the planet at heart.
But each time, actually, they’re asked about whether that is the future of humanity or whether they think that these risks could kill humanity, there’s a sort of shrugging of the shoulders and, “We’ll just keep going because we want to make money,” I guess.
It has been reported in the British press that there are members of Parliament, some of whom are working on committees to do with technology, who still don’t really understand what AI is. And clearly you’re not one of them because you’re aware of the dangers of this issue. But do you feel working across parties that you’re still having to explain technology and its dangers and possibilities to people who are making laws, or should be making laws, to protect the public from AI?
Well, look, I don’t think that’s only the case about AI. We are humans after all, and we have to deal with every single subject that exists under the sun. We have to get our heads around things that we’ve never heard of before.
A bit like being a journalist actually.
That’s true. But you have to then make laws and decisions. So, I don’t want to be unfair to my colleagues.
You may be a specialist in housing policy and you then need to get your head around AI. But I would say that this is the most important issue in front of anybody in parliament or politics at the moment, and therefore, everyone needs to get their head around AI.
My background is in social policy for women and children. But because we did quite a lot of work on the Online Safety Act when I was working for a children’s charity, we campaigned to get the age verification ban for children in pornography into the OSA. And indeed, created quite a strong piece of legislation in respect of that.
We had to get our heads around online safety on the online space. The problem was, of course, that act didn’t include AI chatbots. There were a number of amendments that tried to get it in and we would’ve been in a much better place had we actually succeeded.
But you know, I’m still not a tech expert even though I had quite a while to try to understand these things. But my view is that this is definitely the new front line of where harms are occurring. We can see that hugely in the increase in AI-generated child sexual abuse material, which is absolutely exploding.
In the end it comes down to the people who create the products. And that’s why we should be seeing digital product regulation in the same way as we would any other product regulation.
I’m very, very hopeful that the government is going to look at it really, really closely because there are always design choices that you can make and that can help to prevent these harms, these harms that are completely knowable. We can predict these harms, and so it should be easy to design them out from the start.
Companies can put in more safeguards. Why don’t they?
Profit. But also, let’s be honest, these are global tools and companies. So unless you have international agreement it is a bit like playing whack-a-mole, isn’t it?
The person who made that horrible video of me being chloroformed lives in the US, so the police aren’t gonna follow it up because they’re out of the country.
Do you know who did it?
I don’t know who they are, but the police did find who they were because it’s a criminal offense what they did. They just weren’t able to bring the charge.
We’ve spoken in the last 40 minutes about the full spectrum of human awfulness. I don’t think there’s any area of it that we haven’t …
Oh, sorry. Welcome to my life.
I’m really struck by how cheerful you are despite this. How do you remain so upbeat and hopeful while dealing with all of this?
Because you’ve always got to have hope for the future. I do have a really strong conviction that with the right group of people pushing toward a goal, you can achieve that. You don’t have to accept that things will always be like this. When people come together, when communities come together, you can act for change.
We’re just about to introduce our ban on strangulation in pornography, which is another thing that I’ve been campaigning for and introduced an amendment last year, which the government accepted.
There are always things that we can do to change. You just need to keep going. And also I would say that when you work with these terribly dark areas, yes, it can be quite vicariously traumatizing. But actually the people who work within the sectors are some of the most hopeful people, partly because if you lose hope, then it’s really bad. And we can’t because we’re talking about protecting vulnerable children, and we are fighting for women and our rights to be free of this harm.

Iranian president, Qatari emir discuss Mideast war, Hormuz in Moscow talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:29:11 UTC

Qatar's ruler and the Iranian president have discussed the Middle East war and the blockaded Strait of Hormuz during a meeting in Moscow, the emir's office said.

Addressing a news briefing in Doha, Hashmi warned that escalating tensions were draining the region’s resources and economies and having repercussions beyond the region.
“Qatar is working intensively with regional and international partners, including China, to revive diplomacy and dialogue and put forward practical proposals addressing the concerns of all parties,” he said.

He also described the immediate reopening of the Strait of Hormuz as an “absolute priority” for Qatar and other countries in the region because of its importance to regional and global economies.
“Using it as a pressure card in this way is rejected and unacceptable to the international community,” he said.

Tallinn mulling 1+1 and 2+1 lane options for Tulika tänav renovation

Tallinn mulling 1+1 and 2+1 lane options for Tulika tänav renovation
Preliminary designs have been released for the renovation of Tulika tänav and the section of Paldiski maantee that intersects with it in Tallinn's Kristiine district, and the street will be rebuilt with either 1+1 or 2+1 traffic lanes.
Ahead of the renovation of Tulika tänav, which connects the Kristiine traffic junction and the Sõle intersection, Tallinn is considering two options: rebuilding the street with either 1+1 or 2+1 traffic lanes.
Both solutions will include new sidewalks, cycle paths and street greenery. A traffic study has been carried out to find a suitable solution, and the final choice will be made after assessing spatial possibilities and the needs of different modes of transport.
Tallinn Deputy Mayor Kristjan Järvan (Isamaa) said that he and Tallinn Deputy Mayor Joel Jesse (Center) prefer the 2+1 option.
"Our clear view is that this location cannot accommodate a 1+1 solution, and our firm preference is 1+2," he noted.
However, no decision has yet been made. "When making the final decision, we will naturally take residents' feedback into account," Järvan said.
The reconstruction will also include the renovation of water supply and sewerage facilities, the construction of a separate stormwater drainage system and improvements to street lighting.
Feedback on both options can be submitted until November 10.

The elections are Israel's first general polls since the start of its genocidal war in the Gaza Strip in October 2023.

Two Russian Starlink rival satellites set to fall from orbit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:28:40 UTC
22:28:40 KST

- Two Rassvet-3 satellites from Russia’s second 2026 batch are expected to reenter within a day or two after failing to raise their orbits.
- Most of the remaining satellites from both 2026 launches have reached a stable altitude of about 500 km, satellite tracker Jonathan McDowell said.
Two satellites from Russia’s Rassvet broadband constellation, the country’s answer to SpaceX’s Starlink, are expected to fall back into the atmosphere and burn up within the next day or two after failing to raise their orbits, Harvard-Smithsonian astrophysicist and satellite tracker Jonathan McDowell said, while most of the other Rassvet-3 satellites have now settled into their working altitude.
“Most of the rest are stable at 500 km,” said Jonathan McDowell, who published an updated chart of the constellation’s orbit raising showing the bulk of the satellites from both 2026 launches flattening out at about 510 km (317 miles), while two satellites from the second batch have sunk below 230 km (143 miles) and are dropping fast.
The two failing satellites come from the second group of 16 Rassvet-3 spacecraft that Bureau 1440 launched on a Soyuz-2.1b rocket from the Plesetsk Cosmodrome on July 19, 2026, and by late August tracking data already showed a pair from that batch heading toward reentry without ever performing orbit-raising maneuvers, after they slipped below 300 km (186 miles).
Their loss would bring the number of Rassvet satellites lost since the program began flying operational spacecraft this year to three out of 32, after the constellation lost its first satellite in June, when Object 4 from the first batch, launched on March 23, 2026, reentered without having made a single maneuver.
McDowell’s chart also shows that a handful of other satellites from both batches are still below the target altitude, with one first-batch satellite holding at about 345 km (214 miles), another climbing past 470 km (292 miles), and one second-batch satellite at about 363 km (226 miles), although it does not indicate whether those spacecraft are still working.
Rassvet is being built by Bureau 1440, a private company that began as a research office inside Russian mobile operator MegaFon, and the system is meant to provide satellite internet across Russia, with partial commercial service planned for 2027, subscriber terminals said to weigh under 15 kg (33 pounds) and the company aiming for 292 satellites by the end of 2027 and up to 900 by 2035.
Neither Roscosmos nor Russia’s Ministry of Defense has announced the Rassvet launches, and in August the constellation was already providing at least two daily coverage windows over Ukraine lasting more than an hour each, raising concerns that Russian forces could eventually use it the way Ukraine’s military relies on Starlink.

PRESS RELEASE 160
Albares takes part in the annual Ibero-American Free Zones Conference, bringing together organisations from both sides of the Atlantic
The Minister for Foreign Affairs, European Union and Cooperation, José Manuel Albares, addressed the annual Ibero-American Free Zones Assembly, which opened in Cádiz on Monday, and called for a strategic awakening of a Europe that speaks with its own voice and works hand in hand with Latin America and the Caribbean, “because only through multilateralism can the world move towards progress”.
The Assembly, organised by the Association of Free Zones of the Americas (AZFA) and the Cádiz Free Zone Consortium, provides a forum for cooperation, knowledge exchange and the creation of opportunities among free zones, institutions, businesses, universities and specialists from Europe and Ibero-America.
Strategic awakening
In his address, the Minister recalled that Europe must pursue genuine sovereignty that allows it to avoid dependence on third parties in strategic areas and to be independent in its decision-making, capable of taking action and determined to defend its values and interests. He stressed that it must do so in cooperation and partnership with other regions, diversifying its economic and trade partnerships, as has been done this year with India and Mercosur.
“In this European strategic awakening, as Europe speaks with its own voice and always brings reason, diplomacy, dialogue and negotiation to the table, we want to work hand in hand with Latin America and the Caribbean, because only through multilateralism can the world move towards progress,” Albares reiterated.
Madrid Summit
This Assembly is taking place at a particularly important time for relations with Latin America and the Caribbean, one week before the Ibero-American Summit to be held in Madrid on 4 and 5 November.
The Minister described it as a Summit “that will strengthen the Ibero-American Community, an essential instrument for all of us, particularly in a geopolitical context as complex and uncertain as the present one. A community that offers us a space for dialogue, cooperation and trust, capable of providing stability and certainty in turbulent times, but also of delivering very tangible improvements in the lives of the millions of citizens who belong to it. A community that demonstrates, once again, that there is far more that unites us, and that many opportunities arise when we Ibero-Americans work together.”
The ocean that unites us
Under the theme “The Ocean That Unites Us”, this year’s event seeks to strengthen partnerships on both sides of the Atlantic and promote Cádiz as a connecting point between the two continents. It has brought together representatives of 53 organisations from 20 countries and territories (Spain, Colombia, Costa Rica, Puerto Rico, the Dominican Republic, Brazil, Panama, Honduras, Curaçao, Guatemala, Cuba, Paraguay, Afghanistan, Uruguay, Aruba, El Salvador, the United Arab Emirates, the United States, Haiti and Peru).
The discussions taking place between 26 and 28 October will focus on the exchange of experiences, economic challenges, attracting investment, conserving resources, transforming research into business activity, competitiveness and transatlantic cooperation.

UK spending on ‘fairytale’ carbon capture tech is a national embarrassment, chancellor told
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:28:00 UTC
22:28:00 KST

Campaigners are calling on the chancellor to cut the government’s £24bn spending plans for “fairytale” carbon capture technologies in favour of funding green schemes that can reliably cut emissions and lower energy bills.
The environmentalist Chris Packham is leading an 11th-hour appeal for the Treasury to use this week’s budget to scale back the government’s “exorbitantly expensive” support for carbon capture, which is now more than the planned spending for the US, the EU, Norway and Japan combined.
He said it was a “national embarrassment” that the government had earmarked £24bn to support a series of carbon capture and storage (CCS) projects developed by big oil companies, including BP and the Norwegian state oil company Equinor, and urged ministers to “put things right”.
“CCS is a tech fairytale,” the naturalist and broadcaster said. “It should be a national embarrassment that the UK is pumping more taxpayer money into it than any other country in the world. This budget is a chance to put things right.”
The intervention comes as the government reportedly plans to reduce the grants available to households hoping to swap their gas boiler for an electric heat pump. This shift is considered crucial to cutting the carbon emitted when heating buildings, which makes up around a fifth of the UK’s total greenhouse gas emissions.
Packham called on the government to safeguard funding promises “that empower households to lower bills” rather than “bankrolling exorbitantly expensive projects with ludicrously uncertain results”.
The leaders of many economies have backed carbon capture technology designed to trap the emissions from fossil fuel infrastructure before they are released into the atmosphere. Proponents believe that piping carbon dioxide into underground storage could provide a permanent climate solution for industries that are unable to replace fossil fuels with cleaner alternatives.
Although there are instances where the technology has worked successfully, many high-cost projects have struggled to progress and there are many examples where carbon savings have proved to be far less than expected. Green groups fear the technology has been promoted by fossil fuel companies to prolong the use of fossil fuels.
Packham said a failure to rein in the planned CCS spending “would be yet another strong signal that this government is putting big oil above people and the planet”.
Aled Dilwyn Fisher, a senior researcher at Oil Change International, said: “It’s worrying that spending on climate is being cut in favour of defence, but cutting support for proven climate solutions while continuing to bankroll unreliable carbon capture projects would add insult to injury.
“This budget should be an opportunity to put public money where it can make a real difference to the climate and help cut people’s energy bills, rather than continuing to gamble billions on the fossil fuel industry’s latest expansion plan.”
Work on the UK’s first CCS projects has begun at the East Coast Cluster near Teesside and Humberside, in north-east England, and at the HyNet Cluster near Merseyside and north Wales, in north-west England.
The second phase of the government’s CCS support plan includes £200m to support the Acorn project in Aberdeenshire, alongside £80m from the Scottish government.
Rosie Hampton, a campaigner at Friends of the Earth Scotland, said over the summer that the government’s climate response was being built on “fantasy plans about turning the North Sea into Europe’s carbon dumping ground” while politicians should be focused on “climate solutions that will improve people’s lives, such as warm homes, better public transport and decent green jobs”.
Martin McCluskey, the parliamentary undersecretary at the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, told an industry event this month that the government remained committed to carbon capture but fiscal pressures may require decisions on the pace of the industry’s development.
The Carbon Capture and Storage Association (CCSA) said the UK’s first projects had already awarded more than £4bn in supply-chain contracts, which could support about 350 UK companies and 5,500 construction jobs.
“Pulling back now would undermine investor confidence, risk leaving infrastructure underused and deepen industrial decline,” said Mark Sommerfeld, the CCSA’s UK director.
“This budget must honour existing commitments, turning today’s progress into lasting growth, energy security and reindustrialisation,” he said.
The government has been contacted for comment.

====================================================================================================

German Ambassador: Russia has at no time in the past four and a half years negotiated in a serious way
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
15:26:00 EET
22:26:00 KST

German Ambassador: Russia has at no time in the past four and a half years negotiated in a serious way
Boris Ruge has been Germany’s new ambassador to Ukraine since August.
Ukraine is not new to him, though. Until recently Ruge was a senior NATO official, serving as Assistant Secretary General for Political Affairs and Security Policy – essentially the third-highest position in the Alliance’s civilian hierarchy. And, of course, he was closely involved with Ukraine and supported closer ties for Ukraine with the Alliance.
Now Ruge speaks on behalf of Berlin.
And when he tells European Pravda in this interview that Germany supports NATO membership for Ukraine, that represents a clear German position. But his statements on EU membership for Ukraine are even clearer and more detailed.
This and much more in the ambassador’s first interview in office.
"We are absolutely determined to stay here"
In your view, what does Ukraine mean to Germany?
Ukraine is a very important partner for Germany – in technical terms we could say a strategic partner, as we agreed in the spring of this year. We understand how important Ukraine is for European security, and we also understand its weight as a major economic player.
You’ve worked at NATO, so you’ll know that pretty much every member is described as "a highly valued ally". It’s the same for Ukraine, isn’t it?
No, it’s not the same for Ukraine. Ukraine is a big country, and it is, unfortunately, at the heart of the largest war in Europe since 1945, which has been going on for more than four years now – tragically so. The outcome of this war will determine Europe’s future security order.
As far as we are concerned, Europe’s future security order should include a Ukraine that is sovereign, independent and democratic – and able to move towards and join the European Union, certainly. And NATO as well: we said a few years ago that the future of Ukraine is in NATO.
All of these things matter. At the core is a fundamental point: Ukraine must be able to exercise its own choices and be part of what, in the old days, we would have called the free world. And I think that is very relevant today – if we look at what Russia represents today, it is definitely not the free world.
So, NATO membership, EU membership, and a democratic Ukraine. Those are encouraging messages at the start of our interview, and we’ll come back to each of them later. But first let me say that I’m particularly happy to see you here in Kyiv after last night’s missile attack [the interview took place on 22 October]. Do you know why I say that?
No.
Because we Ukrainians remember 2022, when one embassy after another was leaving Kyiv. Can we be certain that this won’t happen again?
Yes. I think you can be absolutely sure. You remember that Chancellor [Friedrich Merz] came to Kyiv on 4 October. And on 3 October, we were told [by Moscow] that all foreigners should leave Kyiv because it was dangerous and we risked losing our lives by staying here.
But the Chancellor was not deterred from coming here.
We are here. We know that the coming months will be difficult – over the past two months, we have already seen the security situation become more difficult. We need to handle that, and we need to look after the security of our people, but we are absolutely determined to stay here. It’s the same for all our European and NATO partners.
"EU membership won’t happen in 2027 or 2028. That's impossible. It's not doable"
You’ve already said that you see Ukraine as a member of the EU. But is that goal achievable within a reasonable timeframe? And what exactly is a "reasonable timeframe"?
That’s a good question. As we all know, to become a member of the European Union, a country has to adapt its legislation, regulations, institutions and so on. That’s not arbitrary, and it’s not something we’ve made up to make things complicated. It’s simply that the European Union is so highly integrated and demands so much of its members. Ukraine needs to go through those steps – and doing so will also make Ukraine a more European country in a broader sense.
I don’t think you will find a government in the European Union that is more forward-leaning on EU membership than Germany. I remember that you interviewed my predecessor, Heiko Thoms, about the letter that Chancellor Merz wrote back in May [on a special format for Ukraine’s integration into the EU].
Among other things, the letter called for full membership for Ukraine – I think it says so three times in a single letter – and, basically, for opening all negotiation clusters now.
And it says that, as Ukraine moves towards the European Union, Ukrainians – representatives of Ukraine – should be brought into the institutions: the Commission, the Parliament, the Council, the European Court of Justice. It’s a very forward-leaning, very positive vision of how we see Ukraine and of our wish for Ukraine to advance rapidly.
How long it will take is a very difficult question.
I think it's a good thing that
people here in Kyiv have moved away from the notion that it will happen in 2027 or 2028.
It will not happen then. It’s impossible. It’s not doable.
We’re now hearing hopes that Ukraine could join by 2030, and this is being discussed in Brussels as well, not just in Kyiv. Is that an achievable goal, even if it is an ambitious one?
2030 is ambitious. First of all, it depends on how Ukraine performs. And then, of course, the reality is that it’s also a very political process, because there are 27 members of the European Union and they all have a say. So it’s difficult to predict, but I think the geopolitical case for Ukraine joining the European Union is very strong.
What matters is that, together, we keep Ukraine on track, moving forward as fast as possible towards full membership – so that people in this country can feel that this is something they can work towards, and that they have a real opportunity to become a member of the European Union within a reasonable time.
Is it theoretically possible for Ukraine to join the EU while the war is still ongoing?
I don't know whether the European Union has taken a position on whether a continuation of the war would stand in the way of Ukraine becoming a full member. I don’t know that. I don’t believe that’s the case.
We should work with Ukraine, even under these very difficult circumstances, to move forward on the path to the European Union. And then we’ll take it from there.
"There's an understanding, but I remind people that this is the case"
The path to EU membership is first and foremost about reforms.
Last week, several laws were passed that are relevant to the European Union and to Ukraine’s membership – including the law on minorities, but many others as well. There’s a whole list of things – I think they’re very well known to the Office of the President, to the government, to the Rada [Ukrainian parliament] – that need to be done. And in some cases, draft laws or executive decisions are relevant to unlocking funding from the European Union for Ukraine, which is hugely important.
And we keep reminding people that, given the overall situation, we can only encourage Ukraine’s institutions to adopt this legislation as soon as possible, so that the funding the European Union has available for Ukraine can be released.
Do you think the Ukrainian government and our MPs understand that all the reforms must be implemented? That cherry-picking reforms is not an option?
I think there’s an understanding, but I can tell you that I do remind people that this is the case. To raise the very significant resources – the massive resources – needed to support Ukraine and help it defend itself, we also need to be able to tell people in the German parliament, the Bundestag, in the European Parliament and in the European Council that Ukraine is doing its part and delivering on the reform agenda.
Is Ukraine making tangible progress on the rule of law and the fight against corruption?
I mean, there are issues with corruption. There were very prominent cases. But at the same time, we can see that Ukraine has institutions, created after the Revolution of Dignity, that are able to investigate and prosecute people even in very high positions. That’s pretty significant. Maybe it’s not perfect, but nothing ever is.
There is real action on anti-corruption, and that’s extremely important because – again, in Germany – to make the case for supporting Ukraine, there has to be a credible anti-corruption architecture in place and credible action against people who misuse funds for their own purposes.
I remember interviewing German and other European ambassadors five or ten years ago, and even earlier. Time and again they would describe how corruption was hurting their investors. Is that still the case today?
I don’t think that is the main problem for German companies today. And that’s good.
"Russia has at no time in the past four and a half years negotiated in a serious way"
I’d like to ask you about the war, but first, let’s talk about what’s happening around these so-called peace negotiations. I think the best word to describe it is a mess. Would you describe it differently?
No, I don’t have another word for it. I think everyone, first and foremost the people in Ukraine, would like to see the war come to an end – after four and a half years of full-scale war and, before that, eight years of a bloody war at a lower level.
I can see that there is an American-led effort to bring the war to an end. But I would also say, as a German diplomat, that it is clear that Europe has to be part of the picture. The first point is that Ukraine and the people of Ukraine have to decide on what basis they are willing to end the war.
We are grateful to America for trying to bring the war to an end. But Europe – and Germany too – certainly has a big stake in how this war ends, and so we will be there and find a way of articulating our European interests and working with Ukraine to make sure that we end up with a result that is acceptable.
Is Europe playing a sufficiently meaningful role in the process right now?
What we can see is that, as you remember, the national security advisors of France, Britain and Germany have been to Kyiv twice most recently in September. We also had some national security advisors in Oslo just now. So there is a presence, recently in Miami as well.
At the same time, we’re hearing criticism from Poland, our closest EU neighbour. Polish officials don’t hide their frustration that they’re never invited to these discussions. What’s the reason for that?
I don’t know whether it’s true that they’re never invited. But Poland is clearly very important. It’s an important member state of the European Union and an important ally in NATO. It is a neighbour, and it is very much impacted by this war. So I think Poland’s desire to be closely involved is important, clearly. I think there are questions about what the formula will ultimately be.
In a sense, we could say that we have not yet entered into a proper negotiation process. And if we’re serious, we can also say that the Russian Federation has at no time in the past four and a half years negotiated in a serious way. They have always stuck to their basic demands, which essentially amount to Ukraine capitulating – so that is not a negotiation. So I would say we’re not yet in a real negotiation process, and we will see what format it takes.
So for now, as far as I understand, you don't see Russia being ready for serious steps.
Exactly. I mean, last night [21 October] is a demonstration that Russia talks in very vague terms about its willingness to engage, to meet and so on – and in the meantime it attacks Ukraine with its jet drones and ballistic missiles, killing civilians, attacking civilian targets and committing war crimes. So that’s not exactly the mindset of peace. I think we have to be very clear about that.
There was a change in the Ukrainian position beginning in 2025, when the president signalled that he would be willing to accept a ceasefire – a full ceasefire. Since then, we have been talking about the Black Sea deals, grain deals and energy ceasefires – all sorts of things. Russia has rejected every single one of them, and I think the record is perfectly clear.
"I wouldn't say NATO is stepping back. Part of the response is not visible"
Is there a risk that Russian attacks could extend beyond Ukraine?
Russia’s strategy consists of fighting on land. But the front line is relatively stable. Ukraine has done quite a good job of slowing Russia down and, obviously, of retaking territory recently as well.
There’s a war happening in the air, with cruise missiles and drones, where Russia is unfortunately having an impact on the energy infrastructure and attacking the economy – the steel industry, for example. And then there’s a third element: Russia’s hybrid campaign against NATO and EU states, which has been going on for years. Russia is not engaging in a military conflict with NATO, but it is pushing the limits of its hybrid campaign.
In my view, when an explosive-laden drone attacks Leipzig Airport, that’s no longer a hybrid attack. It’s more like a conventional attack, isn’t it?
In the case of Leipzig, Germany made an attribution. We did our homework: we didn’t go out the next morning and say it was Russia – our intelligence services did their homework, and then we attributed it to Russia. And then we took a number of measures: we closed the consulate in Bonn, we closed the Russian House in Berlin, and we did a number of other things to push back.
But you still consider it a hybrid attack?
You know, people argue about hybrid, and I accept that hybrid is perhaps a problematic term. You could say it’s grey-zone – a kind of grey-zone campaign that they’re waging.
But Russia is not engaged in a large-scale military campaign against NATO. And why is that? Because NATO’s deterrence against Russia has worked. So they have been trying to operate below the threshold of an actual military attack.
They've been testing us. And we have to find ways of pushing back.
I was in Berlin at the beginning of September for our ambassadors’ conference. Mark Rutte was there to speak, and he said – and I agree entirely – that if Russia engages in these hybrid operations, the response should be more support for Ukraine, not less, because Russia’s objective is to undermine our support for Ukraine.
And you could see it when Chancellor Merz came here on 4 October with a package of one billion [euros] in military support for Ukraine. So maybe people in Moscow should register that, despite Leipzig and everything else that has been going on against EU states, NATO states and Germany, our support for Ukraine has not gone down. It has gone up.
And yet I’m seeing attacks that ten years ago would have been considered conventional acts of military aggression – Russia is striking NATO member states with drones, targeting Turkish ships, and sinking ships in the territorial waters of Bulgaria or Romania. And nothing happens! There’s no response from the Alliance. So Russia keeps raising the stakes, and NATO is stepping back.
I wouldn’t say NATO is stepping back, but I can tell you that I’ve talked to many Ukrainian colleagues and I know that this is the perception here: that Russia is pushing and NATO has not come up with a strong response. I think part of the response is not visible. But I’ve been telling colleagues from NATO, my former colleagues, that this is the perception here and that they should think about it: The impression that NATO is not responding strongly enough to Russia’s campaign. I think that’s a point people should reflect on in Brussels.
"Germany wants Ukraine to be as close to NATO as possible"
I’m glad to hear that you see Ukraine as a future NATO member. But there’s one opponent to us joining, and that’s the United States. Do you think Ukraine will join the Alliance despite that opposition?
For Ukraine to join NATO, you need all 32 NATO allies to agree. And if you look at the procedure, there are actually several steps where 32 ambassadors need to raise their hand and say "Yes, we agree."
What we said in Washington – and that is the NATO position, as Mark Rutte has reminded people – was that the future of Ukraine is in NATO and that Ukraine is on a… I can’t come up with the adjective right now. Незворотній is the Ukrainian term.
Yeah, absolutely! Незворотній.
Irreversible! Sorry.
So you know the Ukrainian word better!:)
Exactly – so I do remember only the Ukrainian word.
It’s on an irreversible path to full Euro-Atlantic integration. When exactly that will happen is, again, a political issue. The difference today, at least from a German point of view, is that it’s very clear that Ukraine is not just the recipient of our assistance, but also a major element of Europe’s defence today.
We need Ukraine, with its armed forces and its expertise in modern warfare, to be part of our defence against a very aggressive and imperialist Russia whose ambitions go beyond Ukraine. That is our analysis.
What is your vision for Europe’s future security architecture, and what role would Ukraine play in it?
In my view, it revolves around NATO. I’m a former NATO person, so maybe that’s logical. But NATO is the organisation in charge of collective defence. I think the role that the United States plays in NATO is changing – we can see that – because of the change in US force posture globally. As you know, that has been going on for 20 years: Barack Obama talked about the pivot to Asia, and that was in the years after 2008. And now China has become even stronger, and the US is required to play its balancing role in the Indo-Pacific.
So Europeans will have to step up and play more of a role. But to my mind, Ukraine is already very, very close to NATO. We have the NATO-Ukraine Council, and we do a lot of things together. We have the Joint Analysis Training and Education Centre in Bydgoszcz, Poland, and we are learning from Ukraine today when it comes to unmanned systems.
We don’t know when Ukraine will be able to join NATO as a full member, but, from a German point of view, we want Ukraine to be as close to NATO as possible, because in reality you are already part of our collective defence.
What are the key elements of a peace settlement that is acceptable to Europe? And please don’t just say that it’s for Ukraine to decide. You have your own position too, don’t you?
Sure. Our position is that Ukraine should survive as a sovereign, independent, democratic nation that can make its own choices.
What about other conditions, particularly concerning Russia? Some people say that to secure a lasting peace, Europe would need to restore ties with Russia and resume supplies of Russian oil and gas through Ukraine. What’s your view on that?
I don’t believe that’s the case. If you look at the German-Russian relationship after 1991, you could say two things.
One is that Germany got it terribly wrong. We were wrong to assume that we could develop a partnership with Russia. Russia walked away from the partnership we tried to establish and turned into an aggressive, imperialist actor that is trying to overturn the entire political order of Europe. That’s one way of looking at it, and I think in many ways it’s accurate.
Another way of looking at it is that Germany and the rest of Europe tried very hard to build a constructive and positive relationship with Russia. You can see it in the NATO-Russia Council, and you can see it in the way we developed the energy partnership with Russia, and so on. So we tried, and it failed.
We made an honest effort to have a positive, forward-looking relationship with Russia, and Russia threw that out of the window and turned to the use of military force, aggression and this hybrid campaign, this manipulation of information and politics.
This attempt of ours was a failure. But what is important is that we sincerely made efforts to build forward-looking relations with Russia. So the people in Europe today, including in my country, Germany, who say we should go back to that and build a positive relationship with Russia have obviously forgotten that we spent 20 years doing exactly that, and it turned out to be a massive failure.
And it turned out to be the biggest failure on energy in particular. The idea at the time was that if Russia had a major market in Western Europe, it would have a stake in maintaining peace and building a positive relationship. But that is not what Mr Putin ultimately decided.
We are not going back to that. I don’t believe you will find a majority in Germany for that. Maybe people in Washington DC think we should re-establish that energy partnership between Western Europe and Russia, but I think in Western Europe you will find precious few people willing to make themselves dependent on Russia in any way today.
Interview by Sergiy Sydorenko
Video by Mykhailo Alekseev

In the trenches, on duty and in shelters: how Ukraine held the National Unity Radio Dictation
Kyiv • UNN
On October 27, Ukrainians took part in the National Unity Radio Dictation based on a text by Artur Dron. It was written by military personnel, officials, schoolchildren and celebrities.
Today, October 27, on Ukrainian Writing and Language Day, the National Unity Radio Dictation was traditionally held in Ukraine, written by politicians, famous stars and military personnel, reports UNN.
Details
Despite another difficult night, when the enemy attacked our cities with ballistic missiles and hundreds of drones, despite the fatigue, hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians sat down together to write a dictation in their native language. The enemy may destroy buildings, but it is unable to destroy what makes us Ukrainians: our language, culture, history and unity. They cannot be broken by missiles, drones or any other weapon. Our resilience and our unity rest on this foundation. And this is our response to every attempt to intimidate or break us. Thank you to everyone who joined the National Unity Radio Dictation today
Olena Ivanovska, the Commissioner for the Protection of the State Language, representatives of the Commissioner in the regions and the Secretariat team also joined the radio dictation.
"A Letter That Does Not End" by Artur Dron brought together millions of Ukrainians in different parts of Ukraine and far beyond its borders. Military personnel and veterans, teachers and schoolchildren, volunteers, civil servants, and Ukrainians scattered around the world by the war all wrote it. It was precisely for the sake of this unity that the tradition of the Radio Dictation was born 27 years ago
Minister of Culture Tetiana Berezhna also showed a photo of herself writing the dictation at the Scientific and Technical Library of the National Technical University "Kyiv Polytechnic Institute."
"Language truly knows no boundaries." Artur Dron's very poignant text for this year's National Unity Radio Dictation is called "A Letter That Does Not End." And I really wanted this letter not to end. I joined the dictation. I have been writing it for many years, and I get nervous every time. This time, I allowed myself the right to make a mistake and enjoyed the text and its reading. I love this tradition very much: in different cities and countries, Ukrainians pick up their pens and listen to the same text. Everyone has their own handwriting, their own doubts about commas, and their own history of relations with the Ukrainian language. And at the same time, there is a shared feeling of closeness. In Artur's text, language protects us when the present is frightening and helps us create the future. It preserves memory, passes on experience, and provides words for what matters most. For a conversation with an entire country and for a personal "I love you"
The mayor of Ivano-Frankivsk, Ruslan Martsinkiv, also showed how he wrote the dictation together with students.
I joined the National Unity Radio Dictation. The most important things we have are Ukrainian statehood and the Ukrainian language! Thank you to our Defenders
As usual, Ukrainian military personnel also joined the radio dictation; in particular, some of them wrote it from the front line, right in the trenches.
And how did your radio dictation go this year?
The soldiers of the 50th Separate Artillery Brigade, the 92nd Assault Brigade named after Koshovyi Otaman Ivan Sirko, the 10th Separate Mountain Assault Brigade "Edelweiss," the 1st Separate Heavy Mechanized Siverska Brigade, the 22nd Separate Unmanned Systems Battalion and the 39th Anti-Aircraft Missile Regiment also joined in writing the dictation at their combat positions.
On Ukrainian Writing and Language Day, service members of Operational Command "West," organized by specialists from the personnel psychological support structure in cooperation with representatives of the communications structure, joined the traditional Nationwide Radio Dictation. It is the same weapon that the enemy tried to destroy for centuries but never managed to break. Today, we are defending not merely our borders, dignity and sovereignty; we are defending the right to speak, think, read and write, and simply to live in Ukrainian on our own land. Our native word is our "friend-or-foe" password, and as long as our commands are heard in Ukrainian over the radios, we will stand, endure and win
Ukrainian border guards also wrote the dictation.
Border guards from various units and agencies of the State Border Guard Service of Ukraine, together with thousands of Ukrainians, joined the 2026 National Unity Radio Dictation. This year's text, titled "The Letter That Never Ends," was written by Ukrainian writer and veteran of the Russian-Ukrainian war Artur Dron. For border guards, participating in the radio dictation is not only an opportunity to test their knowledge of their native language, but also a chance to join a shared tradition that unites Ukrainians regardless of their profession, location, or circumstances
In addition, the Strategic Communications Center of the Armed Forces of Ukraine showed how service members from various brigades wrote the dictation at their positions, including soldiers from the Presidential Brigade, the 128th, 82nd, and 29th brigades, the 20th Corps, and cadets of the Military Institute of Taras Shevchenko National University of Kyiv.
Celebrities also joined in writing the dictation. In particular, war veteran and public figure Oleksandr Teren showed a photo of himself writing the dictation together with singer "Leleka," actress Maryna Koshkina, bloggers Dasha Kubik and Vlad Shevchenko, as well as chef Yevhen Klopotenko.
By the way, Yevhen Klopotenko shared his alphabet of Ukrainian cuisine on Instagram.
I love how simply and logically we name dishes. You study food—you discover new words

Ukrainian singer and model Dasha Astafieva shared an intimate photo on social media of herself on horseback. "I'm flying to you," she captioned the photos ahead of the National Unity Radio Dictation.

Giant metal 3D printer to build hypersonic systems in Indiana
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:24:52 UTC
22:24:52 KST

- Kratos has bought an AMCM M 8K large-format metal 3D printer with eight 1.2-kilowatt lasers for its hypersonic payload facility in Odon, Indiana.
- The system will support MACH-TB, the U.S. Department of War hypersonic test program for which Kratos is the prime contractor.
Kratos Defense & Security Solutions has bought one of the largest metal 3D printers on the market, an AMCM M 8K additive manufacturing system, for its new hypersonic payload facility in Odon, Indiana, where the company prepares the experimental test vehicles it flies for the Pentagon’s MACH-TB hypersonic test program.
Germany’s EOS, whose AMCM unit builds the machine, announced the sale on Oct. 27, 2026, saying the printer will be installed at the Kratos Indiana Payload Integration Facility near Naval Surface Warfare Center Crane Division, though neither company disclosed the price or when the system will begin producing parts.
The M 8K was developed for space and defense work and can print metal parts inside a build volume of 800 by 800 by 1,200 millimeters (31.5 by 31.5 by 47.2 inches) using eight high-power 1.2-kilowatt lasers, with built-in thermal management, gas flow control, filtration and in-process monitoring meant to keep large, complex components accurate and consistent from one build to the next.
“As we change the paradigm on low-cost, high-cadence hypersonic testing for programs like MACH-TB, this type of capability is critical to achieve the goal,” said Mike Johns, senior vice president of Kratos SRE.
Kratos is the prime contractor for MACH-TB 2.0, the U.S. Department of War’s effort to run frequent, affordable flight tests of hypersonic technologies, under a contract worth up to $1.45 billion awarded in January 2025, and printing large metal parts in-house is meant to help the company build test hardware faster and in greater numbers than traditional machining allows.
The printer will join a site that is still ramping up, after Kratos finished the $50 million, 68,000-square-foot (6,317-square-meter) Indiana Payload Integration Facility ahead of schedule in July 2026, with room to prepare up to six hypersonic payloads at once and plans for more than 100 high-tech jobs in its first phase.
“The M 8K was built for exactly these kinds of applications, large, complex parts where scale, precision, and process reliability all matter,” said Martin Bullemer, managing director of AMCM.

Iranians brace for renewed attacks after Israeli, US elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:23:32 UTC
22:23:32 KST

Iranians brace for renewed attacks after Israeli, US elections
The US and Israel have teased strikes around their elections, particularly against Iran’s civilian infrastructure.
Israelis have gone to the polls to decide whether Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu will remain in power. On November 3, midterm elections in the United States will take place and likely impact President Donald Trump’s final years in office.
Many Iranians are watching both elections closely, knowing that the way Israelis and Americans vote could have serious consequences for their future. Since Israel and the US launched an unprovoked war on Iran on February 28, Iranians have experienced bombings, a blockade and sanctions.
But despite a sharp decrease in US and Israeli attacks since a memorandum of understanding was reached between Washington and Tehran in June, the threat of war has re-emerged. Many political commentators believe that the US and Israel could restart the war after the elections, and Iranians are anticipating further strikes.
“I haven’t followed the Israeli election very closely. But I think there will be more fighting whether Netanyahu wins or Eisenkot or someone else,” 37-year-old Tehran resident Sajad told Al Jazeera, asking to remain anonymous due to security reasons.
He believes that the rhetoric of Israeli officials signals that their ambition in the war is still for the overthrow of the Islamic Republic, which has controlled Iran since a 1979 revolution.
This has gained some support from Iranians inside and outside the country, who are opposed to the government. But cyber intelligence operations by both Israel and Iran make it difficult to accurately gauge online reactions to the prospect of Netanyahu winning another election.
Iranian authorities have described pro-Israeli Iranians as “homeland sellers” and continue to severely punish any perceived cooperation with Israel based on national security charges.
They also fully blame the US and Israel for Iran’s nationwide protests in January, during which thousands of civilians are believed to have been killed. The United Nations says Iranian security forces committed crimes against humanity while cracking down on the protests.
Shayan, a 32-year-old Tehran resident, said he believes that any Iranians who might have hoped for the overthrow of the government at the start of the war are disillusioned after witnessing US and Israeli conduct since then, with thousands of civilians killed and the US blockade and sanctions hitting most people’s incomes.
“I think some people’s viewpoints adjusted after some of the comments from the US and Israel, and after they bombed infrastructure that we need to live, like oil and gas, power and steel,” he told Al Jazeera.
“I think most Iranians don’t have a choice in the matter, but want some stability and peace.”
President Trump has threatened to bring about the “death of a civilisation” in Iran and suggested the country’s map may look different after the war.
He has also repeatedly threatened to launch more major strikes against Iran’s power plants, bridges and other civilian infrastructure if hostilities resume. US media report that the country’s military is prepared to attack over the coming days if an order is given.
The other option Trump has threatened is prolonging a naval blockade of Iran’s southern ports in place since July, which has stopped the country’s oil exports and significantly disrupted trade. Together with some of the most stringent sanctions imposed against any country, the US measures have made Iranians poorer and more isolated from the international community.
The Netanyahu government has also threatened to strike Iranian infrastructure again, including energy facilities. Defence Minister Israel Katz has repeatedly said in recent months that he wants to send Iran “back into the Stone Age”.
His election opponents and other prominent opposition figures, including Eisenkot, Naftali Bennett, Yair Lapid and Yair Golan, have all cheered the US-Israeli attacks on Iran both during the current war and during last year’s 12-day war.
They have also been united in wanting to remove Iran’s enriched uranium stockpiles from Iran and dismantle the country’s nuclear programme. Another goal is eliminating the Tehran-backed “axis of resistance” of armed forces who oppose Israel and the US across the region.
Israeli politicians, both the government and opposition, are generally united on the war aims of overthrowing the Iranian establishment, but differ on the method.
Eisenkot, for instance, has supported Netanyahu’s military strikes against Iran and praised Trump’s decision to launch attacks as courageous. But he also says that military operations cannot realistically overthrow the Islamic Republic, and that change must come from Iranians themselves.
Some Iranians have been mentally preparing themselves for conflict when the elections end.
Some Iranians said they have established groups with friends living in different parts of the country to warn each other of imminent strikes if they hear fighter jets flying overhead.
Some of the groups are in domestic messaging apps or over text message since Iranian authorities have said they will impose more internet and communication shutdowns if deemed necessary.
“In all seriousness, 90 million people have our eyes to the sky to see when there will be war. Damn this life we’ve lived,” a user named Ali wrote on X.

Top Indian media dispute Modi's new data privacy rules in top court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:23:00 UTC
22:23:00 KST

India's Supreme Court Tuesday ordered the government to respond to a challenge by news publishers who argue that new data privacy rules threaten press freedom.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government introduced rules last year to implement a personal data protection law, but critics say their sweeping scope risks undermining public interest reporting.
The new rules "fail to provide any exemption for journalistic activity" and "threaten the full spectrum of journalistic activity," a petition from the Digital News Publishers Association (DNPA) said. The DNPA represents some of India's biggest news organizations.
Members include Network18, part of the Reliance conglomerate led by billionaire Mukesh Ambani and NDTV, owned by the Adani Group, founded by Gautam Adani. Both tycoons are close to Modi.
"We think it could impact investigative journalism and compromise sources," Sujata Gupta, with the DNPA, said.
Data privacy laws in many parts of the world, including the European Union, include specific exemptions for journalism.
The law's requirement to disclose all personal data processed, without a public interest exemption, would "seriously hinder investigative reporting and could discourage whistleblowers from coming forward," Reporters Without Borders, an international media watchdog, said.
Independent activists and smaller news organizations also challenged provisions removing exemptions for personal information sought under India's Right to Information (RTI) transparency law.
"The removal of the public interest override ... of the RTI Act now allows information offices of the government to withhold information that is deemed 'personal' even if it has significant connection to a public activity or public interest," a legal challenge filed by investigative news website The Reporters' Collective argued.
Critics have long accused Modi's Hindu nationalist government of undermining press freedom, a charge the government denies. The court will hear the matter next on Nov. 17.
