Russia tries to drag a village north of Kupiansk into no-man’s-land after its losses in Ukraine’s underground operation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:22:33 UTC
22:22:33 KST

Russian troops are trying to drag Radkivka, a village on the northern edge of Kupiansk in Kharkiv Oblast, into the gray zone so their infiltration groups can keep reaching the city, Viktor Trehubov, spokesperson for Ukraine’s Joint Forces Grouping, said on national television on 27 October, Ukrinform reported. Russian forces made three attempts to advance toward Radkivka on 26 October, Ukraine’s General Staff reported.
Russia has tried for more than a year to retake Kupiansk, a city on the Oskil River, largely by slipping small groups through a disused gas pipeline under the river. They kept using it even after Ukraine said in September 2025 that it had flooded three of the four pipe strings, until Ukrainian troops went into the pipes themselves in Operation Veles, announced on 22 October.
Russian groups now have to move above ground
The pipe Russian groups used to seep toward Kupiansk has been put out of action, so they now have to go through Radkivka or neighboring Holubivka, Trehubov said. They move along the bank of the Oskil and a nearby tree line, but the foliage will soon be gone, which will make that much harder.
On the western bank of the Oskil, Russian forces took losses from Ukraine’s Khartiia Corps and in Operation Veles, and their logistics have “suffered noticeably,” Trehubov said. Advancing there is now harder for them than it was a month ago, he added.
Everything now depends on how the fights for Holubivka and Radkivka end, Trehubov said.
“If Ukrainian control can finally be established there, the Russians will have nowhere much to crawl through,” he said.
Several dozen Russian soldiers remain in low-rise buildings in northern Kupiansk, and Ukrainian forces are working to cut off their rotations, Trehubov said on 23 October.
Each side wants the other off its bank of the Oskil
On the eastern bank, Russian forces keep pushing toward the village of Podoly and Kupiansk-Vuzlovyi, a railway junction town southeast of Kupiansk, aiming to wipe out Ukraine’s foothold there, Trehubov said. Ukraine wants to destroy the Russian foothold on the western bank.
“For that, we will need to at least somehow throw them out of Dvorichna,” Trehubov said, referring to a town north of Kupiansk.
The US-based Institute for the Study of War (ISW) assessed that Russian forces conducted no offensive operations on the Kupiansk axis on 26 October, likely because Ukraine now controls the pipeline, a view at odds with the General Staff’s report for that day.
Ukraine reported confident control of Kupiansk as early as February, yet Russian groups kept slipping into the city for months afterward. Trehubov’s latest assessment stops short of declaring that threat over: Russia will still try to advance, he said.

How to balance a career and a master’s in the Netherlands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:22:11 UTC
22:22:11 KST

Partner content
How to balance a career and a master’s in the Netherlands
Working full time while studying for a master’s can be a tough balancing act. Melina Gkiolma, a sustainability consultant and currently a student on the Online Master Sustainability Management at Rotterdam School of Management, Erasmus University (RSM) in Amsterdam, talks about how she handles the burden.
For many internationals in the Netherlands, going back to university means fitting lectures and assignments around a full-time job, family commitments and trips back home. Finding the time and the energy is often the biggest hurdle.
Melina, who is originally from Athens, has worked in the sustainability sector for five years, having spent the past 2.5 years as a sustainability consultant at Kōan, a boutique consultancy in Amsterdam. She started her career at Deloitte Luxembourg. She helps organisations deal with sustainability reporting requirements and changing regulations across Europe and beyond.
She wanted a part-time course she could follow online, so she could keep working while building her academic background in a field where she sees her long-term career. “This programme seemed like the perfect fit because it met all the criteria I was looking for,” she said.
Finding a routine
Returning to study took some adjustment. “I admit that returning to academic study after several years in the workplace was a little challenging at first,” she said, “but I’ve found a balance that works for me.”
She tries to join the live class every week and usually studies in the evening after work, when she is “already in a productive mindset”. She also puts in some time at weekends, but makes a point of keeping time free to relax.
Weekly updates from the programme managers on upcoming activities and assignment deadlines help her stay on top of the workload, she said.
Studying on the move
Because the course is entirely online, Melina can keep studying wherever she is – at home, on work trips or visiting her family in Greece.
She also found it more sociable than she expected. “People often assume online learning can feel impersonal, but my experience has been the opposite,” she said. Live classes, discussion forums and informal virtual coffee chats have helped her build strong ties with classmates around the world.
The international mix is one of her favourite parts of the course, with students from almost every continent. “It’s eye-opening to hear about people’s different experiences depending on where they live and their different professional backgrounds,” she said.
Theory into practice
Melina has been able to use what she learns at work straight away. Earlier in the programme, students were asked to develop key performance indicators (KPIs) for a logistics company. When a new client later asked her for help setting KPIs for its carbon emissions, she drew on the research she had done for that assignment.
“The master’s has also helped me broaden my horizons in sustainability. Because I work in sustainability reporting, there are many topics I hadn’t explored in depth before. One module I found particularly interesting focused on ethics and leadership. It made me reflect on what I want to stand for in my work, my moral compass, and the purpose behind the things I do. It really got me thinking.”
“Be kind to yourself”
Her advice to anyone thinking of combining a job with a part-time master’s is to go easy on themselves. “Working full time while studying for a part-time master is a significant challenge, but you can find the balance that works for you,” she said.
“And remember, pursuing further education while advancing your career is a major achievement in itself.”
Applications for the Online Master in Sustainability Management at RSM are now open for cohorts starting in 2027. Find out more about the programme and apply here.

China Is Learning to Sell Japanese Culture Better Than Japan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:22:00 UTC
22:22:00 KST

What would Japanese youngsters respond when asked about Chinese culture? Chances are that they will point to the neon-lit streets of Yokohama Chinatown, the culinary tradition that invented gyoza and mapo tofu, and perhaps something they overheard from friends, classmates, and coworkers who are part of the 900,000-strong Chinese diaspora in Japan.
But what about Genshin Impact, the role-playing video game created by Shanghai-based miHoYo?
It certainly is wildly popular. After launching in 2020, it earned $10 billion in revenue by the end of 2025, becoming the fastest mobile game ever to reach that milestone. In Japan, it was ranked first in popularity as late as 2024, and remains within the top 20 for new downloads, more than six years after launch.
While created by a Chinese firm, Genshin Impact draws heavily from Japanese pop culture. Its graphics use the typical nijigen visuals perfected through the country’s anime and manga industries, while the gameplay features gacha mechanics of obtaining mystery items, so culturally rooted in Japan’s gachapon capsule toy vending machines.
MiHoYo, branded internationally as Cognosphere, had been publishing games for China’s otaku community since its founding in 2011. The co-founders stated that their inspiration for creating games came from personal love for Japanese anime and technology. However, their business has expanded far beyond those roots. Only 5 percent of Genshin’s total downloads come from Japan despite the game’s popularity in the country. And as miHoYo increasingly expands globally, its games now mix Japanese, Chinese, and Western elements to attract a more diverse audience, as the transnational visuals of its successful Honkai series attest.
Translating Japanese cultural vocabulary for the global audience has become a source of success for other Chinese firms too. Toymaker PopMart manufactured a global fad for its Labubu dolls by applying that same gacha mechanics to its blind boxes, compelling fans to buy more to chase those rare varieties. Consumer goods retailer Miniso – much derided in Japan as “(Daiso + Muji) / 2” – has become an international promoter of Japanese characters such as Chiikawa and Hello Kitty through licensing agreements.
Notably, Miniso has more than 8,000 stores in 110 countries. With Japanese firms largely absent from large swathes of Africa and South America, Chinese firms have become the first point of contact local consumers have with Japanese aesthetics.
Now, these Chinese firms are ready to sell Japanese culture back to Japan. If miHoYo’s success in Japan through Genshin was accidental, the next wave of Japanified Chinese products will be anything but.
Following PopMart’s entry into the Japanese market in 2022, Miniso-owned toymaker TopToy entered Japan in 2025 using the same formula. Mellojoy, leveraging Japan’s love for punipuni, engineered a craze among young Japanese women for its own handmade squishies. Even Miniso itself is making a return to Japan through a pop-up shop in collaboration with renowned idol Lisa.
Japanese firms will now be in an unusual situation of competing for Japanese consumers in products they have long believed to be idiosyncratically Japanese. The case of the BYD Racco is illustrative. The Chinese electric vehicle giant became the first foreign company to ever launch a dedicated Japanese kei car, a class of ultra-compact cars found only in Japan. Japanese carmakers long considered the kei class to have a technological, cultural, and regulatory moat deep enough to deter foreigners. After the Racco sold more than 1,000 two weeks after its launch, domestic rivals were driven out of their complacency and compelled to respond. Suzuki’s recent launch of the e SKY, an electric kei car using BYD-made batteries, will surely ignite more competition in the previously insular market.
As that competition heats up, Japanese firms may come to discover that consumers no longer really care what it means for a product to be culturally Japanese. A coordinated effort to promote the country abroad through the Cool Japan Fund’s investments in media and retail proved a costly failure, while Miniso plans 900-1,000 new stores every year and BYD is readying the Racco for the international market.
As Genshin Impact showed us, people are interested in a Japanese aesthetic that anyone can access affordably. That means commercialized and scalable products, rather than ones completely made by Japan.

Court orders Egyptian website closed in case seen as test for independent media
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:21:36 CET
22:21:36 KST

CAIRO, Oct 27 (Reuters) - An Egyptian court convicted the editor-in-chief of leading independent news website Mada Masr of running it without a licence on Tuesday, ordered the site closed and held her in custody for five hours, her lawyers and the outlet said.
Lina Attalah of the online newspaper Mada Masr, which has won numerous international awards for its reporting, was fined 3 million Egyptian pounds ($53,400), her lawyers told Reuters. She was released after Mada Masr paid the fine, the newspaper said.
The ruling targets the most internationally prominent independent outlet in a media landscape mostly dominated by the state, and it comes a month after authorities arrested the entire newsroom of the fact-checking outlet Matsaddash. Rights groups have criticized the case against Attalah. Mada Masr, which was founded in 2013, regularly publishes stories on politically sensitive topics.
Her lawyers said the court rejected their requests during Tuesday’s session to review the case file and submit additional evidence and instead issued her a court-appointed lawyer despite her objection. State authorities did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The court gave her the maximum penalty, ordering the website to be shut down and its equipment confiscated, Mada Masr said in a statement.
The independent outlet said in a separate statement that during release procedures, Attalah was informed of a one-year prison term handed to her in absentia in 2024 on charges of disseminating false news and managing an unlicensed website. It said a retrial of the separate case was set for November 11 after her lawyers took steps to challenge the 2024 ruling.
Prosecutors referred Attalah to trial last Thursday.
A group of 119 rights groups and media outlets, including Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and the Committee to Protect Journalists, called the case an “unprecedented attack on press freedom.”
US Senator Chris Van Hollen, a Maryland Democrat, said in a statement on the social media platform X on Friday that the charges were baseless and that “journalism is not a crime.”
Egyptian authorities say the state is committed to upholding freedom of expression but that the media must operate within the law, respect national security and counter misinformation.
YEARS OF LEGAL BATTLES
Egyptian authorities have blocked Mada Masr inside the country since 2017. Mada Masr says six cases have been brought against it and its journalists over the last six years, though rights groups say this is the first of its kind to be referred to trial.
Attalah was named one of the world’s 100 most influential people by Time magazine in 2020.
Mada Masr says it has asked for a licence from the Supreme Council for Media Regulation repeatedly since 2018 but heard nothing back and learned of a rejection only when prosecutors raised the issue during an earlier case in 2022.
The outlet contested that decision in court and said its latest application has been awaiting a response since 2023.
The council has not commented on the case but has said that it facilitates procedures for outlets that meet official requirements and is keen to promote freedom of expression.
In September, the US waived rights conditions, which include protecting media freedoms, on a portion of the roughly $1.3 billion of military aid it sends Egypt each year.
(Editing by Alexander Dziadosz, Aidan Lewis and Matthew Lewis)

The Crta election monitor said last week that television stations with national reach gave three-quarters of the time allotted to politicians to government representatives. The Student List was portrayed negatively more than 80% of the time it was discussed, Crta added.

Spain deports African, Asian asylum seekers to Morocco amid rights group outcry

By Corina Pons
MADRID, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Spain has returned to Morocco more than a dozen sub-Saharan African and Asian migrants who reached the Spanish enclave of Ceuta and were turned down for asylum, the first deportation of its kind from the enclave since a mass border crossing in July.
The Interior Ministry said the group had been sent back to Morocco after it agreed to receive them and they remained on Moroccan territory at present. It declined to give numbers or nationalities but migrant and rights charities operating in Ceuta said 16 people from Senegal, Nigeria, Yemen, Cameroon and Bangladesh were deported.
The NGOs claim such returns fail to take into account the risks associated with Morocco’s treatment of migrants from other countries and fly in the face of the values espoused by Spain’s leftist government.
Virginia Alvarez, an Amnesty International researcher, said Spain’s posture was hypocritical.
“Spain, despite its (progressive) speeches in Europe, is not ensuring that human rights guarantees are met for people who cross its borders in Ceuta and Melilla,” she said. “Morocco does not respect many human rights.”
Neither Morocco’s Interior Ministry nor the International Organization for Migration, which cooperates with Moroccan authorities on voluntary return programmes for third country nationals or migrants, responded to Reuters requests for comment.
A spokesperson for Spain’s Interior Ministry told Reuters that Morocco is considered by the EU to be a safe country, and deportations are carried out “with all the necessary safeguards”, without providing further details.
Over 48 hours in July, some 80,000 people crossed from Morocco into Ceuta, a tiny enclave that along with Melilla represents Europe’s only land borders with Africa.
While most returned within days, thousands remain and Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s government is under pressure from the EU and a frustrated populace to fix the Ceuta crisis before elections on November 29.
Spanish authorities are housing 8,000 migrants in reception centres and processing asylum applications lodged by the majority of people remaining in Ceuta.
Several NGOs including Amnesty International have complained to the Spanish ombudsman that some of the more than 13,000 people the government says have returned to Morocco voluntarily since the middle of August were forced to leave, including non-Moroccans.
(Reporting by Corina Pons, editing by Aislinn Laing and Keith Weir)

MEGA, the robot bringing cheer to municipal police inspections in central Türkiye

2026-10-27

At a market in Türkiye's central Kayseri province, a humanoid robot moves between inspecting products and chatting with shopkeepers, checking price labels one moment and joking about bananas the next.
Named MEGA, the AI-powered robot accompanies municipal police officers on inspections in the Melikgazi district, where its unusual interactions with shopkeepers and customers have brought new energy to the market.
At Carsi Melikgazi, the robot scans shelf labels, compares displayed prices with those charged at checkout and provides information about product shelf lives and hygiene standards. It also relays its findings to relevant municipal departments in real time.
But MEGA's duties go beyond inspections. It reminds shopkeepers to label their products, informs shopkeepers with deficiencies about the applicable rules and thanks businesses that comply with regulations.
Acquired by Melikgazi Municipality, MEGA is part of the local government's efforts to adapt to emerging technologies.
Melikgazi Mayor Mustafa Palancioglu told Anadolu that the country, its cities and districts were seeking to adapt to technological advances, adding that robots could eventually be used in fields ranging from security and disaster response to cleaning and public information services.
Noting that robots were increasingly becoming part of everyday life, Palancioglu said those used in police, security and military services in various countries could also take on roles in the work of local governments.
"As Melikgazi Municipality, we use our robot in different areas to serve our citizens. Today, it is conducting inspections at Carsi Melikgazi as a municipal police officer and informing citizens. At the same time, it makes people smile and boosts morale," he said.
“Shopkeepers have welcomed encountering a robotic municipal police officer that makes suggestions and issues warnings to help maintain order," he added.
Palancioglu said AI-powered robots needed to be trained in advance to perform specific tasks, noting that staff from the municipality's research and development and information technology departments were working on MEGA.
"The robot we acquired is becoming increasingly involved in public services, taking on new tasks and interacting with our citizens. If you use technology for good, it can bring about many different benefits,” he said.
He also highlighted the municipality's efforts to train young people in technology through high schools and workshops, saying projects such as Gokturk Melikgazi aimed to equip them with skills to develop unmanned aerial vehicles and robotic systems.
Greengrocer Ahmet Murt said MEGA had brought new activity to the market and established a friendly rapport with local businesses.
“There has been quite a change since MEGA came to the market. It inspects us and even comments on our hair and beards. It tells us to put labels on products that don’t have them,” he said.
“Customers really like it and chat with it,” he added. “For example, when they offer it something to eat, MEGA says it only uses oil and cannot eat or drink. That makes us laugh.”
Another greengrocer, Mahmut Ozgoncu, said MEGA's arrival had brought more activity to the market.
He said children were interested in the robot, their families could shop comfortably and customers were happy to see MEGA.
Ozgoncu added that the robot also checked the produce on his stall.
“It paid attention to me and looked at the pomegranates and mandarins on my stall. It said, ‘You have very nice products.’ It was pleased that our products were of good quality. I offered it a banana, and it said, ‘I have diabetes, I can’t eat it,’” he said.

Egypt: Court order to shut down and fine Mada Masr a devastating blow to media freedom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:18:54 UTC
22:18:54 KST

Responding to the news that the New Cairo Misdemeanours court today convicted editor in chief Lina Attalah on charges of operating an unlicenced website, ordering the shutdown of prominent independent outlet Mada Masr and taking her into police custody pending payment of the maximum penalty of three million EGP fine (54,467 USD) Amnesty International’s Senior Director for Regional Impact, Yasmine Ahmed, said:
Today’s decision represents a crushing blow to press freedom in Egypt and marks a dark day for independent journalism in the country.
Yasmine Ahmed, Amnesty International
“Today’s decision represents a crushing blow to press freedom in Egypt and marks a dark day for independent journalism in the country. By imposing a 3 million EGP fine, ordering the closure of Mada Masr and the seizure of its property, and detaining Lina Atallah until payment is made, the Egyptian authorities are sending a clear and ruthless message: critical, independent reporting will not be tolerated.
“This draconian ruling is the culmination of years of relentless harassment and unjust proceedings designed to shut down one of the country’s last remaining independent media voices. Lina Atallah should never have been prosecuted for exercising her right to freedom of expression and doing her journalistic job. The Egyptian authorities must immediately overturn this outrageous verdict, halt the forced closure of Mada Masr, and end the systematic persecution of journalists.
“Mada is one of the most fearless and staunchly independent media outlets in the country, and they have continued to report professionally and operate in full transparency. The media outlet has repeatedly attempted to apply for a licence since the new media law was passed in 2018, but the authorities have continuously denied or failed to respond to their application.
“The speed with which the investigation and trial were scheduled and the judge’s refusal to adjourn today’s session to give defence lawyers adequate time to prepare and his refusal of all other requests by the defence, including to submit additional documentation or to summon witnesses, raises serious due process concerns.
“Under no circumstances is shutting down a media outlet a proportionate response to operating without government authorization. International human rights standards are clear on the fact that registration systems should not be used as a mechanism of prior restraint or to pick and choose which media outlets governments like and which they wish to silence.
“Today’s verdict comes at a time when independent journalism in Egypt is under assault and just weeks after the arbitrary detention of six journalists from the Matsadaash fact-checking platform amidst the continued blocking of hundreds of news websites and civil society organizations across the country.
Background
Mada has for years operated in full transparency as a non-profit company, while actively attempting since 2018 to register under the 2018 Law Regulating the Press, Media, and the Supreme Council for Media Regulation. Mada applied for a licence twice in 2018 and 2020 but received no response from the Supreme Council for Media Regulation (SCMR), the government body overseeing the media.
In 2022, Mada learned that the SCMR rejected their application without providing reasons. In the same year, Mada appealed the rejection in court but later lost the case. At a hearing in 2023, the SCMR stated its grounds for the first time. Mada reapplied this year and submitted all the documents the SCMR said were missing but never received a response.
The ruling follows years of harassment and intimidation against Lina Atallah as editor in chief of Mada Masr who has faced six criminal investigations over the past six years over their reporting. Most recently, on 4 August 2025, the authorities summoned Atallah for questioning on unfounded charges, including “spreading false news” and “operating a website without a license,” over an article published on 31 July 2025 about deteriorating detention conditions in Badr 3 prison. She was released on bail pending investigation.
At least 18 journalists are currently imprisoned in Egypt according to the Committee to Protect Journalists. Hundreds of websites remain blocked in the country, including Mada Masr, other media outlets and independent NGOs.

Germany’s Helsing Unveils Low-Cost Highspeed Drone Interceptors
Unknown

2026-10-27
13:17:49 UTC
22:17:49 KST

Helsing, a German military AI company, unveiled its Contra AI-controlled autonomous air defense system via a video posted on X on Monday. Helsing described it as a cost-effective system optimized to tackle jet-powered drone and missile attacks.
Helsing’s Contra system is intended to solve the existing air defense conundrum where the only current way of effectively intercepting jet-powered drones such as Russia’s Geran 4s and 5s is the use of multimillion-dollar interceptors.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Contra is intended to control two relatively inexpensive interceptor missiles: the AD-1 Inferno and AD-2 Ambush said to cost less than $100,000 each compared with Patriot PAC-3 missiles at $4-5 million a unit and the NASAMS (AMRAAM / AIM-9X) at around $1million a throw.
The military issues website Defense News cites recent intelligence reports, that Russia is increasing jet-powered drone and cruise missile production, to as much as 4,000 units a month, which, along with launch sites, could bring parts of the EU within range.
Artificial intelligence and interceptor speed, the key
While still at the developmental stage, Helsing bills Contra, based on its well-proven Altra C2 platform, as an autonomous AI-based operation that will allow the real-time detection and engagement of hundreds or more drone and missile threats into a single air defense picture.
It is anticipated to be “field-ready” by late 2027, with Helsing saying its seekers rely on European supply chains and is free from Chinese components.
Russia Says Three Tankers With Diesel En Route to US
Intercepts would be achieved through a combination of two, advanced radar guided, container-launched missile interceptors whose performance is designed to overlap and supplement each other’s capability.
The AD-1 “Inferno,” which Helsing Chief Executive Gundbert Scherf says is intended as the “workhorse” of the counter-drone system, is powered by a jet engine, and flies at around 700 kph (435 mph) at a range of around 20 kilometers (12 miles). It can loiter over a defended area, swarm with other interceptors, and make repeated passes.
The AD-2 “Ambush,” intended as a rapid interceptor against drones and missiles that break through the AD-1 “net,” has a solid rocket motor and is said to have a flight speed of Mach 2.5 (1,900 mph, 3,000 kph) at a range of in excess of 20 kilometers (12 miles).
Both systems are able to be redirected mid-course by the Contra ground stations with an onboard radar-seeker for all-weather terminal guidance. While designed for, and capable of, stand-alone operation, Helsing said the system is set up to rapidly integrate with third-party counter-drone systems including missile interceptors, lasers, and guns. The company said Contra has already demonstrated such hardware integrations to multiple military customers.
Niklas Köhler, Co-Founder and President of Helsing, says: “Contra ends the air defense dilemma: slow fair-weather drones, or million-euro missiles fired at cheap, mass-produced targets. Our AI links existing sensors and effectors in real time and adds our interceptors, AD-1 and AD-2. With jet and rocket propulsion, a low-cost all-weather radar seeker, and two independent European supply chains, they deliver autonomous fire superiority up to ten kilometers (6+ miles) high – affordable and at industrial scale.”

The dual nationality dilemma: what Dutch News readers say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:16:36 UTC
22:16:36 KST

The dual nationality dilemma: what Dutch News readers say
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Earlier this month we asked Dutch News’ readers for their thoughts on taking Dutch nationality, given that in many cases they would have to give up their original passport.
Legislation due to be discussed in parliament in early December should change that, but it now seems likely that foreigners will be excluded from the new rules – which will then only apply to the native Dutch who take on a second nationality.
The rules on dual nationality are complex and discriminatory. If you are married it is easier to become Dutch and retain your original passport, for example. It also gets easier once you reach the age of 65. But many readers are caught up in the complexity of the current “naturalisation” process. They want to become Dutch, but giving up their original nationality will create a new range of problems.
Over 80 readers told us their stories. Here is a selection of their experiences.
An impossible choice
“What I find difficult is that many people who have lived, worked, and contributed to Dutch society for years are forced to make a choice that other Dutch citizens are not required to make. I would gladly embrace Dutch citizenship, but not at the cost of losing an important part of my identity and connection to my family and heritage.” Ahmed, from Egypt
Bureaucratic nightmare
“I’m Chilean and have been living in the Netherlands for around 10 years. A few years ago, I decided to become Dutch. The Dutch naturalisation process itself was clear and straightforward for me. What I could never have imagined was the nightmare I would face in Chile afterwards.
“Renouncing Chilean nationality is effectively irreversible. Once you give it up, you cannot simply apply to get it back …The renunciation brought very serious practical consequences that I was not prepared for. My Chilean nationality was removed and I was deleted from Chile’s national registry.
“This means that I can no longer obtain basic documents such as a birth certificate in the normal way, despite having been born in Chile. Every time I need to deal with something in Chile, including matters concerning my own family and inheritance, I find myself unable to prove that I am the person who appears in their records. I have no Chilean identity documents anymore, and because I have been removed from the registry, I simply no longer exist in the country where I was born.
“The Dutch government describes the renunciation as something you do ‘voluntarily’. But I struggle with that description. If acquiring Dutch nationality means that I have to give up my original nationality in order to become Dutch, how voluntary is that choice really?” Jonathan, from Chile
An easy decision
“I have lived here for 32 years – over half my life. I was born in Ireland but moved here in 1994. My wife is Dutch-born, our kids were born here and my life is here. I became a Dutch citizen about 15 years ago and gave up my Irish citizenship. I regard myself as culturally more Dutch now than Irish and choosing for a single nationality was a very easy decision.” Jim, from Ireland
Global freedom
“My wife loves it here, I’ve passed my inburgering exams, love my job, and contribute over €100k annually in taxes. But despite loving our life here, we’ve decided to leave soon. With the 30% ruling ending for me and the Netherlands requiring naturalising citizens to renounce their original nationality, staying no longer makes sense. My original passport represents my roots, family, and identity – I will never give it up.
“However, I do want the global freedom and security of a second passport. We’ve made the hard decision to move to Canada or the UK, where we can naturalise in five years or less without dropping our original nationality. It’s a sad move for my wife and a tough choice for both of us, but the current legal framework leaves high-contributing expats with very few practical alternatives.” John, from Jordan
Where to retire?
“I have lived in Europe since 2001 and moved to Amsterdam in 2018 as I wanted to remain in Europe. As I am coming into the end of my career we are contemplating where we want to retire but have no mobility as our permanent residence is tied solely to the Netherlands.
“Right now, given the political situation in Canada, it pains me to surrender my nationality as I am a proud Canadian, but I must contemplate our future as a family that wishes to remain in Europe with the option to reside in a sunnier climate. It is also a shame given the long history between Canada and the Netherlands and the increasing closeness of Canada to the EU. After 25 years in Europe I am firmly European, but it feels unfair to force me to deny that I am also Canadian.” Adele, from Canada
Discrimination
“As I am not married, I am not able to apply for Dutch citizenship without renouncing my Australian citizenship. I find this quite disappointing and even discriminatory, given that, if I had a partner or spouse, I’d be allowed to have both. For that reason I have remained an Aussie, even though I’m not planning on moving back to there anytime soon.” James has lived in the Netherlands for more than 20 years.
Sister separation
“I have given up my nationality (British) and am now Dutch. The complete irony is I’m an identical twin so now I’m an identical twin where my sister has a different nationality. After Brexit I worry about how that may impact us when we are 80 and are less able to travel.” Tina, from Britain
Rise of the far right
“I declined on three occasions an invitation to attend the naturalisation ceremony because I found it difficult to give up my Filipino citizenship. The Philippines allows dual nationality while the Netherlands requires full allegiance.
“In the end, I had to make what felt like a very hard decision of renouncing my Filipino citizenship because PVV was the biggest party at the time. I was worried that living in the Netherlands would be difficult on account of the radical right leaning becoming the biggest political party.” Brian, from the Philippines
Family ties
“I would love to apply for Dutch nationality, but because I still have family in the US, including an adult child and aging parents, I cannot give up my American passport.
“Sometimes the US does not allow people who have relinquished their passports to return, because they are considered a greater risk for overstaying their visas when compared to other visitors. I cannot risk being unable to visit my family, so I am applying for permanent residency instead of a Dutch passport.” Rick, from the US
Practical reasons
“I come from another EU country, and for me there is currently no possibility of becoming a Dutch citizen without renouncing my original nationality. As someone from a small country, this is not an easy decision. It is difficult not only for emotional reasons, but also for practical ones.
“I was born and raised in my country of origin, and my entire family still lives there. My nationality is therefore more than just a passport or a legal status; it is an important part of my identity and my connection to my family and where I come from.
“At the same time, my children were born and raised here in the Netherlands. They speak Dutch, attend Dutch schools, and grow up with Dutch traditions and culture. The Netherlands is their home. Yet, despite being fully part of Dutch society, they are not Dutch citizens and therefore cannot enjoy all the rights that come with citizenship, most notably the right to vote in national elections.
“This creates a difficult situation for families like mine. We can be deeply integrated into Dutch society and consider the Netherlands our home, while still facing a choice between retaining the nationality we were born with and becoming Dutch citizens.
“For me, this is not about rejecting my country of origin or refusing to become part of Dutch society. It is about wanting to preserve both parts of my identity and, at the same time, fully belong to the country where my children are growing up.” Anon
Some names have been changed to protect the privacy of the individuals concerned.
Our thanks to everyone who got in touch, and we will be contacting more of you in the coming period.
If you would like to comment on this article, or have any additional thoughts, don’t hesitate to get in touch via editor@dutchnews.nl. We will be publishing a series of articles focusing on dual nationality in the coming months.

India-China border face-offs test Modi six years after deadly clash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:15:32 UTC
22:15:32 KST

India-China border face-offs test Modi six years after deadly clash
Despite diplomatic thaw between New Delhi and Beijing, clashes along undemarcated border pose challenge to Modi’s strongman image.
New Delhi, India – India’s armed forces are locked in multiple ongoing face-offs with the Chinese army along the border in the northeastern state of Arunachal Pradesh, the chief of India’s paramilitary border force guarding the Himalayan frontier with China has said.
The remarks late last week by Shatrujeet Kapur, the director-general of the Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) paramilitary force, come nearly four months after local civil society groups in the remote northeastern region told Al Jazeera that Chinese forces were increasingly encroaching on Indian territory and denying Indian troops access to patrolling points, angering locals.
Chinese President Xi Jinping was in New Delhi last month – his first trip to India in seven years – for the BRICS summit, where he met Prime Minister Narendra Modi on the sidelines, as the two capitals pursued a cautious thaw in bilateral ties. That thaw is partly driven by United States President Donald Trump’s trade war, which has pushed nuclear-armed rivals Beijing and New Delhi closer.
Yet the alleged Chinese incursions into India underscore how, despite warm handshakes in New Delhi, tensions along the 3,500-kilometre (2,200-mile) border between the neighbours threaten to undercut efforts to normalise ties.
They also pose a major political challenge to Modi, who has built an image as being strong on national security, but who has in recent years faced difficult questions about the relationship with China.
The face-offs with Chinese forces in Arunachal Pradesh – that “still continue”, according to Kapur – come six years after at least 20 Indian troops were killed in hand-to-hand combat with Chinese forces in mountainous Ladakh.
Though satellite imagery and multiple accounts, including from within the Indian security establishment, have since pointed to China effectively taking control of parts of previously disputed territory since that fight, the Modi government has refused to concede that it has given up any land.
And five days after Kapur’s comments on recent standoffs, the Indian government is yet to confirm the nature of the border tensions, instead offering more boilerplate criticisms of China.
Unresolved, lingering dispute
Kapur, the ITBP chief, was speaking at a felicitation ceremony for the paramilitary force’s personnel, where he revealed that commandos have been active in the continuing confrontations on the border with China.
Arunachal Pradesh’s remote Upper Subansiri region – where the ongoing face-offs are reported – had seen the first clash between independent India and China in August 1959, which killed at least two Indian soldiers.
Then-Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru spoke of the remoteness of the region in his account of the clash, when he told Parliament that the border post under Chinese attack was roughly three weeks’ march from the nearest roadhead.
The decades-long India-China border dispute is rooted in a British-drawn border, called the McMahon Line. In 1914, British India and Tibet, not under Chinese control at the time, signed the Simla Convention, demarcating their border. Since gaining independence in 1947, India has treated the McMahon Line as its border with China. But China, which came under communist rule in 1949, rejects the line as the boundary with India, arguing that Tibet lacked the authority to conclude the agreement independently.
Beijing claims the entire state of Arunachal Pradesh and refers to it as “South Tibet” or “Zangnan”. China also controls Aksai Chin, a slice of the disputed Kashmir region that India and Pakistan claim in full.
With their territorial claims unresolved, India and China signed an agreement in 1993 to maintain peace along the Line of Actual Control (LAC), their de facto boundary from 1962, pending a final border settlement. They continue to disagree over its precise alignment.
Those differences were never bridged in the following years, keeping the disputed frontier a persistent flashpoint in relations between the two nuclear-armed neighbours.
The dispute erupted again into a deadly confrontation in June 2020, when Indian and Chinese troops clashed in the Galwan Valley in eastern Ladakh, with both sides accusing the other of crossing the LAC. At least 20 Indian soldiers were killed, and China later acknowledged four deaths among its troops.
Praveen Donthi, a senior analyst at the Brussels-based International Crisis Group, said that border tensions amid a thaw in bilateral relations now appear as “part of a pattern” – “likely a pressure tactic by Beijing,” he added.
And due to the undemarcated border, “stand-offs are bound to occur from time to time, some of which may go out of hand”, Donthi warned.
‘Chinese army on top of mountain’
But the 2020 clash also pushed Modi into a corner domestically, as the opposition parties pressured the government over its opaque handling of China. The Modi government also faced opposition complaints over restrictions on parliamentary scrutiny, questions about whether intelligence agencies had detected the Chinese troop build-up, and limited disclosure of operational details.
Contradictions between the government’s own stand and Modi’s claims also prompted accusations that he was trying to minimise – or even hide – the scale of the crisis along the border.
On June 17, 2020, soon after the Galwan clash, Indian Foreign Minister S Jaishankar spoke to his Chinese counterpart Wang Yi.
“The Chinese side sought to erect a structure in Galwan Valley on our side of the LAC,” the Indian Ministry of External Affairs said after the phone call. “While this became a source of dispute, the Chinese side took premeditated and planned action that was directly responsible for the resulting violence and casualties. It reflected an intent to change the facts on ground in violation of all our agreements to not change the status quo.”
Yet two days later, Modi said on Twitter, now X, that “neither has anyone been able to enter our territory, nor is anyone still on our territory” – an assertion that disputed the foreign ministry’s account. If no Chinese troops had crossed the LAC, why had Indian soldiers been forced to fight them, the opposition and other strategic analysts asked?
The government has never answered those questions, with Modi’s office only issuing a clarification that the prime minister meant that there were no Chinese troops still in Indian territory after the clash.
Six years since the Ladakh clash, the Chinese incursion has returned to challenge Modi’s strongman image at home – which has already taken a hit from youth-led protests in the country that forced out Modi’s education minister in July this year.
In his address, ITBP chief Kapur also recalled the 2020 clash, outlining a specialised training programme “to better equip personnel to deal with” a Ladakh-like situation.
Kapur, who is due to retire this week, also warned that China’s frontier military capabilities had advanced – and Indian forces may not be able to take a fight head-on by traditional methods.
The Crisis Group’s Donthi said that the Modi government “presents an image of a hard security state with zero tolerance for national security failures”. but “the power differential with China is quite sharp, so it tends to downplay any event that reflects poorly”.
The opposition Congress party’s top leader in Arunachal Pradesh state, Bosiram Siram, said that Chinese troops have intruded nearly 50km (31 miles) deep into Indian territory in remote Upper Subansiri.
A Siram-led party delegation visited border areas in August after initial reports of China’s incursions, and Siram added that “Chinese personnel are stationed up there”, referring to Indian territory.
“You can see the [Chinese] Army. They are on top of the mountains, while we are down below,” Siram added.
In response to the ITBP chief’s remarks, India’s foreign ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said that “the situation in India-China border areas gets disturbed from time to time when Chinese forces diverge from established patrolling patterns”. He did not comment on the ongoing face-offs.
No lasting solution in sight
BR Deepak, a professor of Chinese studies at Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU) in Delhi, said that the reports of Chinese incursion pose a challenge to Modi’s “credibility and accountability”.
Since 2012, India and China have relied on an official channel that deters border disputes from snowballing, without resolving the underlying question of where their Himalayan boundary lies.
The so-called Working Mechanism for Consultation and Coordination on India-China Border Affairs (WMCC) has officials from both countries and operates alongside military channels.
Its latest round, the 36th WMCC, was held on August 6 – nearly a month after reports of Chinese incursion first emerged in Arunachal Pradesh. In September, a first-ever commander-level meeting was held in Arunachal Pradesh.
Deepak said that “the continuing face-offs show that these diplomatic efforts have not eliminated the friction.” He argued that “meetings at the military or local level can provide temporary relief and help prevent escalation, but they cannot, by themselves, deliver a lasting solution to a border dispute rooted in decades of historical, political and strategic differences”.
And in the absence of “clear political guidance and a coordinated response” in both capitals, Deepak said, any border-level arrangements will “remain fragile and reversible, as seen in [Ladakh] and now in Upper Subansiri in Arunachal Pradesh”.

Zabuzhko: Ukraine had culture in 1995, but had lost it by 2005
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
15:13:29 EET
22:13:29 KST

Ukraine was under information and cultural occupation in the decade between the 1990s and 2000s, writer Oksana Zabuzhko said.
"In 1995, we had culture. In 2005, we no longer had it. We were a branch of the 'great Russian world,' which was engaged in the information occupation of Ukraine throughout the entire pre-war decade, starting around the turn of the 1990s and 2000s. This was the same preparation of Ukraine for co-optation into Russia, carried out on a massive scale and quite successfully in the information and cultural spheres. Accordingly, we were invisible to the outside world. The visibility of any nation is cultural visibility. As long as the political class does not understand this, this country will be condemned to struggle somewhere in the third ranks, among the countries of the Third World," Zabuzhko said at the 12th Kyiv International Economic Forum, themed "People. Business. Economy. What Next?", in Kyiv, answering a question about whether Ukraine had achieved a cultural breakthrough.
She said that before the full-scale war, no one abroad was interested in engaging with the culture of "some invisible country whose future was still unknown."
"But once our glorious armed forces gave a thorough beating in the spring of 2022 to those who were considered the world's second army, my dream finally came true. In October 2022, Lesya Ukrainka's Cassandra premiered to great acclaim at London's Omnibus Theatre," the writer said.
In her view, the most relevant definition for Ukraine today was one given by political figure Vyacheslav Lypynsky: "The sum of values that, in the course of a community's life, have proved most conducive to that community's survival is called culture."
"Motivation wins, spirit wins, and so does what the Ukrainian soldier has and the Russian soldier lacks. That is a cultural difference. It is a sense of defending the values of one's community. Ask our soldiers what they are defending: their home, their land. At the level of one's home, one's land and one's family, at this level of rootedness, we have already defeated the Soviet regime and Russia in what they wanted to do to our ancestors during the Holodomor," Zabuzhko said.
Returning to the notion of a Ukrainian cultural "renaissance," she stressed that an artist would succeed with a domestic audience only if they articulated the collective unconscious. That was when queues would form for cultural products, as had happened with the play The Witch of Konotop at the Ivan Franko National Academic Drama Theatre.
"The state's role is to obtain information from experts about this very wild-growing garden: where to graft and where to water, which areas need watering, and where to put in money and later recoup it, whether through the state budget, patrons or fundraising. That is an entirely separate matter. What grows on its own does grow on its own, as we have seen over the past decade. They introduced quotas for Russian music on FM radio, and suddenly it turned out that a great deal of Ukrainian music had grown wild in the meantime, having spent the previous decade being considered unsuitable for the format," Zabuzhko said.
As reported, Deputy Prime Minister for Humanitarian Policy and Culture Minister Tetiana Berezhna said that, given the vastly unequal resources available for culture in Ukraine and Russia, Ukraine needed to act asymmetrically. She also said there was currently demand among Ukrainian consumers for Ukrainian culture, demand among creators to produce it, and a need to introduce Ukrainian culture to international audiences.

Norway and Finland leaders hold rare call with Putin
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:12:24 GMT
22:12:24 KST

Norway and Finland leaders hold rare call with Putin
- Published
The leaders of Finland and Norway have held a joint call with Vladimir Putin - rare contact between the Russian president and European leaders.
Finland's President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said the aim of the call had been to "convey messages directly regarding future negotiations" towards peace. An end to the conflict in Ukraine "will not be achieved through silence," Stubb said.
Neither side suggested the needle had been moved on ending the war, which began when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Although the Finnish leader said the conversation with Putin had been "frank and substantive," Støre added that there were "big differences in views" with Putin.
Several European leaders have recently shown willingness to engage with Russia directly, but both Stubb and Støre pointed out their initiative was taken in their capacity as neighbours of Russia, rather than on behalf of Europe as a whole.
"We've not set out to speak on behalf of anyone other than ourselves," Støre said.
Stubb added the call had been prepared in consultation with Ukraine and the US following a meeting between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, the Nordic leaders and US special envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo last week.
The first trilateral US-Ukraine-Russia talks since the start of the year are tentatively planned for early November in Abu Dhabi.
Zelensky later confirmed Stubb and Støre debriefed him after the call and said he was grateful for their "active support", while his Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the call had been "the right approach".
Finland and Norway, which border Russia, initiated the 90-minute call - held from Helsinki - to "discuss Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine and the diplomatic efforts to end the war and promote peace and stability in Europe", the leaders' offices said.
Støre added: "The war comes with enormous human and material costs... The suffering and destruction will impact generations."
The Kremlin said Putin told the leaders that "a just and lasting peace" would only be possible if Russia's interests were considered.
Putin also reaffirmed to the Nordic leaders what he views as the "root causes" of the conflict - his frequent shorthand for Ukraine's desire to exist as a sovereign state.
"A fair long-term peace settlement is possible only if Russia's legal interests are taken into account fully and unconditionally", Putin said.
All three parties reportedly agreed to continue their direct phone communication.
There was no official EU reaction to the talks. The dialogue had not been coordinated with other European leaders, the Danish and Swedish prime ministers said. "I think Europe should stick together rather than going solo," commented Sweden's Ulf Kristersson.
Meanwhile, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Stubb had informed him that Europe's position on the upcoming talks in the United Arab Emirates was "moderately optimistic".
Relations between the US and Ukraine and its European allies have soured since US President Donald Trump agreed to lift some sanctions from Russia, allowing Moscow to export oil to the America.
As the Trump administration's position on Russia has softened, several European leaders have said Europe should be trying to re-establish direct contacts with the Kremlin.
Stubb and Støre are the first European leaders to contact Putin since French President Emmanuel Macron's conversation with him in July 2025.
Soon after, Putin visited Alaska for a summit with Trump, and from then on Europeans were further sidelined from Ukraine peace talks. Moscow regularly mocks European leaders and accuses the EU of prolonging the war by supplying Ukraine with weapons.
But last weekend, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said having a European negotiator at the peace talks table would be "good".
And although he said Moscow did not view Finland and Norway as speaking on behalf of Europe, on Tuesday Peskov conceded that Stubb and Støre's talks with Putin had been "very constructive and practical talks with the leaders of two key neighbouring states."

Japan moves to expose foreign government lobbying
A Japanese government panel began discussing a foreign agent registration system on Monday. The proposal marks a first step toward planned anti-espionage legislation, Qazinform News Agency reports, citing Jiji Press.
The proposed system would cover individuals and organizations lobbying in Japan for foreign governments. Those acting under their instructions or contracts would need to register with Japanese authorities. Tokyo aims to make these activities more transparent.
The panel will draft recommendations ahead of the government’s planned national intelligence strategy. That strategy could be compiled as early as this fiscal year.
The government hopes to submit related legislation during parliament’s regular session next year.
Monday’s meeting took place at the prime minister’s office, the panel’s second gathering. A National Police Agency official called for penalties for malicious acts.
The official said attempts to influence political and administrative processes had increased in recent years. This made legislation an urgent priority.
The government also presented examples of similar systems in the United States, Britain and France.

Mercedes-Benz now expects its 2026 core profit to remain flat at €5.8 billion, abandoning its earlier forecast of 15% growth, further signaling the severe structural crisis threatening Germany's automotive industry.
Mercedes-Benz became the third major German carmaker to lower its full-year outlook on Tuesday, citing challenging market conditions in China and rising material costs.
The company now expects its core profit for 2026 to remain flat at around €5.8 billion, despite previously forecasting an increase of at least 15%.
It also lowered its expected profit margin for its core car business to between 2% and 3%, down from its earlier forecast of 3% to 5%.

Mercedes-Benz shares fell over 4% following the announcement, while Volkswagen and BMW both declined about 2%.
Both BMW and Volkswagen have already lowered their full-year forecasts, as weak demand and fierce competition from Chinese rivals such as BYD and Xiaomi continue to weigh on profits.
Mercedes-Benz's vehicle deliveries in China fell by a further 29% in the first nine months of 2026, after hitting their lowest level since 2016 last year.
Mercedes-Benz CEO Ola Kallenius has urged German employees to work additional hours without extra pay, while expanding production in Hungary, where he says costs are around 70% lower than in Germany.
Volkswagen plans to cut 120,000 jobs worldwide by the end of the decade, in what would be the largest restructuring in automotive history, surpassing the 50,000 jobs lost following General Motors' bankruptcy in 2009.

Frontex gets power to track migration talk on social media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:07:12 UTC
22:07:12 KST

The role of social media platforms in spreading information that contributes to illegal migration was central to the crisis in the Spanish exclave of Ceuta. | Tomohiro Ohsumi/Getty Images
The EU's border agency, Frontex, will be able to monitor social media for information about migration flows.
The European Commission on Tuesday unveiled a revamp of Frontex, strengthening its capabilities and capacity to tackle illegal migration. It will play a more prominent role in deporting people with no legal right to remain in the EU, including new powers to carry out return operations beyond the bloc’s territory and new oversight on social media.
The role of social media platforms in spreading information that contributes to illegal migration was central to the crisis in the Spanish exclave of Ceuta, where thousands of migrants illegally crossed the border within a few hours in July.
Advertisement
The new rules will create within Frontex "an online monitoring and response center to monitor publicly accessible social media content to detect developments relevant to external border management, and also to support action against illegal online content linked to border security risks," EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen told reporters on Tuesday.
The agency will also "be acting as a trusted flagger under the Digital Services Act, flagging illegal content to online platforms, and requesting national authorities to issue removal orders where appropriate," the Commission said in press material.
Being a "trusted flagger" under the DSA, the EU's landmark social media rules, is a special status granted by national digital regulators. Content flagged by entities with this status is put on a fast track to be dealt with by online platforms.
Virkkunen said Frontex will apply for this status with national authorities, and she expected the border agency to be approved because of its "special expertise."

Where is the disconnect between Bulgarians and Presidential elections?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:06:36 UTC
22:06:36 KST

Author
Yoan Kolev
News
Presidential Election 2026
Where is the disconnect between Bulgarians and Presidential elections?
Parvan Simeonov: Low voter turnout is a signal to keep fighting for Bulgaria’s democratic process
Tuesday 27 October 2026 13:14
Tuesday, 27 October 2026, 13:14
PHOTO BTA
Font size
The first round of the presidential election is over, but record-low voter turnout raises serious questions: Why is electoral momentum declining? Is Bulgaria’s democratic process at risk? And why is the figure of the president failing to motivate people to vote?
Parvan Simeonov
PHOTO BTA
“If the presidential election managed to draw just 1.5 million voters to the polls, despite an electoral surge in April this year, we need to give serious thought to how the institution of the presidency and the person of the president are viewed in Bulgaria'', sociologist Parvan Simeonov of Myara polling agency, BNR’s partner in covering the election, told Radio Bulgaria.
''Certainly, the incident involving journalist Sonya Koltuklieva, the murders (of two high-profile businessmen in Sofia and Plovdiv-editor’s note), and the drones in the Black Sea shaped a campaign that did not favour the Bulgarian government. Some of these events occurred after polling agencies published their latest figures, so we were unable to measure their impact. However, they appear to have demobilised supporters of Iliana Iotova while mobilizing those backing Andrey Gyurov and Kostadin Kostadinov, who finished third in the race.”
PHOTO BGNES
“Unprecedentedly low voter turnout of around 22% in the first round should serve as a warning sign that we need to start worrying about the state of the democratic process in the country”, Parvan Simeonov stressed. Despite the uncertainty surrounding the outcome of the second round on November 1, the presidential election has a positive agenda, the analyst believes.
“When we voted in the parliamentary elections in April this year, part of the agenda was negative, meaning it was about opposing the status quo. The presidential election, by contrast, is largely about choosing who should become president. This makes it somewhat more difficult to vote against something or cast a protest vote. Of course, researchers still need to determine what has caused the ‘disappearance’ of two million voters. Around 3.45 million people voted in April, compared with approximately 1.45 million in the presidential election. Those two million voters were part of an electoral surge that is now absent. This makes the outcome of the runoff difficult to predict.”
PHOTO BTA
The sociologist also commented on the exceptionally low voter turnout among our compatriots in Türkiye, where only around 7,000 ballots were cast.
“These are not parliamentary elections, which traditionally generate greater interest because people can see what is at stake for them locally. Candidates run their own campaigns and gather preference votes. Presidential elections, however, are a more abstract choice. So what incentive is there for individuals and political organisations to get involved, especially those motivated by pragmatic considerations? That is why I believe this is a very interesting symptom of Bulgaria’s democratic process. It seems that something is breaking down in the connection between voters and the presidential election”, Parvan Simeonov said, noting that the 2021 presidential election was held alongside snap parliamentary elections, while the 2016 vote coincided with a referendum.
‘We haven’t had a presidential election held on its own for quite some time. What we have seen this time raises many questions.”
Andrey Gyurov
PHOTO BGNES
The sociologist said he was not surprised by Andrey Gyurov’s decisive victory among Bulgarians voting abroad.
''Voters abroad generally support either a new political formation or the pro-Western liberals with the exception of Türkiye, where the situation is different. With no new political formation in the current race, the pro-Western liberals have received stronger support. That is how I explain the fact that Andrey Gyurov is leading among voters abroad, while Iliana Iotova is ahead in Bulgaria. Of course, we will have to wait and see what happens in the runoff, where two competing narratives about the country will go head-to-head''.
Iliana Iotova
PHOTO BGNES
This is why the upcoming debate between the two candidates is so eagerly anticipated, although Simeonov expects it to see two predictable narratives clash. He does not believe the debate will attract many new supporters for either candidate. Rather, it will serve to rally their existing supporters. The current government, represented by Progressive Bulgaria, will play a significant role through its presence and support. The party will need to demonstrate its support for Iliana Iotova, pointing to an increasingly heated contest in what has been dubbed the political tiebreaker.

Russia says 4th tanker with Russian diesel for US expected to depart Wednesday
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:06:26 UTC
22:06:26 KST

Elena Teslova
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
A fourth tanker carrying diesel fuel to the US as part of a Moscow-Washington deal earlier this month is expected to depart on Wednesday, Russia's deputy prime minister said Tuesday.
Speaking on the sidelines of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum in Moscow, Alexander Novak said Moscow had already dispatched three tankers.
"There are currently three ships. The fourth has not yet departed. We expect it on the 28th," he said.
The official said he was surprised by the stance of US politicians who oppose the diesel deal with Russia.
"In general, of course, the position of the Democrats is surprising, who speak or even act not in the interests of the residents of the US," he said.
Russia is also ready to resume gas supplies to Europe if European countries want them, Novak noted.
"For our part, we are ready. We have always been reliable suppliers," he said.
The official said Russia can sell all of its gas volumes in other markets if Europe turns them down.
"If Europe does not buy, we have somewhere to sell our gas. You know that in recent years, we have developed infrastructure for supplies to those countries that are most actively increasing consumption, where the economy is growing. So, Russia has no problems with selling gas in this regard. It is rather Europe’s problem," he said.
Turning to China, he said liquefied natural gas is more expensive for Beijing than Russian pipeline gas.
"From the point of view of economics, of course, it is much more costly for them today. With a shortage of gas and cheap energy resources, consumers overpay because of the deficit and rising prices, and buy more expensive liquefied natural gas with longer logistics costs and so on," he said.
On the future of the Nord Stream pipelines, he said Europe is likely to need them in the long term.
"Looking ahead, in principle, the development of pipeline infrastructure that took place from the 1970s and continued in this century is beneficial both to Europe, European countries, and to Russia, because Russia is energy independent and able to ensure the energy security of other countries that do not have their own energy resources, in particular Europe. So, I think that in the long term, strategically, these pipelines are most likely to be in demand," he said.
Earlier this month, US President Donald Trump unveiled a diesel supply agreement following a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, under which Moscow agreed to “immediately supply” more than 300,000 tons of diesel fuel to the US and global markets.
According to Trump, Russia would supply another 500,000 tons of diesel fuel in November, followed by 1 million tons "immediately thereafter."
He said an additional 3 million tons would be delivered "within a short period," depending on the condition of Russian diesel refineries.
Putin said Russian diesel supplies to US and global markets would benefit the world economy, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy criticized the deal, warning that easing restrictions on Russian diesel exports could help finance its war effort.

Spain deports African, Asian asylum seekers to Morocco amid rights group outcry
- Spain deported more than a dozen African and Asian asylum seekers from Ceuta to Morocco after their claims were rejected, the first such move since the July mass crossing.
- Rights groups, including Amnesty International, said the returns ignore risks in Morocco and clash with Spain’s human rights claims. Spain said Morocco is a safe country and the deportations used “all the necessary safeguards”.
- The Ceuta crisis continues after about 80,000 people crossed from Morocco in July. Spain is housing 8,000 migrants, while pressure grows on Pedro Sanchez’s government before the Nov 29 elections.
AI generated
MADRID - Spain has returned to Morocco more than a dozen sub-Saharan African and Asian migrants who reached the Spanish enclave of Ceuta and were turned down for asylum, the first deportation of its kind from the enclave since a mass border crossing in July.
The Interior Ministry said the group had been sent back to Morocco after it agreed to receive them and they remained on Moroccan territory at present.
It declined to give numbers or nationalities but migrant and rights charities operating in Ceuta said 16 people from Senegal, Nigeria, Yemen, Cameroon and Bangladesh were deported.
The NGOs claim such returns fail to take into account the risks associated with Morocco’s treatment of migrants from other countries, and fly in the face of the values espoused by Spain’s leftist government.
Virginia Alvarez, an Amnesty International researcher, said Spain’s posture was hypocritical.
“Spain, despite its (progressive) speeches in Europe, is not ensuring that human rights guarantees are met for people who cross its borders in Ceuta and Melilla,” she said.
“Morocco does not respect many human rights.”
Neither Morocco’s Interior Ministry nor the International Organisation for Migration, which cooperates with Moroccan authorities on voluntary return programmes for third country nationals or migrants, responded to Reuters requests for comment.
A spokesperson for Spain’s Interior Ministry told Reuters that Morocco is considered by the EU to be a safe country, and deportations are carried out “with all the necessary safeguards”, without providing further details.
Over 48 hours in July, some 80,000 people crossed from Morocco into Ceuta, a tiny enclave that along with Melilla represents Europe’s only land borders with Africa.
While most returned within days, thousands remain and Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s government is under pressure from the EU and a frustrated populace to fix the Ceuta crisis before elections on Nov 29.
Spanish authorities are housing 8,000 migrants in reception centres and processing asylum applications lodged by the majority of people remaining in Ceuta.
Several NGOs including Amnesty International have complained to the Spanish ombudsman that some of the more than 13,000 people the government says have returned to Morocco voluntarily since the middle of August were forced to leave, including non-Moroccans. REUTERS

Font size
The Bulgarian short film Gadje by director Georges Vanev and producer Nevena Semova has won the Audience Award at the 19th edition of the CinEast Film Festival in Luxembourg. Audiences also singled out another Bulgarian title, In Hell with Ivo, directed by Kristina Nikolova.
PHOTO Facebook /Embassy of the Republic of Bulgaria in Belgium
Bulgaria was a special focus of this year’s festival in Luxembourg. The “Focus on Bulgaria” programme showcased contemporary Bulgarian cinema and culture through seven feature films and two short films, meetings with Bulgarian directors and artists, a Bulgarian-themed evening, two concerts, a photography exhibition and Bulgarian cuisine. The Bulgarian Embassy in Belgium partnered with the festival and co-organised some of the accompanying events.
PHOTO Facebook /Embassy of the Republic of Bulgaria in Belgium
Gadje is the debut film of young director and screenwriter Georges Vanev. Born in Sofia, he has lived in Belgium for 30 years. He studied French literature before going on to study cinematography and earned a master’s degree in screenwriting in 2022. Although he was only two years old when he moved to Belgium with his parents, Vanev has maintained a strong connection with Bulgaria. His short film was shot in the Bulgarian village of Bosnek. A contemporary love story reminiscent of Romeo and Juliet, it explores themes of racism and discrimination.
PHOTO IMDb
The other Bulgarian film to capture audiences’ attention at CinEast, In Hell with Ivo, offers a compelling portrait of an artist who defies conventional boundaries. Directed by Kristina Nikolova, the film follows queer performance artist and songwriter Ivo Dimchev, who transforms personal and social hardship into provocative public and intimate spectacles, boldly exploring sexuality, identity, faith and activism in a liberating celebration of queer visibility.

MEPs from various political groups in the European Parliament, including Emil Radev of GERB/EPP, are urging EU transport ministers to resume discussions on ending the seasonal clock change across the European Union. In a letter to the ministers, they call for an EU-wide solution after more than seven years of stalled progress on the European Commission’s legislative proposal. Public opinion polls conducted in various countries show broad support for scrapping the clock change.
“On Sunday, we turned our clocks back by an hour, and the issue may once again be forgotten until March, when we switch to daylight saving time. We have been waiting for years for Europe to put an end to this outdated practice”, Emil Radev commented. He added that changing the clocks twice a year is an outdated and ineffective practice that negatively affects people’s biological rhythms and health and disrupts their daily activities.

A recent cyberattack on the computer systems of Italy’s Chamber of Deputies affected the email accounts of several lawmakers, including Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, Italian news agency ANSA reported Tuesday.

Sources at the Chamber of Deputies said the incident did not constitute an emergency, adding that such attacks occur daily.

The measures may include the temporary deactivation of certain computer system functions, which the sources described as standard practice.
They also said similar attacks and pressure on IT systems appeared to have intensified in recent days, including against other national, European and international institutions.
