The Vanderbilt Report’s Sub-Report on Philosophy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:04:21 UTC
22:04:21 KST

“Academic philosophy is generally healthy in most respects relevant to the work of the Commission.”
That commission is the group of ten scholars (including three philosophers from NYU and one from Princeton), who, at the request of the Chancellors of Vanderbilt University and Washington University, this summer produced a “Report on the State of Scholarship in the Humanities and the Humanistic Social Sciences,” which came to be known as the Vanderbilt Report.
Despite the generality of the report’s title, readers may recall that the commission took as its focus just one type of potential threat to the state of today’s humanistic scholarship: politicization, or, more specifically, “a distinctive form of politicization in which the scholarly enterprise is taken to be subordinate to, or in the service of, political (social or moral) goals beyond the advancement of knowledge and understanding.”
The Vanderbilt Report was followed by several discipline-specific reports, and the last one, on philosophy, was released earlier this month. You can read it here.
The quote at the top of this post is the opening line of the report. In regard to their concern with politicization, academic philosophy is “generally healthy,” say the authors, Kit Fine (NYU) and Gideon Rosen (Princeton). There is mainly just one exception to this, they think: the philosophy of sex and gender. Fine and Rosen write:
For roughly a decade now, this relatively new field has been marked by what amounts to a de facto orthodoxy around a cluster of substantive ideas: that socially relevant sex and gender categories are socially constructed, that sex in human beings is not binary, and most importantly, that trans women are women and should be treated as such for every social and legal purpose. Scholarship that questions these assumptions is routinely met with the sort of opposition that is designed, not to challenge objectionable positions on substantive grounds, but to suppress discussion… [H]eterodox scholars are anathematized, excluded from conferences and other academic forums, and demonized on social media. Journals and academic presses that move to publish heterodox scholarship are met with intense pressure against publication, both from scholars and from a wider public. The chief worry is not that published scholarship in these areas amounts to the sort of advocacy that distorts the facts, much less the sort of “post-truth” repudiation of scholarly norms one sometimes sees elsewhere. It is rather that the scholarly ecosystem that normally serves to vet academic work has been distorted in these areas by a pattern of extraordinary pressure whose cumulative effect is to suppress dissent.
The authors then discuss several cases they think support their concern about this area of scholarship.
One factor that I think is missing from the analysis Fine and Rosen present is today’s communication environment. Because trans identity is currently a live, heated, political topic, it has not been uncommon for scholars working in the area to also be activists engaging in political debates and advocacy. Because of the internet, this brings together two kinds of discourse that work against each other.
The relatively mild discursive norms characteristic of truth-seeking academic work are quite different from the rough, rude, and highly aggressive discursive norms of the vicious point-scoring typical of today’s politics. While each set of norms might seem like it would function well in its respective domain, today’s communication technology erases the borders of those domains, presenting everything in “uni-context“, to use Agnes Callard’s helpful phrase. It’s not as if someone can be an activist in the streets and a scholar in the sheets (of paper). Philosophers are taking to the internet ( X.com or wherever) to post about their latest journal article one minute and their latest political screed the next. So we get everything altogether all at once. When these different forms of discourse are crowded into the same channel, there is no space for the pretense of the shared end of academic inquiry—truth—that in turn facilitates civil academic discourse and charitable engagement with those with whom you disagree.
In plainer terms, in their activist voices, some so-called “gender critical” philosophers have been shockingly horrible to trans women, including trans women philosophers. There has been malicious misgendering, mockery of appearance, various personal insults and cruelty online for anyone to see. And similarly, in their activist voices, some philosophers who are pro-trans activists have publicly said awful, aggressive, and vilifying things to and about those with “gender critical” views, including other philosophers. Even if you think such rhetoric is fine in a political or activist context, its reach is not so limited. Philosophers are people, too. They are unlikely to be able to silo the hateful rhetoric directed at them as a mere political device such that it doesn’t affect their judgments about the person saying it and the kind of thinker they are. People who have been called deluded perverts or transphobic Nazis by each other in political discourse online are unlikely to convince themselves of their opponent’s ability to engage in good faith debate elsewhere. And perhaps they shouldn’t. And if they shouldn’t, then some of the actions Fine and Rosen identify as problematic (e.g., non-co-platforming) may be rational (even if, in some ways, they are still regrettable).
By the way, the point of the foregoing is not to “both sides” the issue. I’m not claiming that those on either side of this debate have been equally bad; I’m not claiming anything about relative badness. Rather, I am just saying that Fine and Rosen overlooked one source of what they characterize as a “distorted” scholarly ecosystem which they find “surprising” and “puzzling”.
Discussion of this and other aspects of the report is welcome.
Comments are moderated. If you haven’t lately, please do look at the comments policy before commenting.

'Don't feel like waiting': Voters complain of long lines at polling stations amid historic turnout
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:04:00 UTC
22:04:00 KST

Voters are facing long waits at polling stations, including in small communities along the Gaza border.
"Well, I don't feel like waiting. I'll come back in the evening," said A., who waited 45 minutes before leaving the polling station.
"One at a time," a security guard at a polling station in Ofakim told a group that appeared to be members of the same family.
"Dad, can I come with you?" asked a girl of about eight as she stood in line.
"No," her father replied. "You have to go into the voting booth alone."
Election Day has drawn tens of thousands of people to polling stations, shopping centers, and entertainment centers.
At the new shopping center in Ofakim, home to the Rachela restaurant that made headlines after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his entourage visited, every business is open and packed with customers.
The supermarket, part of a major chain, is bustling, as are the electrical appliance store, the nuts and sweets shop and the baby products store. Residents are making the most of Election Day, both to cast their ballots for the Knesset and to shop for groceries, electrical appliances and baby cribs.
The corner café, which also operates a bakery, is packed with customers. The usually short line at the cashier stretches as shoppers clutch bags filled with baked goods, cakes, yeast pastries and colorful cookies.
Around midday, a family with three children enters the café. Their political allegiance is immediately apparent: The children's shirts feature a ballot slip bearing their preferred party's letters.
At a small table in the outdoor seating area, another family sits close together as the father explains the meaning of democracy to his daughter.
Political discussions can be heard at almost every table, with conversations covering a range of topics, including the conduct of outgoing ministers and Knesset members.
"I'm waiting for a call to drive someone to a polling station," said one of those seated at a table.
"Are rides to polling stations still a thing?" someone asked.
"Apparently so," the driver replied.
Bribing others to vote for certain parties
Meanwhile, updates about events in communities across the region are circulating through every available channel, including WhatsApp, text messages, email and social media.
One woman shared an unusual account from Yeruham, along with a phone number. When contacted, the woman on the other end of the line spoke with an accent suggesting she was originally from one of the former Soviet republics.
"Before we went into the polling station, I was offered 500 shekels to vote for a certain party. Of course I didn't agree."
Near a polling station next to a high school, a woman with a megaphone makes a final effort to convince passersby to vote for her preferred party.
In her view, it is the only party worth supporting. She considers the others to be people who understand nothing and undermine efforts to manage affairs properly.
The polling station itself, in the meantime, is packed with voters.

Exhibition held in Namibia to raise funds for Cuban health centers
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
21:02:50 CST
22:02:50 KST

WINDHOEK, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- Around 30 Namibian artists are using their work to help provide medical supplies and solar power kits for Cuban health centers, bringing a message of solidarity to a fundraising exhibition in Windhoek, the Namibian capital.
The exhibition, Art for Cuba, opened Monday evening at the Bellhaus Atelier and Galerie and runs through Friday, with a fundraising target of 100,000 Namibian dollars (about 6,000 U.S. dollars).
The initiative supports the national campaign, Namibians in Solidarity with the People of Cuba, with funds intended to help health centers maintain services amid electricity and medical supply shortages, according to the organizers.
For visual artist, musician and cultural activist Ndasuunje "Papa" Shikongeni, the exhibition is a way to acknowledge Cuba's support for Namibia's liberation struggle.
"This initiative is just to show solidarity," said Shikongeni, a contributor and organizer. "It is good to show other countries what Cuba has done for us during the revolutionary struggle of Namibia."
Among the participating artists is Libolly Nekundi, whose painting "Mother's Love" was purchased on the opening night.
Nekundi said the work was inspired by a woman he saw beneath a tree while traveling with photographers, a scene he wanted to capture as an expression of everyday African life.
Having exhibited both locally and in Europe, he said he was pleased that the sale would contribute to supporting the Cuban people.
The opening also brought together diplomats, politicians and community members, with Namibia's Vice President Lucia Witbooi, highlighting the friendship underpinning the initiative.
Witbooi, who officially opened the exhibition, said it honored the enduring ties between the two countries and acknowledged Cuba's contributions to Namibia's development.
"True friendship is measured not only by the support we receive in times of need but also by our willingness to extend that same support to others," she added.
Cuban Ambassador to Namibia Sergio Luis Vigoa de la Uz thanked the organizers and artists, saying the initiative "demonstrates how culture and human sensitivity can be placed at the service of a cause rooted in solidarity."
Namibia and Cuba established diplomatic relations in 1990, following ties forged during Namibia's struggle for independence. Cooperation subsequently expanded into areas including health and education. ■

Israel reports highest election turnout in 53 years amid strong Arab, opposition participation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:02:35 UTC
22:02:35 KST

Voter turnout in Israel’s general elections reached 31.5% by noon local time (1000GMT) on Tuesday, the highest level recorded at that hour since 1973, according to the Central Elections Committee, Anadolu reports.
A total of 2.39 million Israelis had cast their ballots by noon, an increase of more than 3 percentage points compared with the previous election, according to the committee.
Extremist Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich attributed the high turnout to exceptionally strong participation among Arab voters and in left-wing strongholds.
In a social media post, Smotrich said the increase in participation was driven by unusually high voting rates in Arab communities and areas traditionally supporting left-wing parties.
Arab Knesset member Ahmad Tibi also reported unusually high participation, expressing confidence in a strong electoral performance.
“Polling stations are packed like never before, and I am confident we will achieve a major victory,” Tibi said in a press statement.
The remarks come amid efforts by Arab political parties and opposition leaders to mobilize voters in a closely contested election that could determine whether Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu remains in power.
According to The Jerusalem Post, the communities of Ein Hod and Sde Nehemia recorded turnout rates of 25.7% and 25.4%, respectively, by 10 am.
READ: Israeli opposition urges voters to turn out to end Netanyahu’s rule
Other communities, including Nes Harim and Odim, reported participation rates of 23.2% and 23%, respectively.
Earlier Tuesday, opposition leaders urged Israelis to vote in large numbers to end Netanyahu’s rule.
Opposition Yisrael Beiteinu party leader Avigdor Lieberman called for an end to the Netanyahu era, while Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the opposition Yashar party, urged voters to support political change.
More than 7.3 million Israelis are eligible to vote in Tuesday’s election to choose members of the 120-seat Knesset.
Polling stations opened at 7 am local time (0500 GMT) and are scheduled to close at 10 pm (2000 GMT).
The election is Israel’s first general vote since the start of its genocidal war in the Gaza Strip in October 2023.
The vote comes amid deep political divisions over Netanyahu’s leadership, the Gaza genocide, Israel’s military confrontation with Iran and the country’s future political direction.
Netanyahu’s Likud-led coalition and opposition parties are competing to secure the 61 seats required for a parliamentary majority.
Recent opinion polls have suggested that neither bloc is assured of a majority, raising the possibility that Arab parties could play a significant role in determining the formation of the next government.

====================================================================================================

Greenhouse gas levels reach record high in 2025: WMO
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
21:02:33 CST
22:02:33 KST

GENEVA, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- Levels of carbon dioxide (CO2) and other major greenhouse gases in the atmosphere reached unprecedented highs in 2025, locking in more long-term temperature increases for the planet, according to a bulletin from the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) released on Tuesday.
The global average surface concentration of CO2 in 2025 was 53 percent above the 1750 pre-industrial baseline, the WMO Greenhouse Gas Bulletin showed. Concentrations of methane and nitrous oxide -- the second and third most important long-lived greenhouse gases related to human activities -- also rose to a new record, with respective increases of 167 percent and 26 percent.
"Another year, another new record," said WMO Deputy Secretary-General Ko Barrett.
"The past 11 years have been the warmest on record and this trend is set to continue. CO2 has a very long lifetime and so will affect the global climate not just for years but for decades and even centuries," Barrett said.
Growth rates of CO2 have tripled since the 1960s, accelerating from an annual average increase of 0.8 parts per million (ppm) per year to 2.4 ppm per year in the decade from 2011 to 2020. From 2024 to 2025, the global average concentration of CO2 rose by 2.8 ppm, above the decadal average but slightly less than the exceptional surge of 2023/2024, according to the bulletin.
"The more modest growth rate from 2024 to 2025 reflects recovery of the land carbon sinks and reduced fire carbon emissions in 2025 after the strong 2023/2024 El Nino," said WMO senior scientific officer Oksana Tarasova.
Nevertheless, a 2.8 ppm annual increase is still a substantial addition of carbon to the atmosphere from fossil fuel burning, she said.
In 2026, the burning of fossil fuels and the development of a supercharged El Nino will impact land carbon sinks as it did in 2023/2024, said Tarasova, warning that "the risks of reduced CO2 uptake by the ocean are also increasing in our changing climate."
The Greenhouse Gas Bulletin, one of the WMO's flagship annual publications, provides authoritative scientific information for negotiators at the United Nations (UN) Climate conference. ■

====================================================================================================

Economic Watch: Desert brine from former "sea of death" feeds fields across China
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
21:02:28 CST
22:02:28 KST

This photo taken on Sept. 5, 2026 shows a factory of the SDIC Xinjiang Luobupo Potash Co., Ltd. in northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region. (Xinhua/Zhang Xiaocheng)
URUMQI, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- Four hours south of Hami, after a long drive across the barren Gobi Desert of northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, a sweep of blue-green water appears on the horizon.
It is not a lake. These are evaporation ponds, stretching across more than 160 square kilometers at a sprawling potash operation in Lop Nur, once known as the "sea of death" for its extreme aridity and forbidding terrain.
The desert is also home to Lop Nur Town. There are no families who have lived there for generations -- nearly everyone went there in the new century because of the potash resources beneath Lop Nur's salt crust.
POTASH BENEATH DESERT
Potassium is a key plant nutrient, helping crops develop stronger stalks and fuller grain. For years, China had relied heavily on overseas potash, with domestic self-sufficiency long below 30 percent.
Exploration in the 20th century uncovered a world-class sulfate-type potassium-rich brine deposit in northern Lop Nur. But finding the resource was one thing, and producing fertilizer from it on an industrial scale was another.
There was no established industrial process elsewhere to copy. The location also posed its own problems. Two decades ago, there were no roads, little fresh water and no settled population.
"When I first came to Lop Nur, the wind blew sand straight into the face. You could go through all four seasons without seeing any green," said Liu Qinyong, who has worked at SDIC Xinjiang Luobupo Potash Co. Ltd. for more than 20 years. "Everything had to be brought in from outside." SDIC is short for the State Development and Investment Corporation.
The first batch of Lop Nur-brand potassium sulfate was produced in 2003. The company later built a production complex with an annual capacity of 1.2 million tonnes, which reached designed capacity by the end of 2011.
The company has so far produced over 27 million tonnes of potassium sulfate, with its products accounting for nearly half of China's potassium sulfate market.
TURNING HARDSHIP INTO ADVANTAGE
Production in Lop Nur relies heavily on both evaporation and time.
Brine pumped from underground moves through a four-stage evaporation system, where different salts crystallize as the concentration increases. It takes nearly two years before potassium-bearing minerals are ready for processing. These minerals then undergo further processing, including purification, crystallization and drying, to produce potassium sulfate.
The extreme evaporation that makes Lop Nur so inhospitable does much of the concentrating naturally.
Water scarcity has also shaped the production system. Fresh water has to be piped in from Ruoqiang, about 240 kilometers away, while liquids left from processing are recycled within the system and brine is not discharged outside it.
Inside the plant, progress has often been measured in fractions of a percentage point.
Dong Guangfeng, head of the potassium sulfate plant, arrived in 2005, when there was only an industrial pilot facility. Over the following two decades, he and his colleagues worked to raise potassium content and develop a wider range of products.
The potassium oxide content of the company's potassium sulfate has risen from 51 percent to a stable 52.5 percent, while a high-end product reaches 53.8 percent. Its product range has also expanded to include granular and water-soluble fertilizers.
China's potash self-sufficiency has now risen to around 50 percent, Dong said, with Lop Nur contributing an important share of domestic supply.
The brine is also yielding another product. In 2023, the company put into operation a line that extracts lithium from residual brine after potash production. The facility can produce 5,000 tonnes of lithium carbonate a year, mainly for use in power batteries for new energy vehicles.
A TOWN TAKES ROOT
The industry has also drawn people.
Chen Liangzhi, from southwest China's Sichuan Province, was among the early arrivals. When he came to Lop Nur in 2000, there were no roads, electricity or running water.
He lived in a semi-underground shelter and ran a restaurant from a prefabricated metal room. At midday in summer, when surface temperatures could reach 50 to 60 degrees Celsius, the room became too hot for cooking. Chen would retreat underground and wait until late afternoon before lighting the stove again.
Today, his restaurant covers more than 100 square meters and serves business travelers.
Lop Nur Town was formally established in 2002. Its water, electricity and heating are largely supplied via facilities operated by the potash company, while garbage and sewage are handled through shared facilities. Medical workers from the People's Hospital of Bayingolin Mongolian Autonomous Prefecture are stationed at the local clinic.
"If you want people to stay, you first have to make them feel secure about living here," said Liu Xiangyu, deputy Party secretary of Lop Nur Town. Over 3,000 people now live in the settlement that grew around the potash industry.
Notably, far beyond Lop Nur, potassium from beneath its salt crust is reaching and nourishing farmlands across China. ■

ADEN, Yemen, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- Forces aligned with Yemen's internationally recognized government launched a fresh ground offensive near the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait on Tuesday, government sources told Xinhua.

====================================================================================================

DR Congo Ebola cases top 10,000 as outbreak tests Africa's defenses
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
21:02:04 CST
22:02:04 KST

KINSHASA, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- Ebola cases in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) have surpassed 10,000, marking a grim milestone in what has become the world's second-largest recorded Ebola outbreak.
The latest figures released Tuesday by the country's health authorities showed that the country had recorded a total of 10,060 confirmed cases, including 4,887 deaths, as of Oct. 25, with the fatality rate at 48.6 percent.
PERSISTENT TRANSMISSION AT EPICENTER
In the DRC, a brief decline in Ebola infections has given way to another rise.
A report released last Wednesday by the World Health Organization (WHO) Regional Office for Africa found that infections rebounded in early October after falling in late September, with recent epidemic evolution suggesting "renewed intensification of transmission."
According to DRC health authorities, the outbreak, which has become the largest and deadliest Ebola outbreak ever recorded in the country, has spread to eight of the country's 26 provinces and 66 health zones, with the eastern province of Ituri remaining the epicenter, accounting for more than 70 percent of confirmed cases.
The outbreak has unfolded against the backdrop of a protracted armed conflict in eastern DRC, where years of violence and mass displacement have already strained an overstretched healthcare system.
The WHO warned that escalating insecurity, continued population displacement and restricted humanitarian access are further disrupting disease surveillance and response operations, raising the risk of infections going undetected.
Health authorities identified persistent weaknesses in early detection, contact tracing and access to treatment as major obstacles to controlling the outbreak.
Only about 12 percent of confirmed cases in the DRC have been identified among previously known contacts, indicating that some chains of transmission remain undetected, Wessam Mankoula, an official with the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC), warned at an online press briefing last Thursday.
VIRUS CROSSING BORDERS
The difficulties in containing Ebola at its source have increasingly become a concern beyond the DRC. Since May, cases linked to the outbreak have been reported in Uganda, France, Kenya and Nigeria, extending the epidemic across three regions of Africa.
In Kenya, 20 contacts of the country's first imported Ebola patient were released from quarantine Monday after completing 21 days of monitoring without developing symptoms. The initial patient, a Kenyan national who had been living in the DRC, traveled to Nairobi via Uganda and died on Oct. 5.
Kenya has since recorded eight additional cases, all linked to the imported patient and detected among people already in quarantine. As of Monday, the country had reported nine confirmed cases, including two deaths, with another 98 contacts remaining under monitoring.
Further afield in West Africa, Nigeria's first Ebola patient was medically evacuated to Switzerland on Monday and was in stable condition, according to Nigeria's Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare Muhammad Ali Pate.
The index patient, who traveled from Uganda to Nigeria on Oct. 3, developed symptoms four days later and was confirmed infected on Oct. 20.
Nigeria currently has no confirmed Ebola patient within its borders, as 52 contacts remain under monitoring, said the WHO on Monday, stressing that the country has not been declared Ebola-free.
The source of the Nigerian patient's infection, however, remains unclear, prompting a joint investigation with Uganda.
Ugandan Health Minister Chris Baryomunsi said on Sunday in a statement that authorities are working with Nigeria and international partners to review genomic sequencing findings and verify the patient's travel history, contacts and movements in Uganda and en route to Abuja.
Uganda, which recorded 20 confirmed cases, including two deaths, before declaring its outbreak over in July, reaffirmed Sunday that it remained Ebola-free. On Friday, the country announced additional precautionary measures, including reinstating mandatory traveler locator forms, tightening border screening, and restricting transit for travelers with a history of travel to the DRC.
Africa CDC Director-General Jean Kaseya on Sunday welcomed Uganda's continued vigilance and cooperation with Nigeria in investigating the source of its imported case, warning that the risk of further cross-border spread persists.
RACE FOR VACCINES
As health authorities struggle to interrupt transmission, scientists are seeking a longer-term weapon against the outbreak.
On Friday, the first participant received a dose of a candidate vaccine in Bunia, the capital of the DRC's hardest-hit Ituri, marking the launch of a pivotal Phase 2/3 clinical trial known as Tumaini, or "hope" in Swahili.
The trial aims to evaluate whether candidate vaccines can safely and effectively protect people against the Bundibugyo virus, for which no vaccine has yet been licensed.
The first candidate being evaluated is Ervebo, a vaccine already approved against a different Ebola virus species. Preparations are underway to include two Bundibugyo-specific vaccine candidates developed by Moderna and by the University of Oxford in collaboration with the Serum Institute of India.
"If successful, this would be the first time we have clear evidence of vaccine efficacy against Bundibugyo virus," said Chikwe Ihekweazu, executive director of WHO's Health Emergencies Program, describing the prospect as "a major advance" that could transform responses to current and future outbreaks. ■

====================================================================================================

China Focus: China's booming embodied AI industry creates new professions
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
21:01:55 CST
22:01:55 KST

CHONGQING, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- New career opportunities are emerging across China's embodied artificial intelligence (AI) industry, from training robotic arms to building virtual training grounds for inspection robots.
In September, China's Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security and other government departments announced 11 new professions, including embodied AI robot application technicians and digital twin engineers.
At Sevnce Robotics in Liangjiang New Area of southwest China's Chongqing Municipality, Tang Zixiang works as an embodied AI robot application technician, training robots to perform tasks.
Tang adjusts the positions and angles of knobs to simulate different working conditions and uses the resulting data to train AI models. He then deploys the trained models on robotic arms for further testing and refinement. Through repeated trials, robots gradually learn tasks in simulation before performing them in real-world settings.
"Our job is to help robots move from the laboratory to a wide range of real-world applications," Tang said.
Sevnce Robotics develops specialized robots for the petroleum, chemical and power industries. Its machines can replace or assist human inspectors in hazardous environments.
In these settings, robots must operate reliably for extended periods. Tang said technicians need to define speed and accuracy requirements, test whether robots can recover from failed operations, and determine when they should stop or require human intervention.
"Our aim is to turn robots that work in the laboratory into machines that can operate safely and reliably over the long term," he said.
Digital twin engineering, another newly recognized profession, also helps prepare robots for real-world deployment.
Jiang Lei, who works in this field, builds virtual environments where inspection robots can rehearse tasks before deployment.
Using 3D reconstruction, Jiang's team creates digital replicas of factories, enabling virtual robots to rehearse inspection routes and check whether their cameras can capture instrument readings. Once tasks are validated in simulation, they can be transferred to physical robots.
Traditionally, technicians would take robots to project sites before mapping the surroundings, planning routes and locating inspection points, Jiang said.
Digital twins, however, allow the work to be rehearsed in simulation beforehand, potentially cutting on-site commissioning time from two or three weeks to two or three days. Simulation also generates data for algorithm testing and training, reducing the time and cost of collecting data in real-world environments.
As the industry chain becomes more specialized, it is opening career opportunities for people with different educational backgrounds.
Jiang, who studied vehicle engineering at university, moved from autonomous driving research to robot development, which requires expertise in 3D modeling, programming and simulation.
Tang, who studied computer science as an undergraduate and postgraduate student and graduated this year, applies reinforcement learning and imitation learning to robot training while continuing to study robot kinematics and motion control.
The industry's growth is also driving demand for specialists in data collection, model training, system commissioning, operations and maintenance.
Figures released by China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology show that the country had over 400 humanoid robot models and produced more than 40,000 units in the first half of 2026.
Efforts to train the sector's workforce are also gaining momentum. Earlier this month, Beijing City University launched a high-skilled talent training program in embodied AI applications and practice, offering industry workers five days of intensive study that combines classroom instruction with hands-on work with real robots.
Tang said he hoped robots would complement human workers rather than simply replace them. "I hope robots will take on more dangerous, tedious and repetitive work," Tang said. ■

Why do we measure root ginger in ‘thumbs’ and centimetres rather than weight? | Kitchen aide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:00:31 UTC
22:00:31 KST

Why do so many recipes state the amount of fresh ginger in “thumbs” or centimetres. With it being so variable in shape, why don’t you use weight?
 
Nick, by email
 
Let’s gather some of the Guardian food troops and ask them to explain themselves. First up in front of the class is our own perfectionist, Felicity Cloake: “That’s a very good question, and I don’t think there is a very good answer,” she says. “Maybe it’s just convention, because sometimes it feels a bit fussy to give a precise weight for the likes of ginger, onions and other staples if you’re not, say, Heston Blumenthal.” Often, it doesn’t really matter that much, either: “If you give a precise weight, people will perhaps think it’s very important and worry if they’re a few grams out,” she adds. In other words, if Nick were to use a smidge more (or less) ginger than Cloake in, say, her dal, it’s unlikely to make or break it.
Cloake’s fellow columnist Georgina Hayden agrees: “Unlike measuring a ratio of risotto rice to stock, or making a cake, the typical recipes I use ginger in, such as curries, don’t have to be precise,” she says. “After all, cooking should be as instinctive as possible, rather than relying on digital scales.” However, Nick is right in that ginger does vary hugely in shape, Cloake says: “If it was a very thick piece, or it wasn’t thumb-shaped, I’d cut it so the cumulative flesh of the ginger was roughly the same as the cumulative flesh of a thumb. You’re just trying to give a rough amount, without being too prescriptive. But he’s right, we should probably move to grams.”
In that same spirit, another columnist, Ravinder Bhogal, nails down the thumb measurement even further, taking it to mean a piece that’s about 5cm long, the length of an average adult thumb, and weighing about 15g. “I get that ‘a thumb’ as a measurement is not exactly scientific, but how much ginger you put in a dish is also up to you – more if you like it stronger and less if you don’t,” Bhogal says. If, for example, a recipe were to call for garlic as well as ginger, she would be inclined to use the same weight of each, although, she adds: “Remember the flavour of ginger softens as it cooks. But a centimetre here or there is not going to make a huge difference, so go with your own personal taste.”
After all, that’s a big part of cooking, right? When Hayden writes a recipe, she says, its purpose is also to empower home cooks to take a bit of creative licence: “A knob of butter, a pinch of salt, a bunch of herbs … sometimes, vague measurements are a good thing. Also, it’s mad to get out the scales for something as small as ginger.”
Cloake, however, imagines Nick “to be a more scientifically minded cook” than she is, so here are some final words: “Essentially, there’s no good reason for it, except to say that it gives an idea that you don’t have to worry too much. It’s just a guideline.” And there’s plenty enough to worry about in this world already right now.
- Got a culinary dilemma? Email feast@theguardian.com

The Bundeswehr is introducing two principal configurations: the G95A1, equipped with a 419 mm barrel, and the shorter G95KA1, featuring a 355 mm barrel. The compact variant is expected to become the primary configuration for most German military personnel. The rifles weigh approximately 3.4 kg and 3.3 kg, respectively, without additional equipment.
Both versions use a short-stroke gas piston operating system with a rotating bolt. Their technical specifications include a firing rate of approximately 850 rounds per minute and a stated effective range of up to 450 meters.
Earlier, Ukrainian Special Operations Forces were reported to be using German-made Haenel HLR 338 sniper rifles, designed for long-range engagements at distances of up to 1,500 meters. Nocturne Is a Slow-Burning Crime Drama That Struggles to Stay Lit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:00:03 UTC
22:00:03 KST

Nocturne is everything you would expect from a 21st century prestige crime drama. Adapted from a series of best-selling Scandinavian mystery novels, the Apple TV thriller, premiering with two episodes on Oct. 30, casts a genuine movie star (Liev Schreiber) as a brilliant yet broken detective immersed in a case that has become an all-consuming obsession. The large ensemble represents multiple law-enforcement agencies, victims, bystanders, and a singular alleged serial killer played by an actor on a hot streak (Stephen Graham). Children’s lives are at stake. A risky undercover operation is undertaken. Relationships simmer, until suddenly they’re at a full boil. Collateral damage piles up. Progress is glacial, with essential bits of backstory meted out in stingy flashbacks. Underlying every scene is an atmosphere heavy with dread, as though this sordid scenario has arisen not merely from the brain of one twisted villain, but out of a rot at the heart of society.
It’s a prototypical slow burn. This format, in which one complex investigation spans a season or more, wasn’t new to American TV when AMC’s Nordic noir adaptation The Killing became a sensation in 2011. (In this respect and many others, Twin Peaks, for one, was ahead of its time.) But the convergence of streaming, an ideal venue for binge-friendly serialized storytelling, and an audience for ambitious television that had been growing for more than a decade facilitated its proliferation as a cinematic alternative to the formulaic procedurals that still predominate on broadcast networks. The most acclaimed and discussed mystery shows of the past 15 years—True Detective, Mare of Easttown, Fargo, even Only Murders in the Building—have been, with few exceptions, slow burns. Yet, as Nocturne’s mixed success suggests, the tropes and limitations of the style become more apparent with each new title.
In one welcome deviation from the norm, whodunit seems clear from the beginning. Confined in the bowels of a Pennsylvania psychiatric hospital, the serial killer Jurek Walter (Graham) calmly coaxes an inmate in the adjacent solitary cell into suicide. When a boy thought to be one of his victims, Michael (Landon Valentin), turns up, filthy and feeble but alive, years after he and his sister went missing, a new hunt for the girl begins. Schreiber’s Jonah Lynn, a Philly cop and military veteran who is now retired and a bit reclusive, was instrumental in the original investigation. Michael’s return draws him back in, along with an FBI agent, Saga (Zazie Beetz), who is a surrogate daughter to Jonah. As Quinn, a rigorous colleague from the bureau (Poorna Jagannathan), and the weary local police chief (Bill Camp) lead the search, Saga goes undercover as a patient at the hospital and Jonah goes rogue, to the surprise of no one who has ever worked with him. They don’t just want to find the sister; they want to catch Jurek masterminding violent crimes from his cell, thereby proving he’s coherent enough to rot in a real prison.
A slow burn can only be as compelling as the personalities and ideas its pace affords it time to explore. Creator Rowan Joffé and his cast, adapting the Joona Linna novels by Lars Kepler (a pen name of Swedish husband-andwife team Alexander Ahndoril and Alexandra Coelho Ahndoril), do craft a few fascinating characters. Beetz’s Saga is a spookily canny mix of actor, detective, and daredevil, inhabiting her cutesy-until-she’s-not patient persona so fully, you might start to doubt she’s fully faking it. Graham weaponizes the soft masculinity that he wielded so movingly as the horrified father of a homicidal teen incel in Adolescence. It’s his cunning performances of compassion that set Jurek apart from the typical thriller psycho and make us believe he has the capacity to pull off logistically inconceivable feats of cruelty. Rory Culkin adds tension as Karl, a sensitive hospital worker whose anger at the way superiors use him as a pawn leaves him vulnerable to Jurek’s manipulation.
What happens outside the institution isn’t nearly as gripping. Strong actors like Camp, Jagannathan, and Chrissy Metz, who plays Michael’s mother Ida, are saddled with underwritten characters. Everything we know about Jonah—that he’s brooding, single-minded, and willing to break rules in pursuit of justice—is a cliché of the genre, as is his odd-couple partnership with the stiff but well-intentioned Quinn. I got the sense, around the season’s midpoint (seven out of 10 episodes were provided for review), that Joffé was holding some of these characters at arm’s length in order to shock us with revelations about them later. But the extended delay in supplying basic context about Jonah, in particular, comes off as too much of a contrivance. It also distances us from the show’s implicit questions about whether laws and protocols enable (or prevent) justice, and how people like Jonah and Saga should weigh the rewards of dangerous, personal missions against the threat of harm these crusades pose.
Nocturne’s small-town Pennsylvania setting is guaranteed to earn it comparisons to Mare of Easttown and its spiritual sequel, Task. Beyond the dutifully adopted (and, to my ears, pretty accurate) accents, though, it lacks the specificity of those shows, both created by area native Brad Ingelsby, with regard to the region and its people. It doesn’t have the same curiosity about or patience in depicting the characters’ lives outside the Jurek case, either. Viewers got invested in Kate Winslet’s Mare because we got to watch her try to keep up with her precocious teenage daughter and endure the harsh words of her judgmental mom. (It didn’t hurt that said mom was played by Jean Smart.) As Robbie in Task, Tom Pelphrey had space to show us a criminal who was also a lonely, newly single father desperate to provide for his beloved children.
As any connoisseur of the hundreds of crime serials TV has produced since The Killing can tell you, there are only so many murder plots. But there are as many unique characters as there are human beings on planet earth. A slow burn that doesn’t make use of such a rich source of fuel is apt to fizzle out.

====================================================================================================

Just a few minutes of speech may offer a window into brain health and aging
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:00:02 UTC
22:00:02 KST

An automated analysis of short voice recordings can produce an estimate of “speech age” that runs older in people with dementia than in cognitively healthy adults, according to a study of nearly 3,000 adults across Latin America published in Science Advances. The gap between this speech-based estimate and a person’s actual age was also linked to brain-scan and DNA-based measures of aging, a blood marker of Alzheimer’s disease, and lifetime social hardship.
To estimate whether a person’s body appears older or younger than their calendar age, scientists use tools known as biological aging clocks. A biological aging clock is a statistical model that analyzes physical or behavioral data to predict a person’s age. The difference between this predicted age and the person’s actual chronological age is called an age gap, where a positive gap is typically interpreted as accelerated aging and a negative gap as healthier, delayed aging.
Most established aging clocks rely on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to measure brain tissue volume and activity, or blood draws to examine chemical modifications to DNA known as epigenetic methylation. While a study covered by PsyPost in early 2026 showed that blood tests can detect dementia-linked proteins in Latin American populations, both neuroimaging and molecular blood analyses remain expensive and logistically difficult to deploy in lower-income regions. Behavioral age clocks based on questionnaires and cognitive exams also require trained specialists and can be skewed by a patient’s literacy level.
Natural speech may offer an accessible, non-invasive alternative for tracking how the brain and body age. Speaking requires the rapid coordination of multiple cognitive and physical systems, which shift during normal aging and break down more rapidly in neurodegenerative diseases. A slower speaking rate and longer pauses between words or syllables are thought to reflect declines in mental processing speed and word retrieval.
Changes in vocal pitch and the emotional tone of words can capture the flattened emotional expression often seen in dementia. Shifts in vocabulary, such as relying on words for physical objects rather than abstract ideas or using less precise terms, point to the erosion of semantic memory, which is the brain’s system for storing general knowledge and facts.
The research was led by Hernan Hernandez of the Latin American Brain Health Institute at Universidad Adolfo Ibáñez in Chile, with senior authors Agustin Ibanez and Adolfo M. García. Ibanez is a professor of global brain health at the Global Brain Health Institute at Trinity College Dublin, scientific director of the Latin American Brain Health Institute, and strategic scientific director at the Barcelonaβeta Brain Research Center. García directs the Cognitive Neuroscience Center at Universidad de San Andrés in Argentina and is affiliated with the Global Brain Health Institute at the University of California, San Francisco, and the Universidad de Santiago de Chile.
They sought to test whether discrepancies between a person’s chronological age and their speech-predicted age could distinguish between different types of dementia and mirror internal biological aging.
“This study grew from two related goals,” Ibanez told PsyPost. “First, our group has been developing multiple aging clocks to capture the cumulative burden of biological, brain, behavioral, and exposome processes across aging and dementia. Second, many established biomarkers are expensive and difficult to scale, particularly in low-resource settings. We therefore wanted to test whether natural speech could provide a low-cost, non-invasive measure that captures several dimensions of aging simultaneously.”
“We wanted to establish whether speech recordings (an affordable, naturalistic, scalable data source) could offer reliable predictions of aging, considering multiple sociobiological factors in both healthy older adults and individuals with dementia,” García added.
The researchers analyzed data from 2,928 native Spanish speakers across five Latin American countries: Colombia, Peru, Mexico, Chile, and Argentina. The participants were recruited through a multi-country research network and had an average age of about 65 years, with women making up 67 percent of the sample. The cohort included 1,504 cognitively healthy individuals and 1,424 patients diagnosed with various neurodegenerative conditions.
Among the patient group, 24 had mild cognitive impairment (MCI), a transitional stage between normal aging and dementia, and 1,068 had Alzheimer’s disease (AD), the most common form of dementia characterized by progressive memory loss. Another 332 patients had frontotemporal dementia, a group of disorders caused by damage to the brain’s frontal and temporal lobes. The team divided the frontotemporal dementia patients into 255 individuals with variants that primarily affect behavior and movement, and 77 individuals with variants that primarily impair language production and comprehension.
Every participant completed seven brief speaking tasks in a quiet room, including describing an animated video, retelling a short story immediately and after a 20- to 30-minute delay, and naming as many words as possible starting with a specific letter or belonging to a category like animals within 60 seconds. The researchers processed the audio recordings using TELL, an automated speech-analysis app for which García serves as founder and chief scientific officer. Its pipeline removed background noise, isolated the participant’s voice from the examiner’s, and generated text transcripts.
From these recordings and transcripts, the team extracted over 700 distinct acoustic and language measurements and grouped them into seven composite categories: speech timing, vocal pitch, emotional content, word frequency, verbosity, semantic concreteness, and semantic granularity (how specific a word is, such as saying “robin” instead of “bird”).
The scientists trained a machine learning model on these seven speech categories to predict chronological age, and then subtracted each person’s actual age from their predicted age to calculate their speech age gap. On average, the model’s age estimates missed participants’ actual ages by about nine years and accounted for roughly 44 percent of the variation in age across the sample; after a statistical correction commonly applied to age-prediction models, predicted and actual ages correlated at 0.74. Verbosity and speech timing were the most influential features indicating preserved or younger-sounding speech, while vocal pitch variations and negative emotional word content were the strongest indicators of accelerated speech aging.
When comparing the diagnostic groups, cognitively healthy adults had the lowest speech age gaps, whereas every patient group showed larger gaps, reflecting older-sounding speech. Patients with language-dominant frontotemporal dementia displayed the largest speech age gaps, followed by those with behavioral or motor frontotemporal dementia, and then those with Alzheimer’s disease and mild cognitive impairment.
These group differences held up in sensitivity analyses that controlled for chronological age, sex, years of education, country of origin, medical comorbidities, and the number of languages a participant spoke. The researchers also examined whether speaking multiple languages was linked to lower speech age gaps in a subset of participants, finding a slight trend toward younger-sounding speech among multilingual speakers that did not reach statistical significance.
In additional comparisons, the full speech clock separated the diagnostic groups more effectively than any isolated acoustic or language category on its own. “Aging leaves a distributed signature across multiple dimensions of speech—timing, lexical choice, semantic properties, prosody, and verbal output,” García explained. “No single feature tells the whole story; the informative signal emerges from their combination.”
“All too often, brain disorders are conceived as primarily affecting or broadly sparing language,” García said. “This usually reflects a poor operationalization of language. When rich characterizations of speech and discourse are used, ensuing signals can improve the detection, differentiation, and characterization of disorders which are traditionally not associated with language anomalies as a defining feature.”
The researchers next examined how these speech age gaps related to cognitive test scores, blood biomarkers, and lifetime social environment. Across the cohort, larger speech age gaps were associated with worse performance on clinical tests of memory, executive function, everyday functional ability, and both verbal and non-verbal tasks. The link was stronger for tests with a verbal component, such as retelling a story, than for tests the authors classified as nonverbal, such as copying and later redrawing a complex figure. In a subset of participants who underwent blood testing, higher speech age gaps correlated with elevated blood plasma levels of phosphorylated tau-217, a protein that accumulates in the brain during Alzheimer’s disease, specifically among the Alzheimer’s patients.
The team also evaluated each participant’s social exposome, a comprehensive measure combining 319 survey items covering lifetime socioeconomic factors such as education, food insecurity, financial stress, healthcare access, and childhood adversity. Higher speech age gaps were linked to a more adverse social exposome among healthy controls and Alzheimer’s patients, suggesting that cumulative social hardship may be reflected in how old a person sounds. This aligns with earlier research covered by PsyPost in 2025, conducted by several members of the same research network, which found that a heavier lifetime burden of social adversity was associated with poorer cognition and disrupted brain connectivity in Latin American cohorts.
“I was particularly struck that speech reflected not only brain and molecular aging but also the social exposome,” Ibanez said. “It suggests that the cumulative environments people live in (their socioeconomic circumstances, education, access to resources, and other life-course exposures) may leave measurable traces in something as everyday as speech.”
To verify whether the speech clock reflected internal biological aging, the authors compared the speech age gaps against established brain and epigenetic clocks in subsets of participants with available neuroimaging and blood DNA data. The speech age gaps showed moderate-to-strong positive correlations with brain age gaps derived from structural MRI scans measuring gray matter volume (correlation of 0.42), functional MRI scans measuring how brain regions communicate at rest (correlation of 0.49), and a combined brain clock (correlation of 0.53) across healthy controls and all dementia groups. In addition, larger speech age gaps were positively associated with accelerated biological aging across three independent epigenetic clocks that measure DNA methylation patterns in white blood cells, particularly among healthy adults and patients with Alzheimer’s disease, though these links were weaker (correlations of about 0.2) than those with the brain clocks.
When the team examined specific brain networks, they found that the speech clock tracked whole-brain aging more closely than the aging of isolated brain circuits, including the brain’s dedicated language network. Only the language network and the salience network, which helps the brain monitor speech and allocate attention, showed small links to the speech clock, while other individual brain networks showed no statistically significant relationship.
“One striking finding was how strongly the speech clock aligned with brain-age measures across several dementia syndromes, despite being derived solely from speech,” García told PsyPost. “We were also intrigued that whole-brain aging measures related more strongly to speech aging than most individual functional networks did. That suggests speech may reflect the coordinated state of distributed brain systems rather than the condition of a single language circuit.”
“Speech appears to contain much more information about aging than we usually assume,” Ibanez noted. “Our speech-derived aging measure was associated not only with cognitive and clinical impairment, but also with brain aging, epigenetic aging, p-tau217, and social exposures. This suggests that a few minutes of speech may eventually provide an accessible window into broader brain and biological health.”
One independent researcher’s assessment highlighted both the scale of the multi-country effort and the nuances of interpreting speech-based aging markers across neurodegenerative conditions. The cohort’s language-dominant frontotemporal dementia group included patients with non-fluent and semantic variants of primary progressive aphasia, which are neurological syndromes that gradually erode a person’s ability to speak or understand word meanings.
“Hernandez et al. have derived a novel marker of aging by analyzing acoustic and linguistic features of speech samples using a machine-learning algorithm to predict age and by subsequently computing deviations of predicted age from actual age,” Mai-Carmen Requena-Komuro, a postdoctoral researcher at the Institute of Systems Neuroscience at the University Medical Center Hamburg-Eppendorf in Germany who was not involved in the study, told PsyPost. “They show that these ‘speech age gaps’ (SAGs) enable us to distinguish healthy elderly people from people diagnosed with dementia in a large-scale Spanish-speaking cohort living across several countries in Latin America.”
“Speech deficits are known characteristics of language variants of frontotemporal dementia (non-fluent variant primary progressive aphasia and semantic variant primary progressive aphasia, both included in the current cohort), although the specific speech domains targeted differ,” Requena-Komuro said. “Speech deficits have recently caught more attention in patients diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease (there is in fact a language variant of AD known as logopenic primary progressive aphasia).”
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider, including how participants were screened. To qualify as cognitively healthy in the study, participants had to demonstrate functional independence and score above 25 out of 30 on the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE), a standard 30-point questionnaire used to screen for cognitive impairment. In addition, the sample sizes for certain subgroups, particularly the 24 patients with mild cognitive impairment and the 77 patients with language-dominant frontotemporal dementia, were relatively small, and not all participants had blood, brain scan, or epigenetic data available. Because the study relied on cross-sectional data collected at a single point in time, it cannot establish whether an older-sounding voice actually predicts future cognitive decline or tracks the speed of aging over the years.
“I do find it admirable that the authors managed to recruit such a diverse and large cohort of people living with dementia across so many countries,” Requena-Komuro noted. “However, there are a couple of points that made me slightly skeptical: (i) the cut-off score of the MMSE for the healthy controls is set at 25, but the questions are relatively easy so I would not expect elderly adults to score anything below 28 (the maximum is 30). Some of these healthy controls may therefore have belonged to the MCI group instead; (ii) it is unclear whether the regression models aimed at predicting the age of participants included both healthy elderly and elderly with dementia; I would expect an initial model focusing on healthy elderly only to then better understand where and by how much elderly with dementia deviate.”
“Not all speech features go in the same direction, yet they all contribute to the ‘speech age gap’ (SAG),” Requena-Komuro added. “I would therefore caution readers not to overinterpret the SAG as an overall marker of degraded speech. Overall, this study is rich in correlation plots, but correlation does not mean causation. The fact that the SAG correlates with many different factors does not provide much more explanation than these individual factors considered individually.”
Another consideration involves how different neurodegenerative conditions progress across the lifespan and how much speech patterns vary from person to person within the same diagnostic category. Frontotemporal dementia often begins at an earlier age than typical Alzheimer’s disease.
“Generally, a more hypothesis-driven study would have been more insightful,” Requena-Komuro explained. “Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) is an early-onset dementia; it is therefore not surprising that the SAG scores for these subgroups are significantly higher than that of the AD group (if the signs of dementia start earlier for FTD patients, when we compare them at the same age of AD patients, their symptoms are likely to be more severe). Perhaps this is one way of validating the SAG, but given the substantial variability in individual trajectories even within the same clinical group, the SAG could not be used as a standalone measurement to establish diagnosis or characterize disease progression. Unlike what the authors claim, I would therefore say that we are not ready to replace standard cognitive and neuropsychological tests for dementia.”
The study’s authors also describe the speech clock as a complement to existing evaluations rather than a stand-alone diagnostic test. “The speech clock captured clear differences between groups and showed especially strong links with brain-age measures, but it is best viewed as a signal that becomes informative when combined with other evidence, not as a stand-alone test of a person’s health or prognosis,” García said. “A positive speech-age gap should not be interpreted as a diagnosis or as proof that someone is literally ‘aging faster.'”
Because the study was conducted entirely among Spanish speakers in five Latin American nations using structured speaking tasks, the speech clock cannot be applied directly to other languages or casual everyday conversations without further testing. Different languages have unique grammatical rules and acoustic rhythms, meaning that the specific features that signal Alzheimer’s or frontotemporal dementia in Spanish may behave differently in other languages, particularly word-based features, which have carried over less well than timing features in earlier cross-language work. Future longitudinal studies tracking diverse, multilingual populations over time will be needed to determine whether automated voice analysis can serve as a routine screening tool in clinics and public health programs.
“Some associations were moderate rather than large, so this should be viewed as a complementary biomarker rather than a replacement for established clinical tools,” Ibanez said. “Aging clocks are estimations, not diagnoses or deterministic measures of how fast a specific person is aging. Importantly, this study was primarily cross-sectional, so we cannot yet infer individual aging trajectories or say that someone whose speech appears ‘older’ is necessarily aging faster over time.”
“A valuable next step is to determine whether speech-age gaps predict longitudinal cognitive and clinical change, especially across different languages,” García added. “Prediction of future states is a fundamental but rarely hit milestone in speech biomarker research.”
Moving forward, the team plans to explore how lifestyle and clinical interventions might influence vocal aging markers and how these tools can expand dementia research in regions with limited medical infrastructure.
“We also want to test whether interventions that improve brain health shift speech aging toward a healthier trajectory, and to validate these models across languages, cultures, and more naturalistic speech,” Ibanez said. “One important aspect of the study is that it included nearly 3,000 participants across five Latin American countries, which are populations that remain underrepresented in dementia research. Speech-based approaches could be particularly valuable in settings where MRI, PET, or sophisticated molecular biomarkers are difficult to access at scale.”
The study, “Speech clocks decode dementia phenotypes, social exposome, and biological aging,” was authored by Hernan Hernandez, Lizeth Katherine Pedraza, Hernando Santamaria-Garcia, Sebastian Moguilner, Agustina Legaz, Pavel Prado, Jhosmary Cuadros, Lucía Amoruso, Liset Gonzalez, Damián Dellavale, Juan Pablo Espinoza–Puelles, Javier Palma Espinosa, Cecilia Jarne, Fabio Mattiussi, Matías Caccia, Alejandro Sosa Welford, Nicolás Pelella, Jeremías Inchauspe, Franco J. Ferrante, Gonzalo Pérez, Marcelo Adrián Maito, Guido Rocatti, Maria Eugenia Godoy, Joaquin Migeot, Paulina Orellana, Ariel Caviedes, Martin Bruno, Leonel Takada, Andrea Slachevsky, Maria I Behrens, Bárbara Bruna, David Aguillon, Lina Zapata, Jose Alberto Avila-Funes, Nilton Custodio, Bruce Miller, Maria Luisa Gorno-Tempini, Stefanie Pina Escudero, Pablo Reyes, Kun Hu, Maira Okada de Oliveira, Carlos Coronel-Oliveros, Josephine Cruzat, Juan Felipe Cardona, Michael Corley, Irene B. Meier, Vaibhav A. Narayan, Enzo Tagliazucchi, Sandra Baez, Claudia Duran-Aniotz, Adolfo M. García, and Agustin Ibanez.

After the dinosaurs died, the massive ‘D. rex’ fungus ruled the woods
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

A pineapple-sized fungus has quietly grown undetected in the forests of southwestern China – until now. The massive mushroom may set a size record for a major branch of the fungal family tree.
The fungus — named Dianjunus rex — may also represent a previously unknown family, researchers report September 28 in Frontiers in Fungal Biology. Fittingly, D. rex is part of a lineage that split off from other fungi right after the dinosaurs — like T. rex — went extinct.
In 2024, researchers in China were conducting a survey of fungal diversity in a tropical rainforest in Yunnan Province when local farmers tipped them off to an unusual fungus in the area. The farmers included photos, says Indunil Chinthani Senanayake, a mycologist at the Kunming Institute of Botany in China. Some of the farmers who’d made the discovery took a bite of the mystery fungus, Senanayake says, and the tipster “wanted to confirm whether it was edible or not.”
When Senanayake and her colleagues went to the location, they found strange, yellowish, tentacle-like and spatula-like mushrooms growing out of decaying tree roots. These were some kind of ascomycete, or “sac fungi”. Sac fungi like morels, truffles and molds make their spores in microscopic bladderlike receptacles, unlike the bowling pin-shaped reproductive structures in club fungi, the group that includes most culinary mushrooms.
The mushrooms we see growing out of the ground are called fruiting bodies and make the spore-producing cells for the often hidden or subterranean fungus. Most sac fungi have relatively small fruiting bodies. But the mushrooms growing off these mysterious Yunnan fungi were enormous, with some reaching 50 centimeters tall. The team took samples of the fungi back to the lab for further study and found that they weighed up to 2.2 kilograms. By their estimates, these are the largest spore-making fruiting bodies among all sac fungi.
Torda Varga — a mycologist at the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew in Richmond, England who was not involved with the research — notes that some truffle species are known to get close to the bulk. D. rex appears to be the largest sac fungal fruiting body he’s aware of. “What I find particularly remarkable is that a fungus with such an enormous fruiting body appears to have remained scientifically undocumented until now,” says Varga, though he adds his experience has mostly been within Europe.
The researchers compared samples of the fungus’s DNA with those from other fungi to determine its evolutionary relationships. They found that it was a relative of species like candlesnuff fungus and dead-man’s-fingers, which make fruiting bodies only a few centimeters tall, but that it was probably in its own, unique family. The team gave the new species the name Dianjunus rex, referencing both the Latin “rex” for “king” and the ancient Dian kingdom of the region.
The team’s genetic analysis suggests D. rex’s family first evolved in the aftermath of the mass extinction at the end of the Cretaceous Period that wiped out the dinosaurs, some 65 million years ago. “During the dark, cold, postimpact years after the mass extinction, fungi that decompose dead organic matter could keep functioning better than light-dependent photosynthesizers,” Senanayake says.
Varga wonders if searching databases for bits of DNA shed into the environment could help uncover other members of D. rex’s royal family in the absence of physical specimens.
“Some of these [genetic] sequences might belong to previously undocumented relatives of Dianjunus rex,” he says. Finding these hidden species could tell researchers more about the biology and evolutionary history of this king of the sac fungi.

Estonia has run out of asphalt, says Tallinn deputy mayor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Estonia has run out of asphalt, says Tallinn deputy mayor
Estonia is experiencing a shortage of asphalt as factories in Sweden and Lithuania are currently not supplying it to the country, Deputy Mayor Kristjan Järvan (Isamaa) has said
"I have to start with some sad news. Namely, Estonia has run out of asphalt," Järvan said at a Tallinn city government press conference on Tuesday.
The official said Estonia usually imports bitumen from two sources in Sweden and Lithuania.
"And for reasons still unknown, the Swedish company decided not to bring any more. It said that the ship that arrived three weeks ago would be the last this year. The next one will come in the spring. The Lithuanian company was delighted, immediately raised its prices, and then its factory broke down. This means that asphalt plants in Estonia can no longer obtain bitumen," the deputy mayor said.
"What this means nationally is that those construction companies that have their own asphalt plants probably have their own contracts covered and, as usual, any surplus asphalt is put on the open market," he added.
Tallinn is affected by the issue as the second supplementary budget set aside money for roadworks this autumn.
"Now both of the City of Tallinn's partners have said that, unfortunately, the market situation is such that asphalt is simply unavailable. And this means that we are in a situation where we can happily announce that we have asphalt for resurfacing Liivalaia. We have to take a positive view of what we have," Järvan said.
Asphalting work on Liivalaia began on Monday, and Tallinn will grant an additional two weeks for this work, the deputy mayor added.
"But this also means that we will not take the risk of milling up Viljandi maantee and Vabaõhumuuseumi tee to lay new asphalt there. We will still avoid a situation where we have streets dug up for the winter and no asphalt to put down in their place," Järvan said.

What сomes after the war: Bosnia's lesson for Ukraine
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
15:00:00 EET
22:00:00 KST

What сomes after the war: Bosnia's lesson for Ukraine
This op-ed was co-authored with Kateryna Kyrychenko, a Ukrainian international lawyer and Head of Ukraine Legal Affairs and Programme Management at the Public International Law & Policy Group (PILPG). Her work covers international criminal law, accountability for Russian war crimes, peace negotiations and transitional justice. She is pursuing a PhD in international criminal law at the National University of Kyiv-Mohyla Academy.
On a sunny September afternoon, Kyiv almost seemed at peace. People sat outside the Food Market, talking and eating. Between meetings, we discussed Bosnia's and Ukraine's shared experience. For one of us, war is a memory shaping life three decades later; for the other, an immediate reality of air-raid alerts, sleepless nights and uncertainty about the next Russian attack. We returned to one question: what does it mean for war to end?
A month earlier in Sarajevo, a meeting with Ukrainian officials and civil-society representatives had focused on how Bosnia and Herzegovina handled post-war return and reconstruction. Families crossed former front lines to reclaim homes; property disputes took years, and people returned to areas governed by forces that had driven them out. These challenges are familiar to Bosnians. For Ukrainians still at war, the question was not simply how people had managed to return, but what it had taken to rebuild their lives in places from which they had once been driven.
Pressure to negotiate is mounting in Kyiv, yet little attention goes to a peace framework with credible guarantees. After more than 12 years of Russian aggression, including nearly five of full-scale invasion, Ukraine's weariness is understandable. Millions have lost homes, loved ones or livelihoods; families have been separated for years, and communities live between air-raid alerts and the next attack. They want the war to end, but exhaustion is not willingness to accept peace at any price. Distant negotiators may see this desire for relief as a chance for a quick deal. What seems a breakthrough in Washington or a European capital can have different consequences for those living with its terms. Bosnia shows the gap between signing an agreement and the reality that follows.
Ending the war is only the beginning
Dayton, Ohio, is remembered for producing the 1995 peace agreement that ended the Bosnian war. Its annexes covered the constitution, military arrangements, elections, human rights and refugee return. Unlike an archived document, it had force behind it: some 60,000 NATO-led Implementation Force (IFOR) troops separated armies, oversaw territorial transfers and enforced military provisions. Peace required troops on the ground, and the money and governments willing to keep them involved after Bosnia left the front pages.
Ukraine knows the limits of a mission without enforcement powers. From March 2014, the OSCE Special Monitoring Mission monitored the security situation, established facts and reported violations, while also facilitating dialogue and supporting local ceasefire arrangements; it had no power to enforce compliance. Its mandate expired on 31 March 2022 because OSCE consensus on an extension could not be reached owing to Russia's position. The Minsk agreements, meant to end hostilities in eastern Ukraine, proved vulnerable to manipulation: repeated ceasefire violations, unresolved security questions and incompatible readings of political provisions. They neither secured peace nor prevented Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022. For Ukraine, the question is not whether another agreement can be signed but what would make it different from arrangements Russia has already violated: who would verify compliance, respond to renewed attacks and impose consequences?
Dayton was possible under different conditions: the parties accepted IFOR's deployment and undertook to facilitate its operations, while the UN Security Council authorised the force. Russia, by contrast, is Ukraine's aggressor and holds a UN Security Council veto. A guarantee it can veto offers little protection. Ukraine's security cannot rest on monitoring or diplomatic assurances: its ability to defend itself, maintain military capabilities and choose security partnerships must be central to any settlement. Restricting its self-defence while Russia can rearm risks another war.
Civilian implementation was equally demanding. Dayton created the Office of the High Representative, but implementation soon exposed serious obstacles. In December 1997, the Peace Implementation Council in Bonn supported the exercise of what became known as the Bonn Powers: the High Representative could impose binding decisions on specified implementation issues and remove officials who obstructed Dayton commitments.
Ukraine faces a less favourable international environment. Beyond Russia's veto, other major powers' interests may not align with its security needs. Those conditions cannot simply be recreated. Proposals for Ukraine must start from this reality, not assume guarantees will enforce themselves.
The unfinished business of peace
Property return showed that work went beyond the text. Annex 7 gave refugees and displaced people the right to return home and have their property restored, or to receive compensation where restoration was impossible. Laws and administrative procedures were developed and enforced, with municipalities monitored and pressed to comply. People could receive house keys yet find the hardest part of return ahead. For some returnees, especially those returning as an ethnic minority, the label "returnee" can be a reminder that the return of property does not necessarily restore their place in society.
Much will be familiar in Ukraine: destroyed or occupied homes, separated families and repeated displacement. The scale of destruction, mines and unexploded ordnance, displacement of millions and Russia's systematic efforts to alter the demographic, legal and cultural realities of occupied territories will compound Ukraine's challenges. Restoring Ukrainian governance requires more than replacing flags or reopening offices. It must address documented pressure to obtain Russian citizenship, property expropriation, the replacement of Ukrainian education and the suppression of Ukrainian identity, forcible transfers or deportations of civilians, including children, to the Russian Federation, arbitrary detention by Russian forces or occupation authorities, and the consequences of occupation.
War's end brings difficulties beyond rebuilding homes and institutions: disputes over education, integration, national symbols, history, heroes and victims. Who decides what schools teach, whose suffering is recognised and whose history becomes official? Bosnia has grappled with these issues since 1995; many remain unresolved. Survivors and victims' families still face denial of the Srebrenica genocide, historical revisionism and glorification of convicted war criminals, according to the Srebrenica Memorial. Reconciliation efforts have sometimes emphasised moving forward rather than confronting the past. Ukraine should heed the warning: ending a war and reconciling societies are different things.
Despite its achievements, Dayton left unresolved questions, notably the struggle over the Bosnian state. Its two entities and political system enabled obstruction and challenged state authority. Bosnia's experience is not a warning against decentralisation or minority rights. Nevertheless, trouble begins when arrangements protecting communities let a neighbouring government prevent a country from deciding for itself. For Ukraine, a Russian veto over defence or European integration would be especially dangerous. Russia has sought to use the status of occupied territories to influence Ukraine's internal affairs. A settlement must not institutionalise that interference as political compromise or minority protection.
What happens after the diplomats leave?
We sought no Ukrainian version of Dayton. and Dayton's unfinished business in Bosnia makes it no blueprint. But it stopped the war, and some people returned and homes were rebuilt because outsiders stayed to enforce commitments local politicians resisted.
Ukraine's partners should ask what they will do on the first day after the war, not just what they will sign, propose or pressure others to accept. Bosnians understand Ukraine's reluctance to accept promises without guarantees: they have been down that road and, in many ways, still are.
These answers will matter years later, when another crisis dominates headlines and Ukraine leaves the global spotlight. Who will remain engaged, provide assistance or step in when agreements are violated or institutions fail?
"At least nobody's shooting" was common in post-war Bosnia. It is a painfully modest definition of peace, hardly a foundation for the future, especially for those living with unresolved consequences.
Nedim Jahić and Kateryna Kyrychenko
