Saab Announces Key Partners for Gripen Canada
Saab plans to work with CAE, IMP and Magellan Aerospace as its principal Canadian industry partners if Gripen E is selected by the Government of Canada.
Saab today confirms its intention to collaborate with several of Canada’s major international aerospace firms in a first step to establish a broad, national ecosystem that will build, deliver and support the Gripen E advanced multi-role fighter, should the Government of Canada proceed with a Gripen acquisition.
If selected, Saab and its Canadian partners will establish a comprehensive, in-country capability for the production, final assembly, support and further development of airpower capabilities. The collaboration would also include in-service support (ISS), training and long-term sustainment capabilities.
“Canada's fighter capability is a long-term national investment. Together with CAE, IMP and Magellan Aerospace we are prepared to establish a strong Canadian industrial ecosystem around Gripen that delivers operational effect, national sovereignty and lasting industrial and technological benefits," says Micael Johansson, President and CEO of Saab.
Saab has signed a new Teaming Agreement with IMP to establish a new final assembly line, for the Gripen fighter in Canada, if Canada decides to acquire the aircraft. IMP will also be responsible for electrical assembly production and ISS for Canada’s Gripens.
Saab has signed a new Memorandum of Understanding with Magellan Aerospace to provide local manufacturing of advanced aerostructures, composite structures and structural assemblies in Canada, if Canada decides to acquire the aircraft.
Saab has previously signed a Memorandum of Understanding with CAE to deliver advanced fighter pilot and technician training, mission systems engineering and support/sustainment capabilities in Canada, if Canada decides to acquire the aircraft.
“We are proud to be selected by Saab to establish a Canadian capability for the production and long-term support of Gripen. While that capability would be established to meet Canada’s requirements, its potential reaches well beyond Canada. We see a real opportunity for IMP to produce and support aircraft for Gripen customers internationally, positioning Canadian industry as an enduring part of the global Gripen program,” says David Gossen, President, IMP Aerospace & Defence.
“As a proud Canadian manufacturer, Magellan Aerospace is well-positioned to bring decades of advanced aerospace manufacturing expertise to the Gripen program, supporting the creation of high-tech jobs and sovereign defence capability right here in Canada," says Haydn Martin, Vice President Business Development, Magellan Aerospace.
“CAE has decades of experience contributing to the mission readiness of fighter pilots around the world,” says Pascal Grenier, President, CAE Defense & Security. “We have a longstanding commitment to the Royal Canadian Air Force and its training needs. Should the Government of Canada select the Gripen, CAE is prepared to work with Saab to support Canada’s future fighter force.”
These partnerships are designed to strengthen Canada’s sovereign defence capability while contributing to the development of advanced aerospace and defence expertise across the country. When activated, they will add significant new jobs and skills in areas such as high-technology manufacturing, advanced materials, and model-based systems engineering. They will also provide Canada with a self-reliant and sovereign capability to deploy, sustain and enhance a critical national asset for decades to come.
Additionally, Saab is engaged with a broad range of Canadian companies, academic institutions and research organizations to further develop a future defence industrial ecosystem in Canada.

Palestinians who fled Gaza for Egypt are being scammed and exploited by fake charities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

Mohammed Odeh Mahmoud, a 60-year-old Palestinian engineer, lost everything to the war in Gaza: his greenhouses, his farm and his three-story home.
He fled the enclave seven months into the genocide, paying Hala Consulting and Tourism, a private Egyptian company, more than $100,000 to get his 22-member family out of Gaza.
But a different kind of hardship awaited him on the other side. He paid $140 per adult for residency permits, but has been unable to renew them. “Hala just left us displaced in Egypt,” he said. “We have nothing left but God’s mercy.”
Now he relies on a monthly parcel from the Egyptian Food Bank and on help from relatives.
More than 115,000 Palestinians had fled Gaza to Egypt by May 2024, according to Palestinian officials. Unable to obtain residency or work legally, many have depended on charity and aid, leaving them vulnerable to those who would exploit them. Since the October 2025 ceasefire, much of that aid has dwindled, deepening their desperation.
In July 2024, Haidar, who had recently arrived in Cairo from Khan Younis and asked to be identified by his first name only, received a call on his mother’s phone from someone claiming to represent a charity called “Muslims Are Brothers.”
Haidar had registered his details through an online link weeks earlier, hoping for a food parcel and 10,000 Egyptian pounds (about $200) in aid. Now, the caller said, the money was ready.
“He said, ‘Do you have Vodafone Cash on this number?’ I said yes. He said, ‘I’ll send you a code. Send it back to me so I can transfer the money,’” Haidar told Mondoweiss. “And he stole the whole balance.”
Instead of receiving 10,000 Egyptian pounds, Haidar lost 60,000 ($1,200), everything in his mobile wallet.
Mondoweiss found no organization called “Muslims Are Brothers” in the Ministry of Social Solidarity register of licensed NGOs or in the government’s other NGO databases, and it has no official page on social media.
How the traps work
Often posted anonymously or from fake accounts, links with the name of little-known charities circulate on WhatsApp and in Facebook groups for the Palestinian community in Egypt, the largest of which has more than 53,000 members. Those links lead to forms that ask for the head of household’s details, the size of the family, their address, a phone number, and photos of their passports. They also ask what help the family needs: rent, school fees, food or clothes.
Then the calls begin. Callers promise food parcels or cash and ask for more details, or, as with Haidar, a code that gives them access to the victim’s mobile wallet.
The links often stop working within weeks. One posted in February 2026 in the name of a purported aid group no longer works.
Victims have few options once they have lost money. A Palestinian in Egypt without valid residency cannot file a police report or take legal action, said Mahmoud al-Roubi, an Egyptian lawyer and legal researcher.
“I expect the scammers know exactly what their victims’ legal status is, and that they won’t be able to pursue them in court,” he told Mondoweiss.
Many of those targeted use SIM cards registered in other people’s names, because they cannot get their own without a residency permit. That makes it even harder to recover stolen money or trace the thief, al-Roubi said.
‘Exploiting the Palestinian cause‘
K.M., a master’s student who asked to be identified only by his initials, is a Palestinian with Egyptian citizenship who spent four months in Gaza during the war.
His Egyptian passport helped him leave. Hala charged him only $650, while Palestinians paid thousands of dollars. But in Egypt, he has been unable to find steady work.
“Every time I apply for a job, either they reject me because my accent shows I’m Palestinian, or they exploit my situation and I work for a terrible wage,” he said.
Short of money, he registered with a Palestinian charity in Egypt. He soon noticed that his details were circulating among groups he had never contacted.
Callers promised food parcels in exchange for his address, the size of his family and details about his home. That information was then used in attempts to get into his mobile wallet.
K.M. never lost money. A programmer by training, he recognized the trap and posted warnings in the WhatsApp groups where the links circulate.
Khalil Kanoun, a Palestinian activist and researcher, arrived in Egypt in March 2024 and registered through so many aid links that he can no longer remember their names. Scammers have repeatedly tried to steal from his mobile wallet, but have so far failed.
“Exploiting the Palestinian cause for personal gain, by individuals or even by states, has a long history,” he said.
Scammers also target those desperate to leave Gaza.
Nasser Najm, 50, has tried to get out of Gaza five times since the war began. Each time, he paid a broker. Each time, the broker disappeared. In total, he has lost $5,000. The last time was in May 2026, and he is still in Gaza.
The scam trades on the medical evacuation system. Each patient approved for travel to Egypt is allowed two companions, and brokers promise to sell those places to strangers for between $1,000 and $5,000. Once they have the money, the brokers vanish, and the patient travels without them.
“All the brokers are swindlers and liars,” Najm told Mondoweiss from Gaza. “Someone who wants to travel goes looking for a person with a medical referral to be added with them, pays, and gets scammed.”
Like K.M., Najm has posted warnings on social media, including two Egyptian phone numbers he said were being used to scam people.
“I warned everyone again and again,” he said. “Don’t pay anyone.”
No safety net
Samar Abu Kweik, 54, lost her home in northern Gaza to an airstrike early in the war. In early 2024, she left the enclave with her husband, 64, who is ill. She borrowed $10,000 to get them out, a sum she has been unable to repay.
In Egypt, the couple lived on food parcels, vouchers and cash aid.
“Here I felt I had put my dignity on the ground,” Abu Kweik said. “I started running from charity to charity asking for a food parcel, when in Gaza I had lived with honor and dignity.”
That help has since dried up. Abu Kweik said they have not received any aid since the ceasefire in October 2025, and now rely on money her daughter sends from Gaza each month.
“From the day they announced a truce, the aid stopped,” she said.
Her experience is far from unusual. Egypt had provided $578 million worth of aid to Gaza by July 2025, according to the health minister, but Palestinians who fled across the border say support for them has dwindled. UNRWA, the UN agency for Palestinian refugees, does not operate in Egypt.
Part of the problem, according to a source at the Palestinian embassy in Cairo, is that the aid system has changed.
“We used to act as an intermediary between charities and Palestinians to deliver aid,” the source said, speaking on condition of anonymity. “But [the charities] obtained lists with people’s details and started dealing with them directly.”
Maryam Abu Daqqa, a Palestinian human rights activist in Egypt, said she receives a steady stream of complaints from Palestinians who arrived after October 7, 2023, and need help. She refers them to the embassy, which she said has scaled back its role over the past year.
“Most Palestinians in Egypt lack basic necessities,” she said. The little aid available goes to medical cases, she added, while families struggle to cover rent, food and daily costs.
Amal Agha, director general of the General Union of Palestinian Women in Egypt, said the union once acted as an intermediary between charities and families in need, but that link has been cut. It has stopped providing food aid, and now covers university fees only for female students, paid for by its members’ donations.
“Care and support have dropped sharply,” she told Mondoweiss.
For some, even marriage to an Egyptian has not been enough to secure legal status.
Taghreed Gamal, 28, entered Egypt on a 45-day temporary permit in early 2024 and later married an Egyptian. She never renewed the permit, and she cannot regularize her status until she pays the fines she has built up for overstaying.
She now owes 65,000 Egyptian pounds (about $1,300) in fines, and renewing her residency would cost another 35,000 (about $700). That brings the total to 100,000 Egyptian pounds (about $2,000), a sum she and her husband cannot afford.
She had hoped that traveling to Saudi Arabia for Umrah might clear the fine, but a passport official told her she could not travel anywhere, not even back to Gaza, until she paid.
“I looked for solutions, like paying in installments or getting a reduction, but there is no middle ground,” she said.

====================================================================================================

The ASEAN-India Trade Agreement and Its Discontents
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
12:57:00 UTC
21:57:00 KST

Even as India has embraced a renewed fervor for free trade agreements, one trade deal remains disfavored in Indian memory. The 2009 ASEAN-India Goods in Trade Agreement (AITIGA) is one of the oldest trade agreements signed by post-liberalization India as well as one of its most controversial. Atypically for an establishment that prefers to settle diplomatic disputes behind the scenes, Indian diplomats and trade officials are publicly trenchant in their criticism of AITIGA.
An oft-repeated narrative has emerged around the agreement: in the early 2000s, inexperienced Indian negotiators walked into an asymmetric deal, opening up their markets while getting little in return. Consequently, India’s trade deficit with ASEAN ballooned. Moreover, China exploited the AITIGA to route its goods into India through Southeast Asia.
This narrative stems from misremembering history. Rather than a powerful tool for ASEAN and China to penetrate the Indian market, the AITIGA is, in fact, a shallow and weak instrument. Moreover, it is shallow precisely because India preferred it that way. By repeatedly telling itself an alternative story, New Delhi has developed irrational fears over economic cooperation with Southeast Asia and injected unnecessary acrimony in the relationship. The myth of AITIGA as a bad deal is costing India diplomatically.
India started running a trade deficit with ASEAN in 1996, 13 years before the AITIGA was signed. The deficit stemmed from Southeast Asia’s shift from agrarian to manufacturing-led economies. The currency devaluations triggered by the 1997 Asian Financial Crisis further boosted the deficit. While the absolute figure of the trade deficit has ballooned over the last three decades, the India-ASEAN imports-to-exports ratio remains broadly similar to what it was in the 1990s.
After the 1997 crisis, ASEAN was looking to economically integrate itself with its East Asian neighbors. In the early 2000s, it began pursuing ASEAN+1 FTAs with its six immediate neighbors: China, India, Japan, South Korea, Australia, and New Zealand. India had been excluded from the first wave of post-1997 regional integration – the ASEAN Plus Three, Asian Bond Markets Initiative, and Chiang Mai Initiative for currency swap. Eager not to miss out on another wave of regional integration, India agreed to negotiate the FTA.
Contrary to the myth, Indian officials were tough negotiators. After all, India had decades of experience negotiating economic deals in the GATT, WTO, and elsewhere. The negotiations were tortuous and took much longer than the other ASEAN+1 FTAs.
Moreover, there was a mismatch of approach. On the one hand, eager to gain access to the Indian market, ASEAN wanted to widen the FTA’s scope. On the other hand, India looked to protect its domestic industry by limiting the scope of the agreement. Indian businesses were lukewarm about seeking out greater market access in Southeast Asia.
India’s tough negotiating ensured that the AITIGA was the shallowest of the ASEAN+1 FTAs. Whereas all other agreements committed parties to tariff elimination coverage of more than 90 percent, the AITIGA’s promised coverage hovered around 79 percent. ASEAN mirrored India’s reluctance to open its markets. For instance, Indian critics of the AITIGA often point to the fact that Indonesia promised only 48.7 percent tariff elimination coverage to India. Notably, Indonesia offered above 91 percent coverage to all other ASEAN+1 partners, including Australia, with which it ran a trade deficit at the time.
AITIGA also ended up with the most stringent Rules of Origin among all the ASEAN+1 FTAs. It is the only agreement that demands dual compliance (35 percent local content and change in tariff subheading) for goods to qualify for preferential treatment. Its complex compliance rules and lower scope resulted in exporters avoiding using the AITIGA.
In AITIGA, India got what it wanted – an agreement that signaled India’s commitment to its Look East policy without exposing its domestic industry to excessive international competition. While economists may argue over whether Indian protectionism is good economic policy, the debate is irrelevant from a diplomatic standpoint. For whatever reasons, Indian economic managers prefer shielding the Indian market. The AITIGA was a natural outcome of such preference.
However, to then construct a narrative of the agreement as a bad deal in which India got duped is diplomatically damaging. To begin with, it erodes India’s credibility in the region as a reliable and competent partner. India began criticizing the AITIGA almost as soon as it was signed. The two sides agreed to open a review of the agreement in 2015 but still haven’t concluded it. Such long-drawn, dangling processes chip away at India’s image.
AITIGA’s beleaguered state becomes a particularly bad look when contrasted with other ASEAN+1 FTAs, especially the one with China. Beijing began negotiating its FTA with ASEAN around the same time as New Delhi. However, it not only concluded the negotiations fairly quickly, but China and ASEAN have since upgraded the agreement twice. Today, the ASEAN-China FTA is a powerful instrument that deals with a range of issues from digital trade to green technology.
The narrative of AITIGA as a loss for India has made New Delhi a less confident economic actor in Southeast Asia. The resultant hesitation has been evident in India’s exit from the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership as well as its reluctance to conclude bilateral FTAs with Southeast Asian countries such as Thailand and Indonesia. Today, even as India seeks out FTAs in the Middle East and Europe, it is too unsure of itself to look for a trade deal in Southeast Asia.
Tellingly, the acrimony over AITIGA has spilled over into other aspects of ASEAN-India economic cooperation, even the ones which are in India’s interests. For instance, the 2014 ASEAN-India Trade in Services Agreement needs urgent upgradation to account for all the advancements in the digital economy. Given that India enjoys a services surplus with Southeast Asia, New Delhi should be eagerly driving the process. However, so far the two sides have not even begun discussing the issue.
The self-created myths around AITIGA have cast a shadow on India’s Look/Act East policy. New Delhi needs to shed them to become a more confident, credible and engaged actor in the region.

Around one in three people in Primorye, a region of 1.8 million, rely on state support across 97 different programs.
Soaring spending on the war continues to strain both the federal government’s budget and those of regions across the country.
Nationwide, Russia’s 2026 budget deficit is expected to reach a record 7.345 trillion rubles (88 billion), nearly twice the previous forecast of 3.785 trillion rubles (45 billion). That new projection represents 3.2% of GDP compared to the previous target of 1.6%.
President Vladimir Putin said last month that the size of Russia’s budget deficit poses no “critical” risk for the economy and that officials will do everything to keep it under control.

Court orders Egyptian website closed in case seen as test for independent media

Court orders Egyptian website closed in case seen as test for independent media
CAIRO, Oct 27 - An Egyptian court convicted the editor-in-chief of leading independent news website Mada Masr of running it without a licence on Tuesday, ordered the site closed and held her in custody for five hours, her lawyers and the outlet said.
Lina Attalah of the online newspaper Mada Masr, which has won numerous international awards for its reporting, was fined 3 million Egyptian pounds ($53,400), her lawyers told Reuters. She was released after Mada Masr paid the fine, the newspaper said.
The ruling targets the most internationally prominent independent outlet in a media landscape mostly dominated by the state, and it comes a month after authorities arrested the entire newsroom of the fact-checking outlet Matsaddash. Rights groups have criticized the case against Attalah. Mada Masr, which was founded in 2013, regularly publishes stories on politically sensitive topics.
Her lawyers said the court rejected their requests during Tuesday's session to review the case file and submit additional evidence and instead issued her a court-appointed lawyer despite her objection. State authorities did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The court gave her the maximum penalty, ordering the website to be shut down and its equipment confiscated, Mada Masr said in a statement.
The independent outlet said in a separate statement that during release procedures, Attalah was informed of a one-year prison term handed to her in absentia in 2024 on charges of disseminating false news and managing an unlicensed website. It said a retrial of the separate case was set for November 11 after her lawyers took steps to challenge the 2024 ruling.
Prosecutors referred Attalah to trial last Thursday.
A group of 119 rights groups and media outlets, including Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and the Committee to Protect Journalists, called the case an "unprecedented attack on press freedom."
US Senator Chris Van Hollen, a Maryland Democrat, said in a statement on the social media platform X on Friday that the charges were baseless and that "journalism is not a crime."
Egyptian authorities say the state is committed to upholding freedom of expression but that the media must operate within the law, respect national security and counter misinformation.
YEARS OF LEGAL BATTLES
Egyptian authorities have blocked Mada Masr inside the country since 2017. Mada Masr says six cases have been brought against it and its journalists over the last six years, though rights groups say this is the first of its kind to be referred to trial.
Attalah was named one of the world's 100 most influential people by Time magazine in 2020.
Mada Masr says it has asked for a licence from the Supreme Council for Media Regulation repeatedly since 2018 but heard nothing back and learned of a rejection only when prosecutors raised the issue during an earlier case in 2022.
The outlet contested that decision in court and said its latest application has been awaiting a response since 2023.
The council has not commented on the case but has said that it facilitates procedures for outlets that meet official requirements and is keen to promote freedom of expression.
In September, the US waived rights conditions, which include protecting media freedoms, on a portion of the roughly $1.3 billion of military aid it sends Egypt each year. REUTERS

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian called on major global energy suppliers on Tuesday to condemn and “effectively counter” US measures threatening the stability of international energy markets.
Speaking at the 8th summit of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) in Moscow, Pezeshkian said geopolitical developments and unilateral measures were creating challenges for global energy security.
“Unilateral US sanctions on Iran, as well as restrictions affecting maritime and air access, could have broader consequences for energy markets,” he said in his comments carried by the official IRNA news agency.
“Major energy suppliers should condemn and effectively counter measures that threaten the stability of global energy markets,” Pezeshkian said.
He also said US military involvement in the Gulf region could affect energy pricing, supply and transportation, with consequences extending beyond the region.
Referring to the ongoing military conflict with the US, Pezeshkian said damage to energy facilities and disruptions to energy transportation could have implications for global energy security and the wider economy.
He called for greater cooperation among GECF members to reduce market vulnerabilities and strengthen the security of energy supply and demand.
Pezeshkian also highlighted cooperation in energy governance, technical and engineering activities, technology development and market management.
“Iran is seeking to expand joint investment across the natural gas value chain, improve efficiency and increase regional and international gas trade,” he said.
According to Pezeshkian, Iran has an annual natural gas production capacity of around 280 billion cubic meters and is prepared to play a larger role in joint investment projects, gas trade and efforts to strengthen global energy security.
He also said Tehran was ready to expand cooperation with foreign investors in upstream and downstream gas projects.
The GECF brings together major gas-producing countries and provides a platform for cooperation on developments in global natural gas markets.
Pezeshkian is scheduled to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow this week.

The call came ahead of planned US-led peace talks, which European leaders are seeking to join.
Why did Denmark criticize the call?
Frederiksen said that Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store had gone "solo.”
"I'm very sceptical about this Norwegian and Finnish initiative. It hasn't been coordinated with any of the rest of us," she told reporters while attending a meeting of Nordics leaders.

"I believe we should keep Europe united, rather than going it alone," Frederiksen said.
Stubb and Store said they had consulted Ukraine before initiating the call.
They stressed that they represented their own countries and were not speaking on behalf of Europe.
What did the leaders discuss with Putin?
Stubb described the conversation as "frank and substantive." Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov confirmed the call, the first between the three leaders.
"The outcome of this war will have a direct impact on our and the broader European security. Ending the war requires direct discussions," Stubb said.
Finland and Norway both border Russia and have supported Ukraine throughout the war.
Store said the leaders had emphasized de-escalation.
"The war comes with enormous human and material costs. The suffering and destruction will impact generations," he said.
How was Ukraine involved?
The call followed an October 20 meeting in Oslo involving Stubb, Store, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and US envoy Steve Witkoff. US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner joined remotely.

Bulgaria Has EU’s Highest Road Death Rate

Germany is criticizing Bulgaria, Hungary, the Czech Republic and Slovakia for refusing to contribute to financial guarantees for a planned new EU loan to Ukraine, with the dispute threatening to complicate negotiations over the bloc’s budget, German newspaper Die Welt reports.
Hungary, the Czech Republic and Slovakia want to be exempt from backing the new loan, as they were from the previously agreed €90 billion package. German diplomatic circles have sharply criticized their position, particularly because the three countries are also seeking substantial funding from the EU budget. Bulgaria has likewise refused to participate, according to Die Welt.
Although frozen Russian state assets could potentially be used to recover the money, there is no certainty that this will happen.
Last week, Bulgarian President Rumen Radev ruled out Bulgaria’s participation in the new financial aid package. “Bulgaria cannot, under any circumstances, participate in this €70 billion [initiative],” he told reporters in Tvarditsa, Die Welt reported, citing the Bulgarian News Agency (BTA).
Radev noted that Bulgaria, unlike Hungary, the Czech Republic and Slovakia, had joined the €90 billion EU loan approved last year for 2026 and 2027. He argued that the war was draining European economies and fueling social tensions and political instability. Radev also urged an end to the conflict as soon as possible, saying, “The outcome will not be achieved through military means,” according to the newspaper.
A German diplomat condemned the countries’ demands for exemptions, saying they exposed a disconnect between their positions on Ukraine and their expectations for the EU budget. “This absurdity shows, once again, just how out of touch with reality some are when it comes to the EU budget,” the diplomat said.
The diplomat questioned why countries refusing to contribute to Ukraine’s defense should receive additional EU cohesion funding. “How can anyone seriously believe that our taxpayers would be willing to transfer even a single extra euro in cohesion funds to those who refuse to participate in the defense against the greatest threat to all of our security?” the diplomat asked, adding, “There is no cohesion in 'free-riding'.”
Cohesion funds are EU subsidies intended to narrow economic and social gaps between regions, Die Welt noted.
The dispute stems from Ukraine’s additional funding needs for the coming year. Kyiv requires another €70 billion in total, of which partners including Canada and Japan could provide approximately €25 billion. European countries would need to supply loans worth up to €45 billion.

‘Children first and competitors second’: Esports industry failing young players’ wellbeing, report warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
12:50:58 UTC
21:50:58 KST

Sleep disruption, mental health pressures and online abuse are among the risks young esports players face, as a lack of common standards leaves their protection fragmented, Save the Children says.
Children’s health and wellbeing are not adequately protected in competitive gaming, according to a new report, “Protecting Child Rights in Esports,” by Save the Children, published on Tuesday.
The report calls on the fast-growing esports industry to put children’s rights, enshrined in the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child (UNCRC), ahead of competitive ambitions.
Young esports players — up to 300 million children worldwide — can face disrupted sleep, musculoskeletal problems, sexism, anxiety, online harassment and depression, while intensive training can leave less time for education, family and friends.
"Esports offers exciting opportunities for children, but participation should never come at the expense of their rights, wellbeing or development,” Theo Toresson, a psychologist at Save the Children and gaming expert, said in a press release.
"As the industry continues to grow, children must be recognised as children first and competitors second,” he added, calling for children's involvement in decision-making and ensuring a future where “every child can participate safely, develop their talents and enjoy the benefits of gaming without being exposed to harm.”
The concern is that children entering structured competitive environments may face expectations associated with professional sport without equivalent safeguards designed around their age and development.
No common standards for healthy competition
Long periods of sitting, inadequate breaks and training schedules that encroach on sleep, physical activity or schoolwork are among the concerns facing young players.
Long sessions and poor posture can also contribute to neck, shoulder and wrist pain, highlighting the need for ergonomic guidance and better-structured training.
Sleep is another concern. Late-night gaming schedules and the demands of competition can disrupt rest, affecting cognitive performance, mood regulation and overall wellbeing, the report says.
A representative of a national esports federation, quoted anonymously in the report, said there were no established guidelines on playing hours or training methods.
“We do talk about screen breaks, healthy diets, sleep, and hydration. But these are practices we've found best from different researchers and brought together ourselves. There isn't yet a centralized body trying to bring this together,” the representative said.
The absence of common standards raises questions about who is responsible for ensuring that competitive gaming remains compatible with children’s physical and psychological development.
The picture is not uniformly negative, however. The report notes that many professional esports players report satisfactory levels of physical activity, with higher-ranking players often placing greater emphasis on fitness. Players may also adopt healthy habits around diet and other aspects of their lifestyles.
Mental health under pressure
The psychological demands of competition are another concern.
“The demanding nature of esports, coupled with online toxicity, can create significant mental health challenges” for Youth Esports Athletes, the report says.
Stress, anxiety and depression can be compounded by intense competition and limited access to appropriate support. This can be further fueled by, for example, sexism and online harassment, as many interact with audiences through in-game chats, Discord communities, livestreaming platforms such as Twitch and YouTube and social media.
These channels can help young players build communities and develop public profiles, but they also expose them to cyberbullying and privacy violations. The report cited an analysis of chatrooms during 302 gameplay segments from the top 20 streamers on Twitch, one of the most popular platforms for esports
and gaming-related streaming, which revealed that 62% of streams included sexist language, 37% included racist language, 84% included ableist language, and 97% included violent language.
Some esports federations and teams require staff to obtain mental health first-aid training, according to the report, but such practices are not widespread across the industry.
The report warns that young players can be thrust into public-facing roles before they have the experience or support needed to navigate online scrutiny, interviews and livestreams.
The report also exposes challenges such as ensuring equal participation, with persisting large disparities based on access, gender, race, LGBTQIA+and disability; children's involvement in decision-making; economic exploitation, as teams, agents, and even parents sometimes exploit young players, taking advantage of non-transparent contracts and unequal power dynamics; and risks at live events without an adequate supervision.

Israel votes on Netanyahu’s future

Unknown Publisher

Netanyahu bloc falls short of majority in Israeli election – exit polls: As it happened
No major political bloc is projected to secure a parliamentary majority in Israel’s first election since the war with Hamas in Gaza broke out in 2023, according to exit polls released shortly after voting closed on Tuesday evening.
Exit polls by public broadcaster Kan 11 and commercial networks Channel 12 and Channel 13 project that the opposition bloc led by former Israel Defense Forces (IDF) chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot will win 52–53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, compared with 50 for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc. Channel 15 projects that Netanyahu’s bloc will win 55 seats, compared with 49 for Eisenkot’s bloc.
A total of 61 seats is needed to secure a parliamentary majority and form a government.
Voter turnout has reached a five-decade high as Netanyahu faces a crucial test of public confidence amid political scandals, corruption allegations, and wars with Hamas and Iran.
Eisenkot is unlikely to significantly alter Israel’s military or foreign policies. Instead, he has positioned himself as a patriotic centrist, seeking to distinguish himself from Netanyahu, whose leadership has been overshadowed by corruption allegations and accusations of putting his political interests ahead of national priorities.
Before the attack, Netanyahu faced corruption probes and was sinking in the polls as protesters took to the streets to oppose his controversial judicial reforms. Although the attack and subsequent war on Gaza bought Netanyahu some political breathing space, his opponents are now questioning how the prime minister could have left Israel undefended on October 7, and whether he ignored forewarnings about the attack.
Netanyahu has also been condemned for putting his interests before Israel’s by attempting to push IDF Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir into a new military operation on the eve of the election, according to a Channel 12 report. Former Defense Minister Avigdor Liberman has demanded that the prime minister be investigated on suspicion of treason over the allegation.
Rising defense spending, higher living costs, and wartime tax hikes have further eroded Netanyahu’s popularity. An October 21 Jerusalem Post analysis of four major surveys put Eisenkot’s Yashar party at an average of 22.5 seats, compared with 19.75 for Netanyahu’s Likud.
Once the official results are announced, Israel is likely to enter a lengthy period of political horse-trading, with Netanyahu’s far-right allies and Arab parties potentially playing a decisive role in determining the country’s next government.

‘We bear the consequences’: Diaspora Jews fear fallout from Israel’s election - interview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
12:46:39 UTC
21:46:39 KST

As Israelis head to the polls, Diaspora Jews are watching with a stake in an election they cannot vote in, fearing its consequences will follow them home.
From Norway to Mexico to the US, several prominent Diaspora Jews told The Jerusalem Post they are “terrified” that the outcome could deepen the conflation of Israel’s government with Jews worldwide, leaving them to bear the fallout of decisions they did not make.
Robert Hercz, the head of B’nai B’rith Norway, told the Post that he has been closely following the elections and is “terrified: not only for the future of Israel, but also for how the election will affect Jewry worldwide.”
“The world - and especially the European countries - are disproportionately [pre]occupied with Israeli politics - and much of what we get served in the media is oversimplified and polarized. And governments and politicians need to feed their Israel-bashing voter bases.”
This means that if Netanyahu wins, Hercz continued, “the politicians and the media in our parts of the world will go crazy, which in turn will have extremely negative consequences for us Jews living outside Israel.”
Israel-Norway relations will not improve while Netanyahu in office
Regarding Norway, Hercz opined that Israel-Norway relations will not improve as long as Netanyahu is in office.
“Not necessarily because of the politics in Israel, but because the Norwegian government and institutions are so over-invested in anti-Netanyahu rhetoric that they will not be able to move over to a different relationship and policy until Netanyahu is no longer in office,” he added.
Mark Freedman has spent 43 years working as a Jewish communal professional. He has also served as North American board chair of the Pardes Institute of Jewish Studies, and chairs the board of Amiti, a US-based nonprofit that works primarily in Israel to help CEOs of Israeli NGOs.
He told the Post that “The sands have shifted beneath our feet.”
“In the past, lay leadership primarily took a neutral role in how it viewed the Israeli government and the elections that created that government.”
“I think the main change now is the emergence of an old form of antisemitism that has renewed itself, the one that deems Jews in North America to somehow have collective responsibility for the actions of the Israeli government.”
“So that naturally makes one feel that [Diaspora Jews] have more of a stake in the outcome of the elections.”
He gave examples of how Israeli domestic politics filters into the Diaspora.
“A lot of it plays out in local elections, where you see discussions about Israel that you’ve never seen before. Local municipalities are now adopting resolutions that are criticizing Israel as racist and genocidal. That would have been unheard of 15, 20 years ago.”
“So naturally this filters down to the local level.”
Freedman does believe that the outcome of the elections could have an impact on global antisemitism, and that a new government could lead to an “incremental shift” in a positive direction.
“If there’s a government in Israel that is willing to align itself with what we view as traditional values in terms of law enforcement, in terms of equal participation in society, that would have an impact certainly on American views.”
He added that, on a personal level, “it’s really heartbreaking,” to see the divisions and issues inside Israel.
“There is so much positive about Israel, as a Jewish state and beyond that as a democratic state, and that’s at risk right now,” Freedman told the Post.
“I think that people in the United States who follow Israeli politics and who care about Israel as a Jewish homeland are just deeply concerned. So tomorrow’s election will have a great deal of impact on the way that the perception will be formed going forward.”
Netanyahu's international image is 'permanent flashpoint'
Arielle Shturman Waiss is a physician from Mexico City and the founder of ConCiencia Project, a science-based sexual and reproductive health education initiative. She leads health programming in the humanitarian aid sector and is active in Jewish communal life in Mexico and the international Jewish world.
She told the Post that Netanyahu’s international image is a “permanent flashpoint” and that “regardless of context, he ends up embodying everything perceived as wrong with Israeli political leadership.”
This perception, by immediate extension, attaches to Jews in the Diaspora, Shturman Waiss added, “because the ability to distinguish between what is Israeli, what is Jewish, and what is legitimate criticism of a government keeps eroding in public debate.”
“For those of us living in the Diaspora, the problem is more specific: his electoral victory imposes a presumption of consensus on us. It is assumed that we endorse his actions and his radical style of leadership, and that we do so by choice. Because he reached power through a democratic process, that presumption becomes nearly impossible to dismantle; any nuance we try to introduce reads as an excuse.”
“But a citizenry’s vote in a complex parliamentary structure is not a mandate over the identity of an entire people,” she stressed.
Israel events affect Diaspora Jews more since October 7
“Whatever happens in Israel reaches us in Jewish communities worldwide,” Venezuelan national and founder of Tikkun Talks, Deborah Apeloig, told the Post.
“That has always been true, but since October 8, 2023, we have seen it and felt it with a different intensity.”
Apeloig spoke of October 8 deliberately, as she says this day marked the moment the narrative “began shifting against Israel, even as we were still trying to comprehend the massacre.”
She added that, as a Venezuelan Jew working across Latin America, she has felt “how quickly events in Israel become judgments about Jews everywhere.”
“Too often, the Israel presented to the world is reduced to black and white. Its complexity, humanity and diversity disappear behind headlines, political statements and social media narratives better known as “TikTok University”. Through Tikkun Talks, I work to reach beyond our echo chamber, build bridges and repair the world, one conversation at a time.”
Apeloig told the Post she has received hundreds and thousands of meaningful messages from non-Jewish people whose perspectives have shifted, alongside comments “demonizing Netanyahu or using inflammatory statements by Ben-Gvir and Smotrich to condemn an entire country and Jews collectively.”
Echoing the words of Shturman Waiss, she said it can feel like we take one step forward in building bridges, and a “radical politician’s words send us 10 steps backward.”
“Those politicians are responsible for their words; the people spreading antisemitism are responsible for theirs. But we in the Diaspora live with the consequences of both.”
Because of this, she said the elections are of great importance to her, even though she cannot vote.
“The decisions belong to Israeli citizens, but their impact reaches far beyond Israel’s borders.”
“I’m hopeful as I watch Israeli democracy unfold, and I hope the outcome brings leadership that strengthens Israel, helps heal its divisions, and builds a brighter future for the Jewish people worldwide,” she concluded.

According to reports received by ACRI, voters were being processed unusually slowly, with long queues forming at numerous polling stations. The association expressed concern that the delays may not be accidental and could undermine Israeli Arab citizens’ ability to exercise their right to vote in Tuesday’s election.
Reports came from numerous localities, including Rahat, Tel Sheva, Laqiya, Segev Shalom, Abu Tulul, Umm Batin, Iksal, Jaljulya, Kafr Kara, Jisr e-Zarka, Kafr Manda, Ar’ara BaNegev, Tamra, Kafr Kanna, Tira, and Daburiya.
Ra’am said that police, coordinating with Otzma Yehudit representatives, had been preventing voters from entering polling stations
Ra'am says Israeli police coordinating with Otzma Yehudit representatives, prevent voters entering polling stations
Ra’am released footage it said showed police officers coordinating and cooperating with representatives of the Otzma Yehudit party at a polling station in the Bedouin town of Hura in the Negev.
According to the party, the Right had been conducting a systematic campaign against Ra’am, fearing that it could secure eight Knesset seats, a result it said could enable the formation of an alternative coalition of 61 MKs and bring down the Right.
Ra’am added that police had taken control of polling stations in Ar’ara BaNegev following a power outage at the site and were preventing voters from entering.
Israeli officers reportedly delay Arab voting in Segev Shalom
One incident was reported at Segev Shalom High School, where large numbers of police officers and Border Police’s National Guard personnel were reportedly preventing voters from entering the polling station compound, citing the need to manage overcrowding.
However, according to the report, only a small number of voters were inside the compound, while approximately 200 people had been waiting outside the school for an extended period as officers blocked their entry.
ACRI warned that without immediate intervention, the delays could prevent large numbers of Arab voters from exercising their right to vote.
The Adalah Legal Center for Arab Minority Rights in Israel also issued an appeal to the CEC on Tuesday, demanding that Arabic-language ballot slips be urgently delivered to polling stations following reports of a lack of Arab-language ballot slips at various polling stations.
Segev Shalom and Ar’ara BaNegev residents arrested for bribery
On Monday, the eve of Election Day, three Bedouin residents from the Segev Shalom and Ar’ara BaNegev communities were arrested for allegedly attempting to bribe voters to choose Ra’am.
The case was transferred to Lahav 433 on Tuesday.
“Three suspects were arrested in possession of envelopes containing cash, along with ballots for [Ra’am party leader] Mansour Abbas,” Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said, calling for a formal investigation into the incident.
Suspects transferred to Southern District Fraud Unit ahead of court hearing
The suspects were transferred to the Southern District’s Fraud Unit for questioning and are expected to be brought before a court today.
Reportedly, the suspects were detained just hours before the polls opened. Israel Police said it had seized, from their homes, envelopes containing tens of thousands of shekels in cash, notes, and additional items likely connected to the investigation.
In response, Ra’am said in a statement, “We categorically reject attempts by elements within the police to link Ra’am to the compromising of electoral integrity.”

A 4-watt video link passed Ukraine’s state tests, its maker says, and could stretch STING interceptors’ radius from 20 km to 30 km
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
12:46:13 UTC
21:46:13 KST

A new video transmitter for Wild Hornets’ drones, including its STING interceptors, has passed state tests, the Ukrainian drone maker told Militarnyi. The module sends a drone’s camera feed to its pilot. The company expects it to widen its interceptors’ operating radius.
Russia launched 140 Shahed-type drones at Ukraine overnight on 26 October and 280 the next night, when its main target was Kyiv, Air Force figures as of the morning show. Interceptor drones, which cost dozens of times less than the Shaheds they hunt, are one of Ukraine’s answers. The STING alone downed more than 3,000 drones in its first seven months of use, Wild Hornets says. If the company’s estimate holds, a 30 km radius would let each ground station cover more than twice the area it covers at 20 km.
What the testers checked
Specialists from the State Research Institute for Testing and Certification of Arms and Military Equipment and the Defense Ministry’s State Quality Assurance Directorate confirmed the module’s declared characteristics on three drone types, the company said. The three were the STING interceptor, the Queen of Hornets cargo platform, and the 10-inch Wild Hornets Digital anti-aircraft drone.
Some of the drones’ figures exceeded the values the company had set for them, Wild Hornets told Ukrainian defense outlet Oboronka, without saying which ones. Those figures will enter the official specifications after further field tests, it said.
More than double the power
The module, called HV VTX Pro, is part of an upgrade to Wild Hornets’ Hornet Vision digital video system. It more than doubles the transmitter’s maximum power, to 4 W. That sends a clear picture farther and makes the feed steadier in crowded airwaves and under electronic jamming, the company said.
Wild Hornets first described the module in August, when it was already in serial production. Its interceptors’ operating radius would grow from around 20 km to 30 km, the company said at the time. That estimate assumed good line of sight and the 360-degree antenna on its ground stations, according to a company statement Interfax-Ukraine quoted. Interception could also become at least 20% more effective against targets flying extremely low, the statement said.
Wild Hornets is a Ukrainian company that designs and builds drones, from strike FPV drones and cargo platforms to the STING, which the company says flies at up to 280 km/h to hunt Shaheds. Its drones serve with more than 100 units of Ukraine’s Defense Forces, from the army and the National Guard to military intelligence, the Air Force, and the border guard, according to Interfax-Ukraine.

Meni Liberty on one side, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz on the other, over whether to continue the operation in Hebron.

'What are they hiding?': UK MP slams Israel's West Bank ban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
12:43:29 UTC
21:43:29 KST

Breadcrumb
'What are they hiding?': SNP MP describes Israeli 'psychological aggression' after West Bank entry ban
Israeli authorities barred a delegation of European politicians and campaigners from entering the occupied West Bank on Monday, detaining its members for eight hours before sending them back to Jordan, SNP MP Lara Bird told The New Arab.
Bird said Israel was deliberately preventing international observers from witnessing its actions against Palestinians, questioning what the authorities were trying to conceal as settler violence and military raids intensify across the occupied Palestinian territory.
"What is abundantly clear is that there is still a very systematic and intentional effort to stop people from coming into the West Bank to witness what is going on in the illegally occupied West Bank," Bird told The New Arab.
"And that’s the thing that needs to be discussed – not our experiences of being denied entry, but what it is that they are so terrified of people seeing."
The Progressive International delegation had travelled to the region to meet Palestinian farmers, students, academics and civil society organisations, and to participate in the annual olive harvest, which has been targeted by escalating Israeli settler attacks.
The delegation included Labour MP Clive Lewis, Scottish Green MSP Kate Nevens, Spanish senator Josu Estarrona Elizondo of the Basque EH Bildu party, and former Labour MP Sam Tarry.
Bird said the group attempted to enter the West Bank through the Allenby Bridge crossing from Jordan but were detained, interrogated and refused entry "with no justification".
"Everyone is safe, which is important, but it wasn’t a particularly pleasant experience," she told The New Arab after returning to Jordan.
Israeli authorities took delegates to a separate section of the crossing and confiscated their passports.
"Within three minutes, they knew a lot of information about me," she said. "Some people were harassed, shouted at, there was a lot of manipulation – a lot of psychological aggression," Bird added, describing the ordeal as traumatic for several members of the delegation.
Lewis also condemned Israel's decision to prevent the delegation from entering the occupied territory, saying its members had travelled to show solidarity with Palestinians following Israel's genocidal war on Gaza.
"What’s happening here in Palestine is unjust. We’ve just witnessed what Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and many others have called a genocide unfold in Gaza," he said.
"We came here to show the world, and to show solidarity with the Palestinian people. The Israeli government didn’t allow that."
Palestinian olive harvest under attack
The delegation's exclusion comes as Israeli military restrictions and escalating settler attacks deprive thousands of Palestinian farmers of access to their land during the annual olive harvest, a vital source of income and a longstanding symbol of Palestinian attachment to their land.
Palestinian communities have reported attacks involving live ammunition, arson, the destruction of centuries-old olive trees and the theft of harvested olives and agricultural equipment.
Israeli settlers have carried out attacks under the protection of, and in some cases alongside, Israeli forces, as Palestinians face mounting pressure on their land and livelihoods.
The United Nations has described attacks on the olive harvest as "yet another tool of displacement and dispossession".
"We know that violence and demolitions and crackdowns are happening more and more in the West Bank, and that experiences of Palestinians in the West Bank are getting more and more horrific," Bird said.
She also warned that the detention and exclusion of international observers and NGO workers was becoming increasingly normalised, further restricting outside scrutiny of Israel's occupation.
Erik Edman, political director of the left-wing European political alliance DiEM25, said the delegation had intended to meet Palestinian farmers facing attacks on their own land, alongside students, academics and civil society organisations living under Israeli occupation.
"This is an attempt to isolate Palestinians and intimidate those who stand with them. It will fail," he said. "European governments must stop supplying the weapons and diplomatic protection that allow this violence to continue."

Israeli elections offer little hope of change, MP warns
The incident took place on the eve of Israel's parliamentary elections, with Bird warning that a change of government would not necessarily bring an end to the occupation, settlement expansion or violence against Palestinians.
She rejected the portrayal of Netanyahu's political opponents as a meaningful alternative for Palestinians, arguing that support for Israel's settlement project extends beyond the prime minister's governing coalition.
"With the Israeli elections going on today, there is a false picture being painted that the opposition to Netanyahu’s party is more left-leaning, is more centrist, could be a better alternative or solution to the occupation and apartheid," Bird told The New Arab.
"But that is completely untrue because both parties have made it clear that they agree that settlers should be allowed to rage terror and violence in the occupied West Bank and they believe in the expansion of settlements."
Bird called for sustained international pressure on Israel regardless of the outcome of Tuesday's vote, warning against allowing a change in leadership to divert attention from the treatment of Palestinians.

Otherwise, she warned, "we risk completely eliminating the Palestinian people, their culture, their history, their right to be on their land".

Months-old US startup accessed Anthropic’s sensitive data in under 12 hours: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
12:41:58 UTC
21:41:58 KST

Berk Kutay Gökmen
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
A cybersecurity startup gained access to sensitive internal data at artificial intelligence company Anthropic in less than 12 hours, according to a report by The Washington Post .
Cathedral, a months-old startup founded by former members of the US Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), identified vulnerabilities in third-party business software used by Anthropic, the maker of the Claude chatbot, according to a draft report reviewed by the newspaper.
The researchers used AI agents to find pathways into Anthropic’s internal systems, gaining access to meeting transcripts, salary and job offer details, and Slack messages discussing advanced AI models, the report said.
The testing was conducted under a program that allows outside cybersecurity researchers to probe Anthropic’s systems for vulnerabilities.
Anthropic confirmed that Cathedral accessed a “limited set” of its sales, human resources and IT systems. 
The company said it had closed the exposed pathways and briefed federal officials about the incident.
An Anthropic spokesperson said Cathedral had spent several days attempting to breach the company’s own software before turning to third-party business tools.
A senior Trump administration official reportedly said the report had circulated within the government and prompted concern over the speed with which the startup accessed sensitive systems.
The official warned that the findings raised questions about whether foreign intelligence agencies could exploit similar weaknesses.

Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Guo Jiakun’s Regular Press Conference on October 27, 2026
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:41:29 CST

CCTV: Themed on “Justice and Peace for All Humanity,” the photo exhibition commemorating the 80th anniversary of the Tokyo Trials was held at the UN headquarters yesterday, with the participation of diplomats from various countries, officials from different international organizations and people of various sectors. What’s your comment?
Guo Jiakun: The Tokyo Trials hold great historical significance and relevance. This photo exhibition brings together a large number of photographs and archives of the Tokyo Trials depicting the true history of Japan’s militarist aggression and the wartime crimes to the international community. The United Nations was born out of humanity’s reflection on the devastation of war, therefore it fully serves the international community’s common pursuit of remembering history and cherishing peace to hold the exhibition in the UN.
The Tokyo Trials constitute a historic trial in which peace subdued violence and justice prevailed over evil. The Trials are an integral part of the postwar international order. Recognizing and accepting the judgement of the Tokyo Trials is the prerequisite for Japan’s postwar return to the international community. Eighty years on, however, it is alarming that Japan’s right-wing forces still defy the historic verdict of the Tokyo Trials and try every possible means to deny and whitewash the crimes of aggression, promote a distorted view of history, and brazenly worship war criminals as “gods.” The international community should jointly push back against these trends. The lessons of history are still fresh in memory. Anyone who undermines peace and challenges righteousness and conscience is bound to be brought once again before the court of history and justice.
As an important force in the World Anti-Fascist War, China stands ready to work with all peace-loving nations and peoples around the world to carry forward the belief in the rule of law and peace, firmly safeguard the truth of history, uphold the postwar international order, and defend international fairness and justice.
AFP: French football star Kylian Mbappé was dropped today by a few major brands in China, after a video circulated online in which he apparently joked about China. I wonder if the foreign ministry has a comment on this incident.
Guo Jiakun: We noted relevant reports. Any rhetoric or action that hurts the feelings of the Chinese people will naturally be rejected across the sectors in China.
Xinhua News Agency: We have noted a security alert issued by the Chinese embassy in the UK advising Chinese citizens to be aware of recent practices in UK border checks. Could you offer more information on this?
Guo Jiakun: Recently, the Chinese Foreign Ministry and the Chinese embassy in the UK have received multiple reports of Chinese citizens being held and examined for extended hours by the UK police when entering and exiting the country, with their electronic devices including mobile phones seized. The Chinese side strongly deplores and is gravely concerned about the UK police’s arbitrary and excessive law enforcement actions. We have lodged serious démarches with the UK and will take all necessary measures to keep Chinese citizens safe and protect their legitimate and lawful rights and interests. We would like to remind Chinese citizens planning to travel to the UK to read carefully the embassy’s alert to avoid any inconvenience or loss.
The Paper: The situation in the Middle East and the Gulf region has been evolving rapidly. The conflict in Yemen and the Red Sea remains highly intense. And there are reports suggesting that the United States and Israel might resume military operations against Iran. What is China’s comment?
Guo Jiakun: China closely follows the developments in the Middle East, the Gulf region, the Red Sea and the Horn of Africa, and expresses deep concerns over the protracted conflicts and their spillover effects. We call on relevant parties to resolve their disputes through dialogue and negotiation and realize lasting ceasefire and cessation of hostilities at an early date. China is committed to promoting peace talks. Our special envoys will soon travel to regional countries to strengthen communication with the relevant parties and promote engagement, dialogue and deescalation to prevent the worsening of the situation. Guided by the initiatives and propositions put forward by President Xi Jinping on promoting peace and security in the Middle East, China will work together with the international community to make unremitting efforts for the early realization of peace and stability in relevant regions.
AFP: U.S. President Donald Trump claimed on Monday that Brazil’s elections were rigged after incumbent Lula’s win. I wonder if the foreign ministry has a comment on what Trump said.
Guo Jiakun: We respect the independent choice of the Brazilian people.
Bloomberg: The European Union is planning potential trade measures that could be proposed early next year to cut imports of chemicals, furniture and machinery from China, people familiar with the matter told Bloomberg. Does the foreign ministry have any comment on this?
Guo Jiakun: As far as China is concerned, the relationship with the EU is essentially a partnership, and the economic and trade ties are mutually beneficial. The success of the recent second meeting of the China-EU Trade and Investment Consultation fully proves that the two sides can properly handle differences in economy and trade through dialogue and consultation. It is in the interest of both sides to step up dialogue and consultation and deepen economic and trade cooperation on the basis of mutual respect, which is also the shared expectation of the business community and people of both sides. It is hoped that the EU will abide by the principles of market economy and fair competition, avoid abusing trade remedies, and take concrete actions to promote the steady and sound development of China-EU relations.

TikTok parent company founder tops China's rich list amid AI boom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
12:40:02 UTC
21:40:02 KST

Zhang Yiming has reclaimed his position as China's richest person, with a €89.4 billion fortune driven by AI, as the country's technology sector booms while traditional industries struggle.
TikTok parent company ByteDance's founder Zhang Yiming has reclaimed his position as China's richest person, fuelled by the company's expansion into artificial intelligence.
Zhang topped the Hurun Report's rich list with a fortune of $100 billion (€89.4bn), up 43%, “almost all of it on the back of AI,” according to its chairman, Rupert Hoogewerf.
“AI is the biggest single wealth engine on this list: 160 Hurun rich listers — 1 in 10 — now make their money from AI,” he added.
The Hurun Research Institute, which has published the ranking annually since 1999, identified a record 1,529 individuals with fortunes exceeding 5 billion yuan (€645mn), up 6.6% from last year.
China now has 1,176 billionaires, up 155 from last year and 176 more than the US, although still below its 2021 peak of 1,185.
The ranking comes as China's economy grew 4.5% year-on-year in the third quarter, supported by strong exports, while weak domestic demand and a prolonged property downturn continued to weigh on growth.
“This year’s gains were polarised — entrepreneurs in AI, semiconductors and robotics surged ahead, whilst those in consumer, real estate and traditional manufacturing saw their wealth shrink — a two-speed economy,” Hoogewerf said.
The property sector's struggles were also reflected in the ranking. For the first time, no mainland Chinese property developer featured among the 100 richest people, with only Hong Kong property-owning families remaining at the top.

Parliament backed a 50% tax on banks’ profits in 2027: how much the budget will receive and what risks the economy faces
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:38:51 EET
21:38:51 KST

Parliament backed a 50% tax on banks’ profits in 2027: how much the budget will receive and what risks the economy faces
Kyiv • UNN
A total of 265 MPs voted for the bill. The additional more than UAH 50 billion is planned to be allocated to security and defense, but banks warn of risks to lending.
The Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine adopted as a basis a bill providing for the extension into 2027 of the increased 50% corporate income tax rate for banks. This was reported by UNN , citing official information from the Ukrainian parliament.
A total of 265 Members of Parliament voted in favor of the decision. The additional budget revenues are planned to be allocated to security and defense needs. At the same time, representatives of the banking sector warn of possible negative consequences for lending to the economy
What the bill provides for
This concerns Bill No. 15262, "On Amendments to the Tax Code of Ukraine Regarding the Specifics of Taxation of Banks with Corporate Income Tax," registered on May 20, 2026.
The document provides for extending into the following year the increased 50% corporate income tax rate for banking institutions. Thus, if the law is finally adopted, banks will continue to pay tax at the rate already applied in 2026. In addition, the bill prohibits banks from reducing their pre-tax financial result by the amount of losses accumulated in previous tax periods.
At the same time, the possibility of taking such losses into account is to be restored from January 1, 2028. This means that during 2027, banks will not be able to use losses from previous years to reduce taxable profit.
The stated purpose of the legislative initiative is to increase state budget revenues to finance the needs of the security and defense sector amid a full-scale war. The document was initiated by a group of Members of Parliament, including Danylo Hetmantsev, chair of the parliamentary Committee on Finance, Tax and Customs Policy.
On June 16, the relevant committee recommended that the Verkhovna Rada adopt the bill as a basis and as a whole, subject to the necessary technical and legal refinement.
How much additional money is planned to be raised from banks
According to estimates by the Ministry of Finance, extending the increased taxation of banks could provide more than UAH 50 billion in additional revenues to the consolidated budget based on the results of the 2027 tax periods. The funds will be received over two budget years.
In particular, in 2027, the Ministry of Finance forecasts additional revenues of UAH 37.8 billion, of which UAH 34 billion is expected to go to the state budget and another UAH 3.8 billion to local budgets. In 2028, an additional UAH 12.6 billion is expected, including UAH 11.4 billion for the state budget and UAH 1.2 billion for local budgets.
In addition, the materials accompanying the draft State Budget for 2027 provide for UAH 38.5 billion in revenues from corporate income tax paid by banks for the first three quarters of the following year, provided the 50% rate is extended.
At the same time, the parliamentary Budget Committee noted that the bill was not accompanied by the financial and economic justification, with the relevant calculations, required by the Budget Code and the Rules of Procedure of the Verkhovna Rada.
Why the authorities insist on increased taxation
One of the main arguments of supporters of extending the increased rate remains the profitability of Ukraine's banking sector. Parliamentary Finance Committee Chair Danylo Hetmantsev previously explained the need for such a decision by the specific features of how banks generate profits during wartime.
According to him, banking institutions also receive a significant portion of their income from transactions involving certificates of deposit issued by the National Bank and domestic government bonds. These instruments enable banks to earn income with a relatively low level of risk compared with conventional lending. Hetmantsev emphasized that the state, which ensures the functioning of the relevant financial mechanisms, has the right to expect additional revenues from the banking sector amid significant defense expenditures.
"The state is taking away from banks part of this profit, which will go toward financing the army," Hetmantsev said in June 2026.
The parliamentarian also drew attention to the high profitability of bank capital in Ukraine compared with European indicators.
The NBU and the banking sector warn of risks
Despite the expected budgetary effect, the continuation of increased taxation met with objections from representatives of the financial sector.
The National Bank of Ukraine had repeatedly drawn attention to the risks associated with increasing the corporate income tax on banks to 50%. In particular, in its December 2025 Financial Stability Report, the regulator noted that the increased tax burden limits banks’ ability to expand their operations and negatively affects the investment attractiveness of the financial sector.
The NBU identified the possible complication of privatizing state-owned banks as a separate risk. In the regulator’s view, excessive profit extraction may also limit financial institutions’ ability to accumulate capital.
In June 2026, several professional and business associations immediately came out against Draft Law No. 15262. Thus, the Association of Ukrainian Banks, the National Association of Banks of Ukraine, the Confederation of Builders of Ukraine, the Association of Ukrainian Veteran Entrepreneurs, the League of Insurance Organizations of Ukraine, and the Ukrainian Chamber of Commerce and Industry appealed to parliament, calling on it not to support the proposed changes.
Representatives of these organizations warned that the prolonged application of the increased rate could negatively affect lending to businesses, investment activity, and the development of veteran-owned businesses. The Association of Ukrainian Banks also cited estimates according to which UAH 20–25 billion in capital could potentially provide UAH 200–300 billion in lending resources for the economy.
How the decision could affect businesses and depositors
For citizens directly, the draft law does not provide for the introduction of new taxes on bank deposits, card accounts, or credit transactions. The increased rate applies specifically to the profits of banking institutions, not to their customers’ funds.
At the same time, banking market experts draw attention to possible indirect consequences.
Profit is one of the sources of banks’ capital replenishment. The ability of financial institutions to expand lending while complying with established prudential requirements depends, among other things, on the amount of this capital. Accordingly, a reduction in the profit remaining at banks’ disposal could potentially limit their ability to finance new projects. This could primarily concern lending to small and medium-sized businesses, the restoration of damaged infrastructure, residential construction, and investment in energy resilience.
At the same time, a tax increase does not automatically mean that loans will become more expensive or that all lending programs will be reduced. The actual consequences will depend on the financial condition of individual banks, demand for loans, the cost of raising funds, credit risks, and the policy of the National Bank.
How bank taxation has changed in Ukraine
Increased taxation of the banking sector has been applied in Ukraine for several years already. In 2023, the Verkhovna Rada established a 50% corporate income tax rate for banks for the first time. The decision was explained by the need to obtain additional budgetary resources amid the war and the high profitability of financial institutions.
In 2024, the same rate was applied again. In 2025, banks paid corporate income tax at a rate of 25%, but at the end of the year parliament returned to the issue of increasing the tax burden.
On December 3, 2025, the Verkhovna Rada adopted a law providing for the application of a 50% rate throughout 2026.
Recall
Somewhat earlier, NBU Governor Andriy Pyshnyi stated that a third increase in bank taxation would have serious negative consequences. He considers the initiative dangerous because it undermines trust in the tax system.

Air Force Spokesperson: Russian forces launch several ballistic missile strikes on Pivdenny Bridge in Kyiv
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:36:43 EET
21:36:43 KST

During the latest attack, Russian forces launched several ballistic missile strikes against the Southern Bridge (Pivdenny) in Kyiv. While such structures are not easily destroyed, repairing the damaged bridge deck will take time, Yuriy Ihnat, a spokesperson for the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, stated during a televised marathon on Tuesday.
"Of course, the bridge deck can be repaired—bridges are not as easy to destroy as some might think. Nevertheless, this does cause certain inconveniences, and repairs will take time," Ihnat said.
According to him, the adversary employed 16 ballistic missiles—either Iskander-M missiles or S-400 surface-to-air guided missiles—during the recent attack. Specialists examining the impact site will determine the exact type of missiles used. "The adversary used two types of missiles today: either Iskander-M or S-400 surface-to-air missiles," the spokesperson noted.
Ihnat emphasized that over the past two weeks, Russian forces have focused their missile strikes on Kyiv, launching ballistic missiles in several waves throughout the night and combining them with drone attacks.
"Previously, ballistic missile strikes might have occurred just once a night. Now, they are spread out over several waves of attacks... They launch these strikes in waves, and all of this is accompanied by drone attacks," he said.
As previously reported, Taras Chmut, head of the Come Back Alive foundation and a military analyst, stated in an interview with DW that the complete destruction of bridges in Kyiv by Russian shelling is a possibility, provided the adversary is willing to commit significant resources. At the same time, he noted that destroying a single section of a bridge does not necessarily lead to the collapse of the entire structure; the critical issue remains how quickly a crossing can be restored, at least in some capacity. According to him, even partial damage to bridges could severely complicate urban logistics, particularly the operation of the metro system and public transport.
"I wouldn't rule out such a scenario; if the Russians are determined enough and willing to expend the necessary resources, they could certainly do it," he emphasized.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported that on Tuesday, the enemy struck the Pivdenny Bridge in Kyiv, damaging metro infrastructure located on the span.
Kyiv Metro has temporarily suspended service between Osokorky and Chervony Khutir stations on the green line due to the damage to infrastructure on the Pivdenny Bridge. Furthermore, with the Pivdenny Bridge closed, both freight and passenger vehicle traffic have been diverted along alternative routes.
