General Assembly weighs US embargo against Cuba ahead of 34th vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

General Assembly weighs US embargo against Cuba ahead of 34th vote
The General Assembly opened its annual debate on the US economic embargo against Cuba on Tuesday. On Wednesday, 28 October, Member States will vote for the 34th time on a resolution calling for it to end.
Every year at around this time, the assembly – where each of the UN’s 193 Member States has one vote – takes up the “necessity of ending the economic, commercial and financial embargo imposed by the United States of America against Cuba”.
And every year, whatever the political climate, the issue generates plenty of diplomatic heat. The debate usually spills over two days as countries and regional groups take the floor to explain their positions.
A 33-vote record
The assembly has called for an end to the embargo, first imposed in 1960, on 33 previous occasions.
Support has grown markedly since the first vote in 1992, when 59 countries backed the resolution, three opposed it, 71 abstained and 46 did not vote.
It peaked at 191 votes in favour in 2015, 2016 and 2017, during the thaw in relations under US President Barack Obama. The United States and Israel voted against in 2015 and 2017; in 2016, both abstained.
Some countries have shifted position as governments have changed, but many have held the same line for decades. Canada, China and Russia have long voted in favour, while the United States, backed by Israel, has voted against every year bar one.
A tightening squeeze
This year’s debate comes as the Trump administration has tightened the embargo – a move that has led to an energy crisis and possible humanitarian collapse, according to the UN Resident Coordinator in Cuba, Francisco Pichon.
The World Health Organization (WHO) has also warned that energy shortages are taking a toll on health.
In May, senior UN officials reported that more than 100,000 surgical procedures had been postponed. Cuban authorities have repeatedly pointed to further damage to the health system, including delays to vaccination programmes and patients with chronic illnesses unable to get a stable supply of medicines.
This year, President Donald Trump has also raised the possibility of military intervention in Cuba.
Successive UN High Commissioners for Human Rights and independent UN experts have condemned the embargo and other unilateral US sanctions, warning that they threaten Cubans’ rights to health, life, food and development.
Tensions spill over
Those tensions were on display in the chamber on Tuesday when Cuba’s Foreign Minister, Bruno Rodríguez Parrilla, interrupted the US Ambassador, Mike Waltz, on a point of order midway through his statement.
The exchange escalated into a heated row between the two, prompting the President of the General Assembly to briefly suspend the session. The debate later resumed without further incident.
Mr. Waltz rejected the premise of the debate, arguing that Cuba’s crisis was the fault of its own government, not the embargo.
“There is no blockade,” he said. If there were, he argued, there would be no explaining US exports to Cuba – which he put at more than $876 million in the first eight months of 2026 – or shipments from Canada, Spain, Mexico, China, Russia, the European Union and UN agencies.
The country’s wealth had not vanished, he said, but had “simply” passed from ordinary Cubans into the hands of the ruling elite.
Mr. Rodríguez is due to deliver his statement on Wednesday.
What the resolution says
As in previous years, the Cuban-drafted text reaffirms the sovereign equality of States and the principles of non-intervention and non-interference in their internal affairs, as well as freedom of international trade and navigation – all enshrined in numerous international legal instruments.
It also voices concern over laws such as the Helms-Burton Act, enacted by the United States on 12 March 1996, whose extraterritorial effects, it says, undermine the sovereignty of other States, the legitimate interests of people and entities under their jurisdiction and freedom of trade and navigation.
It calls on all States to refrain from adopting such measures and urges those that still apply them to repeal them.

The UN project services agency in the field (UNOPS) reported three incidents affecting its convoys and premises over three consecutive days in the past week alone.
Executive Director Jorge Moreira da Silva said these included close-proximity explosions, drivers detained at checkpoints, and multiple small-arms rounds striking one of the procurement agency’s guesthouses.
The safety of UNOPS staff has been compromised too many times, he said, stressing that all parties to the fighting in Gaza must uphold their obligations to protect civilians and humanitarian personnel.
Guterres condemns West Bank attacks
Meanwhile, Secretary-General António Guterres continues to express his deep alarm over the intensifying violence in the West Bank as an Israeli offensive in Hebron continues.
Associate Spokesperson Daniela Gross told journalists at the daily briefing in New York that the UN chief is following the situation there closely.
“He is deeply alarmed for this offensive…the intensifying violence in the West Bank. He condemns the violence. And he also firmly opposed the settler attacks in the region.”
Between January 2025 and the end of September 2026, 331 Palestinians, including 77 children, were killed in the West Bank, and more than 42,000 have been displaced, according to the UN aid coordination office. OCHA. Over the same period, 21 Israelis were killed in the West Bank.
OCHA also recorded 3,684 attacks by Israeli settlers during the period that resulted in casualties or property damage.
Flood risk
Despite restrictions and funding shortfalls, the UN and its partners continue to bring limited supplies into Gaza. On Monday, UN teams brought in food, blankets, winter clothes, school items and fuel, according to OCHA.
Over the past week, partners distributed school bags to more than 8,000 children. The week before, they provided stationery to about 22,000 boys and girls and furnished some 300 classrooms supporting around 60,000 children.
Many families are living in deteriorating tents and shelters with little protection from the cold, wind and rain. Around 950,000 people are living in displacement sites at medium to high risk of flooding, and stocks of supplies to support them are insufficient, a shelter assessment found.
Media under attack
Also on Tuesday, Francesca Albanese, the UN Special Rapporteur on the situation of human rights in the Palestinian territory occupied, briefed journalists virtually on her latest report, which focuses on the media.
She reminded reporters that she was unable to attend in person because of sanctions imposed on her by the United States.
According to Ms. Albanese, nearly 300 journalists and media workers have been killed in Gaza, citing UN sources, and more than 100 have been detained, many of them tortured.
Some 150 media centres and offices – 80 per cent of Gaza’s media infrastructure – have been destroyed, she said, while in the West Bank more than 139 attacks on journalists have recently been recorded.
She also criticized Israel’s ban on foreign journalists entering Gaza and said there had been no accountability for the killing of Palestinian journalist Shireen Abu Akleh.
“The update is impunity,” she said.
Her report also documents intimidation and repression of Palestinian journalists by Hamas in Gaza and the Palestinian Authority in the West Bank, she said.

Four in five domestic workers lack formal job protections, UN finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Four in five domestic workers lack formal job protections, UN finds
An estimated 66.5 million domestic workers – representing more than four out of five domestic workers worldwide – were informally employed in 2025, a new report by the UN’s labour organisation has found.
This makes them more than twice as likely as other employees to lack effective labour and social protection, making them more vulnerable to working anti-social hours on meagre pay.
Many of those being exploited are domestic workers who “make millions of lives possible,” ILO director Sahra Razavi, briefing journalists in Geneva on Tuesday.
Invisible, undervalued
“[They] clean our homes, prepare our meals, look after our children, care for older persons and support those with disabilities. […] And yet these workers often remain invisible. Their contribution is taken for granted, their work is undervalued,” she stressed.
An estimated 80 million domestic workers were employed worldwide in 2025, up from 75.6 million in 2019.
However, domestic work remained stable as a share of total employment at around 2.2 per cent, indicating that the increase largely reflects growth of overall employment rather than an expansion of the sector itself.
Regional variations
About half of domestic workers globally are located in Asia and the Pacific, and Africa saw the biggest surge in domestic workers since 2019 with an additional 4.2 million joining the sector.
Informal jobs lacking any benefits or protection remain particularly widespread in Africa, where 93.3 per cent of domestic workers are informally employed, and is “nearly universal” in the Arab States, according to the ILO.
Europe and Central Asia have the lowest regional informality rate, yet more than one in three domestic workers continue to be paid informally – which means they also contribute nothing in terms of tax on wages.
The ILO also stressed the gender dimension of the issue: women accounted for 77.2 per cent of domestic workers globally and were heavily concentrated in cleaning and care occupations.
Difficult hours and low pay
Wages are a major concern. Domestic workers earned on average just over half (53.3 per cent) of the monthly wages of other employees, falling to 48.7 per cent for those in informal employment, and the gap has been widening since 2019.
Domestic workers are also particularly vulnerable to extreme hours.
On one hand, many endured very long days. More than one-third of domestic workers worked at least 49 hours per week, while nearly 15 per cent worked 60 hours or more, the report found.
On the other hand, domestic workers were also more likely than other employees to work short hours for little pay, which can reflect underemployment and having to move between multiple households to make a living.
Some progress
Despite these grim figures, some progress has been noted. Among countries with comparable data, more than half have reduced informality among domestic workers since 2019.
40 countries have also ratified ILO Convention No. 189, which sets standards to ensure decent work for domestic workers.
Still, Ms Razavi stressed the need to increase the level of ratification – a formal commitment under international law to apply those standards – particularly in Asia and the Arab States where it is particularly low.
“Domestic work is work, and domestic workers deserve the same rights and the same protections as other workers,” said Ms Razavi, referencing the principles of the convention.

World News in Brief: ‘No safe place in Ukraine’, IAEA calls for Iran nuclear inspections, Kenya hosts thousands of Ethiopians fleeing clashes
The UN refugee agency (UNHCR) on Tuesday urged continued international support for Ukraine’s population as Russian airstrikes intensify and humanitarian needs grow in advance of another bitterly cold winter.
The “relentless” attacks are targeting critical energy infrastructure, leaving millions without heat and electricity, and limited access to water and other essentials.
“The increase in long-range missile and drone strikes means there is no safe place in Ukraine,” said UNHCR director, Philippe Leclerc, adding that humanitarian operations have also come under attack.
Evacuations continue
Between September and mid-October, several security incidents affected agency personnel and partners, aid facilities or clearly marked vehicles involved in relief efforts.
UNHCR said displacement within Ukraine is expected to continue as evacuations from frontline areas increase, while nearly 5.2 million Ukrainian civilians continue to live across Europe as refugees.
UN nuclear watchdog still unable to verify Iran’s nuclear material
The UN’s nuclear watchdog still cannot confirm that none of Iran’s safeguarded nuclear material has been diverted, its chief told the Security Council on Tuesday – more than a year after Israeli and US military strikes cut off inspectors’ access.
“This can and must be rectified,” said IAEA Director Genera Rafael Grossi, adding that we know from our past work with Iran that constructive engagement is possible.”
Inspectors have not been able to return to the sites hit by Israeli airstrikes in June 2025 and joint Israeli and US attacks in early 2026.
The agency has seen no sign of work to repair or rebuild them, Mr. Grossi said, but satellite monitoring is no substitute for access on the ground.
The one exception is the Bushehr nuclear power plant, where inspectors are currently at work.
Iran’s atomic energy agency has cooperated in delivering the safeguards equipment needed to verify spent fuel there before it is moved to dry storage, expected early next year, Mr. Grossi said.
Normal inspections on hold
Normal inspections have not resumed, and Iran has not provided the information and access needed to verify previously declared nuclear material at its safeguarded facilities – both those hit in the attacks and those that were not – the IAEA chief said.
Of particular concern is Iran’s declared stock of 440kg of highly enriched uranium. The agency is also seeking access to the Isfahan Fuel Enrichment Plant, which Iran declared just before the June 2025 strikes.
“Only diplomacy, underpinned by IAEA verification, can prevent nuclear proliferation in the long term,” Mr. Grossi said.

Kenyan authorities are at the fore of an emergency response plan to host more than 36,600 Ethiopian refugees who have fled escalating insecurity in the south, the UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) said on Tuesday.
Recent fighting has triggered waves of displacement following a decades-long battle between forces from southern Ethiopia’s Somali and Oromia regions over boundary demarcations and resources.
Thousands of displaced Ethiopians are living with host communities.
Rapid needs assessment
UN agencies have joined the Government-led response – assessing needs and providing emergency supplies and technical support – including the World Food Programme (WFP) and UN migration agency, IOM, together with UNHCR.
On Tuesday, UNICEF in Kenya said therapeutic nutrition supplies had been delivered to a local hospital and the agency is supporting malnutrition screening, infant and young child feeding, safe water and hygiene services.
UNICEF has also provided four 10,000-litre water tanks and hygiene kits for about 1,000 households, alongside additional nutrition and sanitation technical support.

‘No one saves the planet if it hits their pocket’: UK heat pump installers fear planned subsidy cuts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:59:42 UTC
20:59:42 KST

When Bill Tuck first started installing air source heat pumps six years ago, other heating engineers were skeptical about whether the green technology would take off. “Now, the conversation is completely different,” he said.
“I’m getting approached by them saying: ‘Mrs Jones, my customer for 15 years, she’s enquiring about a heat pump. What can you tell me?’ The whole narrative has changed.”
But despite a surge in interest in cheap and sustainable ways to warm homes, the government is understood to be slashing the amount of money available to subsidise heat pumps as it looks for ways to cut spending in Wednesday’s budget.
Businesses that install the renewable systems are fearing the worst. “It’s going to damage us as a company,” said Tuck, the operations director at Sustain Homes in Watford. About 75% of his customers pay for their pump using the government subsidies. “It’s the foundation of the business. If that’s to go, it’s extremely damaging.
“Of course, we will do what it takes to keep everybody’s jobs going and the business afloat. But it’s a tough one – I don’t know how we will do that.”
The boiler upgrade scheme (BUS) was introduced in 2022 to help people decarbonise their homes and businesses. It provides upfront grants worth up to £9,000 to help property owners replace fossil fuel and direct electric heating systems with low-carbon alternatives such as heat pumps and biomass boilers.
Heat in buildings is responsible for approximately nearly a fifth of the UK’s greenhouse gas emissions, the latest government data shows. The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero has described the 2020s as a “critical decade for decarbonising heat”, but now appears to be putting the cost of decarbonising on to the consumer. The UK lags far behind other European countries with heat pump installation; Norway, the global leader, has 632 installed for every 1,000 households, while the UK has a paltry 3.5.
Jim Lacey, who has been installing renewables with his business JLN Plumbing & Heating for 20 years, said: “No one’s going to save the planet if it really hits their pocket.”
“We can go in [to homes] now and go: ‘It’s a few hundred pound more than having a normal boiler, but you save so much on your energy usage.’ That whole argument’s gone.”
Adam Killa, the founder of Ask Renewables in Burscough, Lancashire, saw what happens when subsidies are removed after the 2022 closure of the Renewable Heat Incentive, a scheme that paid households for generating clean heat.
“As soon as that stopped, we went from doing six, seven, eight [installs] a week down to zero. The customers say: ‘Well, I know they’re good, but 15 grand – I can buy a new boiler for three grand. What’s the point?’
While the government continues its drive to increase numbers of young people earning while learning, heat pump installers say cuts to the subsidy will put their apprentices – and the future of the industry – are at risk.
“Unless we start bringing the young generation through, we’re going to have a huge lack of installers, repair engineers, and more importantly, heat pumps as well,” said Tuck.
A nascent industry, installers fear manufacturers will go under too. According to the Heat Pump Association, about a third of heat pumps sold in the UK in 2024 were produced domestically.
“This isn’t just down to us fitting the heat pumps, it’s the people delivering them, it’s the people manufacturing them, it’s all the associated trades that go with it that make the little bits, the little bobs, everything,” said Lacey. “There’s so many knock-on effects”
James Meadway, an economist and co-director of the green thinktank Verdant, said removing money from green jobs and manufacturing would damage Andy Burnham’s mission to effectively reindustrialise Britain. “It’s at a point where his blank spot on climate is working hard against other things he wants to do,” he said.
Lacey said that, while he had not thought the grant would last for ever, he had expected business and consumers to be weaned off gradually as the technology became more widespread and production costs fell. “But to suddenly axe some off the BUS grant or get rid of it completely is just catastrophic for all the work that we’ve put in so far,” he said.
A government spokesperson said: “We do not comment on budget speculation.
“We remain committed to bringing down bills for families now, while investing in the clean, homegrown energy and warmer homes that will protect households from volatile fossil fuel prices for good.”

India rejects ‘second-class’ permanent UN Security Council seats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:59:36 UTC
20:59:36 KST

India rejects ‘second-class’ permanent UN Security Council seats
India has demanded equal veto rights for all permanent members of an expanded United Nations Security Council (UNSC), warning that creating a second tier of permanent seats would reinforce existing inequalities in the global body. 
New Delhi opposes proposals for long-term membership without veto powers, which would create “second-class” members while preserving the authority of the existing five, India’s Permanent Representative to the UN, Harish Parvathaneni, said during talks about reforming the UN in New York on Monday.
The Security Council currently has five permanent members – Russia, China, the US, the UK, and France – with veto powers, alongside ten non-permanent members elected for two-year terms. The council’s only expansion, in 1965, increased the number of elected seats from six to ten without changing its permanent membership.
In 1997, the then-UN General Assembly President Razali Ismail of Malaysia proposed expanding the Council, including adding five more permanent members but without veto powers.
“Fairness and justice demand that all permanent members enjoy the same rights and responsibilities,” Parvathaneni said, reiterating that veto powers must extend to new permanent members as long as the system exists.
📹 No Second-Class Permanent Seats: India Demands Veto Parity In Reformed UN Security Council Ambassador P. Harish emphasized that New Delhi’s position remains firmly aligned with the Common African Position, insisting that basic fairness and justice demand identical rights and obligations for all permanent members.
— RT_India (@RT_India_news) October 27, 2026
The Asia-Pacific region accounts for more than 60% of the world’s population, but has only one permanent seat; Africa and Latin America remain without permanent representation. The African Union formally presented its reform model, which calls for at least two permanent UNSC seats for Africa, carrying veto rights, earlier this year.
India and its G4 partners – Brazil, Germany, and Japan – have also called for negotiations on expanding both permanent and non-permanent membership.
The reform push has received backing from Russia. Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov reaffirmed Moscow’s support for permanent seats for India and Brazil during the UN General Assembly in September, calling for greater representation of Asia, Africa, and Latin America.
Changes to the UN Charter would require ratification by two-thirds of UN members, including all five existing permanent members.

INTERVIEW – UN envoy likens spread of Islamophobia in Europe to 'metastasis'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:59:29 UTC
20:59:29 KST

- Moratinos urges stronger laws, education, monitoring to counter anti-Muslim hatred
- ‘You cannot close the door to the one who represents the whole of humanity,’ he says of Israel’s entry ban on UN chief
From threatening graffiti on mosques to attacks on worshippers, anti-Muslim hatred has left communities across Europe fearing for their safety. A deadly shooting near Paris on Friday has heightened those concerns.
The attack killed one person and injured five others, including a 12-year-old girl wearing a headscarf whose mother said she was shot eight times. Trappes Mayor Ali Rabeh described it as “objectively a racist attack, probably Islamophobic.”
Against that backdrop, the UN's envoy on Islamophobia warned that hostility toward Muslims was becoming embedded in Europe's political discourse and spreading through its institutions, likening its spread to a "metastasis."
“Europe, I think, is the most complicated case because Islamophobia has been introduced in the political discourse,” Miguel Angel Moratinos, the UN special envoy to combat Islamophobia, told Anadolu on the sidelines of the 9th Mediation Conference in Istanbul.
In England and Wales, police recorded 5,132 hate crimes targeting Muslims in the year ending March 2026, up 15% from the previous year, according to Home Office figures.
In Germany, monitoring organization CLAIM documented 4,096 anti-Muslim incidents in 2025, compared with 3,080 a year earlier. 
Its tally includes discrimination, threats and verbal abuse as well as physical violence, with two homicides and 214 cases of bodily injury.
“Normally in political elections you discuss economy, security, about the main concerns, but why we are discussing Islam? Why do we have to have this kind of concern about the Muslim communities?” he asked.
His concerns extend beyond Europe to the United States, Asia and parts of Africa.
In the US, President Donald Trump attacked Michigan's Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed at a rally Sunday, calling him a "jihadist" who was "on the side of terrorists" and suggesting he should face special security screening before entering the Senate.
El-Sayed, who would become the country's first Muslim senator if elected, accused Trump of mocking his name and faith to distract voters from the effects of the president's policies.
Moratinos urged governments to challenge rhetoric that normalizes hostility toward Muslim communities and turn commitments against discrimination into action.
Having recently visited France, the UK, Germany and Spain to encourage stronger institutional responses, he called for legal protections, investment in education and better monitoring of Islamophobic incidents. 
 
Challenging prejudice
Outlining steps to combat Islamophobia, Moratinos said governments should strengthen legal frameworks and invest heavily in education to challenge prejudice and misinformation.
“Most probably the reason people are anti-Muslim is because they are ignorant,” he said.
“They don't know what is Islam, they don't know what a Muslim community is, they have not been informed, they have not been educated in respecting each other,” he added.
He also called for “monitoring mechanisms” to collect reliable data on Islamophobic incidents, helping authorities identify the sources of discrimination and decide how to respond.
The UN International Day to Combat Islamophobia represents progress, he said, but awareness must lead to practical measures.
“The UN can do what it can, member states can do what they can, civil society has to engage, religious leaders – everybody has to contribute to eliminate this plague,” he said.
 
Rethinking the post-9/11 approach
Moratinos also questioned the emphasis on security that has shaped international policy since the Sept. 11, 2001 attacks.
Drawing on his experience as the EU’s special representative for the Middle East peace process from 1996 to 2003, he said the attacks marked a shift away from political engagement and negotiations.
“From 9-11, we changed the approach and we chose security,” he said. “And security has led us to this catastrophic situation.”
Prioritizing military and security objectives over dialogue had deepened instability across the Middle East, he argued.
“Because when you try to get more security, you are more insecure,” he said. “Security for Israel, security for Lebanon, security for the Gulf, security for Iran, security, security, security, and security brings war, brings instability.”
Moratinos called for a return to negotiations that take account of the interests, concerns and aspirations of all parties, warning that military force cannot substitute for political engagement.
 
‘The force of law’
Turning to Palestine and other conflicts, Moratinos defended the importance of international law, arguing that crises make upholding shared principles more urgent.
“If we lose our soul, if we lose our values, the international community will be lost,” he warned. “The force of law will be much more sustainable than the law of force.”
He also called for changes to the way the UN operates, pointing to the power of its five permanent Security Council members – China, France, Russia, the UK and the US – to block action through their vetoes.
Moratinos called for updated rules to ensure the UN secretary-general can pursue diplomacy worldwide without governments denying his entry.
He described Israel’s decision to bar UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres from entering the country as “unacceptable.”
“He is the Secretary-General. He has to be welcomed in any capital, at any moment,” he said. “You cannot close the door to the one who represents the whole of humanity.”

Foreign military personnel have been given until May 10, 2027, to apply for a residence permit. A three-month period will apply after the conclusion or termination of a contract.
The Ukrainian parliament extended the deadlines for processing residence permits for foreign military personnel. UNN reports this, citing the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine.
The new law adopted by the lawmakers establishes the rules for the lawful stay of military personnel after signing a contract and being discharged from service.
Details
On Tuesday, October 27, Parliament adopted as a basis and as a whole Draft Law No. 16094, "On Amendments to Certain Laws of Ukraine Concerning the Grounds for the Stay in Ukraine of Military Personnel Who Are Foreigners and Stateless Persons." The decision was supported by 282 members of parliament. No parliamentarian voted against it, while 26 more MPs did not vote.
The document concerns foreigners and stateless persons serving under contract in the Armed Forces of Ukraine, the National Guard, and the State Special Transport Service. According to the bill’s authors, the main purpose of the legislative changes is to eliminate the risk that service members could lose lawful grounds for staying in Ukraine because they were unable to complete the necessary documents in time due to combat missions or other circumstances.
What changes the adopted law provides for
One of the main innovations is the extension—from six months to one year—of the transitional period for applying for a temporary residence permit for the relevant categories of foreign military personnel. Under the bill’s provisions, for military personnel covered by the transitional rules, the deadline for applying for a residence permit is extended until May 10, 2027.
In addition, the document provides for a separate three-month period of lawful stay in Ukraine for foreigners and stateless persons after signing a contract for military service. During this period, the service member will be able to submit documents to obtain a temporary residence permit.
At the same time, the one-year transitional period and the three-month period after signing a contract apply to different legal situations. This does not mean that every foreigner who joins the military will be able to refrain from applying for a residence permit for one year.
Certain provisions also concern foreigners who have been discharged from service. For specified categories of such persons, an additional period of lawful stay in Ukraine is established, during which they will be able to regulate their migration status. In particular, this includes the possibility of staying for three months after termination of the contract in cases provided for by law, including for certain former service members who hold passport documents that have expired.
Why the deadlines needed to be extended
The issue of the legal status of foreign defenders of Ukraine became especially relevant ahead of November 10, 2026. On that date, the six-month period was to expire during which foreigners and stateless persons already serving in the military were required to apply for temporary residence permits. However, some service members were unable to meet this requirement on time.
As explained by the relevant parliamentary committee, the reasons were primarily related to the specifics of military service. Foreign military personnel take part in combat operations, carry out tasks to protect Ukraine’s territorial integrity, and do not always have the physical opportunity to personally apply to units of the State Migration Service.
Without legislative changes, such circumstances could have created legal uncertainty regarding their continued stay in the country. In particular, service members who continue to perform their duties could have faced difficulties when confirming the legality of their stay in Ukraine, processing documents, and receiving administrative services. That is why, on October 15, the Parliamentary Committee on Human Rights, the De-occupation and Reintegration of Temporarily Occupied Territories of Ukraine, National Minorities, and International Relations recommended that the Verkhovna Rada adopt the bill both as a basis and as a whole.
How residence permits are currently issued to foreign military personnel
The updated procedure for processing documents for foreigners serving in Ukraine’s Defence Forces came into effect on May 10, 2026. It was introduced pursuant to Law No. 4730-IX of December 17, 2025, and Cabinet of Ministers Resolution No. 573 of May 6, 2026. Under these rules, a temporary residence permit is issued for the entire duration of the military contract, as well as for six months after its termination or cancellation.
This additional period allows former service members to resolve issues related to their further residence in Ukraine, obtain other documents, or travel abroad.
To obtain a residence permit, applicants must contact a territorial office of the State Migration Service, the state-owned enterprise "Document," or the relevant Administrative Services Center.
The documents to be submitted by foreign military personnel include a military registration document or service ID, a military service contract, and an undertaking by the military unit to notify the migration service of the early termination of the contract.
At the same time, certain administrative procedures have already been simplified for this category of foreigners. In particular, when processing a residence permit, the migration service does not verify the residential address. In some cases, legislation also permits the use of passport documents whose validity has expired.
What rights does a temporary residence permit provide?
A temporary residence permit is a document confirming the legal grounds for a foreign citizen’s stay in Ukraine. In particular, the document makes it possible to confirm legal status when dealing with government institutions, opening bank accounts, and obtaining financial, notarial, and medical services.
The absence of properly оформed documents can complicate such procedures even for foreigners who are officially serving in the military under contract.
The Ministry of Defence previously emphasized that the changes to the documentation procedure are intended to reduce the bureaucratic burden on foreign defenders who have to resolve migration issues while simultaneously performing their service duties.
What will change after a foreign national is discharged from military service?
The authors of the new law devoted particular attention to the legal status of foreigners who have completed their military service.
The problem is that after the termination of a contract, a person may need time to determine the further grounds for staying in Ukraine. This may concern service members undergoing treatment or rehabilitation, planning to obtain another legal status, or preparing to return to their homeland.
The draft law provides additional transitional mechanisms for certain categories of discharged service members so that they do not lose their legal grounds for staying in Ukraine immediately after completing their service. At the same time, it is necessary to distinguish between the three-month transitional period for cases specified by law and the six-month validity period of an already issued residence permit after the termination of the contract. These provisions regulate different situations and do not replace one another.
Reminder
At present, around 16,000 foreign volunteers from 72 countries are defending Ukraine.

Arakan Army Firms Up Relocation Plan For Villages on Bangladesh-Myanmar Border
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:57:00 UTC
20:57:00 KST

The Arakan Army (AA) is preparing to relocate some villages from the restive Bangladesh-Myanmar border at a time when the outfit is also deeply engaged in fierce battles against the Myanmar military’s renewed attempts to reclaim territories in Rakhine State.
The plan being fine-tuned will move residents of select villages from the border to areas in different parts of Maungdaw district in Myanmar’s Rakhine State that are well connected by roads and rivers.
In an interview on March 2, Arakan Army (AA) chief Twan Mrat Naing told this correspondent about the relocation plan, which would focus on “remote villages” along the border, many of which are inhabited by the Buddhist Mro community.
Twan Mrat Naing explained that concern for “better security arrangements” for the residents was the primary reason for the decision to shift residents of a few villages to other zones. “Many villages are isolated and scattered. We will have to ensure that this isolation comes to an end. We will have to relocate them and move them to a place where we can provide security and keep an eye on them,” he said.
The AA chief did not spell out any deadline for completion or details of the project. But the concerns he expressed over the security of some villages has multilayered connotations for the current situation along the Bangladesh-Myanmar border and AA’s plan to take control of it.
The 271 km-long Myanmar-Bangladesh border includes a riverine border of 64 km, where the Naf River serves as the boundary between the two countries. In Myanmar, the border runs along the districts of Maungdaw in Rakhine State and Paletwa in Chin State, contiguous to Cox’s Bazar in Bangladesh.
The two districts are both under AA’s control, but the focus of the relocation is on the border villages in Maungdaw, where the population of Rohingya Muslims is over 90 percent.
There is no clarity on how many villages there are along the Bangladesh-Myanmar border. Observers believe there were more Rohingya-inhabited villages before the ”clearance operations” of 2017, when many settlements were destroyed and ceased to exist. Currently, there are over a hundred villages, mostly inhabited by non-Rohingya communities such as Rakhine Buddhists, Mro, Khami, and Chakma.
ARSA’s Presence Along the Border
Underlying the AA’s decision to relocate border villages is its inability to establish absolute control along the border, unlike other parts of Rakhine State that it captured from the military two years ago.
Besides, the AA has to contend with the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (ARSA), a Rohingya Muslim militant group, which is seeking to carve out a distinct region for the community in northern Rakhine State.
In 2016-17, ARSA carried out a series of attacks on police and military outposts in northern Rakhine State. The military retaliated with the “clearance operations,” resulting in the death of thousands of Rohingya and the displacement of over 700,000 people, now lodged at refugee camps in Bangladesh.
The situation changed in late 2023 when the Myanmar military joined hands with Rohingya rebel outfits, including ARSA and the Rohingya Solidarity Organization (RSO), to stall the AA’s campaign to capture Maungdaw. While the military could not prevent the AA from taking control of Maungdaw, the violence resulted in more Rohingya and rebel functionaries crossing over to Bangladesh.
ARSA has support in the Rohingya villages in north Maungdaw. It mounts operations intermittently against the AA and residents of non-Rohingya villages. Its functionaries also frequent the Mayu mountains, which cut across the townships of Buthidaung, Maungdaw, and Rathedaung.
ARSA has clashed with the AA often. It has also abducted and murdered non-Rohingya residents from villages located either near the border or the Mayu mountains. Its victims were mostly from the Rakhine Buddhist, Mro, Khami, Thet, and Chakma communities.
On November 12 last year, ARSA abducted and killed three people, including a 10-year-old girl from Kone Chaung village in Maungdaw. “They were in a group of six people. Three men managed to escape with injuries,” Soe May, a resident of the village, whose daughter was killed, told The Diplomat.
Possibility of Battles on Multiple Fronts
Currently, the AA is engaged in a fierce battle against the Myanmar military in Sittwe and the adjoining region. The Myanmar military unleashed a renewed offensive codenamed Operation 4926 to claw back territories it had lost to the AA in Rakhine State.
However, so far, the military has met with little success. Functionaries of the AA and its political wing, the United League of Arakan, who spoke to this correspondent, were of the view that the military might equip ARSA with weapons to launch more attacks against the AA in north Rakhine State. Reports have emerged of ARSA stepping up its campaign along the border even as the military offensive in Rakhine State deepens.
The AA is concerned about the vulnerability of non-Rohingya border villages to ARSA attacks. Residents of these villages often visit Bangladesh to purchase essential commodities and for medical treatment; this could cease if ARSA trains its guns on them.
A senior ULA functionary pointed out that the most vulnerable to ARSA attacks are about 20 villages located between border pillars 50 and 57, most of which are inhabited by the Mro and Rakhine Buddhist communities.
ARSA, along with the RSO, could target the AA and border villages from camps it has established on the Bangladesh side of the border. Traders from Maungdaw town who frequent the border, including some Rohingya, told The Diplomat that they have seen ARSA and RSO camps at Bandarban in Bangladesh’s Chittagong Hill Tracts.
“Some of these camps are not far from the outposts established by the Bangladesh Border Battalion. The border around Tombru in Bangladesh is the area where the ARSA is most active,” said Kyaw Aye Than, a trader based in the border village of Waylartaung, who occasionally lives in Maungdaw town.
The AA has diverted most of its resources to fight the military for control of Sittwe, the capital of Rakhine State. In addition, it has cadres stationed in the Bamar heartland such as Sagaing Region, Magwe, and Ayeyarwady, where it has teamed up with the local People’s Defense Forces (PDFs) in the movement against the military. The outfit would be overstretched if it were to divert more resources to confront ARSA along the border.
Two months ago, the AA launched its second compulsory recruitment drive under a special law called the National Emergency Defense Provision to increase its cadre strength.
The AA has reportedly learned of the “intimate ties” between ARSA and a section among the non-Rohingya villages, Twan Mrat Naing told me. A sustained collaboration between them could extend to information sharing, which would weaken the AA further in the border areas.
In addition to relocating villages, the AA plans to use technology to surveil the border areas. Drones, camera, and other equipment are being actively considered, the AA chief said.
Border Residents Have Started Relocating
Some non-Rohingya households from the border villages have started relocating to safe areas in Maungdaw, even as the AA is giving final shape to its relocation plans.
On February 10, I saw four huts being constructed near Kine Gree village, located about 20 km north of Maungdaw town. The residents, who belonged to the Mro community, hailed from Don Nyou village near pillar 52 on the border.
An elderly man named Kaing Htauk was among the group engaged in building the huts. He said that since last year 85 households had begun the process of relocating from Pyar Re and Kyauk Lone villages near border pillars 55 to 58. They are now building new homes on plots of land allocated by the ULA. He cited safety concerns as the reason for the move.
“ARSA camps and training facilities across the border in Bangladesh are not very far from our village,” Kaing Htauk said. “We were told by ARSA functionaries to join hands with them. They warned us of dire consequences if we did not.”
Two incidents prompted these residents to arrive at the momentous decision. In April last year, ARSA burnt an AA outpost. Five months later, six farmers, who crossed the border at pillar 52 to visit a market in Bangladesh, went missing. Alarmed villagers then began relocating from their villages.
“Residents of four villages comprising around a thousand people have already shifted to different areas in Maungdaw. More residents from other villages, mostly Mro, Rakhine Buddhists, and Khami, plan to do the same,” said Aung Hlaing, vice chairman of Mro Affairs Committee. He relocated three years ago from the border in a group of 30 people.
Most of the residents of the border villages were engaged in shifting cultivation or petty trade dependent on merchandise from Bangladesh. They face hardships in finding a livelihood in the new location, as it meant adapting to new occupations. While some of them have become daily wagers, others are cultivating food crops such as rice and vegetables and selling them in shops.
There is no fear of ARSA for these residents anymore, but they are now grappling with poverty, which they did not face in their former villages. Aerial attacks by the military are a constant threat they face, like other residents across Rakhine.

Finland, Norway Push Putin for Peace
Unknown

Russian President Vladimir Putin told Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre on Tuesday, Oct. 27, that President Volodymyr Zelensky should come to Moscow for direct talks, reiterating an earlier invitation that Kyiv rejected as it sought to meet on a neutral ground.
Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov told Russian state broadcaster Vesti that Stubb and Støre had passed on Zelensky’s wish to speak with Putin directly, to which he responded by repeating Moscow’s long-standing offer.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Our boss repeated that if Zelensky really wants to hold direct negotiations, let him come to Moscow, where he will be provided with all conditions, including in terms of security,” Ushakov said, adding that the meeting between the two leaders would be most meaningful once the negotiating process is complete.
“Some documents will be worked out, namely in the context of a long-term settlement in Ukraine, and after that the leaders of the two countries could meet. The negotiators would be ready to present the documents to them, and the leaders in turn would be ready to sign them,” Ushakov continued.
In early June, Zelensky addressed Putin publicly and directly, in a rare open letter. He proposed ending the war through a face-to-face meeting at a bilateral summit hosted by a neutral country, backed by broader security guarantees from Europe and the United States.
POW Dispute: South Korea Pulls 8 Diplomats From Ukraine
The Kremlin dismissed the proposal at the time, repeating Zelensky could come to Moscow if he wanted to meet.
Finnish, Norwegian leaders urge an end to the war
Stubb and Støre called Putin from Helsinki earlier on Tuesday, urging an end to Russia’s war against Ukraine and the resumption of negotiations.
According to Finland’s presidential office, the two leaders initiated the call in consultation with Ukraine, following their Oct. 20 meeting in Oslo. The conversation was linked to upcoming talks in Abu Dhabi.
Stubb and Støre reaffirmed that their countries would maintain support for Ukraine.
“The discussion was frank and substantive,” Stubb said. “Ending the war requires direct discussions.”
The Finnish president stressed that the war’s outcome would directly affect both neighboring countries and European security.
Støre highlighted the conflict’s human and material costs, warning that its consequences would extend across generations and emphasizing the need for de-escalation.
The leaders spoke for their respective countries rather than Europe as a whole, the official statement said.
Kremlin: Peace must reflect Russia’s interests
The Kremlin, in its own readout of the call provided by Russian state-owned media TASS, confirmed that the discussion was held at the request of the Finnish and Norwegian leaders.
The statement suggests Moscow remains engaged in the US-brokered process ahead of the trilateral talks planned for November with Ukraine, while simultaneously welcoming the agreement to hold negotiations on Ukraine in Abu Dhabi.
Putin reiterated Moscow’s position, giving his assessment of the situation in the conflict zone, while pointing to what the Kremlin calls the war’s “root cause.” According to the Russian president, a just and lasting peace in Ukraine was possible only if Russia’s interests were taken into account.
In his view, NATO and EU countries were pursuing a confrontational policy that was essentially only prolonging the conflict.
According to the readout, Putin had also informed the two leaders of the ongoing humanitarian operation in Russian-occupied Oleshky, in the Kherson region. However, no further details were provided.
Security in the Baltic Sea region and Northern Europe was also on the agenda, the Kremlin confirmed, affirming the importance of international maritime law and freedom of navigation.
All three leaders agreed to keep in direct contact by telephone, going forward.
Zelensky briefed on the call
Zelensky confirmed that he was briefed in great detail following the leaders’ call, noting that Stubb and Støre “made it clear to the Russian leader that real de-escalatory steps are needed.”
As both Finland and Norway border Russia, they have a particular interest in reliable security arrangements, he argued, noting that various formats for engagement with other partners in Europe were on the agenda as well.
“There must be peace, de-escalation is needed,” Zelensky concluded.
Stubb and Støre met Zelensky and US envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo a week earlier, before Witkoff traveled to St. Petersburg for talks with Putin.
Following that meeting, the Kremlin said Russia was prepared to resume US-mediated negotiations with Ukraine in November.

Turkish communications chief highlights COP31 as opportunity to advance climate diplomacy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:56:51 UTC
20:56:51 KST

Türkiye's upcoming hosting of the UN climate summit COP31 will provide an important opportunity to share the country's vision for climate diplomacy with the international community, Communications Director Burhanettin Duran said Tuesday. 
"COP31, to be held in Antalya on Nov. 9-20, is an important opportunity for our country to share its vision in the field of climate diplomacy with the international community," Duran said at a panel titled From Zero Waste to COP31: Türkiye's Climate Diplomacy, held at the Communications Directorate. 
Duran said that climate challenges, including biodiversity loss, ocean pollution, desertification, water-related problems, global warming and waste management, had long exceeded the capacity of individual countries to address them using national resources alone. 
"Climate diplomacy is a concept we use precisely for this reason," he said, adding that government policies could become meaningful only through international negotiations, cooperation, and shared commitments. 
Duran said a climate diplomacy book prepared by the Communications Directorate aims to bring together Türkiye's experience, efforts, and vision in the field and contribute to policymaking and further work. 
- Scientific knowledge 'must also be reflected positively in political decision-making processes' 
Emphasizing that the consequences of the climate crisis were already being felt, Duran said international policies must balance countries' sovereign rights with their global responsibilities. 
He said countries with greater responsibility for climate change were expected to build greater capacity for technology transfer and climate finance, while a fair negotiation framework was needed to reconcile national interests. 
"Scientific knowledge is not enough. It must also be reflected positively in political decision-making processes," he said. 
Duran cited political scientist Joseph Nye's description of climate change as a "threat multiplier" rather than merely an ecological crisis, saying the issue was directly linked to global justice and equity. 
He also argued that conflicts in different parts of the world had serious environmental and climate consequences. 
"Israel's unlawful attacks on Gaza not only threaten human life but also deepen the climate crisis through the intensive greenhouse gas emissions they release into the atmosphere," Duran said. 
He added that carbon emissions caused by Israel's attacks since October 2023 had exceeded the annual emissions of hundreds of countries and the consequences extended beyond regional peace and security to the global climate.  
Türkiye's climate policies and Zero Waste initiative 
Duran said that Türkiye had adopted a comprehensive approach to combating climate change, ratifying the Paris Agreement in 2021 and setting a 2053 net-zero emissions target under President Recep Tayyip Erdogan. 
Priority areas include improving energy efficiency, expanding renewable energy, reducing industry's carbon footprint, developing sustainable agricultural practices, and protecting natural areas, he said. 
He also highlighted the Zero Waste initiative led by first lady Emine Erdogan, saying the UN General Assembly's designation of March 30 as International Zero Waste Day, with support from 105 countries under Türkiye's leadership, reflected the country's efforts. 
Duran said the initiative had given Türkiye a distinctive form of soft power in climate diplomacy by helping turn the Zero Waste approach into a global norm. 
He stressed the need to support climate efforts with legal frameworks and warned that inadequate public communication could leave them vulnerable to disinformation and social resistance. 
"My personal view is that conducting politics through social vulnerabilities will not carry us into the future," he said. 
Duran said the Communications Directorate's Center for Combating Disinformation monitored misleading campaigns on climate issues and other subjects, adding that authorities needed to build a bridge of communication between legislation and society. 
He also urged the media to focus not only on the risks of climate change but also on solutions, warning that repetitive negative messaging could increase public anxiety and lead to "green fatigue." 
Long-term communication strategy 
Duran said climate change was a long-term issue that would affect future generations even more than the present one, calling for hopeful messaging across communication platforms. 
He said Türkiye envisioned a multifaceted, long-term climate communication strategy, including age-appropriate environmental education for children through experiments, trips, books and stories. 
He stressed the role of Turkish public broadcaster TRT in promoting environmental awareness through children's programs. 
Duran also cited Anadolu's "Green Line" project, launched in 2022, to provide accessible coverage of environmental and climate issues, and a joint statement on Mediterranean forest fires signed by news agencies from Italy, Spain, and Greece. 
He said environmental awareness needed to become part of everyday life, including home heating, transport, consumption habits, packaging and waste management, rather than remaining limited to expert opinions. 
COP31 to promote shared solutions 
Duran said Türkiye's vision for COP31 was based on restoring trust through dialogue and translating commitments into concrete results on the ground.  
"Our goal is to help turn climate pledges into measurable and lasting action," he said, adding that Türkiye aimed to accelerate the implementation of international commitments, strengthen cooperation among countries, and support tangible results in climate action. 
The Communications Directorate was organizing environmental and climate media tours, accrediting national and international journalists for COP31 and helping plan and establish the media center at the conference venue, he said. 
"Of approximately 3,000 members of the press, the procedures for 1,400 have been completed," Duran said. 
He expressed confidence that the summit, to be hosted by Türkiye, would bring countries with different circumstances and priorities together around shared solutions, and wished the conference success.

Greenhouse gas levels set records again in 2025, U.N. says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:55:59 UTC
20:55:59 KST

Greenhouse gas levels set records in 2025, U.N. says, expressing alarm
Geneva — Greenhouse gas concentrations in the atmosphere rose to record highs in 2025, locking in climate impacts that will persist for centuries, the United Nations said on Tuesday.
Levels of the three main greenhouse gases -- the climate-warming carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide -- all rose to unprecedented figures in 2025, the U.N.'s weather and climate agency said.
The World Meteorological Organization said the rise would lead to more long-term temperature increases for the planet.
The WMO's 22nd annual Greenhouse Gas Bulletin comes ahead of the COP31 U.N. climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, from Nov. 9 to Nov. 20.
"Another year, another new record," said WMO Deputy Secretary-General Ko Barrett.
"Greenhouse gases are trapping an unprecedented amount of heat in the atmosphere, providing energy for more extreme weather and associated risks to our economies and societies.
"The past 11 years have been the warmest on record and this trend is set to continue. Carbon dioxide (CO2) has a very long life-time and so will affect the global climate not just for years but for decades and even centuries."
El Nino's impact
The bulletin looks at greenhouse gas concentrations -- the amount of those gases in the atmosphere -- rather than new annual emissions amounts as the world burns more coal, oil and gas.
In 2025, carbon dioxide concentrations were at 426.8 parts per million (ppm); methane at 1,948 parts per billion, and nitrous oxide at 339.1 parts per billion.
That takes them, respectively, to 153%, 267% and 126% of the pre-industrial levels witnessed before 1750.
Of the three major greenhouse gases, CO2 accounts for about 66% of the warming effect on the climate.
Around half of the total CO2 emitted each year remains in the atmosphere; the rest is absorbed by the land and oceans.
From 2024 to 2025, the global average concentration of CO2 rose by 2.8 ppm -- smaller than the record surge from 2023 to 2024 of 3.6 ppm.
WMO senior scientific officer Oksana Tarasova said this reflected the "recovery of the land carbon sinks and reduced fire carbon emissions in 2025 after the strong 2023/2024 El Nino," the naturally occurring, climate-warming weather phenomenon.
"However, a 2.8 ppm annual increase is still a substantial addition of carbon to the atmosphere from fossil fuel burning."
It is also above the average growth rate for the past decade of 2.6 ppm -- a figure that stood at 0.8 ppm in the 1960s.
"We can expect to see a further increase in concentrations in 2026 because of fossil fuel burning and the development of a powerful El Nino which will impact land carbon sinks, as it did in 2023/2024," Tarasova warned.
Methane accounts for about 16% of the warming effect on our climate by long-lived greenhouse gases, though it has a much shorter lifetime than CO2.
Around a third of methane emitted into the atmosphere comes from natural sources like wetlands, with the rest from anthropogenic sources such as cattle, rice farming, landfills and biomass burning.
The bulletin said that as countries shift their energy systems toward decarbonization, more attention should be paid to two potent but less abundant trace gases closely related to electricity production and distribution: molecular hydrogen (H2) and sulfur hexafluoride (SF6).
SF6 has been rising steadily over the past three decades. It is used primarily as a spark suppressant in electricity distribution.
Why hydrogen levels have increased over the past decade is unknown but it has begun to be used as an energy storage medium.

1st 4 participants vaccinated in DRC trial testing Ebola jab's effectiveness against Bundibugyo virus: WHO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:55:07 UTC
20:55:07 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
The first four participants in a clinical trial launched in the Democratic Republic of Congo have been vaccinated to assess whether an existing Ebola vaccine can reduce severe illness and deaths caused by the Bundibugyo virus, the World Health Organization (WHO) said Tuesday.
WHO Director of Science for Health Meg Doherty told reporters in Geneva that the trial, named TUMAINI, meaning "hope" in Swahili, began Friday.
The first vaccine being evaluated is Ervebo, which is known to be safe and effective against Ebola caused by the Zaire virus. Its effectiveness against the Bundibugyo virus disease remains unknown.
Doherty clarified that researchers are examining whether the vaccine reduces severe disease or death, rather than whether it prevents infection.
The trial uses a ring-vaccination approach involving people who have been in close contact with confirmed Ebola patients or otherwise exposed to the virus.
Two vaccination rings have already been established, with several more being prepared. Eligible participants can be vaccinated between one and 21 days after exposure, although researchers do not yet know whether the timing affects outcomes.
"We do not yet know for certain when results will begin to emerge. We expect it will take several months," Doherty said.
The trial is led by Congolese researchers and managed by the country's National Institute for Biomedical Research, with support from WHO and international partners.
Designed as a platform trial, TUMAINI can evaluate multiple vaccine candidates within a single research framework.
WHO advisory groups also reviewed two vaccines developed specifically against the Bundibugyo virus last week: ChAdOx1, developed by the University of Oxford with the Serum Institute of India, and Moderna's mRNA-1469.
Recommendations on those vaccines are expected this week, according to the science director.
Doherty said community members were already approaching the trial site seeking to enroll, underscoring the urgent need for an effective vaccine.
The trial builds on the ring-vaccination strategy used during the West African Ebola outbreak a decade ago, which helped establish Ervebo's effectiveness against the Zaire virus.

Parliament panel launches discussions on Mecca Pact
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:54:54 UTC
20:54:54 KST

(AA Photo)
A parliamentary panel has approved the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement that paves the way for the establishment of the Türkiye-Pakistan-Saudi Arabia Mecca Alliance.
The Turkish parliament’s Foreign Affairs Committee was convened on Oct. 27 under the leadership of the committee leader, ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) deputy Fuat Oktay and with the participation of Deputy Foreign Minister Levent Gümrükçü.
The leaders from three founding members signed the agreement on Aug. 7 in Riyadh. Türkiye is mulling over providing defensive support to Saudi Arabia after the parliament ratifies it and authorizes the government to send troops abroad.
The commission approved the agreement with the votes of the People’s Alliance, composed by the ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) and the Nationalist Movement Party (MHP).
The agreement will later be brought to the General Assembly as part of the ratification process.
Deputy Foreign Minister Gümrükçü, in his explanations about the agreement, stressed that this is purely defensive. “This agreement is not an alternative to NATO but complementary to it,” he said.
“The Mecca Agreement, which is entirely defense-oriented, does not target any country. It is open to the participation of all regional countries that respect international law, particularly the principles of respecting the sovereignty and territorial integrity of states, refraining from the use of force except for self-defense, and non-interference in internal affairs, while pursuing the goal of ensuring regional peace and security,” he stated.
In his opening statement, Oktay also recalled that the trilateral agreement is aiming to establish peace and stability in the region through boosting collective security and deterrence. He stressed that this agreement is purely defensive and not against any third party.
“On the contrary, our country is a party to defense agreements aimed at peace and stability that will increase deterrence and fortify our geography,” he stated.
The opposition lawmakers from the New Party, Democracy and Equality Party (DEM) and the Good Party, however, questioned the motives of the Mecca Alliance, especially at a moment when Saudi
Arabia is in an armed conflict with Yemen-based Iran-backed Houthi groups.
Yeni Party Deputy Utku Çakırözer explained that the main opposition will vote against the Mecca Alliance and the defense agreement with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia saying, “We are of the opinion that this agreement will add additional risks to our country’s security.”
“We don’t want to see that our soldiers are deployed to Yemen,” he stated.
The agreement is expected to be brought to the parliament’s General Assembly in the first week of November.

Parties sidestep app ban inside polling stations, asking voters outside to identify themselves
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:54:34 UTC
20:54:34 KST

Parties barred from using voter-tracking apps inside polling stations found other ways on Tuesday to track which of their supporters turned out to vote.
Under this election's rules, parties may not use voter-management apps such as Elector inside polling stations. The restriction aims to stop party systems from collecting voter information inside polling stations and to protect voters’ privacy and the integrity of the vote.
Parties, including Likud and United Torah Judaism, have apparently found a workaround. Representatives and activists stationed outside polling stations are reportedly asking voters to identify themselves, then logging in to party systems to record that those voters have cast their ballots. Voters can choose to do this freely, within the limits of the law.
WhatsApp allegedly being used to track vote
WhatsApp is also allegedly being used to track the vote. When contacted, Likud’s Elector operation said its system was working normally and that it was encouraging supporters of the “national camp,” as the right-wing bloc calls itself, to vote.
The instructions sent over WhatsApp were detailed: open the app, go to the “Contacts” tab and mark supporters. A follow-up message asked recipients to use the app to message all their supporters.
So while the app has been kept out of polling stations, parties are still running a digital operation just outside them, updating voter information, reaching supporters, and managing their Election Day effort.

Belgian government “considering nationalisation of nuclear power stations”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:54:28 UTC
20:54:28 KST

Belgium’s federal government is reportedly making little progress in negotiations with French energy company Engie regarding the takeover of Belgium’s nuclear power stations. It is questionable whether both parties will meet the 4 November deadline they had set themselves to reach an agreement.
Belgian government “considering nationalisation of nuclear power stations”
According to the newspapers De Tijd and L’Echo, the federal government is already preparing a Plan B: nationalisation. Draft legislation is reportedly ready to expropriate Engie in Belgium and compensate the company accordingly. The offices of Energy Minister Mathieu Bihet (Francophone liberal MR) and Prime Minister Bart De Wever (Flemish nationalist N-VA) declined to confirm this to VRT NEWS.
Since April the government and Engie have been negotiating over the takeover by the Belgian state of all Belgian nuclear power stations and the bill, running into billions, for their decommissioning. The fact that the possibility of nationalisation is now coming to light may well serve as an additional means of exerting pressure on the negotiations. Should it come to nationalisation, this would be a highly exceptional step for Belgium.

Arakhamia named the duration of the ceasefire in occupied Oleshky
Kyiv • UNN
The ceasefire in occupied Oleshky will last until 22:59 on November 1. It is needed to deliver aid and evacuate civilians.
One of the Ukrainian negotiators at the peace talks, Member of Parliament Davyd Arakhamia, named the timeframe for the ceasefire regime as part of the humanitarian mission in Oleshky, in the temporarily occupied territory of Kherson region, UNN writes.
As part of an initiative by U.S. First Lady Melania Trump to unblock Oleshky, the largest-scale ceasefire regime on the largest section of the front in southern Ukraine began today at 3:00 a.m. Kyiv time. This is the largest de-escalation since 2022. The ceasefire regime will last from October 27 until 10:59 p.m. on November 1. Each such de-escalation effort brings the long-awaited peace in Ukraine closer
What is known about the humanitarian mission in Oleshky
Ukraine announced a ceasefire regime in a designated area of temporarily occupied Oleshky in Kherson region, effective from 3:00 a.m. Kyiv time on October 27. This is necessary to carry out a humanitarian operation, deliver aid to the city's residents, and prepare for the safe evacuation of civilians.
Head of the Office of the President Kyrylo Budanov announced the start of the humanitarian mission in Oleshky on the morning of October 27.
Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights Dmytro Lubinets went to the site and will be responsible for coordinating the process.
Lubinets said overnight: "Oleshky: the ceasefire regime has begun; the Ukrainian side is fulfilling its commitments."
Ukrainian Navy Marine Corps spokesman Pavlo Drohal stated later that, as of 9:00 a.m. on October 27, the enemy was observing the ceasefire regime as part of the humanitarian mission in Oleshky.
Meanwhile, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine urged citizens to rely exclusively on official statements regarding the humanitarian operation.

'We know everything': SC on pleas alleging unilateral decisions by CEC, gives petitioners 10 days to reply
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:53:40 UTC
20:53:40 KST

The three-judge bench adjourned the hearing to November 17.
NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Tuesday said that it would examine all aspects of the Election Commission of India's (ECI) decision-making process amid allegations that key decisions, including those related to the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls were taken without the unanimous consent."We know everything. We will examine," Chief Justice of India Surya Kant said while hearing a batch of petitions challenging the functioning of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar and the poll panel, Live Law reported.The three-judge bench, comprising CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana, adjourned the hearing to November 17.The top court granted the petitioners 10 days to file rejoinders to the ECI’s counter-affidavit, which was submitted on Monday and asserted that the decisions in question were unanimous.The CJI's remark came after senior advocate Abhishek Manu Singhvi, appearing for leader of opposition on Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi and other INDIA bloc leaders, urged the court to direct the ECI to preserve file notings and internal communications related to its decisions.Singhvi argued that the records were crucial to determining whether the decisions concerning the SIR were taken unanimously or unilaterally."This whole issue depends on the decision-making process, consultation, and whether the decision was unanimous or not unanimous.
Let file notings, etc be preserved," Singhvi added.The petitions challenge the functioning of Gyanesh Kumar alleged that several ECI decisions, including those related to the SIR, were issued without the concurrence of the other two Election Commissioners.The bench also issued notices to the ECI and other respondents on a fresh petition filed by Rajya Sabha MP Dola Sen. The plea alleges that changes were made to Form 6 during the Bihar SIR without the Supreme Court’s approval.Senior advocate and MP Maneka Guruswamy, appearing for Sen, told the court that the poll panel had wrongly claimed that the changes to Form 6 were approved by the top court.The CJI said the court would examine all the issues and asked senior advocate Vikas Singh, appearing for the first petitioner, Rakesh Kumar Singh to file a rejoinder within 10 days to the ECI’s reply affidavit.Earlier on Monday, in its 248-page affidavit, the ECI strongly defended the SIR and rejected allegations that Form 6, the statutory form used for voter registration, had been amended."The attempt to make aspersions against the Election Commission is unfortunate," the affidavit, filed by Deputy Election Commissioner Bhanu Prakash Yeturu on behalf of the ECI said, PTI reported.The poll panel also maintained that no changes had been made to the statutory Form 6. It said the affidavit itself had been approved for filing through a unanimous decision of all three Election Commissioners.
The petitions followed a report published by The Indian Express on September 25, which said Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had recorded objections at least 14 times over the preceding 10 months to decisions and orders concerning the SIR.According to the report, the two commissioners had objected that the decisions were issued without their knowledge or recommendation.The allegations triggered protests by opposition parties and the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), which demanded the removal of CEC Gyanesh Kumar.The Supreme Court will take up the matter again on November 17, after the petitioners file their rejoinders to the ECI's affidavit.

Her reporting also focuses on policy, governance and economic developments, with a close lens on how decisions in corridors of power affect everyday lives and community well-being.

Australia’s ABC to demand One Nation remove violent Bluey cartoon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:53:15 UTC
20:53:15 KST

Dilara Hamit
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
Australia's national broadcaster ABC said Tuesday it would demand that the right-wing populist One Nation party remove a violent political cartoon featuring the popular children's character Bluey.
ABC Managing Director Hugh Marks described the animation as "a shocking use of Australia's most loved character" and "disrespectful to the children of Australia."
Speaking at a Senate estimates hearing, Marks said the broadcaster had sought legal advice after learning of the video last week and would send a cease-and-desist letter.
“We will be taking further action, I can assure you,” Marks said.
The three-minute cartoon, titled The State of Melbourne, was released in 2024 as part of One Nation leader Pauline Hanson's animated Please Explain series.
It depicts caricatures of former Victorian Premier Daniel Andrews and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese in an SUV that hits Bluey and Australian conservationist and television presenter Robert Irwin.
The politicians then put the victims' bodies in the trunk. Later, Bluey takes the wheel and drives into cartoon versions of Andrews, Albanese and Irwin in revenge.
Marks said One Nation had not sought permission to use Bluey and argued that the video did not qualify as a parody of the original program.
"It's not a parody of any Bluey work," he said. "It's not a minor use of the intellectual property. In my view, it is an infringement of the intellectual property."
The ABC has contacted Bluey's international distributor, BBC Studios, and Brisbane-based production company Ludo Studio about the video.
Marks said the letter would demand the video's removal and that the broadcaster could also seek damages.
The controversy comes amid scrutiny of political violence following an alleged attack on independent lawmaker Helen Haines, who was struck by a vehicle outside her electoral office on Oct. 19 and lost both legs.
Labor Senator Varun Ghosh called One Nation's use of Bluey "heinous" in light of the incident.
One Nation lawmaker Barnaby Joyce defended the cartoons as satire and warned against excessive restrictions on political expression.
“You get to a point where you are sanitizing beyond satire,” he said.
The video, which has received more than 1.3 million views, remained available on YouTube as of Tuesday.

GECF countries account for about 40% of global gas exports — Putin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:52:36 UTC
20:52:36 KST

MOSCOW, October 27. /TASS/. Member countries of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) account for approximately 40% of global gas exports, Russian President Vladimir Putin stated at the GECF summit.
The Russian leader highlighted that the GECF’s core characteristics - openness, clarity, and objective assessments - are highly significant for both gas producers and consumers, as well as for the global energy sector as a whole.
"Especially considering that, collectively, the Forum’s members hold 70% of the world’s natural gas reserves and account for about 40% of global gas exports," Putin emphasized.
This means that GECF member countries make a significant contribution to ensuring global energy security and the balanced development of states and macro-regions, Putin noted. "This primarily concerns new centers of economic growth in Asia, Africa, and Latin America, where energy consumption is rising, cities are rapidly expanding, industrial facilities are being built, and electricity is increasingly being used in industry, transport, and the digital economy - including in data storage and processing centers," the president explained.

Israeli police arrested a man carrying a large knife on Tuesday after approaching opposition politician Yair Golan during an election-day campaign appearance in Tel Aviv in a suspected stabbing attempt, Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper reported.
The incident occurred during a voter mobilization tour at Railway Park in Tel Aviv, the Democrats party, which Golan chairs, said in a statement.

As the guards moved toward him, a large knife fell from his clothing, prompting the security team to restrain him and call police, according to the report.
Police subsequently arrested the suspect, the newspaper said.
The Democrats party said Golan’s security team prevented the man from acting and that no one was injured.
The suspect’s intentions have not been independently established, while police have yet to release details of the investigation.
Golan blamed political incitement for the incident.
“Incitement and violence will not deter us,” he said, while urging Israelis to vote in Tuesday’s elections.
The incident came as Israelis voted Tuesday in general elections for the 120-seat Knesset, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former army chief Gadi Eisenkot heading the main rival political camps.
Neither bloc is assured of securing the 61 seats needed for a parliamentary majority, raising the prospect of coalition negotiations after the vote.
