Kyiv’s South Bridge Hit as Russian Ballistic Missiles and 280 Drones Hammer the Capital
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:16:58 UTC
20:16:58 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Kyiv’s South Bridge Hit as Russian Ballistic Missiles and 280 Drones Hammer the Capital
Russian ballistic missiles struck Kyiv’s South Bridge during a massive overnight assault that also sent 280 drones toward Ukraine, forcing the bridge to close and disrupting metro service across part of the capital.
Russia launched a massive overnight attack against Ukraine, sending 280 drones—including 69 jet-powered Shaheds—along with ballistic missiles, with Kyiv identified as the main target.
The strike damaged the capital’s South Bridge, forcing authorities to close it to traffic and suspend metro service across part of the city, according to Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko on October 27.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Klitschko said specialists were inspecting the South Bridge to determine the extent of the damage following the Russian attack.
Traffic across the bridge has been completely suspended while the assessment is underway.
The strike also disrupted Kyiv’s Green Line metro service, with trains temporarily halted between Osokorky and Chervonyi Khutir stations. Authorities have not yet said when either the bridge or the affected section of the metro will reopen.
Klitschko also released the first photographs showing damage to the bridge following the attack.
Russia is increasingly targeting Kyiv’s seven bridges across the Dnipro River in an effort to divide the Ukrainian capital and disrupt transport connections across northern Ukraine.
Disrupting crossings over the Dnipro could effectively split the city in two, with consequences extending far beyond the capital.
According to Ukraine’s military, Russia launched Iskander-M/S-400 ballistic missiles from Russia’s Bryansk region as well as 280 strike and decoy drones from multiple locations in Russia, the occupied Donetsk region, and occupied Crimea.
The drone force included Shaheds, Gerberas, Parodiya decoys, and other types. Sixty-nine of the Shaheds were jet-powered variants. Kyiv was the primary target of the attack.
Ukrainian fighter aircraft, surface-to-air missile units, electronic warfare teams, drone units, and mobile fire groups were all involved in repelling the strike.
By 9 am, Ukrainian air defenses had shot down or suppressed 257 aerial targets, including two Iskander-M/S-400 ballistic missiles and 255 drones.
Among the intercepted UAVs were 56 jet-powered Shaheds.
Several attack drones were still airborne when the preliminary figures were released, and air-defense operations remained underway.
Ukraine reported Russian strikes at 25 locations, while debris from intercepted targets fell at another 16 sites.
This is not the first Russian strike on one of Kyiv’s bridges. Previously, a Russian Shahed drone struck Kyiv’s South Bridge as a metro train crossed.
Passengers reported hearing an explosion and seeing a flash as the drone hit near the roadway. Smoke then appeared inside the carriage, ash entered through the ventilation system, and several windows were blown out.

DR Congo Ebola cases top 10,000 as outbreak spreads across Africa
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
19:16:49 CST
20:16:49 KST

KINSHASA, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- The Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) said Tuesday that it has reported more than 10,000 confirmed Ebola cases since the outbreak began in May, according to data released Tuesday by the country's health authorities.
The latest report showed that the country had recorded a total of 10,060 confirmed cases, including 4,887 deaths, as of Oct. 25, with a case fatality rate of 48.6 percent.
The outbreak has affected 66 health zones across eight of the DRC's 26 provinces.
The eastern province of Ituri remained the epicenter, accounting for 71.7 percent of all confirmed cases, the report said.
The current outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo Ebola virus, was declared in the DRC on May 15. It has since spread to five countries, including four in Africa. The other three are Uganda, Kenya and Nigeria. France reported one imported case.
Unlike the more common Zaire strain of Ebola, the Bundibugyo virus has no approved vaccine or specific treatment.
The current Ebola outbreak has become the largest and deadliest ever recorded in the DRC and the second-largest Ebola outbreak globally, after the 2014-2016 West Africa epidemic. ■

Iraqi court sentences six French nationals to life for IS group membership
Six French men were sentenced to life in prison by an Iraqi court on Tuesday for membership of the Islamic State (IS) group, according to a source. They are among 47 French IS group suspects transferred from detention facilities in Syria to Iraq last year under an arrangement coordinated by US forces and Iraqi authorities.
An Iraqi court on Tuesday sentenced six French nationals to life in prison and a seventh to 15 years after convicting them of membership of the Islamic State (IS) group, a Reuters witness inside the courtroom said.
The men were among 47 French IS group suspects transferred from detention facilities in northeast Syria to Iraq last year under a broader relocation arrangement coordinated by US forces and Iraqi authorities.
Read moreFrench jihadist who claimed 2016 Nice attack to be tried in Iraq, source says
The presiding judge said the sentences were imposed under Iraq's counterterrorism law for joining the IS group and spreading fear. He added that the court had opted for life imprisonment rather than the death penalty because the defendants were young.
A seventh French national, aged 23, was given a 15-year sentence, according to the Reuters witness.
Abbas al-Maliki, one of the lawyers for the defendants, said the group would appeal the sentence in the Court of Cassation.
Iraq opened the trial of the French nationals last month.
The IS group seized large parts of Iraq and Syria in 2014 before being driven from its self-declared caliphate by a US-led coalition and local forces in 2019. Many of the group's militants were detained, although remnants of the jihadist organisation continue to operate.
The US announced in January that it had begun transferring IS group detainees from Syria to Iraq amid concerns about the security of detention facilities in northeast Syria after Kurdish-led forces lost control of parts of the region.

how light and materiality shape spaces in EDRA MAGAZINE issue six
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:16:17 UTC
20:16:17 KST

how light and materiality shape spaces in EDRA MAGAZINE issue six
the sixth issue draws a parallel between the way light shapes spaces, brings them to life and changes their atmosphere, and the ability of furniture to do the same.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
The philosopher and writer Ralph Waldo Emerson suggested that getting to know someone meant looking at their books. The ones they read, leaf through and display in their homes as a reflection of their interests. The volumes they have chosen to open their minds to the light of knowledge.
Light is precisely the subject of the sixth issue of Edra MAGAZINE. In its latest edition, this magazine, which feels closer to a reference book than a brand catalog, draws a parallel between the way light shapes spaces, brings them to life and changes their atmosphere, and the ability of furniture to do the same.
Why light is central to Edra Magazine Issue No. 6
Throughout its history, Italian design brand Edra has used light both as an inspiration for its furniture and as a tool in its design process. The yarns, polycarbonate, crystals, mirrors and metals in its collections absorb, reflect and multiply light, directly affecting how we perceive the colors and depth of spaces. This ongoing relationship, together with an exploration of how the behavior of light determines our perception of places, explains why the sixth issue of Edra’s printed magazine is dedicated to this vital element.
Across its pages, the volume, with editorial curation by Laura Arrighi and graphic design and photography direction by Stefano Pasqualetti, offers readers a collection of architectural spaces. Here, light and Edra furniture convey meaning and help define the character of each setting. The magazine further broadens its exploration of light by featuring contributions from Jacopo Foggini and Francesco Binfaré, alongside essays by Pierluigi Masini on art and Silvana Annicchiarico on light and the Edra collection.
Contributions from writers Patrizia Piccinini, Chiara Pasqualetti Johnson and Jasmin Jouhar, alongside architect and designer Chiara Tassano, complete the publication. It is conceived to encourage reflection, serve as a lasting reference and even take pride of place on a coffee table or bookshelf.
Inspiring spaces in Edra Magazine Issue No. 6
A section of the magazine presents carefully photographed examples of real spaces. The publication’s two central elements take the lead: light and Edra furniture.
We begin at Swarovski Kristallwelten in Wattens, where crystal transforms light in a new version of the wunderkammer. We then travel to Ca’ del Bosco, a winery in Franciacorta where light radiating from glass bottles illuminates the large dome. Our next stop is the Italian Embassy in Berlin, where natural light fills the interiors and Edra furniture adds a contemporary dimension.
Turning to residential architecture, the magazine features three homes. One in Saint-Tropez, where the connection between indoors and outdoors offers a reference for projects closely connected to nature; a country house in Ostuni, built in stone, whose white walls sit in dialogue with the surrounding olive trees; and a Brutalist villa in Ibiza, where the severity of concrete contrasts with the seascape beyond.
image © Pietro Savorelli
Edra milestones in its latest magazine
The magazine then revisits Edra’s presence at Casa Italia Milano Cortina 2026 as Official Partner of CONI. The collaboration began in 2016.
The brand’s cultural dimension finds expression in the Edra Evening of Honour at Teatro alla Scala in Milan, dedicated to the Campana Brothers. Held on April 23, 2026, the event created an ethereal, suspended world on the historic stage, where music, dance and Edra furniture came together in an artistic performance.
Finally, the magazine reviews the latest initiatives at Edra Palazzo Durini in Milan and in the surrounding area. Here, Edra’s collaborators take center stage through their exhibitions, publications and reflections.
The light of inspiration in Edra Magazine Issue No. 6
Conceived as a printed publication and intended to become a permanent resident on the bookshelves of design enthusiasts around the world, this issue establishes a kind of metaphor. While we often associate light with the flame of knowledge and inspiration, here it is captured within the pages and the spaces they depict.
Light is a tool in artisanal production and works alongside Edra furniture to shape atmospheres and define places. Beyond the pages, this publication casts that light back toward the architects , designers and crafters who will create tomorrow’s collections.

Poland and UK support strong transatlantic alliance, Polish minister says
WARSAW, Oct 27 - Both Poland and the United Kingdom are in favour of strengthening the transatlantic alliance as there is no alternative to cooperation with the US, Polish Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said on Tuesday.
"We share a similar view of the alliance with the United States. Both Poland and the United Kingdom support strengthening this alliance," the Polish Defence Minister said during a joint press conference with British Defence Minister Wes Streeting.
He said both countries backed efforts to strengthen Europe's defence capabilities and strategic autonomy, but not at the expense of ties with Washington.
"There is no alternative to transatlantic cooperation. Any other solution is simply worse, it is bad. But our capabilities, British capabilities, Polish capabilities, and European capabilities must be strengthened for production, for collective defense, for cooperation," he said.
Poland and Britain signed a three-year defence cooperation plan on Tuesday covering joint military exercises and the development of defence capabilities.
Kosiniak-Kamysz also said Poland would seek to ensure that Britain could benefit from the European Union's SAFE defence financing programme and assured that Poland will strive to "bring the United Kingdom closer to the European Union". REUTERS

Remediable Service Statement Delivery Update
Update on Advocate General for Scotland v Milroy
The Ministry of Defence (MOD) can confirm that it has been granted permission to appeal in the case of Advocate General for Scotland v Milroy.
The appeal will now proceed through the next stage of the legal process. As the matter remains before the courts, it would not be appropriate to comment in detail.
Further updates will be provided in due course.
Mr Milroy originally made a claim against MOD in June 2020 on the grounds that the way in which MOD calculates the attendance-based pay divisor for Volunteer Reservists and the failure to provide access to an occupational pension for reserve service before 1 April 2015 amounted to less favourable treatment of part-time workers.
In April 2023 the Employment Tribunal heard the case. The judgment of the Employment Tribunal was in favour of the claimant.
MOD subsequently appealed the judgment and that appeal was heard in December 2025 at the Employment Appeal Tribunal. In January 2026, the Employment Appeal Tribunal dismissed MOD’s appeal and upheld the Employment Tribunal’s findings.
Following the judgement MOD submitted a request for leave to appeal directly to the Employment Appeal Tribunal. This was refused by the judge of the Employment Appeal Tribunal in February 2026.
An application for leave to appeal was subsequently submitted to the Inner House, Court of Session, which was heard at an oral hearing on 8 October 2026. MOD can confirm that it has received permission to appeal following the oral hearing.
Early Leavers – Pension Rights Notice
A world class pension scheme for your military service
When a member of the armed forces reaches their retirement age, they receive one of the most generous pensions available in the UK. This fairly reflects the unique sacrifice they have provided their country throughout their career.
All members of the armed forces are automatically enrolled into the Armed Forces Pension Scheme. Unlike all other public schemes, members pay 0% in contributions each month. The scheme is unfunded and paid from the public purse.

Transfers in and out of the schemes
If you have built up pension benefits elsewhere before joining the armed forces you have the option to transfer in the value of your other benefits to receive a service credit in your Armed Forces Pension Scheme.
Before you apply to DBS Veterans UK for a transfer in, you need to obtain details of the amount of your transfer value from your previous pension scheme, and then an estimate from DBS Veterans UK of the additional pension that this will buy. If you decide to go ahead with the transfer, you should make your application to DBS Veterans UK in writing.
You must be serving in the armed forces to be eligible to transfer in and once you have committed yourself to a transfer from your previous pension scheme, you cannot change your mind and you will have given up forever your rights and those of your dependants under the previous schemes.
Transfers into AFPS 15 must be completed within one year of joining the scheme. For members who remain solely in AFPS 75 and AFPS 05 who may still make transfers in from a non-public service scheme. AFSP 75 the transfer in must be made before your 54 birthday and in AFPS 05 the transfer in must be made before the beginning of your final year of service before your pension is due.
If you leave without receiving immediate pension benefits (including leaving with an Early Departure Payment (EDP) under AFPS 15 or AFPS 05) you have the option to transfer the value of your deferred pension benefits to other defined benefit schemes. A pension in payment cannot be transferred.
However, the government has prevented transfers from unfunded public service defined benefit schemes (such as the AFPS to funded defined contribution schemes in UK or abroad. The Pension Schemes Act 2015 and the Taxation of Pensions Act 2014 made this rule. Application for pension transfers should be made to:

Resettlement Grant
Resettlement Grants assist those leaving the regular armed forces to resettle into civilian life after completing a substantial period of service. A Resettlement Grant is not a pension.
It is a tax-free lump sum paid to regular service personnel, who, at the time they leave the services, are not eligible for Early Departure Payment benefits, an Immediate Pension or ill health award (or any other immediate pension benefits) and they meet Resettlement Grant qualification criteria, which are:
- AFPS 2015 and AFPS 2005: all personnel need to have 12 years’ relevant service (from date of entry)
- AFPS 1975: Officers to have at least 2 years’ Commissioned service and have 9 relevant years of reckonable service from age 21
- AFPS 1975: other ranks to have 12 relevant years of reckonable service from age 18.
The value of the Resettlement Grant at April 2025 is:
- AFPS 2005 and AFPS 2015: £14,059
- AFPS 1975: £20,397 (Officer) and £14,058 (Other Rank)
Please see the latest tri-service codes published each year on gov.uk.
The Resettlement Grant is increased each year at the same rate as armed forces pensionable pay.
Only 1 resettlement grant is awarded, for those who have service in more than one scheme. If personnel are re-employed after leaving they may have to re-pay some or all of the grant. See the re-employment booklet for more details.

DR Congo reports over 10,000 Ebola cases as the outbreak spreads abroad, with no approved vaccine or specific treatment for the Bundibugyo virus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:15:00 UTC
20:15:00 KST

Cases top 10,000 in DR Congo Ebola outbreak
October 27, 2026
Health authorities in the Democratic Republic of Congo reported that Ebola cases had risen to 10,060, with 4,887 deaths since the outbreak was identified in mid-May.
The outbreak involves the Bundibugyo virus, for which there is no approved vaccine or specific treatment. The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention has described it as the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history.
Where else have cases been reported?
Kenya has confirmed nine infections, including two deaths, after a patient traveled from DR Congo through Uganda to the capital, Nairobi.
Nigeria also confirmed an infection in a Swiss woman, the wife of a Swiss diplomat, who fell ill after visiting Uganda. Authorities are investigating where she contracted the virus. She was evacuated to Switzerland.
Why is the outbreak difficult to contain?
Ebola spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of an infected person. It can cause fever, diarrhea and, in some cases, bleeding.
Early symptoms can resemble malaria, potentially delaying isolation and treatment.
The lack of an approved vaccine or specific treatment against the Bundibugyo virus further complicates efforts to control the outbreak.
Are vaccines and treatments being tested?
Clinical trials of two antiviral treatment approaches have been underway since July.
Two further trials are investigating whether the Ervebo vaccine can protect against the Bundibugyo virus. The vaccine is currently approved and recommended only against Ebola virus, formerly known as Zaire ebolavirus.

Finnish and Norwegian leaders call Putin, urge restart of peace talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:14:19 UTC
20:14:19 KST

The leaders of Finland and Norway held a phone call with Vladimir Putin to restart the peace process. The overture comes as Brussels prepares for face-to-face contacts with the Russian side.
Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre held a call on Tuesday with Russian President Vladimir Putin, signalling Europe's increasing willingness to engage directly with Moscow to end the war in Ukraine.
The two leaders urged Putin to end the full-scale invasion and engage in meaningful negotiations to reach a stable, peaceful settlement.
"The discussion was frank and substantive. We are neighbouring countries of Russia. The outcome of this war will have a direct impact on our and the broader European security. Ending the war requires direct discussion," Stubb said in a read-out.
"The war comes with enormous human and material costs. The suffering and destruction will impact generations. In the call, we stressed the importance of de-escalation," Støre said.
Norway and Finland are among the largest donors of military aid to Ukraine, a support the two leaders told Putin would continue unabated.
Security in the Baltic Sea region and the High North was also discussed.
According to the Kremlin, Putin told Stubb and Støre that "achieving a just, long-term peace is only possible with full and unconditional consideration of the legitimate interests of the Russian Federation", a wording that suggests maximalist demands.
The call was made at the initiative of the two Nordic leaders. Afterwards, they exchanged with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
"Alex and Jonas made it clear to the Russian leader that real de-escalatory steps are needed regarding our energy and infrastructure," Zelenskyy said, thanking them for their "active" diplomatic support.
"Russia must stop dragging out the war."
The conversation was framed as a "follow-up" to the last round of peace talks in Oslo, which Stubb and Støre jointly organised. The meeting was attended by senior officials of Ukraine, the US, the UK, Germany, Italy, the European Commission and NATO.
Russia was not included, but US special envoy Steve Witkoff flew to St Petersburg to brief Putin on the outcome of the discussions.
A new round of talks is expected to take place early next month in Abu Dhabi in a format similar to Oslo, but with the participation of the Russian delegation.
Brussels has already expressed readiness for having European and Russian officials sit at the same table, which has never happened in the context of the negotiations.
The European Commission and the European Council are working to establish a combined team to represent the EU position. The two institutions are believed to have been told in advance of the Stubb-Støre call with Putin.
"On the EU side, we are adamantly committed not just to putting an end to the war but to achieve peace that will be just and sustainable. That is our aim and that is the stance we are defending in the ongoing talks," a Commission spokesperson said.
The two Nordic leaders underlined that they were not acting as a special European envoy, a topic that has split countries for over a year now.
"Stubb and Støre took the call as leaders of their respective countries and did not speak on behalf of Europe as a whole," the read-out said.
In a rare sign of Nordic divide, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen quickly criticised the Stubb-Støre overture, complaining it had not been coordinated.
"I actually don't know what they think you can achieve with this," she said. "We have previously also emphasised in clear terms to the rest of Europe, when others have gone solo and travelled to Moscow, that it is important that we Europeans stand together."

Russian Commander Complains NATO Testing Drones on Ukraine’s Front Line
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:13:20 UTC
20:13:20 KST

In an interview with Russia’s state news agency TASS on Tuesday, Oct. 27 the commander of Moscow’s Akhmat special forces unit, Lt. Gen. Apti Alaudinov complained that NATO nations were using the war in Ukraine to test drone technology in combat against Russia.
He commented that large numbers of Western manufactured unmanned aerial vehicles (UAV) were being encountered: “We see that drones manufactured in all these countries, which are members of the NATO alliance, are being tested against us on the line of engagement.”
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Alaudinov claimed that these included drones of every type, capability and operational ranges. According to him, this not only included first-person view (FPV) drones used to attack Russian forces and equipment on the front line but also included long-range UAVs that were being used to carry out deep strikes against towns, cities and infrastructure inside Russia.
The West learning from Ukraine’s experience of drone warfare – a two-way street
In March 2022, in the earliest days of the war, the US Council on Foreign relations commented on how Ukraine relied on drones sourced from Turkey, the Bayraktar TB2, as a means of disrupting Russian tank columns on their march towards Kyiv. Their appearance on the battlefield seemed at first to be a game changer, but it was not long before their vulnerability was exploited by Moscow’s air defenses.
However, the value of drones in taking the war to the enemy and the need for countermeasures was soon appreciated by both sides which led to the battlefield dominance UAVs currently enjoy.
What Israel’s Election Could Change for Ukraine and Relations With Russia
Recent statements by Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense and reports in the Western mainstream and social media seem to partially confirm Alaudinov’s assertions. Ukraine is cooperating with both government and commercial drone-related programs, not only using “attack” and surveillance drones but also to develop counter-drone technology and tactics.
A July report by the Ministry of Defense explained how it was working with NATO’s Allied Command Transformation (ACT) agency using its battlefield experience to support NATO in developing ways to combat drones. The report says this shows that “Ukraine is not only receiving support from its partners but is also actively shaping their approaches to modern warfare.”
On Monday the US publication The Hill reported on comments made by US Air Force Gen. Alexus G. Grynkewich, SACEUR, at a meeting in Poland. This followed on from an earlier report by Bloomberg on plans to use artificial intelligence (AI) enhanced drones to defend the alliance. The general laid out a possible strategy in the event of an attack by Russia, the concept of “blunt, block and break.” The articles suggested that the mass use of UAVs would be key to the success of Grynkewich’s plan and suggested that virtually every military was developing UAV-based concepts supplemented with AI for warfighting.
A week ago, the Wall Street Journal reported on how Ukraine’s “Kill Zone” was being used to test and develop the use of AI in drones. This followed a report in the defense issues website the Defense Post that discussed how Ukraine had been deploying AI tools developed in the NATO-Ukraine Joint Analysis, Training and Education Centre (JATEC) to both plan and control its UAV operations and to predict Russian drone activity. It said a prototype system was undergoing real-time validation by Ukrainian forces.
CBS reported in September that Washington and Kyiv were in the process of agreeing on a policy that would allow the two countries to expand the testing and production of Ukrainian defense technology in the US. It was given new impetus by the use of Iranian drones against US forces in the Middle East.
The report cites experts saying the experience gained by Ukraine in developing drone software and operations, as well as the speed with which it could adapt to battlefield changes, were likely to prove invaluable to the use of drones by the US and its allies.
Deborah Fairlamb, partner in a US venture capital firm that is investing in Ukrainian defense technology, told CBS: “The West needs to start understanding better is that it’s not just about having the tech. It’s about how the tech is used. And this is where Ukraine’s knowledge, skills, experience really need to be transmitted.”
In a separate report on its YouTube channel in July, CBS reported on how Ukraine was deploying US drone technology, such as the “Shield AI” V-Bat vertical take-off and landing (VTOL) reconnaissance and targeting UAV, to support long-range strikes into Russia.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party plans to deploy teams to film Arab voters outside polling stations during Tuesday’s general elections, potentially using the footage to support claims of electoral fraud if the party suffers major losses, Haaretz daily reported.
The newspaper said Likud has spent millions of shekels recruiting and paying workers to monitor polling stations in Arab communities, record voters and report developments to party headquarters in real time.
The teams, established in recent weeks, will operate outside polling stations rather than inside them, allowing them to avoid the strict regulations governing official election observers.
According to the report, senior Likud officials have also discussed launching a campaign alleging that the elections were rigged if the party suffers significant losses.
Sources close to Netanyahu said some party officials have been pressing the prime minister to adopt the strategy and that he is considering the proposal.
However, there is no evidence that Netanyahu personally attended meetings where the plan was discussed.
READ: Israel votes Tuesday in closely contested election as Netanyahu faces challenge from Eisenkot
The proposed campaign resembles US President Donald Trump’s allegations of widespread electoral fraud following his defeat in the 2020 presidential election.
A senior Likud official involved in election operations described the party’s allegations of voting irregularities during Israel’s 2022 election as preparation for the current vote.
“2022 was a trial run for the current election,” the official said.
Likud sources also indicated that footage collected outside polling stations could be circulated as purported evidence of electoral fraud, despite the teams having no legal authority to verify voters’ identities.
Separately, party observers across Israel are expected to report unusual incidents to a dedicated election fraud monitoring center.
The allegations come as Israelis vote in the country’s first general election since Israel launched its genocidal war on the Gaza Strip in October 2023.

Weak EU Demand Hits Bulgarian Exports as Firms Seek New Markets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27

20:07:00 KST

Weak EU Demand Hits Bulgarian Exports as Firms Seek New Markets
Bulgaria ranked third in the European Union for the steepest annual decline in industrial production in August 2026, with output falling by more than 9.4%, as weaker European demand put pressure on Bulgarian exporters and forced businesses to seek new markets and cut costs.
The slowdown in the European economy has hit Bulgarian companies as growth in the eurozone averaged below 0.8%, reducing demand from key trading partners and weighing on exports.
National Statistical Institute (NSI) data show that Bulgaria’s total exports of goods decreased by 3.2% in 2025, while exports of goods and services fell by 1.9% compared with the previous year. Shipments to EU member states dropped by 3.8% to 53.88 billion levs.
The latest industrial figures extend a contraction already seen in 2025, when value added in mining, manufacturing and energy fell by 5.0%.
The slowdown among Bulgaria’s main trading partners, Germany, Romania, Italy, Greece and France, which together account for nearly 64% of Bulgarian exports to the EU, has also affected domestic subcontractors. Exports to Germany, traditionally Bulgaria’s leading export market, declined by more than 7.5% in the first half of 2026. Shipments to Italy fell by 6.2%, while those to Romania decreased by 4.8%.
In 2025, the sharpest decline among European export sectors came in “Miscellaneous Manufactured Articles,” where exports contracted by 14.7%. The category includes a broad range of consumer goods whose demand is particularly sensitive to inflation, averaging 4.5% across Europe, and growing uncertainty among European households.
Machinery and equipment exports also suffered, falling by more than 5% as Western companies froze capital investment. Exports of raw materials and supplies to non-EU markets weakened in 2026 as well, with the “Articles classified chiefly by material” category recording an 8.4% decrease.
With demand from the EU remaining weak, Bulgarian businesses have increasingly looked beyond the bloc. During the first eight months of 2026, exports to countries outside the EU rose by 4.4%, exceeding 21 billion levs.
Companies expanded sales to Turkey, where exports increased by 7.1%, and the United States, where they grew by 5.5%. Serbia, China and the United Kingdom have also become target markets for Bulgarian exporters.
Businesses are also seeking growth through new product categories. Exports of “Animal and vegetable oils, fats, and waxes” to EU countries rose by nearly 44% in 2025. In early 2026, exports of these products to non-EU countries surged by 175%, generating more than 1.2 billion levs in revenue.
These figures point to the agility of Bulgaria’s agricultural and industrial food sectors in exploiting market opportunities created by global shortages.
Despite gains in some markets, the country’s overall trade position remains under pressure, with imports exceeding exports. Bulgaria recorded a trade deficit of more than 6.6 billion levs with the EU in 2025, while its total trade deficit surpassed 10.5 billion levs.
The economic slowdown has also prompted companies to tighten spending, with approximately 15% of planned investment in tangible fixed assets frozen this year. To improve its long-term competitiveness, Bulgarian industry needs to invest in innovation, automation and higher value-added production.
The existing economic model, based largely on low-cost labor and contract manufacturing for major German and French companies, is showing its limitations as competition from Asia and North Africa intensifies.

Israel elections 2026: 10 factors that could shape the vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:06:51 UTC
20:06:51 KST

Breadcrumb
Israel elections 2026: 10 factors that could shape the results
Israelis headed to the polls on Tuesday in what Israeli media report to be one of the country's most dramatic elections in recent years, with the political future of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu hanging in the balance.
The vote comes against the backdrop of Israel's genocidal war on Gaza, growing political divisions and uncertainty over whether Netanyahu's right-wing coalition or the opposition, also rightwing politically, can secure enough seats to form the next government.
But the outcome will depend on more than which party wins the most votes. Turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel, the mobilisation of ultra-Orthodox voters and the performance of smaller parties could all influence the balance of power in the 120-seat Knesset.
The counting process could also take longer than usual, with an unprecedented number of special ballots expected to delay a clear picture of the results until Wednesday afternoon.
The following are 10 factors that could shape the election results:
1. How high will voter turnout be?
Voter turnout is one of the most closely watched indicators in Israeli elections, particularly because it can affect the prospects of smaller parties seeking parliamentary representation.
Turnout in the previous election stood at around 70%, while estimates suggest it could rise to 75% this time.
A higher turnout increases the number of votes a party needs to cross the electoral threshold, making it more difficult for smaller parties to secure seats.
This could have significant implications for both Netanyahu's coalition and the opposition, particularly if parties aligned with either camp fail to enter parliament.
2. Which cities will turn out in the largest numbers?
Beyond the national turnout figure, the geographical distribution of voters could provide important clues about the election outcome.
Traditionally, peripheral towns and settlements such as Ofakim, Yeruham, Kiryat Shmona and Sderot have been strongholds of Netanyahu's Likud party.
By contrast, more liberal cities, including Herzliya, Ramat Hasharon, Tel Aviv and Kfar Saba, have been more closely associated with the opposition's so-called "change camp".
That camp includes prominent political figures with military and security backgrounds, such as Gadi Eisenkot, Naftali Bennett and Yair Golan, alongside Yair Lapid and Avigdor Lieberman.
Turnout figures in these areas could reveal where political enthusiasm is strongest and where voter apathy may affect the results.
3. Why could special ballots delay the results?
Around 650,000 special ballots, known as "double envelopes", have been registered for this election, an unprecedented figure.
These ballots are used by eligible voters who cannot cast their votes at polling stations near their registered addresses.
They include soldiers, diplomats, Foreign Ministry employees, people with disabilities and settlers evacuated from their homes.
The special counting procedures mean that a clearer picture of the election results may not emerge until Wednesday afternoon.
The unusually large number of these ballots could also affect the final distribution of seats, potentially pushing some smaller parties above the electoral threshold.
4. Could Palestinian voters determine the balance of power?
Turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel is expected to be one of the most consequential factors in the election.
The Joint List, led by Yousef Jabareen, and the United Arab List (Ra'am), led by Mansour Abbas, are running separately but have both launched extensive campaigns to encourage Palestinian citizens to vote.
Their performance could affect the prospects of both Netanyahu's coalition and the opposition.
If Arab parties secure more than 14 of the Knesset's 120 seats, analysts believe it would represent a significant achievement, while potentially making it harder for either political bloc to form a government.
However, concerns have emerged over the conduct of voting in Palestinian towns and cities. Several polling stations in Arab communities were delayed in opening on Tuesday morning.
According to sources speaking to The New Arab, some polling committee members claimed to have lost their way in Arab towns, while residents in certain areas alleged that the delays were deliberate.
Arab voters also complained about the absence of Arabic-language ballot papers at some polling stations, raising concerns about accessibility for citizens who are not proficient in Hebrew.
Another controversy concerns the presence of armed election observers.
On Monday, Israel's Supreme Court rejected a petition filed by the Haifa-based legal rights organisation Adalah and the Joint List seeking to prohibit observers from carrying weapons inside polling stations.
The petition followed announcements by Likud and Religious Zionism that they intended to deploy approximately 2,000 observers in Arab towns and mixed cities.
Petitioners warned that the presence of armed representatives from right-wing parties could intimidate Arab voters and provoke confrontations.
The Israeli authorities argued that there was no operational or security justification for banning weapons, saying armed observers would receive specific instructions limiting their use to self-defence.
The court declined to intervene in the decisions of the police and Central Elections Committee, saying the concerns raised had been considered in election security preparations.
Adalah criticised the ruling, arguing that it failed to address the potential intimidation of Arab voters by organised groups of armed right-wing activists.
5. Will young Israelis turn out in greater numbers?
Young voters could play a more prominent role in this election following a campaign heavily conducted on social media.
According to Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper, political parties believe their online campaigns have encouraged greater engagement among younger Israelis, including those who previously showed little interest in electoral politics.
Celebrities and social media influencers have also joined the campaign, with several publicly revealing which parties they intend to support.
Their endorsements have generated debate among followers and helped bring political discussions to audiences that might otherwise have remained disengaged.
Party estimates suggest that younger voters could turn out in greater numbers than usual, potentially increasing their influence on the results.
6. How will ultra-Orthodox voters respond?
Israel's ultra-Orthodox, or Haredi, community has traditionally voted in large numbers, often following the guidance of religious leaders.
However, analysts and prominent figures within the community say voting patterns are particularly difficult to predict this year.
One major source of dissatisfaction is the government's failure to pass legislation exempting ultra-Orthodox men from military conscription during the current parliamentary term.
The emergence of new Haredi parties challenging established political organisations has also created uncertainty.
Meanwhile, United Torah Judaism, which represents sections of the ultra-Orthodox community, has undergone a leadership change, with Knesset member Yaakov Asher replacing veteran politician Moshe Gafni.
According to Yedioth Ahronoth, it remains unclear whether ultra-Orthodox voters will maintain their traditional party loyalties or use the election to register a protest vote.
Their decisions could have significant consequences for Netanyahu, whose governing coalitions have long relied on ultra-Orthodox parties.
7. Does winning the most seats guarantee power?
Not necessarily.
Although considerable attention is focused on which party will emerge as the largest in the Knesset, winning the most seats does not automatically give its leader the right to form a government.
Under Israel's political system, the president assigns the task of forming a government to the candidate considered most capable of assembling a governing coalition.
The president has considerable discretion in making that decision.
As a result, a party could finish first in the election but still find itself in opposition if another political leader can secure broader parliamentary support.
The ability to negotiate alliances and build a viable coalition may therefore prove more important than the number of seats won by any single party.
8. Why does the first mandate to form a government matter?
The candidate tasked with forming a government initially has 28 days to assemble a coalition.
That period can be extended by a further 14 days.
However, securing the first mandate is important for reasons beyond coalition negotiations.
According to the report, the candidate who receives the initial mandate also gains influence over the Knesset's Arrangements Committee, which plays a central role in parliamentary procedures before permanent committees are established.
Control over parliamentary arrangements can allow political factions to advance legislation and potentially replace the Knesset speaker.
This means the first candidate given the opportunity to form a government could influence parliamentary developments even if their coalition negotiations ultimately fail.
9. What role could the Elector app play?
Political parties are also relying on technology to mobilise supporters and monitor turnout throughout election day.
One tool attracting particular attention is Elector, a sophisticated voter-management application reportedly worth hundreds of thousands of shekels.
According to Israeli news website Ynet, the application contains information gathered about individuals who have declared support for particular parties or have been identified as potential supporters.
It allows campaign teams to monitor whether those voters have cast their ballots, providing parties with a clearer picture of their mobilisation efforts.
The system can help parties identify supporters who have not yet voted and focus their efforts on encouraging them to reach polling stations.
However, its use has raised questions about consent and the collection of personal information.
Central Elections Committee chairman Judge Noam Sohlberg expressed reservations about the application but ultimately permitted its use.
The effectiveness of parties' voter mobilisation operations could prove important in closely contested races.
10. Could the weather affect the result?
Even the weather could play a role in determining turnout.
Political parties are closely monitoring forecasts for rain in several Israeli cities on election day.
Rainfall could discourage undecided voters or those with little enthusiasm for participating from travelling to polling stations. This could be particularly significant for parties that depend on mobilising less committed supporters.

Amid Legal Uncertainty, US Lawmakers Warn Banks, Ports Over Russian Diesel Imports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:06:48 UTC
20:06:48 KST

WASHINGTON -- A bipartisan group of US lawmakers have warned American banks, port authorities, and fuel-industry groups against facilitating imports of Russian diesel, raising the prospect of congressional investigations and legal action over President Donald Trump’s decision to ease restrictions on Russian fuel.
In letters sent to the chief executives of major US banks and the heads of several port authorities, the lawmakers warned that importing Russian diesel could violate federal law and expose companies to civil and criminal liability.
They also said the imports would raise national-security concerns by providing Moscow with revenue to help finance its war against Ukraine.
The intervention comes after Trump recently announced an arrangement with Russian President Vladimir Putin under which Moscow would supply hundreds of thousands of metric tons of diesel to the United States, with additional shipments planned in the coming months. The US Treasury Department subsequently issued General License 135, granting a six-month exemption from certain sanctions restrictions.
The letters signal a potential new front in the political and legal battle over the administration’s Russia policy. Democrats could gain significant investigative powers if they regain control of one or both chambers of Congress in the November midterm elections.
“Any importation of Russian diesel into the US raises significant legal questions and may be subject to legal action, as well as congressional investigations,” the lawmakers wrote.
The group includes Democratic Senators Jeanne Shaheen, Ron Wyden, Sheldon Whitehouse, Chris Coons and Elizabeth Warren, as well as outgoing Republican Senator Thom Tillis and Representative Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee.
They urged companies not to facilitate the purchase, transportation, importation, unloading, storage, financing, or distribution of Russian-origin diesel until the relevant legal requirements had been met.
The lawmakers also demanded that the companies preserve records of proposed or completed transactions, including contracts, shipping documents, payment records, port reservations and communications with suppliers and US government officials dating back to September 1.
Recipients were asked to confirm by October 28 that they had implemented the required preservation measures and to disclose whether they had knowledge of any proposed or actual Russian diesel imports.
The letters went to the chief executives of major US banks, including Goldman Sachs, as well as the port authorities of Houston, Corpus Christi and Beaumont in Texas and New York/New Jersey.
Public reporting and vessel-tracking data cited by the lawmakers indicate that ships carrying Russian diesel could arrive at Beaumont and New York/New Jersey as early as the end of October.
At the center of the dispute is whether the administration’s licensing action is consistent with restrictions established by Congress.
The lawmakers cited the Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act of 2022, which generally prohibits imports of Russian-origin energy products unless the president certifies to Congress, following a period of consultation, that Russia has ceased military hostilities in Ukraine, poses no immediate military threat to NATO members, and recognizes Ukrainians’ right to choose their government.
They also argued that Section 216 of the Countering America’s Adversaries Through Sanctions Act requires congressional review before certain licensing actions that significantly alter US foreign policy toward Russia. The lawmakers said the administration had not fulfilled that requirement.
The administration maintains that its action is lawful and consistent with previous decisions by the Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control, which administers US sanctions.
The White House dismissed the lawmakers’ initiative as politically motivated.
“The Democrats are already telegraphing that, once again, they have no agenda to improve the lives of Americans and will instead continue their decade-long obsession with investigating President Trump,” spokesperson Taylor Rogers said.
The letters do not establish that any company has committed a crime. Instead, they warn that participating in the transactions could expose companies to legal challenges and investigations despite the administration’s assurances that the waiver is valid.
Representative Jamie Raskin, the top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, separately warned major fuel-industry associations that companies importing Russian diesel could face civil and criminal penalties, including up to 20 years in prison.
Raskin argued that Trump’s move could not override statutory prohibitions and warned that companies could be held accountable “whether in this administration -- or the next.”
Experts say the warnings could complicate the administration’s plans even if the waiver reduces the risk of sanctions violations under US executive-branch rules.
Michael Wain, a senior international trade policy adviser at the law firm Akin, told RFE/RL that the congressional pushback was noteworthy but that US imports represented only part of the picture.
“General License 135 covers a broad range of Russian diesel transactions and substantially reduces US sanctions risk for foreign firms that stay within its terms,” Wain said. However, he added, companies must still consider British, European Union and other jurisdictions’ sanctions rules.
A key question, he said, is whether foreign buyers previously reluctant to handle Russian fuel will now feel more comfortable doing so -- an outcome that may be part of the administration’s objective.
Glen Howard, president of the Saratoga Foundation and a longtime Russia strategist, said the letters could make major US banks reluctant to finance the transactions.
“It is very significant because it was sent to each of the major US banks and will likely cause them to freeze in place any efforts by the Trump administration to proceed with the sale,” Howard told RFE/RL.
He said the move suggested the administration had failed to adequately consider the deal’s legal obstacles and strategic implications. Howard speculated that the decision had been made by a small group of advisers without broader consultation across the administration.
The potential consequences extend beyond the immediate shipments. Banks and other intermediaries may be wary of congressional subpoenas, requests to testify or future legal challenges, even if they believe a transaction is permitted under the Treasury license.
Rachel Ziemba, a senior fellow at the Center for a New American Security, said the warnings reinforced her view that most Russian diesel cargoes would be sold outside the United States.
“These warnings reinforce my view that most of any Russian diesel cargos will go to countries outside the US and that it is mostly diplomatic theater,” Ziemba told RFE/RL.
She said a meaningful increase in diesel supplies would likely require an energy cease-fire, which she said Russia was wary of agreeing to. Ziemba also said the administration believes its waivers are sufficient to overcome the legal obstacles identified by lawmakers, but that uncertainty could still deter American buyers and financial institutions.
“The concerns from the senators may give some US banks and buyers pause about purchasing the diesel, which is en route to the US as we speak,” Ziemba said.
Some cargoes could consequently be resold to other countries in the Americas, where demand for fuel remains strong.
Russia confirmed the arrangement after Trump announced it on October 9. Trump said Moscow would initially deliver more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel, followed by another 500,000 tons in November and a further 1 million tons afterward. He said Russia could supply an additional 3 million tons, depending on the condition of its refineries.
Traders said the Russian government had begun granting exemptions to its diesel export ban on October 1 to allow shipments under the arrangement. Industry sources said Russian diesel production fell from about 175,000 tons a day in September to 160,000 tons a day in the first half of October, before recovering toward 180,000 tons a day after new export quotas were introduced.
The shipments could provide Russia with additional revenue, but legal uncertainty may deter some US buyers and redirect cargoes to other markets.

Tallinn's new cinemas are still working to build their audiences
Two new movie theaters, which opened earlier this year in Tallinn, are working to differentiate themselves from the competition and build their audiences.
In the spring, Kai Cinema, previously part of Sõprus Cinema, began operating independently, while at the beginning of the summer, Cinamon, which had operated at T1 in Ülemiste, relocated to Kosmos.
Kai Cinema, which is part of the Kai Art Center, has now been operating independently for approximately six months. Program Manager Katariina Rebane said Kai Cinema does not compete directly with the capital's other arthouse movie theaters.
"If we think about what the market share of arthouse movie theaters is in general today, it is rather small. And Kai Cinema is also contributing to increasing the share of arthouse films and their audiences," Rebane said.
The cinema's program has become more extensive after the venue became independent, she added. There have been more special programs and screenings, benefiting both the art center and the local community.
However, Rebane admitted the movie theater is not currently profitable and she does not support raising ticket prices.
"We would rather people could still come to the movies at a lower price, get out of their homes and watch a film together with other people. Taking the economic situation into account, we certainly do not want to raise ticket prices at the moment. We hope the situation improves, and for now we are running the movie theater out of a sense of mission and enthusiasm. We want there to continue to be a movie theater here," she added.
In June, Kosmos Cinema reopened its doors in the city center. As a mainstream movie theater, Cinamon competes directly with Apollo.
"We try to do things differently from Apollo. Our difference lies not only in the location, but perhaps also in the emotional significance of the place. We show various cultural films, such as Japanese and Indian films, and organize various events for children and families," said Cinamon CEO Andac Bagioglu.
The theater manager said attendance figures depend largely on which films are currently being released.
"One of the drawbacks of the movie industry is that you have no control whatsoever over what you sell. When good films, such as 'Spider-Man' or 'The Odyssey,' or a good animated film reach the screen, everyone comes to the movies. But when it comes to average or lower-quality films that can also be watched on streaming services, people do not come to the movies," he acknowledged.

World's climate pledges would cut emissions a tenth of what's needed: UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:04:31 UTC
20:04:31 KST

Supporters of the first federal youth climate trial in Canadian history hold up signs during a rally outside the Vancouver Art Gallery in Vancouver, British Colombia, Canada on October 26, 2026. (AFP Photo)
The latest climate pledges put forth by nations will cut global greenhouse gas emissions just six percent by 2035, a U.N. report said on Oct. 27, weeks before COP31 talks in Türkiye.
That is a tenth of the roughly 60 percent reduction from 2019 levels that scientists say is needed to limit warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius, significantly down from last year's estimate after the United States withdrew from the Paris Agreement.
The report by U.N. Climate Change is a synthesis of 154 countries' nationally determined contributions (NDCs) — obligatory submissions under the 2015 Paris deal — received between January 2024 and August 2026, covering 71 percent of global emissions.
It found that if the countries fully implemented their plans and also met conditional targets, emissions cuts would still amount to just 9 percent.
The U.N. last year estimated a 10 percent cut by 2035, but that was before a large number of NDCs had come in, leaving it to model the missing pledges, and before the U.S. was taken out of the equation.
Under President Donald Trump, the U.S. has left the Paris Agreement for a second time and is pursuing policies that heavily favor fossil fuels.
Last week, the United Nations Environment Program found that global commitments to cut planet-heating emissions put the world on course for 2.6 degrees Celsius warming this century.
Scientists warn that every additional fraction of a degree above 1.5 degrees Celsius increases extreme weather events and the likelihood of irreversible changes to the planet, from dying coral reefs to melting permafrost.

German prosecutors reject motion to dismiss case on Nord Stream pipeline sabotage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:03:34 UTC
20:03:34 KST

HAMBURG, October 27. /TASS/. The German Federal Prosecutor’s Office has rejected a motion to dismiss the case against Ukrainian citizen Sergey Kuznetsov, who is accused of participating in the sabotage of the Nord Stream gas pipelines.
"The defense’s motion cannot be granted," a TASS correspondent quoted senior public prosecutor Stefan Schmidt as saying at a hearing of the Hanseatic Higher Regional Court in Hamburg. The prosecutor rejected the arguments of Kuznetsov’s defense that it was allegedly impossible to ensure the defendant’s "effective defense" because he is a Ukrainian special forces officer and is prohibited by Ukrainian law from disclosing military secrets.
The trial on the merits began in Hamburg on October 27 in the case involving the sabotage of the Nord Stream and Nord Stream 2 gas pipelines. The first court hearing took place on October 14. At that hearing, the defense requested that the case be dismissed. According to the defense, a fair trial cannot be guaranteed because the defendant is a former military officer who allegedly has no right to disclose the contents of orders, who issued them, or other information - not even to his own defense attorneys. Neither the prosecution nor the defense has questioned his involvement in the sabotage during the trial.
The German Federal Prosecutor’s Office charged Kuznetsov with war crimes, including carrying out explosions, destroying buildings, and disrupting public utility operations. Investigators believe he and his accomplices devised a plan to blow up pipelines on behalf of the Ukrainian government. Another Ukrainian was recently detained in Croatia. Prosecutors assume that the saboteurs used forged documents to rent a sailboat from a German company to transport explosives to the Nord Stream pipelines. Kuznetsov was detained in Italy in August 2022 and extradited to Germany.
On September 27, 2022, Nord Stream AG reported "unprecedented damage" on three strings of the offshore gas pipelines of the Nord Stream system. Later, Swedish seismologists said they had identified two explosions on the route of the Nord Stream pipelines on September 26, 2022. Following the incident, the Russian Prosecutor General’s Office initiated a criminal case on charges of international terrorism. Russian Ambassador to Germany Sergey Nechayev stated that all of Moscow’s initiatives to investigate the sabotage of the gas pipelines are being ignored, and numerous requests essentially remain unanswered.

Syria on Tuesday expressed "condemnation and rejection, in the strongest terms" over Jordanian strikes on southern Syria in response to a deadly church attack in Jordan.
In a Syrian foreign ministry statement released a day after the Jordanian strikes, Syria said they were "an unacceptable violation and breach of Syrian airspace without any prior coordination". It also said the attack was "a blatant violation of the principles of good-neighbourliness and Syrian national sovereignty".
Syria said the strikes killed seven people, including three children and a woman. Jordan regretted the civilian casualties, Government Communication Minister Mohammed al-Momani said in a post on X.
The Hashemite Kingdom’s air force Monday evening carried out air strikes in Syria in retaliation for last week’s attacks on a funeral at a Greek Orthodox Church in the southern Jordanian city of Karak that killed nine people. Earlier that day it announced it arrested the three gunmen, but did not disclose their affiliation.

The numbers given in remarks by Momani differ from what Syrian first-responders reported. Syria's civil defense said it only recovered the bodies of seven civilians killed in Jordanian strikes in the southern Daraa and Sweida provinces. Five of those were a family, including three children and a woman; two of the men who were killed were elderly.
Syria’s government said the strikes were carried out without prior coordination or notification.

Amman and Damascus maintained strong bilateral ties following the downfall of the Assad dynasty in December 2024 and the emergence of interim President Ahmad al-Sharaa’s Islamist-led government.
Jordan said on Tuesday it was keen to safeguard its ties with Syria. "Jordan holds great respect for the Syrian state and its brotherly people, and coordination between Jordan and Syria in fighting terrorism and weapons and drug smuggling is ongoing and has been for years," Momani said.
Masoud al-Salim lost his wife, son, and three grandchildren in one of the strikes that hit his home in the Syrian border village of Al-Tuff in Daraa province.
“I came running and found there was no house anymore, no tent, nothing. I couldn’t find anyone,” al-Salim said, rummaging through children’s schoolbooks and toys in the rubble. “I started looking under the rubble. I thought they might be buried there.”

Three Arab states back Greece in dispute over Turkey-Libya maritime accord

Three Arab states back Greece in dispute over Turkey-Libya maritime accord
ATHENS, Oct 27 - Egypt, Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates aligned with Greece to denounce a Turkey-Libya maritime accord as a threat to regional security and international legal order in a long-standing dispute over sea borders in the eastern Mediterranean Sea.
Libya's eastern parliament last week approved a maritime boundaries deal with Turkey, originally agreed in 2019, drawing swift condemnation from Greece and Cyprus, which say it infringes on their own maritime claims.
In a joint statement delivered by Greek Foreign Minister George Gerapetritis at the United Nations in New York on Monday, Greece and the three Arab countries said the maritime accord raised "serious concerns for regional security and stability" and could set a bad precedent by allowing "arbitrary bilateral arrangements" to undermine established rules of international law.
Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan said on Monday that reactions from the European Union and others to the approval of the agreement had no legitimate basis, defending Ankara's policy in the eastern Mediterranean.
The Arab support to Greece signals efforts to turn a bilateral dispute into a broader regional push for respect of maritime rules, increasing diplomatic pressure on Turkey and Libya over maritime zones and future energy projects in the Mediterranean Sea.
Since the 2019 Libya-Turkey deal, Greece has awarded a Chevron -led consortium a licence to look for gas off the island of Crete and has sought a separate agreement with Libya on demarcating their maritime zones.
Gerapetritis said on Monday that Athens stood ready to continue the effort and called on Libya to foster good relations with neighbours in line with maritime rules as part of a political transition.
Libya broke apart into rival eastern and western administrations more than a decade ago during a civil war after a NATO-backed uprising toppled longtime Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi.
The Libya-Turkey accord was agreed by Libya’s internationally recognised government in Tripoli in the west, but the rival eastern administration under military commander Khalifa Haftar had withheld its approval for years.
Turkish support was crucial to repelling an assault by Haftar's forces on Tripoli in 2019-2020.
But relations have steadily improved in recent years, with Turkish officials paying regular visits to Haftar’s de facto capital, Benghazi, and investing heavily in construction and other sectors. REUTERS
