Why we’ll never have another Black Death
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:50:10 UTC
19:50:10 KST

Scientists disagree over how scared we should be by the mysterious death of a worker at a Russian plague lab. A young laboratory technician died earlier this month of an undisclosed illness after working on research at the Irkutsk Antiplague Research Institute of Siberia and Far East. Although officials have not released details about the cause of death, scientists agree that if it was caused by ordinary plague, the wider world has little to worry about. This bacterial illness is infamous for the explosive killing spree known as the Black Death, which wiped out between a third and half of the population of Europe between 1347 and 1353. Today, however, plague is curable and extremely unlikely to blow up into a new pandemic, experts say. That’s thanks to a combination of antibiotic development, scientific understanding and luck.
Experts who study plague are reluctant to say it’s been completely conquered. The World Health Organization (WHO) recently reported approximately 3,800 infections and 423 deaths from plague between 2019 and 2025. And scientists haven’t cracked all the mysteries behind the plague bacterium, known as Yersinia pestis—one of the biggest being how it hides for years in cryptic reservoirs only to spring out in unpredictable new waves of infection in humans or other animals.
The disease is endemic in rodents living in the Americas, Central Asia and Africa, says David Wagner, a plague expert who directs the Pathogen and Microbiome Institute at Northern Arizona University. “It’s constantly cycling between rodents via fleas, and it just does that in perpetuity in a manner we poorly understand, despite 100 years of research.”
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Studies of ancient DNA show plague-infected prehistoric hunter-gatherers in Siberia 5,500 years ago. Plague is known for causing three major pandemics: in addition to the one that started with the Black Death, which peaked between 1347 and 1351 and was followed by outbreaks into the 18th century, there was the plague of Justinian from C.E. 541 to 549 and a third pandemic that started in the 1800s and spread to every inhabited continent by 1900. That last pandemic was accelerated by a boom in rail and steamship travel but was eventually quashed by advances in science.
In 1894 French-Swiss bacteriologist Alexandre Yersin isolated the plague bacterium and connected rat infestations to the disease. Rat eradication campaigns followed around the world, drastically slowing the spread of plague, Wagner says. Though it was really the fleas that spread the disease to people, rat control worked because fleas are very specific about hosts. Different animal species have their own flea species, so rats and plague-carrying fleas traveled together.
Quarantines also helped, Wagner adds, because doctors started to recognize that the bacteria could sometimes spread from person to person through respiratory droplets. In the 1940s, when antibiotics had become widely available, doctors started curing plague cases with the drugs. Several vaccines have been developed over the years and deployed in severe outbreaks, in which they offered partial protection. No vaccine has been deemed effective enough to gain approval from the WHO or the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, but labs in Russia and the U.S. continue to work on them.
Today most plague cases occur in Madagascar. Because food can be scarce there and people fear theft, individuals will store rice in their dirt-floor homes, Wagner says, allowing close contact with the rats that infest the island.
Though fleas are picky about their hosts, plague-carrying fleas in the U.S. are commonly found on prairie dogs, thanks to the animals having some functional similarities to rats. The plague bacterium now infects all five known species of prairie dogs and is one of the factors that contributed to a population decline in these social, burrowing rodents of about 98 percent from their historical levels. Because prairie dogs are a food source for other animals, including the critically endangered black-footed ferret, plague has been wreaking ecological havoc.
Even now it’s not clear where Y. pestis hides out between detectable outbreaks, Wagner says, and it’s surprising that it can be transmitted both by respiratory droplets and through fleas. But important clues about how the sickness operates are emerging from the latest studies of bacterial DNA in ancient bones and teeth.
The plague bacterium appears to have emerged as a human pathogen more than 5,700 years ago, evolving from a soil bacterium called Yersinia pseudotuberculosis, says Hendrick Poinar, a biologist at McMaster University, who works with ancient DNA. For the next 3,000 years, it infected Late Stone Age hunter-gathers and Bronze Age herders. Scientists suspect it was transmitted from human to human via respiratory droplets or via contaminated food because it hadn’t yet acquired the genes needed to travel through fleas.
Despite the versatility of Y. pestis, we’re lucky it can’t spread between humans unless an infected person is very sick and the contact is very close. Because of this limitation, even the emergence of an antibiotic-resistant strain won’t necessarily spark a new pandemic, Wagner says, noting that such strains have already shown up in Madagascar.
Though most scientists aren’t too alarmed about the situation in Russia, some are speculating that the death was caused by some highly genetically modified version of the plague bacterium or a different germ entirely. There’s no evidence for this, though the lack of transparency from Russia is unnerving. Regardless of the cause, the death of the worker is tragic. But if it was caused by the plague we know, the rest of us need not worry.

GM will switch to Nasdaq from the NYSE on Nov. 17
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:49:45 UTC
19:49:45 KST

DETROIT — General Motors plans to transfer shares of its common stock from the New York Stock Exchange to the Nasdaq as the automaker attempts to position itself more as a technology-focused company.
The Detroit automaker said Tuesday that it expects to begin trading as a Nasdaq-listed company on Nov. 17. Its ticker symbol is expected to remain "GM," the company said.
"GM's customer-focused, technology-driven strategy is creating value for our stockholders, making Nasdaq a natural home for our listing as we grow," GM CFO Paul Jacobson said in a release. "We're grateful for our long-standing partnership with the New York Stock Exchange and its remarkable legacy."
GM noted the move will provide eligibility for potential inclusion in the Nasdaq-100 Index.
Current shareholders do not need to take any action with respect to the transfer, the company said.
The switch marks a notable loss for the NYSE, as GM first listed on the exchange in 1911. The Detroit automaker also relisted on the stock exchange in 2010 following a government-backed bankruptcy.
GM follows other companies such as Walmart, DoorDash and Palantir Technologies that have transferred from the more traditional NYSE to the historically technology focused Nasdaq in recent years. Hilton Worldwide Holdings last week also announced plans to move trading from the NYSE to Nasdaq.
The key drivers for a listing transfer differ from company to company, but the Nasdaq in 2024 said common reasons include "index inclusion opportunities, cost effective fee structure, brand visibility partnership, access to Nasdaq's event space, and Nasdaq's suite of investor relations and ESG products."
GM's decision comes a week after the automaker held a technology-focused event where executives laid out the company's roadmap for artificial intelligence and self-driving vehicle technologies.
Shares of GM, which has been aggressively buying back stock, have more than doubled since 2024. GM stock closed Tuesday at $80.54 a share, up 5%. The company's market cap is roughly $64.4 billion.

By Essi Lehto
HELSINKI, Oct 27 (Reuters) - The leaders of Finland and Norway phoned Russian President Vladimir Putin on Tuesday to urge him to end the war in Ukraine, breaking with a longstanding practice among Western European leaders of shunning direct contact with the Kremlin.
The call by Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Stoere was an attempt to influence the diplomatic process after US President Donald Trump shifted his position in favour of Russia and US ties with Ukraine hit their lowest point in 18 months.
Stoere said he and Stubb had spoken to Putin for about 90 minutes, and then to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy.
In a joint statement, they linked the initiative to planned peace discussions between Russian, Ukrainian and US officials in Abu Dhabi next month, their first since February.
Moscow and Kyiv remain far apart on how to end the war that began with Russia’s invasion in February 2022, and long-range airstrikes by both sides have increased this year while battle lines have remained largely static.
“The discussion (with Putin) was frank and substantive. We are neighbouring countries to Russia. The outcome of this war will have a direct impact on our and the broader European security. Ending the war requires direct discussions,” Stubb said.
Stoere said he and Stubb had “stressed the importance of de-escalation.” Both voiced strong support for Ukraine.
In later comments to Finnish journalists, Stubb said all Western allies were consulted on the initiative, adding that Ukraine had sought the opening of a new communications channel and Europe could no longer be a bystander to peace efforts giving Russia “the silent treatment”.
NO SIGN OF KREMLIN COMPROMISE
The Kremlin’s readout of the call did not suggest any softening of Putin’s position.
“It was emphasised that achieving a just and long-term peace is possible only if the legitimate interests of the Russian Federation are fully and unconditionally taken into account,” it said.
“At the same time, attention was drawn to the confrontational policies of EU and NATO countries, which are contributing to the prolongation of the hostilities.”
Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said Tuesday’s call had offered nothing new on the Ukraine conflict, with an information war likely to escalate, and that European countries were simply seeking a role in the negotiation process.
Western European leaders have mostly refused to talk to Putin, hoping to isolate him. But they have been sidelined in peace efforts led by US President Donald Trump, who is seen in many European capitals as unpredictable and prone to side with Putin at Ukraine’s expense.
That perception has been reinforced by deals this month in which Putin agreed to supply Russian diesel to the United States and Trump eased sanctions on Russia. Ukraine has also complained of disruption to intelligence-sharing by the US and to satellite internet services on which its military relies.
Gerhard Mangott, an Austrian political analyst, said European governments had “manoeuvred themselves into a dead end” when it came to finding a solution to the war, and Tuesday’s call was an effort to establish a channel for dialogue.
He drew attention to remarks by Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov on Sunday suggesting Europe should be part of discussions.
“I interpret this as a shift in Russia’s position, given that Moscow had previously consistently rejected the idea of discussing a settlement of the war in Ukraine with the Europeans,” Mangott said.
DANISH LEADER’S CRITICISM
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the call had been coordinated with Kyiv and was “the right approach”.
“We welcome such active support for our diplomatic efforts and peace process,” he said, adding that he also hoped a local ceasefire around the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky could “pave the way to other steps in the peace process.”
But Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said she saw no signs that Russia wanted peace, adding: “I think Europe should stick together rather than going solo.”
Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson said other European leaders were not informed of the talks.
“My impression is that everyone wants peace, except for Putin himself. I have quite low expectations for this type of conversation,” Kristersson told Swedish daily DN.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said he had told Stubb and Stoere that “absolute caution and vigilance are necessary in such contacts”.
Stubb and Stoere said they acted as leaders of their respective countries and not on behalf of Europe, and had “consulted thoroughly with all our partners.”
Russia has frequently accused European governments of stoking the war by arming Ukraine and refusing direct talks.
A source close to the Kremlin said French President Emmanuel Macron had been the last EU leader to speak with Putin — in a summer call that yielded no results and was not made public.
The source said Putin told Stubb and Stoere that the European involvement was welcome and that the war needed to end “taking into account the realities on the ground”.
Asked what this meant, the person said it signified that Russia would not compromise over its aim to capture the whole of Ukraine’s Donbas region. The Europeans responded by saying a “just” peace was needed, the source said.

Ukraine improves jet-powered drone interception rates, but Starlink disruptions threaten progress
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:49:20 UTC
19:49:20 KST

Ukraine made significant progress in countering Russia's jet-powered drones, with some air defence units reporting interception rates around 80%. But recent restrictions on US satellite services exposed Kyiv's reliance on US technology as it races to develop cheaper, more effective interceptors.
Ukraine's improved interceptor drone technology has helped it counter Russia's jet-powered drones, but disruptions to US Starshield satellite services threaten those gains.
According to the Institute for the Study of War (ISW), Ukraine's interception rate fell slightly from 77% to around 74% during disruptions to the military-grade satellite service between 14 and 24 October.
The figures nevertheless represent a marked improvement on early September, when Ukrainian officials reported intercepting around 60% of Russia's jet-powered drones.
Some Ukrainian air defence units have reported interception rates exceeding 80%, although these figures reflect individual units' performance rather than nationwide results.
The Starshield restrictions, which affected high-speed drone operations, were lifted on 24 October, according to Ukrainian officials. However, the disruption highlighted the country's dependence on US satellite communications to sustain its air defences.
ISW warned that maintaining and improving interception rates would require Ukraine to develop and deploy affordable, high-speed interceptor drones on a much larger scale.
Russia has increasingly turned to jet-powered versions of its Shahed-type attack drones, which travel considerably faster than conventional propeller-driven models, leaving Ukrainian air defence crews with significantly less time to detect and intercept them.
Ukraine relies on a combination of interceptor drones, fighter aircraft and ground-based systems to counter the threat.
Interceptor drones have proved particularly effective, according to ISW, but many depend on Starshield connectivity to operate at the speeds required to engage faster Russian targets.
Ukrainian forces also use F-16 fighter jets, either firing air-to-air missiles or engaging targets with onboard guns. Both approaches have drawbacks: missiles are expensive and scarce, while gun engagements demand considerable pilot skill and expose aircraft and crews to additional risks.
Using fighter jets against drones also increases maintenance requirements and diverts aircraft from other missions.
Ukraine has installed ground-based gun turrets in Kyiv and the surrounding region, although expanding these systems nationwide would require considerable time and resources.
The race for cheaper interceptors
The growing threat has accelerated efforts by Ukrainian manufacturers to develop faster, more affordable interception systems.
One such project is the F-Jet 80, a jet-powered interceptor being developed by Ukrainian company F-Drones, which plans to incorporate artificial intelligence into its guidance system.
The company aims to keep the unit cost at approximately $7,000, compared with an estimated $20,000 to $70,000 for other high-speed interceptor drones and around $1 million for an air-to-air missile launched from an F-16.
Although the F-Jet 80 remains under development, its manufacturer says it has already successfully intercepted several Russian drones.
For Ukraine, the challenge extends beyond developing effective technology to producing it in sufficient numbers to counter Russia's expanding use of jet-powered drones.
ISW argues that integrating affordable interceptor drones into Ukraine's existing air defence network offers the strongest prospect of sustaining high interception rates as the country approaches another winter of Russian aerial attacks.

By Marco Aquino
ZAÑA, Peru Oct 27 (Reuters) - As Pope Leo prepares to return to South America next week, many Peruvians remember him as the priest who helped feed hungry families, delivered aid after floods and walked alongside migrants in the country he would eventually call his own.
When the pandemic emptied the streets of northern Peru and one of the world’s longest quarantines left many struggling to eat, Bishop Robert Prevost, as Leo was known, helped launch a soup kitchen in 2020 in the small town of Zaña.
“He gave us an example of human charity, and we prepared the ‘aguadito con fe’,” recalled former cook Betty Burga Campos, referring to the traditional soup of rice, meat and vegetables that volunteers served.
Prevost left Peru for Rome three years later after Pope Francis tapped him to lead the Vatican office that recommends candidates for bishop appointments worldwide.
After rising from missionary and bishop in Peru’s far north to cardinal and ultimately pope, Leo, 71, is set to revisit the country where he became a citizen and built some of the relationships that defined his ministry, weeks after undergoing surgery for lung cancer. The Vatican confirmed on Monday that his November 6 to 17 South America tour remained on schedule.
Across northern Peru, regional governments are refurbishing churches and residents are preparing celebrations for his visit, which also includes earlier stops in Uruguay and Argentina.
For many Peruvians, memories of the Chicago-born head of the Catholic Church are less about Vatican titles than muddy boots, long drives across the country’s rugged north and a hands-on approach to helping people.
“He had become Peruvian, even in the way he spoke. He no longer had much of that American accent,” said José Manuel Zamora Romero, a priest in Lambayeque who knew him for years.
The share of adults in Peru who identify as Catholic has fallen from 76% to 67% over the decade to 2024, according to Pew Research Center. The decline is often linked to social changes and distrust of institutions, following years of political instability that have caused Peru to cycle through nine presidents in a decade.
A BISHOP ON THE MOVE
Prevost arrived in Peru in 1985 at age 30. After years based in the United States and Rome with his Augustinian order, he returned in 2014 and became bishop of the Peruvian city of Chiclayo in 2015. In 2023, Pope Francis brought Prevost to the Vatican. Francis named him a cardinal later that year and he was elected pope in 2025.
Across northern Peru’s sun-baked farm belt, residents and priests recall a churchman constantly on the move.
For the future pontiff, “the distances were not limits, the distances were opportunities,” said David Farfán, a priest in Zaña, one of the towns on the pope’s upcoming itinerary.
Many remember Prevost riding horseback to isolated Andean communities. Others recall him driving hundreds of kilometers himself across Peru’s rugged north.
“His hobby was driving,” Zamora Romero said. “And I know he taught some priests to drive so they could get their licenses … and they all passed the test.”
That practical approach became evident during emergencies.
When severe flooding linked to the El Niño climate phenomenon inundated northern Peru in 2023, photos circulated on social media of Prevost wading through knee-deep water in rubber boots as he helped deliver aid.
When natural disasters occurred, “he was on the front lines to bring the help that the population needed,” said Rev. Jorge Villegas of Chiclayo, where the pope will spend two full days.
Residents pointed to moments like those as evidence of a bishop who preferred action over visibility.
“He wasn’t very focused on being with the press; he was more with the poor and in social conflicts,” said Verónica Castillo, a journalist in Chiclayo who witnessed his intervention during a 2015 labor conflict.
“He was a bishop who intervened, who took action, and people remember that,” she added, recalling how Prevost helped mediate the prolonged protest by workers against a sugar company, which turned violent.
‘PUT HIMSELF IN SHOES OF A MIGRANT’
Migration has reshaped much of Latin America over the past decade, as millions of Venezuelans fled economic collapse and political turmoil. Peru hosts the world’s second-largest Venezuelan diaspora community, with more than 1.5 million migrants. Many arrived without proper documentation and live with inadequate access to healthcare and basic services.
Prevost founded a Catholic organization in Chiclayo in 2018 to assist newcomers.
“He put himself in the shoes of a migrant first and foremost and knew what the situation was like,” said Augusto Martínez, who leads the organization.
The group has assisted thousands of Venezuelans.
As pope, Leo has called for migrants to be treated with dignity, condemned human trafficking and warned traffickers to repent or face divine judgment. He has criticized anti-immigration policies, including measures pursued by US President Donald Trump.
“He supported migrants on how to have a dignified life here in Peru,” said Lisbeth Coromoto Díaz, who received help through the Chiclayo organization and said he held Masses in honor of migrants.
Leo’s planned return to Peru has revived hopes among Catholics in Eten, near Chiclayo, that he could advance a long-running campaign to secure Vatican recognition of the town’s reported Eucharistic miracle. As bishop, he supported the cause, presenting historical records and thousands of testimonies of faith in Rome, linked to a 1649 apparition in which devotees say the image of the Christ Child appeared in a consecrated host.
Tourism officials are promoting routes tied to the places Leo lived and worked. Souvenir shops are stocking shelves with pope-inspired hats, key chains and pins.
In a shop window in the capital Lima’s Gamarra textile district, an image of Leo on a T-shirt depicts him smiling while enjoying a plate of Peruvian food.
“We’ve got the pope looking spirited; we’ve got the pope as a foodie, enjoying delicious ceviche and rotisserie chicken. We even have the play on words: ‘The Pope and the papa (potato) are Peruvian’,” said clothing maker Victoria Quiñones.
Quiñones predicted a 200% increase in her workload and was running low on fabric for the T-shirts.
Nearby, Maria Rodriguez, 70, was shopping for pope T-shirts.
“I’m buying several,” Rodriguez said.
“I’ll be wearing them all through November because I am Catholic: Roman and Peruvian,” she added.
(Reporting by Marco Aquino; additional reporting by Alfredo Galarza, Carlos Valdez and Joshua McElwee; Writing by Cassandra Garrison in Mexico City; Editing by Lucinda Elliott and Rod Nickel)

Exclusive-Alleged Israeli spy company heavily targeted Starlink users, sources say
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:48:45 CET
19:48:45 KST

By Raphael Satter
WASHINGTON, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Experts at a digital defense firm recently found that an Israeli ad tech company was heavily targeting users of Starlink’s satellite internet service in a likely effort to spy on them, according to six people familiar with the matter.
Researchers at TrendAI, a unit of Tokyo-based cybersecurity company Trend Micro, concluded the Israeli company Discover-Tech was one of the biggest sources of digital ads shown to users of SpaceX’s Starlink service and that the ads were likely being used to geolocate or otherwise surveil them, according to the six people.
The researchers, who drew on digital advertising data in TrendAI’s telemetry for their conclusions, found that Discover-Tech had become one of the world’s leading bidders for ads aimed at Starlink users and that it was the No. 1 bidder on Starlink traffic in more than 100 countries, including several where Starlink itself was banned or restricted. Bidding refers to the complex auction system by which advertisers secure space inside people’s browsers and apps.
SpaceX did not respond to requests for comment. Discover-Tech and its chief executive did not respond to requests for comment over the past two weeks.
TrendAI released a report on October 15 about the targeting of Starlink users but did not name Discover-Tech, instead saying the party responsible was “an ad tech entity” which it called “Shadow-Earth-79.” The six sources said Shadow-Earth-79 is TrendAI’s codename for Discover-Tech.
TrendAI did not directly address questions about why its report did not identify Shadow-Earth-79 by name, saying in a statement that its approach to attribution was aimed at reducing the risk of mistakes and avoiding “hype-driven labels” or “unstable actor names that can mislead defenders, distort risk prioritization, and trigger inappropriate response actions.”
Finding ways to track Starlink users has become a cottage industry as governments around the world try to get a grip on the spread of satellite internet terminals. Because they route data through SpaceX-operated satellites rather than nationally regulated telecommunications firms, the terminals can sidestep local internet restrictions, communicate in hostile areas or coordinate action across battlefields. Starlink has become a particularly important resource in Ukraine, whose military relies on the service for frontline communications and directing drone strikes.
In May, Israeli newspaper Haaretz and the website Intelligence Online separately reported that Israeli-owned businesses were pitching clients on ways to identify and track Starlink users. Haaretz said exploiting ad data appeared to play a key role in the process.
DISCOVER-TECH ACCUSED OF WIDER SPY EFFORT
The same day that TrendAI published its report on Shadow-Earth-79, Canadian cyber watchdog Citizen Lab and New York advertising technology firm Confiant outed Discover-Tech by name.
Both groups said the Israeli company abused the ad bidding process, which can leak data about internet users back to the bidder.
Over time, bidders can collect that leaked data, collate it and merge it with other information to de-anonymize users, follow them around the web and, in some cases, set them up for targeting with surveillance software.
Citizen Lab and Confiant said the ads had been shown inside dozens of sensitive networks belonging to media organizations, governments and tech firms.
In response to the investigations, Google, Comcast and other companies said they had removed Discover-Tech from their ad platforms.
At least one big US tech company and one international organization recently launched internal inquiries into whether Discover-Tech’s ads targeted their employees, according to one of the people and a seventh person familiar with the matter.
TOP ADVERTISER IN YEMEN, SOUTH SUDAN
TrendAI’s report cited suspicious bidding patterns that suggested Shadow-Earth-79 was running “targeting and tracking infrastructure rather than a commercial advertising operation.”
In addition to noting the “obvious skew” towards buying ads aimed at Starlink users, the report said that Shadow-Earth-79 was the top buyer of ads in Syria, Libya, Yemen and South Sudan and was the No. 2 ad buyer in Afghanistan even though “the demand for legitimate Western advertising in sanctioned or active-conflict states is effectively zero.” It said the entity won “an implausibly dominant share” of bids in several countries including Hungary, Israel, Egypt, Azerbaijan and Venezuela.
TrendAI researchers were convinced Discover-Tech was behind the suspicious bidding activity and discussed naming the company in TrendAI’s report, according to the six people familiar with the matter. But they eventually dropped the idea of publicly attributing the activity to a named company after TrendAI executives raised legal concerns, five of the sources said.
Self-censorship is common in the cybersecurity industry, especially when executives fear that exposing surveillance operations could draw retribution, industry experts say.
Earlier this year, US cybersecurity company Palo Alto stripped explicit references to China from a report on a global cyberespionage campaign even though its researchers were confident the hacking could be pinned on Beijing, Reuters reported at the time. Reuters said the report was watered down over fears that calling out China would cause problems for Palo Alto’s operations there, which were already under scrutiny following a Beijing directive ordering domestic companies not to use its products. Palo Alto said the lack of attribution in its report was not correlated with “procurement regulations in China” and that any suggestion otherwise was “speculative and false.”
(Reporting by Raphael Satter; editing by Chris Sanders and Rod Nickel)

Swiss house prices continued to rise over summer
House prices in Switzerland have continued to rise unabated. The upward trend continued in the third quarter of 2026 for both detached houses and flats.
From July to September, the Swiss Residential Property Price Index (IMPI) rose by 1.7% compared with the previous quarter to 129.8 points, as announced by the Federal Statistical Office (FSO) on Tuesday. Year-on-year, prices have climbed by as much as 4.4%.
At national level, prices for detached houses have risen by 2.1%. Prices for flats have also increased by 1.3% compared with the previous quarter.
The sharpest rises in property prices were seen in urban municipalities within a small conurbation or outside a conurbation (+3.4%). The smallest price increase, at 0.6%, was recorded in so-called intermediate municipalities, which exhibit both urban and rural characteristics.
More
Buy or rent? Find out where you can afford to live in Switzerland
Significant year-on-year increase
In the longer term, the upward trend in the property market is continuing despite prices already being high. Compared with the previous year, both detached houses (+3.3%) and flats (+5.4%) have risen significantly in price.
The IMPI is a relatively new indicator: it has only been published quarterly since the third quarter of 2020. According to the FSO, it is calculated based on an average of around 7,000 transactions from all regions of Switzerland. The FSO obtains data from the 28 largest mortgage lenders in Switzerland. These cover a very large market share, as the vast majority of property purchases are financed by a mortgage.

Why Jordan has struck Syria: What we know
Syria says Jordan did not coordinate with Damascus before launching operation in rural Deraa and Suwayda.
Jordan said its air force conducted retaliatory attacks on what it called “dens of terrorist organizations in southern Syria”, linked to suspects accused of being behind last week’s attack on a Greek Orthodox church in the kingdom.
In a post on X, the Jordanian Armed Forces said: “Fighter jets from the Royal Air Force destroyed a number of terrorist sites in southeastern Syria.
“The operation resulted in the killing and wounding of many elements of the terrorist organizations and the destruction of a number of their vehicles,” Jordan’s Armed Forces added.
“The armed forces said the operation was conducted in coordination with Damascus.” Jordan’s military said in a further post on X.
ISIL (ISIS) has claimed responsibility for the October 23 church attack.
Jordan did not specify the locations of the attacks or provide casualty figures.
What is Syria saying?
Syria has contradicted Jordan’s account of the overnight attacks.
In a statement, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs informed Jordan of its “complete reservation” over the attacks, which took place “without prior coordination or notification with the Syrian side”.
A Foreign Ministry official told Al Jazeera’s Heidi Pett that the strikes were a “treacherous attack”.
Pett reported from Syria that authorities have said seven people were killed, including three children, in Jordanian air attacks on Deraa and Suwayda countryside.
Syria’s Ministry of Emergency and Disaster Management said its teams had responded to attacks in four sites.
Syria’s civil defence agency said it had recovered the bodies of those killed in attacks. They include five members of one family, including three children and a woman who were killed together in a strike on a tent in the village of al-Taff, in the Lajat area of northeastern Deraa province. Three other members of the family were injured, it said.
In the al-Shayah farms near Nassib, in Deraa countryside, a strike on a farm killed Riyad Karrad, 80. His body was taken to Deraa National Hospital.
In Muzayrib, in the Ein al-Basal area of western Deraa countryside, a strike hit a home. No casualties were reported.
In the town of Shuhayb, in northern Suwayda countryside, a strike on a home killed Mutlaq Abu al-Khail, 60. Rescue teams were still working to recover his body from the rubble when the report was issued.
There was no immediate comment from Jordan on Syria’s accusations that civilians – not armed fighters – were killed.
Shortly after the attacks, Syrian customs authorities on Tuesday closed the Nassib border crossing with Jordan, the only passenger and commercial traffic pathway between the neighbours.
Why did Jordan attack Syrian sites?
Jordan said its attacks on Syrian territory were in response to an attack on a Greek Orthodox church in Karak governorate.
On Monday, senior government security officials said Jordanian security forces had arrested two brothers and their brother-in-law after a shootout over the violence that killed nine people in a rare attack on the minority Christian community in Jordan on Friday.
Major-General Obaidullah al-Maaytah, Jordan’s director of public security, named the three detained suspects as Hazza Zaidan Mohammed, Meshal Zaidan Mohammed and Ahmad Sami Hussein.
The attack during a funeral prompted Jordan’s King Abdullah II to order security forces to respond with an “iron fist”.
Jordan’s Interior Minister Mazin al-Farrayeh said he was launching an investigation “examining all the circumstances that lead young people towards extremism”.
“The file has not yet been closed; investigations are still ongoing. As of today, there are no indications of any links between them and other cells,” al-Farrayeh added.
Has Jordan struck Syrian territory in the past?
Jordan has conducted multiple air attacks on Syria since 2023, saying it was targeting drug and arms smugglers.
The operations have sometimes hit civilians.
Human Rights Watch demanded accountability after Jordan launched attacks that killed women and children in January 2024.
“Cross-border airstrikes that kill civilians demand scrutiny regardless of the threat posed by drug smuggling from southern Syria,” Human Rights Watch said.
The Jordanian Armed Forces said its operations along its border were aimed at armed groups reportedly carrying narcotics, arms, and explosives that it suspected are linked to Iran-allied groups.
How will Syria respond to Jordan’s latest attack?
Syria’s Foreign Ministry said it was in contact with Jordan to establish the circumstances of the operation.
Damascus said it will address the aftermath of the attacks while “safeguarding Syria’s security and sovereignty”.

Common drugs may help dangerous viruses spread through the body
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:46:21 UTC
19:46:21 KST

Common drugs may help dangerous viruses spread through the body
- Date:
- October 27, 2026
- Source:
- Norwegian University of Science and Technology
- Summary:
- A surprising discovery reveals that widely used anti-inflammatory drugs may unintentionally help dangerous viruses spread through the body. Scientists found that JAK inhibitors, prescribed for rheumatoid arthritis and other inflammatory diseases, can weaken a crucial immune defense against influenza, COVID-19, and other infections. By suppressing genes that normally fight viruses, these medications may leave patients more vulnerable to infection.
- Share:
Medications are designed to treat diseases and relieve symptoms, but some can also produce unintended effects that put patients at risk. While side effects are common with many treatments, researchers have identified a particularly concerning possibility involving drugs used to control inflammation.
Scientists at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU) have discovered that a widely used class of anti-inflammatory medications may make it easier for certain viruses to infect cells and spread throughout the body.
"We have found a surprising and potentially serious side effect of a class of anti-inflammatory drugs. They can help viruses spread more easily in the body," says Denis Kainov, a professor at the Department of Clinical and Molecular Medicine at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU).
Common Anti-Inflammatory Drugs May Help Viruses Spread
The medications at the center of the findings belong to a class called Janus kinase inhibitors, or JAKs. These drugs are widely prescribed to control inflammation, but their effects on the immune system may also leave the body more vulnerable to viral infections.
"Among the viruses that more easily affect the body with the help of these drugs are Rift Valley fever virus, influenza A, adenovirus and SARS-CoV-2, the virus that causes COVID-19," Kainov says.
These viruses can cause significant illness, making any treatment that potentially increases their ability to spread a serious concern.
Why Arthritis Drugs Can Weaken Antiviral Defenses
In a new study published in NAR Molecular Medicine, Kainov and his colleagues investigated how JAK inhibitors influence the body's ability to defend itself against viruses.
"JAK inhibitors are often prescribed for autoimmune diseases and inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis," says Erlend Ravlo, a PhD research fellow at NTNU and first author of the article.
Although these medications can be highly effective at reducing inflammation, their benefits come with an important trade-off. By suppressing certain immune responses, they can also interfere with the mechanisms that normally protect the body from viral infections.
"In particular, the drugs suppress an important immune signalling pathway that helps protect healthy cells from viral attacks," Ravlo said.
This pathway plays a central role in coordinating the body's response when viruses attempt to infect healthy tissue.
Scientists Discover How JAK Inhibitors Disrupt Immune Protection
The research team found that JAK inhibitors, including the medication baricitinib, can reduce the activity of genes involved in fighting viral infections.
"These genes play a crucial role in the body's response to viral infections," said Aleksandr Ianevski, an NTNU researcher and coauthor of the new paper.
When JAK inhibitors interfere with this immune signaling system, they weaken an important layer of antiviral protection. Without the usual defensive response, viruses may find it easier to establish an infection and spread between cells.
To investigate these effects, the scientists combined advanced virology methods with gene expression analysis and organoid technology. Their experiments included cells from the lungs, eyes and brain, along with miniature organ models grown in the laboratory.
These approaches allowed the team to examine how the drugs affect antiviral defenses across different types of human tissue.
"Although JAK inhibitors are effective in the treatment of inflammation, this shows that they can pose a hidden risk for patients who have latent or active viral infections," says Ravlo.
What the Findings Mean for Patients and Future Treatments
The results highlight the importance of carefully considering the risks associated with JAK inhibitors, particularly when patients may already have a viral infection or when outbreaks are occurring.
Researchers suggest that healthcare professionals should exercise caution when prescribing these medications during periods of increased viral transmission.
However, the same immune-suppressing properties that create potential risks for patients could also offer advantages in certain research settings. Under controlled laboratory conditions, these effects may help scientists develop vaccines or evaluate potential antiviral medications.
The researchers hope their findings will encourage greater awareness of how JAK inhibitors influence the immune system and support further investigations into their safest and most effective uses.
"We recommend further studies to better understand how the drugs can be used optimally, especially during virus outbreaks or pandemics," says Ianevski.
Professor Magnar Bjørås of the Department of Clinical and Molecular Medicine provided significant scientific expertise and secured most of the funding for the research. Additional financial support came from the Central Norway Regional Health Authority, the South-Eastern Norway Regional Health Authority, the Research Council of Norway and the Swedish Research Council.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Norwegian University of Science and Technology. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Erlend Ravlo, Aleksandr Ianevski, Marius Nårstad Skipperstøen, Hilde Lysvand, Jørn-Ove Schjølberg, Ole Solheim, Wei Wang, Miroslava Kissova, Marthe Vestvik, Olli Vapalahti, Teemu Smura, Hanna Vauhkonen, Valentyn Oksenych, Friedemann Weber, Mårten Strand, Magnus Evander, Janne Fossum Malmring, Jan Egil Afset, Magnar Bjørås, Denis E Kainov. JAK inhibitors remove innate immune barriers facilitating viral propagation. NAR Molecular Medicine, 2025; 2 (2) DOI: 10.1093/narmme/ugaf017

Verkhovna Rada approved budget conclusions for 2027 State Budget - what this means and when the final vote will take place
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
12:46:12 EET
19:46:12 KST

Verkhovna Rada approved budget conclusions for 2027 State Budget - what this means and when the final vote will take place
Kyiv • UNN
A total of 232 deputies voted for the budget conclusions. The document contains 90 proposals concerning 5,236 amendments ahead of the first reading of the budget.
On October 27, the Verkhovna Rada adopted as a basis a draft resolution on the Budget Conclusions (No. 16000/P) as part of the consideration of the draft State Budget of Ukraine for 2027. This was reported by Parliament, UNN writes.
Details
The motion was supported by 232 members of parliament. This is the first stage in adopting the draft state budget in the first reading.
The document contains 90 proposals, which the Verkhovna Rada Budget Committee formulated on the basis of 5,236 amendments submitted by members of parliament, committee chair Roksolana Pidlasa said while presenting the document in the session hall.
"According to a preliminary estimate, taking the submitted amendments into account would require an additional UAH 13.5 trillion — that is almost two more budgets for next year. Many proposals do not meet the regulatory requirements: they are unbalanced, or the proposed sources are not supported by calculations and are unrealistic. Therefore, we rejected such amendments," Pidlasa explained.
After their adoption by the Verkhovna Rada, the Budget Conclusions become a list of changes that the government must take into account or consider when revising the draft budget for the second reading.
"The committee recommends that the Verkhovna Rada adopt the resolution on the Budget Conclusions as a basis and send the budget draft to the government for preparation for the second reading. Together with the government, we will eliminate the main shortcomings of this budget," Pidlasa said during the consideration.
As reported by the Verkhovna Rada, the committee's main proposals include:
-  increasing military personnel's financial support and doubling state guarantees for defense-industry enterprises, to UAH 60 billion;  
-  additional funds for medicines for patients with rare diseases, on top of the UAH 21 billion already allocated;  
-  allocating 4% of personal income tax to community budgets;  
-  increasing funding for housing for internally displaced persons;  
-  expanding the program for insuring war risks and supporting farmers, as well as banning the payment of the "National Cashback" from the UAH 9.4 billion production and entrepreneurship support program. 
What happens next
As explained by MP Yaroslav Zhelezniak of the Finance Committee, the Rada adopted the proposals and conclusions on the Budget as a basis — "not to be confused with the first reading of the Budget, which is tomorrow (October 28)."
"Now the Rada is moving on to consider the 5,236 amendments from MPs. Forty-seven MPs have signed up to speak on them. Tomorrow there will be a vote on the remaining amendments taken into account and the first reading of the 2027 Budget. It will then be sent to the government, and the second reading and final adoption are planned for November 23–26," Zhelezniak reported on social media.
Reminder
The 2027 Budget draft envisages a deficit of 15% of GDP and debt exceeding 110% of GDP. UAH 4.885 trillion is planned to be allocated for security and defense.

Climber falls nearly 5,000 feet to his death on Nepal mountain after reaching summit
A German climber fell about 1,500 meters (nearly 5,000 feet) to his death on Monday, a day after reaching the summit of Ama Dablam mountain, according to a trekking company operator.
Wolfgang Waschiczek, 57, was reported missing from Camp 3, which lies at around 6,200 meters. He had been resting after reaching the 6,812-meter summit on Sunday, before his planned descent.
"After a successful summit, he spent a night at Camp 3 on Sunday, and on Monday morning, his guide found him missing," Gokul Thapa, head of the trekking company Real Himalaya, told AFP.
Thapa said Waschiczek's personal trekking guide, Sonam Lama, had left him in the tent for a few minutes to return borrowed equipment, telling him to stay inside. When he returned, Waschiczek was missing.
Waschiczek's body was spotted by another Sherpa at Camp 2 at around 8 am on Monday at an altitude of about 4,600 metres, Thapa said.
The body was retrieved by helicopter during the afternoon and taken to Lukla, a town known as a gateway for mountaineers and trekkers heading to the Everest region.
It was then flown to the capital, Kathmandu, where a postmortem will be performed at Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital.
"Once the postmortem is done, the body will be handed over to his family members through the embassy," Thapa told AFP.
He said this was Waschiczek's second visit to Nepal.
"He had come to Nepal in 2024 for a trek, and his passing saddened us," he added.
Two Japanese climbers died last week on another peak in west Nepal, the Reuters news agency reported.
Ama Dablam lies in Nepal's Khumbu region and is considered a technically challenging mountain with steep faces.
This is the first fatality on the mountain this year.
Last October, two climbers, one French, aged 65, and the other South Korean, aged 66, died during expeditions there.
This climbing season, more than 300 climbers are attempting to scale Ama Dablam.
Mountaineers have died on other peaks this year.
In July, famed British Nepali climber Nirmal Purja and nine other climbers were killed after being swept away by an avalanche on Pakistan's Broad Peak.
In May, two Indian climbers died on Mount Everest during a record-breaking period of ascents via Nepal's southern route.
In May, American climber Shelley Johannesen died in an avalanche on Nepal's Mount Makalu. Johannesen, co-founder of U.S.-based outfitter Dash Adventures, had successfully reached the 27,838-foot summit before she was struck by an avalanche at around 23,600 feet while coming down.

NASA’s Oldest Martian Spacecraft Have Been Running for Decades. Here’s How
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:45:00 UTC
19:45:00 KST

NASA’s Mars Odyssey spacecraft has been operating for so long, it can rent a car without any fees. The spacecraft arrived at the Red Planet on October 24, 2001. It, along with its 20-year-old sibling, the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO), have operated longer than anyone watching their launches could have dreamed possible.
Having such a long record of observations from above the Martian surface has rewritten the story of water on the planet, past and present alike. Keeping the wizened orbiters going for so long has been possible only thanks to great engineering and constant problem solving—and a little luck. But scientists wonder whether, despite their storied legacies, Odyssey and MRO will be the last of their kind, at least for the Red Planet.
“Both Odyssey and MRO are some of the most productive spacecraft that have ever existed,” says Briony Horgan, a planetary scientist at Purdue University who isn’t affiliated with either mission, calling them “critical” to NASA’s overall Mars research program. Odyssey’s observations of the planet’s ice, for example, and MRO’s ability to see surface features change over time have each given scientists unprecedented insight into Mars as a vibrant planet rather than a lump of rock. Odyssey and MRO also connect humans to every NASA rover, which can’t communicate with Earth directly. It’s an impressive legacy for a pair of orbiters that were only meant to last just a few years.
Space is a notoriously harsh environment that takes luck and resilience to survive for decades. Particularly tricky is the barrage of high-energy particles hitting machinery; a powerful enough strike to a delicate enough apparatus can be fatal. And whereas engineers can keep constant tabs on satellites orbiting Earth, bandwidth to Mars is more limited—science spacecraft might only check in once or twice a week, says Rob Lillis, a planetary and space physicist at the University of California, Berkeley, who has worked on a range of more recent Mars orbiters.
“A Mars craft has to be able to manage by itself,” he says.
Losing an instrument is bad, but losing the power or computing systems can brick the whole craft. NASA often doubles up on vital parts of a spacecraft to ensure that if something important fails, the mission can run off the spare until engineers can troubleshoot a problem.
In the MRO’s case, one challenge it’s faced is ironically due to its staying power. The orbiter determines its precise location and orientation by comparing what its cameras see with a stellar atlas onboard—with just one hiccup. “MRO is actually old enough that some of those stars have moved across the night sky—very slightly, but they have moved,” says Paul Fieseler, an engineer at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory and chief engineer for MRO. The tiny misalignments confused the spacecraft, and last year, engineers had to send up an updated map to keep MRO oriented into the future.
Odyssey’s greatest risk right now is simply running out of propellant it uses to make tiny adjustments to maintain its orientation in space. The spacecraft doesn’t have a fuel gauge–without gravity to push the fuel down, there’s no volume to measure–so NASA can’t be sure how much juice it still has. Engineers have improvised new ways to fully operate the spacecraft on just a few drops at a time in a bid to extend its life.
Experts say both spacecraft benefited from failures during NASA’s infamous “faster, better, cheaper” era. In 1999, NASA lost two missions arriving at Mars: First the Mars Climate Orbiter burned up in the atmosphere, and then, just months later, the Mars Polar Lander botched its arrival and slammed into the surface. Each catastrophe, investigations determined, was caused by what might in more pedestrian realms be dubbed careless mistakes. The first was due to miscommunication between a ground system relying on imperial units and the flight system using metric, while the second was due to a software error not caught during testing.
“Those failures were very much on the mind of the team pulling together the Odyssey spacecraft,” says Glen Havens, an engineer at JPL and project and mission manager of Mars Odyssey. With those losses stinging, NASA invested more in perfecting the Odyssey and MRO spacecraft before launch, designing each to be as resilient as possible and testing every tiny component and every system configuration.
One key principle is what NASA calls “margin”—the spacecraft equivalent of carrying a snack, just in case.
“Unexpected things might happen, and you want to make sure the spacecraft will survive,” says Nilton Renno, a spaceflight engineer at the University of Michigan who hasn’t worked on either mission. MRO launched with a larger battery and more propellant than it strictly needed, Fieseler notes, and that margin is now keeping the mission going, with NASA hoping to operate it for another decade.
But orbiting Mars, it’s wise not to take anything for granted. Just last year, NASA lost the 11-year-old Mars Atmosphere and Volatile Evolution—its youngest Red Planet orbiter—after the spacecraft unexpectedly lost power on the far side of the planet. As Odyssey and MRO continue to age, questions linger about what Mars orbiters come next for NASA.
The agency has hired Blue Origin to build a dedicated communications satellite to beam scads of data back to Earth for at least five years—but unlike its forebears, which began as science missions before turning to communications work, this orbiter will only relay signals for other spacecraft.
NASA’s Mars science agenda includes only relatively limited projects. One mission, which Lillis leads, features two orbiters currently on their way to study how the planet responds to the constant stream of charged particles flowing off the sun. But even he calls the mission “right on the edge of being too small to do good science.” Then, there’s Skyfall, the trio of small helicopters meant to launch aboard the first nuclear-propelled spacecraft within just two years—a shockingly rapid timeline, and for a mission with minimal ability to answer meaty research questions.
To scientists, none of these initiatives quite build on the legacy of Odyssey and MRO and may even raise the specter of the infamous Mars failures that came before. “Certainly they’re pushing for faster, cheaper,” Horgan says. “It’s going to be a lot more challenging to do good science in that environment.”

Brazil handed Washington a setback it won’t forgive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:43:43 UTC
19:43:43 KST

Brazil handed Washington a setback it won’t forgive
In Brazil, the incumbent left-wing president, Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva – known simply as Lula – has decisively won a dramatic run-off election against his challenger from the right – and US favorite – Flavio Bolsonaro. As his de facto sponsor, US President Donald Trump, has signaled that he won’t openly intervene, Bolsonaro, after initially refusing to concede, had to effectively accept the result.
A result that we can call historic even now. In terms of the domestic politics of Brazil, it confirms Lula as a master politician and major statesman. Heading into his fourth term, he has defied his age as well as vicious American attempts to undermine him by economic warfare, sanctions, and social-media foul play.
Lula has also broken the traditional patterns of Brazilian presidential elections. Before he won the second round, he lost the first one; a comeback victory had never happened before and seemed improbable. Now, thanks to a rapid revamping of his campaign, including a belated discovery of social media, and a surge in voter mobilization across the whole country, Lula is the first one to pull it off.
For Brazil, this was a fateful election that could have turned fatal. If Bolsonaro had won, the country would certainly have lost its sovereignty to a policy of enthusiastic subordination to America’s Donroe Doctrine. What has been imposed by violence and treason on Venezuela would have been achieved by elections under pressure in Brazil. It would have joined the recent Latin American shift to the right and deeper submission to Washington.
It is almost as certain that Flavio Bolsonaro would also have found ways to end democracy at home. His father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, already tried. No member of the powerful Bolsonaro clan has ever uttered a word of regret for Bolsonaro’s proven coup attempt. On the contrary, Flavio and his now US-based brother, Eduardo, have been out for revenge. Add Flavio’s nasty reputation of connections to organized crime and even death squads, acknowledged even by the reliably right-wing Economist, and his victory could have spelled doom for many Brazilians.
Many bullets – some quite literal – were dodged. Yet surviving danger is different from conclusive victory. This has not happened. Lula’s victory is solid, outdistancing Bolsonaro by well over three percentage points, but this does not change the fact that the latter still won over 48% of the vote. Bolsonarism has been defeated but not crushed.
The same holds true for the biggest and most dangerous ally of the Bolsonaro clan, Washington. There is no doubt that the US has suffered a setback, most of all in geopolitical terms. Its project to lock Latin America into the cage of Donroe Doctrine imperialism has taken a hit.
And that hit is painful, for Brazil is Washington’s central target in South America. By location, size, demography, and economic performance, as well as potential, Brazil is so important that no revamped American ‘backyard’ empire will ever be complete without it.
Consider a few basic indicators. According to the World Bank, Brazil has a population of 213 million, which makes it the seventh-most-populous country in the world. It is also thoroughly urbanized, with almost 90% of the population living in towns and cities. It is technologically advanced, with almost 93% of Brazilians having access to at least 3G and almost 85% using the internet.
Economic metrics are notoriously tricky and difficult to compare, but Brazil clearly has the largest economy in South America. Globally, it also ranks high. The International Monetary Fund projects its 2026 GDP (adjusted for purchasing power) to reach almost $5.3 trillion, which makes it the eight-largest national economy in the world, leaving behind, for instance, the UK, France, South Korea, and closer to home, Mexico.
Brazil also has substantial reserves of crude oil and is the single biggest oil producer in South America. Bringing these riches under US control and adding them to what Washington is currently trying to loot from Venezuela would have been a wet dream for both American geostrategists and business. Especially as around half of Brazil’s oil production is currently being sold to China, America’s most feared rival.
More importantly, China is Brazil’s most important trade partner by far. Chinese-Brazilian trade is at record levels and growing, while Brazil is the top destination for Chinese foreign direct investment. The Donroe Doctrine was designed not just to restore US domination in Latin America, but specifically to keep China out.
And if all of the above is not irritating enough for the hemispheric empire fans in Washington, Brazil is also a major power in the realm of critical minerals. Indeed, according to American data, Brazil’s reserves of critical minerals rank second behind China and far outdistance those of runners-up, such as India and Australia, not to mention the US itself.
Add to this the fact that Lula’s Brazil has also been a main player in BRICS, the projects of multipolarity and dethroning the dollar, and the resistance to Israel and its crimes, including genocide against the Palestinians, and Washington could not be more eager to subdue this giant thorn in what it considers its southern underbelly.
What a prize to win! And to lose. For now, the US has lost. But precisely because Brazil is so crucial, Washington will not give up. On the contrary, the strong showing of its favorite, Flavio Bolsonaro, and the fact that his party will dominate the Brazilian Congress, will only harden America’s resolve, with numerous opportunities to sow division, subversion, and dirty regime-change tricks yet to be exploited.
Brazil has won a vital reprieve. But the struggle is not over. The empire will strike back. It always does. This means that Lula and his domestic allies will have to continue and broaden the modernization of their approach that started during the second round, for instance, by pursuing a consistent policy of securing Brazilian sovereignty in the social media sphere. It also means that Brazil’s friends in the world, especially those equally invested in the project of multipolarity, such as China and Russia, must think very hard about how to support Brazil more against US pressure.

Funeral homes, morgues and autopsy rooms: Halloween fans seek the ‘real’ thing on paranormal tours
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:42:44 UTC
19:42:44 KST

From former psychiatric hospitals to funeral homes, US attractions offer ghost hunts and overnight stays for Halloween fans seeking an otherworldly encounter.
Fright night is upon us and Halloween fans are plucking up the courage for scary experiences that promise to send a shiver down their spines.
For some travellers, the prospect of paranormal encounters is also shaping their holiday plans, with Booking.com including “Trip to the Beyond” among its travel trends for 2027.
In its survey of more than 28,000 travellers across 32 countries and territories, 65% expressed interest in paranormal experiences, while 48% would seek an experience in the hope of speaking to someone on the “other side”. Half were curious about experiences exploring questions around the afterlife, death or spirituality.
But while Booking.com is tipping the trend for next year, paranormal tours are already a popular choice in 2026 – especially in the US, where former psychiatric hospitals and funeral homes are attracting many visitors.
‘We believe it’s super haunted’
It’s not enough these days for some Halloween enthusiasts to be scared by actors dressed up in spooky getups at makeshift haunted houses: They want the “real” thing.
At a former psychiatric hospital in suburban Detroit and a former funeral home in Toledo, Ohio, visitors can embark on guided paranormal investigations or even set out on their own with rented equipment, such as a handheld electromagnetic field (EMF) metre.
“Guests that come here on our paranormal tours, they get touched, they get grabbed, handprints on clothing, whistled at,” said Justin Cox, founder of Michighost Paranormal, which leads paranormal investigation tours of the Eloise Asylum attraction’s upper floors, where patients were treated. “Everything that you can imagine has happened here, and we’ve heard it all.”
The facility began as a 19th-century poorhouse and operated under various names as it expanded into a complex with dozens of buildings. By the late 1920s, it was one of the nation’s largest public health facilities.
“In the paranormal field, we believe that trauma leaves energy, which creates hauntings,” Cox told AP. “This place had a lot of tragedy, a lot of trauma, so we believe it’s super haunted.”
Family members of patients and others with ties to Eloise have argued against offering for-profit amusement at a site where vulnerable people suffered.
The upper floors of the asylum feel alive
Most of the complex’s buildings were razed in the 1980s, but a five-story, red-brick structure that came to be known as the Kay Beard Building still stands and is home to Eloise Asylum.
It’s there that Cox and his team lead guests on tours of the upper floors, including a room with a bathtub used in hydrotherapy sessions. It’s not uncommon for guests to get in the tub.
And if you "think you can handle the night here, we offer that as well”, Cox said about their overnight stays.
Eloise Asylum haunted attraction’s lead makeup artist and scare actor, Lexi Carter, has gone on the paranormal investigation tour. She said the upper floors feel alive.
Paranormal investigators use spirit boxes to scan radio frequencies for sounds they believe could be messages from spirits. They also use EMF readers to measure changes in electromagnetic fields that some associate with paranormal activity.
Carter said it was wild “watching those go off.” She said: “Oh, my God. It blew me away. I was like, ‘No way. This is real. 'This is so cool.'"
Visits to embalming and autopsy rooms
Eight kilometres south sits the former Urbanski Funeral Home, which hosted thousands of viewings and services from 1926 until its sale last year. Now called Mortuary Manor, the 5,580-square-metre building serves as a funeral home museum and much more.
Paranormal investigators can check out the embalming and autopsy rooms, as well as a morgue where it is standard practice for guests to take pictures of themselves lying on a slab that juts out from a basement wall.
Mortuary Manor will host its first wedding in November on Friday the 13th, of course. And guests who stump up $200 (€179.51) can spend the night in a five-room suite. Operations manager Cory Leibenguth lives in a neighboring upstairs apartment.
He said the building has modern amenities like indoor plumbing, heating, air conditioning and Wi-Fi. He says that "sets us apart from some of these other abandoned locations that don’t have any of that. And then there’s not a lot of funeral homes you can go investigate, either.”
Mortuary Manor visitors can also watch a horror movie projected onto the wall of the main sitting room while surrounded by caskets.
It’s all part of elevating the Halloween experience for hard-core fright fans.
“In today’s world where everybody is so stressed out … Halloween is a time that everybody can just relax and just enjoy the time with their friends and their family, maybe get scared along the way,” Cox said.

Russia’s energy revenues plummet despite surging global oil prices amid drone attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:40:59 UTC
19:40:59 KST

Russia’s oil and natural gas revenues have plunged amid a strong ruble and the impact of subsidies in the fuel sector despite surging oil prices, while Ukrainian drone attacks on refineries have affected production and exports.
Russia’s federal budget revenues from oil and natural gas dropped 17.2% year-on-year in January-September to 5.47 trillion rubles ($67.7 billion), resulting in a loss of around $14.1 billion in the energy sector, according to the Finance Ministry.
Total budget revenues climbed 10% to $367 billion over the same period, while non-energy revenues surged 18.8% to $299.3 billion, the data showed.
Energy revenues dropped while conflicts in the Middle East drove up energy prices. High prices could potentially boost the value of Russian exports, but the amount reflected in the budget is determined not solely by the sales price but also by the indicators used in tax calculations.
The average price of Urals, the country’s main export crude, exceeded $92 a barrel in September, rising from $56.8 in the same month last year to $92.1 a barrel last month.
While the 62% surge bolstered oil producers’ foreign currency revenues, this was not reflected to the same extent in the budget.
Russia prices oil exports primarily in foreign currencies, but production taxes and budget revenues are calculated in rubles.
The ruble’s appreciation against the US dollar meant that the same amount of export revenue converted into fewer rubles.
The decline in the average dollar exchange rate was cited as one of the reasons for the nine-month energy revenue shortfall.
The Russian Central Bank said the official dollar exchange rate stood at $1 as of Oct. 24, below the $1.14 per dollar assumption used in the 2026 federal budget.
The Finance Ministry expects the positive impact on the budget to become more obvious in the coming months due to the delayed reflection of recent increases in oil prices in tax collections.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian plants and energy infrastructure disrupted processing operations.
Russia’s 32 major refineries have a combined daily capacity of around 6.5 million barrels, but this volume fell to 3.8 million barrels per day in June, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA).
The 30% annual drop marked the lowest level in over 20 years, the report showed on Sept. 17.
Russian refineries were reportedly affected by a drone attack every three days during the first eight months of the year.
As of the end of August, only five of the 32 major plants had been unaffected by these attacks.
Gas production, on the other hand, also dropped around 20% year-on-year, while diesel production shrank 30% over the same period, the IEA reported.
Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak recently said these attacks were ongoing, but the damage had been reduced through protective measures. He added that repairs had been accelerated and modernization schedules at some plants might have to be postponed.
Moscow extended restrictions on exports of gas and certain petroleum products until Jan. 31, 2027, with exceptions for diesel shipments under inter-producer and intergovernmental agreements.
While these restrictions limit the benefits firms can derive from high fuel prices in foreign markets, the Economic Development Ministry expects petroleum exports to decline from 125.8 million tons last year to 98.5 million tons this year. It also anticipates crude oil exports will rise from 230.8 million tons to 244.7 million tons.
The fuel damper mechanism Moscow implemented to cap domestic fuel prices provides payments from the budget to refineries during periods when global market prices are more favorable than domestic prices.
The scheme encourages firms to sell their products domestically, but it also leads to higher public spending.
Some $3.78 billion was paid to oil firms under this scheme last month, exceeding the $2.44 billion paid in August. The figure hit its highest level since April 2022 and contributed to the decline in annual energy revenues, according to Finance Ministry data.
Oil and natural gas revenues for the first nine months fell below the baseline level set under the budget rule. While high oil prices supported public revenues, they failed to eliminate the pressure from the exchange rate and the subsidy mechanism.
This prompted the Finance Ministry to lower its 2026 estimates for oil and natural gas revenues from $110.46 billion to $93.87 billion, reducing the full-year forecast by $16.59 billion.
The Economic Development Ministry anticipates oil and gas condensate production will fall from 511.4 million tons last year to 494.2 million tons this year, before rising to 500 million tons next year.
As the Russian federal budget deficit widened to $64.27 billion in January-September, Moscow raised its year-end budget deficit forecast from 1.6% of national income to 3.2%.
The future trajectory of energy revenues will depend on oil prices, the exchange rate, the recovery of plant production and the amount paid in fuel subsidies.

Russia’s Defense Ministry reported that its forces had stopped firing on the Kherson axis at 04:00 Moscow time, at the same moment.
Russia has kept Oleshky cut off for months. In June, the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine documented worsening shortages of food, medicine, and medical care there and in neighboring Hola Prystan. As of 8 October, Lubinets’ office still saw no practical breakthrough toward an organized evacuation, with 358 residents verified as needing help to leave. The ceasefire is the first step that has to hold before aid can go in and residents can leave, an operation Marc Beckman, the first lady’s chief adviser, expects to take five to seven days.
By 09:00 on 27 October, Russian forces were still observing the ceasefire, according to Pavlo Drohal, spokesperson for Ukraine’s 30th Marine Corps. Kyrylo Budanov, head of the Presidential Office, announced that the mission had begun and that Lubinets had gone to the site to coordinate it.
Ceasefire brought forward by two days
The White House announced on 23 October that First Lady Melania Trump had secured a localized ceasefire, set to begin on 29 October. The same evening, Russia’s chief of General Staff Valery Gerasimov announced a ceasefire on the Kherson axis from 27 October, with engineering reconnaissance and a secured route for a humanitarian convoy. Ukraine’s General Staff followed, introducing a ceasefire in a designated area from the same hour.
Beckman told Ukrinform on 26 October that Russia had moved the ceasefire two days earlier and extended it beyond Oleshky into Kherson Oblast. Lubinets said on 23 October that the mission should effectively begin on 29 October, after demining, adding that the date was not a matter of principle for either side.
A day after the announcement, Lubinets and his Russian counterpart Yana Lantratova, who lead the two negotiating groups, confirmed the timing in an online meeting, he said. According to Lubinets, the agreement covers demining the road to Oleshky, delivering food, water, medicine, and hospital equipment, and safe movement for civilians.
Newsmax to document the operation
Meanwhile, Melania Trump said she had secured an “impartial American media organization” to accompany the Russian and Ukrainian teams. Beckman named it as Newsmax. He said he had worked directly with the channel’s owner, and that its journalists would record testimony as what he called neutral American observers.
Residents could leave for Ukraine or Russia, or stay, Beckman said. He added that Russia had assured Kyiv and Washington it would respect their choice of destination. Both governments asked him not to disclose what guarantees Russia gave or how violations would be handled, he said. He expects the operation to take five to seven days after 29 October, with an extension possible if both sides agree.
Diplomat doubts the truce will move peace talks
At the same time, Kostiantyn Yelisieiev, Ukraine’s ambassador to the EU in 2010–2015, told Radio NV the truce became possible only through the personal involvement of Donald and Melania Trump. The US president, he said, sees it as a way to show Americans he is bringing peace closer. He said he expects Russia to attempt provocations aimed at pushing residents toward the Russian side.
Yelisieiev said he does not share the optimism of those who think Oleshky could push the wider peace process forward. He compared it to the Black Sea grain corridor, a one-off arrangement that no longer works. He warned of a “diplomatic smokescreen”: Russia imitates negotiations while it keeps fighting, hoping Ukraine and its partners weaken over time.
A town under blockade
Oleshky lies on the left bank of the Dnipro, about 4 km from Kherson, and has been occupied since February 2022, Radio Svoboda reported. The White House says it had about 24,000 residents before the war and estimates 1,700 to 2,000 remain, mostly elderly, including about 50 children. Russian troops have also seized food dropped by Ukrainian drones, a local official said.
