Remembering Adnan Kivan: a Legacy With a Future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:40:04 UTC
19:40:04 KST

Two years have passed since Adnan Kivan left us on Oct. 27. I write this as the Chief Executive Officer of the Kyiv Post, but also as someone who misses a trusted friend and mentor.
Whenever we discussed why he bought the newspaper in 2018, he returned to the same principles: defending democracy, protecting free expression, and standing against totalitarianism.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
I believed in his sincerity, but I also owe him an honest admission. Having spent decades in advertising and communications, I had grown used to business leaders speaking about purpose in grand, inspiring terms. Part of me wondered whether these were simply noble ideals – larger than what any single individual or publication could realistically deliver. Only after his passing did I realize how deeply personal those words were.
I eventually learned more about the experiences that shaped Adnan’s youth in Syria: his involvement in student opposition to the Assad regime, the exile that followed, and the terrible price his family paid, with 27 relatives kidnapped, tortured, or killed. That history changed how I understood our conversations.
When Adnan spoke about authoritarianism, he was not debating political theory; he was speaking from direct, painful experience. When he spoke about freedom, he understood intimately what its absence cost.
He saw that same spirit in Ukraine. He recognized the demand for human dignity among the Ukrainians who stood on the Maidan, insisting that their voices mattered and their future was theirs to decide.
Russian Missiles Strike Kyiv University Campus – 1 Killed, 15 Wounded, Mostly Students
Adnan had arrived in Ukraine as a student and built a remarkable life here. Through KADORR Group, he became one of the country’s most successful business leaders. Yet Ukraine was far more to him than a place of business – it was the home where he raised his family and planted his roots.
                                                                                                                                                                         Adnan Kivan (L) and CEO Luc Chénier (Photo by Kyiv Post)                             
That success brought a quiet obligation to give back: supporting charitable initiatives, aiding Ukrainian defenders, and investing in independent media platforms, including Channel 7, USI News, and Kyiv Post.
When he bought Kyiv Post in 2018, he acquired an institution with a proud history and a civic role extending far beyond a balance sheet. As he put it then: “Without freedom of the press, you cannot have a democracy.” He also saw broader potential for the paper –launching a Ukrainian-language edition, expanding into digital and video journalism, and highlighting Ukraine’s strengths and promise alongside its challenges.
Sustaining a newsroom requires more than goodwill. Salaries must be met, investigative work funded, and operations maintained through peace and crisis. Adnan committed millions of dollars to acquire and sustain Kyiv Post. When Russia launched its full-scale invasion, he provided immediate additional support, ensuring our journalists could continue reporting reliably from the ground for readers around the world.
                                                                                                                                                                         Adnan Kivan (L) and Chief Editor Bohdan Nahaylo (Photo by Kyiv Post)                             
Crucially, he respected editorial independence. As Bohdan Nahaylo, our chief editor since the reorganization in late 2021, recalls: “Adnan was a gentleman and a rare breed. He told me at the outset: ‘You’re a veteran journalist – I trust you. Make Kyiv Post bigger and better and make it Ukraine’s global voice. Show that Ukraine has good things to offer, not simply gloom and doom. That’s all I ask.’ After that, his support was consistent.”
Honoring Adnan’s legacy means looking forward. A newspaper cannot thrive on past gratitude alone; every edition must earn the reader’s trust, and every generation of journalists needs the resources and independence to do their job.
When I think of Adnan now, I wish I had asked more questions during our conversations and recognized sooner how much of his own life informed his support for Kyiv Post. I cannot revisit those moments, but we can honor the trust he placed in us by carrying the work forward with his son Ruslan Kivan, who now continues his father’s legacy with the integrity and purpose.
Adnan, I miss you, my friend.
So, on behalf of everyone at Kyiv Post, our millions of global readers, and everyone in Ukraine and Syria, thank you, Adnan for your dedication, support, and example.

E5 reaffirms unwavering support for Ukraine by all available means
This is stated in a joint statement by the defense ministers of the five European countries (the Group of Five/E5) following their meeting in Paris on October 26, Ukrinform reports.
“We will maintain our unwavering commitment to supporting Ukraine in its fight back against Russian aggression. Ukraine’s ability to defend itself now and in the future is critically important to Euro-Atlantic collective security. We stress the need to keep supporting Ukraine by all available means – politically, militarily and financially,” the statement says.
The ministers also reaffirmed their determination to continue countering the activities of Russia’s shadow fleet in accordance with international law and in coordination with partners.
In addition, the five countries expressed support for Ukraine’s pursuit of a lasting peace backed by reliable security guarantees. “We stand united with Ukraine in its determination to secure a lasting peace, underpinned by robust security guarantees. The Coalition of the Willing will contribute to robust and credible security guarantees once a cease-fire or a peace agreement is in place,” the document says.
The defense ministers of the five European countries separately emphasized that Russia poses the most acute and long-term threat to Euro-Atlantic security and stability. The statement notes that Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine, violations of NATO members’ airspace, acts of sabotage and the increasingly active use of hybrid attacks do not weaken the Allies’ unity but, on the contrary, strengthen their determination to defend Alliance territory.
The statement also stresses that Europe must take greater responsibility for its own security. To this end, European Allies plan to strengthen political and military leadership within NATO, modernize their armed forces and deepen defense-industrial cooperation based on common and standardized requirements.
At the same time, the ministers emphasized that the United States remains an indispensable ally and that its continued involvement in ensuring European security is essential to a strong and credible NATO.
The E5 also called for strengthening European defense capabilities within NATO and the European Union, stressing that EU initiatives should complement the Alliance’s activities, avoid duplication and provide opportunities for cooperation with NATO countries that are not members of the European Union.
As reported by Ukrinform, Minister of Defense of Ukraine Yevhenii Khmara addressed representatives of the defense ministries of the E5 countries – Germany, the United Kingdom, France, Poland and Italy – and outlined the critical priorities for supporting Ukraine.

Upgraded Russian cruise missile crashes in Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:38:35 UTC
19:38:35 KST

- Photos show Russia’s upgraded Geran-5 K5-K light cruise missile, serial number ANS-3031, lying in a field in Ukraine’s Odesa region.
- The new version has a redesigned airframe and modern navigation equipment, and the cause of its crash is not yet known.
Photos have emerged of Russia’s newest version of the Geran-5 light cruise missile, known as the Geran-5 K5-K and often described in the media as a jet-powered drone, lying in a field somewhere in Ukraine’s Odesa region after it came down during an attack, with the serial number ANS-3031 visible on the airframe.
It is not yet known why the Geran-5 K5-K crashed, whether it was hit by Ukrainian air defenses, brought down by electronic warfare or failed on its own, and Ukrainian officials have not commented publicly on the find.
The K5-K is an upgraded version of the Geran-5 cruise missile with a noticeably different design from the first versions of the weapon, and Ukrainian sources say the new variant has a modified fuselage, smaller swept-back wings, a tail without wingtips and an engine moved from an external pod into the fuselage, along with more modern navigation equipment.
Russian forces began using the new version in late September, and Ukrainian defense technology adviser Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov has said it carries autonomous optical navigation that compares images of the ground below with stored data to correct its course without satellite signals, which makes it much harder to throw off course with jamming, while its designers are reportedly aiming for speeds of up to 900 km/h (559 mph).
Russia first used the original Geran-5 against Ukraine in early January 2026, when Ukraine’s military intelligence described it as a turbojet-powered weapon with a conventional cruise-missile layout, a warhead of about 90 kg (198 pounds) and an advertised range of roughly 1,000 km (621 miles), and said its design was substantially similar to Iran’s Karrar.
Ukrainian intelligence data give the baseline Geran-5 a length of about 6.5 meters (21 feet), a wingspan of 3.2 meters (10.5 feet), a takeoff weight of up to 850 kg (1,874 pounds) and a cruising speed of 450 to 600 km/h (280 to 373 mph), using a Chinese-made Telefly turbojet, a Kometa anti-jamming satellite navigation receiver and cellular modems.
Ukraine’s Defence Intelligence has said Russia produces about 3,000 Geran-4 and Geran-5 weapons a month at the Alabuga plant in Tatarstan, and that Moscow has been building additional production facilities there since May 2026.

Finnish, Norwegian Leaders Call Putin Ahead of Ukraine Peace Talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:36:39 UTC
19:36:39 KST

Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre held a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Tuesday to discuss ongoing efforts to end the war in Ukraine, a move that, while coordinated with Kyiv, some European leaders criticized.
Moscow confirmed the call shortly after officials in Helsinki and Oslo released statements about the conversation, which marks the first time a leader from one of Ukraine’s European allies spoke to Putin since French President Emmanuel Macron’s phone call with the Kremlin chief in July 2025.
Stubb’s office said he and Støre initiated the call in order to “discuss Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine and the diplomatic efforts to end the war and promote peace and stability in Europe.”
It said the aim of the outreach, made in consultation with Ukraine, was “to convey messages directly regarding future negotiations to help to end the war to President Putin,” adding that it was also “related to the upcoming meetings to be held in Abu Dhabi.”
“In the call we stressed the importance of de-escalation,” Støre’s office said in its statement about the call with Putin.
Both Finland and Norway said their leaders were speaking as representatives of their respective countries and did not speak on behalf of Europe as a whole.
Still, the phone call with Putin was met with criticism from some European leaders.
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said she was “very skeptical” of the initiative and did not believe Russia wants peace with Ukraine or Europe.
“I think we should keep Europe together instead of going solo,” Frederiksen said, according to Danish media. “We should stand together and speak with one voice and defend ourselves against Russia.”
In its own statement, the Kremlin said Putin “reiterated the root causes” of his decision to order the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
He also “drew attention to the confrontational policies of EU and NATO member states, which he noted serve to prolong the hostilities,” it added.
Stubb, Støre and Putin discussed security and stability in the Baltic Sea and Northern European regions, the Kremlin’s readout added. The three leaders agreed to maintain direct contact moving forward, it said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he spoke to Stubb and Støre following their call with Putin, adding that he was “grateful for the detailed briefing and for their active support for our diplomacy and the peace efforts we are pursuing together with all our partners.”
Zelensky emphasized that the Finnish and Norwegian leaders told Putin that concrete steps needed to be taken in order to de-escalate the war, especially when it comes to attacks on energy infrastructure ahead of winter.
“Russia must stop dragging out the war,” he wrote in a post on social media.
Tuesday’s phone call comes a week after Stubb and Støre met with U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff and Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky in Oslo. The purpose of the Oslo talks was to mend strained relations between Kyiv and Washington, as well as to seek a new path out of the war.
Witkoff later met with Putin in St. Petersburg to report on progress in efforts to end the conflict. The Kremlin said it is willing to resume U.S.-mediated peace negotiations in Abu Dhabi as soon as next month, though no exact dates have been set.

French teachers say government education measures to quell protests fall short
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:36:11 UTC
19:36:11 KST

French teachers say government education measures to quell protests fall short
PARIS, Oct 27 - French teachers said on Tuesday that education reforms aimed at ending weeks of protests were insufficient and would not be enough to quell students' anger.
The French government on Monday announced a raft of proposals, including capping some class sizes at 28, billions of euros in loans for building renovation and a revamp of the university admissions system, to try to ease popular anger.
But Sophie Venetitay, the secretary general for teachers' union SNES-FSU, told reporters that the measures did not go far enough, saying the size of more classes should be capped and more people should be hired to improve learning conditions for students.
"Today, what the ministry has said is only the beginning of a response," she said. "It will not be enough to extinguish the anger."
High school students initially blockaded their schools to protest against inadequate staffing and resources, in a movement that has since broadened to encompass general trade unions and the so-called "Yellow Vests" to express anger about weakening public services and cost-of-living increases.
The French government, under pressure from bond markets to reduce its debt level, has little spare cash to respond to protesters' demands.
Budget Minister David Amiel said on TF1 the measures announced on Monday were expected to cost €5 billion ($5.6 billion) and would be offset with spending cuts elsewhere.
Student leaders also said the government's concessions were a good first step, but vowed to continue demonstrations, on Saturday and on November 5.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told RTL that there would be a heavy security presence on Saturday, which will come two weeks after large nationwide protests gave way to violence and looting that shocked the country and have spurred curfews and bans on large gatherings in France.
The turmoil has boosted the fortunes of French far-right leader Marine Le Pen, who is favoured to top the first round in the presidential election next spring. REUTERS

====================================================================================================

CRE debt is due, presenting a 'massive' opportunity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:35:51 UTC
19:35:51 KST

A version of this article first appeared in the CNBC Property Play newsletter with Diana Olick. Property Play covers new and evolving opportunities for the real estate investor, from individuals to venture capitalists, private equity funds, family offices, institutional investors and large public companies. Sign up to receive future editions, straight to your inbox.
A massive wall of commercial real estate debt is coming due now and over the next two years, and today's high interest rates will make refinancing significantly more expensive. For some, that is cause for concern, but for others that presents an opportunity.
For 2027, an estimated $733.2 billion in commercial real estate loans will come due, according to Trepp. Roughly $800 billion was estimated to come due this year, albeit at lower interest rates earlier in the year.
"Elevated interest rates have made it increasingly difficult to refinance maturing commercial real estate debt, with little relief in sight," said Lonnie Hendry, chief product officer at Trepp. "As lenders pull back on loan extensions and modifications, more realized distress is likely to emerge, leading to greater loan losses while creating opportunities for investors to acquire assets at attractive valuations."
Industry Reaction
"If I had debt, I'd be petrified," said Richard LeFrak, executive chairman of the LeFrak Organization, on a recent Property Play podcast. "The extend and pretend party is over, and banks are being more aggressive about either selling off the loans or trying to dispose of the assets in one way or the other."
Over the past few years, lenders have been giving borrowers more time, expecting that interest rates would come down. Much of that is coming to an end, and lenders are starting to be more aggressive.
Office and multifamily are seeing the biggest comeuppance of all the sectors. The office delinquency rate in commercial mortgage-backed securities hit 12.16% in September, according to Trepp. But the office recovery is accelerating now, in both occupancy and valuations.
Multifamily is still in distress, working through a recent oversupply and weaker rents. Borrowers, many of whom refinanced their apartment buildings in 2021 and 2022 when interest rates were very low, would now have to refinance at about twice their original rates.
"We have the largest amount of multifamily debt that we've ever seen before, period, that is coming due, and one of the main points is that most of that debt was on floating rate mortgages," said Ari Rastegar, founder and CEO of Rastegar Capital.
This means borrowers will have to put in more cash because interest rates are higher and rents are lower, making the properties less valuable. Lenders will require more equity.
"So imagine if you originated a piece of multifamily debt on a bridge that was a two year bridge that had two one-year extensions, which is a very simple thing that a lot of bridge lenders have. Well, that rate would have originated around 4%, and now rates are up 525 basis points. It's at 9%," said Rastegar.
As rates go up, borrowers need more cash flow to justify the debt service, and some just don't have it. That presents the play on distressed assets.
"We are preparing for a massive buying opportunity, starting a global roadshow to be in front of people, both retail and institutional investors, to say exactly this story. When this happens, we need to be ready to buy everything, and that's what we're preparing to do," said Rastegar.
Borrowers are opting, in some cases, for cheaper, shorter-term financing. That, however, just pushes the problem down the road a few years. Multifamily financing is traditionally meant to be in place for ten years. The hope, however, is that property fundamentals will improve and interest rates will come down, but that is by no means guaranteed.
"We're starting to see some improvements in fundamentals, which should offset some of the distress that we're talking about," said Jason Morgan, co-CEO of Morgan Properties, one of the nation's largest apartment owners and managers. "But not nearly to the level that what someone would need from a 2021 and 2022 valuation perspective."
He said transaction volume has really come to a standstill, and deals that aren't under contract are falling out or getting repriced somewhere up to about 10%, anecdotally.
"So I would agree that the maturing debt, you know, situation within the multifamily sector is going to lead to a lot of opportunities for groups to come in and get bargain pricing compared to what they were a handful of years ago," said Morgan.
The problem, however, is that while the deals are getting repriced in favor of potential buyers, transactions are not moving. Sellers are unwilling.
"It still hasn't been a tidal wave of new opportunities because sellers haven't, you know, come to that reality, which is going to take place over the next few months," Morgan said.

Israelis flock to polls to pass wartime judgment on Netanyahu
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:33:00 UTC
19:33:00 KST

Israelis voted Tuesday at the highest rate in 45 years, delivering a wartime verdict on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in what many called the nation's most consequential election.
Voters will go to polls for the first election since the Oct. 7, 2023 Hamas incursion and Israel's consequent genocidal war on Gaza, as well as in Lebanon and Iran.
Policies of Netanyahu's right-wing coalition have been divisive at home and have deepened Israel's international isolation, but he has defended his record as the only leader with the mettle to face Israel's foes.
Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving leader with 19 years in office, is an unmatched political survivor and his nationalist politics are increasingly entrenched.
Israel's fragmented system makes it difficult for an array of opponents to force out his coalition of right-wing, far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties.
His main rival Gadi Eisenkot, a military ex-chief of staff and security hawk, aims to unseat him with the support of parties on the right and center, as well as the rump of an increasingly marginalized left. Opinion polls show a close race, with neither leader facing an easy path to power.
Voters began casting ballots after polling stations opened at 7 a.m. (5 a.m. GMT). The polls close at 10 p.m. (8 p.m. GMT).
The Central Elections Committee reported that 16.7% of eligible voters had already cast their ballots within the first three hours, the fastest early turnout rate since 1981.
"I think these elections are the most important of all the ones I’ve known," said Ruth Epstein, an 81-year-old longtime left-wing voter in Ramat Gan near Tel Aviv, who voted for the opposition Democrats.
"I’m really scared about what will be here."
Netanyahu supporter Louis Lipsky of Jerusalem said he was voting to keep the prime minister in power, crediting him with normalizing relations with several Arab states under the Abraham Accords of 2020.
Netanyahu has campaigned on his wartime leadership and an endorsement from U.S. President Donald Trump, his ally in war against Iran, who has said they should "finish the job."
If neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot can form a governing coalition in the 120-seat parliament, Netanyahu could stay on as caretaker until another election is held.
His opponents have managed to wrest him from the premiership only once since 2009, and that took four inconclusive elections in two years. He was back 18 months later.
For many of Netanyahu's opponents, the election turns on accountability for the security failures of Oct. 7. Opposition groups have promised to hold a national inquiry, which Netanyahu's government has resisted.
"I am convinced that by the end of today, we will see a change – a new spirit for the State of Israel – that will serve as a rectification for the past three years and for that terrible day," Eisenkot said during a visit to kibbutz Nir Oz in southern Israel.
He walked to the polls with Gadi Mozes, one of 251 people kidnapped by Hamas and taken to Gaza during the Oct. 7 attack that caused 1,200 deaths.
Eisenkot says Israel's response – a genocidal war which health authorities say killed more than 74,000 Palestinians – was a failure because Hamas remains in charge. International community and U.N.-commissioned experts agree the Israel committed "genocide" against the Palestinians living in Gaza.
He repeated his commitment to dismantle Hamas' military and governing power in Gaza within 18 months of forming a government.
In his first public commentary on election day, Netanyahu shared an article on X about an incident in which police said three people were arrested over an election bribery attempt.
"Right-wing voters, dear Likud voters, in the face of attempts to undermine the integrity of the elections, we must go out and vote en masse, vote Likud for the sake of our country," he said.
Netanyahu's critics have said the prime minister may try to cast doubt on the integrity of the voting process, which his office rejects.
Itamar Ben-Gvir, leader of a far-right party in Netanyahu's coalition, cast his vote in the Kiryat Arba settlement in the occupied West Bank early Tuesday. He predicted Netanyahu would return as prime minister and his own party would serve as the right-wing anchor of the government.
Voters from Israel's Arab minority – Israeli by citizenship but Palestinian by heritage – were voting in "unprecedented" numbers, Palestinian candidate Ahmed Tibi said.
Eisenkot has ruled out partnering with Arab parties, citing a lack of shared values, although some experts envision them propping up a minority government to ensure Netanyahu is removed from office.
"My expectation is that we will have only a slight majority either way. No landslide," said Israeli political analyst Amotz Asa-El of the Shalom Hartman Institute.
Eisenkot joined Netanyahu's war cabinet after the Oct. 7 incursion but quit after eight months, criticizing his leadership.
Israel flattened much of Gaza in the genocidal war after Oct. 7 and now occupies around two-thirds of the enclave under a year-old U.S.-brokered cease-fire.
Israel also dealt heavy blows to Iran-backed Hezbollah in Lebanon and traded strikes with Iran, culminating in a 12-day aerial campaign against Iranian nuclear sites in 2025 and this year's joint U.S.-Israeli war.
Like nearly all Jewish-led parties in Israel, Eisenkot opposes the two-state solution that underpinned decades of peace negotiations with the Palestinians.
But he has criticized illegal Jewish settler violence against Palestinians in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, which has surged since 2023 and strained Israel's ties with Western states. And he opposes Netanyahu's far-right coalition partners.

10:31:55 UTC
19:31:55 KST

Romania has uncovered a sabotage network coordinated by Russian intelligence services that attempted to set fire to the Carfil arms factory in Brașov on 14 September, the Romanian Intelligence Service (SRI) announced on Monday.
"Coordinators from the Russian Federation had assigned the group an extensive list of targets across the region, including state-owned and private arms manufacturers, as well as other facilities of military and industrial significance," Reuters quoted the SRI statement as saying.
The suspects include two Belarusian citizens and one Ukrainian citizen. Two were arrested in Germany while preparing similar acts of sabotage, while the third is being sought in Poland, according to Romanian television channel Știri.
Bucharest is seeking their extradition to Romania.
A year ago, Poland and Romania arrested eight people suspected of involvement in a Russian plot to send parcels containing explosives to Ukraine.
Romanian Foreign Minister Dan Neculăescu described the fire in Brașov as "part of a broader sabotage campaign across Europe" targeting the defence industry.
The SRI explained that individuals involved in such operations are typically recruited through social media, initially being offered money for "seemingly harmless tasks", such as "monitoring or photographing specific facilities".
"Later, the assignments become increasingly serious and may involve vandalism, arson or even murder," the intelligence service stated.
Russian President Vladimir Putin personally ordered an escalation of sabotage operations against NATO countries, The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) reported on 20 October, citing three European officials familiar with US intelligence findings.
According to the newspaper, an unsuccessful drone attack on Germany's Leipzig Airport on 4 August was among the first operations carried out as part of the sabotage campaign.
WSJ sources revealed that following the incident, Russia warned the German government through an unofficial communication channel that Leipzig would not be the last target.
Russia reportedly decided to intensify its covert operations at a time when its armed forces were making little significant progress in Ukraine, while Ukrainian forces were increasingly carrying out strikes against targets deep inside Russian territory.
A series of further incidents followed across Europe after the Leipzig attack.
In August, drone manufacturing facilities in Estonia and Poland were set on fire.
During the same period, Slovak authorities announced that they had prevented an attack on a similar facility.
Poland, Lithuania and Bulgaria also reported acts of sabotage targeting stations associated with the Starlink satellite system.
According to Western officials, the sabotage operations are organised by the Special Tasks Department of the Main Directorate of the General Staff of the Russian Armed Forces, established following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The unit is headed by Colonel General Andrey Averyanov.

Ministry cuts police and ISS access to bank data register over tracker
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:31:00 UTC
19:31:00 KST

Ministry cuts police and ISS access to bank data register over tracker
The Justice Ministry has suspended the Police and Border Guard Board's (PPA) to the Enforcement Register after they failed to implement a mandatory data tracker.
The Internal Security Service's (ISS) has been hit by the same access restriction and for the same reason.
The Enforcement Register (Estonian: Täitmisregister) is a state channel for authorities to query bank account data and place attachments. In 2025 the Chancellor of Justice found agencies had accessed bank secrecy data without a proper legal basis.
The required data tracker once functioning allows private citizens to see who has queried their bank data. Of authorities required to install the tracker, the Tax and Customs Board (MTA) and various bailiffs met the October 1 deadline and so can continue to access the register.
The PPA and the ISS, known in Estonian as Kapo, cannot as things stand.
Minister of Justice and Digital Liisa Pakosta (Eesti 200) told ERR that bank data is very sensitive data, necessitating additional security measures like the data tracker when it is viewed automatically by investigative agencies.
"From the data tracker you can see who has viewed your data, and so control is in the person's own hands. The Riigikogu gave investigative authorities access to the Enforcement Register only on condition that people whose accounts are queried can see it from October 1," Pakosta said.
"This means the Enforcement Register can be used to query data protected by bank secrecy only if the investigative authority is connected to the data tracker. The data tracker ensures that the person can check the state, not the state check the person."
Pakosta praised the Tax and Customs Board (MTA) and the bailiffs who joined the data tracker by the deadline - they will be able to continue to use the enforcement register. Initially the MTA had been barred from using it, as the PPA and the ISS continue to be.
"The worry is with the Police and Border Guard Board and the Internal Security Service, who did not get the necessary software solution ready by the deadline. Until it is ready, their use of the Enforcement Register in criminal proceedings is suspended," she continued, echoing a ministry announcement last week.
The Enforcement Register holds data on enforcement proceedings and acts as a channel for authorities to query bank account data. In July 2025 the Chancellor of Justice found agencies were accessing confidential bank data without a proper legal basis. This led to the suspension of the MTA's access, now restored as noted. The Financial Intelligence Unit's (FIU) access was also suspended at the time. The FIU primarily investigates money laundering.
The fix to the issues was the mandatory data tracker, letting people see who queried their data, which in turn followed the passing of the relevant legislation.
"It has now emerged that the Police and Border Guard Board and the Internal Security Service have not made the necessary integrations, and therefore their access to the Enforcement Register and e-arest must be closed," the ministry had announced last Thursday.

Israeli elections offer scant hope of change for Gaza: analysts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:30:06 UTC
19:30:06 KST

Breadcrumb
Israeli elections offer scant hope of change for Gaza, analysts warn
In the Gaza Strip, where three years of Israel's genocidal war have devastated Palestinians, expectations surrounding Tuesday's Israeli Knesset elections vary widely.
Some Palestinians hope the vote will bring about the end of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, while others believe that any incoming Israeli government will not differ much from its predecessor.
The anticipation reflects the narrow range of alternatives available to Gaza's Palestinian residents, amid stalled political processes, continuing suffering and the absence of a clear prospect for ending the war and its impact.
While Israelis await the ballot results to determine their next government, Palestinians find themselves closely connected with the outcome, hoping that something might change in their dire reality.
The contradiction is particularly stark given the postponement of Palestinian elections, while Palestinians follow the Israeli vote and await its results as a potential factor in changing conditions in Gaza.
While Palestinian elections are supposed to serve as a means of renewing political legitimacy and determining national priorities, Palestinians find themselves compelled to look towards another electoral contest in search of a possible way to stop the war or alleviate its consequences.
Yet this anticipation does not mean the results will deliver what Palestinians hope for.
A change in the Israeli government may alter some calculations, but it does not guarantee an end to the war, the lifting of restrictions or the launch of a comprehensive reconstruction process in Gaza, unless it is accompanied by actual shifts in policy and international pressure capable of influencing Israeli decisions.
Differing hopes in Gaza
For Palestinian Mohammad Zakaria, who lives in a tent in Deir al-Balah in central Gaza after being displaced from Beit Lahia in the north, the upcoming Israeli elections represent an opportunity he hopes will lead to the downfall of Benjamin Netanyahu's government, which he holds responsible for what Palestinians have endured during the years of genocide.
Zakaria told The New Arab that the departure of the current government could open the door to a different approach towards the Gaza Strip and give residents a chance to escape the reality of killing, destruction and siege, and recover the minimum conditions necessary for life.
However, this hope is not shared by all Palestinians.
Ibrahim Hammad believes the problem extends beyond Netanyahu and his government to the nature of Israeli society and its current political tendencies. He argues that the rise of the right and the growing prevalence of extremist rhetoric make relying solely on a change of government insufficient.
Hammad told TNA that Palestinians have no guarantees that the arrival of a new Israeli government will lead to a genuine change in the policies pursued towards them.
He noted that positions concerning Gaza, the occupied West Bank and displacement cannot be reduced all on Netanyahu as an individual. He also argues that a change in political figures may not alter the substance of these policies, as long as large sections of Israeli society continue to support hardline positions towards Palestinians.
Saeed al-Aila, meanwhile, views the Israeli elections from a different perspective, one linked to the exhaustion and despair experienced by Gaza's residents after years of war.
Al-Aila told TNA that Palestinians being compelled to follow Israeli elections and link their fate to their results reflects the extent of their inability to influence their own circumstances, as well as the absence of a Palestinian political horizon capable of offering solutions or pathways out of the crisis.
"Gaza's residents can't endure further waiting and suffering, at a time when the necessities of life are deteriorating and basic needs are increasing," he said.
"Perhaps the painful irony lies in the postponement of Palestinian elections, while Palestinians await the Israeli elections to find out whether changes will occur in their lives, as if determining their future has become more dependent on the decisions of the Israeli voter than on their own political will."
A consensus that extends beyond Netanyahu
Political writer and analyst Mustafa Ibrahim told TNA that Palestinian hopes pinned on the Israeli election results reflect a state of despair stemming from the absence of a clear political horizon for solutions, amid the continuation of the war and a lack of sufficient indications that it can be ended through existing political channels.
Ibrahim said the elections could produce an Israeli government that is less hardline on certain issues or create greater room for the opposition and sections of Israeli society calling for an end to the war.
However, he stressed that this does not necessarily mean a fundamental change in Israeli policies towards Palestinians.
He emphasised that any genuine shift will require real international pressure to push the Israeli government to stop the war and commit to clear standards for ending it.
He also highlighted the importance of European and international positions, alongside US pressure, in pushing the political process towards tangible results.
According to Ibrahim, the Israeli elections do not appear to be an independent factor capable of changing the Palestinian reality. Rather, they represent one of several variables that could interact with external pressure and broader political positions.
The change Palestinians are waiting for depends not only on the identity of the next prime minister, but also on the willingness of influential parties to impose a different course from the policies that have led to the continuation of the war and the worsening humanitarian crisis.
For his part, Israeli affairs analyst Adel Shadid argues that a change in the Israeli government will not necessarily lead to a fundamental shift in policies towards Palestinians or a tangible improvement in their circumstances, even if different political forces come to power.
Shadid told TNA that Palestinian, Arab and international reliance on the Israeli elections as a gateway to change revealed the absence of alternatives and the tendency to await transformation from within Israeli society, rather than building effective political and international pressure to force Israel to change its policies.
He noted that Netanyahu's re-election could amount to the legitimisation of the continuation of the existing political approach, and potentially even its intensification.
However, the arrival of another premier would not guarantee fundamental change in Israel's treatment of Palestinians and their rights.
Regarding Gaza, Shadid pointed to broad Israeli consensus on several key issues concerning the territory, making expectations of a major shift simply through a change of government uncertain.
He argued that the next government could adopt even harsher policies towards Gaza, even if Netanyahu does not remain prime minister.

ICE Does Not Belong at the Polls
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:30:02 UTC
19:30:02 KST

During the presidential election of 1863, at the height of the Civil War, federal troops reportedly descended on polling places in Delaware, Kentucky, Maryland, and Missouri and prevented people they deemed disloyal from voting. This prompted a fierce national debate that culminated in Congress passing an 1865 law barring federal “troops or armed men” from “any place” where an election is being held. The central goal of this law, according to its proponents, was “to prevent the President and his officers from interfering in elections,” which are run by the states. Keeping armed federal officers away from the polls, they argued, was necessary to preserve democracy, even in the midst of civil war.
This has been the clear law, and the respected policy of every presidential administration, for over a century.
Until now.
Ahead of the midterms, top Trump Administration officials have publicly refused to rule out the possibility of sending federal agents to the polls. In September, Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin claimed that immigration officers could be sent to polling places to “serve a warrant” as part of immigration enforcement operations or if “there is a threat” to those polling places, adding “we’ll be where we need to be.”
“ICE isn’t there to patrol the polling places,” hedged Mullin. “We’re there to enforce specific threats.”
Federal Bureau of Investigation Director Kash Patel similarly said, “If there’s a reason to go there because there’s been a violation, we will, otherwise we won’t.”
It is clear to us, and to legal experts, that barring extreme circumstances, sending ICE or FBI agents to the polls would be flatly illegal under the 1865 law, and several others. As Daniel Caine, Chair of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, pointedly said this August, any request to send military troops to election sites would be an “unlawful order.” The same holds true for any other armed federal agents.
The only exception to the prohibition is to “repel armed enemies of the United States.” The Congress of 1865 originally included a second exception, allowing armed federal agents to “keep the peace at the polls.” But Congress repealed that exception in 1909 because lawmakers feared that federal authorities could point to any kind of disturbance as a pretext to deploy federal forces.
In other words, unless a hostile foreign power attacks voting sites using weapons, it is a crime for any armed federal agents to go to those sites, even to quell a disruption. And they are certainly not allowed to show up for routine policing or immigration actions.
If sending ICE to the polls is so plainly illegal, then why do top administration officials keep refusing to rule it out? Context is important. The federal government has been conducting indiscriminate and often violent immigration enforcement actions in communities across the country. At the same time, the administration has been peddling conspiracy theories about widespread illegal voting, often targeting communities of color. The administration has redirected thousands of homeland security agents away from critical transnational security threats to hunt for elusive noncitizen voters.
These efforts are not uncovering any significant problems. Federal and state law already bar noncitizens from voting in federal and state elections, and our election system does a terrific job of ensuring that only eligible citizens vote, with vanishingly rare exceptions—as dozens of studies, election reviews, and painstaking investigations have already confirmed.
This intimidation campaign is taking a toll. According to a University of California, San Diego poll conducted last month, a staggering 40% of voting-age American citizens expect ICE agents to be at the polls this November. Black, Hispanic, and Asian American voters are three to four times more likely than white voters to worry that they will be questioned by ICE at polls or that members of their racial or ethnic groups will face intimidation at the polls. This fear is real.
But despite all the administration’s threats, voters should not be intimidated. The law protecting election sites from federal forces is ironclad. Anyone who violates that would be committing a federal crime. Federal and state laws also prohibit any effort to intimidate voters, wherever it occurs. A broad array of civil rights groups and labor unions have already filed lawsuits to hold the federal government accountable for its intimidation efforts—including The Brennan Center, where we work. Other lawyers across the country are poised to run to court to protect elections if federal agents do unlawfully show up to polls.
Outside court, election officials, state government officials, law enforcement, and voter protection organizations are prepared to respond to any instance of voter intimidation. That includes de-escalation and backup plans, including changing voting sites if needed, to ensure that all Americans can continue to vote safely. Voters are determined and undeterred, as millions so far have already cast their ballots by voting early and by mail.
Our advice to concerned voters: make a plan to vote as early as you can. Voters have multiple options to vote with confidence. In addition to voting at the polls on election day, they can vote early in person or vote by mail ballot, dropping it off in secure ballot drop boxes, at an election office, or by mail. You can also go vote with a trusted group of loved ones or neighbors.
It is an outrage that the federal government has refused to rule out the idea of federal agents at the polls. In our view, it is part of a campaign to intimidate voters and undermine our elections.
The only way it will succeed is if voters don’t show up.

Photos reveal walkable Oxford Street as first phase of pedestrianisation begins
Almost a kilometre of Oxford Street in central London has been permanently closed off to vehicle traffic as pedestrianisation of the major shopping street and thoroughfare began yesterday.
Nearly a kilometre of the two-kilometre-long street – the stretch between Orchard Street and Great Portland Street – is now fully pedestrianised.
Traffic, including cars, buses, taxis and private hire vehicles, cycles, scooters and pedicabs, will not be allowed on this part of Oxford Street and will instead be routed via side streets.
Photographs from the unveiling yesterday show the road decorated with a large sign reading “Oxford St” and green bollards keeping out traffic.
The design for the pedestrianisation was made by local architecture studio East, which is working with landscape architecture studio JL Gibbons and urban design studios Gehl and Publica on the project.
Meanwhile, architecture studio Hawkins\Brown has been developing a long-term vision for the entirety of the street, which stretches from Tottenham Court Road to Marble Arch.
This first pedestrianised section is now undergoing a transition period, during which the East team will add new signage, seating and planters to make the area more visitor-friendly. The full transformation is expected to begin in 2027 and be completed by 2028.
“As we have seen from Borough High Street to Eltham, from Croydon to Green Lanes, London’s high streets are the public face of the city in all its diversity, its greenery and its energy,” East director Julian Lewis said.
“We design to preserve and support this energy, maintaining the ebbs and flows of these places which make our neighbourhoods unique.”
The transformed section of Oxford Street will feature two new squares, one close to Holles Street and the other close to Duke Street. These will be marked with a new surface dressing that will make the ground level across the carriageway.
Trees will also be added in “sculptural pots”, East said, before being planted into the ground for the permanent scheme.
London mayor Sadiq Khan had originally announced plans to make Oxford Street traffic-free almost a decade ago, in 2017, but they were blocked by Westminster Council.
East revealed updated renders of its vision for the final scheme earlier this month.

One killed in Ukrainian strike on passenger bus – governor
A Ukrainian drone strike on a passenger bus bound for Moscow has killed one person and wounded several others, according to Evgeny Balitsky, the governor of Russia’s Zaporozhye Region, where the attack took place.
The attack was reported on Tuesday morning near the town of Primorsk, on the Sea of Azov between the towns of Melitopol and Berdyansk. The area, which Ukraine claims as its territory, lies within the zone of so-called “middle strikes,” where Ukrainian forces have regularly launched drone attacks on purported Russian military and logistics targets using the Starlink satellite system for guidence.
Balitsky said 31 people were aboard the bus, which was traveling from Simferopol, the capital of the Crimean Republic, to Moscow. He said the wounded were taken to hospital, while other survivors were provided with food and accommodation.
The incident comes amid a dispute between Kiev and Elon Musk over Ukraine’s use of his Starlink satellite communications network for military purposes.
Musk has accused Ukraine of abusing Starlink for deadly “middle strike” operations, saying the system was intended as a civilian communications service rather than an offensive military tool. He contrasted it with Starshield, SpaceX’s military-oriented satellite service developed for US government customers.
Media reports and statements by officials have offered conflicting accounts of whether Kiev has direct access to Starshield or relies primarily on civilian Starlink terminals. Kiev has accused Musk and US President Donald Trump of imposing speed restrictions on Starlink terminals that effectively prevented their use on fast-moving platforms involved in middle strikes. Russian media reported a sharp decline in such attacks this month.
While the Ukrainian military depends heavily on Starlink communications, it has other means of conducting strikes deep inside Russia, where Starlink does not normally operate. Long-range drones and missiles can follow pre-programmed routes and use AI-driven final stage guidance to strike Russian energy infrastructure and other stationary targets.
The Starlink dispute has unfolded amid wider tensions between Washington and Kiev over Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil facilities. The Trump administration has repeatedly asked Kiev to curb strikes on refineries amid concerns about rising fuel prices, while Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky has rejected claims that Ukraine’s campaign is contributing to the increase.
Global energy markets are under pressure from several factors, including the US war on Iran, the Ukraine conflict and depleted strategic reserves amid tight crude supplies.

Instagram Is a Streaming Service Now
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

I’ve never listened to a full episode of the Happy Wife Happy Life podcast, hosted by Jordan Myrick and Kendahl Landreth, but I’ve sure seen all the clips.
My Instagram Reels algorithm recently served me, along with 5 million other viewers, a brief rant from Myrick about feeling bamboozled by the health care system. Then, I spent the next hour scrolling through the show’s other snippets on Reels, loving the couple’s snarky banter. Still, I never followed the duo to a different platform to watch the full-length podcasts.
On Monday, Instagram announced plans that might have turned me into a regular listener of the show. Instagram will expand tests in the US that let creators upload long-form content up to 90 minutes and flip a video’s orientation to horizontal. Creators can also link their short clips directly back to full-length videos.
“Our belief here is that entertainment and creativity are not limited to a three-minute video,” Tessa Lyons, vice president of product at Instagram, tells WIRED. She wants to build the “best place for social entertainment” with this overhaul of Instagram video. The social media platform may soon feel like a streaming service, as more viewers watch longer videos on their big screen.
Instagram is also expanding its creator tools for turning Reels into episodic content. “We want to be able to say, ‘Wow, Reece loved episode 3. So, as soon as episode 4 drops, we've got to make sure to show it to him,’” Lyons says. This Reels feature, called “Series,” is already available for some creators in the app, and it's being tested for TV viewing as well.
Instagram is focused on the experience of watching videos on your TV. It's hunting for ways to make that TV experience feel social, like showing your connections what you’ve been watching via the Friends tab. The company also plans to turn your smartphone into a TV remote.
Lyons sees the video-focused update as avoiding one of IGTV’s core mistakes—IGTV was the company’s previous attempt at more expansive content. In that instance, many viewers desperately wanted to flip the screen. IGTV failed to connect with users, in part, because it only allowed vertical videos. Meta discontinued the app a few years after its 2018 launch.
While Instagram’s latest changes challenge YouTube’s TV dominance, they also try to leverage its current strength as a platform for clips. Bite-sized clips, often of two people sitting behind podcast microphones, feel inescapable on social media right now, with many creators using them to boost visibility. Even WIRED’s own podcast now records videos for social media clipping.
Instagram is streamlining a viewer’s potential fandom journey. Rather than viral clips and long-form content existing on different platforms, Instagram is positioning itself as a centralized experience where I can stumble on Myrick’s health care rant in the morning and then open the app on my TV later that night and get a nudge to stream the full podcast episode.
“What we're seeing right now is that a lot of great short-form content is vertical, and a lot of great long-form content is horizontal, and we have the design challenge of figuring out how to make that all work cohesively in one product,” Lyons says. “TV becomes a great destination for watching long-form, horizontal content, and mobile becomes a great place for discovering that content.”

AI giant eyes record IPO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:29:10 UTC
19:29:10 KST

AI giant eyes record IPO
US artificial intelligence giant Anthropic has formally filed for a potentially record-breaking initial public offering (IPO), according to regulatory documents. The developer of the Claude chatbot could become the first publicly traded company focused primarily on advanced AI models, even as it warns that its own technology could threaten humanity.
The San Francisco-based company submitted its public registration statement to the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) on Monday, revealing plans to list on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT. The offering could take place as early as November, although its size and share price have yet to be announced.
“The advent of machine intelligence is one of the seminal moments in human history,” Anthropic declared in its prospectus, presenting AI as a technology capable of transforming the global economy.
The company is reportedly seeking a valuation of up to $2 trillion and could raise as much as $100 billion, potentially surpassing the record set by Elon Musk’s SpaceX earlier this year. The figures remain preliminary and were not confirmed in the public filing.
SpaceX completed the largest IPO in history in June, raising $85.7 billion at a valuation of around $1.8 trillion. However, the record-breaking listing drew criticism over its lofty valuation. Investment research firm Morningstar estimated the company’s fair value at just $63 per share, less than half its $135 IPO price.
Similar questions are emerging over Anthropic’s valuation. The company reported $16.3 billion in revenue in the first half of 2026 but posted a net loss of $80.7 billion, largely driven by accounting adjustments. Its IPO filing also disclosed hundreds of billions of dollars in future infrastructure commitments, raising concerns about whether its rapid growth can justify a valuation of up to $2 trillion.
The company itself has warned that its business is highly capital-intensive and that it may never achieve sustained profitability. Its prospectus also acknowledges intense competition, uncertain demand, and the possibility that the enormous sums invested in computing infrastructure may not generate sufficient returns.
Anthropic’s IPO prospectus also contains stark warnings about the technology underpinning the company’s business. Around 80 pages of the 261-page filing are devoted to risk factors, with the company admitting that advanced AI could “pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”
The dangers outlined include the use of AI to develop biological and chemical weapons, the loss of human control over increasingly powerful systems, and lasting damage to human mental health and cognitive abilities. Anthropic also acknowledged that its own AI models have displayed behavior resembling blackmail and resistance to shutdown during testing.
The warnings follow a string of incidents involving rogue AI agents, including an Anthropic model submitting a false homicide tip to police and OpenAI agents disabling safety monitors and hacking external systems.

Putin holds call with leaders of Norway, Finland – Kremlin

Putin holds call with leaders of Norway, Finland – Kremlin
Russian President Vladimir Putin has held a phone call with Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store, discussing efforts to resolve the Ukraine conflict, the Kremlin announced on Tuesday.
The conversation was initiated by the Finnish and Norwegian sides and followed last week’s meetings involving US special envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg, and the Oslo discussions between Stubb, Store, and Vladimir Zelensky.
The Kremlin said the Nordic leaders welcomed the agreement to resume trilateral talks between Russia, Ukraine, and the US in Abu Dhabi in the first half of November. The negotiations will address security arrangements for Russia and Ukraine after the conflict ends, among other issues.
During the phone call, Putin emphasized the root causes of the Ukraine conflict, stating that a just and lasting peace requires Russia’s legitimate interests to be fully and unconditionally taken into account.
He also criticized the confrontational policies of EU and NATO countries, saying they are prolonging the fighting.
The three leaders also discussed security and stability in the Baltic Sea and Northern Europe. According to the Kremlin, Stubb and Store reaffirmed the importance of upholding international maritime law and the principle of freedom of navigation.
Putin also informed his Nordic counterparts of the start of a US-mediated humanitarian operation near Alyoshki in Kherson Region, Russia, with a temporary ceasefire introduced in the area.
The conversation ended with a mutual agreement to maintain direct telephone contact, the Kremlin said.
The call was a rare direct exchange between Putin and European leaders, most of whom have shunned contact with Moscow since the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022.
Stubb described Tuesday’s phone call with Putin as “frank and substantive,” stressing the importance of direct discussions. “We are neighboring countries to Russia. The outcome of this war will have a direct impact on our and the broader European security.”
Store also emphasized that good relations with Moscow are important for Norway’s security and said that Oslo will work to maintain friendly ties with its neighbor, with which it shares an expansive maritime border.
The two Nordic leaders said they took part in the call as leaders of their countries and were not speaking on behalf of Europe. They added that the call was held in consultation with Ukraine to convey its position ahead of the Abu Dhabi talks, and vowed to continue to support Kiev.

German court rules neo-Nazi convicted in racist murders must remain jailed until at least 2035

Ayhan Şimşek
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
A German court ruled Tuesday that convicted neo-Nazi terrorist Beate Zschape must remain in prison until at least 2035, rejecting her bid for early release.
The Munich Higher Regional Court set her minimum detention period at 24 years and declined to suspend the remainder of her life sentence on probation, German news agency DPA reported.
Zschape, 51, was a key member of the far-right terrorist group National Socialist Underground (NSU), which murdered 10 people between 2000 and 2007, including eight Turkish immigrants, a Greek citizen and a German policewoman.
She was sentenced to life imprisonment in 2018 for her involvement in the group's crimes.
Last year, Zschape applied to the EXIT rehabilitation program, which helps individuals disengage from far-right extremism, in an effort to secure early release.
Relatives of the NSU victims strongly opposed her release, arguing that she had shown no genuine remorse and had refused to provide investigators with information about the murders, the group's wider support network or possible links to intelligence informants and security officials. 
NSU's racist murders
The NSU carried out a series of racially motivated killings, bombings and robberies across Germany between 2000 and 2007.
The group's existence and responsibility for the murders came to light on Nov. 4, 2011, when two of its members, Uwe Mundlos and Uwe Bohnhardt, died by suicide following a failed bank robbery.
Evidence subsequently uncovered by investigators linked the group to the killings.
For years, German police and intelligence agencies had largely dismissed possible racist motives, instead investigating victims' families and alleged connections to organized crime and drug trafficking.
Media investigations later revealed that Germany's domestic intelligence agency, the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV), and its regional branches had numerous informants with past contacts with NSU suspects.
Authorities, however, maintained that they had no prior knowledge of the terror cell's existence or its involvement in the murders.
The scandal sparked a nationwide debate over institutional racism and failures within Germany's security and intelligence services, which faced criticism for underestimating the threat of far-right extremism.

A CERN innovation hub is to be established at the Corda Campus, a large technology and business innovation campus in Hasselt (Limburg Province). CERN is the leading European centre for particle physics, based in Geneva (Switzerland). Over the past few decades, a great many new technologies have been developed there. The hub aims to make this knowledge more accessible to businesses in Limburg and the rest of Belgium.
CERN develops technologies that are among the best in the world. Although they are primarily intended for fundamental research, they also have applications outside particle physics, for example in medical imaging, advanced sensor technology and data processing.
The new innovation hub at the Corda Campus in Hasselt is designed to strengthen the link between CERN and the Belgian business community. The focus is on connecting CERN’s expertise with the needs of businesses and research institutions.
For example, both partners aim to launch new research and development projects and to stimulate the development of innovative products and applications.
First region in Europe
Limburg is the first region in Europe to have such an innovation hub. “This is an important recognition of our ambitions,” says Tom Vandeput, chair of the provincial development agency of Limburg province POM Limburg and provincial executive member for Innovation Policy.
The province is allocating an additional 3.6 million euros to the Big Science Hub over the coming years. The collaboration with CERN is a first concrete step within this broader initiative. Our aim is to give our innovative SMEs better access to international knowledge and technology and to strengthen their competitiveness.”
“This CERN innovation hub is the first of a limited number of hubs we are establishing this year to test the new collaboration model in practice,” adds Han Dols, Head of Innovation and Technology Transfer at CERN.
“Together with a partner that is strongly committed to regional innovation, we want to help businesses and researchers apply CERN’s knowledge to challenges in a wide range of fields. In this way, this hub can strengthen the Belgian innovation ecosystem, stimulate socio-economic growth and create tangible social added value.”
Through the Big Science Hub, POM Limburg aims eventually to become a permanent link between Belgian industry and major international research infrastructures.
This should enable Limburg province to secure a stronger position within the international Big Science landscape, opening up new opportunities for innovation, entrepreneurship and employment.

Fabrizio Parrulli, commander of the CUFAA (Carabinieri Forestry, Environmental, and Agri-Food Units Command).
                                    
Indeed, peacebuilding and peacekeeping also depend on the protection of the environment and biodiversity. UNESCO has been active in this field since the 1970s through the “Man and the Biosphere” program, which aims to reconcile the needs of environmental protection with those of sustainable development. The program, for which Italy currently holds the rotating vice-presidency, manages a global network of nearly 800 Biosphere Reserves—21 of which are in Italy—that together cover 5% of the Earth’s surface. 
   “Here at UNESCO, the Carabinieri are known for their role in safeguarding cultural heritage. Today, it is also important to highlight their work—less well-known internationally but equally important—in defending biodiversity. This work benefits the community, and Italy wishes to present it as a best practice and a model that can be replicated on a global scale,” stated Ambassador Liborio Stellino, Italy’s Permanent Representative to UNESCO, addressing a large audience of diplomats and international officials.

Israel reports highest election turnout in 53 years amid strong Arab, opposition participation

Şahin Demir
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
Voter turnout in Israel’s general elections reached 31.5% by noon local time (1000GMT) on Tuesday, the highest level recorded at that hour since 1973, according to the Central Elections Committee.
 
A total of 2.39 million Israelis had cast their ballots by noon, an increase of more than 3 percentage points compared with the previous election, according to the committee.
 
Extremist Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich attributed the high turnout to exceptionally strong participation among Arab voters and in left-wing strongholds.
 
In a social media post, Smotrich said the increase in participation was driven by unusually high voting rates in Arab communities and areas traditionally supporting left-wing parties.
 
Arab Knesset member Ahmad Tibi also reported unusually high participation, expressing confidence in a strong electoral performance.
 
“Polling stations are packed like never before, and I am confident we will achieve a major victory,” Tibi said in a press statement.
 
The remarks come amid efforts by Arab political parties and opposition leaders to mobilize voters in a closely contested election that could determine whether Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu remains in power.
 
According to The Jerusalem Post, the communities of Ein Hod and Sde Nehemia recorded turnout rates of 25.7% and 25.4%, respectively, by 10 am.
 
Other communities, including Nes Harim and Odim, reported participation rates of 23.2% and 23%, respectively.
 
Earlier Tuesday, opposition leaders urged Israelis to vote in large numbers to end Netanyahu’s rule.
 
Opposition Yisrael Beiteinu party leader Avigdor Lieberman called for an end to the Netanyahu era, while Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the opposition Yashar party, urged voters to support political change.
 
More than 7.3 million Israelis are eligible to vote in Tuesday’s election to choose members of the 120-seat Knesset.
 
Polling stations opened at 7 am local time (0500 GMT) and are scheduled to close at 10 pm (2000 GMT).
 
The election is Israel’s first general vote since the start of its genocidal war in the Gaza Strip in October 2023.
 
The vote comes amid deep political divisions over Netanyahu’s leadership, the Gaza genocide, Israel’s military confrontation with Iran and the country’s future political direction.
 
Netanyahu’s Likud-led coalition and opposition parties are competing to secure the 61 seats required for a parliamentary majority.
 
Recent opinion polls have suggested that neither bloc is assured of a majority, raising the possibility that Arab parties could play a significant role in determining the formation of the next government.

Jordan carried out air strikes in southern Syria late on Monday, killing at least five civilians, including women and children, according to Syrian state media. Meanwhile, Amman said the operation targeted Daesh sites following a deadly church attack in Jordan.
The Syrian Arab News Agency (SANA) reported strikes on several locations in Daraa province, saying seven people were killed. Two injured people in Muzayrib, in the western countryside, were taken to Tafas National Hospital, according to the provincial health director.
Among those killed was a 65-year-old man from Daraa city’s Tariq al Sadd neighbourhood who died from shrapnel wounds, the provincial health director said.
Jordan’s army said earlier that it had struck sites belonging to “terrorist organisations” in southern Syria linked to Friday’s attack on mourners at Hamoud Church in Jordan’s Karak province, which killed nine people.
The army said the strikes killed and wounded members of the groups and destroyed sites and vehicles, but did not identify the organisations or provide locations or casualty figures.
Jordan says strikes targeted Daesh
Jordanian government spokesman Mohammad al Momani said on Tuesday that the strikes killed more than 20 Daesh members and destroyed a major weapons depot.
He said the operation followed a period in which Jordan had “run out of patience” with terrorist group movements and threats to its national security.
“The operation was based on field intelligence aimed at neutralising confirmed threats and planned terrorist attacks against Jordan,” Momani said.
He expressed regret over civilian casualties, saying Jordan had avoided striking locations where intelligence indicated civilians were present.
Jordanian security forces arrested three suspects in the church attack on Monday after a shootout in Karak. All three were wounded, while no security personnel were injured, according to Jordan’s Public Security Directorate.
Damascus condemns strikes
Syria on Tuesday condemned the strikes by Jordan. A foreign ministry statement expressed "condemnation and rejection, in the strongest terms", calling the strike "an unacceptable violation and breach of Syrian airspace without any prior coordination".
It also said the attack was "a blatant violation of the principles of good-neighbourliness and Syrian national sovereignty".
The Syrian government also said that the Jordanian strikes were conducted without prior coordination and that an investigation was under way.
Damascus said it was supporting those affected and had conveyed its objections to Jordan, stressing the need for joint security and field coordination on operations in border areas to safeguard Syria’s sovereignty and the security of both countries.
Jordan said it respected Syria and its people and that coordination between Amman and Damascus on counterterrorism and weapons and drug smuggling had been ongoing for years.
Momani said Jordan and Syria would establish a joint committee to follow up on the consequences of the operation and strengthen coordination against Daesh while protecting civilians.
He said Jordan supported Syria’s security, unity and internal stability and was committed to developing cooperation in confronting shared challenges.
“Jordan’s security and Syria’s security are one,” Momani said, adding that countering terrorism remained a shared objective.
The Syrian authorities said the strikes had killed seven people, while SANA reported five civilian deaths and two injuries in the attacks.

Eesti 200 MP: Casino tax cut needs time, over-regulation is the real issue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:24:00 UTC
19:24:00 KST

Eesti 200 MP: Casino tax cut needs time, over-regulation is the real issue
A controversial online casino tax cut needs time to work out, Eesti 200 MP Tanel Tein said.
It is over-regulation and not the lower tax rate, which Tein's party sponsored, which is behind lower than hoped-for tax revenues, the MP went on.
The tax cut, passed last December, lowered the online casino rate from 6 percent to 4 percent, in increments over a two-year period. Receipts fell 9.7 percent in the first seven months of 2026, while the Cultural Endowment, one of the main recipients of the tax revenues, has forecast a €6–7 million shortfall for next year, directly as a result of the lower revenues.
Speaking to "Aktuaalne kaamera," Tein called comparing six months of receipts to a four-year strategy short-sighted, adding the Finance Ministry's forecasts do not represent money in the budget.
The gambling tax cut was your big mission in politics — do you concede failure?
Its aim was to bring extra funding to sport and culture; a private funding foundation and a sports facilities fund were set up at the Cultural Endowment for that purpose. The tax strategy is set up over four years, so assessing it after six months is very short-sighted.
Why do you say that? It can already be seen that the state budget has received half as much tax revenue.
No. If we compare the tax base we had in 2025, in 2026 it has grown noticeably. When we hiked the gambling tax from 5 to 6 percent, growth in the tax base fell sharply — and that is a very important signal that we need to grow the tax base, so there is something to tax.
The Ministry of Finance disagrees with you, while the Cultural Endowment's forecast is something else entirely compared with what you promised at the start of this year.
The Ministry of Finance's forecast is just that, a forecast; it is not money in the budget. And we have to ask why in earlier years growth in the tax base was nearly 40 percent, and during the tax rise it fell sharply to zero. That is a very important point, and it is the market participants themselves who must be asked. It is known that nearly two-thirds of tax revenue comes from foreign operators. To my knowledge, the Ministry of Finance has not spoken to them about what they will do if the tax rises or falls. But the bigger problem is over-regulation.
It is very convenient to blame other officials and institutions for over-regulating. You seem to think pawn brokers are over-regulated too. But the forecast has not matched reality.
A forecast is not money in the state budget. Take the simple example of the car tax: the forecast said €130 million would flow into the state budget, and in fact around €50 million did — so forecasts are very often wrong. We need to know the substance: why that taxpayer and that tax revenue comes to Estonia, what we need to do for it, what other countries are doing so that we are in the international market and competitive. I would very much listen to what the sector and the market participants themselves say on this point — and today they say we over-regulate.
Your own forecasts were €95 million in online casino tax revenue by 2029. Today it's clear that won't happen — what forecasts are you still waiting for?
Let's settle one thing: that was not a forecast, it was an assumption. It was a simulation of what would happen if we succeeded in bringing ten licenses a year to Estonia — and now we have to ask what we should do to bring those ten licenses a year.
What needs to be done? The Cultural Endowment says there is no money to fund projects.
At the Cultural Endowment we have to look at what other tax receipts have fallen. Alcohol and tobacco excise have fallen, [state lottery] Eesti Loto has fallen — all of them. And now the remote gambling tax is being made the political culprit, which in my view is not right. In previous years the remote gambling tax has continued to cover shortfalls in other areas, and that hasn't been talked about.
In your view, should the Riigikogu reverse the legislative amendment?
If our tax base falls, then that tax percentage could be 30. We won't get more tax from it; we need to get more companies here, and for that we need to know what we have to do. We must not over-regulate.
Background:
The tax cut was passed last December and lowers the rate from 6 percent to 4 percent by 2029. The Ministry of Finance forecast a €6–37 million shortfall across 2026–2029. Prime Minister Kristen Michal has said the government will revisit the cut if it brings no extra revenue.
