Massive Groups of Volunteers Are Ready to Face Down ICE at the Polls
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:15:00 UTC
19:15:00 KST

The Franklin County board of elections building at 1700 Morse Street in central Columbus, Ohio, is an early voting site for next week’s midterms. It is also located in the middle of the large Somali American community that was targeted by the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency’s Operation Buckeye last December. The campaign was designed, the agency said, to find “the worst of the worst criminal illegal aliens.”
The result was a paltry number of arrests, months of sustained harassment, and a lingering feeling that ICE agents could return at any minute, especially around election time.
“Here in central Ohio, our early voting location is located in a neighborhood that's been the hardest hit by ICE, and it's an immigrant community neighborhood,” Liliana Rivera Baiman, an organizer with the 614 ICE Watch group and the Ohio Good Neighbor Network, tells WIRED. “So we knew that that neighborhood was at risk and that people were going to be going to vote there, and a lot of the community there, like our Somali community that can vote, our Latino community, they walk to the location.”
Baiman’s group is responding to the threats from the Trump administration to target immigrant communities during the midterms. Dozens of volunteers are already patrolling near early voting sites in Columbus every day, Baiman says, and the figure will rise to around 250 on Election Day. They have been trained to document, record, and report any sightings of federal immigration agents, sharing the information in dozens of Signal and WhatsApp groups.
“We teach people that they have to observe the behavior. We show them what to look out for, what does ICE look like, this is the type of uniform that agents wear, these are the types of vehicles that they drive,” Baiman says. “We show them examples so that they can get familiar with what they might see.”
These efforts are being repeated in towns and cities across the country. WIRED spoke to a dozen people taking part in this effort, whose groups are working together to combat what they see as an existential threat to American democracy. Central to this response are training sessions run by massive national groups like Common Cause, the American Civil Liberties Union, and Indivisible, as well as local groups like Living United for Change in Arizona and NorCal Resist, that have created massive groups of people who can document and record what ICE is doing, understand voters rights, and in many cases, prepare for worst-case scenarios.
Officially, the Department of Homeland Security has said that it has no plans to deploy ICE agents to polling locations on Election Day. “ICE is not planning operations targeting polling locations,” a DHS spokesperson tells WIRED, but added: “ICE conducts intelligence-driven targeted enforcement, and if an active public safety threat endangered a polling location, they may be arrested as a result of that targeted enforcement action.”
For the past six months, President Trump and his allies have declined to rule out possible deployments to voting locations during the midterms, even though they would be illegal under federal law. When asked in May if he would deploy the National Guard or ICE during the midterms, Trump said: “I’d do anything necessary to make sure we have honest elections. We have to have honest elections.”
“Why are there objections to sending ICE officers to polling places?” Todd Blanche, then acting attorney general, said in July. “Illegals can’t vote.” The White House did not respond to requests for comment.
Some election experts simply don’t believe it will happen: “ICE and troops will not be at the polls,” David Becker, a former Justice Department trial attorney who is now head of the Center for Election Innovation and Research, said at a recent media briefing. “It won't happen. If it happens at all, it will be isolated. It will be accidental. It just won't happen.”
But for organizations on the ground interacting with voters in communities that have been targeted by ICE during Trump’s second term in office, the reality feels very different. Hundreds of different groups are part of the fight against possible ICE intimidation at the polls, and they are all working in coordination with each other.
“I've been up and down this state, in and out of Reno, in and out of Las Vegas, into our rural counties, and the number one question I get is about federal agents at polling locations,” Cisco Aguilar, the Nevada secretary of state, tells WIRED.
Beatriz Lopez, the executive director of Voto Latino, a group encouraging Hispanic and Latino citizens to register to vote, agrees, particularly when it comes to the communities her organization is focused on.
“We know that Latino voters are in the crosshairs of this administration because we know our electorate, our voting bloc, is what's going to shape and determine the elections of so many competitive races,” Lopez tells WIRED. “There is legitimate fear among our community.”
Lopez’s group, like many others WIRED spoke to, will be operating a war room on Election Day, with the specific goal of identifying and debunking viral disinformation that could dissuade citizens from voting. But they are also preparing for more troubling, real-world concerns.
“One of the scenarios that we're anticipating is that at the same time that we're trying to get people out to vote, there might be home raids by ICE in some of these neighborhoods, which has a real chilling effect on people,” Lopez said.
To combat this scenario, groups like 614 ICE Watch in Columbus are organizing patrols in neighborhoods near polling locations. “We send our folks in pairs or in groups. We never want to send anyone alone; we always want to have multiple people there so they can help take control of the situation,” Baiman says, adding that they have trained volunteers in a unique method of de-escalation: “If it starts to get very tense, we teach our folks to hum, to sing, to calm themselves down.”
The goal is not to interact with ICE agents but to document what they are doing so that events can be properly recorded and shared publicly. In January, just days after Alex Pretti was shot and killed in Minneapolis, more than 200,000 people logged into an “Eyes on Ice” Zoom training session, designed to teach people how to properly document ICE activities. Those skills are now being deployed during the midterm elections, Ezra Levin, cofounder of Indivisible, a group founded to stop the rise of authoritarianism in the US, tells WIRED.
On a much smaller scale, Living United for Change in Arizona has been training volunteers to become “constitutional defenders” in person, as the group prepares for next week’s vote. To track ICE activity, the group created a heat map that volunteers use to log and track ICE activity. The map is not available publicly, but WIRED was given access to the website and reviewed hundreds of recorded incidents of ICE activity in Maricopa and Pima counties.
Groups are also using social media to draw attention to what is happening. Last week in Sutter County, California, six ICE vehicles showed up in the parking lot of the Yuba City board of elections building, where a ballot drop box is located. Following a call from a local resident, NorCal Resist, a mutual aid organization, was able to send one of its trained volunteers and post an alert on Instagram.
“They don't like the attention, [and] when there's more community attention, they do often leave,” Giselle Garcia, programs director with NorCal Resist, tells WIRED.
DHS denied it was conducting immigration enforcement at a polling location, and said its agents were conducting a targeted enforcement operation against an illegal immigrant from Mexico. “ICE parked in front of a polling center—with permission from a representative of the center—while waiting for the target to exit the courthouse,” Chandler Rebel, a DHS spokesperson tells WIRED.
Much of this work, however, is being done in private, a move Lopez says is necessary to protect the online infrastructure they have put in place over the course of the past two years. Levin said that Indivisible’s leadership team would be hunkered down in an Airbnb in an undisclosed location on Election Day, on alert to deploy their sizable resources wherever they are needed.
Despite the fear that pervades minority communities about what Trump and his federal agents will do next week, every group leader, activist and volunteer WIRED spoke to in recent weeks has repeated one central belief: They are prepared.
“You have all this traditional election protection infrastructure that's really, really robust, but then there is this grassroots infrastructure,” Jill Garvey, executive director of States at the Core, which combats authoritarianism and political extremism, tells WIRED. “They've done all this tactical documentation training. They know how to be constitutional observers, and I'm pretty confident that when and if we have an uptick in federal enforcement at the polls, it's going to get documented really, really quickly, and it's going to be beamed out to the world that it's happening.”

AFP boss warns boys as young as 12 being radicalised at home
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:13:56 UTC
19:13:56 KST

AFP boss reveals new youth radicalisation data, with warning signs for teen boys
In short:
AFP boss Krissy Barrett says new youth teen radicalisation data shows the evolution of youth extremism, revealing warning signs and shattering previous assumptions.
Commissioner Barrett has also revealed that female parliamentarians are three times more likely to receive abuse or threats, showing a clear gender divide.
What's next?
Commissioner Barrett will raise security for politicians at an upcoming meeting with state and territory police commissioners.
Australia's top cop Krissy Barrett has warned teenage boys as young as 12 are being radicalised in their bedrooms, lured by a chaotic blend of violent jihadism, white supremacy and anti-government rage.
A statement from Commissioner Barrett tabled at Senate Estimates details an internal AFP analysis of 55 radicalised children aged 12 to 17, revealing a chilling evolution in modern extremism.
All of the subjects were male, and every single one was radicalised all or in part online.
While violent jihadism remained the most prevalent belief system, it was closely followed by anti-authority and white supremacist ideologies, with an increasing number of boys displaying no clear ideology at all.
"The ideological presentation in youths has shifted over the past two years, with fewer presenting with clearly defined ideologies, and an increasing number having mixed/hybrid ideologies, unclear/ incoherent ideologies, a superficial understanding of ideologies and ideological fluidity," she said.
The data shatters long-held intelligence assumptions that youth extremism is confined to broken homes, revealing that boys from stable families with secure parental bonds are increasingly being weaponised by digital algorithms.
While more than one-quarter did not have a stable male role model and about one-third had witnessed or experienced violence from their caregivers, Commissioner Barrett said there "were also youth cases where there was a secure bond to one or both caregivers."
"This shows kids who come from stable family environments and have few vulnerabilities are also becoming radicalised and manipulated,"
she said.
Commissioner Barrett did point to some clear warning signs among the cohort, including 13 per cent being suspended or expelled in primary school, with more than a third kicked-out from high school.
"In three out of five cases, the youths had received support, treatment or intervention for a mental health condition," she said.
She also warned presentations were not clear-cut and increasingly complex, with "no single profile of a radicalised young person and no one pathway to violent extremism."
She said she hoped the study would help the federal police and policy makers intervene earlier to prevent youth offending.
Parliamentarian security
In the wake of last week's attack on independent MP Helen Haines, Commissioner Barrett told Senate Estimates the AFP handled nearly 800 protective security reports targeting parliamentarians in the first six months of the year.
She warned basic policy debate is increasingly triggering direct threats against politicians.
"At times there is an almost immediate link from a policy announcement or comment, to a threat being sent," Commissioner Barrett said.
"It would be wrong to think only inflammatory comments are creating the flood of threats. In some cases, just the debate causes the hate."
Detailing the drivers behind the harassment, the commissioner said AFP caseloads showed hostility is typically triggered by four factors: policy, perceived performance, profile, and personality.
"In some cases, parliamentarians are being targeted because of their accent, what they look like, or their political party," she said.
The evidence presented to the committee exposed a stark gender divide in the abuse directed at elected officials with female parliamentarians three times more likely than their male colleagues to receive sexualised or gender-based threats.
That toll is highest for female MPs from culturally and linguistically diverse backgrounds, who report the most frequent and varied attacks.
Male parliamentarians are also subject to gender-based abuse, with Commissioner Barrett noting that threats directed at men frequently rely on "accusations of weakness, femininity or subordinate masculine traits."
Facing pressure from MPs and senators over the adequacy of current protection measures, Commissioner Barrett acknowledged the AFP needed to "do better" in demonstrating how seriously threats are managed.
She committed to implementing more consistent officer training and confirmed she would raise parliamentarian security at an upcoming meeting with state and territory police commissioners.
Social media and technology
The surge in threats against politicians is unfolding against a broader, more alarming shift across Australian society, one Commissioner Barrett warned is driven by an "instant pipeline" of digital hostility home-delivered into everyday lives.
"The threats are instant and voluminous. And they instantly shock and cause legitimate fear," she said.
"Perceived or real anonymity have given cowards courage."
Pointing to a dangerous convergence between digital platforms, social hostility, and ideological obsession, the commissioner warned that online abuse is spilling into physical violence.
"The contagion of online hate has breached the digital compound and is spilling into the physical world. This is corroding our communities and has normalised violence — and it continues to impact on many, most notably, the Jewish community," she said.
Crucially, Commissioner Barrett warned that hyper-connectivity and artificial intelligence have erased the geographic isolation that historically shielded Australia from global threats.
"Across the world, we are witnessing a trend where violence emerges with little or no warning, particularly where individuals do not have a protection intelligence footprint," she said.
"Lone actors are being motivated by a convergence of personal grievance, mental health vulnerabilities and ideological concerns. What helped keep us safe in recent times, such as our geography, analogue systems and far away criminals, has been impacted by fully-integrated technology, social media and artificial intelligence."

OPINION - Brazil has chosen, and Lula must deliver
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:13:02 UTC
19:13:02 KST

Marcus Vinicius De Freitas
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
Marcus Vinicius De Freitas is a visiting professor at the China Foreign Affairs University and a senior fellow at the Policy Center for the New South, based in Morocco.
Brazil’s voters have given President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva another chance to govern. His victory also preserves the country’s freedom to negotiate its international partnerships. The election results leave Lula responsible for demonstrating what he can deliver in a fourth term. Whether an octogenarian president in a Latin America that is turning conservative can do so is a defining question for the next four years.
Lula won 51.79 percent of valid votes, compared with Flavio Bolsonaro’s 48.21 percent, reversing a 1.87-point deficit from the first round. Almost half of voters cast valid ballots for his opponent. A fourth presidential victory demonstrates extraordinary personal resilience, but it cannot be read as an endorsement of his entire record.  
Anatomy of a comeback
The comeback required mobilization beyond Lula’s loyal base. National abstention fell from 21.08 percent in the first round to roughly 19.2 percent. Lula’s campaign stepped up its outreach to those who had stayed home or remained unconvinced.
The electoral geography is clearer. Gains in Sao Paulo, Minas Gerais, Rio de Janeiro and Bahia together brought Lula millions of additional votes compared with the first round, widening his overall margin over Bolsonaro. Lula recovered Minas Gerais and reinforced his advantage in the Northeast. He also won the city of Sao Paulo, although Bolsonaro carried the state. The decisive expansion therefore went beyond familiar Workers’ Party strongholds.
Pre-election polling had shown Lula stronger among poorer voters and women. These constituencies help explain his coalition, but claims about specific vote transfers require further evidence. Politically, the result suggests that dissatisfaction with Lula did not automatically translate into confidence in a Bolsonaro successor. Voters could demand change while remaining uneasy about the alternative.  
Foreign interference and national autonomy
Foreign involvement complicated that choice. Donald Trump’s pressure, Javier Milei’s campaigning and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s endorsement gave Bolsonaro international visibility. What Flavio Bolsonaro expected to be a decisive asset for his campaign proved instead to be a poisoned chalice. It enabled Lula to link his defense of sovereignty to a tangible concern: whether Brazil’s next government would negotiate independently or import foreign patrons’ priorities.
Foreign involvement helped Lula politically by giving his sovereignty argument a concrete target. Establishing the precise electoral effect of this foreign pressure, however, is harder. The result alone cannot tell us how many voters rejected Bolsonaro because of outside backing. Nevertheless, economic pressure gave the president grounds to frame autonomy as a protection for Brazilian livelihoods, including those affected by tariffs, rather than as an abstract diplomatic ambition.
The election offers a difficult lesson. Jair Bolsonaro's decision to promote his son reinforced the movement’s dependence on one family. A modern conservative alternative needs credible programs for security and public spending, as well as leaders with executive experience. Social media reach helped conservative candidates compete, but winning national office requires proving that their organisations have the competence to govern.
Lula faces a related succession problem. His fourth victory confirms how heavily the Brazilian left depends on him. He should use this term to strengthen party institutions and groom leaders capable of carrying his platform beyond his presidency. Repeating past achievements will not satisfy younger voters seeking better education, productive employment and protection from violence.  
Pragmatism abroad
Abroad, the outcome favours continuity of strategic autonomy. Brazil should negotiate constructively with Washington on trade and security while maintaining its partnerships with China and the wider Global South. Chinese demand sustains key Brazilian export sectors, where the United States is actually a direct competitor, particularly in soybeans. Sacrificing commercial opportunities to demonstrate political loyalty would cost Brazilian producers.
BRICS gives Brazil a forum to help shape institutions alongside other major developing economies. Lula should use that position to secure finance and technological cooperation that support development at home. International prominence needs practical results to retain domestic support.
The immediate political task is reconciliation. The late extension of voting hours, amid transport and weather difficulties, requires a transparent explanation. Institutions should answer questions with evidence and follow lawful procedures to protect confidence in the result and prevent grievances from hardening into a permanent refusal to accept electoral defeat.
Lula’s legacy will ultimately depend on confronting corruption, improving learning outcomes and making communities safer. That requires investigations that reach politically connected offenders, schools that teach pupils to understand what they read and security policies that protect residents from organized crime. Success must be visible in public services and opportunities, including for those who voted against him. Political parties must also recruit and prepare capable public servants rather than treating online popularity as a sufficient qualification. The next four years offer Brazil an opportunity to begin renewing both political camps. Voters have entrusted Lula with another mandate; the country now needs a government that can turn that mandate into improvements people can recognize.
*Opinions expressed in this article are the author's own and do not necessarily reflect the editorial policy of Anadolu.

Russian ballistic missiles hit a Kyiv university campus, then return before dawn for the Southern Bridge again
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:12:36 UTC
19:12:36 KST

Russia attacked Kyiv with ballistic missiles and drones in two waves, killing one person, injuring civilians, and damaging university dormitories and apartment blocks, the city military administration said. Russian strikes also killed two people in Kharkiv on the evening of 26 October and wounded civilians in four other oblasts overnight. Daytime attacks on 26 October killed people in Donetsk, Dnipropetrovsk, and Kharkiv oblasts.
Russia's war against Ukraine grinds on along the front, where on 26 October alone Russian forces dropped 247 guided bombs and used 9,679 kamikaze drones, the General Staff reported. Behind the front, Russian missiles and drones keep hitting Ukrainian cities, while Washington presses Kyiv rather than Moscow. Ukraine was reportedly told to spare Russian refineries or lose US intelligence and arms. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused US President Donald Trump of trying to pressure Ukraine into capitulating, and a Ukrainian diplomat argues that Trump treats Ukraine as the weak link to be squeezed.
Two ballistic waves hit a Kyiv campus, the center, and the Southern Bridge
Shortly after 22:00 on 26 October, Russian missiles hit near a metro station in Kyiv's left-bank Desnianskyi district, Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported. An ambulance crew that had arrived at a call came under fire, and two medics were injured.
The missiles struck the grounds of one of Kyiv's universities, its campus, Kyoto Park, nearby homes, and the area beside a metro station, Zelenskyy wrote. “There is no military facility nearby,” he said.
In Dniprovskyi district, the blast wave blew out windows in a medical facility's intensive care unit, Klitschko said. A three-story non-residential building in the district partly collapsed.
The evening strike also damaged the metro between two left-bank stations and the exits of Lisova station, Klitschko said.
Kyiv gets no warning of the first of two Russian ballistic waves, hours after Zelenskyy said US alerts were back
A second wave followed before dawn on 27 October. Missiles hit an administrative building in Podilskyi district, Klitschko reported, and at 05:04 he said Russia had hit the Southern (Pivdennyi) Bridge and the metro infrastructure on it.
Police closed the bridge to traffic, and green-line trains stopped crossing it. Russian strikes had already damaged metro infrastructure on the same bridge on 22 October.
The overnight attack set two non-residential buildings on fire in Obolonskyi district, and two more people were injured.
By morning, a 46-year-old woman was dead and 15 people were injured, among them dormitory residents and two medics, the Kyiv City Prosecutor's Office said. Prosecutors counted at least 12 damaged apartment blocks, as well as a burns center, a shopping mall, and a tram.
Kyiv was the main target of the night, the Air Force said, as Russia launched Iskander-M/S-400 ballistic missiles and 280 drones. Air defenses downed two of the missiles and 255 drones.
Zelenskyy put the night's total at 16 ballistic missiles and called the attack “a serious escalation in the Russian operation against our logistics.” He blamed delays in deliveries of interceptors for Patriot and NASAMS air defense systems.
“Artificial and lengthy delays in the delivery of interceptor packages for Patriots and NASAMS, which unfortunately have been happening lately, directly help Russia achieve the goals of its terrorist campaign. Every such delay is a new Russian hit on one target or another.”
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy
Russian strikes kill two in Kharkiv and wound civilians across Ukraine
Russian strikes on Kharkiv's Novobavarskyi district on the evening of 26 October killed two men and injured four people, including a 17-year-old girl, oblast head Oleh Syniehubov said. On the morning of 27 October, a Russian missile hit Izium, damaging eight houses.
In Zaporizhzhia, a Russian strike on a gas station wounded two people, and a later strike on a car wounded a 17-year-old boy, the oblast administration said. In Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, Russian drones and aerial bombs injured three women in Synelnykove district overnight.
In Chernihiv Oblast, Russian attacks set homes on fire and injured six people, including a child, the oblast administration said. In Chernivtsi Oblast, a drone attack damaged an energy facility, cutting power until 02:15 and injuring two security guards, oblast head Ruslan Osypenko said. Russian attacks have also critically damaged electrical equipment in northern Khmelnytskyi Oblast, the regional power company said.
Over the past day, Russian attacks killed civilians in Donetsk, Dnipropetrovsk, and Kharkiv oblasts
On 26 October, Russian attacks killed three people in Donetsk Oblast and wounded 22, oblast head Vadym Filashkin said. His breakdown puts 16 of the wounded in Yasnohirka, where Russian aircraft dropped guided bombs. A Russian drone strike on Pavlohrad killed one person and wounded seven, and a drone killed a woman in Shevchenkove, Kharkiv Oblast. In Kherson, a Russian drone hit a health facility and wounded a nurse. Most of Konotop in Sumy Oblast has been without power since Russian strikes on 24 October, with no forecast for its return, the mayor said.
Patriot systems are the only ones in Ukraine that reliably stop Russia's Iskander-M ballistic missiles, and their missiles have waited almost a month for a US signature. Every week of that wait leaves cities like Kyiv facing waves like this one with fewer interceptors, which is why Kyiv is also asking Lockheed Martin directly for more.

Asian Indoor and Martial Arts Games in Saudi Arabia postponed
TEHRAN - The Olympic Council of Asia (OCA) has officially announced the postponement of the 6th Asian Indoor and Martial Arts Games, originally scheduled to take place in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, in December 2026.
According to the new schedule, the Games will be held from March 28 to April 8, 2027. The decision was made following consultations between the OCA, the Local Organizing Committee, national Olympic committees, and other relevant stakeholders.
Organizers explained that the postponement was necessary to address logistical and operational requirements, improve coordination, and ensure the widest possible participation of Asian countries.
Despite the change, Saudi Arabian officials emphasized that preparations remain on track and that the country is fully committed to delivering a successful international sporting event.
More than 4,500 athletes representing over 45 National Olympic Committees are expected to participate in the competition.
The Games represent an important milestone for Saudi Arabia, marking the country’s first opportunity to host a multi-sport event under the Olympic Council of Asia.
The postponement also provides additional time for participating nations to finalize their preparations and logistical arrangements.
Organizers remain confident that the rescheduled event will strengthen sporting cooperation across Asia and contribute to Saudi Arabia's Vision 2030 objectives.

French senate rejects constitutional bill on autonomy for Corsica island
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:08:59 UTC
19:08:59 KST

İlayda Çakırtekin
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
The French Senate rejected a constitutional bill on autonomy for the island of Corsica on Monday evening, marking a setback for a process launched in 2022, according to Les Echos newspaper.
The Senate voted against the bill by 181 votes to 134 following a debate in which the right-wing majority substantially rewrote the original text passed by the National Assembly.
The revisions included removing a reference to an “island community” from the proposed constitutional text and reducing the scope of the exceptional powers envisaged for Corsica.
Following the vote, Paul-Toussaint Parigi, a senator from the autonomist Femu a Corsica party, announced that his political movement would withdraw from the Beauvau process.
The process was launched in 2022 under former Interior Minister Gerald Darmanin at the request of President Emmanuel Macron with the aim of granting the island autonomous status within the French Republic.
"An archaic majority chose tonight to destroy a balanced political agreement that was painstakingly built and offered hope […]. Under these circumstances, we are withdrawing from the Beauvau process,” Parigi said.
Gilles Simeoni, mayor of Bastia and a prominent Corsican autonomist, said the island’s representatives had sought to find a political solution but faced opposition to the process.
The Corsican Nation Party (PNC) also announced that it was withdrawing its support for the process, criticizing what it described as the senators’ “contempt.”
The compromise had been approved by the Corsican Assembly in 2024 and subsequently received support in the National Assembly in June 2026.
However, the Senate’s rejection reportedly left the reform’s future uncertain, as constitutional amendments in France must be approved in identical terms by both houses of Parliament before being approved by three-fifths of lawmakers in a joint session of Parliament.

Kyiv Regional State Administration, in collaboration with the Ministry of Social Policy, is developing a new standard for a social service designed for those affected by missile strikes, announced Ihor Meschan, Director of the Department of Social Protection of the Population at the Administration.
"Kyiv region is constantly suffering from barbaric Russian air strikes and missile attacks. In effect, we must provide services to those affected. This is, in fact, a brand-new type of service; together with the Ministry of Social Policy, we are currently developing a new standard for services intended for victims of missile strikes," he stated during a press conference at the Interfax-Ukraine news agency on Tuesday.

"Each community is unique; some are very robust and organize social services exceptionally well, in full compliance with all legal requirements. For others, we—along with Caritas Kyiv—provide ongoing guidance to help them meet the state standards established by the Ministry of Social Policy," Meschan said.

"However, these are pre-war figures; we estimate that the actual number of people living in Kyiv region now exceeds 2 million... It is worth noting that 544,320 of these individuals receive pensions or disability payments. Clearly, this presents a massive challenge, as one in four people is unable to work, and the state must ensure they are cared for," Meschan said.
According to data from Kyiv Regional State Administration, the region is home to 133,832 war veterans, 68,976 combatants, over 13,000 family members of those who died, and 10,451 individuals with disabilities resulting from the war. "Consequently, social services have set as their primary objective the task of supporting the families of the fallen and those who have been wounded, most of whom, unfortunately, subsequently develop a disability," emphasized Meschan.

Russian attacks across Ukraine kill four, injure 57 over past day, as Kyiv comes under ballistic missile assault
Russian attacks across Ukraine have killed at least four and wounded at least 55 others over the past day, Ukrainian authorities said on Oct. 27, as Russia launched an overnight missile and drone blitz against the capital, Kyiv.
Russian attacks hit Kyiv's Southern Bridge, disrupting metro services, as well as a university campus, an administrative building, and medical centers.
At least one person was killed, and 15 people were injured in the latest Russian attack on the capital, Ukraine's State Emergency Service (DSNS) said. Those injured in the attack include a paramedic, a medical technician, and a 20-year-old university student.
According to the Ukrainian Air Force, Russia attacked Kyiv with an unspecified number of S-400 and Iskander ballistic missiles, launched from Bryansk Oblast, and with 280 strike drones of various types, 69 of which were jet-powered.
Two ballistic missiles and 255 Russian strike drones, including 56 jet-powered drones, were shot down by Ukrainian air defense or suppressed by electronic warfare.
There were 25 locations reported struck by Russian munitions in the capital, as well as 16 locations that were struck by falling debris from downed missiles and drones.
In Chernihiv Oblast, six people, including a 12-year-old child, were injured in a number of Russian attacks, according to regional authorities.
In Chernivtsi Oblast, two men were lightly njured in a Russian drone strike, according to regional authorities.
In Donetsk Oblast, three people were killed and 22 people were injured in a number of Russian attacks, according to regional authorities.
In Kherson Oblast, four people were injured in a number of Russian attacks, according to local authorities. These included a 62-year-old nurse who was injured when a Russian "Molniya" drone struck a hospital in the city of Kherson.
In Sumy Oblast, three people were injured in Russian drone strikes, according to regional authorities.
In Zaporizhia Oblast, five people were injured as a result of Russian attacks, including a 17-year-old boy, according to regional authorities.

French consumer confidence sinks to 13-year low in October amid protests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:06:56 UTC
19:06:56 KST

Bahattin Gönültaş
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
Consumer confidence in France fell to a 13-year low in October amid escalating protests, rising unemployment concerns and higher prices, official data showed on Tuesday.  
The consumer confidence index dropped five points month-on-month to 80 in October, its lowest reading since June 2013, according to the National Institute of Statistics and Economic Studies.
The figure missed market expectations for the index to remain unchanged at 85 and stayed well below its long-term average of 100 recorded between January 1987 and December 2025.
Protests launched by high school students in mid-September demanding better education conditions quickly expanded into broader mass demonstrations against the government's economic policies.
Alongside social unrest, cost-of-living pressures weighed on household sentiment, with the share of consumers who believe prices rose sharply over the past 12 months jumping eight points in October.
Households' outlook on their personal finances also deteriorated, as the sub-index measuring future financial expectations fell nine points and assessments of past financial situations dropped six points.
Both indicators moved further below their historical averages, while the proportion of consumers considering it a suitable time to make major purchases declined four points.
Unemployment fears rebounded by five points in October after recording a temporary dip in September.
Household saving intentions also weakened, with the share of respondents viewing the current period as a "good time" to save falling six points.
Expectations for future saving capacity slipped three points, while assessments of current saving ability remained unchanged; despite the decline, the overall savings climate index held at 118, above its long-term average of 100.

“Significant minority” feel disadvantaged in Dutch society – SCP
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:06:27 UTC
19:06:27 KST

“Significant minority” feel disadvantaged in Dutch society – SCP
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
A “significant minority” of people in the Netherlands believe other groups in society gain an unfair advantage at their expense, according to a survey for the Dutch government’s social research agency SCP.
Around 30% of people say they feel disadvantaged in the housing market, while 28% believe their views are not properly represented in politics. A smaller group of around 7% thought the justice system was biased against them.
The report found that people with minority ethnic backgrounds and white Dutch people with non-academic qualifications were most likely to feel they were being treated unfairly.
“Dutch people who feel they have drawn the short straw are often in a less favourable position in the housing or labour market,” the report’s authors said.
“They are also more likely to be dealing with other disadvantages such as a lower income, a smaller network or poorer health.”
The SCP tracks people’s perceptions of whether they are fairly treated on issues such as housing, justice and observation of traditions on a monthly basis, using focus groups and surveys.
Traditions
The agency said there was evidence that both people with recent migrant backgrounds and white Dutch people were disadvantaged, but both tended to perceive that the other group was better off.
Native Dutch people felt that traditions such as Sinterklaas were being diluted in favour of festivals such as Eid al-Fitr, while recent migrants said there was almost no recognition of their traditions outside a few major population centres.
The lack of trust in institutions also influenced people’s voting behaviour, with those who felt disadvantaged more likely to support far-right parties such as the PVV and FVD.
The report said the majority of people did not feel disadvantaged, while around one in five people perceived themselves to be privileged over others. They were more likely to be university educated and vote for progressive parties such as D66 and Pro.
“In contrast to many graduates, people with vocational educations are more likely to see society as a place where groups compete with each other for scarce resources, attention and recognition,” the report said.
“Moreover, they are more likely to feel that their own group systematically gets more than other groups and place the responsibility for this mainly with the political system and the government.”

Pope Leo to return to his adopted home on South America tour
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:06:11 UTC
19:06:11 KST

Pope Leo to return to his adopted home on South America tour
ZAÑA, Peru Oct 27 - As Pope Leo prepares to return to South America next week, many Peruvians remember him as the priest who helped feed hungry families, delivered aid after floods and walked alongside migrants in the country he would eventually call his own.
When the pandemic emptied the streets of northern Peru and one of the world's longest quarantines left many struggling to eat, Bishop Robert Prevost, as Leo was known, helped launch a soup kitchen in 2020 in the small town of Zaña.
"He gave us an example of human charity, and we prepared the 'aguadito con fe'," recalled former cook Betty Burga Campos, referring to the traditional soup of rice, meat and vegetables that volunteers served.
Prevost left Peru for Rome three years later after Pope Francis tapped him to lead the Vatican office that recommends candidates for bishop appointments worldwide.
After rising from missionary and bishop in Peru's far north to cardinal and ultimately pope, Leo, 71, is set to revisit the country where he became a citizen and built some of the relationships that defined his ministry, weeks after undergoing surgery for lung cancer. The Vatican confirmed on Monday that his November 6 to 17 South America tour remained on schedule.
Across northern Peru, regional governments are refurbishing churches and residents are preparing celebrations for his visit, which also includes earlier stops in Uruguay and Argentina.
For many Peruvians, memories of the Chicago-born head of the Catholic Church are less about Vatican titles than muddy boots, long drives across the country's rugged north and a hands-on approach to helping people.
"He had become Peruvian, even in the way he spoke. He no longer had much of that American accent," said José Manuel Zamora Romero, a priest in Lambayeque who knew him for years.
The share of adults in Peru who identify as Catholic has fallen from 76% to 67% over the decade to 2024, according to Pew Research Center. The decline is often linked to social changes and distrust of institutions, following years of political instability that have caused Peru to cycle through nine presidents in a decade.
A BISHOP ON THE MOVE
Prevost arrived in Peru in 1985 at age 30. After years based in the United States and Rome with his Augustinian order, he returned in 2014 and became bishop of the Peruvian city of Chiclayo in 2015. In 2023, Pope Francis brought Prevost to the Vatican. Francis named him a cardinal later that year and he was elected pope in 2025.
Across northern Peru's sun-baked farm belt, residents and priests recall a churchman constantly on the move.
For the future pontiff, "the distances were not limits, the distances were opportunities," said David Farfán, a priest in Zaña, one of the towns on the pope's upcoming itinerary.
Many remember Prevost riding horseback to isolated Andean communities. Others recall him driving hundreds of kilometers himself across Peru's rugged north.
"His hobby was driving," Zamora Romero said. "And I know he taught some priests to drive so they could get their licenses ... and they all passed the test."
That practical approach became evident during emergencies.
When severe flooding linked to the El Niño climate phenomenon inundated northern Peru in 2023, photos circulated on social media of Prevost wading through knee-deep water in rubber boots as he helped deliver aid.
When natural disasters occurred, "he was on the front lines to bring the help that the population needed," said Rev. Jorge Villegas of Chiclayo, where the pope will spend two full days.
Residents pointed to moments like those as evidence of a bishop who preferred action over visibility.
"He wasn't very focused on being with the press; he was more with the poor and in social conflicts," said Verónica Castillo, a journalist in Chiclayo who witnessed his intervention during a 2015 labor conflict.
"He was a bishop who intervened, who took action, and people remember that," she added, recalling how Prevost helped mediate the prolonged protest by workers against a sugar company, which turned violent.
'PUT HIMSELF IN SHOES OF A MIGRANT'
Migration has reshaped much of Latin America over the past decade, as millions of Venezuelans fled economic collapse and political turmoil. Peru hosts the world's second-largest Venezuelan diaspora community, with more than 1.5 million migrants. Many arrived without proper documentation and live with inadequate access to healthcare and basic services.
Prevost founded a Catholic organization in Chiclayo in 2018 to assist newcomers.
"He put himself in the shoes of a migrant first and foremost and knew what the situation was like," said Augusto Martínez, who leads the organization.
The group has assisted thousands of Venezuelans.
As pope, Leo has called for migrants to be treated with dignity, condemned human trafficking and warned traffickers to repent or face divine judgment. He has criticized anti-immigration policies, including measures pursued by US President Donald Trump.
"He supported migrants on how to have a dignified life here in Peru," said Lisbeth Coromoto Díaz, who received help through the Chiclayo organization and said he held Masses in honor of migrants.
Leo's planned return to Peru has revived hopes among Catholics in Eten, near Chiclayo, that he could advance a long-running campaign to secure Vatican recognition of the town's reported Eucharistic miracle. As bishop, he supported the cause, presenting historical records and thousands of testimonies of faith in Rome, linked to a 1649 apparition in which devotees say the image of the Christ Child appeared in a consecrated host.
Tourism officials are promoting routes tied to the places Leo lived and worked. Souvenir shops are stocking shelves with pope-inspired hats, key chains and pins.
In a shop window in the capital Lima's Gamarra textile district, an image of Leo on a T-shirt depicts him smiling while enjoying a plate of Peruvian food.
"We've got the pope looking spirited; we've got the pope as a foodie, enjoying delicious ceviche and rotisserie chicken. We even have the play on words: 'The Pope and the papa (potato) are Peruvian'," said clothing maker Victoria Quiñones.
Quiñones predicted a 200% increase in her workload and was running low on fabric for the T-shirts.
Nearby, Maria Rodriguez, 70, was shopping for pope T-shirts.
"I’m buying several," Rodriguez said.
"I’ll be wearing them all through November because I am Catholic: Roman and Peruvian," she added. REUTERS

Nordic Leaders Urge De-escalation in Call With Putin
Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre spoke by phone with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Tuesday at their own initiative to discuss Russia’s war against Ukraine and diplomatic efforts to end the conflict, according to European Pravda, citing Stubb’s office.
The conversation followed a meeting in Oslo on October 20 and was held in consultation with Ukraine, Stubb’s office said. The two Nordic leaders sought to advance diplomatic efforts to end Russia’s war of aggression and promote peace and stability in Europe.
The Finnish president’s office said the purpose of the call was to convey messages directly to Putin about future negotiations aimed at ending the war. The discussion was also linked to upcoming meetings in Abu Dhabi, where trilateral talks involving Russia, Ukraine and the United States are expected to take place in early November.

The statement highlighted the two countries’ shared security interests as neighbors of Russia and firm supporters of Ukraine. “Norway and Finland have always promoted peace and security in our region. The two countries have a shared interest in stability and predictability in the Baltic Sea region and the High North. This was highlighted in the call,” the statement said.
Stubb described the conversation as “frank and substantive,” adding that ending the war requires direct discussions with Russia.
Norwegian Prime Minister Støre stressed the devastating consequences of the conflict and the need to reduce tensions. “The war comes with enormous human and material costs. The suffering and destruction will impact generations. In the call we stressed the importance of de-escalation,” he said.
Stubb’s office also clarified that the Finnish and Norwegian leaders participated in the conversation as representatives of their respective countries, not on behalf of Europe as a whole.

Fire Point refuted the fake claim about halting production of the FP-5 &quot;Flamingo&quot; cruise missile
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
12:05:05 EET
19:05:05 KST

Fire Point refuted the fake claim about halting production of the FP-5 "Flamingo" cruise missile
Kyiv • UNN
Fire Point CEO Iryna Terekh refuted information alleging that production of the FP-5 "Flamingo" cruise missiles had been halted. The manipulation arose from the dissemination of a fragment of her interview taken out of context.
The CEO of Ukrainian defense company Fire Point, Iryna Terekh, denied reports that production of FP-5 "Flamingo" cruise missiles had allegedly been halted. The wave of manipulations was prompted by a fragment of her old interview that was taken out of context and circulated in an edited form. In fact, she was not talking about abandoning "Flamingo," but about having no plans to create additional cruise missile models, UNN reports.
Iryna Terekh personally responded on the social network X to the spread of inaccurate information, explaining that the company was not abandoning "Flamingo" but, on the contrary, planned to continue improving the missile.
"We do not plan to develop additional cruise missile models; instead, we are focusing on developing the existing model, while directing the greatest efforts toward two ballistic models," Terekh wrote.
At the same time, the spread of fake reports concerning Ukrainian long-range weapons may go far beyond ordinary information speculation. As military cybersecurity expert Kostiantyn Korsun explained in a comment to UNN, discrediting Ukrainian arms manufacturers may be one of the tools of Russia's information warfare.
"Discrediting Ukrainian manufacturers of long-range weapons, especially those producing truly effective weapons, may be one of Russia's tools for countering the development of Ukraine's defense-industrial complex. The goal is to establish narratives in Ukraine that are advantageous to Russia: supposedly, this is bad, it is fake, and programs for developing and producing such weapons have no prospects," the expert said.
According to Korsun, the aim of such information campaigns may be to shape a negative public attitude toward Ukrainian defense developments. In particular, this may be done by imposing the idea that they are allegedly ineffective and that funds spent on their production are wasted.
The expert explains that such operations do not always begin with blatantly false messages. A much more effective tool may be the use of real facts that are subsequently distorted or presented in a context favorable to the adversary.
Against the backdrop of these accusations, Iryna Terekh also separately responded to allegations that state funds had been used to create the weapons.
"The state spent zero hryvnias and zero kopecks on the development of each of our product models; this applies to FP-1, FP-2, FP-4, FP-6, FP-7, FP-9, and will continue to apply to all further developments. This is an atypical approach, but it is our additional contribution to the country," Terekh wrote.
Recall
Earlier, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy also spoke about the scale of Russian influence on the information space. During a speech at the Warsaw Security Forum, he said that following Ukrainian strikes on the data centers of Russia's "Yandex," there were noticeably fewer bots, hate, and provocations on social media.
Later, the Center for Countering Disinformation under the National Security and Defense Council published a study according to which, following the attacks on October 8 and 12, the number of messages from the accounts studied that displayed signs of inauthentic behavior on Facebook and Telegram decreased by 83.6% and 42.6%, respectively.

On October 20, a meeting was held in Oslo between Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. Finnish President Alexander Stubb also took part. After this meeting, Witkoff traveled to St. Petersburg, where he met with Putin — then he returned to Oslo and flew to the U.S. from there. Following these talks, the parties agreed to hold a new trilateral meeting between Russia, the U.S., and Ukraine. It will take place after November 4 (that is, after the U.S. midterm elections) in Abu Dhabi.
After this latest stage in the return to peace talks between Ukraine and Russia, European countries began looking for a representative who could take part on the EU’s behalf. Among the candidates for this role, The Telegraph named Stubb and Støre, as well as Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, Czech President Petr Pavel, and Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen.

‘It’s magical’: London’s iconic Oxford Street goes vehicle-free
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:03:32 UTC
19:03:32 KST

‘It’s magical’: London’s iconic Oxford Street goes vehicle-free
The cars have gone, and so have the buses, but while retailers expect a boost, residents worry about change.
London, United Kingdom – “It’s magical,” says biology teacher Muneera Alfadhel from under her umbrella.
In fact, it is a characteristically rainy, grey day in London, but the weather is doing nothing to dampen her mood. She is among the first to walk down the middle of the iconic Oxford Street following its pedestrianisation.
For generations, shoppers have bustled along Oxford Street next to bikes, cars, black cabs and red double-decker buses. But on Monday, from Great Portland Street to Orchard Street, the road is now a pedestrian-only zone.
On Monday morning, by force of habit, most pedestrians are still sticking to the pavement. Mark Arbouine, a forensic scientist out for a stroll, is one of the few breaking ranks: “I saw there was no traffic today, so I thought, why not walk in the middle of the street and take advantage of it? I just think it’s great for the environment, great for shopping. It’s just so much easier to move around the street.”
This tiny strip of real estate is big business: about 1 percent of the UK’s annual gross domestic product (GDP) is generated along this 1km (0.6 miles) stretch of street. But despite its outsized importance, Oxford Street has in recent decades been hit by lower consumer spending, as well as falling rents and footfall, which is now just 57 percent of what it was in 2006, according to New West End Company, a retail trade body.
The Greater London Authority, also known as City Hall, believes pedestrianisation could, therefore, offer a lifeline.
City Hall analysis suggests the partial pedestrianisation of Oxford Street could generate more than $109m per year and support an additional 700 jobs. Following a weekend trial in October 2025, two-thirds of businesses in the area said they had higher or similar sales figures during the pedestrianisation.
This is the first step in a multi-phase regeneration project to add two public squares, 50 trees and hundreds of public seating.
Barbara Stoll, a leading campaigner on the benefits of greener, more walkable cities, was smiling as she observed the street. The air already feels cleaner, she noted.
“It’s amazing coming here this morning. Walking down the street, it was already so uplifting that the noise is considerably lower,” she said. “People are excited. I saw people coming up from the tube and looking around. Seeing that, it’s almost like children when it’s Christmas Day.
“So I think it’s absolutely wonderful, and so needed for London.”
Residents ‘haven’t really been listened to’
On Saturday, ahead of the change, not all shoppers were convinced. A French tourist said he would avoid Oxford Street altogether if buses and cabs were no longer allowed through.
“People with disabilities who cannot walk a lot – that would be really helpful if the buses move on and they don’t discontinue [them],” a shopper told Al Jazeera.
“It would be good. Sometimes you’re tired; sometimes it’s raining.”
The pedestrianisation of Oxford Street has been years in the making, and not without controversy.
London Mayor Sadiq Khan first tried it in 2017, following a manifesto pledge. But the plan fell apart in 2018, when Westminster Council – the local government authority responsible for Oxford Street at the time – withdrew its backing, saying residents did not support it.
Following a public consultation, Khan created the Oxford Street Development Corporation, taking responsibility for the street away from local officials and transferring it to the Greater London Authority and Transport for London.
With this second, successful attempt at pedestrianisation, doubts from local authorities have not gone away.
Residents are not being listened to, said Councillor Tim Barnes, the deputy leader and cabinet member for growth and planning for the City of Westminster.
“There has been a communication process with residents, but it’s been pretty much one way. Mostly, they are being told what’s going to happen to them and how it’s going to happen; what the format of the process is going to be in future. But realistically, those who know the street best haven’t really been listened to.”
He believes the economic benefits are overstated and do not consider the impact of displacing bus routes from a major road to the surrounding, smaller streets. That fear is shared by resident Nerma Cridge, who said London’s West End will become “completely unliveable, too crowded and too noisy at night”.
“We think all of this should be done in a much more productive relationship with communities,” she told Al Jazeera over the phone.
‘People just take back the space’
Concerns over the change will fade once residents see the real-world results in the coming months, Stoll believes.
“Examples from across Europe and the world, where such projects have already happened, prove that this only makes life better overall for local residents,” she said.
“Retail gets a boost. More people linger, more people come to the street, more people spend money in the shops, and even local shop vacancies reduce. The local air pollution significantly reduces, and as activity increases, people just take back the space.”
The Oxford Street Development Corporation will be testing and reviewing the results of the pedestrianisation in the coming months, and reviewing its findings early next year. Transitioning the rest of Oxford Street into a permanent, traffic-free public space is expected to go ahead by the end of next year.
Ahead of mayoral elections in 2028, the pedestrianisation could be one of the last major initiatives that Sadiq Khan signs off. A landmark project that will also become his legacy.

Limiting sugar in the first 1,000 days of life is associated with later dementia onset, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:00:34 UTC
19:00:34 KST

Limiting exposure to added sugar in the womb and during the first two years of life is associated with a lower risk of developing dementia decades later, according to a new study published in Neurology. By examining adults born around the end of post-World War II food rationing in the United Kingdom, researchers found that early-life sugar restriction corresponded with delayed dementia onset, healthier brain structure, and better scores on some cognitive tests in their 60s. The findings suggest that nutritional conditions during the earliest stages of human development may play a lasting role in how the brain ages.
Dementia is an umbrella term for progressive neurological conditions that impair memory, thinking, and the ability to perform everyday activities. The most common form is Alzheimer’s disease, which involves the gradual breakdown of brain cells and the buildup of abnormal proteins, followed by vascular dementia, which occurs when reduced blood flow damages brain tissue. Although lifestyle habits in middle and old age are well-known factors in cognitive decline, growing evidence points to the importance of the “first 1,000 days” of life, the developmental window spanning from conception to a child’s second birthday.
During this early period, the brain undergoes rapid growth, forming neural connections and building the structural foundation for lifelong thinking and memory. High sugar intake during pregnancy and infancy may disrupt this process by triggering inflammation or interfering with how cells respond to insulin. For instance, research covered by PsyPost in 2016 indicated that rats fed sugary drinks early in life developed changes in the hippocampus, a seahorse-shaped brain region essential for memory, that resembled the biological effects of early-life stress. In humans, observational studies have similarly linked higher maternal sugar consumption during pregnancy and breastfeeding to altered brain tissue organization in newborns and slightly lower cognitive scores in young children.
Studying how infant diets affect human brain aging is difficult because tracking people from birth into their 70s rarely happens in controlled experiments. To overcome this challenge, scientists have turned to a historical policy shift in the United Kingdom: the end of wartime sugar rationing. Introduced in July 1942 during World War II, the rationing system strictly limited added sugar and sweets to levels comparable to modern dietary guidelines while keeping overall calories and basic nutrients sufficient, unlike historical famines that caused severe starvation. When the British government abruptly ended sugar rationing in September 1953, national sugar consumption jumped by more than 50 percent, even as total calorie intake rose by only about 5 percent and other food groups remained relatively stable.
Researchers have used this sudden dietary shift to examine how early sugar limits relate to adult health, starting with a 2024 study by another team that linked rationing exposure during the first 1,000 days to lower adult rates of type 2 diabetes and high blood pressure. Extending this approach to respiratory health, a study covered by PsyPost in 2025 found that rationing exposure during pregnancy and infancy was tied to better adult lung capacity and lower rates of asthma. In the realm of mental health, a 2026 cohort study of British adults found that experiencing sugar rationing across the first 1,000 days of life was associated with a reduced preference for sweet foods and a lower risk of adult depression and anxiety.
Building on this line of inquiry, the new study was led by Jiazhen Zheng, an assistant professor at the School of Life and Health Sciences at Shenzhen University of Advanced Technology in China, who also led the 2025 lung-health study. Zheng conducted the research at The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou) alongside co-corresponding author S. W. Ricky Lee of the same institution and their colleagues, examining whether early sugar restriction also relates to long-term dementia risk, brain structure, and cognitive ability in older age.
“While growing evidence suggests that early-life nutrition can shape long-term health, remarkably little is known about whether sugar exposure during this period is associated with dementia many decades later,” Zheng told PsyPost. “We were particularly interested in addressing this knowledge gap because most dementia prevention research focuses on risk factors in middle and older age. The end of sugar rationing in the United Kingdom in September 1953 provided a unique natural experiment to investigate this question.”
The researchers analyzed data from the UK Biobank, a large health study that recruited middle-aged and older British adults between 2006 and 2010. Starting with 74,213 participants born between 1951 and 1956, the team excluded 6,582 people born outside the United Kingdom, 2,424 from multiple births such as twins or triplets, 79 adoptees, 208 people already diagnosed with dementia at recruitment, and 108 who withdrew from the project. This left a final sample of 64,737 adults who were an average of 54.6 years old at enrollment, 56.4 percent of whom were women.
Using each person’s birth date relative to the September 1953 policy change, the authors sorted participants into groups reflecting how long they experienced sugar rationing during their first 1,000 days from conception. In total, 40,963 participants experienced rationing: 10,682 were exposed in the womb only, 15,025 were exposed in the womb plus up to one year after birth, and 15,256 were exposed in the womb plus one to two years after birth. The remaining 23,774 participants were born after July 1, 1954, meaning they were conceived after rationing ended and grew up in an environment of unrestricted sugar.
The team tracked hospital admissions and death registries through July 1, 2023, to identify new diagnoses of all-cause dementia, Alzheimer’s disease, and vascular dementia. To account for other differences between the groups, the statistical models controlled for age, sex, race, birthplace, birth month, inflation-adjusted food prices, average national fat intake at birth, maternal smoking, breastfeeding, and parental dementia history. The researchers also adjusted for adult household income, neighborhood socioeconomic status, smoking, alcohol consumption, physical activity, and chronic illnesses such as heart, kidney, and liver disease.
In addition to tracking dementia diagnoses, the authors examined a subset of more than 7,500 participants who underwent magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain scans at an average age of 61.8 years, alongside roughly 6,400 to 20,600 participants who completed computerized cognitive assessments. These brain scans measured total brain volume, gray matter (the outer layer of brain tissue rich in nerve cell bodies), white matter (the deeper nerve fibers that connect different brain regions), the hippocampus, and white matter hyperintensities, which are bright spots on a scan that indicate small blood vessel damage and tissue wear.
Building on the 2024 research linking rationing to metabolic and vascular health, the team also tested whether adult type 2 diabetes and high blood pressure explained the link between early sugar restriction and dementia, and they checked two conditions considered unlikely to be affected by early sugar intake, type 1 diabetes and melanoma (a form of skin cancer), as negative controls.
Over the follow-up period, 504 out of 23,774 unexposed participants (about 2.1 percent) were diagnosed with all-cause dementia, including 227 cases of Alzheimer’s disease (about 1.0 percent) and 178 cases of vascular dementia (about 0.75 percent). In raw numbers, the rationed groups had slightly higher dementia rates, largely because they were born earlier and were more than two years older on average than the unexposed group, with 251 dementia cases among the 10,682 people rationed only in the womb (about 2.3 percent), 388 cases among the 15,025 people rationed through age one (about 2.6 percent), and 456 cases among the 15,256 people rationed for one to two years (about 3.0 percent). Once the researchers adjusted for age and other background variables, the rationed groups showed a lower risk of developing dementia at any given age, though the association for those exposed only in the womb was smaller and not statistically significant.
Compared with adults who never experienced rationing, those exposed to sugar rationing in the womb plus their first year of life had a 21 percent lower hazard (the rate at which new cases appear at a given age) of developing all-cause dementia and a 23 percent lower hazard of developing Alzheimer’s disease. The association was slightly stronger for those exposed in the womb plus one to two years after birth, who showed a 23 percent lower hazard of all-cause dementia and a 28 percent lower hazard of Alzheimer’s disease.
For vascular dementia, the estimates pointed in a similar direction, though the results were not statistically significant. Looking at the timing of diagnoses, experiencing rationing from conception through ages one to two was associated with delaying the onset of all-cause dementia by 2.55 years, Alzheimer’s disease by 2.87 years, and vascular dementia by 2.49 years.
“The magnitude of the associations was particularly noteworthy,” Zheng said. “These are population-level estimates rather than predictions for any individual, but even modest shifts in dementia occurrence could have meaningful public health implications given the growing global burden of the disease.”
The results were less robust in one additional analysis. When the researchers accounted for the possibility that participants would die of other causes before developing dementia, rationing exposure was still linked to a roughly 15 percent lower likelihood of all-cause dementia, but the associations with Alzheimer’s disease and vascular dementia were no longer statistically significant.
The link between early sugar rationing and dementia was stronger in women than in men, which the authors noted might relate to biological differences in how female neural circuits respond to early nutritional environments. The results held steady regardless of whether participants carried genetic variants of the apolipoprotein E gene that heighten Alzheimer’s risk. Mediation analyses indicated that lower rates of adult type 2 diabetes and high blood pressure accounted for 18.0 percent and 11.6 percent of the association, respectively, or 25.5 percent when combined, while birth weight accounted for just 2.7 percent. As expected, rationing exposure showed no association with type 1 diabetes or melanoma, and the primary dementia patterns were supported by a validation analysis in an independent British aging study, with an American cohort serving as a comparison group.
The brain imaging and cognitive test results aligned with the clinical dementia findings. Compared with the unexposed group, participants who experienced early-life sugar rationing had larger total gray matter volumes, averaging 618.9 cubic centimeters versus 618.5 cubic centimeters (an adjusted increase of 3.27 cubic centimeters), and smaller volumes of white matter hyperintensities, averaging 3.72 cubic centimeters versus 3.84 cubic centimeters (an adjusted reduction of 0.64 cubic centimeters).
Rationed participants also performed better on tests of complex processing speed, verbal and numerical reasoning, nonverbal pattern reasoning, and a timed test of visual attention that involves connecting numbered circles in order. Differences in total brain volume, white matter volume, hippocampal size, working memory, verbal memory, and a harder version of the connect-the-dots test that requires switching between numbers and letters were not statistically significant. These differences were modest: the gray matter difference amounted to about half a percent of total gray matter volume, and the cognitive differences were similarly small.
“What struck us most was how strongly early-life nutritional exposure appeared to be associated with brain health more than half a century later,” Zheng explained. “Beyond dementia diagnoses, we also observed favorable differences in brain MRI measurements, including greater gray matter volume and fewer white matter hyperintensities, alongside better performance on certain cognitive tests. The convergence of these findings across clinical, structural, and cognitive outcomes was especially interesting and suggested that the associations might reflect broader processes of brain aging.”
These results are consistent with research covered by PsyPost in December 2025, which tracked broad diet quality across the lifespan starting at age four rather than isolating sugar restriction during the first 1,000 days of life, and similarly found that healthier early nutritional habits were associated with better cognitive performance and a lower risk of late-life dementia. They also align with another study covered by PsyPost in November 2025, which examined how chronic sugar consumption caused memory impairment and Alzheimer’s-related brain pathology in adult rats rather than how early-life sugar restriction affects long-term dementia risk in humans, yet similarly linked high sugar exposure to neurodegenerative decline.
“Our findings suggest that the nutritional environment during pregnancy and early childhood may have consequences for brain health that extend across an entire lifetime,” Zheng told PsyPost. “The key message is not that people should eliminate sugar entirely, but rather that limiting excessive added sugar during these sensitive developmental periods may be beneficial. Importantly, our findings demonstrate associations, not definitive causation.”
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider when interpreting these findings. Because this was an observational study that relied on birth dates during a historical policy change, the researchers did not have direct measurements of how much sugar individual pregnant mothers or infants actually consumed. Although national surveys confirm that household sugar purchases surged right after September 1953, personal eating habits within both the rationed and unrationed groups likely varied from family to family. Because exposure was determined entirely by birth date, the rationed participants were also older, so the findings depend on statistical adjustments for age; the authors checked this by confirming that dementia risk did not drift among never-rationed participants born at different times after the policy ended.
“One important distinction is that our study does not prove that reducing sugar intake in infancy directly prevents dementia,” Zheng noted. “Other dietary, social, or environmental differences associated with the rationing period may also have influenced the results. Furthermore, our findings should not be interpreted as advocating extremely restrictive diets during pregnancy or infancy; adequate and balanced nutrition remains essential for healthy development.”
Another consideration is the age and makeup of the study population. Because participants were born in the early to mid-1950s, they were only in their late 60s and early 70s by the end of the tracking period in 2023, meaning the study primarily captured relatively early cases of dementia rather than diagnoses occurring in the 80s and 90s.
In addition, the UK Biobank consists of volunteers who survived into middle age and tend to be healthier, wealthier, and predominantly white (over 96 percent of this sample), which may limit how well the findings apply to more diverse or disadvantaged populations. The authors suggest that future randomized trials testing practical nutritional counseling to limit added sugars during pregnancy and infancy could help establish how early dietary habits shape brain development and long-term cognitive resilience.
“We hope to better understand the biological mechanisms linking early-life nutrition with brain aging and neurodegenerative diseases,” Zheng said. “In this study, type 2 diabetes and hypertension together statistically accounted for approximately one-quarter of the observed association, suggesting that metabolic and vascular health may play a role. Future research should examine additional biological pathways, clarify the most sensitive developmental windows, and determine whether these findings can be replicated in other populations with more detailed dietary information. Ultimately, we hope this work will help inform evidence-based nutritional recommendations across the life course.”
“I believe one of the broader implications of our work is that dementia prevention may need to be considered from a much earlier life-course perspective,” Zheng added. “We often think of dementia as a disease of old age, but some of the factors associated with vulnerability or resilience may originate decades before symptoms appear. Understanding these early influences could open new opportunities for preventive research and public health strategies.”
The study, “Association of Sugar Restriction in Utero Through Age 2 Years on Dementia Risk Later in Life,” was authored by Jiazhen Zheng, Gregory Y.H. Lip, Zhuoni Zhang, and S. W. Ricky Lee.

These four elections could change the world in 10 days – Stateside with Kai and Carter
