Love with nowhere to go
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Listen to this essay
23 minute listen
I have been grieving my mother for years, even though she is still alive. Sometimes before falling asleep – in that liminal space between waking and sleeping where the self becomes porous – I’d see the image of the sweet and caring woman who would come to say goodnight, her cheeks covered in thick layers of night cream. Then, out of nowhere, the image would flip into the raging woman who was so entangled in her own suffering that she turned her frustration on us. Over the years, that second woman slowly swallowed the first, as she got pulled into my brother’s addiction. It’s hard to say where her own unhappiness ended and my brother’s suffering began, but together they drifted into a parallel reality, cut off from the world beyond their heads. There was no funeral for this. No condolence cards. No flowers. No phone calls. No leave of absence. What was I supposed to mourn?
And yet what I felt for them, what I still feel, has the unmistakable gravity of mourning. Can there be grief without death? I have come to think that we grieve much more often than we realise, and that death is grief’s most visible occasion rather than its essence. If that doesn’t match your experience, it may be because we rarely call these other losses by their name. Most of our losses arrive without a funeral. That is the human predicament: we are creatures built to attach, living in a world where nothing stays. Sooner or later, we lose the things we care about. And since we are complex beings with a body, a mind, a community and an environment – beings who love many different things – there is a great deal we can lose, from our physical health to our sense of who we are, from relationships to homelands to the natural world we share with other species. For creatures like us, there is no way around heartbreak: to live is to lose. Grief is what love does when its object is gone. It is love with nowhere to go.
Over the past few years I have accumulated many such losses. There is the psychological loss of my father as I knew and loved him: a brutal stroke rendered him incapable of walking and cycling, and cycling was the only thing that could ‘make his thoughts liquid’, as he used to say. There is the loss of old friendships. First you are no longer part of each other’s lives – you just update one another about your life – and then, one day, it becomes awkward to reach out at all. There is the gradual softening of an academic identity I’d spent the most vital years of my life constructing. It was a genuine vocation, a life of the mind that taught me to think slowly and carefully. But it was also, as I came to realise, a way of living safely at one remove from where actual life takes place. What is slipping away is a future in which being an academic philosopher would be the whole answer to the question of who I am.
There was the woman whose calmness, clarity and silence embodied the qualities I have come to like so much about the Nordics since moving to Norway. Like a magical stranger, she entered my life unexpectedly, but at the same time her arrival felt so natural, her presence so obvious, that it was as if she had always been there. After our first meeting, which lasted almost 24 hours, I wrote in my journal: Ze is gekomen om te blijven. ‘She had come to stay.’ And she did, for nine intense months. She tried to teach me to ski. We listened to the music of Nils Frahm, which reminded her of melting snow. And she made me see that the deepest form of intimacy happens in the space between the words.
But despite the depth of our bond, she left, abruptly, as if she had never been there. She had fallen in love with another man. I was left behind, dazed and disoriented, and although my heart was broken, this kind of loss did not have a name that matched how shattered I felt. It was ‘just a breakup’, and it didn’t even deserve that name: we had been dating, but it never technically became a relationship. It was also a romantic connection that ran alongside another one, a long partnership that was open by mutual agreement and conscious design. Much about it wasn’t legible to most people around me. I faced the grief largely by myself. No scripts, no rituals, no recognised form, no legitimacy, no shared language, no way to make sense of what had happened to me.
Part of what made the experience so disorienting was a narrow idea of what grief is. In psychology, in philosophy and in our Western culture at large, grief has been treated almost exclusively as a response to the death of someone we love. It’s a neat, tidy understanding. The most celebrated grief memoirs – think of The Year of Magical Thinking (2005) by Joan Didion and A Grief Observed (1961) by C S Lewis – are concerned with the loss of a life partner. And Michael Cholbi’s Grief: A Philosophical Guide (2021) – one of the most extensive philosophical treatments of the emotion – focuses mostly on the grief we experience at the death of someone we love or who otherwise matters to us.
Restricting grief to bereavement is like restricting pain to cluster headaches
Death is visible and final: it has a body, a date, a medical certificate. The other losses are blurrier: they have no physical object, no clear beginning or end, no tangible proof they happened. We also have an infrastructure for death: funerals, condolence cards, flowers, casseroles, bereavement leave – a whole social script. Perhaps the infrastructure defines what counts: if there is no social and cultural scaffolding to digest the experience, it must not be real grief.
The prime reason for the single-minded focus on death loss, however, must be that bereavement is simply the most striking instance of a broader emotional phenomenon that comes in degrees. But restricting grief to bereavement is like restricting pain to cluster headaches, anxiety to panic attacks, sadness to depression, or pleasure to ecstasy – it is taking the most extreme instantiation of something and making it the essence of that thing.
If grief isn’t just about death, what is it about? What do all these cases of grief share? A good way to answer this question starts from the observation that every emotion has a characteristic thing it is about. Fear is about danger or threat; anger is about offence or injustice; happiness and joy are about flourishing or harmony between self and world. What is grief about? If you say ‘death’, you are doing something weird: you are defining the emotion by the particular thing that sets it off, rather than by what that thing means to us. In technical philosophical jargon, you are making the mistake of conflating an emotion’s material object with its formal object. Fear of sharks, fear of public speaking and fear of heights aren’t three different emotions – shark-fear, public-speaking-fear and heights-fear. All three count as fear because they are about danger: their aim is to tell you something is threatening.
Grief clearly has something to do with loss. Although this gets us somewhere, it doesn’t get us far enough. Mere loss is necessary but not sufficient. If I lose a pen or an old sweater, I am not experiencing any grief. If I have any emotional reaction at all, it will be a slight ripple of annoyance. Perhaps we should add that for there to be grief we must lose something we care about or love, but, again, this is necessary but not sufficient. If I lose a book I really like or don’t get a dream job I applied for, what I experience is frustration or disappointment, sadness perhaps, but not grief.
What sets grief apart is how deeply the loss reaches into the fabric of your life: grief begins where your identity is disrupted. What is lost in the case of grief is not just some concrete, historical object, but a cluster of (future) possibilities that are tightly woven into your sense of identity, life structure or experiential world. When they go, you don’t just lose something: you lose a version of yourself, your life is turned upside down, and you come to inhabit, in a real sense, a different world. This is why death is grief’s most extreme instance, rather than its only one. When someone we love dies, every possibility – not only our own possibilities with them, but their possibilities too – is wiped out. As Matthew Ratcliffe and Louise Richardson, academic philosophers at the University of York, put it in their paper ‘Grief Over Non-Death Losses: A Phenomenological Perspective’ (2023):
Grief is thus distinctive insofar as it involves recognising and comprehending the implications of lost possibilities for the structure of one’s life or world, and – over time – coming to reorganise one’s life accordingly.
This reorganisation is not merely cognitive. It lives in many other places: in the body (the hand that still reaches for the phone to text someone who no longer answers your messages), in how you experience your surroundings (the café you used to visit together that now feels alien or even hostile), or in your autobiographical memories (the shared joke that simply doesn’t land with other people).
‘I am grieving the future children I imagined and believed I would have but am unable to’
My mother is still alive. No one has died: there is no concrete, historical object that has been pulled beyond my grasp. But a whole set of possibilities that had been woven into the structure of my life and world, all bound up with having a mother who was present, responsive, good enough – those are gone. It has become impossible to call her and poke that mind of hers, so unusually free and unusually deep.
The same goes for my father. Sure, he survived the stroke. But the man whose restless mind needed to cycle to make his thoughts liquid – the future I had with that man, the shared cycling trips in the south of France, the conversations that needed repetitive, cyclical movement to come alive – that future was negated. The same structure holds for the woman whose disappearance collapsed an experiential world that felt like a home I had only just found, and for the academic identity I had built over almost two decades. As other vocations began to call more insistently, a single, all-consuming way of being in the world – the thinker, the life of the mind, the person whose future would be organised around reading and writing – loosened its hold.
The case that makes this way of thinking about grief most compelling, though, is one where there is no concrete object of loss at all. Ratcliffe and Richardson’s central example is involuntary childlessness – grief for a child who never was, a future that was imagined, anticipated and deeply woven into one’s sense of self, but that never materialised. Here, no one died and no one left. There is nothing tangible to point to: no grave, no anniversary, no recorded name, no memorial service, no shared practices to give words or meaning to the loss. And yet, as one respondent in their study put it: ‘No one can understand what it’s like to carry this loss. In their minds, no baby meant no loss.’ Another respondent simply called their grief by its name: ‘I am grieving the future children I imagined and believed I would have but am unable to.’ And a third spoke, chillingly, of ‘the death of a future life’.
They lack the interpretative resources to understand and share significant aspects of their experience
‘No baby meant no loss.’ Many forms of non-death loss are what the family therapist Pauline Boss calls ‘ambiguous loss’. These are losses without clear boundaries, without a definite beginning or end – cases where someone is physically present but psychologically gone, or physically gone but psychologically still there. Think of an Alzheimer’s patient whose self has been erased by the disease or of a soldier missing in action. Because many non-death losses are ambiguous, the grief that follows them is not openly acknowledged, socially validated or publicly mourned – what the grief scholar Kenneth Doka has called ‘disenfranchised grief’.
Those whose grief is disenfranchised because their losses are ambiguous don’t just lack scripts or rituals or traditions. They lack the interpretative resources to understand and share significant aspects of their experience. When we lack the concepts to name what it is like to be us, what it is we are going through, we suffer what the philosopher Miranda Fricker calls a ‘hermeneutical injustice’ – an inability to make our own experience intelligible to ourselves and to others. This is not because we are confused, but because the shared language or conceptual apparatus – the frameworks we use to make sense of ourselves – hasn’t caught up. As two of Ratcliffe and Richardson’s respondents put it: ‘It took me a while to understand that what I was feeling was grief’; ‘I never realised this was grief until I found others in a similar situation.’
The same happened to me: when the magical stranger disappeared, my loss was ambiguous – she still existed, we were never officially together, I had another partner – and my grief went into hiding. In a culture where the end of a relationship is ‘just a breakup’ and monogamy is the unspoken rule, I lacked the rituals to digest the grief and the hermeneutical resources to conceptualise and communicate what had happened to me. For ‘self-interpreting animals’ like us, in the words of the philosopher Charles Taylor, the result is that we end up in the dark, as strangers to ourselves.
The narrowing of grief to bereavement is more than a conceptual mistake. It does real damage. What the writer and grief counsellor Stephen Levine called ‘unattended sorrow’ doesn’t dissolve but goes underground, hiding in the shadows, later resurfacing as unexpected symptoms. I have been there. A mechanical tightness in the chest and a hard belly, like wearing a harness to brace against life. Harrowing dreams. Attempts to numb what is too painful to feel alone. And, worst of all, cynicism and a slow erosion of trust. Not just in other people, but in your own feelings, your own intuitions about the depth, sustainability and future of any new connection. When no one around you recognises your grief, you begin to wonder whether you were wrong to feel it at all.
Sigmund Freud understood this, though he read it as pathology. In the essay ‘Mourning and Melancholia’ (1917), he contended that grief is healthy and normal, but only if it is intelligible and bounded. The job of mourning, he argued, is to detach you from the lost object and reinvest your emotional energy elsewhere. If you can’t complete that job, if the loss is unclear or unnamed or ambiguous, you are no longer mourning. Instead, you are suffering from an illness called melancholia. For Freud, grief that cannot do its work calcifies into something darker, something more elusive.
If you deny someone the right to grieve, you deny them access to themselves
But the damage runs deeper than that. When we cannot grieve a loss, we lose something else along with it: the chance to register what mattered to us. Grief is how we come to know what we loved in the presence of its absence. Or as the psychotherapist and grief worker Francis Weller puts it in The Wild Edge of Sorrow (2015):
Grief and love are sisters, woven together from the beginning. Their kinship reminds us that there is no love that does not contain loss and no loss that is not a reminder of the love we carry for what we once held close.
Your grief tells you that you had the courage to love, that you allowed someone or something else to enter ‘the core of [your] being and find a home in [your] heart’. If you deny someone the right to grieve, you deny them access to what they loved and valued, which is to say that you deny them access to themselves. You don’t just rob them, then, of their love; you also rob them of self-knowledge.
The tradition I spent most of my life in – the lineage of Western thinkers who asked how a human being should live – was the first place I looked to understand what was happening to me. These thinkers had a lot to say about grief, but most of it was suspicious and sceptical. Plato believed a good man is the most self-sufficient of all, and least shaken by loss. In the Phaedo, Socrates’ wife Xanthippe is led away wailing before the philosophy can begin, and towards the end of the dialogue, Socrates rebukes his weeping friends for behaving like women. A similar sentiment can be found among the Stoics. Epictetus, in the Enchiridion, compares the loss of a wife or child to a jug breaking. And Marcus Aurelius, who lost many of his own children, reminds himself in his Meditations not to pray that he might keep his child, but to pray that he might not fear losing him.
Behind this way of thinking lies an expensive belief: that attachment is a liability, and that a wise person – someone who has figured out how to live the best possible life – does not need anything that can be taken away from him. If grief is love with nowhere to go, a tradition that treated such love as an error was never going to know what to do with it.
Christianity kept the verdict the ancients had arrived at. In his Confessions (397-400 CE), Saint Augustine looks back on his devastation after a friend’s death, and diagnoses it as a spiritual mistake: ‘Why had that grief penetrated me so easily and so deeply, if not because I had poured out my soul onto the sand, loving someone who would die as if he never would?’ Baruch Spinoza – not religious in any conventional sense of the word – reached the same conclusion. Sadness, he writes in his Ethics (1677), is the mind’s move to a lesser perfection, a loss of its power to act. This means it can never be a good in itself, and its typical source is too much love for things that are impermanent. The cure for grief – and this puts him squarely back into the ancient intellectualist tradition – is understanding: the moment it dawns on us that what we lost could never have been kept, our grief will relax.
The sense that part of oneself has been lost now appears in psychiatry’s most important manual as a mark of disorder
Arthur Schopenhauer, unlike many before him, did not despise grief. In The World as Will and Representation (1818), he values sorrow for one reason only: great personal suffering breaks the will and leads to self-renunciation (Selbstverneinung). Grief is worth having, then, because it has the power to cure us of wanting the world at all, which means that, in the end, he is not so far from the thinkers who came before him. A good life, for all of them, is a matter of loosening our attachments to what is impermanent and fragile.
What began as a doctrine of philosophers leaked into the wider culture. In his landmark study Death, Grief, and Mourning in Contemporary Britain (1965), the anthropologist Geoffrey Gorer found that mourning was increasingly seen as ‘a weakness, a self-indulgence, a reprehensible bad habit instead of as a psychological necessity’. In the 1970s, the historian Philippe Ariès traced the same shift across the industrial West: death, once familiar, had become shameful, something to be hidden. Meanwhile, medicine had entered the debate. In 1961, the psychiatrist George Engel asked, half provocatively, whether grief was a disease. In 2000, the philosopher Stephen Wilkinson answered: yes. In one of academic philosophy’s leading journals, he argued that even normal, healthy grief qualifies as a mental disorder because it meets the standard definition of one. Like all mental disorders, it involves significant distress and interrupts normal functioning. In 2013, the fifth edition of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders removed the clause that had excluded the recently bereaved from receiving a diagnosis of major depressive disorder. Then, in 2022, the revised edition added prolonged grief disorder, whose possible symptoms include identity disruption, such as the feeling that part of oneself has died. The sense that part of oneself has been lost now appears in psychiatry’s most important manual as a mark of disorder – though, tellingly, only when someone has actually died.
But the Western tradition had it backwards. Suppressing, eradicating, denying or pathologising grief doesn’t protect the good life; it sabotages human flourishing by cutting us off from the things we love. More than that, it cuts us off from each other. Grief named and disclosed is grief that can be met, grief that can be placed between you and another person, where the two of you can look at it and hold it together. That shared vulnerability lets one person recognise another in their common humanity. Grief, as Weller reminds us, was never meant to be carried alone; it was meant to be held and processed by a whole village. Strip it of its name and you strip people of the possibility of being seen in their loss, of discovering that the wound they thought was theirs alone is in fact shared by those around them.
Recently, while in the Netherlands, I visited the Kröller-Müller Museum with my father, the same father whose future was negated by a stroke. I looked at him from a distance, the man who once built his life around cycling – to France, to Rome, to Spain’s Santiago de Compostela – now hunched behind his rollator. We stood together in front of Vincent van Gogh’s painting At Eternity’s Gate (1890): an old man, face buried in his fists, clearly hurting. A sorrowful man, looking at a sorrowful man, looking at a sorrowful man painted by a sorrowful man. Years before he painted it, when he first drew the same figure for a lithograph, Van Gogh wrote that there can be an ‘unutterably moving’ quality, ‘something precious, something noble’, in the expression of an old man like that.
I didn’t know my father loved Van Gogh as much as I do. We stood there for a long time – somehow in contact with the magic of grief – and something opened up between us that had no name but felt important, exquisitely alive. We didn’t talk about my mother, or how our family had unravelled, or what the stroke had taken from him. We didn’t have to. The painting said what neither of us could.

Radev's "Care Basket" Initiative: Retail Markups and Cheese With 70% Water Are “Killing the Consumer”

Bulgaria Has EU’s Highest Road Death Rate
Bulgaria recorded the European Union’s highest road fatality rate in 2025, with 71 deaths per million inhabitants, according to final figures released by the European Commission
Cheese sold in Bulgaria with water content exceeding 65% and retail markups of up to 140% is raising concerns about food quality and pricing, according to Dimitar Zorov, chairman of the Association of Dairy Processors and the National Union of Cattle Breeders, and Bogomil Nikolov of the Active Consumers association.
An Active Consumers inspection of products offered under the “Care Basket” initiative found cheese with unusually high water content, in some cases reaching 70%.
Nikolov said the association began checking the products after noticing unusually low prices during the initiative’s first week. “In the very first week, we noticed prices that were suspiciously low. We thought this couldn't be right, so we took samples. It turned out that the low price came at the expense of water content,” he explained.
He said one way manufacturers increase the water content is by cutting the cheese’s maturation period short. “If the production process requires the cheese to mature for 45 days, but you bring it to market on the seventh day, it hasn't yet shed its excess water,” Nikolov said.
Zorov said the standards he cited put the normal water content of white brined cheese at around 54%. Comparing prices becomes misleading when a product contains 70% water, he argued, adding that such cheese does not provide the same nutritional value as properly produced and matured products.
He also attributed the deterioration in quality to pressure on producers to supply goods at ever-lower prices, while retail markups continue to increase.
“A key factor is the pressure on producers to lower their prices, while at the same time, retail markups are rising,” Zorov said during an appearance on bTV.
He noted that markups on some dairy products in Bulgaria range from 80% to 140%, considerably higher than those in other European countries.
“In Europe, we hear of markups around 25–30%. In Bulgaria, it’s 100-140%. What are we doing? We are killing the consumer,” Zorov said.
He argued that demands for lower wholesale prices could encourage the production of products that resemble cheese but do not meet expected quality standards. This also puts honest Bulgarian producers at a disadvantage when competing against cheaper goods with a different composition, he said.
Zorov called for limits on retail markups and wholesale margins, pointing to Greece, where measures restrict markups on certain products.
“It is not free market competition when you control over 80% of the retail trade, especially in large cities,” he said.
Nikolov cautioned that the problem was more complicated than the relationship between producers and retail chains alone. He called for the development of alternative sales channels, including farmers’ markets and direct sales from producers to consumers.
“The more we shift toward a single dominant form of retail, the worse it gets. We need to encourage other models to ensure greater competition,” Nikolov said.
He cited farmers’ markets in Greece as an example of a system in which consumers can buy goods directly from producers.
Nikolov also linked the problems in the sector to long-standing policies, including the way agricultural producers receive subsidies.
“Milk production has been steadily declining for decades. Vegetable production is falling, and fruit production is falling as well,” he said.
Bulgaria’s “Care Baske” initiative, launched in June 2026, is a government effort (the Radev Cainbet) encouraging major retail chains to voluntarily reduce prices on essential food and hygiene products, with a focus on Bulgarian-made goods. Participation reportedly grew from eight to 14 retail chains, but the scheme has faced criticism over its effectiveness and calls for stronger oversight. Rumen Radev’s role has been to defend the initiative’s approach in Parliament, arguing that voluntary commitments by supermarkets were not enough and should be backed by legislation, regulatory oversight and a centralized electronic food-price registry to identify unfair practices and unjustified price increases.

Leaders of Finland and Norway hold direct talks with Putin

Finnish President Alexander Stubb shakes hands with Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre in Oslo on Oct. 20, 2026. | Cornelius Poppe/NTB/AFP via Getty Images
Finland’s President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre held a joint call with Russian leader Vladimir Putin on Tuesday as part of international efforts to secure an end to the war in Ukraine.
“The discussion was frank and substantive,” said Stubb in a statement after the call. “We are neighboring countries to Russia. The outcome of this war will have a direct impact on our and the broader European security. Ending the war requires direct discussions.”
The conversation was held in consultation with Kyiv and the two leaders — who are firm allies of Ukraine — were not speaking as official representatives of Europe as a whole.

But the call comes at a delicate moment in the four-year-long war as European officials bid for a place at the negotiating table, with U.S. President Donald Trump pushing for a peace deal. Two EU officials said the President of the European Council, António Costa, had been told of the planned call in advance.
Støre said the two European leaders stressed the importance of de-escalation in the call with Putin. “The war comes with enormous human and material costs. The suffering and destruction will impact generations,” he added.
Stubb’s office described the call as a follow-up to talks in Oslo on Oct. 20, in which the two European leaders were joined by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff, who then traveled to meet Putin in Russia the following day.
The Kremlin issued a dry statement simply confirming that “the sides exchanged views on the resolution of the Ukrainian crisis,” and that settling the conflict was the main topic of Tuesday’s call. The statement added that the outcome of Putin’s talks with Witkoff was also taken into account, according to Russia’s state-owned TASS news agency.
Stubb and Støre are close friends and speak frequently, and they were together in Helsinki for the conversation with Putin. According to a statement from the Finnish president’s office, the two leaders wanted to tell the Russian leader directly that they would continue supporting Ukraine and that peace negotiations must resume, looking ahead to the planned meetings in Abu Dhabi.
Advertisement
They also told the Russian leader that they had a shared interest in the stability of the Baltic Sea region and the High North.
Stubb and Støre briefed Zelenskyy after the call. “I am grateful for the detailed briefing and for their active support for our diplomacy and the peace efforts we are pursuing together with all our partners,” the Ukrainian president said in a post on X. “Alex and Jonas made it clear to the Russian leader that real de-escalatory steps are needed regarding our energy and infrastructure.”
“We discussed preparations for the trilateral meeting planned for November at the team level — Ukrainian, American, and Russian,” Zelenskyy said. “Finland and Norway, as countries that border Russia, have a particular interest in sound and reliable security arrangements. We also discussed various formats for our engagement with partners in Europe that could be useful in further supporting diplomacy, our defense, and our shared security.”
Not everyone was impressed with Stubb and Støre’s move. Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said she was “very skeptical” about the initiative. European countries had not been involved in coordinating the call, she said, adding: “I believe we should keep Europe united rather than going it alone.”
Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson said peace must come through “strength” rather than “appeasement” of Russia, and if the talks lead to this then they will be welcome. But previous attempts to talk to Putin have not delivered progress and there are no signs he wants a truce, Kristersson added.
Paula Pinho, spokesperson for the European Commission, said: “We take note of the call, which took place solely on a bilateral basis, and is a follow-up of the meeting in Oslo.” The EU side is “united in our commitment not only to put an end to this horrific war but to achieve peace that will be just and sustainable,” she said.
Advertisement
“That is our aim and that is the stance we are defending in the ongoing talks. These negotiations are happening in different formats, different places and different levels involving heads of states and government, ministers, senior diplomats and officials. The EU is involved.”
The last staunch European supporter of Ukraine to speak to Putin at leader level is believed to have been French President Emmanuel Macron in July 2025. Some EU leaders like Slovakia’s Prime Minister Robert Fico and former Hungarian premier Viktor Orban have maintained semi-regular contact with the Russian president in recent years, despite the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
EU diplomats and officials have been considering how to ensure Ukraine’s allies in Europe can play a meaningful part in negotiations on a ceasefire and longer term peace agreement. Stubb’s name emerged as one of the potential leaders who could take on the job of representing Europe and bolstering Ukraine in face-to-face talks with Trump and Putin.
He is one of the few EU leaders and Ukraine backers who has maintained a healthy relationship with Trump at a time of strained relations across the Atlantic. Finland also shares a 1,300 kilometer border with Russia, meaning Stubb and his officials already have valuable experience of dealing with a threatening and unpredictable neighbor.

Taiwan power semiconductor makers target AI data center upgrades
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:59:09 UTC
18:59:09 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The shift toward higher-voltage power systems in AI data centers is creating opportunities for Taiwanese power semiconductor makers as rising electricity needs drive infrastructure upgrades, CTEE reported Tuesday.
AI server racks are drawing increasingly large amounts of electricity, with power requirements climbing from tens of kilowatts toward megawatt-scale levels. Conventional 48-volt and 54-volt systems are approaching their limits, prompting the industry to explore higher-voltage architectures such as 800-volt direct current (800VDC), according to Business Today.
This transition is reshaping the market for power semiconductors. These specialized devices regulate electricity, convert power between voltage levels, and protect equipment against electrical faults, according to Sinotrade.
Panjit International Inc. is positioning its rectifiers and power metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistors (MOSFETs) to meet evolving requirements. Rectifiers convert alternating current (AC) into direct current (DC), while MOSFETs act as electronic switches that control the flow of electricity, according to Sinotrade.
Panjit's bridge rectifiers feature low forward voltage drops, helping reduce energy losses in AI and cloud servers. Its superjunction MOSFETs are designed to improve power conversion efficiency.
Taiwan Semiconductor Co. offers rectifier diodes, MOSFETs, and circuit protection components for data center power systems. While the shift to 800VDC increases distribution voltage, power still needs to be converted to lower voltages for servers and individual components, supporting demand for products used in these conversion stages alongside devices built to handle higher voltages.
Eris Technology Corp. sees additional opportunities in circuit protection as data centers adopt higher-voltage power systems. The company focuses on transient voltage suppressors, which protect electronic equipment against sudden voltage spikes, as well as MOSFET packaging.
The company said the shift toward high-voltage DC power in AI servers will increase demand for upgraded protection components. It is developing products with higher voltage ratings to meet these requirements.
Meanwhile, rising production costs and pricing adjustments by international manufacturers such as Onsemi are prompting domestic suppliers to consider price increases. Higher costs for wafers, lead frames, and packaging materials are adding to the pressure.
Supply chain sources said some manufacturers plan to raise prices for products not covered by existing contracts in the fourth quarter.
In conventional data centers, electricity is distributed as AC before being converted to lower-voltage DC at server racks. The 800VDC architecture distributes higher-voltage DC power closer to the servers, reducing the number of conversion stages and the current needed to deliver the same amount of power.
This helps reduce energy losses and improve overall efficiency, according to Sinotrade.

The poll used computer-assisted telephone interviews, including 696 landline and 379 mobile phone respondents, according to Mirror Daily. The margin of sampling error was plus or minus 3 percentage points at a 95% confidence level, and results were weighted by gender, registered county or city, age, and education.

Western media pushing anti-Russian propaganda in Africa – expert
Western media outlets are increasingly spreading anti-Russian narratives in Africa, Mayya Nikolskaya has told RT.
Speaking ahead of the third Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow, head of a research program at the Institute for International Studies at Russia’s MGIMO University, pointed to CNN, BBC, RFI and France 24 as examples of Western broadcasters whose coverage has shifted away from development initiatives toward criticism of Moscow.
“They [Western media] used to focus more on development projects, now they’re talking mostly just about how Russia is bad,” she said, suggesting that this creates opportunities for Russian media to offer alternative perspectives.
Nikolskaya also criticized France’s approach to Africa, arguing that Paris had become an increasingly unpopular partner in African states.
“There is a far-reaching consensus in the policy advice circles that Paris is currently very toxic, quote-unquote,” she noted.
According to the expert, former colonial powers must rethink their relations with Africa and consider “not just what they can take from Africa but also what they can give it.” She added that African nations now have greater freedom to choose international partners, including Russia and China, based on their own priorities.
Nikolskaya made the remarks during the Russia-Africa Media Forum, which opened in Moscow on Monday. Organized by RT in cooperation with Sputnik and TASS, the event brought together more than 200 media professionals and experts from 46 African countries to discuss media cooperation and Africa’s representation in international news coverage.
The forum comes ahead of the third Russia-Africa Summit, scheduled for October 28-29 in Moscow. Russian President Vladimir Putin is expected to co-chair the plenary session with Burundian President Evariste Ndayishimiye, the current African Union chair.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Taichung Water Resource Bureau said Monday that it is using satellite images, drones, and ground patrols to crack down on unauthorized slopeland development.

From Baku’s waterfront to the Greater Caucasus: a new winter destination within reach
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:58:13 UTC
18:58:13 KST

Modern ski resorts, competitive prices and a growing calendar of international competitions are putting Azerbaijan’s mountains on the winter tourism map.
Baku is the lowest-lying capital city in the world. Yet a few hours’ drive from its Caspian Sea waterfront, the Greater Caucasus mountains offer a very different landscape, with modern ski resorts set among the peaks. “Very few people know that Azerbaijan actually has mountains,” says Florian Sengstschmid, CEO of the Azerbaijan Tourism Board. “This is where the conversation starts.”
At the London Snow Show, where Azerbaijan exhibited for the first time, Sengstschmid says visitors were repeatedly surprised to discover the country had mountains. The challenge now is to turn that surprise into interest in what Azerbaijan offers in winter, both on and off the slopes.
A compact country with a wide range of experiences
Azerbaijan’s geography allows visitors to experience strikingly different landscapes within a relatively short journey. Sengstschmid describes it as “a compact and remarkably diverse country where Europe meets Asia”, with terrain ranging from high mountain peaks to subtropical landscapes.
“You can ski in the morning and have lunch in Baku,” Sengstschmid says. “You crisscross the country from subtropics to the high mountain peaks within a few hours’ driving.”
A winter trip can also take in a traditional hammam, a spa visit or dinner in a mountain village, where fresh-caught trout features on the menu. Khinalig, close to Shahdag, is one such village. Further afield, visitors can explore UNESCO World Heritage sites such as the Walled City of Baku, the Gobustan rock art landscape and the historic centre of Shaki, as well as natural fire temples, ice caves and waterfalls. Wine and food routes offer another way to discover the country, alongside its Silk Road heritage.
Modern resorts at competitive prices
Two of Azerbaijan’s resorts, Shahdag and Tufandag have invested in modern ski infrastructure, including Austrian technology. Sengstschmid, himself Austrian, says he is proud to see it in place. Snowmaking at both resorts uses less water than it once did, while accommodation ranges from guesthouses to five-star hotels. Sengstschmid also highlights the après-ski scene as another attraction.
“It is exciting to see what technology can do,” Sengstschmid says, “but it’s also our responsibility to ensure future generations can enjoy the mountains as much as we have.”
Price is another draw. A day’s ski pass costs around £25, a two-hour private lesson £50, a beer £3 and lunch £10. For British and European skiers facing rising costs in the Alps, those numbers stand out.
Sandra Spitz, Sports and Events Director at the International Ski and Snowboard Federation (FIS), has visited Shahdag herself. She describes the skiing as “very nice, smooth”, with “really space on the slopes”. She also praises the resort’s setting and its appeal to families, describing it as “not too expensive” and “incredible, beautiful”.
For Sengstschmid, one of the biggest advantages is the space on the slopes. “You have no crowds, you have no queues, and you just enjoy the sound of the snow.”
Building a winter sports culture
Azerbaijan has been affiliated with FIS since the 1990s. Its more recent five-year partnership with the organisation goes beyond hosting competitions, focusing on developing local talent, training coaches and creating pathways into professional winter sports.
Skiing and snowboarding are still relatively new sports in Azerbaijan. Sengstschmid wants young people to see a future in them, whether as athletes, coaches or in other roles across the industry.
This season, Azerbaijan hosts the FIS Alpine European Cup in February, followed by the FIS Freestyle World Cup finals from 5 to 7 March. The country has also built national teams in ski mountaineering with the International Ski Mountaineering Federation (ISMF), a discipline that made its Olympic debut at Milano Cortina earlier this year.
For FIS, the opportunity lies in bringing more people into the sport. “Azerbaijan is very important for us,” Spitz says. “It’s an emerging market in skiing and snowboarding, and this is the playground where we can actually get new skiers loving skiing and snowboarding.”
Shahdag also provides equipment free of charge to children in its clubs, a model Spitz holds up as an example of how resorts can encourage participation.
Azerbaijan already has experience hosting international sporting events. Baku marked ten years of Formula 1 in September, and Sengstschmid says F1 “put Baku and Azerbaijan on the map of sports”. The FIS partnership aims to do the same for winter sports.
A destination beyond the ski season
Summer accounts for around half of the resorts’ visitors, according to Sengstschmid. Hiking, trail running, multi-day treks, birdwatching in Shahdag National Park, horse riding and mountain coasters attract visitors during the warmer months. A longer season can also help resorts maintain employment and support businesses in nearby communities beyond winter.
Sengstschmid makes a wider case for visiting lesser-known places. He points to figures suggesting that 80% of travellers visit just 10% of destinations, arguing that the Caucasus could help spread tourism beyond the busiest hotspots.
Spitz says she would not have known four years ago that you could ski in Azerbaijan. “But now I know it,” she says, “and every single destination is worth a visit.”
For Sengstschmid, Azerbaijan’s appeal extends well beyond the ski season. Wine, food, industrial heritage and the Silk Road offer reasons to explore the country beyond its mountains. But for visitors discovering Azerbaijan for the first time, the slopes may be the starting point.

18:56:58 KST

LONDON, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Two men appeared in a London court on Tuesday charged under Britain’s National Security Act following last month’s security incident at the RAF Fairford military base, with prosecutors alleging one tried to assist Iranian intelligence in Britain.
RAF Fairford had been used by US bombers to carry out strikes on Iran, but they were withdrawn on security grounds shortly after five British men were arrested outside the base in southwest England in the early hours of September 27.
The circumstances of the incident, which remain largely unexplained, attracted huge international attention, coming at a time of heightened concern about the security implications for Western states of the war between the United States and Iran.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said earlier this month that the activity at RAF Fairford was likely to have been coordinated in Iran, which Tehran’s ambassador to Britain has denied.
British national Mohmed Abdulkarim, 24, was charged with engaging in conduct that was likely to materially assist a foreign intelligence service between August 31 and September 28.
Abdulkarim appeared at Westminster Magistrates’ Court alongside Nouman Essghir, a 24-year-old dual British-Iranian national who was first arrested outside RAF Fairford on September 27 and is charged with entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK on August 22.
SUSPECT CALLED POLICE
Prosecutors said Abdulkarim, who was in a wheelchair in court, arranged for five men to take three vans and drive to RAF Fairford at the behest of a man called “Ali”.
The five men bought around £300 ($400) worth of petrol, which was stored in drums, prosecutor Louise Gray said.
“One of them was told there was a bomb in the van … (and) one of them called 999,” Gray added, with police arriving shortly after.
Gray said Essghir had conducted reconnaissance of the base on instructions from “Ali” in August, adding that he was also in one of the vans which drove to RAF Fairford the following month.
After the five men were told there was a bomb, Gray said Essghir sent a message to “Ali” asking “wtf (what the fuck) is going on” but received no reply.
Abdulkarim was granted bail ahead of his next court appearance in November. Essghir has been remanded in custody.
Police said that six other people, four of whom are British nationals who were arrested outside RAF Fairford on September 27, remain on police bail.
The decision to bail suspects after an apparent major incident had drawn scrutiny, but on Tuesday police said that decision had helped secure charges against the two men.

The backlash highlighted the risks for athletes and brands in the lucrative China market, where satire about Mao, modern China’s founding leader who ruled the country from 1949 until his death in 1976, remains a social taboo.
LaLiga President Javier Tebas said that he held a meeting with the ambassador of China in Spain to address the situation and “seek solutions that allow us to overcome this episode.”
“Our commitment is to keep working together so that an individual episode does not harm the important advances achieved nor affect the millions of Chinese fans who follow our competitions,” Tebas said in a statement posted to social media. “China is and will continue to be a strategic partner for LaLiga.”
Other major organisations that have incurred the wrath of Beijing and Chinese netizens include fashion brand Dolce & Gabbana, Swiss watchmaker Swatch and the National Basketball Association.
Some recovered quickly while others took years.
CHINA STATE TV HALTS BROADCASTS
Brands including dairy companies Mengniu and Shanghai Milkground Food Tech as well as Eastroc Beverage said they were ceasing all cooperation with Mbappe effective immediately.
The companies said they “firmly oppose and have zero tolerance for any words or actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people.”
China’s state television has halted broadcasts of all matches and events involving LaLiga and Mbappe, and all advertisements involving Mbappe have been removed, state-backed media outlet the Paper reported on Tuesday.
“Mbappe’s team knew, or should have known, what the true cost of Chinese brand endorsements was all about,” said Terrence Burns, sports sponsorship expert and CEO of the T. Burns Sports Group.
Swiss-based On Holding, which signed Mbappe in September after he had spent two decades at US rival Nike, welcomed his apology and said it had “deep respect” for China.
Accor did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Denmark’s Lego, which has a Mbappe building set on sale in China, said it could not comment. The Mbappe set still featured on Lego’s Chinese website on Tuesday.
‘WHAT DID HE SAY?’
Chinese state media outlet China Daily said Mbappe’s remark had “triggered a backlash among his Chinese fans, threatened his lucrative commercial relationships and offered a sharp reminder of the limits of celebrity influence”.
“What did he say? Many Chinese would rather not repeat it,” the state-backed Global Times added. “The message from Chinese consumers is clear: Respect is not optional; one doesn’t get to profit from China while disrespecting it. Not a chance.”
On Chinese social media platform Weibo, one user wrote about the apology; “Not accepted. Not forgiven!!”.
State broadcaster CCTV struck a more conciliatory tone, however, saying it would listen to what Mbappe had to say after his apology, and “even more importantly” watch what he does.
“We hope La Liga, Real Madrid, and Mbappe himself will genuinely learn a lesson from this, offer a sincere apology, and thoroughly correct their mistakes,” CCTV said in a statement.
Real Madrid declined to comment.
Tebas issued an apology earlier on Tuesday on X and said his organisation deeply regretted the alleged comments that have caused discomfort and offence in China.
“We are taking the measures within our reach and working directly with our partners and interlocutors in China to overcome this situation,” Tebas wrote. “A relationship built over so many years cannot be damaged by a single episode.”
TRENDING ON WEIBO
As of 0700 GMT, four topics related to Mbappe were still among the top 10 trending searches on Weibo. Some netizens called for China to blacklist Mbappe and reduce his commercial value to zero. These comments received hundreds of likes.
Fans have been creating memes superimposing Mbappe’s face on images of military and political leaders to suggest that he has the power to influence decisions at the teams he plays for.
Mbappe has been nicknamed “the dictator” in the European press.
“In attempting to laugh at himself and his reputation of being a dictator in the locker room, he apparently crossed a red line he didn’t know was there,” said Brian Jacobsen, chief economic strategist at Annex Wealth Management.
In an interview with L’Equipe last month, Mbappe said that although aspects of the meme trend were harmless fun, the viral ones depicting him as a dictator showed “a lack of political and human awareness”.
A spokesperson for China’s Foreign Ministry said words and actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people “will naturally be met with joint opposition from all sectors of Chinese society”.

Open, check, store: What changes once a packaged food is opened
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:56:42 UTC
18:56:42 KST

That satisfying pop of a jar lid, the snap of a foil seal, or the smooth peel of a fresh film, we’ve all experienced it. It’s that reassuring moment that says, 
“
This food is fresh, untouched, and safe.”
But here’s the catch: the moment you break that seal, the safety bubble vanishes. While modern food packaging uses clever barrier technology and vacuum sealing to keep food pristine on store shelves, it isn’t bulletproof once opened. Opening a package starts the countdown, shifting the responsibility of keeping food safe straight into your hands.
What the numbers tell us about food safety at home
Improper post-opening handling isn't just a minor oversight. It's a major driver of global food waste and foodborne illness:
- 60% of global food waste happens at home: According to the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) Food Waste Index Report [1] , households account for over 60% of all food wasted worldwide, equivalent to over 600 million tonnes of food per year. Misinterpreting date labels and letting opened food spoil prematurely are two primary drivers.
- 1 in 10 people fall ill annually: Estimates from the World Health Organization (WHO) [2] highlight that roughly 1 in 10 people worldwide fall ill every year from consuming contaminated food. A common contributor in domestic kitchens is improper temperature control and cross-contamination after packages are unsealed.
- The ‘best before’ confusion: Data from the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) shows that 30% to 40% of the food supply is lost or wasted [3] . A significant portion stems from consumer confusion surrounding unopened "Best Before" dates versus actual post-opening shelf life.
What happens when you break the seal?
Inside an unopened package, food lives in a controlled environment. Once the package is opened, that protection is broken, and three key changes can begin to occur:
- Air enters (oxidation): Oxygen in the air reacts with fats, oil and certain vitamins. Overtime, this can cause food to become rancid, colours to fade and flavours lose their punch.
- Moisture changes: Dry foods, such as chips or cookies, can absorb moisture from the air and lose their crispness. Other foods may lose moisture and gradually become dry or stale.
- Microorganisms are introduced: Mold spores, yeasts, and bacteria naturally present in the environment can come into contact with the food. Given the right conditions, these microorganisms may grow and contribute to spoilage. 
The simple open-check-store checklist
Keeping food fresh after opening doesn't require complex science. It only requires just a few quick habits:
Quick hacks for common kitchen staples
- Sauces & dips: Some condiments, such as ketchup, can remain shelf-stable until opened, but mayonnaise, pesto, and cream-based dressings belong in the fridge the second they are opened. Always check the label for storage instructions.
- Canned goods: Have leftover tomatoes, beans or other canned foods? Never leave them in an open metal can in the fridge. Transfer them into a clean glass or food-grade plastic container before refrigerating. This helps preserve quality and prevents unwanted flavour changes.
- Dairy & milk: Store opened milk and dairy products on the inner shelf of the refrigerator where temperatures are more consistent. Avoid storing them on the door shelves which experience greater temperature fluctuation.
- Grains & spices: Store spices, flour, rice and cereals into sealed glass jars to keep pantry pests and humidity away.
Packaging helps keep food safe and fresh until it reaches your kitchen, but proper handling after opening is just as important. Paying attention to storage instructions, resealing products carefully and maintaining good kitchen hygiene, ensures every bite stays as fresh and safe as it should.

HSL raises ticket prices and introduces a fare cap for contactless payments
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:56:37 EET
18:56:37 KST

Helsinki Regional Transport (HSL) is introducing a price cap for contactless payments. The change is meant to make it easier for passengers to choose between a single ticket and a day ticket. The change takes effect on Monday, 2 November.
The cap is calculated starting from the first ticket purchase. The system then adds up the prices of all tickets bought with the same payment method.
However, HSL notes that a physical payment card and mobile payments linked to the same card are treated as different payment methods.
Once the combined total reaches the price of a day ticket, no further charges are made for additional journeys.
The fare cap depends on the zones you travel in during the 24 hours. A two-zone 24-hour ticket is €10.60.
In a press release, HSL said the cap means passengers no longer have to estimate how many trips they will make during the day.
The fare cap applies only to adult single tickets paid with contactless payment — it doesn't cover tickets bought through the HSL app or with an HSL card.
Fares rise
The HSL board meanwhile decided on Tuesday to raise ticket prices by an average of 1.8 percent at the beginning of 2027. In the most popular AB zone, the price of an adult single ticket will go up by 1.5 percent, from €3.30 to €3.35.
Children's single tickets and single tickets in the 50 percent discount group will stay the same in all zones.

Swiss bankruptcies set to reach record levels in 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:56:00 UTC
18:56:00 KST

Swiss bankruptcies set to reach record levels in 2026
Economic concerns, high energy costs and rising interest rates are taking their toll on businesses. This is leading to a rise in corporate insolvencies worldwide.
In Switzerland, bankruptcies are even likely to reach a record high, as a study by Allianz Trade shows. The new Swiss insolvency law is also contributing to this.
Allianz Trade’s experts expect the sixth consecutive rise in Swiss corporate insolvencies in 2026. With 15,000 cases, this would mark an all-time high. This would represent a doubling compared with 2022, and even a tripling compared with pre-pandemic levels. These findings are set out in the Insolvency Report published on Tuesday by the trade credit insurer.
However, this “unprecedented” wave of insolvencies can only be partly attributed to the macroeconomic and financial challenges facing companies. “The new insolvency law, which has been in force since 2025, is largely responsible for the high number,” said Jan Möllmann, head of Allianz Trade in Switzerland, according to the press release.
More
Bankrupt debtors to get second chance in Switzerland
Möllmann went on to say that the insolvency law automatically leads to an increase in the number of companies against which insolvency proceedings are initiated. “We currently expect the situation to stabilise at this new, high level in 2027 and 2028.”
According to the study, corporate insolvencies worldwide are likely to rise by 5% in 2026 and by a further 1% in 2027, having already risen by 6% in 2025. Due to the persistently uncertain geopolitical and macroeconomic environment, the expected peak in insolvencies is shifting by one year to 2028. After that, the number of corporate insolvencies is likely to fall slightly.

Pärnu property prices unaffected by Rail Baltic delay

Unknown Publisher

Pärnu property prices unaffected by Rail Baltic delay
Real estate agents have said the postponement of the Rail Baltic deadline until 2032 is still too recent to be reflected immediately in Pärnu's real estate market. Projects already underway are continuing as planned.
This is not the first time that the completion deadline has been pushed back, and entrepreneurs and residents hope they will be able to travel on the track from Tallinn to the summer capital Pärnu by 2032.
Ingmar Saksing, a real estate agent at LVM Kinnisvara, said investors have factored this into their plans.
"Today we can talk about growing interest in the area where a terminal will be built, as in Ülemiste in Tallinn. Following the same logic, it is clear that property prices in this area and interest in the area are higher than before," he said.
The Part spa hotel will be completed by next autumn, adding 450 hotel beds to Pärnu. Sari Sopanen, head of the major development project, said the railway delay has not changed the hotel's development plans, but the completion of Rail Baltic would certainly help increase the number of customers.
"If Pärnu were connected to two international airports, Tallinn and Riga, then of course that would be a very, very big advantage for our industry and for us as well," Sopanen said.
"We believe in Pärnu, our location is ideal, it is a very good spot on Pärnu beach," she added.
Property prices in the summer capital have been steadily rising by two to three percent annually over the past decade, including inflation. The delay in Rail Baltic's completion has not caused any major jumps in prices, in either direction.
"People consider other reasons much more when deciding to change their place of residence, plus the fact that the arrival of the railway in Pärnu does not mean that everyone will want to move to Pärnu. Perhaps they will just come during the day and travel back home in the evening," said Terje Võrk, a real estate agent at Arco Vara.
In recent years, new real estate developments have sprung up in several parts of the city. Saksing said this is welcome, because when supply emerges, demand will follow.
"In total, 400 apartments are under construction and on offer, and at the current pace it will take up to two years to sell them, assuming no more are added," Saksing said.

Privacy group files complaints against Scale AI over alleged worker surveillance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:56:00 UTC
18:56:00 KST

Privacy group files complaints against Scale AI over alleged worker surveillance
- Privacy group noyb filed five complaints against Scale AI in four EU countries over alleged illegal worker surveillance on Outlier, a platform used to create AI training data.
- The complaints say up to 19 trackers recorded keystrokes and mouse movements, and workers faced repeated ID and face checks that may break EU biometric rules.
- noyb wants fines and a review of task assignment. DiPLab also found bonuses and game-like rewards pushed workers to complete many tasks fast.
AI generated
European digital privacy advocacy group NOYB filed five complaints against Scale AI in France, Italy, the Netherlands and Austria on Oct 27, alleging it illegally monitored freelance workers who produce training data for artificial intelligence models.
The complaints target Outlier, a platform it operates on which more than 900,000 freelancers perform various tasks that are recorded to create AI training data for clients such as Meta, OpenAI and Google. Meta owns 49% of Scale AI.
NOYB is asking regulators to fine Scale AI and examine how the platform assigns tasks.
“You don’t work when you want,” said Thomas Le Bonniec, who spent two years studying the platform for Paris-based research collective DiPLab. “You work when the platform wants you to and there are tasks available.”
Scale AI did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The complaints seen by Reuters said up to 19 trackers follow workers while they work, including recording keystrokes and mouse movements every few seconds. An investigation by DiPLab found the resulting file could be rebuilt into a video that replays a work session from start to finish.
Workers must also submit identification documents and face video to identity verification firm Persona. The complaints said the checks were invasive, repeated without explanation, and broke European Union rules on biometric data.
Outlier also uses game-like mechanisms, and bonuses are a key part of its incentive system, DiPLab found.
Outlier offered bonuses of US$100 (S$128) to US$200 for completing 200 tasks in 24 hours, Le Bonniec said, citing interviews with workers during his investigation. Italy’s data protection authority fined delivery platform Glovo in 2021 over similar gamification, he added.
Four workers asked Outlier for copies of their data between December 2025 and May 2026. None received an answer, the complaints said. REUTERS

Jordan says it killed more than 20 Islamic State militants in airstrikes on Syria

Unknown Publisher

Jordan says it killed more than 20 Islamic State militants in airstrikes on Syria
Oct 27 - Jordan said on Tuesday its forces had killed more than 20 Islamic State militants in airstrikes on southern Syria the previous evening, following a deadly church attack in Jordan that authorities linked to militants operating across the border.
The strikes, which followed a rare attack in Jordan, have inflamed tensions between the two US allies.
Jordan has been a longtime partner to the US in its fight against extremism, while the Islamist-led government of Syria's President Ahmed al-Sharaa, who wants to restore the country's relations with the West after overthrowing longtime ruler Bashar al-Assad in 2024, said it was seeking to curb extremism.
Syria said the strikes killed seven people, including three children and a woman. Jordan regrets the civilian casualties, Government Communication Minister Mohammed al-Momani said in a post on X.
Jordan said on Monday its air force had struck what it described as militant hideouts in southern Syria after determining that the suspects behind last week's church attack were linked to "terrorist groups" based there. Jordanian security officials said separately that security forces had arrested two brothers and their brother-in-law following a shootout linked to the church attack, which killed nine people.
Local resident Salah Mahwash, speaking to Reuters during the funeral of four people including three children in Al-Mismiyah in southern Syria, said:
“At around 10 p.m., there was an explosion and the sound of aircraft overhead. We went to the site, and it was a poor family whose father had gone missing during the events and was in Sednaya prison.
"Today, as you can see, these are people just trying to make a living, tending to their sheep and goats and doing manual labour. We condemn what happened in the Jordanian state, of course.”
Attacks such as the church shooting are rare in Jordan, a relatively stable US ally in the Middle East. No group has claimed responsibility for the shooting, although Jordan said the militants it targeted in Syria were members of Islamic State.
Monday's strikes have nevertheless sparked anger in Syria. While the Jordanian military said they were conducted in coordination with Damascus, Syria's government said they were carried out without prior coordination. It also said it would hold an investigation.
Statements in recent days by Jordanian authorities that there appeared to have been no prior planning of the church attack have added to the confusion, seemingly at odds with Jordan's justification for Monday's cross-border strikes.
Syria's Foreign Ministry condemned the strikes as a violation of the country's sovereignty.
It said, however, that Damascus was coordinating with Amman and would establish a joint security committee to strengthen border security and prevent similar incidents.
Last year, Jordan and Syria agreed to form such a committee to secure their border, combat arms and drug smuggling and work to prevent any resurgence of Islamic State militancy. REUTERS

Nord Stream Trial Resumes as Prosecutor Challenges Defense Bid to Halt Proceedings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:54:55 UTC
18:54:55 KST

The Nord Stream sabotage trial resumed in Hamburg on Tuesday, with the court rejecting a defence bid to halt proceedings. The judges ruled that Ukrainian military secrecy obligations did not, in themselves, prevent Serhii Kuznetsov from receiving a fair trial.
The dispute dominated the second day of proceedings against the Ukrainian former military officer, who is accused of helping organise the September 2022 operation that damaged three of the four Nord Stream pipeline strings beneath the Baltic Sea.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The defence supported its position with a sworn statement from Kuznetsov’s superior confirming that he was bound by secrecy obligations. The court nevertheless held that restrictions arising from those obligations did not, in themselves, bar his prosecution in Germany. It also noted that Kuznetsov had not sought an exemption allowing him to disclose protected information.
                                                                                                                                                                         Serhii Kuznetsov (center) with his German lawyers Lars Brögeler (left) and Jes Meyer-Lohkamp (right) at the Nord Stream sabotage trial in Hamburg, Germany, on Oct. 27, 2026. (Photo by Korbinian Leo Kramer / Kyiv Post)                             
Federal prosecutor Stefan Schmidt had urged the judges to reject the defence’s interpretation of the European Convention on Human Rights. Its protections, he argued, could not be understood to allow a state to prevent a prosecution simply by withholding permission for a defendant to disclose information covered by secrecy obligations.
US Reportedly Proposes Nord Stream Revival in Ukraine Peace Talks
The court also said it would seek improvements to Kuznetsov’s detention conditions. Proceedings were continuing at the time of writing.
At the trial’s opening on Oct. 14, Kuznetsov’s lawyers sought to have the proceedings discontinued, arguing that his obligations under Ukrainian military secrecy rules left him unable to answer the allegations and mount an effective defence. They also disputed the evidence of his alleged leadership role and challenged the prosecution’s characterisation of the pipelines as civilian infrastructure.
Kuznetsov faces charges including causing an explosion, destroying structures, disrupting public services and committing a war crime involving an attack on civilian objects. He denies involvement.
His lawyers argue that Nord Stream served Russian military and strategic interests, raising a question that extends beyond reconstructing the sabotage itself: how should the pipelines be classified under the laws of war?
The prosecution alleges that the operation was carried out on behalf of Ukrainian state authorities. Ukraine has denied responsibility for the attacks.
                                                                                                                                                                         Serhii Kuznetsov at the Nord Stream sabotage trial in Hamburg, Germany, on Oct. 27, 2026. (Photo by Korbinian Leo Kramer / Kyiv Post)                             
Tuesday’s ruling allows the trial to proceed despite the defence’s contention that Kuznetsov remains unable to speak freely about information relevant to his case.
The case leaves several central issues to be resolved:
- What evidence establishes Kuznetsov’s individual role in the alleged operation?
- Were the pipelines civilian objects or a lawful military target?
- Can the defence obtain the information and authorisations it says it needs from Ukraine?
The ruling leaves Kuznetsov’s lawyers facing the difficulty at the heart of their application: how to answer the prosecution’s allegations when, they say, their client cannot discuss the information needed to challenge them. The court has declined to treat that constraint as grounds to halt the trial.
In August, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk criticized the trial.
“I will not change my mind here, and I believe that those who built this pipeline should be ashamed, not those who disabled it,” he said.
The Nord Stream pipeline, which carries natural gas from Russia to Germany, was first negotiated in the 1990s, with agreements signed in the 2000s by Russian President Vladimir Putin and then-German Chancellor Gerhard Schröder.
The first Nord Stream pipeline was completed in 2011, while Nord Stream 2 was built a decade later. After leaving office, Schröder, with close ties to Putin, soon joined the board of the Russian state-owned oil conglomerate that negotiated the pipeline.
In mid-October, Washington reportedly talked with Moscow about restarting the pipeline as part of the peace negotiations.

US President Donald Trump has offered a $1 million reward for reporting voter fraud in past elections or the upcoming November 3 midterms, provided the tip leads to an arrest and conviction.
Trump announced the offer on Truth Social on Monday, repeating it to reporters ahead of a rally in Corinth, Mississippi.
“Anybody reporting Voter Fraud in the past Elections, or the upcoming 2026 Midterm Election, will be paid $1,000,000 upon the arrest and conviction of those that created the Fraud!” he wrote.

Trump has long alleged widespread election fraud, notably refusing to accept his 2020 defeat to Joe Biden and repeatedly calling the vote “rigged” and “stolen.”

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency found no evidence of fraud capable of changing the outcome, while Trump’s own attorney general at the time, William Barr, publicly rejected his claims.
The million-dollar bounty adds to Trump’s growing list of cash incentives ahead of the midterms, as Republicans fight to keep Congress. The biggest carrot so far was his proposed $5,000 ‘Trump Dividend’ for every American adult citizen if Republicans retain both chambers. Announced at a Republican gathering in Dallas last month, the giveaway would cost roughly $1.3 trillion for an estimated 260 million adults, drawing bipartisan criticism. Trump has suggested congressional approval might not be necessary, although lawmakers, including House Speaker Mike Johnson, and policy analysts say such a massive payout would require legislation and congressional funding.
Trump has also cheered a separate multibillion-dollar giveaway by ally Elon Musk, who promised every US child a share of SpaceX next year. The pledge followed Musk’s renewed backing of Trump and the Republicans after their public feud last year over the president’s spending legislation. According to the New York Times, Musk has donated more than $276 million to Republican groups since July, bringing his 2025-2026 election-cycle contributions to roughly $366 million.
The cash promises come as Trump’s ratings sink amid frustration over the prolonged Iran conflict, gasoline topping $6 a gallon, and persistent inflation despite his pledges to cut living costs, while Republicans face increasingly grim midterm prospects. A Reuters/Ipsos poll last week put his approval at 31% – the lowest of either presidential term – with Democrats leading Republicans 47% to 35% among registered voters on a hypothetical congressional ballot. A separate New York Times/Siena University poll put Trump’s approval at a record-low 36% among likely voters, with Democrats ahead by 11 points in congressional races, 52% to 41%.
Republicans currently hold a slim 218-214 House majority and a 53-47 Senate advantage. However, polls indicate they face unexpectedly tight Senate races in Kansas, Texas, Iowa, Alaska, and Ohio – all states Trump comfortably carried in 2024. Democrats need a net gain of four seats in both the House and Senate to take control.

Somali army kills over 75 al-Shabaab militants after convoy attack: Defense Ministry

Mohamed Dhaysane
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
Somali forces killed more than 75 al-Shabaab militants and wounded another 56 during an hours-long battle in the country's southwestern Bay region, the Defense Ministry said Tuesday.
The fighting erupted after al-Shabaab militants attacked a Somali military convoy carrying supplies between the towns of Leego and Burhakaba in South West state.
The ministry said troops operating under Operation Banooda fought to repel the attack and protect the convoy.
During the battle, al-Shabaab militants drove an explosives-laden vehicle toward a Somali army position, but it detonated before reaching its target, the ministry said.
The ministry said the army would continue pursuing al-Shabaab militants and those providing them with support or shelter.
The casualty figures could not be independently verified.

The UN Security Council renewed AUSSOM's mandate in December 2025, extending its authorization until Dec. 31, 2026.

- KNDS Deutschland is promoting the Boxer RCT30, known in Germany as Schakal, as suited to countering modern threats such as drones.
- The vehicle combines the Boxer chassis with the Puma’s unmanned RCT30 turret and a 30 mm cannon that can fire airburst rounds.
KNDS Deutschland is promoting its Boxer RCT30 wheeled infantry fighting vehicle as a weapon against drones, saying the 8×8 combat vehicle, which Germany and the Netherlands are buying in large numbers under the name Schakal, combines mobility, protection and firepower in a design suited to countering the latest airborne threats.
In a post this week, the German company said the Boxer RCT30 was built to handle a wide range of rapidly changing challenges and is “ideally suited for countering state-of-the-art threats, such as drones,” though it did not describe any new counter-drone equipment, software or ammunition added to the vehicle, or any recent test against drone targets.
The Boxer RCT30 pairs the Boxer’s eight-wheeled armored chassis with the unmanned RCT30 turret from Germany’s Puma tracked infantry fighting vehicle, which carries a 30 mm automatic cannon that can fire programmable airburst rounds that explode near a target and scatter fragments, a type of ammunition armies have increasingly looked to for hitting small drones.
Germany and the Netherlands are already among the largest customers for the vehicle, and in 2025 they signed a €4.5 billion contract for 270 additional Boxers, including 222 Schakal infantry fighting vehicles, along with ambulance and training variants, through the multinational ARTEC joint venture of KNDS Deutschland and Rheinmetall.
The two countries added 69 more Boxer RCT30s in August 2026, with 35 for Germany and 34 for the Netherlands, bringing the Royal Netherlands Army’s planned fleet of wheeled infantry fighting vehicles to 106, while Germany’s order for the Schakal has grown to about 185 vehicles.
