A Remarkable Recovery: The Return of China’s Last Wild Horses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:51:32 UTC
18:51:32 KST

The long journey back to the wild: The return of Przewalski’s horses
Author: Chen Ziqi, a reporter from CGTN
In the vast steppe of northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, small herds of Przewalski's horses, the world's last surviving wild horse species, roam the Kalamaili Nature Reserve.
They search for food and water, navigate harsh weather and gallop freely across the open land, sending clouds of dust into the air. The scene would have been impossible to witness just two decades ago.
After disappearing from the wild in China by the 1970s, the horses have gradually returned through four decades of conservation efforts, with their population growing both in captivity and in the wild. The challenge now is shifting from rebuilding population to ensuring their long-term survival.
Learning to live wild again
In 1985, China brought 11 Przewalski's horses from Germany and the United Kingdom to Xinjiang and established the Xinjiang Wild Horse Breeding and Research Center to to help the species recover. The first foal was born at the center three years later. By 2000, around 100 foals had been born there.
Keeping the horses alive and increasing their numbers was only the beginning. The ultimate goal was to return them to the wild, where survival would depend on more than human care.
In 2001, 27 Przewalski's horses were released directly into the Kalamaili Nature Reserve in the Junggar Basin. Without a preparatory period, the attempt proved unsuccessful: three horses died after struggling to adapt to the sudden change. Harsh weather, scarce food and water, and competition among stallions all posed challenges to survival.
Zhang Yanbao, who monitored the horses for seven years after their first release in 2001, remembers a story from the early days of the reintroduction.
A mare and her three offspring were released into the wild together. When the mare died, her two daughters stayed close to their younger brother and protected him when conflicts arose within the herd.
The young stallion, known as No. 147, faced another challenge as he matured. Dominant stallions typically drive away younger males once they become rivals for mates. But No. 147 remained in his herd longer than expected.
“His sisters shielded him whenever he needed and kept him close. With their support, the young stallion grew strong and healthy. In the same year he was finally driven from the herd, he succeeded in forming a group of his own with mares, which was a remarkable achievement,” Zhang says.
The early setbacks helped shape a more gradual approach to reintroduction. Today, the wild horses selected for release spend about six months to a year in a transitional area covering roughly 20 square kilometers within the reserve. There, they learn to find food and water, become familiar with the landscape and adjust to life with less human assistance.
At the breeding center, the horses are fed twice a day. In the transitional area, food is provided only once every three to five days, encouraging them to forage more independently.
“Horses have very keen senses,” says Xue Jiannan, an animal science engineer at the center. “Even before leaving the enclosure, they can detect where grass and water are more abundant outside. They also seem to know how far they’ll need to travel to reach those places.”
Even with this preparation, survival is not guaranteed. In winter, heavy snowfall can bury grass beneath the snow, while insufficient snowfall can leave water sources frozen. Rangers monitor the herds and intervene when necessary, providing food or water during extreme weather and calling veterinarians when injuries or illnesses threaten an animal’s life.
Entemahan Azhanhan (middle) gives treatment to the stallion injured during a fight with another stallion. [Photo:courtesy of Entemahan Azhanhan]
One particularly urgent case in 2016 remains vivid for Entemahan Azhanhan, a senior veterinarian at the breeding center. Two stallions had fought fiercely, and one bit the other’s genitals. The wound became infected, leaving the injured horse unable to walk when it was found. Entemahan knew he had to act quickly. 
“After administering anesthesia, I removed the infected tissue and stitched the wound. For ten days, we treated him with topical medication, anti-inflammatory injections and painkillers. Thankfully, the stallion survived and retained his ability to reproduce,” he recalls.
The protection, however, is not to shield the horses from every danger, but to give them the best chance of surviving on their own. By January 2026, about 180 Przewalski’s horses raised under human care had been returned to the wild in Xinjiang.
The people behind the return
Protecting wild horses in the remote reserve can be as demanding as the conditions the animals face.
In the early 2000s, monitoring equipment was limited and digital communications unreliable in the Kalamaili Nature Reserve. Rangers often worked in pairs, tracking animals across a vast landscape where wolves and other dangers were never far away.
Zhang Yanbao still remembers a summer afternoon when his vehicle broke down in the reserve. He and his colleague could not repair it, and remaining there overnight was not an option as there were many nocturnal predators.
They set off on foot.
“We ran for seven hours straight, without resting or drinking water,” Zhang says. “I never imagined I could run for so long.”
They eventually reached a herdsman’s home at around 11 p.m., where they were given food and water. After a short rest, they continued walking for another hour or two before finally leaving the reserve.
Today, technology has made monitoring easier. The team uses camera traps, thermal cameras, drones and GPS-enabled collars to track the horses’ movements. Collars fitted to lead mares use China’s BeiDou satellite navigation system to help researchers understand where herds spend their time.
Yet technology has not replaced the value of experience. Rangers still draw on years of observation to locate the horses, assess their condition and decide when intervention is necessary.
For Entemahan, the connection with the animals began long before he became a veterinarian. Raised in a herdsman’s family, he grew up around horses and learned from his parents how to care for them.
The center discourages staff from forming overly close relationships with the horses, helping preserve their natural wariness of humans. For Entemahan, however, such emotional attachment is difficult to avoid.
He remembers a night in 1999 when a mare gave birth to a foal that could not open his eyes. As he tried to help the newborn, the mare became protective, biting and kicking at him until he scrambled over a fence to escape injury.
Three or four years later, he took part in releasing that same mare into the wild. As the team prepared to let her go, she lingered near their vehicle, seemingly reluctant to leave.
Entemahan wondered whether she remembered the man who had helped her foal. The moment stayed with him.
He had spent years caring for the animals, yet the purpose of that care was to prepare them to live beyond it.
“I worried whether they could adapt, whether they would find enough food and water. But at the same time, they are returning to their true home. It’s such a relief seeing them run freely across the steppe,” Entemahan said. 
Protecting a future in the wild
The return of Przewalski’s horses depends not only on preparing individual animals but also on protecting the landscape they inhabit.
The Kalamaili Nature Reserve covers more than 14,000 square kilometers, spanning Gobi and desert terrain. The region is rich in resources including coal, oil and gold. Oil wells and mining sites once dotted parts of the landscape.
To improve conditions for wildlife, more than 280 oil wells had been sealed and the land restored to grassland by the end of 2018, according to the conservation team.
Habitat restoration is only one part of the work. The population must also retain enough genetic diversity to remain healthy over generations.
Between 1985 and 2005, the center introduced 24 Przewalski’s horses from countries including the United States, the United Kingdom and Germany. These additions helped broaden the genetic pool.
Today, breeding decisions are informed by DNA analysis of hair and fecal samples, which allows researchers to assess how closely related potential breeding pairs are.
The center has reduced the coefficient of relatedness used in its breeding decisions from around 0.2 to 0.01 or lower, according to Xue Jiannan.
The team is also studying artificial insemination, which could make it possible to introduce new bloodlines without transporting live horses over long distances.
The effort reflects a shift in priorities. In the early years, increasing the population was the main objective. Now, the focus is increasingly on maintaining genetic diversity and ensuring that the horses can sustain healthy populations over time.
The progress has been substantial. China’s Przewalski’s horse population now exceeds 900, accounting for about one-third of the global population. Roughly 560 live in Xinjiang, in both captive and wild settings.
The long-term goal is to establish a population capable of surviving and reproducing in the wild, with minimal intervention.
For Xue Jiannan, seeing the wild horses in the nature reserve is a tangible sign of their conservation efforts.
“When I see wild horses running freely on the steppe, or drinking at a water hole not far from us, that’s when I truly understand the meaning of what we’ve done,” Xue said.
His greatest hope is also the simplest: that one day the breeding and research center will no longer be needed to protect an endangered species.
“That will be the moment we know our mission is complete and that we have done our job well.”
Protecting biodiversity beyond Przewalski’s horses
The return of Przewalski’s horses to the wild is one example of the broader effort required to protect biodiversity: restoring habitats, safeguarding threatened species and ensuring that ecosystems can sustain life over the long term.
That challenge is also at the center of the 17th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17), being held in Yerevan, Armenia, from October 19 to 30.
The conference marks the first global review of progress under the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, adopted in 2022, which sets 23 targets for 2030. The review aims to assess how far countries have come and what more is needed to meet their commitments.
Among the framework’s key goals is conserving at least 30% of the world’s land, inland waters, coastal and marine areas by 2030. It also calls for urgent action to halt human-induced extinctions, recover threatened species and reduce human-wildlife conflict.
At the opening ceremony of the “China Corner” at COP17, China’s minister of ecology and environment Huang Runqiu noted that despite growing international commitment, progress remains insufficient to meet global biodiversity targets. He has called on countries to take concrete action and pursue more transformative measures to accelerate implementation.
The experience of Przewalski’s horses illustrates what such efforts require on the ground. Reintroducing a species is only the beginning. Its long-term survival depends on suitable habitats, continued monitoring and the ability to withstand the pressures of life in the wild.
As countries work toward the 2030 biodiversity targets, the challenge is not simply to make commitments, but to turn them into lasting results for wildlife and the ecosystems on which all life depends.

Norway's prime minister, Finland's president in phone call with Putin

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27

18:50:51 KST

Two Nordic leaders urge Putin to end Ukraine war in rare direct contact by Europeans
HELSINKI, Oct 27 - The leaders of Finland and Norway phoned Russian President Vladimir Putin on Tuesday to urge him to end the war in Ukraine, breaking with a longstanding practice among Western European leaders of shunning direct contact with the Kremlin.
The call by Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Stoere was an attempt to influence the diplomatic process after US President Donald Trump shifted his position in favour of Russia and US ties with Ukraine hit their lowest point in 18 months.
Stoere said he and Stubb had spoken to Putin for about 90 minutes, and then to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy.
In a joint statement, they linked the initiative to planned peace discussions between Russian, Ukrainian and US officials in Abu Dhabi next month, their first since February.
Moscow and Kyiv remain far apart on how to end the war that began with Russia's invasion in February 2022, and long-range airstrikes by both sides have increased this year while battle lines have remained largely static.
"The discussion (with Putin) was frank and substantive. We are neighbouring countries to Russia. The outcome of this war will have a direct impact on our and the broader European security. Ending the war requires direct discussions," Stubb said.
Stoere said he and Stubb had "stressed the importance of de-escalation." Both voiced strong support for Ukraine.
In later comments to Finnish journalists, Stubb said all Western allies were consulted on the initiative, adding that Ukraine had sought the opening of a new communications channel and Europe could no longer be a bystander to peace efforts giving Russia "the silent treatment".
NO SIGN OF KREMLIN COMPROMISE
The Kremlin's readout of the call did not suggest any softening of Putin's position.
"It was emphasised that achieving a just and long-term peace is possible only if the legitimate interests of the Russian Federation are fully and unconditionally taken into account," it said.
"At the same time, attention was drawn to the confrontational policies of EU and NATO countries, which are contributing to the prolongation of the hostilities."
Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said Tuesday's call had offered nothing new on the Ukraine conflict, with an information war likely to escalate, and that European countries were simply seeking a role in the negotiation process.
Western European leaders have mostly refused to talk to Putin, hoping to isolate him. But they have been sidelined in peace efforts led by US President Donald Trump, who is seen in many European capitals as unpredictable and prone to side with Putin at Ukraine's expense.
That perception has been reinforced by deals this month in which Putin agreed to supply Russian diesel to the United States and Trump eased sanctions on Russia. Ukraine has also complained of disruption to intelligence-sharing by the US and to satellite internet services on which its military relies.
Gerhard Mangott, an Austrian political analyst, said European governments had "manoeuvred themselves into a dead end" when it came to finding a solution to the war, and Tuesday's call was an effort to establish a channel for dialogue.
He drew attention to remarks by Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov on Sunday suggesting Europe should be part of discussions.
"I interpret this as a shift in Russia's position, given that Moscow had previously consistently rejected the idea of discussing a settlement of the war in Ukraine with the Europeans," Mangott said.
DANISH LEADER'S CRITICISM
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the call had been coordinated with Kyiv and was "the right approach".
"We welcome such active support for our diplomatic efforts and peace process," he said, adding that he also hoped a local ceasefire around the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky could "pave the way to other steps in the peace process."
But Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said she saw no signs that Russia wanted peace, adding: "I think Europe should stick together rather than going solo."
Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson said other European leaders were not informed of the talks.
"My impression is that everyone wants peace, except for Putin himself. I have quite low expectations for this type of conversation," Kristersson told Swedish daily DN.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said he had told Stubb and Stoere that "absolute caution and vigilance are necessary in such contacts".
Stubb and Stoere said they acted as leaders of their respective countries and not on behalf of Europe, and had "consulted thoroughly with all our partners."
Russia has frequently accused European governments of stoking the war by arming Ukraine and refusing direct talks.
A source close to the Kremlin said French President Emmanuel Macron had been the last EU leader to speak with Putin — in a summer call that yielded no results and was not made public.
The source said Putin told Stubb and Stoere that the European involvement was welcome and that the war needed to end "taking into account the realities on the ground".
Asked what this meant, the person said it signified that Russia would not compromise over its aim to capture the whole of Ukraine's Donbas region. The Europeans responded by saying a "just" peace was needed, the source said. REUTERS

Kazakhstan’s economy ranks 47th globally with GDP near $400 billion

Kazakhstan’s economy ranks 47th globally with GDP near $400 billion
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has estimated Kazakhstan’s nominal gross domestic product (GDP) at nearly 398 billion US dollars for the year, placing the country 47th among the world’s largest economies, according to the fund’s October World Economic Outlook. Visual Capitalist compiled a global ranking based on the IMF’s estimates, Qazinform News Agency reports.
The ranking is based on GDP measured in current US dollars at market exchange rates.
Kazakhstan ranks just below Chile and Peru, while Portugal, Finland and Greece are positioned lower on the list.
Kazakhstan’s economy grows in global ranking
The IMF’s estimates for Kazakhstan have increased significantly over the past year. A year ago, the country was at the lower end of the world’s 50 largest economies, with GDP estimated at approximately 320 billion US dollars.
In the spring, the fund revised its projections upward, moving Kazakhstan one position higher. At that time, the country overtook Finland, New Zealand and Hungary in terms of economic size.
The latest estimates have moved Kazakhstan further up the ranking, placing it ahead of Portugal. Overall, the estimated size of the country’s economy has increased by nearly a quarter over the past year.
Economic growth outpaces global average
According to the IMF, Kazakhstan’s real GDP is projected to grow by 4.4 percent this year, exceeding growth expectations for the United States, the Eurozone, Germany, Russia and Japan.
Among the major economies highlighted in the report, only India and China are expected to grow faster than Kazakhstan. Global economic growth is projected to reach 3.1 percent.
Kazakhstan remains Central Asia’s largest economy
Kazakhstan continues to have the largest economy in Central Asia by a considerable margin. Uzbekistan, the region’s next-largest economy, ranks 61st in the IMF’s October estimates.
Kazakhstan’s GDP is more than twice the size of Uzbekistan’s economy. The fund’s spring estimates also indicated that Kazakhstan’s economy was larger than those of the other Central Asian countries combined.
GDP per capita in Kazakhstan is expected to exceed 19,000 US dollars by the end of the year, placing the country significantly ahead of its regional neighbors on this measure.
Non-resource sectors drive economic expansion
Growth in non-resource sectors is making a substantial contribution to Kazakhstan’s economic expansion. According to the Ministry of National Economy of Kazakhstan, the non-resource sector grew by 5.4 percent between January and September.
Construction recorded the strongest growth, expanding by 11.5 percent. Manufacturing, transportation and trade also reported notable increases in output.
The structure of the economy is gradually changing as well. In the first half of the year, manufacturing’s share of GDP rose to 14.1 percent. Machinery manufacturing, the chemical industry and pharmaceuticals were among the fastest-growing segments.
IMF forecasts stronger growth in the coming years
The IMF expects Kazakhstan’s economic growth to accelerate to 4.9 percent next year. The fund also projects a slowdown in inflation and a slight decline in unemployment.
The country’s external position is expected to strengthen, with the current account projected to record a surplus equivalent to 0.5 percent of GDP this year.
The IMF’s medium-term outlook, published in the spring, projected that Kazakhstan’s nominal GDP would exceed 500 billion US dollars by the beginning of the next decade. GDP per capita is also expected to increase significantly over the same period.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported in its review for Republic Day that Kazakhstan had achieved significant socio-economic progress and demographic growth following a seven-year period of national transformation.

Rada has begun reviewing the 2027 State Budget with a record 5,236 amendments

Rada has begun reviewing the 2027 State Budget with a record 5,236 amendments
Kyiv • UNN
The Verkhovna Rada is considering the 2027 budget in its first reading. Lawmakers submitted a record 5,236 amendments, with the vote on the bill in principle scheduled for today.
On October 27, the Verkhovna Rada began considering the draft law on the State Budget of Ukraine for 2027. Details of the process were provided by members of parliament, UNN reports.
Details
"The Rada has now proceeded to consider the state budget," said MP Yaroslav Zhelezniak from the Finance Committee, explaining the stages of consideration:
-  first, the presentation, followed by a vote (226+), to proceed to consideration of the amendments; 
-  then the amendments and a vote to confirm the amendments and approve the bill in the first reading. 
"The procedure for consideration was supported by 215 votes," Zhelezniak noted, adding that the draft 2027 state budget is being considered in the first reading.
The MP also quoted his colleague, Chair of the parliament's Budget Committee Roksolana Pidlasa:
-  5,236 amendments — “a record for the past 24 years.” To take them into account, an additional UAH 13.5 trillion would be needed, “almost two budgets”; 
-  90 proposals have been taken into account; 
-  the government was instructed, before the second reading, to work on increasing servicemen's financial support, doubling state guarantees for the defense industry to UAH 60 billion, and providing housing for servicemen; 
-  additional funds for medicines for patients with rare diseases, beyond the UAH 21 billion already allocated. 
The vote on the bill in principle will take place today
We remind you
The 2027 Budget draft envisages a deficit of 15% of GDP and debt exceeding 110% of GDP. UAH 4.885 trillion is planned to be allocated for security and defense.

Finnish and Norwegian leaders call Putin, then Zelenskyy
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:50:00 EET
18:50:00 KST

Finnish and Norwegian leaders call Putin, then Zelenskyy
On Tuesday 27 October, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre held a phone call with Russian leader Vladimir Putin on their own initiative.
Source: European Pravda, citing Stubb's office
Details: The Finnish president's office said in a statement: "The call was a follow-up of the meeting in Oslo on 20 October and held in consultation with Ukraine."
Stubb and Støre initiated the call to discuss Russia's war against Ukraine and diplomatic efforts to end the war and promote peace and stability in Europe.
The statement also underlined that Stubb and Støre took part in the phone call "as leaders of their respective countries and did not speak on the behalf of Europe as a whole".
Stubb and Støre emphasised that Finland and Norway would continue their longstanding support for Ukraine. They stressed that the war must end and negotiations must continue.
"The discussion was frank and substantive. We are neighbouring countries to Russia. The outcome of this war will have a direct impact on our and the broader European security. Ending the war requires direct discussions," Stubb said.
Støre emphasised that during the phone call, the two leaders "stressed the importance of de-escalation".
Updated at 11:51: Dmytro Lytvyn, an adviser to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has reported that the Ukrainian leader is currently holding a call with Stubb and Støre.
Background:
- Earlier, Yuri Ushakov, an aide to Putin, said that Europe should be involved in talks between Russian, Ukrainian and US officials.
- The Telegraph recently reported that Russia may try to use the upcoming round of peace talks on the Russia-Ukraine war to secure concessions from NATO.
- On 20 October, Zelenskyy, Støre and Stubb held talks in Oslo with US President Donald Trump's envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
- Afterwards Witkoff travelled to St Petersburg to meet Putin, whom he described as a "humanitarian".
- On 23 October, Zelenskyy spoke with the US president's special envoys and said that a trilateral meeting at team level on ending Russia's war against Ukraine was planned for the first half of November.
- Ushakov claims that Russia is ready to resume trilateral talks with the US and Ukraine on ending the Russia-Ukraine war after 4 November.

Germany news: Fall of global order threatens Europe, Asia, Merz says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:49:00 UTC
18:49:00 KST

Germany news: Merz in Asia says middle powers must 'assert ' interests
Published October 27, 2026last updated October 27, 2026
What you need to know
- German Chancellor Merz is on a multi-day tour of Asia to promote new forms of cooperation and trade
- Germany's defense minister calls for 'a stronger Europe within a stronger NATO'
- Court rules to proceed with case against Nord Stream sabotage suspect
This blog is now closed. Below is a roundup of the top stories in Germany on Tuesday, October 27, 2026:
Don't want to miss our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google.
'Act with confidence' in Chinese market, Steinmeier tells German companies
On the first day of his farewell tour in China, German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier urged the German business community to act with confidence in the Chinese market.
"When you travel in China, you're amazed at how highly Germany and German technology are still valued here," he said in Hefei. "That's why we can act with confidence in these markets."
Steinmeier did not bring any companies with him to China as part of his delegation, as his final trip was intended to focus on culture and science.
Nevertheless, the first day of the trip in Hefei, the capital of Anhui Province, revolved primarily around the economy. Steinmeier visited the Volkswagen China Technology Company (VCTC). About three years ago, Europe's largest automaker opened a research center for electric mobility there, which today employs 3,000 people.
Johannes Volkmann, a lawmaker accompanying Steinmeier in China, warned that the German economy must not "lose its leadership in innovation."
"I'm taking this call to action with me from here to do more to improve competitive conditions at home," he said, adding that Germany must avoid creating new dependencies "by allowing innovation and value creation to take place only outside Europe."
Steinmeier called for Europe to reposition itself and reorganize its economic instruments with its growing trade deficit with China in mind.
"The trade surplus that China is accumulating naturally causes us concern because the successful model of economic cooperation is becoming unbalanced," he said. "We must strive to ensure that economic cooperation does not come to an end, but that it continues — to the mutual benefit of both sides."
Germany's trade deficit with China amounted to just under €90 billion ($100 billion) in 2025. According to the Federal Statistical Office, China exported goods worth €170.6 billion to Germany, and German exports to China amounted to €81.3 billion.
Across the 27-member EU, the deficit amounted to almost €197 billion in the first half of 2026, according to EU Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic.
Additional reporting by Rosalia Romaniec in Hefei.
Court rejects bid to end case against Ukrainian over Nord Stream blasts
A German court denied a defense request to end the trial of a former Ukrainian army officer who stands accused of sabotaging the Nord Stream gas pipelines.
Serhii Kuznietsov, 50, went on trial this month at the Hamburg state court, charged with causing an explosion, damaging property, disrupting public services and being an "accomplice to war crimes" by attacking civilian infrastructure.
Prosecutors accuse him of being the ringleader of the destruction, considered one of Europe's biggest acts of post-World War II sabotage. He is alleged to have carried out the explosions together with six others.
His lawyers said the charges should be dismissed, arguing that, as a former soldier, Kuznietsov was obligated by Ukrainian law not to speak for national security reasons and could face severe penalties in Ukraine if he did. They argued that, under German law, anyone who cannot speak on his or her own behalf cannot be convicted.
The Hamburg court ruled Kuznietsov's defense was not limited under German law and that freedom to testify is not limited by a foreign country's conditions of service.
The undersea explosions on September 26, 2022, damaged the Nord Stream 1 pipeline, which brought Russian natural gas to Germany until Moscow cut off supplies in August 2022.
The blasts also damaged the Nord Stream 2 pipeline, which never went into service. Germany suspended the pipeline's certification process shortly before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Italian authorities detained Kuznietsov last year. He was publicly named in extradition proceedings that led to his transfer to Germany in November.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has denied allegations that his country was involved in the pipeline blasts.
Mercedes cuts outlook for 2026 profit margin
German carmaker Mercedes-Benz has cut its forecast for 2026, with difficult market conditions in China and higher fourth-quarter cost expectations set to negatively impact profits, the company said on Tuesday.
Markets were quick to take note of the announcement, and Mercedes shares dropped 3.4% in trading on Tuesday morning.
The move makes Mercedes the third big German carmaker to lower its outlook for 2026 after BMW and VW took similar steps.
Mercedes-Benz CEO Ola Kaellenius has called on German employees to work more without pay while also expanding manufacturing operations in Hungary, where he said costs are about 70% lower than in Germany.
Mercedes currently expects an adjusted car profit margin of 2% to 3% in 2026, compared to the 3% to 5% in the previous guidance.
Like many German automakers, Mercedes has faced weak sales in China. German carmakers have struggled in the world's largest car market with sluggish demand and increased competition from local manufacturers.
Mercedes vehicle deliveries in China — last year already at their lowest level since 2016 — fell a further 29% in the nine months to the end of September.
Mercedes also released third-quarter figures earlier than planned, which showed that the company generated just €172 million ($191 million) in free cash flow from its vehicle business, down on the €422 million forecast by financial market experts.
Before interest and tax, Mercedes posted an operating profit of €1.77 billion — more than double the €750 million recorded a year earlier, according to the preliminary figures. But last year's stats were significantly impacted by one-time expenses, especially related to job cuts and legal disputes.
Adjusted for one-off items, the operating profit margin in the passenger car business stood at 2.5%, down on the 4.8% recorded a year earlier.
Some 5% of Germany potentially suitable for long-term nuclear waste storage
The German agency responsible for finding a final repository for nuclear waste (BGE) has eliminated five states from its search.
Berlin, Hesse, Rhineland-Palatinate, Saxony and Saarland were deemed unsuitable for long-term radioactive waste storage.
In a report issued Tuesday, the BGE said it had limited its search to 5% of Germany, down from 25% in 2025. The federal agency aims to suggest suitable locations for final evaluation by the end of 2027.
Regions in northern, northwestern, southern and eastern Germany remain under consideration as locations for final storage facilities.
Germany's nuclear waste is currently stored in 16 above-ground interim storage facilities.
The BGE assessments evaluate regions' geological conditions and their ability to safely contain highly radioactive material. Granite, salt, and clay are generally considered potentially suitable types of rock and areas with damaged or compromised subsurface conditions, places with mines or volcanos have been active, are not eligible as final disposal sites.
Germany needs to find a repository for approximately 27,000 cubic meters of highly radioactive nuclear waste generated over more than 60 years of nuclear power generation. The site is expected to ensure safety for 1 million years. The last German nuclear power plants were decommissioned in April 2023.
BGE said its goal remains finding the site that offers the highest level of safety for highly radioactive waste.
The agency's recommendations, however, are not legally binding and it will be up to German lawmakers to determine the final disposal site.
NSU terrorist Beate Zschäpe to stay in prison until at least 2035
Convicted right-wing terrorist Beate Zschäpe's request for early release from prison was denied with a court ruling that she would remain behind bars for at least nine more years.
Munich's Higher Regional Court on Tuesday set her minimum term at at least 24 years and refused to suspend the sentence to probation. By determining her guilt to be particularly severe, the court effectively ruled out her release after 15 years, which, including her time in pretrial detention, would have expired this year.
The Munich court said Zschäpe, currently 51, still had a good chance of leaving prison alive.
The decision is not yet legally binding, and the defense and the Federal Prosecutor's Office can appeal.
Zschäpe had been sentenced to life in prison in 2018 as an accomplice in the National Socialist Underground (NSU) murders that killed 10 people, mainly individuals with an immigrant background as well as a police officer.
The terror group went undetected for a decade. Zschäpe's fellow NSU members, Uwe Mundlos and Uwe Böhnhardt, injured several people with bomb attacks in Cologne and killed themselves to avoid arrest in 2011.
Under normal conditions, a convict who receives a life sentence in Germany can apply for parole after 15 years.
IN DEPTH: Harry Kane breaks Bayern and Bundesliga's Ballon d'Or drought
Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane has won football's most prestigious individual prize, beating Kylian Mbappe and Lamine Yamal. Kane has developed even more in the Bundesliga despite an uneven league.
Pistorius wants 'stronger Europe within a stronger NATO'
German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius, along with his counterparts from France, Italy, Poland and the UK, authored an op-ed calling Russia "the most acute and long-term threat to Euro-Atlantic security and stability."
In the article, published online and in Tuesday's Tagesspiegel newspaper, the defense ministers wrote they "share a deep conviction" that European countries need to do more to ensure their own security and aim to build "a stronger Europe within a stronger NATO."
The ministers, however, added that the United States would remain an "indispensable ally."
The pronouncement comes as many in Europe are wary of US President Donald Trump's commitment to the NATO military alliance.
The US leader has threatened to leave the group and to seize control of Greenland, a territory of fellow NATO member Denmark. US presidents have repeatedly called for European NATO members to contribute more to the alliance's military capabilities.
As US support for Ukraine also appears to waver, the five defense ministers reiterated their political, military and financial support for Kyiv as it fights of Russia's full-scale invasion.
Merz: Collapse of global order threatens middle powers in Europe and Asia
In Singapore, to start a four-day business-oriented trip that will also bring him to Japan and South Korea, Chancellor Friedrich Merz said it was up to European and Asian nations to find their spot amid a changing global order.
"We must assert our interests in an international environment shaped by renewed great-power rivalry," Merz said.
With a view to unpredictable tariffs imposed by the United States under President Donald Trump and trade restrictions from China, Merz emphasized the stability offered by Germany and the rest of Europe.
"This is a deliberate counterpoint to what we are currently seeing. We want to do things differently, and we want to show that there is a better way," Merz said, adding that Europe sought to expand partnerships to increase free trade with open competition, reliability and a rules-based order.
He also called for increased international investment and cooperation.
"Under the federal government I lead, investment opportunities will be continuously improved," Merz said following a meeting with Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong. "I encounter a great deal of confidence here in Germany and in Europe as locations for investment."
The German leader called for a new free-trade agreement between the 27-member European Union and the Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP), comprising 12 countries across five continents, including Australia, Canada, Japan, Mexico and the United Kingdom. Neither the United States nor China is part of the CPTPP.
For his part, Wong said investment in Germany and Europe would continue.
"Many of our investors, including our sovereign wealth funds, have been investing in Germany for a long time," Wong said. "They will continue to invest because they are confident that, in the long term, Germany and Europe have potential."
Merz and Wong agreed their nations would work to expand cooperation in security and defense as well as trade, investment, sustainable energy and artificial intelligence.
Welcome to our coverage
Guten Morgen and welcome to our daily coverage of what's making news in Germany.
While we follow the news here in Berlin and Bonn, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is in Singapore, speaking about international cooperation among middle-power countries in Europe and Asia amid a "renewed great-power rivalry."
Today, we're also expecting a decision on whether to proceed with a case against a Nord Stream sabotage suspect and a report on Germany's ongoing search for a nuclear waste storage facility.
Not to mention a car ramming last night near the northern German city of Hannover that has left several people with serious injuries, while the suspects are still on the run.

Smithsonian scientists just recreated the first 2 billion years of the Universe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:48:35 UTC
18:48:35 KST

Smithsonian scientists just recreated the first 2 billion years of the Universe
New model gives astronomers a powerful tool to understand discoveries from NASA's James Webb and Nancy Roman space telescopes.
- Date:
- October 27, 2026
- Source:
- Smithsonian
- Summary:
- Scientists have created one of the largest and most detailed simulations of the early universe ever made, offering an extraordinary new glimpse into the cosmos shortly after the Big Bang. Called Lumina, the groundbreaking simulation recreates the universe’s first 2 billion years, showing how dark matter, gas, and radiation interacted to give rise to the earliest stars, galaxies, and black holes.
- Share:
Scientists have created one of the largest and most detailed simulations of the early universe ever developed, offering a remarkable new way to explore how the cosmos evolved after the Big Bang. Known as "Lumina," the simulation was built by researchers at the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian to help astronomers interpret observations from powerful instruments such as the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and Nancy Roman Space Telescope.
The research, published in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, reconstructs the universe's first 2 billion years by modeling the interactions between ordinary matter, dark matter, and radiation. By comparing Lumina's predictions with observations from JWST, Roman, and other telescopes, scientists can evaluate how well existing theories explain cosmic evolution and identify discoveries that might challenge their understanding of the universe's fundamental laws.
Astronomers have spent centuries studying the sky and developing explanations for the formation of stars, galaxies, and other cosmic structures. Modern supercomputers now make it possible to turn these ideas into detailed simulations that predict how the universe should behave. When telescope observations agree with those predictions, they strengthen confidence in current theories. Unexpected differences, however, may point toward physical processes that scientists have yet to fully understand.
"With JWST, the early universe has become an exciting new frontier in astrophysics," said lead author Oliver Zier, an ITC Fellow at the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian. "To understand what we are seeing with this telescope, we need to translate our theories into detailed predictions. After several years of work, with plenty of ups and downs, it is incredibly rewarding to see the simulation results and watch our predictions come to life in video."
Recreating the Universe's First 2 Billion Years
Lumina is the largest cosmological radiation hydrodynamics simulation ever produced. In simple terms, it uses powerful computers to calculate how gas, dark matter, and light influenced one another as the young universe developed. By following these interactions across the first 2 billion years after the Big Bang, researchers can examine how the earliest galaxies formed and how their activity changed the enormous clouds of gas surrounding them.
The simulation models a volume of space more than 100 times larger than those covered by earlier comparable projects. Its virtual universe spans a cube approximately 1.5 billion light-years on each side, providing a view of cosmic evolution on a scale comparable to the vast regions that today's most advanced telescopes can study.
Another major advance is Lumina's treatment of helium reionization, a process in which radiation strips electrons from helium atoms. For the first time, a simulation of this kind follows that transformation as it unfolds while simultaneously accounting for how it affects the surrounding universe. This allows scientists to study the relationship between evolving galaxies, radiation, and the gas that fills the space between them.
"We feel incredibly fortunate to be building simulations like Lumina," said Aaron Smith, an assistant professor of physics at the University of Texas at Dallas and an author on the paper. "For the first time, we can follow along as both hydrogen and helium changed into their modern form across such an enormous volume of the universe, while still resolving the galaxies and other luminous objects driving that transformation."
A Massive Supercomputer Powers the Virtual Cosmos
Recreating such an enormous portion of cosmic history demanded extraordinary computing resources. The team used more than 15,000 graphics processing units on Frontier, one of the world's fastest supercomputers, housed at Oak Ridge National Laboratory in Tennessee.
That processing power enabled the researchers to simulate an exceptionally large region of the early universe without sacrificing the fine detail needed to investigate individual galaxies and other important structures. As a result, Lumina can capture the broader evolution of the cosmos while also tracking processes involved in the formation of stars, galaxies, and black holes.
Testing the Mysteries of the Early Universe
Beyond recreating cosmic history, Lumina provides a powerful new framework for investigating how the universe developed. Researchers plan to use it to explore the movement of gas between galaxies, the influence of radiation left over from the Big Bang, and the emergence of regions where stars formed at especially high rates.
By placing these predictions alongside observations from the James Webb Space Telescope, the Nancy Roman Space Telescope, and other instruments, scientists hope to build a more complete picture of the universe's earliest chapters. Any unexpected differences between the simulated cosmos and the real one could provide valuable clues, potentially revealing where current theories need to be refined or reconsidered.

According to the ministry, Ukrainian drones killed or wounded the highest number of the Russians in March and the lowest in February. The monthly casualty statistics for 2026 are:
- January – 29,572
- February – 26,204
- March – 33,989
- April – 33,961
- May – 30,548
- June – 27,072
- July – 30,272
- August – 29,554
- September – 32,739
In the first 25 days of October, Ukrainian drones killed or wounded a further 27,829 Russian soldiers.
The Ministry of Defence reported that each hit is video-recorded in the Delta battlefield situational awareness system and verified by the Brave1 defence innovation cluster.
Quote from the Ministry of Defence: "Targeting enemy military personnel with drones makes it possible to exhaust its human resources, reduce the combat capability of their units and restrain the pace of the offensive. In addition, the wiping out of enemy manpower using UAVs helps to preserve the lives of Ukrainian servicemen by making it difficult for the enemy to approach our positions."

U.S., UK and Australia test Saronic drone boats together
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:46:41 UTC
18:46:41 KST

- Saronic Technologies fielded three Corsair autonomous boats with U.S., British and Australian forces at Maritime Big Play Pacific in San Diego.
- The boats ran pier resupply partly under denied communications and a trilateral sense-decide-effect mission within a mixed uncrewed fleet.
Saronic Technologies’ Corsair drone boats, the same type the U.S. military used to strike an Iranian naval base in July, have operated alongside forces from the United States, the United Kingdom and Australia at Maritime Big Play Pacific, the AUKUS partners’ largest demonstration of uncrewed and autonomous technology, held in San Diego this October.
The Texas company said it fielded three Corsairs across the three nations and that the boats ran several mission scenarios, including resupplying a pier with parts of the mission carried out while communications were denied, and a trilateral “sense, decide, effect” mission in which the Corsairs operated as part of a mixed fleet of uncrewed surface vessels supported by uncrewed aircraft.
Saronic said the boats were controlled through its Echelon software, integrated into the Common Control System used to command uncrewed vessels, and it credited the U.K. Royal Navy with giving the company the opportunity to take part, though it did not say which navy operated each boat or how long the boats ran without human input.
Maritime Big Play Pacific brought more than 40 government and industry technologies from the three countries to San Diego under AUKUS Pillar 2, the part of the partnership focused on advanced military technology, with the program organized around anti-submarine warfare, integrated lethality, contested resupply, and subsea and seabed warfare, while the Royal Navy led the anti-submarine warfare strand with its own uncrewed surface vessels, underwater gliders, drones and subsea vehicles.
The Corsair is a 7.3-meter (24-foot) autonomous surface vessel that can carry up to 453 kg (1,000 pounds) of payload, has a range of about 1,852 km (1,000 nautical miles) and a top speed above 35 knots, and the U.S. Navy awarded Saronic a $392 million production contract for the boats in December 2025.
Task Force 59 began fielding Corsairs in the Middle East in late March 2026, mostly for surveillance and support, and on July 12, 2026, three Corsairs struck Iran’s Bandar Abbas Naval Base, targeting a submarine and ship maintenance facility, in what U.S. Central Command called the first time American forces had used sea drones in combat operations.

Jordan says strikes in Syria killed over 20 ISIS members as Damascus condemns attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:46:19 UTC
18:46:19 KST

Lina Altawell and Sahin Demir
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
Jordan said Tuesday that its airstrikes in southern Syria killed more than 20 ISIS (Daesh) terrorists and destroyed a major weapons depot, while Damascus condemned the operation as a violation of its sovereignty and reported several casualties.
 
Jordanian government spokesman Mohammad al-Momani said the strikes were conducted after Amman had “run out of patience” with the movements of terrorist groups and threats to its national security.
 
“The operation was based on field intelligence aimed at neutralizing confirmed threats and planned terrorist attacks against Jordan,” he said.
 
“Initial results of this operation indicate significant losses among ISIS, estimated at more than 20 members, as well as the destruction of a major weapons depot belonging to the group,” Momani said.
 
He expressed regret over civilian casualties, saying Jordan refrained from striking locations where intelligence indicated civilians were present.
 
“Jordan takes precautions to avoid harming civilians and attaches the same importance to the lives of innocent civilians outside its borders as it does to the lives of Jordanians,” he said.
 
Momani said Jordanian authorities were following up on the matter with their Syrian counterparts.
 
He said the two countries would establish a joint committee to examine the consequences of the operation and strengthen coordination in combating ISIS while protecting civilians.
 
The spokesman stressed that Jordan values its relations with Syria and remains committed to developing cooperation in confronting common challenges.
 
“Jordan’s security and Syria’s security are one,” he said, adding that combating terrorism remains a shared objective.
 
Momani also linked the security threats to a recent attack on a church in Jordan’s Karak governorate that killed nine people.
 
He reiterated Jordan’s support for Syria’s security, unity and stability, particularly in the country’s south.
 
Syria condemns strikes
 
Syria’s Foreign Ministry strongly condemned Jordanian airstrikes targeting several locations in the southern Daraa province a day earlier, saying they were carried out without prior coordination with Damascus.
 
In a Tuesday statement, the ministry said the attacks killed and injured several people, describing the operation as an “unacceptable violation” of Syrian airspace and national sovereignty.
 
Syrian authorities had earlier reported that seven people were killed in the strikes.
 
Damascus also condemned Friday’s attack targeting St. George Greek Orthodox Church in Jordan, offering condolences to the victims’ families and wishing the injured a speedy recovery.
 
However, the ministry stressed that the Jordanian military operation inside Syrian territory was unacceptable and violated the principles of good neighborliness and bilateral coordination.
 
It warned that certain parties were seeking to undermine relations between the two countries and fuel tensions, without elaborating.
 
The ministry said coordination was underway with Jordan to establish an urgent joint civilian and security committee to investigate the incidents, prevent their recurrence and strengthen security cooperation along their shared border.

Iraqi court sentences six French men to life in prison for Islamic State membership
BAGHDAD, Oct 27 - An Iraqi court on Tuesday sentenced six French nationals to life in prison and a seventh to 15 years after convicting them of membership in Islamic State, a Reuters witness inside the courtroom said.
The men were among 47 French Islamic State suspects transferred from detention facilities in northeast Syria to Iraq last year under a broader relocation arrangement coordinated by US forces and Iraqi authorities.
The presiding judge said the sentences were imposed under Iraq's counterterrorism law for joining Islamic State and spreading fear. He added that the court had opted for life imprisonment rather than the death penalty because the defendants were young.
A seventh French national, aged 23, was given a 15-year sentence, according to the Reuters witness.
Abbas al-Maliki, one of the lawyers for the defendants, said the group would appeal the sentence in the Court of Cassation.
Iraq opened the trial of the French nationals last month.
Islamic State seized large parts of Iraq and Syria in 2014 before being driven from its self-declared caliphate by a US-led coalition and local forces in 2019. Many of the group's militants were detained, although remnants of the jihadist organization continue to operate.
The United States announced in January that it had begun transferring Islamic State detainees from Syria to Iraq amid concerns about the security of detention facilities in northeast Syria after Kurdish-led forces lost control of parts of the region. REUTERS

Justice Department Files More Charges Against James Comey
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:45:00 UTC
18:45:00 KST

The Justice Department has brought charges against former FBI Director James Comey for the third time in 13 months, this time related to alleged leaks of national security information to the media.
According to court documents filed earlier this month and unsealed on Monday, federal prosecutors are accusing Comey of “willfully” mishandling information related to national defense in October 2016, resulting in the information appearing in media reports.
“Having reason to believe such information could be used to injure the United States and to the advantage of any foreign nation,” the court document said Comey “knowingly and willfully communicated, delivered, transmitted, and caused that information to be communicated, delivered, and transmitted to a person not entitled to receive it.”
The inquiry is the latest attempt to prosecute Comey, who is a prominent critic of President Donald Trump. Trump fired Comey in 2017 while Comey was leading the FBI investigation into potential ties between Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign and Russia. The first Trump Administration cited a memo related to Comey’s handling of the FBI investigation into Democratic presidential candidate Hillary Clinton’s emails. Since then, Trump has publicly called for criminal investigations into Comey and celebrated the indictments he’s faced.
In a video posted on Monday, Comey said the latest investigation was an attempt to politically persecute him.
“They’re back, again,” Comey said. “It would almost be funny if it weren’t such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice, one that we cannot become numb to.”
“I’m still innocent. I’m still not afraid of these people,” he added.
Comey’s attorneys argued in court filings that the alleged leaks had already been investigated twice during the first Trump Administration in 2017 and 2019, and neither had resulted in charges.
The Justice Department has pursued a number of investigations and indictments against prominent Democrats in recent weeks, appearing to break with the unofficial “unwritten 60-day rule” of avoiding filing new charges or taking public investigatory action that could influence an approaching election. Earlier this month, the Department secured a search warrant for the home of Rep. Ilhan Omar (D, Minn.), who called the effort “the latest escalation in [Trump’s] campaign of political intimidation.” The DOJ also secured an indictment against Virginia Senate Leader Louise Lucas, who led the Democrats’ counter-effort against Republican gerrymandering, on drug trafficking and money laundering charges. Lucas denied the allegations and said she would fight back against an attempt by “people in power … to silence those who stand up to them.”
What to know about the new Comey charges
According to court documents, prosecutors allege that around Oct. 4 and 5, 2016, Comey directed FBI staff to speak with the New York Times “about specific accuracy concerns” related to “misinformation which had appeared” in a Reuters report about Yahoo’s cooperation with U.S. surveillance.
In doing so, prosecutors contend, Comey “illegally transferred classified information.”
The Times article had described how Yahoo had adapted its existing email filtering system, used to detect spam, malware, and child sexual abuse material, to comply with a secret surveillance order to search messages for a computer “signature” associated with communications by a foreign, state-sponsored terrorist organization. The article said the Justice Department had obtained the order from a Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court judge in 2015 and that Yahoo was barred from disclosing it.
A spokesperson for the Times said the newspaper “does not comment on the sourcing behind our reporting, but we know from experience that prosecutions like this one are designed to discourage sources from providing journalists with the kind of valuable and illuminating information that the public needs to know.”
Comey’s lawyers argued in a motion to dismiss the case that the Trump Administration did not file an indictment within the 10-year statute of limitations. On Oct. 5, prosecutors filed the charges in a criminal information under seal in Federal District Court in Washington, which does not require approval from a grand jury or a judicial finding of probable cause, but have not obtained an indictment.
Previous charges against Comey
The Justice Department has brought multiple charges against Comey during Trump’s second term. It secured an indictment against him in September 2025 over allegations that he made false statements to Congress in 2020 related to alleged leaks to the media. The charges were thrown out by a federal judge in November, concluding that the prosecutor, Lindsey Halligan, had been unlawfully appointed.
Comey was also indicted in April over allegedly making a threat against Trump by posting on Instagram a photograph of seashells on a North Carolina beach arranged to spell “86 47.” Prosecutors argued that the arrangement was intended as a threat “to kill” Trump, who is the 47th President. Comey, who deleted the post after initial backlash, said he did not intend the photograph to be a threat against Trump, and that he understood the numbers to be a “political message.” The numbers “86” have commonly been used to mean “to throw out” or “to refuse service to,” according to Merriam-Webster, but have also been used in some instances to mean “to kill.”
That case is set to go to trial in North Carolina in February 2027.
Earlier on Monday, a federal judge in New York ruled that the Justice Department had unlawfully fired Comey’s daughter, Maurene Comey, in July 2025. The judge ordered her retroactive reinstatement with back pay, concluding that the Trump Administration had violated the Constitution and federal law by claiming the President had executive authority to fire civil servants.

Flavio Bolsonaro Reportedly Flees Brazil Amid Election Loss and Money Laundering Investigation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:45:00 UTC
18:45:00 KST

The Trump Administration is set to grant a visa to right-wing Brazilian Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, who has reportedly left Brazil to travel to the U.S. after refusing to comply with an order to surrender his passports as part of a criminal investigation into an alleged money laundering operation.
"The State Department will issue visas to Flavio Bolsonaro and his family and allow them entry into the United States," Administration officials told multiple outlets on Tuesday.
Bolsonaro, who lost the country’s presidential election on Sunday, initially said that he would comply with the Supreme Court’s order to turn over his travel documents and not flee Brazil.
"I have never thought about leaving the country," he said on Monday. "I will hand over my passports and defend myself against this travesty, which is a clear attempt to intimidate me."
But Bolsonaro did not comply with the order to hand over his passport by the end of the court’s 24-hour deadline on Tuesday morning, and multiple outlets have reported that he departed the country with the intent of heading to the U.S. Outlets in Argentina and Brazil have reported that he crossed the border into Argentina, though the Argentinian government has said it has no record of him entering the country.
Bolsonaro is being investigated for alleged links to a Brazilian lawyer, Willer Tomaz, who is accused of laundering more than $1 billion through a fraud scheme, the New York Times reported.
In a ruling that became public on Monday, a day after Bolsonaro, the son of jailed former President Jair Bolsonaro, lost the presidential election to incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes ordered police to confiscate the senator’s passports as part of the probe.
Bolsonaro, who has cast the investigation as political persecution, said in a social media video on Monday afternoon that the seizure of his travel documents was an attempt at intimidating him after he lost the election.
The situation could inflame political tensions amid claims from Brazil’s right wing and abroad that the election was unfair. Bolsonaro initially said he would seek to annul the vote, although his Liberal Party later conceded defeat. In the video posted Monday, the right-wing senator said he would now seek to have Lula’s ticket disqualified, citing alleged disinformation and “vote buying.” He also said he would organize the opposition in Congress to Lula’s government.
“I wasn’t the one who lost,” he said. “The system won.”
Donald Trump, an ally of the Bolsonaros, said on Monday that the election appeared “rigged.” The U.S. President did not provide evidence for his claim.
“I didn’t take sides, but it looked like another rigged election,” Trump said.
“I just think it had a very bad look, the election, the way it was tabulated,” he added. “The extension given was very strange.”
Brazil’s Supreme Court had granted a two-hour extension to voting on Sunday, citing transport issues raised by Lula’s campaign. Bolsonaro’s campaign had separately requested a two-hour extension due to heavy rainfall in certain areas. Lula won the election by more than 4 million votes. Roughly 0.03% of the total votes—or less than 35,000 votes—were recorded in the extra two hours. Vice President Geraldo Alckmin told Rede Vanguarda that Trump’s claims were “completely wrong.”
Bolsonaro is also being investigated over alleged links to a disgraced banker connected to a corruption scheme. Bolsonaro allegedly raised millions of dollars from the banker to fund a biopic about his father.
Here’s what to know about the investigation.
What to know about the money laundering inquiry
The inquiry into Bolsonaro stems from a federal probe into unauthorized deductions from pension payments made by Brazil’s social security agency. The broader operation, launched in April 2025, investigated associations suspected of collecting unauthorized membership fees from pension benefits.
Evidence from the probe led investigators to examine suspected money laundering involving betting platforms and financial transactions linked to Tomaz, who denies wrongdoing.
Police reportedly discovered that Bolsonaro had “master user” access to bank accounts belonging to Alcazar Holdings, a company owned by Tomaz. In May 2025, a person working for Tomaz asked the bank to remove Bolsonaro’s access to the accounts, local media outlets BPMoney and Times Brasil reported earlier this month, citing police findings. Both Bolsonaro and Tomaz deny having a joint account or financial ties.
The order required Bolsonaro to surrender his passports and barred him from contacting Tomaz. Bolsonaro said he would comply with the order and that he had “never considered” leaving Brazil. He said that the ruling came after his brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, had said on a podcast last week that he should leave the country if he lost the election.
Criticisms of Brazil’s justice system
Bolsonaro has repeatedly criticized Brazil’s judiciary and described the investigations into him as politically motivated. The country’s Supreme Court generally assigns cases through a lottery system, and the money laundering investigation was assigned to de Moraes on Oct. 16.
De Moraes was the lead justice in last year’s trial of Jair Bolsonaro, who refused to accept his election loss in 2022. A five-member panel of Supreme Court justices convicted Jair Bolsonaro, by a 4-1 vote, of attempting to overturn his election defeat and sentenced him to 27 years and three months in prison, which he is serving under house arrest due to poor health. Prosecutors alleged that the plot included plans to assassinate Lula. Jair Bolsonaro denies wrongdoing.
In June, a Supreme Court panel unanimously convicted Eduardo Bolsonaro of coercion in judicial proceedings. Prosecutors alleged he had attempted to lobby the Trump Administration to use tariffs and sanctions, including on de Moraes, to pressure judicial authorities to drop its prosecution of Jair Bolsonaro. He was sentenced to four years and two months in prison, but remains in Texas, where has lived since 2025.
De Moraes has also faced scrutiny over reported ties to Daniel Vorcaro, the former owner of Banco Master, whose financing of a film about Jair Bolsonaro is the subject of a separate inquiry into Bolsonaro. The New York Times reported, citing a police dossier, that Vorcaro sent text messages to de Moraes asking for help to avoid arrest. In messages to other associates, Vorcaro reportedly mentioned paying millions to the law firm of de Moraes’s wife. De Moraes has denied wrongdoing and said he never acted to favor Vorcaro or Banco Master.
De Moraes also clashed with tech billionaire Elon Musk in 2024 over court orders to block accounts on Musk’s social media platform X. De Moraes temporarily suspended the platform in Brazil after it failed to comply with judicial requirements, which Musk had described as “the most draconian demands of any country on Earth.”

BRICS parliaments call for unilateral sanctions to be lifted
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:43:57 UTC
18:43:57 KST

NEW DELHI, October 27. /TASS/. BRICS parliamentarians are calling for the removal of unilateral economic sanctions, as such measures undermine international law, according to a joint statement approved at the 12th BRICS International Parliamentary Forum.
"We condemn the use of unilateral coercive measures that are contrary to international law and reiterate that such measures, particularly in the form of unilateral economic sanctions and secondary sanctions, have wide-ranging adverse effects on human rights, including the right to development, as well as the health and food security of people in the countries concerned. We call for the removal of such unlawful measures, which undermine international law and the principles and purposes of the United Nations Charter," the document says. TASS has obtained a copy of the statement.
BRICS parliamentarians also firmly denounce all violations of international humanitarian law, including deliberate attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure, including on the territories of member states. They also denounce the denial of humanitarian access and attacks on humanitarian personnel. "We stress the need to ensure accountability for all violations of international humanitarian law," the joint statement says.

Kiev makes new demand for European interceptors
Ukraine has asked five European nations to release 10% of their interceptor missile stockpiles to ease the shortage of air defense ammunition.
Defense Minister Evgeny Khmara presented the proposal by video on Monday to his counterparts from France, Germany, Italy, and the UK, and Polish Deputy Defense Minister Pawel Zalewski, who met in Paris. He said their Patriot and IRIS-T stocks can be replenished from future deliveries contracted for Ukraine with foreign funding.
Khmara floated a similar proposal for advance deliveries of Patriots last month. Kiev also accused Washington of delaying deliveries of the interceptors. US officials cited the competing military needs of their own forces and denied any change in policy toward Ukraine.
The five countries’ joint statement made no commitment to supply additional interceptors, though they reiterated their support for Ukraine “by all available means – politically, militarily and financially.”
Poland and the Netherlands have said they have no Patriot missiles to spare; Greece has warned that aid must not undermine its own defenses. Germany, a key donor, has pledged additional older PAC-2 interceptors from its military stocks. Other European countries have reportedly held back PAC-3 missiles to preserve their own reserves.
The shortage comes amid an escalating exchange of long-range strikes. Kiev intensified drone attacks on Russian oil refineries and retail warehouses over the summer in what Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky called a “40-day pressure campaign.” Russia has said its increased strikes on Ukrainian targets are retaliation. Ukrainian forces are struggling to intercept Russian ballistic missiles and faster, jet-powered long-range drones.
Kiev is also seeking additional financial support after overspending this year. Zelensky has asked European donors for at least €70 billion ($78 billion) to cover military and budget needs; Western governments are struggling to agree on how to finance additional aid.
The EU, which borrowed €90 billion ($100 billion) last year to prop up the government in Kiev for 2026-2027, is facing tensions among member states, with the Czech Republic, Hungary, and Slovakia saying they won’t take part in a potential new loan proposed by the European Commission.

Benelli shotgun gets Israeli computerized anti-drone sight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:42:31 UTC
18:42:31 KST

- SMARTSHOOTER has integrated its SMASH computerized fire control sight with a Benelli shotgun, adding a new weapon type to the system’s range.
- SMASH tracks a designated target and releases the shot only when a hit is likely, helping troops engage small, fast-moving drones.
Israeli company SMARTSHOOTER has fitted its SMASH computerized fire control sight to a Benelli shotgun, taking a system best known for helping soldiers shoot down small drones with rifles and putting it on a weapon that fires spreads of pellets at close range.
The company announced the integration this week, saying it shows the flexibility of the SMASH design across different weapons and operational requirements, but it did not say which Benelli model was used, whether the pairing has been tested against drones or other targets, or whether any military or police customer requested it.
SMASH sights work differently from a normal optic, because the shooter marks a target and the onboard software tracks it, calculates a firing solution and releases the shot only when it judges that the chance of a hit meets its programmed threshold, which is meant to help troops hit small, fast-moving drones that are hard to engage with iron sights or a standard scope.
U.S. forces already train with the rifle version, and in February 2026 U.S. soldiers, airmen and Marines, along with Belgian troops, qualified with the SMASH 2000 at Grafenwoehr in Germany during the U.S. Air Force’s Joint Multi-Domain Counter Unmanned Aircraft Systems Operator Course.
SMARTSHOOTER has steadily moved the technology onto heavier and larger weapons, and during the UK-U.S. Project VANAHEIM/FLYTRAP trials in 2025 it mounted the SMASH 3000 on a heavy machine gun for the first time, with the systems reportedly intercepting drones at ranges of up to 400 meters (1,312 feet), while its SMASH Hopper remotely controlled weapon station was fitted to a reconnaissance vehicle.
Benelli Armi, the Italian shotgun maker based in Urbino, builds semi-automatic shotguns used by military and law enforcement units around the world, including the M4 model adopted by the U.S. Marine Corps as the M1014, although SMARTSHOOTER did not identify the Benelli shotgun shown in its announcement.
