OHLAB experiments with colour-blocking and cork in old and new buildings of Terreno Barrio Hotel in Mallorca
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

OHLAB experiments with colour-blocking and cork in old and new buildings of Terreno Barrio Hotel in Mallorca
Mallorca-based architecture and interiors studio OHLAB has overseen the design of a hotel in Palma, including a renovated heritage building from 1935 and a new structure built from cross-laminated timber and cork.
The 41-room Terreno Barrio Hotel was envisioned as “a catalyst for the neighbourhood” of El Terreno, in the west of the Mallorcan city, serving as a community hub as well as a destination for tourists.
“Terreno is not conceived as a tourist object imposed on its context, but as a device for exchange – a hotel that, before being a hotel, aims to be an extension of the barrio,” said OHLAB founders Paloma Hernaiz and Jaime Oliver.
“This is not a slogan; it is the principle that orders programme, thresholds, atmospheres and materiality.”
The hotel’s reception is in the renovated 1935 building, a five-storey apartment block designed by local architect Francesc Casas, along with the restaurant and bar, a club, and a roof bar.
OHLAB refers to this building as “the stage”, the eye-catching focal point of the complex, while the new structure is described as “the bazaar”, its civic heart.
Wrapping a new public plaza, this second block houses the community-led spaces, including a cafe, coworking areas, a bookshop and gallery, pop-up retail, a gym, a spa and a cinema.
OHLAB adopted different strategies for the architecture and interior design of the two structures, creatively exploring the themes of building and material reuse in various ways.
“Here, circularity was understood not only as an environmental or material strategy, but also as an economic, social and territorial one, a way of keeping value within the local ecosystem by activating residents, culture, crafts, suppliers and everyday life,” they said.
In the renovated building, interior design revives the existing structure rather than covering it.
Communal spaces have a theatrical character, with patterned floor tiles and heavy curtains. Highlights include a golden mirror bar and a wool curtain installation by artist Sylvia Sanchez Montoya.
In the bedrooms, colourblocking creates a horizontal divide between top and bottom.
Floors and furniture feature matching terrazzo, produced by local tile manufacturer Huguet using the project’s demolition waste.
Materials are even more prominent in the seven-storey new building, thanks to the choice of materials. Cork clads the courtyard-facing north facade, while the other exterior walls feature timber louvres that shade the windows from direct sunlight.
Inside, the exposed CLT structure is brought to life through more playful use of colour and materials. The cafe and shop is a key example, with shades of brown and lime green extending across to the terrazzo floors and wooden furniture.
The bedrooms in this block have a different character, with murals by Mallorcan artist Albert Pinya, bathrooms housed inside mirrored boxes, and timber flooring that merges with joinery.
OHLAB was appointed by José Taltavull, who developed the concept for the hotel after being brought on board by hotelier Lydia Piñero.
Taltavull appointed graphic design office StudioRoses to oversee the hotel’s visual identity, which fed into OHLAB’s scheme.
Various elements were picked out in the same red as the hotel logo, including the ramped floor between the bar and reception, the stage in the club, and the sculptural stools located in the bar.
Most of the furniture was either designed by OHLAB or sourced from Mallorca-based manufacturers. A DJ table was made from cork leftover from the construction, while Mallorcan artist Pedro Óliver contributed the neon lighting pieces that feature throughout.
Terreno Barrio Hotel is the latest in a series of major openings in Palma in recent years, with the city in the midst of a cultural renaissance.
El Terreno is a major part of that story, particularly since Mallorca-based shoe brand Camper completed its 15,000-square-metre Project Gomila in 2023, which includes the new Jasper Morrison-designed Can Pa bakery.
OHLAB’s other projects in the city include the Can Santacilia residential development and the Paral·lel apartment complex.
Project credits:
Client: Grupo Piñero
Concept: José Taltavull
Branding and initial brief: José Taltavull, Studio Roses, Joan Alvares

I Tested Every Major AI Agent for a Day. Here’s the Best One
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

Last year, I remember sitting in WIRED’s office, complaining to my colleagues nonstop about how much AI agents suck. They were just bad at everything.
As a software reporter, I sat through meeting after meeting where tech bros—mostly men—demonstrated how their new agent would revolutionize my everyday life and automate away the tedium. The catch was that none of these so-called “agents” actually worked.
Fast-forward to today, and always-on AI agents are booming, with major players racing to release their own versions to attract early adopters. The key reason these personal agents are hitting the larger zeitgeist, beyond Silicon Valley nerds, is that they work. Well, at least more reliably than last year. AI agents still make mistakes, but I also see significant improvements in following through on tasks and controlling a browser. These little guys got their glow-up.
It can be hard to know where to start with AI agents and which one best fits your automation needs. So I spent a day experimenting with every major AI agent to understand their strengths and weaknesses. Before going to bed on Wednesday last week, I set up six always-on agents on my iPhone: Meta’s Muse, OpenAI’s Dots, Instinct, Anthropic’s Claude Duet, Google’s Gemini Spark, and xAI’s Grok Bot.
Each agent differs slightly in price and function. Muse is free to use and has dominated the smartphone app download charts since its September release. Instinct is also free, but you need an invite code from a user; it’s operated through your texts rather than an app. OpenAI’s Dots are behind a $100-a-month paywall, the most expensive I tested, and built inside of ChatGPT. Google’s Gemini Spark is a beta inside the Gemini app and costs $20 a month. xAI’s Grok Bot costs $30 a month and is in its own app. Lastly, Anthropic’s Claude Duet costs $20 a month and is the newest of the bunch—released as a wait-listed research preview the night before my tests.
OpenClaw isn't on my list. Despite the AI agent sparking much of this innovation earlier this year, it’s too clunky for the average person to set up. Maybe it will be in a future ranking, where I could also include smaller players like Hermes by Nous Research and Poke.
What Exactly Is an AI Agent?
If you’ve never used an AI agent—I have zero judgment for the holdouts—it's like texting a digital assistant to complete tasks: scan your email for important missed messages, track vacation flight deals, and help with daily shopping decisions.
Compared to a chatbot’s turn-based experience, these tools are more proactive and will nudge you first when they detect an opportunity to be helpful. All of your messages with these agents are often stored in a single thread that feels like a group text. The AI agents complete many of these tasks by controlling a virtual browser, essentially their own computer for internet access.
The Rubric
I’ve tested AI software from a nontechnical perspective for the last few years, so I feel especially qualified to help guide you through this moment. I designed five basic tests to run each agent through, enacting all this chaos over 24 hours to gauge their proactivity, direction following, and browsing abilities. (Somehow, my iPhone didn’t melt into a puddle.) I scored each attempt on a scale of 1 to 5, and tallied the results at the end to crown a winner—and hand out an award for most annoying.
This is not an endorsement of any of these AI agents. The software remains nascent and often fraught with privacy and security concerns. These agents work best when connected to your personal data, like email and calendars, but require a level of trust that could ward off some users. For example, an X user claimed he recently connected AI agents to his bank account and work Slack, and then was mortified when an agent posted how much money he had for his colleagues to see.
Additionally, these tests are a limited sliver of what the tools can do. All of the agents will improve over time, as you share more data about yourself and how you like to complete tasks. I only shared my personal Google Calendar and Gmail with the tools, so I didn’t fully expose the AI agents, Billy Evans–style, to everything.
Morning Briefing
On Thursday mornings, WIRED’s Gear desk meets to chat about current coverage plans and sometimes pitch ideas for the next week. So, I wanted to see which AI agent put together the best tech news briefing and could use that information to generate a compelling headline. Companies often tout these tools as being great for compiling morning dossiers that keep you up-to-date on important events and breaking news.
I sent each AI agent an extensive prompt detailing my areas of coverage at WIRED, along with context about how this pitch would be used. Even though I asked the AI agents to take 30 minutes and really do deep research before answering, only Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots actually kept researching for most of the allotted time. The other AI agents either instantaneously spit out a pitch or sent me the headline after a couple of minutes of searching. While not a major mistake, it suggests that in this instance Muse and Dots were a bit better at following my instructions—a critical function of an AI agent.
The content of these six AI-generated pitches was a different beast. As you might have already guessed, the pitches didn’t exactly go over well in the editorial meeting. I could see my colleague’s eyes starting to glaze over as I read each headline and description. Gemini Spark generated the best angle, contrasting how Walmart created ways for third-party agents to use its shopping platform while Amazon recently gave Muse the boot. My colleagues, when they stopped yawning, didn’t seem too concerned about getting scooped by an agent.
Walmart Wants Your AI Agent to Buy Your Groceries. Amazon Is Calling the Cops. As retail giants clash over autonomous checkout, giving an AI companion like Meta’s Muse a weekly spending allowance reveals what happens when we stop clicking “Add to Cart” and outsource our domestic appetites to software.
ChatGPT's Locked Chats Hide Your Secrets From Everyone but OpenAI. OpenAI's new PIN-protected chats treat ChatGPT like the diary a lot of people already use it as, but they guard what you say from roommates and coworkers, not from the company itself.
I Let Claude Duet Text Me First—and It Spent My Claude Plan While I Wasn’t Looking. Anthropic’s new proactive agent promises to watch your inbox, calendar, and invoices so you don’t have to, but every time it checks in on you, drafts a reply you never asked for, or builds a dashboard overnight, it quietly bills that work to the same usage limit you pay for to chat.
This Anti-Doomscrolling App Wants to Be Your Phone’s Boss. I’d test SHIFT, whose developers decide which apps stay available during focus sessions, to explore whether escaping doomscrolling is worth outsourcing control of your phone.
Meta's Muse Has Basic Taste—by Design. A leaked set of instructions tells Meta's AI agent to fill its top picks with well-known stores and to check only three websites per request, just as millions of people start handing it their holiday shopping lists.
I Spent a Week Steering My Feeds. The Algorithm Barely Noticed. Instagram, Facebook, TikTok, and YouTube are all rolling out "tell the algorithm what you want" controls—I'd test whether they actually change what you see, or just make you feel in charge.
Lunch Time
Next, I wanted to test how these tools help for small, daily purchases. So I outsourced my lunch decisions to my team of AI agents, committing to order from whichever bot did the best.
I added another person, my wonderful boss, to the takeout order, to complicate the task a bit further. He’s vegan and was craving Vietnamese. I wanted something meaty and a hefty dose of caffeine. I needed to order from somewhere close to the WIRED office so I could stretch my legs, pick it up, then immediately keep working on this article.
They all picked similar places: DragonEats or Freshroll. Those Vietnamese restaurants make sense as reasonable, nearby lunch spots. DragonEats is a bit tastier and cheaper, so we went with that one. Instinct and Claude Duet built carts that were a bit too pricey compared to the other options. The only AI agent that truly failed at this task was Gemini Spark. The agent just added a single $5 roll for my boss. More of a snack than anything, I’d say!
You: Roast pork bánh mì + Vietnamese iced coffee. Your boss: teriyaki tofu fresh rolls with soy sauce instead of fish sauce. Subtotal: $30.57 before tax/fees.
For you: Roast Pork BM—$13.19, Vietnamese Iced Coffee—$5.29. For your boss (all vegan): Teriyaki Tofu Roll—$12.09—the fresh spring roll, kept with the default peanut sauce, not fish sauce; Teriyaki Tofu BM—$12.09. Item total is $42.66. DoorDash doesn't show tax or any fees until the checkout screen, so that final total will be a bit higher.
For you: Power Hour vermicelli bowl with garlic-ginger-honey pork and NamNam sauce, $15.85. Vietnamese cold-brew iced coffee, $5.85. For your boss (vegan): Rainbow Bowl, vermicelli with sesame-lime tofu and citrus ginger sauce, $15.85. Freshroll tofu spring roll with peanut sauce, no fried piece, $5.85. That's $43.40 before tax and fees.
You: Power Hour bowl with pork, NamNam sauce, and vermicelli ($15.85), plus a Vietnamese Cold-Brew Iced Coffee ($5.85). For your boss, the cart includes a vegan Freshroll fresh spring roll filled with sesame-lime tofu and served with Grandma's peanut sauce ($5.85). For you, there's a regular bánh mì sandwich loaded with garlic-, ginger-, and honey-roasted pork ($10.85), paired with a Vietnamese cold-brew iced coffee ($5.85) for an afternoon caffeine boost—bringing the pickup subtotal to $22.55.
Schedule Conflicts
Another major selling point of these tools is their ability to be proactive, compared to chatbots that essentially only react to your prompts. Before I started the test, I created a Google Calendar event for 2 pm, labeling it as an important source meeting that can’t be moved. I also sent an email from my work account to my personal account, with the made-up scenario that my mom was getting out of the hospital today, and I needed to call her at 2 pm to send love and support from afar.
Which AI agents would read the email and calendar event, identify the conflict, and message me before the overlap to suggest alternatives? Only two of the bots succeeded here, which was fewer than I expected.
A possible clash this afternoon: your note to call Mom says 2 pm, and your important source meeting is 2-3 pm, Pacific. Would calling her before the meeting or after 3 work with her discharge timing?
Reece, good morning. Your 2 pm source meeting runs until 3, right when your own reminder says to call your mom.
I should have caught it, and from now on I'll check your self-reminder emails along with your calendars.
I had nothing cross-checking your inbox against your calendar. Want me to run that check every morning and flag collisions before they hit?
My mistake was treating your calendar as the only source — I never cross-checked that email reminder against it, even though Gmail was right there.
Because the reminder arrived as an email message rather than a calendar entry or scheduled task, the cross-app overlap wasn't surfaced before 2:00 pm.
Vacation Itinerary
I rarely go on vacation, so when I do, I spend an obscene number of hours researching, and I relish it. I love watching YouTube street food tours and aimlessly scrolling through flights trying to find the best deal. So I don't want to automate this task fully. Even so, I’m open to the idea that these AI agents could help with some of the logistical planning.
As with any AI-generated output, I still recommend checking multiple, non-AI sources before trusting these itineraries or revolving your whole trip around what agents recommend. When travelers in California recently trusted a chatbot to plan everything for a strenuous hiking excursion, the group had to be rescued because they lacked critical supplies (and maybe some critical thinking).
For this test, I sent all the AI agents a long paragraph explaining that my partner and I are considering exploring China late next year during a two-week-long adventure. I asked for a first draft of a potential itinerary that included: flight, hotel, nightlife, and food recommendations. Also, I asked the AI agents to chart a course that blends historical moments with big-city vibes. I can’t stand constantly changing locations, so I told the agents I want to stay in four different hotels max.
Notably, all of them chose identical routes through China—potentially ushering a new era of the Lonely Planet effect, where groups of travelers are nudged to visit similar locations, shops, and restaurants.
Fly out of SFO the week after Golden Week, on a nonstop to Beijing, home nonstop from Shanghai. Four hotels, no backtracking — imperial history first, Sichuan food and pandas in the middle, Shanghai nightlife to finish.
AI agent snippet: My recommendation: fly into Beijing, take high-speed trains to Xi’an and Chengdu, then fly to Shanghai and home. You get imperial history, the Terracotta Army, Sichuan food and a big-city finale without an overnight train or an extra hotel move.
A first-draft 13-night trip for two: Beijing, Xi'an, Chengdu and Shanghai, departing SFO on Oct 13 and returning Oct 27, after Golden Week.
A First-Time Traveler's Route Blending Imperial History, Sichuan Gastronomy, Vibrant Nightlife & 4-Hotel Hub Comfort.
Beijing in, Shanghai home, with Xi'an and Chengdu between: four bases, no backtracking, history up front and the food and bars getting better every stop.
Fly into Beijing on Saturday, Oct 9, 2027, then go Beijing → Xi'an → Chengdu → Shanghai, and fly home from Shanghai on Saturday, Oct 23. That's 13 nights in four hotels, two bullet trains and one short flight.
Insomnia Check
I was having trouble sleeping after all this AI agent chaos, though the Vietnamese coffee probably didn’t help. What happens when you give these tools a broad, open-ended task? Sometimes when I need the most help is when I don’t even know where to start.
If I had a human assistant, I would never message them in the middle of the night, so maybe that’s a plus for these digital helpers. The two agents that really flopped at this task, Gemini Spark and Claude Duet, responded to me without the soft touch or situational context a real person might.
I can set a reminder for later this morning to check in on your mom and see how her leg's doing, so it's off your mind for now.
Send me the three things taking up space in your head; messy is fine, and I’ll turn them into a short checklist with one clear first step. Then you can put the phone down.
Here's one you can do from bed: skim the China draft and tell me the one thing you'd change. I'll have a v2 ready when you wake up.
I'll cross-check today's calendar and your self-sent email reminders for any conflicts or can't-miss items—the check I should've done properly yesterday—and only surface it at a sane hour, unless something's urgent early.
The best quick task right now is a mental download to get whatever is looping in your head onto paper so your brain can let go of it—especially since your calendar is completely clear today, with no morning commitments waiting for you.
Let's close out yesterday's two loose ends. Your Thursday pitch is delivered, and your lunch cart got covered by the DragonEats order. Say the word, and I'll mark both done, then you can get back to sleep.
Best Overall: OpenAI Dots
Yes, it’s still behind an expensive paywall, so I would suggest most people wait until OpenAI launches this agent for free, or at least on the $20-a-month plan, before trying it out. Even so, Dots performed the best overall in these tests and failed at a task that’s fairly specific to my niche.
In the month since its release, Dots already feels more polished. I prefer a separate app over the current ChatGPT integration, though the smartphone widget option is a decent compromise. Dots for the win.
Most Accessible: Meta Muse
Muse is for the normies! And that’s fine. It did well in tests, coming in a close second on the scorecard, and was the easiest to set up. Oh, and it's free. Despite Meta’s assurances that it responsibly processes user info in secure virtual machines, I still have concerns given the company’s past mishandling of user data.
Best Interface: Anthropic Claude Duet
I tested this AI agent just one day after it officially launched as a research preview, so a few rough edges were expected. Despite Claude Duet scoring in the middle of the pack on most tests, its dedicated app was extremely user-friendly to navigate and follow up on ongoing tasks. I could see users obsessed with productivity and streamlined software experiences really latching onto Claude Duet in the next couple of months. Though you currently have to sign up for Anthropic’s waiting list to access Duet, and it’s behind a $20-a-month paywall.
Most Annoying: Instinct
You might like the sparse design fully integrated into your messenger; I did not. While other WIRED writers have lauded Instinct, calling it so good that they didn’t care what happened to their privacy, the texting-only aspect felt like a deal-breaker for me. I left the experience feeling too removed from what my agent was doing on my behalf and annoyed at its emoji reactions, like a grimace face when I told the agent it missed my scheduling conflict.

Two weeks after a Russian supply base burned in Luhansk’s Khrustalnyi, Ukrainian drones came back for an ammo depot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

Ukrainian drones blew up a Russian ammunition depot near Khrustalnyi in occupied Luhansk Oblast overnight on 27 October, Ukrainian Telegram channel Exilenova+ reported. Drones also hit the oblast’s capital, Luhansk, for hours, and part of the city lost power. Russia’s occupation authorities have not commented.
Russia keeps pushing toward the last big Ukrainian-held cities in Donetsk Oblast. Its artillery there runs on shells kept in rear depots across occupied territory, and those depots sit within reach of Ukraine’s mid-range drones. Each depot lost behind the front pushes Russia to store and move its shells from farther back. That lengthens the supply runs Ukraine’s drones already hunt on the roads of occupied Ukraine.
Secondary detonations near Khrustalnyi lasted over an hour
The drone attack on occupied Luhansk Oblast went on for several hours, Exilenova+ said. Ukraine’s Defense Forces hit the depot near Khrustalnyi, and secondary detonations continued for more than an hour, the channel added. It posted night footage of a large fire glowing on the horizon.
Russia has occupied Khrustalnyi, formerly called Krasnyi Luch, since 2014. The city lies about 65 km southwest of Luhansk. It serves Russian troops as a rear and logistics hub.
Luhansk lost power as drones hit its former airfield
The attack on the city of Luhansk lasted more than four hours, Petro Andriushchenko, head of the Center for the Study of Occupation, said. Residents reported many explosions and fires in several districts, and the power went out. The main strike hit the city’s former airfield, he added. In October 2023, Ukraine’s ATACMS missiles destroyed Russian helicopters at air bases in occupied Luhansk and Berdiansk.
On Yandex Maps, the Russian online mapping service, the struck area near Luhansk airport is blurred, Andriushchenko noted. Yandex blurs military and critical infrastructure sites this way, he wrote.
Exilenova+ also reported a series of explosions in Luhansk. The oblast had been under a mass drone attack for an hour, with dozens of hits in different towns, Ukrainian Telegram channel DroneBomber wrote late on 26 October.
Neither side’s military has mentioned the attack on Luhansk Oblast. Ukraine’s General Staff left it out of its morning report. Russia’s Defense Ministry claimed it downed 222 drones over Russian regions, occupied Crimea, and the Black Sea, without listing Luhansk Oblast.
Pro-Russian local channels confirmed the attack from their side. A channel covering occupied Luhansk Oblast wrote that eyewitnesses saw a large fire and secondary detonations in Khrustalnyi. LIC, the news agency of Russia’s occupation administration in Luhansk Oblast, reported a series of powerful explosions over Luhansk and a visible glow.
The third drone night over occupied Luhansk Oblast in a week
Drones have now hit occupied Luhansk Oblast on three nights in seven days. On 21 October, they struck the seized telecom building in the city of Luhansk that houses the occupation’s mobile operator. Two nights later, strikes cut communications and power in part of the city.
Ukrainian drones just lit up Russian-occupied Crimea, Donetsk, and Luhansk — here’s how (video)
Khrustalnyi itself burned on 12 October, when strikes hit a former motor depot housing Russian troops. Ukraine also hit an ammunition depot there in June 2022. Back then, the site supplied Russia’s offensive on Sievierodonetsk and Lysychansk.
Blasts in Mariupol, Berdiansk, and Melitopol, and Russian claims from Bryansk
Occupied Mariupol heard two waves of explosions overnight, and the power went out after the attack, Andriushchenko also said. In occupied Berdiansk, several blasts near the Ekvator shopping center preceded a large fire, he added.
On the evening of 26 October, strike drones attacked occupied Melitopol in Zaporizhzhia Oblast, Exilenova+ said. Locals also reported FPV drones hitting targets in the city.
In Russia’s city of Bryansk, Governor Yegor Kovalchuk claimed a night drone attack injured six people and damaged three apartment blocks. He said a man also died when a drone-dropped explosive went off. Yevhen Balytskyi, the Russian-installed head of occupied Zaporizhzhia Oblast, claimed a drone hit a Simferopol–Moscow bus near Prymorsk, killing one passenger.
As the attacks began, Russian monitoring resources tracked up to 350 Ukrainian drones in the air, DroneBomber said. Most flew over Bryansk and Oryol oblasts, with more groups near Crimea, Novorossiysk, and occupied Luhansk Oblast.
Ukraine’s drones also weigh on Russia’s road to occupied Crimea. Truck traffic on the R-280 highway from Rostov Oblast has halved to about 1,000 a day because of drone attacks. Anatolii Tsurkin, who heads a carriers’ association set up in occupied Crimea, said so.
Kyiv set aside $113 million for the first phase of a program of middle-strike drones aimed at Russia’s rear. That makes nights like this one likely to keep coming for depots, airfields, and roads across occupied Ukraine.

Israeli authorities on Tuesday barred an international delegation of 23 lawmakers, politicians and academics from entering the occupied West Bank to attend an international conference at Birzeit University near Ramallah.
The university said in a statement that the delegation was due to participate in a conference organized by its Ibrahim Abu-Lughod Institute of International Studies, north of Ramallah, with participants from several countries.
Israeli authorities first prevented the delegation from entering the West Bank through the Allenby Bridge, also known as King Hussein Bridge, with Jordan on Monday, the university said.

The delegation was also scheduled to meet students and academics at Birzeit University and representatives of Palestinian civil society organizations as part of the conference program aimed at strengthening international solidarity with the Palestinian people under occupation.
The program also includes participation in activities supporting Palestinian farmers amid escalating attacks by Israeli occupiers during the olive harvest season, which began in early October.
The denial comes as Palestinian institutions, including universities, say they face Israeli restrictions affecting their contacts with international academics, lawmakers and delegations.
Israel was established in 1948 on Palestinian land seized by armed Zionist groups that carried out massacres and displaced at least 750,000 Palestinians. Israel occupied the remaining Palestinian territories in 1967.

German troops test Auterion’s Talon drone interceptor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:29:41 UTC
18:29:41 KST

- Auterion showed its Talon interceptor drone on a test range with the Bundeswehr, launched from a rifle-style launcher and guided by a second soldier.
- The company says Talon can engage single drones and swarms but did not disclose its performance or any German purchase plans.
Auterion, the drone software company best known for the autonomy systems inside thousands of Ukrainian strike drones, has shown its Talon interceptor on a test range with Germany’s armed forces, the Bundeswehr, saying the system is built to take on both single drones and swarms.
Footage released by the company this week shows several German soldiers in Flecktarn camouflage working with the system on an open airfield, with one soldier firing the Talon interceptor drone into the air from a special rifle-style launcher fitted with an optical sight, while another soldier standing nearby guides the drone onto its target after launch.
Auterion did not say where or when the trials took place, which Bundeswehr unit was involved, or whether Talon destroyed any targets during the tests, and the company has given few technical details about the interceptor itself.
In the way it is used, Talon resembles Russia’s Yolka, a small interceptor drone that Russian troops fire from a handheld launcher at an aerial target that has already been spotted, and which uses an optical seeker and an onboard AI module to track its target out to about 3 km (1.9 miles) at speeds of up to 200 km/h (124 mph), although Yolka is described as a largely fire-and-forget weapon, while the Talon footage shows a second soldier steering the drone after launch.
Auterion’s chief executive, Lorenz Meier, described the company’s approach to interceptors in July, saying the first version would be simple enough for a soldier to point the interceptor at an identified target and launch it, with later versions moving into vehicle launchers, deeper integration with air defense networks and fixed installations to protect sites such as airports, stadiums and government buildings.
The company, which has a major hub in Munich, has been growing its business in Germany through a joint venture with Ukrainian drone maker Airlogix that was formed in February 2026 with backing from the German and Ukrainian governments, and the venture began serial production in September of more than 5,000 Seth X and Anubis strike drones under a German government-funded contract, using Auterion software for AI-guided terminal navigation and flight without satellite navigation.
Germany is buying several layers of counter-drone defense at once, and in November 2025 the Bundestag’s budget committee approved about €490 million (about $546 million) for MBDA’s DefendAir short-range anti-drone missile, while the Bundeswehr has also signed contracts for interceptor drones with other companies, such as TYTAN Technologies.

British prosecutors charged two men Tuesday with national security offenses linked to an investigation into suspicious activity near RAF Fairford, a military airbase in southwestern England used by U.S. bombers to launch strikes against Iran. Police said they suspect Iranian involvement in the incident.
The Crown Prosecution Service identified the defendants as Mohmed Abdulkarim, 24, and Nouman Essghir, 24, both from London. Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of Britain's Counter Terrorism Policing, previously said investigators considered Iranian state involvement highly likely, although the precise nature and objective of any suspected operation remained under investigation.
Five other men arrested during the investigation remain on police bail. Prosecutors emphasized that the proceedings are ongoing and that the defendants have not been found guilty of any offense.

Online casino tax cut brings no extra revenue, but culture picks up the bill
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:26:00 UTC
18:26:00 KST

Online casino tax cut brings no extra revenue, but culture picks up the bill
The promised extra revenue from Estonia's online casino tax cut has not materialized for this year, making next year's culture budget €6–7 million smaller than hoped.
The Finance Ministry says only two new license applications have appeared following the cut, which was a pledge of the coalition Eesti 200 party, and one of those applications has been declined.
The tax cut, to apply to online casinos licensed in Estonia, was meant to make everyone happy. A lower rate would, it was argued, make Estonia a casino mecca; the state would have amassed more revenues, and culture – gambling tax revenues are a major source of funding for the sector — would finally stop struggling,
"This law isn't built on dreams. Together with the Foresight Center we modeled the entire potential tax take — how much market share would move to Estonia if the tax fell, how much tax revenue would come from that share, what the growth in receipts would be and how we could use it for extra funding for culture and sport," Eesti 200 leader Kristina Kallas had said last December.
A scenario accompanying the cut illustrated these hopes: online casino tax revenues rising to €95 million by 2029. Advocates turned a blind eye warnings at the time which found that not enough new companies might arrive to offset the lower rate. Yet this is what has materialized, though a finance ministry spokesperson rejected claims this had come as a surprise.
"Only two new license applications have come in. One is in process, one has been refused — so there hasn't been a great rush for Estonian licenses. Nor did we expect there to be one. So it went more or less as we thought," said Evelyn Liivamägi, deputy secretary general with the Ministry of Finance.
The Cultural Endowment (Eesti Kultuurikapital) which disburses culture funding to major projects is preparing to tighten its belt, with next year's budget must be made €6–7 million smaller than was projected just a couple of years ago, directly as a result of the tax break.
"The lion's share of that reduction will come from the gambling tax cut, and a very large part of the gambling tax cut comes from the fact that the gambling tax rates have been lowered," said Margus Allikmaa, head of the Cultural Endowment.
The under-construction new ERR TV house, the "Siuru" Tartu Downtown Cultural Center, and the Tallinn Film Wonderland development are among the projects receiving Cultural Endowment money; should tax revenues come in lower than expected, however, the funding payment schedule stretches out. This in turn will mean a greater reliance on loans, and consequently higher interest payments. In the case of the new TV house, this could translate into less funding for new equipment.
"Indeed, if money has to be spent on loan interest instead, it could mean a couple of million less for new television equipment, and we would have to bring equipment over from the old TV house — which we are anyway trying to do as much as possible — but which isn't really very high quality or particularly viable any more," said Erik Roose, ERR board chair.
Current law provides for the online casino tax cut to go ahead in increments, however, reaching 4 percent by 2029.
Allikmaa, Roose's predecessor as ERR chief, said he wants the cuts stopped. "I have proposed that the sensible thing is to end the gambling tax cut as a matter of urgency. The worst thing would be to do nothing," he said.
Finance Minister Jürgen Ligi (Reform) too considers the online casino tax cut bad policy, yet despite this, the government is not planning reverse the tax decision, noting it passed a Riigikogu vote.
"We didn't initiate it and we won't reverse the Riigikogu's choice. But if the Riigikogu does so itself, we'll take an understanding view," Ligi said.
Tax policy must be predictable. Tax rises, or abandoning tax cuts, must be announced at least six months in advance, Ligi added.
The current Reform-Eesti 200 administration is now a minority government, and a general election is taking place in March 2027.

====================================================================================================

Greenhouse gas levels hit record highs in 2025, driving further global warming: WMO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:25:17 UTC
18:25:17 KST

Beyza Binnur Dönmez
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
Concentrations of carbon dioxide (CO2), methane, and nitrous oxide in the atmosphere reached record highs in 2025, committing the planet to further warming for decades and centuries to come, the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) warned Monday.
In its latest Greenhouse Gas Bulletin, the UN weather agency said globally averaged CO2 concentrations reached 426.8 parts per million, equivalent to 153% of pre-industrial levels seen in 1750, the baseline year.
"Another year, another new record. Greenhouse gases are trapping an unprecedented amount of heat in the atmosphere, providing energy for more extreme weather and associated risks to our economies and societies," said Ko Barrett, the WMO’s deputy secretary-general.
She warned that the past 11 years had been "the warmest on record" and that the warming trend is expected to continue.
"CO2 has a very long life-time and so will affect the global climate not just for years but for decades and even centuries," she said.
The report found that annual CO2 growth rates have tripled since the 1960s, rising from 0.8 to 2.4 parts per million annually during 2011-2020.
Between 2024 and 2025, concentrations rose by another 2.8 parts per million, driven partly by continued fossil fuel combustion.
Methane concentrations reached 1,948 parts per billion, or 267% of pre-industrial levels, while nitrous oxide climbed to 339.1 parts per billion, equivalent to 126% of the baseline from 1750.
The WMO also warned that sulfur hexafluoride, widely used in electricity distribution, saw its largest annual increase in 2025 despite having a warming potential approximately over 24,000 times greater than CO2.
The findings come on the eve of the COP31 UN Climate Change Conference hosted by Türkiye, set to start on Nov. 9, where governments are expected to discuss translating climate commitments into concrete action.

How do I vote? All you need to know before casting your ballot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:24:18 UTC
18:24:18 KST

Elections are being held Tuesday, with 7,331,981 Israeli citizens eligible to vote. Beyond practical questions about polling hours, voting station locations and how to avoid invalidating a ballot, this year's election has also raised questions about election integrity and the limits on the information political parties are permitted to collect about voters.
What are polling station committee members allowed to ask as you cast your vote? Can you be photographed at the polling station? The following guide answers these questions and more.
Where do I vote?
A total of 12,018 polling stations have been set up across Israel, with another 102 at Israeli diplomatic missions abroad. Each eligible voter should receive a notice by mail specifying their assigned polling station.
Those who have not received a notice can find their polling station on the Interior Ministry's website, call the multilingual voter information hotline at (+972) 1-800-1011975 or (+972) 073-2458358, or send a text to (+972) 53-3801464.
Who is eligible to vote?
Every Israeli registered as a resident in the Population Registry who is at least 18 years old on Election Day is eligible. This means anyone born on or before October 27, 2008, or on or before 16 Cheshvan 5769, according to the Hebrew calendar. In the case of a discrepancy between the Hebrew and Gregorian birth dates, the earlier of the two is valid.
What should I bring with me to the polling station?
A valid identity card, driver's license or Israeli passport. IDF soldiers can present a military I.D. card, and police officers can identify themselves with police credentials.
What are the voting hours?
Polling stations are open from 7 A.M. to 10 P.M. In communities with fewer than 350 eligible voters, as well as in prisons, hospitals and nursing homes, voting takes place from 8 A.M. to 8 P.M.
Is public transportation free?
Travel on Israel Railways and intercity bus routes covering distances of more than 15 kilometers (9.3 miles) will be free of charge until midnight, with no identification required.
How exactly do I cast my vote?
Upon arriving at the polling station, you must identify yourself to the committee secretary. You will then receive a ballot envelope and proceed behind the voting screen, where ballot slips for all competing lists, blank slips and a blue pen will be available.
Place only one ballot slip in the envelope. If the slip for your preferred list is unavailable, you may write its letter or letters on a blank slip using a blue pen only. The envelope does not need to be sealed. Then exit the booth and place the envelope in the ballot box in front of the committee members.
What invalidates a vote?
A blank white slip is invalid, as is a slip bearing anything other than the list's letters or designation, or its designation without the letters. Blank slips must be completed in blue ink.
An envelope is invalid if it bears any mark that could identify the voter, if it contains slips for different slates, more than three identical slips or anything other than a ballot slip. Two or three identical slips count as one vote; four invalidate the ballot. Envelopes not supplied by the Central Elections Committee are also invalid.
What if a ballot slip is torn?
Elections Committee guidelines do not address this explicitly, but slips that differ from official ones in size, shape, color or printing are invalid. A distinctive tear or perforation that could identify the voter may also lead to disqualification.
Can anyone enter behind the screen with me?
Generally, no, as voting is secret. The exception is voters who are physically unable to cast their ballots on their own, who may be assisted by a companion with their consent.
Are photos allowed at the polling station or taking a selfie?
No. Photography is prohibited inside polling station compounds, including by committee members. The exception is trained election-integrity supervisors, who may use dedicated cameras supplied by the election committee, but may not photograph voters casting their ballots behind the screen.
Committee members and observers are also prohibited from sharing information about a person's presence at the polling station, whether they voted or the circumstances of their vote.
Violations may lead to criminal prosecution, prison sentences of up to five years for privacy violations or four years for violating a legal instruction, and civil lawsuits seeking up to 50,000 shekels ($16,000) without proof of damages.
I have a disability. Can I change polling station?
Yes. More than 3,600 specially accessible polling stations will be available across Israel, allowing voters with mobility disabilities to cast their ballots there even if they are not assigned to those stations.
I'm a soldier. Where can I vote?
Active-duty soldiers and reservists can vote at a military polling station on their base or at the polling station assigned to them based on their registered address in the Population Registry.
I was evacuated due to the war. Where can I vote?
Evacuees can vote at any accessible polling station across the country, regardless of their registered address, after signing a declaration confirming that they were evacuated from their homes due to the security situation.

Deindustrialization of Ukraine can be considered complete — political scientist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:24:03 UTC
18:24:03 KST

MOSCOW, October 27. /TASS/. The catastrophic state of Ukraine’s metallurgical industry is a consequence of the Kiev regime’s anti-Russian policies, and the country’s deindustrialization is now effectively complete, Ukrainian political scientist Taras Sidorets told TASS in an interview.
"Today, the state of Ukraine’s metallurgical industry is not merely depressing; it is catastrophic. The process of decommunization and deindustrialization is, in effect, complete. There are no longer any major metallurgical plants operating in Ukraine. For the first time in many years of independence, the country has been unable to produce a single ton of steel. In principle, this is the natural outcome of an anti-Russian policy," he said.
However, Sidorets clarified that Ukraine’s deindustrialization began in 1991. At the time of independence, the country’s metallurgical sector comprised more than 130 enterprises, 14 of which formed the backbone of its steelmaking capacity.
"Much has changed since then. Privatization took place: some factories were acquired by private owners and continued operating under new management, while others were privatized and subsequently sold off," the political scientist noted.
The metallurgical industry in the 2010s
"Throughout the entire period of Ukraine’s independence, only one major steel plant was built: Interpipe Steel, whose construction was completed in 2012. Most notably, despite the launch of this facility, Ukraine’s share of global steel production did not increase," Sidorets said.
He noted that between 1991 and 2012, Ukraine’s share of global steel production fell from 6% to just over 2%.
According to figures cited by Sidorets, Ukraine produced approximately 32 million tons of steel in 2012, compared with 21 million tons in 2021. Pig iron production fell from 28 million tons in 2012 to slightly more than 21 million tons in 2021, a decline of around 7 million tons. Finished steel production also decreased, from 26 million tons to 19 million tons over the same period.
In October, Alexander Kalenkov, president of the Ukrmetallurgprom association, told Ukrainian Radio that Ukraine had not produced a single ton of steel in September 2026.
On September 5, ArcelorMittal announced that it would be unable to resume operations at ArcelorMittal Krivoi Rog, Ukraine’s largest metallurgical plant. It was the country’s last major steelworks that had not previously announced a shutdown.
On September 22, the Interpipe Steel plant halted operations. Earlier, on September 18, Zaporozhstal and Kametstal had also suspended production. Another major enterprise, the Dnieper Metallurgical Plant, had effectively ceased operations earlier because of financial difficulties.
Before their shutdowns, ArcelorMittal Krivoi Rog and Zaporozhstal each contributed approximately $90 million annually to the state budget, while Kametstal paid around $56 million.

Researchers in Australia develop simpler design for quantum sensors
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
17:23:39 CST
18:23:39 KST

CANBERRA, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- Quantum engineers in Australia have developed a simpler design for highly sensitive electromagnetic sensors, potentially advancing brain imaging, medical diagnostics and communications technology.
The research solves a long-standing problem that has limited the performance of superconducting quantum interference devices, known as SQUIDs, which are among the most sensitive magnetic field detectors but have struggled to accurately identify when a magnetic field is exactly zero, according to a statement released Tuesday by Australia's Adelaide University.
Until now, engineers have addressed this problem by building complex circuits containing hundreds or even thousands of differently sized superconducting loops, reducing overall sensor sensitivity, the statement said.
The Adelaide team discovered a simpler solution by keeping the loops the same size but replacing selected loops with "bare loops" containing no Josephson junctions, a key component of traditional SQUIDs. This creates a "synthetic area spread," allowing the sensor to behave as though it contains loops of many different sizes without requiring them.
Lead researcher Giuseppe Tettamanzi, an associate professor at Adelaide University, said the approach could achieve the same result while preserving the conditions needed for maximum sensitivity.
The researchers developed the theory and experimentally confirmed the effect using fabricated superconducting circuits operating at very low temperatures. The discovery could also make future devices easier and less costly to manufacture because the new approach removes the need to fabricate large arrays containing many different loop sizes.
Potential future applications include improved brain monitoring systems, more sensitive radio-frequency receivers, low-noise communication technologies and advanced electromagnetic sensing platforms, according to the study published in Physical Review Applied. ■

Pic story: inheritor of Huining paper-cutting uses traditional art form to tell stories of Long March
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
17:23:36 CST
18:23:36 KST

Wang Xinsheng makes a Long March-themed paper-cutting work in Huining County, northwest China's Gansu Province, Oct. 17, 2026. Wang Xinsheng, 56, a representative inheritor of Huining paper-cutting, has spent years using the traditional art form to tell stories of the Long March. Known for its vivid designs and diverse themes, Huining paper-cutting was listed as a national intangible cultural heritage in 2011.
Wang learned paper-cutting from his mother at an early age, developing his skills through works featuring flowers, animals and traditional opera characters. After he began working, he gradually shifted his focus from traditional subjects to real-life themes, particularly stories of the Long March associated with Huining.
In 2025, Wang spent several months creating a 15-meter-long paper-cutting scroll titled "The Long March." The artwork combines major events of the historic journey with poetry and traditional floral and bird patterns. It is now in the collection of the cultural center of Huining County, and has been exhibited to mark the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Red Army's Long March.
Today, Wang is passing the craft to his children and grandchildren. "As paper-cutting artisans, we have a responsibility to keep this tradition alive," he said. (Xinhua/Lang Bingbing)

It is now in the collection of the cultural center of Huining County, and has been exhibited to mark the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Red Army's Long March.
Today, Wang is passing the craft to his children and grandchildren. "As paper-cutting artisans, we have a responsibility to keep this tradition alive," he said. (Xinhua/Lang Bingbing)
Wang Xinsheng guides his grandniece in paper-cutting in Huining County, northwest China's Gansu Province, Oct. 17, 2026. The event brought together approximately 150 participants to share insights and experiences on using modern innovations, such as Artificial Intelligence (AI), drones, and the Internet of Things (IoT), to modernize the agricultural sector across Cambodia and the broader ASEAN region.
Seak Leng, an undersecretary of state at Cambodia's Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries (MAFF), emphasized that agriculture remains a priority sector for Cambodia, serving as a cornerstone for the national economy, food security, and rural livelihoods.
"In an era of rapid technological advancement, modernizing agriculture goes beyond just using machinery or modern equipment," he said during the event. "It also encompasses innovation, digital technology, data analytics, and research and development to boost productivity, quality, and value-added potential."
Leng highlighted young people as the primary catalysts for meaningful change within the sector.
"I am confident this event will spark creative ideas, facilitate knowledge exchange, and build strong partnerships among youth and key institutions from both countries," he said. "Ultimately, this will help transition Cambodia's agricultural sector into one that is more modern, efficient, climate-resilient, and highly competitive."
The dialogue was organized by China's Guangxi Radio and Television Station in collaboration with Cambodia's MAFF, Ministry of Information, National Television of Cambodia, and Royal University of Agriculture.
Nguon Samnang, vice president of the Cambodia Agricultural Science Academy, said the dialogue arrived at a pivotal moment, emphasizing that embracing innovations like AI, drones, and IoT is vital for modernizing the agricultural sector and ensuring sustainable growth.
"Many of the agricultural technologies and innovations developed in China can be adopted across the ASEAN region, including Cambodia, to boost farmers' livelihoods and support agricultural communities," he said.
He added that cooperation between China and ASEAN can be expanded through active exchanges among experts, youth, and young researchers, noting that the participation of both the younger generation and local farmers is essential for future agricultural development.
Leang Seiha, a fourth-year student at the Royal University of Agriculture in Phnom Penh, described the dialogue as a unique opportunity to exchange techniques, share ideas, and learn about China's modern agricultural practices.
"I would like to thank China for working closely with Cambodia to share its technical knowledge, as well as organizing training programs and seminars," she told Xinhua. "These platforms allow us, as students, to explore new technologies that can help modernize Cambodia's agriculture."
Thong Mengdavid, deputy director of the China-ASEAN Studies Center at the Cambodia University of Technology and Science, said Chinese agricultural technologies-including spraying drones, IoT soil sensors, and high-yield crop seeds-are essential tools for modernizing farming across Cambodia and the wider ASEAN region.
"Adopting these scalable solutions helps local farmers boost yields, cut labor costs, build climate resilience, and meet global export standards," he told Xinhua.
He emphasized that China and ASEAN should prioritize expanding cooperation in key areas, including digital and smart agriculture platforms, agri-e-commerce supply chains, and green technologies like climate-resilient breeding.
Additionally, both China and ASEAN should establish dedicated youth agri-tech exchange hubs while increasing investments in vocational training and technical education for rural communities, Mengdavid added. ■

Over 3,000 Australians died by suicide in 2025: statistics bureau
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
17:22:48 CST
18:22:48 KST

CANBERRA, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- Over 3,000 Australians died by suicide in 2025, according to official data published on Tuesday, with males accounting for a significant majority.
The Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) said that 3,283 of the 188,421 deaths registered nationally in 2025 were classified as being due to suicide, making it the 15th most common cause of death.
The figure was a slight decrease from the 3,326 suicide deaths reported in 2024, but the ABS noted that the number is expected to rise as ongoing coronial investigations progress.
It said that 73.9 percent of all people who died by suicide in 2025 were males.
The median age at death for those who died by suicide was 45.0 years. For males, it was 45.5 years, and for females it was 43.8 years.
By comparison, no other cause of death that ranked in the top 20 nationally in 2025 had a median age at death lower than 65.5 years.
The ABS said that suicide was the leading cause of death for Australians aged 15-44 in 2025 and was the overall leading cause of premature mortality, with suicide victims accounting for 108,674 combined years of potential life lost. ■

====================================================================================================

Israel election results 2026: When will we know who won and what’s next?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:22:45 UTC
18:22:45 KST

Israel election results 2026: When will we know who won and what’s next?
Exit polls are expected soon after voting closes late on Tuesday, but a final verdict might take days.
Israelis are voting in a closely watched election to decide on the direction of the country, three years after the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack on southern Israel that set off the genocidal war on Gaza.
The first election since those attacks comes at a time when Israel’s pogroms in the occupied West Bank have escalated, and amid mounting tensions with several of its neighbours, many of whom it has attacked in the past three years.
But the vote also comes amid growing domestic questions that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu faces over alleged failures that allowed the October 7 attack, his government’s handling of efforts to retrieve captives taken to Gaza, alleged corruption and disputes over ultra-Orthodox military service.
In final polls published Friday, Netanyahu’s coalition is expected to be neck and neck with – or trail slightly behind – the opposition bloc led by former Israeli military chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot.
According to Israeli news outlet Haaretz, which has collated polls from Israeli news channels, as of Friday, an average of Channels 11, 12 and 13 predicts Netanyahu’s bloc will win 50 seats while Eisenkot’s opposition bloc will take 54 seats. The Israeli parliament, known as the Knesset, has 120 seats in all, so 61 is the mark that a grouping needs to reach a majority.
Here’s what you need to know about the election.
When do polls close in Israel?
On Tuesday, polls opened at 7am local time (05:00 GMT) and will end at 10pm (20:00 GMT).
About 7.3 million Israelis will be eligible to vote, including 1.2 million Palestinian citizens of Israel. Israelis living abroad cannot vote because the country does not have a general absentee ballot, requiring voters to be physically present on election day.
Diplomats and state emissaries are the exception and cast their ballots at Israeli missions on October 20.
When will Israel’s election results be announced?
News channels will broadcast exit poll results once the election ends, with the first indications likely within a few hours of polls closing, but it could take days or weeks to get a clear result.
Results will also be live on the Central Elections Committee website once polls close.
While a clear picture of the election results may come out quickly, if no party or coalition secures a majority, it could take much longer.
The final vote tally is expected by Friday, and official election results are formally published a week after the election, on November 4.
How does the electoral system work?
Under a proportional representation system, Israelis vote for a single party, not individual candidates.
The number of seats the party gains in the Knesset is linked to the proportion of the vote it receives. For example, if Netanyahu’s Likud party secures 50 percent of the national vote, it would take 50 percent of the Knesset’s 120 seats.
A majority requires 61 of the 120 seats.
For a party to enter the Knesset, it must secure at least 3.25 percent of the national vote.
About a dozen parties are widely thought to have a chance of crossing the threshold, so the final tally and seat allocation will take time.
How is Israel’s next prime minister chosen?
Once the final count is in, President Isaac Herzog will speak with party leaders about who they want as prime minister, then tap the candidate he believes has the best chance of forming a government.
The person nominated then has up to 42 days to form a government. As it stands, no single party in Israel has ever won an outright majority, so governments are formed by a coalition of parties, and negotiations on forming a government often take weeks.
What happens if Netanyahu or his rivals cannot form a government?
If no government emerges, the current cabinet, Netanyahu’s government, will remain as a caretaker government.
But before that point, whoever gains the most votes will have different options to assemble support from smaller parties, including forming a minority government or working with another political leader to alternate as prime minister under a power-sharing arrangement.
If all negotiations fail, and no grouping is able to cobble together a workable government, new elections will have to be called.

Scientists uncover how living cells in human milk use nutrients
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
17:22:43 CST
18:22:43 KST

SYDNEY, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- Advanced nanoscale imaging has revealed the diversity of living cells in human milk, how these cells are structured, what they contain, and how they use nutrients, according to an Australian study.
The study provides a new view of the cellular and metabolic complexity of human milk by combining correlative imaging, stable isotope tracing and single-cell analysis to examine major cell populations, including milk-producing cells and immune cells, according to a statement released Tuesday by the University of Western Australia (UWA).
Lead author UWA PhD candidate Lin Qiongxiang said human milk is an incredibly complex biological system containing many different types of living cells, and stable isotope tracing showed that cells in human milk use nutrients in very different ways.
"When we tracked where sugar (glucose) ended up, we found it was being turned into fat droplets inside macrophages in milk, and those cells were switching on genes involved in handling fat," Lin said.
The findings, published in ACS Nano, showed that human milk cells have distinct functions to enable optimal milk composition and volume. The study also identified high levels of sulfur and iron in neutrophils, a type of immune cell that contributes to the killing of bacteria and helps protect infants from infection.
The researchers said the platform could help investigate how human milk cells vary between individuals, throughout lactation and under different maternal health conditions, including gestational diabetes. The findings could improve understanding of the biological roles of living cells in human milk and their potential importance for maternal and infant health. ■

Defense ministers from the United Kingdom, Germany, Italy, Poland, and France met in Paris on October 26 as members of the E5 group — the countries with the largest defense budgets — to discuss support for Ukraine ahead of winter.
After the meeting, the ministers named Russia the main long-term threat to European security and pledged to keep supporting Ukraine despite Washington’s warming relations with Moscow.
“Our countries share the assessment that Russia represents the most acute and long-term threat to Euro-Atlantic security and stability,” the final statement reads. Russia’s war against Ukraine and intensifying hybrid attacks in Europe “do not undermine our unity, solidarity and cohesion. On the contrary, they strengthen our determination to pursue the efforts already undertaken to safeguard the integrity and security of Allied territory,” the ministers said.
The ministers pledged to continue backing Ukraine but announced no new military or financial aid packages, Bloomberg said. During the meeting, they limited themselves to reaffirming earlier commitments.
German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius stressed that the allies would work to preserve U.S. support for Ukraine: “We will do everything we can to ensure that the U.S. also supports Ukraine with supplies, as well as with intelligence and satellite data.”
The latest deterioration in relations between Ukraine and the United States is forcing Europe to consider how to help Ukraine without American support, Bloomberg said. Pistorius said the E5 countries are also working with Ukraine on their own air defense system meant to supplement the U.S. Patriot systems.
Relations between Kyiv and Washington have deteriorated sharply amid a fuel crisis. Donald Trump first demanded that Ukraine stop striking Russian fuel infrastructure, and when a cease-fire could not be reached, he eased sanctions against Russia, allowing diesel fuel to be sold on the world market.
In response, Volodymyr Zelensky accused Trump of trying to force Ukraine into capitulation, saying the United States is delaying shipments of missiles for Patriot air defense systems and restricting the operation of Starlink and Starshield in Ukraine.

====================================================================================================

What Marco Rubio’s sidestepping of New Delhi says about the US’s stance on India
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:21:33 UTC
18:21:33 KST

When the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, visited India for the second time this year, headlines concentrated on who he met and where he went.
The fact that Rubio bypassed New Delhi and did not meet the prime minister, Narendra Modi, during his trip last week, and instead traveled to the financial capital, Mumbai, where he met India’s foreign minister, Subrahmanyam Jaishankar (pictured top with Rubio), and business leaders, did not go unnoticed. Nor did his decision to travel to Jamnagar, the small Gujarati town that is home to Reliance Industries’ colossal oil refinery complex.
Bilateral ties between the two countries have come under strain under the second Trump administration, particularly over tariffs and India’s purchase of Russian oil. Yet, Rubio’s return to India just five months after his first visit as secretary of state signals that the country remains useful for president Donald Trump’s ambitions after all.
As director of the South Asia Program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, Milan Vaishnav has spent a decade tracking India’s place in the world, particularly its ties with the US. Vaishnav has described Trump 2.0 as “unbound” marking a new era in India-US relations.
Tracking foreign affairs, he told me, is a minefield right now. From the White House’s transactional approach to global alliances, ongoing conflicts in the Middle East and consequential elections around the world, politics is changing at a pace that means all predictions are off the table. “I think anyone who tells you they know exactly what is going on and how it fits into their neat theory of the world is lying to you,” says Vaishnav.
I asked him about the many confusing aspects of the US-India relationship, from the hostile political rhetoric to the US embrace of Pakistan, as well as Rubio’s latest visit.
Trump the deal-maker
Ahead of Rubio’s visit, several commentators noted the secretary of state’s “unusual” itinerary. Vaishnav thought the pre-visit chatter about Rubio skipping Delhi to visit Mumbai and Jamnagar was overblown. “Not every bilateral meeting has to take place in a national capital,” he says.
But that doesn’t mean it wasn’t noteworthy. “I do think the choice of venues was intentional. This administration and, particularly, this president, sees foreign policy through the lens of ‘deal-making’. And if you’re trying to drum up business deals, what better place to visit than Mumbai?” he says.
The Jamnagar visit, where Rubio met Mukesh Ambani, the chair of Reliance, also indicates some politicking. “At a time when petrol prices are extremely high in the United States and are likely to be a major issue in the 3 November midterm elections, the administration wants to show that it is doing everything it can to bring them down. India is a major consumer of oil, but it is also a major exporter of refined petroleum products,” says Vaishnav. “One of Rubio’s objectives was to encourage Reliance and, by extension, India to process more Venezuelan crude [oil],” he added.
While this could present an opportunity for India to advance relations, it’s not a given: the US president remains, after all – and to put it lightly – mercurial.
“The biggest plot twist for me has been the Trump administration’s embrace of Pakistan after the May 2025 conflict with India,” says Vaishnav. Pakistan’s standing in Washington had eroded over the years, especially under Joe Biden, who left office without ever having made a presidential phone call to his counterpart in Pakistan. “Many officials in Congress had grown exhausted with Pakistan’s double game, speaking the language of partnership on the one hand while undermining US interests on the other,” says Vaishnav.
But, after coming to power the second time, Trump thanked the country for its help in nabbing a suspect linked to a 2021 bombing in Afghanistan that killed 13 US service members. This reversal in Pakistan’s fortunes gathered pace after the May conflict with India, which Trump took credit for ending. In June, he welcomed Asim Munir, Pakistan’s army chief, to the White House, after Munir called for the president to be nominated for the Nobel peace prize.
“I chalk up the reversal to a few factors: Trump’s well-known strongman envy, Pakistan’s savvy diplomacy, and the prospect of energy and crypto deals involving members of Trump’s inner circle,” says Vaishnav. For him, it isyet another demonstration of how much weight Trump places on deals, transactions and short-term wins. “For New Delhi, this means Modi’s personal rapport with Trump and 25 years of investment in the bilateral relationship offer no guarantee against a 180-degree reversal in US policy,” he adds.
In a recent piece, Vaishnav’s colleague Sameer Lalwani pointed out that the US relationship with India remains more resilient than the political rhetoric may suggest with quiet, but nonetheless strategic, progress being made.
As Lalwani points out, bilateral trade reached a record high between India and the US in 2025; nearly $68bn worth of AI infrastructure investment in India has been pledged by US technology companies; and the two countries have carried out record number of joint military exercises this year.
The way forward
Despite these wins, in terms of future bilateral relations, “there are at least three reasons for caution,” warns Vaishnav. First, he points to the onslaught of US actions that have dented Indian interests. Trump had imposed a punitive 50% tariff on India in 2025, which was reduced to 18% earlier this year, but without a comprehensive trade deal being reached. Second, on immigration, the White House’s H-1B visa and green card restrictions have disproportionately affected Indian workers in Silicon Valley.
“This has created a real trust deficit on the Indian side, and with good reason,” says Vaishnav. The frustration was on display earlier this month, when New Delhi branded remarks made by the US vice-president, JD Vance, about Indian professionals as “deeply offensive”. Furthermore, Vaishnav argues that while governments and private sector firms might be great at making announcements, they’re not always a guarantee of delivery.
His final caution is how political tensions can have a chilling effect. The trade negotiations offer a telling example: in January, the US commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, blamed the lack of a trade deal on Modi’s failure to phone Trump, a characterisation that New Delhi has disputed. Vaishnav says: “Much of the progress we are seeing is the product of decisions made years ago. It is one thing to keep existing projects moving, but turbulence in the relationship could make new initiatives a heavier lift.”
If India is serious about making its ambition to be a global powerhouse a reality, Vaishnav thinks there’s a clearcut way to win. “I would argue that the most important investment is political – ensuring India remains a robust, inclusive, participatory democracy,” he says. “On the economic front, India has made massive new investments in physical and digital infrastructure. But the returns on those investments will be limited unless the government doubles down on reforms: more efficient dispute resolution, an impartial legal system, even-handed tax enforcementand regulatory certainty.”
Ultimately, neither side can afford to treat the other as expendable. The test now is whether strategic foundations can hold at a time of global political upheaval.

Vibe check
Prarthna Singh has consistently placed the female identity at the heart of her artistic practice, documenting Indian women’s aspirations and acts of rebellion in male-dominated spaces. When commissioned to photograph rkivecity’s menswear line, made from discarded clothes reworked into new garments, she turned that same gaze outward. The setting was the acclaimed 151-year-old Mayo College boys’ school in Ajmer, Rajasthan – Singh attended the linked girls’ school, and credits it with shaping her rebellious spirit.
“I was thinking about how I could bring a sense of intimacy and camaraderie of boarding-school life to the images, because that exists,” she told me. One image shows a pair of hands holding another boy’s jacket, the faces left out of the frame, so the garment stands in for the familiarity they share. Seeing this work against the backdrop of students taking to the streets to fight for their rights lends the series a lasting significance. “This was just my way of showing all of this is connected. These worlds are not existing separately,” said Singh.

Is it too early for kūčiukai?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:21:00 UTC
18:21:00 KST

With two months to go until Christmas, Lithuanian bakeries and supermarkets are already starting to sell kūčiukai, traditional pastries eaten on Christmas Eve. Some businesses say early sales have proved successful and others planning to wait until after All Saints’ Day.
The small, crunchy pastries made from leavened dough and poppy seeds are a staple of the Lithuanian Christmas Eve – Kūčios – as even the name suggests. Granted, most of us indulge in them throughout the holiday season.
Lina, a resident of Panevėžys, tells LRT TV she buys kūčiukai as soon as they hit supermarket shelves because she misses their taste and enjoys the festive mood they bring.
“It’s really nice that kūčiukai are already available and we can enjoy them and taste them until then. Is it too early? Definitely not. Nothing is ever too early; sometimes it’s just too late,” she says.
The Velželio duona bakery in Panevėžys is among the first to begin production each year. Its production manager, Marius Sarapas, said starting early helps attract customers eager for the traditional treat.
“People have been looking forward to them. There’s that initial purchase, when they’re not available anywhere else yet, but we already have them,” Sarapas said.
He added that early sales also allow the bakery to build up its seasonal business and give customers a chance to compare its products with those of competitors entering the market in the following weeks.
The first kūčiukai have also appeared in some supermarket chains.
Rimi Lietuva communications director Luka Lesauskaitė-Remeikė said the retailer was gradually bringing forward the start of sales to see whether customers would buy the pastries earlier.
“We can see that kūčiukai could be part of our assortment all year round. People like them as a snack, almost like sunflower seeds. We sometimes joke that you can watch a movie while eating them,” she said.
Last year, the pastries appeared in Rimi stores much later than this year, she added. This year, they arrived last week as the retailer experiments with earlier sales to gauge customer interest.
However, shoppers will not find kūčiukai in all major supermarket chains just yet. Lidl, Iki and Maxima plan to start selling them in November, after All Saints’ Day.
Consumers are divided over whether the early appearance of Christmas treats is welcome.
Some say selling them in October is premature and risks overshadowing the holiday season. One woman interviewed by LRT TV said Christmas preparations should begin after Halloween or the early November period of All Saints’ Day and All Souls’ Day.
Others are indifferent because they make the pastries themselves rather than buying them in stores.
“I’m 96, and I’ve always made everything for the holidays myself,” one woman said when asked whether she baked kūčiukai at home. “When you buy them, they’re made by someone else.”
Meanwhile, the price of kūčiukai in supermarkets is expected to rise by about 7% this year, according to estimates by retailers.

Two men charged in Britain with helping Iran over RAF Fairford incident

- Police said six others remain on bail, and Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor said the earlier decision helped secure “swifter progress” and “better evidence”.
AI generated
LONDON – Two men were charged on Oct 27 under Britain’s National Security Act following September’s security incident at the RAF Fairford military base, with prosecutors accusing one of them of trying to assist Iranian intelligence operations in Britain.
RAF Fairford had been used by US bombers to carry out strikes on Iran, but they were withdrawn on security grounds shortly after five British men were arrested outside the military base in south-west England in the early hours of Sept 27.
The circumstances of the incident, which remain largely unexplained, attracted huge international attention, coming at a time of heightened concern about the security implications for Western states of the war between the United States and Iran.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said earlier in October that the activity at RAF Fairford was likely to have been coordinated in Iran, which Tehran’s ambassador to Britain has denied.
British national Mohmed Abdulkarim, 24, was charged with engaging in conduct that was likely to materially assist a foreign intelligence service between Aug 31 and Sept 28, with police saying the country is believed to be Iran.
Nouman Essghir, a 24-year-old dual British-Iranian national who was first arrested outside RAF Fairford on Sept 27, was charged with one offence of entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK on Aug 22.
The pair will appear at London’s Westminster Magistrates’ Court later on Oct 27.
Police said that six other people, four of whom are British nationals who were arrested outside RAF Fairford on Sept 27, remain on police bail.
The decision to bail suspects after an apparent major incident had drawn scrutiny, but on Oct 27 police said that decision had helped secure charges against the two men.
“We know the decisions made during our investigations can sometimes appear illogical to those on the outside, but I want to make it very clear that there will always be a good reason or rationale behind them,” said Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of National Counter Terrorism Policing in Britain.
“In this case, this decision-making has led to swifter progress, better evidence, and ultimately us securing the charges that I have announced today.” REUTERS
