Aeon unveils 140,000-square-foot missile plant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:19:26 UTC
18:19:26 KST

- Aeon Industrial unveiled the Armory, a 140,000-square-foot factory for missile systems, interceptors, fuzes and seekers, targeting initial production in the coming months.
- The Texas company says its high-voltage fuzes are in volume production and were demonstrated at the Pentagon’s Drone Dominance program.
Aeon Industrial, a Texas company that already makes low-cost drone fuzes in volume, has unveiled the Armory, a planned 140,000-square-foot (13,000-square-meter) factory for missile systems, interceptors, high-voltage fuzes, seekers and other critical components, saying it wants to add production capacity where the U.S. munitions supply chain depends on too few suppliers.
The company said the Armory is its first manufacturing site and is targeting initial production in the coming months, and that it is already developing a second site, Armory-2, to expand production further, though it did not say where either facility is located or how many missiles or interceptors it expects to build there.
Aeon is based in Austin, Texas, with offices in Oklahoma and Alabama, and it says its plans rest on proven hardware and contracts worth “eight figures,” meaning at least $10 million, although it did not name the customers or programs behind those contracts.
The company’s most mature product is MERC, a low-cost, high-voltage electronic safe-and-arm fuze that decides when a warhead detonates and keeps it safe until then, and Aeon says it is in volume production with 10,000 units on the line, after Aeon and warhead maker Mountain Horse Solutions said in September that their combined warhead and fuze package had flown on drones from several top-performing companies at the Pentagon’s Drone Dominance Gauntlet at Fort Carson, Colorado, where one-way attack drones were put through competitive testing.
The Drone Dominance program is the U.S. Department of War’s effort to buy large numbers of cheap attack drones quickly, and in October it led to orders for 60,000 attack drones from nine companies, after earlier rounds in which five companies led the scoring in the $1 billion program, while fuzes like MERC are designed to work across quadcopters, fixed-wing drones, missiles and interceptors, which lets one component supply several of these weapons at once.
The company is also pushing into air defense, and its joint low-cost interceptor proposal with European missile maker Destinus was selected on Sept. 30, 2026, as one of 10 finalists in the U.S. Army’s xTech Apex Intercept competition, which is looking for cheaper weapons to supplement the Patriot air and missile defense system against cruise missiles, short-range ballistic missiles and other aerial threats, with the U.S. Army planning to pick up to three winners in that category by Dec. 31, 2026.
Christopher “Gus” Jennings, Aeon’s director of growth and a former U.S. Army Special Forces soldier, said the company is building “next-generation weapon systems,” but Aeon has not identified which missile or interceptor designs will be built at the Armory first.

AI chip boom tripled South Korea's economic growth in the third quarter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:19:18 UTC
18:19:18 KST

South Korea's economy grew faster than expected in the third quarter. However, analysts warned that its heavy reliance on the chip industry leaves the country vulnerable to a slowdown in global AI spending.
South Korea's economy grew more than three times faster than expected in the third quarter, fuelled by strong demand for semiconductors, according to central bank data released on Tuesday.
GDP rose by 1.0% in the July-to-September period compared with the previous quarter, preliminary figures from the Bank of Korea (BOK) showed.
The figure surpassed the central bank's August forecast of 0.3% growth.
The reading was boosted by a 2.3% rise in exports, "led by semiconductors, machinery and electrical equipment", the BOK said.
Investment in facilities rose by 4.1%, largely driven by spending on machinery used in semiconductor production.
The data validates the "BOK's upbeat assessment...that booming demand for chips is keeping exports and investment strong", said Kwon Hyo-sung of Bloomberg Economics.
Semiconductor exports soared by 218.7% year-on-year to $148 billion (€127bn) in the third quarter, according to government figures.
On an annual basis, the economy grew by 3.4%, slightly below the 3.7% recorded in the previous quarter.
Real gross domestic income (GDI), which measures purchasing power, surged by 18.8% year-on-year, marking its fastest increase in nearly 49 years, supported by rising semiconductor prices.
South Korea's economy had already recorded its fastest growth in more than five years in the first quarter, expanding by 1.7% quarter-on-quarter amid strong demand for semiconductors.
Growth remains 'heavily concentrated' in chip sector
However, analysts cautioned that South Korea's economic growth remained heavily reliant on the semiconductor industry.
"The risk is that growth stays heavily concentrated in the semiconductor sector, leaving South Korea exposed to a slowdown in global AI spending," said John Bromhead, a senior economist at Moody's Analytics.
The surge in semiconductor demand has also helped push the country's current account surplus to record highs.
South Korea posted a current account surplus of $116.6 billion (€100bn) in the second quarter.
Meanwhile, semiconductor exports soared by 218.7% year-on-year to $148 billion (€127bn) in the third quarter, according to government figures.

Russia and Ukraine Trade Deadly Strikes as Oleshky Ceasefire Begins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:18:28 UTC
18:18:28 KST

Russia and Ukraine have begun a local ceasefire in the occupied town of Oleshky in southern Ukraine, both sides said Tuesday, but strikes continued elsewhere across Ukrainian and Russian territory, with several people being reported killed.
The ceasefire, which the Trump administration announced last week, should enable deliveries of humanitarian aid as well as evacuations from the frontline town as its residents grapple with acute shortages of food and medicine.
U.S. First Lady Melania Trump said later Tuesday that the ceasefire had been expanded beyond Oleshky within the wider Kherson region to allow safe passage for humanitarian convoys.
“Timing was accelerated two days ahead of schedule to protect the safety of civilians and to facilitate the delivery of critical humanitarian aid,” she said in a post on X. “The ceasefire’s geographic area has expanded beyond Oleshky, within the Kherson region, to provide safe passage for the humanitarian convoys.”
Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine’s parliamentary commissioner for human rights and head of its negotiating team, confirmed in a Facebook post that Kyiv was observing the ceasefire.
On Telegram, Russia’s Defense Ministry said it stopped shelling in the area of Kherson as it prepared for the ceasefire around Oleshky, which is located nearby.
Despite the local ceasefire, Ukraine and Russia continued to trade strikes elsewhere overnight.
In western Russia’s Bryansk region, Ukrainian drone attacks killed two people and wounded at least six others, Governor Yegor Kovalchuk said Tuesday.
The first victim was killed when an explosive was dropped from a drone, Kovalchuk said. He later confirmed the death of a 67-year-old man in the same area.
Elsewhere, authorities in the Belgorod region said one woman was killed and seven people were injured over the past 24 hours.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said it intercepted 222 Ukrainian drones across Russia and annexed Crimea between Monday night and Tuesday morning.
In Ukraine, a Russian missile attack on Kyiv killed at least one and wounded 15 others, including students in a dormitory. Overnight Russian attacks also killed and injured people in the cities of Kharkiv and Pavlohrad.
Meanwhile, in the partially occupied Zaporizhzhia region, Kremlin-installed authorities said one person was killed and 30 others were injured when a Ukrainian drone struck an inter-regional passenger bus.
Reuters contributed reporting.

====================================================================================================

Africa is more than its crises, but the West won’t let you see it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:16:02 UTC
18:16:02 KST

Africa is more than its crises, but the West won’t let you see it
When it comes to media in all its formats, Africa does not lack voices. It has thousands of newspapers, radio stations, television channels and digital platforms. What it often lacks is equal power to shape international conversations about its own affairs, and the resources to ensure that African perspectives reach audiences beyond the continent. The real challenge is who sets the agenda, the background and chooses the frames through which events are understood, breaking out of the stereotypes. And above all, who decides which voices deserve to be heard.
There is an important distinction between challenging an unequal international media landscape and achieving genuine media independence. The real test of the emerging Russia–Africa media cooperation will be whether it strengthens African media institutions’ ability to investigate, hold power to account and tell stories on their own terms.
Research published by the European Council on Foreign Relations in October 2025 reported that more than 1,000 African journalists had completed RT Africa training courses across 35 countries. Although the report presents this as part of Russia’s expanding media influence on the continent, the figure illustrates the reach of RT’s professional engagement with African journalists. It does not, however, establish that the journalists share Moscow’s political objectives or are becoming Russian mouthpieces. Far from it.
Separately, BBC Monitoring reported, citing the South African Institute of International Affairs, that as many as 4,000 African news websites republish content from RT and Sputnik, a Russian news agency. This is an estimate of the network’s potential reach, not a measure of audience size or editorial allegiance.
However, the underlying issue is not simply whether Russian media are gaining a foothold in Africa, but whether greater access to international content and training can strengthen African journalism’s independence. Research by Africa No Filter, analyzing 60 African news outlets across 15 countries in 2020, found that approximately one-third of stories in the surveyed outlets about Africa were sourced from non-African news services. The findings point to a structural problem: African newsrooms often rely on external sources to cover the continent itself simply because they lack the means to do the field work themselves.
A 2024 Global Media Index for Africa, produced by the University of Cape Town, South Africa, in partnership with Africa No Filter and The Africa Center, analyzed more than 1,000 articles published by 20 international news organizations over six months.
Its findings offer grounds for questioning how major Western outlets portray the continent. Africa is covered through a narrow set of crises, while the lives, ideas and achievements of its people receive less international attention.
The Washington Post, for example, scored just 29% for diversity of topics, while the Wall Street Journal covered the fewest African countries among the outlets assessed, with a score of 31%. The study also found that reporting across the sample privileged political and business elites over ordinary Africans.
The relationship between media and power has a long history that predates today’s digital platforms and geopolitical competition. During the era of slavery and European colonial expansion, newspapers helped shape how readers understood Africa, its people and the economic systems, built around their exploitation. Their positions were not uniform: some publications campaigned against slavery, while others defended the interests of enslavers or opposed more radical demands for emancipation. The Manchester Guardian, for example, supported abolition but also argued that enslavers should be compensated for losing “their property.”
This reveals a wider contradiction: abolition was championed even as the interests of slaveholders and traders were protected. The historical question, therefore, is not whether all Western media defended slavery or colonialism, but how economic and political power shaped the stories told about Africa – and whose voices were given authority. Literal slavery is here being minimized as a human issue in the first place.
The same question of whose perspective shapes the story is relevant to contemporary demands for reparative justice. African and Caribbean governments and campaigners have long argued that slavery and colonial rule were systems whose consequences continue to shape economic and social inequalities. Yet these demands can be presented in international coverage primarily as disputes over money, political controversy or diplomatic embarrassment, rather than as challenges to the historical and legal foundations of the present order.
Jamaica’s September 2026 petition to King Charles III offers a concrete example. It asked the King to refer questions about the legality of the enslavement of Africans, possible breaches of international law and Britain’s obligation to provide a remedy to the Privy Council; it did not demand a specified payment. Nevertheless, some coverage framed the issue around the prospect of a multibillion-dollar bill, prompting Jamaica’s culture minister to stress that the petition was about legal questions, not a monetary claim.
This is where Russia-Africa media cooperation can be assessed by more than the number of journalists trained or alternative outlets made available. Challenging Western dominance of international news is not, by itself, the same as securing media independence. Russian media can offer African audiences and journalists perspectives that differ from those of Western outlets, but the same scrutiny must apply to their ownership, funding, editorial priorities and relationship with political power. The meaningful measure of cooperation is whether it helps African newsrooms develop the professional freedom to investigate their own governments, question foreign partners and report beyond the narratives promoted by either side.
Maybe what should be ask is this: not whether Africa should choose between Western and Russian narratives, but whether African journalists have the freedom to develop their own narratives, bring home know-how and strengthen their media institutions at home. That requires investment in African-owned media, stronger local news networks and editorial independence from both foreign powers and domestic authorities.
Africa’s media landscape should no longer be viewed through the prism of Cold War rivalries, in which facts risk being distorted to serve one side at the expense of the truth. Nor should Western media dominance, with its persistent stereotypes and narrow framing of the continent, remain the norm. Africa does not need another outside power to speak for it; it needs the conditions in which its own journalists can be heard, taken seriously and trusted to hold power to account.
The statements, views and opinions expressed in this column are solely those of the author and do not necessarily represent those of RT.

In short:
Olympic gold medallist Tom Slingsby says Tribeca Loyal could break the Sydney to Hobart race record "by a lot" if it gets the right conditions in this year's race.
Tribeca Loyal, owned and skippered by Anthony Bell, is a renamed version of last year's line honours winner and race record-holder, Comanche.
What's next?
The Sydney to Hobart will begin in Sydney Harbour on Boxing Day.
A decade after his last appearance in the Sydney to Hobart Yacht Race, Anthony Bell has unveiled a new Loyal boat to challenge for line honours in this year's race.
But it's not a new boat — it's an old one.
Bell was first to Hobart in 2011 with Investec Loyal and in 2016 with Perpetual Loyal, setting a then-race record in the latter race of one day 13 hours, 31 minutes and 20 seconds.
On Tuesday in Sydney, Bell revealed his boat for this year's edition of the bluewater classic — the race record-holder and last year's winner, Comanche.
Bell spent up big to buy the five-time line honours-winning boat, which will race on Boxing Day as Tribeca Loyal.
Bell, the owner and skipper of the supermaxi, is aiming to lift the J.H. Illingworth Challenge Cup for a third time.
He has again recruited America's Cup and Olympic gold medallist Tom Slingsby to serve as the crew's sailing master.
The three-time world sailor of the year is delighted to be working on a yacht with the quality and power of Comanche.
"It's the most powerful supermaxi there is in the world," Slingsby said in Sydney.
"There's times there where we actually try to slow the boat down because it's got so much power and the waves could be too big that you're flying off the waves too fast.
"It averages really high speeds, it loves it when it's windy, so it's an exciting boat. You wouldn't want to choose any other boats to do the home run on.
"This boat already owns the Sydney Hobart race record, but … if we get the right conditions, we can break that record by a lot."
Despite his past success with Loyal, the 2012 Olympic gold medallist admits sailing on the open seas is a long way from his comfort zone.
"I'm not an ocean racer," Slingsby declared.
"I'm more of the short-course stuff.
"It's not something that I'm good at and really want to do, but I love coming back."
A major motivation for Slingsby and the crew is the continuing partnership with the Humpty Dumpty Foundation, which raises money for life-saving infant medical equipment for Australian hospitals.
The worthy cause is why Loyal will once again take on some celebrity deckhands to boost its fundraising profile.
Former Wallaby turned Rugby Australia chief executive Phil Waugh and Sydney Roosters great Anthony Minichello are among the famous names heading south.
"I certainly don't miss the contact of playing rugby league, but the camaraderie, and everyone being laser-focused on achieving a goal, that's the stuff you do miss when you retire from professional sport," Minichello said.
This year's star-studded crew continues the tradition for Loyal to rely on some unconventional athletes taking up a new sport.
"We've had 21 people who represented Australia, won world surfing titles, gold medals, played for the Wallabies, played rugby league, and we have two TV Week Gold Logie winners as well," Bell said.

ABC to demand rightwing One Nation party stop using Bluey in ‘shocking and disrespectful’ cartoon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:14:18 UTC
18:14:18 KST

Australia’s national broadcaster will send a cease and desist letter to the rightwing populist party One Nation for using Bluey in a “shocking and disrespectful” cartoon which sees the beloved character repeatedly ramming politicians with an SUV.
The ABC’s managing director, Hugh Marks, told Senate estimates on Tuesday he became aware of One Nation’s potential breach of intellectual property last week and sought legal advice. “We will be taking further action, I can assure you,” he said.
The legal dispute came to light after the Western Australian Labor senator Varun Ghosh asked the ABC if it had sought legal advice over the 2024 political cartoon, called State of Melbourne, which has had 1.3m views on YouTube so far.
“I appreciate it was published two years ago, but has a particular poignancy in the last week,” Ghosh, the communications committee chair, said.
Estimates was held a week after the alleged attack on independent MP Helen Haines outside the politician’s northern Victorian electorate office, which led to her losing both legs.
Marks said he believed the use is a clear breach of intellectual property and “a cease and desist letter should be issued”.
He revealed the ABC had been in contact with Bluey’s international distributor, BBC Studios, and the Brisbane-based creators Ludo. He said Pauline Hanson’s party had not sought permission to use the children’s character in the hit show. The BBC, Ludo and One Nation have been approached for comment.
“It’s not a parody of any Bluey work,” Marks said. “It’s not a minor use of the [intellectual property]. In my view, it is an infringement of the intellectual property, number one. But it’s also a shocking use of Australia’s most loved character.”
“In fact, probably the globally most loved character in a video. That is both shocking and disrespectful to the children of Australia who love that character so much.”
The animation shows Bluey behind the wheel striking a depiction of the former Victorian premier Daniel Andrews and the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, with an SUV, as well as TV host and conservationist Robert Irwin. Before he is run over, the Albanese character says to Bluey: “You’ve got that crazy look in your eyes”.
In one scene in the three-minute video, Andrews is at the wheel, Albanese is his passenger and the car deliberately runs over Bluey and Irwin. The politicians are then shown putting the bodies of Bluey and Irwin in the boot of the SUV.
On Tuesday, Australia’s senators also heard evidence on other matters concerning the ABC in addition to the beloved cartoon.
Marks told estimates the ABC’s former news director Justin Stevens received a termination payout of $353,230 because he did not want him to work out his notice.
“Following Mr Stevens’s resignation, we had the option to ask Mr Stevens to continue to work through his notice period, or for me to ask him not to work out his notice period,” Marks said.
“I felt it was important, given what had happened, that I asked him not to work out his period, and to pay him his contractual entitlement to do so.
“I felt it was important that we move forward with new leadership. So I didn’t want to continue Mr Stevens in that role.”
Stevens, whose total remuneration for the financial year was $864,394, was replaced by Reuters executive Simon Robinson last month after a 19-year career at the public broadcaster. His base salary was $529,202, according to the annual report.
Marks told senators “mistakes” were made in the production of programs by former Four Corners reporter Mahmood Fazal but the entire leadership of Four Corners had now been replaced.
The ABC has removed several programs made by the sacked bikie turned journalist because of concerns over his use of anonymous interviewees.
“We did a review of Mr Fazal’s work and found substantial flaws in much of that work,” he said.
“I think we can take confidence that there are many great people who do work for Four Corners. And with new editorial leadership, we are obviously very confident as to its future.”
The ABC said it was reviewing its editorial guidance about the use of anonymous sources in light of the Fazal incident.
Sally Neighbour, a former Four Corners executive producer, alleged in the Monthly that “an associate of Fazal played different roles in different stories, disguised behind a mask”.
Fazal has previously said he stands by his reporting. In July, he said he was “shocked” by the removal of the two Four Corners episodes and that he believed the ABC’s process and decisions “set a worrying precedent for the organisation’s independence and commitment to public-interest journalism”.

UK prosecutors charge two after RAF Fairford incident
Unknown

UK prosecutors charge two after RAF Fairford incident
British Iranian dual national Mohmed Abdulkarim and British citizen Nouman Essghir charged under the National Security Act.
British prosecutors say they have charged two men with offences under the National Security Act following an incident in September at RAF Fairford, an airbase in England used by the United States.
British Iranian dual national Mohmed Abdulkarim and British citizen Nouman Essghir, both aged 24, were charged under the National Security Act, the Crown Prosecution Service said. They are due to appear in court later on Tuesday.
Abdulkarim is charged with engaging in conduct that was likely to materially assist a foreign intelligence service. Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of the United Kingdom’s Counter Terrorism Policing, said police believed the country Abdulkarim was assisting was Iran.
Essghir was charged with entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK.
Both men live in Westminster, a district in London.
The airbase in Gloucestershire, southwestern England, had been used by US bombers to carry out attacks on Iran this year.
Essghir was arrested outside the base on September 27, when armed police officers and army bomb-disposal experts swarmed the rural area. Dozens of residents were evacuated from their homes as police and experts searched for explosives.
Abdulkarim was arrested in the past week. Six other men remain on bail, all living in London and aged between 23 and 25, as investigations continue.
Shortly after the incident at the base, US B-1 bombers were withdrawn from the site.
“We have seen a range of incidents in recent months that we believe have been directed by the Iranian state and, as the Director General of MI5 said just the other week, we are working together to intervene, identify and respond to that threat,” Taylor said in a statement.
Al Jazeera’s Camille Nedelec, reporting from London, said police initially commented that they were considering all avenues and that they were not ruling out a state actor.
“But at the time, they didn’t go so far as to point towards Iran – although US President Donald Trump and British Prime Minister Andy Burnham were fairly quick to say they believed that there was credible evidence to suggest Iran was involved,” she said.
“It’s only in the past few days that police who have been in charge of this investigation have increasingly said they believe there is evidence that Iran is involved,” she added.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham last week said the activity at RAF Fairford was likely to have been coordinated in Iran, which Iran’s ambassador to the UK has denied.
Last year, the UK said there had been 20 credible Iranian-backed threats to kill or kidnap individuals based in the UK.
In July, Britain used new powers to ban support for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and a linked group, Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (HAYI), which had claimed responsibility for seven attacks earlier this year at locations linked to Jewish and Israeli communities and Persian-language media.

Israel’s election is on a knife-edge as voters head to the polls today, with the final surveys showing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu neck and neck with his main centrist challenger, Gadi Eisenkot.
It is the country’s first general election since the Hamas-led attack of 7 October 2023. Some 7.3 million people are eligible to vote, including hundreds of thousands casting a ballot for the first time, while tens of thousands of Israelis living abroad are thought to have flown home to take part.
Netanyahu, 77, is Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, having held the post on and off for more than 19 years. He has campaigned on his security record and his close relationship with US President Donald Trump, arguing he is best placed to keep the country safe.
Eisenkot, 66, a former military chief and political newcomer, leads the Yashar party and an informal bloc stretching from the right to the centre-left. He has pledged an independent state inquiry into the security failures surrounding the 7 October attack, something the current government has resisted.
Voters at polling stations reflected the divide. “He’s a man who’s not afraid to take action,” said 85-year-old Zipporah Bennett, explaining her support for Netanyahu. In Jerusalem, 65-year-old Alexandra said: “I want change in our country.”
Arab-majority parties, which represent around 21% of the population, could prove kingmakers if the result is as tight as expected, though neither leading candidate has publicly said he would partner with them.
The vote is being closely watched in Europe. The EU is Israel’s largest trading partner, but relations have come under strain over the war in Gaza. In April, Spain, Ireland and Slovenia renewed a push to suspend the EU-Israel Association Agreement at a meeting of foreign ministers, but Germany and Italy blocked the move. alqudsWikipedia
Analysts caution that replacing Netanyahu would not necessarily mean a break with the policies driving European criticism, pointing out that Eisenkot has opposed Palestinian statehood. He has, however, promised to crack down on violent settlers. Al Jazeera
Polls close at 22:00 local time (21:00 CET). Final results could take days, and no party is expected to come close to the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-member Knesset, meaning coalition negotiations could last weeks or even months.

Actual Swiss wages increase by 0.5% in 2026
Actual and minimum wages in Switzerland are set to rise by an average of 0.5% and 0.8% respectively in 2026. This was announced on Monday by the Federal Statistical Office (FSO), based on the provisions of the main collective labour agreements (CLAs).
The average increase of 0.5% in actual wages, agreed by the social partners in the main collective labour agreements, was broken down into 0.3% at individual level and 0.2% at collective level. According to inflation forecasts for 2026 (+0.6%), real wages in sectors covered by collective agreements are not expected to rise this year. The agreements on actual wages cover just under 700,000 people.
In detail, the increase in actual wages was 0.2% in the secondary sector and 0.8% in the tertiary sector. Among the economic sectors, the largest increases were recorded in transport and storage (+1.2%), Financial and insurance activities (+1%) and professional, scientific and technical activities (+0.8%). Manufacturing and construction saw more modest increases, of 0.3% and 0.2% respectively.
More
Median annual salary in Switzerland rose to CHF87,000 in 2025
As regards minimum wages, the average increase of 0.8% in 2026 follows rises of 1% in 2025 and 2% in 2024. More than 1.85 million people are covered by a collective labour agreement (CLA) that includes statutory provisions on minimum wages and for whom agreements have been concluded.
Minimum wage increases varied by sector: +0.3% in the secondary sector and +0.8% in the tertiary sector. Among the sectors, ‘unclassified activities’ (commercial employees and sales staff) stood out with +2.3%, followed by ‘financial and insurance activities’ (+1.8%) and ‘other service activities’ (+1.5%). The lowest increases were recorded in manufacturing (+0.1%) and accommodation and food service activities (+0.2%).

Putin to host 22 African leaders in Moscow
Russian President Vladimir Putin will host 22 African leaders at the Russia-Africa summit in Moscow this week for talks spanning economic cooperation, energy, and global affairs, Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov has said.
Putin’s schedule includes 24 bilateral meetings across the Russia-Africa gathering and Tuesday’s eighth Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) summit, Ushakov told reporters on Monday.
Five are scheduled for Tuesday, with the presidents of Mozambique, Equatorial Guinea, and Iran, as well as Qatar’s emir and Libya’s Presidential Council chairman. Another 11 are planned for Friday, including talks with representatives of Ghana, Mali, Mauritania, South Sudan, the Central African Republic, DR Congo, Togo, Eritrea, Somalia, and Comoros.
Ushakov said the discussions will emphasize “national sovereignty and fair access to food, resources, fertilizers, and modern technologies,” adding: “We have a busy... extremely packed week ahead.”
According to the Kremlin aide, delegations from 48 of Africa’s 54 countries have confirmed that they will take part in the October 28-29 gathering. Putin and Burundian President Evariste Ndayishimiye, the African Union chair, will co-chair the summit at the Grand Kremlin Palace.
He said the Russia-Africa summit will adopt a cooperation action plan for 2027-2029 and two declarations, one setting out joint positions and the other covering cooperation in AI. Another 33 intergovernmental, interagency, and commercial documents are set to be signed with African countries.
The accompanying Economic and Humanitarian Forum will cover agriculture, energy, mining, finance, and technology, with around 4,000 Russian and African entrepreneurs invited.
The gathering follows the 2019 Sochi summit, attended by 43 African heads of state or government, and the 2023 St. Petersburg summit, which drew delegations from 48 African countries, including 17 heads of state. Russia completed the delivery of 200,000 metric tons of free grain to six African countries in February 2024, fulfilling Putin’s pledge at the 2023 summit, according to the Agriculture Ministry.
The Russian Foreign Ministry said earlier this month that Western governments are attempting to pressure African states, including through financial blackmail, to deter them from attending the Moscow summit. Russia has positioned itself as a strategic ally to African countries, with governments across the continent seeking closer ties in education, energy, and security despite Western criticism.
Malian Foreign Minister Abdoulaye Diop defended his country’s partnership during Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov’s February 2023 visit to Bamako, saying, “We are not going to continue to justify our choice of partners.”
Ghanaian President John Dramani Mahama, who is in Moscow for the Russia-Africa summit, reaffirmed his country’s nonaligned foreign policy in London last week, saying partnerships should deliver investment and fair returns rather than being determined by competition among outside powers.

Some semiconductor wafer manufacturers have already begun discussing their PC requirements for 2027 with Asus, he said. “The commercial market still has strong demand,” Liao said.
He added that many organizations had not fully allocated their budgets in 2025, while businesses and government agencies were now considering larger budgets for 2027. Unexpectedly rapid PC price increases had left some organizations unable to purchase all the equipment they needed, prompting them to plan more carefully for future procurement, per UDN.

Ukraine’s Ambassador to the United Kingdom and former Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (2021–2024), Valeriy Zaluzhny, believes that the war in Ukraine persists due to the weakness of the Western world and its security system—a system that requires a new military doctrine reflecting the realities of modern warfare.
"The West needs to step out of its comfort zone and into the reality of what war looks like in 2026; it must shed the illusion that outdated guarantees and doctrines can truly protect it and its children," Zaluzhny wrote in a Facebook post.
According to him, the Western security system remains rooted in a World War II-era doctrine, merely supplemented by expensive, high-precision weaponry whereas modern conditions demand a comprehensive overhaul of approaches to combat operations.
Zaluzhny emphasized that for the West to ensure its own security, it is not enough to simply procure new weapons or adjust tactics to account for the use of drones.
"The West needs a new doctrine to defend itself. For us in the military, a doctrine is a 'Bible of war'—it integrates all components of the armed forces—weaponry, tactics, structure, training, and funding—into a unified system," he noted.
Zaluzhny stated that such a doctrine would enable the assessment of the impact of new technologies, adaptation to change, and the planning of joint operations. "A relevant, up-to-date doctrine means security for your children and for your state. No other commitments will save you," he wrote.
He added that the West still possesses sophisticated and costly technologies that could help build a new security system; however, the key factor remains the willingness to step out of one’s comfort zone and take collective action. According to Zaluzhny, only by working together can the war for the future of our children be won.
Zaluzhny also mentioned that he addressed officers from various nations at the Joint Services Command and Staff College of the UK Defence Academy, where they are preparing for senior command roles, and noted the participation of Ukrainian military personnel with firsthand combat experience in the training program. Among them is a Hero of Ukraine, Lieutenant Colonel Serhiy Roschin, a squadron commander who has been defending the Ukrainian skies since 2022.

Migrant workers urge Taiwan to strengthen protections for pregnant caregivers

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:10:55 UTC
18:10:55 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Migrant worker groups protested outside the health ministry Tuesday, calling for stronger labor protections and better home care services amid concerns over pregnant caregivers, CNA reported.
Taiwan relies too heavily on families hiring migrant caregivers directly, worker groups said, leaving both workers and employers with too much responsibility. They urged the government to provide more affordable and flexible home care services.
The Taiwan Care Workers' Union said many migrant caregivers work long hours without clear limits. It urged the government to gradually replace direct household employment with a system in which professional care organizations hire caregivers and provide services to families.
Taiwan prohibits employers from firing migrant caregivers because they become pregnant. However, household caregivers are not covered by the Labor Standards Act, and their maternity leave is unpaid, per the labor ministry.
At a separate protest outside the labor ministry, employers and families raised concerns about finding replacement caregivers. They said families caring for people with severe disabilities could be left without enough support for months when their regular caregivers cannot work.
The Taiwan Association of Families with Disabilities and Migrant Caregiver Employers called for a government agency to oversee recruitment, insurance, training, and job placement to help families maintain care.
The labor ministry said that if a caregiver cannot perform the required work, both sides may agree to end the contract, allowing the employer to apply for a replacement under existing rules.
The health ministry said it would work with the labor ministry to improve care services and support for families. Since September 2025, households employing migrant caregivers have had greater access to government-supported services, including care provided outside the home.
The labor ministry said the government has allocated about NT$2 billion (US$63 million) for respite and short-term care services. Eligible households can receive a combined total of up to 52 days of support annually when regular caregivers are unavailable, per Liberty Times.

The court said NT$7 million in bail and travel restrictions would be sufficient to deter him from fleeing or interfering with the investigation.

Prosecutors detained Wu at a Kaohsiung hospital on Monday after he failed to physically appear at a detention hearing that morning. Asked by the media about the incident, Wu said he had applied for two days of leave to prepare for heart surgery scheduled for Wednesday, per China Times.
Wu accused prosecutors of overstepping their authority, describing the incident as an erosion of human rights protections. After the presiding judge granted bail, Wu’s family posted the NT$7 million bond and took him back to the family residence, per ETtoday.
Wu’s defense team objected to his treatment, questioning whether prosecutors had obtained a medical assessment to determine if he was fit to leave the hospital, per SETN. The team emphasized that the court had approved his leave, adding that Wu had agreed to attend the evening hearing in person after prosecutors objected to his absence.
Wu’s lawyers questioned whether prosecutors’ insistence on detaining him at the hospital was intended to create what they described as the false impression that he was evading court proceedings.
The Taitung District Prosecutors Office responded by highlighting its efforts to verify whether Wu needed to remain hospitalized for further treatment, per Tai Sounds. It said the detention decision took both Wu’s health and the ongoing investigation into account.
Prosecutors also noted that the subsequent court proceedings would determine the legality of the detention.
Wu Chun-li manages Wu Hsiu-hua's Taitung County magistrate campaign.

Congo's Ebola cases surpass 10,000 as fears grow of wider African spread
Oct 27 - The number of confirmed Ebola cases in Democratic Republic of Congo has risen above 10,000, government data showed on Tuesday, a milestone that coincides with growing fears the epidemic could spread to more African countries.
The latest situation report from Congo's public health institute put the number of cases at 10,060, with those killed by the virus reaching 4,887.
The outbreak, caused by the rare Bundibugyo species of Ebola, was announced in mid-May and has since become the largest and deadliest in Congo, surpassing a 2018-2020 epidemic.
It is now the second-largest and second-deadliest on record behind only the 2014-2016 West African Ebola outbreak, which infected over 28,600 people and killed more than 11,000, mainly in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone.
Earlier this month, Kenya reported its first case and went on to announce nine cases in total, after a man who had travelled from Congo via Uganda died in Nairobi.
Last week, Nigeria became the fourth African country to report an Ebola case.
Health officials have been seeking to work out how and where the patient — the wife of a Swiss diplomat, who had not travelled to Congo — contracted the disease. The Swiss government said she was believed to have contracted it in Uganda.
The woman and her husband were flown to hospitals in Switzerland on Monday.
Uganda reported 20 cases in May and June, mostly imported from Congo, but the World Health Organization declared the country Ebola-free in August.
Ugandan officials say the country does not have any Ebola cases.
Uganda's health minister said on Sunday that Ugandan citizens returning to the country with a history of travel to Congo would be quarantined for 21 days. REUTERS

Bunun people’s farming practices featured in COP17 report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:10:31 UTC
18:10:31 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The traditional farming practices of the Bunun people have been highlighted in the latest edition of Local Biodiversity Outlooks, a report presented at the COP17 biodiversity conference in Yerevan, Armenia.
The report, presented last week, examines 56 cases of how Indigenous and local communities around the world preserve and sustain biodiversity. One features a collective of Bunun farmers in Zhuoqing Village, Hualien County.
Tse-Xin Organic Agriculture Foundation, which has collaborated with the farmers for more than a decade to revive traditional agricultural practices, said the case study from Taiwan underscores “the key value of Indigenous agricultural wisdom in conservation and sustainable development,” per CNA.
Zhuoqing Village sits at the edge of Yushan National Park, and according to recent government data, the vast majority of its 1,235 residents are Bunun.
Research shows the Bunun’s relationship with the land has gone through a profound change over the past century due to colonization and forced resettlement, with farming shifting from diversified cultivation to rice monoculture.
The revival of traditional farming practices began in 2013, when a young man who had returned to the village took over his family’s rice paddies and persuaded fellow farmers to pursue organic cultivation, according to the report.
The farmers began working with the foundation in 2014, focusing on documenting traditional practices and preserving local crop seeds, especially legumes.
One way the farmers and the foundation preserve Indigenous knowledge is through a mentorship program that pairs six elders with six young participants. Each month, the young participants visit their mentors’ gardens to record crop types, planting arrangements, plant growth, and surrounding wildlife.
Over 12 years, 20 hectares of farmland in the village have been converted to organic production, conserving local varieties of beans and grains, the foundation said.
“Indigenous peoples and local communities are by no means passive aid recipients,” the foundation added. “They are the most important rights-holders and guardians in achieving global biodiversity goals.”

French consumer confidence hits a 2013 low in October amid protests
- French consumer confidence fell to 80 in October, its lowest since June 2013, as protests, political unrest and austerity fears hit sentiment, INSEE said.
- Households grew more worried about prices, jobs and finances. Views on saving weakened, and Bloomberg Economics warned weak sentiment could hurt spending and fourth-quarter growth.
- The government announced school and university reforms to calm unrest, but protests and strikes are set to continue. Inflation may rise to 3.6%, with growth near 0.1%.

French consumer confidence fell by five points to 80 in October, its lowest level since June 2013, amid widespread protests in the country, official statistics agency INSEE said on Oct 27.
The country is being hit by a wave of protests, which began with small student demonstrations in suburban Paris in September to denounce school conditions and swiftly broadened into a wider demonstration against the government’s economic policies.
Economists surveyed by Reuters and Bloomberg had expected confidence to be around 85, the same as the revised September number and the latest figure is below any economist forecast.
The latest consumer confidence level is well below a long-term average of 100 between January 1987 and December 2025. The reading has been below 100 for five years amid bouts of inflation and political and budget instability and consumers are gloomy over a host of indicators.
The backdrop has worsened significantly in recent weeks with the minority government entering another showdown over austerity measures, a surge in borrowing costs as investors dump French bonds and an escalation of student protests.
The tensions boiled over on Oct 17 with violence breaking out around cost-of-living demonstrations, looting across the country and thousands of arrests.
INSEE’s latest consumer confidence measure does not reflect the full impact of the upheaval: while the cut-off was Oct 19, most of the responses are collected at the start of the three-week survey period.
“Weak sentiment is likely to weigh on spending as political uncertainty increases. This brings further downside risks to our fourth-quarter growth forecast,” said Jean Dalbard, economist at Bloomberg Economics.
In an attempt to calm the unrest that began with students blocking high schools, the French government announced on Oct 26 that it will overhaul the system for allocating university places, limit some class sizes and provide loans for building renovations.
But protests are set to continue on Saturdays as well as a day of demonstrations and strikes on Nov 5 that is backed by the country’s biggest trade unions.
The proportion of consumers who believe that prices have risen sharply over the past 12 months has risen by eight points, having already gained six points in September.
Data on Oct 30 is expected to show inflation accelerated further to 3.6% this month. A reading of gross domestic product, also due that day, will likely reveal that the economy expanded only 0.1% in the third quarter after stagnating in the previous three months and contracting at the start of 2026.
The INSEE survey found that households’ sentiment towards their past and future personal financial situations has dropped by nine and six points, respectively.
Fears over the trend in unemployment are on the rise again, up by five points following a fall in September.
The proportion of households considering this a good time for savings has fallen by six points, while views on their current ability to save remain stable. REUTERS, BLOOMBERG

EU Plans to Expand Frontex Powers for Deportations Outside Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:08:00 UTC
18:08:00 KST

Bulgaria Has EU’s Highest Road Death Rate
Bulgaria recorded the European Union’s highest road fatality rate in 2025, with 71 deaths per million inhabitants, according to final figures released by the European Commission
The European Union plans to expand Frontex’s powers to help deport irregular migrants from one non-EU country to another, extending the bloc’s migration operations beyond its borders, several EU officials told Euronews anonymously.
The European Commission is due to present the reforms on Tuesday, granting the Warsaw-based agency broader operational authority outside EU territory in changes likely to draw criticism from civil society organizations.
Frontex currently assists national authorities in returning irregular migrants from EU member states to their countries of origin, while also patrolling the bloc’s external borders and coastlines.
Under the proposed rules, the agency would also be able to help authorities in third countries, including North African governments, return Central African nationals to their countries of origin before they attempt to reach Europe.
“The more people you return before [they reach Europe], the less you have to return after,” an EU official told Euronews.
Frontex personnel would also be permitted to participate in deportations from return hubs that EU member states are now allowed to establish in non-EU countries under recently approved legislation. Five EU governments are negotiating plans to establish the first such hub, which is expected to begin operating in 2027.
Migrants whose asylum claims or rights to remain in the EU have been rejected and who are accommodated at these facilities are ultimately expected to be sent back to their countries of origin. Frontex’s participation could play a key role in arranging these final transfers.
Josephine Solanki, a researcher at the Amsterdam-based Transnational Institute think tank, described the agency’s evolving role during a press briefing ahead of the reform. “It's no longer only an agency supporting EU countries at their borders. [...] It's a deportation agency, increasingly operating far away from the actual border of the EU,” she said.
Several nongovernmental organizations and civil society groups are calling for any extension of Frontex’s mandate to come with stronger oversight and accountability safeguards to protect migrants’ fundamental rights. They argue that the agency has already been linked to rights violations during operations within Europe.
Cooperation with any non-EU country would nevertheless require a specific agreement with the government concerned, similar to the status agreements Frontex has already concluded with several countries outside the bloc, including Albania, Serbia and North Macedonia.
Such agreements allow Frontex personnel to be deployed for designated tasks on partner countries’ territory, including joint operations and rapid border interventions.
The EU is currently negotiating an agreement with Senegal. In 2023, Frontex appointed a liaison officer for Senegal whose expanded remit also includes Mauritania and Gambia, under informal “working arrangements.”
The reform would additionally establish a rapid-response force for sudden, large-scale arrivals of irregular migrants and an online surveillance unit responsible for monitoring social media to prevent mass movements.
The measures are intended to prevent a repeat of the mass entry into Ceuta last July, when around 90,000 migrants forced their way across the border between Morocco and the Spanish exclave.
European Commission Vice-President for Security Henna Virkkunen and Home Affairs Commissioner Magnus Brunner are expected to unveil the reform following the Commission’s weekly College meeting on Tuesday.
Frontex is also expected to receive €12 billion under the EU’s next seven-year budget, twice its previous allocation.

Israeli army offensive in Hebron displaces nearly 5,000 Palestinians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:07:44 UTC
18:07:44 KST

The Israeli army continued a large-scale offensive in the occupied West Bank city of Hebron for a fifth consecutive day on Tuesday, forcing nearly 5,000 Palestinians from their homes.
Hebron municipality said 4,969 Palestinians from 780 families had been forcibly displaced from the Deir Bahha and Al Jilda areas since the campaign began on Friday.
Among those displaced are 336 infants, 441 elderly people, 216 pregnant and nursing women, 44 people with disabilities and 312 people with chronic illnesses, the municipality said, warning of growing humanitarian consequences.
The army has shut entrances to Hebron and surrounding villages since Friday, following a shooting attack that killed two Israeli soldiers.
Anadolu footage showed Palestinians being stopped, searched and mistreated by Israeli forces at military checkpoints near Al Jilda Roundabout. Witnesses said reinforcements arrived in Ein Deir Baha, where troops took over Palestinian buildings and turned them into military posts.
The Palestinian Prisoner Society said the army had arrested 85 Palestinians across Hebron governorate since Friday.
Raids and closures across the West Bank
Elsewhere in the occupied West Bank, Israeli forces arrested at least nine Palestinians during raids and closed all main entrances to Ramallah.
In the northern West Bank, troops raided Jenin’s eastern neighbourhood and the towns of Meithalun, Jaba and Qabatiya, arresting at least six Palestinians, according to local sources.
In the central West Bank, Israeli forces closed Ramallah’s main entrances, including the Ein Sinya and Atara checkpoints, the Rawabi gate and the Nabi Saleh and Aboud gates, and set up additional checkpoints on alternative roads.
In Al Bireh, troops turned a Palestinian home into a military post, held four residents inside and confiscated their phones, local sources said.
Farmers were also expelled from their land in Turmus Ayya, while troops raided Tuqu, southeast of Bethlehem, with tracked military vehicles.
In Hebron governorate, troops repeatedly raided Taffuh and searched the homes of former prisoners. Israeli forces also assaulted and arrested a Palestinian man and his son in the Hawara area south of Hebron, according to local sources.
Illegal settler attacks and outposts
Separately, Israeli occupiers set fire to three Palestinian vehicles early Tuesday in Umm Safa, west of Ramallah.
Village municipal chief Marwan Sabah told Anadolu that attackers entered around midnight and set the vehicles ablaze. Residents confronted the group, forcing it to withdraw, he said.
Sabah said Umm Safa had repeatedly faced attacks involving assaults, vehicle arson, intimidation and harassment, adding that occupiers had seized large areas of village land.
Israeli occupiers also established a settlement outpost at Al Bireh’s northern entrance, overlooking the Al Balou neighbourhood, the Bedouin rights group Al-Baidar said.
According to the Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission, occupiers attempted to establish 21 new settlement outposts across the West Bank in September, including 10 in Ramallah and Al Bireh governorate.
The incidents come amid intensified Israeli army raids and attacks by Israeli occupiers across the occupied West Bank since Israel launched its war on Gaza in October 2023.

Israel election turnout hits 45-year high at 16.68% by 10 a.m.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:07:25 UTC
18:07:25 KST

Voter turnout in Israel's parliamentary election reached 44.9% by 2 p.m. Tuesday, surpassing the 38.9% recorded at the same hour in the previous election, the Central Elections Committee announced. According to official figures, 3,290,480 Israelis had cast their ballots by that time. "We've broken all records," said attorney Din Livne, the committee's acting director-general, as long lines formed at polling stations across the country.
Turnout was also high among military personnel. The IDF Spokesperson's Unit reported that 48% of service members had voted by 1 p.m., compared with 44.4% at the same hour during the election for the 25th Knesset.
A breakdown of turnout by city revealed significant differences across the country. By noon, 28.8% of eligible voters in Tel Aviv had cast their ballots, compared with 27.1% in Jerusalem, 27.3% in Haifa, 29% in Rishon LeZion and 27.4% in Be'er Sheva.
Among the municipalities included in the committee's figures, Modi'in-Maccabim-Re'ut recorded particularly high participation at 36.7%, followed by Modi'in Illit at 33.2%. Turnout reached 31.4% in Kiryat Ata, 30.4% in Ashdod and 30.3% in Sderot. Lower figures were recorded in Netanya at 23.8%, Nazareth at 24.9% and Eilat at 22.2%.
The midday figures followed an already strong start to voting. By 10 a.m., turnout had reached 16.68%, the highest recorded at that hour since 1981. More than 1.2 million Israelis had cast their ballots during the opening hours, an increase of 0.78 percentage points compared with the same stage of the previous election, when turnout stood at 15.9%.
Voting was also significantly higher among military personnel. According to the IDF, 48% of eligible service members had voted by 1 p.m., compared with 44.4% at the same hour during the previous election.
A total of 7,331,981 Israelis are eligible to vote in the election for the 26th Knesset, with 36 parties competing for seats in the 120-member parliament. Some 12,018 polling stations are operating nationwide, with most remaining open until 10 p.m.
Early reports indicated considerable voter interest, with long lines forming at polling stations in Ra'anana, Ramat Gan and other cities. At a school in Ra'anana, one voter expressed surprise at the unusually large morning crowds, saying she had never encountered such a long line so early on election day.
Livne acknowledged the lengthy queues, saying the high turnout had inevitably led to delays as election officials carefully verified each voter's identity. He urged citizens to remain patient and promised that everyone who arrived before the deadline would be able to vote.
"We promise that everyone will get to vote," Livne said, explaining that polling stations would remain open beyond 10 p.m. if necessary to accommodate voters already waiting in line by that time.
Central Elections Committee Chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg acknowledged the inconvenience caused by the queues, noting that voters were waiting between 15 and 20 minutes at some polling stations. However, he said the strong participation demonstrated that Israelis were determined to exercise their democratic rights despite the country's political divisions.
President Isaac Herzog, who voted in Jerusalem alongside his wife Michal, urged Israelis to participate in the democratic process. He described election day as a celebration of democracy and called on citizens not to allow political divisions to undermine the vote.
"This is our day to go out, make a difference and vote," Herzog said, emphasizing that all citizens have an equal voice at the ballot box.
Shin Bet Director David Zini also addressed the Central Elections Committee's control center, saying the election was being conducted safely and under close supervision despite attempts by some individuals to disrupt the process.
The committee separately dismissed reports of systematic damage to ballot slips belonging to political parties, saying it had found no evidence of widespread tampering. Officials stressed that individual complaints were being examined immediately and urged voters to rely on official information.
Voting is taking place under unsettled weather conditions. The Israel Meteorological Service issued a yellow warning for thunderstorms and lightning between 10 a.m. and 2 p.m., with rain, strong winds and possible hail forecast across parts of the country. Flash floods are also possible in southern Israel.
Although most polling stations will close at 10 p.m., when television networks release their exit polls, the final outcome may remain uncertain for several days. Between 600,000 and 650,000 Israelis are expected to cast special double-envelope ballots, primarily soldiers, reservists and displaced residents voting away from their registered polling stations.
Those ballots could affect the distribution of approximately 15 parliamentary seats and potentially change the balance between competing political blocs. Election officials expect to complete the full count by Thursday afternoon, meaning the final allocation of seats may remain unresolved beyond election night.
First published: 11:07, 10.27.26

EU readying for major Australian resources investment, ambassador says
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:07:16 CET
18:07:16 KST

By Melanie Burton
SYDNEY, Oct 27 (Reuters) - The European Union expects a wave of investment into the Australian critical minerals sector as it pushes to diversify its supply chain away from China, the bloc’s ambassador to Australia Lawrence Meredith said on Tuesday.
Australia and the European Union struck a free trade agreement in March after eight years of negotiations, removing tariffs on almost all goods and easing EU access to Australian critical minerals.
Once both parties sign and ratify that agreement, expected early next year, a 5.5% EU tariff on critical minerals will be removed.
“It is going to be a game changer,” Meredith said.
In parallel, talks are “very close” for Australia to sign a memorandum of understanding with the European Investment Bank, which would act as the bloc’s funding vehicle, Meredith added.
“The European Union will be massively investing in critical minerals. Since we wish to diversify away from China, then one of the most likely partners has to be Australia,” he said.
EU policy proposals have laid out as much as €10 billion ($11.2 billion) for critical raw materials within the larger €409 billion competitiveness fund, as the EU debates its budget from 2028 to 2034.
Australia is one of several critical minerals “superpowers” in which the EU is looking to invest, including Brazil, South Africa and Canada. The EU also expects to invest along the supply chain, including in processing, Meredith said.
Australia said on Tuesday it would refresh its critical minerals strategy to place greater emphasis on refining and processing, as competition for investment intensifies and supply-chain concerns persist.
The bloc is looking initially at the minerals that Australia will prioritise for its strategic reserve: gallium, antimony and rare earths.
Australian companies going faster through the early project development would speed the investment process, he said.
“(The FTA) is a signal that Europe wants to do far more with Australia. We also have a security and defence partnership. A lot of that is dual technology, and it requires precisely these critical minerals,” he said.
The European Union plans to mobilise €800 billion into defence under ReArm Europe by 2030.
Australia is also on track to join the EU’s flagship funding program for research and innovation, Horizon Europe, next year.
Meredith said 2026 had been a “transformational” year for Australian-EU relations.
“You’ve seen a big surge in EU-Australia in 2026, and I’m very confident we will go to the next level in 2027.”
($1 = 0.8961 euros)
(Reporting by Melanie Burton: Editing by Sharon Singleton)

Congo’s Ebola infections surpass 10,000, government says
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:07:12 CET
18:07:12 KST

Oct 27 (Reuters) - The number of confirmed Ebola cases in Democratic Republic of Congo has risen above 10,000, government data showed on Tuesday, a milestone that coincides with growing fears the epidemic could spread to more African countries.
The latest situation report from Congo’s public health institute put the number of cases at 10,060, with those killed by the virus reaching 4,887.
The outbreak, caused by the rare Bundibugyo species of Ebola, was announced in mid-May and has since become the largest and deadliest in Congo, surpassing a 2018-2020 epidemic.
It is now the second-largest and second-deadliest on record behind only the 2014-2016 West African Ebola outbreak, which infected over 28,600 people and killed more than 11,000, mainly in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone.
Earlier this month, Kenya reported its first case and went on to announce nine cases in total, after a man who had travelled from Congo via Uganda died in Nairobi.
Last week, Nigeria became the fourth African country to report an Ebola case.
Health officials have been seeking to work out how and where the patient — the wife of a Swiss diplomat, who had not travelled to Congo — contracted the disease. The Swiss government said she was believed to have contracted it in Uganda.
The woman and her husband were flown to hospitals in Switzerland on Monday.
Uganda reported 20 cases in May and June, mostly imported from Congo, but the World Health Organization declared the country Ebola-free in August.
Ugandan officials say the country does not have any Ebola cases.
Uganda’s health minister said on Sunday that Ugandan citizens returning to the country with a history of travel to Congo would be quarantined for 21 days.
(Reporting by Nilutpal Timsina and Anait Miridzhanian; Editing by Robbie Corey-Boulet, Alexander Winning, Barbara Lewis and Joe Bavier)

The manifesto pledge on equalisation still applies, but it was always clear it would happen over time and we would take into account, as the minimum wage uprating each year always does, the relative strength of the labour market and other pressures …

NAIROBI, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Tanzanian opposition leader Tundu Lissu, who was charged with treason last year, has started a hunger strike to protest his inability to access his lawyers, his party said.
Lissu, who leads the CHADEMA opposition party and came second in the 2020 presidential election, began refusing food on Monday after his lawyers were denied entry to the prison where he is being held, party spokesperson Brenda Rupia wrote on X.
Tanzania Prisons Service spokesperson Elizabeth Mbezi said it would give an update on Lissu soon. Government spokesperson Gerson Msigwa did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Lissu was charged with treason over what prosecutors said was a speech calling on the public to rebel and disrupt last year’s general election. He pleaded not guilty to the charges, which his lawyer has said are politically motivated.
Tanzania’s electoral commission had barred CHADEMA from participating in the polls after it failed to sign a code of conduct document.
The election was marred by protests and unrest, with a government-appointed commission of inquiry saying the violence that broke out afterwards killed at least 518 people and blaming the protesters for the violence.
CHADEMA’s chief legal counsel, Rugemeleza Nshala, told journalists on Saturday that Lissu had planned the strike because he was denied privacy during talks with his lawyers in violation of a court order.
The court is due to deliver its judgement in Lissu’s case on November 6.
Lissu’s detention, along with the alleged abductions of government critics, has shone a spotlight on the human rights record of President Samia Suluhu Hassan, who won the 2025 election.
The government has rejected accusations of widespread rights abuses and said it is committed to respecting human rights. It ordered an investigation into reports of abductions in 2024, though no official findings have been made public.

Finnish drone electronics maker raises $2.8M in five days
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:06:27 UTC
18:06:27 KST

- Finnish drone electronics maker Arctic RAVN secured €2.5 million in convertible loan commitments in five days, exceeding its €2 million target.
- The company aims to build tens of thousands of speed controllers by the end of 2026 and eventually up to two million circuit boards a year.
Finnish drone electronics maker Arctic RAVN has secured €2.5 million (about $2.8 million) in convertible loan commitments in five days, passing its €2 million (about $2.2 million) target before it has officially launched a single product, and it plans to use the money to scale up production of the circuit boards that power and steer military drones.
The company said on Oct. 27, 2026, that it opened the round in October and that the financing will go toward ramping up manufacturing and product development, as it already holds follow-up orders and is in talks with several leading European defense manufacturers.
Arctic RAVN builds electronic speed controllers, the boards that regulate power to a drone’s motors, and flight controllers, the onboard computers that keep the aircraft stable and carry out its pilot’s commands, and it says every product is designed and manufactured in Finland with components sourced entirely from Europe and NATO-allied countries.
“Investors committed to the round within days, even though we have not yet officially launched a single product. Follow-up orders and discussions with several leading defence manufacturers indicate a need for high-performance European drone electronics. We are now scaling our manufacturing capabilities for industrial-level output and strengthening Europe’s ability to produce critical drone electronics,” said Matti Vansén, chief executive of Arctic RAVN.
The company has already put more than €1 million (about $1.1 million) into scaling up production of its speed controllers and aims to build tens of thousands of units by the end of 2026, with a significant share already reserved by customers, before shifting its next production ramp-up to flight controllers and, over the longer term, expanding capacity to as many as two million circuit boards a year.
Its current lineup includes the AR41ESC, a four-in-one speed controller that runs on 6S to 12S lithium-polymer batteries and handles at least 60 amps of continuous current per channel, with 90-amp bursts, and the AR32FC flight controller, which accepts 4S to 14S battery input, carries two inertial measurement units and runs custom firmware.
Arctic RAVN is one of the studio companies of Finnish Defence House, a defense technology venture studio that finds, funds and builds new companies, and it joins a growing number of Finnish firms working on military drones, including Summa Defence, which delivered its first batch of Zeus FPV drones to the Armed Forces of Ukraine in December 2025.

‘Coward’ premiered in Belgian cinemas on 21 October and has already attracted considerable international attention. The film won awards and was enthusiastically received at Cannes, received rave reviews in both domestic and international media, and was selected as Belgium’s entry for the Oscars.
In the film, Dhont approaches the First World War in a unique way. Alongside the violence and destruction, he emphasises beauty, art and the love between two soldiers at the front. He also highlights aspects of ‘the Great War’ that have been forgotten over the years.

From 7 November onwards, a pop-up exhibition will showcase costumes, props, archive footage and clips from the film. This will give visitors an insight into how historical sources and museum collections were brought to life on the silver screen. The exhibition also places the film within a broader historical context.
