Israel Heads to the Polls as Netanyahu Battles to Stay in Power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:05:00 UTC
18:05:00 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his main rival, former Israel Defense Forces chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot, appear short of an outright victory, initial exit polls indicate.
The polls show Eisenkot’s opposition bloc with a narrow edge over Netanyahu and his allies, though they suggest that neither side will emerge with a clear path to a governing majority.
Still, opposition leaders cast the initial poll results as an evident rebuke of Netanyahu, the country’s longest-serving Prime Minister, who is facing one of the most consequential tests of his political career.
Eisenkot wrote on social media shortly following the release of the preliminary exit polls that “the preliminary poll results point to complete distrust in Netanyahu” and contended that “if these are the final results, this is a victory.”
Opposition leader Yair Lapid and Yair Golan, the leader of Israel’s Democrats party, treated the initial polls as an even stronger marker of the opposition’s success.
“Don't let them confuse you: The Netanyahu bloc suffered a harsh defeat,” Lapid posted. "This is a total collapse and the public told them to get lost and go home.”
“The public has spoken, it has fired the Netanyahu government,” Golan wrote.
Itamar Ben-Gvir, Israel's national security minister and head of the far-right Otzma Yehudit party, meanwhile expressed hope that Netanyahu's bloc would ultimately prevail, pointing to differences between exit polls. “The night is still young,” Ben-Gvir said Tuesday evening.
Israelis flocked to polling stations earlier in the day to decide Netanyahu’s political fate.
From 7 a.m. to 10 p.m. local time on Tuesday (1 a.m. to 4 p.m. EDT), Israelis were able to cast votes for representatives in the Knesset. Numbers from Israel's Central Elections Committee reflected a strong turnout, with 77.7% of eligible voters reported to have cast their ballots by 10 p.m., local time—the highest turnout logged since 1999.
Netanyahu was joined by his wife Sara as he cast his own ballot just after midday, at a polling station in a Jerusalem school. “This is a very moving and fateful moment. My wife and I are truly overwhelmed,” Netanyahu told reporters after voting. “We know what is at stake, and since I am not allowed to say things explicitly, I will say: Vote correctly.”
Not long after, Netanyahu told his supporters that "buses are heading to the polling stations and huge lines are being reported in the Arab settlements." Complaining that "the right-wing strongholds are not waking up," he again urged people to go out and vote.
Netanyahu’s Likud party said in a statement that it had submitted a request to the Central Elections Committee to extend voting hours past 10 p.m. The committee later announced it would not be extending voting hours past the scheduled closing time.
This is the first election in the country since the Oct. 7, 2023 terrorist attacks by Palestinian militant group Hamas and the subsequent Israeli war in the Gaza Strip. Since then, Israel under Netanyahu has pursued an aggressive military campaign across the Middle East—going to war with Iran, backing settler attacks and displacement in the West Bank, and carrying out strikes against militant groups in Lebanon and Yemen.
The election was widely seen as a referendum on Netanyahu’s leadership and Israelis’ willingness to change course amid uncertainty.
Read More: Israel's Choice
“I hope this will be a true holiday for democracy,” Isaac Herzog, the Israeli head of state, told reporters from a polling station in Rehavia, where he and his wife voted. “No one can be allowed to spoil or undermine it.”
Here’s what to know:
Who is in the running?
Two main political blocs are contending to form Israel’s next government. The first is the pro-Netanyahu coalition led by Netanyahu’s Likud party. The coalition includes far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties, such as Otzma Yehudit (Jewish Power) led by national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Religious Zionism-Zehut led by finance minister Bezalel Smotrich. Their ultranationalist policies have found an audience in younger right-wing Israelis.
On the other side are the Jewish-led opposition movements—with Eisenkot and the centrist Yashar (Straight) party at the forefront. Eisenkot, who entered politics in 2022, joined Netanyahu’s emergency war cabinet after the Oct. 7 attack on Israel. But after having lost a son in combat in Israel’s wars, Eisenkot left his post in 2024. Two of his nephews also died fighting in Gaza, a prominent campaign talking point.
The opposition also includes a joint ticket led by former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett and Knesset opposition leader Yair Lapid, the secular nationalist party Yisrael Beiteinu (Israel Our Home) led by former finance minister Avigdor Lieberman, and the Democrats led by former IDF deputy chief of staff Yair Golan.
The Democrats party on Tuesday said Golan had been “approached in a threatening manner” by a man who was found to be carrying a knife. The lawmaker was attending a voting-day mobilization tour in Tel Aviv's HaMesila Park at the time of the incident.
"Golan’s security guards blocked the man, and as they moved toward him, a large knife slipped from beneath his clothing and fell to the ground," the party said in a statement shared with the Guardian. "Police were called to the scene and arrested the suspect." Golan, in his own statement, vowed that "incitement and violence will not deter us" and encouraged people to go out and vote.
Meanwhile, some polls had suggested that Eisenkot’s Yashar party may garner slightly more support than Netanyahu’s Likud, but they also projected that neither the Prime Minister’s right-wing bloc nor the opposition were likely to win the 61 Knesset seats needed to form a government.
Including Arab parties such as United Arab List (Ra’am) and the Joint List, or fringe parties, could be necessary to form a government. Both pro-Netanyahu and anti-Netanyahu coalitions have so far ruled out teaming up with the Arab-led parties. Arab citizens of Israel make up about 20% of the population, though they receive fewer government services and endure higher poverty and unemployment rates. Discrimination and disappointment have historically depressed Arab-Israeli voter turnout. However, on Tuesday, there appeared to be strong turnout in some of Israel’s largest Arab-majority towns.
Netanyahu touts Trump endorsement
Netanyahu has brought attention to the support he received from his longstanding ally, U.S. President Donald Trump, who only announced his endorsement days before the election as conflict in the Middle East has tested their friendship.
In a late-night TV appearance on Oct. 25, Netanyahu boasted of Trump’s endorsement and said that Trump was willing to take action “that would finally, finally, remove the Iranian threat” so long as Netanyahu stayed in power. Netanyahu added that he has already instructed Israel’s national intelligence agency Mossad as well as the IDF to “bring down” the Iranian regime. Trump remains very popular in Israel.
By contrast, U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance declined to endorse Netanyahu for re-election, just a day after Trump put his “complete and total” support behind the Israeli leader.
“The President has the most effective endorsement in American, or international, political history,” said Vance, when asked in an interview if he would also be extending an endorsement of his own. “I endorse American candidates and that’s where I'm focused on, is the midterms, so I'm not getting involved in the Israeli elections.”
When pushed for an answer, Vance added: “I'm not anti-endorsing [Netanyahu], I'm not pro-endorsing him.”
A high-stakes election for Netanyahu
At stake for Netanyahu could be more than his continued leadership. The premier faces an international arrest warrant for alleged crimes related to the Israeli military campaign in Gaza. And even domestically, critics have demanded an inquiry into Netanyahu’s decision-making around Oct. 7. The attack, which resulted in over 1,200 people in Israel killed and around 250 hostages taken, is considered by many to be indicative of a major security failure.
The Gaza health ministry reports that since Oct. 7, 2023, more than 74,000 individuals have been killed. In the absence of independent monitoring on the ground, Gaza’s health ministry is the primary source for casualty data relied upon by humanitarian groups, journalists, and international bodies. Its figures do not differentiate between civilians and combatants and cannot be independently verified by TIME.
Another issue driving the election is public fury over ultra-Orthodox communities’ exemption from military conscription for men engaged in religious studies. Despite a shortage of soldiers, less than 10% of eligible ultra-Orthodox men enlist, amid demands from Netanyahu’s allies to exempt them. Eisenkot, Netanyahu’s main rival, has promised to end the de facto exemptions.
Netanyahu’s repeated attempts to reform the judiciary have also factored into this election, with critics slamming his undermining of democratic institutions and connecting it to his legal interests. Netanyahu is in the middle of a yearslong corruption trial, which he and his allies—including Trump—have claimed is politically motivated. He sought, but didn’t receive, a presidential pardon from Herzog.
When will we know the results?
About 7.3 million Israeli citizens were eligible to vote on Tuesday. The election fills the Knesset’s 120 seats through proportional representation—which means parties, not personalities, are on these voters’ ballots.
After polling stations closed at 10 p.m. (4 p.m. EDT), local media broadcasted initial exit polls. The final vote tally is expected by Oct. 30, with official results published on Nov. 4.
But getting a clear picture of the Israeli government is likely to take longer.
No single party has ever claimed 61 seats to form a government, meaning Israel has always been governed by coalitions. Such alliances can take weeks or months to form, and what those coalitions may look like will depend on the election outcomes for smaller parties, which each need 3.25% of the votes to secure a seat in the Knesset.
Once the election winners are determined, President Herzog will refer to party leaders to choose a preferred Prime Minister and will ask the strongest candidate to form a government within 42 days. If a coalition cannot be formed after multiple attempts, the current Likud-led coalition government will continue to serve as caretaker before another round of elections is held in the coming months.

Nausėda: Lithuania-China diplomatic ties should not hinge on Taiwan office name
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:04:00 UTC
18:04:00 KST

Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda said restoring full diplomatic representation between Lithuania and China should not be directly linked to changing the name of Taiwan’s representative office in Vilnius, stressing that normalising relations is a pragmatic goal.
“Such efforts are fully justified, and I do not think they should be linked very directly to the name of the Taiwanese Representative Office. We simply want neither more nor less – we want to restore relations with China to a normal level,” Nausėda told the radio Žinių Radijas on Tuesday.
He said Lithuania could initially accept a lower level of diplomatic representation, with the interests of either country represented by a deputy head of mission rather than an ambassador.
“This is a completely pragmatic goal to normalise diplomatic relations. That is something we should do in any case,” the president said.
Nausėda said it was too early to determine whether ongoing discussions with Beijing would yield tangible results. Meetings scheduled for November could help clarify the prospects for negotiations, he added.
Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius has previously said he hoped Lithuania and China would achieve a breakthrough by the end of the year.
Lithuania’s ruling majority aims to normalise relations with China and restore diplomatic representation to the level maintained by other European Union member states. The goal is also included in the government’s program.
Relations between Lithuania and China deteriorated in the autumn of 2021 after Vilnius allowed Taiwan to open a representative office under the name “Taiwanese”. Similar offices in other countries generally operate under the name Taipei, which Beijing prefers because it does not imply recognition of Taiwan as a separate state.
China responded by unilaterally downgrading its diplomatic representation in Lithuania from ambassador to chargé d’affaires. Lithuania subsequently stopped issuing new accreditations to Chinese diplomats, leaving China without accredited diplomats in the country since May last year.

Number of UK businesses in financial distress ‘at two-decade high’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:01:07 UTC
18:01:07 KST

The number of UK businesses in financial distress has hit its highest level in more than two decades, as pressure grows on the chancellor to provide more support to the private sector in Wednesday’s budget.
There were 738,144 businesses in “significant” financial distress in the third quarter of this year, up 1.6% compared with the same period last year, according to BTG. That is the highest level since the administrator’s closely watched “red flag” report began in 2004.
The UK’s support services, construction and real estate sectors were among the most vulnerable, with the highest numbers of businesses in significant distress – at 118,695, 108,340 and 99,908 respectively.
The hospitality industry was hardest hit this year, with a 5% rise in the number of bars and restaurants in distress to 18,866. Struggling food and drug retailers rose by more than 7% to 19,269, according to BTG, which is one of the UK’s biggest insolvency practitioners and changed its name from Begbies Traynor in February.
The growing strain on UK companies comes as the chancellor, John Healey, prepares to give his first budget on Wednesday, against an increasingly volatile backdrop as the war in the Middle East disrupts the global economy, putting pressure on public finances and reigniting the cost of living crisis.
The chancellor has vowed to use the budget to provide households and businesses with more “breathing space”.
Mark Fry, the chief executive of BTG, said British businesses were “battling a combination of rising employment costs, inflationary pressures, higher energy prices and elevated borrowing costs.
“Crucially, these pressures are not only affecting small businesses’ ability to operate, but also larger businesses’ ability to compete on a global stage,” he said.
A freedom of information request by BTG also found that British businesses still owed £27.3bn in arrears to HMRC in VAT, corporation tax and PAYE at the end of August.
About £24bn has been recovered since arrears reached a peak of £51.3bn during the Covid pandemic, compared with a pre-pandemic total of £11.4bn.
“With £27.3bn owed to HMRC, high levels of recovery activity and record financial distress across the economy, many companies are approaching this budget from a position of financial weakness rather than strength,” Fry said.
“We hear from businesses that structural hurdles, weight of red tape, employment legislation and the tax burden alongside high interest and energy costs will need to be tackled if this is to be a budget for business.”
Last week the prime minister, Andy Burnham, promised that his government would “slash red tape” for businesses, with plans to make compliance guidance clearer, simplify the UK’s corporate reporting requirements and extend import tariff suspensions on products favoured by businesses.

Türkiye completes EU machinery safety harmonization to boost $10 bln in exports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:59:51 UTC
17:59:51 KST

The Turkish Trade Ministry has announced the signing of a declaration confirming Türkiye’s alignment with EU machinery safety legislation, fulfilling customs union requirements.
The regulatory harmonization “paves the way for the Turkish machinery sector to benefit from the free movement of goods across European markets.”
Ankara can now designate accredited notified bodies within Türkiye, enabling Turkish machinery exporters to conduct their conformity assessment and certification procedures at home instead of relying on foreign institutions.
The local assessments will be recognized under the same conditions as those performed by EU manufacturers.
The deal marks a major milestone in simplifying technical and administrative processes that Turkish exporters deal with when accessing the European single market.
The financial costs and administrative burdens associated with these regulatory procedures will be significantly reduced.
The alignment will reportedly benefit more than $10 billion worth of Turkish machinery exports to the EU per year.
Machinery sales make up 10 percent of Türkiye’s total export volume to the EU, according to the ministry.

GDELS and ARMMO team up on mobile anti-drone system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:58:47 UTC
17:58:47 KST

- ARMMO and Santa Bárbara Sistemas launched and flew the Bandit-X interceptor drone from an ASCOD Heavy Mission Carrier during Spain’s ATLAS 26 exercise.
- ARMMO says Bandit-X exceeds 360 km/h, flies for 20 to 25 minutes and has an estimated range of 40 to 50 km.
Spanish drone maker ARMMO Defense Technologies and General Dynamics European Land Systems’ Spanish unit, Santa Bárbara Sistemas, launched and flew ARMMO’s Bandit-X interceptor drone from an ASCOD Heavy Mission Carrier tracked armored vehicle during the ATLAS 26 counter-drone exercise in Huelva, Spain, turning the heavy vehicle into a mobile launcher for drones that hunt down other drones.
The two companies announced the demonstration on Oct. 27, 2026, along with a cooperation agreement to develop and integrate autonomous systems on armored vehicles and other ground platforms, and they said the launch was carried out in front of senior Spanish and NATO officers, including Spain’s Chief of the Defence Staff, Adm. Gen. Manuel Teodoro López Calderón, and Adm. Pierre Vandier, NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Transformation.
The launcher had already been spotted at the exercise, when Defence Blog reported that a tracked ASCOD carrier was seen with box-shaped launch containers marked with ARMMO’s logo on its open rear deck at the Médano del Loro training range, where ATLAS 26 ran from Oct. 19 to Oct. 23 under the direction of the Spanish Army’s Anti-Aircraft Artillery Command.
Bandit-X is a high-speed interceptor built to find and destroy hostile unmanned aircraft, and ARMMO says it flies at more than 360 km/h (224 mph), with plans to push that to 420 km/h (261 mph), stays in the air for 20 to 25 minutes and has an estimated operational range of 40 to 50 km (25 to 31 miles), depending on conditions and mission profile.
The company says the drone can navigate on its own when satellite navigation is jammed or denied, resists electronic interference and guides itself autonomously in the final phase of an intercept, and that it was validated during NATO experimental activities in Slovakia in 2026 and has been assigned a NATO Stock Number, which lets allied militaries identify and order it through their common logistics catalog.
The ASCOD Heavy Mission Carrier is a modular tracked platform from Santa Bárbara Sistemas that can be fitted for ground-based air defense, artillery, fire support, heavy recovery, logistics, electronic warfare, medical evacuation and counter-drone missions, and it uses the NEVA open digital architecture, built to NATO’s Generic Vehicle Architecture standard, so that systems from other companies can be added to the vehicle.
ARMMO, which operates an industrial site of more than 30,000 square meters (323,000 square feet) in Zafra, in Spain’s Badajoz province, also builds unmanned ground and surface vehicles and electronic warfare systems, and the agreement with Santa Bárbara Sistemas sets up a framework for putting its autonomous technologies on a range of ground vehicles.

Natural History Museum launches new tender for permanent exhibition project
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:58:00 UTC
17:58:00 KST

Natural History Museum launches new tender for permanent exhibition project
The Natural History Museum has launched a new €3 million tender to find a contractor for one of the largest projects in Estonia's museum sector in the past decade.
The museum is seeking a contractor to design the new permanent exhibition and to implement it based on that design at the newly built wooden Nature House in Põhja-Tallinn. The two-part tender has a total value of €2,812,950.
Egle Hecht, acting director of the Estonian Museum of Natural History, said she hopes to see companies from both Estonia and abroad that have previously carried out similar museum projects among the bidders for the permanent exhibition tender.
"This is a very large international tender for Estonia's museum sector, the likes of which was last carried out more than 10 years ago when the Estonian National Museum was established," she said.
The previous tender failed.
"A total of three bids were submitted for the first tender for the core exhibition, but unfortunately none of them qualified. As these were predominantly some of the world's leading creative agencies specializing in exhibition construction, which often do not participate in public procurement tenders, it turned out that they misunderstood the tender conditions and made mistakes when submitting their bids. With the new tender, we hope to avoid similar situations," Hecht said.
The acting director said the museum's new core exhibition will tell the story of the coexistence of nature and humans through Estonia's natural environment. It is hoped it will be "more ambitious and exceptional than before in terms of its concept, size and execution."
"In every chapter, humans are one of the characters, equal among others. Alongside well-known and visible species, we emphasize the richness of microscopic life and its coexistence with other living organisms. We talk about different relationships in nature, also touching on, for example, how rich biodiversity influences culture and language, and vice versa. The new permanent exhibition offers something for all age groups, being accessible and taking different visitors into account," Hecht said.
The museum is also planning a separate children's exhibition, where they can learn about nature in a way that supports their natural curiosity.
Natural History Museum to fully open in 2028
The tender consists of two parts: the permanent exhibition and the exhibition for young children.
"We will open the children's exhibition together with the museum's first temporary exhibition in 2027, meaning there is less time to complete it, while the permanent exhibition will open in 2028. That is why the tender has been divided into two parts," Hecht said.
The acting director said the museum will open its doors with its first exhibition in 2027, as planned from the outset, although the exact date is not yet clear.
"Once the Taru Nature House is completed, the museum will only then begin moving into the building and constructing and setting up the exhibitions. The completion of the building will allow us to begin creating the exhibition," Hecht said.
The expected final deadline for the design and exhibition construction work under the procurement contract is April 6, 2028.
The deadline for submitting bids is in one month's time, on November 23. The work will be financed from external funds (the Cohesion Policy Funds Implementation Programme 2021–2027) and the Environmental Investment Center's environmental program.

By orders of the Head of State, Yerzhan Seitkulov has been relieved of his duties as head of the Information Resources Protection Department of the Executive Office of the Kazakh President, with Nurbolat Magzumov appointed as his successor, Qazinform News Agency reports, citing Akorda.
Born on April 4, 1979, in Almaty region, Seitkulov graduated from the Faculty of Mechanics and Mathematics at Lomonosov Moscow State University in 2001. He also completed a research internship at New York University and holds a Candidate of Sciences degree in Physics and Mathematics.
Seitkulov began his career in 2002 as a mathematics lecturer at the Kazakhstan branch of Lomonosov Moscow State University in Astana, where he worked until 2007. He then joined L.N. Gumilyov Eurasian National University, serving as a senior lecturer, associate professor, and deputy dean for research at the Faculty of Information Technology until 2011.
In 2012, he became director of the university's Research Institute of Information Security and Cryptology, a position he held for a decade. He later headed the Engineering and Technical Center under the Administrative Office of the Kazakh President, serving in that role between August 2022 and November 2023.
Seitkulov joined the Executive Office of the Kazakh President in November 2023 as deputy head of the Department of Informatization and Information Resources Protection. He was appointed head of the department in December of that year before taking charge of the Information Resources Protection Department in August 2024.
Nurbolat Magzumov has been appointed as the new head of the Information Resources Protection Department of the Executive Office of the Kazakh President.
Previously, Qazinform reported Kanat Kulshmanov would head the Central Communications Service.

EXPLAINER - Israel election: What to expect after polls close
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:56:58 UTC
17:56:58 KST

Polling stations in Israel’s closely contested general election will close Tuesday at 10 pm local time (2000GMT), beginning a counting and coalition-building process that could determine whether Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu remains in power.
Around 7.3 million voters are eligible to elect the 120 members of the Knesset in Israel’s first general election since the Oct. 7, 2023 attacks and its first held on schedule since 1988.
Final opinion polls placed former military chief Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party ahead of Netanyahu’s Likud, but projected neither political bloc securing the 61 seats normally required to form a government.
Here is what to expect after voting ends.
Israeli broadcasters Kan 11, Channel 12, and Channel 13 are expected to release separate exit polls immediately after polling stations close.
The surveys will provide the first estimates of how many seats each party may receive and whether Netanyahu or Eisenkot has a possible route to a governing majority.
Exit polls, however, are projections rather than counted votes. Small differences between the surveys could prove significant because several parties are polling close to the 3.25% electoral threshold.
A party falling slightly below the threshold would receive no representation, potentially shifting several seats between the rival blocs.
Final pre-election surveys projected Yashar winning 22 or 23 seats and Likud receiving between 19 and 21.
Netanyahu’s right-wing and religious alliance was projected to secure around 50 seats, while the main opposition parties were forecast to receive between 52 and 56. Palestinian-led parties were expected to win a combined 14 to 16 seats.
Votes cast at ordinary polling stations will be counted locally after voting ends, with results transmitted to regional counting centers and the Central Elections Committee.
The first official figures are expected to emerge during the night, gradually replacing the television projections.
A clearer picture should be available Wednesday morning, but closely contested seats may remain unresolved.
Israel allocates parliamentary seats nationally through proportional representation. Votes cast for parties that fail to reach the electoral threshold are excluded before seats are distributed among the qualifying lists.
This means the balance of power may change sharply as the count reveals which smaller parties have entered parliament.
The initial count will not include all ballots.
Soldiers, diplomats, hospital patients and staff, prisoners, election workers and voters using specially accessible polling stations cast their votes through a double-envelope system.
Officials first verify the voter’s identity and ensure that the person has not also voted at an ordinary polling station. The identifying outer envelope is then separated from the anonymous ballot before counting.
Approximately 650,000 such ballots are expected, representing enough votes to affect around 14 parliamentary seats.
Their counting is expected to take between 24 and 36 hours and could move parties above or below the electoral threshold, change individual seat allocations and alter the coalition arithmetic.
The final tally is expected by Friday, while the official results are scheduled to be published on Nov. 4.
Finishing first does not guarantee that a party leader will become prime minister.
Once the results are official, President Isaac Herzog will consult representatives of every party elected to the Knesset. Each faction will recommend the lawmaker it believes should be asked to form a government.
Herzog will then assign the task to the member of parliament considered most capable of assembling a coalition, regardless of whether that person leads the largest party.
The first nominee will receive 28 days to form a government and may request an extension of up to 14 days.
If the attempt fails, Herzog may give another lawmaker 28 days to try. If that candidate is also unsuccessful, 61 lawmakers can propose a third candidate, who would have 14 days to build a government.
Failure at every stage would dissolve the Knesset and trigger another election. Netanyahu’s current government would remain in office in a caretaker capacity throughout the process.
Government formation in Israel has taken between 20 and 100 days, and no new government has been sworn in less than 50 days after an election during the past two decades.
Netanyahu’s established alliance consists of Likud, the far-right Otzma Yehudit and Religious Zionism parties, and the ultra-Orthodox Shas and United Torah Judaism parties.
Final polls consistently projected the bloc at around 50 seats, leaving it 11 short of a majority.
To remain in power, Netanyahu would need his alliance to outperform the polls or persuade lawmakers from outside the bloc to support him.
He could seek an agreement with a right-wing opposition party, encourage defections or pursue a broader unity government.
However, most opposition leaders have pledged not to join a Netanyahu-led coalition.
Eisenkot’s potential alliance includes Yashar, the Bennett-Lapid-led B’Yachad party, Yair Golan’s Democrats and Avigdor Lieberman’s Yisrael Beytenu.
Although projected to finish ahead of Netanyahu’s bloc, these parties are also expected to fall short of 61 seats.
Support from the Palestinian-led Joint List or Ra’am could provide Eisenkot with the necessary parliamentary numbers, either through formal coalition participation or outside backing.
But such an arrangement faces major political obstacles.
Lieberman has ruled out serving in a government dependent on Palestinian-led parties, while Eisenkot has avoided committing himself to such a coalition. Netanyahu has also sought to mobilize right-wing voters by portraying Palestinian parties as potential kingmakers.
A minority government could theoretically take office if it received more votes in favor than against during the Knesset confidence vote, but it would face immediate questions about stability.
If neither bloc can assemble a workable majority, pressure could grow for a national unity government involving Likud and one or more opposition parties.
Such an agreement could involve Netanyahu leaving office, a rotating premiership or a limited-term government focused on security and constitutional issues.
Eisenkot and other opposition leaders have rejected serving under Netanyahu, making a unity arrangement difficult unless Likud changes its leadership or accepts a power-sharing formula.
The remaining possibility is another election.
Israel held five general elections between 2019 and 2022 after repeated coalition deadlocks. A similarly fragmented result could return the country to political paralysis, with negotiations rather than Tuesday’s vote determining who ultimately governs.

Kazakhstan completes over 820 gasification projects in 7 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:56:51 UTC

Kazakhstan completes over 820 gasification projects in 7 years
Kazakhstan has expanded access to natural gas to 772 settlements over the past seven years, increasing the number of people with access from 9.5 million to 13.1 million, Qazinform News Agency reports.
During this period, Kazakhstan invested 612.3 billion tenge from the national budget and Samruk-Kazyna funds in gasification, completing 821 projects and building more than 31,500 kilometers of gas networks.
These efforts increased the share of the population with access to natural gas from 51.47% to 64.2%, an increase of 12.73 percentage points.
Kazakhstan continues to expand its gas infrastructure by building main and distribution pipelines to ensure a reliable supply of natural gas to more settlements, homes, and businesses.
In 2025 alone, more than 354,000 people in 94 settlements gained access to natural gas, with approximately 2,000 kilometers of distribution networks built across the country.
Work is continuing in 2026, with 40 gasification projects underway, including seven carried over from previous years and 33 new projects. Once completed, they are expected to provide natural gas access to another 36,000 people.
To reach its target of providing natural gas access to 80% of the population by 2035, Kazakhstan's Ministry of Energy plans to expand major pipelines, regional gas networks, and the country's natural gas resource base.
A key project is the Ishim–Astana gas pipeline, backed by a memorandum signed between the Kazakh Government and Russia's Gazprom. The pipeline is expected to supply natural gas to Astana, Kokshetau, and Petropavlovsk, while also diversifying supply routes to northern Kazakhstan.
Another major project involves the construction of a second line of the Beineu–Bozoy–Shymkent main gas pipeline. The expansion aims to increase the capacity of Kazakhstan's gas transportation system, improve supply reliability, and meet growing demand for natural gas in the country's southern and central regions.
In Zhetysu region, the 302-kilometer Taldykorgan–Usharal gas pipeline was completed and commissioned in 2025, paving the way for up to 84 settlements to be connected to the gas network.
Kazakhstan also plans to expand gas supply and distribution networks in Almaty, Turkistan, Kyzylorda, Zhambyl, Kostanay, Karaganda, and other regions.
These projects are expected to extend natural gas coverage across the country, giving more people and businesses access to natural gas.

Russia and Ukraine began a regional cease-fire Tuesday to launch a humanitarian mission in occupied Oleshky, though fighting persisted elsewhere, including the capital of Kyiv.
The cease-fire is intended to enable aid deliveries and evacuations from the frontline southern Ukrainian town, which faces acute shortages of food and medicine.
"As head of the Ukrainian negotiating team, I confirm that the Ukrainian side is honoring its commitments," Dmytro Lubinets, the parliamentary commissioner for human rights, said on Facebook, confirming the halt's timing.
On Telegram, Russia's Defense Ministry said it stopped shelling toward the Ukrainian city of Kherson starting at 4 a.m. Moscow time (1 a.m. GMT) to prepare for the Oleshky effort; Oleshky faces Kherson across the Dnipro River.
Lubinets added the deal was reached in coordination with U.S. first lady Melania Trump and Russia's commissioner for human rights, Yana Lantratova.
New strikes Tuesday hit the Southern Bridge and subway infrastructure in Kyiv, forcing traffic suspension, city officials said. A Reuters witness heard explosions.
Oleshky lies on the Dnipro's eastern bank in Ukraine's southern Kherson region, opposite Kherson, held by Ukrainian forces.
Russian troops have controlled the town since seizing it in the early days of their February 2022 invasion.
White House envoys talked with both sides in recent days to find a solution as the U.S. seeks to mediate a peace deal to end the war, Europe's deadliest conflict since World War II.
Friday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said peace negotiators from Ukraine, Russia and the United States agreed to meet at a technical level in early November in Abu Dhabi to continue the talks.
Since Monday evening, a Russian missile attack on Kyiv killed at least one person and injured 15, including students in a dormitory. The attacks also killed and injured people in Kharkiv and Pavlohrad.
On Telegram, the Russian Defense Ministry said it hit transport infrastructure in Kyiv, a logistics hub in Kharkiv region, as well as industrial facilities and cargo vessels elsewhere it said were being put to military use.
A drone attack killed one man and wounded six others in the western Russian city of Bryansk, near the Ukrainian border.
A drone hit a bus, killing another person and injuring 30 in the Russian-controlled part of Ukraine's southeastern Zaporizhzhia region, local officials said.
Reuters could not immediately verify the reports. Russia and Ukraine deny deliberately targeting civilians.

reclaimed timber frames shape skroget coastal sauna and community hub in norway
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27

reclaimed timber frames shape skroget coastal sauna and community hub in norway
rare collectiv constructs skroget, a 40-meter-long arctic sauna and gathering pavilion in båtsfjord built from nineteen reclaimed timber portal frames resembling a ship-like hull.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
RARE COLLECTIV BUILDS HARBOR PAVILION and sauna IN BÅTSFJORD
Located nearly 500 kilometers above the Arctic Circle in Båtsfjord, Norway, Skroget is a coastal sauna and community pavilion conceived by Rare Collectiv, a group of fifteen international architecture students from the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU) under the Design in Context course. Commissioned by the local municipality to establish an accessible public harbor hub, the project was designed in two days and constructed in ten days, translating reclaimed materials and site-specific environmental conditions into a functional community infrastructure.
RECLAIMED LUMBER FORMS THE SKELETON AND INTEGRATED FURNITURE
Extending nearly 40 meters along the shoreline, the pavilion’s structural system references the skeletal frame of a ship’s hull. The volume is organized around nineteen identical timber portal frames that establish a clear programmatic and climatic orientation: sloping downward toward the water to frame sea views, while opening toward the south to create wind-sheltered outdoor seating that maximizes solar gain. The structural grid organizes a linear progression of amenities, linking an open-air fire pit, communal seating areas, changing facilities, and showers to a central sauna. The entire structure by Rare Collectiv design group, along with its integrated benches and tables, is fabricated from reused 3×7-inch municipal timber, employing uniform member dimensions and angled joinery to maintain structural continuity across the harsh coastal terrain.

designer: Rare Collectiv
location: Båtsfjord, Norway

Kyiv hopes for ‘new momentum’ in peace talks after Finnish and Norwegian leaders’ call with Putin – as it happened
Alexander Stubb and Jonas Gahr Støre held ‘substantive’ talk with Russian president on peace negotiations, but faced sceptical reactions from some European leaders
Sybiha confirms Putin phone call was 'coordinated' with Ukraine as Kyiv hopes for 'new momentum' in peace talks
Ukraine’s foreign minister Andrii Sybiha has confirmed the Finnish and Norwegian call with Putin was coordinated with Ukraine, saying it was “the right approach” to any engagement with Putin.
Speaking alongside Finnish and Norwegian foreign ministers in Helsinki, Sybiha said:
“We welcome such active support for our diplomatic efforts and peace process. This call was, as it was mentioned, coordinated with us, and this is the right approach. … I will say this once again, Ukraine wants to end this war. We have doable proposals and solutions. We are ready for partial ceasefires and a full end to hostilities. Of course, everything needs to be fair. We will not take any one-sided steps.”
Sybiha said that Ukraine was looking for “a new momentum” in peace talks with Russia, and to “define new role for Europe in our peace efforts.”
“So president Zelenskyy shared with his vision which signals our friends should convey directly to the Putin, and these signals were conveyed. Ceasefire … and another signal meeting with Putin. We are ready to meet with him. … Probably the only way to get …. new quality in our talks is a meeting at the level of president Zelenskyy and Putin.”
He later said that the negotiators can only discuss things up to a certain level, but key decisions can only be made by the heads of states.
He also added that Kyiv was “ready for the trilateral meeting” in the UAE next month, and “we will use every opportunity to bring peace closer.”
He also welcomed the limited ceasefire in Oleshky, saying it could “pave the way for other steps in the peace process as a confidence-building measure.”
But conceded that “the reality on the ground in Ukraine remains very tough” as a result of relentless Russian strikes.
And, on that note, we will be closing the blog for today.

Finland’s Stubb welcomed the “frank and substantive” phone call, insisting that “ending the war requires direct discussions” with Russia.
Støre insisted “all our partners and allies were informed in advance” (13:43), despite scepticism or outright criticism from the Danish, Estonian, Polish and Swedish prime ministers (11:26, 14:03, 15:01, 15:53).

But the Kremlin readout revealed that Russia’s Vladimir Putin blamed the EU and Nato for “confrontational policies” and demanded “full and unconditional recognition of the legitimate interests of the Russian Federation”(11:53).
The phone call took place just hours after a localised ceasefire kicked in the Ukrainian city of Oreshky after intense calls for humanitarian aid to be made available to the city’s residents (9:55, 17:08).
Elsewhere,

Oleshky ceasefire has been expanded territorially to guarantee safe passage of humanitarian convoys, Melania Trump says
The US first lady, Melania Trump, has issued a brief statement confirming the humanitarian ceasefire in Oleshky, Ukraine, which she was involved in organising.

She also added that “the ceasefire’s geographic area has expanded beyond Oleshky, within the Kherson Region, to provide safe passage for the humanitarian convoys.”
'Every decision which supports peace efforts is timely,' Ukraine's Sybiha says in response to Putin call criticism
Ukraine’s Sybiha has also pushed back against suggestions that it’s not a good moment for having a call with Putin.
“If you are at war, every decision, every step which support peace efforts is always timely. So that’s why we welcome such type of steps, efforts to speed up our negotiations.”
He also added that the European channel should not be seen as “the alternative” for the US-led talks, but “a supplementary track.”

Romania summons Russian ambassador over alleged arson attack on defence plant last month
Romania has summoned the Russian ambassador today, blaming Moscow for a fire at the state-owned Carfil defence plant in Brașov.
The fire damaged the premises of several commercial entities. Three people are being investigated for their involvement in the incident.
The Romanian security intelligence SRI confirmed yesterday that it had “identified a coordinated sabotage network from the Russian Federation” to be behind the arson attack, with “other attempts on targets in Romania. including international military facilities or those used for training the Ukrainian armed forces.”
“MFA Romania summoned the Russian Ambassador today to convey a firm protest over the September 14th sabotage in Brașov. Evidence proves Russia’s responsibility for this unacceptable hybrid attack.
We also condemned Russia’s systematic strikes on commercial vessels in the Black Sea, a deliberate escalation violating international law and freedom of navigation, with global consequences.”
Earlier today, Romania’s president, Nicușor Dan,condemned the incident, calling it “a grave violation” of Romania’s sovereignty.
“Let it be clear: these are not isolated, unrelated incidents; rather, they are part of a premeditated and coordinated campaign aimed at sowing division within our societies and undermining the commitment of European states to their own security and to collective defence.
We must not delude ourselves regarding the nature of this threat. This hybrid war has been ongoing for years, manifesting in various forms, all with the same objective: to weaken European states from within and erode the solidarity among them.”
'Every contact with Russia must convey Europe's unity and determination to support Ukraine,' Estonia's FM says
Estonia’s foreign minister, Margus Tsahkna, does not seem to be convinced by the idea of talking to Putin either.
In a post on X, he said:
“Only increased pressure on Russia will make it take peace negotiations seriously.
Every contact with Russia must convey Europe’s unity and determination to support Ukraine and maintain pressure on Russia, while making clear that Europe will not negotiate away the fundamental principles underpinning its security.
Ukraine wants peace, and Estonia supports all efforts to achieve it. But there is no indication that Russia has changed its strategic objectives or is genuinely interested in negotiations.
Russia’s goal is not merely to seize parts of Ukraine, but to subjugate the entire country and undermine Europe’s security order, founded on NATO and the EU.
A just and lasting peace requires increased pressure on Russia, tighter sanctions, action against sanctions evasion, Russia’s international isolation and unwavering support for Ukraine. We must show Russia through concrete action that, as long as its war continues, pressure will remain strong and Ukraine’s supporters will not abandon it.”
Sweden's Kristersson insists any peace deal must be achieved on Ukraine's terms
Sweden’s prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, has insisted that any peace “must be achieved on Ukraine’s terms,” joining a growing chorus of sceptical voices after an earlier call between Finland and Norway’s leaders and Russia’s Vladimir Putin.
Talking to reporters, Kristersson said that any peace settlement “must be brought about through strength, and not through appeasement towards Russia.”
“If talks lead to that, then talks are good. But my experience so far – based on the reports we received from German and French attempts at dialogue [with Moscow] – is that the results have been very, very modest.”
Kristersson added that given Russia’s continued aggression against Ukraine, “I see nothing to suggest that they are seeking peace.”
“But we will surely receive an update on those discussions later today, and I am interested in that,” he said.
No solution to end the war can be found without Ukraine's involvement, Merz says
German chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Tuesday that attempts by the US and Russia to end the war in Ukraine “can never find solutions without Ukraine” and said any talks must also include European countries.
Merz was speaking at the Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore as he described diplomatic efforts to build a negotiating format with Moscow.
He said the end of the war depended “only on one person” and framed continued backing for Kyiv as a defence of Europe’s political order.
He said “as long as he [Putin] does not want to end the war, we will support Ukraine” and that Europe was not just defending Ukraine’s territorial integrity but also “the entire political order of the European continent”.
Merz added that Russia, Ukraine, the United States and European countries should be at the negotiating table and warned against a scenario where “Russia, perhaps China and the United States of America” end the war without Ukraine.
Stubb talked of 'very restrained optimism' about constructive peace talks in Abu Dhabi, Tusk says
Poland’s prime minister Donald Tusk has also responded to Stubb and Støre’s engagement with Putin, giving a detailed account on the European consultations ahead of and after the call.
Speaking before the cabinet meeting in Warsaw, Tusk said the call followed “consultations with me, among others, but primarily with president Zelenskyy and the US side … that it would be good for European politicians to have a working contact given the planned ceasefire talks that may take place in Abu Dhabi.”
He said the UAE talks between Russia, Ukraine, and the US are provisionally planned for 4 November.
Tusk confirmed he had been briefed on plans for the call beforehand, with Norway’s Støre assuring him that he and Stubb were ready to take political responsibility for this rare engagement with Putin, and would stick to the agreed position of the coalition of the willing.
He said Finland’s Stubb then briefed him after the call, saying “both sides maintained their positions,” and that “the European side’s impression during the call was one of very restrained optimism” about the chances of making progress in Abu Dhabi.
Tusk said he was “very cautions” about engaging with Russia and urged Stubb and Store to be “vigilant” in their talks with Putin, as “Russia’s agenda and interests are quite precisely defined, and that one should harbour any illusions about getting an agreement.”
He said Stubb and Støre also told Putin that the security of Nato’s northern and eastern flanks were “non-negotiable”.
Poland’s PM also stressed that despite the resumed dialogue, “nothing changes” in Europe’s “full support for Ukraine,” or collective views on “the [broader] security architecture and security guarantees for Ukraine.”
Summing up the talks, he said:
“We should not have any illussions; it is clear what the Russian side is playing at, but I will remain in constant contact with all those who possess the good will and the belief that an agreement is possible – or at the very least, a ceasefire before winter.”
Without specifying the source of his claim, Tusk said that “three, four nights ago,” “Russia lost 2,500 men” during one night. “This gives us an idea of just how dire the further consequences of this war could be.”
Norway's Støre defends Putin call, but acknowledges 'significant' differences in opinions
Jakub Krupa
Norway’s Jonas Gahr Støre has offered a bit more colour on his and Stubb’s call with Russia’s Putin in a huddle with journalists in Helsinki just now.
He and Stubb had been initially given only 20 minutes to talk to Putin, but ended up speaking for 90 minutes, in a conversation he described as “substantive, focused on the issues at hand, and professional.”
“Much of what he said was already known – he [Putin] recalled his views on how the conflict evolved since 2014 – and we stated our positions. These are well-known views, which we were able to acknowledge and respond to,” he said.
The talks touched on what can be done to tackle most pressing issues, including attacks on energy infrastructure and in the Black Sea.
But Støre conceded “there remain significant differences in our respective positions,” reiterating Norway’s continued support for Ukraine.
“We stand with Ukraine, defend its right to self-defence, and emphasise the need for a diplomatic path to end this war in a lasting and just manner,” he said.
Støre also stressed that he and Finland’s Stubb spoke on behalf of their two countries only, “and no one else.”
Responding to criticism of their call from Denmark’s Frederiksen(11:26), he said that “all our partners and allies were informed in advance and received a detailed account afterwards.”
Pushing back further, he added:
“If one assumes that the current situation – where communication from the American administration to Moscow serves as the sole channel for discussing Ukraine outside of Ukraine – is the only way, then one is entitled to that view. I believe it is important that other voices are heard as well.”
Støre also stressed that the importance of the meeting in Abu Dhabi, first agreed as a result of the Oslo consultations that he and Stubb hosted.
In a brief section of the briefing in English, Støre again focused on pushing back against Frederiksen’s criticism:
“I believe that talking, having the right messages, is not wrong. Today these messages [are] coming out of the American administration; that is the only thing reaching Moscow. So [now] there are [also] voices from two neighbouring states, speaking on behalf of Finland and Norway, not speaking on behalf of others, but … in full compliance with the coalition of the willing who share view on the nature of this war and how it has to end.”
Russia is exploring the possibility of cooperation with partners from the United States in the resource-rich Arctic, president Vladimir Putin told a conference of gas-exporting countries in Moscow.
Putin did not specify whether the joint projects under consideration would involve extracting natural gas or other resources.

Rogue AI, cyberattacks and weapons: the risks Anthropic is warning investors about ahead of its IPO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:52:25 UTC
17:52:25 KST

The AI company’s IPO paperwork warns of potential harms from increasingly autonomous systems, alongside financial and regulatory challenges.
Rogue AI systems, cyberattacks and the potential use of artificial intelligence to develop dangerous weapons feature among the risks Anthropic has disclosed to investors as it prepares for a stock market debut.
Of the 335 pages outlining Anthropic’s finances, executive compensation, dividend policy and the like, 93 pages are devoted to “risk factors” — things that could hurt potential shareholders’ investments. Rival SpaceX’s listed risk factors, in comparison, took up 38 out of more than 250 pages.
The disclosures are required as part of the IPO process, giving potential investors a clearer picture of the risks they face by buying into the company.
In pitching itself to investors, Anthropic presents its own initial public offering as a step toward mitigating the risks it believes AI poses.
“To build AI is to harness cognition itself, and anything so powerful can be used for ill as well as good,” write the company’s founders in a letter to prospective shareholders in the IPO filing. “Anthropic is a deeply values-driven organisation, founded in large part to help the world realise AI’s benefits and avoid its dangers.”
Still, the risks are many. They range from the mundane — the possibility it won’t be able to retain key staff or navigate regulatory roadblocks — to involvement in cyberattacks and the spread of dangerous misinformation.
Here is a look at some of the risks Anthropic details:
The technology’s rapid development
Anthropic said it’s possible its models could develop so quickly the company won’t be able to implement adequate safety measures, “which could increase the likelihood of safety incidents, regulatory intervention, or reputational harm, and could adversely affect our business.”
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei warned in September that within six to 12 months AI could be capable of leading a swarm of agents that could take over the entire internet.The warning, and now Anthropic’s move to sell shares, comes amid growing concern inside and outside the industry about increasingly powerful systems that can solve problems beyond human capacity but could also act on their own to carry out harmful tasks.
As AI systems “become more autonomous and capable of taking consequential actions with less human oversight,” the SEC filing said, there’s a risk that such systems could “take harmful actions independently and at scale without human intervention.”
“Even if our own models do not cause such harm, a significant safety incident involving any frontier AI could trigger broad reputational damage to the AI industry, public backlash, and sweeping regulatory responses that could adversely affect our business,” Anthropic said.
Now that the AI models are themselves contributing to Anthropic’s own research and development, it’s possible that AI could progress “beyond our ability to evaluate and safeguard new models,” according to the filing. This, the document said, could adversely affect Anthropic’s business.
Malicious actors could cause mayhem with the technology
The filing discussed concerns that advanced AI systems, if not developed and operated with enough safeguards and oversight, “pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such systems were misused, replicated, weaponised, or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy.”
The company said it would be harmed if use by bad actors causes damage, “or if our model guardrails or safeguards fail to prevent such misuse.”
Anthropic sketched out the prospect of bad actors using AI models to build chemical weapons or authoritarian rulers turning to the technology to crack down on their citizens. In September, the company disclosed that it had blocked efforts to use its AI models for malicious activity such as cyberattacks, surveillance and research that could have led to biological weapon development.
The company could run up against limits on processing power
Compute — the computing power or resources needed to build, test and improve AI models — is expensive and in high demand. Anthropic notes that if it’s unable to secure adequate compute, or if “we fail to direct our compute effectively across our workloads, we may be unable to train models that remain competitive with those of our competitors or adequately serve our customers.”
Anthropic mentioned community opposition to data centres as a risk to its business. Data centre development “has prompted public controversy and regulatory scrutiny regarding environmental impact, land and water use, and the allocation of limited power resources,” the filing said, adding that if regulators impose new requirements or charges as a result, its ability to do business could suffer.
In addition, the company relies on a small number of customers, including SpaceX and Microsoft, and distribution channels for a large portion of its revenue. This means that even if just one of its big customers decides to scale back — or drop the company altogether — Anthropic said it could see its prospects and finances suffer.
Mitigating the risks
In some ways, AI’s enormous risk, combined with its enormous potential, is Anthropic’s main selling point. The company has tried to position itself as a responsible AI company, and courts business customers by emphasising safety-mindedness.
“We believe that frontier AI companies must invest in safety and alignment to help ensure the responsible diffusion of this technology,” the filing said.
Brian Mulberry, chief market strategist at Zacks Investment Research, said IPO deals have to display “very clearly” what risks people face when they invest their money in a newly public stock.
“That’s one of the things that’s great about our capital markets here domestically is the level of transparency that you must commit to, to be a publicly traded corporation on a U.S. exchange requires you to outline those risks in a very clear way, so that people understand if they want to participate by offering their hard-earned money and help finance this type of a deal,” he said.

Number of millionaires in NL skyrockets as house prices rise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:52:15 UTC
17:52:15 KST

Number of millionaires in NL skyrockets as house prices rise
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Over 81,000 households achieved millionaire status last year without needing to do anything to earn it – the rise in house prices has quietly boosted their wealth.
The figures come from national statistics bureau CBS, which counted 547,000 households with net assets of at least €1 million at the start of 2025 – 6.6% of all Dutch households.
A year earlier the number stood at 466,000. In 2011 it was 170,000. The main driver is the rise in asset valuations – namely house prices.
Two-thirds of millionaire households have between €1 million and €2 million, and 3% have over €10 million.
Those who got rich this way tend to be older – the average millionaire is 61, and fewer than 3% are under 35. For younger people, entrepreneurship and ownership in company shares is the more common way to millionaire status. CBS does not say what role inheritance plays here.
Where you live, of course, makes a big difference. In Bloemendaal and Laren, close to two in five households are now millionaires. In Kerkrade, Zuid-Limburg, it’s closer to 1 in 100. Groningen, Flevoland and Friesland are all below 5%.

NATO simulates war with a million troops on each side
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:51:22 UTC
17:51:22 KST

- NATO and U.S. Army commanders ran the Avenger Triad 26 simulation from Wiesbaden, Germany, from Oct. 6 to Oct. 15, 2026, with one million simulated soldiers on each side.
- Palantir’s Maven Smart System was the central system tested to give commanders a full operational picture within seconds.
NATO commanders spent 10 days in October rehearsing how they would fight a war against an enemy army of one million soldiers, running the alliance’s Avenger Triad 26 computer-assisted exercise from a command center in Wiesbaden, Germany, where about 150 officers from several countries tracked a simulated attack on alliance territory around the clock on a live map of Europe.
The exercise ran from Oct. 6 through Oct. 15, 2026, at headquarters in Germany, France, Poland and the Netherlands, with Wiesbaden, home of U.S. Army Europe and Africa, coordinating the effort, and the simulated scenario pitted one million soldiers on each side against each other, local news outlet Merkurist reported after a press tour that gave it rare access to the command center.
Merkurist reported that about 20,000 troops took part in the field, including 4,000 U.S. soldiers, although Avenger Triad 26 was mainly a simulation for command staffs and not a traditional field training exercise, with headquarters from NATO’s 32 member countries practicing how to run joint operations in a crisis, share information and make decisions quickly.
U.S. Army Europe and Africa and NATO’s Allied Land Command worked as a single integrated headquarters during the exercise, which brought in U.S. Army V Corps, the 2nd Polish Corps, the 1st French Corps and the 1st German-Netherlands Corps under an Article 5 collective defense scenario, in which an attack on one ally is treated as an attack on all.
All incoming information was pulled together in Wiesbaden, where a map of Europe showed NATO bases and enemy positions in real time, and one of the main goals of the exercise was to cut the time it takes commanders to react to an attack, partly by using artificial intelligence, so that in a real emergency they could see a complete picture of the battlefield within seconds.
“We must connect the information technology of the 21st century with the military capabilities of the 20th century,” said British Army Lt. Gen. Jez Bennett, acting commander of NATO’s Allied Land Command.
The central system tested in Wiesbaden was the Maven Smart System, the data and targeting platform built by U.S. company Palantir, which uses artificial intelligence to sort through large amounts of data quickly, and the plan is to eventually feed information from reconnaissance drones, ground sensors, radars and cameras into one common network. The U.S. military is also building new tools on the same platform, with U.S. Navy and U.S. Marine Corps developers demonstrating a Maven-based air-defense dashboard at Marine Corps Air Station Yuma, Arizona, in October.
“In the past, a military commander had to wait for a messenger on horseback. Now information reaches us at lightning speed,” said German Army Maj. Gen. Björn Schulz.
Lessons from the war in Ukraine were also built into the exercise, and U.S. Army Maj. Ben Schiff said that Ukraine, which was invaded by Russia, has advanced military drone technology faster than any other country.
During a preliminary exercise in Wiesbaden the week before Avenger Triad 26 began, soldiers were shown several new systems, including unmanned vehicles built to search for mines and drones meant to defend against enemy aerial weapons, and some of that technology is being researched and developed in laboratories at the Wiesbaden-Erbenheim installation.

“Fifteen Tulips” and countless hits: Mimi Ivanova celebrates 80 with a concert
Tuesday 27 October 2026 10:15
Tuesday, 27 October 2026, 10:15
Mimi Ivanova
PHOTO Facebook/ Mimi Ivanova and Razvigor Popov
Font size
One of Bulgaria’s most popular singers over the past six decades, Mimi Ivanova, is celebrating her 80th birthday with an anniversary concert entitled “When I Was a Girl – Mimi at 80.” On October 28, the festive evening at Hall No 1 of the National Palace of Culture in Sofia will feature golden hits, new songs and special musical collaborations.
Mimi Ivanova and Razvigor Popov
PHOTO Facebook/ Mimi Ivanova and Razvigor Popov
Joining Mimi Ivanova on stage will be much-loved Bulgarian performers, who will perform songs from her repertoire as well as works by her longtime creative partner and husband, composer Razvigor Popov. Among the special guest performers are Veselin Marinov, Margarita Hranova, Elvira Georgieva, and DesiSlava. The concert will also feature appearances by Yordanka Hristova, Vasil Naydenov, Georgi Hristov, Orlin Goranov, the Argirov Brothers, Toni Dimitrova and Stefan Diomov.
Born on December 28, 1946, Mimi Ivanova began singing at a very young age. Her musical journey started at a music school in her hometown of Hisarya. She later graduated from the Music School in Plovdiv and went on to study in the estrada department of the Music Academy in Sofia, where she was taught by the renowned singer Irina Chmihova.
While still a student, Mimi became a soloist with the Sofia Orchestra, performing alongside fellow singers Pasha Hristova, Maria Neykova and Boris Gudjunov. The artists later recorded songs together that won prestigious awards, including the Golden Orpheus and Spring music festivals. Throughout her career, Mimi Ivanova has received numerous awards in Bulgaria and across Europe, released a number of albums, and won the hearts of many fans.
PHOTO Facebook/ Mimi Ivanova and Razvigor Popov
Mimi Ivanova’s partnership with the Bulgarian National Radio began in the early 1970s, when she worked extensively with the Radio’s Big Band, led by conductor Vili Kazasyan. This longstanding partnership has continued throughout her career. Songs performed by Ivanova have won awards six times at BNR’s Spring music contest.
Among the award-winning entries is “Fifteen Tulips” (1978), with music and arrangement by Razvigor Popov and lyrics by Yordan Yankov. The song has since become one of Mimi Ivanova’s signature hits.

U.S. Marine Corps tests kamikaze drones in Japan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:47:17 UTC
17:47:17 KST

- The U.S. Marine Corps tested Neros Archer kamikaze drones with live warheads at Camp Fuji, Japan, for the first time on Oct. 20, 2026.
- Junior enlisted Marines from Battalion Landing Team 1/1 destroyed targets in two scenarios, including an anti-armor ambush, with no unexploded drones left behind.
The U.S. Marine Corps has tested kamikaze drones in Japan, flying Neros Archer one-way attack drones armed with live explosive warheads at Combined Arms Training Center Camp Fuji, at the foot of Mount Fuji, on Oct. 20, 2026, the first time the drone has been used in its live kinetic form at the range.
Marines from Battalion Landing Team 1/1 of the 31st Marine Expeditionary Unit flew the drones into targets in two separate training scenarios, one of them an anti-armor ambush, and both flights ended with the targets destroyed and no unexploded drones left on the range for the Explosive Ordnance Disposal team to recover.
“This week is the first time, here at CATC Camp Fuji, that we’ve deployed the Neros Archer in a live kinetic variant,” said Chief Warrant Officer 2 Stephen Bilbo, Camp Fuji’s Gunner and Range Control Officer. “Neros Archer is the current Marine Corps’ program of record for one-way attack drones flown by a first-person view pilot.”
The Archer is a small first-person-view strike drone built by Neros Technologies of El Segundo, California, and flown by a pilot wearing a video headset who steers it directly into the target, and the Camp Fuji flights follow the U.S. Marine Corps’ first live-fire FPV attack drone training, held in South Korea on July 30 and Aug. 5, when Marines from the 3rd Marine Division struck armored and personnel targets with Archers at ranges of up to about 20 km (12.4 miles).
The Marines in Japan are testing how the drone fits into small ground units, and the battalion described the exercise as a different kind of training from what 1st Battalion, 1st Marines had previously done at its home station at Camp Pendleton, California.
“This scenario is going to be a little bit different than we’ve done in the past, this is going to be a proof of concept tied to our hunter-killer teams. The goal of this is to be an extension of our hunter-killers’ capabilities with defeating armor and a means of ground line communication within our adversary force,” said Master Sgt. Glenn Dayton, company operations chief of Weapons Company, Battalion Landing Team 1/1.
The pilots are junior enlisted Marines, from lance corporal to sergeant, who are hand-picked by their unit leadership for a three-week operator course, and the only prerequisite is that they have no previous drone experience, which the U.S. Marine Corps says lets them learn the Archer’s flying skills without old habits to unlearn.
“All this is handled by noncommissioned officers and non-NCOs,” said Dayton. “You’re looking at the heart and soul of our ground force. This is not executed by staff NCO or officers, I think that’s a huge aspect. Our lower enlisted are the ones we rely on to master this craft.”
A few dozen observers watched the two flights, and the Camp Fuji EOD technicians were there because an armed drone that fails to detonate is treated as live ordnance lying on the range.
“The drone carries an explosive payload, if for any reason it’s not able to function as designed with the controller and it goes down [without exploding] it counts as unexploded ordnance or UXO and then that falls under our bread and butter,” said Staff Sgt. Francisco Melandez, a CATC Camp Fuji explosive ordnance technician.
The U.S. Marine Corps signed a $17 million contract for 8,000 Archer Strike drones, while the U.S. Army has turned to the same company for its own FPV needs, awarding Neros a contract worth up to $500 million in 2026 after selecting it in November 2025 as one of three primary manufacturers for its Purpose-Built Attritable Systems program.

Norwegian media companies take Meta to court over new commercial terms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:42:06 UTC
17:42:06 KST

Ilayda Cakirtekin
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
Major Norwegian media companies have taken Meta to court over its proposed new commercial terms, raising concerns about the potential use of news content to train artificial intelligence models, broadcaster NRK reported Tuesday.
Members of the Norwegian Media Association (MBL) argue that the new terms would grant Meta the right to scrape every article, photo and video published by editorially controlled media outlets.
Major media organizations, including NRK, TV 2, Schibsted, Amedia, Polaris, Aller, DN, Mentor Medier, NTB and Hordaland Folkeblad, have asked the Oslo District Court to suspend Meta’s new terms pending a judicial review of their legality.
“We believe that this should be legally assessed to see if this is actually in line with Norwegian law,” said Lene Eltvik Vindfeld, chairwoman of the MBL.
NRK’s legal director Olav Nyhus also said they “in no way” want Meta to be able to use their content to further strengthen platforms such as Facebook and Instagram.
Nyhus added that it would not be easy to terminate agreements with Instagram and Facebook, as the platforms have become important channels for disseminating information.
“What Meta is doing is destroying the entire financial basis for journalism,” he said, adding: “We believe that Meta’s conduct and terms are a clear violation of competition law.”
Meta recently revised its commercial terms to remove language that raised concerns about the potential use of news websites to train artificial intelligence models.
The revised terms specify that automated website crawling is intended to develop, improve, research and maintain advertising and business products.
The provisions still allow Meta to use automated tools, including web scrapers, bots and crawlers, to access and collect content from websites associated with businesses using its platforms.
An earlier version of the proposed terms included language about using collected material to “train” Meta products, prompting concerns among publishers and legal experts over the potential use of copyrighted news content for AI development.
Meta subsequently removed the reference and clarified that the crawling provisions apply to advertising and business products.

EU readying for major Australian resources investment, ambassador says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:40:59 UTC
17:40:59 KST

EU readying for major Australian resources investment, ambassador says
SYDNEY, Oct 27 - The European Union expects a wave of investment into the Australian critical minerals sector as it pushes to diversify its supply chain away from China, the bloc's ambassador to Australia Lawrence Meredith said on Tuesday.
Australia and the European Union struck a free trade agreement in March after eight years of negotiations, removing tariffs on almost all goods and easing EU access to Australian critical minerals.
Once both parties sign and ratify that agreement, expected early next year, a 5.5% EU tariff on critical minerals will be removed.
"It is going to be a game changer," Meredith said.
In parallel, talks are "very close" for Australia to sign a memorandum of understanding with the European Investment Bank, which would act as the bloc's funding vehicle, Meredith added.
"The European Union will be massively investing in critical minerals. Since we wish to diversify away from China, then one of the most likely partners has to be Australia," he said.
EU policy proposals have laid out as much as €10 billion ($11.2 billion) for critical raw materials within the larger €409 billion competitiveness fund, as the EU debates its budget from 2028 to 2034.
Australia is one of several critical minerals "superpowers" in which the EU is looking to invest, including Brazil, South Africa and Canada. The EU also expects to invest along the supply chain, including in processing, Meredith said.
Australia said on Tuesday it would refresh its critical minerals strategy to place greater emphasis on refining and processing, as competition for investment intensifies and supply-chain concerns persist.
The bloc is looking initially at the minerals that Australia will prioritise for its strategic reserve: gallium, antimony and rare earths.
Australian companies going faster through the early project development would speed the investment process, he said.
"(The FTA) is a signal that Europe wants to do far more with Australia. We also have a security and defence partnership. A lot of that is dual technology, and it requires precisely these critical minerals," he said.
The European Union plans to mobilise €800 billion into defence under ReArm Europe by 2030.
Australia is also on track to join the EU's flagship funding program for research and innovation, Horizon Europe, next year.
Meredith said 2026 had been a "transformational" year for Australian-EU relations.
"You've seen a big surge in EU-Australia in 2026, and I'm very confident we will go to the next level in 2027." REUTERS

India ramps up oil imports from Middle East – media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:40:20 UTC
17:40:20 KST

India ramps up oil imports from Middle East – media
India’s imports of Middle Eastern crude have surged to more than half of its total oil purchases, as steep Gulf discounts and soaring freight costs make Russian supplies less competitive for Indian refiners.
Middle Eastern crude accounted for 54% of India’s oil imports in September, up from 32% in August, while Russia’s share fell to 33.5% from 46.6%, according to ship-tracking data reported by Reuters. Russia nevertheless remained India’s largest individual oil supplier.
The shift is reflected in purchases by state-owned Bharat Petroleum Corporation Limited (BPCL), which expects Russian crude volumes to decline significantly in November. Russian oil accounted for around 37% of BPCL’s crude sourcing during July-September.
India increased Russian oil purchases when the US-Iran war disrupted Middle Eastern supplies. However, Gulf shipments have since recovered to prewar levels, with producers offering steep discounts to attract buyers.
The conflict has driven up global tanker rates, making the longer voyages from Russian ports increasingly expensive. Average crude freight costs have risen nearly sevenfold over the past year, from around $3 per barrel to more than $20, according to Goldman Sachs. The bank cited war-risk premiums, higher fuel expenses, and costly ship-to-ship transfers.
Freight costs for Russian Urals crude shipped to Asia reached around $30 per barrel or more in early October. Transporting a tanker shipment from Russia’s Black Sea ports to India currently costs $27 million-$30 million, compared with approximately $19 million in September, Reuters reported.
Meanwhile, some Iraqi cargoes are being offered at discounts exceeding $25 per barrel against the Dubai benchmark before shipping, while selected Saudi shipments have been discounted by as much as $10, Bloomberg reported, citing traders. Russian crude, which previously sold at steep discounts, was being offered at around a $2 premium to the separate Dated Brent benchmark.
“Due to the increase in freight, we are not getting good offers from Russia,” BPCL finance director Vetsa Ramakrishna Gupta told analysts on Monday.
Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited (HPCL), another state-owned oil company, is also adjusting its procurement strategy, increasingly buying crude on a delivered-price basis to manage shipping costs. HPCL Chairman Vikas Kaushal also confirmed that Gulf producers are offering discounts to offset the elevated freight rates.
Indian Petroleum Minister Hardeep Singh Puri said on Tuesday that Middle Eastern supplies are increasing, and noted that Russian oil purchases depend on pricing and discounts compared with other grades.
Asked whether Washington had pressured India to reduce Russian oil imports, Puri said, “I never felt anything.”
