Spring sets course for autumn in trees, says Swiss study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:21:00 UTC
17:21:00 KST

Spring sets course for autumn in trees, says Swiss study
A warm spring causes some trees to shed their leaves several weeks earlier in autumn, according to a Swiss experiment involving three native tree species.
The findings could help to better predict the impact of climate change on forests and the carbon cycle, the Swiss National Science Foundation (SNSF) announced on Tuesday.
A research team led by Yann Vitasse from the Swiss Federal Institute for Forest, Snow and Landscape Research (WSL) studied young hornbeams, small-leaved lindens and Norway maples. To do this, it exposed half of the trees to temperatures around 5°C above the ambient temperature from January to mid-June.
Under these conditions, the hornbeams and small-leaved lindens budded two to four weeks earlier than the control plants. Leaf senescence also began three to four weeks earlier in these trees. Furthermore, both tree species grew more vigorously and had already stored more starch as an energy reserve by the start of summer.
The Norway maple reacted differently: although it also sprouted earlier, its growth and starch storage did not accelerate. Its leaves therefore did not age any earlier than those of the control plants.
More
How drought affects Swiss forests
Implications for the carbon cycle
For a long time, researchers assumed that falling temperatures and shorter days in autumn were the main triggers of leaf senescence. The new findings show that spring conditions also play a role, according to the SNSF.
It is still unclear which factor triggers the earlier leaf senescence. The researchers therefore intend to carry out further experiments and analyse field observations as well as satellite data.
The findings are also relevant for climate models. Trees absorb carbon dioxide (CO₂) from the atmosphere via their leaves. If the growing season ends earlier, the period during which they sequester carbon could be shortened. The extent to which this affects forests depends, among other things, on the tree species and the respective environmental conditions.
The Swiss National Science Foundation emphasised that the 5°C warming simulated in the experiment is not a direct prediction of future climate trends. However, unusually warm conditions in spring could occur more frequently in the future.

U.S. Air Force puts its first hypersonic missile into production
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:20:32 UTC
17:20:32 KST

- The U.S. Air Force awarded Lockheed Martin a $694 million contract to produce and field the ARRW hypersonic missile.
- The service withheld quantities and delivery dates, three years after it had planned to cancel the weapon without production buys.
The U.S. Air Force has put its first hypersonic weapon into production, awarding Lockheed Martin a $694 million contract on Sept. 29 to build and field the AGM-183A Air-Launched Rapid Response Weapon, or ARRW, a missile the service had planned to abandon just three years ago, the Department of the Air Force announced on Oct. 26.
The service withheld how many missiles the contract covers and when deliveries will begin, citing operational security, but said the award formally moves the weapon out of prototyping and flight testing and into production. The contract was placed through the Department of War’s Enterprise-Wide Agile Acquisition Contract.
ARRW is a boost-glide weapon that rides a solid-fuel rocket booster to more than five times the speed of sound, about 6,100 km/h (3,800 mph), before releasing a glide vehicle that maneuvers toward its target, which makes it far harder to track and intercept than a conventional ballistic missile. The U.S. Air Force says it will let aircraft strike time-sensitive, heavily defended and high-value targets from long range, outside the reach of enemy air defenses.
“This is a turning point in our advanced weapons roadmap. By moving ARRW from test to production, we’re providing our combatant commanders with a credible, high-speed strike weapon capable of penetrating the most advanced anti-access and area-denial systems,” said Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink.
The missile is too large for most fighters and will initially be carried by the B-52 Stratofortress bomber, Air & Space Forces Magazine reported, and it has also reportedly been tested on the B-1.
“Fielding ARRW enhances our ability to hold targets at risk anywhere around the world. This hypersonic weapon provides the Joint Force a flexible and rapid response option for highly contested environments,” said Chief of Staff of the Air Force Gen. Ken Wilsbach.
The production decision caps a troubled development history. Lockheed won the design contract in 2018, but the first three flight tests starting in 2021 failed before the missile flew successfully in May 2022, and in March 2023 the service’s then top acquisition official, Andrew Hunter, said the program would end without any production buys as the U.S. Air Force shifted its focus to the smaller Hypersonic Attack Cruise Missile. The service reversed course in 2025, when then-Chief of Staff Gen. David Allvin told Congress the U.S. Air Force would buy ARRW.
The program received $362 million in fiscal 2026, and the U.S. Air Force has requested $452 million for production in fiscal 2027, although that request is stalled in Congress while the Pentagon operates under a continuing resolution at 2026 funding levels. Budget plans call for $556 million to $621 million a year for ARRW procurement from 2028 to 2031, with missile quantities marked as controlled unclassified information.

Anduril unveils family of air defence interceptors
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:17:33 GMT
17:17:33 KST

Anduril has revealed Steelfin, a family of surface-to-air interceptor missiles built on a common two-stage architecture so that one production line can turn out versions for everything from point defence to upper-tier ballistic missile defence, according to the company.
The company set out the problem it is addressing, saying adversaries have invested in large volumes of low-cost, mass-producible offensive weapons and that air defence batteries are too often forced to expend exquisite interceptors against lower-cost threats, straining stores of the most critical defensive weapons and putting defenders on the losing side of the cost exchange.
Steelfin pairs a first-stage booster, which can take different solid rocket motors to suit range, launch configuration or packing density, with a second-stage terminal interceptor sharing the same airframe, avionics, software, flight control system and interfaces across every variant. Open interfaces between the subsystems in that terminal stage let different seekers and mission systems be fitted without redesigning the missile.
Because the variants share an architecture and components, they move through the same production line using the same tooling, technicians and facilities, and Anduril said it is planning to produce on the order of several thousand Steelfin variants a year in the short term, with capacity designed to flex to demand. The same open interfaces allow commercial off-the-shelf components and competition between vendors, widening the supplier base.
The missiles are compatible with launch infrastructure already in service, including the M903A2 launcher used by Patriot, the Mk 41 vertical launching system fitted to warships, Typhon and emerging containerised launchers, and are designed to integrate with fielded fire control systems such as Aegis and IBCS. Anduril has completed ballistic testing with representative air vehicles and will begin flight testing next year.
The American company has built a European presence over the past two years, with Latvia selecting its Barracuda cruise missile family and a United Kingdom arm working on autonomy, counter-drone systems and command software. Its approach of designing weapons around mass production and common components is the same argument being made by Helsing, which launched its own pair of low-cost interceptors this week.

Fishing quotas for the Baltic Sea approved for 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:16:59 UTC
17:16:59 KST

Fishing quotas for 2027 in the Baltic Sea and the Gulf of Riga have been approved this week at a meeting of the European Union (EU) Agriculture and Fisheries Council in Luxembourg. 
Following discussions among industry experts from the Baltic Sea Fisheries Forum (BALTFISH) in Luxembourg on the evening of 25 October, and subsequent negotiations at the Agriculture and Fisheries Council late on Monday evening, a compromise was reached on fishing opportunities in the Baltic Sea for next year.
The final decision largely reflects the common position agreed upon by the Baltic Sea countries.
Under the agreement, Latvia will be allocated a herring fishing quota of 4,581 tonnes in the Baltic Sea for 2027, representing a 71% increase compared with 2026. The European Commission (EC) had initially proposed an increase of 49%.
The cod bycatch quota will remain at 10 tonnes, unchanged from this year. Cod may only be caught as bycatch.
The European Commission had initially proposed reducing cod fishing allowances by 90% in subdivisions 22–24 and by 50% in subdivisions 25–32.
In the Gulf of Riga, the herring fishing quota has been approved at 20,550 tonnes, an increase of 11% compared with 2026.
Meanwhile, Latvia's sprat fishing quota will reach 40,340 tonnes, representing a 44% increase.
The salmon catch allowance in the Baltic Sea will remain unchanged at 3,366 fish.
The Ministry of Agriculture explained that the compromise revised the European Commission's initial proposals concerning cod bycatch limits and restrictions on recreational salmon fishing, including angling and fishing for personal consumption.
The permitted cod bycatch volumes and conditions will remain identical to those in force in 2026.
According to the ministry, these limits correspond to actual bycatch levels and therefore no longer threaten the continuation of fishing for other species along Latvia's Baltic Sea coast.
The Baltic Sea countries also rejected a proposed complete ban on recreational salmon fishing.
The ministry explained that there was no justification for prohibiting the catching of hatchery-raised salmon, which are identified by their clipped adipose fins.
Latvia's greatest concern was the European Commission's original proposal to reduce cod bycatch allowances by 50%, which the country considered unacceptable.
Negotiators successfully secured changes to that proposal.
The discussions also resulted in a 71% increase in fishing opportunities for herring in the central Baltic Sea, in line with scientifically permitted catch levels, compared with the European Commission's initial proposal for a 49% increase.
The Ministry of Agriculture noted that fishing opportunities in 2027 will also increase by 44% for sprat and 11% for herring in the Gulf of Riga.
Ģirts Krūmiņš, State Secretary at the Ministry of Agriculture, said the decisions are important for ensuring the responsible use of fish resources available in the Baltic Sea rather than leaving them to Russian fishing operations.
According to Krūmiņš, Russia has significantly exceeded its allocated fishing quotas for many years and has failed to respect the condition of fish stocks.
"I am very pleased that both sprat and herring quotas will increase substantially next year. We should make the most of these opportunities to generate the greatest possible economic benefit and added value," Krūmiņš said.
He emphasised that the increased quotas would strengthen Latvia's coastal communities and support local fishermen and fish processors, whose livelihoods depend directly on the resources provided by the sea.
Krūmiņš stressed that the most important achievement during the negotiations was preserving the existing cod bycatch quota, which the European Commission had sought to reduce.
"I believe our decisions must not threaten the survival of fishing in the Baltic Sea or the traditional coastal way of life, as adopting the European Commission's proposal would have done," Krūmiņš said.
He added that the agreement would help protect the livelihoods of Latvia's coastal fishermen and ensure they can continue their work.

Scandals and losses force revamp of Swiss supermarket chain Migros
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:16:29 UTC
17:16:29 KST

Scandals and losses force revamp of Swiss supermarket chain Migros
Supermarket chain Migros, one of the largest employers in Switzerland, wants to call time on its tradition of decentralised operations by merging its regional cooperatives.
How did this come about and what happens next?
Migros group’s core business is barely profitable any more, and its supermarkets are struggling with low margins. This is evident from an analysis of the results of the ten regional cooperatives.
Last year, the Zurich regional co-operative made a loss of CHF180 million. Migros in Ticino, in southern Switzerland, is also in the red. Supermarkets in Ticino and Geneva face competition from low-cost chains based in neighbouring countries.
By dissolving the regional societies and merging them into a group cooperative, Migros aims to make savings and streamline operations.
More
Retail giant Migros confronts its complicated history with alcohol
The previous Migros structure gave each cooperative a great deal of power, giving rise to the term “regional prince”. Each regional cooperative has its own management with its own chair and keeps its own accounts with separate annual reports.
This decentralised organisation has led to several scandals. For a long time, for example, there was turmoil within the Neuchâtel-Fribourg cooperative.
+ How a new kind of Swiss store changed the way we shop
The Neuchâtel-Fribourg internal conflict escalated seven years ago when its then president was accused of fraud and embezzlement.
Migros group headquarters in Zurich attempted to remove the Neuchâtel-Fribourg leadership, which led to a vote of the 50,000 local cooperative members.
Irregularities occurred during the vote, involving forged ballot papers. The case highlighted the weaknesses of the decentralised organisation.
The regional cooperative in Zurich failed in a foreign venture that squandered several hundred million francs. In 2013, Migros Zurich took over the organic supermarket chain Tegut in Germany. But this resulted in financial losses and the German chain being put up for sale.
This example, too, highlighted the shortcomings of the decentralised organisation.
The Migros group merger will now centralise completely different cooperativee, both large and small. In terms of sales figures, the Zurich cooperative is the largest, with a turnover of around CHF4 billion.
The Eastern Switzerland cooperative, on the other hand, has the most employees, at 8,466. The smallest cooperative is in Ticino. However, all ten cooperatives support the merger.
It remains to be seen how many jobs will be cut following the merger. Since 2018, Migros has shed or outsourced almost 15,000 posts.
Migros has sold off a number of subsidiary companies, including Hotelplan, Globus, Melectronics, SportX, Micasa and Mibelle. The sale of Tegut in Germany will result in the loss of a further 7,000 jobs this year, with the employees transferring to the new owner.
The regional cooperative merger needs the blessing of Migros’s 2.3 million cooperative members who will vote on the proposal. A turnout of at least 25% and a two-thirds majority are required.

SEOUL, Oct 27 (Reuters) - A fire broke out on Tuesday in Guryong village, a shantytown in Seoul’s upmarket Gangnam district, affecting 77 households and 107 people, South Korea’s Yonhap news agency said.

Prison sentences of up to one year for fraudsters who conned Prince Laurent and Princess Claire

Four defendants who defrauded Prince Laurent (pictured left), King Filip’s brother, and Princess Claire, his wife, of 17,000 euros have been sentenced to prison terms of up to one year. The couple, who live in leafy Tervuren (Flemish Brabant), clicked on a link in a fake text message in 2021.
Prison sentences of up to one year for fraudsters who conned Prince Laurent and Princess Claire
On 23 December 2021, Princess Claire received a message on her mobile phone purporting to be from Cardstop. Card Stop is the central 24/7 service in Belgium used to immediately block lost, stolen, swallowed, or compromised payment methods. The text stated that she needed to block her bank card. She had lost her card a few days earlier and didn’t suspect anything. She clicked on the link and entered her personal details on a fake website.
When Princess Claire became suspicious, she closed the website, but a few days later she realised she could no longer make any payments. Her bank confirmed that she had been the victim of phishing. A total of 17,776 euros was withdrawn from Prince Laurent and Princess Claire’s accounts. The account into which the prince receives his allowance was also affected.
Identity of fraudsters still a mystery
Almost five years later, the public prosecutor’s office has not managed to map out the fraudsters’ entire network. However, four so-called ‘money mules’ were tracked down. They had made their accounts available to the fraudsters to channel the money and were due to appear in court today.
One of the money mules will not face any punishment. The other three were given suspended prison sentences of between six and twelve months. Together, they must also repay 10,765.75 euros.
'Fake'
The investigators were also able to establish that the fraudulent message had been sent by a woman from Antwerp, but she pleaded not guilty.
Her lawyer, Walter Damen, argued that the woman’s telephone number had been spoofed. This is a technique used by fraudsters to display a false number with a message, in order to impersonate someone else. The woman was acquitted.

Coalition spokesperson Turki al-Maliki said the operations aimed to dismantle the group's ballistic missile network and disrupt its supply routes.
The renewed fighting between the two sides has shattered a 2022 U.N.-brokered truce that largely halted attacks between the Saudi-led coalition, which backs Yemen's internationally recognized government, and the Houthis, who control the capital Sanaa.
The escalation has also opened another front in regional conflicts involving the U.S., Israel and Iran.

Live: Polls open in first Israeli election since October 7 attack
Unknown

2026-10-27
08:15:50 UTC
17:15:50 KST

Live: Israeli exit polls show narrow edge for opposition but no clear majority against Netanyahu
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Exit polls on Tuesday showed that the opposition bloc led by Israeli opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot gained a narrow edge over Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud bloc in the Knesset, setting the stage for weeks of jockeying to form a government. The day's vote was marked by decades-high turnout in the country's first election since the October 7, 2023 attacks. Follow our liveblog for the latest updates.
Eisenkot says Israel has chosen change, hopes to form government
Israeli opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot said early Wednesday said Israel had chosen change after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and that he would seek to form a new government.
In remarks to supporters, Eisenkot also issued a veiled warning to Netanyahu who has stepped up warnings in the final days of the campaign that he will attack Iran -- an emergency that could potentially delay efforts to form a coalition.
"Netanyahu, don't you dare use Israel's security for your political needs," Eisenkot said.
Exit polls showed the opposition bloc led by Eisenkot with a tiny edge over Netanyahu's right-wing bloc in Tuesday's election but with neither side securing a majority.
"The people have spoken against the continuation of Netanyahu's rule," Eisenkot said. "In an election with such a high turnout, it would be a mistake to go to another round of elections."
Eisenkot warns Netanyahu not to 'use Israel's security' for political ends
Israel's elections: What happens next?
Here are four possible scenarios:
1. Coalition
The parties will immediately begin negotiations to try to reach a 61-seat majority in the 120-member Knesset, but the path forward is far from clear.
President Isaac Herzog will name a candidate who has the best chance to form a government -- not necessarily the party with the most seats, which the initial exit polls showed to be Netanyahu's Likud.
The Arab Israeli parties, particularly Raam, have voiced openness to working with Eisenkot's bloc, but the camp has kept them at arm's length, perceiving their support as a liability during the campaign.
For Netanyahu's bloc, however, there is no obvious place to pick up more seats after some smaller right-wing parties failed to meet the vote threshold for entering parliament.
2. Minority government
If no bloc manages to secure 61 seats, a candidate could attempt to govern without a majority but rather through support on an ad hoc basis from other lawmakers.
In this scenario, lawmakers from the Arab Israeli parties -- whose community makes up 20 percent of the population and generally identifies as Palestinian -- could play a critical role.
Raam, led by Mansour Abbas, has been a kingmaker in the past, having been the first Arab party to join an Israeli government in a short-lived 2021-2022 coalition led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid.
Another Arab movement, the Joint List, has said it would be unlikely to join a coalition government outright, but has offered to provide a "safety net" for any one that ousts Netanyahu from power.
3. National unity government
Considering Israel's extreme polarisation, a national unity government would appear fanciful, but it could theoretically create a less extreme government.
Israeli commentators have often mused on the possibility of a national unity government in which Netanyahu would jettison his provocative far-right allies as well as ultra-Orthodox parties and team up with Eisenkot, who shares Netanyahu's views on many security issues.
Such a grand coalition would also exclude Arab parties.
4. Deadlock and new elections
If no candidate manages to form a government, Israel will have to return to the polls.
The country held four elections between April 2019 and March 2021 due to the inability of politicians to forge a lasting coalition.
The candidate designated by the president will, in principle, have 28 days to form a coalition, with a possible 14-day extension, although there are other procedural ways to prevent an immediate calling of new elections.

The stalemate could work in Netanyahu's favour, allowing the prime minister to remain in power in a caretaker capacity while parties try to forge a governing coalition.
Final results could take days, and Israel's fragmented political system leaves smaller parties potential kingmakers. No single party has ever won 61 seats outright in the 120-seat Knesset, making coalitions the norm.
Israel's Eisenkot says election results show 'lack of confidence' in Netanyahu

Strong gains for Arab-majority parties in Israel vote, exit polls show
The first exit polls from Israel's pivotal general election showed strong gains for the country's Arab-majority parties, whose voter base turned out in high numbers, likely giving them a critical role in the next parliament.
Exit polls from the main Israeli television channels showed the two Arab lists, Raam and the Joint List, winning 17 or 18 seats in the 120-member parliament between them, up from 10 in the last election in 2022.
While Raam and the Joint List do not belong to the opposition bloc, they have expressed openness to supporting it.

On October 28, the Kyiv Security Forum will hold a special event in Brussels to support Ukraine

Unknown Publisher

10:14:50 EET
17:14:50 KST

On October 28, the Kyiv Security Forum (KSF) will hold a special event in Brussels entitled ‘Support Ukraine – Defend Europe’, bringing together Ukrainian and foreign politicians, diplomats, military personnel and experts. The event will focus on how to help Ukraine withstand the winter, maintain its defence capabilities and prevent Russia from achieving its strategic objectives.
Speakers include:
- Arseniy Yatsenyuk – Chairman of the Kyiv Security Forum; Prime Minister of Ukraine (2014–2016);
- Henna Virkkunen – Executive Vice-President of the European Commission for Tech Sovereignty, Security and Democracy;
- Radmila Shekerinska – Deputy Secretary General of NATO;
- Vsevolod Chentsov – Deputy Prime Minister of Ukraine for European and Euro-Atlantic Integration;
- Theo Francken – Minister of Defence of Belgium;
- Alyona Getmanchuk – Head of the Mission of Ukraine to NATO;
- Taras Kachka – Head of the Mission of Ukraine to the EU;
- Ivanna Klympush-Tsintsadze – Chairwoman of the Verkhovna Rada Committee on Ukraine’s integration into the European Union;
- Maksym Timchenko – Chief Executive Officer of DTEK.
Members of the Kyiv Security Forum Security Council will also participate in the event: Kurt Volker – former U.S. Special Representative for Ukraine Negotiations; Natalie Jaresko – Chair of the Board of Trustees of the Aspen Institute in Kyiv and former Minister of Finance of Ukraine; Admiral Rob Bauer – former Chairman of the NATO Military Committee; Admiral Sir Tony Radakin – former Chief of the British Defence Staff; Danylo Lubkivsky – former Deputy Foreign Minister of Ukraine; as well as serving members of Ukraine’s Defence Forces.
The discussions will be moderated by Mark Lobel, journalist and BBC presenter.
Participants will also discuss how to respond to nuclear threats and further escalation by Russia, as well as how Europe can shift to a stronger model of defence, readiness and unity.
This will be the first high-level security event organised by the Kyiv Security Forum EU Office in Brussels, which was established on the initiative of Arseniy Yatsenyuk. The Office recently began its work in Brussels, continuing the Kyiv Security Forum’s efforts to build Ukraine’s ties with international partners since 2007.
The KSF EU Office in Brussels will serve as a permanent platform for political and expert dialogue with EU and NATO institutions, the governments of partner countries, parliaments, think tanks and civil society.
The work of the KSF’s EU Office will focus on helping to achieve Ukraine’s key strategic objectives: victory over Russian aggression; accession to the European Union and NATO; post-war recovery and reconstruction; accountability for Russia’s aggression and reparations for the damage it has caused; full participation in shaping Europe’s new defence architecture.
The registration of the international non-governmental organisation ‘European Office of the Kyiv Security Forum’ in Belgium was approved by a relevant Royal Decree signed by King Philippe of Belgium.
The Kyiv Security Forum (KSF), founded by the Arseniy Yatsenyuk ‘Open Ukraine’ Foundation, is Ukraine’s leading international platform on issues of war and peace. The KSF events are attended by heads of state and government, politicians, diplomats, military commanders, experts, civil society figures and journalists. The platform’s activities are aimed at keeping Ukraine at the centre of the global agenda, expanding its circle of international partners and building expertise on pressing security issues.

The Trump administration is backing Orbán, who blocked a €90 billion EU loan to Ukraine, for UN secretary-general and is counting on support from Moscow and Beijing, WSJ says

The Trump administration has encouraged former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán to run for UN secretary-general and discussed a joint US-Russia-China candidacy with Moscow and Beijing, the Wall Street Journal’s (WSJ) editorial board wrote on 25 October, citing sources in three countries. Russia’s biggest ally in the EU, Orbán has been out of office since May, when Péter Magyar became Hungary’s prime minister.
The UN secretary-general can influence the war through diplomatic negotiations, mediation, and by drawing the Security Council’s attention to Russia’s aggression. António Guterres’s term ends on 31 December, so the council has to settle on a successor within weeks.
According to the WSJ, US officials discussing the next UN chief kept saying they wanted “someone like Orbán,” and their Russian and Chinese counterparts agreed. The US then brought the idea to Orbán himself. Russia and China are believed to support his bid based on those earlier talks with Washington, and the plan is for him to be the three countries’ joint candidate.
Ukraine warns of Orbán’s veto tactics at the UN
Orbán is receptive but has not decided, and he does not want to enter the race unless he is sure he can win, the editorial board wrote. A State Department official counted eight Security Council votes as safe for him and 10 within reach. A candidate needs nine of the 15 votes and no veto from a permanent member. The editorial board asked whether Britain and France, typically cautious in using their veto, would stand in the way. Any announcement is being held until after the 3 November US midterm elections.
Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha wrote on X that Orbán as secretary-general would put to good use “the masterful veto and blackmail skills” he developed over years of derailing major EU decisions. Ukraine, he added, could share its “great experience of taking him out for coffee at the right moment,” a reference to the December 2023 EU summit, where Orbán left the room so the other leaders could open accession talks with Ukraine without his veto.
Orbán ran Hungary for 16 years as Putin’s closest EU partner
Orbán’s 16 years of “illiberal democracy” eroded democratic values in Hungary. Since 2010, Fidesz has built an enormous partisan media ecosystem. Before the vote, it amended the electoral law twice and gerrymandered more than a third of the electoral districts, so the opposition might need around 55% of the popular vote to win a simple majority. Orbán still lost the 12 April election. Magyar’s Tisza won 138 of 199 seats, a two-thirds majority in parliament.
Orbán kept close ties with Moscow throughout the full-scale war. When he met Putin in Beijing in October 2023, he spoke of “the military operations and the sanctions” rather than a war. In summer 2024, while Hungary held the EU Council presidency, he flew to Moscow on what he called a peace mission, and the EU distanced itself from the trip. In November 2025, he went back to Moscow, seeking to keep Hungary’s access to Russian oil and gas. He is widely considered Putin’s closest partner among EU leaders. After that visit, he said the only solution was for Ukraine to become a buffer state again, and that the longer peace was delayed, the more people and territory Ukraine would lose.
He used Hungary’s veto against Ukraine until his last weeks in office. In February, Orbán vetoed a €90 billion EU loan to Ukraine amid the disruption of Russian oil supplies through the Druzhba pipeline to Hungary and Slovakia. Hungary lifted its veto in April after repairs to the pipeline were announced. Foreign Minister Péter Szijjártó phoned Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov from EU meetings for years with “live reports on what’s been discussed,” a European security official told The Washington Post. Szijjártó did not respond to the Post’s request for comment.

The family, who have already lost their other children in the war, quickly learn that their daughter's foot can only be amputated without anesthesia.

"The film was accepted in states I would never dream about. It shows people are changing towards Gaza. For us to have a chance to show these audiences a story from Gaza is a success by itself," Hajjaj said.
In his post-screening discussions with audiences, many people comment on how realistic it looks—and are surprised to learn that it was filmed in southern California. Hajjaj spent months creating an authentic set and wardrobe to depict Gaza, where he has family he speaks with nearly daily. Many have died in Israeli airstrikes.
“In the discussions, as a filmmaker, they ask how I did it, where I filmed it. I always say I do have family in Gaza. The feelings I portrayed in those scenes are real feelings. I lived in that environment. I lived through that war. I experienced it through my family,” he said.
Hajjaj, who grew up in the border city of Rafah, has spent decades in Hollywood. His screen credits include "Ms. Marvel", "Will and Grace", and "Black Monday". Through his work, he hopes to be an ambassador of Palestinians for American audiences through the accessible medium of film.
"I'm their ambassador. I've accepted this message and mission. I am trying to fulfil this mission I have," he said.
"It's a lot of work. I am in Hollywood and I'm going against the current. We might have seen a lot of celebrities change their perspective, but that control in Hollywood has not changed. We're still facing the same issues." He said.
"Surprisingly, I haven’t had anybody get up and speak against the film and what I say. The story of a girl in Gaza could happen to anyone," he said. "People are hungry for these kinds of stories."

Kazakhstan, China plan to boost security at Khorgos Border Center

A draft law to ratify the agreement has been published on Kazakhstan's Open Legal Acts portal for public discussion. The agreement would establish a legal framework for cooperation between Kazakh and Chinese authorities to maintain security and public order at the Khorgos center.

Speaking on the BBC programme, broadcast on Oct. 23, William discussed Kazakhstan’s saiga conservation efforts and the Altyn Dala Conservation Initiative. He said the species had recovered from critically endangered status to numbers in the millions, noting that Kazakhstan’s government had recognized its importance to the country and conservation efforts.
“They threw their full weight behind it,” William said, referring to the government’s support for the initiative.

According to the Earthshot Prize, the saiga population grew from around 40,000 to more than four million over two decades, following a severe decline caused by poaching and disease. The initiative brings together Kazakhstan’s government, the Association for the Conservation of Biodiversity of Kazakhstan and international conservation partners.
The initiative’s work also extends to other endangered species, including Przewalski’s horses, as part of broader efforts to restore Kazakhstan’s natural ecosystems.

OpenAI says AI has made breakthroughs in three scientific fields
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:07:38 UTC
17:07:38 KST

OpenAI says AI has made breakthroughs in three scientific fields
OpenAI says its AI models have produced proofs that challenge established ideas in mathematics and computer science and address a major problem in physics, Qazinform News Agency correspondent reports.
One claim challenges a long-standing belief about how quickly computers can solve difficult problems. OpenAI says its AI system disproved the Exponential Time Hypothesis, which researchers have used for decades to estimate how much computing power certain tasks require.
The hypothesis suggests that some problems become so difficult as they grow that solving them quickly is impossible. Researchers have relied on it to assess the limits of algorithms in fields ranging from biology to computer science.
If OpenAI's proof is correct, scientists may need to rethink these limits and explore faster ways to solve some problems. The finding does not mean all difficult computing problems can now be solved quickly.
In mathematics, OpenAI says its models proved a 1991 conjecture about how waves behave when they focus. The result also settles two related mathematical problems, according to the company. These findings could help researchers better understand wave behavior and advance other areas of mathematics.
In physics, OpenAI says its models produced mathematical proofs concerning theories that explain how fundamental particles interact. One describes the strong force, which holds quarks together inside particles such as protons and neutrons. The work also addresses a problem involving Yang-Mills theory, one of the questions included in the Clay Mathematics Institute's Millennium Prize Problems.
OpenAI has published the mathematics and computer science proofs for examination. Independent experts will review the computer science claim, while a separate team led by Nobel Prize-winning physicist David Gross will examine the physics findings.

India evacuates tens of thousands as ‘very severe’ Cyclone Arnab nears
The cyclone is due to make landfall on Wednesday, with more than 12 million people living along its projected path.
India is evacuating tens of thousands of people from its eastern coast as a strengthening Cyclone Arnab bears down on its coastal states.
The cyclone has intensified since Monday and is expected to make landfall by Wednesday morning.
The India Meteorological Department has issued a warning for the coastal states of Andhra Pradesh and Odisha, saying the “very severe” cyclonic storm was centred only 260km (160 miles) southeast of the port city of Visakhapatnam, the most populous in Andhra Pradesh.
The department expects Arnab to turn northwest and cross the coast by 11:30am local time (06:00 GMT) on Wednesday, with sustained winds of 115-125km/h (71-78mph) and gusts of up to 140km/h (87mph).
Arnab formed over the Bay of Bengal, which is among the world’s main breeding grounds for tropical cyclones, frequently affecting India’s eastern coastal regions.
More than 12 million people live along the cyclone’s projected path, which runs inland and north across India, according to Andhra Pradesh’s disaster management authority.
Nearly 50,000 people had been moved to shelters from vulnerable areas of the state by Monday night, out of an estimated 400,000 in need of evacuation, the authority’s managing director, Prakhar Jain, told the Reuters news agency.
“Evacuation is continuing,” Jain said.
Railway authorities in the region said on social media that at least 12 trains had been cancelled in eastern India and services on 53 routes along the southern coast had been suspended for Tuesday and Wednesday.
In Odisha, authorities have announced plans to evacuate 48,000 people out of harm’s way, according to local newspaper The Hindu.
Authorities in neighbouring Nepal have advised tourists to stay away from high-altitude areas over concerns that Arnab could trigger heavy rain, snowstorms and avalanches in the Himalayas from Thursday night to Saturday.
The advisory comes after a Himalayan flash flood in August killed about 1,500 people in the country.

EU Inc: Why the Commission's perfect startup plan might be falling apart
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:00:50 UTC
17:00:50 KST

EU Inc, the Commission’s promise to strengthen the EU’s startup market and keep startups from moving abroad, is facing roadblocks that make its adoption by 2026 difficult. Will the 28th regime survive?
The European Parliament's Committee on Legal Affairs (JURI) failed to vote on its draft report on EU Inc on October 19.
Known as the “28th regime,” EU Inc. creates unified company rules to reduce fragmentation across the EU’s 27 legal systems, making it faster and cheaper to launch and scale businesses. It would give startups a single pan-European digital company form without changing national company, tax residency or social security rules.
But it faces strong opposition. The European Trade Union Confederation (ETUC) warns that loopholes in the current proposal trigger a race to the bottom in pay and workers’ protections, while EU Inc’s founders say months of negotiations are watering down the reforms’ core.
What EU Inc promises
EU Inc is an EU-wide company type with a single, harmonised rulebook. It would be optional and complement existing national company laws and forms, giving founders another option when starting a business.
Under the regime, businesses can register in one member state via the central EU interface takes 48 hours. Minimum capital is €1, and no opening deposit is required. All procedures, including formation, filing, governance, share issuance, and liquidation, are fully digital and incur no notary or chamber fees. Fast, fully digital access to insolvency procedures is included. Existing companies can convert into an EU Inc without dissolving and reincorporating.
With a harmonised European Employee Stock Option, Eu Inc would change how equity compensation works, ensuring employees receive options under the same rules and tax principles, wherever they live.
Some aspects won’t change. Contracts, working time, dismissal protection, collective bargaining, and works councils remain governed by the country where employees work. Social security remains determined by where they physically work. The proposal creates no new tax regime or changes to tax residency, as companies remain taxed where their effective management sits.
Workers’ rights drive the deadlock
The Commission presented its proposal on 18 March 2026 and aims to reach an agreement by year-end.
The Council adopted its position on 23 October. It supports the proposal’s objectives while simplifying the framework, streamlining digital and employee stock-option provisions, strengthening safeguards, and aligning it with EU internal market freedoms.
Parliamentary negotiations have stalled after JURI failed twice to secure a majority for rapporteur René Repasi’s (S&D) draft report. Repasi named no sticking points, but workers’ rights appear to be the biggest issue.
“We have made progress, but we still need to find the right balance for a final agreement Repasi said. For EU Inc to be a “seal of quality”, it needs legal certainty and safeguards for workers against misuse which, he pointed out, has been "entirely absent from the Commission proposal".
Should EU Inc become a “vehicle for circumventing labour law rather than a driver of high-quality innovation, it will have failed to deliver on its promise", the rapporteur added.
On 24 September and 20 October, ETUC protested the proposal’s lack of safeguards in Brussels and Strasbourg. ETUC Deputy General Secretary Isabelle Schömann warns EU Inc could encourage “regime shopping”. Companies may register in states with weaker labour protections and collective bargaining, then operate elsewhere to evade stronger laws and enable social and fiscal dumping.
ETUC says the proposal lets companies avoid informing and consulting workers. Since employees’ board representation varies by country and depends on a company’s registration location, firms could register where it doesn’t exist, excluding workers from decisions.
Businesses could replace wages or employment contracts with stock options, as no clear ban prevents paying workers in shares or supplementing low wages with them, Schömann said. For Repasi, options are valuable for attracting and retaining talent, but he warned that “such schemes should never replace fair wages, pensions or social security contributions”.
EU Inc companies could use fast-tracked liquidation, even if they have outstanding payments. This means unpaid wages, severance, or social security contributions for laid-off workers, while social security authorities have only limited time to review and object, according to ETUC’s own legal analysis report.
“Faster procedures can reduce unnecessary administrative burdens, but speed must not come at the expense of creditors’ rights, employees’ claims or the effective enforcement of legal obligations”, Repasi warned.
Negotiators want to reach an agreement by year-end. However, this will depend on the "willingness of all parties to work constructively,” the rapporteur said, calling on the Commission to be “an honest broker”. “It must facilitate a fair process and help both co-legislators find common ground, without favouring one position over the other”, Repasi told Euronews.
For Schömann, negotiators are overlooking one crucial aspect.
Access to investment is the biggest obstacle for startups and scale-ups, and it is essential to keeping them in Europe, she said, but “we don't see where these new businesses will get access to investment” through the EU Inc reform.
Is EU Inc still keeping its promise?
Although trade unions are pushing for stronger worker protections, EU Inc's founders are warning that months of negotiations are watering down the reforms' core. On 15 October 2026, the EU-INC campaign issued an urgent warning to European leaders, accusing policymakers of weakening the proposal through months of negotiations.
Backed by more than 26,000 founders, investors and entrepreneurs across Europe, including figures associated with Stripe, Klarna, Mistral AI and Atomico, the campaign declared: “The EU Inc you championed - one that will enable Europe to compete at scale - no longer exists.”
Simon Schaefer, co-initiator of the EU-INC campaign, told Euronews that the original ambition had been to create a genuinely European legal framework, rather than one dependent on national courts. "Instead, the commission has chosen the version in which national member state courts [are] responsible for dispute resolution. And that alone is [...] not the major moonshot that we originally asked for because it does have 27 flavours to a degree", he said.
According to the campaign, allowing member states to introduce national exceptions and different requirements risks creating 27 variations of the same framework. Schaefer argues that, if a fully unified European system is no longer achievable, startups must at least be able to choose the member state offering the most suitable corporate framework.
"The company or corporate law, company law, labor law, tax law, all of these things are so intertwined and so complex that we believe the best possible outcome of the current proposal of the commission is for 1 2 3 member States in Europe [to] build the possible framework for startup[s]", he said.
One major disagreement is about the proposed central European company registry, which was removed from an initial Council compromise draft. Founders argue that a single register for standardised company information is essential for simplifying banking, investment and compliance procedures across borders.
They also oppose restrictions on employee stock options, including limits based on company size and turnover. Such restrictions could prevent growing businesses from benefiting from the framework.
But the question of who should benefit from EU Inc is also raising concerns. Although designed primarily for startups, the Commission's proposal contains no general restrictions on company size or age. Large, established businesses could also choose EU Inc, raising questions about whether simplified rules intended for young companies could be used by corporations seeking more favourable governance arrangements.
The proposal also has a central contradiction: companies could register in one member state while being managed from another. Because tax residency remains governed by national rules, a company registered in Ireland but operating from Germany could still face German tax obligations and cross-border compliance questions.
For Schaefer, however, this is one of the proposal's most important advantages: "The free choice of administrative HQ would make the same possible for within Europe. So, you could register your company in any choosing in any country of member state of your choosing, but you could still physically be in another member state and pay your taxes there."
A single registration process would not necessarily mean a single legal environment. National laws would also continue filling gaps in the European framework, potentially preserving differences between member states, even if the rules for setting up a company are harmonised.
Another issue is the legal basis. The Commission relies on Article 114 of the EU treaties, which allows the alignment of national legislation to improve the single market. However, the European Company Law Experts group questions whether this provision can legally support a separate, optional company structure.
Then there's the problem of the speedy digital registration process, which has raised concerns about fraud prevention. The proposal retains certain administrative, judicial or notarial checks, but Germany's Federal Chamber of Notaries argues that identity verification and legal safeguards are insufficient, potentially increasing the risks of shell companies, fraud and money laundering. The Commission, however, maintains that safeguards against abuse will still be in place.
And responding to trade unions' concerns that EU Inc could weaken workers' rights, Schaefer argued that safeguards should target abuses directly, including preventing businesses from using stock options to circumvent minimum wage requirements.
"We are available and willing and wanting to design the right tools to prevent fraud. We're in unison with the trade unions that we do not want to abuse workers' rights. It should never happen", Schaefer said.
The EU-INC campaign wants EU leaders to restore five essential elements: freedom to register in any member state, access for companies of all sizes and sectors, a single European registry, harmonised stock options taxed when shares are sold, and national tax and employment obligations linked to actual economic activity.
But if the negotiations compromise those demands, the campaign could seek to delay the legislation rather than accept a watered-down version, Schaefer warned.
"If we see an indicator that it will not or that there's too much compromise then we will try to Find a way to delay it and to do it proper. For us speed is not the main decisive factor. For us getting it right is almost more important right now than the actual speed."

- Eisenkot joined Israel’s war cabinet in 2023, participating in decision-making during Gaza war
After a 41-year career in the Israeli military, former army chief Gadi Eisenkot is seeking to unseat Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Tuesday’s legislative elections, in a contest between two figures whose careers have been closely tied to Israel’s military and political establishments.
Eisenkot, 66, is running at the head of the Yashar party, which he founded in 2025, promising to form a “change” government that would end the rule of Netanyahu, 77, who has served as prime minister for a combined period of more than 17 years.
Opinion polls show Yashar, contesting elections for the first time, ahead of Netanyahu’s Likud party.
At the same time, polls indicate that neither man’s bloc is expected to secure the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-member Knesset.
That means the contest is unlikely to be decided simply by which party finishes first, with post-election alliances expected to play a decisive role in determining who becomes the next prime minister.
 
Moroccan roots
Eisenkot was born in 1960 in Tiberias to a Jewish family of Moroccan origin and grew up in the southern Israeli city of Eilat.
His father was born in Marrakesh, while his mother was born in Casablanca.
He joined the Israeli army’s Golani Brigade in 1978, beginning as a soldier in the 13th Infantry Battalion before rising through the ranks to command the brigade, according to his party’s website.
During his military career, Eisenkot served as military secretary to two prime ministers and commanded the occupied West Bank division during the Second Palestinian Intifada, which began in 2000.
He later headed the Operations Directorate, commanded the Northern Command and served as deputy chief of staff.
In 2015, he became the Israeli army’s 21st chief of staff, remaining in the post until 2019.
 
‘Dahiya Doctrine’
Eisenkot’s name is closely associated with the so-called “Dahiya Doctrine,” which advocates the use of disproportionate military force against infrastructure used by Hezbollah in Lebanon.
According to Yashar’s website, Eisenkot developed the doctrine while serving as head of the Northern Command and the Operations Directorate following the 2006 Lebanon war.
The doctrine calls for expanding the use of military force against infrastructure during confrontations with Hezbollah beyond directly targeting military positions.
As chief of staff, Eisenkot oversaw implementation of the multi-year Gideon Plan, aimed at strengthening the Israeli army’s ground, air, naval, intelligence and cyber capabilities.
His party biography also says he introduced measures in 2015 to confront stabbing attacks in the occupied West Bank and tunnels along the Gaza and northern borders.
 
From military to politics
After retiring from the army, Eisenkot headed the David Ben-Gurion Heritage Institute, which focuses on preserving the legacy of Israel’s first prime minister and developing the Negev. He also held positions in the private sector.
He was elected to the Knesset in 2022.
In August 2023, while serving on the Knesset’s Foreign Affairs and Defense Committee, Eisenkot warned that Israel’s deterrence and regional standing were eroding, blaming government policies and deep internal divisions.
In October 2023, Eisenkot joined Israel’s war cabinet as a minister and participated in decision-making over the war on Gaza.
His son Gal was killed on Dec. 7, 2023, during Israeli attacks on Jabalia in northern Gaza. Two of his nephews were also killed during fighting in the Gaza Strip.
Since October 2023, Israel’s war on Gaza has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and injured over 175,000 others, while around 90% of the enclave’s civilian infrastructure has been destroyed.
Despite a ceasefire agreement in effect since Oct. 10, 2025, Israeli attacks involving bombardment and gunfire have continued, causing further casualties.
 
Challenge to Netanyahu
Eisenkot holds a bachelor’s degree in history from Tel Aviv University, a master’s degree in political science from the University of Haifa and a master’s degree from the US Army War College.
He was awarded an honorary doctorate in 2019 by Reichman University.
Eisenkot founded Yashar party in 2025 as a vehicle for challenging Netanyahu for the premiership.
The party presents itself as an alternative government and says its goal is to preserve Israel as a “Jewish, democratic, secure and strong state.”
Although Eisenkot presents himself as a candidate for change, his record includes commanding the Israeli army and serving in the war cabinet during the Gaza genocidal war.
The electoral contest with Netanyahu centers on who will lead the next government. His party positions do not indicate a fundamental departure from Israel’s military approach toward the Palestinians.
Netanyahu is seeking to retain the premiership, while Eisenkot hopes to capitalize on his lead in opinion polls to bring Netanyahu’s rule to an end.
With polls giving neither bloc a parliamentary majority, each side’s ability to assemble a coalition of at least 61 lawmakers is expected to determine who can form the next government.

Admit it: the English love affair with European food has grown stale – we need a native cuisine we can be proud of | Lewis Bassett
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:00:05 UTC
17:00:05 KST

No discerning dinner party host in England would dream of serving their guests a traditional English ham. You might find jamón ibérico, of which Spain is so proud, but never stuffed chine, a shoulder cut of salted pork marbled with parsley, once a delicacy in Lincolnshire. It sometimes seems as if the English middle classes are so concerned with other countries’ proud artisanal products that they miss the potential of our own.
We’re more likely to find cookery writers and experts in nutrition advocate for Japanese foods than traditional English fare. The Chinese diet, too, has its passionate advocates in England. We barely need to mention the English middle classes’ long love affair with France and Italy and Spain.
Many well-to-do English eaters project ideals of rustic authenticity on to southern Europe, giving us the “modern European” cooking that has dominated the menus of many smart restaurants in England for decades. Yet perhaps this culinary culture is running out of road? Is it not a little dull to see aioli, burrata and fresh pasta almost everywhere? What happened to salad cream and whitebait and pickled herring and steamed puddings? Where did all the bath buns and sally lunns go? Are croissants really all we want from our bakeries? When did England’s middle classes fall out of love with English food?
My book The Full English explores these topics from the first-person perspective of a chef-cum-sociologist. I describe the history of England’s break with the tastes once shared by elites across medieval Europe, which provided us with our first recognisably national cuisine. For Georgian Britons, food, especially beef, spit-roasted and served with simple garnishes, was everything that France was not. France was said to be popish and tyrannical, and the courtly tradition of French food reflected that. France was viewed by British patriots as weak, because its population supposedly subsisted on weeds and frogs. Beef, by contrast, was hearty, honest and rooted in the self-reliance of the English country gentleman. Many middling and upper sorts in Georgian England, from William Hogarth to William Gladstone, joined clubs whose patriotic motto was “beef and liberty”.
But by the late 19th century, among a generation with no direct memory of the Napoleonic wars, elite food preferences changed again, no less because the elite itself had changed. Britain had already become a majority urban nation in 1851 (some 100 years ahead of southern Europe), and in English cities, merchants, financiers, capitalists and their associated professions – groups whose power came from money, rather than land or title – demanded French cooks and French restaurants as a modern move away from the country cooking of the older upper classes, one which reflected Britain’s new ease with France.
Later, in postwar Britain, an expanding middle class underwent a lifestyle revolution. Stiff hats, starched shirts and rigid table manners were out and the supposed informality of Mediterranean food was in, along with bare brick walls, furniture from Habitat, bric-a-brac and olives; all markers of what the cookery writer Elizabeth David deemed a new taste for “the luxury of authenticity”.
And why not? Fourteen years of rationing had undermined a native food culture already hindered by urbanisation and industry, both of which were enabled by our dependence on imported food. Then, on top of these features of Britain’s peculiar modernity, has been the long shadow cast by Georgian patriotism – which deemed French food as effeminate, and so committed us to a view that refinement in food is “posh”. No wonder the middle class in this country projected a greedy gaze upon an idealised, provincial France and Italy.
But might it be time to turn our hungry dreamings back to England? The other nations that make up the union have their own culinary traditions and often proud relationship to national identity. But in England, patriotism is often assumed to be a blight. Outside international football tournaments, one senses that flags are flown mostly out of fear and hatred, and almost never out of pride. A positive, prouder version of national identity could become a powerful way to rebuild connection in our increasingly fragmented society.
Nations are inventions, thus so too are national foods. Take the case of British bread. The modern artisanal sourdough loaf – so adored by today’s tote-bag yoga-ing classes – has its roots in France and California and was introduced to England in the mid-1990s. And yet its popularity has seen an explosion of native craft baking across the UK, producing a proud generation of artisans who have brought about a better, and at this point, recognisably British bread.
We need such inventions more than ever, since ours is a country with some of the most unhealthy and unsustainable eating habits in Europe. Roast beef or overfished seafoods cannot be the way to go. Old dishes and familiar ingredients can be adapted, and new traditions can be invented. Yet as the new British artisanal sourdough shows, middle-class trends can be unaffordable for many. Such exclusivity can breed resentment, in turn fuelling the popularity of foods and brands, such as Greggs, which reproduce our anti-posh, anti-artisanal culture and our habits of unhealthy, industrial eating.
For England to find a popular new culinary heritage, one centred on the dignity of craft production as much as health, will require state policy capable of lifting up our culinary standards across the board.
And here, pride can form a common ground for any politics leaning in that direction. As a chef, I know that when I have made a custard tart with a satisfying wobble or perfectly dressed a crop of garden beans with a pouting spike of vinegar, I feel a sense of self-respect. Investing in British culinary craft is a way to lend pride to our struggling nation; a decent native cookery culture will be one positive thing worth raising the flag for.
- Lewis Bassett is a chef and the host of The Full English Podcast, and the author of The Full English

"Things start in really simple gestures" says Es Devlin of her Design Museum retrospective
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:00:00 UTC
17:00:00 KST

British artist and designer Es Devlin explains how ambitious creative projects begin with simple ideas in this exclusive video interview with Dezeen, filmed at Es Devlin: Other Worlds, her first European retrospective at London’s Design Museum.
“This is literally my favourite project. A book which took me seven years to make and it contains everything I’ve ever made,” Devlin told Dezeen, referring to a companion book created to coincide with the exhibition.
The book, as well as the exhibition, brings together three decades of Devlin’s work across theatre, opera, concert stage design and large-scale public installations.
The exhibition explores how Devlin’s projects develop, from early drawings and models to monumental installations experienced by audiences around the world.
In the interview, she explains how she hopes the presentation will demystify the creative process and encourage visitors to pursue their own ideas.
“I really hope that when people leave this exhibition, they’ll see objects and traces of things which make them say, ‘Oh, I could do that’,” she said.
“It’s not a mystery. It doesn’t come by magic. It comes step by step, with attention, curiosity, work and collaboration.”
The exhibition begins with a replica of Devlin’s studio in Peckham, complete with her books, objects, models, drawings, tools and paints.
“I love visiting other artists and designers’ studios,” she said. “I think it’ll make people feel something about what these rooms feel like, where creativity is allowed to happen at all times.”
From the studio, visitors encounter Come Home Again, Devlin’s installation originally presented outside Tate Modern in 2022.
The original work featured illuminated cut-outs of endangered wildlife arranged within a cross-section of the dome of St Paul’s Cathedral.
Reconfigured beneath a mirrored ceiling for the Design Museum exhibition, it is followed by A 30-Year Desk, a series of concentric circular desks displaying archival objects, drawings and models from across her career.
The archive includes material relating to her designs for the 2018 theatre production The Lehman Trilogy, the Forest of Us installation in Miami and the closing ceremony of the London 2012 Olympic Games, alongside more than 30 models of projects that have previously been exhibited in Britain.
The exhibition culminates in An Infinite Library, an eight-metre-wide rotating sculpture containing more than 2,000 books that have shaped Devlin’s worldview.
The artwork was originally installed on the beachfront of the Faena Beach hotel in Miami Beach and has been reimagined for the Design Museum retrospective.
Arranged in bands of colour above a circular mirror, the books are illuminated by projections and accompanied by recordings of Devlin reading selected passages.
Devlin began her career designing sets for small-scale theatre productions in 1996 before moving into opera, dance and concert stage design. Over the past decade, she has increasingly focused on large-scale public artworks and installations.
For Es Devlin: Other Worlds, she brought together material spanning her career, including childhood experiments and paintings made shortly before the exhibition opened, to reveal the ideas and processes behind her finished projects.
“I began to develop an attitude on how to take things that are amassed in piles and are somewhat overwhelming, to spread them out along a timeline and make them digestible and legible to an audience,” she said.
“Actually, these things that seem huge and overwhelming and complicated, they start in really simple gestures.”
Es Devlin: Other Worlds runs at the Design Museum in London until 4 April 2027.

‘Unacceptable’: condemning writers over AI detector scores
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:00:00 UTC
17:00:00 KST

‘Unacceptable’: condemning writers over AI detector scores
When a detector flagged a bestselling novel as AI-generated, it sparked a controversy that had serious consequences for the author. Swiss experts and artists examine how much these tools can really prove and what their verdicts mean for creative work.
Haitian-Canadian writer Thélyson Orélien had a promising career ahead of him. His novel C’était ça ou mourir (It was either that or die), a critical and commercial success, was in the running for some of France’s most prestigious literary prizes, including the Goncourt. That was until an anonymous account on X accused him of writing almost the entire book using artificial intelligence (AI).
Orélien denied using AI to write the novel. But to his accusers, the evidence seemed unequivocal: Pangram, one of the most popular tools for detecting AI content, had classified more than 95% of the book as AI-generated.
From there, things took a turn for the worse for Orélien. His novel was removed from the Goncourt selection, also amid revelations by the press of plagiarism in earlier works, for which he apologised. His Canadian publisher cut ties with him after an external analysis uncovered further evidence of AI use. Orélien continued to deny having written the book with AI, while acknowledging that he had turned to it for historical research during the creative process.
From the beginning, the controversy divided the literary world between those who defended the author and questioned the reliability of AI detectors, and those who criticised him.
Beyond Orélien’s case, Swiss filmmaker, screenwriter and lecturer Manuel Flurin Hendry believes it’s unfair to damage a writer’s reputation based on a software-generated score. “The idea that you feed a text into Pangram and then socially execute a writer feels unacceptable,” Hendry told Swissinfo in an interview at the AI+X Summit in early October. Hendry defends artists’ freedom to choose their own tools.
Other Swiss writers and artists have openly experimented with AI. Author Charles Lewinsky incorporated entire passages generated by ChatGPT into his novel Täuschend echt. Photographer Matthieu Gafsou has used image-generation tools such as DALL·E in his artistic work.
These are just a few transparent examples of how AI has entered creative work in Switzerland. But deciding how to respond to undisclosed and potentially extensive use of AI is far more difficult. As is determining how much AI-generated material is acceptable in a work of art, and whether tools like Pangram can really be trusted as a definitive proof of fraud.
How reliable is Pangram?
For Hendrik Strobelt, a senior researcher at IBM in the United States, the question of Pangram’s reliability is complex. In 2019, Strobelt and his colleagues developed GLTR, one of the first experimental tools designed to help identify text potentially generated by language models.
At the time, OpenAI had just released GPT-2, the model on which GLTR was based. AI models tended to produce rather dull texts that were very similar in style, because this type of content was the most common, Strobelt explains.
Identifying whether a text might have been produced with the help of AI was therefore relatively straightforward: it was enough to look for the most likely words.
Then language models became more sophisticated. Strobelt believes that, with today’s advanced AI systems, it has become extremely difficult to establish clear rules to distinguish AI-generated text from human writing.
“Now these models are significantly larger. They can imitate styles if you prompt them accordingly,” the IBM researcher says.
Software such as Pangram uses a method known as “supervised classification”. It compares and classifies texts written before generative AI became widespread – which is presumed to be human-written – with “mirror” versions on the same topic, generated by different commercially available language models. During training the software learns to identify the differences between them.
The logic is that if a system can distinguish between texts that are very similar in subject matter, its predictions will become more accurate.
“You want to train on things that are very close to each other, to be sure that you get the hard tasks trained first,” Strobelt explains.
Pangram claimsExternal link an accuracy rate of 99.98% and a false-positive rate of 0.01%. Its high performance has also been supported by independent researchExternal link, including a studyExternal link published this year.
According to Paolo Italiani, an AI and machine-learning researcher at the Università della Svizzera italiana (USI), the longer a text is, the more reliable a detector’s assessment tends to be.
“It’s quite probable that at least a portion of [the text] is AI-generated,” he says.
The limits of AI detectors
Yet it remains difficult to understand exactly which features of a text these tools rely on to make their classifications, says Lonneke van der Plas, professor of natural language processing at USI.
Interpretability studies would be needed to gain more understanding, she explains. But because commercial tools such as Pangram are largely black boxes whose internal workings are not accessible to independent researchers, it is challenging to study how they reach their conclusions.
In theory, certain clues such as an overly linear argumentative structure could help determine whether a text was more likely written by AI or by a human, researchExternal link co-authored by Van der Plas highlights. But such features, she cautions, are not sufficient to establish a text’s origin with certainty.
Van der Plas also points out that detection tools tend to perform less reliably in languages other than English and in more specialised genres that may have been less well represented in their training data.
The problem becomes even more complicated when a text is the product of collaboration between humans and AI. Some tests showExternal link, detectors’ accuracy drops by around 20 percentage points in such cases. Pangram’s own technical reportExternal link also indicates that the software loses accuracy when faced with content that alternates between human-written and AI-generated sentences.
“This software has been mostly trained on either completely human-generated or machine-generated texts. As soon as they get something that it’s in between, they get into trouble,” van der Plas says.
A score is not sufficient proof
From a legal perspective, results produced by tools such as Pangram do not constitute proof that an author has committed fraud.
“A legal decision cannot simply rely on those technologies because they can be inaccurate” says Jacques de Werra, professor of intellectual property law at the University of Geneva.
If a case like Orélien’s were brought before a court, de Werra explains, other evidence alongside detector scores should be considered, including original manuscripts, successive drafts and even exchanges with AI systems. De Werra also points out that AI involvement in creative work does not automatically invalidate an author’s copyright claims.
“If a person can demonstrate that there is a sufficiently close creative link between the input, creative prompting, and the output, it could be possible to claim human creativity,” he says.
The key is whether the author’s creative contribution is sufficient. De Werra stresses, however, that there is no fixed numerical threshold that determines how much of a text must be written by a person for a work to be considered their own.
If a book moves you, does it matter if AI helped write it?
For Manuel Flurin Hendry, however, the issue goes beyond legal protection.
Hendry openly uses AI-based technologies, some of which he has developed himself, for various aspects of his work, from analysing screenplays to assisting his academic research.
Technology, he explains, opens new channels of inspiration, sometimes suggesting approaches he had not previously considered. It also frees up more time for the creative process.
“True human writing is thinking in action. It requires friction and to enter a state where one can just concentrate on their flow of thoughts,” he says.
And he poses a provocative question: why should it matter how much AI contributed to a work? “If it moves you. If you find it interesting. If it makes you think, what is the argument?” he asks.
What’s important, Hendry argues, is learning which tasks to delegate to AI and which are better done personally. Rather than rejecting technology, artists should be transparent about how they use it.
“If I pretend this is mine, but it’s totally AI generated, then it’s fake,” Hendry says.
What is at stake is not only an artist’s reputation, but above all the relationship of trust with their audience.
