Novartis back on track for growth in third quarter
At Swiss pharmaceuticals giant Novartis, the negative impact of generic medicines continued to ease in the third quarter. For the full year, management is revising its previous outlook for core operating profit upwards.
According to a statement released on Tuesday, Novartis generated revenue of $14.5 billion (CHF12 billion) in the third quarter. This is 4% higher than in the same period last year. At constant exchange rates, revenue also rose by 4%.
This means that Novartis’s business performance is continuing to gain momentum: after the group had reported a decline in revenue in the first quarter due to the launch of generic versions of key blockbuster drugs, it had already returned to a growth trajectory in the second quarter.
Novartis had recently emphasised on several occasions that the erosion caused by generic medicines was likely to have peaked. Key revenue drivers such as Entresto, Promacta and Tasigna lost their patent protection last year. Group CEO Vas Narasimhan had emphasised that the negative impact is likely to be significantly greater in the first half of 2026 than in the second.
More
Big Pharma steps up race for AI-discovered drugs
Research setback weighs on results
In terms of operating profit, the Basel-based company recorded a slump of 59% to $1.8 billion. The bottom line was a consolidated profit of $1.2 billion, down from $3.9 billion in the same period last year. The reason for the sharp decline is the partial write-down of $1.9 billion relating to the failed product candidate Del-Desiran. Novartis has recently been grappling with various setbacks in late-stage research.
For analysts, however, the core operating profit – adjusted for various factors – is the key figure. At $6 billion, this figure rose compared with the previous year and exceeded the AWP consensus of $5.6 billion.
For the full year, Novartis is revising its previous profit guidance. Core operating profit is now expected to remain stable or show a slight increase. Novartis had previously forecast a decline in the low single-digit percentage range. Management continues to expect revenue growth at constant exchange rates to be in the low single-digit percentage range.

European automakers urge EU to protect Türkiye investments
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
07:32:57 UTC
16:32:57 KST

The European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA) has called for targeted exemptions to protect European manufacturers’ existing operations in Türkiye under the EU’s proposed “Made in EU” rules, warning that exclusion could weaken their competitiveness.
The call follows a Franco-German negotiating position that leaves Türkiye outside the proposed automotive framework while allowing for Britain’s inclusion.
The Industrial Accelerator Act, which seeks to strengthen European production against Chinese competition, has yet to be adopted.
Maria Linkova-Nijs, ACEA’s executive head of policy and strategy, told Daily Hürriyet that the association supported strengthening production in Europe but said manufacturers that had invested in good faith under existing rules should not be penalized.
“Investments by ACEA members operating in countries such as Türkiye and Morocco, particularly in the heavy commercial vehicle segment, must be taken into account in the ongoing negotiations,” she said.
ACEA members produced 29,000 trucks and 8,500 buses in Türkiye in 2025, according to Linkova-Nijs.
Excluding those operations could undermine competitiveness, put long-term investments at risk and create uncertainty over future production and investment decisions, she warned.
The association supports targeted exemptions for existing operations in neighboring countries closely integrated with Europe.
These should protect investments without creating loopholes or undermining the legislation’s objectives, she said.
Cengiz Eroldu, chairman of Türkiye’s Automotive Manufacturers Association (OSD), also criticized the Franco-German position, saying it did not reflect Europe’s production and supply networks and lacked economic justification.
He said Türkiye and the EU were important suppliers and markets for each other.
Their customs union had supported three decades of industrial integration extending beyond trade to joint investment, manufacturing, engineering and research.
Excluding Türkiye would therefore risk harming European manufacturers with investments in the country as well as Turkish producers, he said.
Eroldu stressed that the Franco-German agreement represented the position of two member states, with negotiations on the final legislation continuing.
Industry representatives reviewed developments with Trade Minister Ömer Bolat on Oct. 19, he said.
OSD and other automotive associations are continuing contacts with EU institutions and member states to seek provisions that preserve joint production and supply chains.

French education reform proposals 'vague': Govt created 'most of the problems' it now seek to solve
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
07:31:55 UTC
16:31:55 KST

French education reform proposals 'vague': Govt created 'most of the problems' it now seeks to solve
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on: Modified:
François Picard welcomes Jean-Rémi Girard, president of the SNALC teachers' union, who places responsibility for France's educational difficulties not simply on demographic change or fiscal constraints, but on years of political decisions that, he argues, have weakened the state education system. Against a backdrop of student protests, budgetary uncertainty and mounting concerns over educational inequality, Girard contends that the French government faces the formidable task of addressing a crisis largely of its own making.
The French education system, Girard argues, is caught between competing imperatives: reducing public expenditure, tackling teacher shortages, accommodating growing demand for higher education and safeguarding equal access to academic opportunity.
His critique is particularly striking in its historical dimension. During French President Emmanuel Macron's first term, Girard points out, the government eliminated 8,000 secondary teaching positions even as student enrolment was rising. "They created most of the problems that everybody is trying to solve now," he argues. Despite declining enrolment in some schools, staffing shortages persist, leaving institutions struggling to replace absent teachers and maintain adequate classroom conditions.
Girard's critique of the current state of French education is all-encompassing. Turning to Parcoursup, France's university admissions platform that was introduced under Macron in 2018, he challenges the tendency to identify the admissions system itself as the principal source of student frustration. "The problem is not Parcoursup per se," he explains. Rather, the deeper contradiction lies in the widening gap between growing demand for university studies and the limited capacity of higher education institutions to accommodate students' aspirations. This raises broader questions about fairness, educational opportunity and social mobility. As Girard succinctly puts it: "We cannot push the walls."
Girard also examines the relationship between educational discontent and wider social unrest. While acknowledging that the student movement has evolved amid broader cost-of-living protests and episodes of rioting, he cautions against allowing the unrest to overshadow the underlying educational grievances. The protests, he insists, have exposed "very big problems" within the national education system – concerns shared by students, teachers and unions alike.
Ultimately, Girard raises a fundamental question about French politics and the socioeconomics of public education: can governments credibly promise educational improvement while confronting severe fiscal constraints, political instability and budgetary policies that risk undermining investment in public education and social mobility for France's youth?
For Girard, the distinction between political announcements and meaningful reform is crucial. Although he acknowledges that the government's latest proposals represent a tentative step forward, he remains sceptical of commitments lacking concrete guarantees and secure funding. Without an approved parliamentary budget, he warns, the promised measures "won't become real".

Egypt&#8217;s regime persecutes journalists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
07:30:20 UTC
16:30:20 KST

The assault on an Egyptian journalist, who was beaten and dragged along the ground outside 6 October Central Hospital, west of Cairo, just days ago, highlighted the risks journalists face in Egypt.
A video (https://h1.nu/1GKSf), widely shared on social media, shows around seven people beating and dragging journalist Mohamed Faisal and detaining him inside the hospital while he was reporting. One of the assailants claims to be an “army officer”, reflecting the wider security crackdown on Egyptians, particularly journalists.
Faisal, who works for the government-authorised website Besraha, received a public apology from Health Minister Khaled Abdel Ghaffar, who also decided to terminate the contract with the security company responsible. The incident, however, reopened old wounds among journalists.
Since Abdel Fattah El-Sisi came to power in a military coup on 3 July 2013, journalists have faced repeated persecution. In 2026, Egypt ranked 169th out of 180 countries in the annual World Press Freedom Index published by Reporters Without Borders (https://h1.nu/1GKSB).
Arrests and Torture
The assault on Faisal came just days after journalists from Matsadaqsh, an independent fact-checking platform, called for medical examinations after being tortured and subjected to electric shocks to extract confessions. The Egyptian Public Prosecution later denied the claims.
On the evenings of 28 and 29 September, Egyptian security forces arrested the platform’s entire editorial team. Their phones and computers were seized from their homes, and their whereabouts were not disclosed. They were also denied contact with their families and lawyers, according to the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), an independent international organisation based in New York.
The detained journalists — Abdullah Qadri, Mohamed Ashraf Abu Omayra, Islam Barakat, Mohamed Adel, Omar Helal and Mohamed Mahmoud — said during questioning that they had been tortured and otherwise ill-treated to force them to record video statements incriminating themselves while in National Security Agency custody. They were subsequently brought before the Supreme State Security Prosecution, which ordered their pretrial detention for 15 days in connection with case No. 8083 of 2026, according to Amnesty International (https://h1.nu/1GKTj).
In a statement titled “Torture of Matsadaqsh Journalists: State Policy, Not Just Individual Misconduct”, the independent Cairo Institute for Human Rights Studies said that the torture, ill-treatment and enforced disappearance of Egyptian journalists reflected a recurring pattern and an almost established practice among security agencies in dealing with detained political opponents, human rights defenders and journalists (https://h1.nu/1GKTr).
READ: Egypt’s parliament approves military support for Saudi Arabia
Systematic Targeting
The two incidents have once again drawn attention to press freedom in Egypt, both domestically and internationally, and sparked anger among journalists inside and outside the country. In two separate statements, the Freedoms Committee of the Egyptian Journalists Syndicate described the assault on a journalist carrying out his professional duties as a crime punishable by law and a violation of the public’s right to know. It also said that the arrest of Matsadaqsh journalists violated the law and the Constitution.
Iman Ouf, head of the Freedoms Committee of the Egyptian Journalists Syndicate, said the arrest of more journalists, while others remain behind bars for years, was “a blatant disregard for the law and the Constitution, and a continuation of the policy of targeting journalists”.
The number of journalists imprisoned or detained in Egypt has reached 25 (https://h1.nu/1GKTZ), with concerns that more could be arrested in the coming period, according to the New York-based Committee to Protect Journalists.
Lina Attalah, editor-in-chief of the independent website Mada Masr, is also facing an uncertain future as she faces trial on 27 October on charges of establishing and running an online platform without a licence. The case is registered under No. 9072 of 2026 with the Supreme State Security Prosecution.
Journalists in Egypt are often pursued on charges with a political character, including (joining a terrorist group, publishing false news, misusing social media, receiving foreign funding and highlighting shortcomings in state institutions).
A Green Light
A security source who spoke to Middle East Monitor on condition of anonymity said that El-Sisi had given the Interior Minister the “green light” to arrest all Matsadaqsh journalists. The source said the move followed a complaint made last month at a meeting with mayors and village representatives about reports published by the investigative platform that questioned the credibility of state institutions.
During his 13 years in power, El-Sisi has never officially visited the Journalists Syndicate’s headquarters in central Cairo. His presidency has also seen security forces storm the premises on 1 May 2016, in an unprecedented incident dubbed “Black Sunday”.
On Wednesday, 4 May 2016, journalists held an emergency general assembly at their syndicate headquarters, demanding the dismissal of then Interior Minister Magdy Abdel Ghaffar, the publication of his photograph in negative, an apology from El-Sisi and the release of journalists imprisoned over their work.
Elected head of the Journalists Syndicate in 2023, Khaled El-Balshy, a left-wing opposition figure, has yet to meet with El-Sisi in an official capacity, unlike previous syndicate heads, who traditionally met with the president. This reflects growing tensions between the presidency and the press in Egypt.
Days ago, El-Balshy reiterated that the syndicate would continue to demand respect for the rule of law and the constitutional guarantees of press freedom and freedom of publication. He also pledged to defend all journalists, whether or not they are members of the syndicate.
READ: Egypt: Authorities Arrest Entire Investigative Newsroom
Persecution Continues
The arrests and persecution of journalists in September were not unprecedented, nor was the targeting of the Matsadaqsh team an isolated incident. Human Rights Watch has documented “repeated arrests and prosecutions in Egypt targeting peaceful critics, human rights defenders, journalists and online content creators”.
On 22 July 2024, Egyptian security forces arrested Ashraf Omar, a cartoonist for the independent website Al-Manassa. Human rights organisations said he was beaten and threatened with electrocution.
Egyptian journalist Yasser Abu Al-Ela has been detained since March 2024. His wife, Naglaa Fathi, and her sister were also arrested on 27 April that year, reflecting a security practice of targeting detainees’ families as a form of collective punishment.
According to political researcher Amr El-Masry, independent journalism poses a threat to the military regime and could bring it down if given the opportunity. He described it as a driving force for social change after social media, noting that journalists are the boldest in expressing their views and criticising those in power, making them the first to be targeted.
The persecution of journalists is expanding to include security summonses, prosecutions, the blocking of newspapers, the takeover of media organisations, the dismissal of opposition journalists, travel bans, exclusion from official positions and restrictions on their sources of income.
Unofficial estimates suggest that more than 600 websites have been blocked in Egypt, including dozens of independent news outlets and human rights organisations. Personal social media pages and websites used to circumvent censorship have also been blocked, reflecting a broader effort to control the flow of information.
The persecution of journalists has intensified as some news platforms have exposed falsehoods in official statements during the Egypt Forum conference, which was held to showcase the government’s achievements. Their coverage of hunger strikes by detainees in several prisons has also contributed to this escalation. According to Qutb Al-Arabi, former assistant secretary-general of the Supreme Council for the Press, these platforms have challenged the single narrative that El-Sisi has succeeded in imposing on Egyptian public life.
The El-Sisi regime is in serious trouble. Imprisoning an entire journalistic team is not so much a sign of strength as an indication that the general’s position is becoming increasingly precarious as he faces a small but defiant journalistic force that refuses to be crushed under the treads of tanks.

Khmara calls on E5 nations to transfer 10% of their air defense missile stocks to Ukraine in exchange for contracted future deliveries
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

09:30:05 EET

In an address to defense officials from the E5 group (Germany, the United Kingdom, France, Poland, and Italy), Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara proposed that these partners transfer 10% of their existing stocks of interceptor missiles for Patriot and IRIS-T systems to Kyiv. In exchange, Ukraine would offer future deliveries—already contracted and financed via a European Union loan—to replenish those stocks. Khmara also proposed establishing joint production of drones within the territories of these allied nations, the Ukrainian Ministry of Defense reported on Monday.
"We are proposing not just to increase procurement, but to scale up the joint production of Ukrainian drones within the territories of other countries. The minister identified the strengthening of air defense as the primary critical priority, noting that an immediate exchange—drawing from allies' existing stockpiles in return for future deliveries under Ukraine’s current contracts—would allow for the rapid protection of Ukrainian cities and serve as a model for other nations. Furthermore, Ukraine has an urgent need for man-portable air-defense systems (MANPADS) to counter Russian jet-powered drones; the country is seeking both the transfer of such systems from partners' existing inventories and funding for new acquisitions.
The head of the defense department identified the development of unmanned systems as the second priority, noting that Ukrainian enterprises have the capacity to double their drone production by 2027, provided that funding is delivered on time.
Khmara emphasized that Ukraine strives for a just and lasting peace—a goal that requires strength, readiness to defend the nation, and the timely provision of necessary weaponry to the armed forces.

Form Follows Formation: How Architecture Works with Geological Shapes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
07:30:00 UTC
16:30:00 KST

A canyon is a space no one designed. Its walls expose layers of rock deposited over millions of years, and the passage between them exists because water slowly wore that rock away. Glaciers shaped valleys in a similar way, leaving slopes behind as the ice retreated. Long before architects began shaping spaces, the Earth was already producing them.
Architects have long looked to the ground for geometry. A cliff can suggest a section, a cavity a room, and layered rock a way of stacking material. Some architects build directly into an existing formation, occupying a slope or a cavity on site. Others study a formation and reproduce some of its characteristics elsewhere, from precise geological data to the general experience of a landscape.

The Convergence of Fintech and Digital Entertainment: UX Benchmarking in the Hybrid iGaming Era
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
07:29:44 UTC
16:29:44 KST

The way we spend our downtime has changed quite drastically over the last few years. It wasn't that long ago that the worlds of finance and digital entertainment lived in completely different zip codes. You had your banking app for the serious stuff and your gaming apps for the fun stuff, and the two rarely met. However, if you look at the current landscape, those boundaries are thinning out. We're seeing a massive crossover where the slick, high-speed user experience (UX) of modern fintech is becoming the standard for the gaming industry.
This shift isn't just a happy accident. It's a calculated response to a more tech-savvy audience that expects everything to happen instantly. Whether you're moving money between accounts or spinning a reel, you want it to be seamless, secure, and intuitive.
 The Macroeconomics of iGaming 4.0
When we look at the numbers, the scale of this industry is honestly staggering. Analysts are projecting that the global gross gaming revenue (GGR) will hit around $81.4 billion by 2025. That's not just a big number for a press release; it represents a fundamental shift in how global audiences value digital entertainment.
What’s driving this growth? It’s a mix of better mobile infrastructure, the widespread adoption of 5G, and a change in how we perceive digital value. We've moved into what many are calling "iGaming 4.0," an era defined by hyper-connectivity and data-driven experiences. In the UK specifically, the market has matured to a point where the focus has shifted from simply acquiring new users to providing a high-quality, sustainable experience for existing ones. This economic weight means there's more investment than ever into the underlying tech stack, making the platforms we use today unrecognisable compared to those from a decade ago.
 Blockchain-Level Security in Legacy Systems
Security is usually the boring part of the conversation, but in the current climate, it’s arguably the most important. The UK is often seen as a global leader in regulation, and for good reason. The UK Gambling Commission has been very clear about the "Consumer Duty," which essentially means companies have a legal and moral obligation to put the user's interests and safety at the heart of their business.
Because of these strict rules, we've seen a rapid adoption of fintech-grade security protocols across the board. We're talking about end-to-end encryption, multi-factor authentication, and even biometric logins that you’d normally associate with a high-street bank. Many platforms are now looking at how blockchain technology can improve transparency. While not every site is running on a decentralised ledger, the principles of blockchain (immutability and verifiable transactions) are being integrated into legacy systems. This level of security is no longer a luxury; it’s the entry price for operating in a regulated market.
 Volatility and the New Wave of Engagement
There is a fascinating parallel between the world of high-frequency trading and modern digital entertainment. If you’ve ever watched someone trade altcoins or navigate a fast-moving stock market, you'll notice they have a very specific set of expectations. They want data to update in real-time, they want zero latency, and they want an interface that doesn't get in the way of their decision-making.
This is where the concept of "high-volatility" engagement comes in. In the financial world, volatility is about the rate of change in prices. In the world of digital entertainment, it's about the frequency and variance of outcomes. Traditional UK operators have had to adapt to this "crypto-native" mindset. For instance, Bally Bet has significantly optimised their online slots interface to cater to these exact expectations. The focus is on speed and a clean UX that mirrors the efficiency of a high-end trading platform.
When we talk about the evolution of Random Number Generators (RNG) versus algorithmic trading, the similarities are striking. Both rely on complex mathematics to ensure fairness and unpredictability. For those interested in the technical side of things, the Bally Bet slots portfolio serves as a bit of a benchmark for regulated, high-frequency digital entertainment. It shows how you can take a mathematically rigorous system and wrap it in a user-friendly package that feels modern rather than dated.
 UX Synergy: Re-engineering for the Web3 Generation
The "Web3 Generation" is a term that gets thrown around a lot, but what does it actually mean for UX design? Essentially, it refers to a cohort of users who grew up with the internet in their pockets. They are used to apps that are minimalist, fast, and highly personalised. They don't have the patience for clunky menus or slow loading times.
Established brands have had to go back to the drawing board to stay relevant. It’s not just about adding a fresh coat of paint; it’s about re-engineering the entire journey. Why does this matter? Because if a user has to click five times to find their favourite game, they’ll probably just go somewhere else. The goal is "frictionless" interaction. This means using predictive search, simplifying the "cashier" process, and ensuring that the mobile experience is just as robust as the desktop one.
I often find that the best designs are the ones you don't notice. When everything works perfectly, you're focused on the entertainment, not the tech. This synergy between fintech efficiency and gaming fun is what's defining the current era of the industry. It’s about creating a space where the user feels in control and the platform feels responsive.
 The Future of Hybrid Payments
Looking ahead, the next big frontier is the full integration of hybrid payments. We've already moved past the days when you had to type in your sixteen-digit card number every time you wanted to do something. The rise of digital wallets like Apple Pay, Google Pay, and PayPal has been a game-changer for the UK market.
But we're likely to go even further. We're starting to see the early stages of "open banking" being used to facilitate near-instant transfers. This is a huge win for the user because it eliminates the "pending" period that used to be so common. In the near future, we might see even more integration with digital assets, though that will depend heavily on how the UK regulatory framework evolves.
The goal for traditional ecosystems is to create a "closed-loop" payment system that is both incredibly secure and incredibly fast. If you can move your balance from your bank to your entertainment account and back again with a single thumbprint, that’s the gold standard of UX.
 Finding the Right Balance
As much as we talk about the tech and the economics, it's important to remember why we're here in the first place. Digital entertainment is supposed to be just that: entertainment. The reason we want better UX and faster payments isn't just for the sake of efficiency; it's to make the experience more enjoyable and less stressful.
The UK has some of the best protections in the world, and it's vital to use the tools available to keep things in check. Most platforms now have built-in features that let you set limits on your time and spending. It’s always a good idea to familiarise yourself with these settings before you start. Responsible play is the only way to ensure that the industry remains sustainable and fun for everyone involved. If you ever feel like you need more information on how to stay in control, sites like BeGambleAware are excellent resources.
 A Natural Evolution
We are living through a really interesting period where the lines between different digital sectors are blurring. The convergence of fintech and iGaming is a natural evolution driven by the demands of the modern consumer. We want the security of a bank, the speed of a trading app, and the entertainment value of a world-class gaming studio.
It's a tall order, but the industry is clearly rising to the challenge. By benchmarking against the best in fintech and listening to the needs of the Web3 generation, operators are creating a new kind of digital landscape. It’s one that’s faster, safer, and ultimately much more user-centric than anything we’ve seen before. Whether you're a tech enthusiast or just someone looking for a bit of fun on a Friday night, these changes are making the digital world a much more seamless place to navigate.

General Staff: Russia has lost 1,581,840 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
07:29:15 UTC
16:29:15 KST

Russia has lost 1,581,840 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Oct. 27.
The number includes 1,400 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report, Russia has also lost 12,448 tanks, 25,609 armored combat vehicles, 167,472 vehicles and fuel tanks, 51,653 artillery systems, 2,241 multiple-launch rocket systems, 1,727 air defense systems, 449 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 3,025 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy.
Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action.
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action.
The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

Russia struck Ukraine with ballistic missiles and 280 drones during the night of October 27. Two ballistic Iskander/S-400 missiles and 255 unmanned aerial vehicles were shot down or suppressed. UNN reports this, citing data from the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
What Russia attacked with and from where
According to the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, during the night of October 27 (starting at 18:00 on October 26), the enemy attacked with:
-  Iskander-M/S-400 ballistic missiles from Russia's Bryansk region; 
-  280 Shahed-type attack UAVs (69 of them jet-powered), Gerbera UAVs, and Parody-type decoy drones from the following directions: Orel, Millerovo, Kursk, Shatalovo, Primorsko-Akhtarsk — Russia; the temporarily occupied territory of Donetsk; and the temporarily occupied territory of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea — Hvardiiske. 
Where Russia struck
"The main direction of the strike was Kyiv," the statement said.
How the air defense forces performed
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare units and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of the Ukrainian Defense Forces.
According to preliminary data, as of 09:00, air defense forces had shot down/suppressed 257 enemy targets:
-  2 Iskander-M/S-400 ballistic missiles; 
-  255 enemy Shahed-type UAVs (56 of them jet-powered), Gerbera UAVs, and drones of other types; several attack UAVs are still in the air, and combat operations continue. 
Hits by the enemy's air-attack weapons were recorded at 25 locations, as well as the falling of downed targets (debris) at 16 locations.

07:25:54 UTC

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The KMT called on the government and anti-nuclear advocacy groups to nominate representatives for debates on a referendum proposing the abolition of Taiwan’s non-nuclear homeland policy.
The Central Election Commission announced in September that it would hold five debates on Nov. 12, 14, 16, 18 and 20, per SETN. The referendum asks voters whether they support adopting nuclear energy to strengthen the economy and abolishing the non-nuclear homeland policy, per Global Views Monthly.
Presidential Office spokesperson Karen Kuo (郭雅慧) said Friday that Taiwan had already achieved its non-nuclear homeland policy. KMT Culture and Communications Committee Chair Chen I-hsin (陳以信) urged President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) on Monday to nominate representatives to defend the policy or apologize for what Chen considers to be the wrong policy for Taiwan.
Pro-nuclear advocate Huang Shih-hsiu (黃士修) reiterated Chen’s call, stressing that the KMT had already submitted its debate representatives, per ETtoday. He noted that the Control Yuan had previously criticized the Cabinet for failing to nominate representatives to defend government policies during the 2018 local elections.
Huang also urged the National No-Nukes Action Platform to nominate representatives, adding that the advocacy group had previously announced Oct. 15 as the date it would release its list of debate representatives.
In addition to calling for the release of the representatives’ names, Huang addressed criticism of the referendum.
Former CEC Chair Chen In-chin (陳英鈐) questioned the proposal’s effectiveness, saying the referendum does not specify whether it seeks to reopen existing nuclear power plants or establish small modular reactors, per Liberty Times. He added that the referendum would have no bearing on the results of nuclear safety inspections.
National Chengchi University Associate Professor of law Lin Chia-ho (林佳和) argued that the referendum, which calls for the abolition of Article 23 of the Basic Environment Law, should have been handled by the legislature, per Environmental Information Center. He said the move would allow lawmakers to shirk their responsibilities.
In response to Chen, Huang said the proposal envisioned using nuclear power to support carbon capture, desalination, or hydrogen production when installing new conventional reactors or small modular reactors.
Responding to Lin, Huang stressed that the referendum concerned abolishing the policy rather than specific legal provisions. He accused former President Tsai Ing-wen’s (蔡英文) administration of ignoring the results of a 2018 pro-nuclear referendum to pursue its non-nuclear homeland policy.
The 2018 referendum sought to repeal the legal requirement that all nuclear reactors in Taiwan cease operations by 2025, per Taiwan FactCheck Center. Although the referendum led to the removal of the relevant provision, then-Premier Lai Ching-te (賴清德) stressed that the government’s policy remained unchanged.
Academia Sinica research fellow Su Yen-tu (蘇彥圖) explained that arguments presented during the preceding debates were intended to inform voters rather than determine the referendum’s legal effect. He noted that the referendum itself focused on abolishing the legal requirement for all reactors to cease operations before 2025.
Former Taipei Bar Association Chair Huang Hsu-tien (黃旭田) suggested that the government could continue pursuing denuclearization if it opposed the use of nuclear energy.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan will expand hospitals, improve medical workers' pay, and strengthen healthcare services under the government's Healthy Taiwan policy, President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) said Tuesday.
Speaking at a topping-out ceremony for a new emergency and critical care building at Taipei Hospital in New Taipei's Xinzhuang District, Lai said the project would improve care for local residents. He expressed hope that the building would open in 2028, CNA reported.
Lai said the government aims to increase average life expectancy by three years by 2032. It also wants to reduce the share of people's lives spent in poor health from 10% to 8%.
The president said Taiwanese are living longer, but the years spent in poor health have not declined. People spend about eight years of their lives with health problems or disabilities that may require medical care or daily assistance.
The government also aims to cut the age-standardized cancer mortality rate by one-third by 2030, Lai said. It has set a similar reduction target for the age-standardized mortality rate from chronic diseases, with prevention efforts focused on high blood pressure, high blood sugar, and high cholesterol, per CTEE.
Lai said achieving these goals would require more funding for hospital facilities, medical equipment, and healthcare services. He also called for higher pay and better working conditions for doctors, nurses, and other medical staff, measures outlined in the government's healthcare policy.
The government's Healthy Taiwan Cultivation Plan will invest NT$48.9 billion (US$1.5 billion) from 2025 to 2029. The program focuses on improving working conditions, training medical workers, introducing smart healthcare technology, and supporting sustainable medical services.
Lai also praised Taipei Hospital for its role during the COVID-19 pandemic, including its quarantine and screening work. He recalled approving the expansion project while serving as premier and thanked successive administrations for helping move it forward, per UDN.
The new building will have 16 floors above ground and four basement levels. The expansion was designed to increase hospital capacity and strengthen emergency and critical care services for residents of Xinzhuang and surrounding areas, per Economic Daily News.

King Charles heads to Caribbean as calls for slavery reparations grow
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:25:21 CET
16:25:21 KST

By Michael Holden
LONDON, Oct 27 (Reuters) - King Charles heads to the Caribbean this week on a tour which comes against the backdrop of increasingly vocal demands from the region that Britain pays reparations for its role in the slave trade.
Charles and his wife Queen Camilla will first visit the Bahamas and Guyana, before heading to Antigua and Barbuda for the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM), the biennial get-together of the international organisation which he heads. The tour runs from October 27 to November 4.
At a previous meeting in 2022 of the leaders of the Commonwealth — a group of 56 nations which were mainly former British colonies — Charles expressed deep personal sorrow over slavery, and the issue is certain to be prominent once again.
Last month, CARICOM, the Caribbean Community, a group of 23 member and associate member states which includes the Bahamas, Barbados and Jamaica, said it would push for reparations to be on the CHOGM agenda.
“The Caribbean has consistently asserted that reparations is fundamentally about justice,” CARICOM’s Secretary-General Carla Barnett said in a speech last month.
“It is about recognition, accountability and transformation, and about building a just and equitable future for the descendants of those who, as the chattel of colonial owners, endured untold suffering, loss of life and freedom.”
While Buckingham Palace has said the monarch would not shy away from Britain’s involvement in the transatlantic slave trade during his tour, he would not formally apologise for it as some have wanted, in keeping with British government policy which also excludes making any financial reparations.
“It is important to note here the work his majesty himself has done over many years both to acknowledge the wrongs of the past and to find creative ways to right inequalities that endure,” a palace spokesperson said.
Shirley Botchwey, the secretary-general of the Commonwealth, which encompasses some 2.7 billion people, said last week the time had come for discussions about reparations, be they financial or in some other form such as the return of artefacts.
As for an apology from the king, who remains the head of state of a number of Caribbean nations including both the Bahamas and Antigua and Barbuda, she told Sky News: “It wouldn’t hurt to have that.”
From the 15th to the 19th century, at least 12.5 million Africans were abducted and sold into slavery by European merchants, with Britain responsible for transporting an estimated 3.2 million people, making it the second most active European nation after Portugal.
(Reporting by Michael Holden; Editing by Xevi Fontdegloria)

Good morning. It’s Tuesday, and this is what’s on today’s docket: Election fever spreads to Israel, Zelenskyy bemoans a lack of American Patriot missiles, and the European continent is only getting hotter, according to the EU climate chief. I’m Angela Skujins. Let’s dive in.
All eyes on Jerusalem: Roughly seven million eligible Israeli voters will head to polling stations today to cast their ballot in the country’s first legislative election since the 7 October attacks in 2023. Incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of the right-wing Likud party has dominated Israeli politics for the last two decades, and another victory would confirm unshakable confidence from his constituents, particularly after three years of war.
A defeat, however, could spell trouble. Netanyahu's main political rivals are led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, whose two sons were killed in combat. “What he is offering is an eternal war,” Eisenkot, the Yashar party leader, said in a radio interview. Although the pair share some policy positions — they both reject a two-state solution and favour a hard-line approach with Iran — Eisenkot is campaigning on a simple premise: he is not Netanyahu.
Yossi Mekelberg, senior consulting fellow with the Middle East and North Africa Programme at Chatham House, just said on Europe Today that a new government led by the opposition would bring about meaningful change. This would be manifested hopefully through a state commission into the 7 October attacks. “The more the (current) government rejects the idea, the more people are suspicious that they have something to hide,” he said. Watch.
Brussels watches: It remains to be seen whether the election will change how the EU engages with Israel. The capitals maintain an EU-Israel Association Agreement, which entered into force in 2000, that, among other measures, establishes a free trade area for industrial goods, agricultural trade preferences, and a framework for political, economic, and cultural cooperation.
According to Amnesty International, however, the EU and all its member states are under a “clear obligation” to prevent trade and investments that assist in the maintenance of Israel’s unlawful occupation of Palestinian territories, as set out in the International Court of Justice’s advisory opinion of July 2024.
Despite the agreement remaining in force, the EU executive has also tried — and failed — to ban trade with illegal Israeli settlements. Meanwhile, relations between the EU’s top diplomat Kaja Kallas and her Israeli counterpart Gideon Sa’ar remain fractious at best.
Hope is in the air: Diplomats wanted to remain tight-lipped when speaking to me about the election occurring just over 3,000 kilometres away, and what it means for relations between European capitals and Israel. However, one EU insider said there was “some hope” to find common ground with the new administration, whomever that may be.
Have I read that right? US President Donald Trump’s top officials allegedly want former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán to be considered as the United Nations’ new secretary-general.
According to a Wall Street Journal report, Washington kingmakers have allegedly tapped the former prime minister for the top job, but nothing is certain yet. As my colleagues Sandor Zsiros and Ferenc Horvath report, the proposal could be a joint US-China-Russia bid, but securing the position is not as easy as it seems.
At least one UN member state has voiced its opposition, too. “I am certain that Viktor Orbán, as UN Secretary-General, would put to good use the masterful veto and blackmail skills he has developed over years of derailing major EU decisions,” Ukrainian Minister for Foreign Affairs Andrii Sybiha opined.
Speaking of Ukraine: Defence ministers from Europe’s biggest military powers — France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the United Kingdom — met in Paris Monday for a meeting centred on support for Ukraine and the spiralling war in Iran.
The strongest commentary to come out from the gathering was NATO Deputy Secretary General Radmila Shekerinska, who stated that the ministers agreed “all allies” must “dig deep and do more — especially with air and missile defence” for Ukraine.
“We need to do it now, because every night the pressure from Russia is felt in almost every Ukrainian city,” she said.
Time goes by: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated on Monday he has waited “nearly a month” for US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth to approve Patriot missiles, among other weapons, to counter Russia’s advances. “Conversations with other countries are also ongoing,” he said.
Over four and a half years into the full-scale invasion, Moscow has shown no signs of abating its relentless aggression. This is abundantly clear with non-stop aerial attacks battering Kyiv and other civilian areas, with the country lacking appropriate air defences to air attacks, such as deadly jet-powered drones.
Efforts by the EU’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas to convince countries to pledge interceptor missiles to help defend against Ukraine have also failed.
Shifting tides: Complicating the matter on the ground is US President Donald Trump’s shifting alliances, manifesting recently through a controversial diesel deal catching Zelenskyy and European allies off guard. Sudden restrictions to Starlink technology, owned by Trump ally Elon Musk, also demonstrates fraying support from Washington.
Should we be surprised? Retired US Army Lieutenant General Ben Hodges recently told Euronews that Trump would always support Russia and that “he was never going to support Ukraine.”
How can Europe step in? Officials in Brussels are examining possible solutions for a widening funding gap of roughly €70 billion for 2027 to continue supporting the ally to the east.
Commission news: The European Commission will unveil new climate rules on Tuesday requiring EU governments to clarify who is responsible for protecting citizens from climate disasters, Climate Action Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra told Euronews.
In an interview with EU news editor Maria Tadeo, Hoekstra warned that the world is heading towards a temporary or potentially prolonged overshoot of the Paris Agreement’s 1.5°C warming limit, making it essential for governments to prepare for more extreme heat and climate disasters, even if efforts to cut emissions succeed.
“It is up to member states to decide where they want to put that responsibility. But what we do make mandatory is that they do have to appoint and articulate where the responsibility is going to lie,” Hoekstra said. Marta Pacheco has more on that important story.
One more thing: The EU executive will also propose new rules today beefing up the bloc’s border security. As part of the pitch, Frontex will be allowed to transfer migrants between third countries, expanding its operations beyond Europe and facilitating deportations from return hubs. Read more of that must-read reporting by Vincenzo Genovese.
Ukraine’s €70 billion shortfall could make or break the next EU budget
The fight over the European Union's next seven-year budget has taken a new twist, one that could very well make it or break it. In an explosive mix, the fraught negotiations have overlapped with the effort to fill Ukraine's €70 billion shortfall for 2027.
The vast scale of the deficit prompted a change of agenda in next month's special summit, which was originally planned to focus exclusively on the draft budget. The meeting has now been expanded to last two days, 26 and 27 November, to allow time for the discussion on Ukraine. New proposals on both fronts are expected.
Technically, the two issues remain separate. But politically, diplomats and officials say, they are becoming rapidly intertwined. Both are about money and both come with a pressing deadline before the French elections in April.
“We need a structural solution for financing Ukraine. We can’t keep scrambling at the end of every year under pressure,” an official said. “It’s good that these discussions are coming together in November.”

Toward the end of his speech, Bennett thanked campaign staff, activists and volunteers. "In all my years in politics, I have never seen anything like this. You worked day and night, with creativity, determination and an enormous love for this people," he said.
"There has never been a campaign like this in the history of the State of Israel," he added, concluding with a call to action: "And now, let's get to work. We have a country to fix! Am Yisrael Chai!"
Bennett arrived at party headquarters alongside Lapid, the No. 2 candidate on his list, who had declared minutes after the exit polls were published: "Don't let anyone confuse you. Netanyahu's bloc has suffered a crushing defeat. This is a complete collapse, and the public has told them to go home."
Bennett and Lapid, who both served as prime minister during the previous change government, joined forces in April with the establishment of the Beyachad party. Until then, Lapid had headed Yesh Atid, the party he founded in 2013.
Bennett returned to politics after taking a break following the end of his tenure as prime minister and amid widespread criticism from the right over his alliance with parties from the opposing political bloc, particularly Mansour Abbas' Ra'am party.
The first political partnership between Bennett and Lapid came after the 2013 election, when they formed what became known as the "brothers' alliance" within Netanyahu's government, in which both served.
When Beyachad was established six months ago, Bennett appeared to be Netanyahu's main challenger for the premiership. But following the formation of Eisenkot's party, Beyachad slipped to become the third-largest party in the polls. Over the past month, however, the polling trend had begun to shift.

Harry Kane is first Bundesliga player since Matthias Sammer to win Ballon d'Or
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
07:24:50 UTC
16:24:50 KST

The Bayern Munich striker's award ends a decades-long wait for a Bundesliga player or Englishman to receive the prestigious trophy.
Just ten kilometres from Brisbane Road, where he scored his first professional goal in England’s third tier, Harry Kane collected the biggest individual prize in men’s football on Monday night at the star-studded London Palladium Theatre.
The Bayern Munich striker becomes the first England player to win the Ballon d’Or since 2001, and English fans were quick to celebrate. Kane could hardly believe it himself.
“Not many people would have thought that, and maybe even I wouldn’t have thought that I could get this far,” he told streaming service DAZN.
He added that he was never the sort of player expected to become a superstar.
Seventy-three goals in 65 matches for Bayern and the England national team was, in the view of the journalists' jury, unsurpassed last season: not by Kylian Mbappé, Lionel Messi, Lamine Yamal or Rodri.
Kane's award also ended a long barren spell for the Bundesliga. The last time a player active in Germany was honoured with the Ballon d'Or was in 1996, when Matthias Sammer won it. For Bayern, Kane is the first recipient since Karl-Heinz Rummenigge, who took the prize in 1981.
Bayern president Herbert Hainer called it a proud day for the club. “Harry Kane can do everything, and he scores goals, goals, goals,” he said, adding that Kane now stands alongside Franz Beckenbauer, Gerd Müller and Rummenigge.
The atmosphere turned emotional when Kane thanked his family. He addressed his words to his in-laws, his parents, his brother Charlie and his wife Katie, who was sitting in the hall.
He also thought of his children at home and sent them a loving greeting.
He also thanked the people who have supported him in recent years. They include Bayern coach Vincent Kompany, who could not travel after collapsing on Friday, and Thomas Tuchel, his former Bayern coach and now England manager.
Tuchel said he ran out of superlatives for Kane’s performances long ago, but was delighted to see the football world recognise them officially.
**"**I ran out of superlatives to describe your performances a long time ago, but I am very happy to see that you have now also been officially recognised by the football world," said German coach Thomas Tuchel.
Even Prince Harry sent his congratulations. "What a fantastic achievement and so richly deserved. A brilliant captain, a remarkable player and someone who has given football fans around the world so many unforgettable moments."
Alexia Putellas Wins Third Ballon d’Or
Meanwhile, in the women's category, Alexia Putellas won the Ballon d'Or féminin. The Spaniard prevailed in the vote for women's footballer of the year ahead of compatriot Clàudia Pina and England's Alessia Russo.
The 32-year-old Barcelona midfielder previously won in 2021 and 2022. She then suffered an ACL injury, and Bonmatí rose to stardom in her absence. Bonmatí completed her hat-trick of wins in 2025 but was left off this year’s shortlist after breaking her leg in December.
The women’s Ballon d’Or only dates back to 2018, when Ada Hegerberg became its first winner. Putellas used her moment to encourage young players to play with “love and passion".
Putellas joined Barcelona in 2012 and described her time at the Catalan club as “something special".
“I’m really grateful for having 14 seasons as a player (at Barcelona),” she said. “What I experienced last year was like a perfect story.”

Indonesia sends oxygen bus to aid residents choking on forest fire haze
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:24:47 CET
16:24:47 KST

By Arief Rahman Septian Prathama
PALANGKA RAYA, Indonesia, Oct 27 (Reuters) - A bus fitted out with oxygen tanks is providing a sanctuary in a city on Indonesia’s Borneo island where people are choking from forest-fire-induced haze and the blazes show no sign of letting up.
Indonesia regularly battles seasonal forest fires, predominantly on Sumatra and Borneo islands, but this year the infernos are the most intense in more than a decade. An intense El Niño weather phenomenon has driven up temperatures, leaving the country’s vast forests and peatlands more vulnerable to fires that have turned skies orange across Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore.
As respiratory illnesses increased in the Central Kalimantan city of Palangka Raya, the local government provided an ‘oxygen bus’ replete with oxygen tanks and medical professionals who offer residents a chance to be hooked up to a small oxygen tube around their nose for 5 to 10 minutes at a time.
“The service is intended to help people access oxygen, particularly those experiencing respiratory problems or who need oxygen support amid unhealthy air quality conditions,” the Central Kalimantan provincial health department said on Instagram this week.
Indonesia’s air pollution index has shown some areas of Borneo and Sumatra registering pollution levels of over 1,000, with readings of 300 or more already categorised as hazardous.
Respiratory illnesses linked to the fires have risen, with about 350,000 cases from August to October 25, the health ministry said. Central Kalimantan reported about 31,000 cases as of October 25.
“This is a disaster from nature and there is not much we can do,” Oktawina, 44, who like many Indonesians goes by one name, said with an oxygen tube hooked to her nose.
Medical staff on the white-and-blue bus recorded patients’ details and administered oxygen to residents reporting breathing difficulties. One of them, Yuda, said most residents who came to the bus coughing or had trouble breathing.
Purnasari, 31, another patient on the bus, said: “If I’ve been out of the house lately I feel tightness and coughing … because this morning the thick yellowish smoke so my breathing feels tight.”
Hundreds of students protested at the office of the provincial governor last week demanding a greater response to the fires, local news website Kompas reported.
(Writing by Stanley Widianto; editing by Lincoln Feast.)

No pressure from US to cut Russian oil imports, Indian oil minister says
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:24:33 CET
16:24:33 KST

By Nidhi Verma
GOA, India, Oct 27 (Reuters) - India has faced no pressure from the US to reduce its Russian crude imports, oil minister Hardeep Singh Puri said on Tuesday at an industry event.
“I never felt anything,” Puri said when asked if there has been pressure to cut Russian oil imports.
Puri said Middle East oil supplies have been rising as the region is able to ship out more cargoes.
He said India was getting 0.2% of its oil imports from Russia before the Ukraine war, while imports have surged since the war started due to discounts on Russian oil.
India’s imports of Middle Eastern crude oil surged in September, returning to pre-war levels, while its refiners cut back purchases of Russian oil amid stiff competition from China, ship-tracking data showed.
The minister said that the purchase of Russian oil is linked to discounts and pricing when compared with other grades. Russian oil imports have been reduced as the refiners are buying more Gulf oil sold at a discount, he added.
“Whatever people say or do, ultimately it is anchored in their self-interest,” he said.
The minister also said India is expanding its refining capacity to help meet local demand and export commitments.
(Reporting by Nidhi Verma; Editing by Thomas Derpinghaus)

MTR Corp reveals linked faults behind 2 disruptions at Lam Tin station in 15 hours
Hong Kong rail operator says failed insulation sparked a fire, leading to a cable overload that disrupted services again
Two service disruptions at Lam Tin station within 15 hours earlier this month were linked, with a failed rubber insulating component causing an overloaded cable connection, the MTR Corporation has said.
In a paper submitted to the Legislative Council’s transport panel on Tuesday, the rail operator said its preliminary investigation found that the component’s failure caused a short circuit and fire in the first incident. This in turn led to an overloaded cable connection, which overheated and caused the second disruption.
The MTR Corp also pledged to offer a special day of fare concessions once accumulated penalties for service disruptions reached HK$25 million (US$3.2 million).

India news: Arunachal sees more violence as anti-dam protests spread

India's east coast braces as cyclone 'Arnab' approaches
The Indian coastal states of Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, took a number of steps including shutting schools, issuing helpline numbers and moving vulnerable people to safety as the severe cyclonic storm "Arnab" approaches.
The Indian Meteorological Department (IMD) on Tuesday forecast isolated by "extremely heavy rainfall" over coastal Andhra Pradesh and Odisha for Tuesday and Wednesday, adding that nearby Chhattisgarh would experience similar conditions on Wednesday.
Much of the rest of India, including Delhi, will also see moderate weather impacts of winds and rainfall due to the cyclone, the press statement said.
Other eastern states including West Bengal and Jharkhand will also see heavy rainfall over the next three days, it added.
The cyclone which formed over the Bay of Bengal on Monday morning is expected to make landfall in Andhra Pradesh on Wednesday.
Odisha shut schools and banned fishing and is preparing to evacuate nearly 50,000 people to safer places to prepare for the storm, local media reported.
Andhra Pradesh also implemented similar measures to ensure "zero loss of life and minimal damage to infrastructure."
Train services were also impacted with India's South Coast Railway suspending 53 train services over October 27 and 28 due to the storm.
India's biggest air carriers IndiGo and Air India said flights to and from Andhra Pradesh's capital city of Vishakhapatnam would be impacted on October 27 due to weather conditions brought by the storm.
They advised travelers to check their flight status and book book alternate flights in cases of cancellations.
Election body defends SIR roll-out in top court ahead of hearing
The Election Commission of India (ECI) on Monday defended its decision to carry out the "Special Intensive Revision (SIR)" of electoral rolls, saying the exercise was undertaken legally and approved unanimously, the Press Trust of India news agency reported.
The defense was made in a counter affidavit filed in the Supreme Court of India ahead of today's hearing on petitions against poll-body chief Gyanesh Kumar.
In September, The Indian Express newspaper published a major investigative report citing irregularities in the voter revision exercise while alleging an internal rift.
The report said Chief Election Commissioner Kumar reportedly made unilateral decisions without informing the other two election commissioners as required under law.
The report led to nationwide protests led by student unions and India's Cockroach movement who argue that Kumar took biased decisions to the benefit of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government, eroding the people's vote in the world's largest democracy.
The protests were met with a massive police response and detentions.
India's opposition parties are also conducting a unified campaign against Kumar and Modi, calling for the former's removal from power and a rollback of voter names deleted under SIR.
India's largest opposition party Indian National Congress (INC), along with its regional allies, is planning a 'Save the Vote' march in Delhi in November. It has called for Indian masses including students, workers and farmers to join in.
Arunachal calls in police reinforcements amid protests
Authorities in Arunachal Pradesh called in reinforcements to the town of Pasighat in anticipation of more protests over a hydroelectric dam.
News outlet NDTV reported that the state police called in dozens of Rapid Action Forces (RAF), a special federal police unit.
More companies of Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) were rushed in from Assam to the Siang Valley Region, the report said, adding that a total of About 34 companies of Central Armed Police Force (CAPF) was deployed in the region.
Regional newspaper Arunachal Times reported that about 30 companies of CAPF, alongside state and paramilitary forces were in the region to manage the tense protests.
The force reallocation comes days after protests against Siang Upper Multipurpose Project (SUMP) turned violent in Pasighat on October 23. Mobs reportedly vandalized lawmakers' houses and set local offices on fire.
Anti-dam protests spread in Arunachal Pradesh
Violent protests broke out against a proposed hydroelectric project in Arunachal Pradesh on Monday in Daporijo town.
Normal life in Daporijo was interrupted as student organizations implemented a 12-hour general strike over the 1,605-megawatt Upper Subansiri hydroelectric plant, also known as the Menga Dam project.
The protesters are demanding authorities permanently withdraw the power project.
Anti-damn protests have been building up in the northeastern mountain state, with locals fearing mass displacement, loss of ancestral land, ecological losses and seismic risks.
News outlets reported that tensions escalated during the strike leading to fresh violence. At least one police vehicle was damaged and a police constable injured, the Arunachal Times reported. The report said that supporters of the strike also allegedly vandalized an office rented by India's flagship hydroelectric power generation company, setting office equipment on fire.
The Times of India also reported that local police conducted a flag march and appealed for peace.
In the village of Taliha, residents voice strong opposition to the Menga Damn project and the related land assessment exercise in motion. Protesters blocked a bridge to restrict movement, Arunachal Times reported, adding that their demonstrations were largely peaceful.
Not the only controversial dam
Protests and related violence shook Pasighat on October 23 after police fired tear gas at youths protesting the proposed 11,000-megawatt Siang Upper Multipurpose Project (SUMP). That's a different, larger but an equally as controversial project as the Menga Dam.
Protesters had allegedly set fire to buildings and vehicles then as well, prompting police forces to arrest dozens of demonstrators.

Lithuania’s Foreign Ministry said Tuesday that two Lithuanian women that were declared missing last week have been detained in Iran and that efforts are underway to provide them with consular assistance.
“The Ministry of Foreign Affairs received official information from Iran on October 26 regarding the detention of Lithuanian citizens,” the ministry said in a comment to BNS.
The ministry said it could not provide details about the circumstances of the detentions but was seeking to “make arrangements to provide the detained individuals with the necessary consular assistance”.
It reiterated its recommendation that Lithuanian citizens avoid traveling to Iran and urged those currently in the country to leave immediately.

The women had travelled abroad for tourism.
Negotiations underway
Lithuania is making diplomatic efforts to secure the return of the two citizens detained in Iran, Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius said Tuesday.
“Active diplomatic work is currently under way to clarify the situation and secure the release of our citizens,” he told reporters in Vilnius.
Sinkevičius said he had more information about the grounds for the women’s detention but declined to comment further, saying this could undermine negotiations for their release. He said officials were in contact with the women’s relatives and were using diplomatic channels to bring them back to Lithuania as soon as possible.

INTERVIEW – Israel faces 4 scenarios for formation of next government after polls
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
07:20:13 UTC
16:20:13 KST

- Scenarios include regular coalition, minority government, national unity government or new elections
Israel could face four possible scenarios for forming its next government if neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nor opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot secures enough support to build a governing coalition after Tuesday’s general elections, an expert on Israeli politics said.
Opinion polls indicate that neither Netanyahu, leader of the Likud party, nor Eisenkot, leader of Yashar party, is expected to reach the 61-seat threshold required to form a government with their respective blocs.
Israel is treated as a single electoral district, with voters electing members of the 120-seat Knesset by voting for party lists.
The prime minister is not directly elected but must be a member of parliament capable of securing the confidence of at least 61 lawmakers.
Since no single Israeli party typically wins a parliamentary majority, governments are generally formed through coalitions of parties with broadly compatible political positions.
Speaking to Anadolu, Wadie Abu Nassar outlined four possible scenarios following the elections.
“The first scenario is that Netanyahu or Eisenkot manages to form a regular government through a coalition with parties that win seats in the polls,” Abu Nassar said.
He described that scenario as “difficult” in light of polls showing neither Netanyahu’s bloc nor the opposition camp reaching 61 seats.
“Still, this scenario cannot be completely ruled out, particularly amid reports that Eisenkot is trying to win over lawmakers from the Haredi parties to support a government he would form,” he added.
 
Minority government
“The second scenario would involve Eisenkot forming a minority government that relies on Arab votes in the Knesset without those parties joining the government,” Abu Nassar said.
Arab parties in Israel have said they could provide Eisenkot with a parliamentary “safety net” in exchange for guarantees for Arab citizens, aimed at preventing the current government — which includes far-right ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich — from remaining in office as a caretaker administration.
The Joint List, an alliance of three Arab parties led by Yousef Jabareen, and the United Arab List, headed by Mansour Abbas, have expressed willingness to support an Eisenkot-led government from outside the coalition.
In return, they have sought measures including halting home demolitions, combating crime in Arab communities and opening a political horizon with Palestinians.
Eisenkot has not taken a definitive position on the proposal, though he has previously ruled out including Arab parties in a coalition he seeks to form.
Polls suggest that 13 electoral lists could enter the Knesset, including two representing Arab citizens, who make up around 20% of Israel’s population of more than 10 million.
The Arab parties are projected to win a combined 14 to 15 seats, according to opinion polls.
 
National unity government
Abu Nassar said the third scenario would be the formation of a national unity government bringing together Netanyahu, Eisenkot and other Israeli parties.
“There are discussions in Israeli circles that if the elections reach a deadlock, meaning neither bloc obtains the required majority to form a government, a national unity government could be formed,” he said.
He said Israeli President Isaac Herzog has been pushing such an option to avoid another election, while reports indicate that figures close to US President Donald Trump also favor the scenario.
“Under such an arrangement, the government would include Likud under Netanyahu and Yashar under Eisenkot, along with other parties, while excluding Ben-Gvir’s far-right Jewish Power party and Smotrich’s far-right Religious Zionism party,” Abu Nassar said.
The main obstacle, he added, is that opposition parties reject joining a government with Netanyahu or one led by him, even though he appears open to a unity government in which he and Eisenkot would rotate as prime minister, provided Netanyahu serves first.
“Opposition parties do not necessarily reject joining Likud in a unity government but object to Netanyahu personally,” Abu Nassar said.
“Some Israeli circles have raised the possibility of Herzog granting Netanyahu a pardon in corruption cases against him in return for his withdrawal from political life,” he added.
Netanyahu has said that he would not leave politics even if he loses the elections.
Netanyahu faces charges of bribery, fraud and breach of trust in three separate corruption cases, known as Cases 1000, 2000 and 4000.
Separately, the International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for Netanyahu on Nov. 21, 2024, accusing him of war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza, where more than 74,000 people have been killed in a brutal offensive since October 2023.
Ben-Gvir has also claimed that Netanyahu has avoided appearing in photographs with him because he is seeking a possible unity government with Eisenkot.
 
New elections
The fourth scenario would see neither Netanyahu nor the opposition succeeding in forming a government, leaving the current Cabinet in place as a caretaker government until another election is held several months later.
“In the fourth scenario, elections would be repeated after several months, and until then the current government would remain as a caretaker government until a new one is formed,” Abu Nassar said.
“This is the scenario Netanyahu would prefer and work toward if he fails to form a government,” he added.
Under Israeli law, Knesset elections are normally held every four years.
The elections are widely seen as crucial for the political future of Netanyahu, 76, who is standing trial on corruption charges, including bribery, fraud and breach of trust, which could result in imprisonment if convicted.
Netanyahu has also been wanted by the International Criminal Court since 2024 over war crimes and crimes against humanity committed against Palestinians during Israel’s genocidal war on the Gaza Strip, where more than 74,000 people have been killed since October 2023.

The Joint List, an alliance of three Arab parties led by Yousef Jabareen, and the United Arab List, headed by Mansour Abbas, have expressed willingness to support an Eisenkot-led government from outside the coalition.
Their demands include halting home demolitions, combating crime in Arab communities and opening a political horizon with the Palestinians.
Eisenkot has not taken a definitive position on the proposal, although he has previously ruled out including Arab parties in a coalition he seeks to form.
Polls suggest that 13 party lists could enter the Knesset, including two representing Arab citizens, who account for about 20% of Israel’s population of more than 10 million.
Opinion polls project that the Arab parties could win a combined 14 to 15 seats.
The third scenario would involve a national unity government bringing together Netanyahu, Eisenkot and other parties, Abu Nassar said.
“There are discussions in Israeli circles that if the elections reach a deadlock, meaning neither bloc obtains the required majority to form a government, a national unity government could be formed,” he said.
Abu Nassar said Israeli President Isaac Herzog has been pushing for such an arrangement to avoid another election. Reports also indicate that figures close to U.S. President Donald Trump favor the option.
Under the proposed arrangement, Likud and Yashar would join other parties in a government led by Netanyahu and Eisenkot, while Ben-Gvir’s Jewish Power party and Smotrich’s Religious Zionism party would be excluded, Abu Nassar said.
The main obstacle is opposition parties’ refusal to join a government with Netanyahu or one led by him, Abu Nassar said. Netanyahu, however, appears open to a unity government in which he and Eisenkot would rotate as prime minister, provided Netanyahu serves first.
“Opposition parties do not necessarily reject joining Likud in a unity government but object to Netanyahu personally,” Abu Nassar said.
Some Israeli political circles have raised the possibility of Herzog granting Netanyahu a pardon in his corruption cases in exchange for his withdrawal from political life, Abu Nassar added.
Netanyahu has said he would not leave politics even if he loses the election.
He faces charges of bribery, fraud and breach of trust in three separate cases, known as Cases 1000, 2000 and 4000. He denies wrongdoing.
Separately, the International Criminal Court (ICC) issued an arrest warrant for Netanyahu on Nov. 21, 2024, over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.
More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed by Israel’s genocidal military offensive in Gaza since October 2023, according to figures cited in the original report.
Ben-Gvir has also claimed that Netanyahu has avoided appearing in photographs with him because he is pursuing a possible unity government with Eisenkot.
The fourth scenario would involve neither Netanyahu nor the opposition succeeding in forming a government, leaving the current Cabinet in place as a caretaker administration until another election could be held several months later.
“In the fourth scenario, elections would be repeated after several months, and until then the current government would remain as a caretaker government until a new one is formed,” Abu Nassar said.
“This is the scenario Netanyahu would prefer and work toward if he fails to form a government,” he added.
Under Israeli law, Knesset elections are normally held every four years, although an election can be called earlier if the political system fails to produce a functioning government or other legal conditions for an early vote are met.
The election is widely seen as crucial to Netanyahu’s political future. The 76-year-old prime minister is standing trial in Iarael on charges including bribery, fraud and breach of trust. A conviction could result in imprisonment.
Netanyahu is also subject to an ICC arrest warrant issued in 2024 over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza during Israel’s genocidal military campaign since October 2023.

UN recognized Russia’s attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure as war crimes and crimes against humanity

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:19:32 EET
16:19:32 KST

UN recognized Russia’s attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure as war crimes and crimes against humanity
Kyiv • UNN
The UN Commission reported Russia’s war crimes against civilian objects and crimes against humanity. It also addressed human trafficking.
The Russian authorities committed war crimes by deliberately directing attacks against civilian objects, as well as crimes against humanity in the form of other inhumane acts by carrying out attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, and also engaged in human trafficking to recruit foreign nationals into their armed forces for subsequent participation in hostilities in Ukraine, the UN Commission of Inquiry stated. This is stated in a UN statement, reports UNN.
The Russian authorities committed war crimes by deliberately directing attacks against civilian objects, as well as crimes against humanity in the form of other inhumane acts by carrying out continuous attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure
The Commission reportedly "also concluded that the Russian authorities recruited into their armed forces men who had become victims of human trafficking in various countries, in violation of international human rights law".
The Commission investigated the impact of the large-scale attacks by the Russian armed forces on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure on the civilian population, including during the difficult winter period of 2025–2026, as well as the cumulative consequences of these attacks since autumn 2022. Over the years, it notes, systematic waves of attacks, during which hundreds of drones and missiles were used simultaneously, became increasingly frequent and intense and covered an ever-wider area, causing significant damage to Ukraine’s energy sector.
According to the Commission’s assessment, "the Russian commanders who ordered the attacks were aware that the heating facilities they selected as targets in large population centers were vital to the civilian population, especially in winter. The Russian authorities officially stated their intention to continue the attacks and referred to plans to carry them out. The Commission concluded that the Russian authorities committed war crimes by deliberately directing attacks against civilian objects".
"The evidence collected indicates that the attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure were carried out deliberately, in accordance with a state policy aimed at depriving the civilian population of electricity and other essential services dependent on energy supplies and causing them suffering. The Commission concluded that the Russian authorities committed crimes against humanity in the form of other inhumane acts," the statement said.
The Commission relied on testimony from 255 people who endured the winter under the conditions described above in the Dnipropetrovsk, Kyiv, Kharkiv, Kherson, Mykolaiv, Odesa, Poltava, Zaporizhzhia and Zhytomyr regions, as well as on information provided by Ukrainian authorities, doctors and non-governmental organizations.
