Europe must prepare for a 3°C warmer world, EU climate chief warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:30:44 UTC
15:30:44 KST

As Brussels warns that Europe must prepare for increasingly extreme weather, new EU rules will require governments to clarify who is responsible for climate preparedness – but no new funding is being offered to help households adapt.
The European Commission will unveil new climate rules on Tuesday requiring EU governments to clarify who is responsible for protecting citizens from climate disasters, Climate Action Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra told Euronews.
The move comes as Brussels warns that Europe must prepare for increasingly extreme weather, including scenarios involving 3°C of global warming by 2100.
Hoekstra warned that the world is heading towards a temporary or potentially prolonged overshoot of the Paris Agreement’s 1.5°C warming limit, making it essential for governments to prepare for more extreme heat and climate disasters, even if efforts to cut emissions succeed.
“It is up to member states to decide where they want to put that responsibility. But what we do make mandatory is that they do have to appoint and articulate where the responsibility is going to lie,” Hoekstra said.
While the EU continues to pursue emissions reductions, the costs of adapting to a hotter world are becoming harder to ignore, from rebuilding after wildfires and floods to protecting homes, roads and public infrastructure.
The Dutch Commissioner estimated the economic damage from this summer's extreme weather at more than €100 billion.
Asked what a 3°C rise above pre-industrial temperatures could mean for Europeans, Hoekstra pointed to heat plans for cities and the need to prepare infrastructure for a hotter future, rather than relying on historical weather patterns.
The reference trajectory is based on scientific research, including work by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change and advanced European climate modeling, he said.
The Commission's projections envisage 2°C of global warming by 2050 and 3°C by 2100 for Europe, reflecting Brussels' assessment that Europe is warming roughly twice as fast as the global average.
The trajectory is intended to be translated into national and local risk assessments, taking account of the uneven distribution of climate impacts.
“Even if we get all of this right, we have no way to avoid more summers than the one we saw last year,” the Commissioner said, arguing that readiness, resilience and preparedness must become the priority alongside emissions cuts.
The proposed legislation would require EU countries to specify whether national, regional or local authorities are responsible for preparing for climate disasters.
Governments would retain flexibility over how they allocate responsibilities, but would have to specify who is accountable — an attempt to prevent political disputes over who failed to prepare when floods or wildfires destroy homes.
The Commission also wants climate scenarios to be considered when planning new roads, bridges and neighbourhoods, recognising that infrastructure designed for past weather conditions may no longer be fit for purpose.
"We want to introduce a culture of preparedness and resilience by design, rather than dealing with the damages in the aftermath, which is often very ad hoc and doesn't always build back better," a senior Commission official said on Monday on condition of anonymity.
No new money
However, the question of how to pay for climate adaptation remains unresolved.
No new financial commitment to household support is expected from the Commission's climate resilience strategy, despite concerns that ordinary citizens may struggle to afford the investments needed to adapt.
Hoekstra pointed to the Commission's proposal to devote 35% of the EU budget to climate and nature.
But the strategy's effectiveness will depend partly on the outcome of ongoing negotiations over the EU's next multiannual budget, with climate spending competing against priorities such as defence, security, competitiveness and agricultural support.
The Commission is also counting on the recently announced €30 billion from the European Investment Bank for climate adaptation through 2030.
Nonetheless, the lack of new funding is a potential weakness in the Commission's ambition.
The Commissioner argued that preventive investment is economically worth it but did not announce a new household support scheme or explain how the EU would ensure that lower-income households could afford necessary improvements.
In an attempt to fill the bloc's climate protection gap, Brussels wants to work with the insurance sector, as Commissioner Hoekstra pointed out that many areas in Europe are underinsured against climate disasters.
According to the senior Commission official, only around 25% of assets exposed to climate impacts are insured, leaving governments and property owners vulnerable to substantial losses.
“The fact that so many areas are underinsured” is one of the issues the Commission will examine, Hoekstra said.
The strategy could therefore expose another fault line between Brussels' climate ambitions and the cost-of-living pressures facing European voters.

RAMSA Unveils Plans for New Welcome Hall at Chicago’s Griffin Museum of Science and Industry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:30:00 UTC
15:30:00 KST

RAMSA (Robert A.M. Stern Architects) has unveiled the design for a new Welcome Hall at the Kenneth C. Griffin Museum of Science and Industry (Griffin MSI) in Chicago, Illinois. The project involves reopening the building's historic North Portico as a year-round entrance and introducing a new glazed volume connecting the portico to the museum's exhibition spaces. The proposal is part of a master plan completed by RAMSA in 2024 that examines the use of the museum's existing exhibition and public areas.
The museum's current entrance route passes through largely subterranean spaces and requires visitors to navigate more than 100 stairs and two elevators to reach the exhibition areas. According to the project team, this journey takes approximately 18 to 25 minutes. The proposed entrance is expected to reduce the arrival time to four to seven minutes by establishing a direct route at ground level, without stairs or elevators along the main path.
The design takes as its starting point the building's original role as the Palace of Fine Arts during the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition. At the time, the North Portico functioned as an entrance in direct relation to the surrounding landscape and public spaces. The new Welcome Hall is positioned as an extension of the North Lawn and remains below the historic plinth across much of its length. Its curved form and glazed walls are intended to maintain views toward the existing portico and its Ionic columns. The proposal also includes Science Gardens, accessible lawns, restrooms, and other amenities that will be available without museum admission. These facilities will provide public access to parts of the museum grounds independently of its exhibition spaces.
Related Article
Google Unveils New Renderings of Chicago's Thompson Center Redesign, Marking Its Escape From Demolition
The design limits physical alterations to the historic façade, which is constructed of limestone and granite. The North Portico intervention is one of two entrance projects planned for the museum. The historic South Portico is scheduled to reopen as an additional accessible entrance in winter 2027, providing access to the ground level of the central pavilion. The design introduces a glazed curtain wall at the existing staircase while retaining the relationship between the historic cheek walls and façade columns. As with the northern entrance, removed stone elements will be preserved for potential future restoration.
The South Portico project also includes a redesigned South Court incorporating the museum's Coal Mine exhibit, which opened in 1933. The North and South Portico projects follow RAMSA's completion of a master plan for Griffin MSI in 2024. Developed over the course of a year, the plan assessed more than 400,000 square feet of exhibition and public space, reviewing existing uses and identifying opportunities to adapt underutilized areas of the historic building and improve its connections to the surrounding campus.
Recent developments in museum architecture also include projects that combine the adaptation of existing buildings with new additions. In Rotterdam, Mecanoo has released images of its renovation of Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen, which involves a new building, the restoration of the existing museum, and the redesign of its gardens. In Ghent, Design Museum Gent reopened following a four-year renovation and expansion by Carmody Groarke, ATAMA, and RE-ST, bringing together restored historic buildings and a new wing. Meanwhile, the Fondation Beyeler in Riehen, Switzerland, is expanding its Renzo Piano-designed museum with three buildings by Peter Zumthor, alongside the restoration and enlargement of its surrounding park. The expanded ensemble is scheduled to open fully on January 15, 2027, following a preview phase beginning September 26, 2026.

Palestine weekly: West Bank under siege as Israelis go to the polls
Israel sealed the West Bank, emptied parts of Hebron and tightened the squeeze on Gaza as its election campaign wrapped up.

The West Bank city has been in a state of lockdown since two Palestinian gunmen opened fire at an army checkpoint at Hebron’s northern entrance on Friday, killing two Israeli soldiers and wounding three. After the suspects were killed, Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ordered the isolation of Hebron and said troops would go house to house in the gunmen’s neighbourhood. “We will act to destroy this place, to change it completely,” he proclaimed.
What followed has been a mass displacement operation in the Hebron area, echoing last year’s military expulsions of three refugee camps, alongside widespread destruction in the neighbourhoods targeted by the army, evoking scenes out of Gaza.

Thousands have been forced out of their homes already, with Defence Minister Israel Katz saying people would not be allowed back “until we’ve finished dealing with all the Hamas issues in Hebron”. By Monday, the governorate’s fourth day under closure, at least 3,171 Palestinians from 488 families had been forced out, according to Hebron Municipality data cited by the Wafa news agency. Hebron Governor Khaled Dudin said Israeli forces had searched more than 500 homes, arrested more than 70 people and fragmented the city with 128 closed gates and 120 checkpoints.
The Palestinian Prisoner’s Society says the displaced include 127 infants, 81 pregnant women and 26 people with disabilities, and that at least 47 people have been detained in Hebron since Friday.
Bulldozers razed a three-apartment building belonging to Riyad Amrish, as well as a tile and ceramics factory, an auto-parts shop and other businesses in Farsh al-Hawa. Israel’s Channel 12 said Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich ordered the demolitions.
Israeli NGO B’Tselem warned the operation amounts to “collective punishment and acts that could constitute war crimes”.
Sieges at every scale
But Hebron is only the most prominent of multiple sieges happening at different scales, with years-long efforts to strategically encircle Palestinian communities in the West Bank now being employed to devastating effect:
- Homes: The three-week siege by Israeli settlers of the family of Yusuf Shanaran in Wadi al-Rakheem, Masafer Yatta continues, with the family unable to leave or receive aid for days at a time without army coordination, Shanaran told Al Jazeera on Monday. In Umm Safa, northwest of Ramallah, village Mayor Marwan Sabah said Mohammad al-Obaiyat’s 1954 house received a demolition order with a November 11 deadline after months with a gate blocking its road. Settlers have since been filmed attempting to break into the family home, which has been besieged for nearly a month, with few supplies entering during that time.
- A village: Madama, south of Nablus, is only just emerging from a two-week siege of its four entrances, with heavy restrictions remaining at its just-opened northern entrance, according to villagers. A kindergarten principal there told Al Jazeera she lifts children over the barrier one by one.
- A region: Twelve Masafer Yatta communities in the southern West Bank were cut off for several days, with about 50 teachers unable to reach their schools, and Wafa reported that Bethlehem governorate’s roads were closed for several days.
- A territory: The Israeli army barred Palestinian workers from illegal Israeli settlements on Sunday and Monday and will close all crossings on election day.
The only Palestinians who can vote – Palestinian citizens of Israel – may face issues at the polls, too; Israel’s Channel 12 reported that Netanyahu’s Likud party was preparing to challenge results from Arab polling stations before a vote had been cast.
Olive harvest attacks
This year’s olive harvest has drawn unprecedented levels of settler pogroms, theft and closed-military-zone orders. The Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission has counted 482 attacks on the harvest by Sunday across nine governorates, Wafa reported.
At the same time, Israel released nine of 10 settlers arrested following last week’s attacks on a foreign journalist and diplomats. The attacks have continued undeterred. Wafa reported 17 attacks on farmers and their property on Thursday, and the commission documented 21 in 12 hours on Friday. The past week’s harvest-related incidents fall into a handful of repeating patterns:
- Theft of olives and equipment in at least a dozen villages, including Sinjil, Silwad, Berin, Beit Iksa, al-Lubban Asharqiya, Kafr Malek, Ein Arik and Deir Ballut, according to Wafa and local reports. Near Immatin, at least 25 masked settlers sent three tractors and two trailers rolling down a hillside, destroying the equipment and olives on board.
- Assaults in at least 15 places, among them Burin, where stones left three farmers with head wounds; Ein Arik, where The Times of Israel reported a farmer suffered fractures; and Beit Iksa, al-Lubban Asharqiya and Kafr Malek, where pickers were pepper-sprayed. Settlers fired live rounds at pickers in Berin and Osarin, and smashed cars and trucks in Marda, Wad Qaddoum and Sinjil, Wafa and local monitors reported.
- Detentions and expulsions in at least a dozen places. Fifteen farmers were detained in as-Sawiya on Sunday. In Beit Iksa, where the harvest had been coordinated with the Israeli Civil Administration, Mohammed al-Kiswani was pepper-sprayed and detained; settlers told farmers they would never harvest “with or without coordination”. Land at Deir Jarir and Turmus Aya was declared a closed military zone without orders shown, Ayed Jafry reported – and far-right influencers were brought to film the expulsions for campaign content.
- Damage to olive trees in at least 10 locations. Settlers burned dozens of trees in Burqa on Friday, keeping Palestinian Civil Defence crews out, according to Wafa; trees were set on fire in Immatin, Salem and Beit Furik; and a bulldozer uprooted hundreds in Madama, according to villagers. Soldiers uprooted dozens more in Deir Qaddis for a settler road and posted a notice at al-Mughayyir ordering hundreds of trees uprooted and in Khirbet Abu Falah for a “security buffer zone”, giving residents 24 hours to object, Jafry reported.
- Arson. In Burqa, settlers set fire on Tuesday to a memorial to Palestinian residents killed and, an hour later, to the home of Jamal Bajes, a Palestinian-American – the second arson at his house in recent months, according to local reports. Local activist networks reported a home was burned in Deir Abu Mishal, and Wafa said settlers tried to set another ablaze in Burin under army protection.
Those joining the harvests in solidarity were targeted, too. United States Democratic congressional candidate Brad Lander was among about 80 volunteers detained near Nahalin on Wednesday and released with a “warning”; Israel’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs accused him of “harvesting headlines”.
Gaza: Managed scarcity as killings continue
The last week in Gaza saw at least 37 more Palestinians killed as Israel’s daily attacks continued. Monday’s daily report from the Gaza Ministry of Health alone recorded 11 deaths – eight newly killed, three recovered from rubble – and 35 wounded, taking the toll since the October 2025 “ceasefire” to 1,559 killed and 5,608 wounded, with a cumulative toll of 74,555.
Among those killed this week:
- Akram Yassin and his wife, Dina Abu Bakr, in a strike on their apartment behind al-Shifa Hospital on Tuesday.
- Majdi Mohammad Fakhri Hassan, a child, shot near the Happy City resort south of Khan Younis; Rafif Raed Lubad, 17, shot in the head in Jabalia; and Fatima Abu Laban, killed in Tal al-Dhahab, northwest of Beit Lahiya on Saturday, according to Wafa.
- Three security guards – Sami Baroud, Ashraf Dahlan and Shadi Abu Ataya – at the Islamic University in Gaza City on Sunday, after an earlier strike wounded seven students. Israel said it was targeting a Hamas operative.
For days, hunger worsened with crossings into Gaza shut: Flour stocks ran out, leaving seven of 20 commercial bakeries open, Abdul Nasser al-Ajrami of the bakers’ association told Wafa, and a tray of eggs reached a price of 60 shekels ($19.50).
The pressure began to ease somewhat on the evening of October 23, as Israel told traders that commercial goods would resume and an Egyptian committee delivered flour, Mohammad Abu Warda of the private sector’s emergency committee said.

Blood test could reveal prostate cancer risk more than a decade before diagnosis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:28:08 UTC
15:28:08 KST

Proteins present in men’s blood could give clues to prostate cancer risk years before diagnosis.
Distinctive proteins in men’s blood can signal a higher risk of prostate cancer more than 15 years before diagnosis, Oxford researchers have found.
“Finding proteins linked to known prostate cancer driver genes in blood collected years before diagnosis gives us new insights into the earliest stages of the disease,” said Karl Smith-Byrne, corresponding author of the study at Oxford.
Prostate cancer is the most common cancer among men in the European Union and second worldwide, after lung cancer. About 330,000 new cases are diagnosed every year and about 75,000 men die of the disease annually, in the EU alone.
Researchers at Oxford University analysed blood samples collected between 1992 and 2000 from more than 2,500 men. They compared baseline samples from 982 men who went on to develop prostate cancer with those from 1,573 men who did not.
The team measured more than 6,000 different proteins in each participant’s blood plasma. Because the samples were taken years before any diagnosis, sometimes more than 15 years, the researchers could look for early chemical warning signs — changes in proteins.
Some proteins were linked to a higher overall risk of prostate cancer, while others were associated specifically with aggressive or fast-growing forms of the disease. At the same time, men with higher levels of certain immune-system proteins, like GZMK and ANXA2, showed a lower long-term risk of prostate cancer, according to the study, published in the journal European Urology
“Many prostate cancers grow slowly and may never cause harm, while others are aggressive and can be life-threatening,” said Zhe Huang, first author of the study and a postdoctoral epidemiologist at Oxford Population Health.
“Ultimately, we hope this will help us understand the biology of aggressive prostate cancer and identify markers that could improve how we assess risk in the future,” Huang said.
The findings are not yet a screening test and need further validation, the researchers noted.
“Together with existing and future genetic evidence, these findings may help us identify biological pathways that could be targeted to prevent aggressive prostate cancer”, said Smith-Byrne.

At least 60 Orthodox Christians killed in attacks in Ethiopia’s Oromia region

2026-10-27

15:27:50 KST

At least 60 Orthodox Christians were killed in separate attacks on October 20 and 24 in Ethiopia’s Oromia region, with more than 20 others seriously wounded and 20 homes burned down, church officials said in a statement late on Monday.
“We have heard with deep sorrow the report submitted by the Diocese Office,” the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church’s Holy Synod said, describing the killings as “extremely tragic cruelty and suffering inflicted on our citizens”.
The church said 14 people were killed on October 20 in Gora Silingo, Angada Kebele, in Merti district, while another 46 were killed on October 24 in Tereta, Chole and Birbo in Shirka district.
Both districts are located in the Arsi Zone of central Ethiopia’s Oromia region.
The Holy Synod condemned the killings, saying the violence violated constitutional protections for life and religious freedom and threatened Ethiopia’s tradition of peaceful coexistence among different faiths.
It called on government institutions to publicly condemn the attacks, strengthen civilian protection and ensure those responsible are brought to justice.
The church also urged security agencies to provide additional protection to affected communities and take preventive measures against further violence.
The Oromia regional government has pledged to pursue those responsible for the killings.
According to local media reports, a local official accused a newly formed rebel alliance that includes the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA) of carrying out the attacks. The OLA has previously denied allegations of targeting civilians.
The killings come amid continuing insecurity in Oromia, Ethiopia’s largest regional state, where government forces have been battling armed groups for years.
In July, the Ethiopian Human Rights Council reported that at least 432 civilians and four local militia members had been killed in targeted attacks across East Arsi between 2021/2022 and June 1.
The Holy Synod said it would seek discussions with senior government officials to address the security crisis.
It also announced prayers for the victims on Monday and directed Orthodox churches and monasteries worldwide to hold similar services on Tuesday, following the Divine Liturgy.
The church expressed condolences to the bereaved families and called for urgent measures to ensure its followers could live and worship without fear.

Prediction markets open new front for US election misinformation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:27:21 UTC
15:27:21 KST

U.S. President Donald Trump delivers remarks during a campaign rally at Crossroads Arena on October 26, 2026 in Corinth, Mississippi. Trump is in Mississippi today to continue campaigning for Republican candidates ahead of the midterm elections. (Getty Images via AFP)
The U.S. midterms are playing out against a controversial new scoreboard, as the nation votes in its first major elections since prediction markets went mainstream.
With hundreds of millions of dollars on the line, experts are warning that the proliferation of live odds into news coverage and on social media could sow confusion — and provide fodder for misinformation.
Concerns range from motivated actors taking extreme measures to sway markets, to voters overtrusting the odds and baselessly blaming fraud where election results differ.
President Donald Trump has already made unsubstantiated allegations of fraud central to his political movement ahead of the November 3 vote.
Polymarket and Kalshi are allowing users to buy and sell contracts on thousands of outcomes related to the midterms, despite surveys showing most Americans oppose betting on elections.
The companies have also partnered with prominent news organizations.
"They're more and more becoming part of how Americans understand elections," said Davina Hurt, government ethics director at Santa Clara University's Markkula Center for Applied Ethics.
"Elections are not games," she told AFP. "My concern is that we've reached a point where financial market expectations carry more weight in the public's mind than the votes themselves."
Prediction market trading has surged amid legal battles over whether they should be regulated as federal commodities or under state gambling laws.
Kalshi said its markets offer unique data distinct from polling, that probabilities do not guarantee outcomes and that efforts to manipulate odds are canceled out by other buyers.
"Kalshi should be seen as a complement to traditional polling," head of communications Elisabeth Diana told AFP. "On prediction markets, you trade what you think will happen. On polls, you say what you want to have happen."
Yet experts expressed fears over markets being misconstrued, especially as Polymarket and Kalshi issue race "projections" on social media.
A high probability "is not a promise," Hurt said. "When the prediction fails, that's not evidence that elections fail. But people are going to read that in."
When Republican Spencer Pratt lost the Los Angeles mayoral primary in June, right-wing influencers pointed to prediction market odds which showed him favored to advance to the general election as evidence of fraud.
Some X posts spreading misinformation carried “paid partnership” tags, prompting backlash and action from Polymarket and Kalshi.
“The June primary reinforced how quickly expectations about election outcomes can become confused with actual election results,” said Michael Sanchez, spokesman for Los Angeles County’s registrar’s office.
For the first time, researchers who monitor election misinformation at University of Washington's Center for an Informed Public are tracking how prediction markets are misrepresented online.
"There's more reason to create these rumors because there's that sort of financial element tied to it," senior research scientist Rachel Moran told AFP.
"It's becoming a significant part of our work."

Kazakhstan allocates over 122 billion tenge in recycling fees to waste management projects
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:26:30 UTC
15:26:30 KST

Kazakhstan allocates over 122 billion tenge in recycling fees to waste management projects
Kazakhstan has allocated 122.6 billion tenge in recycling fees to finance 34 projects aimed at developing modern waste management infrastructure across the country, Qazinform News Agency reports via the country’s Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources.
With the ministry’s support, Zhasyl Damu joint-stock company is funding initiatives that include the construction of new recycling facilities, the establishment of waste sorting complexes, and the purchase of specialized equipment.
A total of 67 projects, worth 440 billion tenge, have been approved by the Investment Headquarters under the Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources. Of these, 34 have already received funding.
Among the funded initiatives, six projects involve the construction of municipal solid waste sorting facilities with a combined annual capacity of 650,000 tons. Another 18 projects focus on expanding recycling capacity by a total of 435,000 tons per year, while 10 projects provide for the purchase of 177 units of specialized equipment.
As of now, 15 projects have been commissioned. Their implementation has resulted in the purchase of 131 units of specialized equipment, the launch of waste sorting lines with a combined annual capacity of 290,000 tons, and the commissioning of recycling facilities capable of processing 19,300 tons of waste annually.
The largest share of funding has been allocated to projects in Almaty, North Kazakhstan, Pavlodar, Aktobe, and Kostanay regions. Initiatives are also being implemented in Atyrau, Akmola, Mangistau, East Kazakhstan, Abai regions, as well as Astana, Shymkent, and other parts of the country.
The projects cover nearly all major areas of the waste management sector, including the recycling of waste paper, PET bottles, used car tires, and other waste materials. They also involve modernizing existing facilities and upgrading fleets of specialized equipment.
Work on new projects is ongoing. Several initiatives are currently at different stages of review, approval, and preparation for funding in accordance with established procedures.
Under Kazakhstan’s Environmental Code, recycling fee revenues are allocated to support such initiatives. Their implementation is expected to strengthen the country’s waste management infrastructure, increase recycling volumes, reduce the amount of waste sent to landfills, and promote the reuse of secondary raw materials in the economy.
Earlier, Qazinform reported Kazakhstan would build waste-to-energy plants.

Retailers say electronic price tags will not lead to sudden price rises
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:24:00 UTC
15:24:00 KST

Retailers say electronic price tags will not lead to sudden price rises
Supermarket chains in Estonia have said the increased use of electronic price tags, which reduce the need for paper, will not be used to suddenly increase prices during peak demand, despite customer concerns.
Observant customers have noticed electronic price tags in various grocery stores for some time now. Selver, for example, has introduced electronic tags for fruit, vegetables and bakery products.
"This certainly makes work more efficient and convenient, and you do not have to print and replace tags. At the same time, it has to be considered very carefully, because the investment is significant," said Selver communications manager Mariann Järvela.
Completely replacing paper tickets with electronic screen tags would cost millions of euros for a major retail chain.
Rimi supermarket chain said its smaller stores have made the switch already. The company's head of sales and business operations, Jelena Litvinovitš, said the investment has not paid off.
"Unfortunately, this technology really is still very, very expensive. To be honest, we are waiting to see whether it might become cheaper, but not yet. The risk is that if we do not find a solution in the coming years, the batteries will run out and then we will have to consider what to do with these price tags," she said.
Electronic tags can be changed in seconds, and customers are concerned prices will rise suddenly during peak demand.
For example, it is theoretically possible to take a packet of coffee from the shelf at one price, and then find it has risen at the checkout. Stores promise that this will not occur.
"I can confirm that there is no such risk at Rimi. It would certainly raise a lot of questions and negative emotions among customers. One of the reasons is that we have not found a good solution for how to change prices during the day and how to explain this to customers," Litvinovitš said.
"Yes, in theory it is possible and it would certainly bring greater profits. We know that it is used elsewhere in the world, but we ourselves have not found a good explanation or ways to do it," she added.
Grocery stores are not the only ones using automated solutions. For example, electronics retailer Euronics introduced electronic price tags in 2023, citing savings on labor costs. The company paid half a million euros for the tags three years ago.
"In the more distant future, we will probably reach a point where there are no paper price tags, but that is probably still some way off. In the near future, there are many advantages, but there are still quite a few disadvantages as well," said Nele Peil, head of the Estonian Traders Association.

B'Yachad reports Likud to CEC over suspected election interference, source tells 'Post'

Yisrael Beytenu filed a petition with the chairman of the Central Elections Committee (CEC) on Tuesday, demanding an immediate halt to the distribution of kippot bearing the image and name of the late Rabbi Ovadia Yosef outside a polling station in Afula.
According to the party, the kippot also featured the inscription "I have chosen the path of faith."
Yisrael Beytenu argued that the distribution constituted prohibited election campaigning and the unlawful distribution of gifts to voters.
"The law applies to everyone, including Shas," Yisrael Beytenu said in a statement.
Reservists-Economic Party report missing, defaced ballots
The Reservists and Economic Party filed a complaint with the CEC on Tuesday following reports of missing and defaced ballot slips at several polling stations across Israel.
According to the party, ballot slips bearing its designated voting symbol were missing from several polling stations, while others had been damaged or marked with pens.
"After Likud's fake news campaign, we received numerous complaints about our ballot slips being defaced or removed," party chairman Yoaz Hendel said.
Yashar party claims systematic attempt to disrupt voting
Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party also filed a complaint with the Central Elections Committee on Tuesday over suspicions of a systematic attempt to disrupt voting for the party and undermine election integrity, following reports of ballot tampering at polling stations across Israel.
According to the party, several incidents were identified in which ballot slips marked "Derech," the party's designated voting symbol, were missing, damaged, or turned over inside voting booths.
The party said it had received a series of serious reports from polling stations nationwide concerning the disappearance, damage, and marking of its ballot slips in ways that could result in votes being disqualified.
"Anyone who tries to steal ballot slips is trying to steal the election. This is a serious violation of election integrity and the fundamental right of Israeli citizens to vote," the party said.
Religious Zionist Party alleges deliberate ballot damage
Earlier on Election Day, the Religious Zionist Party claimed they had received numerous reports that ballot slips belonging to the party and Likud had been deliberately damaged at several polling stations across Israel, potentially rendering them invalid.
According to reports received by the party's election-day headquarters, small tears had been made along the edges of ballot slips from both parties, raising concerns that votes cast using those slips could be disqualified.
The party called on the Central Elections Committee to intervene immediately and instruct election integrity inspectors at polling stations to conduct frequent checks of ballot slips to ensure they remain valid.
Yisrael Beytenu and People of Israel say slips missing
Yisrael Beytenu and People of Israel filed separate complaints with the Central Elections Committee on Tuesday after receiving reports that their ballot slips were missing at several stations after voting began in Israel's 26th Knesset election.
According to a statement issued by Yisrael Beytenu, ballot slips bearing its electoral symbol were allegedly not placed at polling station No. 45, located at 10 Gamla Street in Kiryat Ono, when voting opened.
The Central Elections Committee released a statement clarifying that the station in question had ballots for the party.
Similarly, People of Israel reported that the party's ballot slips were missing, and its headquarters received reports from both military and civilian polling stations that its ballot slips had been turned over, making them appear to be blank voting slips.
Haredi Public ballots missing, hidden, voters say
Voters said that ballots for the Haredi Public party had been removed from polling stations in Bnei Brak, Modi'in Illit and Jerusalem, with the Civil Election Watch organization saying it had received 23 reports regarding ballots being removed in entire stacks or hidden beneath ballots of other parties, Kan News reported on Tuesday.
According to the report, voters could not find ballots for the party at their polling stations, and had to request them from election officials. In Modi'in Illit, one voter said the party's ballots had been hidden beneath those of other parties.
"A stack of Haredi Public ballots disappeared instantly," an election observer at Modi'in Illit said, according to Kan.
A Bnei Brak voter expressed concern that if voters are forced to request the correct ballots to be provided or found as his wife did, not every woman will do so.
"Not every woman will feel comfortable asking polling station officials, all of whom are Haredi, why ballots are missing."
B'Yachad files claims that Netanyahu engaged in electioneering, Likud reps tracked voters
The B’Yachad party, led by former prime minister Naftali Bennett, submitted an appeal to the CEC accusing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of illegal electioneering after Netanyahu spoke on haredi (ultra-Orthodox) radio program Kol Barama and urged the public to vote for Likud.
Later on Tuesday, B’Yachad said it had received reports from its representatives on the ground that the Elector app was being used at polling stations in a moshav in the Lower Galilee. The party did not name the moshav.
Following the reports, the party filed a second complaint with the Central Elections Committee.
Elections Committee rejects first B’Yachad claim
The Central Elections Committee declared that claims circulating regarding Likud representatives in polling booths across the country illegally tracking voters using an app were false after B'Yachad issued a formal complaint shortly after Election Day kicked off.
“An isolated report was received concerning photography at a polling station in Moshav Yarhiv. The polling station committee member who took the photographs understood her mistake after the guidelines were explained to her and stopped taking pictures," the CEC stated.
“The committee reiterates that party representatives at polling stations are prohibited from providing their parties with information about whether an individual has arrived at a polling station or cast a ballot, including through apps. These guidelines are binding on all parties and their representatives.”
The Likud party denied any wrongdoing, stating that the party has set up booths outside of polling stations and that voters can volunteer the relevant information.
"This has nothing to do with the polling station ‘representatives,’ to whom voters are required to identify themselves,” the party stated.
Polls opened at 7 a.m. Tuesday at 12,018 polling stations for the country’s 7,331,981 eligible voters, with 36 lists competing for the Knesset’s 120 seats. Neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc nor the opposition is assured of a majority, and Netanyahu will remain caretaker prime minister until a new government is sworn in, whatever the outcome.

Palestinian citizens of Israel can vote, but cannot expect change
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:15:48 UTC
15:15:48 KST

Palestinian citizens of Israel can vote, but cannot expect change
Elections cannot stop the accelerated process of ‘recolonisation’ of 1948 Palestinian communities.
For the majority of Israelis, the general election on October 27 is a choice between Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and the forces that oppose him, led by former general Gadi Eisenkot. But for the Palestinian citizens of Israel, who make up 20 percent of the population, the upcoming polls present a different dilemma.
As the political mainstream in Israel continues to shift to the far right, Palestinian citizens face growing threats to their political and collective rights. Palestinian communities in Israel experience increased violence, while settlers are encroaching on their boundaries. The recent push to expand policing and militarisation of civilian life is another source of growing anxiety within the Palestinian population.
In this context, the anti-Netanyahu bloc does not seem to offer the prospect of policy reversal or change. Therefore, the question on many Palestinian minds is whether voting in the Israeli elections can make any difference at all.
Recolonisation of 1948 Palestine
Since the Nakba of 1948, the Palestinians who managed to remain in their homes in what was declared as territory of the new State of Israel have had a different fate than the Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza. In 1952, they were granted Israeli citizenship, and in 1966, the martial law under which they were forced to live was lifted.
Although Palestinian citizens of Israel have the right to vote and participate in politics, citizenship has not shielded them from the broader system of dispossession and attempts to reshape their Palestinian identity and national belonging.
Through land confiscation and the regulation of education and culture, the Israeli state has sought to detach Palestinians from their historical roots and collective past, promoting instead a model of the “Arab Israeli” as a citizen whose identity is separate from its Palestinian and Arab national context.
Formal citizenship has not secured substantive equality for Palestinians as they face discriminatory laws, systemic underfunding of basic services, and political and socioeconomic marginalisation.
Instead of engaging in direct violence towards Palestinian citizens – as it has done in the West Bank and Gaza – the Israeli state has instead “outsourced” brutality to criminal networks.
As a result, Palestinian communities have faced killings, shootings, bombings and arson while Israeli law enforcement has largely ignored the problem. More recently, this problem has escalated, as organised crime groups obtained advanced weapons reportedly stolen from Israeli army stockpiles or smuggled across borders. This growing militarisation of organised crime has claimed hundreds of lives.
In parallel, Israeli settlements next to Palestinian communities have expanded, accompanied by accelerated seizure of land. This process of “recolonisation” began in mixed cities, such as Jaffa and Lydd, where religious-nationalist settler groups started establishing themselves in Palestinian neighbourhoods in 2021.
Since October 2023, this process has accelerated. In August, Israel’s Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich unveiled his party’s plan to “Judaise” the Naqab and northern Israel. He proposes to add one million Jewish residents to the two regions, establishing 40 new settlements and dozens of farms, expanding existing settlements, and creating hundreds of thousands of new housing units.
The idea is to extend the model of territorial control from the occupied West Bank into the Naqab and northern Israel, where Palestinian communities are concentrated.
There are also indications that the policing of Palestinian towns and villages could increasingly fall under the National Guard, established under National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir.
The idea of creating the force was prompted by the May 2021 protests, known as the Dignity Uprising, which spread across Palestinian communities in Lydd, Haifa, Umm al-Fahm, and dozens of other towns and villages.
Ben-Gvir has advocated expanding the state’s capacity to suppress such unrest. Although the National Guard’s precise role and operational framework remain under development, its potential deployment against mass protests raises serious concerns about the right to protest and the protection of democratic freedoms.
The government has strengthened settler security squads and integrated them into a broader security framework, raising concerns about the growing role of armed civilian groups in enforcing control over Palestinian communities.
At the same time, Ben-Gvir has widened access to personal firearms, issuing 300,000 gun licences since taking office.
Together, these measures normalise civilian policing and deepen the militarisation of everyday life, reinforcing the unequal distribution of coercive power in a society structured on the dispossession and subordination of Palestinians.
The Palestinian response
Parties seeking to represent Palestinian citizens of Israel, such as the United Arab List (Ra’am), led by Mansour Abbas, have long argued that parliamentary participation and support for the anti-Netanyahu camp can help remove the far right from power and halt its settler-colonial agenda. But the party’s own track record proves this premise wrong.
Ra’am joined the coalition government formed after the elections in 2021, which excluded Netanyahu, but it failed to bring about fundamental changes in the conditions of Palestinian citizens. The coalition was fragile and often rocked by deep ideological contradictions.
In 2022, Mazen Ghnaim, a member of Ra’am, publicly acknowledged that he could not push through policies that would benefit the Palestinian population, despite his party being part of the ruling coalition and despite promises being made that such policies would be accepted. He also lamented the heavy criticism he faced whenever he was visiting Palestinian communities.
Ra’am’s experience in that coalition illustrated the challenge of sustaining Palestinian political participation in a government whose other constituent parties uphold exclusionary nationalist policies.
The problem, therefore, extends beyond Netanyahu himself: Palestinian support for the anti-Netanyahu camp cannot translate into meaningful policies that challenge the broader structures of discrimination and dispossession Palestinian citizens of Israel face.
Voting may offer a way to slow down this project, but it cannot reverse the deeper transformation taking place within Israeli society. The cultural shift towards fascism extends beyond the government and its political leadership, becoming increasingly embedded in social attitudes and everyday life.
That said, I believe another four years of far-right rule would pose an immediate threat to Palestinian communities and their rights. Therefore, I will vote in Tuesday’s election.
But Palestinians need to recognise that electoral participation must be accompanied by a more radical political response capable of confronting the structures and ideologies driving this transformation. This requires, among other things, reforming the High Follow-Up Committee for Arab Citizens of Israel and rooting it more firmly in Palestinian society through popular committees and grassroots organising.
It also demands a broader commitment to democratisation and de-Zionisation across historic Palestine, as part of a larger political project aimed at building a different future through alternative institutions, mechanisms, and forms of collective action.
Whatever the Israeli state might claim, the fate of the Palestinian citizens of Israel is tied to the fate of the rest of the Palestinian population. That is a realisation that Palestinian political leaders must finally embrace.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

How you can access free public transportation to get to polling booths on Election Day - explainer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:15:44 UTC
15:15:44 KST

Free intercity public transportation is available across Israel on Tuesday, Election Day for the 26th Knesset, with the benefit extending to all passengers, not just eligible voters, according to Walla. The service is funded by the Central Elections Committee.
Free travel began at 8 p.m. on Monday and will continue until public transportation services conclude Tuesday night.
The benefit applies to about 660 intercity bus routes longer than 15 kilometers, up from 600 routes during the 2022 elections, as well as all Israel Railways lines.
However, city buses, light rail services, the Metronit bus rapid transit system, and Haifa's Carmelit underground railway will continue to charge regular fares.
Passengers can check whether a specific intercity bus route is included in the arrangement by calling the Transportation Ministry's information hotline at \*8787.
How can passengers travel for free?
Intercity buses: Passengers can board eligible buses free of charge without presenting identification, obtaining a ticket, or validating a Rav-Kav public transportation card.
Israel Railways: Passengers must obtain a special paper ticket from station ticket counters or ticket machines. To avoid unnecessary charges, they should not use tickets or passes loaded onto their Rav-Kav cards or public transportation apps.
Additional trains on Jerusalem-Tel Aviv route
Due to anticipated demand, Israel Railways will run three trains per hour in each direction between Jerusalem's Yitzhak Navon Station and Tel Aviv from noon until 8 p.m. Tuesday, up from the usual two trains per hour.
Some of the additional services will begin and end at Tel Aviv's HaHagana Station.
In addition, police have restricted the number of passengers traveling to and from Jerusalem. Passengers are therefore required to obtain a personal travel voucher in advance for their selected train.
Due to expected congestion, railway staff will enforce the voucher requirement. Vouchers can be obtained free of charge through the Israel Railways website.
Will travel to Eilat also be free?
Different eligibility requirements apply to passengers traveling to and from Eilat.
Free travel on these routes is subject to an eligibility check based on the passenger's registered residential address and advance registration through Egged's information center at \*2800.
Rail passenger numbers could break 2022 election record
During the previous elections for the 25th Knesset on November 1, 2022, Israel Railways recorded a roughly 33% increase in passenger numbers, rising from 249,146 on a typical weekday to 331,706 on Election Day.
That record is expected to be broken this year.
The free transportation initiative is estimated to cost NIS 3.5 million and will be funded by the Central Elections Committee through the Transportation Ministry.
Passengers are advised to check updated schedules and service changes through the Israel Railways website, its official app, the \*5770 information hotline, or the railway's official WhatsApp channel.

Finance Ministry prepares plan to prevent increase in deficit, fund defense, for next government
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:15:36 UTC
15:15:36 KST

Even before the exit poll results of today's elections are known, the Finance Ministry has already prepared a plan that includes a series of harsh economic measures, intended, among other things, to finance the defense budget and prevent an increase in the deficit and the debt-to-GDP ratio.
Some of the measures were planned in cooperation with the Bank of Israel. The next government will be responsible for implementing the policy.
In addition, after Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich subsidized gasoline prices by NIS 1 per liter over the past two months to prevent price increases, the subsidy, which has cost more than half a billion shekels, will end Saturday night. As a result, gasoline prices will surge by at least NIS 1 per liter at midnight on Saturday, and may rise further as global fuel prices climb.
The price of a liter of self-service 95-octane gasoline is expected to reach NIS 8.90. However, the dollar's roughly 1% decline against the shekel yesterday will help moderate the increase.
Higher fuel prices are expected to trigger price increases across a range of other goods and services whose rates have so far been frozen at the government's initiative, including electricity, water, and public transportation. This is expected to drive up the Consumer Price Index.
The freeze on adjustments to income tax brackets, tax credit points, and National Insurance contributions, along with the current VAT rate, will remain in place in 2027 under existing automatic budgetary provisions.
Revenue from these measures is estimated at NIS 10 billion. In addition to ending the gasoline subsidy, further tax measures will be proposed to boost state revenue.
These include mandatory reporting of income from residential property rentals and taxation of rental income from the first shekel earned. Currently, rental income of up to NIS 5,654 per month is exempt from tax. Some of these legislative initiatives have been held up in the Knesset Finance Committee.
Another proposal would impose a tax on international content providers operating in Israel, commonly referred to as the "Netflix tax." Another measure expected to be implemented is a reduction in tax benefits on pension contributions, along with a recommendation to eliminate VAT exemptions for sectors that currently benefit from them.
Economic measures aim to fund increased defense budget
Broader macroeconomic measures are aimed at finding sources of funding for the required increase in the defense budget, which is expected to reach NIS 187 billion.
One almost certain source of funding will be sharp cuts to coalition funds, alongside sweeping efficiency measures across government ministry budgets.
The main challenge facing the coalition forming the next government will be the immediate need to pass a 2027 budget, or potentially a two-year budget covering 2027 and 2028. The budget must include comprehensive reforms under the Economic Arrangements Law.
As a result, the Finance Ministry is unlikely to secure approval by the end of 2027, so it will need to prepare a continuing budget.
The timetable for implementing these measures is tight, and the parties that make up the new coalition will have to begin taking action even before the next government is formed.
Stock exchange unfazed by Netanyahu crypto economy warning
Meanwhile, the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange appeared unfazed yesterday by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's dire economic warnings over the weekend concerning the crypto economy.
Trading opened lower yesterday, the final trading day before the elections, against the backdrop of Netanyahu's statements warning of possible sanctions, cuts to US aid, and the prospect of a shift toward a shadow economy.
However, the trend quickly reversed, and the stock market moved into positive territory, with the exception of banking stocks.
The stock exchange has declined since the beginning of the month amid uncertainty over the elections. Now, however, traders appear to be cautiously optimistic about the possibility of change.

Palestinian citizens of Israel fear they’re next target if far-right wins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:12:04 UTC
15:12:04 KST

Palestinian citizens of Israel fear they’re next target if far-right wins
Majd al-Krum’s peaceful protests have forced settlers to withdraw, but fears of further provocations loom after elections.
Majd al-Krum, Israel – The police closed the road to al-Rus, so the villagers found other ways up there.
Beginning on September 13, local Palestinian citizens of Israel made the steep climb to the pine-covered hilltop above Majd al-Krum using horses, off-road vehicles and on foot. A couple of weeks earlier, settlers from the occupied West Bank had begun building an outpost there, on village land – one of the first such attempts on this side of the Green Line, the name used for the boundary between Israel and the occupied West Bank.
The young Israeli settlers said they were there to graze livestock with a Jewish National Fund (JNF) permit. But there was no livestock, noted Hussein Mannaa, 50, a lawyer and member of the town’s Popular Committee. Within a week, the camp had grown from a handful of people to between 25 and 30, according to villagers, with a kitchen, a toilet, a water line and electricity.
Villagers rushed to the scene, so police closed the road to the site. Yet local Palestinians came in droves nonetheless.
Anas Sgaier, a 21-year-old law student and youth organiser, made the nearly hour-long climb up the mountain. “I remember one moment: I’m going up and it’s hard for me to breathe,” he said. “And to my right, I saw an older woman, in her 80s, with her husband … walking up 50 minutes, just to show her presence.”
After almost a week of peaceful protests that saw hundreds of Palestinians from Majd al-Krum and across the region come every day, the JNF ordered the settler tents removed. By September 16, the site was cleared out.
The village had won, for now.
A ‘pilot’ experiment
A little more than a month later, Israelis head to the polls on Tuesday, and Palestinian villagers fear al-Rus was a prelude to what may come next. Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich is campaigning on a promise to “Judaise” the Galilee, where Palestinian citizens of Israel make up a large proportion of the population, and says he will repeat there “the revolution we carried out in [the occupied West Bank]”.
“The al-Rus experiment is like a pilot … experiment: ‘come on, let’s see the reaction’,” said Husein Khalaily, 50, an economic consultant, while sitting at his home in Majd al-Krum.
Reaction was swift: the village’s Popular Committee met as soon as the rumours of the settler outpost were confirmed and, with the local council, called daily demonstrations. “The popular struggle alongside the legal track is what bore fruit,” said Mannaa, a mainstay at the weeklong demonstrations at the site.
It was young people who drove the protests, villagers said. “Bring your coffee and come,” beckoned Sgaier in Instagram posts alongside his cousin. “We’re only going up to drink coffee, because that’s our land.”
“Not only the people of Majd al-Krum: Deir al-Asad, al-Bi’na, Sakhnin, Arrabeh … from the Naqab they came,” recalled Mannaa. Some left-leaning residents of nearby Jewish communities also turned up. “There was this incredible solidarity,” said Khalaily.
Hanan, a Palestinian Christian from a nearby village, said the outposts she read about in the occupied West Bank had felt far away – until Majd al-Krum. “I never saw the Arab community so united and really fighting for their lands,” she said.
Smotrich came to Majd al-Krum, a village long known for its political activism, to campaign with a police force and a water cannon. “The young people were hot-blooded and wanted to go out and confront him,” Khalaily said, but the local committees and political parties talked them down.
But the targeting continued. On September 18, police announced the arrest of a 32-year-old Majd al-Krum resident over alleged contact with a Lebanese agent. Smotrich seized on it, saying Galilee residents were “in the atmosphere of October 6”, a reference to the October 7, 2023 attack on Israel.
‘The language is clear’
On August 27, Smotrich posted a plan promising one million more Jews and 40 new Jewish communities in the Galilee and al-Naqab, another area of Israel where many of the residents are Palestinian. His party then released an AI-generated video in which a West Bank Palestinian frantically warns a relative in the Galilee that “the Jews are coming” to “do to you what they did to us”.
Sgaier said he and his friends laughed at the absurdity of the video. Then they watched it come to life at al-Rus.
“He came here and said it clearly: ‘I want to Judaise the Galilee,’” said Khalaily. “Back in the day, they used to say, ‘we want to develop the Galilee.’ Today – the language is clear.”
Villagers believe the recent provocations are intended to create a pretext for making that happen, where Palestinian citizens hold rights that Palestinians under military occupation in the West Bank do not, making dispossession a harder proposition. “Building the outposts, they wanted to lead the people into a confrontation,” said Mannaa. “They want to impose a state of chaos because chaos benefits them.”
The settlers pointed to a grazing permit granted on the land of al-Rus from the quasi-governmental JNF. But according to Khalaily, the plot, about 8.4 dunams (roughly two acres), is half privately owned by his cousin, and half administered by the Israel Land Authority, which has long refused to partition it so the owner can tell which part is his.
“They chose Majd al-Krum because it’s hard to break,” said Mannaa, pointing to the village’s history of defiance since the Nakba in 1948, when many villagers were expelled from their homes. “If they break Majd al-Krum,” said Khaled Kewan, 27, a singer from the village, “[it’s] going to happen all over the Galilee”.
The JNF later said the “grazing” initiative would move to another plot about 500 metres away on land villagers consider theirs. But the village rejects any relocation, “even one tent”, Mannaa said.
Al Jazeera has reached out to the JNF, the Israeli police and the Israeli Finance Ministry for comment, but has yet to receive a response.
‘Coming not just for Majd al-Krum’
Whether Smotrich remains in power depends on the election results on Tuesday – where the Palestinian vote will likely figure prominently. Polls suggest neither of the main Zionist blocs can reach 61 seats without support from the Arab parties.
Turnout by Palestinian citizens of Israel has hovered between 45 and 65 percent in recent years. However, organisers believe the demographic’s turnout may hit 70 to 75 percent, a level last seen in 1999.
After the settlers’ attempts and provocations in Majd al-Krum, Mannaa boldly predicted the town “will go past 80 percent”.
Khalaily, a longtime boycotter who has only ever voted once, now urges turnout at every talk he gives. “These prominent racists who are there now have to be removed, even if just for a stage,” he said. He sees little difference between Netanyahu’s government and its likely replacement, “except that Smotrich and [far-right National Security Minister Itamar] Ben-Gvir won’t be in it”.
After October 7, fear kept Palestinian citizens away from demonstrating. “People got busy with other things,” said Khalaily. “Busy with fear, with making a living.” Crime in the town made it worse. “I’ll be sitting here at night and I hear the sound of shooting,” said Khalaily, who has children who witnessed three men murdered. “Nothing moves. It’s become normal.”
Palestinian citizens have more rights than those in the West Bank, leaving them caught between a system they oppose but must live in. “We here have the most to lose,” he said, “because we’re settled on our land and we stayed on it.”
As a result, many stayed quiet in recent years. “We left Gaza alone, left the West Bank alone, left Lebanon alone,” said Sgaier. “I said after that our time is coming.”
“I just didn’t expect it to come this early.”
However, after Smotrich’s rhetoric and the settlers’ local incursions, “the people who were indifferent about the elections, who didn’t want to take part or vote: the matter provoked them,” said Mannaa. “They know well what awaits us if this government returns to power.”
Some, like Sgaier, will still boycott. “What happened in Majd al-Krum, we solve it by going out [to] the street – not through the Knesset [parliament] and the laws,” said Sgaier, who sees little difference between the two Zionist political blocs. “They don’t want Palestinians here.”
Sgaier believes there was a real change where it counts: on the streets. During the protests at al-Rus, he saw people he never expected. “They are not politically engaged,” he said, “but they came, too”.
The settlers’ tents are gone, leaving only sparse remains and Hebrew graffiti proclaiming “the nation of Israel lives”. Nonetheless, villagers keep trekking up the mountain every day. Families barbecue there, and schoolchildren draw and play music.
During the weeklong protests, Khaled Kewan would leave al-Rus in the evenings to go to a recording studio. He and fellow musicians from the town made the song “Ibn Bladi”:
“Oh, land of mine, land of my ancestors!” he sings. “No matter how many walls they build across my country … I am a son of this land, a son of my own country.”
The inspiration was clear, but Kewan deliberately chose not to name Majd al-Krum explicitly. “Haifa’s my town too, Akka’s my town too, Sakhnin’s my town too, Arraba’s my town too … I love the whole homeland,” he said.
The settlers’ “Judaisation” efforts, he said, “are coming not just for Majd al-Krum, but for the whole Galilee.”

The programme will be implemented through six central government institutions under the Drug De-addiction Programme (Representative Image)
NEW DELHI: With the Centre targeting a drug-free India by 2029, the health ministry has launched a nationwide capacity-building programme to train 10,000 healthcare professionals in the prevention, diagnosis and treatment of substance use disorders, including addiction to alcohol, opioids and other drugs.Union health minister J P Nadda launched the programme on Monday under the Vision Document on Narcotic Control 2026-2029, stressing that tackling substance abuse requires coordinated action by healthcare, social welfare and law enforcement agencies. The ministry aims to train 2,000 personnel in the current financial year, followed by 3,000 in 2027-28 and 5,000 in 2028-29.The programme will be implemented through six central government institutions under the Drug De-addiction Programme, with the National Drug Dependence Treatment Centre (NDDTC), AIIMS, serving as the coordinating centre. The other institutions are NIMHANS, Bengaluru; PGIMER, Chandigarh; Central Institute of Psychiatry, Ranchi; Dr Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital, Delhi; and AIIMS Bhubaneswar.The training will combine live online sessions, self-paced courses and in-person programmes. Doctors and medical officers will undergo a 12-week online training course featuring lectures and clinical case discussions, while nurses, community health officers, auxiliary nurse midwives, counsellors and psychologists will have access to specialised modules.
The curriculum will cover substances ranging from alcohol and cannabis to opioids, sleeping tablets and inhalants, as well as addiction among vulnerable groups, including women and adolescents.More than 800 nominations have already been received through the health ministry and the National Health Mission for online and offline training. Around 150 personnel from de-addiction centres supported by the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment are also expected to undergo in-person training over the next two months.Nadda said fragmented efforts among government departments had created gaps in coordination and service delivery. Effective implementation of the narcotic control strategy, he said, would require clearly defined responsibilities, sustained inter-ministerial coordination and collective accountability. He also stressed the need to strengthen de-addiction centres through training, institutional support and adequate resources.
At the launch, Nadda released the second edition of Substance Use Disorder: Manual for Physicians (Management of Addictive Disorders). First published in 2005, the revised manual incorporates advances in the understanding and treatment of addiction and is intended to help doctors manage substance use disorders in both specialised facilities and general healthcare settings.The initiative follows the Vision Document on Narcotic Control unveiled by Union home minister Amit Shah in June 2026. Besides enforcement against drug trafficking, the strategy assigns the health ministry the task of expanding access to evidence-based addiction treatment by strengthening the skills of medical and allied healthcare personnel.Officials said the programme would draw on the clinical expertise and training infrastructure of the six institutions to improve the availability and quality of addiction care across states and Union territories.

Her deep dives into heritage topics are well-researched, resulting in captivating narratives that resonate with her audience. Russia's assault on Ukraine's energy grid is a war crime, UN says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:05:16 UTC
15:05:16 KST

The United Nations has determined that Russia's frequent and intentional attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure constitute a war crime, a U.N. inquiry report said on Oct. 26.
In recent months, Russian forces have strategically escalated attacks on Ukraine's energy grid in the lead up to the freezing winter months to wipe out power plants, substations, and gas infrastructure, despite U.S. President Donald Trump having called for an energy ceasefire.
"Russian commanders ordering the attacks had the knowledge that the heating facilities they targeted in large civilian agglomerations were indispensable to the civilian population, in particular during the winter," a report from the UN's Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine concludes.
Last winter, the Kremlin also focused its attacks on energy sources, leaving millions of Ukrainians without power in temperatures as low as minus 21°C.
Based on interviews with 255 people who endured these conditions across Ukraine, the commission concluded that "Russian authorities have committed the crimes against humanity of other inhumane acts."
One interviewed man described how, during winter, he would attempt remain awake through the night out of fear of falling asleep and dying from the cold. "The scariest thing was to fall asleep and not to wake up; it was like torture to be scared of dying from cold," he said.
"The waves of attacks by Russian authorities against Ukraine's energy infrastructure were carried out with intent and pursuant to a state policy to deprive the civilian population from essential energy supplies and cause suffering," the report outlines.
In addition, the report outlines how Russia's recruitment of soldiers from third countries also violates human rights law. Recruitment from 29 other countries through lies and coercion counts as human trafficking, the report finds.

Court rejects eastern border bunker procurement tender appeal
The Supreme Court of Estonia on Monday rejected a company's appeal challenging the tender to procure concrete bunkers to be installed along Estonia's eastern border.
The court decided on Monday not to hear a cassation appeal by Nordic Shield Group AB, in which the company sought to challenge a tender organized by the Estonian Center for Defense Investments (RKIK) for the procurement of concrete bunkers.
RKIK's Baltic Defense Line project manager Armin Siilivask told ERR that Monday's court decision means the procurement process can now proceed.
"Now that the court has made its decision, our aim is to continue with the procurement according to the planned schedule, so that we can, if possible, reach the signing of a contract as early as March next year. To do this, the necessary procurement procedures must be carried out: conducting bidding rounds, holding negotiations, carrying out checks and evaluations and, if everything goes smoothly, signing a contract with a suitable bidder," Siilivask said.
Nordic Shield Group's appeal focused on the tender's production quality standard and the required ISO certificate.
RKIK said the certificate submitted by Nordic Shield Group did not meet the requirements set out in the tender conditions.
Estonia's aim is to install 600 concrete bunkers along its eastern border by the end of 2027 as part of the Baltic Defense Line. RKIK announced a tender for the procurement of the bunkers in 2025.

====================================================================================================

Animal panic and air pollution: Why Switzerland is set to vote on a nationwide firework ban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:02:12 UTC
15:02:12 KST

Fireworks were banned in the Netherlands earlier this year on safety and environmental grounds.
Swiss citizens are gearing up for an explosive vote: whether to ban noisy fireworks.
Spurred on by animal welfare and environmental groups, the citizen-proposed ‘popular initiative’ will be put to the ballot on 29 November.
“For pets, wild animals, and farm animals, fireworks are not a celebration, but pure stress,” says non-profit Schweizer Tierschutz STS (Swiss Animal Protection), which is supporting the initiative.
The proposal also calls for better protection for people and the natural environment against noise, air pollution, litter, accidents and fires caused by fireworks.
An initial Swiss Broadcasting Corporation (SBC) poll released on Friday (23 October) showed promising support for the ban, with 69 per cent of voters backing it.
While the proposal proved most popular among left-wing voters, it received majority support across the political spectrum, and particularly among women.
Votes like these are common in Switzerland, where any citizen or group can launch an initiative by gaining 100,000 valid signatures from eligible voters. Recent examples include the neutrality initiative, rejected in September, and the pending nuclear disarmament initiative.
Would it mean a complete ban on fireworks in Switzerland?
The proposal seeks to “significantly restrict particularly loud and disruptive fireworks” in private settings by banning the sale of noisy pyrotechnics. Quieter alternatives would still be permitted, such as sparklers and fountain-style volcano fireworks.
It would also allow ‘cantons’ (local areas) to grant exemptions for events of “supra-regional significance”, such as 1 August (Swiss National Day) and New Year’s Eve, but still with a focus on quieter alternatives.
Currently, Swiss cantons and communes may restrict or ban the sale and use of fireworks on a local level. Age limits and licensing requirements also govern their use.
STS says the initiative, ‘For a restriction on fireworks’, would create a clear rule for the entire country.
But industry association the Swiss Fireworks Coordination Office (SFK) argues that the proposal is a “threat to Swiss tradition”, while some politicians have said that it would infringe on citizens’ personal freedoms and should be left up to the cantons to govern.
The Swiss People’s Party, the Centre Party and the Swiss Trade Association have launched a campaign to vote against the measure, warning of its impact on business owners and potential to fuel a "prohibition culture".
After initially being submitted in 2023, the proposal received over 137,000 signatures. A failed counter-proposal in summer means it will now be followed by a public vote.
If successful, it could see Switzerland follow in the footsteps of the Netherlands, where a broader firework ban came into force this summer, primarily for safety reasons but also on animal and environmental welfare grounds. Other countries in Europe have their own rules and restrictions, such as Belgium where the use of large, powerful fireworks is restricted to professionals only.
How do fireworks impact the environment?
When fireworks explode, they release tiny dust particles, which are rich in toxic metals from the gunpowder and colouring compounds they contain.
According to the Swiss Federal Office of Police, between 1,000 and 2,000 tonnes of fireworks – three-quarters of which is made up of packaging – are used annually in Switzerland, producing between 200 and 400 tonnes of particulate matter per year.
This accounts for two-to-three per cent of the country’s annual particulate matter emissions, according to the Federal Office for the Environment (FOEN).
As well as contributing to air, water and soil pollution, these fine particles can be inhaled with harmful health impacts, particularly for vulnerable people with existing conditions.
Unfavourable weather conditions can heighten the harms, such as fog which can trap particles in the air for longer, or hot and dry conditions which can increase wildfire risk.
FOEN urges responsible disposal of used fireworks, which can be placed in regular household waste once cooled down, while packaging should be recycled as normal.
Fireworks trigger ‘fear, panic and disorientation’
Animal welfare groups have been vocal in their support of a firework ban.
“The sudden noise triggers fear, panic, and disorientation [in animals],” says STS. “The consequences range from flight behaviour and acute stress to injuries or even death. Protecting animals from unnecessary noise is therefore a central concern of animal welfare.”
Speaking in a campaign video for the initiative, Swiss veterinarian Maruschka Blaser says that animals hear high-pitched sounds and loud bangs more acutely than humans. Giving horses as an example, she says “things can become dangerous very quickly when they run uncontrollably because of fireworks”, either for people in crowds or other animals in fields.
“When it comes to domestic animals such as cats and dogs, they sometimes need to be given medication to calm them down days in advance” of firework displays, says Blaser. “I also know families who spend the night in an air-raid shelter with their pets, but somehow that isn’t a solution either,” she adds.
“Millions of pets live in Switzerland. For many of them, fireworks trigger stress or panic,” says Casimir von Arx, President of the Bern branch of Schweizer Tierschutz STS (Swiss Animal Protection SAP) in a campaign video. “We can only protect them if, as a society, we show consideration for one another.”

BISHKEK, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- The Communist Party of China (CPC) possesses unique qualities that enable effective long-term governance of China, an experience a Kyrgyz political analyst said is enlightening and inspiring to other nations.
Noting that the fifth plenary session of the 20th Central Committee of the CPC focuses on strengthening full and rigorous Party self-governance, Mars Sariev believes that the core, unique advantages that underpin the CPC's long-term governance include strict Party discipline, a high sense of political responsibility, a resolute anti-corruption drive, and a commitment to maintaining the integrity of its personnel.
"For the CPC, this is of fundamental importance," Sariev said. "A party that aspires to govern a nation for the long term cannot allow private interests to infiltrate its political decision-making system."
Sariev believes the CPC's governance experience is particularly worth studying because it implements its policies in a consistent, systematic way.
Using the CPC's anti-corruption campaign as an example, he noted that the effort remains ongoing rather than temporary.
"Corruption is capable of adapting to changing realities, which is why the system of oversight must also be constantly refined and improved," he added.
He believes another important lesson from the CPC's experience is its strong emphasis on training highly qualified personnel.
"For long-term governance, what matters is not only the professional competence of officials, but also their personal integrity, their ability to adhere to discipline, and their willingness to prioritize long-term national interests over short-term personal gain," he noted.
In Sariev's view, the CPC's ongoing pursuit of and a commitment to "self-reform" are also vital.
"The Party's 'self-reform' reflects the system's ability to regularly eliminate factors that could lead to its gradual degradation over time," he said.
Sariev added that this process involves not only combating corruption but also fighting unnecessary formalities, bureaucratism, hedonism and extravagance to prevent them from escalating into corruption. ■
