Dating costs in Europe: Which cities are cheapest and most expensive?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:00:48 UTC
15:00:48 KST

Dating can be costly across Europe. Some cities are incredibly expensive, but the picture changes when salaries are taken into account.
Do you think about money when planning a date? And does your financial situation affect whether you feel ready to start a relationship?
Romance is not only about feelings. Dating also costs money. A coffee, a drink or a dinner can put pressure on your wallet. And for some people, money may affect not only where they go on a date, but whether they want to start a relationship at all.
So, how much does dating cost across Europe? The answer varies widely from city to city according to the Mapping the World’s Prices 2026 report, published by Deutsche Bank Research Institute.
What is included in the Cheap Date Index?
The Cheap Date Index includes one bottle of wine, one pair of jeans, one dress, two coffees, one meal for two people in a mid-range restaurant, two cinema tickets, two one-way public transport tickets and a 5km taxi trip.
As the index includes a pair of jeans and a dress, clothing can account for a large share of the total cost. So, it may not reflect only the cost of the date itself.
The prices come from Numbeo, which is not an official data source. Its prices are crowdsourced from users.
Switzerland most expensive, Turkey cheapest
Among 28 European cities, two Swiss cities rank at the top. The cost of this date basket is €407 in Geneva, and Zurich closely follows at €400.
Istanbul is the cheapest city for a date, but the basket still costs €168. It also costs less than €200 in the Italian capital, Rome (€195).
The simple average across the 28 cities is €270. The figures reflect prices in mid-2026.
Dating is also quite expensive in the Nordic countries. Oslo and Copenhagen share third place at €323. Stockholm ranks sixth at €310, while Helsinki is eighth at €296.
The UK is more expensive than other major economies
Among Europe’s largest economies, London is the most expensive city at €317. Another British city, Birmingham, is also in the top 10 at €290.
Paris is close to the European average at €279. In Italy, the date basket costs €278 in Milan but just €195 in Rome, showing significant differences within countries.
The three German cities on the list are all below the European average and very close to each other. A date costs €260 in Munich and €254 in both Berlin and Frankfurt.
The two Spanish cities are also among the cheapest. The date basket costs €219 in Madrid and €213 in Barcelona.
Among other cities, the cost is €294 in Dublin, €290 in Edinburgh, €271 in Brussels, €263 in Amsterdam, €250 in Vienna, and €225 in Warsaw and Lisbon. It is €222 in Athens and €214 in Prague.
Europe at the top
Eight of the 10 most expensive cities are in Europe. Europe also has 14 of the top 20 and 20 of the top 30. Istanbul is the only European city among the 20 cheapest.
A cheap date costs €270 on average across the 28 European cities whereas it costs €195 in the other 41 cities.
Globally, Tel Aviv-Yafo ranks third at €365 and is the only non-European city in the top five.
New York ranks eighth (€308), Los Angeles 13th (€288) and San Francisco 14th (€281). Sydney (€270) is close to Amsterdam (€263), while Dubai (€243) is close to Berlin (€254). Singapore and Madrid both cost €219.
Tokyo (€161) and Seoul (€163) are cheaper than Istanbul (€168). Hong Kong (€196) is also close to Rome (€195).
When income is considered, the rankings reverse
The nominal prices alone tell only half the story. Zurich and Geneva have the most expensive cheap dates, but they also have the highest salaries. That means a date takes the smallest bite out of pay there: 5.6% of a monthly net salary in Zurich and 6.4% in Geneva.
Luxembourg (6.6%), Amsterdam (6.7%) and Frankfurt (7.2%) follow.
The picture reverses in southern and central Europe. A cheap date in Athens costs €222. This is just over half the price in Zurich. Yet it takes 19.6% of an average monthly net salary of €1,132, the highest share among the 28 European cities. Istanbul (16.7%), Lisbon (16.3%) and Budapest (15.6%) come next.
The salary figures are city-level estimates from Numbeo cited by Deutsche Bank. Still, they are broadly in line with the shares calculated using Eurostat’s annual net earnings for a single person without children earning the average wage. Eurostat figures are national averages, rather than city-level data.
Using Eurostat data, the share of the date cost would be 7.2 percentage points lower in Athens at 12.4%. In Lisbon, it would be 12.6%, rather than 16.3% using Numbeo’s salary estimate.
Examining the link between income and readiness for a relationship using US data, Johanna Peetz and Geoff MacDonald found that the financial well-being of young adults is linked with romantic desire, perceived readiness for relationships, and actual transitioning into intimate partnerships.
Chen-Hao Hsu and Henriette Engelhardt also found that temporary employment and unemployment negatively affected the probability of union formation for single women and men in Europe.
Another study found that temporary employment and unemployment negatively affected the probability of union formation for single women and men in Europe.

Seeking guaranteed snow? These are Europe’s most reliable ski resorts and regions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:00:32 UTC
15:00:32 KST

A new study has ranked Europe’s most reliable ski resorts and regions. Here are the top destinations to consider for your next active winter getaway.
Choosing where to go on a ski holiday involves more than finding a great resort, especially if you have a need for speed, slopes and adventure.
Snow conditions, the reliability of snowfall throughout the season and whether lifts and slopes are open can make a huge difference to your ski holiday.
Although no destination can completely promise perfect conditions, Inghams Ski has analysed more than 100 popular ski resorts and regions in the Northern Hemisphere to create the “Reliable Ski Score” ranking, with scores out of 100.
The travel operator measured each resort for mountain running (35%), which looked at the average percentage of lifts and slopes operating during the core season; and for snow adequacy (25%), which looked at the percentage of core-season days with 30cm or more at the base station.
Other factors included consistency (20%), or how steady mountain running was from season to season; downside protection (12%), which is the gap between the average season and the worst one; as well as average snow depth of the mountain (8%).
Each resort and region’s historical performance was studied during the core season period of 5 January to 20 March across seven Northern Hemisphere winter seasons between 2017-2018 and 2025-2026, with the exception of the seasons impacted by Covid-19.
The results see Italian, Austrian and French destinations dominate the top 10 ranking of Europe’s most reliable ski resorts and regions.
Top 10 most reliable ski resorts and regions in Europe
How the destinations scored out of 100 in the study:
- 1. Pontedilegno-Tonale, Italy: 93.1
- 2. Obertauern, Austria: 92.9
- 3. Les Arcs, France: 92.2
- 4. Les 3 Vallées, France: 91.1
- 5. Alpe d’Huez, France: 90.5
- 6. Kitzsteinhorn, Austria: 89.6
- 7. Filzmoos, Austria: 89.5
- 8. Tignes-Val d'Isère, France: 89.4
- 9. Espace San Bernardo (La Rosière/La Thuile), France: 89.2
- 10. Damüls Mellau, Austria: 89.1
A look at the top three most reliable ski resorts and regions
Pontedilegno-Tonale, Italy
According to the Inghams study, Pontedilegno-Tonale in northern Italy is Europe’s most reliable region for skiing.
The mountainous area between Valle Camonica in Lombardy and Val di Sole in Trentino is a standout destination for its glaciers, nature reserves and high-altitude areas. It was highlighted for its consistent performance across reliability factors, giving skiers “practically hiccup-free exploring alongside snow-sure slopes”.
The ski area is home to 46 slopes, with the highest point of the resort sitting at 3,016 metres above sea level. Ponte di Legno’s slopes take skiers through dense pine and spruce forest, while Passo del Tonale sits at the foot of the Presena glacier and the skiing area features more than 44km of slopes.
During selected dates of the ski season, Inghams recommends taking advantage of the “Alba in Quota”, or “dawn at high altitude” window of opportunity. Here, lifts open earlier for skiers to experience sunrise skiing before the slopes officially open for the day.
Obertauern, Austria
In Austria’s Salzburg region, at 1,752 metres, the Obertauern ski resort emerged as the second most reliable in Europe.
It offers beginners and advanced skiers alike more than 100km of slopes across a long season from November through to May. And, as Inghams highlighted, the area is made up entirely of ski-in/ski-out hotels, giving visitors direct access to pistes from their accommodation.
Obertauern is also replete with cross-country ski trails, with routes ranging from six to 23km, including the medium-difficulty Gnadenalm. At an altitude of 1,350 metres, the trail sits halfway between Obertauern and Untertauern, earning the name "snow basin" because of its unique location.
Les Arcs, France
Rounding up the top three is Les Arcs. The French ski resort nestled in the heart of the Alps is set amid alpine meadows, glaciers and a peak that reaches 3,226 metres.
The mountain resort features 200km of ski trails with a winter season set to start on 12 December this year and will last until 24 April 2027.
Part of Paradiski, one of the world’s largest interconnected ski areas, Les Arcs is described as an “excellent choice for both freestyle enthusiasts as well as those looking for reliable conditions”. Les Arcs is also connected to Peisey-Vallandry and La Plagne via the iconic Vanoise Express cable car. Paradiski features 425km of slopes and 258 ski runs between the three linked resorts.

Ukraine's €70 billion shortfall could make or break the next EU budget
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:00:28 UTC
15:00:28 KST

Brussels faces a highly charged mix as the fight over the next EU budget overlaps with the efforts to plug Ukraine's €70 billion gap.
The fight over the European Union's next seven-year budget has entered a critical new phase, one that could make or break the deal.
In a striking coincidence, the heated negotiations have overlapped with the effort to fill Ukraine's €70 billion shortfall for 2027.
Brussels had long suspected that Kyiv's accounts would show a sizable gap next year, as Russia escalates its war and devastates the levers of the domestic economy. But it was not until this month's summit that the €70 billion figure was validated.
Leaders then asked the European Commission to present possible options for providing the additional financing, with joint debt immediately emerging as the most feasible path.
The bloc is expected to cover two-thirds of the request, roughly €46 billion. Other allies, such as the UK, Canada, Norway and Japan, should take up the rest.
The vast scale of the deficit prompted a change of agenda in next month's special summit, which was originally planned to focus exclusively on the draft budget.
The meeting has been extended to two days, 26 and 27 November, to accommodate discussions on Ukraine. Fresh proposals are expected on both fronts.
Technically, the two issues remain separate files. But politically, diplomats and officials say, they are becoming rapidly intertwined.
"These are the most pressing issues for the remainder of the year, definitely," a diplomat said, cautioning it was still too early to talk about one big package.
Two key reasons explain the entanglement.
First, the two are about money.
The budget battle pits the so-called “Frugals”, or “Sensible Six”, against the “Friends of Cohesion”, with the two camps clashing over which budget envelopes should be cut and by how much. The "Frugals", which happen to be the net payers, demand steep reductions across the board, while the "Friends" want to preserve bigger volumes.
Second, the two face a pressing deadline set by the French election.
Marine Le Pen, the candidate of the far-right National Rally, who is firmly ahead in polls, has vowed to cap her country's contribution to the budget at €5 billion a year and warned sealing a deal before the election would be a "democratic scandal".
The incumbent, Emmanuel Macron, told his fellow leaders that reaching a deal between January and April would be "complicated".
The same logic now applies to Ukraine. As part of her programme, Le Pen has promised to halt all French support for the war-weary country.
"This funding will stop, and it is a matter of honesty to tell (Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy) the truth," she said earlier this month.
Easier or harder?
The prospect of a Le Pen win in the spring weighs heavily on officials and diplomats in Brussels, who admit both open issues – the budget and Ukraine – must be resolved by the end of the year before the window of opportunity closes.
The closer the election, the narrower the space for high-stakes decisions.
"Our internal cohesion is fragile. If that starts to unravel, the consequences for Ukraine could be even greater than anything Trump says or does," a national official said, referring to the US president's recent shift to Russia.
"We need a structural solution for financing Ukraine. We can't keep scrambling at the end of every year under pressure. Support for Kyiv needs to be properly built into the next budget. It's good that these discussions are coming together in November."
However, it is not yet clear whether Ukraine would make it easier or harder to agree on the budget, which remains stuck in maximalist red lines from the opposing camps.
One school of thought holds that reaching a deal may be easier because the “Frugals” includes some of Ukraine's largest bilateral donors – Denmark, Finland, the Netherlands, Sweden and Germany – who have a vested interest in locking in the fresh funding.
A strong collective decision on Ukraine could make it more politically palatable for them to accept – or rather, tolerate – a bigger budget than they might have wished.
"It might be helpful to get it done," another diplomat said.
But an alternative view is that the “Frugals’” continued push to cut funding for agriculture and cohesion policies could make it impossible for some “Friends of Cohesion” to back a deal on Ukraine without triggering a backlash at home.
The Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia are signalling they will exempt themselves from any joint debt to support Kyiv. Bulgaria, a vocal critic of weapons deliveries, is expected to follow suit. All of them sit in the cohesion group.
Making matters more difficult, the talks will unfold against a bleak backdrop of elevated energy prices, high borrowing costs and public discontent across Europe.
"It would be very dangerous, and I want to make this absolutely clear, if anyone tried to link the financing of Ukraine to the budget," Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico said.
"It would be a miracle if we reached an agreement in December."

Ukrainian media face pressure as they step up scrutiny of authorities in wartime
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:00:17 UTC
15:00:17 KST

How free is Ukraine's press in wartime?
President Volodymyr Zelensky speaks during a press briefing in Kyiv, Ukraine, on April 22, 2025. The president has not had a major press conference open to all media since February 2025. (Evgeniy Maloletka / AP)
Over the past year, Ukrainian independent media have stepped up investigations into corruption among top officials and abuse in the military, despite the constraints and risks of Russia’s full-scale invasion.
Yet this work is coming at a cost. Ukrainian media have faced a wave of lawsuits, controversial court rulings, threats, and smear campaigns on social media.
"An environment is gradually taking shape in which it is becoming increasingly difficult for journalists to do their jobs," Inna Vedernikova, a journalist at the Ukrainian newspaper Dzerkalo Tyzhnia, told the Kyiv Independent. "The space for freedom of speech is shrinking."
Despite the pressure and nearly five years of working under the full-scale invasion and martial law, the journalistic community remains robust. In the Reporters Without Borders' 2026 World Press Freedom Index, Ukraine climbed seven places to 55th worldwide — above the U.S. and some European countries.
But Ukrainian journalists and editors describe a less optimistic reality, pointing to persistent threats that make it difficult to hold power to account.
From wartime consensus to scrutiny
When Russia’s full-scale invasion began in 2022, Ukrainian journalists put the criticism of the government on hold, as the country rallied behind the war effort.
"(The war) has led to an unprecedented rise in self-censorship," Yurii Nikolov, a journalist at the media outlet Nashi Hroshi, told the Kyiv Independent.
In their turn, the authorities were expected to play by the rules and act responsibly.
At the same time, to unify the nation’s media policy amid the invasion, the authorities also merged all major television channels into one state-controlled pool. It has stayed that way ever since.
But several months into the invasion, the wartime consensus began to unravel. The first corruption investigations appeared before the end of 2022.
In recent years, a series of major corruption scandals has erupted, prompting independent journalists to step up their scrutiny of the government and bringing criticism of the authorities back into the public sphere.
Vedernikova said, despite the invasion, "it quickly became clear that a journalist's role — asking direct questions and pointing out problems — had not gone away."
As independent media resumed their investigations, those under scrutiny began to retaliate.
After a series of scandals in 2023-2024, when some journalists faced surveillance and persecution by law enforcement, the pressure shifted toward other arenas, including the courts and online smear campaigns.
Inna Biletska, head of investigations at the public broadcaster Suspilne, said that “the underreformed law enforcement sector and judiciary create fertile ground for those implicated in investigative reporting to push back."
There is also a growing number of SLAPP lawsuits (Strategic Lawsuits Against Public Participation), according to Kateryna Dyachuk, head of freedom of speech monitoring at the Institute of Mass Information, a non-profit watchdog tracking press freedom.
Courts and lawmakers
The most direct pushback has come through the courts and parliament, and it risks changing what journalists can publish.
One of the defining moments came in July, when a Ukrainian court banned the Anti-Corruption Action Center, the media outlet Slidstvo.info, and journalist Alina Stryzhak from publishing a specific investigative report. The report focused on the brother of Oleksiy Sukhachov, head of the State Investigation Bureau. It exposed him as the owner of a staggering real estate portfolio.
Although courts had previously upheld libel lawsuits against Ukrainian media, a ban on an investigative report before publication appeared to be unprecedented.
Maksym Savchuk, a journalist at Slidstvo.info and a co-author of the report, said the ban did not apply to him, so he sent the investigation to other media for publication. It was published by 27 other outlets in an organized effort.
"The investigation that the court tried to suppress went on to receive 4 million views, and I doubt it would have reached anything close to that number had it not been for the court order and the publicity surrounding it,” Savchuk told the Kyiv Independent.
Libel suits have long been a tool of pressure. Hromadske’s head of investigations, Yaroslava Volvach, said the outlet faced enormous pressure from the late Andriy Portnov, a former ally of pro-Russian ex-President Viktor Yanukovych who was widely seen as wielding immense influence over Ukraine’s judiciary.
In 2023-2024, Portnov sued both Hromadske and the Kyiv Independent’s editor-in-chief for libel. Lower courts initially upheld the suits, but the Supreme Court rejected them in May 2026. Portnov was shot dead in Madrid in May 2025.
Another blow to free speech came in October 2025, when the Supreme Court restricted what media can report about criminal cases. Back then, the court banned Dzerkalo Tyzhnia from naming a suspect in a criminal case and ordered the outlet to remove his name.
In August, Dzerkalo Tyzhnia reported that Dmytro Borzykh, a lawyer and former prosecutor, was also seeking a court order barring the publication of his name as a suspect until a guilty verdict against him enters into force.
"This approach is fundamentally at odds with European standards," Dzerkalo Tyzhnia’s Vedernikova said. "A journalist cannot declare someone guilty of a crime before a court has convicted them. But informing the public that a specific person has formally been named a suspect by law enforcement… is an entirely different matter."
Parliament may add to the pressure.
In April 2026, the Ukrainian parliament approved a draft of a new Civil Code in the first reading. The draft would allow individuals to request the removal of information about them from search engines and databases if it has "ceased to be of public interest."
A separate clause would introduce the concept of a company's “digital image" and require the company’s consent for data processing. This could make due diligence harder and limit corporate transparency.
"If journalists once investigated something — a corruption case, for example — all of that material would eventually have to be removed from the internet altogether," Dyachuk said.
The draft of the new Civil Code was met with public outcry over several controversial provisions. It is still being revised, and no final vote has been scheduled.
Risks of investigating the military
Investigating abuse in the military has brought a different kind of pressure: direct threats, often with little response from law enforcement.
In February, the Kyiv Independent and the Brazilian TV channel SBT published an investigation into alleged abuse and torture within a Brazilian unit of Ukraine’s International Legion, which led to the death of a Brazilian recruit. The same month, the unit’s commander threatened journalists from both outlets, accusing them of taking money from Russia and saying they would be “identified” and “located.” Ukraine’s military intelligence (HUR), which oversees the unit, said in March that the unit’s command had ordered a probe into the threats.
In a separate incident, a Security Service (SBU) official came to Kyiv Independent CEO Daryna Shevchenko’s apartment building in September 2025 and attempted to collect information about her. The SBU said the official’s activities were not linked to Shevchenko, and that it was a misunderstanding. A month earlier, the Kyiv Independent published an investigative story about Fire Point, Ukraine’s biggest new defense producer, and the company’s management threatened to report journalists to the SBU over it.
Other outlets have faced the same and more.
In June, the Ukrainian media outlet Babel published a report on alleged excessive battlefield losses, inadequate medical care, coercion, and physical abuse at the Skelia assault unit.
Following the publication, Mykola Kharkhan, a soldier at the unit, released a video accusing the author of the report of working for Russian money and saying such reports would not stay "unpunished.” Skelia's press office said that such threats are unacceptable.
Kateryna Kobernyk, Babel's chief editor, told the Kyiv Independent that the outlet is mostly afraid not of Skelia's leadership but of "retaliation and unpredictable behavior by specific individuals within Skelia."
Babel said in July that it had reported the threat to the State Investigation Bureau and the police, who initially failed to react and open a criminal case. The bureau later said it had opened an investigation.
"I believe that, from what I know, law enforcement agencies are currently working very slowly and somewhat unprofessionally," Kobernyk said about the case.
Also in July, the State Investigation Bureau searched the facilities of drone maker Vyriy, whose co-founder Oleksii Babenko holds a 75% stake in Babel. Some interpreted the searches as an effort to pressure Babel, although Babenko himself denied this.
Kobernyk said that Babel's editorial operations are independent of Babenko but "Babel's reporting may have served as a trigger" in an attempt to deal a blow to Vyriy.
The Kyiv Independent has requested comment from the State Investigation Bureau.
Ukrainian freelance journalist Anna Kaliuzhna, who covers the front line, has faced pressure over her investigations of the military.
Kaliuzhna said she had received death threats in 2024 from a battalion commander at the 3rd Assault Corps, after she accused the brigade's leadership of using its political influence to get better battlefield conditions.
The police investigation into the threats "is not making any progress," she said.
"They haven't questioned any of these people or ordered any forensic examinations to confirm that the messages were actually sent from those phones," Kaliuzhna told the Kyiv Independent. "No one has been charged."
In March 2026, Kaliuzhna published a post criticizing alleged violations at the Skelia and 225th Assault Regiments. She said she had received around 150 messages pressuring and insulting her from fighters of the two regiments.
In July, the Ukrainian outlet Texty published her investigation into the 225th, alleging soldiers were beaten, shot at, jailed, and even killed. Both regiments said they could not comment. The police told the Kyiv Independent they are investigating the threats, but no charges have been brought yet.
The Kyiv Independent has also requested comment from the 3rd Assault Corps.
"I just hate the fact that I don't feel any safer behind the front lines than I do at the front," Kaliuzhna said.
Conscription as leverage
The authorities also have quieter tools, and conscription is one of them. A number of media outlets, including independent ones, have the “critically important” status, granted by the government, which allows them to obtain draft exemptions for their staff. So far no independent media outlet has lost that status, but some fear it could become a pressure tool.
“We have seen the fact that Ukrainska Pravda has critical infrastructure status… increasingly used in the rhetoric of Telegram channels and bloggers affiliated with the authorities, as well as by bots on social media,” Andriy Boborykin, CEO of the Ukrainska Pravda media outlet, told the Kyiv Independent. “It was entirely predictable that the conscription exemptions granted to journalists at independent media outlets would become a target for manipulation.”
In the past, officials have used conscription as a means of exerting pressure on the media.
In 2024, military enlistment officials attempted to draft Yevheniy Shulhat, then a journalist at Slidtsvo.Info who was investigating the wealth of a top SBU official. The media outlet identified that the enlistment officers were getting instructions from a subordinate of the SBU official Shulhat was investigating.
A green light to disregard media
President Volodymyr Zelensky and his office have also come under fire for failing to communicate with the media about policy changes, corruption scandals, and other pressing domestic issues.
The president and his office often ignore journalists’ requests for comment, and Zelensky does not give interviews to independent Ukrainian media. Instead, the president opts to send voice messages via a WhatsApp group chat with reporters run by his team and to hold closed-door briefings with groups of journalist. (Editor's note: The Kyiv Independent is often invited to these briefings). After a briefing, Zelensky’s team picks which quotes can be published, with the rest being off-limits.
According to two people who have long worked with the president, he doesn’t want to face anticipated questions about corruption, domestic political crises, and reforms that would arise in a sit-down interview with independent Ukrainian media.
The last time Zelensky held a major press conference was in February 2025. In August, Ukrainian journalist Danylo Mokryk, a reporter with the Kyiv Independent’s War Crimes Investigations Unit, filed a petition for Zelensky to hold a press conference and invite independent media. The petition was blocked for unclear reasons. Several more petitions were filed by Mokryk’s followers, until eventually one was accepted and published. It gathered the necessary 25,000 votes in late September, giving the president 10 working days to respond. Zelensky ignored the petition.
“The country’s current leadership is trying to create an environment in which the doors are closed to journalists who criticize the government and point out its mistakes,” Savchuk said.
Yevhen Buderatskyi, a deputy chief editor at Ukrainska Pravda, said that the outlet “has no access to government officials.”
“They keep telling us that the President’s Office doesn’t really allow them to talk to us,” he added. “It’s difficult to obtain information. It’s hard to speak of any real progress for freedom of speech.”
The President’s Office has not responded to the Kyiv Independent’s request for comment.
Smear campaigns online
Another threat to journalists comes from social media.
Telegram, one of the most popular sources of news for Ukrainians, is often used for smear campaigns against journalists and activists, and some of the channels are reportedly linked to the authorities and top officials.
“Telegram channels can reach huge audiences and say virtually anything they want,” Dyachuk said. “They can take money to publish paid-for content, while at the same time facing no real accountability for the information they put out.”
Sevgil Musayeva, chief editor of Ukrainska Pravda, also told the Kyiv Independent that the outlet “is very often targeted by online bots or supporters of various political parties.”
Difficulties with funding
Financing independent journalism is another challenge.
A major blow to Ukrainian journalism came in 2025, when U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration ended most of the projects of the United States Agency for International Development (USAID). USAID had been a major source of funding for many Ukrainian independent media.
Journalists interviewed by the Kyiv Independent said, however, that they had adapted by shifting their focus to European grants and other sources of funding.
Another source of funding — the advertising market — has shrunk due to the war. But advertisers have also faced political pressure.
Musayeva said in 2024 that the President’s Office had been pressuring advertisers to stop dealing with her outlet. In June 2026 she said that the pressure had ceased after Andriy Yermak, then Zelensky’s chief of staff, was forced to resign in November 2025.
The ousting of Yermak revealed one of the stranger attempts to pressure journalists. At his arrest hearing in 2026, prosecutors revealed that the former head of Zelensky’s office texted his psychic the names of Musayeva and another Ukrainska Pravda journalist, in what appeared to be a request to curse them.
Musayeva also said in 2024 that Ukrainska Pravda’s owner Tomas Fiala had received offers to sell the outlet, and that she believed it to be a form of pressure by the authorities.
“The pressure (on the media) is growing, and the most frightening thing is that it is becoming the norm,” Musayeva told the Kyiv Independent.
“You don’t even take these threats seriously anymore because they are essentially constant.”

Landowners could scupper free Land Registry access plans, campaigners warn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:00:04 UTC
15:00:04 KST

Plans by the government to give the public free access for the first time to information on who owns England’s land are at risk of being scuppered by landowners, campaigners have said.
On Tuesday the government set out its proposals to lift the paywall on the Land Registry, arguing that opening it would help the UK build more houses, protect nature and improve strategic planning. The plans will be open to public consultation for eight weeks.
The Guardian has previously revealed that there are internal rifts between the government and the Land Registry – an “arm’s length body” that comes under the oversight of the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government but acts largely independently – over how far to open it to scrutiny.
Guy Shrubsole, author of Who Owns England?, urged people to get involved. “The government has put forward a bold but sensible proposal to open up the Land Registry and reveal who owns the vast majority of land in England and Wales – a question that goes back to the Domesday Book and has always been entwined with wealth and power,” he said.
“But the country’s biggest landowners may still try to scupper these plans at the last hurdle. It’s up to us peasants to stage the most gentle of revolts, by submitting our views to this public consultation.”
The proposals would for the first time allow public sector bodies, including government departments and local authorities, to access the information free of charge. This should make it easier for councils to identify sites for new homes, schools, hospitals, environmental assets, water infrastructure and public transport.
A new free public dataset would identify the owners of significant land-holdings, covering the vast majority of land in England and Wales, but excluding ordinary homeowners. More sensitive information might also be available to investigators, civil society groups and regulators who can demonstrate a clear public interest.
A government spokesperson said: “We are improving access to the Land Registry’s database to help fill in the gaps on who really owns land in England – with at least 10% currently unknown. By driving up land transparency we can make smarter decisions on building the homes and infrastructure we need, while delivering a crucial win-win for the economy and nature.”
Campaigners welcomed the move. Roger Mortlock, chief executive of the Campaign to Protect Rural England, said: “Our finite land supply is facing an unprecedented squeeze. Making it easier to find out who owns what will help us make the most of every hectare, whether for homes, infrastructure, food or nature’s recovery.”
Gavin Lane, president of the Country Land and Business Association, which represents landowners and rural businesses, warned of the possible impact of opening the register further.
“Making more personal information public could leave families vulnerable to fraud and other risks, especially as AI makes it easier to steal and misuse people’s identities,” Lane said. “Greater transparency should not come at the expense of people’s privacy, security and safety.”
Many landowners have been reluctant to have their holdings made public, and are likely to fight the proposals. Shrubsole said: “Centuries of secrecy over who owns our land might finally be coming to an end – but only if enough members of the public respond to this consultation.”

‘It’s the smell of freedom’: Belgrade cleans up after Student List triumph
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:00:04 UTC
15:00:04 KST

Student List cleaned up at Serbia’s parliamentary elections. So it was only fitting that the morning after a night of raucous celebrations, the movement’s supporters were gathering, bin bags in hand, at Pioneers Park, opposite the national assembly building in Belgrade.
For the previous 18 months, this small patch of greenery – with its established trees and playground – had been a no-go zone. A pro-government camp known as Ćaciland had taken over the space with convicted criminals living there in white tents, happy to attack journalists, or anyone else who came too close. Police stood by but did nothing to prevent the violence.
On election night, it seemed that thuggery might be on the cards again. Half an hour before the polls closed, large numbers of masked, black-clad men started gathering in and around Pioneers Park. Their intimidating presence gave credence to pre-poll predictions that the governing Serbian Progressive party (SNS) would not hand over power without a struggle.
What happened next took almost everyone by surprise. Shortly after the polls closed – and before any projections of the results had been published – Aleksandar Vučić told supporters at SNS headquarters that they had suffered a comprehensive defeat to the Student List. As cheers rang around the heart of Belgrade, he added that he did “not want unrest” or “anything like that on the streets”.
The riot police stood aside and the barriers blocking access to the area around Pioneers Park were removed. The goon squad made a rapid exit – and Student List supporters joyfully ransacked Ćaciland, setting fire to some of the tents.
But this is not a movement that likes to leave a mess. Over the two years of anti-corruption protests that led to the Student List’s victory, participants have always cleaned up after themselves. So the call went out for volunteers to restore Pioneers Park to something approaching its previous state.
Hundreds of people answered the appeal and joined municipal workers to remove the remains of Ćaciland. Some dismantled the mangled white tents, while others painstakingly cleaned and disinfected the climbing frames, swings and slides in the children’s playground.
Radomir Dalic painstakingly combed over the grass to remove cigarette butts and other rubbish. Apparently relishing his labours, he said he was overjoyed that the park was finally rid of “criminals with violent intentions towards us”.
“Yesterday was a big victory, so today is the smell of freedom,” he added. “We are in garbage, but it’s the smell of freedom.”
Tamara Tomic wore yellow rubber gloves for the occasion – and radiated similar pride in taking part. “Gathering here and cleaning this place just shows that we want to live nicely,” she said. “We want to enjoy the city, enjoy a normal life without violence and without anyone torturing us.”
For now, nobody is asking too many questions about how the Student List will govern. In fact, Serbian voters have taken something of a leap into the unknown – because this is a movement that operates unlike a traditional political party. It has no hierarchy and no leader. Its candidates were chosen by a series of student assemblies, with nominations ranging from academics to athletes, economists to engineers.
The Student List did publish an 11-point plan. Most of these points deal with anti-corruption measures – ironically, the pitch that secured victory in 2012 for Vučić and the SNS. Other commitments include judicial reform, media freedom, affordable housing and improved access to healthcare, with the promise of “a doctor in every village”.
But beyond the domestic priorities – in essence, a clean-up for public institutions – little is clear. The Student List went into the elections without naming a candidate for prime minister, let alone a possible cabinet.
Kurt Bassuener, co-founder of the Democratization Policy Council, said he was concerned about what that might mean when the euphoria of victory died down, and the serious business of forming a government began.
The thinktank chief added: “I’m hoping that there is a dream scenario plan here – they have portfolios and people who have credibility in particular issue areas and they can hit the ground running. Because the danger of a broad coalition like this is that the fissures will show soon after victory.”
Ilija Srdanović, the candidate ranked first on the Student List, has played down the potential for strife. A cardiologist at the university in Novi Sad, the city where a deadly roof collapse sparked the student protests, he has protested alongside the students since the early days. However, he was keen to emphasise that his ranking on the list did not mean he would become prime minister.
“The student movement is fully democratic,” he said, adding that the aim was to buck Serbia’s history of “creating the cult of personality or leadership”.
The 250 candidates on the Student List were “equal subjects in this struggle”, Srdanović insisted, with “numerous candidates who can be chosen for the prime minister position or any other position”.
But his confidence does little to reassure those who have noticed that the broad spread of views held by Student List candidates could lead to trouble. Despite Vučić’s warnings that a Student List government would impose sanctions on Russia and recognise Kosovo’s unilateral declaration of independence, the movement’s foreign and regional policy remains opaque.
“We have not seen seas of EU flags at demonstrations by students or the marches across Serbia,” said Michael Davenport, a former EU and UK ambassador to the country.
“There are massive policy areas where there is no consensus among the Student List or those have been elected. The approach towards accession to the European Union is not clear, nor is the position with regard to regional issues like Bosnia and Herzegovina and, very particularly, Kosovo.”
Many people are happy to leave these concerns for another day. Vučić and the SNS have fallen – and the cacophony of car horns continued throughout Monday as drivers passed the clean-up crew in Pioneers Park.
One visible symbol of the old regime has been swept away. The Student List voters are hoping more will follow.

‘It’s a better experience’: shoppers praise Oxford Street pedestrianisation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:00:04 UTC
15:00:04 KST

To the east of Oxford Circus, there is chaos. A steady stream of red London buses swing round the last junction before the newly pedestrianised Oxford Street begins. The streets are crammed with pedestrians, some squabbling over who poked whom with their umbrella first.
To the west, pedestrians walk freely through the temporary bollards on to a green welcome banner rolled along the tarmac, declaring Oxford Street traffic-free.
It may be a wetter Monday morning than London’s mayor would have dreamed of, but Sadiq Khan hailed it a “momentous day”. Almost a kilometre of the capital’s most famous shopping street has now been pedestrianised, banishing the buses, bikes, taxis, e-scooters and pedicabs along with private cars.
Shoppers who spoke to the Guardian shared their enthusiasm for Khan’s project, revelling in how the extra space to walk the street and browse the shops meant they were no longer crammed so tightly that they jostled one other off the pavement.
Daniel Te, who had moved to London from the US in July, was so moved by the scene that he whipped out his sketchpad to memorialise the moment. “I’m trying to capture the sheer mass of people going down the street,” he said, observing that despite the pedestrianisation, most people continued to walk on the pavement.
“It’s an entirely new place now, isn’t it?” he said. “My first impression was I remember getting off the Oxford Circus tube stop and seeing the scramble crossing and all the people walking around, and I was like, ‘wow, that’s really cool.’ So now to see the whole street become kind of like the scramble crossing is really exciting.”
Te added that on a typical day he would avoid the street because it was “too busy”. “Now there’s more space to walk around, I’m more inclined to come,” he said.
A former city planner, he considered it “a really big achievement when a street becomes pedestrianised”, adding that he would love to see neighbouring streets become car-free. “Covid taught us a lot about what we can do with our spaces,” he said, noting that although he thought the bus rerouting might make some journeys more inconvenient, “it’s a small price to pay”.
Raquel Cox, who was on holiday from Ireland, came to the street after watching a news item on the pedestrianisation. “We couldn’t believe it. We said, ‘We have to go there and experience it first-hand’.”
Although she acknowledged there could be negative impacts on the surrounding streets, which will become busier as a result, she felt that as a shopper, “it’s a better experience”.
After decades of discussion, the closure to traffic has come into effect in time for the busy Christmas shopping period, although the bigger transformation of the street – a £150m project including trees, seating and level “plazas” for events – will start taking shape from spring 2027.
Abbas Shigival, who runs a kiosk selling tourist souvenirs at the start of the pedestrianised section, said it would take time to determine the impact on his business, though he thought the morning had been a little busier than usual. “It’s a more pleasant environment,” he said. “People are happier because they can walk around.”
His views were echoed by Khan – whose first jobs were in retail in stores in the street – in a speech at John Lewis on Monday morning. The mayor said: “We’ve seen over the last couple of decades this street in decline … Pedestrianising the street with great public transport links, more greenery, more seating, will link to a better experience all round.”
The permanent plans will depend on feedback in the first phase and testing, and Khan said London “would be closely monitoring these changes to make sure they are working for everyone”. He added: “I want this to be a proof of concept – that investing in people rather than traffic leads to better footfall and spend.”
About half of the 1.2-mile (1.9km) street is now vehicle-free, roughly from Oxford Circus station to Marble Arch. Many of London’s doubledecker buses will now be diverted into neighbouring roads.
Claire Mann, the chief operating officer at Transport for London, said there would still be “plenty of capacity for passengers” and it should not affect reliability. “We’ll be monitoring to see if it does have an impact on ridership – but Bond Street and the Elizabeth Line does give you a way to arrive in style,” she said.
Not everyone agrees, however. Ben McMullan, a taxi driver, said traffic was “definitely worse on the surrounding streets, and accessibility is a huge problem”, noting that he had “got stuck in areas I wouldn’t have got stuck in before”.
He had already dropped off several customers that morning who had struggled with no direct access to the street by car, including a mother with a pram and a woman with walking difficulties. “I could only get her so far and she was really disappointed,” he said.
McMullan feared the change might have a negative impact on his business. “Once people realise they can’t get to where they need to go, I think automatically that just shuts them off from getting in the cab,” he said.
Jack* was one of many cyclists stopped by security guards over the course of the day as he cycled down the street, on his way home from a construction job. “I’ll be completely honest with you. I’m not going to listen to no one. I’m going to ride down this road, whether they like it or not,” he said, adding that an alternative route would make his commute longer. “It’s not going to work for me.”
He disagreed with pedestrianisation on principle. “We live with loads of low traffic neighbourhoods. It makes it harder for people to actually have vehicles.”
*Name has been changed.

My advice for Burnham’s first budget? Hit the banks – and hit them hard | Polly Toynbee
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:00:03 UTC
15:00:03 KST

Vibes matter. We live by how we feel – an idea that orthodox economics gets wrong and Andy Burnham’s first budget looks set to get right.
This walking good-vibes maestro is spreading a confetti of small good deeds. These may not shift the dial yet on 40 years of neoliberal economics, but they show the way he’s heading. Eyecatching everyday things – from capping bus fares to that small but resonant sum of £45 VAT on average off electricity bills – get people talking, alongside bigger plans for a national care service, electoral reform and a possible journey back to the EU.
Though his first budget is billed as unradical, one tax rise stands out for its Burnham vibes. After years of no penalties, no apologies, no payback for their bailout from the crash they caused, banks face a tax rise. The Tories’ cuts to the bank levy and bank profits surcharge were left in place by Rachel Reeves. No longer.
UK profits from the country’s four biggest banks were reportedly £13bn for the first half of this year, 16% up on last year.
Don’t undervalue the toughness it takes to ignore bankers’ intimidation, as the boss of their pressure group UK Finance writes to the chancellor saying a tax rise will encourage banks to move to competitor countries. The group’s claim that London has the highest bank taxes is a fabrication: only Ireland has a lower rate among western European countries. Paris’s is far higher, according to the authoritative Tax Policy Associates.
Jamie Dimon, the chief executive of JP Morgan, has said that any move against bank profits could cause him to scrap plans for a £3bn London headquarters, a tower in Canary Wharf to house more than half of the bank’s 23,000 UK staff. He threatened Reeves likewise, and announced the tower go-ahead only after she left banks in peace in her 2025 budget.
Pause here to examine Dimon, the essence of the business power that Labour governments are always up against. Forbes lists his net worth as $3.1bn, and he took home $43m last year. In 2009, when the then chancellor, Alistair Darling, imposed a 50% levy on bankers’ bonuses over £25,000, Dimon called him to protest. In his memoir, Back from the Brink, Darling recalled that a “very, very angry” Dimon had threatened that JP Morgan might reconsider its UK investments. “He said that his bank bought a lot of UK debt and he wondered if that was now such a good idea.” And, yes, again Dimon reportedly warned that he might not build a new London office.
This year, documents released in the Epstein files revealed how the then business secretary, Peter Mandelson, had urged Dimon to “mildly threaten” Darling over the tax. That’s their milieu and how they operate. But Darling didn’t back down, though he was besieged by bankers with identical scripts. He stood firm, and JP Morgan built its London office and didn’t stop buying UK government debt. The BBC’s Faisal Islam recounts that episode as told him by Darling as “an incredible live example of the relative power of government and financial markets, of the actual dynamics of the ‘bond vigilantes’”.
The bank payroll tax raised an estimated £2.3bn in four months. But it was dropped. Are you surprised to learn that what was billed as a bonus levy was paid by the banks, never by the bankers? Or by their lack of shame or collective responsibility as they bargained squalidly over bonuses even in the aftermath of a crash they caused?
Officially the bank bailout cost the public £23bn, after some asset sales. But that’s trivial compared with the colossal lasting damage right across the economy. Official estimates cite a loss of up to 7.5% of GDP; others suggest double that amount.
Bankers hiss at any hint of plucking a few feathers off them, but we wait to know how much John Healey dares take. Dimon visited No 10 last month to warn them off a tax raise, but Burnham only “dropped into the meeting briefly”.
So, how much? Returning the corporation tax surcharge on banks to its original 8%, from the 3% to which the Tories cut it, would yield £2bn. It’s a puny sum, and the banks owe the country much more. But nonetheless, Burnham resisting their bullying would send a self-confident message.
TUC polling finds strong support for a bank windfall tax, as it does for higher gambling and wealth taxes. Raising capital gains tax is popular, too. In the air, more long-term, is a money-raising idea backed by the Institute for Fiscal Studies and Resolution Foundation, to merge national insurance and income tax and no longer exempt pensions, rent and share income from NI.
Burnham knows the trick to raising tax is linking it to good spending, such as ending the triple lock to invest in social care. So banks, shedding jobs by the thousand, could be funding Alan Milburn’s upfront costs to get Neets (young people not in education, employment or training) into work.
Good vibes greet this budget. Though inflation is up, so is employment, growth, business investment and average pay. Earnings inequality jumped up for the first time in a decade, but from Friday, trade union reps get the right to recruit in every workplace, a gamechanger in anti-union companies. Union membership is the surest way to raise pay, by a reported 4-5%, so ignore Tories raging about the “red tape” of workers’ rights.
A budget signals a government’s way forward. Willingness to defy bank bullying, even a bit, is a good early sign. Watch out for more Burnham emblems.
- Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist

‘We want a full apology for slavery’: Commonwealth at a crossroads as king heads to the Caribbean
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:00:03 UTC
15:00:03 KST

King Charles’s upcoming Caribbean tour could accelerate moves to remove him as head of state in several countries unless he does more to confront the monarchy’s historic links to slavery, campaigners have warned.
The king will embark on a nine-day tour on Tuesday, visiting the Bahamas and Guyana before travelling to Antigua and Barbuda, and will attend the Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm).
Patrick Vernon, a cultural historian and UK representative of the Global Jamaica Diaspora Council, said the stakes for this trip could not be higher for the future of the royal family’s standing in the region, warning: “I think it’s the biggest crossroads for the Commonwealth since its creation.”
Charles is expected to deliver three significant speeches during the trip, but will follow government advice not to issue a formal apology for Britain’s role in the transatlantic slave trade. The British government has also ruled out paying reparations.
The visit is expected to be met with protests over the monarchy’s colonial legacy and demands for a formal apology and reparations. It comes four years after the Prince and Princess of Wales’s controversial 2022 Caribbean tour, where images of the couple greeting Jamaican children through a wire fence sparked widespread criticism across the region.
Although Charles has gone further than his predecessors in acknowledging the monarchy’s historic links to slavery, he arrives in a region transformed.
Recent developments include a UN resolution, tabled by Ghana, declaring the transatlantic slave trade the gravest crime against humanity and calling for reparatory justice, as well as Jamaica’s unprecedented slavery reparations petition to the king, which is due to be heard by the UK-based privy council next March.
“I think his visit is pivotal,” Vernon said. “If the visit does not meet the needs and expectations of a lot of the Commonwealth heads, it raises a big question about the future of the Commonwealth. What’s the point of being in the Commonwealth when one of the biggest crimes against humanity, which has been recognised at international level, where you can’t even have a proper dialogue, conversation and exploration?”
The Labour MP Bell Ribeiro-Addy, who chairs the all-party parliamentary group for Afrikan reparations, said the royal family and UK government had failed to reckon with a sea change happening across the world on this issue.
“I think it would be wrong to think that we can continue with platitudes. You’ve got ‘atrocity’, ‘deep regret’, ‘sorrow’, and now they’re going to say ‘darkest days’,” she said. “I think the king needs to realise that people wouldn’t keep raising it if what he was doing was anywhere near enough.
“You can tell that the Commonwealth means something to the monarchy, and I’m sure he would not want to be the monarch under which it crumbles.”
Prof Robert Beckford, a theologian at the University of Wolverhampton, said: “I think what’s at stake fundamentally is credibility: credibility in the monarchy and that leadership based on his ability to empathise and lead as the head of the Commonwealth. And the credibility rests on the ability to empathise with Caribbean history.”
While there were widespread calls for apologies, Beckford, also a broadcaster, said a “creative way” for the king to navigate the reparations debate would be to back a national truth and reconciliation commission examining Britain’s role in slavery.
“It would also provide us with the opportunity to take the nation on a journey into history, and understanding how slavery and colonialism operated as systems of extraction,” he said.
Protests over slavery reparations during royal visits to former colonies in the Caribbean are not a new occurrence. High Priest Richmond McKinney, a Rastafarian leader who is organising a protest during Charles’s visit to the Bahamas on Tuesday and Wednesday, was involved in demonstrations against Queen Elizabeth II in the 1980s.
“The cry remains the same: freedom, redemption and international repatriation. So we see it fitting to agitate and lobby and even have a protest against the crown now that it’s her son King Charles,” McKinney said. “You say you regret slavery, but your regret is not good enough. We want a full apology from you.”
Guyana’s president, Irfaan Ali, has made it clear ahead of the king’s visit that he wants progress towards reparations, beginning with an apology.
Currently, there are no formal agenda items on reparations at this year’s Commonwealth leaders’ summit in Antigua.
However, the chair of the Caribbean community reparations commission, Prof Sir Hilary Beckles, has said: “I can assure you that [for] everyone in the Caribbean right now, everyone who’s going to be at that meeting from the Caribbean, with an interest in the Caribbean, from Africa, and an interest in the global African movement, this will be the number one item on the table.”
Dr Niambi Hall Campbell-Dean, the committee’s chair, said: “We [are] spending hundreds of thousands of dollars to host the person who is responsible for the enslavement and colonisation of our ancestors, and what are we really getting out of it? So I think that the protests are twofold. It’s one for the king to be aware that we are still demanding that reparations be made, and then two to just [raise] awareness of more Bahamians and to cause us to really question our relationship to this crown.”
For Ribeiro-Addy, a successful trip would include an apology that quickly jumped to questions of “How do we move forward from this?”
“And the most important point to make is that the Netherlands’ king apologised. Their world didn’t end,” she said.

Fritters and chocolate cake: Thomasina Miers’ recipes for cooking with pumpkin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:00:03 UTC
15:00:03 KST

It would be lazy to write, with a rueful shake of the head, that Halloween gets bigger every year. Halloween is huge. I have seen it grow, vicariously, through my children year on year and, despite previously approaching it with a Scrooge-like attitude, something in me has shifted. Perhaps it’s simply the pleasure I see light up in all toddlers through to teens; they can’t get enough of the fandango of dressing up, mixed with its unmistakable, irresistible sprinkle of wickedness. So now I am in. Last year, we had 60 14-year-olds dancing the night away, and I wish I’d made them the recipes here, both of which play on the deliciously sweet, wonderfully savoury nature of pumpkin, that most brilliant of Mexican fruit. Quick, utterly delicious and the perfect finger food. Happy Halloween!
Pumpkin and carrot fritters with green chilli and coriander relish (pictured top)
Delightfully crisp, rich in flavour and delicately spiced, these are simple to throw together but look and taste spectacular, especially with the zippy relish for dipping.
Prep 15 min
 
Cook 40 min
 
Makes 14, to feed 4-6 as a starter
200g squash or pumpkin wedges (delica, crown prince, butternut), peeled
 
200g carrots, scrubbed clean
 
2 tsp olive oil 
 
8 spring onions, trimmed and finely chopped 
  
2 tsp coriander seeds 
  
2 tsp cumin seeds 
  
1 tsp ground cinnamon 
  
Salt and black pepper
 
 
2 fat garlic cloves, peeled and finely grated or minced
 
15g ginger, peeled and finely grated or minced
 
120g gram flour 
  
Neutral oil, for frying
 
Greek yoghurt, to serve
For the relish
 
1-2 green chillies, to taste, stalks discarded, then roughly chopped (remove the pith and seeds first if you prefer less heat)
  
1 bunch coriander
  
Juice of 1 lime
 
 
1 tbsp apple cider vinegar
 
1 tsp runny honey
  
1 garlic clove, peeled and roughly chopped
 
1 shallot, peeled and finely chopped
 
Coarsely grate the pumpkin and carrot, then wrap them in a clean tea towel or kitchen paper, and squeeze hard to push out any excess moisture.
Put a frying pan on a medium heat, add the oil and spring onions, and cook, stirring, for two to three minutes. Grind the coriander and cumin seeds in a mortar, then add to the pan with the cinnamon and a few generous pinches of salt, and cook for a few minutes more. Add the garlic and ginger, and cook, stirring all the time, for a couple of more minutes. By now, the onions will have softened and the mixture will be smelling irresistibly fragrant. Tip the lot into a large bowl, then add the grated pumpkin and carrots, and the gram flour. Season with a little more salt and plenty of black pepper, then mix to combine.
To make the relish, set aside half the chopped chilli, then put the rest in a food processor with all the remaining relish ingredients and a tablespoon of cold water. Blend to a smooth sauce, then taste, season with salt and pepper, and add more chilli, if need be, or more lime juice for acidity.
Heat 2cm of neutral oil in a medium pan until hot. Scoop out rounded dessertspoons of the pumpkin mixture and, using your hands, shape them into round patties; wet your hands with cold water to stop the mix sticking. Working in batches, slide the patties into the hot oil and fry for a few minutes on each side, until golden and crisp. Keep the cooked fritters in a warm oven while you fry the rest.
Serve the hot fritters with the relish and scoops of yoghurt on the side.
Pumpkin, cardamom and dark chocolate slice
Part blondie, part sponge cake, these delicious slices are full of sweet nuttiness from the squash, the gentle scent of cardamom and rich chunks of dark chocolate that melt in the mouth.
Prep 10 min
 
Cook 1 hr 20 min
 
Serves 9
250g squash or pumpkin (delica, crown prince, butternut would all work), or 200g pumpkin puree
 
200g unsalted butter 
  
200g soft brown sugar
  
2 large eggs 
  
250g plain flour, or a mix of plain and emmer, einkorn or spelt
 
2 tsp baking powder 
  
Fine sea salt
  
12 green cardamom pods, bashed to open and seeds crushed
 
100g dark chocolate, roughly chopped
 
Flaky sea salt
  
Icing sugar and ground cinnamon, to serve
  
Heat the oven to 180C fan (160C fan)/350F/gas 4 and line a 20cm square baking tin with greaseproof paper.
Cut the pumpkin/squash into a couple of wedges, remove and discard the seeds, then arrange the wedges on a baking tray. Sprinkle with a few teaspoons of water, then roast for 25-30 minutes, until completely soft. Scoop the flesh into a bowl, then mash with a fork until mostly smooth – don’t worry about any small lumps here or there, because they add a pleasing texture to the slices. You want 200g cooked flesh.
Melt the butter in a small pan and cook over a medium heat until the solids begin to brown and toast. Once smelling nutty and delicious, take off the heat and add the sugar, stirring until it melts. Tip the brown butter mix into a large bowl, add the cooled pumpkin puree and stir to combine. Whisk in the eggs one at a time, until smooth.
Sieve the flour and baking powder into a second bowl, season with a generous pinch of fine sea salt and add the ground cardamom seeds. Gently stir half the dry ingredients into the wet, then stir in the rest of the flour mix. Stir in the chopped chocolate, making sure there are no pockets of flour remaining, then pour into the prepared tin. Bake for 25-30 minutes, until springy to the touch.
When the tin comes out of the oven, sprinkle over some flaky sea salt, then leave to cool completely. Remove from the tin and cut into squares. If you like, dust the slices with a little icing sugar scented with a pinch of cinnamon to serve.

MVRDV designs Essen Central Library as public "living room" in Germany
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:00:00 UTC
15:00:00 KST

MVRDV designs Essen Central Library as public “living room” in Germany
Red bookshelves fill the multipurpose interiors of this city library, created by Dutch studio MVRDV in a former department store in Essen, in collaboration with architecture practices Includi and Meyer Architekten.
Named Essen Central Library, the 11,000-square-metre civic building was designed as a “vibrant cultural and educational hub” for the German city and to offer more than a traditional archive.
MVRDV said this aims to ensure the building’s longevity and usefulness in the information age, while also providing opportunities for social interaction in Essen.
“Of all the building functions out there, the library is possibly the one that has had the biggest challenges to adapt to the new millennium,” said MVRDV partner Fokke Moerel.
“Essen Central Library offers a response to this challenge. The library remains an important civic building, yet it offers much more than just a place to find books – it becomes a living room that is open and inviting for all of Essen’s diverse citizens,” she continued.
“It offers a solution to the social atomisation and isolation that has also been growing in the past decades.”
Essen Central Library, which opened to the public on Saturday, relocates a former library to a more central location. It spans all six storeys of Boeckerhaus, the former department store on Kennedyplatz that it occupies.
MVRDV and Meyer Architekten said their design draws on a theory by sociologist Ray Oldenburg about third places, which are free and informal social environments for people to enjoy beyond their homes, schools and places of work.
As such, it is hoped the library can feel inclusive to everyone in the city, whether they are visiting “without a specific purpose” or looking for a specific collection. To achieve this, the team collaborated with third place design specialist Includi on the interior.
Externally, the building is marked by large bands of glazing, allowing views of the library’s interior, including bands of study spaces on the perimeter of each floor.
MVRDV said this allows “the activities taking place within the library to become part of its expression towards the city”.
“The activated facade acts as an interface between the city and the library, connecting the public realm with the everyday experience of the library users,” said the studio.
“The different heights and uses create a lively view of people reading, working, talking, or relaxing, with visitors adding even more character to the space.”
Throughout the interior, bookshelves are used to define different spaces and combined in clusters on each floor, making collections “concentrated and identifiable”.
These clusters, named “media villages”, also define soft play spaces on the first floor, gaming pods on the second, and hobby zones on the third floor. They are all red in colour, but lighten in tone with each level.
The bookshelves are complemented by a palette of warm and natural wood finishes, plant pots and seating areas suited for socialising or focusing. Blue signage helps with wayfinding on each landing.
Completing the project is a ground-floor cafe intended to entice passersby and a rooftop events space with panoramic city views. There are also “makerspaces”, music rooms and areas to use technologies such as 3D printers, virtual reality and robotics.
MVRDV was founded in 1993 in Rotterdam. Its other recent projects include a proposal for a “new world wonder” in the Netherlands and a Bordeaux housing scheme with people-shaped portals.
Other libraries recently featured on Dezeen include a demountable timber structure in Amsterdam that was also conceived as “a living room for the neighbourhood” and a former commercial building in Norfolk that was overhauled and wrapped in a skin of cement shingles.

====================================================================================================

‘Learning the language is hard’: Adewuyi on life in Lithuania, racism and missing Africa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:00:00 UTC
15:00:00 KST

When Olugbenga Adewuyi decided to move from Nigeria to Lithuania, he did not speak Lithuanian and knew almost nothing about the country. Over the past seven years, he has reached A2 level in the language, obtained a permanent residence permit and grown accustomed to life there. But when discussing integration, he says language is not the only challenge.
For a non-white foreigner trying to become part of Lithuanian society, avoiding racism can be difficult – from offensive comments online to situations in which you feel unwelcome.
First shock: the weather
Adewuyi was given the opportunity to take part in an EU project for IT specialists and arrived in Kaunas in October 2019. At the time, he did not know he would settle in the country for the long term.
“I had lived in Nigeria all my life and really wanted to try something new. Many of my colleagues had found jobs in various European countries, so I started looking for an opportunity to do the same,” Adewuyi told LRT.lt.
His first impressions of Lithuania had less to do with a new city or a different culture than with the weather. On the day he arrived, the temperature was just 4C.
“Where I come from, the temperature almost never drops below 20C. I went outside wearing just a T-shirt because I wanted to find out what a Lithuanian autumn was like. I quickly realised it was not a good idea,” he says with a laugh.
Today, he works as a software developer and says he is satisfied with his standard of living in Lithuania.
“IT specialists are paid well here. Of course, I considered opportunities to move to another country, but for now, things have worked out in such a way that I am staying in Lithuania,” he says.
After living in the country for several years, Adewuyi has obtained a permanent residence permit. However, he admits that he is seriously considering spending part of his time in Africa.
“I miss Africa. Here, I always stand out from the crowd. Sometimes you just want to be among people who look like you,” he says.
‘I thought I would never learn Lithuanian’
One of the biggest challenges Adewuyi has faced in Lithuania is the language. His native languages are English and Yoruba, spoken by one of Nigeria’s largest ethnic groups.
Lithuanian seemed completely unlike any language he knew.
“When I first heard Lithuanian, I thought I would never learn it. The hardest part is the grammatical cases. In English, everything is much simpler: we use prepositions, whereas here you have to change word endings. For someone who speaks English, that is very unusual,” he says.
He began learning Lithuanian almost as soon as he arrived. His employer paid for his first language courses.
Adewuyi says his progress really took off when he began studying independently in preparation for the state Lithuanian language examination.
“I passed the A2-level exam. That is enough for everyday life – I can find my way around the city and deal with daily practical matters. But, for example, visiting a doctor and communicating in Lithuanian is still a difficult task,” he admits.
Adewuyi’s circle of friends now includes Lithuanians, Belarusians and people from other countries. One Lithuanian friend helped him prepare for the exam by speaking to him exclusively in Lithuanian and correcting his mistakes.
“Even now, when I write to him in English, he replies in Lithuanian. I still find grammatical cases particularly difficult to understand,” Adewuyi says.
He has noticed that many migrants are in no hurry to learn Lithuanian because they are unsure whether they will stay in the country for long.
“Most foreigners think they will live here for a while and then leave. So they are not always motivated to learn the language. But when they need to obtain a permanent residence permit, their attitude changes,” he says.
Adewuyi identifies the changing seasons, the way public institutions operate and the sense of security as the main advantages of living in Lithuania.
He says that when you approach a government institution, you generally get what you need “without unnecessary formalities or having to know the right people”. He has also grown quite fond of Lithuanian cuisine.
“I like variety. I often visit different cafes and restaurants and try new dishes. The food here suits me perfectly,” he says.
Nevertheless, Adewuyi believes cultural differences are one of the most challenging aspects of living abroad.
“Where I come from, people are generally very open and welcoming. Lithuanians are more reserved, so it takes time to make friends. Being a foreigner is probably difficult in any country, but here you feel it particularly strongly,” he says.
Racism and difficulties finding accommodation
Speaking about attitudes towards people with a different skin colour, Adewuyi acknowledges that during his seven years in Lithuania, he has experienced both positive encounters and unpleasant situations.
He says discrimination is far from always being obvious.
“The thing about discrimination is that it is often impossible to say for certain whether it has taken place. You cannot always prove that you were treated differently specifically because of your skin colour,” he says.
The most painful experience for Adewuyi has been looking for accommodation. This year, while searching for a new flat, he became acutely aware that, in his view, foreign nationals with a different skin colour have to make considerably more effort than local residents.
“If your skin colour is different from that of the majority of the population, you automatically find yourself at the bottom of the list of potential tenants. That was probably the most unpleasant experience I have had recently,” he says.
Nevertheless, Adewuyi says he has experienced few instances of overt aggression during his years in Lithuania. He recalls hearing racist insults on several occasions, but says such incidents have been rare.
“Yes, I have been called the N-word, but those incidents were very rare. In general, I cannot say that I constantly encounter this kind of attitude,” he says.
According to Adewuyi, he feels safe in everyday life. In public places, at events and in clubs, people tend to show curiosity and friendliness rather than hostility.
“When I go out, people are usually friendly and interested in where I come from. I do not feel that I am in danger, and I am not afraid to walk around the city,” he says.
Online comments cause concern
Speaking about religion, Adewuyi says he grew up in a religious family but now describes himself as an agnostic.
“I grew up first in a Muslim environment and later in a Christian one. But I am not religious now. I am an agnostic,” he says.
He says that over the past year or two, he has found some public debates in Lithuania particularly difficult to watch, especially those concerning religion and attitudes towards people from different cultural and religious backgrounds.
In particular, he is referring to the debate surrounding the burning of the Quran. Online comments and public discussions about migrants have had a significant impact on his emotional wellbeing.
Further reading
“The past year or two have been quite difficult. Sometimes you open the news or social media and see a huge number of negative comments. This is especially true when the discussion concerns events attended by Black people. Posts like these almost always trigger a wave of hatred,” he says.
He believes such rhetoric also influences how people perceive others in real life.
“After reading comments like these, you start wondering: if someone looks at you in the street, what are they really thinking? Perhaps the person is simply looking at you, but you have already started to doubt yourself. It really does have an impact,” he says.
One incident at a city fair has stayed in Adewuyi’s memory. He says he was standing in a queue at a market stall when the vendor, having served other customers, simply walked to the back of the stall without acknowledging him.
“To this day, I cannot explain it any other way. After that incident, I found it much harder to attend similar events. Perhaps someone will say it was a trivial matter, but when you live far from home and do not have the support of your family nearby, such seemingly small things hurt much more,” the Nigerian says candidly.
Despite these experiences, Adewuyi stresses that he does not consider Lithuania a dangerous country for foreign nationals.
However, he admits that he sometimes feels tired of standing out.
“Sometimes you just want to be among people who are similar to you. There are many foreigners, Ukrainians and Belarusians living in Vilnius, but I still stand out very clearly. Over time, you begin to understand how important it is sometimes to feel like part of the majority rather than an exception,” he says.
