Eisenkot is viewed by supporters as a capable leader with sterling security credentials who, along with his likely governing partners, could act as a bulwark against creeping illiberalism. As someone personally touched by the conflict – his son and two nephews were killed in Gaza – his backers believe that he feels deeply the pain that still courses through Israel three years after the attacks.
Parties that would likely throw their support behind Eisenkot have vowed to improve Israel's international standing and work to conscript ultra-Orthodox men while bolstering the independence of the judiciary.
'Not afraid to take action'
Zipporah Bennett, an 85-year-old retiree, said she was voting for Netanyahu "because he has had the experience of navigating the country through a lot of difficult seasons".
"He has the full support of the American government," she said, "and I believe he's a man who's not afraid to take action."
Netanyahu returned to power in December 2022, bringing into his coalition far-right ultra-nationalists who have since seen their political clout skyrocket.
The opposition has scorned the premier for his backing of ultra-Orthodox parties fighting to keep exemptions for religious Jewish students from drafting into the military, which faces personnel shortages.
But one of the biggest criticisms levelled at Netanyahu is his failure to take responsibility for the October 7 attack, the deadliest day in the country's history.
Eisenkot, 66, has pledged to establish an independent state commission of inquiry into the security failures that led to the attack, something Netanyahu's government has resisted.
Seeking to unseat the premier is an informal bloc of parties led by Eisenkot's Yashar and spanning from the right to the centre-left.
Eisenkot has vowed to prevent the creation of a Palestinian state and expressed support for Israeli settlements, but has promised to crack down on violent settlers.
Neither Eisenkot nor Netanyahu have publicly said they would partner with the predominantly Arab lists, which represent some 21 percent of Israel's population and who could become kingmakers if the results are as close as expected.
Final results could take days to trickle in and it is highly unlikely that any single party will come close to the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-member parliament.
Cobbling together any coalition could take weeks or months, with possible new elections on the horizon if negotiations fail.

Election Day 2026 is a day for democracy and a chance for unity - editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
04:09:34 UTC
13:09:34 KST

Israelis heading to the polls on Tuesday will be making choices shaped by three extraordinary years. The October 7 massacre, the wars that ensued, and the strain on families, soldiers, and communities have changed the questions voters are asking of their leaders.
Political disagreements have become deeply personal, and the next government will inherit decisions with consequences far beyond one Knesset term.
Even so, Election Day deserves a measure of joy.
Across Israel, citizens will walk into polling stations, choose a ballot, and exercise their democratic right. Some will vote with conviction, others with reservations.
First-time voters will join parents and grandparents who have cast ballots through decades of upheaval. The results will divide winners from losers, but the act of voting belongs to everyone.
The agenda waiting for the next government ranges from accountability for October 7 to Israel’s security and place in the world.
One of the next government’s first tests will be how to investigate the failures that allowed Hamas’s October 7 attack.
Demands for a state commission of inquiry have become a central election issue, particularly for bereaved families who want answers and accountability. The argument over the form of that investigation will not disappear when the votes are counted.
The dispute over haredi military service is equally consequential. After years of fighting and repeated reserve call-ups, the burden of service weighs heavily on many households. Parties remain divided over exemptions, enforcement, and the kind of draft legislation the next coalition should pursue. What leaders agree to in coalition talks will affect both the IDF and Israeli society.
Decisions await on the future of Gaza and the peace plan
Beyond Israel’s borders, decisions await on the future of Gaza and the peace plan intended to shape its recovery and security. Israelis must consider what arrangements could prevent Hamas from again threatening their communities, who should govern Gaza, and what role international partners should play.
The Palestinian question also remains unresolved. Debates over a possible Palestinian statehood, settlement expansion, and violence in the West Bank carry direct implications for Israel’s security and relations with its allies.
International pressure, including the threat or use of sanctions, adds another dimension to choices that cannot be postponed indefinitely.
This also explains why the ability to vote should inspire pride. After so much loss and uncertainty, Israelis still have the power to influence who will make those decisions. A citizen can fiercely disagree with a neighbor over Gaza, conscription, or the government’s record and still respect that neighbor’s equal place at the ballot box.
The Jerusalem Post also calls for a modest widening of the political camps and the formation of a broad Zionist government. Israel’s challenges demand leaders willing to work across familiar dividing lines.
Cooperation will require difficult compromises, but the next coalition should strive to represent a wider range of Israelis and offer the country a measure of stability.
That appeal should remain in voters’ minds beyond Election Day.
Once the ballots have been counted and the parties know how many seats they have won, the democratic marathon enters its next stage. Seat totals will establish the balance of power in the Knesset, but coalition negotiations will determine the priorities, partnerships, and commitments of the government that emerges.
The public should remain part of that conversation. Israelis can continue asking their elected representatives what they intend to do about an October 7 inquiry, military service, Gaza, and relations with the Palestinians and the wider world. They can make clear that a broad Zionist coalition, if it is achievable, should be pursued with seriousness and goodwill.
Israelis should allow themselves to enjoy the day
Results may come quickly; building a government will take longer. Its quality will be judged by the agreements reached and the decisions that follow, long after election-night speeches have faded.
For now, Israelis should allow themselves to enjoy the day. Bring children to the polling station. Talk with friends and relatives, including those voting differently. Appreciate the chance to participate in a national decision even when the outcome is uncertain.
Cast a ballot with hope, then keep paying attention as the next government takes shape.

Scientists discover a surprising clue to why some brains resist Alzheimer’s
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
04:02:26 UTC
13:02:26 KST

Scientists discover a surprising clue to why some brains resist Alzheimer’s
- Date:
- October 27, 2026
- Source:
- Netherlands Institute for Neuroscience - KNAW
- Summary:
- Why do some people stay mentally sharp even when their brains show signs of Alzheimer’s disease? Scientists in the Netherlands may have uncovered an important clue hidden in a rare group of immature brain cells. Researchers discovered that these cells remain present even in people over 80, but their behavior differs dramatically between those who develop dementia and those who remain cognitively healthy.
- Share:
Some people have the brain changes associated with Alzheimer's disease but never develop dementia. While others experience worsening memory and thinking problems, these individuals remain mentally sharp despite signs of the disease in their brains. Scientists have long struggled to explain why.
Now, researchers at the Netherlands Institute for Neuroscience have uncovered a promising clue. Their findings suggest that a rare group of brain cells, known as immature neurons, may behave differently in people who resist Alzheimer's symptoms. Rather than simply replacing damaged cells, these neurons could help protect the brain from the harmful effects of the disease.
This remarkable ability is known as cognitive resilience. It describes how some people maintain their memory and thinking abilities even when their brains show signs of damage or disease.
"Around 30 percent of older adults who develop Alzheimer's disease never experience its symptoms," says Evgenia Salta, senior author of the research. "We really don't know why. That's a big mystery, and a very important one."
Understanding this mystery could transform how scientists approach Alzheimer's, shifting attention from what causes brain cells to deteriorate toward what allows certain brains to remain healthy and functional.
Can the Aging Brain Repair Itself?
One possible explanation for cognitive resilience is that some brains have a greater ability to repair or protect themselves as Alzheimer's progresses.
"Perhaps they can add new brain cells to a network that is degenerating," Salta says.
This possibility involves a biological process called adult neurogenesis, which refers to the production of new nerve cells (neurons) in an adult brain. Neurons are specialized cells that transmit information throughout the nervous system, allowing us to think, learn, remember, and respond to our surroundings.
Scientists have established that adult neurogenesis occurs in several animal species. Whether it continues to happen in the adult human brain, however, has been a subject of scientific debate for decades.
If the human brain can produce new neurons later in life, those cells might help maintain important connections as aging and disease damage existing networks. However, finding immature neurons does not necessarily prove that they were recently formed.
To investigate this possibility, Salta and her colleagues examined donated human brain tissue obtained through the Netherlands Brain Bank, a research resource that collects and preserves brain samples.
The researchers compared three groups: people without detectable brain pathology, patients who developed Alzheimer's dementia, and individuals whose brains showed Alzheimer's pathology but who remained cognitively resilient.
The team concentrated on a small region within the brain's memory center, an area believed to be among the few locations where new neurons might develop.
Finding the relevant cells was far from straightforward.
"These cells are extremely rare, so we had to develop new ways to find them," Salta says. "We really zoomed in on the exact spot where we expected them to be."
The researchers also developed new approaches to analyzing their data, allowing them to identify the cells more precisely without relying heavily on assumptions drawn from animal studies.
Scientists Find Immature Neurons in Brains Over 80
The search revealed something remarkable. Immature neurons were present across all three groups, including in the brains of older adults.
These cells resemble neurons that have not yet fully matured, suggesting that the aging brain may retain cellular features associated with development and adaptability.
"Even at an average age of over 80, we still found these immature neurons in all groups," Salta says.
But the most intriguing discovery came when researchers compared the brains of people who had developed dementia with those who had remained mentally sharp despite Alzheimer's pathology.
Initially, the scientists expected resilient individuals to have substantially more immature neurons. If these cells help replace damaged neurons, having greater numbers might explain why some brains withstand the disease.
Instead, the difference in cell numbers was much smaller than anticipated.
That unexpected result pointed toward another explanation. The important distinction might not be how many immature neurons a brain contains, but how those cells respond when the brain comes under attack.
A Hidden Defense Against Alzheimer's Damage
When the team examined the activity of immature neurons more closely, they identified striking differences between the groups.
In cognitively resilient individuals, the cells showed signs of activating biological processes associated with survival and protection against damage.
"In resilient individuals, these cells seem to activate programs that help them survive and cope with damage," Salta says. "We also see lower signals related to inflammation and cell death."
Inflammation is part of the body's normal defense system, but when it becomes persistent in the brain, it can contribute to damage and interfere with communication between neurons. Cell death, meanwhile, gradually disrupts the networks responsible for memory and thinking.
The findings suggest that immature neurons in resilient brains may be better equipped to withstand these harmful conditions.
More surprisingly, their role might extend beyond protecting themselves.
"It might not be (only) about replacing lost neurons," Salta explains. "It could be that these cells support the surrounding tissue and help the brain stay functional and 'youthful'. They may act as a sort of fertilizer in a garden that has started falling apart."
In other words, rather than serving only as replacements for dying neurons, immature cells could potentially help maintain the environment surrounding existing brain cells.
Such support might allow neural networks to continue functioning even as Alzheimer's related damage accumulates.
Why Scientists Are Cautious About the Discovery
Although the results offer an intriguing explanation for cognitive resilience, Salta emphasizes that the researchers have not established exactly what these immature neurons do.
Their conclusions about the cells' possible protective roles are based on patterns observed in brain tissue, not direct experiments demonstrating those functions.
"We assume the cells' function based on the data, but we cannot confirm it in this type of study," she explains.
That distinction is particularly important because research on adult neurogenesis has attracted considerable public attention, sometimes leading to claims that go beyond what scientists have demonstrated.
The presence of immature neurons does not establish that new neurons are continuously being produced in older humans, nor does it prove that these cells are responsible for preventing dementia.
Other biological mechanisms almost certainly contribute to cognitive resilience as well.
"This is one piece of a very large puzzle," Salta concludes. "There will never be just one factor that explains resilience."
Could Alzheimer's Research Shift Toward Protecting the Brain?
The findings raise a broader question about aging: Why do some people's brains remain relatively stable while others experience progressive cognitive decline?
"Somewhere along this trajectory, there's a kind of decision point," Salta explains. "Some people remain stable, others develop dementia. We want to understand what drives that difference."
To explore this further, the researchers plan to investigate how immature neurons communicate and interact with neighboring brain cells. Understanding those relationships may reveal whether the cells actively contribute to resilience and how their protective responses might work.
The research also reflects a growing change in how scientists think about Alzheimer's disease.
Traditionally, much of the field has focused on understanding the processes that damage the brain, including the accumulation of abnormal proteins and the loss of neurons. Increasingly, researchers are also asking why some brains remain functional despite those changes.
By identifying the mechanisms behind this natural resistance, scientists hope to uncover new ways to preserve memory and cognitive abilities as people age.
"Cognitive resilience is extremely exciting," Salta says. "If we understand what protects these brains, it could eventually lead to new therapeutic strategies."
Although practical treatments remain a distant possibility, the discovery suggests that even in old age, the human brain may possess protective abilities that scientists are only beginning to understand.

Zelensky Outlines Three Security Options as US Pushes for November Talks With Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
04:01:27 UTC
13:01:27 KST

President Volodymyr Zelensky said Washington was willing to discuss security guarantees that could include an American military response to renewed Russian aggression, but insisted that any agreement must spell out exactly what US forces would do and receive congressional approval.
In an extensive interview with TSN’s Alla Mazur, Zelensky said Ukraine was considering several postwar security arrangements, including NATO membership, direct US guarantees and a European-led coalition backed by Washington.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
He stressed that the terms could not be dictated by Moscow and that Ukraine would not accept neutrality or restrictions on its armed forces.
“What are the US prepared to do? In what numbers? Aviation or ground operations, if Ukraine needs to be defended quickly?” Zelensky asked.
He said the current US administration was prepared to discuss such arrangements, but the details had to be written into a binding agreement rather than left to political promises between presidents.
Congress must approve any US guarantees
Zelensky said a bilateral security agreement must survive changes in political leadership in Washington and Kyiv.
“Congress must vote for the security guarantees,” he said, rejecting another arrangement resembling the Budapest Memorandum, which failed to prevent Russia’s aggression against Ukraine.
The president outlined three possible security frameworks: Ukrainian membership in NATO, bilateral US guarantees, or a European-led Coalition of the Willing involving more than 30 countries with American support.
Ukraine Confirms Honoring US-Brokered Truce in Russian-Occupied Oleshky
NATO membership remained his preferred option, but he acknowledged that direct US guarantees without formal accession could provide a compromise.
However, he said key questions remained unanswered, including whether American forces or military installations could be stationed in Ukraine and how Washington would respond if Russia invaded again.
Zelensky said the same uncertainty applied to a European military presence, which Moscow has repeatedly opposed.
‘We are not exchanging anything for anything’
The president rejected suggestions that Ukraine had agreed to trade territory for security guarantees as Washington prepared for renewed negotiations with Russia.
“We are not exchanging anything for anything. We are ready for discussions,” Zelensky said.
He insisted that territorial questions could be addressed only by national leaders, while technical delegations could negotiate other aspects of a settlement.
Zelensky said US negotiators had presented several proposals following talks in Oslo on Oct. 20, which American envoy Steve Witkoff subsequently took to Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg.
He emphasized that the document was not a completed peace plan submitted to Putin for approval.
“Russia does not decide,” Zelensky said, explaining that the proposals were intended for discussion among the parties involved in ending the war.
He added that Russian demands could not determine Ukraine’s security arrangements.
“The limitation of our army and Ukraine’s neutrality are not up for discussion,” he said.
Ukraine wants to retain 800,000 troops
Zelensky said the size of Ukraine’s postwar armed forces would remain an internal decision, dependent on financing and the security arrangements eventually agreed upon.
“If I have enough money, I want to maintain an army of 800,000,” he said.
He stressed that he would not negotiate the size of Ukraine’s military with Russia or, for that matter, with the US.
The president said NATO membership could change Ukraine’s military requirements, but the decision would depend on the alliance’s readiness to help finance and equip Ukrainian forces.
Without NATO membership, Ukraine would require other credible guarantees alongside a large, well-funded army equipped with modern weapons and technology.
He said Washington’s proposals also covered economic questions, reconstruction and territorial matters, although he declined to reveal all details because of understandings with American negotiators.
US says Putin agreed to November trilateral talks
Zelensky said the Oslo negotiations had also helped reopen a diplomatic channel with Moscow.
According to the Ukrainian president, US officials traveled to St. Petersburg after the meeting and subsequently informed Kyiv that Putin had agreed in principle to trilateral negotiations involving Ukraine, Russia and the US in November.
Abu Dhabi was among the locations discussed, although Zelensky said the talks could also take place elsewhere in the Middle East or Europe.
Kyiv wants European representatives involved and hopes technical negotiations can lead to a meeting between national leaders.
Zelensky said such a meeting could address territorial disputes, while other discussions could explore an energy ceasefire, a maritime ceasefire to protect Ukrainian exports and imports, and further prisoner exchanges.
He welcomed the return of 270 Ukrainian prisoners but said a comprehensive all-for-all exchange would require negotiations at the leaders’ level.
The president said Russia was also seeking security guarantees in discussions with Washington. He acknowledged that he did not know the full details of Putin’s conversations with American envoys, including whether economic issues influenced Moscow’s position.
Oslo talks restore intelligence and satellite capabilities
Zelensky described the Oct. 20 Oslo meeting as productive, saying it helped resolve two of Ukraine’s three immediate disputes with Washington.
He identified the problems as limited US intelligence sharing on Russian ballistic missile launches, restrictions affecting Starlink and Starshield satellite capabilities, and shortages of air defense systems.
According to Zelensky, intelligence sharing on ballistic threats had been fully restored, while satellite capabilities returned to the speeds required by Ukrainian forces.
He said that during overnight checks with defense officials, the satellite service had resumed operations at speeds corresponding to 420 kilometers (261 miles) per hour, following earlier restrictions.
Ukraine’s military welcomed the restoration, he said.
The president thanked American officials and Ukraine’s negotiating team for resolving both issues, adding that public attention may also have helped.
However, the shortage of air defense weapons remained unresolved.
Zelensky said the Oslo meeting had produced tangible results but warned that the situation could change, particularly amid US domestic political developments.
Witkoff and Kushner did not visit Bucha
Zelensky also disclosed that he had invited US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner to visit Bucha during their earlier trip to Kyiv, but they did not go.
The president said he had taken them to St. Sophia Cathedral to show them Ukraine’s historical heritage and the reality of life in a country resisting Russia’s invasion.
He wanted the American delegation to experience Ukraine firsthand rather than rely on narratives emerging from its contacts with Moscow.
Zelensky said he had also hoped to show the envoys Bucha, the Kyiv suburb where Russian atrocities occurred in 2022.
“We offered,” Zelensky said when asked whether the Americans had been invited.
He said he wanted them to see both the consequences of Russian occupation and how communities were rebuilding.
“They did not find the time, but they found time for many other things,” he said.
The president acknowledged that the reasons for not visiting Bucha could have varied.
Nevertheless, he said showing the envoys Kyiv’s historic sites and the resilience of its residents had helped create an emotional connection with Ukraine.
He noted that St. Sophia Cathedral predates Moscow itself, underscoring Ukraine’s long history and independent identity.

Study finds that producing methanol on the red planet from carbon dioxide in the atmosphere ‘is technically feasible to a certain extent’

Chinese space scientists are working out how future astronauts on Mars could make their own fuel out of thin air, a sign that Beijing is serious about one day sending people to the red planet.
A team at the state-funded Deep Space Exploration Laboratory in Hefei has developed a catalyst that turns carbon dioxide – which makes up more than 95 per cent of the Martian atmosphere – into a liquid fuel called methanol.
“Methanol can serve as fuel to generate electricity, provide heating and power Mars rovers, and it can also be used as a chemical building block for making antifreeze, building materials and other products,” space resources scientist Zhang Zhe and his colleagues wrote in a paper published online in the Journal of Deep Space Exploration.

Dammed Between Energy and Water Scarcity: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam and the Nile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
04:00:00 UTC
13:00:00 KST

Every large dam divides as much as it connects, and the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam is no exception. A monumental feat of architecture and engineering, the mega-dam has brought everyone together, for better or worse, to interrogate who gets to declare sovereignty over the riches of the river, be it water or momentum, and to challenge colonial-era Nile treaties.
Inaugurated in September 2025, the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam, or GERD, is a grand concrete structure on the Blue Nile in western Ethiopia within the Benishangul-Gumuz region, just 30 kilometers upstream along the river and east of the border with Sudan. It is built as a major source of hydroelectric power, being consistently ranked in the top 3-30 globally, and symbolizes Ethiopia's national sovereignty, rise to exponential economic development, and technological self-determination. So, why has it become the center of a protracted dispute over regional water security and international law between Ethiopia, Sudan, and Egypt?
The Architecture of the Dam
Related Article
Ecologies of Repair: Reconciling Our Relationship with Water
To understand the debate, the architecture must first be outlined. The GERD, a gravity mega-dam built under the management of civil engineering company Webuild (née Salini Impregilo) for the Ethiopian Electric Power, is comprised of a roller-compacted concrete (RCC) main dam, a concrete-faced rockfill saddle dam, and a system of spillways and hydroelectric power stations at the base. Designed for a 6,000 MW capacity, documented as 5,150 MW in recent literature, and meant to double the country's electricity generation, the dam is 1.8 kilometers long and rises to a 175-meter height. The main dam, located only 14 kilometers from Sudan, holds back a reservoir that can contain 74 billion cubic meters of water — named Lake Nigat — that is 3.5 times the surface area of Addis Ababa.
Moreover, the 5-kilometer-long, 50-meter-high saddle dam crescents a lower area of the surrounding reservoir basin for passive water retention, where the average annual outflow of the entire reservoir amounts to approximately 50 billion cubic meters of water. The two hydroelectric power stations, flanking the river bank on both sides and consisting of 13 Francis turbines, produce an average of 15,700 GWh/year.
The system of spillways provides safety for the dam by discharging floodwater without causing damage as well as maintaining the reservoir level below the designated threshold. They include a main service-gated spillway, a free-flow crest spillway, and an emergency side-channel ungated spillway capable of handling severe flooding.
Webuild's internal laboratories tested and manufactured the materials for long-term structural stability and mechanical performance. This was achieved through an advanced, internally and internationally researched RCC mix designed with a low cement, low water content, and extended setting times. In addition, an integrated network of galleries in the main dam accommodates high-sensitivity precision instruments including vertical pendula, to monitor hydrostatic pressure, structural shifts, joint integrity, and turbine performance in real-time. This continuous operational data is channeled directly into a centralized database at the right bank control center, allowing engineers to conduct proactive maintenance and ensure maximum structural reliability.
The structural resistance of its reservoir allows the GERD to alter seasonal water patterns, manage floods, and generate hydropower. However, considering its location on an international and transboundary river system, filling the reservoir raises questions regarding water requirements and storage timelines. The project's multi-stage filling cycles have proceeded unilaterally, without transparency between the upstream country and its downstream neighbors, fueling geopolitical tensions. Operating the GERD depends on hydrological regulation, as lack of coordination in operations and transparent data-sharing could disrupt existing downstream infrastructure — a prime example being Sudan's Roseires Dam, due to its proximity to the GERD.
Egypt argues that Ethiopia's unilateral operations can cut down water flow, which is a national threat to its people and economy. It also supports its claims by addressing Ethiopia's "unilateral exploitation" of its transboundary waters in the Omo, Jubba and Shebelle basins, and the harm it causes its neighbors, Somalia and Kenya.
Resolving this issue peacefully would foster vital regional cooperation on the White Nile too, where uncoordinated dam releases from Uganda have triggered downstream flooding in South Sudan, increasing people's displacement and disease outbreaks.
But how did we get here, anyway?
Historical Hegemony
During the initial survey for the GERD, carried out in the 1960s, Ethiopia lacked the internal stability to progress with it. It was kept discreet until sufficient work was done because it was known that its development would carry a heavy geopolitical weight, especially on downstream countries in the basin.
This weight is amplified, considering the Nile Basin countries are 11, some of which are upstream, downstream, or both in relation to other countries. The solely upstream nations include Burundi, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Rwanda, Uganda, Tanzania, Kenya, Eritrea, and Ethiopia, while the sole downstream nation is Egypt. Sudan and South Sudan are both upstream and downstream, with South Sudan being upstream relative to Sudan and Egypt, and downstream relative to Uganda, since the White Nile is sourced by rivers flowing into Lake Victoria. The Blue Nile, supplying 85% of the Nile River, originates at Lake Tana in the Ethiopian Highlands, where it flows into Sudan and finally converges with the White Nile at Khartoum to form the main Nile River flowing through Egypt into the Mediterranean Sea.
Historically, Nile Basin hydropolitics have been shaped by Egypt's hydrohegemony, a legal history formed from a century of colonial-era 'treaties' — the Nile Treaties — towards a multilateral agreement that still conflicts with water rights. The 1902 Anglo-Ethiopian Agreement originally secured Egypt's control of the Nile by restricting Ethiopia from modifying the Blue Nile without British consent. This was further amplified by the 1929 Anglo-Egyptian Treaty — an exchange of notes more than a treaty, which essentially allowed Egypt to veto upstream projects or embark on unilateral development — and the subsequent 1959 Nile Water Agreement, which granted exclusive annual allocations of 55.5 billion cubic meters to Egypt and 18.5 billion cubic meters to Sudan. Reality, however, is more nuanced: while these inequitable, colonial-era treaties should be abolished or reassessed, Egypt remains a water-scarce nation, where the Nile supplies more than 90% of its freshwater needs, and approximately 95% of its population lives along its course.
Also, unlike other riparian nations in the basin — excluding Eritrea, an observer in the Nile Basin Initiative, due to its minimal hydrological footprint, and Sudan, facing severe infrastructure collapse — Egypt relies on the Nile as an existential lifeline. Since the GERD sits on the Blue Nile, which supplies the vast majority of the Nile's total flow, it signifies a major shift in regional power that ends the 'monopoly' of the river and creates a threat to downstream countries' agriculture and water security, especially during multi-year droughts. To challenge asymmetric control, the Nile Basin Initiative (NBI) was launched in 1999, with the Cooperative Framework Agreement (CFA) following soon after in 2010, one year before the Renaissance Dam's groundbreaking in 2011.
Preoccupied with the internal politics of the Arab Spring, Egypt was unable to effectively oppose or block the project. Its isolation deepened when Sudan softened its earlier objections into a moderate neutrality. Sudan's position has since shifted repeatedly, from rejection to neutrality or support and back again, driven largely by internal fragmentation and domestic politics. The debate over the dam's benefits and drawbacks has also shaped these shifts. On the one hand, the dam promises more stable irrigation, lower dredging costs, and better flood management. On the other, it carries serious long-term risks: floodplains depleted as sediment builds up in the reservoir basin, disrupted local ecosystems, and a lack of cooperation between the three countries.
The pressure culminated in the 2015 Declaration of Principles on GERD, which remains the primary trilateral framework between Ethiopia, Sudan, and Egypt. In it, the three countries acknowledged the dam and committed to the principles of international water law. They have still not reached a binding agreement on how the reservoir is filled or on how to manage droughts.
Divisions persist on a wider scale too. When the Nile Basin Cooperative Framework Agreement (CFA) came into force in October 2024, Egypt and Sudan refused to sign it. Both want to protect their access to a vital resource and the veto rights they claim under colonial-era treaties.
The Architecture of Geopolitics
Concrete structures can control physical water flows, but they rarely can resolve political friction. Ethiopia positions GERD as a shared resource built for its people and neighbors, vowing to export surplus to promote its own economy as well as support the continent, but hydrological uncertainty remains the biggest issue in the absence of a clear, definitive binding agreement meant to operate the dam. An exemplar model for sustainable and equitable transboundary water governance can be found in the Senegal River Basin Development Authority (OMVS) — Organisation pour la mise en valeur du fleuve Sénégal — that utilizes a framework of collaborative benefit-sharing and joint infrastructure ownership.
Ultimately, unlocking the GERD's true potential as a driver of East African economic integration hinges on overcoming impasses to secure its downstream neighbors and provide a new example of equitable water governance, environmental safety and sustained trilateral cooperation. Otherwise, how can shared river basins foster a nation's right to build its economic future against the security of its neighbors?

Taiwan rebuffs China’s commemorations for post-World War Two ‘restoration’ of island
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
04:59:31 CET
12:59:31 KST

TAIPEI, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Taiwan’s defence minister on Tuesday said China was waging “cognitive warfare” after Beijing marked the anniversary of Japan’s handover of the island to Chinese rule with satellite images of Taipei and a military propaganda poster.
Japan took over Taiwan from China’s Qing Dynasty in 1895 and ruled it until 1945, when it transferred the island to the Republic of China government. Both Beijing and Taipei commemorate the event, now in its 81st year.
On Sunday’s anniversary of the handover, China released high-resolution satellite pictures of Taipei, including the train station and the National Palace Museum. The museum holds a vast collection of treasures brought to Taiwan in 1949, when the Republic of China government fled there after losing a civil war to the communists.
The Chinese military’s Eastern Theatre Command also published a poster with a map of Taiwan superimposed on images of fighter jets and warships, with the title “Remember the history of the restoration”.
Speaking to reporters at parliament in Taipei, Taiwan Defence Minister Wellington Koo said China was using the anniversary to carry out “cognitive warfare”.
“We must stress that the People’s Republic of China was established in 1949. The War of Resistance has absolutely nothing to do with the People’s Republic of China — this is a clear, objective fact,” he added, referring to World War Two and the Japanese invasion of China which began in 1931.
Taiwan’s military marked a different anniversary, the start of an unsuccessful late-October 1949 invasion attempt by the People’s Liberation Army of Kinmen, islands which sit next to the Chinese coast and remain under Taiwan control to this day.
Koo said that was a date much more worthy of remembering.
“This reminds us once again that China’s determination to annex the Republic of China and Taiwan by force has never changed. We should be even more vigilant,” he added.
Beijing has never renounced the use of force to bring Taiwan under its control. The democratically elected government in Taipei rejects Beijing’s sovereignty claims.
Neither government formally recognises the other, and their shared World War Two history is a frequent source of tension.

Harry Kane ends England’s 25-year Ballon d’Or wait

The Bayern Munich striker accepted the prize at a ceremony at the London Palladium on Monday, following a prolific season for club and country.
According to England Football, Kane scored 73 goals in 65 matches during the season, including 61 for Bayern and 12 for England.
He becomes the fifth Englishman to win the award, following Stanley Matthews, Bobby Charlton, Kevin Keegan and Owen.

The 33-year-old also received the Gerd Müller Trophy, which recognizes the season’s leading goalscorer for club and country.
“It was the best season of my career without a doubt,” Kane said, thanking his Bayern and England teammates and coaches for their contribution.
England head coach Thomas Tuchel congratulated Kane, calling the award deserved and praising his performances.
Kane is the first player representing a Bundesliga club to win the Ballon d’Or since Borussia Dortmund’s Matthias Sammer in 1996, according to the Bundesliga.

Wei Chuan Dragons win sixth Taiwan Series title with 6-0 shutout

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Wei Chuan Dragons defeated the CTBC Brothers 6-0 in Game 6 of the Taiwan Series at the Taipei Dome on Monday, securing their sixth Chinese Professional Baseball League championship with a 4-2 series victory.
Starting pitcher Cristopher Mercedes delivered a dominant performance, throwing eight scoreless innings, striking out six, walking two, and surrendering just two hits. Relievers Lin Tzu-yu (林子昱) and Lin Kai-wei (林凱威) combined to finish the shutout in the ninth inning, per CNA.
The Dragons won the first three games of the best-of-seven series before the Brothers rallied to win the next two, forcing a sixth game. The Dragons broke open a 1-0 game with five runs in the bottom of the eighth, including a two-run home run by catcher Jiang Shao-hong (蔣少宏).
The victory marked the Dragons’ sixth Taiwan Series title overall and their second since returning to top-flight competition in 2021. The team previously won championships in 1990, 1997, 1998, and 1999 before disbanding, then claimed its fifth title in 2023.
Manager Yeh Chun-chang (葉君璋) secured his third championship as a manager and his second with the Dragons since their return. His championship record also includes titles won during his playing career.
Yeh became emotional while speaking to reporters after the game, saying the team’s success stemmed from everyone’s efforts to improve the club.
“This team has achieved good results because everyone worked together. Everyone and every aspect of the team tried to make this team better,” he said. “Thinking about all of this, it’s impossible not to be emotional.”
Mercedes was named Taiwan Series Most Valuable Player after winning Games 2 and 6. Across his two starts, he pitched 14 innings and allowed one earned run, finishing with a 0.64 earned run average.
The Dominican pitcher did not allow a hit until the sixth inning of Game 6. After previously pitching for Japan’s Yomiuri Giants and Taiwan’s Uni-Lions, he achieved his championship goal with the Dragons.
“This game was the best I have ever pitched in my career,” Mercedes said. “I am so excited. I have never won a championship like this before.”
Dragons center fielder Kuo Tien-hsin (郭天信) said the experience of winning the 2023 championship had changed how he approached this year’s title run. He hoped to help younger teammates manage their nerves and learn from the experience, per CNA.
“Last time (2023), I just blindly fought hard and eventually won the championship. This time is different,” Kuo said.
“There are quite a few players younger than me on the team, and I hope they can learn something and be less nervous on the field. I am also someone who thinks a lot, and I hope to help them as much as possible.”
This year’s Taiwan Series, dubbed the “Dragon-Elephant showdown,” was the first championship series between the Dragons and Brothers. All six games were held at the Taipei Dome, with the schedule disrupted by a typhoon.
The six games drew a combined attendance of 230,615, setting a record for a single Taiwan Series. Games 1, 4, and 5 each drew 40,000 spectators, per UDN.

He also pressed for developing a shared toolkit to address key issues including hybrid threats, foreign agent registration, supply chain security, and the extraterritorial reach of Chinese law, the DPP said.
Chen said his invitation to participate in the forum and attend the European Democratic Party’s annual congress reflected European recognition of Taiwan’s democratic achievements. He described it as another step toward institutionalized cooperation through direct party-to-party dialogue.
The DPP will continue to pursue value-based diplomacy and expand Taiwan’s international space through party diplomacy, Chen said.

New report tracks how Russia helps China build better drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
03:54:05 UTC
12:54:05 KST

Russia's defense cooperation with China extends far beyond imports of dual-use goods, with evidence pointing to sharing drone design technology, providing testing services, and joint research, according to a new report from U.S. think tank C4ADS.
The report adds to earlier findings by the Kyiv Independent regarding China's military collaboration with Russia throughout the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
C4ADS, a Washington-based nonprofit that investigates security threats, released a report in October that maps lesser-known layers of cooperation between the two countries' defense industries, drawing on Russian trade records, corporate filings, leaked documents, and academic papers.
The investigation found that Russian designs for rocket-launched drones likely helped shape weapons China unveiled in 2025 and that Russian wind tunnels kept testing aircraft models for China's top arms maker after the invasion of Ukraine.
The report also documents how researchers from the two countries are jointly developing algorithms that could underpin combat drone swarms. Moreover, it shows that some suppliers to Russia's defense industry are moving production to China.
Beyond China’s well-documented supplies of components, raw materials and machine tools to the Russian defense industry, and Russia's recently revealed sales of airborne combat vehicles and munitions to China, the two industries increasingly work together further upstream, sharing designs, testing services and research.
read also
Joint drone development
A notable example involves the Science and Production Association SPLAV, Russia's leading maker of multiple-launch rocket systems (MLRS). SPLAV is subject to multiple international sanctions and export controls.
Trade records show SPLAV sent Chinese arms giant Norinco technical documents for a "reconnaissance rocket" in 2014–2015, and apparently again in April 2022, less than two months after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The rocket is most likely SPLAV's 9M534, which releases a reconnaissance drone in mid-flight.
In March 2025, China unveiled the Feilong 60A, a loitering drone launched from Norinco's SR-5 rocket system and reportedly capable of operating in swarms. Three months later, Norinco tested Sky Eye, a drone fired from a cannon. Both drones are similar to the Russian 9M534.
C4ADS believes the Russian technical documents helped speed up Norinco's work on both systems, though it notes that this conclusion rests mainly on how closely the Chinese and Russian systems resemble each other.
Russia's aerospace testing base is also working for Norinco, which now faces U.S. sanctions and Japanese and Taiwanese export controls.
The Russian state-owned Central Aerohydrodynamic Institute (TsAGI), which is under multiple Western sanctions, tested Chinese scale aircraft models in its wind tunnels and returned them to Norinco with the test data at least nine times between 2022 and 2024. The work comes as Norinco has been expanding into military drones over the past decade.
read also
The cooperation also extends to universities and research institutes. Drones have become a growing focus of joint research by Chinese and Russian scientists, according to C4ADS.
Researchers from the two countries co-authored 86 academic papers on drones and other unmanned systems between 2022 and 2026, an average of about 17 a year. In the dozen years from 2009 to 2021, they produced only 36 such papers, or about three a year.
Evgeny Neretin, a department head at the Moscow Aviation Institute, has co-authored multiple papers with researchers tied to Chinese defense laboratories — labs that also funded the work. The papers deal with algorithms for autonomous drone combat and, more recently, for keeping several drones in formation while they track targets, a likely building block for drone swarms.
In June 2025, the Chinese government approved the creation of a joint educational institute between the Moscow Aviation Institute (sanctioned by the U.S. and EU), and China's military-linked Northwestern Polytechnical University (subject to U.S. and Japanese export controls).
read also
Russian weapons, made in China
The C4ADS report also indicates that some Russian makers of machine tools and chips are moving production to China.
Stankomashstroy, a sanctioned Russian machine-tool maker, plans to move production of advanced five-axis machine tools to an industrial park in China's Shaanxi province.
In 2025, the company sold equipment to the Votkinsk Plant, which builds ballistic missiles, and to Izhevsk Electromechanical Plant Kupol, a producer of air defense systems and long-range attack drones.
Illustrating Moscow's reliance on Beijing for chips, Russia's sanctioned state-owned chipmaker Element set up at least four subsidiaries in China in 2025 and began assembling chipsets there. In 2026, Element also bought power electronics intellectual property from the Chinese defense contractor Shijiazhuang Tonhe Electronics.
According to C4ADS, these moves would likely help Element produce military-grade microelectronics despite Western sanctions and export controls. They also fit a recent Kremlin initiative to build up Russia's chip industry.
A deepening alliance
The C4ADS report adds fresh details to previous findings by the Kyiv Independent regarding China and Russia's military partnership.
While China officially claims neutrality in Russia's war against Ukraine, Beijing remains Moscow's key trading partner, economic supporter, oil buyer, and provider of dual-use equipment.
According to leaked Rostec documents, China bought Russian airborne combat vehicles, ammunition, and parachute systems after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Dozens of Chinese officers and arms industry staff visited Russia during the war to negotiate the deals.
Separate Kyiv Independent investigations found that Chinese suppliers have helped keep Russia's missile and drone production pipelines running.
Machine tools shipped mostly from China fueled the expansion of the Votkinsk Plant, which makes ballistic missiles — including intercontinental ones.
Chinese and Hong Kong companies also supplied parts to the maker of Russia's Lancet attack drones and remain the main channel for Western chips used in Russian weapons.

Meta merges apps and device accounts under one system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
03:53:47 UTC
12:53:47 KST

Did you wake up to an email from Meta recently about your new Meta Account?
Or maybe you received a pop-up message on your Facebook or Instagram account?
Well you're not alone.
In April, Meta announced it would be unifying access to its accounts across the company's apps with some Australians already seeing the changes.
Here's a rundown of what's changed and how it affects you.
What's changing and why?
Meta is changing its current Accounts Centre with an updated system called Meta Account.
The idea of the new system is to bring account management for the company's various apps and devices under one system.
These include:
- Messenger
- Threads
- Meta AI
- AI glasses
- Meta Quest headsets
Meta says WhatsApp will not be added to a Meta Account by default. It will only be in your Meta Account if you choose to add it or you've previously added it to your Accounts Centre.
The switch should not change your profiles or how you use these apps.
Meta says it's designed to make "signing in and managing your settings easier".
Here are a few updates you can expect, according to Meta:
- One password
- Easy set up for new apps and devices
- Boosted security with passkeys
- 24/7 protection
- Personalised security recommendations
Can you opt out?
No.
The change is automatic and being rolled out gradually.
You should receive a notification on your social media platform and email when your account is updated.
But Meta says you can still control and choose which profiles are in your Meta Account at any time.
For example, you can have a Meta Account for your Facebook and another Meta Account for your Instagram profile.
Settings that are specific to each app will also remain independent.
"For example, who can see your Facebook posts is a Facebook setting," Meta's website says.
"Similarly, whether someone can tag you in a photo on Instagram is an Instagram setting."
So how can I keep my apps separate?
Here's a step-by-step guide to create separate Meta Accounts for each of your apps:
- Click your profile picture in the top right of Facebook
- Select Settings & privacy, then click Settings
- Click Meta Account, then click Manage account
- Click Manage on your app of choice
- Click Move out of this Meta Account
When it comes to your passwords, Meta should use the same login info you use currently. It's up to you if you want to create a single password or passkey to use across all apps and devices.
Is it safe to put all your apps under the same Meta Account?
Macquarie University cyber security lecturer Jennifer Williams says while the new account system is likely no more or less secure than the old one, a breach of the new system would have a greater impact.
"An attacker would be able to gain access to all of your private messages on Instagram, Facebook, and, for those who have connected it to their Meta account, WhatsApp," Dr Williams says.
"They could use information from those messages to blackmail the user, impersonate them and send messages to their friends and family, or make posts on their behalf."
But Dr Williams says in the end, security comes down to the user's practices.
"If they do not use strong, unique passwords or two-factor authentication, then there is a greater risk of a breach of their account."
Ryan Ko, director of the Cyber Research Centre at the University of Queensland, says the more significant question is privacy.
"A unified identity makes it easier for Meta to track and profile its users, which then enables them to sell on to their clients," Professor Ko says.
"When Meta Account users' profiles connect activity across services, it creates a richer and more comprehensive profile of the user.
"The security risk is concentrated access; the privacy risk is concentrated knowledge of the user."

Ukraine and Russia begin Oleshky ceasefire for aid mission
October 27, 2026
Russia and Ukraine began a localized ceasefire early Tuesday to allow humanitarian aid into the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky in southern Ukraine.
Both sides confirmed that the truce took effect at 3 a.m. local time (0100 GMT), following an agreement brokered by US first lady Melania Trump.
Russia's Defense Ministry said its forces had stopped shelling in the Kherson sector to prepare for the humanitarian operation.
Ukraine's human rights commissioner Dmytro Lubinets also confirmed that Kyiv was observing the agreement.
"As head of the Ukrainian negotiating team, I confirm that the Ukrainian side is honoring its commitments," he wrote on Facebook.
However, it could not be independently verified whether fighting had decreased.
What is the humanitarian situation in Oleshky?
Around 2,000 people, including up to 50 children, remain trapped in Oleshky, according to Ukrainian and US estimates. The town had about 24,000 residents before Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.
The United Nations says residents face severe shortages of food and medicine. Mines and drone attacks have made it difficult for them to leave.
Former residents told news agency AFP earlier this year that people remaining in the town were starving, sometimes hunting pigeons or surviving on food grown in their gardens.
"They've forgotten what bread is. You need flour for bread, and there's not even flour left," said Olga, who was in contact with two families still in Oleshky.
Oleshky lies across the Dnipro River from the Ukrainian-controlled city of Kherson.
Russian troops captured the town during the first days of the invasion in 2022. It suffered further destruction in June 2023 when the collapse of the Kakhovka dam caused widespread flooding.
What role did Melania Trump play in the ceasefire?
The White House said last week that Melania Trump had helped secure the agreement after holding talks with civilian negotiators from Russia and Ukraine.
Her office said the first lady had also met United Nations officials who briefed her on conditions in Oleshky.
Announcing the agreement on Friday, Trump said civilian officials from both countries would visit residents to assess their needs.
Doctors, food, drinking water and medicine are expected to reach the town before evacuation corridors are opened.
"Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine," Melania Trump said.
Ukraine has accused Russia of preventing residents from leaving, an allegation Moscow denies.
Neither side has provided details about who will monitor the ceasefire. Reports have also differed over its duration, with one account saying it could last through Saturday.
What happened in Kyiv after the ceasefire began?
Russian missile attacks continued elsewhere in Ukraine as the localized ceasefire began.
Explosions shook Kyiv shortly after 3 a.m. local time Tuesday, according to witnesses, while air raid alerts sounded across several regions.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the attacks had damaged the Southern Bridge and associated subway infrastructure. City authorities said traffic on the bridge had been suspended.
On Monday, a Russian missile attack on Kyiv killed at least one person and injured 10 others, including students at a dormitory. Further attacks caused casualties in Kharkiv and Pavlohrad.
"It is important that the world sees that Russia is showing nothing but a desire to kill and continue waging war," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote after the attacks.
Could the Oleshky ceasefire help revive Ukraine peace talks?
The limited truce in Oleshky comes ahead of another round of US-mediated peace talks between Washington, Moscow and Kyiv, expected in November.
Negotiations have been effectively frozen since the United States and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran in February.
Previous attempts to establish ceasefires have repeatedly failed amid deep mistrust between Russia and Ukraine.
More than four and a half years after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, hundreds of thousands of soldiers and civilians have been killed, while millions have been forced to flee their homes.

Malaysia’s 2027 Budget: Fiscal Consolidation Continues Apace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
03:51:00 UTC
12:51:00 KST

The Malaysian economy is coasting these days. Growth for 2026 will be around 5 percent, with similar levels projected for 2027. Investment in manufacturing and digital services is flowing in, and the current account and trade balance are running large surpluses thanks to booming exports. The deficit is shrinking, even as fuel subsidies rise to cushion consumers from spiking energy prices. Inflation is stable, and fiscal reforms have succeeded in widening and diversifying the tax base, reducing exposure to volatile petroleum rents. For Malaysian fiscal planners, 2027 is coming up roses.
This kind of stable, sustained economic growth is music to the ears of fiscal forecasters because it means tax revenue will continue to grow in proportion to GDP. Not only that, but it will grow in a largely predictable manner. This is obviously important when making a budget because decisions about future spending and borrowing depend on how well you forecast revenue and growth. If growth misses the forecast, revenue comes in below target and the deficit widens. This has been a recurring theme in the Philippines in recent years.
It seems unlikely Malaysia will have a similar issue. Steady, predictable growth means more accurate revenue forecasts, making it easier to control spending and trim the deficit, something Malaysian fiscal planners are particularly fond of. Government expenditures mostly focus on maintaining and upgrading systems and services, and it is unusual to see big budget-busting social or infrastructure programs. As soon as the economy stabilized after the pandemic, Malaysia pivoted toward fiscal consolidation and sought to get the deficit under control through a combination of spending cuts and tax hikes.
This has continued apace in recent budgets, and it is working. The deficit in 2026 is projected at 3.6 percent of GDP, a steep decline from the high of 6.4 percent in 2021. Fiscal consolidation continues in 2027, with the deficit shrinking to 3.3 percent of GDP. That would be the lowest level since 2017. This is expected to happen even as approved government spending for 2027 rises to 458 billion ringgit ($112 billion), a 3.7 percent increase year over year.
Such is the power of tax reform. Historically, Malaysia has been highly dependent on dividends and taxes derived from extracting, refining, and selling petroleum products such as natural gas and oil. In 2019, dividends from state-owned oil and gas firm Petronas and excise and other taxes on petroleum-related activities accounted for 32 percent of government revenue. By 2026, it had fallen to 15 percent, and is expected to remain around that level in the 2027 budget. More than 80 percent of government revenue now reliably comes from non-petroleum sources, mainly taxes.
This is good news because while rents from natural resources like oil and gas can be an important contributor to government operations, they are unpredictable. Prices go up and down, and as the world pivots toward cleaner energy, any government that relies excessively on exploiting fossil fuels to shore up its revenue could be left holding the bag in a couple of decades when renewables are more dominant. By then, it will be too late.
Tax reforms, particularly a recent hike in the sales and service tax, have shifted revenue toward a more sustainable and diversified tax base. Revenue from this tax is set to increase from 10.5 percent of the total in 2019 to 19.2 percent in 2027. The sales and service tax is expected to contribute 73 billion ringgit in 2027, around $18 billion. Few people are happy to pay higher taxes, but during disruptive and uncertain transitional periods, such as the one we are currently living through, expanding the tax base and shoring up the country’s fiscal health is boring but sound medicine.
Evidence of this can be found in the one major line item where Malaysia continues to spend big: subsidies. Malaysia spent around $18 billion on subsidies in 2026, and is targeting roughly the same amount for 2027. A lot of this will go toward cushioning consumers from spiking energy prices. Fiscal planners would prefer to see subsidies go in the opposite direction. Indeed, they started cutting subsidies soon after the post-pandemic economy began stabilizing.
But with an unexpected shock to global energy prices that most rational people would not have seen coming, tax reforms and prudent fiscal management give Malaysia sufficient policy space to increase spending and shell out $18 billion in subsidies in successive years while still narrowing the deficit. That is the kind of fiscal math finance ministers in some neighboring countries can only dream about.

Scientists video REM-like sleep in Australian jumping spider species
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
03:49:29 UTC
12:49:29 KST

Scientists video REM-like sleep in Australian jumping spider species
In short:
A new study has found a species of jumping spider, Portia fimbriata, experiences at least two sleep stages, including a REM-like stage.
An Australian expert says the study is the "most complete behavioural case for sleep in any arachnid".
What's next?
The team is now looking at how spiders sleep in the wild, including across Australia.
While not everyone gets to enjoy some peaceful shut eye, it seems that more creatures than we thought enjoy a good kip.
Subtle eye flickers and leg curls captured on video confirm a small Australian jumping spider experiences the same kinds of movements we do during sleep, according to a new study.
Study co-author Daniela Rößler, a behavioural ecologist from the University of Bonn, said the sleep patterns of Portia fimbriata were structured in at least two parts.
"Spiders have distinct sleep stages, and that the architecture of their sleep mirrors key features of vertebrate sleep far more closely than anyone expected," she said.
The research, which the team hopes can help scientists understand how sleep has evolved through the animal kingdom, was published today in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
How to wake a spider
Portia fimbriata, which is found across Northern Australia, is a "dream species" for studying sleep, study co-author Nadja Geiger said.
"She is diurnal, highly visual and famously clever,"
Ms Geiger said.
"She also has a very clear night-time resting posture, sleeping upside down in a little web … this makes sleep easier to identify and study."
The team recorded the arachnids throughout the night, then carefully analysed the footage to identify the stages.
The spiders groomed themselves while they snoozed and drooped down slowly over the course of the night in a phase the researchers called quiescent.
This was followed by a REM-like sleep stage, complete with leg curls, eye movements and arm twitching as the spiders dosed.
Loading...
Once the researchers had observed these two different phases, they could see what happened when they tried to wake the spider up.
"A hallmark sign of sleep is … [responding] slower or not at all to external stimuli," Ms Geiger said.
They woke the spiders up with a loud noise while they were still for more than 15 minutes in the quiescent stage, as well as when they showed signs of REM-like sleep and when they were visibly awake.
Similar to humans who have been woken from a nap, it took the spiders longer to respond when they were in this quiescent and REM-like state.
"This effect was particularly strong during the REM-like phase," Ms Geiger said.
"Responses were significantly delayed, and some spiders did not respond at all."
Spider sleep a (not so) controversial idea
Thomas White, an entomologist at the University of Sydney who studies invertebrate behaviour, said some people might think associating similar behaviours to animals that were so distantly removed from us was controversial.
"With spiders, you're talking about animals that have diverged 500 million years ago from all other vertebrates," Dr White said.
But he noted that scientists were becoming less hesitant as evidence mounted that similar behaviours occurred.
"We readily see our dog lying down and its eyes are twitching and it's kicking its little paws. Essentially what [the researchers] are showing here is that something similar," he said.
"Yes, [spiders] diverged a very long time ago, but if we're willing to extend that inference to our dogs, our cats, or even animals that are quite unlike us like reptiles, then what's stopping us from extending that inference … in animals that are very unlike us?"
Dr White said that the study built on research from the same team a few years ago that found some possible REM-like sleep in jumping spiders.
"But this goes a step further in mapping out different behavioural facets of sleep-like behaviour," he said.
"This paper is far and away the most complete behavioural case for sleep in any arachnid."
What can spider sleep tell us?
According to Dr Rößler, understanding how spiders sleep may help researchers explain why sleep exists at all.
"If animals with such different brains and sensory worlds show structured sleep with REM‑like phases, it suggests that the basic architecture of sleep may be far older and more widespread than we thought," she said.
"Comparing sleep across such different animals can help us understand how sleep evolved, which features are ancient, and what functions different sleep stages may serve."
The researchers are now looking at studying sleep in spiders in the wild, including fieldwork in northern Queensland and Western Australia.
"This allows us to ask how natural conditions and anthropogenic changes, such as artificial light and habitat disturbance, influence sleep outside the laboratory," Dr Rößler said.
"We'd love for this kind of research to help spread a little more curiosity and appreciation for these charismatic animals."

Macklemore vows to fight until 'last breath' at opening of 'Free Palestine' tour
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
03:45:16 UTC
12:45:16 KST

American rapper Macklemore vowed to continue to speak out loudly against Israel's war in Gaza at the opening of his "Free Palestine" concert tour, organized after he was dropped as the opening act for Ed Sheeran over pro-Palestinian remarks.
The Grammy-winning rapper received a deafening ovation in Dublin, where fans in the overwhelmingly pro-Palestinian country came draped in Palestinian flags, black, red and green football jerseys and keffiyeh scarves being sold by vendors outside.
"I am proud to stand here on stage in solidarity with the Palestinian people. We will continue to fight for collective liberation until our last breath," Macklemore said on stage, where he waved a Palestinian flag for much of his set.
"Six weeks ago, two words is all that it took," he said, referring to the rallying cry of "Free Palestine" and his criticism of the Israeli government's actions in Gaza and the West Bank at New Jersey's MetLife Stadium that led to his removal from Sheeran's US tour.
"Those two words are so threatening to some people that we'd rather silence those two words than confront what they actually mean... Somehow those words have become more controversial than the suffering that made them necessary."
The crowd, who snapped up the 13,000 tickets for Dublin's 3Arena within minutes, chanted "Free Free Palestine" throughout.
Macklemore a 'speaker for our time,' concert attendee says
"We need a speaker for our time. It has to be somebody like that who can reach out to people. He made it feel so alive, and I've come out feeling I want to be part of something," said Siobhan Lyons from Dublin, who attended the concert with her daughter.
Irish artists who have spoken out against Israel's actions played in support on Monday, including "Take Me to Church" singer Hozier, rap group Kneecap and Beoga, one of the acts who quit Sheeran's tour in solidarity with Macklemore.
Palestinian singer Lina Makhoul and Palestinian American DJ Habibeats also performed, and pro-Palestine activists such as Game of Thrones actor Liam Cunningham spoke between sets.
Sheeran, one of the world's top-selling recording artists, said stadium owners on the remaining dates threatened to bar any further shows with Macklemore on the bill.
Palestinian authorities say more than 74,000 people have been killed in Israel's assault on Gaza, launched after Hamas-led fighters killed about 1,200 people in southern Israel on October 7, 2023. Israeli officials deny their actions in Gaza amount to genocide.
The "Free Palestine" tour will continue in Paris and London this week, with US dates due to be announced later, Macklemore has said.

G Flip and Chrishell Stause have broken up and like many in the queer community, I’m in mourning  | Rebecca Shaw
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
03:44:59 UTC
12:44:59 KST

In this current bummer of a world, we often wake up to bad news. This morning, it was devastating. I picked up my phone and saw multiple texts asking me how I felt about the fact that … Chrishell Stause and G Flip have broken up.
If those names seem like some sort of gibberish to you, I won’t expect you to understand the seismic shift. While I was sleeping soundly in Australia in the knowledge that love exists, Strause, from the LA “real estate” show Selling Sunset, posted a vulnerable and deeply sad video where she revealed that she and Australian drummer G Flip have parted ways after being married for several years.
Her clear, genuine sadness, her talk of feeling like a failure – it moved me. I posted about it on Instagram and in came the flood of responses: Nooooo. Love is dead. Love isn’t real. Whose fault is this. I’m devastated. I’m in mourning. And so on and so forth. Many queer people in particular have been sliced in the heart by this news. Every group chat I’m in is talking about it (not all instigated by me).
I’ve started seeing comments under posts about the breakup such as “Who?” or worse, “Who cares?” and I have to tell you that I care. We care. To me, and people like me, this relationship was a beautiful queer success story.
Chrishell comes from a poor background, and her previous marriage ended in a brutal public dumping by actor Justin Hartley. She joined Selling Sunset as a real estate agent and soon became the main character as she compellingly rebuilt her life. During the process she met and fell in love with a non-binary drummer from Australia.
Watching someone from such a hyper heterosexual world like Los Angeles real estate, from a hyper heterosexual show like Selling Sunset, begin to dip her toe into the queer world was amazing. Watching her experiencing a truly fulfilling romantic relationship and falling for someone who loved her back and encouraged her to be her true self was a balm. Bringing that queer dynamic to the world of reality TV was also deeply enjoyable.
I think everyone tuned into this public relationship was happy to see Chrishell glowing. She and G Flip travelled together, their love always seeming to become stronger and more joyous. Chrishell seemed to love Australia, and in fact became part of Australia, endearing herself by travelling to all sorts of places G Flip’s music took her, such as Wollongong. When she ordered a flat white in a Selling Sunset scene at a cafe, I felt national pride. When the show introduced wide American audiences to their relationship, and to Chrishell’s hyper femme love for the non-binary G Flip, the couple received homophobic hate. But their love endured.
Until now.
Of course, we don’t know what happened. We know that Chrishell seems heartbroken, posting a video because she felt she owed it to the fans of their relationship, the ones who have been so supportive. We know that she seems confused, saying it won’t be hard for her to be respectful of G Flip “because I am in love with this person”, and adding she doesn’t “have all the information and the reasons” for the breakup.
We know that G Flip posted, saying that their head and heart feel very heavy. Ultimately, as much as I would love a full investigative report, a timeline, perhaps a podcast series, we are strangers to these two people and their relationship. Their love seemed genuine and real, and as we all know, that sometimes isn’t enough. Chrishell also said she is “definitely never doing this again”. I hope she doesn’t mean true love, I hope she means that after her public marriage breakup with Justin Hartley and her very visible relationship with G Flip, she won’t be bringing an audience along with her next time.
It must be pretty exhausting to have your romantic life turned into a spectator sport, even if the spectators are mostly well-meaning strangers, such as lesbians who love your love.
So for now, I and many others will be in a short period of mourning. It’s yet another loss of a nice thing. I will be lighting a candle and accepting condolences. And then, I will be trying to get on with my life, just as Chrishell and G Flip will. Love may not be dead, but it certainly had a difficult morning.
- Rebecca Shaw is a writer based in Sydney

'Determined to make sure we do everything': Albanese reacts to MPs' calls for duress alarms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
03:43:04 UTC
12:43:04 KST

IN BRIEF
- Anthony Albanese told Labor MPs on Tuesday he understood they wanted tighter security at both the office and home.
- The prime minister said an independent review, particularly focusing on safety and security, would be fast-tracked.
Labor MPs have proposed duress alarms as a security option with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese after raising concerns following a colleague's horrific injuries from an alleged attack.
Concerns from MPs have sparked daily reviews after independent Indi representative Helen Haines was struck repeatedly by a four-wheel drive outside her Wangaratta office.
Haines has lost both her legs in hospital and remains in a serious but stable condition.
Police are examining the motive of the alleged attack.
Albanese told Labor MPs during a party room briefing on Tuesday he understood they wanted tighter security whether at the office or at home.

Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
He said the government would fast-track an independent review, with safety and security recommendations a particular focus.
"You've all dedicated so much to the safety of others in the workplace," Albanese told colleagues.
"I'm determined to make sure we do everything for your safety and the safety of your staff as well."
Opposition leader Angus Taylor told a Coalition party room meeting political violence had largely been avoided in Australia because of a "robust parliamentary system".
"The foundation of the Westminster system was to stop violence and wars," he said.
Parliament House security to be stepped up
At least nine MPs will have security crackdowns accelerated for their electorate offices, Finance Minister Katy Gallagher confirmed, after they raised concerns last week.
Security in Parliament House's public places will also be stepped up.
"It's very legitimate that we have a look at that and respond," she told ABC Radio.
Security is handled across several departments: the Australian Federal Police is responsible for assessments and security details, the Department of Home Affairs looks after home security, and the Department of Finance handles offices and transport.
All three coordinate to share information, Finance secretary Matt Yannopoulos confirmed in a late-night Senate estimates sitting on Monday.
But the updated protection would not be enough to shield women in the public eye from abuse, Gallagher warned, urging social media companies to take action when threats are posted on their platforms.
Debate on proposed social media reforms set to return
Her comments come before the government's Digital Duty of Care bill returns for debate in the lower house.
Under the proposal, social media platforms would be forced to protect users under 18 from content that promotes crime, eating disorders, pornography or misogynistic content, as well as posts that cause distress.
Representatives from the media regulator and the eSafety commissioner will likely field questions about the proposed legislation during Senate estimates on Tuesday.
MPs from across the political divide paused proceedings on Monday for a full day of tributes to Haines.
'I felt like I couldn't breathe'
As the sun set over the capital, Labor backbencher Ali France described learning of the attack.
"I felt like I couldn't breathe, my chest hurt, and like the speed of light, my brain went straight to her fight for life," France recounted in parliament.
"The flashes of fear that she may have had, the confusion of not knowing what was hurt or who was hurt, the urgency and the heroism of bystanders, her staff, and first responders.
"I went there because I know it."
France was seriously injured saving her youngest son Zac from an out-of-control vehicle in a shopping centre car park in 2011 and had a leg amputated.
