Egyptian man breaches Israeli border fence as IDF warns of heightened security concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
03:41:22 UTC
12:41:22 KST

An Egyptian national crossed the border fence from Egypt into Israel early Tuesday in the Nitzana area and was detained by IDF troops dispatched to the scene, the military said.
According to the IDF, the suspect was spotted by military surveillance systems and apprehended after crossing the border fence. He was taken for further questioning by security forces.
"The IDF views the incident with severity and continues to maintain a high level of defensive readiness in the area," the military said, adding that the incident is under investigation.
On August 3, IDF troops and undercover Border Police officers intercepted a smuggling cell along the Egyptian border in two separate operations, arresting two suspects. In one incident, members of the cell were spotted attempting to smuggle weapons and drugs. A large drone believed to have been used for cross-border smuggling was found in their possession. In another operation, security forces seized an off-road vehicle carrying a large quantity of substances suspected to be drugs.
On September 29, 2025, military surveillance personnel spotted a cell of at least two suspected smugglers near the Egyptian border and dispatched troops to the area. As the suspects attempted to flee, their vehicle overturned, killing one of them. The suspects were believed to have been involved in an attempted drone-smuggling operation. Another suspect managed to escape.
The IDF did not initially report the incident. In response to an inquiry from ynet, the military said: "During an IDF operation, surveillance personnel identified suspects near the Egyptian border, and troops were dispatched to the location. As the suspects attempted to flee, their vehicle collided with an IDF vehicle and overturned. There were no casualties among our forces."
Toward the end of last year, following IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir's directive to establish a special unit to combat drone smuggling from Egypt after months of limited enforcement, Defense Minister Israel Katz ordered the military to designate the area adjacent to the border a closed military zone.
Katz also announced that the rules of engagement would be "adjusted accordingly", declaring: "We are declaring war. Anyone who enters the prohibited area will be harmed."

DONETSK, October 27. /TASS/. Russian troops have evacuated 87 civilians from Kupyansk-Uzlovoy in the Kharkov Region, Russian Foreign Ministry Ambassador-at-Large Rodion Miroshnik said.
"Service members from the 153rd Tank Regiment of the 47th Tank division, led by the regimental commander, callsign Trinadtsaty, and the assault team commander, callsign Rumyn, carried out a large-scale humanitarian operation to evacuate civilians from the liberated city of Kupyansk-Uzlovoy. A group of civilians was found in the basement of an apartment building in the southern part of the city, which until recently was controlled by the enemy. Troops led by a commander with the callsign Maga used electronic warfare equipment and drones to establish a corridor stretching more than 20 kilometers, providing passage and cover along a route where Ukrainian forces had remotely planted landmines," he wrote on Telegram.
Miroshnik added that Ukrainian forces had carried out a series of mortar and drone attacks on civilians during the evacuation, causing casualties. A total of 87 people were evacuated over three days.

Russian strikes on Kyiv overnight into Tuesday, Oct. 27, prompted traffic restrictions on the South (Pivdennyi) Bridge, a major transport crossing connecting the capital’s eastern and western banks of the Dnipro River.
The Kyiv City Military Administration (KMVA) announced the restrictions following the attack and warned residents to account for disruptions when planning their journeys.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Service on the Green (Syretsko-Pecherska) metro line was also disrupted, with trains operating separately between Syrets and Vydubychi stations and between Osokorky and Chervonyi Khutir, according to the KMVA.
South Bridge is being inspected for damage following a Russian attack, Kyiv Mayor Vitalii Klitschko later said in a Telegram post. Specialists are assessing the extent of the damage, and the bridge is currently closed to traffic.
Klitschko also released the first photos showing the aftermath of the Russian strike on the bridge.
There is currently no information on when the bridge will reopen to traffic or when metro service on this section of the line will resume.
The South Bridge carries both road traffic and a section of the Green Line, making it a critical connection across the Dnipro.
The disruption follows repeated Russian attacks on the crossing earlier in October, including strikes that damaged metro infrastructure and forced temporary suspensions of road and rail traffic.
In a separate development overnight, Klitschko reported that Russian ballistic strikes hit an administrative building in Kyiv’s Podilskyi district and non-residential buildings at two other locations.

The latest attack followed Monday evening’s missile strikes on a university campus and residential neighborhoods, which killed one person and injured 10 others, most of them students.

mockups before fuckups at museo franz mayer opens the archives of jorge diego etienne, revealing nearly 15 years of sketches, prototypes, and material tests behind the monterrey-based designer's practice.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
JORGE DIEGO ETIENNE (JDE) EXHIBITS 15 YEARS OF PHYSICAL PROTOTYPES
Presented at the Museo Franz Mayer in Mexico City, Mockups Before Fuckups surveys nearly 15 years of design practice by Monterrey-based consultancy JDE, founded by industrial designer Jorge Diego Etienne. On view from October 16th, 2026, through February 14th, 2027, the exhibition focuses on the iterative processes preceding market production, exhibiting preliminary sketches, scale models, working prototypes, material experiments, 3D printed studies, and unreleased design concepts.
EXPANDED ARCHIVE BRINGS UNRELEASED DESIGNS AND COLLABORATIONS
The exhibition layout is structured around the studio’s five methodological stages and fifteen core design principles, framing physical prototyping and error mitigation as fundamental risk-reduction tools. Spanning varied typologies, including tableware, furniture collections, public spaces, and urban infrastructure, the displayed works feature Etienne’s early aluminum pen holder Choose Your Bullets, custom tableware developed for Michelin-starred restaurant Pangea, and research pieces from the Galeana collectible design series, alongside corporate collaborations with TANE, Libbey, Coca-Cola, Tupperware, and Cemex. Curated with the assistance of Roble Vargas, this expanded edition follows an earlier presentation at Centro Cultural Plaza Fátima in Monterrey and is accompanied by a monographic publication edited by designaholic (books).

EU gas prices hit four-year high
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
03:31:28 UTC
12:31:28 KST

EU gas prices hit four-year high
European natural gas prices have surged to their highest level in four years amid the Iran war and the EU’s continued push to phase out Russian energy, according to data from online aggregator Trading Economics.
On Monday, wholesale prices briefly surpassed €97 ($108) per megawatt-hour, reaching levels not seen since December 2022. The increase came as gas storage facilities in the EU were just 74.62% full as of October 25, well below seasonal averages.
Liquefied natural gas (LNG) shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, which accounted for around a fifth of global LNG trade before the start of the US-Israeli war against Iran earlier this year, remained around 80% below pre-conflict levels.
Some EU countries have already begun drawing on stored gas as temperatures drop. Trading Economics forecasts that European gas prices will reach €98.20 per megawatt-hour by the end of the fourth quarter of 2026.
In the UK, the month-ahead gas contract rose by 4% to its highest level since December 2022, according to The Guardian. Brent crude, which climbed to $117 per barrel last week, has since eased slightly but remains at around $115.
British households could face a 27% increase in energy bills in January, pushing the average annual dual-fuel bill to nearly £2,200 ($2,940), according to a forecast by energy supplier EDF. An earlier forecast by Cornwall Insight projected a 16% increase to £2,000.
In August, The Guardian reported mounting concerns in the EU over low gas storage levels and soaring prices ahead of winter. In September, EU Energy Commissioner Dan Jorgensen warned that the bloc faces its worst energy crisis since 2022.
In mid-October, German media reported that Berlin plans to make households and businesses pay for a national emergency gas reserve costing more than €3 billion over ten years. The government-controlled stockpile would be reserved for emergencies, including sabotage and infrastructure failures, rather than being used to lower gas prices.
The opposition Alternative for Germany (AfD) party called for energy ties with Russia to be restored, following US President Donald Trump’s example. On October 13, AfD co-leader Alice Weidel said Germany should seek its own diesel deal with Russia, praising Trump’s agreement with the country as a pragmatic approach.
Following the EU’s sweeping sanctions on Russia in 2022, the bloc experienced one of its worst energy crises in decades. Gas prices soared above €300 per megawatt-hour, driving up costs for industries and households and contributing to surging inflation.
The EU has continued its efforts to phase out Russian energy. While Russia accounted for around 45% of EU gas imports in 2021, the share fell to around 12% by 2025.
Moscow has described the EU’s efforts to sever energy ties with Russia as “suicidal.” Last week, Russian presidential investment envoy Kirill Dmitriev argued that the bloc would eventually have to restore ties because “cooperation with Russia economically will be inevitable.”
Dmitriev blamed the EU’s problems, including high energy costs, on its leaders, saying they refuse to acknowledge and correct their mistakes.

This article was first published on October 27, 1971.
Hongkong’s royal welcome for Princess Anne
Princess Anne, radiant in a stylish knee-length beige suit and a matching wide-brimmed hat, flew in yesterday (October 26, 1971) to a warm welcome from the people of Hong Kong.
She begins her official visits today (October 27, 1971) – a public holiday – when thousands of people will be able to see her during her calls at places like the Tung Wah Hospital, the Po Leung Kuk and the ancient Man Mo Temple.
The Princess, who has heard a lot about this “Pearl of the Orient” from her father, will do a little sightseeing, and perhaps a little shopping too in Sheung Wan, a district which boasts a history almost as long as that of the Colony itself.

DOJ charges ex-FBI Director James Comey in new case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
03:30:04 UTC
12:30:04 KST

Former FBI Director James Comey has been charged for the third time with federal crimes, according to a court filing unsealed Monday in U.S. District Court in Washington, D.C., at Comey's request.
Comey is accused in the new case with knowingly communicating information related to national defense to a person not entitled to receive it.
He is also charged with conspiring with others to violate the law against sharing such information.
The charging document, known as an information, says Comey, "through one or more co-conspirators," directed an unnamed individual "to disclose national defense information to a reporter for a national news publication."
Comey is seeking to dismiss the new case, according to a court filing by his lawyers, which says the information relates to the "alleged disclosure of classified information" to The New York Times on Oct. 5, 2016.
Comey's lawyers told a judge in that filing that the alleged disclosure "was investigated by two separate U.S. Attorneys over the past ten years. Both declined to prosecute."
Comey has been repeatedly targeted by the Department of Justice under the administration of President Donald Trump, who fired him as FBI director in 2017. Both men have been fierce critics of one another since then.
"For the third time in little more than one year, the Department of Justice has attempted to charge Mr. Comey with a federal crime. Mr. Comey steadfastly maintains his innocence," his attorney, Patrick Fitzgerald, said in a statement, according to The Associated Press.
The DOJ filed the information against Comey on Oct. 5 and asked a judge to seal it, citing the risk that an ongoing criminal investigation would be compromised by the charges becoming public. Judge Trevor McFadden granted that request that day.
Attorneys for Comey, whom the DOJ agreed should be notified of the information, filed a motion to dismiss the case on Oct. 9, arguing that the 10-year statute of limitations to file a grand jury indictment relating to events of Oct. 5, 2016, had expired.
Comey's lawyers accused the DOJ of filing "a faulty information under seal" in an effort to put the statute of limitations on hold.
The attorneys on Monday asked McFadden to unseal the information, and the judge agreed to do so.
Comey separately is currently seeking the dismissal of an indictment obtained by the DOJ in North Carolina federal court on charges of threatening Trump's life by posting a photo of seashells on a beach on social media. He previously successfully won dismissal of another indictment accusing him of falsely testifying to Congress.
The new criminal complaint came to light hours after a federal judge in New York ruled that the Department of Justice had unlawfully fired Comey's daughter, Maurene Comey, last year as an assistant U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York.
"Well, they're back — again," James Comey said in a video message on Substack addressing the new case.
"It would almost be funny if it weren't such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice, one that we cannot become numb to," he said. "Nothing's changed with me. I'm still innocent. I'm still not afraid of these people, and I still believe in the independent federal judiciary."
"And I'm still lucky to have an amazing family and an incredible group of lawyers that will stand up in court and fight the latest and whatever comes after this," Comey said. "The next couple of years are going to be hard for all of us. It's really important that we stand straight and keep the faith in America."
In the pending indictment in North Carolina, Comey in late April was charged with threatening Trump's life by posting on Instagram a photo of seashells on a beach arranged to form the numbers "86 47."
Prosecutors claim that the number "86" — which is often used in restaurants to indicate a menu item is no longer available — was code for suggesting someone kill Trump, who is the 47th U.S. president.
Comey has denied any wrongdoing in that case and is seeking to have the indictment tossed out by a judge.
Comey was first indicted in September 2025 by a federal grand jury in Virginia on charges of making a false statement and obstruction, in connection with testimony he gave before the Senate Judiciary Committee on Sept. 30, 2020.
Comey, in that testimony, denied authorizing another person at the FBI to serve as an anonymous source in news reports regarding an investigation of Hillary Clinton and her emails when she was the Democratic presidential nominee in 2016.
That first indictment was dismissed by a judge on Nov. 24, 2025, after the judge ruled that Lindsey Halligan, a then-interim U.S. attorney who obtained the indictments, had been invalidly appointed.
On the same day the judge tossed Comey's case for that reason, the same judge dismissed an unrelated indictment obtained by Halligan against New York Attorney General Letitia James, who had been accused of bank fraud and making false statements to a financial institution in connection with a home mortgage she obtained in 2020.
James, like Comey, has been a staunch critic of Trump, and a target of the president's ire.

US judge halts tree-cutting at Trump’s Washington golf course project
- A US judge stopped more tree-cutting at East Potomac Golf Links in Washington, after hundreds of healthy trees were already removed for Donald Trump’s golf course plan.
- Judge Ana Reyes ordered no more tree damage and said the government must give ten business days’ notice before any major changes, pending the lawsuit.
- Trump wants the public course remade for championship events, but environmental groups and local golfers oppose the work and say the course has been badly rushed.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – A US federal judge ruled on Oct 26 to halt tree-cutting at a public golf course in the heart of the capital, after hundreds of trees were felled in President Donald Trump’s pet project.
As an avid golfer who owns courses around the world, Trump has called for Washington’s East Potomac Golf Links, a public course with affordable rates, to be remodelled into a facility capable of hosting major championship-calibre events.
The early demolition for the overhaul had charged ahead despite an environmental group’s lawsuit, and opposition from local golfers who argue the 100-year-old course is a rare spot where they can affordably play the sport.
“The Court ENJOINS defendants from removing or damaging additional trees on East Potomac Golf Course and ORDERS them to provide ten business days’ written advance notice before making any irreparable modification to any forms or features of East Potomac Park, pending the outcome of this litigation,” District Judge Ana Reyes wrote in the 70-page order on Oct 26.
“The Government felled hundreds of trees from the East Potomac Golf Course without real notice even though it knew of the scheduled removal at least a week prior,” Reyes wrote, adding they were “healthy, non-hazardous trees”.
Earlier in October, Trump said construction was set to start in November on the 18-hole course.
He insisted on Oct 26 that the site would close for renovation as scheduled on Nov 15 and pledged to appeal Reyes’ decision.
“The judge has absolutely no right to hold up this very important and beautiful Project,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.
More than 500 trees have already been cut down, the judge wrote.
The court “does not speak for the trees,” Reyes wrote in her order, in reference to the Dr. Seuss book The Lorax.
“It speaks only for the rule of law,” she said. AFP

Flavio Bolsonaro drops bid to annul Brazil's presidential runoff
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:26:32 CST
12:26:32 KST

RIO DE JANEIRO, Oct. 26 (Xinhua) -- Defeated Brazilian presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro has abandoned plans to seek the annulment of Sunday's presidential runoff, but will pursue separate legal action against incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's campaign over power abuse, Brazilian media reported Monday.
Lula won Sunday's runoff with 51.79 percent of valid votes, defeating Bolsonaro, who received 48.21 percent, according to results released by Brazil's Superior Electoral Court.
Bolsonaro, the candidate of the right-wing Liberal Party, refused to concede defeat in remarks in Brasilia late Sunday, saying he would seek to have the election annulled.
Earlier Sunday, Brazil's Supreme Federal Court ordered polling stations nationwide to extend voting by two hours in response to disruptions caused by public transport stoppages and heavy rain.
The extension applied only to polling stations that were still open when the decision was made by the Superior Electoral Court. Stations that had already closed were not reopened.
Bolsonaro argued that the measure disadvantaged voters in areas where polling stations were not reopened and said his legal team would challenge the election results.
However, his allies and lawyers persuaded him to drop the plan, arguing that a challenge to the validity of the election had little legal basis and was unlikely to succeed in the country's electoral and supreme courts, Brazilian newspaper Folha de S.Paulo reported.
Instead, Bolsonaro plans to file an Electoral Judicial Investigation Action, seeking to have Lula's ticket disqualified over alleged abuses of political and economic power during the campaign, CNN Brazil reported, citing members of Bolsonaro's campaign.
"What he did was an unprecedented abuse of political and economic power, creating a complete imbalance in the electoral contest," Bolsonaro said in a video posted on social media.
Valdemar Costa Neto, president of the Liberal Party, said Monday that the party had recognized the election result.
Supreme Federal Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes has ordered Bolsonaro to surrender his passports to the Federal Police and barred him from leaving the country.
The ruling is part of an investigation involving Bolsonaro and lawyer Willer Tomaz, according to Brazil's public news agency Agencia Brasil.
Moraes also prohibited Bolsonaro from contacting Tomaz, Brazilian media reported. Both men are under investigation by the Federal Police on suspicion of money laundering and illegal foreign exchange transactions. ■

S. Korea's real GDP grows 1.0 pct on quarter in Q3
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:26:01 CST
12:26:01 KST

SEOUL, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's economy delivered a better-than-expected performance in the third quarter, driven by a semiconductor export boom, strong facility investments and significant growth in government spending, central bank data showed Tuesday.
The seasonally adjusted real gross domestic product (GDP), adjusted for inflation, expanded 1.0 percent in the July-September quarter compared to the previous quarter, according to the Bank of Korea (BOK).
It was more than three times higher than the 0.3 percent growth forecast estimated in August by the central bank, which projected an annual growth outlook of 3.3 percent for 2026.
The quarterly growth rate rebounded sharply from negative 0.1 percent in the fourth quarter last year to 1.8 percent in the first quarter this year, before maintaining positive momentum with an increase of 0.6 percent in the second quarter and 1.0 percent in the third quarter.
Outbound shipments of the export-driven economy mounted 2.3 percent quarter-on-quarter in the third quarter thanks to strong demand for semiconductors, machinery and electrical equipment.
Soaring demand for locally-made semiconductors was led by expanding global investments in artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure.
Imports gained 2.4 percent due to higher inflows of crude oil and semiconductor manufacturing machinery.
Facility investments jumped 4.1 percent on the back of robust demand for semiconductor manufacturing equipment, while construction investments added 0.7 percent in the third quarter after falling 0.1 percent in the previous quarter.
Investments in intellectual property products grew 2.3 percent due to increased spending on software and research and development (R&D).
Private consumption, another growth engine of the Asian economy, showed a slight setback with a decrease of 0.2 percent amid lower expenditure on both goods and services.
Fiscal spending climbed 1.9 percent, affected by higher government spending on health insurance benefits.
Amid the better-than-expected economic increase and the still high inflationary pressure, the BOK delivered a back-to-back rate hike in July and August, raising its benchmark interest rate to 3.00 percent.
By industry, the seasonally adjusted production among manufacturers swelled 2.0 percent in the third quarter on a quarterly basis, spearheaded by computers, electronic and optical devices.
Output in the service industry rose 0.2 percent, and production in the construction sector advanced 2.0 percent on an expansion in civil engineering projects.
Those in the agriculture, forestry and fishing, and the electricity, gas and water supply sectors increased 5.9 percent and 3.7 percent, respectively.
Real gross domestic income (GDI), which measures the actual purchasing power of income generated from domestic production activities, expanded 3.4 percent in the third quarter compared to the previous quarter.
From a year earlier, the real GDI surged 18.8 percent in the July-September quarter, representing the fastest growth in nearly 49 years since the fourth quarter of 1977.
It was powered by soaring global prices of locally-made semiconductors that improved the country's terms of trade. ■

====================================================================================================

‘A national emergency’: Bay Area Israelis fly home to vote in pivotal election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
03:13:03 UTC
12:13:03 KST

This article was produced by J.–The Jewish News of Northern California in partnership with the Jewish Telegraphic Agency.
Ayelet Frank was one of the first people to check in on Sunday, Oct. 25, for a nonstop flight from San Francisco to Tel Aviv. A resident of Redwood City, California, since she left Israel in 1984, she is flying back for one reason: to vote in the Oct. 27 election.
It’s the first time in her more than 40 years abroad that she is going back to cast a ballot.
Election about Israel's very existence, Frank says
“This election is unique. It’s very different than any other,” she told J. “It’s about Israel’s very existence. This election is between the destruction of the country, or building it up in a positive way.”
A native of Kibbutz Ein Harod in the Jezreel Valley, she is spending only two days in Israel before returning to California. It’s a long way to travel just to vote, but, she said, “It’s that important.”
Frank was one of 271 passengers on El Al flight 48, which landed in Israel less than 24 hours before the polls open. It was the first nonstop flight from San Francisco to Israel since the Oct. 7, 2023 Hamas attack. Many on board were part of what one organizing group estimates is a wave of 67,000 Israelis abroad flying home for an election widely seen as a referendum on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. In a tight race, the Israel Democracy Institute said that many voters could swing nearly two Knesset seats.
Those travelers are spending thousands of dollars for the chance to cast their ballots in what many are calling the most consequential election in Israel’s history.
The mood in the boarding area at the San Francisco International Airport was buoyant. Lots of people seemed to know one another and were running up to hug friends and chat excitedly. There were families with children and plenty of babies in strollers and carriers. There were a smattering of black kippahs as well as one Hasidic family. There were also Israeli residents returning home from vacation in the Bay Area. But judging from the conversations as well as from people interviewed by J., most passengers were Israeli expats flying back to vote.
Capitola resident Udi Pardo left Israel in 1983, a year before Frank. Most of his family still lives in Israel and he visits twice a year. But for him, this was his first time flying home for an election.
“I never tried to go and vote before because I don’t live there,” he said. “But now it’s a national emergency. I can’t not go.”
“Israel is on the verge of an abyss,” he continued, saying that he has not yet decided between Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar and Naftali Bennett’s B’Yachad — both center-right parties opposed to Netanyahu’s government. “We need to bring back sanity to Israel and to Israeli politics and reestablish liberal democracy because it’s about to disappear.”
First election since October 7 Massacre
The Oct. 27 election is the first since the Hamas attack and the war that followed. The stakes are so high, pundits say, that Israelis living abroad are flying home to vote in what appear to be unprecedented numbers. Israel does not allow absentee voting, except for diplomats and other state employees posted abroad, so expats who want to cast a ballot must do so in person.
The 67,000 estimate comes from Fly & Vote, a project of the U.S.-based America Israel Democracy Coalition to help expats navigate the logistics of participating in the election. The group cautioned that the figure is based on a voluntary August survey and its own registration data, not a count of arrivals. No comparable data exists for previous elections.
Israel’s Likud-led government has tried to impede Fly & Vote’s efforts with legal action, which was blocked in October by Israel’s Supreme Court. The government reportedly also considered closing or slowing down traffic at Ben Gurion International Airport in the days before the election. Analysts say this is because Netanyahu and his allies believe that many, if not most, of those responding to Fly & Vote’s initiative will vote against the current government.
Indeed, that seemed to be true of most of the expats on this El Al flight from San Francisco. Every person interviewed spoke about the “need for change” in Israel’s government, and those who declared their support for candidates mentioned either Eisenkot or leaders of other anti-Netanyahu parties. The Silicon Valley-based Israeli expat group UnXeptable, which emerged to protest Netanyahu’s judicial overhaul and has become a major anti-Netanyahu voice globally, had a large presence on the flight, with about a dozen key members sporting light blue T-shirts emblazoned with the date of the election and the Hebrew words for “Flight for Change.”
They were handing out shirts to any other passengers who would take them, some of whom put them on right away. Local TV stations showed up for an UnXeptable press conference held at the check-in counter.
Roni Bar-Niv of Sunnyvale is one of several people interviewed who is spending just a few days in Israel, in her case enough time to vote, turn around and fly back to the Hebrew-language school she runs near her Silicon Valley home.
In the 26 years since she left Givatayim, a suburb of Tel Aviv, Bar-Niv said, she visits Israel four or five times a year but she, too, has never flown back to vote until now.
“I thought I didn’t need to vote because I don’t live there,” she said. But everything changed, she added, after Oct. 7. “If we pay taxes — we have an apartment there — and if we send money for the war effort, and if we have children there — my daughter made aliyah five years ago — we need to go and vote,” she said. “The direction our country is going is very bad, for Israelis living there and for us also.”
Berkeley resident Rivka Amado left Jerusalem 22 years ago. A retired ethics professor and Ladino singer, she said it’s the duty of Israeli expats to show up.
“This election is critical, and it’s important for every Israeli to vote, whether you live here or there,” she said.
The surge in emigration since Oct. 7 has also swelled the pool of Israelis abroad. Some 82,800 Israelis left the country in 2024, according to Israel’s Central Bureau of Statistics, up from 55,000 in 2023. More than 69,000 left in 2025, the Times of Israel reported, the second straight year that emigration outpaced immigration.
Gilad Kariv, an opposition lawmaker from the Democrats party who chairs the Knesset’s Diaspora Affairs Committee, has warned of a “tsunami of emigration,” according to the Jerusalem Post. He has called it a “strategic threat to the future of Israel” tied to the government’s conduct.
J Street regional director Shimrit Braun Kamin (left) hugs Galit Lipsitz Goldental near the El Al counter at San Francisco International Airport, Oct. 25, 2026. (Aaron Levy-Wolins/J. Staff/Report for America)
Experts point to the war in Gaza and opposition to Netanyahu’s judicial overhaul as driving forces, suggesting that many recent emigrants are critical of the government.
Thirty-seven parties are on the Oct. 27 ballot, but only about a dozen are expected to clear the 3.25% electoral threshold needed to win Knesset seats. With Netanyahu’s Likud party polling neck-and-neck with his main opponent, Eisenkot’s Yashar party — the final pre-election polls show Yashar winning 22 to 23 seats to Likud’s 19 to 21 — every seat matters.
Neither party is projected to win a clear majority, meaning either one will have to negotiate intensely to form a governing coalition.
That’s why these expats have ponied up the dough, packed their bags and jumped on planes.
Eyal, a tech designer in his 40s who has been living in Mountain View since 2004, declined to give his last name because of his former job in the Israeli military. This, too, is his first trip home to vote.
In general, he said that he agrees with Israelis who believe expats should not have a voice in elections that no longer affect them personally.
“But in this particular election, I think a lot of Israelis want us to come and vote,” he said. “I know my parents do.”
Shlomi from Sunnyvale, who left Israel more than 15 years ago and also declined to give his last name, is worried that if there is not a new government, Israel’s brain drain will accelerate.
“We are in the final moments,” he said, likening Israel’s political situation to a soccer game. “If the government doesn’t change, I think a lot of good people who contribute to the future of the country will leave Israel.”
Shlomi is also worried that Israel will lose its partnership with the United States.
“It’s not about right or left,” he said, declining to say how he’ll vote. “It’s about dignity, about taking responsibility, about leaders that actually make decisions for the people rather than their personal benefit.”
Iddo Tal, a Jerusalem native, has lived in Palo Alto for 15 years, where he is a tech entrepreneur and teaches fundraising to startup founders around the world. He has launched “five start-ups and two kids,” he said, joking that “the kids have been a huge success.”
Unlike most of those interviewed, he has traveled back to vote before. He made the trip to visit his parents but timed it around an election.
“They always say every election is historic, and they’re always right,” he said.
Tal believes expats should vote, saying it keeps Israelis at home and abroad closely connected. “There’s something very exciting about making the Israeli diaspora part of Israel [proper], by coming back to fight, to raise money, to vote,” Tal said.
Hadar Aviram teaches law at UC Law San Francisco while studying to become a rabbi through Hebrew Union College. Born in Israel, she grew up “all over the world” and landed in San Francisco in 2001 for grad school. She wore one of the blue UnXeptable shirts and has joined some of the group’s protests.
“Let’s start with taking accountability for the Oct. 7 massacre and the ensuing war,” she said. “And long before that, we were all hostages to this hateful, bigoted, corrupt government.… I’m flying to release us from him, and him from us.”
She bristles at people who don’t understand why Israelis like her feel so strongly about this election.
“If some of those ignorant folks ask what Zionism is, I invite them to look around at all the people here who have packed their bags and emptied their savings accounts because they want to save their country,” she said, waving at the crowded boarding area. “When you love something very, very, very much, you are willing to go to great lengths to save it.”

Exit poll update: Second news outlet projects Eisenkot-Netanyahu tie; Opposition needs Arab support to form coalition
A second Israeli news outlet has projected a tie between the blocs led by Gadi Eisenkot and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, with both at 51 seats. The Arab parties garner a joint 18 seats, meaning no bloc can form a coalition without them.
According to Kan's exit poll, the Democrats drop from 10 to nine, and Otzma Yehudit falls from seven to six.
Eisenkot urges against second election, warns against Netanyahu using war for political gain
Opposition frontrunner Gadi Eisenkot (Yashar) warned against calling another election, urging Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu not to use war for his own political gain.
"I will do everything in my power to build a Zionist, pro-IDF enlistment government," he said. "Doing everything to fulfill the people's will is my personal duty. Calling another election will be a mistake."
Speaking to Netanyahu, Eisenkot said, "Don't you dare to use Israel's security for your own political gain."
Neither Netanyahu's bloc nor the anti-Netanyahu bloc has the necessary 61-seat majority needed to form a government, with exit polls projecting the two Arab-majority parties with 16-18 Knesset seats, nearly double the 10 seats they had in the outgoing Knesset.
Channel 13 exit poll update: Eisenkot bloc tied with Netanyahu coalition, Likud wins 27 seats
Channel 13 updated its exit poll, now projecting a tie between the coalition and the bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot at 51 seats. The Likud remains the largest party, rising to 27 seats.
Yashar loses one seat, falling to 22, while United Torah Judaism loses one seat and is left with six.
Lapid hints at minority gov't, Bennett: 'Will do anything for Zionist coalition'
Opposition leader Yair Lapid said his goal was forming a Zionist government, hinting at a possible minority government.
"We may not have a broad coalition on the first day, but we'll expand it later," he said. Lapid added that the exit polls show that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has suffered a crushing defeat. "The people of Israel have won. We are the majority. In a democracy, the side that receives more votes wins, and it should form a government. It can do so, and it has a duty to do so," he said.
Former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, who co-leads the Together party with Lapid, said "the leaders of the reform bloc are in touch with one another" and that they would do everything possible to establish "a Zionist government of those who serve, a government of doers that will run the country responsibly and serve all the people of Israel."
Bennett has previously ruled out forming a government that relies on the Arab parties. According to the exit poll results, he would struggle to form a government if he maintains that position, but he did not address the issue in his speech Tuesday evening. He said the exit polls show that "the alliance of soldiers has defeated the alliance of draft dodgers today," adding, "We will patiently await the official results, because a lot can still change."
Ultra-Orthodox Sephardic party Shas sees significant drop in support, according to exit polls
According to exit polls, Shas, the ultra-Orthodox Sephardic party, has seen a significant drop in support from the 11 seats it holds in the current Knesset.
Judy Maltz recently visited the western Negev town of Netivot, which has long been a stronghold of Shas, and found residents who feel increasingly alienated by the party's hardening ideological stance, particularly its emphasis on full-time yeshiva study over military service and participation in the workforce.
Smotrich says party 'won't let' Arab Israelis celebrate record turnout
Far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich said his party "won't let" Arab Israelis celebrate the record number of votes exit polls project the two Arab-majority parties winning.
"I can see on some of the screens that the Arabs are celebrating tonight. So I'm telling you and them: We won't let them celebrate," he said, speaking at his Religious Zionism party's event after exit polls showed the Joint List and United Arab List winning 16-18 seats, almost double the 10 seats the two parties had in the outgoing Knesset.
"They think they'll be able to reverse the settlement revolution in Judea and Samaria, and I'm telling them they won't succeed."
He added, "Right now, it looks like the Holy One, blessed be He, still wants us to act through natural means, and we have seven seats. It's possible that the soldiers' votes will give us more seats."
Ben-Gvir tells supporters to 'pray' for final results, 'full-on right-wing government'
Far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir criticized what he said is a move to form a unity government with opposition frontrunner Gadi Eisenkot, telling his supporters that he hopes the final results will bring about a "full-on right-wing government."
"Unfortunately, tonight we're hearing people talk about forming a unity government with Eisenkot. This is exactly the scenario we warned against – it would be a terrible mistake," he said.
"We hope that this evening will be considered the best evening in the world, so we'll wait for the final results," he said. "Pray to God that we wake up tomorrow to a new morning, a morning of good news for the people of Israel," he told his supporters. "With God's help, we'll establish a full-on right-wing government."
"Regardless of the final results, we are very proud of what we have done, and especially of the major reforms we promised the public and worked to implement," listing the law mandating the death penalty for Palestinians convicted of terror, alongside home demolitions, Israel's new national guard and lax gun laws.
Unaligned Reservists' chief: Both blocs are deadlocked, we're heading for another election – that's bad
Yoaz Hendel, chairman of the Reservists party, responded to exit polls predicting that his party would fail to cross the electoral threshold, decrying the surge in seats for Arab parties, projected to win 18 seats.
"We all need to be humble and wake up tomorrow to the real results," he said. "I would like to see Winter cross the threshold too, to break this dichotomy. It's not good that anti-Zionist parties have 17 seats."

Russia-Ukraine ceasefire brokered by Melania Trump takes effect in Oleshky
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
03:10:19 UTC
12:10:19 KST

A localised humanitarian ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine has taken effect in Oleshky city, following a diplomatic initiative brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump to allow emergency aid deliveries and civilian evacuations.
The ceasefire started at 01:00 GMT on Tuesday. The White House confirmed that the first lady served as the "exclusive intermediary" in securing the operational pause.
The arrangement addresses critical shortages of food, potable water, and medical supplies in the frontline settlement, situated on the eastern bank of the Dnipro River in Ukraine's southern Kherson region.
The remaining population faces mined roadways, recurring military bombardments, and severe electricity shortages.
"The situation in Oleshky is dire. Oleshky is a front-line war city on the brink of disaster," Melania Trump said.
"It was abundantly clear that without my intervention, the possibility to bring humanitarian aid into the city and to evacuate the elderly would be impossible."
Military implementation
Russian Chief of General Staff Valery Gerasimov announced that Moscow would observe a "regime of silence" from 4 am Moscow time on October 27.
"To ensure the safety of the population and the delivery of essential humanitarian supplies, engineering reconnaissance will be conducted, and the safe passage of a humanitarian convoy to the settlement of Oleshky, Kherson Region, will be facilitated," Gerasimov said.
Ukraine's General Staff confirmed it would observe the ceasefire from 3 am Kiev time to facilitate aid deliveries and guarantee safe passage for departing civilians.
Under the framework, civilian representatives from Ukraine and Russia will assess local requirements.
Residents choosing to leave will receive transport to destinations in either country, with an American media organisation accompanying field teams to record proceedings.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov noted the mission could last several days.
Oleshky, seized by Russian forces in 2022, had a pre-war population of roughly 24,000.
Today, only 1,700 to 2,000 residents remain, predominantly elderly individuals unable to flee earlier.
The town suffered catastrophic damage in June 2023 when the destruction of the Nova Kakhovka Dam triggered massive flooding across the Dnipro basin, an act for which Kiev and Moscow continue to trade blame.

Nicknamed “Asian Elvis,” Tang entered the final ranked second in qualifying, scoring 14.566 points with a difficulty score of 6.000 and an execution score of 8.566, per Nownews. For the final, his coaching team raised his routine’s difficulty score to 6.600, helping propel him to the top of the podium.
Tang delivered a fluid routine featuring his signature aerial twists and earned an execution score of 8.366. His total of 14.966 points secured the gold medal.
The championships ran from Oct. 17-25 in Rotterdam, Nownews reported. Tang’s victory marked a historic milestone for Taiwan, which had previously won two silver medals and one bronze at the world championships.
President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) congratulated Tang on his achievement, praising his performance on the world stage and his contribution to Taiwan’s sporting success. He also encouraged the rest of the national team to continue striving for top honors.
Since the Asian Games in Nagoya last month, Tang has worked with coach Huang Bo-rui (黃柏瑞) and a sports psychologist to refine his mental approach, treating finals more like practice sessions, per UDN. He said he aimed to compete in a relaxed state, without adding too much ceremony or pressure, allowing him to perform with greater composure.
Tang, who turned 30 last month, has overcome multiple serious injuries during his career, including three surgeries on his right elbow and a ruptured left Achilles tendon during a domestic trial three years ago. He won bronze in the men’s horizontal bar at the 2024 Paris Olympics and helped Taiwan claim bronze in the men’s team event at the Asian Games last month.
Those medals and his world championships gold have boosted his confidence ahead of the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.
His wife, Tseng Jo-yu (曾若語), traveled to Rotterdam to support him at the world championships, as she did when he won his Olympic medal in Paris, UDN reported. Tang described her as an “invisible coach” whose support motivates him to continue improving.

Trump, ignoring polls, predicts economy to help Republicans in midterms
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
04:05:07 CET
12:05:07 KST

By Trevor Hunnicutt
CORINTH, Mississippi, Oct 26 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump campaigned on Monday in deeply Republican Mississippi, predicting victory for a Republican Senate candidate based on what he deemed to be a booming US economy, while also repeating his claim that oil prices would soon plummet.
Trump, a Republican, has been on a campaign blitz through normally safe Republican states ahead of the November 3 vote, with party strategists telling Reuters they are on edge about races from Alaska to South Carolina, in part because of voter discontent over how Trump’s tariffs and the Iran war have fueled inflation.
Sounding hoarse from his recent series of campaign rallies, Trump remarked, “God didn’t make your vocal cords to do a rally every day.”
Trump is expected to visit Texas, Ohio, South Carolina, Florida and Iowa in the final days of the campaign, with voter concerns over affordability likely to weigh on Republicans, pollsters say.
Trump acknowledged the war in Iran has pushed up oil prices, but said it was a small price to pay to stop Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon.
“I thought the price of oil was going to go much, much higher,” Trump said.
“It’s worked out fine and it’ll be over soon,” Trump said about the war.
All 435 seats in the US House of Representatives and 35 of the 100 Senate seats are on the ballot, with public opinion polls suggesting the Democrats will regain control of the House and have a chance to retake the Senate.
A Republican victory would preserve Republican control of Congress, which Trump has enjoyed since returning to the White House after the 2024 election, while a Democratic victory could impede the president and trigger congressional investigations into his administration.
In Mississippi, an unexpectedly competitive US Senate race has given Democrats a rare opening ahead of next week’s congressional elections.
Democrats last won a Senate seat in Mississippi in 1982. Trump carried the state by nearly 23 percentage points in 2024, and he won the northeastern Mississippi county he was set to visit on Monday by 68 percentage points.
But several election analysts no longer regard US Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith’s reelection as a sure bet. The Trump-endorsed Republican faces Democrat Scott Colom, a district attorney from the Columbus area, and independent Ty Pinkins, a military veteran and attorney who previously ran statewide as a Democrat.
“Cindy’s doing great but I’ve just got to make sure,” Trump said. “I can’t take a chance.”
After listing a series of economic achievements, many of them exaggerations or unverifiable claims, Trump said, “I can’t help Cindy Hyde-Smith any better than that.”
Senate Majority PAC announced a $1.2 million ad campaign in support of Colom last week, and Democrats have dispatched big-name figures from former Vice President Kamala Harris to former presidential primary candidate Pete Buttigieg to campaign alongside the Democratic candidate.
Colom came to Corinth on Monday, posting pictures of himself meeting with voters outside the venue where some 5,500 Trump supporters gathered inside.
“Walking the line outside the Trump rally in Corinth, I was reminded that more unites us than divides us here in Mississippi,” Colom said on X. “When I’m elected to the U.S. Senate, I’ll represent every Mississippian — whether you voted for me or not.”
Democrats are contesting all three Republican-held House seats in Mississippi, but none is viewed as a likely pickup opportunity. A fourth seat, represented by US Representative Bennie Thompson in a heavily Black district, is considered safe for the Democrats.
(Reporting by Trevor Hunnicutt in Corinth; Additional reporting by Daniel Trotta; Editing by Colleen Jenkins, Howard Goller and Stephen Coates)

You bought it, but do you control it? The hidden power behind smart devices
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
03:01:59 UTC
12:01:59 KST

You bought it, but do you control it? The hidden power behind smart devices
When a stolen smartphone can be remotely disabled and a connected car can be tracked or prevented from starting, the question of who controls a device after it is purchased becomes more complicated. Recent reports of stolen iPhones being blocked in France have brought this issue into focus. How far does a manufacturer’s control over a connected device extend, and where does the owner’s right to control their property begin? Qazinform News Agency examines how remote security technologies are reshaping the concept of digital ownership.
How technology can stop stolen devices
On Oct. 17, shops in Paris, Marseille, Lille, Bordeaux, Lyon and other French cities were targeted during looting alongside demonstrations. Electronics, including smartphones and tablets, were among the goods stolen.
A video shared on social media showed a message on a stolen iPhone instructing the holder to return it to an Apple Store in Lille. The message said the device had been locked and was being tracked, warning that local authorities would be notified.
According to French media outlet BFM Tech, manufacturers can remotely disable stolen smartphones and tablets, while mobile operators can blacklist their International Mobile Equipment Identity (IMEI) numbers to prevent them from connecting to cellular networks. A blacklisted phone may, however, remain usable over Wi-Fi.
Yernar Yeleuov, a cybersecurity engineer at the School of Cybersecurity at Astana IT University (AITU), said anti-theft protection works through several mechanisms, including account-based locks, remote commands and network blocking.
Apple’s Activation Lock and Android’s Factory Reset Protection can prevent someone from setting up a stolen phone after a factory reset without the previous owner’s credentials. Services such as Find My and Find My Device allow owners to lock a screen, display a message or erase data remotely.
But these systems are not foolproof. A remote command may not reach a phone that remains disconnected from the network. IMEI blocking also depends on the networks and databases involved, while stolen devices may be dismantled for parts or targeted through phishing attacks designed to steal account credentials.
“These mechanisms are a strong deterrent that reduces the value of a stolen device, but not a guarantee that it will be returned,” Yeleuov said.
From smartphones to connected cars
The same principle is increasingly relevant to vehicles. In April 2026, Stellantis announced an expanded connected-services offering that includes Stolen Vehicle Tracking Assistance through its Connect PLUS package. In July, Ford Canada expanded the availability of vehicle theft-prevention features to selected models, including theft alerts, recovery assistance and a remote Start Inhibit function that can prevent a vehicle from starting remotely under specified conditions.
However, the technology that helps recover stolen property can also create new cybersecurity risks.
“If a vulnerability is found not in a single car but in the manufacturer’s servers or API, the entire fleet is at risk at once,” Yeleuov said.
Connected vehicles also collect location data that can reveal where people live, work and travel. If these systems are compromised, the consequences may extend beyond vehicle theft to unauthorized access and privacy violations.
Yeleuov said critical vehicle systems, including brakes and steering, should be isolated from infotainment systems and external communication channels. Remote commands must be securely authenticated, and an immobilization function should never stop a moving vehicle.
Who controls a device after purchase?
A smartphone or connected car is more than a physical product. It also depends on software, online accounts and services that may remain under a manufacturer’s control.
“The honest answer is that buyers today almost never get full control,” Yeleuov said. “Legally, you own the hardware, but the software that makes this hardware useful is usually licensed rather than sold.”
This distinction matters when companies change software, discontinue services or restrict features. A device may remain physically intact but lose some of its functionality if it depends on a manufacturer’s servers or subscription.
The end of software support can create a further risk: devices that no longer receive security updates may retain vulnerabilities that attackers can exploit.
Yeleuov distinguishes between protective measures, such as security updates and anti-theft tools, and commercial restrictions that can limit repairs or access to features. Both can affect how much control consumers retain after purchasing a product.
Balancing security and ownership
Remote blocking and tracking can make stolen devices harder to use, but consumers also need protection against mistaken restrictions, unauthorized tracking and sudden service shutdowns.
Yeleuov said safeguards should include transparent policies, secure authentication, notifications when remote actions are taken and accessible procedures for appealing incorrect blocks. Consumers should also know before buying a connected product which functions can be controlled remotely and how long software support is expected to last.
“The keys to a device should be in the owner’s hands, not the manufacturer’s,” he said.
Kazakhstan’s IMEI registration system provides a mechanism for managing mobile devices on local networks, but the broader issue extends beyond stolen phones. As more products become connected, ownership increasingly depends on the software and services that determine how they can be used.
The challenge is to ensure that technology protects consumers without making them unnecessarily dependent on the companies that manufacture their devices. Buying a product gives consumers its physical hardware, but meaningful ownership also requires transparency, security and clear limits on remote control.
The issue is part of a broader debate over digital security in Kazakhstan. In September, Qazinform reported that more than 100 experts gathered in Astana for KazHackStan 2026 to discuss emerging cyber threats and the future of cyber resilience.

South Korea’s GDP grows 1% in Q3 on strong exports and investment
The growth in July-September accelerated from 0.6 percent in the previous quarter and surpassed the central bank’s August forecast of 0.3 percent. On a year-on-year basis, the economy expanded 3.4 percent.
South Korea’s export performance was driven by booming global demand for semiconductors amid the expansion of artificial intelligence infrastructure. Exports reached a record $120.9 billion in September, up 83.5 percent from a year earlier, with semiconductor shipments exceeding $60 billion.
Facility investment rose 4.1 percent from the previous quarter, while construction investment increased 0.7 percent. Government spending also advanced 1.9 percent. However, private consumption declined 0.2 percent amid stock market weakness and sluggish automobile sales affected by strikes at major automakers.
The BOK said South Korea’s economy grew a cumulative 3.6 percent during the first three quarters of 2026.
“If the economy maintains the on-quarter growth pace in the fourth quarter, GDP will likely grow 3.6 percent for the full year,” said Lee Dong-won of the BOK’s statistics department.
The central bank may revise its August full-year growth forecast of 3.3 percent upward, with updated projections scheduled for release next month.

Azerbaijan secures $40 million ADB loan to boost women-led businesses and farming
The Asian Development Bank (ADB) and Bank Respublika Open Joint Stock Company have signed a $40 million loan agreement to expand access to financing for micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) and agricultural borrowers in regions outside Azerbaijan’s capital, Baku, Qazinform News Agency cites the press service of ADB.
Under the agreement, at least 20% of the loan proceeds will be allocated to women-owned MSMEs, while at least 50% will support borrowers engaged in agricultural production, processing, and trade. The funding is expected to facilitate the adoption of modern drip irrigation systems and encourage the cultivation of crops and fruits suited to varying weather conditions.
The initiative aims to promote business growth, create jobs, increase incomes, strengthen resilience to natural hazards, and contribute to the diversification of Azerbaijan’s economy.
“This financing aligns well with ADB’s country partnership strategy for Azerbaijan, 2025–2029, by promoting private sector-led growth, strengthening food security, improving resilience, and expanding access to finance for women-led businesses in areas outside the capital,” said Sunniya Durrani-Jamal, ADB country director for Azerbaijan.
She added that the project builds on the bank’s existing cooperation with Bank Respublika and expressed ADB’s commitment to deepening the partnership to achieve these objectives.
Established in 1992, Bank Respublika is Azerbaijan’s fifth-largest bank by assets, holding a 4.4% market share. It serves retail, MSME, and corporate clients through a network of 40 branches, 24 of which are located outside Baku.

'Veto should be held by all permanent members': India at UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
03:01:03 UTC
12:01:03 KST

Parvathaneni Harish called for comprehensive Security Council reforms, arguing that all permanent members of an expanded Council must have equal rights and responsibilities
NEW DELHI: India has called for comprehensive reforms of the United Nations Security Council (UNSC), saying all permanent members of a reformed Council must have the same rights and responsibilities, including the power of veto.Delivering India's statement at the United Nations, India's permanent representative Parvathaneni Harish said the veto should be exercised with restraint and must not become a tool for narrow political interests, particularly on matters concerning international peace and security.
India also opposed proposals to create a separate category of permanent members without the veto or with fewer powers, arguing that such an arrangement would deepen existing inequalities within the Council."India's position on the veto is principled and well known. It is aligned with the Common African Position. We reiterate that as long as the veto exists, it must be held by all permanent members of a reformed Council. Fairness and justice demand that all permanent members enjoy the same rights and responsibilities," news agency ANI quoted Harish as saying."A new category of permanent members, with or without the veto, would only further complicate a discussion that is already difficult, and would further entrench the very inequity we are seeking to correct.
Periodic elections and the concept of permanency are fundamentally contradictory," Harish added.Harish said the veto had been used 331 times on around 200 resolutions during the UN's history. He noted that most vetoes, or threats to use them, had come from three of the five permanent members -- China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States."The record of the Veto is stark. Over the life of this Organisation, the veto has been exercised 331 times on around 200 resolutions. We also note that two out of the five permanent members have not exercised a veto for over three and a half decades, and most of the vetos or threats of vetos have emanated from only three of the P5," he said.He also questioned the effectiveness of accountability measures introduced in 2022, under which the UN General Assembly holds a debate whenever a permanent member exercises its veto. The continued use of the veto since the mechanism was adopted showed that it had not brought the expected change, he said.
He also highlighted what he described as an “effective or de facto veto” in the Council's working methods. Under the practice of consensus, a single member can block presidential statements, press statements and decisions of sanctions committees, sometimes without providing an explanation, he said."The veto is not only what is cast in the open. There is also the 'effective or de facto veto' that every Council member, elected and non-elected, holds over presidential statements, press statements and the decisions of sanctions committees, where the unwritten rule of consensus allows a single member to hold or block a proposal, most often without explanation," Harish said.
Aastha Jha is a writer at The Times of India, covering politics. She also writes on business, global affairs, social issues, with a focus on policy, governance and their impact on everyday lives. Her work brings together reportage and analysis, tracking developments in India and abroad while examining the broader social and economic currents shaping public discourse.

BAROMÈTRE DU REJET : Le Pen, toujours moins rejetée
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
03:00:00 UTC
12:00:00 KST

BAROMÈTRE DU REJET : Le Pen, toujours moins rejetée
La nouvelle édition de l'enquête mensuelle de Cluster 17 pour POLITICO montre que Marine Le Pen est encore moins rejetée par les Français qu'au mois de septembre. Reste un mince motif d'espoir pour le bloc central.
Par SARAH PAILLOU et PAULINE DE SAINT REMY à Paris
Les mobilisations et violences d’octobre ont renforcé le rejet de Jean-Luc Mélenchon et amoindri celui de Marine Le Pen.| Joel Saget/AFP via Getty Images
Les candidats du bloc central, Edouard Philippe et Gabriel Attal, sont bien placés pour le savoir : s’ils peinent à progresser dans les sondages d’intentions de vote — voire, s’ils reculent — c’est qu’après deux quinquennats d’Emmanuel Macron, l’heure est au dégagisme.
Comme le montre la dernière enquête de l’institut Cluster 17 pour POLITICO, parue lundi 26 octobre, ce sont les incarnations d’une rupture radicale avec le macronisme qui, à ce stade de la campagne, ont le vent dans le dos : Marine Le Pen et Jean-Luc Mélenchon.
Mais les représentants du camp central ne souffrent pas que d’un simple désir d’alternance : s’ils décrochent, c’est qu’ils suscitent désormais chez les Français un rejet aussi fort, voire plus puissant, que le Rassemblement national ou La France insoumise. Impossible donc, pour les partis ayant déjà exercé le pouvoir, de continuer à parier sur des électeurs prêts à tout pour barrer la route de l’Elysée aux “extrêmes”.
Advertisement
Pour l’emporter en 2027, un prétendant à la présidence doit donc formuler un nouveau vœu : plutôt que de rêver d’être majoritaire dans le pays, se contenter d’espérer être le moins exécré des compétiteurs. Ce que mesure notre baromètre mensuel du rejet, réalisé par Cluster 17 pour POLITICO, dont la deuxième livraison montre que les grandes tendances observées en septembre s’accentuent et témoigne d’un moment de la campagne “plutôt favorable aux droites” (traditionnelle et extrême), analyse Jean-Yves Dormagen, le président de l’institut.
Logique : notre enquête a été menée du 19 au 22 octobre, juste après les casses et pillages du 17 octobre.
Cluster 17 a, de nouveau, demandé à 3 000 personnes quelle était la probabilité, sur une échelle de 0 à 10, qu’elles votent “un jour” pour chacun des candidats à la présidentielle testés — 0 correspondant à une impossibilité totale de glisser ce bulletin dans l’urne, 10 indiquant que les sondés jugent “tout à fait possible” de le faire.
Seul motif de satisfaction pour Edouard Philippe et Gabriel Attal : la priorité des Français est davantage de faire barrage au camp RN ou au camp Insoumis plutôt qu’au bloc central. | Daniel Perron/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images
Tous les candidats testés demeurent rejetés par une majorité de Français. Les plus répulsifs restent les mêmes, mais ils voient augmenter le taux de Français excluant totalement de voter pour eux. L’Ecologiste Marine Tondelier arrive ainsi toujours en tête du classement du rejet, à 71% (+3 par rapport au mois dernier) — à égalité cette fois avec Eric Zemmour, non testé dans notre précédente enquête.
Mélenchon de plus en plus repoussoir
Même logique pour Jean-Luc Mélenchon. Toujours en deuxième position des personnalités les plus rejetées, l’Insoumis l’est encore plus qu’en septembre. Les interrogés sont désormais 69% à juger inimaginable de choisir un bulletin au nom de l’Insoumis (ils étaient 66%).
Les violences du week-end des 17 et 18 octobre ont “radicalisé sur la droite un certain nombre de personnes”, juge Dormagen. Et ainsi conforté l’image négative de “JLM”, augmentant la perception de LFI comme “un mouvement radical, qui incarne une rupture brutale”.
Advertisement
Le moment profite, en miroir, aux figures supposées incarner l’ordre, la fermeté, l’autorité, au premier rang desquelles Marine Le Pen. La candidate RN est désormais celle qui réunit le moins de sondés estimant strictement impossible de voter un jour pour elle : ils ne sont plus “que” 52% (- 4).
A ses côtés au même score : le social-démocrate Raphaël Glucksmann. L’eurodéputé Place publique se maintient quasiment à son niveau du mois dernier.
Misant sur une promesse du retour de l’ordre lui aussi, l’ancien ministre de l’Intérieur Bruno Retailleau est lui aussi moins repoussé qu’en septembre. Les sondés sont 54% (-4) à refuser catégoriquement de voter pour lui. Il rejoint ainsi le mouchoir de poche des personnalités les moins rejetées, avec Marine Le Pen et Raphaël Glcuksmann.
Edouard Philippe est à peine plus rejeté que ces personnalités. Avec 56% de Français excluant à jamais de voter pour lui, il se voit doublé de peu par le sénateur vendéen.
Le bulletin Gabriel Attal est, en revanche, de moins en moins envisagé par les interrogés comme une possibilité. Les sondés sont 59% à trouver inimaginable de voter pour le candidat Renaissance — une augmentation de trois points, comparé à notre sondage précédent. Supposition de Jean-Yves Dormagen, qui ne parie pas sur une hostilité des sondés à son égard : outre le rejet qu’il suscite, “la candidature d’Attal se heurte depuis le début à un enjeu de légitimité. Y compris dans son espace électoral potentiel, les gens ont du mal à comprendre pourquoi il est candidat.”
Le député des Hauts-de-Seine est ainsi quasiment aussi inenvisageable pour les Français que… François Hollande, nouvellement testé. L’ancien président, qui rêve d’un retour en grâce dans le cœur des Français, a visiblement du pain sur la planche : 61% des sondés jugent impossible de voter pour lui.
Advertisement
Un espoir pour le camp central ?
Reste, malgré tout, une (petite) raison d’espérer pour les anciens Premiers ministres d’Emmanuel Macron. Cluster 17 a cette fois demandé aux sondés quelle était leur priorité (à l’exclusion des deux autres) : empêcher la victoire du RN et de ses alliés, de LFI et de ses alliés, ou des partis ayant soutenu le président ?
Réponse : les Français ne sont que 14% à dire que leur objectif principal est une défaite du camp “macroniste”. Alors que faire barrage au camp Insoumis est prioritaire pour 43% d’entre eux, et celui du RN pour 30%.
De quoi laisser penser, donc, que si tous les camps restent majoritairement rejetés — fût-ce d’une courte tête —, tout espoir pour un représentant du bloc central de faire “barrage” à l’extrême droite n’est pas complètement vain. Encore faudra-t-il accéder au second tour.
(*) Etude Cluster 17 pour POLITICO réalisée auprès d’un échantillon de 3 000 personnes, représentatif de la population française grâce à la méthode des quotas, interrogées par questionnaire autoadministré en ligne, du 19 au 22 octobre 2026. Les données ont fait l’objet d’un redressement sociodémographique, à partir des données de l’Insee, ainsi que d’un redressement politique fondé sur la reconstitution des votes au premier tour de l’élection présidentielle de 2022 et aux élections européennes de 2024. La marge d’erreur se situe entre 0,8 et 1,8 point.
